Overall the proposed rule will help somewhat in expediting some Design-Build projects.

Specific comments/concerns with the proposed rule are as follows:

The Design- Build contractor could only do "Preliminary Design" prior to NEPA approval (636.109). Preliminary Design is defined as all design activities necessary to complete the NEPA alternatives analysis and review. We believe this is too restrictive and in fact is more restrictive than what we can do currently. Currently, we can do permitting, mitigation and work to comply with other related laws relative to permitting such as the 404 permit. Also, FHWA has been lenient by allowing work items such as surveying, utility identification, hydraulic analysis, hazardous material investigation, traffic studies, early geotech, etc. during this phase. In addition we should be able to do any work necessary to support the RFQ and RFP. This is the biggest issue with the rule, and FHWA needs to fix it in the final rule.
In the commentary of the proposed rule it states the design-builder is not allowed to proceed with final design activities for a specific alternative, even on an "at-risk/nonparticipating basis". We feel this is overly restrictive and takes away flexibility the states should have. The major benefit of Design-Build for the traveling public is the time savings, and this restriction limits the overall time reduction. We suggest FHWA change this requirement.
The rule would require that the preferred alternative can't be the required alternative in the RFP. We believe this is overly restrictive when it is obvious that the preferred alternative will be the selected alternative. The states, at their risk, should have the option of using the preferred alternative in the RFP.
When the issues of a traditional type Design-Build contract are intertwined with the issues of Design-Build in Public Private Partnerships, it is confusing. We believe the two issues should be separated in the rule as the issues are different with different methods of delivery.
In Design-Build Public Private Partnerships we believe the developer should be able to prepare the NEPA document with State and FHWA oversight.

One additional comment. Although it probably would not occur in Florida because we don't foresee ever doing a Design-Build when many alternatives are still on the table in the NEPA process, we oppose letting a Design-Build project without price being a consideration.

Comment on [Docket No. FAA-2005-23500; Directorate Identifier 2005-NE-46-AD] RIN 2120-AA64

This proposed AD involves a component identified by nomenclature as an air seal for the second stage high pressure turbine of V2500 engines. The part is not identified by part number.

According to our records there may be a part approved under CFR 14 § 21.303 that can replace the OEM part. That part is identified as P/N M2A2335-01 approved as a replacement for the IAE P/N 2A2335-01 under McClain International PMA Supplement no. 63, dated 5/20/2002 at page 3. The design approval method is “Test and Computation” indicating that the PMA part may be similar, but not identical to the OEM part. (The PMA supplement page is submitted herewith.)

The intent of the proposed AD is therefore unclear whether or not it is contemplated to apply to this particular part numbered part, and if so, whether it applies to just the OEM part or to the PMA part as well. We request clarification of intent.

We might also suggest that part numbers be cited in AD's whenever possible and appropriate to reduce or eliminate ambiguity. Bear in mind that not everyone has ready access to the service bulletins so adding the part number to the AD helps MARPA, MRO’s and part purveyors to monitor defects.

Jack Buster
AD Committee
Modification and Replacement Parts Association (MARPA)

Docket No. FAA-2005-22413; Directorate Identifier 2005-NM-167-AD
/Quote/
Corrective Actions
(h) If a cracked thrust link is found ...., do the actions in paragraph (h)(1) of this AD.
(1) Replace the cracked thrust link .... i.a.w Part 2 of the SB;
/Unquote/
Part 2 of the SB(page 28) requires engine removal as a preparation of thrust link replacement. There is no load on the thrust link at static condition and the thrust link can be replaced without engine removal, by removing engine exhaust sleeve only. This is agreed by Boeing message No. 1-38515891-9 dated 16-Sep-2005, saying "Boeing agree with JAL that it would be an appropriate alternate procedure to accomplish thrust link replacement without engine removal, by removing the engine exhaust sleeve."

/Question/
If JAL replace the thrust link without engine removal, does FAA consider that the deviation in the procedure is minor which does not require AMOC ?
By omitting engine removal, JAL can minimize the workload of thrust link replacement.

Paragraph (f) of the NPRM references Bombardier Alert Service Bulletin A601R-28-064, dated April 21, 2005, but since then, this service bulletin has been superseded by Bombardier Alert Service Bulletin A601R-28-064, Revision A, dated September 15, 2005 with updated information.

RECOMMENDATION: Reference the latest service bulletin in the AD which is Bombardier Alert Service Bulletin A601R-28-064, Revision A, dated September 15, 2005.

Dear Sir;
I am a powerplant engineer in charge of V2525-D5 powered MD-90 aircraft at Japan Airlines International.
First of all, I am understanding the importance and effectiveness of vibration monitoring recommended by IAE SB V2500-ENG-72-501 and actually,?I am monitoring our fleet/engines using IAE SB recommended criteria day by day. It is not so difficult to do if it is to be done as the supplement trend monitoring of the aircraft / engine /systems. However, it will be so hard to do if this will be a mandatory AD requirement.
There are two main reasons why I feel the difficulty.
1)No Licence / Certification is currently provided for this trend monitoring;
It may cause the problem how/who judge a trend data is good or not good.
I do not concern so much, if this is a just monitoring supplementary performed , but we must demonstrate /report our compliance to the AD to our local authority.
If it does not require difficult judgement, we do not show this concern.
However, this trend monitoring is not such simple and the judgement will be differed by each person. In other words, the final judgement of this trend monitoring entirely depends on how we read the data which may shows scattering each flights. I believe this condition is not appropriate for the action required by AD.
Therefore, suitable training for this monitoring and issuing a licence / certificate will be required for this special monitoring.
2) Need to maintain ground monitoring system for this new requirement:
Engine flight data trend monitoring utilizes various ground hardware /software/ systems which have to be maintained separately from aircraft routine maintenance.
This monitoring system may fail or may having a problem for various
unexpected reasons even though the aircraft onboard vibration monitoring /indication system itself is working properly.
There is no certain way to judge the ground system is working properly.
It will be too difficult to create those criteria for ground system, but I believe the necessity of them shall be discussed and considered because this will be the AD requirement.
Also, maximum inactive period of this vibration trend monitoring shall be clearly documented if this have to be the mandatory actions by AD.
MD-90 MMEL allows inability of (onboard) engine vibration monitoring
system up to ten (10) consecutive calendar days.
Therefore, more than ten(10) days of inactive periods for this trend monitoring shall be approved and it should be clearly documented.
IAE SB is totally not clear at this point.

Thank you very much for your kindness to accept my long comments on this subject in advance.

Faithfully Yours,

N. Tsurusawa

RE:Docket ID number EPA-HQ-OPPT-2005-0049

Dear Members of the EPA,

Members of the Board of the Children?s Health Forum (CHF), a non-profit
organization devoted to the prevention of childhood diseases that
disproportionately affect poor and minority communities, respectfully submit these
comments regarding the Environmental Protection Agency?s (EPA) Lead,
Renovation, Repair and Painting Proposed Rule. The proposed rule, issued under
the authority of Section 402(c)(3) of the Toxic Substances Control Act, is
designed to minimize the introduction of lead hazards resulting from the
disturbance of lead-based paint during renovation, repair and painting activities in
most housing built before 1978. The rule proposes the types of work practices
that should be used and would require renovators to be trained in and use lead-
safe work practices and to be certified in the use of those safe practices.

The EPA?s proposed rule excludes several important issues that we have
addressed in our comments below. CHF has been working since 2002 with the
Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), state and local officials,
community organizations, and national leaders to combat childhood exposures to
harmful lead hazards and prevent instances of elevated blood lead levels. We
believe that by excluding these provisions, the EPA will hinder the progress being
made by advocates to eliminate childhood lead poisoning by 2010. We would like
to work with the EPA as you enact requirements that will reduce exposure to lead
hazards and protect children from harmful exposures.

Childcare facilities
Unfortunately, the proposed rule does not include protections for daycare centers.
This omission cannot be overlooked. Many children spend each day attending
childcare facilities where they may be exposed to lead hazards, such as dust or
peeling and chipping paint, just as they are in their homes. For these children,
addressing the home environment is not enough. The EPA must include daycare
facilities as applicable under the proposed rule in order to protect the health of all
children.

Work Practices
The proposed rule does not prohibit dangerous work practices as they are
addressed by HUD and rolls back the basic EPA prohibitions currently in place for
abatement practices. Dangerous work practices such as open flame burning,
torching, machine sanding, abrasive blasting, dry sanding, dry scraping, and
hazardous paint stripping should be prohibited under the proposed rule, as they
contribute to an unsafe environment for current and future occupants and workers.
Use of these practices releases lead dust into the air, and causes significant
environmental hazards, posing risks to children and families, workers, and others.

HUD has already adopted the prohibition of these dangerous work practices as
part of their lead safety regulations that cover renovation, repair and painting
activities similar to those addressed by this rule because current research has
shown that these practices endanger human health. Many other federal, state,
and local agencies have also prohibited these work practices and identified lead-
safe practices in order to help prevent cases of childhood lead poisoning. These
rules should not be undone by EPA?s rule, nor should agencies enact regulations
that cause confusion to homeowners and contractors. Instead, EPA should
conform to existing standards governing dangerous work practices.

Clearance Testing
The proposed rule includes a visual ?white glove test? for cleaning verification once
renovation, repairs, and painting work has been completed. This method is not
consistent with the standard clearance dust testing and has not been sufficiently
proven to protect occupants from hazards. White glove testing has not been
connected to blood lead levels and visual tests are not sufficient to determine the
safety of a unit.

Upon completion of renovation activities, specific clearance dust testing should be
required by the EPA?s proposed rule for all homes. According to the National
Center for Healthy Housing (NCHH), clearance dust testing is the only objective
methodology for determining the safety of a unit following renovation. It is
consistent with federal, state, and local requirements under HUD rules for federally-
assisted housing and has been used by countless housing agencies serving
millions of units. CHF believes that an independent clearance dust examination
should be required by the EPA to ensure that occupants are protected from
renovation, repair, and painting work that disturbs lead paint.

Recommendations
?Address childcare facilities under the proposed rule;
?Prohibit dangerous work practices; and
?Make clearance dust testing mandatory for all units applicable under
the proposed rule.

Finally, we urge the EPA to enact rules that are consistent with HUD?s
established standards governing renovation and lead safety issues. By speaking
with one voice, the federal government eliminates inconsistent or duplicative
standards, thereby avoiding confusion and lowering the overall costs to
consumers. Consistency in rulemaking benefits the children we are trying to
protect, as well as the adults who must work within these rules.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this important regulation.
Under the Toxic Substances Control Act, this rule was to have been issued by
October 28, 1996. We understand the barriers that can postpone implimentation
of a rule of this nature, but surely all of us recognize that we are 10 years too long
in inacting this. Once the commenting period is completed and the EPA approves
the final rule, its policies must be implemented without delay to protect children
from harmful exposures to lead hazards and lead dust. We hope you will act on
this rule immediately.

Sincerely,

Benjamin L. Hooks, Chairman of the Board
Secretary Jack Kemp, Co-Chair of the Board
Dean Kurt Schmoke, Member of the Board
Secretary Henry Cisneros, Member of the Board

re:Comments on EPA?s Lead Renovation, Repairs and Paint
Proposed Rule
Docket ID number EPA-HQ-OPPT-2005-0049

The Gateway Green Education Foundation requests that the U.S. Environmental
Protection Agency make the following changes in its January 10, 2006 EPA
proposed requirements to minimize the introduction of lead hazards resulting from
the disturbance of lead-based paint during renovation, repair, and painting activities
in most housing built before 1978 (71 FR 1588):

1. Please apply all rules to child care centers and prohibit dangerous practices on
all building exteriors that could elevate children?s blood lead levels.

2. Please continue the dust wipe method of measuring lead contamination in
buildings (including homes) and discontinue consideration of the white glove
method.

3. Please continue the definition of dangerous work practices regarding paint
removal currently used the the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban
Development and disregard recommendations to relax standard made in the Small
Business Review Advocacy Panel Report.

4. Please redefine the term ?childhood lead poisoning? to include children who have
any lead in their blood (> 0 mcg/dL).

These requests are all based on the article below which should be used to clarify
any ambiguities in the above requests.

Sincerely,

Don Fitz, Ph.D., President
Gateway Green Education Foundation

EPA Going Lead Wild

by Don Fitz

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) supposedly helps protect the
environment, especially from toxins that endanger human health. But maybe not.
Lead activists from across the country charge that the federal agency is missing
the chance to reduce exposure to lead in paint and is actually undermining
existing standards of safety.

At issue is the EPA?s proposed ?Lead Safe Work Requirements to Protect
Children during Renovation, Repair and Painting.? Blood lead levels of many
children have increased after remodeling homes built before 1978 (when lead was
banned from paint). Disturbing lead-based paint can release dust in lead or
fumes.

Thus, Section 402 of the Toxics Substance Control Act of 1992 required the EPA
to draft standards for home repairs that would minimize exposure to lead. Though
Congress instructed the EPA to compile rules for lead safe practices by 1996, the
agency failed to act for nearly 10 years. After being threatened with a lawsuit and
receiving a warning from Senator Barak Obama, the EPA finally published a
proposed rule on lead hazards on January 10, 2006.

The 10 year tardy proposal is silent on major issues that affect childhood health.
According to the Sierra Club?s Ed Hopkins, ?EPA?s rule ignores 14,200 child care
centers that have significant lead-based paint hazards.? These centers care for
470,000 children.

Additionally, the proposed rule says nothing concerning dangerous work practices
on building exteriors. This is important for children?s health because practices
such as sandblasting on building exteriors can spread lead dust in streets,
schoolyards and playgrounds.

It remains unclear whether lack of attention to these areas is a blessing in
disguise, since so much of the EPA proposal could prove harmful. A storm of
controversy is brewing over how to determine if home renovation has created a
lead hazard.

For years, the accepted method for measuring the degree of lead danger in
buildings has been ?dust wipe samples.? A cloth is used to wipe dust from key
areas of a house and it is then sent for laboratory analysis. Multiple studies have
confirmed that the amount of lead in dust wipes correlates with blood lead levels of
children living in the homes. The more lead dust there is on the cloth, the more
lead poisoned the children are.

EPA?s proposed rule would toss out this tried and scientifically accepted method.
And what would replace it? The EPA hopes to initiate its own ?white glove
methodology,? which Rebecca Morley of the National Center for Healthy Housing
(NCHH) calls ?baby wipes on a mop.? The white glove method involves wiping
windowsills and floors with white disposable cleaning cloths and then looking to
see if dust is visible on the cloth.

Both the dust wipe and white glove test gather dust on cloth. The major difference
is that dust wipes are sent to a lab for analysis and the EPA proposes training
inspectors to make a visual determination of the presence of lead from a white
glove test.

It?s not hard to figure out that a chemical analysis from a lab is more accurate than
a person eyeballing a cloth. In fact, lead research demonstrates conclusively that
visual examinations are insufficient to determine the quantity of invisible lead dust
present. A 2002 NCHH study found that 54% of housing units passed a visual
lead test but failed clearance levels for lead.

When the EPA developed the white glove test, it only collected data on bare
floors. Consequently, the EPA specifies that the white glove test would only be
used on bare floors and that carpeted rooms would only require a visual inspection
for the presence of lead.

Visual inspections for lead are notoriously unreliable, with a two-thirds rate of
failure to adequately identify lead dangers. About 54 million houses built before
1978 contain some wall-to-wall carpeting, with 47 million having living room
carpeting and 46 million having bedroom carpeting. In all of these, the EPA?s rule
would expose children to lead poisoning by not requiring dust wipes following
home repair.

Perhaps the most insidious aspect of the white glove test is that it could
undermine laws mandating property owners to disclose records of lead
contamination to buyers or renters. Since the EPA rule would not require
renovation firms to provide owners with written documentation of white glove tests,
there would be no records to give to buyers or renters. This loophole could result
in people moving into homes with no information on their degree of lead
contamination.

Even worse than not drafting rules that would require adequate testing for lead, the
EPA proposes to relax rules concerning ?dangerous practices.? This goes to the
heart of the difference between corporate and environmental approaches to
dangerous materials. Whatever the toxin in question, industry spokespersons
suggest ways to control and contain it. Environmentalists argue that it makes
more sense to not make toxic messes than it is to assume the mess will be made
and ponder how to clean it up.

For years, the EPA, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
(HUD) and several other federal agencies have agreed that the best way to control
the release of lead during home repair is to ban dangerous methods of paint
removal. Prohibited methods of paint removal include (a) open flame burning or
torching; (b) machine sanding or grinding or abrasive blasting or sandblasting
without a HEPA local exhaust control; (c) heat guns operating above 1100 degrees
Fahrenheit; or, (d) dry sanding or dry scraping (with some exceptions).

Using heat to remove lead paint is a good example of why a work practice can be
dangerous. Lead volatilizes into a fume at temperatures typical of flame torches.
A fume is not a gas. It is composed of tiny particles that are more easily
absorbed into the human body than are larger particles. This is why techniques
such as heat that were frequently used to remove lead paint between 1970 and
1990 often resulted in an increase (rather than a decrease) of blood lead levels of
children living in the home.

EPA argues that prohibiting dangerous practices could make many jobs, such as
preparing a surface for repainting, very hard or impossible. This contention is
astounding, given that prohibition of dangerous practices has been increasing as
people discover more and better alternatives.

It is hard to overemphasize the health hazards of going backwards and legitimizing
practices that are known to generate large amounts of lead dust and fumes.
Rebecca Morley is the Executive Director of the National Center for Healthy
Housing (NCHH). Reviewing the potential long term effect of the proposed
changes, she emphatically concluded that ?The failure to prohibit dangerous work
practices means that many more homes will be unnecessarily contaminated,
posing risks for future generations who will occupy these homes.?

On its web site, the EPA points out that there are over 310,000 children with
elevated blood lead levels and over 38 million homes with lead-based paint in the
U.S. Then why would it overlook the massive scientific data indicating that it is
trying to move in the wrong direction? Ever since it was founded during the reign
of Richard Nixon, the EPA has been criticized for being far too receptive to
spokespersons of the industries it is supposed to be regulating.

In proposing its rules on lead, the EPA lent a long ear to recommendations of the
Small Business Review Advocacy Panel Report. Instead of promoting a
continuation of bans on dangerous work practices, the Panel urged the EPA to
emphasize training, containment and clean-up concerning lead removal.

The after-the-fact thinking of the small business Panel was incorporated into the
EPA proposed rule on lead. So much so that portions of the EPA proposed rule
are no more than paraphrases of the business Panel?s recommendations. Dr.
Jack Leonard of the Environmental Management Institute noted that ?No scientist
who conducted the research that is the basis for much of the rule were permitted
to comment on the recommendations of the Panel.?

The EPA missed a great chance to offer a new definition of what ?lead poisoning?
means. The standard measurement is the number of micrograms of lead per
deciliter of blood, or mcg/dL. As decades have gone by and bodies of research
have revealed that lower levels of lead damage human health, the blood lead level
used to define lead poisoning has repeatedly dropped.

The current definition of lead poisoning used by the Centers of Disease Control
(CDC) is 10 mcg/dL. Since this standard was published, multiple studies have
documented damage to children?s reading and math ability at levels below 10
mcg/dL. In fact, there is more incremental damage for children?s intelligence
scores for the range 0 ? 10 mcg/dL than for any other 10 point range. It is now
time to redefine childhood lead poisoning to mean finding any lead in a child?s
blood.

Throughout U.S. schools, children frustrated by poor academic skills show
behavioral problems. Barbara Chicherio, who is on the National Committee of the
Green Party USA, is also a social worker in the public schools. She believes
that ?There is no question that many of the difficulties we see in children are
directly or indirectly caused by their exposure to lead at an early age.?

The approach of industry is always to try to convince the public that there is
some ?acceptable? level of toxins. Lead is one of many poisons now known to
have no safe level in the human body. Proposing new rules on lead safe work
requirements during renovation, repair and painting gave EPA heads a perfect
opportunity to redefine lead poisoning and to draft rules based on the goal of
eliminating lead from our environment. Predictably, the EPA failed to live up to the
challenge.

Office of Pollution Prevention and Toxics (OPPT)
Environmental Protection Agency
1200 Pennsylvania Ave., NW.
Washington, DC 20460–0001
(Re: Lead; Minor Amendments to the Renovation, Repair, and Painting Program)

To Whom It May Concern:

As a student in the Environmental and Occupational Health program at the
George Washington University’s School of Public Health & Health Services, I have
become familiar with the toxic effects of lead and its corresponding regulatory
history. I am pleased to see that progress continues to be made on this front,
although I do believe that more can be done in the future to address the problem of
lead in our environment. In order to contribute to the public health discussion, I
have extensively reviewed the Lead Renovation, Repair, and Painting Program
(RRP) rule that went into effect in June of 2008, and its proposed amendments
(Lead; Minor Amendments to the Renovation, Repair, and Painting Program) that
were published in the Federal Register on April 22, 2009. I have prepared the
following comments for your consideration regarding the feasibility and
appropriateness of requiring accredited training providers to submit digital
photographs of successful trainees along with post-course notifications, while also
taking the time to highlight additional areas of improvement for such regulations.

The RRP rule, by establishing the Renovator and Dust Sampling Technician as
two new training disciplines in the field of lead-based paint and developing an in
depth accreditation and certification program for those who perform these tasks,
has improved the level of protection from environmental lead exposure for families
with children across the United States. It created necessary work practice
standards that are to be employed during renovation, repair, and painting
activities. Such a rule is a sure sign of progress as lead abatement regulations
alone left much of the issue unresolved. Through this effort, the Environmental
Protection Agency has developed an approach that not only minimizes the costs
and burdens associated with regulation, but also provides adequate protection
against lead-based paint hazards created by renovation activities, of which the
EPA itself estimates to regularly exceed 8 million projects annually.

By requiring that all renovations subject to this rule only be performed by certified
firms, EPA has put in place a system of high standards that will promote safer
and more effective work practices. Such a system also allows for EPA to
establish a more progressive way to classify a firm or individual renovator as being
properly certified and to ensure that these standards are upheld. The requirement
that the RRP puts forth for the completion of accredited training and certification
process for both renovators and dust sampling technicians is further facilitated by
the fact that they must possess a copy of the course completion certificate at the
job site.

However, as EPA officials rightfully concluded, the possession of a certificate
alone would not be sufficient with regard to EPA’s compliance monitoring efforts.
In order to expedite the process of determining a worker’s training/accreditation
status, EPA, through this amendment, proposes the required submission of post-
course notifications and digital photographs of every successful trainee by the
accredited training program provider upon completion. The notifications and
corresponding photos are to be included in a database record, ensuring that the
individual has met training requirements.

As the requirement for post-course notification was inadvertently omitted from the
final RRP rule’s text, such an amendment would be expected. Furthermore, as
described within the proposed rule’s summary, the amendment to remove the
requirement for accredited lead-based paint activity training providers to submit to
a digital photograph of each successful trainee to the EPA, along with their post-
course notification is only necessary because EPA already receives such photos
through other means. But when considering the proposal to move forward with
digital photograph for both renovators and dust sampling technicians, one does
not find this to be the most effective approach.

As mentioned above, certified renovators are currently mandated to carry a copy
of their training certificate which can be presented to each new employer as proof
that they have received training and are certified in the required work practices.
Rather than require workers to carry around a copy of this certificate and use the
photo for database purposes alone, though, I would suggest issuing photo
identification cards (using the same photo as would be provided in the database)
as a way for the worker to demonstrate his/her certification both on and off the
worksite. I have found that similar suggestions were provided during the public
comment period for the overall RRP, however, there was little explanation as to
why such an approach would not be adopted.

The EPA itself had determined that including a digital photograph in the
notification would not be an added cost to training providers because the cost
would be recouped as part of the fee charged for the course. Such a measure
could surely be dealt with in a similar manner. Certainly this would raise the initial
cost of such training courses by a small margin per worker, but through the
practicality of this approach there is an opportunity to cut costs in the long-term
as such photo identification is not only easier to carry from day to day, but is also
much more likely to last the duration of the accreditation period (5 years),
compared to a paper certificate.

Detailed in the supplementary material that details of the RRP rule itself, the firm
must document that a certified renovator was assigned to every renovation project,
that he/she provided on-the-job training for workers, that the certified renovator
performed/directed tasks required, and that they performed the post-renovation
cleaning verification. Such documentation must be accompanied by a copy of the
certified renovator’s training certificate. As this relatively young system becomes
more advanced, such cards as mentioned above could be used in conjunction with
innovative on-the-job technology that could save time, money and resources by
enabling such reports to be submitted from the worksite, directly into the
database (as seen today with such professions as package delivery companies).

Additionally, there are no corresponding documents that can be used to verify on-
the-job training by a previous employer. EPA has acknowledged that under the
current regulations, renovation firms will generally have to provide training each
time a new non-certified worker is used when this information is not readily
available. Yet, it is the renovation firm’s responsibility to adequately document the
elements of on-the-job training provided to each worker on each project within the
Federal Lead Paint Program (FLPP) database. A further weakness of this system
that has been recognized, though, is that this database will only contain
information about certified renovators working in federally administered
jurisdictions. In concurrence with the photo identification card proposal, I would
offer the suggestion of developing a system wherein workers can be identified
based on their level of on-the-job training and years of experience. Such a system
would allow for more practiced individuals to earn a higher grade as they continue
to improve their skills. With a uniform system in place, not only would firms not
have to waste man-hours training a new individual who already has on-the-job
experience due to a lack of documentation, but also the workers themselves will
be able to have increased mobility within their respective professions, on both the
federal and state level.

I do acknowledge the fact that while the RRP rule in its entirety addresses
significant environmental health and safety risks, this proposed amendment does
so only indirectly as it focuses primarily on administrative requirements
surrounding this regulation. But clearly, while I support the direction the EPA is
going in regards to the RRP rule, I do feel as if there are additional steps that
could be taken (and amendments that could be made) in order to maximize the
benefits of such regulation. In addition to supporting efforts to widen the
amendment’s reach regarding photo identification procedures, one area of concern
would have to involve whether renovators are required to formally report homes that
do house children and/or pregnant women and have not yet gone through the
process of lead abatement. If so, are there any rules in place to require a follow up
in regards to lead abatement/education efforts? Additionally, though it is stated
that work practices for renovation are designed to minimize exposure to lead-
based paint hazards created by the renovation, I would also be interested to learn
what uniform steps are actually being taken to ensure that renovators being
protected from the heightened risk of lead exposure brought about through their
work. Finally, when considering that the withdrawal of a renovator or firm’s
certification is the most significant penalty mentioned in this rule if the regulatory
standards are not upheld, one has to ask, couldn’t these penalties be more strict?

I support the fact that the RRP rule actively extends training, certification, and
work practice requirements to renovation and remodeling projects in target
housing and child-occupied facilities. The EPA, after reviewing the existing
abatement regulations with great care has put forth excellent regulation that
reflects the differences between abatement and renovation activities, yet allows for
progress to continue steadily. In my opinion, though, while moving forward,
further ‘renovation’ of the regulation itself is what is needed. The rule is structurally
sound, but it could use improvement that would help not only with aesthetics, but
also in terms of practicality. The EPA should not be content with such minor
amendments, when so much more could be done today.

Sincerely,

Joseph M. Blankenship

Disclaimer: My comments do not in any way represent the position of the
Southern Nevada Health District (SNHD). The official position of the SNHD, if any,
will be made by the Chief Health Officer, SNHD.

My comments are submitted as a concerned citizen focusing on the health and
well-being of our children. I am the Project Director, however, of the SNHD
Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Program (CLPPP). In addition, I am a
Certified Industrial Hygienist (CIH) with over 20 years of experience developing and
implementing programs to ensure the protection of the health of the workforce
from exposure to a vast number of "airborne contaminants," including airborne
lead. As you may be aware, the airborne standards that govern the
workforce/occupational exposures, are based on an 8-hour day, 40-hour week for
a "healthy adult." Public exposures are typically an "order-of-magnitude" or more
less than the occupational exposure standard.

The current NAAQS for lead, as you know, is 1.5 mcg/m3 averaged,
arithmetically, over a 90-day period. Assuming evenly distributed daily (24-hour)
exposures, the equivalent value to maintain compliance with the NAAQS is
approximately 0.017 mcg/m3.

Faced with the problem of trying to identify the plausible sources and routes of
childhood lead exposure, I conducted a study to see if "inhalation of airborne lead"
was a plausible route and contributed significantly to the blood-lead level (BLL) of
lead poisoned or lead exposed children. From a review of the scientific literature, I
was able to find a mathematical model relating "air lead level/concentrations" (i.e.,
ALL) to "blood-lead levels/concentrations" in children less than 6 years of age.
The model was described by Hayes, et.al. as follows: ln(BLL) = 0.24*ln(ALL) +
3.17. In my study, I conducted air monitoring in pre-1978 homes of children
diagnosed with elevated blood-lead levels. The children's "actual" BLL results as
determined by Quest Diagnostic Laboratories compared quite favorably with
the "predicted" BLL results obtained using the Hayes, et.al. model. The
differences seen between "actual" and "predicted" BLL results were not significant
(p = 0.78).

Using the Hayes et.al. model, ln(BLL) = 0.24*ln(ALL) + 3.17, and assuming an
evenly distributed daily (24-hour) exposure value of 0.017 mcg/m3 to achieve
compliance, the predicted BLL is 9 mcg/dL. This predicted BLL is lower than the
current CDC "level of concern" (i.e., 10 mcg/dL), but it is still higher than what we
would like.

Clearance testing: I feel air sampling for airborne lead levels should be part of the
clearance testing procedure. The proposed regulation (study used) sites 2 mcg
as the limit-of-detection (LOD). I feel this value is too high, unless a huge volume
of air is drawn through the filter. Using the Hayes, et.al., model, the LOD should
be less than 10-E6 mcg/m3 or even as low as 10-E9 as shown below:

TO Whom it May Concern:

I am writing in opposition to the proposed regulations that would establish more
stringent requirements on remodeling and renovation activities on a pre-1978
property.

While I recognize the importance of protecting children from lead based paint
hazards, I believe the proposed regulations fall short of their intended objective.
Specifically, by using a remodeling contract as the primary triggering mechanism
for reducing exposure, you do nothing to limit lead exposure that currently
threatens children.

The regulation appears to be premised on the notion that remodelers cause higher
levels of lead exposure as a result of our actions. However, a recent NAHB study
demonstrates that professional remodelers, following proper work practices,
actually reduce lead based paint levels.

By exempting homeowners from the regulations, you are contradicting the very
foundation of the proposed regulation (i.e., remodeling/renovation results in added
exposure). Why is it acceptable for homeowners to increase lead exposure
(according to the EPA premise) by engaging in unregulated home renovation or
remodeling activities?

As a small businessperson, an important factor in remaining competitive, even
viable, is the ability to accurately project and control costs. I am deeply
concerned that these new regulations will increase my liability exposure, which
could lead to higher insurance premiums, if insurance even remains available.
Again, as costs go up to provide our services, homeowners will be more likely to
undertake the renovations themselves, or engage a contractor less worried about
following proper work practices.

Finally, in order to better identify and remediate true safety concerns, I believe
there needs to be more clarity and better testing procedures to assess lead
hazards, as the test kits are not reliable in making accurate determinations.

In closing, I urge the EPA to delay implementation of the regulations and work
with all interested parties in developing a system that will truly protect our children.

Sincerely:
Bill Kidd, President Missouri Siding and Window

I am writing in opposition to the proposed regulations that would establish more
stringent requirements on remodeling and renovation activities on a pre-1978
property.

hazards, I believe the proposed regulations fall short of their intended objective.

RESPONSE TO THE EPA PROPOSED SUPPLEMENTAL RULES TO INCLUDE
CHILD-OCCUPIED FACILITIES UNDER THE PURVIEW OF THE REGULATIONS
Submitted by the National Association of the Remodeling Industry (NARI)
JULY 5, 2007

About National Association of the Remodeling Industry (NARI)
NARI is a non-profit trade association with national headquarters based in Des
Plaines, IL (northwest Chicago) and with 58 Chapters in most major metro areas
nationwide. NARI is comprised of almost 7,000 member companies ? remodeling
contracting companies, local suppliers and national suppliers. NARI?s Core
Purpose is to advance and promote the remodeling industry?s professionalism,
product and vital public purpose. NARI members voluntarily subscribe to a strict
Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice. NARI provides rigorous programs of
study with hands-on training through its chapter structure. With passage of
examinations demonstrating competence, certifications holding national
recognition are awarded (e.g., Certified Remodeler, Certified Lead Carpenter,
Certified Kitchen and Bath Remodeler, etc.). These programs are a NARI
hallmark and exemplify NARI?s commitment to its Core Purpose.

NARI?s Role in Lead-Safe Work Practice:
Contractor Training
NARI demonstrates a ten-year history of strong support for government initiatives
on lead-safe work practices. Since lead came to the forefront as an environmental
and health hazard, NARI has taken a proactive position training both remodeling
contractors and informing consumers. Between 1996 and 1998, NARI worked
with both EPA and HUD and conducted two-day training seminars throughout the
country on Lead-Safe Remodeling. The outreach was broad and offered to all
remodeling contractors, not just NARI members. NARI continues to work to
ensure that its members employ lead-safe work practices. NARI certification
programs and skill training are consistently updated to reflect most current lead-
safe work practices.

Consumer Education
NARI strives to ensure that the public remains informed about the hazards of lead
and about hiring contractors trained in lead-safe work practices. NARI provides a
brochure entitled ?Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home.? The brochure is
available in both Spanish and English. NARI contractors are aware that they are
to provide, as required by law, this brochure to homeowners prior to commencing
a remodeling project in homes of pre-1978 construction.

NARI?s Position
As noted in our preliminary testimony submitted on May 22, 2006, and
subsequent comments submitted in April, 2007, NARI is in strong opposition to
the new EPA proposed rules governing lead as announced on December 29,
2005. Our opposition is not diminished with the proposal to include child-
occupied facilities under the purview of these regulations.

We would like to reinforce our belief that the EPA?s regulatory approach toward
mitigating lead based paint hazards places undue burdens on the remodeling
industry, while turning a blind eye on homeowner repairs. As the supplemental
regulation maintains a similar approach to the initial regulation, we believe that
many children could needlessly be placed in harms way, primarily because owner
occupants will not be held to the same standards as professional remodelers.

SPECIFIC ISSUES REGARDING THE SUPPLEMENTAL NOTICE:

NARI has very specific concerns regarding the proposed supplemental regulation,
including: The definition of a child-occupied facility; the lack of definition of child
care; exemptions for owner occupied housing; and the onerous disclosure
requirements layered on remodelers.

The proposed definition of a child-occupied facility is as follows: a building or a
portion of a building, constructed prior to 1978, visited regularly by the same child,
under 6 years of age, on at least two different days within any week (Sunday
through Saturday period), provided that each day?s combined visit lasts at least
three hours and the combined weekly visits last at least 6 hours, and the
combined annual visits last at least 60 hours.

We believe that the proposed definition is overly broad, vague, and could end up
including virtually any pre-1978 property, as there are many instances where
friends or relatives provide child-care, or where children frequently visit each other
simply to play. Situations where relatives and friends are providing some level of
child care is happening much more frequently, as the cost of enrolling children in
traditional child-care centers escalates.

Is it the EPA?s intent to include such arrangements under the regulations? In
using the proposed definition of the child-occupied facility, the EPA casts such a
broad net that in the final measure it could be difficult, if not impossible, to
successfully implement the regulation.

In addition, as more individuals and companies are captured under this definition,
it is conceivable that child care facilities in areas lacking trained lead based paint
testers and contractors will have a difficult time complying with the regulation. As
a result, you may end up with companies/homeowners doing the work
themselves, or using untrained companies to perform the renovations.

Further compounding the confusion would be the lack of a definition of child care.
In the prior example, would two children who are frequent playmates at each
other?s homes trigger these regulations? Does the child-care provider need to be
compensated, in order to meet the standards of having provided child care?
Should it even matter if the child-care provider is compensated, as renovation or
repair activities, if not done properly, could expose children to lead hazards? If the
end goal is to minimize risk to children, we believe all renovation work for pre-1978
structures should be included, whether or not compensation is provided for child
care.

As stated in our prior comments, we are extremely concerned that the relatively
small scale renovation or remodeling work that triggers the lead work standards
will create an economic disincentive to use professional remodelers. Further, the
regulations do little to protect the children in owner occupied housing where
hazardous conditions are present, and where conditions could get worse if the
owner occupant conducted repairs on their own.

Finally, with respect to the notification requirements, NARI is opposed to section
745.84 as proposed. As renovation and remodeling experts, we accept the
responsibility to inform prospective clients about lead based paint hazards. We
do not believe however, that remodelers should be responsible for providing
notices to our clients' customers or child-care recipients. This section presents
an additional level of accountability and liability that should be limited to the child-
care provider.

In closing, we want to reiterate our opposition to the proposed regulations and
pledge our willingness to be part of a constructive dialogue that results in a
common sense solution for our all parties impacted by lead based paint hazards.

On behalf of the American Architectural Manufacturers Association, the Associated General Contractors, the Institute of Real Estate Management, the National Association of the Remodeling Industry, National Association of REALTORS®, the National Lumber & Building Material Dealers Association, the Painting & Decorating Contractors Association, Plumbing-Heating-Cooling Contractors Association, Real Estate Roundtable, the Vinyl Siding Institute, and the Window and Door Manufacturers Association, please find attached our comments on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s proposed amendments to the rule for the Renovation, Repair and Painting (“RRP”) Program as it applies to target housing and child-occupied facilities (the “Rule”).  EPA has proposed amendments to the Rule - published in the Federal Register (Volume 75, No. 87) on May 6, 2010 - to require dust wipe testing and clearance testing in specified circumstances.

The Childhod Lead Action Project (Project), founded in 1992, works to eliminate
childhood lead poisoning through education, parent support and advocacy.
Childhood lead poisoning remains the most pervasive, yet preventable
environmental health problem in Rhode Island. It is one of the most insidious
indicators of environmental injustice ? children of color continue to have alarming
rates of poisoning. Over the years, the Childhood Lead Action Project has come
to be recognized as a leading education and information resource by the
community and as a catalyst for social change. The Project is the only
organization in Rhode Island devoted exclusively to this critical issue.

The Project has considerable experience working with Property Owners,
Contractors, Human Service Providers and Building Officials. Since May of 2004,
the Project has successfully trained over 660 people with the Renovator/
Remodeler Course. Regulated under the RI Department of Health, we provide a
program similar to that proposed under EPA?s new requirements to reduce
exposure to lead hazards created by renovation, repair, and painting activities that
disturb lead-based paint. Therefore, our specific concerns and suggestions are
included in this letter. We have also attached our point-by-point response to the
specific questions posed in the EPA document Renovation, Repair, and Painting
Proposal: Points to Consider.

?The Project believes that the proposed 40 CFR 745.90(b) has a large
loophole in the ?supervision? requirement regarding the presence of a certified
renovator during renovation activities. This section would only require that a
certified renovator be physically present on the site during initial posting of signs
and construction of containment, as well as during clearance testing. At other
times, the work could be performed either by a certified renovator or by individuals
that have been trained by a certified renovator in accordance with the EPA
specified training (i.e., no formal certification of these other individuals or training
by authorized provider) as long as a certified renovator is ?available? by telephone
[40 CFR 745.90(b)(5)]. However, while trainers in formal courses must meet
specific knowledge and experience criteria, anyone who completes a certified
renovator class (regardless of their qualifications as a trainer) would be authorized
to ?train? any number of workers for their firm and turn them loose to perform
renovations that are for (all practical purposes) unsupervised. We see this as a
major weakness of the overall certification process because it would allow a single
certified renovator to ?supervise? any number of projects at the same time without
being physically present at any of them. Therefore, we would suggest that 40
CFR 745.90(b) be amended to require the on-site presence of at least one certified
renovator during all phases of the renovation activity.

?The Project believes that the manner in which some proposed
implementation timelines are described may be a source of confusion. For
example, there is a general statement [745.81(a)] that training, certification and
accreditation requirements and work practice standards will become effective one
year after publication of final rule in all states without a currently delegated
renovation program (i.e., directly administered by EPA). However, other aspects
of this proposed rule appear to have implementation dates up to three years after
the publication of the final rule.

?The proposed work practice standards in 40 CFR 745.85 would allow
acceptable clearance to be determined by use of a ?cleaning verification card?
rather than by dust wipes. The Project finds the information provided by EPA in
support of this proposal to be less than compelling. Although one study appeared
to indicate that there were no false negatives (i.e., acceptable clearance by this
method when dust wipes showed a project would NOT have been cleared), several
other studies appeared to have a considerably higher (and unacceptable) false
negative rate. In addition, our experience has shown that even if EPA contractors
under ideal/simulated field conditions could properly use the ?cleaning verification
card?, most renovation contractors would not exercise the same degree of caution
and would be more prone to ?accidentally? misread the card in an attempt to clear
the job in a more rapid manner. Therefore, we believe that use of a ?cleaning
verification card? poses an unacceptably high possibility of a false negative
clearance for an area undergoing renovation, and that traditional dust wipes should
remain as the only acceptable clearance method.

?The proposed initial renovator [40 CFR 745.225(d)(6)] and dust
sampling technician [40 CFR 745.225(d)(7)] courses are both specified as at least
8 training hours, including at least 2 hours of hands-on training activities.
However, the actual course requirements are only described in fairly broad terms.
It seems apparent from their posting on the EPA Lead web site that either the
Joint EPA/HUD Training Curriculum (July, 2003) or the EPA Model Renovation
Training Course (September 2000) are the preferred formats for presenting this
training. As a provider of the Renovator / Remodeler Training Course we believe
that EPA should be consistent with their other lead training programs and
specifically identify a ?model course? (or courses) which contain the essential
training elements that must be included.

The attached paper demonstrates mathematically that the two-sided EPA criterion for a test kit to be acceptable for use under the RRP rule (as currently operationalized: no more than 10% false positives at a lead level of 0.8 mg/sq cm and not more than 5% false negatives at 1.2 mg/sq cm), imposes extremely stringent requirements on the false positive rate at lead levels lower than 0.8 mg/ sq cm. It is questionable whether any test kit, or even laboratory analysis of paint chips, can meet these false positive requirements. However, the paper also shows that the false positive requirement could be significantly relaxed while still meeting the overall goal of achieving a low false positive rate in the current US housing stock built before 1978.

QuanTech, Inc.

First, I want to tell you that I am an extremely alert and safety conscious parent and have always made my children adhere to any safety regulations as put forth by our state which includes mandatory seat-belt use. In the over 35 years that I have been driving I have never gotten one ticket for any traffic violation moving or otherwise.

Second, having worked on special needs school-buses as a monitor and holder of a school bus passenger CDL I have first hand experience with riding on buses where seat belt use was required and thus can tell you first hand the advantages and disadvantages of seat-belt use.

DISADVANTAGES:

Problems with observation, enforcement, litigation, impact on route planning, staffing and finances, sanitation, vandalism, seat-belt inflicted injuries and maintenance issues.

First, Because of the compartmentalized seats where the seat back is high it would be virtually impossible for the driver alone on the larger buses to observe the students to insure that any regulations regarding mandatory seat belt was being complied with.

Second, in light of issue number one it would be necessary to hire additional monitors to assist the driver to insure that the children were being compliant with the law. The hiring of enough monitors alone would not only be a financial burden, but in our county there are barely enough monitors to cover the special needs buses. Many times even those buses have to go without. The larger buses may require more than one monitor to adhere to compliance. See number three.

Third, even if a monitor were placed on each bus due to the high seat back it is impossible to observe all the children at any one time on the larger buses. On the smaller buses this can be managed somewhat between the monitor and driver by making good use of the rear view mirror and direct observation from an alert monitor. Take special note of the word "alert".

Fourth, it would still be impossible to observe all the children without the monitor continually walking the aisles and subsequently putting the monitors safety in jeopardy.

Granted roaming the aisles is somewhat a given with the hazards of the job territory to check on students for various reasons, but let's keep the monitors in their seats as much as possible.

Fifth, it may be argued that the driver could just make sure
the children had the belt on initially. Without a monitor the driver would then have to get out of his/her seat to insure each child was strapped in before departing the stop.

At some bus stops a significant number of children can be picked up thus adding a tremendous amount of time to the run and heat to drivers anger that are impatiently waiting behind the stopped bus.

Though most of our students are capable of buckling themselves in, many of our younger children do require assistance. This in itself can be a problem.

Sixth, there are some parents out who will be ready to sue if you so much as touch their child even to assist them with their belt. I have witnessed this first-hand. The parent was standing right there watching to see that their child was not touched in any way while buckling their belt. This has the possible impact of causing additional run time lost by a child either defiant of buckling up or too young to manage by him or herself.

While it is true that an IEP can require this "no assistance action" to be taken it was not the case in this instance. On a main-stream bus there would be no IEP, but potentially there could be parents out there ready to insist the driver or monitor was abusing their child by assisting them with the application or their child's seat-belt.

Seventh, some drives see the unbuckling of students in an emergency as an issue. Unbuckling of the belt by a student requires very little time and could be done in most cases before the driver ever got to them. I think in most cases this would not be a significant issue unless a child were unconscious or very young and in a shoulder strap safety vest, car seat, or a wheel chair. That is one of the many needs for monitors on the special needs buses.

Eighth, enforcement of the belt use and insuring compliance would become a major but "necessary" headache. Necessary? Yes, because in the event of an accident in this crazy sue happy world if children were found not wearing one it could end up being a litigation, financial and insurance nightmare for the county and driver and "anybody and their uncle" that the sue happy thinks they can get money out of. The driver and county can find themselves in a "no-win" situation. Whether a child get hurt with the belt by a careless toss or found without a seat-belt in an accident, if use were mandatory it would just be another way parents could get money from a legal suit.

I personally feel having ridden the buses myself as a driver and monitor and with occasional opportunity to be thrown in a sudden emergency stop without a seat belt that the high back padded seats do offer adequate protection.

I can also say from first hand experience the seat-belt use in the hands of some children can potentially cause more trouble then any help they serve.

Ninth, vandalism could no doubt be another issue. The belts could in the hands of a vandal be another temptation item for destruction. Over the course of the years we have had broken fire extinguishers, slashed seats and broken windows and mirrors and many other assorted things students can do to destroy parked buses and buses on the run. Seat belts would be one more thing for the vandals to tamper with even with simple things such tying knots in the straps of the belts fallen through the seat in front of them.

Tenth, the seats on our buses have gaps between the seat back and seat proper in which the seat belt often slips down through the crack in back of the seat sometimes gets hung up and difficult to pull back through. If the belt is knotted in the back by some bored child this again would take more time out of the run to sort that mess out. On some of our older buses just the act of trying to retrieve the belt could cause cuts and scrapes on the hands.

Eleventh, I had an occasion to witness an child quickly getting up from his seat and upon removal of his belt without thinking gave the belt straps a good toss. Needless, to say what happened to his seat mate was a good bop in the mouth and a bloodied lip from a flying belt buckle. Fortunately no major bodily harm was done, however, I could see where a belt eagerly tossed off could potentially cause a few chipped teeth, stitches required in the lip or cuts and bruises to the face or eye injury to a seat mate.

Twelfth, I have never seen a bus seat belt that I have felt comfortable with that would work properly in event of an accident. I don't know why that is. Perhaps, it's a design flaw with the type of pull through buckle belt we are using. From the start I have complained about them because they continually loosen up. Nothing has ever been done to correct or research the problem. It could have something to do with the age of the belt.

Though the pre-trip inspection calls for checking out the proper condition of the equipment there is no way to test whether or not a belt is going to hold unless one sees the child in a belt that actually loosens up. I don't have to tell you, it's scary and I've seen it happen too many times. I would seriously question the belt's effectiveness. On our special needs buses it can be a "royal pain" insuring that each child's belt is not only on, but remains tight. If a child wiggles too much the belt slips and loosens up. So not only would the driver and or monitor would have to insure the child not only kept the belt on during the trip, but also kept it tight.

Again, it is simply not possible for the driver to be alert to the road and traffic conditions while constantly watching the students in the rear view mirror to insure that not only is the belt on, but on properly.

Thirteenth, do parents know how many kids that not only like to lick the windows also like to put the belt ends in their mouth? Do they know how many times the belt straps have fallen on the filthy floor? Do they know how many children get sick to the stomach on a bus and would no doubt get some of the regurgitated liquid on the belt? It is enough times that would make any parent sick on the stomach themselves and think twice about the sanitation issues the belts alone would cause not with just their child putting their belt into their mouth, but even handling it.

I don't know that we've ever had anyone pass along a germ making another child sick and have no way of finding that out, but I would think the potential could certainly be there, particularly if en mass seat-belt use were required. It would be interesting to conduct a bacterial test on the belts to see what germs are harboring on them.

It would also be interesting to compare sick days in states where belts were mandatory against a non use state.

I would think maintaining a belt with any amount of safe sanitation would be very difficult for the driver. We have had infant seat belt straps we were able to take out and scrub clean but anchored in seat belts would be another matter. What would the disinfectant be, bleach? How many children would be sensitive to any cleaning products used?

Fourteenth, in this age of budget cut-backs, increasing gas prices and more schools being added thus doing "more with less" retro fitted seat-belt installation would also be an additional financial burden to the already cash-strapped county. Purchasing additional buses with seat-belts would also add to the expense.

Fifteenth, do they make extensions for heavier children? This may be a problem. While riding the bus as a monitor I like to wear my belt because it is there, not because I think it will give me any more protection than the seat in front of me. However there was a brief period of time when I weighed in at the low 200 lbs point. I could not get that belt around me. I have a feeling in this age of obesity that there are many students that weigh significantly more. This could possibly necessitate more administrative action or finding a specialized belt.

ADVANTAGES:

One, when buses are carrying the max load of students particularly at the high school level seating can be quite cramped. The belts do offer an additional security to keep one in their seat.

While serving as a monitor I have experienced this from both angles.
As an adult I sometimes have to sit on the very edge of a two seat-er that is very cramped with an older or larger child. I once lost my balance and fell out of my seat. I was not injured, but ever since that time wearing of the belt has afforded me much more security.

Two, I have also discovered that there are a few kids in the younger grades who enjoy playing around take great delight by intentionally throwing themselves on the floor if the driver takes a corner a little too rough. Never any injuries, but the recount of the tale to the parents at the end of the day gives them something else to complain about. Having that child wear a seat belt cured that problem.

Unfortunately, since then the reg has changed and now states that unless a child has it on his or her IEP the child is not required to wear a seat-belt and the driver could get into trouble if he or she has the student put one on. Students are allowed to put on their belt with self initiation if they so desire.

This may not be a bad way to go should the requirement for buses to be out-fitted with seat-belts occur. Do not make the law mandatory, but have them there if the child wants to wear them.

I believe this was an issue presented by one parent that their child was traumatized from riding in a car having to wear the belt and not having any on the bus. Personally, I think the child will get over it if the parent does.

In all the years my children rode the bus this transition was never a problem for any of them nor have I been made aware that it has been for any children on the buses I have personally carried and observed.

In closing I think there still remains many questions to be answered that would serve to strengthen the case one way or the other.

In addition to preforming a bacterial count and type on seat belts currently installed in buses I think it would also be interesting to hear from any drivers that have been in an accident with children wearing belts and could make a hypotheses as to how much more they think their riders were protected.

It would also be interesting to hear from any drivers that have found themselves in a position where they had to release all the belts in an emergency as opposed to those who are imagining such an occurrence.

It would be interesting to know if any crash tests have been done with buses using mannequin's with and without belts.

My hypotheses is that in the event of a roll-over I could see belts being very helpful. Unfortunately, it would probably be the flying cargo causing the most injury and I think providing bus storage areas for books, bags and musical instruments would be more helpful from the manufacturers of school buses. Of course that would also add considerably to the bus purchase price.

How much the high padded seat backs alone would help is questionable in certain types of crashes without actual testing to know, but I suspect that in a head-on or rear end crash the seat backs would offer great protection in themselves.

With side crashes in most cases the bus is built high enough and strong enough to withstand most of the impact of most vehicles. Belts may or may not be helpful if hit by a lesser vehicle. I suspect they would not contribute that much to any injury prevention and any injuries received would most likely be minor.

On the other hand if a bus takes a direct hit anywhere from a larger and heavier and fast moving vehicle be it truck or train I doubt the addition of seat belts other than for the driver would afford any more protection to those in the direct path of the hit. Only testing could tell for sure and case studies.

It is my hope that in defense either way of the belt someone qualified in physics, gravitational force and knowing the material the buses are made of will be able to lend a scientific reasoning behind either support for the belt or not enough to warrant the changes in the regulation.

I do believe that the statistics attest for themselves on the safety of buses over the private vehicle. I also would hope that statistically incidents of specific types of accidents would be looked at and some percentage of belt protection would be able to be drawn.

Logistically there are loads of reasons not to have seat-belts installed on buses, but if the belt saves the life of one child particularly if it is mine or yours what would be the worth. Could we even begin to assign a dollar amount in addition to the amount of inconvenience experienced by the drivers and transportation staff.

Not only seeking opinions or testimony by a physical scientist or engineer but also medical lab personal and maybe even ER personnel that have case records of injuries treated and as to whether seat belt use was in effect would not be out of order.

There are many questions to be answered; chiefly, are we doing enough to protect our children? Where do we draw the line out of reason or compassion?

One final interesting thing to know would be of those who advocate seat belt use for bussed children, how many put their own children in jeopardy by things they do at home, things they teach their children about other important life lessons such as respect for authority, religious belief, family values and what they do in their own car when driving with their kids. I would hope that none of those advocating seat-belt use have ever run a bus red light, but you never know. People are full of inconsistencies in what they allow as acceptable or not.

God bless you with wisdom in this most touchy subject. In most things we all do in life, we weigh doing what is considered as obtaining reasonable and affordable security and or protection against the likely-hood of an unfortunate event occurring. If we think we may be burgled and the subject may come in with a gun and shoot us in the process we could go as far as living in a steel box with no windows. But how many go that far? No one I know. Some who live in especially notorious areas for crime may go as far as investing in iron bars for their doors and windows, but even that wouldn't protect against a drive by shooting that sadly all but too often happens. Others because of where they live feel iron bars would be too tacky looking or the HOA may not approve so they invest in ADT. Others would like to have it either one of those protections but can't afford it so they lock their doors.

We can only go so far and do what is reasonable within our resources to protect us against what we feel will really happen. I dare say nine times out of ten we are right nothing happens. To the one that does end up losing there is still solace in knowing that protection was given to the level that was reasonable for that person to have.

Manufacturers put protective devices in our cars, but sadly sometimes it's not enough. If we have money we can read the stats and purchase a car we feel will structurally offer us the most crash protection. If we don't have the money we buy some tiny little car to get us around town and wear our seat belt. How many of us have put up the money to drive the streets in Sherman tanks to protect our family against a drunk driver? Nobody I know. Even if we had the money and it was legal we would be afraid of being socially ostracized. We all have our criteria within which we make decisions about our health and welfare.

How many seat-belt on bus advocates are there who are constantly bombarding their children with second-hand smoke. Mt mother never having smoked in her life died from complications of second hand smoke. Dad was almost a chain smoker for most of his life and then she got it at the office wherein she worked. This was before the no-smoke rules came about and to go to work you might as well have been in a pool hall.

The fact remains we can't do it all and if we could we wouldn't for various reasons. Every day people will die on our highways. Every day people will die in violent crimes that technically they could have protected themselves from, but chose not to out of taking what they thought were reasonable precautions. Every day people will die from medical complications from unhealthy food choices. Yet these people knew the risks and chose to do nothing because they enjoyed the choices in food they made. In their mind they chose not to starve themselves, but chose not to go the extra mile in spite of the statistics.

I think the seat-belt issue on buses is going to boil down to the same thing. I don't think we have all the stats available to us that there could possibly be, but there is enough to make a good educated guess. We know compartmentalization works. In deciding if we need to do more we will be faced with first Is it doable and then is it reasonable to do more in light of other precautions we have already taken. What do the stats that we have tell us about the risk equated with doing what is reasonable in that situation?

We weigh our chances and hedge our bet on how much to do that is within our resources and any other requirements one may have when deciding how far to go with our own safety and protection. Should any more be asked of our leaders in the care of our protection?

Without getting into theology, no matter what we do in life physical death will come sooner or later in some way and there is no way any of us are going to ever be able to stop it. Death is no respector of age either. Things can and do happen to anybody at any time and some of those things are unanticipated freak events.

A few years back there were a couple of serial killers in our area. Anybody who was deathly afraid of getting shot might have chosen to never leave their house, but I dare say for most people it was business as usual. A few lost the bet, but they did what was reasonable in light of what they felt the chances of them becoming one of the victims.

Officials who find themselves in charge of our protection should not be expected to do any more. While they are being paid to perform their work, their task is to use their connections and resources to make informed decisions as would anyone else. The only difference is our safety officials are trusted to be more informed through access to different resources and statistics the average person does not have. Thus, it might be said that for our officials it is their business to find out the facts and make intelligent decisions based on what they know and do what is reasonable in that light.

Nobody ever wants to lose a child and conscientious parents will do what they can to protect their children, but even they will only go so far using the same reasonable criteria.

It seems to me that the purpose for the light sport aircraft category is to provide access to the air with some limits to the use of aircraft, by airmen not trained or necessarily physically qualified for private pilot operations or above. The limitations are there in part because of pilots experience, but more so for limited utility and flight area limitations for safety and airspace congestion.

Attendant to the limitations of light sport aircraft are use restrictions on the aircraft that principally reduce the utility of the aircraft to that of recreation. Limitations on aircraft configurability would only have limited or no effects on the utility of the aircraft within the rules of operation of light sport aircraft, and in the case of repositionable undercarriages and cockpit controlled adjustable propellers particular, there are negative implications on safety. These controls are as important to safe flight as the mixture control.

In the case of aircraft that operate from water or land, safety issues regarding the use of an in flight and on water adjustable propeller pitch seems to provide increased safety without any utility negatives . Take off distances can be shorter reducing fatigue on the airframe. Landings may be slower. Certainly taxi operations will be safer. The gain in performance in the air for aircraft so configured and powered per class limits is minimal and limited by the basic airspeed limits of the class.

The use of repositionable gear for an aircraft that can operate from land or water, is essential to the fundamental definition of the capability. As an normal experimental aircraft, these configurations would be expected on such a plane. Again airspeed limitations are not an issue. Operations with undercarriages that are not repositionable increases the potential for incorrect landing configurations as a result of inflight failure of the engine.

In both cases there are two reasons for possibly limiting the use or existence of those functions – operator inability, or issues associated with failure of the systems in question. Operator inability is an issue for training – not aircraft limitations. System failure can only be addressed through training and maintenance, just like engine failure.

Qualification/training can be managed much like the endorsements for operation of complex aircraft.

The Administrator should allow flight activities for the LSA amphibian aircraft in the light sport aircraft category with the full capability of the aircraft offered to the pilot, but ensure the pilot receives a complex aircraft endorsement for the class aircraft.

I fully support LSA’s petition to allow LSA certification under the ASTM consensus standards of amphibious aircraft with retractable landing gear.

The ability to reposition the land gear is an integral part of an amphibian aircraft. I also understand that the purpose of the LSA category is to keep the aircraft flow by sport pilots as simple to fly as possible. It seems that a logical solution to the problem would be to allow private pilots and above to reposition the gear in flight within current regulations. Sport pilots that choose to fly an amphibian would not be able to reposition the gear until they received instruction and were signed off by a qualified instructor. This issue has recently become not only a regulatory question but also a matter of unfair competition and restraint of trade by the FAA. One LSA certified amphibian aircraft has been given the approval for pilots other than sport pilots to reposition the gear in flight. Another LSA certified amphibian aircraft has been arbitrarily denied this approval. This creates a hugh competitive advantage for the one aircraft which appears to have received unfair preferential treatment by the agency.
