Comment on [Docket No. FAA-2006-25891; Directorate Identifier 2006-NM-186-AD] RIN 2120-AA64

This proposed action requires replacement of certain parts deemed to be not airworthy with “new and improved” parts pursuant to certain OEM and/or manufacturer service documents. The Modification and Replacement Parts Association (MARPA) submits the following comments:

Item #1
Frequently airworthiness directives are derived from service information originating with the type certificate holder or its suppliers. Manufacturer service documents are privately authored instruments generally enjoying copyright protection against duplication and distribution. When a service document is incorporated by reference pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 552(a) and 1 CFR part 51 into a public document such as an airworthiness directive, it loses its private, protected status and becomes itself a public document. If a service document is used as a mandatory element of compliance it should not simply be mentioned, but should be incorporated into the regulatory document. Public laws by definition must be public which means they cannot rely for compliance upon private writings. Moreover, the legal interpretation of a document is a question of law and not of fact. Therefore, unless the service document is incorporated by reference a court of law will not consider it in interpreting the airworthiness directive. We are concerned that failure to incorporate essential service information could result in a court decision invalidating the airworthiness directive.

Incorporated by reference service documents should be made available to the public by publication in the Document Management System (DMS) keyed to the action that incorporates them. The stated purpose of the incorporation by reference method of the Federal Register is brevity; to keep from expanding the Federal Register needlessly by publishing documents already in the hands of the affected individuals. Traditionally, “affected individuals” has meant aircraft owners and operators who are generally provided service information by the manufacturer. However, a new class of affected individuals has emerged since the majority of aircraft maintenance is now performed by specialty shops instead of aircraft owners and operators. This new class includes maintenance and repair organizations (MRO), component servicing and repair shops, parts purveyors and distributors and organizations manufacturing or servicing alternatively certified parts under 14 CFR § 21.303 (PMA). Further, distribution to owners may, when the owner is a financing or leasing institution, not actually reach the persons responsible for accomplishment of the airworthiness directive.

We therefore request that the service documents deemed essential to the accomplishment of this proposed action be (1) Incorporated by reference into the regulatory instrument, and (2) published in the DMS.

Item #2
Type certificate holders in their service documents universally ignore the possible existence of PMA parts. This is especially true with foreign manufacturers where the concept may not exist or be implemented in the country of origin. Frequently the service document upon which an airworthiness directive is based will require the removal of a certain part numbered part and the installation or a different part numbered part as a corrective action. This practice runs afoul of 14 CFR § 21.303 which permits development, certification and installation of alternatively certified parts (PMA).

Mandating the installation of a certain part numbered part to the exclusion of all other parts is not a favored general practice. Such action has the dual effect of preventing in some cases installation of perfectly good parts while at the same time prohibiting the development of new parts permitted under 21.303. Such a prohibition runs the risk of taking the airworthiness directive out of the realm of safety and into the world of economics since prohibiting the development, sale and use of a perfectly airworthy part has nothing to do with safety. Courts could easily construe such actions as being outside the statutory basis of the airworthiness directive (safety) and, as such, unenforceable. [Courts are reluctant to find portions of a rule unenforceable since they lack the knowledge and authority to rewrite requirements and are thus generally inclined to simply void the entire rule.] We believe that specification of a certain part numbered part to be installed should be viewed as one, but not the only method of addressing the problem.

This action, as written, also does not comply with proposed FAA Order 8040.2 which states as follows:

Parts Manufacturer Approval (PMA). MCAI that require replacement or installation of certain parts could have replacement parts approved under 14 CFR § 21.303 based on a finding of identicality. We have determined that any parts approved under this regulation and installed should be subject to the actions of our AD and included in the applicability of our AD.

The Small Airplane Directorate has developed a blanket statement that resolves this issue by adding the phrase “or FAA-approved equivalent P/N” to the part number mandated to be installed. The following language, as set forth in 2006-CE-29-AD, is also included:

(f) 14 CFR 21.303 allows for replacement parts through parts
manufacturer approval (PMA). The phrase ``or FAA-approved equivalent
P/N'' in this AD is intended to allow for the installation of parts
approved through identicality to the design of the replacement
parts. Equivalent replacement parts to correct the unsafe condition
under PMA (other than identicality) may also be installed provided
they meet current airworthiness standards, which include those
actions cited in this AD.

Typically the Engine Directorate and the Rotorcraft Directorate avoid the issue by specifying “airworthy parts” be installed leaving the determination of exactly which parts to the installer.

Because this proposed action differs markedly in treatment of this issue from other directorates, the mandates contained in Section 1, paragraph (b)(10) of Executive Order 12866 are not being met. This paragraph requires that all agencies act uniformly on a given issue.

We therefore request that the proposed action be modified to consider and permit the use of PMA parts pursuant to existing laws and regulations.

Jack Buster
Chairman, AD Committee
Modification and Replacement Parts Association

Further, distribution to owners may, when the owner is a financing or leasing institution, not actually reach the persons responsible for accomplishment of the airworthiness directive.

To further enhance and promote aviation safety we therefore request that the service documents deemed essential to the accomplishment of this proposed action be (1) Incorporated by reference into the regulatory instrument, and (2) published in the DMS.

Type certificate holders in their service documents universally ignore the possible existence of PMA parts. If the part numbered part determined to be defective has been replaced by a PMA part carrying a different part number, the AD will not mandate its removal. The FAA has frequently stated that defective PMA parts, if known, will be identified in the regulatory action. However, the FAA’s state of mind or intent is not a probative element in the formulation of written rules. As stated previously, the interpretation of a document is a question of law and factual elements, such as the FAA’s knowledge at the time, will not be considered. Therefore, if a part number is used to designate the parts determined to be defective there needs to be language that would also embrace any defective PMA parts that carry different part numbers, but share the same defects.

Parts Manufacturer Approval (PMA). MCAI that require replacement or installation of certain parts could have replacement parts approved under 14 CFR § 21.303 based on a finding of identicality. Including the above statement from 8040.2 would resolve the issue of possible defective PMA parts being installed and not affected by the proposed action.

The Small Airplane Directorate has developed a blanket statement that resolves the replacement issue by adding the phrase “or FAA-approved equivalent P/N” to the part number mandated to be installed. The following language, as set forth in 2006-CE-29-AD, should be included:

14 CFR 21.303 allows for replacement parts through parts manufacturer
approval (PMA). The phrase ``or FAA-approved equivalent
P/N'' in this AD is intended to allow for the installation of parts
approved through identicality to the design of the replacement
parts. Equivalent replacement parts to correct the unsafe condition
under PMA (other than identicality) may also be installed provided
they meet current airworthiness standards, which include those
actions cited in this AD.

Typically the Engine Directorate and the Rotorcraft Directorate avoid the issue by specifying “airworthy parts” be installed leaving the determination of exactly which parts to the installer.

Because this proposed action differs markedly in treatment of this issue from other directorates, the mandates contained in Section 1, paragraph (b)(10) of Executive Order 12866 are not being met. This paragraph requires that all agencies act uniformly on a given issue.

We therefore request that the proposed action be modified to consider possibly defective PMA parts and permit the use of PMA parts meeting the “new and improved” criteria pursuant to existing laws and regulations and the issues set forth in the current proposed regulatory action.

Jack Buster
Chairman, AD Committee
Modification and Replacement Parts Association

As a former 14 year Air Force pilot and current 42 year old commercial airline pilot I am writing in support of raising the minimum retirement age for commercial airline pilots from 60 years old. In support of my request I've found the information in a researched article written by Dr. Robin Wilkening, a leading occupational medical expert in the nation on Age 60 and frequent testifier before Congress on the issue, to be very informative. I will quote the summary of this article that was published in the prestigious Journal of Aviation, Space and Environmental Medicine (Aviat Space Environ Med 2002; 73:194-202.

Methods: An extensive review of the medical literature was accomplished using MEDLINE. Pertinent Federal Regulations were examined. Legal proceedings and public domain documents were noted. Letters and personal communication were solicited where necessary information could not be ascertained by other means.

Results: The Age 60 Rule was not based on any scientific data showing that airline pilots aged 60 and older were any less safe than younger pilots, and there is evidence to indicate that the choice of age 60 was actually based on economic rather than safety considerations. Airline pilots consistently exceed general population norms for longevity, physical health, and mental abilities. Fear of an adverse pilot health event causing a crash in standard multi-crew operations is not justified. For decades, airline pilots under age 60 have been granted the means to demonstrate their fitness for flying by taking medical, cognitive, and performance evaluations that are denied to airline pilots when they reach age 60. Actual flight experience demonstrates that older pilots are as safe as younger pilots. International aviation experience indicates that abolishing the age 60 Rule will not compromise aviation safety.

Conclusion: There appears to be no medical, scientific, or safety justification for the AGE 60 Rule, where age alone is used as the single criterion of older pilot fitness, represents age discrimination in commercial aviation.

This article was written back in 2002 but its validity continues to be historically proven today. Older non commercial pilots, due to increased experience continue to maintain a slight better safety record than those of their younger peers. The new ICAO standard, due to go into effect this Nov, also indicates the international aviation communities’ support for this as well.

The Age 60 Rule developed as a political tool but was described (with out any supporting data)as a safety issue. This was initially protested by the pilot unions. As future contracts developed that allowed for substantial pilot retirement benefits, the pilot unions began to support it. I feel through my research and actual experience as a pilot that this rule is still supported for political and personal reason while hard medical data is being overlooked. November 23, 2006, the ICAO Council will ammend it's charter to allow one pilot in a two-pilot crew to act as pilot in command until reaching the age of 65.

At the same time, a State may wish to impose a lower maximum age limit than that specified by ICAO. It however, cannot prevent an aircraft operated by a PIC holding a license from another State, who is below the ICAO upper limit, from operating in its airspace.

What this means is that after November 23, 2006, foreign pilots will be allowed to fly in US airspace, acting as pilot in command until they reach the age of 65. At the same time, under present FAA regulations, US pilots will be forbidden from conducting similar operations after reaching the age of 60.

The majority of aerospace physicians believe that when the Age 60 Rule was established, an arbitrary number was chosen without substantial evidence correlating age to safety.

After 2-plus years of study, the Aerospace Medical Association's Civil Aviation Safety Subcommittee found in 2004 that there is insufficient medical evidence and/or accident record to support airline pilot restrictions based on age alone.

The Subcommittee thus suggests that the Association abandon its 20-plus year prior policy of support, and recommends that the FAA abandon the Age 60 Rule altogether, change the cutoff criteria, or raise the age limit. This was one of the sources cited by ICAO in justifying it increase of the age limit for airline pilots.

For the sake of fair and equitable treatment of US pilots, consistent with the studies conducted by Aerospace medical experts, the current FAA Age 60 Rule should be ammended to conform with the new ICAO standard.

I am a 28yr Captain with a major airline. I have watched many healthy, highly competant, and highly experienced pilots be pushed out of their career field while still very capable to perform the job they have pursued and trained for their whole lives.
The archaic age 60 requirment that was put in place in the early 50's was strictly an economic decision with labor factors at that time. It was never, and still is not, about safety...as ALPA would like us to believe. In fact, ALPA at one time fought vigorously to have that rule changed.
The international community at the end of this year (ICAO), will change their charter to allow their members to fly to age 65 - including into and out of the US. The internationl members that have already been flying past age 60 have over 33 million man hours of incident and accident free flying.
Almost ALL of the recent accidents and incidents in the US aviation community have involved younger, less experienced pilots. NONE...have had any impact due to any age related factor. NONE!
Let's be perfectly honest about why ALPA is resisting the change to age 65. It is due to the young age of their membership who wish to move up the seniority ladder more quickly - unfortunately at the expense of senior members, many who have lost their pensions and major parts of their income in the 'restructuring' of the aviation industry since 9/11.
I personally was not in favor of changing the rule in the past...not because I felt there was any safety factor involved, but because those we're the rules when I signed on in 1978'. I felt I would have my career and then get out of the way for the next generation. But with the loss of the pensions, that is no longer a realistic option. Many of my bretheren have families, children in college, and some have serious medical issues in their families. I guarantee the pilots that want to fly, REALLY want to fly! That would not be a factor, because they would be doing what they really love.
We are evaluated several times a year, both skill wise, and medically. Any pilot who cannot pass muster should not be allowed to continue. But in this modern day and age, when people are living longer, healthier lives, people should not be discriminated arbitrarily by their age.
I submit, and hope, that this committee will be able to see past the 'political' position of the people who oppose this long ovedue change.
In the last 70's and early 80's, ALPA (of which I am a lifetime member), used incredible political, and financial capitol, defending having a 3rd pilot in the Boeing 737 cockpit. The US has always 'LED' the avition industry in innovation and safety. This time we seem to be the 'dead weight' holding down common sense, and good judgement.
Thank you for listening to my input, and I hope the people who make the decision on this long overdue change, have the strength and vision for the future of our industry, and our profession.

While I understand the desire to align the Coast Guard's proposed Prohibited Items with TSA's Prohibited Items List for aviation, I believe it is inappropriate to do so due to the vast distinction between aircraft and cruise ships. I believe an excellent distinction was recognized in that on board a cruise ship, items that might be prohibited from boarding the vessel might already be located within the vessel for recreational and other purposes, i.e., items such as steak knives or ice axes. I think the biggest distinction that this proposed amendment does not reflect accurately is the distinction of the two industries, in that air travel is primarily used for transporting oneself from point A to point B, while cruise ships carry thousands of individuals for extended periods of time.

In addition, allowing cruise ships to prohibit additional items or substances not listed on the Prohibited Items list that they deem a threat to safety in effect produces inconsistencies between ships screening standards and therefore will lead to even greater uncertainty and confusion as to appropriate screening procedures for cruise ships. Similarly, the Coast Guard allows for flexibility in revising the Prohibited Items list in order to protect the public from security threats that can change rapidly. However, if the list is able to be revised, modified, and revised again, the probability of conflicts arising at the ports are even higher, thus delaying the screening process even further. Under the Maritime Transportation Security Act of 2002, the National Maritime Transportation Security Plan shall provide for efficient, coordinated, and effective action to deter and minimize damage from a transportation security incident Implementing screening procedures similar to those executed at an airport would thus deter this effectiveness and efficiency standard causing undue delay and burden to passengers.

If a screening process similar to that of TSA were to be implemented for cruise ships, the delay in boarding would be infinitely greater due to the vast difference in vessel capacity. Unlike air travel, cruise ships are primarily used for vacation and special occasions. Requiring individuals to sit through a process similar to what TSA has adopted, might lead into a decline of travel via cruise ships, which will in turn decline revenue for these cruise companies. Additionally, cruise lines have dedicated security forces that function as police on the ship as opposed to the minimal presence on an aircraft. Currently, TSA works alongside these cruise companies to implement extensive security techniques involving canine teams, explosive experts, advanced imaging technology machines and terrorist watch list matching. Thus, there is no need to further scrutinize the screening process for cruise ships.

If the Coast Guard is adamant about creating screening procedures reflective of TSA's, they need to take into consideration the vast difference in size of those on board a cruise ship versus those on board an aircraft, and these considerations should be reflected in the proposed regulations. Moreover, cruise ships should be allowed to formulate their own screening methods that they deem most efficient, subject to approval by the U.S. Coast Guard. Therefore, the proposed regulation and accompanying Prohibited Items list should serve as guidance and should be tailored to more accurately reflect the nature cruise ship industry. Unlike the aviation industry, cruise ships are more resilient than aircraft which should result in the development of specific screening requirements for the cruise ship industry. Therefore, despite the proposal of new regulations on the cruise ship industry, the low probability of a terrorist attack on cruise ships should result in less stringent screening requirements at cruise ship terminals.

The Great Lakes Cruising Coalition (GLCC) is a bi-national organization that advocates for passenger cruising on the Great Lakes. Its members represent American and Canadian port cities and towns, port authorities, several U.S. states and the Canadian province of Ontario, visitor and convention bureaus, the Canadian St. Lawrence Seaway Marketing Corporation and the U.S. Department of Commerces St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation. Its disparate membership is unified in the coalitions mission to revive the fledgling, yet historic, Great Lakes cruising industry.

Since its inception in 1997, the GLCC has worked closely with federal, state, and local agencies on both sides of the border to insure safe and successful Great Lakes cruising experiences for its international clientele, and to expand its reach.

The changes proposed in the U.S. Coast Guards Consolidated Cruise Ship Security Regulations fail to recognize the uniqueness of the Great Lakes as a cruise destination and pose a serious threat to the efforts and investments that have been made to revive this emerging trade.

Very few dedicated passenger cruise terminals exist in the Great Lakes basin. Many facilities that have received cruise ships over the years are no more than municipal parks with waterfront docks. While facility security plans (FSPs) are in place to accommodate cruise ship visits, the imposition of additional standardized regulations to require terminal screening programs (TSPs) at these sites is wholly impractical. Few entities in our region have the financial wherewithal to afford the additional cost of either the required screening equipment or the personnel to operate it.

Currently all vessels trading in the Great Lakes are subject to rigorous inspection protocols imposed by the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Canadian Border Services Agency (CBSA). Both of these Federal agencies are satisfied with the disciplined and compliant nature of the ports and cruise ships that enter their jurisdictions and recognize the Great Lakes as being a unique destination.

We believe the proposed regulation needs to be rewritten to in a way that cannot be interpreted as imposing additional economic hardship on terminal facilities acting as cruise ship ports of call. We believe the screening functions should remain with the cruise lines. The system now in place has worked successfully. There is no need for a duplication of screening methodologies.

To Whom It May Concern:

The North Atlantic Ports Association Inc. (NAPA), founded in 1949, is one of the oldest and most active associations of commercial seaports. Our member ports in the United States stretch from Maine to Virginia, and our goal is to promote commerce in a reasonable manner. Each one of our members is dedicated to the movement of cargo and passengers in a safe, secure and efficient manner in order to strengthen the local and national economies. Many of our ports have a limited cruise ship season and some ports are Port of Call ports.

The proposed new rule on Consolidated Cruise Ship Security needs more clarification on the transfer of responsibility for security and screening on cruise days. Cruise ship operations vary from port to port. In some ports the cruise line operates the terminal. In others, its the port authority that is the terminal operator. A closer investigation in to the financial aspects of the cruise industry, especially in the northern climate ports, will reveal the terminal owner/operators are operating at a break even basis.

The financial beneficial impact to the port community is to service providers and businesses related to tourism such as restaurants, attractions and shops. We believe that these costs could be significant and may be hard to absorb by the operator/ owner, especially in those ports with short windows of operation. Should these costs be too burdensome, they could only be passed onto the passenger taking the cruise. This pass through charge in the form of Port Security Fees would be marked up and collected by the cruise line from the passengers. The net result will be to transfer the burden and costs to U. S. terminal owners /operators and the U.S citizen passengers while relieving the foreign corporations, which own the cruise line, of any security related financial burdens.

This new regulation has the potential of not only increasing cost but also liability. By amending the regulation, the USCG will shift the screening process for passengers and baggage to the terminal operator or owner. This places all the liability, training and maintaining of the screening equipment onto the terminal operator and / or owner. The result is the cruise terminal operator/owner will be subject to civil penalties if goods and devices are discovered onboard the cruise ship.

Under existing cruise ship security regulations, terminal owners/operators and cruise ship operators collaborate to ensure proper security measures are in place to screen cruise ship passengers and their baggage. The terminal owners/operators and the ship operators coordinate the particulars of the screening process, as outlined in NVIC 4-02, and confirm each other's screening responsibilities in the signed Declaration of Security. This system has worked very well and we see no need to change.

In conclusion, NAPA is concerned that the proposal could be interpreted to subject cruise terminal operators to civil penalties for dangerous goods and devices discovered onboard a cruise ship after the vessel is out of its control, require facility operators to assume the cost and liability for the screening of personnel, baggage and personal items, and place an unfair financial burden on the facility operator or owner to acquire and maintain the security screening equipment. We request that you withdraw this proposal as written.

NAPA would like to thank you for this opportunity to comment on this proposed rulemaking and welcome any questions you may have.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Sincerely,
F. Bradley Wellock

The members of the industry do not release gas to test their systems, they call in expert, certified technical representatives who do the system testing and certification for them, usually using very safe compressed air to make the tests of the delivery system, not the system’s charge of CO2. There is no risk to this industry’s personnel here.

In the event of a real fire and deployment of the CO2 system to save the vessel and it's occupants the system is already equipped with a very dependable strobe light triggered by the release command and an audible alarm, powered by the system itself that sounds in the protected compartments prior to the discharge of a significant amount of the gas. This is way more dependable than odorizing the gas which could easily be misinterpreted as a whif from a well coiffed passenger as she went past the ventilation intake.

This proposed rule may well put more people at risk. It proposes the installation of lockout valves into the extinguishing system. This, in a day of very high energy conservation consciousness yet we cannot get crew to turn out the light when they leave the head, and now we are going to expect that these same crew members will remember and bother to turn the CO2 system back on each time they exit a protected compartment? Come on now, let's get real here!! Eliminating all risk is not achievable. In the U.S. there are 2500 left handed people each year who are killed trying to operate machines that are designed with the right handed majority in mind. #1 is starting a chain saw and #2 is using a cutoff saw. Until this number becomes significant and results in corrective regulation you cannot possibly justify attacking the safety record of the U.S. small passenger vessel fleet which has a record of zero losses.

As usual, the cost predictions used in preparing this proposal are far below those bid by our local supplier of fire protection services. The document predicts $1,475 for a lockout valve in piping smaller than 2". Our supplier bids $2,895.00. To inject scent into discharged gas, not to detect leaks in the system at rest, is bid at $3,225.00. This compared to the predicted cost in the document of $551.00. If the goal were truly to protect crew from passive system leaks then all tanks must be removed from the vessel, serviced and recharged with odorized gas. This is bid at $25,329.00 for the eight tanks in our principle system.

This is a poorly thought out, unnecessary regulation being foisted upon a very safe and safety conscious industry that simply cannot afford this sort of foolishness just to justify a few regulatory industry jobs. Stop the process now and work on a new regulatory proposal that makes sense and that will help to preserve this industry. Require that in the preparation of regulatory analysis the cumulative cost of regulations enacted over the preceding 15 years must be taken into consideration when trying to justify a new increase in costs of operations. Look to the past for reference. In recent history we have been tasked with Passenger Weight (reduced our earning capacity 13% fleetwide), ADA, TWIC, GMDSS, AIS, ECDIS, Port Security, EPIRB, STCW, EPA Vessel General Permit, Non Tank Vessel Response Plan, and on and on... Each one taken as the only expense added to the industry is in its own right probably affordable, but taken cumulatively the burden suddenly becomes overpowering for the average small passenger vessel operator trying to survive on the minimal profit margins offered by this industry.

IMO FSS Code Ch 5 Sec 2.2.2 requires two controls to active co2 flooding systems and provides for the use of a lock box to prevent accidental activation of the flooding system. Use of the lock box and key is a readily available off the shelf system which will provide protection from unintended activation of flooding systems. Use of this type of protection will lessen the burden on owners and operators of existing systems as some will already comply.  Other systems which do not can be easily retro fit by existing vendors who are already familiar with the lock box. Cutting into existing systems to install valves will be costly.  It will also be difficult to define a place for these valves in systems which were not designed to have them. Often real estate on vessel can be difficult to find for the retro fit of things even as simple as a single valve. As the lock box is designed to work with an existing system controls it will be easier to install and maintain.

We commend the proposed rulemaking in providing a substantial improvement in safety for all vessels and platforms using total flooding carbon dioxide systems. Both lockout valves and odorant devices are widely used low-cost methods for reducing the risk to personnel in spaces protected with carbon dioxide. In addition, the changes in the proposed rule regarding the use and requirements for clean agent systems will help clarify the acceptability and use of such systems in applications regulated by the Coast Guard.

My specific comments are below:

1) I suggest including a statement in the rule or in the commentary that specifically references the EPA SNAP program. This program is specifically required under NFPA 2001 Standard for Clean Agent Extinguishing Systems, which is adopted by reference in the proposed new part 162.161 so a reference to SNAP in 162.161-2 may be useful.

2) I suggest the USCG further limit the installation of new Carbon Dioxide Total Flooding Systems using the same criteria contained in NFPA 12, 2008 edition, 4.1 Restrictions for Normally Occupied Enclosures, specifically 4.1.1 with exceptions noted in 4.1.1.1-4.1.1.5.

3) Table 76.05 refers to “Carbon Dioxide Alternative Systems” whereas the balance of the NPRM refers to “Clean Agent Systems “or “Fixed Clean Agent Fire Extinguishing Systems”. The reference section, Subpart 95.16 is titled “Fixed Clean Agent Fire Extinguishing Systems”. In addition the term “Carbon Dioxide Alternative Systems” is not defined or used elsewhere in the document. I suggest replacing the term “Carbon Dioxide Alternative Systems” with “Clean Agent System” throughout Table 76.05.

The two proposals do not appear to be backed by evidence that they will eliminate or even reduce casualties. A better approach for life safety would be to prohibit new installations of carbon dioxide systems.

There does not seem to be much value in the use of an odorant in the carbon dioxide agent. Three factors argue against the introduction of an odorant. 1) Systems for large spaces are already provided with audible alarms. The proposed addition of an “olfactory alarm” would be redundant to the audible alarm, except for the smaller spaces without audible alarms. 2) It is doubtful that an early warning by olfactory means would help reduce injuries and fatalities associated with carbon dioxide systems. The EPA commissioned a study, released in 2003, titled “Review of the Use of Carbon Dioxide Total Flooding Fire Extinguishing Systems.” This study did not explicitly address whether alarms would have reduced casualties, but the casualties cited in the study were primarily due to inadvertent discharge with people trapped in the space and unable to exit. Put another way, the problem was NOT that the victims were unaware of the agent discharge. 3) As an issue of human factors, there is no convincing evidence that an odorant detected by a person would signify the release of a dangerous gas. If USCG is intent on the concept of an odorant, then the particular odorant should be specified and then publicized, so that its meaning would be unambiguous.

The benefit of a lockout device does not appear to be compelling. Many of the casualties cited in the EPA study mentioned above were due to inadvertent release, when the system would not have been locked out. Other casualties have occurred during maintenance or inspection. The deaths on Cape Horn occurred when the inspectors thought the actuation system had been disabled. The point is that another lockout device is not guaranteed to solve the problem.

The proposed Rule for towing vessels in, Notice of Proposed Rule Making (NPRM), Docket No. USCG-2006-24412, RIN 1625-AB06, Inspection of Towing Vessels, has no requirement for hot work requiring a Marine Chemist or Coast Guard Authorized Person as appears elsewhere in 46 U.S.C. 3301 for other U. S. Coast Guard inspected vessels. The Coast Guard should include a requirement for hot work operations in the proposed Rule for towing vessels.

The Coast Guard requires the use of a Marine Chemist or Coast Guard Authorized Person for inspection and testing of certain hazardous areas or spaces on inspected vessels before hot work operations may commence. Uninspected towing vessels are currently regulated by the U. S. Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). OSHA 29 CFR 1915.14 requires the use of Marine Chemists on uninspected vessels for hot work operations which has resulted in fewer fire and explosion incidents during hot work on these vessels. Since the Coast Guard has proposed classifying towing vessels as inspected vessels, then it is reasonable that minimum safety requirements for hot work continue to apply to towing vessels in the same manner as these requirements apply to other inspected vessels that are under the Coast Guard’s authority. It is recommended that the Coast Guard adopt regulatory language for the proposed towing vessel Rule that is consistent with hot work requirements for cargo vessels found in 46 CFR 91.50-1.

Should the Coast Guard agree with this recommendation, a reference to NFPA 306, Standard for the Control of Gas Hazards on Vessels, 2009 edition (or current edition at the time of adoption) be included in 46 CFR 136.112, Incorporation by Reference, section of the proposed Rule.

It is imperative that US regulations move away from a six and six two watch system. Having worked under the two watch and the three watch system, The ability to avoid sleep deprivation and fatigue is greatly diminished in the two watch system.

To champion the old system as an acceptable work environment flies in the face of the research that has been collected.

In a perfect world, it may just be possible to break up one's sleep into two parts. However, in this world, the mariner must have above average discipline to go to sleep immediately after the completion of his or her watch. Then the mariner must carefully schedule his or her time during the second rest period to eat, take care of personal hygeine and personal business, interface and recreate with fellow crew members, and get a nap that brings his total rest to 7.5 to 8.0 hours of sleep.

Lets now throw in loading and discharging, making and breaking tow, docking and undocking, taking on stores, and all the other activities that are part of ship life, but are not part of the navigation watch, and one can see that a carefully crafted schedule would be severely upset by regular vessel duties.

A career in the maritime industry is demanding an ever increasing professionalization. With new security, health, and training requirements, the basic competency of the modern mariner is being stretched to levels that would have been unheard of in 1978 when I began my maritime career. At that time, a z-card and the ability to stand was sufficient to be hired as a deck hand on a Gulf OSV.

If we understand that the modern mariner must be more professional and better trained to meet the contemporary maritime challenges, then why do we think that a watch system that probably was never really any good when it was established, can meet the human needs of that same modern mariner?

If we expect more from our professional mariners, we must also give him or her the proper work environment to perform those expectations

As per requirements set forth in Table 142.240, Carbon Dioxide Cylinders utilized in Fixed Fire Fighting Systems must be weighed and recharged if weight loss exceeds 10% of weight charge.

For your guidance, similar works aboard non-US Flag vessels allows for the use of Ultrasonic Liquid Level Indicator Units ( LLI ). We utilize a LLI approved in accordance with British Standard EN ISO 9001:2008 for use with CO2, Halon and Industrial Fluid.

As per NFPA 12, 1.2.2 "Nothing in this standard is intended to restrict new technologies or alternative arrangements, provided the level of safety prescribed by the standard is not lowered."

As the size of cylinders used in various types of suppression systems increases ( some cylinders are in excess of 600 lbs ), the method of physically handling them in order to ensure their contents ( weight ) becomes increasingly impractical. In addition to the increased time and physical labor required, a real risk of damage to the system exists. Not to mention the potential safety risks to personnel involved in the handling of these heavy cylinders. The use of a properly calibrated LLI not only reduces the labor time by at least 40%, it also provides a reliable means of determining cylinder content levels which is safer for personnel and equipment alike.

This "new technology or alternative arrangement" accurately determines if cylinder(s) content is in compliance, meeting the intent of NFPA 12 and 46 CFR; all while reducing the risk of physical injury, property damage, accidental discharge and labor time.

Given same, the benefits of utilizing a properly maintained and calibrated LLI allows for a fiscally sound means of enhancing personnel and equipment safety. Use of LLI units should be allowed to determine CO2 cylinder content levels as outlined Table 142.240.

Thank you for your time, effort and intelligent consideration of this matter.

Best Regards,

Peter O'Shea
Sea Safety Services, Inc.

Western corn rootworm is one of the key pests of field corn in Colorado. This species
and its congener, the northern corn rootworm, are significant pests throughout the corn
belt. Rootworms were controlled for many years through the use of soil insecticides,
which were a significant concern in terms of avian hazard, groundwater contamination
and applicator exposure. The recent trend in rootworm management has been towards
the use of transgenic corn hybrids and neonicotinoid seed treatments. The
development of resistance to the Bt toxins (Cry3Bb1 and 34Ab1 + 35Ab1) expressed in
available hybrids is of great concern given these species? long track record in
developing resistance to a variety of control tactics (e.g., organochlorine soil
insecticides, OP and carbamate adulticides, corn/soybean crop rotation).

The expected result of Bt toxin failure would be that corn producers would need to turn
to seed treatment, crop rotation or soil insecticides for rootworm control. The most
likely of these is soil insecticides, given that seed treatments are known to perform
poorly in the presence of high rootworm abundance and that variant corn rootworm
populations have been problematic in areas where crop rotation is widely practiced. In
other words, resistance to Bt toxins would likely return us to the environmental concerns
associated with widespread soil insecticide use.

While resistance management strategies, particularly the use of crop refuges, have
been employed since the introduction of transgenic corn hybrids expressing rootworm
toxins, the development of resistance remains of great concern. The use of additional
effective resistance management strategies is highly desirable, particularly given the
debate regarding adequate refuge size for the rootworms. One effective strategy is
the deployment of multiple toxins. The registration of MIR604 (mCry3Aa) would result in
three toxins available in the corn hybrid market, which should greatly reduce the
likelihood of failure of the Bt technology and reversion to reliance on soil insecticides.

RE: Environmental Assessment for Proposed Determination of Nonregulated
Status for Corn Genetically Engineered for Insect Resistance

To Whom It May Concern:

The Iowa Farm Bureau Federation, the state?s largest general farm organization
with more than 143,000 members, is pleased to see the Animal and Plant Health
Inspection Service has prepared a positive Environmental Assessment in response
to a petition from Syngenta Seeds, Inc. regarding the regulatory status of
genetically engineered corn rootworm resistant corn derived from transformation
event MIR604.

The estimated to cost U.S. corn farmers from crop damage due to corn rootworm
is as much as $1 billion annually. Corn rootworm is traditionally a problem in
acres planted to corn each year. In continuous corn patterns, as much as 50-60
percent of total U.S. corn acreage has traditionally had some chemical control
applied for corn rootworms. In Iowa, as much as 22 percent of corn acres in some
years have been treated with a corn rootworm soil insecticide. These products
must be handled with care to protect human health and the environment. What?s
more, these treatments can cost as much as $16 per acre, putting farmers at a
competitive disadvantage.

Another traditional control method is more corn-soybean crop rotations, but this
has not always performed as an effective management tool because of the
development
of a variant of the western corn rootworm that lays eggs in soybeans.

More recently, farmers have adopted the new transgenic corn rootworm hybrids,
but product choices for farmers within the marketplace are limited. Having
additional Bt events and varieties for Iowa farmers to choose from for corn
rootworm management is important for both economic and environmental
reasons. While planting Bt corn for protection against rootworm doesn't guarantee
that there will not be rootworm injury, science supports the use of Bt corn
rootworm hybrids as a safe, effective insect management tool that can be used
responsibly by Iowa farmers.

Protection provided by event MIR604 is similar to other new transgenic corn
rootworm products on the market. Examination of the docket indicates that it
provides excellent control of corn rootworm and is not dependent on the weather.
APHIS approval of this event will help Iowa farmers remain competitive while also
providing environmentally safe management options.

Sincerely,

Rick Robinson
Environmental Policy Advisor

TO: USDA-APHIS

FROM: Michael S. Davis, DVM PhD Dipl ACVIM

RE: Docket No. 99?014?2 (Proposed rule change for the transport of warm-
blooded animals)

The purpose of this communication is to comment on the proposed rule changes
for the climatic and environmental conditions for the transportation of warm-
blooded animals. I am a veterinary internist and physiologist with specific
interests in exercise and stress physiology, and as such have both a scientific
and practical interest in this topic (the latter being the result of the transportation
of athletic animals). Furthermore, I am currently assembling a research program,
at the behest of the American Kennel Club, to address the specific physiology of
transportation-related morbidity and mortality amongst brachycephalic canine
breeds.

I applaud the efforts of the USDA-APHIS to be proactive in the implementation of
performance standards for the transport of warm-blooded animals. However, I fear
that the actual implementation of such standards is premature and, in a few
critical areas, flawed or likely to have unintended adverse consequences.

The current regulations promote a ?one size fits all? approach that neither
recognizes the ability of certain animals to thrive outside the theoretical ideal
climatic conditions, nor acknowledges the inability of other animals to maintain
homeostasis within these same conditions. The current regulations allow, on an
individual basis, the accommodation of the former through an acclimation
certificate issued by a veterinarian. As the proposed rule change highlights, this
provision is not without pitfalls, as it is difficult, if not impossible, for a veterinarian
to predict the future behavior and health of an animal based on a single physical
examination (this point being the critical difference between an acclimation
certificate and a health certificate, the latter simply testifying to the immediate
status of the animal). The effect of an acclimation certificate is to transfer the
liability for an adverse event to the veterinarian. A previously proposed change to
allow the owner of the animal to accept that liability through their own acclimation
certificate was not enacted due to concerns regarding the possible misuse of such
authority by unscrupulous owner/shippers. An additional concern (apparently not
raised during the public comment period of this previous proposed amendment) is
that there is no guarantee that the typical animal owner is capable of determining
whether the animal is acclimated to a specific set of conditions. Such a
determination requires detailed knowledge of an animal?s history, specifically with
respect to its environment, as well as the ability to determine whether an animal is
maintaining homeostasis. It is unlikely that the majority of shippers that would be
permitted to issue an acclimation certificate would have that knowledge, just as it
is unlikely that the majority of veterinarians would have that knowledge of the
animals that are presented for a veterinary acclimation certificate. Thus, it is clear
that although an acclimation certificate is a useful approach in theory, in practice it
likely creates greater hazard.

The proposed rule change towards implementation of a performance standard,
although scientifically sound, is unlikely to result in practical improvement of the
transport conditions of animals at this time. The idea of a performance standard is
deceptively simple, in that if an animal is maintaining homeostasis under a
particular set of environmental conditions, then those conditions are by definition
acceptable and safe. If, however, an animal is not maintaining homeostasis, then
immediate action must be taken to improve that environment. Certainly there are
animals that can withstand large ranges of environmental conditions without
compromise, just as there are environmental extremes that few animals can
withstand for any appreciable amount of time. It is entirely appropriate that these
environmental extremes are specifically recognized in the proposed rule change.
Examples of these specific directives include Section 3.19 (and elsewhere)
(1) Shelter from sunlight and extreme heat. Sufficient shade shall be provided to
protect the dog or cat from the direct rays of the sun.
(2) Shelter from rain and snow. Sufficient protection shall be provided to allow the
dogs and cats to remain dry during rain, snow, and other precipitation.).
These conditions should be included in any rule change.

The remainder of the performance standard is vague, with the admonition
that ?Transportation of all live animals shall be done in a manner that does not
cause overheating, excessive cooling, or adverse environmental conditions that
could cause unnecessary discomfort or stress.? While capturing the essence of
the risks to homeostasis during transportation, the application of such a guideline
is impractical or unlikely. Overheating and excessive cooling are conditions that
can only be determined accurately by personnel trained in veterinary biomedicine,
and it is unlikely that the majority of transportation personnel have or will be
provided with the training necessary to facilitate their greater role as animal health
monitors (if this rule change is enacted). ?Unnecessary discomfort or stress? is
very subjective statement, thus placing the decision making authority for
alteration or intervention (and the liability for action or inaction) in the hands of
someone without the veterinary training to make informed judgments on these
issues. In summary, the proposed regulations, as written, transfers ALL liability
for the health and well-being for animal cargo to the transportation companies,
specifically the baggage and cargo handlers, without providing specific guidelines
on which to base their decisions.

In the absence of specific guidelines (as the current regulations provide), the
transportation industry is unlikely to accept full liability for the health and well-
being of live animal cargo and will cease to carry such cargo, or severely restrict
such carriage to the substantial detriment of the animal-owning public. The
current regulations do not explicitly recognize the inability of some animals to
maintain homeostasis within the stated guidelines, and this shortcoming has led
to self-regulation by the transportation industry. Rather than implementing a
performance standard based on the moment-to-moment condition of the animals
(analogous to the proposed rule change), the airlines have instead opted to refuse
to carry these animals. Currently, only 3 of the major US airlines permit, in some
manner, the transportation of brachycephalic dogs and cats, with the remaining
airlines maintaining a virtual or absolute embargo on the transportation of these
animals. These actions have been instituted in the absence of any scientific data
suggesting that some or all of these breeds are less capable of withstanding
transportation stress, and instead have been instituted based on perceived risk
and/or individual airline experiences. The fact that the transportation industry has
demonstrated the willingness to substitute their own, more stringent regulations for
those currently in place through USDA-APHIS in order to limit their liability forms
the basis for my concern of unintended, and undesirable consequences arising
from the performance standard rule change as written.

Successful implementation of a performance standard, defined as a standard that
permits and realizes the transportation of any animal that can be transported
safely, while restricting the transportation of any animal that is likely to suffer as a
result of that transport, will require two items. First, scientific data must be
gathered on the different environmental conditions associated with the ability of
broad classes of animals to maintain homeostasis during transportation, as well
as the environmental conditions associated with animal class-specific adverse
events. Assembly of such data will permit, and must result in, the construction of
guidelines specific to different animal classes that are incorporated into the APHIS
rules and provided to the transportation companies. Second, the construction of
more dynamic guidelines will not alleviate the need for a performance standard.
Therefore, the sensitivity and specificity of clinical signs of adverse events
(overheating, excessive cooling, undue discomfort or stress) that can be
recognized during shipping (i.e., from outside a cage or other animal enclosure by
lay personnel) must be determined, and training in this type of monitoring be
provided to the transportation personnel to permit more informed recognition of
appropriate homeostasis and/or the need to intervene in the animal?s environment.

I strongly support the proposed changes to the regulation concerning climatic conditions for the
transportation of animals. This proposed rule would relieve the burden on veterinarians of
issuing certifications of acclimation for extremes in temperature, would place the liability for
animal injury upon the owners rather than the veterinarians, and would provide an economic
balance between animal owners and animal carriers.

First, this proposed rule would relieve the burden on veterinarians of issuing certificates of
acclimation. Currently, the rule does not require that the certifying veterinarian have actual
knowledge of the animal?s acclimation. Rather, it implicitly allows the veterinarian to take the
animal owners at their word that the animal has been acclimated. I do not believe this is lying
on the part of the veterinarians; rather, it is merely a loophole that they are free to pass through
if they choose to take the owners at their word. Further, why would an unscrupulous veterinarian
care? They are not the owners of the animals, and are merely getting paid to issue the
certificates. If anything, they are encouraged to certify unknown animals under the current rule.

Further, the issue of liability for animal injury should fall on the owners, not the veterinarians who
issue these certificates. As stated earlier, many veterinarians issue acclimation certificates
without actually knowing if the animal has been acclimated to these temperatures. And again,
this may be due to the veterinarians taking the owners at their word. Here is the problem with
the current rule, however: the owners should be liable for this misrepresentation, not the
veterinarians. I do not mean to suggest that many animal owners intentionally mislead their
veterinarian in order to specifically harm their own animals. However, I do believe that this is an
unfortunate byproduct of the owners? desire to get the necessary documentation for the pet to
travel, for whatever reason ? to accompany the owner to a new home, sale of animals to new
owners, for show, etc. Even if the owner?s motive is not to harm the animal, it may still happen
if the owner intentionally misleads the veterinarian into providing a certificate of acclimation for
an animal which is not acclimated. By removing this certification requirement, and instead
requiring standards appropriate to the animal?s welfare, this proposed rule ends the practice of
deception in order to obtain travel certifications for animals who may not actually be acclimated
to these claimed temperatures, and it removes the burden from the veterinarian.

Finally, this proposed rule goes further than the current rule to protect animal welfare, by
considering the humidity, ventilation, and other climatic factors that the animals may be
subjected to during transport. Although the supporting material seems to suggest that this new
rule would not detrimentally affect the carriers, I believe that it could lead to an increase in
animal transportation costs. However, I believe that increased transportation costs are perfectly
permissible, as it represents an economic balance between the interests of those affected here:
the carrier and the owner. It is true that these regulations might require the transporters to adjust
or restructure their current methods of shipping, thereby causing a financial burden. However,
since the animal owner is entrusting the carrier with their animal (perhaps their pet), and since
the goal is to transport the animals safely, then certainly the owners will be willing to pay a bit
more for this safe transportation. Therefore, I think this proposed rule is the perfect compromise
between carriers, veterinarians, and owners, and keeps the animals? welfare as the focus, as
was intended all along.

Re: Proposed Amendment to Animal Welfare Act

E-Submission to Federal E-Rulemaking Portal

To Whom It May Concern:

I support the proposed changes with regard to the transportation of live animals
other than marine mammals. The transportation of animals over great distances
is often stressful and traumatic for the animal itself. As humans, pet owners, and
ultimately those responsible for the domestication of most animals, it is our duty
to see to it that we do as much as possible to provide for the care of these
animals. This is especially important when we place these animals in situations
that are difficult for them and cause undue stress.

The one element of the proposed amendment to the Animal Welfare Act that I
appreciate the most is that it allows for a standardization of the requirements for
the transportation of live animals other than marine mammals. This
standardization places the responsibility of the temperature regulation on those
that are actually transporting the animal. This is in contrast to the earlier
requirements that placed some of the responsibility on the pet owner and some on
a veterinarian to sign-off on a certification. This earlier certification placed too
much responsibility on a veterinarian who may have not ever treated the animal.

The earlier rules also allowed for too much time in between legs of the animal?s
journey, where the temperatures could rise or fall beyond what would be
considered a comfortable level. In most cases, this would only lead to added
stress for an animal in an already stressful situation.

Concerning Docket No. 99?014?2.

I think the attempt to simplify animal transport law and protect all species is noble
but may inadvertently lead to over-simplification of the rules and create harm to
some animals. If I read the proposal correctly, the transport of any warm-blooded
animal would be included in the ruling. I am a poultry veterinarian for a

farms to processing facilities. Cages are not covered (drafts, direct sunlight, etc.)

during winter transport to prevent excessive wind-chill. Current practice has
evolved from over 50 years of trying to improve transport, primarily for economic
reasons, but also for maximal animal husbandry (minimize death loss, broken
bones, etc.). Requiring total different hauling vehicles, e.g., "no direct sun-light",

The Humane Society of the United States (HSUS) welcomes the opportunity to
comment on the APHIS proposed rulemaking for regulations on temperature
requirements relating to the transportation of animals.

The HSUS opposes the proposal to replace the current ambient temperature
requirements with a ?single performance standard.? The proposed, single standard
is too vague and open to many interpretations, and thus unenforceable until the
animal has already suffered and/or died. The HSUS is also concerned that
some breeds, such as brachycephalic breeds, are more susceptible to high heat
and humidity, than others. Therefore, The HSUS requests that APHIS keep the
current ambient temperature requirements, but also urges the addition of
provisions that animals should be monitored closely to ensure that the existing
temperature requirements are not compromising an individual animals? welfare and
that if climatic conditions are found to be detrimental, appropriate adjustments and
care must be immediately provided. This approach maintains a temperature range
to guide handlers, but also allows USDA to take enforcement action if cases are
found in which an animal?s welfare is compromised due to climatic conditions.

The HSUS supports the measure in APHIS? proposed rules that would remove
provisions for acclimation certificates. Acclimation certificates allow animals to be
transported in conditions that may not be safe. Transporting animals in
temperatures below the minimum of 45 degrees and above the maximum of 85
degrees poses a threat to their health and well being. The veterinarians asked to
sign the certificates are usually unfamiliar with the animal and/or with the animal?s
normal living conditions (and thus temperature acclimation status) and are unable
to make a valid determination. We understand that they are concerned about
liability if an animal with an acclimation certificate suffers harm while in transit, but
they should be held liable if they approve an animal to be transported in unsafe
conditions.

Therefore, I respectfully urge APHIS to withdraw the proposal to replace the
regulatory temperature requirements with a single performance standard. Thank
you for your time and consideration.

meet animal welfare standards. The proposed text is:

"Paragraph (f)(1) of the proposed performance standard would state that
transportation of all live animals shall be done in a manner that does not cause
overheating, excessive cooling, or adverse environmental conditions that could
cause unnecessary discomfort or stress. When climatic or environmental
conditions, including temperature, humidity, exposure, ventilation, pressurization,
time, or other environmental condition, or any combination thereof, present a
threat to the health or well-being of a live animal, appropriate measures would have
to be taken immediately to alleviate the impact of those conditions. The different
climatic and environmental factors prevailing during a journey would always have
to be considered when arranging for the transportation of and when transporting
live animals."

Given that animal transporters are not likely to be veterinarians, how are they
expected to know when an animal is experiencing "discomfort or stress";
moreover, if the transporter believes an animal is experiencing discomfort or
stress, how are they to know if the discomfort or stress is caused by "overheating,
excessive cooling, or adverse environmental conditions"? The transporter could
use such arguments to evade this rule.

In addition, the word "unnecessary" weakens this rule, as a transporter could
argue that EVEN IF the transporter recognized an animal was experiencing
discomfort or stress, and EVEN IF the transporter believed the discomfort or
stress was caused by overheating, excessive cooling, or adverse environmental
conditions, the transporter is not responsible because the discomfort or stress
was NECESSARY.

Further, how can a layperson be expected to know what poses "a threat to the
health or well-being" of any particular animal without guidance?

This language needs revision to make it objective and enforceable. I suggest:

1. Eliminating the word "unnecessary" so it reads, "transportation of all live
animals shall be done in a manner that does not cause overheating, excessive
cooling, or adverse environmental conditions that could cause discomfort or
stress."

excessive cooling, adverse environmental conditions, discomfort, stress, health,
well-being, and immediately. These definitions should include reasonable, specific
upper and lower limits that could never be exceeded. Without concrete
measurements, this regulation is subjective and difficult to enforce.

animal welfare in transportation.

To Whom It May Concern:

It is interesting to note that while many comments already submitted regarding this Proposed
Rule endorse replacing the engineering standards of the regulation (i.e., the temperature
specifications) with the performance standard contained in the proposed change, many of these
same comments criticize the new language for lack of specificity!

All the more reason to adopt the approach we recommend in our original comments (APHIS
2006-0150-0075.1), which would install the new performance standard (including dispensing with
the acclimation certification) while retaining the ambient temperature requirements in the current
regulation. We think that the rewritten rule puts much needed emphasis on assessing all travel
conditions—alone and in combination--in terms of the overall welfare of the animal. As with all
performance standards, especially in the initial phases of enforcement, we recognize the
potential for more or less strict interpretation and disagreements. But there is no arguing with
whether the ambient temperature does or does not comply with what is allowable. Keeping this
engineering standard provides a necessary back-up to the performance standard.

It is disingenuous to argue that this is an inappropriate approach when in fact the Animal Welfare
Act regulations are replete with both performance and engineering standards for the same
activity. For example, § 2.131, Handling of animals, has subparagraphs that direct licensees,
among other things, to handle animals “as expeditiously and carefully as possible in a manner
that does not cause overheating…” and, during public exhibition, to handle them “so there is
minimal risk of harm to the animal and to the public.” But it also includes the specific
(engineering) directive that “performing animals shall be allowed a rest period between
performances at least equal to the time for one performance.”

Similarly, and most apropos of the proposal at hand, § 3.3, Sheltered housing facilities, has
performance and engineering standards in the same paragraph:

“(a) Heating, cooling, and temperature. The sheltered part of sheltered housing facilities for dogs
and cats must be sufficiently heated and cooled when necessary to protect the dogs and cats
from temperature or humidity extremes and to provide for their health and well-being. The
ambient temperature in the sheltered part of the facility must not fall below 50° F (10° C) for dogs
and cats not acclimated….Dry bedding, solid resting boards, or other methods of conserving
body heat must be provided when temperatures fall below 50° F (10° C). The ambient
temperature must not fall below 45° F (7.2° C) for more than 4 consecutive hours when dogs or
cats are present, and must not rise above 85° F (29.5° C) for more than 4 consecutive hours
when dogs or cats are present. The preceding requirements are in addition to, not in place of, all
other requirements pertaining to climatic conditions in parts 2 and 3 of this chapter.”

Other examples include, but are not limited to, Sections 3.6, 3.10, 3.26, 3.28, 3.53, 3.78, 3.79,
3.83. A number of provisions under the AWA regarding primary enclosures mandate specific
minimum space requirements (engineering standards), but also require the performance standard
that animals are able to “make normal postural adjustments with adequate freedom of
movement.”

Therefore, there is sufficient legal precedent to allow for the use of both a performance and an
engineering standard with respect to regulating the climatic and environmental conditions in
which animals may be transported.

Sincerely,
Cathy Liss
President
Animal Welfare Institute
