The Michigan Department of Agriculture (MDA) issues a large number of
phytosanitary export certificates for a variety of commodities, including lumber,
dry beans, corn, soybeans, ornamentals, and fruit. We appreciate the efforts of
USDA, APHIS, and PPQ in streamlining the certification system with the
development of PCIT and the need to provide for the financial stability of the
certification program.

The Michigan Department of Agriculture understands and supports the user fee
increases for export certification as a means to recover costs for trade facilitation.
MDA utilizes a separate inspection fee structure for cost recovery which we plan
to continue to utlilize. Unfortunately, the current PCIT system allows for
collection of the administrative fee for exporters utilizing the system, but it does
not allow for collection of the inspection fee itself in Michigan. This means an
exporter is charged two fees for each inspection under this system that are going
to two collection agencies. We cannot support this type of dual charge system.
For states such as Michigan that utilize a separate certification fee system, the
burden of collecting, tracking, and remitting for administrative fee for USDA is left
with the state which has no way to cover the costs for these activities. We
cannot support this type of unfunded burden.

With respect to reissueing certificates, we have observed that many certificates
are voided and reissued due to changing capacities of vessels, resulting in
splitting of lots which requires issueing new certificates. In most cases, this need
to reissue new certificates is out of the control of the exporter. It appears in these
cases, exporters would get charged for administrative fees twice on the same
shipment.

It appears that USDA is anticipating collecting approximately $2.5 million in
administrative fees
for the issuance of certificates by state and county partners. Frankly, this is a
relatively small amount of revenue compared to the burden and hassle that this
additional fee will impose on state and county agencies. For years states and
counties have assisted USDA, free of charge in issuing these certificates and
facilitating trade. It
would seem that this partnership, and the advantage to USDA, would be worth far
more than $2.5 million per year.

Therefore, the Michigan Department of Agriculture requests that the proposed $16
administrative fee for certificates issued by state and county agencies be
eliminated from this amendment.

The proposal to raise the fee for APHIS-issued phytosanitary certificates (phytos)
by 100% is excessive. This increase further squeezes agricultural, horticultural
and forest commodity producers and reduces their profitibility to the point that
some producers will reduce or quit exporting. Further, this increase will send
more producers to the state and county officials that already issue most of the
certificates. Many states will need to follow suit and raise fees as well. At a time
when the country is trying to restore some "balance" to the balance of trade, this
proposed fee increase is going in the opposite direction.

Second, the proposal to charge state and county cooperators $16.00 for each
certificate they issue is inappropriate for several reasons:

a. Most state phyto fees are set in statute. To change a fee involves a process
that can take up to two years to complete.
b. A special fund would have to be set up to hold these fees separate from the
state general revenue fund and special spending would need to be authorized to
utilize these fees to pay APHIS. This would require another lengthy legislative
process.
c. The extra spending authority required for paying these fees to APHIS will be
counted against our division's total annual authorized spending, thus causing the
legislature to reduce access to our already limited funds.
d. The collection of the fees, depositing into special account, tracking and
transferring to APHIS will cause extra work for state staff, further reducing our
resources.
e. It is wrong that the state must pay APHIS this fee. APHIS already receives, for
free, state and county employees who complete this important APHIS mission.

If a $16.00 fee must be collected for each phyto, APHIS personnel should do the
billing and receiving of the fee. Then, funds received are in the agency for which
they are destined. Each state can provide a listing of every phyto issued to the
local APHIS office to be used to generate billing. If a shipper does not pay the
federal fee, let the state know and they can deny that shipper any additional
phytos until the bill is paid.

We are cognizant of the cost of APHIS' export certification program and it's
shortfall of revenue. We also appreciate the excellent job APHIS does with all the
preparatory work (training of cooperators, maintenance of EXCERPT, printing and
distribution of various certificates, etc.) that occurs prior to an inspection or
issuance of a phyto--work that is unseen by the average phytosanitary certificate
receiver. However, this program may not be able to be run as a zero-sum
operation, where fees pay for all costs. The USDA may need to pay more than
the program recovers. The overall positive effect of a robust ag, hort and forest
product export climate more than compensates for the shortfall--in jobs, income
taxes and well-being of our citizens.

General comments to Docket No. APHIS-2006-0137

1. APHIS contends that the increase in user fess is justified by increasing costs.
At the same time, APHIS encourages industry participation in programs to
improve efficiency and reduce costs. Many of these programs are 'voluntary.'
Where these programs directly assist in the export certification process it would
seem appropriate that credit be given to those organizations that do participate
since they require less support from APHIS and State/Country cooperators.

In particular, those entities involved in the National Seed Health System (NSHS)
have reduced the resource requirements of both APHIS and State cooperators,
and as such should be entitled to a lower cost of certification. ACOs supporting
exports from these companies recognize that NSHS members make the issuance
of FPCs faster and more economical. For these companies, the FPC rate should
be reduced.

2. PCIT was originally billed as a means to increase efficiency (among other
things.) Those who use PCIT should be entitled to share in the reduced cost to
APHIS of issuing phytos, and their fees should be adjusted downwards
accordingly.

3. Many exporters receive multiple FPCs at any one time. The existing and
proposed fee structures are the same whether you get one (1) FPC or 10. The
incremental effort to sign additional FPCs has never been recognized in the fee
structure. Now is the time to do so. Many exporters shipping on a regular basis
hold back requests for FPCs to 'batch' them and make it easier and more
economical in terms of the time required by ACOs.

This disparity becomes even more pronounced with PCIT. APHIS cannot justify
charging $100 for the 10th FPC when their incremental cost is much less.

4. The definitions of commercial vs. noncommercial shipment and the threshold
value of $1,250 need some clarification.

Many exporters ship research and parent seed to ?winter? production locations in
the tropics or southern hemisphere for an additional breeding cycle or for
multiplication. This seed then returns to the US for the next breeding cycle or is
used to produce a commercial seed crop. This seed is 'noncommercal' in the
sense it is not sold for planting and the production of a commercial/marketable
crop. This seed is used to develop new varieties.

Many of these shipments have customs values exceeding $1,250 and are ensured
as such.

The rule should be amended to ensure that research (or breeder) seed and 'parent'
seed receives the lowest possible export certification fee.

5. The incremental fee increases will cause confusion. Set a rate somewhere in
the middle and leave it static for the period in question. Initial overages and later
shortfalls can be buffered by the reserve fund.

6. Requiring the states/counties to collect fees and remit monies to APHIS will
cause problems. Some states (and perhaps counties) have no legal facility to
collect and remit these funds, nor are their legislatures likely to enable them to do
so in the near future. APHIS needs to address this problem with agreement by the
states before the rule is enacted. To do otherwise will cause confusion and may
slow down or interrupt the issuance of FPCs resulting in harm to exporters.

Regards,

John Stevens
Phytosanitary Issues Manager
Pioneer Hi-Bred International Inc

The following are the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship?s
general comments concerning Docket No. APHIS-2006-0137.

1. Requiring the states/counties to collect s $16 administrative fee, and remit to
APHIS, will cause major problems for the state/county organizations that are
writing the federal phytosanitary certificates (PC). Some states (and perhaps
counties) have no legal facility to collect and remit these funds, nor are their
legislatures likely to enable them to do so in the near future. APHIS needs to
address this problem with agreement by the states before such a rule is enacted.
To do otherwise will cause confusion and may slow down or interrupt the issuance
of PCs resulting in harm to exporters. Is APHIS ready to immediately assume PC
duties in those states where the administrative fee cannot be collected by the
local PC issuing authorities?

The 2004 Kadix Systems Report, which is the underpinning of this propose rule,
shows that states/counties are issuing approximately three-quarters of all federal
PCs. What the report does not delve into detail, is why are exporters working with
local officials rather than federal officials to obtain PCs. However, the report does
articulate what may be a key point, ?In 2002, a major reorganization involving the
USDA and DHS redirected substantial staff and funding away from the USDA,
leaving fewer USDA personnel and money available to accomplish export
certification tasks. In addition, agricultural exports have continued to increase
since 1996, with a corresponding increase in demand by industry for export
services.? I surmise that USDA cannot meet clients? (exporters) needs, but that
state and county officials are doing so. Instead of taking a look within to see how
APHIS can better serve the clients and thus maintain a level of PC issuance that
translate into a suitable revenue stream, APHIS is choosing to tax the local
government entities that are doing a good job.

2. APHIS contends that the increase in user fess is justified by the increasing
cost of providing export certification while meeting the cost-recovery requirement
of APHIS operations. At the same time, APHIS encourages industry participation
in programs to improve efficiency and reduce costs. Many of these programs
are 'voluntary.' Where these programs directly assist in the export certification
process it would seem appropriate that credit be given to those organizations that
do participate since they require less support from APHIS and State/Country
cooperators.

In particular, those entities involved in the National Seed Health System (NSHS)
have reduced the resource requirements of both APHIS and State cooperators,
and as such should be entitled to a lower cost of certification. Accredited
Certification Officials (ACOs) supporting exports from these companies recognize
that NSHS members make the issuance of PCs faster and more economical. For
example, if one key Iowa exporter, who is accredited with the NSHS program,
were to cease being NSHS accredited, the Iowa Department of Agriculture and
Land Stewardship would have to hire at least two ACOs to meet the PC needs of
that exporter alone. For companies that are NSHS accredited, the federal PC rate
should be reduced because they do significantly reduce ACO workloads.

3. PCIT was originally touted as a means to increase efficiency. Those who use
PCIT should be entitled to share in the reduced cost to APHIS of issuing phytos,
and their fees should be adjusted downwards accordingly. If APHIS is serious
about wanting PCIT to be adopted by exporters, then APHIS should pass on the
cost savings of the PCIT system to the exporters actually implementing PCIT.

4. Many exporters request multiple, and often similar, PCs at a time. The existing,
and proposed, fee structures are the same whether you get one PC or 10. The
incremental effort to sign additional PCs has never been recognized in the fee
structure. Now is the time to do so. Many exporters shipping on a regular basis
hold back requests for PCs to 'batch' them and make it easier and more
economical in terms of the time required by ACOs.

This disparity becomes even more pronounced with PCIT. APHIS cannot justify
charging $100 for the 10th FPC when their incremental cost is much less.

5. The definitions of commercial vs. noncommercial shipment and the threshold
value of $1,250 need some clarification.

An ?Iowa example? of the need to clarify can be taken from agricultural seed
production facilities in this state. Many seed companies ship research and parent
seed to winter production locations in the tropics or southern hemisphere for an
additional breeding cycle or for multiplication. This seed then returns to the US for
the next breeding cycle, or is used to produce a commercial seed crop. This
seed is 'noncommercial' in the sense it is not sold for planting and the production
of a commercial/marketable crop. This seed is used to develop new varieties.
However ? this seed could be the next biggest hybrid on the market ? or it may
never make it to commercial market. Is it worth $1,250, or not? Clarification is
needed by APHIS is how to determine a shipment?s worth. Conversations with
APHIS staff indicate that it is up to the exporter to declare the worth of the
shipment ? but how is this value-declaration validated?

6. The incremental fee increases will cause confusion ? as well as a bookkeeping
and outreach/communication nightmare each time an incremental step is
implemented.. Set a rate somewhere in the middle and leave it static for the
period in question. Initial overages and later shortfalls can be buffered by the
reserve fund.

Regards,

Robin Pruisner
Iowa SPRO, State Entomologist, & Entomology & Plant Science Bureau Chief

I would like to make a few comments on the proposed amendment to the Animal Welfare Act
concerning contingency planning:

1) The proposed amendment makes the release of detailed emergency response information
possible through FOIA and state public records laws. This is an unacceptable threat to the
security of research animal facilities.

2) Detailed animal evacuation instructions or shelter-in-place instructions are not desirable or
necessary for most large research institutions. They have multiple facilities and extensive
resources at their disposable, and hold practice sessions in flexible disaster recovery.

3) Throughout most of the country disasters are limited to spontaneous, unpredictable events.
Advance animal evacuation by preplanned pathways is not an option. It is during the recovery
phase that law enforcement will allow personnel to return to facilities to care for animals. It
seems that only facilities located in the floodplains of major rivers where flood crests
are predicted days in advance, and perhaps hurricane prone areas, would have enough advance
warning to systematically evacuate animals from facilities before it becomes too dangerous.

In light of the fact that a high percentage of those who refused to evacuate during Hurricane
Katrina did so because they would not leave their pets behind, and the resulting nightmare that
ensued for both human and animal rescuers trying to save those stranded, this clearly points to
the need for disaster planning to include animals.

It's clear we can't rely on people and facilities to do the right thing for their animals voluntarily.
After all, people were left behind in nursing homes. So what hope is there for animals, unless the
law requires -and enforces- a detailed plan?

As for the unfortunate animals in research facilities, one could argue that they'd be better off
dead. But I suppose any regulation that forces researchers to treat these living creatures as
something more than expendable capital is a step in the right direction.

Thank you for allowing public input, and please take this opportunity to do what's morally right.

RE: Handling of Animals; Contingency Plans

To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on a proposed rule to amend the
Animal Welfare Act regulations by adding new requirements for contingency
planning and training of personnel employed by licensees and registrants. (Docket
No. APHIS-2006-0159). The proposal would require research facilities, dealers,
exhibitors, intermediate handlers, and carriers to “develop, document, and follow
an appropriate plan to provide for the humane handling, treatment, transportation,
housing, and care of their animals in the event of an emergency or disaster (one
which could reasonably be anticipated and expected to be detrimental to the good
health and well-being of the animals in their possession).” The proposal specifies
a general set of criteria to which contingency plans would have to adhere.
According to the proposal, contingency plans must:

(i) Identify situations the facility might experience that would trigger the need for a
contingency plan, including emergencies such as electrical outages, faulty HVAC
systems, fires, and animal escapes, as well as natural disasters the facility is
most likely to experience;

(ii) Outline specific tasks required to be carried out in response to the identified
emergencies or disasters including, but not limited to, detailed animal evacuation
instructions or shelter-in-place instructions and provisions for providing backup
sources of food and water as well as sanitation, ventilation, bedding, veterinary
care, etc.;

(iii) Identify a chain of command and who (by name or by position title) will be
responsible for fulfilling these tasks; and

(iv) Address how response and recovery will be handled in terms of materials,
resources, and training needed.

After a careful review of this proposed rule, which appeared in the October 23,
2008 Federal Register, 73 Fed. Reg. 63085 (2008), the National Association for
Biomedical Research (NABR) generally supports the objectives embodied in the
proposed rule. NABR believes contingency plans are an important component of a
well-managed animal care and use program. However, we have several concerns
we urge the Agency to consider prior to finalizing this proposal.

Adequacy and Assessment of Contingency Plans

The proposed rule is silent on how Agency inspectors or other Agency officials will
evaluate the adequacy of these plans. The Federal Register notice states that
plans will be reviewed by APHIS personnel as part of the routine inspection
process. However, the proposed rule provides no guidance or explanation for the
criteria to be used by Agency personnel when assessing the adequacy of these
plans. NABR is concerned Agency inspectors may inappropriately cite regulated
entities for failing to include specific items in their plans, even though the
purported basis for such citation is not specified in this proposed rule and
subsequent Agency regulations.

We therefore urge the Agency to provide additional information on how these plans
will be evaluated, and permit additional comment prior to finalizing this proposed
rule. NABR remains concerned about the use of Guidance documents or additions
to the Animal Care Policy Manual to impose new requirements not specified in the
regulations.
In the alternative, we request the Agency add additional language to both the
proposed rule and the Agency Inspection Guide making it clear licensees or
registrants cannot be cited for the failure to include specific actions in their plans
that are not explicitly required by the regulations as codified in the Code of
Federal Regulations.

Distinction Between Emergencies and Natural Disasters

The proposed rule contemplates contingency planning for emergencies such as
electrical outages, faulty HVAC systems, fires, and animal escapes. While the
assessment of risks related to potential emergencies and the resulting plan that
would be developed as result of that assessment is relatively straightforward, the
same cannot be said when attempting to develop plans to respond to natural
disasters.

NABR believes regulatory language addressing these two disparate events must
recognize the difference between emergencies and natural disasters and should
not hold the facilities to the same level of accountability for contending with these
events. Many unforeseen events can occur during a natural disaster and often
circumstances change with little notice to decision makers. Contingency plans
cannot cover every potential scenario related to a natural disaster. Often the
severity of damage related to a natural disaster cannot be adequately predicted.
The proposed rule should clearly acknowledge this and provide for a best efforts
approach when making contingency plans for unpredictable natural disasters.

Exemptions for Entities Covered by State Contingency Requirements

Individual states may require similar contingency planning requirements. Many
licensees and registrants therefore will have plans developed to comply with these
state requirements. We request the proposed rule be amended to provide an
exemption from the proposed requirements for those licensees and registrants
that have plans in place that meet existing state requirements.


Intermediate Handlers and Carriers

NABR strongly recommends that intermediate handlers and carriers be excluded
from the requirements outlined in this proposed rule. It is extremely unlikely that
carriers and intermediate handlers would encounter the types of situations
contemplated by this proposed rule. Carriers and handlers would, as a matter or
practice, avoid entry into an area under potential threat of an impending natural
disaster (i.e., weather-related event). In the case of other potential natural
disasters, such as an earth quake, there is little relief that any potential planning
might provide. Existing regulations already cover other potential emergency
situations unrelated to natural disasters.

We therefore believe that any contingency planning by these particular entities
would provide little or no benefit to the animals, but would impose significant and
unnecessary costs on intermediate handlers and carriers. Because of the many
other regulatory burdens imposed on intermediate handlers and carriers, the
number of such entities willing to transport research animals is dwindling. We are
concerned that additional regulation, which arguably has minimal value to the
animals, will further reduce the number of entities willing to perform this vital and
important function. Codification of the requirements proposed in this rule could
easily result in the loss of access to air and ground transportation for research
animals.

Training

As currently written, the training requirements specified in the proposed rule are
too broad and therefore unnecessarily burdensome. NABR believes the training
requirements should be amended to allow more reasonable compliance
requirements. We agree that identifying a chain of command by name or by
position title of those who will be responsible for fulfilling the tasks specified in the
plan is an important and essential component of such a plan. However, as
worded, the training requirements appear to apply to all employees, rather than
only those employees identified by the facility as responsible for implementing the
plan. It is very unlikely that a new employee would be given such an important
responsibility. Therefore, we urge the Agency to amend this provision by
specifying that it only applies to those individuals identified in the plan as having a
designated role in the contingency planning and execution process.

Executive Order 12866 and Regulatory Flexibility Act

NABR has reviewed the Preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis and Initial
Regulatory Flexibility Analysis and has several concerns about the information
contained in that document. As a general matter, the discussion in this section
appears to contemplate more extensive requirements than what is specified in the
preamble of the proposed rule.

Introduction - As part of the analysis, assumptions are made as to how many
regulated animals were impacted by the events surrounding hurricane Katrina.
Since the total number of regulated species reported to have been used in the
entire state of Louisiana for FY 2005 is less than 13,000, the conclusions reached
in the analysis appear to be inconsistent with this fact.

Proposed Rule and Contingency Plan Components – This section indicates that
all potential emergencies must be addressed no matter how remote the possibility
of the emergency arising. This requirement is not consistent with the fundamental
principles of a risk assessment based management system and appears more in
line with a risk avoidance management system. If this is indeed the case, the
estimated impact in terms of both time and cost to prepare the proposed
contingency plan has not been accurately assessed. We request the Agency
clarify in any final rule that contingency plans cannot be expected to address all
potential emergencies no matter how remote the possibility of the emergency
arising.

Specific Facility Considerations – In the subsection Research Facilities, reference
is made to informing disaster mitigation agencies to ensure that animals are cared
for after evacuation. It is unclear to NABR which agencies could provide support to
ensure the continued care of animals maintained in research facilities. Since
moving animals on experimental protocol could serve as a significant non-
experimental variable and thus negate the future use of those animals on the
research project, the only option available may often be euthanasia. The fact that
this is not recognized in the analysis is of concern to NABR as it relates to the
Agency’s understanding of the complexity of managing animals maintained in
research facilities.

Expected Benefits and Costs of the Rule – This section is lacking specific
information and we therefore question how, on the basis of this information, a
realistic cost benefit analysis could have been produced. We request the Agency
revise this section by adding significantly more detail and then permit additional
comment by affected parties.

Significant Alternatives to the Rule

NABR agrees with the Agency that the submission of contingency plans to
APHIS for review as required for marine mammal facilities is not a cost effective
option and therefore should not be pursued.

Additional Comments

NABR agrees that preparedness for disasters can reduce harm to animals but
may not reduce the loss of life. The fact that euthanasia may be the only option in
the event of a major disaster and thus will be a key component of a contingency
plan must be recognized by the Agency. NABR also questions the need to train
all facility employees as opposed to training those identified with responsibility for
implementing the plan. We also question the assumption that there will be
minimal cost involved with the development of the proposed contingency plans. To
be effective such plans may require the availability of resources currently not in
place and thus result in major costs to the research or breeding facility. The
additional training requirements alone will involve substantial additional costs to
regulated entities.

Specific Comments on the New Proposed Regulations

While NABR requests the Agency provide additional information on how these
plans will be evaluated, and permit additional comment prior to finalizing this
proposed rule, we offer the following comments on the specific regulatory
proposals specified in the proposed rule.

In 2.38(l)(1) the requirement that a plan would have to be followed would appear to
imply that failure to do so would result in a facility being found to be in
noncompliance regardless of the nature of the disaster and the circumstances
that surrounded the facility’s inability to follow to the letter their contingency plan.
We would suggest that the word “follow” be replaced by the word “implement.” The
language contained in parenthesis appears to be in conflict with language
contained in the Preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis and Initial Regulatory
Flexibility Analysis, which indicates that all potential emergencies be addressed
no matter how remote the possibility of the emergency arising. The same can be
said for the language contained in 2.38(l)(1)(i).

In 2.38, (l) (1)(ii), we recommend that the phrase “backup sources of” be deleted
and that the phrase “as described in the contingency plan” be inserted after the
phrase “as well as sanitation, ventilation, bedding, veterinary care, etc.” We
believe this is necessary because all of the components described in 2.33(b) for
veterinary care may not be possible to maintain during a disaster.

In 2.38, (l)(3), we recommend deleting the second and third sentences –
delete “Training of facility personnel” through “within 30 days of their start date.”.
The very prescriptive nature of these two sentences is not consistent with training
requirements in other sections of the regulations.

In 2.134 similar changes as recommended above should be made.

NABR appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule to amend the
Animal Welfare Act regulations by adding requirements for contingency planning
and training of personnel by research facilities and by dealers, exhibitors,
intermediate handlers, and carriers.

Dear Sir/Madam:

I hope this correspondence, respectfully submitted on behalf of People for the
Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) and our more than two million members and
supporters, finds you well. PETA is pleased that the Animal and Plant Health
Inspection Service (APHIS) Animal Care (AC) at the U.S. Department of
Agriculture (USDA) has proposed to amend the Animal Welfare Act (AWA) to
require USDA-inspected facilities to develop contingency plans for protecting
animals in an emergency. The amendment is long overdue.

The failure of animal facilities to formulate adequate contingency plans to ensure
the welfare of animals in their care has resulted in animals drowning, starving, and
dying of dehydration or exposure. In the aftermath of natural disasters, power
outages can also result in failures of heating, cooling, and ventilation systems,
causing animals to literally cook, freeze, or suffocate to death.

A dramatic example is that of Louisiana State University (LSU). In the wake of
Hurricane Katrina, all 8,000 dogs, monkeys, mice, and rats in the university’s
laboratories died—the great majority trapped in their cages as the waters rose
around them. Yet nearby, when the levee near the Louisiana SPCA was breached,
submerging the entire shelter under water, no animals were harmed. They had
been evacuated to Houston days before, thanks to plan developed years earlier. If
a nonprofit animal shelter is capable of developing and implementing a successful
evacuation plan for animals, the state’s largest public university system, with
more
than $130 million in federal funds from National Institutes of Health alone, should
certainly be compelled to do the same.

Presently, animal experimentation facilities are expected to include contingency
planning in their animal care programs and the Institutional Animal Care and Use
Committee (IACUC) is expected to ensure that these plans are in place before it
approves the animal care program. However, in the absence of a legal
definition of “animal care program” in the AWA, we have seen that many facilities
do not have adequate contingency plans in place. This is the case not only for
extreme disasters such as floods, tornadoes, fires and hurricanes, but indeed,
even for far more modest challenges such as malfunctions in alarm, heating and
watering systems. A strong federal mandate, requiring animal facilities to develop
detailed contingency plans, would safeguard animals more than the current
nebulous guidelines and suggestions are doing.

The contingency plans developed by research facilities should include, at
minimum, the following elements:

1. Location and Facility-Specific Vulnerabilities: The location of the facility and
probable location-specific emergency situations, such as wind, fire, blizzards,
earthquakes, tornadoes, floods, wildfire, and hazardous material spills, should be
identified and thoroughly evaluated. Also, a detailed survey of any facility-specific
vulnerability, such as structural integrity and safety features, should be identified
and addressed.
2. Priorities: The safety and welfare of all animals in the facility must be given top
priority, greater than any research equipment, data, or vials containing valuable
biological materials. In case of emergency, animals must be moved or secured for
safety first.
3. Moving Animals to Safety: Detailed instructions on animal evacuation to an
internal safe area or outside the facility must be developed and all laboratory
personnel must be trained on evacuation protocols.
4. Responsibilities and Tasks: All tasks necessary for ensuring the welfare of
animals in the laboratory must be itemized. The amount of time required for each
task should be estimated and with this, staff members should be assigned
responsibility for specific tasks. Backup personnel should be assigned to each
staff member; these lists should be updated as necessary and all staff members
should be trained to ensure that they are able to carry out their responsibilities. A
clear chain of command and coordinated lines of communication should be
established to ensure that contingency plans are carried out effectively and
efficiently.
5. Resources and Training: The created contingency plan must be fortified by
ensuring that all materials, resources, and training necessary to carry out the plan
are in place. The facility should conduct inventory checks to ensure
that it has enough vehicles to transport animals, extra caging for transportation,
first aid kits for animal during evacuation, food and water provisions for animals
and
other such resources. Training of personnel on the specifics of the contingency
plan, along with quarterly disaster drills to eliminate any flaws from the system,
are also critical.

We appreciate the opportunity to provide input. If you should have any questions
or
concerns, please contact me at AlkaC@peta.org or 703-920-2022. Thank you.

Respectfully submitted,

Alka Chandna, Ph.D.
Laboratory Oversight Specialist
Laboratory Investigations Department
People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals

The proposed regulation requiring a contingency plan in the event of a disaster
sounds on the surface to be valid. However, it appears this proposed regulation
has been hastily and poorly thought out. The cost/benefit analysis has not been
accurately researched and established. This is of great concern to us as our idea
of what this regulation will cost is obviously higher than what the USDA is
thinking. The USDA’s idea that the time and cost to implement a contingency
plan by their regulated facilities will be minimal is proof that there has not been an
appropriate study done to provide the answer to this important question. The
proposed regulation is at this point so vague that there is not a way to estimate
the cost to the industry. There is a long, long list of questions that this proposed
regulation brings up that simply needs to be addressed before any regulations are
actually written.
1) What is going to be accepted as a plan? Will it need to be the size and scope
of some of the plans that are floating around the internet? The plans I have
checked out are several pages in length and would cost thousands of dollars to
develop. It is not difficult for someone to draw up a plan that is not assigned to any
particular situation as there is no accountability in making up general plans.
However, when a plan is established for a particular facility there will come with it
a certain level of scrutiny and accountability. Therefore, a great deal of time, effort,
and expense will need to go into planning for things that are more likely NOT to
happen than TO happen. There is an infinitesimal benefit to the tremendous cost
of putting a plan in place for every possible disaster that could happen. The
different scenarios would be so varied that it would be next to impossible to plan
for them all without a great deal of time and expense involved. As an example: If a
tornado were to come close to a facility, there are so many levels of damage that
could occur and each scenario would require a different plan. The same would
apply if the electricity would be out for varying lengths of time such as days as
opposed to hours. Each would require a much different plan.
2) Will we be required to maintain a separate approved facility that could house
our animals in the event of a disaster that would require evacuation? If not, what is
going to be acceptable to USDA regulation on a very temporary basis? Is USDA
ready to shoulder some of the costs? Is USDA ready to provide transportation,
emergency housing, or at least give some relaxation of regulations until the facility
can be at least temporarily repaired?
3) Does the USDA understand the consequences of regulations on small
businesses? As USDA has stated, most of the facilities that would need to
comply with this regulations are small businesses according to federal
definitions. I disagree that this indicates that the cost of putting a plan in place
would then be minimal. On the contrary, depending on what USDA will consider to
be acceptable as a contingency plan, the cost could be prohibitive. Small
business does not equate to small contingency plan. Indeed, the cost for a
contingency plan per unit of output will rise dramatically compared to a large
business’ cost per unit, putting these small businesses at a great disadvantage.
4) Is this plan going to be available on EFOIA? That would be the worst of
situations as some disasters are intentionally man made. If anyone intent on
causing havoc would have access to the disaster plan, they would also be able to
thwart the recovery phase.
5) Is the purpose of the plan to help the animals or to just increase accountability
if the plan were not followed in the case of an emergency? The concern here is
valid…..no matter how much time, thought and money is put into developing a
plan to use in the event of an actual disaster, the circumstances will always be
such that plans will need to be adapted to fit the particular circumstances. If the
contingency plan is not followed exactly, will the facility and operator be held
accountable to the plan?
The list of questions could go on for a long time. The purpose of these comments
and questions is not to say that some type of a disaster contingency plan is a
bad idea, but rather to say that the USDA needs to do the necessary and required
background studies before proposing this regulation. The research to accurately
estimate the time and cost involved in complying with this regulation has not been
done. Proposing a vague regulation is not acceptable.
Respectfully submitted,
Joe Gerst, Chairman
Iowa Federation of Animal Owners,
Promoting the responsible ownership of animals.

7 CFR part 319 (Docket No. APHIS-2006-0125) Importation of Emerald Ash Borer Host Material
From Canada
Proposed action: amends regulations to prohibit or restrict the importation of emerald ash borer host
material from infested areas of Canada consistent with those imposed by Canada on the materials
from infested areas of the United States. I support the prohibition of importation into the United
States of all ash trees, regardless of size, that originate in regions regulated by the CFIA for
emerald ash borer. A concern is that the regulations might not be updated frequently enough. It
would be better to include infested areas of Canada. Wood or bark chips less than 1 inch in
diameter are allowed since larval growth are apparently not supported by chips this size or smaller.
However, adults could be within that size of wood and carry emerald ash borer to the U.S. I do not
support this inclusion of wood chips greater than 1 inch as an allowable imports.
Counties bordering ones quarantined for emerald ash borer may have populations not yet detected
since it is difficult to survey reliably for this pest. Even in official surveys, reliable techniques are
not available to detect early infestations in an area. I would not allow firewood or ash wood and logs
in neighboring counties to be enterable with only an import permit; again official surveys are not
reliable to detect early infestations. Stronger regulation and tracking of firewood would be helpful.
Preventing long distance shipment of firewood would help to slow the spread of invasive wood borer
and other wood associated insects. At the least even though importer documents may be required
to accompany some shipments, prior notification of receiving states that shipments from infested
states are on their way would be more helpful and should be required.

Kathleen Johnson, Insect Pest Prevention & Management Program Supervisor

wellbeing of animals under its care. Charles River also provides a wide range of
preclinical services, principally through its contract research facilities, that are
designed to support drug development activities. Charles River has developed
substantial experience over many decades in the safe production and transport of
animals as well as their responsible and humane use in biomedical research.
Charles River is a strong proponent of good animal welfare and responsible use of
animals in biomedical research. As a corporation we are supporters of
appropriate risk base emergency preparedness programs for animal facilities and
as such applaud the USDA’s interest in helping the regulated community prepare
for events that may threaten the environment and health of animals.

Unfortunately, After a careful review of this proposal, which appeared in the
October 23, 2008 edition of the Federal Register (Volume 73, Number 206, pages
63085-63090), Charles River strongly recommends that the USDA reconsider this
proposal and withdraw it in favor of preparing a more manageable and applicable
proposal in keeping with the risks and practicalities of responding to emergencies
and natural disasters. The proposal as it stands leaves open too many questions
as to the level of detail, the process by which the adequacy of contingency plans
will be judged, the agency’s approach toward failure to follow a contingency plan
due to exigent circumstances, and the mechanism to ensure consistency of
evaluation of plans and outcomes in the event of emergency situations or
disasters. While contingency plans can be made based upon a risk analysis that
is institutionally specific, other statutory authorities at the local, state or national
level may impose restrictions, requirements or other interventions that would make
it impossible to implement some or all of the contingency plan from being
executed in the face of a disaster. The proposed regulation does not address how
these differences will be addressed and whether the institution will be found in
noncompliance under such circumstances, especially if animals are lost.

The USDA’s responsibilities cover many animal activities involving dealers,
exhibitors, research facilities and animal transport providers. While certain
disasters over recent years have adversely affected pet animals, the agency has
not provided information on the number of animals in other categories that have
been negatively impacted by disasters or emergencies in facilities that would be
covered by this proposed rule change. Given the amount of burden placed on the
agency currently as well as the significant financial impact that, in Charles River’s
opinion, will be placed on the regulated community, it is important that the agency
lays a sound case for undertaking a proposal of this nature. The proposal does
not contain sufficient evidence to support the contention that USDA regulated
species suffered harm or died as a result of the lack of or implementation of
contingency plans. In its present form Charles River views the proposal to be
unwieldy, costly and lacking sufficient details to be fairly applied and
administered. The following sections address some of the areas of concern.

Intent of the Proposal

The agency’s position is that as a result of the events experienced in the 2005
hurricane season all licensees and registrants should be required to develop a
contingency plan for all animals regulated under the AWA in an effort to better
prepare for potential disasters. This contention was further reinforced by the
experience with Hurricane Katrina wherein provisions for pets, as well as
presumably animals in regulated categories, had not been made resulting in harm
or death to animals. While Charles River believes contingency plans are an
important component of a well-managed animal care and use program, we are
concerned that the intent of the agency is not clear in the proposed language. In
Charles River’s view there is a difference between emergency situations and
disasters. An emergency is an unexpected, serious occurrence or situation
urgently requiring prompt action. In the case of animals and their environment, it
likely involves the failure of a system or structural component of a facility. A
disaster is an occurrence causing widespread destruction often resulting in
multiple and unpredictable failures to the physical facilities and the animal care
program resulting from external conditions imposed on the facility such as severe
weather, earthquakes, and floods.

If the intent behind the proposed rule on contingency plans is to better prepare
facilities for emergencies and for disasters, while simultaneously allowing
institutions to formulate a plan that best suits their needs, then the lack of specific
details as to what elements must be included in all contingency plans is
appropriate (assuming that all contingency plans require the same elements).
Thus, the agency would assure that a risk analysis and forethought had been
given to likely emergencies and natural disasters that might befall a facility and
that planning had gone into averting harm or death to the animals during such
occurrences. Unfortunately, such planning assumes a number of things. Most
importantly, it assumes that more than one emergency or disaster does not occur
simultaneously and that necessary resources and personnel are in the appropriate
places and can administer to the problem when it occurs. In the event of certain
natural disasters, access to electrical power, water required for drinking and
sanitation, and personnel access to the facilities may simultaneously not be
available. Electrical generators and transfer switches may break during
emergency operation requiring parts or special technical personnel to repair such
equipment that are not available or accessible. While basic risk analysis and
contingency planning can provide some level of protection of animal welfare during
such emergencies or disasters, there are too many variables to assume that all,
or even most, situations will be covered. This may cause the plan to be modified
or even completely scrapped in the face of an emergency or a disaster due to the
inability to implement one or more components of the plan. Alternative actions
put in place which may rely on certain components of the original plan may or
may not be completely successful. Certainly, the planning process can be
valuable and help personnel consider what options could be available and what
materials could be placed on hand to work through the emergency or natural
disaster; but some animal injury or death could still occur no matter how thorough
the planning process or alterative actions taken.

If the intent, however, of agency is to hold facilities accountable for following
contingency plans to the letter, regardless of the nature of the disaster or
emergency, then the lack of specific detail and expectations by the agency is
problematic and unacceptable. If a regulated entity does not have a contingency
plan for a specific event or group of events because it was an unforeseen event or
if the contingency plan was in place but lacked the level of detailed required to
implement it under the specific circumstances or if the plan would likely be
unworkable due to a specific set of circumstances, would that entity be in
noncompliance? Would the judgment regarding noncompliance be affected by
whether the animals were harmed in any way regardless of what actions the
facilities took? What will be the criteria for before or after event acceptability?

Components of the Plan

Identification of Risks

In this component of the plan as proposed by the USDA, the identification of
events that would trigger the need for a contingency plan, including emergencies
such as electrical outages, faulty HVAC systems, fires, and animal escapes, as
well as natural disasters that the facility is most likely to experience, would need
to be assessed. While the assessment of risks related to potential emergencies
and the resulting plan that would be developed as a result of that assessment is
relatively straightforward, the same cannot be said when attempting to develop
plans to respond to natural disasters. As outlined above, there is a level of
complexity and uncertainty as to how many emergency related risks can occur
during a single natural disaster as well as their sequence and magnitude. Unlike
emergency items, the availability of external support to rapidly correct multiple
emergency situations is an uncertainty that is unlikely to be addressed in
advanced by planning. Charles River believes that the regulatory language
addressing these two disparate events must recognize the difference between
emergencies and natural disasters and should not hold the facilities to the same
level of accountability for contending with these two different classifications of
events.

Task Required

The second component of the plan is to outline specific tasks required to be
carried out in response to the identified emergencies including, but not limited to,
detailed animal evacuation instructions or shelter-in-place instructions. The
requirement that this part of the plan be in an outline format implies such a plan
would not require a great deal of detail and thus be open to subjective
interpretation by both the regulated community and the regulatory enforcement
personnel. Charles River is particularly concerned about the language indicating
the need for detailed evacuation or shelter–in-place instructions. Unlike zoos,
exhibitors and certain regulated entities, many of Charles River’s functions are in
the contract research organization environment and are governed by Good
Laboratory Practices (GLP) requirements in order to meet standards imposed by
the FDA and EPA. Changes in environment or facilities and even the movement of
animals to other locations within the same facilities that could result in breaches
in the health status of animals or changes in their environment would negate the
animal’s usefulness in that study. The only recourse would be to euthanize the
animals should the environment not be able to be satisfactory stabilized or the
facilities or their mechanical systems be somehow compromised. It is unclear
whether large scale euthanasia under such a proposal would be acceptable. It is
also unlikely that the practical issues needed for maintaining the large scale
supplies of the controlled drugs required to undertake such a massive task on a
moment’s notice could be addressed in a reasonable manner. Moreover, in the
case of nonhuman primates, dogs, and farm animals, there may be no practical
way to move them to other accommodations even if their movement would not be
of consequence to the studies in question or to breeding operations. The
availability of appropriate and safe transport for large numbers of these animals on
short notice is very unlikely and problematic during a natural disaster. To relocate
animals in an acceptable manner would require substantial additional facilities that
are kept empty at another location outside of a disaster area so that they would
be available to receive evacuated animals. The cost for such arrangements would
be substantial and impractical.

Identification of Chain of Command

The third component of this proposal involves identifying a chain of command by
name or by position title of those who will be responsible for fulfilling these tasks,
which is clearly an essential component of such a plan. Charles River is
concerned with the highly prescriptive requirements for training individuals
responsible for carrying out the plan. As it is currently worded, the training
requirements appears to apply to all employees, rather than only to employees
identified by the facility as responsible for implementing the plan. It is extremely
unlikely that a new employee would be given such important responsibilities in
this chain of command, especially if the employee was not charged with decision
making during an emergency. As a result, the 30 day requirement for training
such individuals seems both unnecessary and not in keeping with lack of
specificity in the rest of the plan. It also raises the question of what is acceptable
training and whether missing the training or retraining deadline by a few days
would be considered a noncompliance. For organizations such as carriers and
intermediate handlers whose turnover rates are often high especially in cargo
related tasks, the training requirement would be so financially burdensome that it
might influence decisions regarding provision of animal transport services.

Addressing How the Response and Recovery will be Handled

The fourth component of the proposed plan includes addressing how response and
recovery will be handled in terms of materials, resources and training needed.
Charles River is concerned about this component as it relates to the requirement
that the contingency plans would have to be in place within 180 days of the
effective date of the final rule. If this component of the plan identifies materials
and resources not currently available within a facility, does the 180 day time frame
mandate the acquisition of materials and resources by the implementation date?
For facilities without existing contingency plans and the necessary materials and
resources to implement them, acquiring such resources within such a short time
period would be difficult, if not impossible.

Unintended Consequences:

The USDA is proposing to add requirements for contingency plans for intermediate
handlers and carriers. Charles River believes that there is substantial potential for
unintended consequences should the present proposal be adopted and applied to
these entities. There are a limited number of ground transporters and air carriers
capable and willing to provide carriage for animals. The level of contingency
planning by carriers and handlers that can be put in place for emergencies and
natural disasters is substantially restricted by the fact that carriers have only
limited fixed facilities with most of the process of carriage being done in
vehicles/aircraft in which the risk profile can be different depending upon routes,
terrain, climate, and traffic. These entities are heavily regulated already through a
number of agencies including the Department of Transportation that limit their
potential actions and activities. While some planning can be made for
emergencies such as equipment failure, the ability to implement such plans in a
timely fashion depends heavily on the location of the equipment and the type of
failure. Due to health requirements that must be maintained during transit, off-
loading animals for an extended period of time at facilities that may or may not be
equipped to maintain the animals’ health status ultimately imposes risks to that
status which in turn impacts the value and usefulness of the animals. This risk
may be unacceptable to the consignee and may ultimately require euthanasia of
the animals as a consequence of what might seem to be a reasonable alternative
action during an emergency or a disaster. In the case of air carriage, only limited
permanent structures in the form of warehouses with limited areas of climate
control are available and in some cases may not be available at certain locations.
As with any perishable cargo, carriers try to make accommodations to maintain
necessary conditions for the animals, but this is not always possible if stays are
extended as might be the case in weather related or natural disasters. However,
few regulated species would likely be in transport through affected areas during
any such event.

Charles River is also concerned, that depending upon how one interprets the
current proposal, carriers and intermediate handlers could either be extensions of
the research or breeding facility or independent agents. It is unclear whether
carriers would need to file separate disaster plans to cover the portion of the time
they handle animals or whether it would be the responsibility of the research
institution or breeding facility to provide such disaster plans. In either case, the
practicality of extending this requirement to carriers is extremely questionable.
Carriers are influenced substantially by the economic climate as to what cargo
they will carry and the limitations placed on that cargo. Imposition of
requirements that would add costs to the carrier’s operation including provision of
special facilities, training costs for large numbers of personnel at many locations,
and the potential to be found in noncompliance with subsequent enforcement
actions by the USDA resulting in fines or other requirements will clearly force
carriers to eliminate the availability or severely restrict the availability of carriage of
USDA regulated animals. It would also have severe consequences in terms of
resources that the USDA would have to employ to fairly implement this
requirement across all of the various sites that can be involved in carriage of
animals.

Proposed Rule and Contingency Plan Components

In this section the agency indicates that all potential emergencies be addressed
no matter how remote the possibility of the emergency arising. This requirement
is not consistent with the fundamental principles of a risk-based management
system and appears more in line with a risk avoidance management system. If
this is indeed the case, the estimated impact in terms of both time and cost to
prepare the proposed contingency plan has not been accurately assessed. Also
included in this section are some suggested general steps that should be taken
by facilities in the development of a contingency plan. Had similar information
been provided in the Background section of the notice in the Federal Register, the
regulated community would be able to provide more substantive comments.
Clearly, there appears to be a disconnect within the proposal as to what level of
contingency planning in terms of emergency as well as disaster planning the
agency is expecting. The level of detail that appears to be suggested within the
proposal given the complexity of possible disaster events as outlined previously
can be quite extensive and may likely provide no more benefit than more general
planning with a clear chain of decision making responsibilities assigned to specific
personnel with back ups.

Specific Facility Considerations

In the subsection Research Facilities, reference is made to informing disaster
mitigation agencies as to facilities needed and status in order to ensure that
animals are cared for after evacuation. This appears to be a clear reference to the
situation involving Hurricane Katrina and the consequences deriving there from. It
is unclear to Charles River which agencies could provide support to ensure the
continued care of animals maintained in research or breeding facilities, especially
given the complex requirements and the number of animals that may be housed in
a single facility. Since moving animals on experimental protocol could serve as a
significant non-experimental variable and thus negate the future use of those
animals on the research project or for any other purposes, the only option
available may often be euthanasia. Other agencies would likely be ill-equipped to
handle such a scenario nor authorized to carry it out. In the case of contract
laboratories, ownership of the animals resides not with the facility but with the
sponsor further complicating legal ramifications following resolution of the
disaster. The fact that the agency has not recognized this complexity in their
analysis with respect to managing animals maintained in research facilities is
disconcerting and an indication that the agency should withdraw the current
proposal and comeback with a more focused proposal with respect to
requirements and reasonable expectation of capabilities tailored to the needs of
individual components of the regulated community.

Expected Benefits and Costs of the Rule

It is Charles River’s view that this section contains little specific information that
could have formed the basis for a realistic cost benefit analysis. Charles River is
concerned that as part of the analysis made by the agency Hurricane Katrina was
used as an example of a disaster in which lives of regulated species were lost.
As part of the agency’s analysis, assumptions were made as to how many
regulated animals were impacted by the events surrounding Hurricane Katrina.
Since the total number of regulated species reported to be used in the entire state
of Louisiana for FY 2005 was less than 13,000, the conclusion reached in the
analysis do not seem to be supported by this number. Clearly, a much smaller
number of animals were present at the time of the disaster and of those the USDA
does not appear to have any firm numbers as to those that survived unharmed
versus those that were injured, died or were euthanized during or after the
disaster. It is important not to confuse the substantial problem during natural
disasters with the pet population not regulated by the USDA with those regulated
entities that may have had animals present at the time of the disaster and may
subsequently be impacted. Charles River believes a much more thorough
analysis is required to justify the imposition of these additional regulatory
requirements.

Significant Alternatives to the Rule

Charles River agrees with the agency that the submission of contingency plans to
APHIS for review as required for marine mammal facilities is not a cost effective or
practical option and therefore should not be pursued.

Additional Considerations

As with any emergency situation, there is always the question of access to
animals and facilities by personnel. Missing from the proposal is a clear
statement that contingency plans should not put the lives of humans at risk in
order to implement the plan or to gain access to the facilities in order to care of
animals. There are a variety of natural disasters that would not permit safe
access to animals nor the implementation of disaster plans/contingency plans
without risking human lives. It is unclear how the agency would handle such
circumstances if they result in loss of animal lives or conversely loss of human
lives directly attributable to attempts to implement the contingency plan.

Comments on Wording of Regulations in Part 2

Charles River believes that the current proposal should be withdrawn and a more
focused proposal developed that will provide a basis for meaningful comment. In
rethinking the proposal, the USDA should consider the following wording changes
in the proposed regulations and modify or adapt language in any new submission
of the proposal in accordance with these suggestions.

In 2.38, (l),(1) the requirement that a plan would have to be followed would appear
to imply that failure to do so would result in a facility being found to be in
noncompliance regardless of nature of the disaster and the circumstance that
surrounded the facility’s inability to follow to the letter their contingency plan. We
would suggest that the word “follow” be replaced by the word “implement.” The
language contained in parenthesis appears to be in conflict with language
contained in the Preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis and Initial Regulatory
Flexibility Analysis, which indicates that all potential emergencies be addressed
no matter how remote the possibility of the emergency arising. The same can be
said for the language contained in 2.38(l),(1),(i).

In 2.38, (l),(1),(ii), we recommend that the phrase “backup sources of” be deleted
and that the phrase “as described in the contingency plan” be inserted after the
phrase “as well as sanitation, ventilation, bedding, veterinary care, etc.” We
believe this is necessary because all of the components described in 2.33,(b) for
veterinary care may not be possible to maintain during a disaster.

In 2.38, (l),(2), we recommend that the first sentence be deleted and the phrase in
brackets be moved to appear after the word APHIS in what is now the second
sentence. This is necessary because if a contingency plan requires the
acquisition of equipment or alteration of existing support services, the 180 day
time frame may not be achievable.

In 2.38, (l),(3), we recommend deleting the second and third sentences. The very
prescriptive nature of these two sentences is not consistent with training
requirements in other sections of the regulations.

In 2.134 similar changes as recommended above should be made.

Charles River appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule to
amend the Animal Welfare Act regulations by adding requirements for
contingency planning and training of personnel by research facilities, dealers,
exhibitors, intermediate handlers, and carriers. We feel strongly that the proposal
should be withdrawn and a more focused proposal perhaps tailored to the
requirements of individual entities and with reasonable expectations as well as
risk management recommendations be developed. The agency should make
clear exactly how it intends to regulate this process, the criteria for judging
compliance versus noncompliance, and the mechanisms by which consistency in
evaluation will be assured. If further clarification of these comments are needed,
please contact Charles River.

Respectfully submitted,

William J. White, V.M.D., M.S., DACLAM, DECLAM
Corporate Vice President, Veterinary and Professional Services

exposed. In today's Registered Dairy Cattle market, this limit simply does not
come close to the value of many animals that could be destroyed. The US
Registered Dairy Herd is the envy of the world, due in large part to the efforts of
USDA to promote improvement through genetics. This has resulted in high
demand for US dairy cattle genetics throughout the world and incredible earning
power of dairy animals that have genetics in demand worldwide. The export
market for elite dairy cattle genetics is the driving force in these high values. So,
while I applaud the work that is done to keep our export markets open through
control and eradication of TB, we must consider the potential financial devastation
that could result to dairy producers whose livlihoods are tied to animals worth far
more than $3,000.

Currently, in the Section 50.3(b) of Subpart A of Part 50 of Chapter I of Title 9 of
Code
of Federal Regulations, from the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service,
USDA
(APHIS), it states, “The Department will in no case pay more than $3,000 for an
animal
that is destroyed.” While the USDA cap of $3,000 an animal may exceed the
value of
many of the cattle that need to be sacrificed for TB concerns, it does not come
close to
compensating the owners for the appraised value of many registered cattle.

The American Guernsey Assocaition. represents 800 members from across the
United States whose cattle represent the most elite Registered Guernsey
genetics in the world.

family farms. The loss of these animals and the limit in compensation for that loss

indemnity rates need to be flexible and compensate the owner for the appropriate
value of the reactor, suspect, or exposed animal. Without a change in the
indemnity paid for registered cattle, all of our members are potentially vulnerable
to financial devastation should a case of TB occur in their herd.

Seth Johnson

ACTION:That the following sentence be repealed and deleted from Section 50.3(b) of
Subpart A of Part 50 of Chapter I of Title 9 of Code of Federal
Regulations: "Additionally, the Department will in no case pay more than $3,000 for an
animal that is destroyed."

COMMENT/SUMMARY:

As you know, for the most part, bovine tuberculosis was virtually eradicated from the
United States until several years ago. Unfortunately, in recent years, we are seeing
new cases.

The value of registered cattle and how it pertains to the indemnity paid for animals
under the current Bovine Tuberculosis Eradication program is the impetus for this
letter. Producers who own cows that are reactors to bovine tuberculosis and/or have
been exposed to it have been traditionally paid an indemnity as part of the depopulation
program. The intent of the indemnity is to compensate herd owners for losses
incurred.

Initially it was believed that the indemnity limits were consistent with the relative market
value of the animal. However, herds that specialize in high quality and valued
registered genetics own animals whose value far exceeds the limit of Federal
indemnity.

Currently, in the Section 50.3(b) of Subpart A of Part 50 of Chapter I of Title 9 of Code
of Federal Regulations, from the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, USDA
(APHIS), it states, “The Department will in no case pay more than $3,000 for an animal
that is destroyed.” While the USDA cap of $3,000 an animal may exceed the value of
many of the cattle that need to be sacrificed for TB concerns, it does not come close to
compensating the owners for the appraised value of many registered cattle.

The Holstein Association USA, Inc. represents 30,000 members from across the United
States whose cattle represent the most elite Registered HolsteinSM genetics in the
world. For example, I’ll give you some statistics from three Registered Holstein sales
held this year.

•The Branson Limited Edition sale held March 8th, averaged $16,447 per
head. The top seller was a calf which was sold for $81,000, and the second top seller
was a cow which sold for $60,000.
•At the Crescentmead Registered Holstein herd dispersal in Wisconsin this
summer, the cows sold averaged well over $6,000 per head.
•At the Global Glamour Sale at Arethusa in Litchfield, Connecticut on July
28th, 54 animals sold for an unofficial average of $97,471 per animal. Thirteen animals
sold for over $100,000, and one sold for $1 million.

Obviously, the sentence that appears in Section 50.3(b) of Subpart A of Part 50 of
Chapter 1 of Title 9 of Code of Federal Regulations which states, “Additionally, the
Department will in no case pay more than $3,000 for an animal that is destroyed"
needs to be repealed and deleted.

In order to keep up with the ever-changing livestock industry, and to increase the
speed at which high-risk animals are removed from the general population, indemnity
rates need to be flexible and compensate the owner for the appropriate value of the
reactor, suspect, or exposed animal. Without a change in the indemnity paid for
registered cattle, all of our members are potentially vulnerable to financial devastation
should a case of TB occur in their herd.

Cordially,

John M. Meyer
Chief Executive Officer

Agency:Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, USDA

Action:That the following sentence be repealed and deleted from Section 50.3
(b) of Subpart A of Part 50 of Chapter l of Title 9 of Code of Federal Regulations:
“Additionally, the Department will in no case pay more than $3,000 for
an animal that is destroyed.”

Comment/Summary

Bovine tuberculosis was all but eliminated in past years in the US. However,
recently there has been an unfortunate increase in the frequency of the disease.
While the vector for each infected herd may vary, the range of possibilities and
control is daunting: human/bovine, bovine/bovine, deer/bison/bovine and the
reciprocals of each. With modern management practices dairy herd owners take
steps to control these vectors, however they are not always successful in
controlling the exposure of their herds.

In the case of registered cattle the herd owners are then faced with the strong
possibility of not being able to be recompensed adequately for their cattle that are
reactors to tuberculin testing. The current Federal indemnity program while
adequate for commercial level cattle at $3,000 simply does not meet the income
potential of cattle with elite genetics. The primary deference is that the income
stream from commercial dairy cattle comes largely from sale of milk and beef at
the end of an animal’s usefulness. In the case of elite dairy genetics there is
added value above and beyond that of milk/beef income from the sale of multiple
offspring for genetic improvement of other herds. In many cases sales of superior
breeding stock equals or exceeds the value derived from sales of milk and beef for
registered dairy producers on an annual basis. It should be noted that many of
these producers are under 200 head of milking cows and are able to maintain their
family operations in part from the extra income derived from sales of genetics.

At this time Section 50.3(b) of Subpart A of Part 50 of Chapter 1 of Title 9 of the
Code of Federal Regulations limitation of $3,000 per animal does not bear any
awareness of this distinction.

The Brown Swiss Cattle Breeders Association of the USA represents 900
members from across the United States and the American Milking Shorthorn
Society represents 400 members. These members focus on developing the
superior genetics that commercial milk producers seek out and are willing to pay a
premium for in acquiring. Recent examples include:

The 2008 National Brown Swiss Convention Sale in which 86 lots
averaged $7,737.
The 2007 National Brown Swiss Convention Sale in which 61 head
averaged $7,208.

In addition in both breeds the sale of embryos by private treaty is also a major
source of income. Elite genetic cows can generate $5,000 to $20,000 a year in
sales in addition to sales of milk.

If the above named section is not repealed the potential economic loss would be
devastating for our members the registered dairy cattle producers if their herds are
impacted by TB.

Cordially,

David J. Kendall
Executive Secretary

The New Mexico Cattle Growers’ Association (NMCGA) supports the goal of
ensuring that proper herd management plans be implemented by herd owners who
are entitled to indemnity payments. However we are concerned that the proposed
rule lacks a defined and workable time table for the development and approval of
that herd management plan. Once a herd owner has destroyed the affected
animals, the financial impacts of that necessary action are immediately felt on
family ranching operations as well as in the community and region that depends
upon them for economic activity.

An affected producer could develop an acceptable herd plan but be left to wait an
undetermined length of time for government approval of the plan. Because no
payment of indemnity would be made until approval, there is an undetermined
length of time wherein the herd owner, having taken all necessary steps to comply
with the program and develop a herd plan, will continue to lose income. The
longer the approval process takes, the greater the risk to the herd owner, and
those who depend upon him for income, jobs and tax base, that the viability of the
entire operation will be lost.

NMCGA believes that thirty (30) days is an acceptable amount of time for the
approval of herd management plan. Additionally, we propose that the majority of
indemnity payments be made upon the submission of a herd management plan by
the affected herd owner as follows: 75% paid upon submission, with a payment of
15% upon approval of the plan, and the remaining 10% upon verification of plan
implementation.

Please see attached letter for comments on behalf of Ken Nobis, President and
John Dilland, General Manager, Michigan Milk Producers Association.

There is no mechanism in regulation that allows the indemnity cap to increase
with market prices of animals. Furthermore, values for cattle have increased since
the $3,000 indemnity cap was put forth in regulation, and it is not unusual for good
quality commercial cattle to eclipse the $3,000 indemnity cap.

Section 50.9 allows additional consideration to be given to additional value of
animals to be destroyed because of their genetic makeup. Increasing the
indemnity cap will only affect a small percentage of animals, i.e., there are few
purebred animals that would even qualify for this additional consideration. In
addition, the animals would need to be appraised. Following the comparsions of
appraisals, negotiations can begin on the true value of an animal. The $3,000 cap
prevents these negotiations from even getting started. From a breeders point of
view, this additional value is critical to recouping some of the future income that
will be lost after the animal is destroyed.

With the widespread concern of the true cost of downgrading a state's TB status
to all affected industries, it seems to be a small concession to increase the
indemnity cap for a handful of animals to expedite the process of restoring a
state's TB-free status. Please consider changing the regulation to allow for higher
settlement prices to be paid for genetically superior animals.
