The NHTSA states that:

Our mission: Save lives, prevent injuries, reduce vehicle-related crashes

On the face of it this initiative (docket 23700) aimed at reducing the increasing toll of motorcyclist injuries and. fatalities through state grants for training etc. is laudable.

However the NHTSA itself is primarily to blame for the increase in motorcycle accidents since
1996 by permitting glaring and distracting daytime running lights (DRL) on motor cars and trucks.

The introduction of DRL permitted by NHTSA in 1997 has put all vulnerable road users at great
danger (including pedal cyclists and pedestrians) and it is not surprising 10 years later, that
casualties are increasing to this group of road users.

In fact, the introduction of DRL has not reduced road accidents in general either in the USA or Europe.
The only comprehensive study of real before and after data was conducted by HILDI which
showed a 3.7% INCREASE in accidents to DRL equipped vehicles (ref HILDI vol15 No.1 December 1997).
There have been subsequent academic studies by Tessmer et al but these all have been
theoretical and not based on real-world data or tests.

The Japanese Government did real tests on DRL and proposed an intensity of 200cd - about the
level of bright parking lights and far below the 800  3,000cd allowed by NHTSA.

The problems associated with excessive glare were recognised by NHTSA and dockets 4124 and
1724 were launched in 1998 and 2004 .

These dockets have received hundreds of complaints about the dangers of glaring DRL, but the
NHTSA has failed to act when other countries, notably the European Union have decreed
that the DRL intensity from headlights is too high and 16watts of tungsten (or LED equivalent) have been adopted.

By failing to act to reduce DRL intensity, the NHTSA are exposing themselves collectively and
individually to lawsuits from pedestrians, pedal cyclists and motorcyclists.

This current initiative on docket 23700 for motorcyclists is too little, too late.

The NHTSA could reduce fatalities to all groups of vulnerable road users at the stroke of a pen by banning or reducing the intensity of DRL to an acceptably low level below 200cd.

I submit that until this reduction in DRL intensity or an outright ban is mandated, that the NHTSA is failing to fulfil its mission to the American people.

Roy Milnes

Has NHTSA not recognized the correlation between the increased use of automobile Daytime Running Lights (DRLs) and motorcycle fatalities? Right about the time that General Motors began fitting all of its US vehicles with DRLs (and refusing to disconnect them) back in 1997, motorcycle fatalities had a sharp increase. Yes, increased cyclist training and addressing motorist awareness are welcomed measures, but let's focus on another cause of motorcycle related fatalities: DRLs.

In NHTSA's own NPRM in docket 4124, it acknowledged that the study by Kirkpatrick, et. al., determined that a significant percentage of drivers would dim their rearview mirrors in the presence of even "moderate" DRL intensities. This reflexive action isn't the only response that drivers show to excessively bright DRLs. This can be translated into a general avoidance of viewing DRLs which leads to an indiffernnce to surrounding traffic.

The NPRM in 4124 would have eliminated high beam DRLs that are currently permitted to run at 7000cd at lab voltages. The high beam implementation is still in widespread use by automobile manufacturers even though they are well aware of the negative safety effects of the excessive glare. It is this excessive glare that has caused the once conspicuous motorcyclists to be lost in the sea of Daytime Running Lights. Given a motorcycle's relatively narrow cross section, one can understand the desire of cyclists to stand out from the crowd. This has resulted in cyclists operating with full intensity high beams or a modulated low/high beam combination. In fact, NHTSA has now permitted such modulators for sale in the US. This is the WRONG way to approach the glare problem.

To address the problem, NHTSA should give hard consideration to Japan's experiments on the effects of automobile DRLs on motorcycle conspicuity - TRANS-WP29-GRE-51-10e. This study is particularly telling. In the presence of just 200cd DRLs, the visibility of the motorcycles is greatly diminished. This number is well below the 1500cd (2000cd at 13.8V) proposed in 4124.

What should NHTSA do?
1) Ban all headlamp based DRLs.
2) Force a recall of all high beam DRL vehicles.
3) Standardize on amber DRLs not more than 250cd for automobiles.
4) The DRLs should be driver controlled with the default state OFF.
5) Ban modulators on motorcyle headlamp assemblies.
6) Start a media campaign for responsible headlight usage: ON at night and in inclement weather; OFF at all other times.

Excessive glare is but one part of the problem. However, removing the light pollution from our streets and highways can only improve conditions for other vulnerable road users.

Respectfully submitted,

Steven L. Johnson, Ph.D.

Section 2010 of SAFETEA-LU authorizes the Secratary of Transportation to "make grants to States that adopt and implement effective programs that reduce the number of single and multiple vehicle crashes involving motorcyclists". This simple statement defines the task NHTSA is required to perform in writing the rules to implement the intent of section 2010 of SAFETEA-LU.
Section 2010 was concisely written, and defines the parameters qualifying States will be required to operate under. I do not see any glaring examples in the rules as written that would interfere with the intent of section 2010. There is adequet flexability built in that allows qualifying States to use the grant money in a wide variety of ways. The agency in each State is allowed to use the grant money in whatever area of their Motorcycle Safety Program that needs the most attention. The WI Motorcycle Safety Program Administrator has defined areas in our program that could use some attention. Those areas are covered nicely in Section 2010, and in the rules to implement it. There are also provisions in 2010 that require programs to be effective in reducing fatalities and crashes in key areas. This should insure that grant money is not given out to support programs that do not show that they are having a positive impact on motorcycle safety. I own and manage the Animal Health Department and Customer Service
Department of the largest pet store group in Arizona.
Our company purchases pure breed and specially bred puppies from the Hunte
Corporation, who is the petitioner in this matter.
We are in favor of the petition, because we feel the classifications set by USDA
are outdated and does not accurately reflect or differentiate our business from that
of a dealer that sells animals for research or for food. With more and more people
rallying for animal rights, it is very important to classify a pet store separate from
an organization that sells pets for research or food. It is difficult to understand
how USDA can group together business with such different objectives, standards,
and relationships and obligations to their customers, employees and animals they
care for. In a pet store, the animals socialization, happiness and well being is
being cared for on a continual basis. When the animals are in their new homes,
the obligation does not stop there.
This petition will not only help the pet store and pet distributors in the eyes of the
public, but will allow USDA to enforce the highest standards in caring for these
pets. The pet industry is regulated by USDA according to federal law, but as a
consumer business, it also is regulated by the market. Breeders, distributors and
pet stores cannot cut corners when it comes to caring and providing for the
puppies that will ultimately become a pet in someone?s home.
The pet industry is damaged when its distribution segment is linked from a
regulatory perspective with a business segment that operates on a completely
different set of principles. This petition is simple and straightforward. It does not
request regulatory changes, it merely requests that the USDA regulatory scheme
refer in a non-discriminatory way to pet distributors, and specifically that the
terminology defining that regime reflect the realities of the businesses being
regulated.

The petition submitted by The Hunte Corporation makes perfect sense and I ask
that it be granted.

Thank you for providing me with the opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,
April Shaw, Animal Health Director

requirement, it may lead animals to be transported at younger ages than intended
by USDA. In order to provide protection for all covered species, USDA should
clarify the term unweaned and identify minimum age requirements for individual
species.

other animals covered under the Animal Welfare Act. Research facilities should
not be given a blanket exemption.

Sincerely,

To whom it may concern,
My company breeds and sells small pets and feeder animals. Ninety percent of
the animals we sell are less than eight of age. Older animals are not desired in
the small animal trade. Small animals such as gerbils, hamsters, rabbits, etc.
are weaned and able to survive on their own at three to four weeks of age. Three
to four weeks of age is when these pets should find a home, so that they can
socialize with their new owners. Older small animals are much less likely to
bond and interact with people, they will very likely bite and be antisocial.
This causes harm to their usually young adolescent new owners and leads to
neglect by said owners. I believe that the proposed amendment is far too broad
to be appropriately implemented. It should, at very best, be specific to
individual species.
Furthermore the terminology suggests at some points within the amendment that
only currently regulated animals will be covered, and then it seems to imply
that all warm blooded animals would be included. The terminology is too unclear
and confusing. If this proposed amendment were to be adopted it could be
interpreted that ALL warm blooded animals would then be regulated under the
animal welfare act. If this would include food and fiber animals this amendment
could be extremely detrimental to the persons who produce food and fiber
animals. The terminology needs to be more explicit. If the purpose of this
amendment is to intentionally cover ALL warm blooded animals, and not just the
currently regulated animals, it should not be passed for any reason.
There are too many flaws within this amendment. For example, how and who will
determine the exact age of all the different species? Will this require
additional documentation and paperwork? On our farm we produce nearly five
hundred thousand animals every year, the added documentation and paperwork would
be an unfair burden to me and my company. Also considering how different species
mature at different rates it seems this proposed amendment could also be
extremely difficult, if not entirely impossible to enforce.
In general I feel this proposed amendment is ridiculous and should not be
adopted. Simply put, it would be a gross waste of the valuable time of our
already over burdened inspectors, and a vulgar misuse of funds that should be
better used elsewhere.

Thank you,
George E. Powers Jr.
President, Backwoods Farm Inc.

RE: Minimum Age Requirements for the Transport of Animals

To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on Docket No. APHIS-2006-0024, a
proposed rule to amend the Animal Welfare Act regulations by:

(1)adding a minimum age requirement for the transport in commerce of all
covered species;
(2)amending the current regulations pertaining to the shipment of
underage animals to research facilities; and
(3)adding a new requirement when covered animals are shipped for the
purpose of receiving medical attention.

After a careful review of this proposal, which appeared in the May 9, 2008 edition
of the Federal Register (Volume 73, Number 91, pages 26344-26349), the National
Association for Biomedical Research (NABR) strongly urges the USDA to
withdraw this proposal. As currently written, this proposed rule does not provide a
basis for meaningful comment. We respectfully request the Agency develop a
more focused proposal that takes into account the biological requirements of the
species involved. We further request the Agency provide documentation on
existing failures in transportation of regulated species below eight weeks of age.
NABR and its members are willing to work with the Agency in gathering the
necessary information to develop such a proposal. The major concerns raised by
the language in the existing proposal are enumerated below.

Background
The Agency’s position is that its regulations governing the minimum age of
animals transported in commerce should be uniform. USDA regulations currently
contain minimum age requirements for dogs and cats transported in commerce,
and the Agency proposes to apply these same requirements to all covered
animals. In principle we agree all covered animals should be governed by species-
appropriate requirements.

We do not agree that particular requirements appropriate for dogs and cats will be
appropriate for all covered species. The biological requirements of the many
species covered by the Act vary. Therefore, it is not possible to promulgate a
uniform set of rules without imposing arbitrary requirements. Furthermore, we do
not believe the Agency has provided adequate justification, based on available
scientific data and husbandry practices, to impose the additional requirements
outlined in this proposed rule. Sixty percent of the covered species used in
research in 2006 were species that are routinely weaned and shipped prior to
eight weeks of age (guinea pigs, hamsters or rabbits). If one included other
frequently-used species such as gerbils, ferrets and pigs, this percentage would
be even greater. Furthermore, guinea pigs, hamsters, gerbils and rabbits used in
research are maintained and ordered based upon body weight and not by specific
age.

To adopt the same standards for the majority of animals used in research is not in
keeping with the long established and accepted practices of veterinary experts
who work in this field. Other federal agencies have recognized that regulations or
standards based on uniform age requirements are not always appropriate. For
example, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Guidelines for Conducting
Toxicity Studies (http://www.cfsan.fda.gov/~redbook/red-ivb1.html )
require, “Testing should be performed on young animals, with dosing beginning as
soon as possible after weaning and following an acclimation period of at least 5
days. Dosing of rodents should begin no later than 6 to 8 weeks of age. When
dogs are used, dosing should begin no later than 4 to 6 months of age.” We
believe that this language underscores the need for the regulations to be
consistent with the biologic differences in the covered species and serves to
support our belief that adopting a single age-based standard for all species is
scientifically inappropriate.

The proposed rule does not provide any background or an underlying rationale for
imposing uniform requirements while ignoring species-specific biological
requirements. Without knowing the Agency’s perceived basis for proposing these
new regulations, it is difficult to provide meaningful input. Have there been past
enforcement issues that have prompted this proposal? The Agency references
past enforcement issues but provides no details on what such issues entailed and
how they are relevant to this proposal. Is this proposed rule based on
acknowledged animal care principles documenting that transportation of more
than two hours is stressful to unweaned animals given that the nursing interval for
many species is much greater than every two hours? What is the source for the
animal care principles embodied in this proposed rule?

Based upon the information provided in this proposal, it would appear the Agency
is unaware how many animals of any species under eight weeks of age or
unweaned are currently shipped to research institutions, and thus has not
documented a need to increase the amount of paper work that is currently
required.

Transportation Plan (required for exception to new requirements)

Since all use of covered species in research, teaching or testing must be
described in a specific IACUC-approved research protocol, adding the proposed
language regarding a protocol to existing requirements is unnecessary. In
addition, it is unclear who would be responsible for the development of the
proposed transportation plan. In the current Standards the language pertaining to
Consignments to carriers and intermediate handlers, the responsibility for
developing the paper trail falls to the consignor. The transportation plan contained
in this proposal would appear to require the consignee to assume this
responsibility, yet they would not have specific transportation details which could
easily change if there was a delay in the approval process. If the responsibility for
the transportation plan falls to the commercial supplier, large commercial breeders
of commonly used small mammals, in our analysis, could each be responsible for
preparing and executing more than 5000 of these plans per year. The process of
review by the USDA at regional locations holds open the potential for delays in
approval because of the need to review information at the receiving institution or
disagreements regarding the appropriateness of arrangements, inconsistently
applied standards or institutional justification of need to use animals less than 8
weeks of age. It is also unclear as to why such a plan would require more than
the signature of the attending veterinarian, who is required by regulations to
oversee the adequacy of the veterinary care provided and other aspects of animal
care and use. It is also not clear what is meant by the receipt of “written approval”
before animals could be transported. Since the request can be made using either
e-mail or facsimile to avoid delay, it does not seem logical that an approval could
not be transmitted in the same manner. Even with all components of the
transportation plan in place, it still will not avoid delays, accidents, misrouting, or
other uncontrollable events which this proposal seeks to address. Given the
extremely low transportation failure rates for regulated and non-regulated species
commonly used in research cited in a recent National Academies of Science
report on transportation, it is unclear how the proposed transportation plan
process with its additional complexities and potential delays will improve the
process and safety for regulated research animals.

NABR believes there are many inconsistencies in this proposal. For example, the
proposal would require a transportation plan for animals under the age of eight
weeks that are shipped to a licensed veterinarian to receive medical care. Given
the basic premise of this proposal to help ensure humane treatment of these
animals, it is unclear as to why a plan would be required for animals shipped
outbound, but not for those that were being returned. If there is indeed a need for
such a plan, would not that need be doubled by round trip shipment?

Executive Order 12866 and Regulatory Flexibility Act
Since the majority of the covered species currently shipped to research facilities
have a biological weaning age of less than eight weeks of age, we have serious
reservations about the regulatory flexibility analysis that was conducted. The
proposed eight week minimum age for animals would have a major impact on the
providers of those species for research and would require a significant increase in
the administrative cost of obtaining those animals.

Benefits and Cost of the Rule
We find it puzzling how the Agency determined this proposed rule would reduce
the frequency of illness and death of young animals in transportation, given that
the agency does not currently know how many licensed animal dealers transport
underage and unweaned animals, much less how many animals are involved. In
fact, the benefit to dogs and cats has not been documented. How one would
calculate the benefits when the current costs are unknown is unclear.

In its analysis, the agency provided some examples of proposed increased costs.
One of those analyses involved guinea pigs that were found to sell for $30.00 and
cost $1.00 per day to feed (NOTE: These costs are not at all reflective of the
current average selling price or fully loaded maintenance costs which are
considerably greater than when the data quoted by the Agency was compiled).
According to the Guinea Pig Fact Sheet contained on the USDA’s Animal Welfare
Information Center (AWIC) website, the weaning age of a guinea pig is 14-21
days. While this weaning range has been quoted in a few publications, guinea
pigs are most commonly weaned by 5 to 14 days of age with no impact on their
welfare. Under the proposed new weaning age of eight weeks, the additional cost
of feeding a guinea pig would add from $35.00 to $42.00 (based on the agency’s
numbers) to the sale price of each animal. This would more than double the cost
of the animal, not to mention increasing the cost of shipping much larger animals.
Having consulted with experts providing purpose bred guinea pigs for biomedical
research we believe the figures used in the analysis do not accurately reflect the
real impact on animals used in research. Purpose bred guinea pigs are raised in
barrier facilities, which adds significantly to the daily cost of maintenance. In
addition, requiring that these animals be maintained by the breeder for an
additional 5-6 weeks would require a significant investment in additional equipment
and facilities. Shipping costs (transportation plus additional containers) would
double since the number of 8-week old animals that could be safely transported in
a container while conforming with existing transport guidelines would be half the
number of younger animals.

Assessment of Alternatives
Given the lack of justification for the proposed change in the current language and
given that the proposed language is inconsistent with the known biological needs
of the majority of the covered species used in research, we believe the first
alternative identified by the Agency (i.e. no change to the existing rule) is justified
at this time.

NABR appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed changes in the
current regulations pertaining to the minimum age requirements for transport of
animals covered under the Animal Welfare Act.

The National Association for Biomedical Research (NABR) is the only national,
nonprofit organization dedicated solely to advocating sound public policy that
recognizes the vital role of humane animal use in biomedical research, higher
education and product safety testing. NABR's membership is comprised of over
300 public and private universities, medical and veterinary schools, teaching
hospitals, voluntary health agencies, professional societies, pharmaceutical
companies and other animal research-related firms.

Respectfully,


Mary F. Hanley
Executive Vice President

Animal Welfare Act regulations (Docket # APHIS-2006-0024) by adding minimum
age requirements for the transport of animals in commerce. I support USDA’s
effort to protect young, unweaned animals in transport. However, I am writing to
urge USDA to create minimum age requirements that are specific and appropriate
for different species of animals.

is vague and not always the most appropriate factor in determining a young
animal’s suitability for transport. Many animals, often primates, rely on their
mothers even after there is no longer a nutritional reason to nurse. These animals,
though technically weaned, may still suffer from premature separation from their
mothers. Additionally, it is common practice for animals used for commercial
reasons to be prematurely and forcibly weaned from their mothers. While an
animal that has been forcibly weaned may meet the proposed transport
requirement, it may lead animals to be transported at younger ages than intended
by USDA. In order to provide protection for all covered species, USDA should
clarify the term unweaned and identify minimum age requirements for individual
species.

In addition, animals used in research deserve similar protection in transport as
other animals covered under the Animal Welfare Act. Research facilities should
not be given a blanket exemption.

Sincerely

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to OPPOSE the proposed rule, Docket No. APHIS-2006-0024, to
amend the Animal Welfare Act regulations by adding a minimum age requirement
for the transport of all covered species and changing current regulations related to
the shipment of underage animals to research facilities.

I strongly urge the USDA to withdraw this proposal because it fails to account for
the biological requirements of the species involved, provides no evidence of
significant existing problems in transportation of regulated species below eight
weeks of age, and includes no scientific rationale for the proposed rule changes.
The USDA’s stated position is that the regulations governing the minimum age of
animals transported in commerce should be uniform and exactly match those of
current USDA regulations regarding minimum age requirements for dogs and cats
transported in commerce. However, the proposed rule provides no underlying
scientific rationale for imposing uniform requirements that ignore species-specific
biological requirements. The biological requirements of the covered species vary
tremendously. Therefore, proposing an arbitrary, uniform set of requirements is
scientifically inappropriate and completely ignores the established and accepted
practices of veterinary experts.

Because the majority of the covered species currently shipped to research
facilities have a biological weaning age of less than eight weeks of age, the
proposed eight week minimum age for animals would have a major negative impact
on suppliers and on the investigators who use these species for important, often
federally-funded, scientific research without providing any measurable benefit with
regard to the safety and welfare of the animals. There is also a major concern that
the significant increase in paperwork and approvals required by the proposed rule
could actually harm animals by enhancing the risk of significant delays during
transportation.

Given the lack of justification for the proposed rule and its inconsistency with the
known biological requirements of most of the covered species used in research, I
believe that the best option at this time is no change to the existing rule.

Sincerely,

Louis A. Rosenthal, Ph.D.
University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health
Madison, WI

RE: Docket No. APHIS-2006-0024
Comments regarding the Minimum Age Requirements for the Transport of Animals

The Center for Great Apes respectfully submits the following comments on
APHIS’ proposed rule on the minimum age requirements for the transport of
animals.

General Comments

The Center for Great Apes was founded in 1993 as a non-profit organization for
the purpose of maintaining a permanent sanctuary for those orangutans and
chimpanzees that have been used in entertainment or kept as pets by private
owners. Currently, the Center houses 42 great apes…twenty-eight chimpanzees
and fourteen orangutans that range in age from 3 years to 50 years. The Center is
not open as a public attraction, does not receive any type of government funding,
and does not breed or sell infant great apes.

We are particularly concerned that the proposed eight-week minimum age for the
transportation of animals in commerce is inappropriate for non-human primates
and may expose them to both acute and chronic health and social risks.

The establishment of minimum age requirements for the transportation of APHIS-
regulated species must take into account the great range and diversity of
behavioral, health and social needs of species concerned. The eight-week
proposed rule presents several areas of urgent concern in regard to non-human
primates.

Short Term Health Risks

If the eight-week age requirement for taking puppies and kittens from their mothers
is based on their nursing period and weaning age, then non-human primates who
have much longer mother-infant dependency periods should be allowed the same
criteria for pulling infants from mothers. Chimpanzee and orangutan infants nurse
for four to six years on their mothers and stay with their mothers for eight or nine
years.

The “pulling” of infant non-human primates from their mothers results in a wide
variety of health risks as these primates are susceptible to most human diseases
including colds, flu, tuberculosis, and other zoonotic diseases. The longer an
infant primate stays with its mother and naturally nurses, the more opportunity the
infant has to build immunity against disease.

Behavioral Consequences

The early months and years that non-human primates spend with their mothers
and social group are critical to the foundation of social learning necessary for
appropriate development into adolescence and adulthood. When non-human
primates are “pulled” from their mothers at too early an age, they are exposed not
only to health risks but also to behavioral challenges that can last throughout their
lives.

Social species, such as non-human primates, require familial interactions in order
to develop social skills that will be used later in life. Early deprivation of same-
species interactions and appropriate role models often leads to social problems
such as aggression and stereotypic behavior in adulthood. We have seen many
great apes that were sold as weeks-old to months-old infants to private pet owners
and to trainers for the entertainment business. Once grown into adolescence and
adulthood, these chimpanzees and orangutans are usually out-placed to facilities
willing to take them.

Those who had the least time with their birth mothers often have the most
behavioral problems and social difficulties interacting with their own species.

Summary

For these reasons, the Center for Great Apes is concerned that the proposed
eight-week minimum age rule for commercial transport of animals can result in
injury, illness, behavioral abnormalities or even death for non-human primates.
Moreover, it is our opinion that great ape infants should not be pulled from their
birth mothers until they are weaned, or at age four or five years.

While the proposed rule change is intended to protect young animals in shipment,
it cannot do that without taking into account the differences in species. The
arbitrary nature of the blanket “eight-week” proposed rule for all species gives rise
to ethical problems that will be impossible to resolve.

Thank you for the opportunity to review and comment on this proposal.

Sincerely,

Patti Ragan
Director

age requirements for the transport of animals in commerce. It is my belief that it is
our responsibility to protect young, unweaned animals in transport.

I am writing to urge USDA to create minimum age requirements that are specific
and appropriate for different species of animals.

The requirement that animals be eight weeks of age and weaned prior to transport
is vague and not always the most appropriate factor in determining a young
animal’s suitability for transport. Many animals, often primates, rely on their
mothers even after there is no longer a nutritional reason to nurse. These animals,
though technically weaned, still suffer from the traumatic premature separation
from seeing their mothers murdered before their very eyes and then forced to leave
their dead bodies.

There are other animals used for commercial reasons to be prematurely and
forcibly weaned from their mothers. While an animal that has been forcibly
weaned may meet the proposed transport requirement, it may lead animals to be
transported at younger ages than intended by USDA. In order to provide protection
for all covered species USDA should clarify the term unweaned and identify
minimum age requirements for individual species.

In addition, animals used in research deserve similar protection in transport as
other animals covered under the Animal Welfare Act. Research facilities should
not be given a blanket exemption.

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing in support of the above referenced PROPOSED RULE (PR) to
amend the Animal Welfare Act regulations by adding minimum age
requirements for the transport in commerce of animals.

I am aware that the current regulations address age limits for dogs and cats,
but that no corresponding regulations exist for rodents not used for
research purposes including but not limited to, rats, mice, gerbils,
hamsters, degus, and chinchillas. They are animals too!

I agree and strongly support your proposal to amend the current
regulations to restrict the transport of all animals including
rodents not used for research purposes that are less than 8 weeks of
age, unless certain conditions have been met, as outlined in the PR.

Establishing federal minimum age requirements for the transport in
commerce of rodents not used for research purposes, and providing for
the transport of all animals that have not met the minimum age of 8
weeks of age, are necessary to help ensure the humane treatment of
these animals.

Thank you,

Becky Brill

Comments Regarding the USDA Proposal to Amend Animal Transport Regulations

To whom it may concern:

In reference to Docket No. APHIS-2006-0024, Minimum Age Requirements for the
Transport of Animals, I respectfully submit that the all inclusive scope of this
proposal gives no consideration to widely varying specie-specific physiological
development and maturity ages and their subsequent relationship to the animal's
suitability for shipment-the premise for the proposed change. This generic
approach regarding shipping age restriction is impractical. It is neither
scientifically-sound, nor is it applicable to long-standing objective husbandry and
animal care-taking experience.

At Marshall BioResources, there is nearly 70 years experience in multi-specie
animal production. I would like to specifically address why it is inappropriate to
generalize ferret and rabbit growth and development with all other species, both of
which Marshall BioResources has extensive experience in raising.

To establish my credentials for this comment, I am currently serving as Senior
Clinical Veterinarian for Marshall BioResources, with over 20 years of practice in
the field of research animal medicine.

Mammals, as a group, are very diverse. Some are predator species while others
are prey species. Some live in complex social groupings while other species live
solitary lives. Similarly, mammalian growth and development follows species-
specific timelines that vary considerably depending on the particular specie. In
general, the rate of growth and development is inversely related to size. In other
words, smaller animal species mature more quickly than those that are larger.
For instance, ferrets and miniature rabbit breeds wean at 5-6 weeks of age
reaching puberty at 4-5 months of age. Larger animals, such as dogs, wean at 6-
8 weeks of age and reach puberty by approximately 10 months of age.

I respectfully submit that the blanket inclusion of all mammals for a minimum age
requirement for transport is not reasonable. Indeed, the shipment failure rate for
young ferrets and dogs under 8 weeks of age from Marshall BioResources is
negligible, at a small fraction of 1%.

Exemptions would have to be applied for in order to transport animals for research
that are less than 8 weeks of age. However, ferrets, dogs and pigs, three animal
species with which Marshall BioResources has ample experience, are routinely
weaned by 6 weeks of age and already live independently from their mothers by
this age.

The all inclusive scope of this proposal is all the more disappointing as it is not a
good way to enforce good laboratory animal practice, with respect to shipping
animals for specific studies. Developing much needed research studies is very
important. Young animals are often required in toxicology studies to help with the
development of medications that are to be used in children, as well as in adults.
The time that it takes to apply for exemptions may lead to the inability to transport
animals to a research facility at the critical age at which they are needed for
study.

Additionally, there is no mention in the proposal of how animal shipments coming
into the United States will be handled. Will animals under 8 weeks of age be
allowed to be transported out of the country? There is potential for a dual
standard to be enforced which is unfair and unjust as well as inconsistent.

In conclusion, I reiterate that different mammalian species wean at various ages
and those that wean prior to 8 weeks of age are able to be safely transported
independent from their mother. To recommend a generic age for shipment of
research animals may very well delay important research and will not be a good
way to enforce good laboratory practice. Age-related transportation restrictions
should only be based upon a species specific, biologically relevant time frame.

The USDA does important work, ensuring the safety and comfort of our important
research animals. Of this, we in the research community are thankful. However,
it is important that biologically relevant data be used in determining the
appropriate age at which young animals can be shipped. A rigid time frame that
imposes irrelevant restrictions on shipment for many species may very well limit
important medical studies from being carried out.

Respectfully,

Felipe Berard

Doctor of Veterinary Medicine
Senior Clinical Veterinarian
Marshall BioResources

Regarding a new federal motor vehicle safety standard that requires all vehicles with a GVW of less than 10,000lbs to have electronic stability control, I do not believe this federal mandate is a good idea. This mandate is going to cost the consumer money and may cause as many accidents as it prevents. Electronic stability control ("ESC") systems are not free and often are a cost option on most makes and models today. If these systems were to be made standard, new car prices would increase across the board.

Additionally, the study on ESC was done under controlled test conditions. Regardless of how closely the tests were monitored or controlled, the fact will always remain that the roads today are NOT predictable and cannot easily be duplicated by a series of tests. ESC may add an element on safety under certain conditions but may also add many unpredictable and unusual characteristics to the vehicle.

I have driven vehicles with ESC. In fact, our family owns one. In our 2000 Mercedes ML320 SUV, the system works quite well. It keeps the behemoth under control and I have experienced no ailments with the system.

However, on other vehicles that may not have AWD or wide tires (255mm in this case), the system may cause pronounced and unexpected problems. In such an instance on OdyClub.com, a member in his 2006 Honda Odyssey was making a legal right turn on red during a rain shower. The road was slick and there were cars coming, so he hit the gas. However, ESC (called VSA by Honda "Vehicle Stability Assist") dialed back the throttle and did not allow the vehicle to accelerate. When the system finally returned full control to the driver, the vehicle shot forward while the wheels were still turned towards the right. As a result of this unintended acceleration, the vehicle almost hit several pedestrians on the curb.

In another case, I was driving a 2006 Honda Accord EX V6 6-speed. I had taken a turn a bit too fast. However, I knew that I was able to handle the situation because I drive a similar Accord. What I didn't expect was that VSA intruded (mine does not have VSA) and the steering bound up, the throttle was killed, and brakes were modulated. This caused the car to plow forward and I lost most control of the car. I stopped just short of hitting the curb.

In another instance, a member on DriveAccord.net had rented a Saturn L-series sedan with ESC. She was not familiar with ESC and had not expected the intrusion it caused when she tried to change lanes on a slick highway. The wheels slipped slightly on the lane divider dots, she corrected the steering slightly with no response, so she cranked the wheel hard. The car ended up flipping several times. In court, under oath, a technician determined that it was the stability control that caused her to flip.

In my opinion, most types of stability controls are still too crude and take away too much control from the driver. It does not help in spirited driving (by adding the surprise intrusions of brakes, sudden on/off throttle, etc) and it cannot overcome the laws of physics - meaning it will not be able to help when a serious emegency arises. IF this becomes law, it should be mandated that the end user (the buyer of the car) has the option to turn the stability control completely off at his or her discretion.

Thank you for your consideration,
Benjamin Cheah

COSVAM COMMENT RE:

{Docket No. NHTSA-2006-25324, Notice 1] - Automobili Lamborghini SpA; Bugatti Automobiles S. A. S. and Bugatti Engineering GmbH; Group Lotus Plc; Morgan Motor Company Limited; Maserati REceipt of |Applications for a Temporary Exemption From Advance Air Bag Rrequirements of FMVSS No. 208

The Coalition of Small Volume Auto Manufacturers, Inc. (COSVAM) represents the interests of small volume auto manufacturers (SVMs) in the US market. In the mid-1990s, the SVM industry was threatened with extinction due to the intensity of the cascade of federal legislation. After COSVAM was formed and a period of intensive negotiation with NHTSA and EPA, the situation altered drastically. Today, the SVM industry is now much healthier in the US market and new flexibilities have permitted endangered companies to apply for exemptions.

Accordingly, the standards set for the determination of eligibility for SVM status are definitive. Only those SVMs who do, in fact, qualify as small companies placed under severe financial hardship by the onset of new regulations for technological innovations should be eligible for exemptions, temporary or permanent.

The docket indicated above includes applications for five companies who manufacture four well known and highly distinguished brands: Bugatti, Lamborghini, Lotus and Morgan.

The applications contain a good deal of meritorious information even though the financial aspects of the individual manufacturers remain somewhat obscure.

The purpose of this comment is to call attention to the question of eligibility which the agency has correctly chosen to depict in the "tentative" terms of the filing for three manufacturers: Bugatti, Lamborghini and Maserati.

Two of the brands, Bugatti and Lamborghini, are owned by major motor manufacturers with sales in the US market exceeding the upper limits allowable for SVM classification. The Volkswagen and Audi corporations share technology, collaborate on the engineering of powertrains, electronics, chassises and vehicle engineering on many levels. The two companies also share technology with the Porsche Group. These corporate policies are matters of the public record.

For these reasons, the rationale for the petitions from Bugatti and Lamborghini remains obscure. Over and apart from this obscurantism is the question of why either of these distinguished companies would wish to project their acclaimed products as spearheading the vanguard of automotive engineering, design and performance, but be unable to comply with FMVSS 208 - a regulation with which other automotive products from their corporate family are (or will be) in compliance.

The relevant facts concerning the corporate ownership of Bugatti and Lamborghini are well known and have been a part of the public record for a number of years. Unless significant new information is made a part of the public record or contained in unpublished portions of the application process, the two should be seen as brands manufactured by major motor manufacturers - Volkswagen (Bugatti) or Audi (Lamborghini).

The case of Maserati is equally problematical - for according to a plethora of public reports this highly illustrious brand has been engineered by Ferrara SpA, and the technology available for compliance with FMVSS 208 should be readily available to them.

At one stage, Ferrari and Maserati certification (homologation) fell upon the same corporate staff occupying the same corporate office within the Ferrari complex at Maranello which is situated in close proximity to Maserati in Modena. The culture of technology-sharing between the two firms has been publicized for years, and their recent corporate separation was defined in the public record as administrative rather than technological. Maserati still uses powertrains and other engineering originally developed by and for Ferrari. Therefore, the reason why they are not able to comply with FMVSS 208 remains obscure as of this writing.

The Morgan Motor Company Limited is an independent firm - and there is no question of its status as an SVM. Morgan is an archetypal SVM. The fact of Morgans presence in one docket of applications for temporary exemptions from federal safety standards may have clouded the issue of eligibility for those individuals not intimately familiar with the SVM industry - especially the European brands and corporate relationships.

For the reasons cited above, it would be greatly appreciated if these facts be taken into consideration by the Administrator and their Chief Counsel before, during and after the consideration of these petitions.

Yours respectfully,

It is our opinion that permitting pilots to log SIC time in aircraft types for which an
SIC is not required, provided that certain circumstances exist and certain
requirements are met, would result in a huge boost in safety and significant
improvements in the training of low time pilots. Many aircraft originally designed to
be operated by two pilots are now in freight service and flown by a single pilot. The
EMB-110, BE-99, BE-1900, DHC-6, SA226 and the SA227 come to mind. In most
cases the autopilots have been removed for reasons of economy and the cockpit
layouts leave much to be desired in single pilot operations. These aircraft are
frequently flown by relatively low time pilots in the early stages of their professional
careers. If the right seat in these aircraft is occupied by a pilot properly trained in
two-pilot operations, safety is bound to be enhanced. If logging time as SIC is
permitted, many of these seats will be filled.

In addition to immediately providing a higher level of safety, a rule change here will
provide present single pilot operators with a better career path to the left seat in
their airplanes. A longer term benefit for the industry will be the increased level of
real world experience pilots will have gained prior to their progression to corporate,
fractional and airline operations. Finally, it appears that we are facing a prolonged
pilot shortage across the industry. Any bona fide means by which we can
accelerate the flow of properly trained, experienced pilots to positions of aircraft
command will be worth the effort.

An operator wishing to obtain approval for what is proposed here would need an
approved training and checking program for two-pilot operations with the
appropriate CRM emphases. Such a program would logically delineate specific
rules for crew pairing as well as approach limitations for lower time pilots.

We support rapid approval of the proposed exemption.

Stephen Mcclure
Director of Operations, AirNow

I strongly support the subject document. The time that a pilot is in the SIC position and is performing duties duly stated as such, notwithstanding the basis of aircraft certification, should be authorized to log such time in total. It is given that an extra pilot can be a significant enhancement to safety if such duties are explicitly defined for the applicable aircraft and for the entire duration of the operation (including preflight), and the pilot is trained and certified accordingly. It is important that his/her accredited time be not fractionalized for the flight since that would be set up a pilot's mindset that his/her duties would also be fractionalized. Hence, the assigned SIC would not be dedicated to performing 100% of his or her time. The consequence would be a degradation of the safety enhancement or even a possible safety in hindrance since such a mindset would surely lead to cockpit crew management issues.
I have flown the Fairchild Metro, BE-99 and DHC-6 aircraft under many single and dual pilot scheduled and unscheduled activities, and done so successfully. However, there were also circumstances such that superstition and luck beyond my skills seemed to carry me through. As pilots we all know that predictable operations are easy to plan and relatively easy to conduct. But we're also aware that the unpredictable and the emergencies are the real killers. And as such, we should never be averse to getting all the help we can, particularly one close at hand - in the right seat. Allowing this exemption is a step in that direction.

Alpine Aviation, Inc. supports the petition as submitted by Ameriflight, Inc. The
first officer assists with workloads during high demand phases of operation and the
position gives pilots seeking more experience the incentive to serve in this
capacity. Loggable time is very important to pilots early on in their career.

Programs that provide qualified pilots the opportunity to log flight time when assigned as SIC in aircraft types that may be operated single pilot benefit the entire aviation community. The FAA has endorsed this approach through 14 CFR §135.101, which requires an SIC for all aircraft when carrying passengers in IFR under Part 135. Consequently, a certificate holder must assign an SIC when conducting such operations if one of the following holds true: (1) the Certificate Holder has not been issued Operations Specification A015; (2) The aircraft is not equipped with a functioning autopilot; and/or (3) the PIC has not been checked IAW 14 CFR §135.297 (g). A pilot assigned as SIC for one of these reasons may log the flight time under 14 CFR §61.55. Under this regulatory construct, an SIC is required if the flight is done in a Beechcraft Baron 58 by an operator that has not been issued A015. The SIC must be properly qualified under the operator’s FAA approved training program and can log the flight time. Yet, if the same aircraft and crew offload the passengers and continue the Part 135 operation with only freight on board, under the same IFR conditions, the pilot serving as SIC may no longer log the flight time. This holds even though the pilot continues performing to the same standards and gains equivalent experience. Moreover, the experience gained during both segments likely surpasses the quality of the experience gained from other less structured, yet time honored methods such as banner towing, or aerial survey.
In addition to the enhancement to direct operational safety provided, allowing pilots to build quality flight time in this manner streamlines career advancement by building flight time faster. Furthermore, it provides exposure to a professional structure and discipline earlier, which enhances overall operational safety.
Providing more expedient means for developing pilots is essential to the health of our Nation’s aviation infrastructure.

Ameriflight's request should be granted. Their statements concerning increasing safety during Single Pilot operations are accurate. The additional crewmember, by their simple presence, will influence the PIC to adhere to SOPs, and the additional crewmember adds greatly to CRM. The additional flight crewmembers gain valuable flight crew experience in real-world operations that will contribute vastly more to their ability to operate in complex environments than towing banners or providing primary instruction in single-engine piston aircraft. Time spent in the right seat of any commercial operation, whether requiring an SIC or not, provides invaluable flight management experience. This is also a way to counter the egregious 1500 hour requirement that was mandated by lawmakers who refused to listen to either the FAA or industry experts who pointed out that logged hours alone mean very little. It is crew operational experience in commercial operations that produces safe pilots, not simple logged hours .

Without such a provision in the regulations that allows a properly trained and checked SIC can log time in a Beech 99, Fairchild Metro, or other similar airplane approved for single-pilot Part 135 cargo operation, the pool of qualified pilots to occupy such PIC positions as are available in the industry will continue to shrink.

The only occupants of that pool would be those who have run up sufficient hours thru typical single-engine operations as flight instructing and other activities in far less-complex aircraft types than Cessna 208s, Beech 99s or Fairchild Metros. So who's the "safer" upgrade to PIC in such a situation - the pilot who's sat right seat for a year or two in that airplane make, model and type or someone moving into the seat either from flying single pilot ops in less complex and certainly different airplane makes, models and types OR from giving thousands of hours of flight instruction in far less complex airplanes?

Additionally, pilots qualified to be PICs are not filling the pipeline from our very-downsized military these days either. Speaking of the military, how is it that the USAF or USN will consider a pilot qualified to be an all-weather fighter/tanker/transport pilot with only 300 hours flight training time and yet the FAA won't consider a pilot with that same # of hours qualified to fly a Caravan or Beech 99?

It is for these reasons that I respectfully request that the FAA/DOT grant this petition and allow properly trained and checked SICs to log time and count SIC flight time in aircraft like Beech 99s, Fairchild Metros, or other similar airplane approved for single-pilot Part 135 cargo operation.

Setting aside the direct safety and public interest advantages of granting this petition, it should be noted that there is currently considerable controversy in U.S. aviation, including among FAA personnel, as to whether logging such SIC flight time is already “legal.”

Many pilots currently log such flight time, and many employers recognize its value and use it as a factor in selection of flight crew candidates.

A grant of this petition will not only unify the FAA’s position on the issue, but also set the stage for other operators to petition for similar exemptions so their properly trained and checked first officers are clearly logging “legal” flight time – and possibly, eventually precipitate minor changes in current rules to eliminate the need for exemptions on this issue.

Comments from FedEx Express:

1. The substantiation presented in the NPRM does not seem to justify the
urgency of an AD, especially with regards to the full impact it will have on all of the
A300-600, A310, A330, B747, B767 and MD-11 fleet operators. The FAA NPRM
only identified a single event within the worldwide fleets of mixed airframe types
that have, in turn, been in operation for a good number of years. In the NPRM
discussion, more than one failure point was implied, of which the unapproved
clevis pin was one contributing factor. If transcowls becoming hazardous debris
on runways is the driving concern, then why were other failure issues not
addressed? Also, the NPRM discussion did not identify any subsequent events in
which [1] any similar unapproved parts have been found in use, [2] have caused
similar unsafe conditions, or [3] have otherwise even been reported since the
original event occurred. FedEx respectfully suggests further investigation would
be prudent before any AD is issued involving the actions prescribed in this NPRM.

2. FedEx concurs with other submitted comments regarding the limited
usefulness of conducting a "rebound hardness test" in an effort to root out, and
eliminate the future installation of, suspect or unapproved parts. What is really
needed is a means to easily and quickly identify unapproved low-strength carbon
steel clevis pins versus approved clevis pins which should otherwise be
manufactured from a stainless steel alloy (ref: GE/MRAS comments). The
rebound hardness test alone cannot do this.

3. The present clevis pin design does not have any part identification information
marked anywhere on it. FedEx would like to see some type of standardized
marking (part no. and some form of post inspection mark) be incorporated on the
clevis pins. Presently, an uninspected pin could still be inadvertently installed
onto a previously inspected reverser. Any person handed an unbagged/untagged
clevis pin might not be able to tell the difference today.

4. If all the rebound hardness testing requirements are retained as written in the
NPRM, some operators will incur an additional burden if they don’t presently
possess rebound hardness test equipment (scleroscope test equipment is not a
typical maintenance tool and is not identified in aircraft/engine/fan reverser
maintenance manuals as a special tool). Such operators will have to implement a
means to test all pins now installed in reversers and in stock as spares, as well
as test all future pin procurements if no terminating actions are defined. This will
likely mean either contracting outside testing services or procuring & integrating
new test equipment into their aircraft maintenance programs. The latter option will
also affect the provisioning, training, and certified calibration programs of the
operator and this then becomes an additional burden that is not included in the
NPRM Cost of Compliance estimate.

5. NPRM/AD paragraph 2.(g)(4) will need to be revised. The GE CF6-80C2
engine maintenance manual (ref: GE pub. no. GEK108746-20 or -30) does not
contain any continued service instructions relative to any CF6-80C2 fan reverser
hardware and, in particular, pertaining to the fan reverser clevis pin. Some
serviceable/repairable limitations, however, can be found in the MRAS CF6-80C2
Fan Reverser CMM (ref: MRAS pub. no. MR92466) or pertinent aircraft
maintenance manuals.

6. If the FAA does issue an AD, FedEx Express requests the FAA not issue a
single compliance period requirement (i.e., 18 months/4,500 FH’s) to be
applicable to all GE CF6-80C2 and CF6-80E1 series engines installed on six
different aircraft types, within which the FAA has listed sixteen model variations.
Instead, it would be more prudent to prescribe (and easier for operators to
implement ) multiple compliance period requirements that are, at a minimum,
differentiated and more applicable to the six aircraft types identified – A300-600,
A310, A330, B747, B767 and MD-11.

In consideration, the six aircraft types identified in the NPRM are neither identical
nor are they all operated in the same manner. They likely have different FAA-
approved maintenance programs relative to capabilities and operator utilization.
Forcing a single-value-fits-all approach will cause aircraft to be removed from
service prematurely on an off-schedule, special visit basis. With multiple
compliance period values assigned, hardware inspections and/or replacements
could be better scheduled to fit into regularly schedule maintenance visits such as
aircraft C-checks, and reduce disruptions to regular service and schedule
maintenance operations.

FedEx Express operates a mixed fleet of 80-90 MD-11, A300-600 and A310-300
series aircraft powered with CF6-80C2 engines. The maintenance programs and
associated scheduling for these type aircraft differ significantly. For one aircraft
fleet type, the C-check schedule is 18 months/6,000 FH’s while it is 30 months/-
3,500 FH’s for another. Applying the proposed 18 months/4,500 FH’s mandate
equally to these fleets will prematurely force many aircraft out of service in order
to comply with the AD mandated maintenance actions under such
scheduling. Whereas, implementing multiple compliance periods will more
effectively permit these aircraft to be worked within already established scheduled
maintenance cycles and still maintain safe aircraft operations overall.

HEALTH HAZARD INFORMATION
Health Effects:
Acute
Swallowed: Moderately toxic. May cause moderate to marked irritation and
possibly
chemical burns of the mouth, throat, oesophagus and stomach. There will be
discomfort or pain in the chest and abdomen, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea,
dizziness, faintness, drowsiness, weakness, circulatory collapse and coma.
Aspiration into the lungs may occur during ingestion or vomiting, resulting in
lung injury.
Eye: Liquid will cause severe and persistent conjunctivitis, seen as excessive
redness
and marked swelling of the conjunctiva with profuse discharge. Severe corneal
injury may develop, which could permanently impair vision if prompt first aid
and medical treatment are not obtained. Vapour will cause stinging sensations
in the eye with excess tear production, blinking and slight excess redness of
conjunctiva.
Skin: Brief contact will cause itching with mild to moderate local redness and
possibly swelling. Prolonged contact may result in pain, severe redness and
swelling, with ulceration, tissue destruction, and possibly bleeding onto the
inflamed area. Contact with solutions of glutaraldehyde may cause harmless
yellow or brownish coloration of the skin.
Inhaled: Vapour is irritating to the respiratory tract, causing stinging sensations in
the
nose and throat, discharge from the nose, possibly bleeding from the nose,
coughing, chest discomfort and tightness, difficulty with breathing and
headache. Heating the solution may result in more severe irritant effects.
Chronic: Repeated skin contact may result in the absorption of potentially harmful
amounts of material. Also may cause cumulative dermatitis. Overexposure to
the vapor of the material will cause signs and symptoms of an asthmatic attack
in hyper-reactive individuals.
First Aid:
Swallowed: DO NOT INDUCE VOMITING. Do not give anything to drink. Obtain
medical advice without delay
Eye: Immediately flush with water and continue washing for at least 15 minutes.
DO
NOT remove contact lenses, if worn. Obtain medical attention without delay,
preferably from an ophthalmologist.
Skin: Immediately remove contaminated clothing and shoes. Wash contaminated
skin
with soap and water. Wash clothing before reuse. Discard contaminated leather
articles such as shoes and belt.
Inhaled: Remove to fresh air. Give artificial respiration if not breathing. If breathing
is
difficult, oxygen may be given by qualified personnel. Obtain medical
attention.
First Aid Facilities: Eye bath, safety shower
Advice to Doctor The hazards of this material are due mainly to its severely irritant
properties on
skin and mucosal surfaces. Moderately toxic by swallowing. Moderately toxic
by absorption across the skin. Due to the severely irritating or corrosive nature
of the material, swallowing may lead to ulceration and inflammation of the
upper alimentary tract with haemorrhage and fluid loss. Also, perforation of the
esophagus or stomach may occur, leading to mediastinitis or peritonitis and the
resultant complications. The stomach should be evacuated carefully in case of
ingestion. Any material aspirated during vomiting may cause lung injury.
Therefore, emesis should not be induced mechanically or pharmacologically. If
it is considered necessary to evacuate the stomach contents, this should be done
by means least likely to cause aspiration (e.g. gastric lavage after endotracheal).

Personal Protection: Use self contained breathing apparatus in high
concentrations. If self-contained
breathing apparatus is not available, a MSHA/NIOSH approved air purifying
respirator equipped with an organic vapour cartridge should be used. Wear
splash proof monogoggles, in conjuction with a face mask, protective clothing
(including a chemical apron, rubber boots) and nitrile gloves. Wash thoroughly
after handling.
Flammability: Not flammable under conditions of use

and evaporation of

Spills and Disposal: Very low concentrations (5ppm or less of glutaraldehyde) can
be degraded in a
biological waste water treatment system. Thus, small spills can be flushed with
large quantities of water. Large quantities or 'slugs' can be harmful to the
treatment system. Thus, large spills should be collected for disposal. It may
also be possible to decontaminate spilled material by careful application of

asphyxiant. Special fire fighting procedures: Use self-contained breathing

I am writing regarding EPA Docket numbers EPA-HQ-OPP-2010-0752 and EPA-HQ-OPP-2010-0753 in support of prohibiting use of sodium monofluoroacetate (Compound 1080) and sodium cyanide.
Compound 1080 and sodium cyanide are extremely dangerous and inhumane.
Death by Compound 1080 is agonizing, excruciating, and slow (it usually takes between 3 and 15 hours). Exposure can result in cardiac failure, progressive failure of the central nervous system, or respiratory arrest following severe prolonged convulsions.
Compound 1080 is one of the deadliest poisons on earth and has no antidote.
The EPA classifies Compound 1080 as an “extremely hazardous” toxin that poses a significant hazard to human health and safety and to non-target wildlife. For these reasons the EPA banned Compound 1080 throughout the U.S. in 1972.
Compound 1080 is a potential terrorist threat to water and food supplies; according to its own records, Wildlife Services cannot account for all the Compound 1080 it has and uses.
In addition to these poisons’ toll on wildlife, they put public safety at risk; hundreds of pet dogs are harmed or killed by sodium cyanide each year, and humans have also been severely injured by accidentally triggering M-44 sodium cyanide ejector devices or handling poisoned pets.
Paradoxically, killing coyotes can increase their numbers by triggering breeding and larger litters.
Rather than killing predators, ranchers should make better use of good husbandry practices such livestock guard animals, electronic sound and light devices, penning animals as night, lambing in structures, promptly removing any carcasses and fencing appropriately.
Scientific research shows that it makes more economic sense to implement long-term predator deterrents than to kill coyotes and other predators.
Thank you for helping to end senseless poisoning of coyotes and other wildlife by Compound 1080 and sodium cyanide!

I wholly support the re-registration of the pesticide Acrolein, as a farmer using
water provided by the East Columbia Basin Irrigation District (ECBID). The water

RE:Reregistration Eligibility Decision for Acrolein

To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the EPA Reregistration
Eligibility Decision document.

In reviewing Section IV, Risk Management and Reregistration Decision, the
District has the following comments in regards to how EPA addressed new
requirements of Acrolein applications:

Occupational handlers/workers:

1.Proposed - Instead of requiring the registrant-provided applicator
training a minimum of every three years, the training requirement will be annual.

Response – This is already being done by Baker Petrolite at our Pesticide
License Recertification classes every year. Baker has been very proactive in
ensuring that all applicators are trained every year. However, changing the
training requirement to a yearly requirement would hamper the District’s ability to
treat with Acrolein, if one of our applicators was sick or unable to attend the once
a year recertification class, basically that applicator would not be able to apply
Acrolein the next year or until Baker was able to provide the training again.
Biannual training would be better fit for the District and would ensure training is
current and up to date.

2.Proposed - During application, two trained applicators must be on site
at all times.
Response - The Quincy-Columbia Basin Irrigation District has always had two
trained applicators on site during the set up and take down of all Acrolein
treatments. This is required because during the set up and the take down, there
is the most potential for exposure to Acrolein. After the set up process is
complete and the treatment is proceeding safely, the second applicator does not
stay within visual distance of the applicator that remains at the application site. If
the applicator at the site needs assistance, she/he has access to a District radio
and many also carry a cell phone with them. They have communication access
to both personnel and their supervisors if help is needed. It is not productive or
economically responsible to have two persons sit and watch a hose and dials for
hours on end. The applicator that stays on site with the treatment has the
responsibility to check pressures and visually inspect the hoses and equipment
while the treatment is in process. If the applicator must make changes or
adjustments during the treatment, she/he must call for assistance before
proceeding. In 2008 the Quincy District had 279 hours recorded for the applicator
(s) that were required to stay on site. The doubling up on applicators would have
both a productivity and economic impact on the District.
With all the safety precautions and practices already in place, both through the
Baker Petrolite Application and Safety manual and/or additional requirements by
the District, there appears to be no need to have two applicators on site during
applications.
3.Proposed - All applications must be made during day light hours.

Response - The District has applied Acrolein for many years. During those years,
the District has reviewed, evaluated and looked at ways to reduce exposure, risk
and to be good stewards of our resource and deliver uninterrupted water service for
our water users During this process we have modified how treatments are made,
when they are made, what rates to apply aquatic chemicals at and where to treat
with aquatic chemicals to get the best results with the least amount of
chemicals. The District has modified treatments and used new approaches that
are found to be more effective while using the least amount of chemical possible
and still achieving an effective treatment.

In order to use Acrolein in the most effective, least obtrusive way, and stay in
compliance with our NPDES permit, the District has implemented a plan for
treating our Canal which does involve some night time applications. The District’s
canal is eighty eight miles (88) and it takes from two to four days (depending on
flow) for water to travel from the beginning of the canal to the end. When the
District is treating the canal we apply Acrolein at the correct strength for the weed
conditions for that section of the canal. District personnel monitor and follow the
Acrolein downstream, tracking the parts per million (PPM) and how far the
chemical travels. District personnel monitor the leading edge of the chemical
during the entire distance of the canal. When the Acrolein PPM drops below the
desired control level to control the weed conditions in that area of the canal, the
District does a boost treatment. These boost treatments are miles downstream
from the original treatment and are limited to boosting the chemical back up to the
desired PPM. They occur hours later and while they are started during the day,
the boost treatment will end after dark, therefore requiring a night treatment.

Our night time treatments are only during the summer months when it does not
get dark until late in the evening. Our treatments usually start around 6 PM and
end about an hour after dark. Our trucks are outfitted with portable lights for our
applicators to give adequate lighting for checking the valves and hoses and to light
up the area. The District also has radio communication for applicators and
personnel monitoring the treatment are close by. Supervisors are checking on
personnel throughout the evening also. The District does whatever is necessary
to ensure the safety of our personnel during both daylight and evening hours.

Exposure to bystanders:

1.Proposed - Certified applicators may only apply at sites where they
have “No Swimming” signs posted.
Response - The District has signs posted on Irrigation right of ways that say, “No
Trespassing”, which suffice to notify people that the area is off limits. The District
also posts signs at the entrance to the treatment site during treatments, to notify
the public of a treatment. These signs are in both Spanish and English.

Ecological Risk Management

1.Proposed – Maximum of eight (8) applications – annually
Response – This needs to be clarified, eight treatments total per canal or section
of canal?

2.Proposed – Minimum two (2) week re-treatment interval per application.
Response – If EPA is intending to limit the treatments to daylight hours and the
Districts needs to do additional treatments on the same canal in order to get an
effective weed control downstream from the original treatment, this would limit the
District’s ability to control aquatic weeds in the remaining portions of the same
canal we treated the day before. The proposed requirements for 2 week re-
treatment intervals needs to be clarified and EPA needs to address the good
stewardship the Districts have already in place before creating requirements that
restrict good use practices

If, as applicators, the District is limited to the eight applications and the two week
intervals, it will force the District to again modify our applications, with the
probability of increased application rates to achieve adequate weed control for
longer distances, therefore raising the amount of chemical needed for each
treatment and the increase in the amount of time needed to treat in order to
achieve the same result.

The Quincy-Columbia Basin Irrigation District has an Aquatic Treatment program
in place which combines all of the requirements of the law including the NPDES

This letter is in response to the Environmental Protection Agency?s request for
comments regarding the Human Health Risk Assessment of Acrolein, docket
number EPA-HQ-OPP-2007-0588. The Washington State Potato Commission
wishes to express its support for the re-registration of the aquatic herbicide,
Acrolein.

The Washington State Potato Commission represents over 300 potato growers in
the State. There were 165,000 acres of potatoes planted in Washington State in
2007. Approximately 87% of the potatoes grown in Washington are processed
into frozen, dehydrated, and refrigerated, value added products. Washington State
is the second largest producer of potatoes behind the state of Idaho. The farm
gate value of the potato crop was $562 million in 2006. Washington State has the
highest average yields in the US. In 2007, the average yield in Washington was
620 cwt. /acre. The US average yield was 390 cwt. /acre.

According to a study by Dr. David Holland of Washington State University, (The
Economic Impact of Potatoes in Washington State, 2006) the value of the potato
industry to the economy of Washington State is over $4.7 billion. Most of this
economic activity is located in the Columbia Basin. The economy of Central
Washington relies heavily on the production and processing of potatoes. Many of
these rural communities would suffer extreme hardship if restrictions prevented the
current level of potato production and processing.

The Federal Reclamation Columbia Basin Project delivers water to nearly 1600
square miles of farm lands. Approximately 60% of all potato production in
Washington State occurs within the Columbia Basin Project. The Columbia Basin
Project has several thousands of miles of canals, laterals, and ditches that
transport water to agricultural lands. The use of Acrolein insures that those
canals, laterals, and ditches are clear of vegetative grown which would prevent the
delivery of water is left unchecked.

There are no effective alternatives to the use of Acrolein in the Columbia Basin
Project. If this product was not available for use in Central Washington State, the
landscape of our environment and economies would be greatly impacted. Our
rural economy would be shattered.

best stewards of Acrolein use in the country. Each treatment site is posted and

personnel provide annual safety training and each application is carefully
monitored, sampled, and reported to the Department of Ecology.

the effective and safe use of Acrolein. They have a long history of safe and
successful use of Acrolein. Their current programs should be implemented across
the country to protect against human and environmental exposure.

The loss of access to this product would be devastating to our potato industry.
Irrigation water would be greatly restricted if Acrolein was not available for use in
Washington State. Thank you for this opportunity to comment on the value of this
product to our industry and reducing human health risk.

Chris Voigt
Executive Director

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY

[EPA-HQ-OPP-2007-0588; FRL-8357-9]


Acrolein Revised Risk Assessments; Notice of Availability and
Solicitation of Risk Reduction Options

AGENCY: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

ACTION: Notice.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: This notice announces the availability of EPA's revised risk
assessments for the pesticide acrolein. In addition, this notice
solicits public comment on risk reduction and alternative options for
acrolein (Phase 5 of 6-Phase Process). The public is encouraged to
suggest risk management ideas or proposals to address the risks
identified. EPA is developing a Reregistration Eligibility Decision
(RED) for acrolein through the full, 6-Phase public participation
process that the Agency uses to involve the public in developing
pesticide reregistration and tolerance reassessment decisions. Through
these programs, EPA is ensuring that all pesticides meet current health
and safety standards.

DATES: Comments must be received on or before June 2, 2008.

ADDRESSES: Submit your comments, identified by docket identification
(ID) number EPA-HQ-OPP-2007-0588, by one of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal: http://www.regulations.gov.

Ave., NW., Washington, DC 20460-0001.
