Re: Docket No. EOUST 101

Dear Sir or Madam:

This is in response to the proposed new final report, final account, and no-asset
report forms. I am a Chapter 7 trustee on Middle District of Pennsylvania panel
and have served in that capacity since the early 1990's. I am particularly
concerned with the no-asset report forms.

The new no-asset report form eliminates the current practice of filing such forms
on-line and in batches. Today, this would mean that Trustees would have to hand-
input the information, at an annual cost estimated by the EOUST of $2100 per
trustee. I believe, however, the actual cost would be higher. Assuming 15 minutes
of staff time are needed to input the information, during an average year I would
see an additional $3,750 in expenses with no increase of revenue to offset it. Add
to that the mechanics of preparing a pdf for each case and ecf filing that takes
only five minutes, and you will add another $1,000 to the Trustee’s overhead.
While I understand the EOUST states that it is “currently exploring alternatives
with the Administrative Office of the United States Courts to enhance the
transmission of electronic data collected by the courts to EOUST” in order
to “reduce or eliminate the need for trustees to manually enter the information.”
Technologically we are not there yet and therefore, the new no-asset report
presents two practical problems for trustees. It also gives no guidance to the
Trustee concerning whether he may rely solely on the debtor’s schedules in
arriving at the figures to be inputted. Frequently they are simply wrong.

The statute on which the proposed new form is based requires the Attorney
General to issues rules “within a reasonable time after the effective date of this
section” and to weigh the “economy, simplicity, and lack of undue burden on
persons with a duty to file reports.” 28 U.S.C. § 589b(c)(2). Until alternatives with
the Administrative Office are worked out that would reduce or eliminate the need
for Trustees to manually enter the information, it would be both reasonable and
appropriate for the EOUST to conclude that the new no-asset report form is too
uneconomical, too complicated, and too burdensome on Trustee to be
implemented under the current state of technical capabilities.

The new final report form also requires a certification that “[a]ll required tax returns
of the bankruptcy estate have been filed.” To establish a tax return filing
requirement governed by EOUST policy, as opposed to IRS policy, would remove
any element of trustee discretion and add to the expense and length of case
administration in many cases. Many of us are not tax experts and if a filing is
required in every case that means hiring another professional and his fees. There
are many situations where it is apparent to the trustee, and would probably not
be
disputed by the tax authorities, that the bankruptcy estate will have no income tax
liability, despite a technical tax return filing requirement. Accountants frequently
screen cases in this position for me at no cost and advise me accordingly. You
are taking away this discretion at the expense of the unsecured creditor’s dividend.

The new final report, final account, and no-asset report forms all contain “penalty
of
perjury” certifications that effectively transform them into affidavits. They reference
Federal Rule of Bankruptcy 5009 as the apparent basis for this language.
However, Rule 5009 merely establishes a presumption that a case has been fully
administered if a trustee files a final report and final account and there is no
objection within 30 days. It does not require or suggest that the Trustee make
any
statement under penalty of perjury. As with EOUST-imposed tax return
requirements, I suggest that such statements be eliminated from the forms.

Thanks for your consideration.

Sincerely,

William G. Schwab

UST. The UST should have the resources to pull this same information from the

My staff needs confirmation from the EOUST that provides a definition of what
each of the new fields mean. For example:

A. Date Last Tax Return Filed – is this the date the return was signed, how do we
know when it was actually filed? Is this the date of the last return filed prior to the
filing of the bankruptcy case or is this to be updated through the closing of the
case to be the date of the last return filed just prior to completion?

B. Total Assets Exempted – is this taken from Schedule C? Is it the net equity of
the exemption claimed or the gross amount claimed? And what if Schedule C is
amended?

C. Assets abandoned pursuant to 11 USC Sec 554 – This is a Chapter 7 concept
where trustees abandon assets. Clarify how this is applicable in Chapter 13. For
instance, occasionally, we get orders that call for the trustee to abandon the
property. Do we update this field? With what amount? Amount of the claim? But
what if there is no claim? Scheduled amount? But what if creditor wasn’t
scheduled because the property was abandoned and foreclosed on just prior to
the bankruptcy filing?

D. Claim Asserted – Our standard procedure is that we put the creditor’s claim
amount as reflected on their proof of claim in this field. However, if we get an order
calling for a different amount does that trigger the need to change the Claim
Asserted field or should the Claim Asserted field remain the amount of the original
claim. What about amended claims? What about split claims? What about
mortgage claims where the claim amount “includes” the arrearages? Do we break
this up and subtract the arrearage amount from the claim amount to determine the
Claim Asserted for each record? And what about tax claims that have a secured,
priority, and general unsecured portion and frequently have an “estimated” priority
and unsecured portion. Do we break those out as well insofar as the Claim
Asserted amount?

E. Modification dates – what constitutes a modification? Is a motion to abate,
motion to incur, motion to sell, motion for attorneys fees considered a
modification?

F. Number of months case was pending – is this the petition date to the date
closed, date of last payment, date of dismissal/conversion order or date order
becomes final?

G. Amount of general unsecured claims discharged without payment – is this
based upon debts scheduled by the debtor or based on actual unsecured claims
filed by creditors. So, if the creditor receives less than 100%, should the unpaid
balance of the claim be included in the category of claims discharged without
payment?

H. In the Receipts section, Total amount refunded to debtor – does this mean only
the amount refunded at time of closing or amounts refunded during the life of the
case? Refunds are triggered by many occurrences such as abatements, tax
refund overpayments, emergency refunds, etc. Clarify what it is we are supposed
to track in this category.

At any rate, ALL the new requirements/fields should be clearly defined, preferably
by taking the Final Report example that the EOUST provided and listing an
explanation next to each field.

Confirm that the changes apply to all cases, even pre-BAPCPA cases.

Lastly, we don’t agree with the EOUST’s estimate that the new final report
changes will increase the cost in the amount of $7.00 to the Chapter 13 Trustee. It
is difficult to estimate the additional staff time it will take to input the information
for all the new fields, but there is no doubt whatsoever that it will be more time
consuming, and certainly more than $7.00 worth of staff time and that’s just on
the front-end. Assuming the Trustee’s Case Analysts make between $40 and
$50k per year, $7 would equate to about 15 minutes of their time.

Then there are modification orders that must be manually loaded, more staff time
and the closing process itself will take considerably longer with more data to
input. And with all the additional work we will be doing regarding completed cases
per USC Sections 522 & 1328 (checking cases 6 months prior to closing,
requesting information, filing pleadings…) more costs in staff, documents, etc. will
be incurred.

Additionally, effective October 1, 2008, we will be administering all mortgage
payments through the plan where debtors are in default when they file their
Chapter 13. This, coupled with the new final report requirement will take
substantial staff time and may require hiring additional staff. W. H. Griffin

I am currently serving as a panel trustee for the District of Kansas. I strongly
oppose the proposed concerning NDR Reports, Final Reports, and Final Accounts.
It appears to me that almost all this additional information will have to be
entered manually by legal assistants. The projected impact on our trustee
staff set forth in the comments accompanying the rule is significantly
understated. I urge you to delay implementation of the rules with respect to
data collection until the use of data enabled forms by bankruptcy petitioners is
mandated. Even then a pilot program should be implemented to actually test the
computer generated data to see if this is feasible. Furthermore, much many of
the terms used in the proposed forms need clarification. For example, in the
NDR form are we to use real values or use scheduled values in determining the
amount of assets abandoned? In the new Final Account, are we to use "filed
claims" or "scheduled claims" when computing claims discharged without payment?
Finally, the Final Report form appears to be greatly expanded. This will result
in a much larger mail out to creditors & increased cost on the bankruptcy
estates. Thank you for your consideration of my comments.

I am an attorney in private practice in Dixon, Illinois. In addition, since 2001, I
have served as a chapter 7 panel trustee for the Northern District of Illinois,
Western Division.

I have serious concerns about the newest burdens being imposed on chapter 7
panel trustees under the proposed rule for Uniform Final Reports, Docket Number
EOUST 101. The chapter 7 trustee’s no-asset fee has been $60.00 since 1994.
The $60.00 fee has not increased to keep up with inflation. The $60.00 fee has
not increased to offset BAPCPA’s significant economical impact on panel
trustees. And the $60.00 fee will not be increased to cover the additional costs
that panel trustees will incur under the proposed rule. Enough is enough!

My concerns are many, but I believe most or all of them have been eloquently
expressed by other commentators. Without limitation, I concur with comments
made by the following:

National Association of Bankruptcy Trustees
David Leibowitz
Marianne T. O’Toole, LLC
Steven R. Neuner
Larry Compton
Kevin R. McCarthy

1. I agree with the comments of each of the panel trustees posted as of this
morning, Friday, April 4, 2008, at 10:35 am MT.

2. P. 6447, column 3, first paragraph, "This rule . . . affects only trustees .
. ." -- The bankruptcy courts and others are also affected. The reports relate
to the courts' work processes and our service to the public. The size of the
reports affect our data storage requirements and customers' cost to purchase
copies.

3. P. 6447, column 3, last paragraph -- "Smart forms." This approach is not
yet a reality. Making assumptions about time and cost savings and about the
effectiveness of interoperability with a number of varied systems based on so
many unknowns seems currently indefensible.

4. P. 6448, column 2, second paragraph -- Cost to the government for developing
these uniform forms and the associated information "system." Do the projected
costs include those which will need to be incurred by the judiciary?

5. P. 6449, column 1, first paragraph -- Eliminating the current process for
filing "virtual" forms and for "batch" filing of those forms (filing them in a
number of different cases at the same time) seems like a leap backwards.
Wouldn't it be possible for the EOUST and the judiciary to work together to
modify the courts' electronic filing system which would meet Congressional
directives while still incorporating current efficiencies?

6. P. 6449, column 2, section 58.7(a). In place of the words, "before the case
may be closed," I suggest substituting the words, "in preparation for closing an
asset case." 28 U.S.C. section 589b(d) does not include requirements for the
report as stated here; the sentence should be reworded for accuracy.

The word, "deadline," should be substituted for the archaic and jargonistic
term, "bar date," in paragraph 6.

7. P. 6449, column 3, section 58.7(b). It might be wise to substitute "the
amount specified in Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2002(f)(8)" for "$1,500" to avoid the need
to update this section in the future if the bankruptcy rule changes.

The Congressional directive does not require the EOUST to require a uniform form
for notice of a report. The content and style of, and the process envisioned
by, the EOUST's proposed form may not meet with the requirements of the courts;
Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2002(m).

8. P. 6449, column 3, section 58.7(d). Is the wording, "All funds have been
returned" appropriate in cases which are converted and funds have been
collected? Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1019(4).

9. P. 6450, column 1, section 58.7(e) and (f). Are there substantive
differences between the final reports of chapter 12 and 13 standing trustees and
case trustees? It is hard to see a need for two different forms for each chapter.

10. General suggestions for the forms.
a. The designation of the paper should not include a form name abbreviation.
b. Stuffy words, legalese, and pompous style should be avoided in favor of
plain English. See The Redbook: A Manual on Legal Style, Bryan A. Garner,
West
Group, St. Paul, MN, 2002.
c. The need to comply with the courts' requirements for signatures (e.g., for
electronic filing) and address/contact information should be noted.
d. Why is the Paperwork Reduction Act statement included on each form?

I concur with the comments and recommendations made by Sam Crocker on

Tucson, Arizona

While I applaud the idea that persons with disabilities should have as much

users within several miles of the motors. Trails that are hard to keep up

already is. Those with disabilities who can actually accomplish their goals
with a modicum of help can be that much more proud of their accomplishments.
Allowing people who never put in the time and effort (that the rest of us do) to
get into the mountains safely by putting them on ATVs is just a bad idea.

what can and can't be done. Passing laws on areas unknown to the lawyers is not
going to help anyone.

The NAD Says:

Stadiums
• Stadiums of all sizes, regardless of use, must caption all aural information,
including emergency and safety information, unless doing so would be an undue
burden
• Captions must be placed in the same lines of sight as the Jumbotrons or other
video displays; handheld captioning devices should not be used
• Captions must be effective: same line of sight as the visual component; sufficient
size and contrast to ensure readability; and be timely, accurate, complete, and
efficient
• Captions benefit everyone

Qualified Interpreter
• An interpreter must be able to interpret both ways – “receptively and
expressively” (ASL-to-English and English-to-ASL)
• Whenever possible, an interpreter must be certified
• List and describe different kinds of interpreters: sign language, oral, cued
language, deaf-blind, certified deaf, and speech-to-speech interpreters
• Qualified interpreters can be provided “on site or through video remote
interpreting (VRI) services”

Video Interpreting Services
• Don’t make up new names – call it “video remote interpreting” (VRI)
• Define as “qualified interpreter services delivered through the use of video
conference technology”
• Explain that VRI is not the same as “video relay services” (VRS)
• Clarify that the rules about technical requirements for VRI are minimum
requirements
• VRI service should be provided only when it is expected to and actually results
in effective communication
• VRI services may not always be appropriate

Other Aids and Services
• Do not add “exchange of written notes” – not effective except for brief,
uncomplicated, and inconsequential communication
• Add “support service providers (SSPs)” for people who are deaf-blind
• Change “computer-aided transcription services” to “computer aided real-time
transcription services” (like CART)

Effective Communication
• Do not delete: “In determining what type of auxiliary aid and service is
necessary, a public entity shall give primary consideration to the requests of the
individual with disabilities.”
• Add: “The type of auxiliary aid or service necessary to ensure effective
communication will vary in accordance with the method of communication used by
the individual, the nature, length, and complexity of the communication involved,
and the context in which the communication is taking place.”

Companions
• Communicate effectively with companions who are deaf or hard of hearing
(companions are family members, friends, or associates of another person)
• Clarify “companions” must include, for example, a deaf wife of deaf husband or
hearing husband; a deaf parent of deaf child or hearing child
• Make absolutely clear that children are not to be used for interpreting or
facilitating communication

Telecommunications
• Add: Public entities should provide TTYs and “other voice, text, and video-based
telecommunications products and systems, such as videophones and captioned
telephones” when they offer the opportunity to make outgoing calls on more than
an incidental convenience basis
• Accept and treat relay calls the same as telephone calls
• Automated answering systems must work with TTYs and relay services, and
should include early option to connect with live person
• Ensure that emergency call centers, including 9-1-1 services, provide direct
access by TTYs and other text and video-based telecommunications products and
systems, to the extent technically feasible and as required by the “next
generation” of 9-1-1 services

Complaints
• Do not change the requirement for agencies to investigate each complaint for
which they are responsible

Detention and Correctional Facilities
• Give deaf and hard of hearing inmates the choice between a integrated setting
with inmates without disabilities, or a specially designed unit that may be at a
different or more distant location
• All options should be fully accessible to deaf or hard of hearing inmates
• Assignment to administrative segregation based only on the basis of the
disability label cannot be condoned

These comments are regarding The proposed changes to The Americans With
Disabilities Act. Specifically Titles II, and III, CRT docket No. 105 and CRT docket
No. 106 regarding the removal of miniature horses as legally being considered
service animals.
I have been a happy guide dog user for over six years. My black Labrador and I
do very well together. I consider myself to be very fortunate to, according to an
article published by the Buzzle Staff And Agencies,
(http://www.buzzle.com/editorials/1-27-2005-64895.asp,) to be one of the lucky
7,000 visually impaired people out of the 1.3 million visually impaired people in this
country to have a service animal. Because of the provisions set forth in the ADA, I
am able to bring my dog in public and live a normal and independent life. I don’t
even wish to imagine what it would be like if guide dogs rather than guide horses
were being considered for removal from the ADA. That would absolutely devastate
me. My independence would be stolen right out from under me. As a person living
with a disability, such independence is precious. There are times when I take for
granted that yes, I can go to the store with my dog and not be questioned.
However, if I were to be approached, I have proof that my dog is indeed a service
dog from a reputable school. I’m required to carry an ID while in public if any
proprietor were to question me about bringing my Labrador into their
establishment.
The matter of whether miniature horses being removed from the ADA shouldn’t
even be an issue. Yes, clearer language should be established regarding the
specific tasks and duties performed by various service animals. It indeed, would
assist in determining which animal holders are clearly taking advantage of the
legislation. It would spotlight those who are not as well. Those who have animals,
such as a guide dog or horse, the animals are trained to be well-behaved and
docile at all times. All service animals, (more specifically dogs and miniature
horses) according to The Guide Horse Foundation,
(www.guidehorse.org/faq_training.htm,) “Aggression is considered undesirable in
any guide animal. It is a common misconception that Guide Dogs are trained to
protect their handlers. In practice, all guide animals are trained to remain passive,
and it is never proper for a guide animal to display aggression, even when
threatened.” To better clarify, the legislation should focus on the BEHAVIOR of the
animal rather than the particular species. This way, if a SPECIFIC animal, whether
it be a dog, horse, monkey, etc, should become aggressive, the SPECIFIC animal
would be dealt with, rather than a species.
IDs, if they are not already issued to all service animal users, could be issued
to all legitimate service animal users. A registrar could be created with the names
and service animals of individuals to, in those instances if a service animal were to
become aggressive or be unable to perform their tasks to serve the needs of their
handler could be removed, and be considered inactive. In forming this directory,
officials at all levels of government would know which service animal users are
legitimate, and which are simply taking advantage of the current legislation. To
handle the matter of privacy, all information in this directory would be considered
confidential, with only certain professionals provided access. Those professionals
might include, the police, the DOJ, The Humane Society, service animal providers
to only name a few. If a proprietor questioned the legitimacy of a service animal,
they could simply call their local law enforcement agency, and for instance, read
off the number provided on the issued ID. No personal information of the handler
would be disclosed, while too, the proprietor would be assured that the service
animal isn’t a stray or untrained.
At this point in my life, I am perfectly content with my dog, but for some
visually impaired individuals, a guide dog simply isn’t an option. According to the
Buzzle article, the user may have allergies. Since a miniature horse only sheds
twice a year, compared to a dog’s constant shedding, for health reasons, a horse
would be a better option. Miniature horses live on average, thirty to forty years,
whereas a dog only lives eight to twelve years. There are some handlers, and
those in society who are afraid of dogs. They might feel more at ease with a
horse. Some handlers, too, may prefer their service animal live outdoors rather
than indoors as is more common with a dog. Adding another point that was not
discussed in this article, for some, a dog is not conducive or even acceptable to
the culture or religion of the handler. A horse would be more acceptable for
someone, for instance, who is a faithful follower of Islam. According to Muslim
veterinarian, Dr Ayoub Banderker, in an article he wrote on the matter of Islam and
dogs, “If the saliva of a dog touches you or any part of your clothing, then it is
required of you to wash the body part touched and the item of clothing touched by
the dog’s mouth or snout.” (http://www.islamicconcern.com/dogs.asp.) One final
point. What if the person doesn't want a dog? What if they're horrible cane users?
Should they be refused the opportunity for independence? Should it be withheld,
or denied if there aren't any other options open to them? That's what would happen
if the miniature horse were removed from the list of acceptable service animals.
The disabled person would need to rely on the assistance of others, rather than
living a full independent life on their terms, instead of on those terms set forth by
legislation.
In closing, more specific provisions should be made in the legislation focusing
more on the behavior of a SPECIFIC animal, rather than any one or several
species. In doing away with the miniature horse being legally considered a service

I am an Appalachian Trail (AT) maintainer and have given more than one thousand
hours of my life to building new treadway and maintaining the AT in good
condition as well as far more hours hiking on the AT and other trails. CRT

CRT Docket No. 105 will not make the trail accessible to the disadvantaged.
There are several reasons for this. Please let me outline some of these facts
that must be understood in order to avoid destroying the trail that you are
attempting to improve.

1. Most of the Appalachian Trail is built in steep terrain. The soil is very
fragile and great care must be taken to build a trail that will sustain foot
travel. We are continually making repairs from the damage done by walkers. We
occasionally have bicycles, horses, and ATVs illegally use the Trail. The
results are always catastrophic. The damage requires volunteers to devote many
hours of hard labor to make repairs. Sometimes the damage is too great and we
have to devote even more hours to relocating to Trail to a fresh location. This
is very hard work! The occasional damage from illegal use from wheeled vehicles
can be stopped by law enforcement. But it is still very taxing on our resources
and very hard on the will and enthusiasm of the volunteers who are the
life-blood of the Appalachian Trail.

2. The Appalachian Trail is an unprecedented accomplishment of volunteers. I
don't think there is anything close to it in the USA.

3. Most of the Appalachian Trail cannot possibly be made accessible to the
physically disadvantaged. Riding an ATV on such steep terrain would be very
dangerous. There would be many ATV users on the Appalachian Trail, but they
would not be the disabled. There are also sections that will never accommodate
any type of vehicle.

4. The Appalachian Trail community supported the thru-hike of blind Bill Irwin
who hiked the entire AT depending only on his service-dog (see the book Blind
Courage), a hiker on crutches from MS who walked the entire 2000-mile Trail
three times, and even two double amputees who thru-hiked the AT. If the AT were
drastically changed then the accomplishments of these heroic people would be
diminished and the challenge for future accomplishment would be eliminated.

4a. There is no need to regulate the use of crutches, braces, or any other kind
of non-vehicular devices as they have always been encouraged and never regulated.

5. If a courthouse has magnificent steps that are not accessible to the
disabled, we build a ramp and/or an elevator to make the courthouse accessible.
We don't tear down the steps. We do not alter the steps so that a wheelchair
can negotiate them. We also don't allow ATVs to use the ramps.

6. The Appalachian Trail community is working with due diligence to make
sections of the Trail accessible where it is feasible. It is inappropriate to
ignore our steady progress and use a heavy hand to force what is not possible.

7. We are all familiar with courthouses and parks. But only those with worn
hiking boots have the experience to decide on CRT Docket No. 105. CRT Docket
No. 105 must not demand that AT Volunteers build that which is impossible to
accomplish nor demand that volunteers tear down the trail on which they have
individually spent thousands of hours. CRT Docket No. 105 could result in the
loss of the Appalachian Trail, a great national asset, rather than its
improvement.

Comments on Workable Standards for Determining Program Access

My name is Victoria Thornton Bruckner. I am a person with a lifelong mobility
disability, and a licensed clinical social worker with thirty years’ experience
working with clients who have all types of mobility, sensory, cognitive and
psychiatric disabilities. I also am a disability consultant and a community
educator concerning the Americans with Disabilities Act. I am submitting my
comments on several of the proposed regulation changes now being considered by
the U.S. Department of Justice.

As a person with a disability and a professional who has conducted seven ADA
Title II self-evaluations for cities and Port Districts over the past ten years,
I am appalled that the Department would consider amending current regulations to
include language suggesting to public entities that making only one facility,
out of several that exist, accessible would constitute providing program access
to local disability communities.

I am sorry to say that, in even proposing this language, the Department is
demonstrating to people with disabilities throughout the United States that it
does not care about protecting their access to public programs and services, or
their right to integration, at all.

The Department must repudiate including such language in any of its regulations.
This language will, in most cases, destroy the concept of program accessibility
as we know it and ensure de facto segregation of people with disabilities. It
would directly and unequivocally contravene the stated purpose of the ADA, which
is to prohibit segregation and exclusion of people with disabilities.

Whenever a public entity, such as a town, city, county or district, provides
multiple facilities that offer programs serving the general population in
different neighborhoods or geographic locations, it is necessary for people with
disabilities to be able to access all of the benefits of such locally provided
programs that are available to others. The ADA makes this obligation clear.

Affording access to only one facility for each type of program in a town, city,
county or district would mean that the only disabled people able to utilize or
benefit from that program would be those who are located in the immediate
vicinity of the accessible facility.

To understand why this doesn’t work at all, imagine if only one public library
in the City of Los Angeles, or one courthouse and one police station in the City
of Chicago, were made accessible. Would that constitute an acceptable standard
of program accessibility for the citizens of those cities? Absolutely not!

While the Department may not have meant to suggest to public entities, in
including this language, that providing a single accessible facility would
always constitute affording an acceptable level of program access, from my
experience with conducting ADA Title II self-evaluations, I can assure members
of the Department that this is exactly how the meaning of this language will be
taken by all public entities facing multiple demands for services in an
environment of serious budget cuts.

The effect on accessibility and availability of public services and programs to
people with disabilities would be devastating. Therefore, use of this language,
and any suggestion of this proposed standard, should be avoided at all costs.

Comments on Changes to Title II Complaint Investigation Procedures

My name is Victoria Thornton Bruckner. I am a person with a lifelong mobility
disability, and a licensed clinical social worker with thirty years’ experience
working with clients who have all types of mobility, sensory, cognitive and
psychiatric disabilities. I also am a disability consultant and a community
educator concerning the Americans with Disabilities Act. I am submitting my
comments on several of the proposed regulation changes now being considered by
the U.S. Department of Justice.

In spite of staff shortages and budget constraints, it is critically important
that the Department not abandon its practice of investigating all Title II
complaints.

Unless all public entities, and the public at large, understand that all ADA
complaints are to be investigated by the Department, cities, counties,
districts, states and other public entities will soon understand that they are
being given “a wink and a nod” to do or not do whatever they wish concerning
affording accessibility, integration and equal participation to people with
disabilities.

One reason that the ADA has been as successful as it has been throughout the
United States is that program accessibility standards have been generally upheld
through the enforcement of ADA regulations. At least, that has been true for
public entities. In the case of Title III entities, lax enforcement of the
readily achievable barrier removal standards through the investigation of
relatively few Title III complaints has led to the proliferation of lawsuits as
the only available means of enforcing readily achievable barrier removal
requirements and enforcing the obligation to provide auxiliary aids and services
to afford effective communication to people with disabilities.

I am sure that Congress, and the Department, never intended to encourage the
existence of this plethora of lawsuits. I know this for a fact because I
participated in the ADA Training and Implementation Project, jointly funded by
the Department and the EEOC in 1992 and 1993. I was one of 400 participants in
this project who received in-depth training in ADA regulations and requirements.
During the training, it was repeatedly stated that the Department wished to
discourage lawsuits and encourage the use of alternative dispute resolution in
all cases. In fact, all of us participants received lectures on dispute
resolution techniques in preparation for our work as community ADA educators.

However, because it eventually became clear that the majority of business owners
faced relatively few consequences from the Department if they did not comply
with Title III, disabled members of the public began using lawsuits as the only
means of showing local businesses that they were serious about holding them to
their barrier removal obligations.

In order to avoid duplicating this litigious situation with state and local
government entities, it is essential that the Department scrupulously uphold its
standard of investigating all Title II complaints.

Comments on Provision of Accessible Routes to Witness Stands

My name is Victoria Thornton Bruckner. I am a person with a lifelong mobility
disability, and a licensed clinical social worker with thirty years’ experience
working with clients who have all types of mobility, sensory, cognitive and
psychiatric disabilities. I also am a disability consultant and a community
educator concerning the Americans with Disabilities Act. I am submitting my
comments on several of the proposed regulation changes now being considered by
the U.S. Department of Justice.

I strongly urge the Department to press for full accessibility of courthouses
and courtroom facilities. Access to due process of law is a fundamental
constitutional right for everyone in the United States. It does not, and should
not exclude individuals with disabilities, who in many communities constitute up
to one-fifth of the population or more.

Community residents come to courthouses as prospective jurors, members of jury
panels, attorneys, witnesses, plaintiffs, defendants, and simply as members of
the public seeking information and guidance. Many of these people have
disabilities, and need access to all the facilities afforded at the courthouse.
They may also need appropriate accommodations, including accessible seating,
assistive listening devices, sign language interpreting, or other auxiliary aids
and services, to attend court proceedings and participate as jurors and witnesses.

Some of these people have hidden disabilities, such as heart conditions and
breathing problems, and therefore have the same or similar accessibility needs
as people with mobility disabilities. Many seniors have these disabilities, and
seniors, when retired, often serve on juries, since they have the time and the
civic interest to do so.

During my professional career I have been deposed, and have had to testify, in
several legal cases. It was highly important to my credibility and effectiveness
as an expert witness in these cases to have full access to the witness stand, in
the presence of the judge and jury. Fortunately for me, the courtrooms in which
I testified had accessible paths of travel to the witness stands and other areas
they contained. Unfortunately, this access isn’t always available, even for some
judges who have mobility disabilities.

Through my work on the Disability Rights Committee of my local Bar Association,
I have also learned of instances in which crime victims, witnesses and attorneys
themselves have not been able to obtain needed disability accommodations in
order to fulfill their roles at trial.

Any consideration given to the remediation of these grave problems must take
into account the fundamental constitutional nature of everyone’s right to due
process, and the absolute necessity of accessibility to all court facilities as
part of that right. It is crucial to ensure that everyone has effective and
meaningful access to our justice system. Limiting efforts to provide this access
in the interest of cutting costs deprives community members of their most basic
constitutional right.

Question 10: service animals
There should not be an exclusion of the types of animals that may serve as

where other animals may not be permitted, a certification should be administered

Question 17: “Are there types of mobility devices that almost always will
require an assessment to determine whether they should be accommodated?” All
terrain vehicles and other vehicles with internal combustions engines will
require an assessment whenever they are used in an environment where they are
not currently used by people without disabilities. They pose safety hazards to
pedestrians; create exhaust fumes and noise, and damage tread ways designed for
pedestrian use.

Question 18: “Should motorized devices that use fuel or internal combustion
engines (e.g., all-terrain vehicles) be considered personal mobility devices
that are covered by the ADA?” No.

“Are there specific circumstances in which accommodating these devices would
result in a fundamental alteration?” The use of motor vehicles on hiking trails
will fundamentally change the aesthetic experience of all other users, be
dangerous, and damage the environment. One needs to look no further than the
severe damage ATV’s cause to hiking trails designed for foot-travel. Pedestrian
paths, walks and trails are unsuitable for motorized vehicle use, regardless of
the operator’s disability. The loud motor noise will disrupt the experience of
the pedestrian trail user. ATV use on equestrian trails will be especially
dangerous in that horses will be spooked and riders injured. ATV’s pose safety
risks to pedestrians, equestrians and cyclists in any setting other than a road
designed for motor vehicle use. The environmental impact of ATV use can be
extreme. Rutting of trails, soil erosion and stream sedimentation are universal
problems from ATV traffic. Obviously, motorized vehicles are dangerous indoors
due to carbon monoxide poisoning from exhaust fumes.

should be excluded from coverage by the ADA as a group. Otherwise, local, state
and federal agencies will have to evaluate their use at every public facility,
and develop site-specific rules or policies. Evaluating thousands of trails,
greenways, exercise paths, etc. is an unreasonable burden. Unlike the example
of the gatekeeper at the county fair, there will not be a park ranger at each
trailhead to determine if an ATV operator is disabled. Allowing ATV use only by
the disabled on pedestrian trails would be impossible to police.

There are many trails restricted to cross county skiing and snowshoeing in the
winter. As proposed, the ADA would allow anyone with a handicap parking tag to
use a snow mobile on these trails.

Question 19: “Should personal mobility devices used by individuals with
disabilities be categorized by intended purpose or function, by indoor or
outdoor use, or by some other factor?” This approach has merit. Certain
vehicles would just be accommodated for outdoor use. This would avoid each
municipality having to develop a policy on driving golf carts through city hall.
The next step would be to amend the ADA to require drive-in elevators.

appropriate for motorized recreational use. As an avid hiker and backpacker,
trails are one of the few places left where I can go to escape the noise and
exhaust of motorized vehicles. Many parks and recreation areas have created or

I write as an attorney and individual citizen regarding the proposed regulations
addressing service animals. I applaud the DOJ for explicitly specifying in the
proposed regulations that that individually trained animals that do work or
perform tasks for persons with psychiatric, cognitive, or mental disabilities
are clearly covered by the ADA. However, I urge you to remove the proposed
exclusion of emotional support and comfort animals from the definition of
"service animal." I also urge you to eliminate exclusions based on species.

The Americans with Disabilities Act requires individual case by case assessment
for determining the reasonableness and necessity for accommodations requested by
individuals. The proposed blanket exclusions for particular types of
accommodations related to animals violates the essence of this requirement and
will result in people with disabilities losing meaningful access to housing and
other accommodations. As a legal aid attorney, I have had several clients with
severe anxiety disorders whose psychiatrists literally prescribed that they
needed to adopt a cat or dog to assist them with anxiety reduction. In one such
case, my client's housing development did not allow pets. I was able to get her
permission to adopt a small dog in accordance with her psychiatrist's
prescription as a reasonable accommodation under the Fair Housing Act. She
adopted the dog and having the dog significantly assisted her with anxiety
reduction. However, the dog was not individually trained, and did not need to be
in order to perform the work prescribed by the psychiatrist. It is harmful and
counterproductive for the DOJ to propose a blanket elimination of the
requirement for this type of accommodation in other settings, such as shelter
services provided by public agencies. Moreover, such blanket exclusion
discriminates against people with psychiatric impairments in relation to people
with physical impairments, as it excludes animals most likely to serve the
functions required by people with psychiatric disabilities

Similarly, the blanket exclusion of particular types of animals unnecessarily
precludes accommodations that may be both necessary and reasonable for an
individual. For some individuals, having a rabbit may be as calming and
psychiatrically beneficial as having a dog, and may be more feasible if the
person has mobility problems or is allergic to dogs and cats. Moreover, an
accommodation may be necessary due to a psychiatrically impaired adult or
child's specific attachment to a particular animal and the significant
psychiatric deterioration that would occur if forced to separate from the
animal. This can occur as easily with a rabbit or hamster or rat as with a dog
or cat.

For these reasons, I urge the DOJ to eliminate the "comfort animal," "emotional
support animal," and species-specific exclusions from the proposed definition of
"service animal."

Thank you for your attention and consideration.

DNA is not a fingerprint - it contains vast amounts of sensitive medical
information about us. The Justice Department's decision not to require
destruction of the biological samples once the DNA profile is uploaded to its
database exacerbates the potential for our genetic privacy to be violated and
opens the door to the potential of familial searching.

The regulations will add a disproportionate number of people of color to the
database, potentially making those communities an increased target for law
enforcement and further aggravating the already existing racial disparities in
the criminal justice system.

The regulations estimate that potentially more than one million new samples will
be added to the database a year, yet the FBI's laboratory is currently receiving
for processing only 75,000 offender samples each year. The requirement to
collect, profile and upload such a massive number of DNA samples will flood the
system and create huge backlogs, which may ultimately hinder criminal
investigations, rather than help them.

The regulations contemplate federal agencies contracting with third parties to
collect and store DNA samples. Outsourcing the handling of this most sensitive
information to multiple collection and storage sites will almost certainly lead
to abuse, the creation of "shadow databases," and error, potentially undermining
public trust in DNA as an effective investigational tool.

persons with little to no upper body strength to make the maneuver.

implemented within the Code of Federal Regulations for public accommodations
within the lodging industries for bed heights that will accommodate persons with
disabilities using accessible rooms. Problems with bed heights being increased
to “luxury heights” include hotel properties with Marriott, InterContinental

management have refused to do anything about the height in accessible rooms
because there is no regulation within the current 28 CFR Part 36.

requiring an accessible room is the continued use of "boxed frames" under the
lower spring mattress, which eliminates the use of a Hoyer lift for persons
requiring this equipment in an accessible room intended for persons with
disabilities. Again, there is apparently no provision for open space below
bed(s) in accessible rooms within the current CFR.

There has been much comment regarding the example given of a
psychiatric service dog helping some individuals with dissociative identity disorder
to remain
grounded in time or place. By including grounding as work performed
by a psychiatric service dog, the Department is providing the basis
for an individual with a psychiatric disability to use a service
animal in place of another human being to interact in a controlled
manner and re-orient the individual to his or her surroundings, and
makes clear that this meets the DOJ definition of a service animal.
Opponents of such work persist in misinterpreting the work of such a
service animal, thoroughly trained to recognize and alert to its
handler's symptoms ithout direct human intervention, and to comport
itself well in public, as merely that of emotional support, companion
or comfort animals that do not meet the Department's definition of a
service animal. Their position also contradicts the basic premise that
a service animal does work to mitigate a disability, rather than just
performing 'tasks' on command, like party tricks. If excluded, this
section will continue to be a source of confusion to the public,
businesses and assistance dog partners. IAADP believes the reference
to grounding should be eliminated, as well as the phrase "do work";
they do not speak for all assistance dog partners, and many of us
would be irreparably harmed by adopting their position.

To further clarify the issue, it would be advantageous to refine the
general statement, "Animals whose sole function is to provide
emotional support, comfort, therapy,
companionship, therapeutic benefits, or to promote emotional
well-being are not service animals." It seems that others who have
left comments, and thus likely the wider population as well, overlook
the word 'sole' and choose to interpret biofeedback and most
psychiatric service animal work as "emotional support." While mood
disorders, such as my clinical depression, are mitigated by my service
dog's work, this is not at all the same thing as the happiness a
neurotypical individual will feel when interacting with a pet. Just
as a dog stopping at curbs for a person with no difficulty perceiving
curbs independently would not make a dog a service animal, making a
person whose emotions fall within a healthy range feel better would
not be the work of a service animal. On the other hand, indicating
curbs for a blind person is an important guide dog task, and
interacting in such a way as to mitigate the symptoms of a
neurochemical disability is vital for a psychiatric service animal.
These methods of interaction will necessarily be highly individual,
with the person and dog learning what works best for them; the
clearest way to rephrase succinctly would be to alter the emotional
support component to, "Animals whose sole function is to provide
NONSPECIFIC emotional support, comfort, therapy, companionship, or to
promote GENERAL emotional well-being are not service animals."

Many have raised the specter of "pets", animals that are not
adequately trained to work in public and cannot be trained to reliably
do work or perform tasks. It would seem far more reasonable to require
standards of BEHAVIOR for service dogs.
Reasonable standards might include:

PUBLIC APPROPRIATENESS:

* Animal is clean and does not have a foul odor.
* Animal does not urinate or defecate in inappropriate locations.

BEHAVIOR:

* Animal shall not make unsolicited contact with members of the
general public.
* Animal's conduct does not disrupt the normal course of business.
* Animal works without unnecessary vocalization.
* Animal shows no aggression toward people or other animals.
* Animal does not solicit or steal food or other items from the
general public.

TRAINING:

* Animal is specifically trained to mitigate (lessen) the effects
of its partner's disability; said disability being any condition as
described by and covered under the ADA that substantially impairs one
or more major life functions.
* Animal obeys the commands of its handler.
* Animal works calmly and quietly on a harness, leash or other tether.
* Animal has been specifically trained to perform its duties in
public and is accustomed to being out in public.
* Animal must be able to lie quietly beside the handler without
blocking aisles, doorways, etc.
* Animal stays within a reasonable distance of its handler at all
times unless the nature of a trained task requires it to be working at
a greater distance. The exact distance may vary depending on factors
such as other mitigating tools used; a wheelchair, for instance,
requires more room between dog and handler than a guide harness.

Thank you for your consideration,

Tracey Martin

Comment on CRT Docket No. 105

We offer comments re one item in the NPRM:

“Other power-driven mobility devices”

This well-intentioned change would have some unwanted effects on trails,
especially footpaths such as the Appalachian National Scenic Trail.

There is no reason to open the door to ATVs or other large devices. The
Appalachian Trail was designed and is maintained to footpath standards. Wheeled
vehicles will degrade the tread. Large wheeled vehicles will widen the treadway,
damaging vegetation

It is vital to maintain the quality of the A.T. experience for all users; this can be
done by providing accessible sections and any maintaining the rest free from any
power-driven mobility devices. This should be the goal for all backcountry, rustic,
footpaths.

For other areas, it is important to restrict the devices to “electric-powered only”,
with a weight limit of 100 lbs and a top speed of 5 mph in order to protect the
resource and limit interference with other pedestrian users.

As written, the proposed wording of your § 35.104 Definition opens the door to
destruction with the catch-all phrase of “other power-driven mobility devices.” An
overly-broad definition is ripe for misinterpretation.

Above all, please do not include internal-combustion powered machines. Engines
would disturb the quiet and primitive nature of footpaths, creating conflict where
none exists now.

The National Trails System Act, passed by Congress in 1968, specifically limits
its use to foot traffic. The existing CFR 36, Section 7.100 says “Appalachian
National Scenic Trail – The use of bicycles, motorcycles, snowmobiles, or other
motor vehicles is prohibited.”

We suggest the following definition:

§ 35.137 Mobility devices

“(e)Device use in restricted areas. Department of Justice reaffirms that in
federally designated wilderness, the only wheelchairs or mobility devices
acceptable must comply with the definition in the ADA Title V Section 507c for
federally designated wilderness: “Wheelchair (or Mobility Device). A device
designed solely for use by a mobility impaired person for locomotion that is
suitable for use in an indoor pedestrian area.”

(f) The Department of Justice further affirms that a wheelchair or mobility device
that meets this definition may be used anywhere foot travel is allowed, and that
this definition also applies in areas with equivalent, non-motorized, land-use
designations in national, state and municipal forests and parks.”

This is not opposition to persons with disabilities. We have been inspired by
accounts backcountry achievements of the blind and paraplegic. This is a plea to
you; do not allow destruction of footpaths in your attempt to allow accessibility.

I commend the Department of Justice for including in its revised proposed
definition of service animal a number of new and essential elements,
particularly emphasis on maintaining control of the service animal in public
settings and the requirement of housebreaking. As an Service Team committed to
fostering the assistance dog movement, I appreciate the Department of Justice's
attempt to clarify the definition of service animal for the general population,
public accommodation representatives and those working with service animals.
However, I believe certain issues need further clarification before being
established as final rules.

In response to the NPRM published in the Federal Register on June 17th, based on
the rationale discussed below, encourages the Department of Justice to:

1.
Eliminate the phrase "providing minimal protection" from the definition of
service animal;
2.
Eliminate the phrase "do work" from the definition because it is redundant
and the example of work given in the NPRM, grounding, undermines the
Department's goal of maintaining a clear distinction between specially trained
service animals and those animals whose mere presence can provide emotional
support, companionship or therapeutic benefits.
3.
Limit the use of other species only to animals which can be trained to
meet the same standards for behavior and training that assistance dogs must meet
to qualify for public access.
4.
Avoid placing a size or weight limit on common domestic animals such as
assistance dogs.

According to the NPRM, widespread misinterpretation of the minimal protection
language has been a problem for the last 15 years. The DOJ notes "Despite the
Department's best efforts, the minimal protection language appears to have been
misinterpreted."

By continuing the use of this language, nothing will change.

Since the mission of the new rules is to clarify and avoid confusion,
maintenance of this phrase undermines this goal.

Minimal protection has been used by some trainers and disabled partners to
justify attack and aggression training for what are claimed to be service
animals. Although the Department does not agree with this interpretation,
continuing to use the minimal protection phrase does nothing to curtail the idea
that attack and aggressive behavior are acceptable tasks performed by assistance
dogs.

The justification for including minimal protection in the original definition
was to guarantee the rights of those with seizure disorders to train their
service dogs for seizure response and alert tasks. Since the new definition
proposed by the Department includes assisting an individual during a seizure,
the minimal protection language is redundant and not needed.

Therefore, in response to Question Nine, I believe that maintaining the
"providing minimal protection" clause is counterproductive to the goal of the
current NPRM.

I applaud DOJ's categorical statement: "Animals whose sole function is to
provide emotional support, comfort, therapy, companionship, therapeutic
benefits, or to promote emotional well-being are not service animals."

I believe it is imperative to make it clear that individuals with disabilities
whose pets or companion animals have not been trained to perform tasks directly
related to their disability do not qualify as service animals. These are
usually referred to as emotional support or comfort dogs when associated with a
person with a psychiatric, cognitive or mental disability. Since individuals
with psychiatric disabilities constitute the largest single category of
Americans with disabilities, the distinction between task training to mitigate
the effects of an individual’s disability on the one hand, and mere presence on
the other should be clear and consistently supported by the Department.

My concern is with the section in the NPRM that reads:

"In contrast, the phrase 'do work' is slightly broader than ’perform tasks', and
adds meaning to the definition." By definition all work is task defined thus to
say "do work" is redundant and not needed.

Another concern is the example given of a psychiatric service dog helping some
individuals with dissociative identity disorder to remain grounded in time or
place. By including grounding as work performed by a psychiatric service dog,
the Department is providing the basis for an individual with a psychiatric
disability to claim the mere presence of a dog, which helps ground him/her,
meets the DOJ definition of a service animal.

This reference contradicts the strong and clear statement that emotional
support, companion or comfort animals do not meet the Department's definition of
a service animal. It also contradicts the basic premise that a service animal
performs a task to mitigate the effects of an individual’s disability. If
included, this section will continue to be a source of confusion to the public,
businesses and assistance dog partners. I believe the reference to grounding
should be eliminated, as well as the phrase "do work".

In response to Question Ten, I commend the Department for recognizing the
concerns expressed by many of the constituents about the use of reptiles and
other species that cannot be reliably housebroken, task trained or, which by
their very nature, pose a threat to public safety. My goal is to promote the
responsible use of access rights and prevent the erosion of societal tolerance
for service animal teams in places of public accommodation.

In response to Question 11 concerning the size and weight of common domestic
animals, I endorse the current Department policy. We believe it is not the role
of the government to limit disabled people's choice of what would be an
effective assistance dog for them.

The size of a common domestic animal like an assistance dog is a matter of
individual choice/necessity and may be related to the nature of the disability.
Limiting size and weight would discriminate against disabled individuals who
because of their height or weight and/or the severity of their mobility
impairment need to work with very large powerful assistance dogs on strenuous
tasks such as providing stability while walking, helping transfer in and out of
chairs, getting up after a fall or pulling a wheelchair. I recommend not placing
limits on the size or weight of a common domestic animal like an assistance dog.

With the incorporation of IAADP's recommendations in the new definitions, I feel
that the current confusion and misinterpretations will be greatly mitigated to
everyone's benefit.

Docket ID: DOJ-CRT-2008-0015
RE: ADA Service Animal Definition and Regulations
I am a guide dog user and have been since 1995. I have been active in advocacy
efforts on behalf of guide and service dog handlers for the past several years.

I support efforts to preserve the public access rights granted by the Americans
with Disabilities Act (ADA) for the next generation. I remain deeply concerned
about the abuses of the ADA taking place due to accidental or intentional
misinterpretation of the original Service Animal definition.
I commend the Disability Rights section in the Civil Rights division of the U.S.
Department of Justice for a number of the changes in wording that have been
proposed. I support the Department's decision to incorporate policies from its 1996
and 2002 interpretative guidance documents into the ADA regulation ( 28 CFR
36.302c) which will give these policies greater standing legally as well as
educationally. I welcome the addition of the housebreaking requirement and the
emphasis on keeping an animal under control in the newly proposed definition of a
service animal. However I believe the effort to end the misinterpretations of the
definition of a service animal falls short of achieving the intended goal in several
areas. Below, I will address an important issue I strongly encourage the DOJ to
reconsider, the retention of “Do Work” in the proposed new definition as illustrated
in the NPRM.

: RETENTION OF "DO WORK" IN THE NEW DEFINITION

I am pleased to see that the Department was receptive to educational efforts
concerning individuals with psychiatric disabilities, autism and other mental
impairments. It is our position that such individuals may significantly benefit from
task trained service dogs and should not be lumped in with those who wrongfully
claim that the ADA sanctions public access for them and their non task trained
pets.
While there is much that is good about the proposed definition in the NPRM,
a serious flaw has come to our attention. It concerns the Department's
explanation titled "Task Emphasis" in the NPRM. The content is so contradictory
to the Department's own interpretative guidance document, "Business Brief:
Service Animals" from 2002 and to the intent of the proposed definition, which is to
eliminate misunderstandings on what qualifies an animal to be a service animal, I
must oppose the retention of the phrase "do work." I refer to the example cited in
the comments of CADO to this NPRM.
I am aware that for years, pet owners with psychiatric impairments have
used the "my pet keeps me grounded" rationale for bringing their non task trained
animals into places of public accommodation.
I am deeply concerned that this "do work" example will be cited in the future
as proof that task training is unnecessary for animals belonging to people with a
psychiatric, cognitive or mental disability. Certainly the idea that work can be a
non physical form of assistance and not a task will further confuse the distinction
between service animals and pets.
Therefore, in the interest of eliminating further confusion and abuse, I strongly
urge the Department to reconsider this "do work" issue. I respectfully point out
the fact that the Department's own interpretative guidance in 2002 excluded the
phrase "do work" from the way it defined a service animal.
For six years, the Department's own emphasis on the fact that Task Training
is fundamental to the definition of a service animal in the Business Brief has been
relied on by the disabled community, businesses, colleges and other interested
parties. The DOJ has educated the public and businesses that the performance
of tasks is the crucial distinction between specially trained service animals and
other animals, whatever their label.

I suggest that the “do work” phrase in the original definition had nothing to
do with a non physical form of assistance. Rather, it merely reflected the fact it
was customary to discuss the trained behaviors performed on command or cue by
guide dogs as "guide work." Guide work is a series of trained tasks performed as
needed, such as leading a blind person around obstacles, halting to indicate
changes in elevation such as a curb, avoiding traffic in the team's path, finding the
location of a building's exit and finding an empty seat in a classroom or on a bus.
These are trained tasks and stand in sharp contrast to the DOJ's example of the
ambiguous concept of grounding.
Unfortunately, due to the impression the average person receives from the NPRM
discussion cited above, the phrase “do work” if defined by a term such
as “grounding” will seriously undermine the Department's profoundly essential goal
of distinguishing between service animals and pets whose presence or
companionship will provide emotional support, therapy, comfort, or other
therapeutic benefits. The controversy will never end.
Based on these considerations, I strongly recommend the elimination of "do
work" in the final rule's definition.

I wish to thank the DOJ for its efforts to help clarify the issues which have
created so much confusion and misinterpretation of the original service animal
definition and regulations.

Sincerely,
Becky Barnes
Mount Kisco, NY

I commend the Department of Justice for including in its revised proposed
definition of service animal a number of new and essential elements, particularly
emphasis on maintaining control of the service animal in public settings and the
requirement of housebreaking. I appreciate the
Department of Justice's attempt to clarify the
definition of service animal for the general population, public accommodation
representatives and those working with service animals. However, I
believe certain issues need further clarification before being
established as final rules.

In response to the NPRM published in the Federal Register on June 17th,
I encourage the Department of Justice to:
* Eliminate the phrase "providing minimal
protection" from the
definition of service animal.

* Limit the use of other species only to animals which
can be trained to meet the same standards for behavior and training
that assistance dogs must meet to qualify for public access.

* Avoid placing a size or weight limit on common domestic animals such
as assistance dogs.


According to the NPRM, widespread misinterpretation of
the minimal protection language has been a problem for the last 15
years. The DOJ notes "Despite the Department's best efforts,
the minimal protection language appears to have been misinterpreted."

By continuing the use of this language, nothing will change.

Since the mission of the new rules is to clarify and avoid confusion,
maintenance of this phrase undermines this goal.

Minimal protection has been used by some trainers and disabled partners to
justify attack and aggression training for what are
claimed to be service animals. Although the DOJ does not agree with
this interpretation, continuing to use the minimal protection phrase does
nothing to curtail the idea that attack and aggressive behavior are
acceptable tasks performed by assistance dogs.

The justification for including minimal protection in the original
definition was to guarantee the rights of those with seizure disorders to
train their service dogs for seizure response and alert
tasks. Since the new definition proposed by the Department includes
assisting an individual during a seizure, the minimal protection language is
redundant and not needed.

I believe that maintaining
the "providing minimal protection" clause is
counterproductive to the goal of the current NPRM.

I agree with DOJ's categorical statement:
"Animals whose sole function
is to provide emotional support, comfort, therapy,
companionship,
therapeutic benefits, or to promote emotional
well-being are not service
animals."

I believe it is imperative to make it clear that
individuals with disabilities whose pets or companion animals have not
been trained to perform tasks directly related to their disability do
not qualify as service animals. These are usually referred to as
emotional support or comfort dogs when associated with a person with a
psychiatric, cognitive or mental disability. Since individuals with
psychiatric disabilities constitute the largest single category of Americans
with disabilities, the distinction between task training to mitigate the
effects of an individual's disability on the one hand, and mere
presence on the other should be clear and consistently supported by the
DOJ.

I commend the DOJ for recognizing
the concerns expressed by many of our constituents
about the use of reptiles and other species that cannot be reliably
housebroken, task trained or, which by their very nature, pose a threat
to public safety. The goal is to promote the responsible use of
access rights and prevent the erosion of societal tolerance for service
animal teams in places of public accommodation.

Concerning the size and weight of common domestic animals, I concur with the
current Department policy. I believe it is not the role of the government to limit
disabled people's choice of what would be an effective assistance dog for
them.

The size of a common domestic animal like an assistance
dog is a matter of individual choice/necessity and may be related to the
nature of the disability. Limiting size and weight would discriminate
against disabled individuals who because of their height or weight
and/or the severity of their mobility impairment need to work with very large
powerful assistance dogs on strenuous tasks such as providing stability
while walking, helping transfer in and out of chairs, getting up after a fall
or pulling a wheelchair. I recommend not placing limits on the
size or weight of a common domestic animal like an assistance dog.

With the incorporation of these recommendations
in the new definitions, I feel that the current confusion and
misinterpretations will be greatly
mitigated to everyone's benefit.

I wish, to submit some comments as a parent of a duaghter who has a wonderful,
incredible Service Dog. The first concern I have is in asking you to delete the

The Atlanta area is currently designated as nonattainment for the 8-hour ozone and particulate matter national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS). Docket ID Number: EPA-HQ-OAR-2009-0022-0066. Federal Register Number: 2018-24649. Subject Heading: Agency Information Collection Activities; Proposals, Submissions, and Approvals: Acid Rain Program (Renewal). Date Posted: Nov 13, 2018. Comments Due: Dec 13, 2018

Dear EPA-HQ-OAR-2009-0022-0066 Docket,
The Acid Rain Program (ARP) under Title IV of the 1990 Clean Air Act was landmark legislation that has since made a profound environmental impact. The 1990 expansion of the Clean Air Act enabled the EPA to expand programs and regulations related to improving air quality. Acid rain, caused by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide particles, is known to harm aquatic environments and organisms, harm plants and trees, and even human health. Though acid rain itself poses no physical threat to humans, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide particles in the air can damage heart and lung functions; illnesses such as asthma, bronchitis, emphysema, and even premature death have been linked to sulfur and nitrogen pollution (Pisupati, n.d.).

ARP determined to safeguard the health of American ecosystems and homes by enforcing emission reductions from fossil fuel run energy plants (the primary producers of sulfur dioxide). The Program was the first to utilize tradable permits as an incentive for energy plants to reduce their emissions and the innovation was largely successful. Since 1980, sulfur dioxide emissions have gone from 17.26 million tons to 1.14 million tons in 2016 (U.S. EPA, 2018c). This monumental reduction was also reflected in nitrogen oxide emissions. In 1990, emissions were 6.42 million tons and in 2016, they were 0.78 million tons (U.S. EPA, 2018b).

The Acid Rain Program has made remarkable improvements in emission reduction and the overall environment. The proposed information collection request will improve the efficiency of the program and allow greater reduction in sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions. Commitment to improving our air quality is imperative, especially considering the increasing federal ambivalence to environmental concerns and general sentiment of market deregulation.

As a program funded through the general appropriations to the EPA by Congress, Superfund sites will most likely continue to be addressed at a slow rate. It is unfortunate that in a time of elevated unemployment rates that additional funding mechanisms such as the previous user tax are not available to support additional assessment and remediation activities of the program. The previous user tax placed a burden on chemical users and created a link between the major chemical users and the funding of clean up activities. Future funding via a tax might be better received if the funding targeted violators of environmental standards rather than broad industries.

Southern and central California are experiencing extreme challenges to the existing water supply due to environmental protection of species in the Sacramento delta and an extended drought. As this trend continues the value of clean water will increase dramatically. Future selection of sites should give additional attention to areas of the country where water resources are at a premium. It appears as if a significant return on investment is more likely in situations where the value of clean water is high or likely to increase at an accelerated rate. None of the selected sites for this rule are located in California.

The time required to complete Superfund projects and the names given to them have resulted in negative perceptions of the program. Additional favorable consideration of future projects should be directed to states, counties, contractors and work groups that demonstrate the greatest ability to implement projects in an efficient and effective manner. Rewarding innovation and success in the program may stimulate growth through efficient use of funds.

Furthermore, it is common for the name of a site to be derived from the town, former business or current property owner. Although this process is practical, it has the potential to add a stigma that may not be entirely accurate at sites with multiple, potential, responsible parties. An alternative naming convention for sites, after initial listing, that signifies growth and renewal might be warranted in order to reflect the goals for a cleaner and healthier environment. A site naming convention integrating the common names of plants, trees or other biological organisms reflective of the area ecology may foster improved public perception. Additionally, it may symbolize the potential for growth and renewal that is anticipated at the location. The use of such names at community meetings and on project documents could support this concept.

Although Superfund is a federal program, the local agencies are informally tasked with keeping community members informed throughout the process. Federal agencies may work with regional contractors and may appear for occasional public meetings, but the need to share information and build relationships with local agency representatives should not be overlooked. Local administrators should be integrated into these types of projects and utilized for their area expertise and ability to interface with constituents. Open dialogue with local officials can facilitate communication channels that are critical when addressing topics such as community exposures, environmental contamination and relative risk.

The environmental protection agency is attempting to eliminate the requirement for large pesticide exporters to provide the proper labeling of their pesticides on every individual product’s package. I personally see this rule proposal to be quite absurd. I have never in my life witnessed a situation where the deregulation of the food industry has been beneficial for the people. We can all remember last year when governments of Europe underwent harsh scrutiny when large proportions of horsemeat were found in mislabeled packages of what was thought to be ground beef. In the food industry the  labeling of all products, especially when it comes to pesticides, is absolutely crucial to public health. The current state of our nation’s food and agricultural systems leave us living in a world were we have very little knowledge as to where our food is coming from, how our food is being made, and even what our food truly is. The lack of labeling for these individual pesticide packages will only make this issue more severe. Under this proposal, these unlabeled pesticides will will be exported and used on agricultural products throughout the world. There has been a mass movement over the past decade in the United States advocating for transparency of the food industry and increased regulation of genetically engineered foods. This deregulation of labeling for pesticides will decrease transparency of the food industry, it will also become that much harder for the regulation of organically grown food. Studies have shown there are many potential risks that come along with genetically engineered foods such as allergies, organ damage, and resistance to antibiotics. Also the prolonged exposure of genetically engineered foods into the environment will lead to the creation of “super weeds”, weeds that develop a tolerance to herbicides. But regardless of these health and environmental factors, large food producers, who’s only interest is to satisfy shareholders, see very large benefits to genetically engineered foods because they increase crop production and maximize profits. This rule proposal will only serve to benefit the large pesticide producers, allowing them to cut the cost of production by not properly labeling everything. The government should not further increase the risk to public health just because these large pesticide exporters want to cut back on expenditures. We must put the people first.
