Dear Members of the Scientific Advisory Panel:

We share the concerns about post- application exposures of bystander workers and residents to volatilized pesticides and contamination of nearby fields expressed in comments from PANNA, NRDC, the Farmworker Pesticide Project and Larry Jacobs.

We also urge you to look within the field at volatilized pesticide exposures experienced by tractor drivers, irrigators and field workers reentering fields during and soon after expiration of restricted entry intervals. For many pesticides, the Worker Protection Standard currently allows some early reentry 4 hour after some pesticide applications have been completed based on the out-of-date assumption that inhalation exposure will be negligible after 4 hours. We have spoken with tractor drivers and irrigators who experienced symptoms consistent with pesticide illness during early reentry work which involved minimal or no contact with treated surfaces. We are also concerned that current restricted entry intervals do not consider exposure to volatilized pesticides, particularly in greenhouses, mushroom houses and poultry and other livestock quarters. Peak short-term exposures to volatilized pesticides need to be evaluated for workers reentering treated fields and enclosures.

On a separate note, during today’s meeting I was concerned to learn that inhalation studies conducted in dogs and primates have been excluded from use in this assessment because they “don’t fit the model”. For a number of fumigants and other pesticides more sensitive toxicity endpoints have been found in dogs or primates than in rats and systematic exclusion of this data will not be protective of public or worker health.

I also disagree with the Agency’s decision not to assess chronic exposure because of “the seasonal nature of agriculture.” On the west coast agriculture pesticide use in agriculture is not so seasonal. The growing season extends year round in coastal areas and inland dormant sprays and soil fumigants are applied during the fall and winter.

Thank you for all the time and effort you are putting into work on this panel on this very important issue of spray drift volatilization.

To: EPA Advisory Committee Concerning Volatilization of Drift of Conventional Pesticides

Thank you for this opportunity to share my personal experience and concern for public health regarding the use of conventional pesticides and drift.

It is possible that I was first exposed to pesticides before I was even born. I lived in the same farm area from 1948 to about 1969 and then again from 1988 to 2005. That is about 38 years on living on my parents' farm. They lived there, all but four years, from 1947 to the time of their deaths. My father passed away August 3, 1999 and my mother April 2, 2001.

As a child I remember having numerous earaches, stomach problems and difficultly learning in school. I also remember that my mother seemed to constantly have the "flu." My father was very healthy except for problems with his heart valve and had to have 3 knee replacements due to the type of work he did. Both parents also had high blood pressure as they aged and my mother had problems with her thyroid and liver.

In 1996 my father developed proteinuria and hematuria, indicating kidney problems. These symptoms can be associated with paraquat exposure, as well as other chemicals used in my area. Near the end of his life, he was also diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, rare waxy casts, became anemic from an upper gastrointestinal bleed requiring blood transfusion and great weakness. These are all symptoms of paraquat exposure according to your EPA manual on Recognition and Management of Pesticide Poisonings. And yes, paraquat was used in the orchard located at the rear of our property. Just a year or two before this illness, my father was packing up a mountain trail for seven miles with his horses. This takes strength and good health to accomplish. He did this 2-3 times a year for his recreation until he suffered the illness caused by paraquat (in my opinion).

I wanted to contact my father's nephrologist to see what he thought of my theory, but his has been dealing with cancer of the lung that has now moved to his brain. My father's nephrologist lost his two parents to cancer and were our neighbors. The lived close to the rice fields.

As I mentioned, my mother seemed to constantly have the "flu." Eventually she developed liver problems, which turned to malignant liver tumors.

In the early 1990's I started studying every possible cause I could think of that might be causing my health problems. Being a very athletic, strong and active person, I couldn't understand why I kept getting so sick. It wasn't until sometime in 2003 that I started looking at the possibility of pesticide exposure. We farmed organically so I really didn't know much about pesticides, but the computer opened doors to information not easily available in the past.
Agriculture expanded in our area over time and so did the use of pesticides. The land is very flat and is prone to have high winds. There are about 9 miles of continuous rice fields to the south of my family's property. There are about 500 acres of almond orchard to the north of the property. This makes it possible to have drift from both rice and almonds, depending on which way the wind is traveling.

I have reviewed the requirements for farm worker protection when they are applying pesticides, but neighbors have no protections at all, don't know what is being sprayed or when it will be applied. I am writing to congratulate the administrator and agency on this long-awaited
ruling. These findings are necessary and long overdue.

I am also writing to make a comment on the EPA's reliance on IPCC and CCSP
reviews, which I believe has wider significance. These scientific efforts are
without a doubt invaluable and should be central to policy discussions. However,
it's important to recognize that these broad reviews represent a kind of lowest
common denominator in scientific judgement. What is deemed true in such
collaborative assessments is those facts for which there is an overwhelming
preponderance of evidence.

certainty. Sometimes, judgement must be exercised to avoid catastrophic risks
even when the science is still incomplete or merely suggestive.

that mean that it is of no concern? Of course not. In fact, our lack of
understanding of current behavior of the ice sheets should be a cause for more
concern, not less. At least it would be, with wise leadership.

Thank you for your tremendously important effort in making this finding. Please
continue with all due speed.

The South Dakota Department of Labor submits the following comments in response to the proposed rule Federal State Unemployment Compensation (UC) Program; Funding Goals for Interest Free Advances RIN 1205-AB53.

The proposal appears to disregard the immediate impact of the recession, the future impact severe recession level benefits will have on the application of the solvency standard and the action of many states to maintain solvency standards.

The majority of states are dealing with record high benefit levels and immediate or near-future insolvency. They are working through the political and financial implications of decisions to restore solvency to their programs and may need cash flow loans over the next several years as a tool in this process. Implementing this new requirement will seriously hamper this process.

South Dakota has never been insolvent but now faces that prospect due to benefit payments at three times normal levels. The State Trust Fund declined to an unacceptably low level in the 2001-03 recession. The state took prompt and responsible corrective action by increasing employer payments to the fund, but the changes did not have enough time in place to correct the problem before the onset of the current recession. Future changes are planned to again restore solvency to the fund, but they could be complicated by the abrupt elimination of favorable loan terms.

The application of the standard could require unnecessary reserves. The South Dakota experience is having an adequate reserve by this measure might be sufficient for current benefit levels, but those high levels have never been experienced in the recent past. Having “sufficient reserves” would have meant significantly higher payments would have been required from employers, and those payments would have remained in the federal trust fund, not needed and not used, for decades. Having favorable temporary loan terms available is a better business practice than taking these funds out of local economies. As the solvency standard is a function of historical benefit payments, the current high payment levels will drive the “sufficient reserve level” even higher.

In summary, South Dakota recommends the entire proposal – necessity, timing and financial requirements – be tabled in light of the length and severity of the current recession.

Federal-State Unemployment Compensation (UC) Program
Funding Goals for Interest-Free Advances: Proposed Rule
Regulatory Information Number 1205-AB53

Comments from the Nevada Department of Employment, Training & Rehabilitation
Employment Security Division

Nevada supports the concepts of prudent trust fund management and agrees with the selection of Approach I as the proposed qualifying funding measure for interest-free advances.

The State does, however, take exception with the proposed time frame of 2 years after its date of publication for implementing the final rule. Given the extraordinary depth and length of the current recession, Nevada believes a phased approach to the funding goals is necessary to provide states with extended time to adjust their financing systems. Linking a 5-year average to the current economic recession should be considered during the development of a reasonable phased approach. Above all, the time frame for the legislation should allow for situations like the present and avoid punishing states that have acted prudently but are faced with extenuating situations before their tax process has a chance to adjust for the difference.

Finally, given the dramatic impact the current recession has had on the majority of state trust funds, Nevada urges an extension of the existing waiver of interest on trust fund loans through CY 2011.

Sincerely,

We are opposed to the proposed interpretation. This change would be dangerous if applied in Alaska. Consider for example a flight from Kaltag to Nulato to Koyukuk to Galena to Fairbanks and return via the same routing. We fly this each day. If I understand the rule correctly, a pilot would no longer be 'good to start, good to finish' for the entirety of their assignment.  I would not be in favor of grounding the pilot on the final leg, or any leg, if that leg were to put them over 14.0 duty, 8.0 hours flight, or whatever.  The reason I would oppose this is because it would add an additional stress from the first minute of the day.  If a pilot knows they will be flying a long assignment, there will be enough fatigue and stress.  I think I'd stay fresher and more focused if I could do my assignment, and then if it was supposed to be 13.5 duty hours but ran over 14.0, oh well.  If a pilot knew they could be grounded on that last leg, realistically they'd feel pressure to rush all day, load the bags quickly, hurry the passengers in the cabin, do an intersection departure, etc.  And if they did get stuck unable to fly home, they may wind up unexpectedly in a hotel (possibly without a toothbrush, change of clothes, underwear, etc.).  They'd probably still have to fly the next day, and would be doing so on poor rest.  I don't think this rule accomplishes its goal.  I would be in favor however of reducing the 14.0 duty day to 12.0 or 13.0.  You could reduce it to 12.0 and have a 2.0 hour buffer following the 12.0.  So 'good to start, good to finish' could apply for the first 12.0 hours.  Then, if they have another leg left but it's been 12.5 hours, they could fly the last leg assuming it will be done by 14.0 (12.0 plus the 2.0 buffer = 14.0).

Since 1966 the Alaska Air Carriers Association (AACA) has represented the interests of aviation businesses in Alaska. Our members own, operate, and service aircraft, providing for the needs of the traveling public through scheduled commuter operations, aircraft maintenance, flight tours, on-demand air charters, fuel sales, parts sales, storage, rental, airline servicing, flight training, and emergency medical evacuation.

For over forty years, AACA and the Alaskan carriers have worked hard to improve the safety record of Alaska operations. Fatigue and rest are paramount considerations here, as we fly in some of the most challenging environmental conditions.

While at first blush, the proposed change of the interpretation may appear to simplify the issue for the FAA, it creates a serious situation for Alaskan pilots. We fly in an airspace of over 3 million square miles. In that area, only 91 airports are even in proximity to shelter. The rest of the 1809 airports and airstrips have no shelter and no services, for the aircraft, the pilot, or the passengers.

A pilot transporting passengers or cargo, faced with head winds or weather conditions can occasionally during the year be faced with expected arrival minutes past the 14 hour duty day. In our environment, and with the limited infrastructure resources, it is far safer for a pilot to exceed the 14 hour duty day, than to set down and expose his passengers or cargo to the elements. In fact, preheating an engine is not even an option at almost all of the 700 airports and 1200 landing strips in the State of Alaska.

The proposed interpretation puts pilots into a lose-lose situation and this in no way contributes to improved aviation safety.

This FAA proposal should be adopted to change FAR Part 135.263 (d) that would not create an exception for flight crewmember rest requirements. As such, if a flight crewmember was to be aware at the time of departure on the last leg of the flight that he or she has not had the required rest, 14 CFR 135.267(d) would prohibit him or her from departing on the last leg of the flight.

It is illogical that the nearly-identical regulatory language in sections 121.471(g) and 135.263(d) is interpreted in two different ways. This proposal would make both regulatory languages agree as regards to required crew rest.

There should be only one level of aviation safety in regards to public expectations. A minimun period of required crew rest should be defined for commercial flight activity under CFR(s) Part 121 and Part 135.

The traveling public is entitled to one level of safety, and the highest consistent level of safety is what the regulations should mandate.

Flight schedules must account for delays that may be anticipated in flight operations and schedule accordingly. To force a crew to fly without the required minimum rest periods is not conducive to safe flight operations.

Comments on Blended versus Block Refuge
Lawrent L. Buschman
Dept. Entomology, Kansas State University

I would like to make two points about Blended versus Block Refuge, one scientific
and based on unpublished data that is still being analyzed, and second an opinion
about grower compliance when RIB requirements become complex.

I. Corn Borer (CB) production is significantly reduced in the Refuge-In-The-Bag
(RIB): It is important to remember that a 5% RIB will not produce as many corn
borers as a 5% block refuge. In SW Kansas, we have two years of data for
experiments where single plants are artificially infested with neonates. The four
surrounding plants are either non-Bt plants (block refuge) or Bt plants (RIB). These
data show that ECB survival in the blended refuge is 20 to 40% for 1st generation
and 17 to 71% for 2nd generation. This agrees with other observations made in the
non-Bt block refuge that 25 to 43% of 1st generation and 26 to 55% of second
generation larvae that survive to the mature larval stage are found on plants other
than the natal plant. In a blended refuge these larvae would have been exposed to
Bt plants and would have died. These data also show that southwestern corn
borers derived from native feral oviposition were not found on blended refuge
plants under moderate population levels in the block refuge (0.3 to 0.6 larvae per
plant). At this time it is not clear if the difference is due to the method of infestation
or to the species, however, this situation is troubling relative to RIB. We will have
additional data for artificial SWCB infestations when it can be analyzed. It is
interesting to note that corn earworm numbers were similar for the blended versus
block refuge plants.

II. Simplifying the IRM Refuge requirements: It is important to remember that
adding seed mixtures to the existing 20% and 5% block refuge requirements will
make following IRM regulations incredibly difficult for growers. When one needs to
read the label on each bag to figure out what the IRM requirements are I think the
growers are not going to be as willing to comply as they have been. Back in the
1990’s we had a confused set of regulations. The EPA was able to harmonize the
IRM requirements in ca. 2000. We have had about 10 good years where growers
knew what they were expected to do for IRM. Now we are entering another period
of confusion where growers will be totally confused about what they need to do for
IRM. They will have a difficult time understanding the difference between single toxin
and multi-toxin pyramided corn that requires 5 % versus 20% block refuge. Then
you also have Refuge-in-the-Bag for corn rootworm but not for corn borers. I think it
is likely that some growers will give up on IRM or will mistakenly (or intentionally)
assume their seed is Refuge-in-the-Bag and not plant a refuge. Other growers may
mistakenly (or intentionally) assume that their corn requires only the 5% refuge
when it should be 20%. Others will assume that IRM is not science but a political
buy-out. I think there will be many growers who will be tempted to quit worrying
about IRM because it is just to confusing. We are in real danger of losing the
grower’s good will and cooperation with respect to IRM. IRM is just becoming too
complex and confusing.

We must figure out some way to simplify IRM requirements. We need a simple set of
IRM recommendations. We certainly do not need to add to the confusion by allowing
RIB for CRW but not for CB. If we are going to allow RIB—it needs to be for both
CRW and CB. It is just too confusing to expect growers to keep it straight that we
can have RIB for one insect but not for the other.

Lawrent "Larry" L. Buschman
4500 E. Mary St.
Dept. Entomology & SWREC
Kansas State University

Garden City, KS 67846
Phone: 620 276 8286
E-mail: lbuschma@ksu.edu

Re: Docket Number FAA-2010-0302

Dear Administrator:

I am writing to comment on the NPRM that recommends the creation of a new rule subpart H to part 93, Mandatory Use of the New York North Shore Helicopter Route.

As a manager of a helicopter part 135 operation, and as a pilot, I am very familiar with establishing routes and having several operators flying along these routes. I am also very familiar with the challenges of balancing noise abatement procedures against those of safety concerns. I have also witnessed first hand the negative effects of changing routes, or forcing operators to use one route only, when transitioning certain areas.

I understand the purpose of this intended rule is simply to reduce the sound effect of helicopter operations along Long Island, with very little regard for the safety of the traveling public. The first sentence in the FAA’s mission statement reads “Our continuing mission is to provide the safest, most efficient aerospace system in the world”. They go on to say; “Safety is our passion. We work so all air and space travelers arrive safely at their destinations.” In reading the background as published in the NPRM, it states that Helicopters while on this mandatory route are to remain offshore and “over the water”. The FAA during the development of the NPRM of part 136, and after its passage with numerous denials of requested exemptions for relief from life preserver requirements, believe it to be so dangerous to be overwater, or even cross a river in the desert of Arizona, that each occupant must be wearing a life preserver. The Administrator has indicated that crossing a shoreline or operating overwater is so hazardous, even if you are within gliding distance of the shore, that a helicopter must be equipped with emergency floats or be in a twin engine helicopter, for the passengers not to be wearing life jackets. It is then self evident, if the agency continues to maintain their belief of the dangers of over water flight, that this route, being over water, is truly not in the best interest of safety, and therefore in direct opposition to their stated mission.

There is a second serious concern of establishing one mandatory transition route, which we have first hand experience with. When part 136 was first enacted, operators who previously used two or four different transition routes were now sandwiched in to one route. The shoreline transition routes, which at most placed the helicopter over the shore line for merely 50 seconds, were deemed by the agency to be to be far too hazardous for commercial air tour operators to use, without equipping their aircraft with $80,000 emergency floatation systems or purchasing tens of thousands of dollars of life preservers that passengers had to wear, for operators to continue flying these routes. Therefore, the majority of operators began using the only arrival and departure route that does not require the aircraft to cross water except for take off and landing. The increased mandatory use of this route, has compacted all the helicopter traffic into one small corridor. When aircraft are compacted into one small area, such as around airports or on “Mandatory Routes”, the risks of midair collisions increase dramatically. This is self evident, and regrettably supported by far too many aircraft accidents. Once again, this seems to be in direct conflict with the FAA’s mission statement.

The other issue that was created as a direct result of compressing all the aircraft into one small route was an increase in noise complaints. It is quite logical that if you push all helicopters that transition Long Island into one small corridor, that corridor will experience a huge increase in noise complaints. Previously, along that route we had one or two people who would contact us and actively worked with the community to mitigate the helicopter noise issues. Once the aircraft were all using the same route we started hearing from people who in the past had never been bothered and the ones calling were wondering what had changed and they are now more despondent than ever. As a matter of fact we actually train our pilots, when not prohibited by terrain obstructions such as mountains or buildings, to vary their approach and departure azimuths when ever transitioning areas, or when arriving and departing landing pads or airports. This technique actually reduces the noise impact on individuals and prevents repetitive disruptions. Creating “Mandatory Routes” will just increase the amount of noise ten fold and impact new people consistently over and over again.

The next area I would like to address is where in the proposed rule under the Authority for This Rulemaking you use 49U.S.C. 44715(a) “provides that to “relieve and protect the public health and welfare from aircraft noise,””. I was very disappointed to see this comparison made. It seems clear by reading 44715(a) controlling the 85 or 90 decibels of an Helicopter, all certified and tested by the Federal Aviation Administration, has little to do with a sonic boom as stated in the statute. The editing of the rule as printed above as it was edited when placed into the NPRM causes me to have some concern of the FAA’s third value of their Mission Statement, which reads;

“Integrity is our touchstone. We perform our duties honestly, with moral soundness, and with the highest level of ethics.”
As you read through 44715(a) and (b) in it’s entirety bellow, I would like to draw your attention to (b(3)) which reads as follows “(3) consider whether the standard or regulation is consistent with the highest degree of safety in air transportation or air commerce in the public interest;” This is the requirement that the FAA must first must meet in order to use this law to create a new regulation. I would say that from any of the arguments above they have failed to meet this requirement and it is mandatory, hence the word “shall”.
Sec. 44715. Controlling aircraft noise and sonic boom
(a) Standards and Regulations. -- (1)(A) To relieve and protect the public health and welfare from aircraft noise and sonic boom, the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, as he deems necessary, shall prescribe --
(i) standards to measure aircraft noise and sonic boom; and
(ii) regulations to control and abate aircraft noise and sonic boom.
(B) The Administrator, as the Administrator deems appropriate, shall provide for the participation of a representative of the Environmental Protection Agency on such advisory committees or associated working groups that advise the Administrator on matters related to the environmental effects of aircraft and aircraft engines.
(2) The Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration may prescribe standards and regulations under this subsection only after consulting with the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency. The standards and regulations shall be applied when issuing, amending, modifying, suspending, or revoking a certificate authorized under this chapter.
(3) An original type certificate may be issued under section 44704 (a) of this title for an aircraft for which substantial noise abatement can be achieved only after the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration prescribes standards and regulations under this section that apply to that aircraft.
(b) Considerations and Consultation. -- When prescribing a standard or regulation under this section, the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration shall --
(1) consider relevant information related to aircraft noise and sonic boom;
(2) consult with appropriate departments, agencies, and instrumentalities of the United States Government and State and interstate authorities;
(3) consider whether the standard or regulation is consistent with the highest degree of safety in air transportation or air commerce in the public interest;
(4) consider whether the standard or regulation is economically reasonable, technologically practicable, and appropriate for the applicable aircraft, aircraft engine, appliance, or certificate; and
(5) consider the extent to which the standard or regulation will carry out the purposes of this section.

Again, it is very troubling that while presenting the authority to justify the ability to create this rule they twice edited the entirety of the wording of the rule and twice removed the “aircraft noise and sonic boom”. I do not believe that when this rule was created they were referring to the common sounds emitted from a helicopter they were however referencing extremely loud jet engines associated with sonic booms, hence that is why the words are almost exclusively in unison throughout the rule. Interestingly enough it appears as though the responsibility of regulating noise is actually that of EPA and not the FAA. I would argue that the FAA under the present justification does not have the legal authority to create this rule. Further it appears that they may only prescribe standards and regulations under this section after consulting with the EPA. I see no mention of this consult ever taking place in the rulemaking.

Lastly, just for a comparison. I do believe the current noise limit for older motorcycles is set by the EPA in the range of 93 decibels. I am uncertain of the exact number of helicopters which transition Long Island during the summer, however, I feel fairly certain the amount of motorcycle noise far outweighs that of helicopters. Further the motorcycles are rarely involved in commerce of any kind, and rarely transport more than one person.

Thank you for you attention to this matter.

Sincerely,
Charles M. Horton

I'm writing to you today in request that my comments will be shared with the Federal Advisory Committee for review for consideration in improving worker and passenger safety in the Sportfishing industry.

I am an avid sport fisherman located in Southern California. I operate an online tackle store and educate anglers not only on fishing techniques and good practices but also the importance of maritime safety when operating their own vessel.

Southern California has a very unique and large fleet of passenger carrying commercial sport fishing, diving and whale watch vessels (approximately 175) that operate in US and Mexican waters. The vessels range from 50 to 125 feet and carry up to 60 passengers or more, the majority of the voyages are in the 24hr to 36hr range.

Over the past several years I have taken notice that there have been several maritime incidents and near misses that make me question my safety as a passenger aboard these vessels and I feel it has been often overlooked. The US Coast Guard is the only governing body (not CAL OHSA, or MACOSH).

Some of the unacceptable trends I have witnessed:
1. Captains turning off AIS systems to try and hide their fishing locations with passengers aboard.
2. Crews working excessive hours or too many days in a row
3. Crews using illegal drugs to stay awake due to lack of rest

Here are some of the incidents:

Shogun Crew Overdoses while in port between trips (2020)
https://www.nbcsandiego.com/news/local/our-crew-members-in-hospital-after-suspected-drug-overdoses-at-fishermans-landing/2411956/

Conception Fire (2019)
https://www.justice.gov/usao-cdca/pr/federal-grand-jury-issues-new-indictment-conception-boat-fire

Pacifica runs aground at harbor entrance (2019)
https://www.nbcsandiego.com/news/local/mission-beach-belmont-park-65-foot-ship-people-found-aboard-sdpd/133033/#:~:text=Nearly%20two%20dozen%20people%20were,the%20San%20Diego%20Police%20Department.

Prowler collides with Attessa IV (2018)
https://www.10news.com/news/10news-exclusive-boat-crash-survivor-recalls-moment-of-impact

Safety Proposals:

1. AIS - Require all commercial passenger carrying vessels to have AIS (Class B) systems regardless of length (currently only over 65 feet). Require them to be on at all times, not just within terrestrial waters (12 miles). The cost impact for this would be roughly $400 per vessel, most of them have the technology integrated into their current marine electronics already but choose not to use it. This would reduce collisions, near misses and improve emergency response times. The single press of the emergency button not only puts out a distress signal quickly, but identifies the vessel and its location instantly without having to converse over VHF with potentially someone who is unfamiliar with the vessel or its location. This would increase response times to first responders, the Coast Guard, and save lives. The second component of this is the Coast Guard needs to audit these records of AIS use in comparison to the ship's voyage log or during onboard inspections. There is currently no oversight other than complaints from civilians to the local Coast Guard sector. Historical AIS data is available to civilians and is easily accessible online from websites like Marinetraffic.com. Even when AIS is switched off, vessels can still be tracked via satellite, and passengers often post their location on social media using chart apps on their phones. For captains to think that their vessels are really traveling undetected is a fallacy.

2. There needs to be a more stringent oversight on the number of hours worked and days worked in a row by captains and crew. I can tell you first hand and speaking with crew members on multiple vessels that this is a huge problem. One crew member aboard a San Diego vessel said he was on his 28th day of working in a row. His girlfriend would do his laundry for him and exchange clothes for him when he was in port for a few hours between trips. I witnessed another crew member start his shift on deck at 5am, work all day and then cut fish/clean the boat until 2am the next day. He would work multiple trips in a row working similar hours and getting little to no sleep. Operating a vessel is much like operating an airplane, when things go wrong they either fall from the sky or sink which results more often than not in death. There are flytime limits for the airline industry, and there should be similar requirements for nautical operations that carry passengers as well.

3. There needs to be more stringent/frequent drug testing of not just captains but deckhands as well. I don't think that the drug use is purely because of recreational use, but it's often a clutch for being overworked as a necessity to stay awake because of consistently working long hours.

Committee members, Ladies and Gentlemen:
Regarding Agenda Items (6) (b) National Recreational Boating Strategic Plan and (11) Boating Safety Related Topics
To wit:
The safety of recreational boaters on the navigable waters of the United States is being jeopardized by the boaters' lack of access to up to date navigational charting information due to the current standard of care being exhibited by the manufacturers of recreational electronic chart display information systems. The electronic charts and associated subscription update services being offered by the manufacturers are navigationally unsafe due to being generally significantly out of date, at some manufacturers by more than one year, and the displayed charts do not provide boaters any traceability to the USCG issued weekly Local Notices to Mariners that have been incorporated.
The worldwide IMO/IHO led transition to Electronic Navigation Charting in support of SOLAS and GMDSS treaty obligations is well underway and effectively supporting the safety needs of the participating large commercial ship mariners. The United States' own National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has been leading the way in architecting a successful transition from traditional paper charts to electronic navigation charts in collaboration with its mission partners. Today, NOAA and the USCG provide ENC and LNM charting updates on a weekly cycle.
The electronic charting update infrastructure exists throughout the worldwide commercial maritime industry and is supported by the commercial manufactures of the GMDSS / ECDIS equipment. These participants access and utilize weekly updates to maritime charting information. Indeed they are mandated to utilize this update process and frequency. This weekly update process is the established international standard for ensuring the carriage of most recent navigation planning charts.
The manufactures of recreational electronic chart plotters and multi-function displays advertise that they provide boaters access to the latest charts via internet subscriptions and one-time memory card updates. The fact of it is that none of the manufacturers comes anywhere close to providing "the most recent charts". The ones that I am personally familiar with and those of my boating associates, is that the updates are generally six months to several years out of date. And even more jeopardizing to boater safety, none of the major manufacturers enables traceability of the viewed chart segment to the USCG LNMs that are incorporated.
The data and infrastructure is available to rectify this safety shortfall. NOAA / USCG provide it now to the GMDSS / ECDIS manufacturers and mariners on a weekly update basis. Not one single recreational navigational display manufacturer provides a recreational version of this weekly update service, at any price to recreational boaters. (To my knowledge)
For the purpose of establishing minimum safety thresholds, governing bodies and governments routinely establish minimum system requirements and manufacturing regulations. With the sunsetting of paper RNCs and the transition to ENCs and electronic displays, the old method of writing LNM updates on paper charts needs to be transitioned into its equivalent for electronic displays. The most likely method for this transition is to utilize the currently available weekly ENC update infrastructure.
The SOLAS participants define navigationally safe chart update frequency to be weekly.
(1) I ask the Committee to adopt the SOLAS definition for navigationally safe chart updates as the standard for recreational boating safety. And thus incorporate into the 2022 – 2027 Plan an Opportunities and Challenges - Technologies strategy. This strategy to evolve the recreational boating electronic manufactures' culture toward a practice of weekly ENC chart update availability for equipment owners. Also within the Plan promulgate associated Performance Initiatives.
The recreational marine electronics industry has not, and is not addressing the described critical navigation data recentcy gap.
(2) I am requesting this Committee, through its powers, cause a remedy to be enacted through appropriate actions being incorporated into the National Recreational Boating Strategic Plan, agenda item (6) (b) and by all other means at the Committee's disposal.

The RBS Program includes Technologies as the second of its four Challenges & Opportunities.

An additional Technology C & O for the RBS Program is evident: Improve education and training of recreational electronic navigation displays and improve boater access to up-to-date ENC data ensuring that the displayed charts are navigationally safe.

I trust that the foregoing comment will be useful to the Committee as it reviews and evaluates the 2022 -2027 RBS Strategic Plan and discusses boating safety related topics.

This is a rule that will provide greater visibility and more appropriate review of awards made under the 8(a) program. Significant taxpayer funds are awarded using 8(a) authority each year and subjecting these awards to competition or appropriate justification of why competition cannot be employed increases transparency of the process and will increase taxpayer confidence that their funds are being appropriately spent.

The parenthetical statement at FAR 6.204(b), "(But see 6.302-5 and 6.303-1 for sole source 8(a) awards over $20 million.)", is completely unnecessary and potentially confusing.  The title of the section is "Competitive 8(a)."  The sentence that precedes the parenthetical statement, "No separate justification or determination and findings is required under this part to limit competition to eligible 8(a) contractors." is always true and nothing in the rule changes that.  The use of the parenthetical statement right after the sentence makes it appear as if the preceding statement may not be true in certain circumstances.  As such, I recommend removing the parenthetical statement at FAR 6.204(b).

FAR Case 2009-043

I congratulate the attempt to clarify what is and isn’t considered a Time & Material (T&M)/Labor Hour (LH). However, the proposed language “Time-and-materials contracts and labor-hour contracts are not fixed-price contracts”, in my opinion, does not (1) clarify the issue. (2) nor, address the fact that what is actually happening is the Contracting Officer is using a Fixed Price Level of Effort (FP LOE) contract without the appropriate approval.

When a Contracting Officer uses a fixed loaded labor rate and a fixed number of labor hours the contract type can be considered either a T&M/LH (FAR 16.6) or a Fixed Price Level of Effort (FP LOE) (FAR 16.207).

Since, the LOE T&M/LH vs FFP issue not only affects contract actions under FAR Part 8 and 12, but also FAR Part 13, 14, and 15, recommend adding a definition to Part 16 that clearly defines a LOE contract and identifies that a LOE contract type is considered to be either T&M/LH, FP LOE or a Cost Plus Term (FAR 16.6(d)(2). Otherwise, Contracting Officers are likely to read the proposed change to FAR Part 16 as something they already knew and continue calling LOE contracts FFP.

Cecilia Davis stated during a telephone conversation that the intended meaning of 25.1103(e) is that 52.225-25 is applicable to ALL solicitations, not only to those for supplies and services.

"The contracting officer shall include the provision at 52.225-25, Prohibition on Engaging in Sanctioned Activities Relating to Iran--Certification, in ALL [emphasis added] solicitations."

That recommended wording will make it clear that 52.225-25 should be included in ALL solicitations, including those for construction. Concerning the question as to whether or not an agency can post a complete contract award online, the answer is yes. They already have all the permissions needed to do so. The FAR does not need to be changed to provide this level of transparency. It would have to be changed to make the posting mandatory.

If the agency has an electronic copy of a contract they can post them on a website recognizing the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) process that must be considered before this occurs. The FOIA process addresses what information should and should not be provided to a requestor. This provides a process to review and remove any information that might be proprietary, classified, sensitive, or personal in nature.

There are several agencies that post their contract award documents in their FOIA Reading Rooms if the contract has been requested at least three times and a redacted copy is available in an electronic format.

In addition, one agency posting contracts online immediately because they make purchases using published catalogs and the prices are exactly the same.

With no further guidance necessary, a contracting officer that desires to post contracts online could establish the Request For Proposals (RFP) in such a way to ask the offerors in their proposals to segregate anything that the vendor feels is proprietary keeping it in its own section or attachment of the RFP. This would enable the majority of the contract to be posted online immediately. If a FOIA is requested for the remainder of the contract, review and redaction would be made simpler by looking over just the section or attachment not posted initially.

The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) is a University Affiliated Research Center that for more than sixty (60) years has been making critical contributions to critical government challenges, under contracts with the government. JHU/APL is generally supportive of the above-referenced interim rule’s objective fostering better openness in government contracting. For the following reasons, however, JHU/APL believes that the requirement for prime contractors to report subcontractor executive compensation data is practically unworkable, and will unnecessarily significant administrative burdens, when a more practical alternative exists.

JHU/APL has dozens, if not hundreds, of subcontractors who meet the criteria established in the rule for required executive compensation reporting. In all likelihood, these same subcontractors also perform under subcontract for many other prime contractors. Under this rule, each prime will have to report the same information for each subcontractor, and each subcontractor will be forced to provide the same information to each prime for which it works, unless the subcontractor otherwise publicly reports executive compensation information. This has the potential to create an unnecessarily complicated and unwieldy reporting process, which will place significant administrative burdens on both primes and subcontractors. As an alternative, we urge the FAR Council to consider modifying the interim rule to require prime contractors to flow down the reporting requirement to their subcontractors, so that the subcontractors can report their executive compensation information directly. In this way the objectives of the rule will still be achieved, and subcontractors and prime contractors will each only have to report their executive compensation once annually.

The Government intends to implement the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act for all Government contracts over $25k through the new FAR Clause 52.204-10. This implementation will place a heavy burden on, and increase costs to, all contractors and subcontractors to the Federal Government. These additional costs will be passed on to the Government through direct and/or indirect costs in future proposals and their resulting contracts, raising the cost of these goods and services to both the Government and the taxpayer.

The Transparency Act mandated a free, public website containing full disclosure of all Federal contract award information. With the government’s annual projected costs for just reporting data to the website at over $21M, this website will not be free to the taxpayer. And, since this cost does not include the collection costs for all data for all subcontracts over $25K, which will be considerably higher for all affected contractors (and passed on to the Government in higher direct and/or indirect rates), as new processes will need to be implemented to collect, track, store, and report this data, nor does it include the Government’s cost to maintain the website, the bill to the taxpayer will be considerably higher than this $21M figure. And with this high price tag, the anticipated benefit to the average taxpayer will be, arguably, zero, as the average taxpayer will never visit or use this website. This website will be funded by the taxpayer and used by others to create statistics to support their various positions regarding Government procurement.

If this rule must be implemented, most of the additional costs incurred by the taxpayer could be saved by altering the proposed rule in many ways, including:
1)Exempt all Commercial Item (FAR Part 12) and COTS purchases – These purchases are based on commercial practices and commercial, market-driven prices. The same rationale for their exemption to FAR Part 15 requirements should be applied here. It can certainly be argued that reporting a purchase of a pick-up truck or other supplies normally purchased by the public was not the intent of the Act. The creation of these classes of purchases was based on the idea of less government regulation and the implementation of this reporting seems to be in direct conflict with this founding premise.
2)Raise the threshold to a more reasonable level – The $25k threshold for purchases will cover almost all activity occurring at the prime and first-tier levels. Using a reasonable approach and applying typical statistical models, the Government could report 80% of all contract activity by selecting only 20% of the largest contracts. This methodology can meet the intent of transparency for the bulk of dollars spent, but without the high cost and burden of reporting all purchases.
3)Eliminate the reporting of 5 highly compensated officers – If the Government awards a contract to a prime contractor, this award would generally be based on either competitive means or best value. Either of these means should eliminate the need for identifying the salary of its officers, as this is part of the competitive cost structure and of no relevance to the price paid by the taxpayer. The need for this data to be made public, which is only required for those entities that do not already report such data to the SEC, is objectionable, at best. Unless the contract is a sole-source, cost-type contract in which the Government will be obliged to pay the full salary of the company’s officers, this information should be protected, as the only reason to publicly display it on a web-site is to appease the curious spectator.
4)Add an exemption for competitively awarded, Firm-Fixed Price contracts – If contracts are competitively awarded on a firm-fixed price basis, the need for transparency is eliminated. Further reporting of these awards and their first-tier competitively awarded subcontracts simply adds no value to the taxpayer.
5)Add an exemption for small businesses – The Government has established Small Business as a special sector of business that needs special attention and nurturing to assist in its growth. Implementing these reporting criteria may especially impact these small businesses, adding costs to their structure and adding extra burden to them and their prime contractors in collecting and reporting information, including salary information, as most small businesses would not be exempt from that part of these reporting requirements. These small businesses would be particularly sensitive to reporting such salary data in the proposed public forum.
6)Clarify that only the allowable portion of the officer’s salaries must be reported – If officer’s salaries must be reported, the reported data should be limited to the allowable portion of those salaries. If a company pays its executives at a competitive rate, but disallows a portion of that salary and benefits in its indirect rate structure, the Government never pays for this portion of these executives’ salaries. As such, reporting the full salary is misleading, as it would lead the viewer to believe that the Government was paying the entire salary. As the Government already disallows certain costs and caps others, reporting of the entire salary and benefits would also conflict with existing Government policies. Finally, all of these salaries are audited by DCAA personnel and are required to be within the mandated Government maximum allowable amounts.

In summary, this proposed rule is over-reaching and creates a heavy burden on the Government’s prime and first-tier contractors. This burden may lead some contractors, particularly commercial and small business contractors, to re-assess the value of dealing with the Government, leaving this sector and, in doing so, eliminating some of the current competition. Please consider the comments above in determining the cost-benefit of implementing any final rule.

As an organization that has documented employer conduct throughout union organizing drives and its impact on workplace efficiency, American Rights at Work (ARAW) has an interest in the proposed amendment to the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) through implementation of Executive Order 13494, Economy in Government Contracting (RIN 9000-AL39, FAR Case 2009-006), and wishes to share its perspective.

ARAW supports the proposed rule implementing President Obama’s executive order forbidding federal contractors from claiming reimbursement for costs associated in any way with persuading employees to exercise, or not to exercise, their rights to organize and bargain collectively.

A 2009 report from Cornell University scholar Kate Bronfenbrenner indicates the proclivity of employers to devote a great deal of an organization’s time and money to persuading employees not to form a union. When faced with an effort by their employees to form a union:
•75% of employers hired anti-union consultants;
•89% of employers mandated employees to attend captive audience meetings during work time;
•70% of employers mailed anti-union literature to their employees;
•77% percent of employers mandated that supervisors meet individually with employees in attempts to dissuade the formation of a union;
•64% of employers interrogated employees about their union involvement and activity.
These various forms of activity represent costs to the employer that should not be imposed on the taxpayer through government reimbursement.

With reports finding that employers spend during union organizing drives anywhere between $600 to $3,700 per employee on consultants and/or lawyers alone to assist with the aforementioned union avoidance tactics, ARAW believes that proposed rule RIN 9000-AL39 will help ensure taxpayers don’t foot the bill for such wasteful spending.

By promoting efficiency, ARAW believes the proposed rule would fulfill the Administration’s goal to eliminate wasteful spending.

Re: FAC 2005-46, FAR Case 2009-028

To Whom It May Concern:
The following comments are directed at the Federal Acquisition Regulations: Encouraging Contractor Policies to Ban Text Messaging While Driving. The rule essentially updates the Federal Acquisition Regulation to include President Obama’s Executive Order 13513. Acknowledging and applying rules associated with text messaging while driving serves to promote public safety. The rule is headed in the right direction but specific language could be changed to maximize its efficiency.

Section 23.1104 (Policy) reads: “Agencies shall encourage contractors and subcontractors to adopt and enforce policies that ban text messaging while driving.” While it is a promising venture to merely “encourage” contractors, it would be a much stronger stance to make it mandatory that all federal contractors and subcontractors “enforce” these policies in states with text-messaging bans.

According to Governors Highway Safety Association (2010) roughly 30 states have already enacted text-messaging bans (www.ghsa.org/html/stateinfo/laws/cellphone_laws.html). The Federal Government could follow suit or pave the way for increased regulation of text messaging. Enforcing measures related to this issue appears to be the national trend. At worst, the enforcement of text-messaging policies could mirror those states that already have text-messaging bans. Encouragement of contractors to ban text messaging could be applied in those states without such policies.

Section 52.223-18 (ii) reads: “Privately-owned vehicles when on official Government business or when performing any work for or on behalf of the Government.” This statement refers to a segment of the population affected by the text-messaging rule. I selected it to parse out the regulations seeming ambiguity. When won’t a contractor claim he or she is on “personal” time? How will government agencies evaluate the effectiveness of their campaign to encourage a ban on text messaging? I doubt there will be a concerted effort on the part of the federal government, individual contractors, and police departments to track the tickets solicited (this doesn’t even consider states without a ban). These considerations are just a few of the many reasons an amendment should be added to the rule specifying that the ban applies to all those Federal contractors and subcontractors currently under contract with the Government. It would reduce the rule’s arbitrary nature and would make for a seamless transition if and when the remaining 20 states adopt similar bans.

Sincerely,
Austin Grout
MSW Candidate 2011
Wayne State University

I am a Foreign Service Contracting Officer with the U.S. Agency for International Development, currently serving at USAID/Russia in Moscow, with over 25 years of overseas experience. I have provided comments to my Agency representative for submission so the remarks below represent my personal view of the problems associated with application of the proposed rule overseas, particularly in the USAID context.

It is not clear why the government is correcting the problem of foreign vendor misuse of the generic DUNS number by requiring CCR registration for contractors with awards over $25,000. CCR registration is a quantum leap from obtaining a DUNS number for a foreign firm or organization. In my experience, while foreign organizations have experienced problems obtaining DUNS numbers, they can be resolved by phone with a local contact who speaks the local language.

This is not the case with CCR registration. It would not be possible for organizations who did not have a near native English speaker with some knowledge of USG procurement to successfully complete CCR registration. In addition, to do so, organizations must also apply for a NATO CAGE code. Most of the CCR fields are not applicable to foreign organizations (although they may not understand that). If this rule is adopted, it will mean that either USAID contracting staff will have to spend hours assisting firms in registering or that firms will decline to do business with USAID. It seems unreasonable for a hotel that is providing conference facilities, for example, to register in CCR.

I suggest that the CCR registration requirement only apply to acquisitions above the Simplified Acquisition threshold and that the CCR registration website be revamped to take into account foreign vendors, either with a simplifed registration form or by blacking the inapplicable fields or by providing access in other languages. I also suggest that the requirement for a NATO CAGE code be deleted for non-DOD awards.

This change obliterates more of the audit trail. Monitoring the scrap in
automated enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, such as SAP, is quite
challenging with its
grouping, pegging, and distribution (GPD) paradigm juggling inventory
between final cost objectives, based on need, and limited contractor
personnel that can readily explain the various inventory movement types. In
SAP, the transfer of material between final cost objectives is not
extraordinary, but rather the essence of the system allowing the contractor
maximum flexibility during the production process. The buy to the group,
peg to the final cost objective, and distribute to the current pegging
sounds simple, but when it is understood that all final cost objectives are
intermediate cost objectives until a point in time that the deliverable is
transacted for delivery, after DD250, does the difficulty of monitoring
emerge. There is no longer borrow/ payback transactions with GPD, if it is
determined that a final cost objective needs material and its associated
labor currently pegged to another final cost objective, it is just a matter
of changing the pegging and redistributing the costs. Since costs can only
be pegged to existing final cost objectives, determining the excess material
is just a matter of seeing the fluidly pegged material in a sea of cost
transfers. If material is currently pegged to a final cost objective it is
not considered excess, even if the requirement for the material is exceeded,
since all material is not transacted for delivery, and there will be no new
final cost objective until after the effort is awarded. So at the point in
time when the knowledge of residual/ excess inventory would be of the most
use to the Government, during proposal evaluation, it is not available. If
small business wants to resolve the tracking of scrap material, they should
do what the big businesses do and run SAP.

Stormwater Rulemaking has been lacking in cross-cutting strategies that more closely tie the stormwater rules to the varying types of land use.

Specifically, the existing stormwater rules focus on a one-rule-fits-all sites (site-based) which has not adequately considered the wide variety of contexts of the built environment. This results in stormwater rules that are typically easy to comply with in low-density developments, and particularly easy in low-density greenfield developments. The corrolary to this is that the rules disincentivize compact development and redevelopment.

The unintended poor consequence is stormwater rules that promote sprawl. These stormwater rules tend to be at cross-purposes with, and trump regional and local Comprehensive Planning and Zoning that attemtps to curb sprawl.

The Stormwater Rules would be more effective environmentally and more effective on restoration of watershed health if they aligned with State and Local anti-sprawl Land Use policiies.

The current regulatory structure in water management is a severe impediment to integrated and innovative infrastructure solutions. The CWA and SDWA were built up around a traditional model of centralized water and sewer lines and treatment plants, a system which is increasingly seen as financially and environmentally unsustainable. However, most of the integrated water, wastewater, stormwater, energy, solid waste, etc. “soft path” solutions that are being proposed for sustainability at building and neighborhood scales are regulated by states or by localities, or by federal agencies other than the EPA, making regulatory reform a challenge for EPA.

Proposed regulatory and non-regulatory solutions to this fragmentation and technological lock-in are described on the Water Alliance website (www.water-alliance.org), in particular in the study “Federal Policies to Advance Decentralized and Integrated Water Resource Infrastructure” (www.sustainablewaterforum.org)

Of particular importance to an “Integration and Innovation” agenda are the following recommendations:
Fund a study group to identify problems and solutions to the current regulatory structure and impediments, including alternatives for both incremental reform and significant new federal legislation
Develop mechanisms for incorporating soft path technologies into municipal point-source wastewater and stormwater permits
Incorporate “adaptive management” and “performance based approaches”
Explore ways to coordinate and integrate enforcement actions in surface water quality, source water protection, drinking water, groundwater, sediment and flood control, coast zone management, estuary protection and endangered species, and streamline the processes by which local communities can meet the requirements;
Develop models for state and local design codes and fund pilot projects
Appoint a Water Commission to study and recommend to the Congress better mechanisms for promoting sustainable infrastructure across agencies

A true implementation of the watershed approach, especially in urbanized watersheds, requires a balance of often competing beneficial uses.  It would be very helpful if water quality regulations recognized this reality and allowed—in cases where a sufficiently sophisticated and inclusive watershed process has been used—compliance to be based on maintaining that described balance.  For example, if an engineered flood control channel accommodates fisheries habitat, has vegetated strips to provide riparian bird habitat, includes trapping basins to implement a watershed-scale sediment management program, has recreational trails for the REC beneficial use and for education, but ultimately also needs to manage these features with a level of maintenance to sustain a planned level of flood management capacity in the channel, then the implementation of a plan that balances these many uses should be considered compliance, should not be difficult to get permits for, and should not require mitigation.

EPA rules and regulations regarding offsets is rooted in ancient history where POTWs were the primary concern. Now that the focus has shifted to non-point sources, offsets offer the best way to improve water quality for the least cost, in the least amount of time. EPA should encourage any remediation project that can offset loads by at least 2:1.

The concept of offsets is at the heart of a collaborative watershed approach, particularly with regard to nonpoint source pollution. The whole idea of stakeholders collaborating on how and where best to solve a shared problem depends on the ability to use an offset approach.

EPA’s claim that water quality-based objectives (and the related TMDL targets) supersede the BMP/MEP standard in MS4 permits should be reconsidered. This policy circumvents the legislative intent of the CWA to treat non-point sources differently.

EPA’s decision to redefine historically non-point sources (e.g. stormwater runoff) into point sources by virtue of the fact that the MS4 has a defined outfall also undermines the original intent of the Clean Water Act and creates more problems than it solves.

The total inability to consider cost-benefit or cost-effectiveness cannot continue in light of current economic constraints on the ability of state and municipal governments. There must be some ability to prioritize environmental risks. EPA’s claim that economic factors cannot be considered (except through the UAA process) is extremely counterproductive. This would change if the cost of compliance had to be shared equally (33% each) between the federal, state and local government. As long as EPA does not have be responsible for the cost, there is no constraint on what they can demand.

The need to prioritize water quality issues is foundational to the watershed approach, which EPA espouses. A central idea to the watershed approach is that there will always be many water quality challenges, and the key is having stakeholder support for prioritization. This is even more important when one realizes that beneficial uses often compete with and limit each other.

EPA should reconsider the utility of using the “most sensitive use” to govern applicable water quality standards in each waterbody. It would be better to consider a “zoning” strategy. Uses often conflict and cannot all be protected equally at each and every location simultaneously. Protecting the most sensitive use (usually COLD or WARM) elevates these uses above all others. In fact, protecting aquatic life may make it impossible to continue using the same waterbody for REC, MUN, PWR or AGR.

One alternative approach would be to allow EPA and other regulatory agencies to sit at the watershed table with other stakeholders, advocate for their interests and offer their resources, and become part of the watershed groups balanced watershed solution. Currently EPA touts the watershed approach, but after stakeholders do the hard work of balancing and prioritizing, regulatory agencies often still seek to require all regulatory requirements to be “highest” priority, which is impossible.

The radon rule was difficult to finalize due to perceived inequities. The definition of "oil in bulk" as used in the proposed regs needs to be articulated. Does the proposed language in 46 CFR 90.05-25(b) apply to flammable & combustible liquids being carried as other than cargo (e.g. for the vsl’s use in gensets, etc)?  Without a definition, the proposed rulemaking is ineffective. After the Seagoing Barge Act was implemented, G-MCO released msg P 181852Z APR 96.  This msg stated that "UNMANNED SEAGOING BARGES CARRYING HAZARDOUS MATERIAL AS CARGO MUST BE INSPECTED."  It also stated that 'UNMANNED SEAGOING BARGES CARRYING OIL IN BULK, NOT AS CARGO, ALSO MUST BE INSPECTED. FOR THE PURPOSE OF THIS EXEMPTION, THE TERM "IN BULK" IS ESTABLISHED AS A MATTER OF POLICY TO MEAN AT LEAST 250 BARRELS." This msg has often been interpreted to mean that ALL seagoing barges that carry hazardous materials, including flammable or combustible liquids, as cargo & in bulk, must be inspected, no matter how much cargo they carry. This msg has also been interpreted to mean that all seagoing barges carrying more than 250 barrels of flammable or combustible liquids such as oil, for the vessel's own consumption (e.g. diesel fuel for gensets, cranes, etc.) are not exempt from the Seagoing Barge Act & must be inspected. Paragraph 3 of the msg indicates that future changes to MSM Vol II will incorporate this policy. However, the current MSM Vol II, Section B, Ch 4, par E.1 doesn’t seem to incorporate the policy.  The regs must incorporate a definition of the term "in bulk" in 46 CFR 90. The term "in bulk" should mean the carriage of any liquid (cargo or otherwise) that is loaded on board a vessel through hoses, pipes, etc, & that is not pre-packaged in pre-determined quantities. Furthermore, the regs should clearly articulate the quantity of flammable & combustible liquid, not being carried as cargo, that would nullify exemption from the Seagoing Barge Act & require inspection. This is currently interpreted to be any amount greater than 250 barrels.

The Coast Guard proposal to finalize the regulation to require vessels to carry adequate discharge removal equipment is obviously much needed.  This proposal would significantly reduce the risk posed by vessels carrying oil or hazardous substances in bulk without creating a significant increase in the cost of business for the transporter.  It is the next logical step to convey the desired effect intended by the Oil Pollution act of 1990 (OPA 90).  OPA 90 currently requires facilities to carry adequate discharge containment and removal equipment, as well as, training and annual certification of that training and equipment.  I believe that this should also be a requirement included in the proposed regulation.    It is not enough that the vessel carry adequate discharge removal equipment on board the vessel.  The vessel also needs to create and submit a "vessel response plan", akin to the facility response plan required for facilities that conduct business of a similar nature.  This vessel response plan should require that the crew is competent in deploying the required discharge removal equipment as well as certification that the discharge removal equipment is in proper and working order.  Simply having discharge removal equipment onboard the vessel does no good if the crew does not know how to implement its use. In the event of a release, the crew of the vessel should be prepared ahead of time, and know their role and responsibility to limit and mitigate that release as well of the hazards of that release.   For example the concentration of a gasoline spill creates an explosive environment and should not be handled the same as a release of diesel.

Much of the pollution in U.S. rivers and streams today comes from the manure generated by CAFOs (concentrated animal feeding operations), which confine thousands of animals on a single site. To determine the extent of the problem and how it might be better addressed, the public and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) need to know more about these facilities and the waste they produce. But unlike many other industries, CAFOs do not regularly disclose facility-specific information to the EPA—and the powerful interests behind CAFOs want to keep it that way.

Under a recent settlement agreement, the EPA promised a regulation that would require CAFOs nationwide to report some basic facts, such as the location of the operation and number of animals housed. The EPA is now asking for public comments on a proposed rule to collect some of this data from the nation’s largest CAFOs. Having this information will vastly improve the agency’s ability to ensure that CAFOs comply with the Clean Water Act and do not contaminate our lakes and waterways.

Gathering this information is about simple transparency and protecting the environment, but industrial animal agriculture is fighting to keep CAFOs shrouded in secrecy. The industry is pressing the EPA to withdraw the proposal or limit its application.

We ask the EPA to finalize a rule that collects information from CAFOs across the country!

To Whom It May Concern:
My name is Cary Spencer and I am a Member of the Snake River Sugar Company LLC (SRSC). The Members of SRSC are growing 181,840 base acres located in Idaho, Oregon and Washington. My farm is located in Canyon County, Idaho and in 2017, I farmed 250 acres. Of these acres, 50 acres were planted to sugarbeets and the rest was divided between grain corn, winter wheat, radish and sweet corn
Sugarbeets are the fourth most important crop grown for human consumption in Idaho, exceeded only by wheat (1,196,000 acres), barley (550,000 acres), and potatoes (320,000 acres). In 2016, the SRSC harvested approximately 7,540,000 tons of sugarbeets, which produced an estimated 1,360,000 tons of pure sugar.
The sugarbeets I produce on my farm are affected by a multitude of pests. However, Curly Top, a viral disease transmitted by the sugarbeet leafhopper severely affects sugarbeets grown in our production area leading to severe crop losses. Yield losses can easily exceed 85%, especially if sugarbeets grown without seed treatments are infected early in their growth stage.
To address this extreme risk, I have to plant sugarbeet varieties that are genetically highly resistant to Curly Top and apply a neonicotinoid seed treatment, including Poncho Beta (Clothianidin 34.3% and beta-Cyfluthrin 4.6%, Bayer CropSciences LP), NipsIt INSIDE (Clothianidin 47.8%, Valent U.S.A. Corporation), and Cruiser 5FS (Thiamethoxam 47.6%, Syngenta Crop Protection, LLC). These seed treatments are highly effective on sugarbeet leafhoppers as they affect their ability to feed on sugarbeets, thus stopping virus transmission for up to 60 days.
Over the last 10 years, growers in my Cooperative have used a combination of genetic resistance and seed treatments and, as a result, losses to Curly Top disease have been negligible. In addition to the control of sugarbeet leafhoppers, neonicotinoid seed treatments offer varying levels of control of other sugarbeet piercing and sucking pests such as aphids (root, green peach and black bean), leaf miner, sugarbeet root maggot and others.
The loss of neonicotinoids, such as Poncho Beta, NipsIt INSIDE, and Cruiser 5FS, would cause the growers in my Cooperative and myself to apply less effective chemicals, resulting in overall higher application rates and frequencies. In addition, alternative pesticides belonging to the groups of carbamates and organophosphates cannot be used as a seed treatment and would need to be applied to the foliage increasing applicator exposure and the risk of targeting beneficial insects and pollinators.
A loss of neonicotinoids and the protection they provide against a multitude of sucking and piercing insects, will cause sugarbeet growers like myself experience reduced crop quality and an overall reduction in grower income.
I know these are preliminary risk assessments. However, I trust the EPA will refine, as necessary, based on sound science and field data and think through IPM and resistance management requirements.
Sincerely,

Cary Spencer

This chemical should be banned immediately in the U.S. due to non-target impacts on honeybees and other sensitive organisms. Germany, France and Italy have already banned Clothianidin because of unacceptable risks to non-target organisms and the U.S. should follow suit. Colony Collapse Disorder (CCD) is a real and growing threat to honeybees around the world that we depend on to pollinate our food supply. Continued approval of chemicals that negatively impact pollinators is unacceptable and should be illegal.
The EPA's own review outlines the toxicity:
"Clothianidin’s major risk concern is to nontarget insects (that is, honey bees). Clothianidin is a neonicotinoid insecticide that is both persistent and systemic. Acute toxicity studies to honey bees show that clothianidin is highly toxic on both a contact and an oral basis. Although EFED does not conduct RQ based risk assessments on non-target insects, information from standard tests and field studies, as well as incident reports involving other neonicotinoids insecticides
(e.g., imidacloprid) suggest the potential for long term toxic risk to honey bees and other beneficial insects. An incident in Germany already illustrated the toxicity of clothianidin to
honeybees when allowed to drift off-site from treated seed during planting."
I urge the EPA to do the right thing and permanently ban Clothianidin in the U.S. Thank you.

My name is Ernie Chandler and I am a Member of the Snake River Sugar Company LLC (SRSC). The Members of SRSC are growing 181,840 base acres located in Idaho, Oregon and Washington. My farm is located in Washington County, Idaho and in 2017, I farmed 1350 acres. Of these acres, 182.5 acres were planted to sugarbeets and the rest was divided between wheat, onions, and corn.
Sugarbeets are the fourth most important crop grown for human consumption in Idaho, exceeded only by wheat (1,196,000 acres), barley (550,000 acres), and potatoes (320,000 acres). In 2016, the SRSC harvested approximately 7,540,000 tons of sugarbeets, which produced an estimated 1,360,000 tons of pure sugar.
The sugarbeets I produce on my farm are affected by a multitude of pests. However, Curly Top, a viral disease transmitted by the sugarbeet leafhopper severely affects sugarbeets grown in our production area leading to severe crop losses. Yield losses can easily exceed 85%, especially if sugarbeets grown without seed treatments are infected early in their growth stage.
To address this extreme risk, I have to plant sugarbeet varieties that are genetically highly resistant to Curly Top and apply a neonicotinoid seed treatment, including Poncho Beta (Clothianidin 34.3% and beta-Cyfluthrin 4.6%, Bayer CropSciences LP), NipsIt INSIDE (Clothianidin 47.8%, Valent U.S.A. Corporation), and Cruiser 5FS (Thiamethoxam 47.6%, Syngenta Crop Protection, LLC). These seed treatments are highly effective on sugarbeet leafhoppers as they affect their ability to feed on sugarbeets, thus stopping virus transmission for up to 60 days.
Over the last 10 years, growers in my Cooperative have used a combination of genetic resistance and seed treatments and, as a result, losses to Curly Top disease have been negligible. In addition to the control of sugarbeet leafhoppers, neonicotinoid seed treatments offer varying levels of control of other sugarbeet piercing and sucking pests such as aphids (root, green peach and black bean), leaf miner, sugarbeet root maggot and others.
The loss of neonicotinoids, such as Poncho Beta, NipsIt INSIDE, and Cruiser 5FS, would cause the growers in my Cooperative and myself to apply less effective chemicals, resulting in overall higher application rates and frequencies. In addition, alternative pesticides belonging to the groups of carbamates and organophosphates cannot be used as a seed treatment and would need to be applied to the foliage increasing applicator exposure and the risk of targeting beneficial insects and pollinators.
A loss of neonicotinoids and the protection they provide against a multitude of sucking and piercing insects, will cause sugarbeet growers like myself experience reduced crop quality and an overall reduction in grower income.
I know these are preliminary risk assessments. However, I trust the EPA will refine, as necessary, based on sound science and field data and think through IPM and resistance management requirements.
Sincerely,

Ernie Chandler
