3. The data demonstrates that existing CCR surface impoundments do not pose an immediate safety threat.
4. The final CCR rule should not require the initiation of closure of a CCR surface impoundment or landfill if the owner/operator of the unit can demonstrate that there is a reasonable basis that the impoundment may be needed to manage wastes in the future.
5. Closure time frames for CCR surface impoundments and landfills should be derived from the facility’s closure procedures and schedules as addressed in a state-authorized closure process that is included in the facility’s operating record or in a closure plan certified by an independent professional engineer.
6. EPA should not apply the location restrictions for new units to “overfills,” nor should these expansions be subject to the liner and groundwater monitoring requirements for new units if these standards are already being met by the underlying unit.

Background

On June 21, 2010, the EPA published a proposal to regulate management of coal combustion residuals (CCRs). On November 19, 2010, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) provided comments on the EPA proposal and stated that existing TCEQ regulations and programs are effective and encourage CCR recycling. Our comments pointed out that subjecting CCRs to the hazardous waste regulations would negatively impact their beneficial use. The TCEQ stated a preference for regulating CCRs under Subtitle D of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act should EPA determine that federal regulation is necessary and appropriate. The TCEQ would like to take this opportunity to reiterate this preference.

On August 2, 2013, EPA issued a Notice of Data Availability (NODA) and Request for Comment in Federal Register/Volume 78, No. 149, pp 46940-46947. EPA is seeking comments on specific issues, including comments associated with the closure requirements for CCR disposal units, as part of the final rule development for CCR management. The TCEQ comments on some of the specific issues included in the August 2013 EPA NODA and Request for Comment are included below:
TCEQ Comments

1.Time Frame to Initiate Closure

The EPA’s proposed rule under the RCRA Subtitle D option requires that the facilities initiate closure no later than one year after the most recent receipt of waste (i.e., if the unit has not received waste for a year, the owner or operator must initiate closure).
The TCEQ recommends that the one-year deadline included in the original proposal in 40 CFR §257.100(j) be increased to at least three years. As the EPA has acknowledged in the NODA, information collected during the structural integrity assessment from several coal-fired electric utilities shows that the one-year time frame required in the original proposal is impractical and would create a number of operational constraints. Further, the NODA notes that information collected from electric utilities indicated that there may be legitimate reasons for a CCR surface impoundment or landfill to be kept idle for two to three years (or more) before waste management in the unit is resumed. Therefore, by requiring closure of the unit to be initiated within one year after the most recent receipt of waste (as originally proposed), EPA would force a facility to close the unit when there is still additional capacity to operate the existing management unit. Based on these observations, the TCEQ recommends that the EPA allow facilities at least three years to initiate closure of a CCR landfill or surface impoundment if the management unit has useful capacity and is planned to be used in the future.

In addition, the TCEQ recommends that 40 CFR §257.100(j) be further revised to include a provision for the owner or operator to request an extension to the proposed three-year time frame and provide flexibility for States to approve such extensions based on a case-by-case review and merit of the request.

2.Time Frame to Complete Closure

The EPA’s proposed rule under the RCRA Subtitle D option required that the CCR landfills and surface impoundments be closed within 180 days following initiation of closure activities.

The TCEQ agrees with the numerous comments received on the proposed rule regarding the impracticability and infeasibility of completing closure of the CCR management units within the 180-day timeline. As the EPA’s NODA and Request for Comment acknowledged, there are many factors, including the site’s operational practices, site physical features and complexities, and market conditions, that influence the closure of CCR management units. The TCEQ supports a tiered approach, based on the size of a CCR management unit, as the basis for the deadline to complete closure activities for CCR landfills and surface impoundments. The EPA’s NODA and Request for Comment includes proposals received from some commenters on such a tiered approach that can be grouped under four categories: (1) units smaller than 20 acres would be subject to a one-year deadline to complete closure; (2) units between 20 and 50 acres would be subject to a two-year deadline to complete closure; (3) units between 50 to 75 acres would be subject to a three-year deadline to complete closure; and (4) units greater than 75 acres would be subject to a site specific deadline to complete closure. The TCEQ supports consideration of such a tiered closure schedule and recommends that a provision be added to provide flexibility for States to approve additional extensions to the deadline based on a case-by-case review and complexity of the site conditions. Towards this, the TCEQ recommends a revision to 40 CFR §257.100(k) in the proposed rule to include provisions for the owner/operator of a CCR surface impoundment or landfill to request an extension to the unit’s closure schedule beyond the timeframes proposed in the tiered approach.

I object to SIP approval of this rule. I believe Federal consent decrees are not applicable requirements under Title V and should not be incorporated into Title V permits. Not all consent decree requirements are necessarily instances of noncompliance with existing requirements. If some consent decree requirements are required to be incorporated into Title V permits and/or construction permits, the consent decree requirements can be included in a permit application as a compliance schedule for the alleged non-compliance cited in the consent decree. There is no need for this additional authority.

It is also curious why the authority is limited to federal consent decrees and not also include state agreed orders.

There is ample time for the public to comment on federal consent decrees after the decree is lodged before it is entered by the court. Any requirements that are required to be put into a permit should be done as an administrative amendment without any comment by the public or EPA. Why create additional un-needed beauacracy.

This notice refers to standards initiatives driven by regulatory frameworks and often supported by accredited standards developing organizations, such as HL7. Clearly these efforts are driven by the electronic data submission programs of the FDA and focus on clinical, non-clinical and more recently pharmacogenomics domains. But currently other several standards initiatives occupy strategic positions in the international scenario (see list at http://biosharing.org/standards_view) that should be considered too, if mature. This group of grass-roots initiatives address particular (omics or other) technologies or defined domains of application (e.g. system biology, pathways) have emerged from the academic community. Such initiatives are focused on supporting tool and data interoperability through the development of three kinds of (de facto) reporting standards: ‘minimum reporting requirements (checklists), terminology and ontologies, and file exchange formats.
Domain-specific initiatives are important because they address ‘real world’ data reporting requirements; but focusing on particular communities’ interests or technologies leads to duplication of effort. The development of largely arbitrarily different standards and the mountain of technical frameworks needed to overcome it severely hinders data integration and discovery.
Above all actions a coordination is needed to help bringing these standardization groups closer to address the fragmentation issue. Although, regulatory-driven initiatives have far stricter guidelines than academia, much could be learned from exchange of ideas and practices of these sectors.

The CEN/ISO 13606 is a European norm in the public domain from the European Committee for Standardization (CEN) also approved as an international ISO standard. It is designed to achieve semantic interoperability in the electronic health record communication.
In the May 2012 ISO/TC215 Vancouver meeting the general opinion was that the 13606 is the best standard encountered in ISO in a long time. There was no discussion whatsoever about the need to have the 13606 renewed. It was decided that the revision process should be executed as swiftly as possible, meaning will take a two year process.
The overall goal of the CEN/ISO 13606 standard is to define a rigorous and stable information architecture for communicating part or all of the electronic health record (EHR) of a single subject of care (patient) between EHR systems, or between EHR systems and a centralized EHR data repository. It may also be used for EHR communication between an EHR system or repository and clinical applications or middleware components (such as decision support components) that need to access or provide EHR data, or as the representation of EHR data within a distributed (federated) record system. Such (federated) record systems can be optimized for both clinical research and population research.
Business case studies and analysis show that using the ISO 13606 in CESIL™ for clinical research, www.e-recordservices.eu, will result in 20B USD extra revenue and cost savings for the top five European Life & Sciences Companies per year. Regarding the Food and Drug Administration's seeking input from stakeholders and other members of the public on questions regarding its regulatory requirements for study data management, we provide our perspective on a subset of the questions formulated. Below we give our view regarding the following questions:

7. Are there other open data exchange standards that should be evaluated? Please explain advantages and disadvantages. What would be the impact (e.g., financial, technical, or in terms of implementation or change in business processes)?

8. What would be a reasonable phased implementation period for each recommended exchange standard? And should supporting multiple, concurrent study data exchange standards be evaluated (please explain advantages and disadvantages of this approach)? What can FDA do to help industry to be more prepared for, or reduce burden of, a migration to a new study data exchange standard?

9. FDA encourages sponsors to design study data collection systems so that relationships between data elements, as well as relationships across data domains, can be captured at the point of data entry. Describe the challenges, to and opportunities for, accomplishing this goal.

10. What other comments would you care to share with FDA concerning the general topic of data exchange standards?

The full text of our comment can be found in the file attached.

These are responses to questions 4 and 8.

4.
Switching to a data exchange standard other than SAS Transport V5 (no matter if that standard is HL7-based, ODM-based or something else) is feasible if:
- There are tools available to instantiate source (SDTM) and derived (ADaM) datasets into those exchange formats. These tools should either be open-sourced or reasonably-priced commercial software
- The new exchange standard is more flexible than the current exchange format.
- The new exchange standard is compatible with industry-standard analysis software such as SAS and R

The data exchange standard is invoked when preparing a submission; the work to ensure that study-level and integrated datasets will fit into that standard has been done prior to the submission activities.

8.
Clinical studies do not currently use any HL7-related standards during conduct or analysis. Therefore, it’s difficult to estimate a reasonable phased implementation period for HL7 standards. Regarding CDISC standards, there exist useful and practical guidance documents, tools, and presentations related to the current standards available for sponsors to follow (including the ODM model).

In general, I find BOEM’s evaluation of the impacts adequate, given what we learned from the Ocean SAMP process, as well as the recent NOPP initiative. One mistake that needs to be corrected in the EA is that green sea turtles are NOT endangered; they are threatened throughout their range except for the breeding population in FL waters where they are endangered (http://www.nmfs.noaa.gov/pr/species/turtles/). In reference to leatherback turtle nesting, it would be helpful to clarify that in U.S. Atlantic waters, nesting occurs on the east coast of FL, the Caribbean and south; rarely in TX, GA, SC, and NC (Wynne and Schwartz, 1999). While hatchling sea turtles are unlikely to occur in our waters, we do know that Kemp’s ridley sea turtles, primarily juveniles, are summer inhabitants here, specifically Cape Cod Bay. Due to the difficulty in sighting, we have very little in-water data on Kemp’s ridleys in the coastal waters of the WEA, save opportunistic sightings and reports. That said, though, the EA recognizing the window for potential impact (June–November) is accurate, so attempts to schedule activities of potential impact outside of that window should minimize the threats. One troubling aspect of the EA sea turtle section is that it tries to suggest that loggerhead and leatherback sea turtles in our region are dispersed, even while referring to a reported concentration area of leatherbacks off central Long Island (Shoop and Kenney, 1992). We have evidence that this is not an anomaly for either species, as recent reports have found both loggerhead and leatherback aggregations in multiple areas in our region. This would increase the potential impact if operations were conducted in the WEA during the June-November timeframe. I will conclude by making a call for research on the distribution of all sea turtle species, especially Kemp’s ridleys and juvenile sea turtles, in the WEA since aerial surveys are inadequate to ID these individuals.

These comments address the lease application by Southern Company to BOEM requesting permission to establish a wind energy data collection site off the coast of Georgia. Sea to Shore Alliance is a non-profit research organization whose staff have been documenting North Atlantic right whale use of the region, the only known calving ground for the species, for over a decade.

In 1994 waters off of Florida and Georgia were designated critical habitat for the right whale. Since that time, copious amounts of data on habitat use and temporal and spatial distribution of right whales in Georgia waters have been collected. While the current critical habitat designation ends 35 nm south of the proposed site, NMFS was petitioned last year to expand the critical habitat boundary to more accurately depict significant habitat. Current best available scientific data indicate the importance of the proposed area to the species. Environmental features such as water temperature, water depth, distance from shore and general distribution of right whale cow/calf pairs support the expansion of critical habitat. Data analysis and model development by NMFS support the view that areas currently outside the critical habitat designation (including the proposed site) are important for calving right whales. Additionally, a gillnet restricted area was established by NMFS in the proposed region as part of the core right whale calving area.

While we generally support the development of wind energy, we strongly request that BOEM choose the no-action alternative for this lease application. The effects of increased noise and vessel traffic resulting from construction at the proposed site would likely detrimentally affect an extremely fragile species during a critical phase of their reproductive cycle. As the only known calving ground for a species with less than 500 individuals, this is an extremely sensitive area and therefore is an unsuitable site for the requested activity.

BOEM should determine "No Action" will be taken that creates a public safety hazard on the waterway; constitutes a "taking" of fishing rights; and fails to provide a fair return to the nation for the use of the public resource.  By a change in use of the waterway, BOEM seeks to terminate existing and historic rights held by the public to the resource on which we depend for our livelihoods and food.

The Blue Cross and Blue Shield Association (“BCBSA”) submits comments on the Request for information (the “RFI”) on “Nationwide Health Information Network: Conditions for Trusted Exchange,” as issued in the Federal Register on May 15, 2012 (77 Fed. Reg. 28543).

Pleases see BCBSA’s detailed responses to ONC’s three overarching questions in our full submitted comments.

The RFI asks three questions: (1) whether it is timely for ONC to act to establish a governance mechanism for the nationwide health information network (NwHIN); (2) the advantages, disadvantages, and anticipated market impact of the potential proposals; and (3) whether ONC should consider any alternatives in place of, or in combination with, the proposals.

First, we do not believe it is timely for ONC to act to establish a governance mechanism as proposed in the RFI. The broad NwHIN definition encompasses many forms of electronic exchange, including private sector electronic exchange associated with payment and delivery reforms such as ACOs and medical homes. The governance mechanism would likely have a chilling effect on innovative private sector approaches to electronic exchange in support of essential payment and delivery reforms.
Second, we anticipate that the market impact of the potential proposals would be negative. The eligibility criteria would deter new entrants and the privacy and security standards would hinder quality improvement activities and critical payment and delivery reforms.
Third, we believe ONC should consider an alternative governance model that addresses interoperability standards – one of the main barriers to health information exchange - in the context of a specifically defined model of community-based health information exchange.
ONC indicates this is intended as a voluntary validation framework. But at least one interested public or private organization will require NVE recognition and make the validation framework de facto mandatory.

The American Health Information Management Association (AHIMA) welcomes the opportunity to comment on the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology’s request for information regarding the Nationwide Health Information Network: Conditions for Trusted Exchange, as published in the May 15, 2012 Federal Register.

The NwHIN RFI is a commendable approach to finally bringing trust to the forefront of the health information technology discussion. Your thoughtful list of specific questions will encourage a more effective conversation. This conversation is a prerequisite to a practical and trusted national network that contributes to the triple aim.

HealthURL takes the perspective of the individual patient-physician interaction in a domain dominated by vendor and institutional interests. Our advocacy is informed by over 20 years of participation in health care standards, telemedicine, and software as a clinical tool. Control of one’s personal biological information is a fundamental human right that transcends technology. Our personal boundary is no longer our skin. Scanners, implants, labs, and medical consultations are now powerful enough to threaten a person’s place in society.

NwHIN governance must balance individual interests with those of vendors and institutions. Strong and clear principles will be the foundation for any governance mechanism that engenders trust in a system as complex and technical as health IT. The Conditions for Trusted Exchange proposed in this RFI are a step in the direction of establishing the core principles, the constitution, that will drive effective governance and regulation.

The attachment presents specific comments from the individual patient-physician perspective. Collectors, amateur and professional are the source of most scientific information we have and that is published. Rare species are often widely distributed over a large or inaccessible area, the rare butterfly often not seen where human have access. The case of charlestonensis revolves around its unknown status in areas not yet surveyed by lepidopterists that should be.

To whom this may concern at USFWS; Like all of those who submitted comments here, I am concerned about the fate of Plebejus shasta charlestonensis. I am insufficiently familiar with it to know whether or not it warrants a listing; however, I am most concerned with the approach being taken to it. A blanket listing of five "innocent bystanders" that each look very little at all like the Blue does nothing to promote its conservation and sets a sloppy and downright dangerous precedent. Is FWS concerned with ideological crusades, or will it remain true to its mission of targeted efforts to protect biota populations that truly need it? In its Proposal bulletin, FWS drew a great deal of attention to the alleged threat to the Blue posed by collecting. However, by its own reported admissions, the collection of the Blue in any numbers over the past two decades has not exceeded the single digits. Nonetheless, many pages were devoted to fearmongering claims of mass commercial collection and poaching--despite absolutely no market existing for such small, drab insects. If anything is threatening P. s. charlestonensis, it is mulching/woodchipping of the slopes for the maintenance of the ski runs; however, a discussion of this was given short shrift. Even less justifiable is the assertion that five dissimilar lycaenids that are not even sympatric with the Blue within the Spring Range require protection from collecting as well. None of these five are uncommon, located near charlestonensis, or even look anything like it beyond being small butterflies. Does FWS really want to discourage scientists and amateur lepidopterists from surveying our native lepidopteran fauna and learning more about these populations and current and future potential challenges they may face? In closing, FWS has a choice before it: will it be motivated by philsophical agendas or hard, fast science?

Brian P. Banker, member of The International Lepidoptera Survey and Southeast Arizona Butterfly Association

Firstly, we don’t really know whether the “Charleston Blue” is truly threatened; its populations have not been adequately assessed to make such a claim valid. Also, the petition to protect suggests that over collecting represents the butterfly’s primary threat, but I can reliably argue that this is not the case. This subspecies was identified as a discrete population many years ago so most collectors who want it already have it, it demonstrates virtually no phenotypic variability that would encourage the need to obtain more than a few specimens, and I would be astonished to learn that it has any commercial value.

Secondly, those who would go to the trouble of searching out I. s. charlestensis will readily be able to distinguish the “real” prize from its common congeners. Although all small blue butterflies may seem superficially alike to the uninformed, those of us who know them well have no real problems making the appropriate distinction based upon microhabitat preferences, flight pattern, etc. As a general principle, to suggest that every butterfly that looks remotely like the target specimen should also be protects is ludicrous. One more comment here. It is abundantly clear from reading others' submissions on this site that there is a great lack of literacy in terminology used for describing populations. *Endangered* and *endemic* and *rare* are three entirely separate things. An endangered animal or plant is one that is facing material threats to its existence from human or natural causes. It might have a very small range or a very wide one. An endemic animal or plant is one that is naturally found in a limited or localized area. It might be very rare, reasonably abundant, or dirt-common. It might be endangered or it might be doing just great. A rare animal or plant is one that is hard for most humans to find. It may be endangered or perfectly stable, and it might be endemic or found over a very broad range. It might be genuinely of low density and it might simply be tough for humans to find owing to peculiar habits/behavior/an unusual lifecycle. Usually, barring habitat destruction, "rare" insects fall into the latter category. Call me an elitist if you will, but I fail to see any value for the public interest in uneducated individuals in the life-sciences making comments about matters they simply do not understand. The only accomplishment that will be had from willy-nilly SoA listings motivated by fear, emotionalism, or (worst of all, a philosophical agenda) is that scientists and concerned amateur entomologists and butterfly watchers will simply cease observing these creatures and monitoring the health of their populations entirely. FWS knows better than that and has a big choice to make in the very near future. Will the agenda win out, or will sound policymaking driven by application of the scientific method alone carry the day? --Brian Banker, member, The International Lepidoptera Survey (TILS) and Southeast Arizona Butterfly Association (SEABA)

As a rational being I would never condone the extinction of a genetically distinct entity. I cannot, however, support the protection of such an entity based largely on anecdotal and/or presumptive evidence. The proposed listing of the Mt. Charleston Blue considers the collection of adults as a crucial threat to this butterfly and justification for the proposed listing of five visually “similar” taxa. Like the Miami Blue (Cyclargus thomasi bethunebakeri, sensu lato), I am disappointed that USFWS is proposing to list yet another poorly-known taxon without strong indication that a collection threat truly exists.

As noted in Calhoun (2011), I strongly disagree with the protection of additional species per the Similarity of Appearance (SOA) provision. Because the collection of adults is not convincingly established as a threat to Plebejus shasta charlestonensis, the protection of “similar” species is of little value and counterproductive to our overall understanding of these butterflies in the region. Moreover, the arbitrary definition of “similar” clearly lacks an understanding of the taxa involved (see Grishin in press). In this case, the proposed protection of additional species per SOA is a hasty attempt to solve an unsubstantiated problem. A greater scientific appreciation of these butterflies would require the very type of research that these proposed listings would preclude.

Literature Cited

Calhoun J. V. 2011. Comments regarding docket No. FWS-R4-ES-2011-0043. http://www.regulations.gov/#!documentDetail;D=FWS-R4-ES-2011-0043-0042.

Grishin, N. in press. Visual keys to differentiating Spring Mountain blues (Lycaenidae: Polyommatinae). News Lepid. Soc. 54:117-120.

The proposed rule is an impressive, well-referenced document containing a wealth of information. It could be considered an excellent foundation for sparking public interest in diminutive butterflies from the Spring Mountains of Nevada, and might develop into an effective conservation program. The main obstacle to conservation efforts is that these attractive insects are still very poorly known, and without better understanding of their biology our well-intentioned efforts to protect them from hypothetical and speculative threats may well prove futile. I would hereby like to draft several ideas that may well be helpful in generating potent conservational strategies and policies.

In summary, after careful analysis of available sources I conclude that the best chance to save the Blues is through designation of critical habitat combined with detailed studies of the biology of the Mt. Charleston Blue and related species through collaborative efforts by many amateur and professional biologists, citizen scientists, naturalists, collectors, photographers, observers, and the rest of the interested public to pinpoint the true reasons for the Blue’s apparent decline. On the contrary, listing of common and abundant species of Blues as "threatened" is highly illogical and serves no purpose but to unduly discredit valuable conservation efforts and the conservationists therein (because such listing makes no common sense to the public), creates obstacles for acquiring further knowledge about these insects by citizen scientists, alienates the public, and detracts from the real causes of the Mt. Charleston Blue’s endangerment--and therefore is seriously detrimental to the honorable goal of nature preservation in general and Lepidoptera conservation in particular.

Rationalizations, evidence and references to support my conclusions are detailed in the attachment.

I am a long-time supporter and scholar of U. S. butterfly conservation. I have been writing on this topic for 45 years. I founded the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, and am the author of the Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Butterflies and other standard butterfly books. I hold a doctorate in butterfly conservation ecology from Yale University.

The listing of the Mt. Charleston blue butterfly may be warranted. However, the auxiliary listing of the lupine blue butterfly, Reakirt's blue butterfly, Spring Mountains icarioides blue butterfly, and the two Spring Mountains dark blue butterflies, on the grounds of similarity to the main species under consideration, is ill-informed and dangerous.

First, there is no intensive or commercial collecting of the taxa under consideration. The situation of a collector or enforcer mistaking the Mt. Charleston Blue for one of these other taxa is hypothetical and imaginary. I have been in the field in the Spring Mountains (Pyle, Mariposa Road, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2010); it is difficult to get into the habitat of the proposed listed species. Virtually no collectors do so.

Second, the supposed similar species are NOT difficult to distinguish from the Mt. Charlston blue. The least bit of attention to suitable field marks, available in any of several field guides, will enable any observer to easily distinguish these taxa. The supposition of mis-ID among these butterflies is a manufactured and fallacious assumption: a straw man.

Finally, the most important tool of butterfly conservation is field survey of species occurrence. The near-random listing of species supposedly similar to genuine rarities has a chilling and ultimately depressive and preventive effect on such basic faunistic data-gathering. This is a blunt object used for a precise purpose, ill-informed and poorly conceived. I oppose it in the most stringent terms.

Dr. Robert Michael Pyle

Ara ambiguus in Panama occurs in canopy forests on the Caribbean slope from Costa Rica to Colombia, on the southern Azuero peninsula and in eastern Panama and Darien provinces. Their numbers are unknown. The Azuero peninsula harbors a small breeding population, perhaps 20 - 30 adults with a similar number of juveniles. It is assumed that the density of this species in intact forests is similar to values shown for Costa Rica. However, Caribbean slope forests, once unaccessible are now being exploited. As well, the new paved Darien road gives easy access to previously inaccessible forests with consequent logging and poaching.

A. ambiguus prefers intact, low disturbance, lowland canopy tropical forests, from semi-dry to rainforest. For nesting, they require large holes at least 90 cm in diameter with preference for species that produce holes well above ground: Cavallinesia platanafolia and Dipteryx panamensis. In Panama, diet includes the seeds and fruits of over 50 species of trees, vines and orchids. However, in nesting season, they forage principally on large seeds with high levels of protein, lipids and carbohydrates, mostly D. panamensis and Hura crepitans. All timber species

Green macaws migrate seasonally in Panama as they do in Costa Rica, but it is not know the extent to which they travel.

Threats in Panama incude: Uncontrolled deforestation, est. 2% per year nationally, but higher in some areas; chick poaching including cutting down large nesting trees to remove chicks thereby eliminating long standing nesting sites; hunting for food; and killing adults for their tail feather to adorn head dresses for the popular folkloric dances in communities on the Azuero peninsula. Adults are killed for their long tail feathers, 2-4 per bird and head dresses may have as many 60 feathers.

Laws exist to protect this species, but generally not enforced. National parks exist but protect mostly forests above 600m whereas GG macaws prefer forests below that.

The comment submitted yesterday (11/20/2012) under my name is in fact not mine. It does not represent my personal views (see below) and it falsely represents the position previously submitted by the Executive Council of the Lepidopterists’ Society (11/19/2012).

Regarding the two proposals, I will speak to what I know:

1. Endangered Species. I have been an avid lepidopterist for 55 years and maintain a collection. However, I have never visited or collected at Mt. Charleston in Nevada. As a researcher I have co-authored a molecular phylogeny of North American Blues (Pratt et al. 2006. Pan-Pacific Ent. 32[3/4]:283-295) that included the Plebejus shasta shasta (W.H. Edwards 1862) population from the Sierra Nevada range in California. This study demonstrated that nominate P. s. shasta clustered with Plebejus emigdionis (Grinnell 1905) in an allozyme phylogeny. These two species belong to separate subgenera within Plebejus. The current taxonomic alignments of members of these subgenera are uncertain and need further study. Continued sampling of their populations and construction of refined distribution maps within the Great Basin are desperately needed. Despite the endemism of P. s. charlestonensis in the Spring Range of southern Nevada and its suggested threatened state, I believe it is premature to apply endangered species status to this population and effectively curtail further research.

2. Threatened Due to Similarity of Appearance. My focused research area is the systematics, distributions, and life histories of the genus Celastrina in North America. While the Celastrina sp. on Mt. Charleston are not included in the list of five other blues proposed for threatened status, I fear that they will be inadvertently lumped with this list and effectively regulated under those rules. It is nearly impossible to separate the Celastrina from those on the proposed list without capture and/or close examination. Currently, the Celastrina on Mt. Charleston [continued]

Currently, the Celastrina on Mt. Charleston are known as the cinereous azure C. echo cinerea (W.H. Edwards 1883). This arrangement is tentative, as suggested in the Pelham catalogue (Pelham 2008. J. Res. Lepidoptera 40: xiv + 658 pp.). Some of the subspecies of echo may be full species. I have visited 46 museums in North America examining thousands of Celastrina and mapping their distributions. Most of these specimens were collected by avid amateur lepidopterists who understood the need to document what occurred where and when. From examination of this vast repository, the possibility of additional unnamed taxa arose. Indeed, I have co-authored three new species-level taxa in the genus Celastrina in the last 14 years (Scott & Wright 1998. Papilio n.s., no.9, 15 pp.; Wright & Pavulaan 1999. The Taxonomic Report 1[9]:1-11; Pavulaan & Wright 2005. The Taxonomic Report 6(6):1-18). There is potentially another azure new to the United States and this may involve Mt. Charleston. I recently discovered an unpublished manuscript in the archives of the Carnegie Museum written by Harry Kendon Clench, famous lepidopterist and curator of insects at the same museum. When Clench died in 1979, he left “several papers in various states of preparation” (Brown 1980. J. Lepid. Soc. 34[2]:66-67.  One of these was a partial systematic analysis of the argiolus group of Celastrina. Based on his analysis of museum specimens, Clench planned to limit the distribution of C. e. cinerea to the western Chihuahua at least and to expand the distribution of the Mexican azure C. e. gozora from Central America & Mexico to western Texas, southeastern Arizona, and Mt. Charleston, Nevada. I believe it would be unwise to apply threatened status to the list of five blues on Mt. Charleston. This action could affect the enforcement methodology of all blues on the mountain and hinder further research on the identity and important life history aspects of Celastrina population(s) in the Spring Range.

As a veterinarian, conservationist, aviculturist, parrot "rescuer", and avian welfare advocate, I am writing to support the listing of the hyacinth macaw (Anodorhynchus hyacinthinus) as endangered under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).
 
The Hyacinth Macaw is at risk of extinction due to habitat loss, capture for the pet trade, reduced nesting sites, and meat and feather collection. Listing these animals under the ESA will help preserve the species by restricting the commercial trade and increasing funding for conservation. Their listing will hopefully result in improved evaluation and regulation of land development that would permanently destroy their habitat. It is crucial that additional regulations be put into place now before it is too late.

Profit should not play a role in determining whether or not they should be listed under the ESA. However, some of my veterinary colleagues who financially benefit from the commercialization and exploitation of these birds, with strong ties to the breeding community, would tell you otherwise. They will insist that regulations are not needed for the survival of this species. So I ask you to evaluate their source of income before determining if their comments should be taken into consideration. In addition the listing would still allow for permits to be acquired for activities that are restricted by the ESA, and allow for legitimate organizatons to continue with "business as usual".
Parrot rescue groups are concerned this would limit their ability to adopt out of state. With the escalating homeless parrot problem in the U.S., it is important rescuers have the ability to place birds wherever homes are available.

Thank you,
Dr. Kim Danoff

To Whom It May Concern: I am writing to support the listing of the hyacinth macaw as threatened or endangered under the Endangered Species Act.As described in the petition, the populations of all of these species are perilously low and the combined impacts of habitat loss, low reproduction, and trapping for the pet trade continue to threaten their survival in the wild. In addition, projects proposed by U.S. government agencies, the World Bank and other multilateral lending agencies that would impact these species if listed under the ESA will receive a higher level of scrutiny if these species are listed under the ESA.The ESA provides broad protection for species of fish, mammals, birds, and plants that are listed as threatened or endangered in the U.S. or elsewhere. Congress deemed the ESA of paramount importance not only “to see that this situation is not permitted to worsen,” but also to “reverse the trend toward extinction, whatever the cost.” While the listing of these species is likely to be opposed by individuals profiting from the commercial trafficking of these species for the pet trade, the decision to list is based on scientific merits and, “without reference to possible economic or other impacts of such determination.”Moreover, there are exemptions that allow individuals to obtain a permit authorizing activities otherwise prohibited under the ESA for scientific purposes, for enhancing the propagation or survival of the species, or for the incidental taking of endangered species,[4] therefore those with legitimate interests and ability to contribute to the protection and recovery of these species will be able to do so after receiving a permit.Once again, I urge the USFWS to add the hyacinth macaw to the list of threatened and endangered species under the ESA.

The Hyacinth Macaw(Anodorhynchus hyacinthinus) is a commonly kept and bred species in captivity. The United States captive population is in the many thousands, and the world captive population is >5,000 birds.

FWS should consider this a distinct population, as they are geographically isolated from wild counterparts. This distinct population is large in number, increasing in number quickly, and in no danger of going extinct due to longevity, high reproductive rates, and virtually unlimited captive habitat. FWS cannot possibly consider this distinct population as endangered for the reasons above.

If FWS does not find the captive population as distinct, then it must consider the wild and captive population together, as a single population. This combined population is large in number, increasing rapidly, and in no danger of extinction due to the above factors and virtually unlimited captive habitat.

If FWS still wishes to exclude the captive population, then the captive population also must be excluded from the affects of a listing, such as a ban on interstate commerce.

Listing the Hyacinth Macaw on the ESA will not provide any benefits to those Macaws in the wild that they do not already enjoy due to being listed under C.I.T.E.S. Our government has no control over what other countries do with their wildlife. Listing these birds on the ESA provides no funds for conservation projects. However, the results of listing these birds on the ESA will have serious negative effects on the Hyacinth macaws presently in the U.S. These macaws are being bred in large numbers in the U.S. Implementing the regulations under the ESA for listed birds will set in place restrictions that will cause the eventual loss of these birds in captivity, in other words, extinction in the U.S. The intent of the ESA is to protect and conserve species, not to cause extinction. The late Dr. Ulyssess Seal, the highly respected scientist in the Species Survival Commission of the IUCN, made the point that saving species requires two actions: conserving the species in the wild and breeding the species in captivity. Listing the Hyacinth Macaws on the ESA will prevent this from happening in the U.S. In 1992 the Wild Bird Conservation Act was passed into law and the Hyacinth Macaws were included under that act, which states in Section 4914 (b) "The Secretary shall seek to ensure that regulations promulgated under this section will not have the effect of deterring captive breeding of exotic birds." The ESA regulations should not be implemented in such a way that the effect results in a deterrence of captive breeding; that was not the intent of the ESA. Breeding, trading, selling for pets, transporting across state lines, should not be regulated as this will definitely deter captive breeding. Selling birds as pets and transporting birds across state lines helps provide the income to enable those breeding the birds to fund the keeping and breeding of the Hyacinth Macaws. Without income from sales, individuals do not have the ability to maintain breeding pairs of Hyacinths.

This proposed regulatory action is economically significant and would be deleterious, particularly to small businesses. The hyacinth macaw is widely bred in the United States and sale of individuals and husbandry supplies across state borders is economically significant.

Listing these birds under ESA will not aid in their conservation because they are already protected under CITES. All it will do is have a deleterious economic impact upon macaw-oriented industries (generally small businesses) such as pet supply businesses and breeders. It will also consume FWS time that would be better used for the conservation of native species where the ESA can make an impact.

I am writing to support the listing of the Hyacinth Macaw (Anodorhynchus hyacinthinus) as threatened or endangered under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

As described in the petition, populations of all this species is extremely low as habitat loss, low reproduction rates, and trapping for the pet trade continues to threaten their survival in the wild. Increasing protections under the ESA for these imperiled parrots species will help preserve them by restricting the commercial use and expanding opportunities for much needed conservation funding and awareness.

The decision to list these species is based on scientific merits and, "without reference to possible economic or other impacts of such determination" (1) will likely draw opposition by individuals who profit from the commercial use of these species for the pet trade.

However, the exemptions that allow for individuals to obtain a permit authorizing activities otherwise prohibited under the ESA for scientific purposes, for enhancing the propagation of the species, or for the incidental taking of endangered species, (2) will enable those with legitimate interests to contribute to the protection and recovery of these species to continue doing so after receiving the required permit.

For these reasons, I urge the USFWS to add the hyacinth macaw to the list of threatened and endangered species under the ESA.

Sincerely yours,
Denise Kelly,
President, Avian Welfare Coalition

(1) 50 CFR § 242.11(b)

(2) 50 CFR § 17.22

Listing these birds under ESA will not aid in their conservation because they are already protected under CITES. All it will do is have a deleterious economic impact upon macaw-oriented industries (generally small businesses) such as pet supply businesses and breeders. It will also consume FWS time that would be better used for the conservation of native species where the ESA can make an impact.

These birds are common in US aviculture and are frequently bred. Familiarity with the species by owners encourages the owners to take ecotourism trips to the range countries and to make donations to conservation programs in the range countries. Discouraging ownership, as this listing will do, will thus actually harm the conservation of the species because ecotourism and donations will decrease.

If they are listed they should be done so under a Special Rule that will not restrict their trade across state lines and no permits for ownership or sale should be required.

Adding these birds will put unnecessary stress on state and federal wildlife officers distracting them from their real focus which is protecting our local wildlife and habitat. More effort from USFWS should be directed to protecting our natural bird populations (such as the various threatened plovers and sandpipers, warblers etc.) and enforcing rules and regulations that protect them.

FWS should change the way they apply the ESA to non-native species, especially those that are already protected under CITES and/or the Wild Bird Conservation Act. There should be NO new prohibitions placed upon dealing with nonnative species. Listing under ESA for non-native species should be an "honorary" listing that shows recognition by the US Government of the precarious state of the species but does not hinder ownership in the US.
Nonnative species listed under ESA receive no additional protection by listing. As a result, the parrot species under consideration for listing are not helped and those in the USA who care about them are hurt: researchers are hurt (gotta get yet another permit to import samples and fewer US admirers of the species to provide donations), vets are hurt (fewer parrot owning clients), pet owners are hurt (harder to obtain the species for pets), aviculturists are hurt (harder to obtain breeders and sell offspring), businesses that provide supplies are hurt (fewer owners to buy supplies), and parrot charities and clubs are hurt (fewer members).

Bird sellers argue that restricting domestic shipment and sale of these animals would increase illegal animal demand. They think that someone who is angry at having to comply with one law will instead do something even more illegal. They're not going to violate the law by carrying a bird across state lines, but will instead buy one imported illegally, without papers at all? Pass the Thorazine. Vendors do have some viable arguments against adding macaws to the list. The single-mindedness of FWS in not recognizing the reality of life here on earth--the fact that humans have been keeping animals as pets for millennia--in making it virtually impossible for normal people to move those animals around, might very well have a negative effect on the genetic makeup of captive breeding populations. The bird lobby claims that is the case; there may be some truth here. Regardless of whether you like it or not, captive populations do represent a reservoir of individuals that might very well be critical in the future to species survival. It makes sense to avoid inbreeding, but, due to the paperwork nightmare, that may have already occurred in some cases.

What we need is to have the birds added to the domestic ESA list, BUT: we need to remove the restrictions on the movement of such birds and we need to lessen the paperwork nightmare. The reality is that those birds are here to stay. We can reduce illegal wildlife trade, as well as keep an eye on inappropriate aviculture, by creating a registry of ALL such animals. It's in the long term interest of the species that we know as much as possible about the remaining individuals: I want more than a registry; I want a genetic database. Just require that every single macaw have documentation, and get off your high horse about some of them being pets; then you'd protect the species even better. If every single bird had to have documentation, the smugglers would be unable to sell their goods at all.

I view listing as a perversion (noun: The alteration of something from its original course, meaning, or state to a distortion or corruption of what was first intended) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and unnecessary, redundant legislation for the following reasons:
1) The hyacinth macaw is already listed and protected under CITES, which the U.S. honors in accordance with Section 2.a.4.F of the ESA.
2) The proposal does not in any way support the purpose of the ESA as defined in Section 2b, as there are no discrete conservation programs associated with this listing, making the listing arbitrary and superfluous in nature, as the U.S. government already supports CITES.
3) The proposal, through lack of associated conservation programs, and by negatively impacting current breeding activities (hence conservation) of the hyacinth species in the US by unnecessarily increasing permitting and restriction of ownership, clearly does NOT support ESA policy defined in Section 2(c).
4) The proposal, through loss of breeders and owners (you can't successfully breed unless there is an outlet for production) would contribute to the further decline of total global hyacinth population, shrinkage of the gene pool in remaining breeding population, loss of small businesses dependent upon the small but viable hyacinth industry, loss of public awareness for conservation efforts, ecotourism, and conservation donations, to name a few of the down road impacts.
5) Most importantly, U.S. listing would do nothing to conserve the hyacinth in its home range of Brazil, Paraguay, and Bolivia or further hamper unsustainable exploitation resulting from remaining illegal trade in those countries. All impact would be negative for the U.S. owners, breeders, and birds (birds would suffer if their firmly established bird-human bonds were severed) of the current U.S. captive hyacinth population. I see no winners in this proposal.

To Whom it May Concern:

There are a number of problems with listing parrot species on the Endangered Species Act.

First, the Act is intended to dedicate funds to the protection of the species on its list. This makes little fiscal or logical sense to do with species that are native to other countries, as their natural habitats are outside of our control. Additionally, we have plenty of native species that are not receiving the attention or funds they need for proper conservation at this time. Any funds that would go to parrots would be taking away from species that are more rightly under US jurisdiction.

Secondly, adding parrots to the ESA has already proven to be harmful to those species. The restrictions on ownership and interstate transport are so severe that breeders can no longer afford to devote their efforts to those species, which ends up by greatly reducing the domestic populations of those birds. This has been shown by the Golden Conure, which was being bred quite successfully in captivity prior to its inclusion on the ESA. Even for those who do continue to breed for conservation, the restrictions affect their ability to preserve genetic diversity by getting new individuals from other breeders, which hurts the species in the long run.

Additionally, if a parrot becomes difficult or impossible to obtain legally, that gives more incentive for poaching and smuggling from their native countries, which further hurts wild populations.

In short, no currently extant parrot species is native to the United States and should not be added to the ESA. If they are, they need to be added with a special rule that allows interstate sales and transport without the harsh restrictions that make it impossible for the species to remain viable in captivity.

Please list Florida bonneted bat as an endangered species. The bat is evolutionarily distinct, geographically isolated, and increasingly rare at a time US bats are under extreme threat from habitat destruction and White-nose Syndrome. Most North American bat species only have a single pup each year, making the risk of extinction greater due to their slow population growth and the need to act all the more urgent. Listed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature as a critically endangered species and on the state endangered species list for Florida, there is no reason to preclude the species from federal protection as well.

This is not the first time this bat has been considered for federal protection. The species has only been found in a handful of counties, including as fossils from the late Pleistocene. Since that time, it is very likely that the range of this species has contracted as urbanization and other threats have continued to mount. Until recently, the Florida bonneted bat was beloved to be a subspecies of a more widespread mastiff bat. However, sufficient evidence now exists that the population of bonneted bats in Florida are unique enough to be considered a separate species. In many ways, we know less about this species than we did when it was first considered for protection. For instance, almost all recorded colonies have been found in artificial roosts or in urban structures and historically known colonies have declined. An acoustic survey in 2006 in Coral Gables found only three calls from the species.

This bat species has already been believed to be extinct several times, most recently in 2002 when a colony was found in Fort Myers. I understand that bats are not popular, but I hope that the FWS will grant this unique species the protection it deserves despite pointless popularity contests. The Florida bonneted bat should be listed as an endangered species because it is evolutionarily distinct, geographically isolated, and increasingly rare. Population estimates number the entire species in the hundreds or low thousands, making it one of the most critically endangered species on the continent. Most North American bat species only have a single pup each year, making the risk of extinction greater due to their slow population growth and the need to act all the more urgent. Listed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature as a critically endangered species and on the state endangered species list for Florida, there is no reason to preclude the species from federal protection as well.

This is not the first time this bat has been considered for federal protection. The species has only been found in a handful of counties, including as fossils from the late Pleistocene. Since that time, it is very likely that the range of this species has contracted as urbanization and other threats have continued to mount. Until recently, the Florida bonneted bat was beloved to be a subspecies of a more widespread mastiff bat. However, sufficient evidence now exists that the population of bonneted bats in Florida are unique enough to be considered a separate species. In many ways, we know less about this species than we did when it was first considered for protection. For instance, almost all recorded colonies have been found in artificial roosts or in urban structures and historically known colonies have declined. An acoustic survey in 2006 in Coral Gables found only three calls from the species.

This bat species has already been believed to be extinct several times, most recently in 2002 when a colony was found in Fort Myers. No less amazing than rediscovery of the ivory-billed woodpecker, I hope that the FWS will grant this unique species the protection it deserves before it suffers a similar fate.

I completely support the finding that E. floridanus should be listed as endangered and that, without conservation efforts, will likely go extinct throughout its range. Data – the materials are extremely thorough and include all information (published and non-published) I am aware of that is relevant to the species. I found that the conclusions drawn were reasonable, possibly even conservative. Given the extremely small population size, small geographical range and low reproductive rate of this species makes extinction highly probable. The proposal also includes all of the potential threats to the species, most importantly: loss of habitat (especially forested areas), lack of regulatory mechanisms particularly when in contact with humans, and likelihood of stochastic weather events in south Florida. I also agree that at this time more information is required to determine critical habitat for this species.
Additional Information – I have two additional comments to the proposal. First, although we do not know what the minimal viable population size of E. floridanus is, I would predict a strong Allee effect at low population sizes for at least two reasons. One – offspring survival in bats is usually highly correlated with maternity colony size due to thermoregulation. Thus, although colony sizes are relatively small in E. floridanus (compared with T. brasiliensis) Low offspring survival is expected if females were roosting solitarily or in even reduced numbers (less than ten individuals). Two – roost sites function as information centers for many species of bats including the molossid Molossus molossus (Dechmann, D.K.N, et al. 2010. PLoS One 5:e0192). My personal observation at one of the colonies at Babcock-Webb is that this species is highly social (much like T. brasiliensis, Bohn, K.M., et al. 2008. JASA 124:1838 - 1848), which may have an effect on its viability at low population sizes. Second, as a resident of Miami-Dade county public education on bats is crucial.
Given their alarmingly low numbers and the critical decline of bats in general, it is very important to protect these last remaining few.  Please list them and protect their habitat and numbers!

The unwarranted listing of Florida Bonneted Bat (Eumops floridanus) (FBB) as an endangered species would result in an irresponsible exposure of the public in south Florida to an increased risk of exposure to West Nile virus, Dengue Fever, Saint Louis encephalitis and Eastern Equine encephalitis and other mosquito transmitted diseases. In my opinion, the publications, unpublished data and survey information outlined in the Federal Register provide sufficient justification to list the Florida Bonneted Bat as Endangered under the U.S. Endangered Species Act of 1973.

The Florida Bonneted Bat is a unique endemic mammal species which has an extremely restricted range in south Florida (Timm and Genoways 2004). It is so rarely encountered by researchers that it was recently presumed to be extinct (Belwood 1992 ).

Relating to the material presented in the Federal Register discussing the Florida Bonneted Bat, I have the following observations:

Also, the Gray Bat (Myotis grisescens) is known from only a half dozen caves in northern Jackson County, and may now be virtually gone from the state (Gore et al. 2012). In addition to data previously provided to the USFWS, from June 2012 to November 2012, I conducted acoustical bat surveys on 39 nights in and around Everglades National Park (ENP).  Eumops floridanus was detected on 4 of these surveys as follows:23 August 2012, L-31N  Proposed FPL Corridor canal, mixed habitat; 5 October 2012, ENP Main Park Road, wet prairie habitat; 11 October 2012, ENP Main Park Road, pine rockland, tropical hardwoods; and 15 October 2012, L-31N  Proposed FPL Corridor, canal, mixed habitat. Please note the following correction needed in Table 1 – Locations and Habitat Types Recorded or Observed for Florida Bonneted Bats (2003 – 2012).  The third site listed, the “L-31N Florida Power and Light (FPL) corridor, eastern boundary ENP”, is a proposed transmission line corridor currently under review and assessment.  The present ownership is public and managed by the National Park Service (NPS) and the South Florida Water Management District (SFWMD). In the interest of refining our understanding of foraging habitat of the Florida bonneted bat, I reviewed all acoustic files available to me, from 2000 to the present, that were identified as belonging to the bonneted bat.  This review did not reveal any definitive “feeding buzzes”, a feature presumed indicative of successful foraging.  I also queried biologists in South Florida conducting acoustic surveys for the Florida bonneted bat, and they confirmed that they had yet to identify a feeding buzz attributable to Eumops floridanus. The ecomorphology of the Florida bonneted bat, and Eumops spp. in general, suggests a bat that flies high, relatively fast, and quite possibly far.  Those characteristics confound acoustic detection, including capturing feeding events as indicated by the “feeding buzz”.  It is not unreasonable to consider that the Florida bonneted bat may forage some of the time (if not frequently) at altitudes beyond the range of detection by acoustic survey equipment.

The Services propose to effectively put into their official policy an interpretation of "destruction or adverse modification" which holds that the Services will examine site specific impacts to designated critical habitat in reference to the entire area of designated critical habitat. This rule would codify the holding of the Ninth Circuit's decision in Butte Environmental Council v. Corps of Engineers, 620 F.3d 936 (9th Cir. 2010).

Under the proposed new rule one of the Services could conclude that, for example, a project eliminating 250 acres of designated critical habitat (as in the Butte case) would not "destroy or adversely modify" critical habitat because loss of those 250 acres would not be sufficient to completely eliminate the recovery function of the entire (and much larger) area designated as critical habitat for a particular species.

There are two problems with definition, one legal and one practical.

As a legal matter, the ESA defines critical habitat as the area essential for the conservation of a listed species. Since conservation means recovery under the ESA, critical habitat means the area essential for a species' recovery. If it is possible to eliminate 250 acres (in the above example) without precluding or significantly delaying development of the physical habitat attributes needed for a species' recovery, such a determination is effectively saying that those particular acres are NOT essential for the species' recovery. This finding is thus the same as concluding that the area being impacted is NOT critical habitat because it is not essential to the species' recovery. In such an instance, the appropriate action by the Service would be to amend its critical habitat designation for the species in question to remove those areas not essential for the species' recovery. However, if those 250 acres of habitat are indeed essential to the species recovery and thus were properly included in the species' critical habitat designation, the plain language of section 7(a)(2) precludes any actions that would "destroy" or "adversely modify" those specific 250 acres of critical habitat -- along with all other acres properly included in the critical habitat designation because they are essential to the recovery of the relevant species. Therefore, the Services' proposed interpretation of "destruction or adverse modification," which would permit elimination of the 250 acres of designated critical habitat so long as it is a small part of a much larger critical habitat designation, is inconsistent with the ESA itself.

As a practical matter, even if the Services' proposed definition of "destruction or adverse modification" were allowed under the ESA (and it is not), the Services have no means to implement this definition. If the Services deem it acceptable to allow elimination or adverse impacts to specific areas of designated critical habitat so long as the entire designated critical habitat continues to serve a recovery function, the Services need two things: 1) a system to keep track of all additive adverse impacts to designated critical habitat, regardless of whether those impacts are caused by federal or non-federal actions; and 2) a clear determination of the bare minimum condition of the entire designated critical habitat necessary for the entire designated area to serve a recovery function for the relevant species. The Services have never -- in the past or present -- developed either one of these necessary elements of their proposed approach to determining destruction or adverse modification of critical habitat. Moreover, the Services lack the resources and information to develop a scheme to keep track of all additive adverse impacts for all designated critical habitats.

The Services should instead develop a definition of "destruction or adverse modification" that focuses on the net adverse impacts to critical habitat. If a proposed agency action would destroy or adversely modify even one acre of designated critical habitat, such an action would be precluded by the plain language of section 7(a)(2). However, if a federal agency developed a means to mitigate this impact such that its action would have no net adverse impact on designated critical habitat, it would not constitute destruction or adverse modification under section 7.

The State of Utah has reviewed the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Services) proposed rule for Implementing Changes to the Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat as published in the Federal Register on May 12, 2014. Most of the proposed amendments will lead to overregulation of both public and private lands without providing substantial benefit or protection to listed species. Rather than clarifying procedures, the Services are simply creating for themselves broad discretionary authority to designate more areas as critical habitat without regard to scientific evidence, or effects on property owners and local economies. The state specifically requests these proposed amendments be withdrawn and the original language set forth by Congress remains intact to define, regulate and designate critical habitat.
The proposed rule would eliminate flexible language governing critical habitat designations. For example, the rule proposes to remove the words where appropriate from the Scope and Purpose section because the Services believe that circumstances when critical habitat designation will be deemed not prudent are rare. This statement is disingenuous, as only 44% of federally listed species currently have designated critical habitat. Therefore, the reverse is actually true, because the majority of federally listed species do not currently have designated critical habitat. There are several practical and scientific reasons why critical habitat designation is not necessary to assist a species towards recovery including, but not limited to: species habitat is currently on protected lands, critical habitat is not found within the borders of the United States, a lack of essential life history information at the time of listing, current threats include disease or overutilization which would not be affected by critical habitat designations, and/or species is a habitat generalist which is not tied to any specific piece of land. Simply said, a case where critical habitat designation is not necessary is not a rare occurrence and is, in fact, a frequent circumstance for federally listed species. The original wording of this section should be maintained, as Congress intended, to allow flexibility in designating critical habitat based on the best available science. The words where appropriate should be maintained in the Scope and Purpose Section because the phrase clearly constrains the Services from designating critical habitat where it is not appropriate, and, as demonstrated above, there are many instances where critical habitat is not appropriate.
The Services propose to define the phrase geographical area occupied by the species as the geographical area which may generally be delineated around the species occurrences, as determined by the Secretary (i.e., range). As this proposed definition is meant to provide clarity and encompass what scientific literature refers to as a species range, the Services should actually use the term and definition of range instead of creating a new term and definition. Also, repeating area in the definition of geographic area occupied by the species is redundant and uninformative. It is generally discouraged to use the same terms in the definition of a phrase that appear in the phrase itself.
More troubling is that the proposed definition leaves broad interpretations of facts to the Secretary and expands the areas that could be designated as critical habitat. As written, the definition will dramatically expand occupied critical habitat designations into areas historically considered unoccupied. In determining the geographical area the Secretary has the prerogative to include areas used throughout all or part of the species life cycle, even if not used on a regular basis (e.g., migratory corridors, seasonal habitats, and habitats used periodically, but not solely by vagrant individuals). Further, the proposed rule also defines occupied as areas that are used only periodically or temporarily by a listed species during some portion of its life history, and is not limited to those areas where the listed species may be found more or less continuously. With this expansive language, the proposed definition conflicts with the ESA's stated purpose to restrict critical habitat designations to habitats that are representative of the historic geographical and ecological distributions of a species. ....
See Attached State Response Letter for complete comments.

The Services' attempt to claim broad discretion to set the scale of a critical habitat designation also conflicts with their obligation to use the best available scientific information in designating critical habitat.

Today, through GIS databases and other computing and analytical tools, the Services are better equipped and able to identify specific areas actually meeting the criteria for designation of critical habitat than ever before. Given these tools, it would be contradictory and arbitrary for the Services now to be unwilling to use satellite data, GIS information and other resources at their disposal to differentiate between areas in which the necessary features are and are not present.

In addition, the exclusion process under section 4(b)(2) requires that the Services review habitat designation at a scale of detail that would allow individually owned parcels to be excluded. Broad scale designations undermine a landowners reliance on certainty regarding which particular area of the landowners lands are within critical habitat designation or excluded from it.

In their description of the purpose of the proposed rule, the Services state that the amendments are intended to add clarity for the public, clarify expectations regarding critical habitat and provide for a credible, predictable, and simplified critical habitat designation process. Instead, these amendments attempt a broad re-orientation of the scope and purpose of a critical habitat designation.

The Perry County Soil and Water Conservation District Board is a strong advocate of conservation practices in all areas of the community. Soil conservation and water quality are the main objectives, but wildlife and other natural resources are also very important to this board. Sediment loads and contaminates attached to the soil are the largest problem for water quality. The soils of the county are very productive but also have a very high potential for erosion. The agricultural production is a significant portion of the community economy. Loss of agricultural products will have a huge impact on the local economy.

Conservation tillage, cover crops, vertical drains, ponds and other conservation practices are commonly used on the vast majority of agricultural production in the area providing runoff to cave systems in this karst area. All of these practices reduce the soil erosion, sediment load, and contaminates moving with those sediments to improve the water quality in those caves and stream where they drain. The goal of health reform through practice innovation and increased transparency requires effective competition, including competition for EHR services. Regulation, so far, has reduced competition as vendors use it to lock-in institutions and institutions use it to restrict practice innovation by physicians and patients.

Stage 3 is the last chance for the highly visible, intrusive and expensive federal regulations to drive real competition, interoperability, and innovation through effective bidirectional access with patient authorization. Vendor lock-in and institutional inertia will respond when EHRs are open to _incremental_ competition from external services for decision support, care coordination, outcomes registries, message filtering, summarization, and alerts.

Stage 3 must enable individual physicians and patients to substitute apps and services for every major clinical function of a certified EHR.

Incremental substitutability is best served by a common access authorization mechanism capable of bidirectional transport and single-sign-on security. Although important, content standards, are secondary. Privacy and security will be enhanced as market forces are enabled by substitutability.

Comment 1: Stage 3 certification should require bidirectional real-time RESTful interfaces based on OAuth 2.0, single-sign-on based on OpenID Connect, and global voluntary patient identifiers based on a Direct address as a low-cost, privacy-preserving and patient-accessible link.

Comment 2: Stage 3 certification should apply RESTful APIs, OAuth, OpenID Connect and Direct patient IDs consistently and uniformly across all of the mandated external interfaces. These include: decision support, registries, patient messaging, referrals, and imaging.

Comment 3: Stage 3 should support the primacy of the physician-patient relationship by enabling individual physicians to “white list” specific external services and patient endpoints that they take responsibility for.

This appears to be language that is derived from the S&I Framework Health eDecisions initiative (for which Zynx is a Committed Member).

Comment #1: In order to fully meet the challenge of making CDS interventions more easily shared, implemented, and updated, EHRs should also be able to export CDS interventions (not just consume/import them). Without the ability for EHRs to export CDS interventions, healthcare organizations will not be able to leverage 3rd party CDS customization tools. Additionally, multi-facility healthcare systems with multiple EHR vendors would be unable to share homegrown CDS interventions across EHR systems. I believe that the spirit of Health eDecisions is to allow CDS interventions to be shared between any 2 entities, and this requires bidirectional flow of information. My recommendation is to call out the need for EHR vendors to both consume CDS interventions from central repositories and to be able to export CDS interventions to facilitate sharing and ongoing editing in 3rd party software systems.

Comment #2: Clarification on "preference-sensitive care lists" would be helpful (I am a physician and do not know what that means). Health eDecisions specifically defines rules (already mentioned in the examples), order sets, and documentation templates within the scope of Use Case 1. If that is the intent, then it would be helpful to say "order sets and documentation templates" (or whatever is intended as the allowable CDS interventions) instead of "preference-sensitive care lists".

RE: ONC08 Questions - A key source of evidence that EHRS and HIE technologies can support exchange and enforcement of standards-based patient consent directives are the ONC Data Segmentation for Privacy (DS4P) pilots.  Three pilot teams led by VA/SAMHSA, SATVA, and NetSmart, which are teaming with providers, vendors, and HIEs, have already demonstrated the ability to used standard terminologies to "tag" a Meaningful Use (MU) compliant C32 and CCDA in accordance with the HL7 Consent Directive CDA.  The pilots have demonstrated or are developing exchange capabilities that conform to DS4P implementation guide.  Notably, both the "Push" and the "Pull" exchange capabilities utilize current and emerging MU exchange approaches for Direct and federated exchange.  In addition, the standards-based semantic labeling (tagging) of clinical facts, which are the discreet elements used to construct a CCDA, with clinical terminologies and provenance is already a MU EHR required capability.  The DS4P pilots demonstrate how these "tagged" clinical facts are consumed by the security labeling services or Access Control System Policy Information Point (PIP).  The PIP also invokes the governing privacy policies and patient consent directive to control enterprise user access and to construct a CCDA for disclosure, which either redacts, masks, or tags a clinical fact (at the CDA header, section, and entry level) with security labels that tells the receiver how to comply with policies that govern the disclosure.
