The NPRM recognizes the need to test and certify the accuracy of Clinical Quality Measure calculations, and has requested public comment on the best way for CQM test data sets to be developed.

Due to the complexity of CQM calculation logic, thousands of test patient records are likely to be required for adequate testing and calculation of each CQM, making manual entry of test patient data impractical. The number of patient records required to adequately test EHRs for certification purposes rises significantly with measure complexity.

One approach ONC may want to consider for CQM accuracy testing would require EHRs to import a set of standard test records that exercise each data element and permutation of measure logic. This ‘Gold Standard Test Set’ would be required for testing and certification of the CQM reporting function.

To achieve this goal, ONC may want to consider:

1) A way for vendors to easily and consistently import large numbers of test patient records. Such an ‘Import Specification’ developed for the purpose of CQM reporting, would populate the record fields that support the content needs for Clinical Quality Reporting testing and certification. Such a test data Import Specification could also form the basis for a minimum data set that captures the information required to accurately calculate CQMs.

2) EHRs should be required to incorporate this CQM test patient data using the ‘Import Specification’ in an automated way.

3) The ‘Gold Standard Test Set’ should be of sufficient quantity and diversity to assure the accuracy required for testing and certification of CQM calculation and reporting.

The stage 2 measure definitions would benefit from more careful scrutiny with regard to pediatric applications. Specific areas of concern include:

1. Small number of measures that cover pediatric core practices as opposed to primarily adult disorders appearing rarely in pediatrcs. Addition of pediatric-oriented measures prior to implementation would benefit both institutions and patients by allowing focus on quality of adoption in ways applicable to the majority of patients seen at pediatric institutions.

2. Denominators for many measures start at 18 years of age, despite the prevalence of target conditions being low at ages under 30-40. Since pediatric practices and institutions commonly see patients into their 20s, and more rarely older patients with "pediatric" diagnoses (e.g. congenital heart disease, embryonal tumors), this is burdensome for pediatric practices in two ways:
a. denominators are small, meaning it is neither a wise investment of clinical nor HIT resources to implement significant screening for conditions with a very low likelihood of positivity
b. small denominators lead to larger variability in measures due to patient-specific "random noise".
Rather than implementing these measures for all populations with any patients >18 yo, consider waiving the measure for practices having <5% or <1% of patients over this age. Similarly, consider including patients >18 years old in child-targeted measures for pediatric practices, as these more accurately reflects the practice's adoption of the EHR and related workflows.

As ranchers, if this rule is finalized, every federal grazing permittee within the area of critical habitat for jaguars will immediately have to have their grazing permits reapproved. Both mountain ranges have been habitat for jaguars in the past, with documented sightings as early as 1904 and off and on since then.
As habitat continues to be developed and the climate continues to change, protection of intact habitat with connectivity to breeding populations will be increasingly important.
The major threat to jaguars in both the Santa Rita and Patagonia mountains is proposed mining. In the Santa Ritas, Augusta Resources, a Canadian-based mining company proposes to excavate a massive open pit copper mine that will be over half a mile across rim-to-rim and more than a half a mile deep. The amount of rock that will be removed will weigh the same as 18,000 aircraft carriers. In the Patagonia Mountains, Forest Service officials are in the early stages of evaluating as many as 11 mining proposals that would affect thousands of acres of national forest lands.
Along with the direct destruction of habitat, these mines will affect water quantity and quality, trigger the development of many new roads and the widening of existing roads, cause significant amounts of noise, vibrations and lights and increased number of people and traffic, all of which will adversely affect jaguars.
Indeed, the Arizona Game and Fish Department has stated that the proposed Rosemont Mine alone would “render the northern portion of the Santa Rita Mountains virtually worthless as wildlife habitat and as a functioning ecosystem, and thus also worthless for wildlife recreation.” The multiple mines proposed in the Patagonia Mountains would significantly exacerbate the problem. Thank you.

I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to expand and make biologically meaningful its proposal for designation of critical habitat of jaguar in the American Southwest. A much greater critical habitat than that currently proposed is necessary for FWS to fulfill its responsibility to facilitate the recovery of the jaguar in America, in which it maintained extensive populations prior to European settlement. The FWS has illegally refused to protect the jaguar for several years, despite the fact that the jaguar ranged across all or most of Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas, and this vast range clearly represented a distinct population under the Endangered Species Act. The interagency Jaguar Conservation Team identified and mapped millions of acres of suitable habitat in 2006, and FWS must designate these areas as critical habitat, a task that is far past due. The draft critical habitat proposal, limited to a few mountain ranges along the Mexican border, does fulfill this habitat need.

The new critical habitat designation must at the very least include the Sky Islands and the Gila/Mogollon Rim regions of Arizona and New Mexico, areas that are conspicuously absent from the draft proposal. The Sky Islands have been the setting to the most recent jaguar sightings, and offer a strong base for recovery. The Gila National Forest and the Mogollon Rim were the location of the last plausible jaguar reproduction in the US several decades ago, and certainly the last known female jaguar until 1963, and offer suitable prey sources. The FWS has also egregiously erred in excluding the Chiricahua Mountains in Arizona from protection, considering the known existence of a jaguar there as recently as 1986, as well as the Animas Mountains, the location of a photographic sighting in 2006.

These most recent locations of jaguars are the animals themselves indicating where their ecological instincts will guide them, and where the FWS must designate critical habitat, regardless of the exploitive wishes of companies that would destroy the jaguars' rightful home. A significant amount of this potential habitat is under imminent threat, including from the "Rosemont" copper mine proposal in the Coronado National Forest. This makes the designation of critical habitat a more compelling obligation of the FWS, not less, as the purpose of this designation is specifically to avert such threats of biodiversity destruction as the Rosemont copper mine.

There still exists hope and potential for the remaining deserts, canyons, and woodlands of the Southwest to welcome the jaguar back to its historic home, if FWS will meet its legal duty to make it happen. Contrary to the assertions of the prior Administration’s FWS leadership, the range of the jaguar across Latin America neither obviates nor interferes with the FWS role in recovering the jaguar in the southwestern US as a substantial reproducing population. Many other wide-ranging species, such as the bald eagle and peregrine falcon, have been listed and recovered in the US, and indeed are icons of the ESA’s efficacy.

As a former resident of New Mexico, I know firsthand the vast habitat offered by the coniferous forests and sprawling mountain meadows of the Gila National Forest, and that its ecological vitality and integrity of the Gila would be greatly enriched by the presence of jaguars. The absence of top predators is a great malaise afflicting western ecosystems, and the Gila is sadly no exception. The Gila would benefit greatly from a renewed jaguar presence that kept deer and elk actively moving, rather than mowing down riparian zones at will, as they are wont to do in the absence of predatory surveillance.

Again, please designate the full extent of the Jaguar Conservation Team’s identified area as critical habitat, and develop a binding recovery plan for the jaguar in America, where it belongs and deserves to live again. Thank you for your attention to this issue.

The designation of critical habitat for the jaguar, a magnificent component of our native fauna, is an extremely welcome event. No critical habitat designation is absolutely perfect. While the currently proposed plan has many positive points, it also excludes certain essential areas, the inclusion of which would greatly bolster the habitat plan and significantly  increase the jaguar's prospects for again becoming a functioning component of our natural environments. The current designations are restricted to the southernmost 'Sky Islands.' These are essential initial points of refuge for any jaguars dispersing northward from Mexico. Even in this first tier of designations, there is at least one important omission:  the Chiricahua - Dos Cabezas mountain complex.  This chain is documented former jaguar habitat, it remains largely in its natural state, is relatively isolated from urban areas, and it provides an important migration corridor into the interior of Arizona. Going beyond the southern tier of Sky Islands, there needs to be habitat plan that at least offers the prospect for a sustainable population of jaguars in the U.S. A population that must cling precariously to a string of mountains virtually on the border, has little prospect for remaining viable over the long term. It would be unduly dependent upon stragglers arriving from Mexico at random intervals, with at least some of those individuals later returning to Mexico, as has happened. There needs to be a second tier of designated regions farther north that offers at least the prospect for population aggregation and stability over time.  The Mogollon Rim region, which is clearly (and repeatedly) historically documented jaguar habitat, would be the preferred area for inclusion in the designated habitat plan.  This area still retains the essential characteristics required for jaguar establishment and survival. Its inclusion would greatly strengthen the plan and increase jaguar prospects for the future.

DATA DO NOT SUPPORT THE PROPOSED LISTING OF LESSER PRAIRIE CHICKEN
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
“CESAR’S review of the proposed listing of the Lesser Prairie chicken applies the clear direction of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that listings be based solely on data and that the conservation efforts of states and local agencies be considered. We closely examined the references cited by the US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS), published literature, regulatory documents, and readily available data. In addition, we performed an independent analysis of the past distributional history of the lesser prairie chicken to provide a deeper-time perspective, and commissioned independent peer reviews of the available population analyses.
Our review identified data that demonstrate lesser prairie chicken populations are increasing and are unlikely to be extirpated either locally or range wide in the foreseeable future. In addition, our review identified analyses that demonstrate lesser prairie chickens have not lost their genetic diversity and are not genetically isolated. These data offer empirical support for the conclusion that local and statewide conservation efforts are and will continue to be effective. These two facts, both supported by data, are prima facie evidence that the lesser prairie chicken is not likely to become in danger of extinction in the foreseeable future.
Based on the information we developed, it appears that the FWS assumed population declines and loss of genetic diversity and used post hoc rationalizations to support listing based on speculative reasons for the nonexistent declines. The best available data on population growth and genetic health demonstrate that the lesser prairie chicken is not in decline throughout all or a significant portion of its range.
In part, CESAR’s mission, “…is to bring scientific rigor to regulatory decisions undertaken pursuant to environmental statutes…”1 Accordingly, this report also addresses the threats identified in the proposed rule based on the FWS reliance on speculation, surmise and opinion. We believe that identifying those portions of the rule that fail to comply with the requirements of the ESA and related laws, regulations, and guidelines, will help improve this proposed rule as well as future rules.
In general, our review identified the following shortcomings in the proposed
rule:
>The proposed rule fails to consider data and analyses demonstrating lesser prairie chicken populations are increasing and that genetic isolation has not occurred.
>The conclusions in the proposed rule are not based solely on the best scientific and commercial data available as required by the ESA, but on an amalgam of opinion, speculation, and surmise.
>The proposed rule inaccurately implies that the states’ ability to protect lesser prairie chicken through existing regulatory mechanisms is inadequate compared to that of the ESA.
>The proposed rule fails to accurately acknowledge the scope and importance of the voluntary conservation contributions made by states and local agencies.
>The proposed rule is internally inconsistent; asserting that sufficient information on habitat needs is available to list the species but that there is insufficient data to identify the characteristics and location of the habitat essential for the conservation of the species.
The ESA is a powerful tool for conserving species. However, it has clearly articulated standards for decision-making, explicitly requiring data and consideration of local efforts in the listing process. This proposed rule fails to meet the basic requirements of a listing determination as articulated in the ESA.”
CONCLUSION
“The FWS has:
>limited or incomplete data on historic habitat loss,
>limited or incomplete data on the habitat requirements of the lesser prairie chicken and
>limited or incomplete data on the available habitat for the lesser prairie chicken.
The best available data find increasing populations across the range of the greater prairie chicken and low extinction probabilities. Genetic analysis demonstrates no loss in genetic diversity and no evidence of genetic isolation.
A review of the state and local efforts to conserve the lesser prairie chicken demonstrates robust statutory authority for protection of habitat on public and private land as well as legislative commitment to conservation of wildlife species and their habitat at the state level. These authorities exist whether the species is listed or even remains a candidate.”
“There are no data that support the FWS assertion that habitat fragmentation and decline with related effects are threatening the lesser prairie chicken. There are data that demonstrate population growth, low extinction probabilities, and genetic robustness.
The FWS has failed to meet the requirements of the Act that listing be based solely on data showing that the species is adversely affected by one or more of the five factors enumerated in the Act.”

I write to make known my strong opposition to the proposal to plant Franciscan manzanita anywhere in San Francisco, and especially in the proposed areas of Bernal Hill, Glen Canyon (which for some reason they call Diamond Heights), Mount Davidson, Twin Peaks, Corona Heights, Bayview Park, and McLaren Park.

My opposition is based upon the following:

1) Regarding the addition of 73 acres of SF city parkland for consideration as critical habitat for the Franciscan manzanita, this is not a case of protecting existing plants, but rather a choice to plant manzanitas in city parks. Please do not allow those advocacy groups who have tried for years to change park usage in San Francisco city parks from active to passive recreation to succeed in their stated goals of taking people out of our city parks.

2) SF is the second densest city in the US. We don't have enough recreational open space as it is. We are surrounded by water on three sides and by densely populated San Mateo Country on the only other side. We have no way to expand our park space into surrounding communities. We have a very limited amount of parkland available in San Francisco. Unlike many cities, San Franciscans do not have backyards in which to play with their kids and their dogs. We rely on our city parks to be our "backyards." Removing access to over 200 acres of city parks to plant the manzanita will have a significant negative impact on the health and well being of San Franciscans who regularly use those parks.

3) USF&WS calls these parks "unoccupied." But these areas contain many trails popular with hikers, bikers, and dog walkers. Thousands of people walk both with and without dogs in these areas every day. They are NOT "unoccupied."

4) Designation as "critical habitat" will lead to restrictions on public access and public use of these areas. The same groups who sued to get the endangered species designation -- the same people trying to kick dogs out of the GGNRA -- have also sued SF to close access at Sharp Park because they claim SF is not doing enough to protect an endangered snake there. They will do the same thing if they think people and/or dogs are "bothering" the manzanita, forcing SF to close access to everyone wherever it is planted. You cannot walk with your dog in an area with endangered plants. You cannot play catch with your child. Your kid cannot go off a trail to follow a butterfly in an area with endangered plants.

5) The Franciscan manzanita requires full sunshine to survive. Designation as critical habitat means that healthy trees will have to be cut down wherever it is planted to let the sun reach the plants.

6) The Franciscan manzanita may be rare in the wild, but you can buy exact clones of it (taken from a plant relocated in the 1940s) at East Bay nurseries. Closing scarce city parkland to plant a manzanita you can easily buy in Berkeley is ludicrous.

7) Designation as critical habitat means that any decisions on changes to these parks -- a new trail, a new picnic area, a new restroom -- will have to be approved by USF&WS, in essence giving the Federal Government control over 200 acres of our city parks, even if no manzanita is ever planted there.

8) If it must be planted in the "wild," it should be planted only in remote areas, with few trails and few visitors, such as Crystal Springs Reservoir.

Please do not plant endangered species in our San Francisco parks. San Francisco is the second densest city in the United States, and we are already very limited in recreational space. These parks are areas heavily used by San Franciscans; the parks are not “unoccupied” land.

Planting endangered species and designating these areas as critical habitat will have profound and deleterious effects on the use of this land, both by those who walk, run and otherwise exercise in and enjoy these areas, and for the trees and other plants already sharing this space. Put endangered plants in areas *away* from human habitation, not smack dab in the middle of busy city parks!

Thank you for your consideration.

The need is less than critical.

Save McLaren Park is a community-based advocacy and stewardship group that works to understand and protect the natural areas of San Francisco’s John McLaren Park. We lead nature and photography walks and sponsor work parties. We also publish a website and a regular newsletter to let folks know what is going on in the park, and to encourage them to get involved in various volunteer activities. Most recently, we sponsored a smartphone-powered bioblitz where we observed, confirmed, and mapped almost 250 species in the park within a three-hour period.

We only recently learned of this revision to the proposed federal ruling concerning critical habitat for Franciscan Manzanita in McLaren Park. We are of course supportive of habitat restoration efforts, and would like to understand more about the project. At the same time, the proposed areas in McLaren Park are frequently travelled and much admired by park neighbors and visitors, and are already home to many species of plants, butterflies, birds, and other critters.

Therefore, we urge that plans which might impact this access, or might impact other established and documented wildlife habitat in the vicinity, be presented and discussed frequently in varied public forums before final decisions are made. We offer our volunteers and organization to facilitate this community dialogue with site visits, public meetings, work days, and so on. We believe this will increase public understanding of the project, while providing invaluable feedback to various agencies working on it. You can contact us and find out more about our organization at www.savemclarenpark.org.

Sincerely,

Ken McGary for the
Save McLaren Park Coordinating Committee

Dear US. Fish and Wildlife Service,
I am a resident of San Francisco and strongly oppose the plan for recovery of the Franciscan Manzanita for the following reasons:
1. The 2003 Recovery Plan for Raven’s Manzanita states that it’s difficult to ascertain a “pure species in Archostaphylos” because of its “many poorly defined taxa and prevalent hybridization.” The provenance of Franciscan Manzanita is murky. It could be a hybrid, in which case we would be expending an enormous amount of public space and money for a plant that is less than unique.
2. Raven’s Manzanita has not been successful by Endangered Species Act (ESA) standards after 33 years, so why should we assume the Franciscan Manzanita is any more likely to have a successful recovery?
3. Burning would be necessary in the Natural Areas of San Francisco’s public parks to trigger germination and to result in the “spontaneously reproducing variable populations” called for by ESA standards. We don’t want burning in our public parks due to air pollution and other risks that would result.
4. Setting aside 6% of City-managed park land is not a reasonable tradeoff in the second most densely-populated city in the US for protected space for this plant. It’s interesting that both the National Park Service and the Presidio have requested that some of their land be removed as critical habitat. Clearly, they have examined these tradeoffs.
Sincerely,
Dee Seligman
SF, CA 94117

1. The Draft Economic analysis is inadequate and incomplete.
1a. It has ridiculously low costs for "consultation" with San Francisco Departments, estimated at $363. To the extent that critical habitat is designated in San Francisco Parks, any significant changes or work done in the areas, or use approval or restrictions, will require consultation, with much higher than disclosed costs.
1b. The designation of Twin Peaks areas, which contain a water reservoir for emergency fire protection of San Francisco in the event of an earthquake, could affect the timing, construction, and availability of this reservoir. No designation of critical habitat should be made which would in any way affect the Twin Peaks reservoir, and resulting earthquake and fire protection of the City of San Francisco.
2. The Draft Economic analysis ascribes no costs to limits on public use of San Francisco parks which might result from critical habitat designation, and is therefore incomplete, despite more than 375 comments in this docket indicating restrictions on use would be harmful and costly to San Francisco residents. It does not appear that the Draft Economic Analysis authors, or the FWS, even reviewed and considered these comments in preparing this incomplete economic analysis. The economic analysis should be supplemented to consider costs of land use restrictions and park access restrictions and resubmitted before any final decision on including San Francisco parkland is made.
3. The Draft Economic Analysis is flawed to the extent it accepts inaccurate field work designations of areas as unoccupied by Franciscan Manzanita currently. As previously commented, and attached in files to this comment, there is currently Franciscan Manzanita in a Native Plant garden at Omar and Myra streets, on Miraloma School Grounds. Franciscan manzanita can therefore be viewed, enjoyed, protected, or otherwise preserved by this location, which is not mentioned in the habitat designation proposed rule or economic analysis. See also the prior comments of Stan Berman and others indicating they know of existing Franciscan manzanita plantings, and the articles indicating it is being successfully propagated in Santa Cruz and Berkeley.

As previously commented, coastal grassland with fog effects is found both North of the Golden Gate Bridge and South as far as Santa Barbara. To use San Francisco parkland as the only critical habitat is botanical egotism and unjustified.
5. Finally, the notion that a linked set of areas will provide genetic diversity and opportunities for hybridization is fundamentally inconsistent with rejection of existing plantings of Franciscan manzanita as exemplars of the species. If Franciscan manzanita will hybridize with other genetically similar plantings, designation of critical habitat is less useful than merely making plantings widely available over a widespread geographic area, without designation of critical habitat. Thus, adding for example 70 acres in Glen Canyon or Diamond Heights will not be justified on any basis, without substantial fieldwork ( which has not been done so far) to establish the real current range and locations of Franciscan manzanita in various forms.

Dear USFWS,

This is further to my earlier comment on designating critical habitat for a. franciscana.

1. The proposed expanded acreage suggests designating over 200 acres of land owned by San Francisco city, and falling under its Natural Areas Program (NAP). The NAP has about 1100 acres of park land in the city. This area is used recreationally by park-goers, and taking 200 acres out is excessive. The only recreation possible on restricted areas is weeding and planting under the supervision of SFRPD staff.

2. The example of the closely-related Raven's manzanita suggests that fire may be needed for the germination of the seeds. Prescribed burns are at present not allowed in San Francisco, nor are they appropriate for the city because of pollution and the risk of the fire escaping its planned boundaries.

3. It will almost certainly require felling of more mature trees that currently occupy or shade the designated areas, with the impacts on carbon sequestration, pollution, run-off regulation, wind, slope-stability, and the aesthetics of the area.

4. There is no demonstrated need to designate critical habitat. The issue for this plant is not the kind of soils; this manzanita has been in the nursery trade for decades, and shown that it can thrive under varied soil and climate conditions. The issue is seed reproduction. This is not an issue that can be assisted by designating habitat, but rather by encouraging natural growth under nursery conditions with the possibility of cross fertilization with the Laurel Hill clone. Designating this acreage is likely to add more rules, more bureaucracy, more pushback from the community, and ultimately have unintended consequences in terms of the treatment of the affected acreage as well as resentment of the entire program.
In other words, it will have a direct as well as an intangible cost with little pay-off in terms of the plant's actual success.

5. Though this effort seeks to designated habitat only within the county of San Francisco, it would seem that habitat that is equally good - and perhaps more popularly acceptable - exists in the Marin Headlands, and in San Bruno mountain.

I hope you will consider these comments in making your determination.

Sincerely,

Rupa Bose

I'd like to submit the following arguments AGAINST designating any part of the San Francisco Parks a critical habitat for the Franciscan Manzanita.

1) SF is the second densest city in the US. We don't have enough recreational open space as it is. Removing access to 196 acres of city parks to plant the manzanita will have a significant negative impact on the health and well being of San Franciscans who regularly use those parks.

2) USF&WS calls these parks "unoccupied." But these areas contain many trails popular with hikers, bikers, and dog walkers. Thousands of people walk in these areas every day. They are NOT "unoccupied."

3) Designation as "critical habitat" will lead to restrictions on public access and public use of these areas. Given special interest groups in the area's history of suing to close access to other critical habitats this designation will effectively force SF to close access wherever it is planted.

4)The Franciscan manzanita requires full sunshine to survive. Designation as critical habitat means that healthy trees will have to be cut down wherever it is planted to let the sun reach the plants. This will impact the wind resistance these trees currently provide.

5) The Franciscan manzanita may be rare in the wild, but you can buy exact clones of it (taken from a plant relocated in the 1940s) at East Bay nurseries. Closing scarce city parkland to plant a manzanita you can easily buy in Berkeley is a waste of efforts and resources.

6) Designation as critical habitat means that any decisions on changes to these parks - a new trail, a new picnic area, a new restroom - will have to be approved by USF&WS, in essence giving the Federal Government control over 196 acres of our city parks, even if no manzanita is ever planted there. Davidson Park for this purpose be undertaken with the understanding and recognition that the park is a recreational resource for us all, who regularly hike and walk our dogs on its trails and enjoy its vistas. I support the possible Wolverine introduction into Colorado. Historically, Wolverines lived in remote, high-elevation areas of Colorado. The continued survival of the lone wolverine 'M56,' who moved from Wyoming into Colorado, leads me to believe that Colorado has good habitat and enough food to support wolverines. As the climate changes, Colorado's high mountain elevations could expect to retain cold and snow, thus creating an ideal environment for wolverines to survive and raise their young.
While I would rather see wolverines returned to Colorado with the full protections of the Endangered Species Act, I am hopeful that the experimental nonessential designation is a compromise that will make broad support for a reintroduction of wolverines in the Southern Rockies region much more likely.

Establishment of a "nonessential experimental" population in Colorado is a great step toward deepening the gene pool of this rare carnivore. Wolverines travel great distances to breed and their genes travel far. As a recent study has shown, wolverines can travel up to 500 miles. This means that genes from a Colorado population could be shared between the Wyoming or even possibly Idaho populations.
If you look a worldwide map of potential wolverine habitats (those with consistent years of deep spring snowpack), you will see a long arm that stretches down the length of the Rocky Mountains. This is the natural range of these animals and should be considered the necessary scope for the success of the species.
The areas between the deep snowpack areas are also important. Through an establishment of an experimental population in Colorado, researchers can establish an understanding of those corridors. Understanding the migratory corridors for wildlife can help us use our protected areas wisely and could potentially pose less of a threat to industry and private land interests while still protecting the wolverines genetic diversity.

In 1973, as a result of several years of attempting to preserve our nation’s natural resources and precious wildlife, Congress passed, and the Richard Nixon Administration signed into law, the Endangered Species Act. The goal of the Endangered Species Act (the “ESA” or the “Act”) is to conserve endangered and threatened species to ensure their long-term survival in the wild. To me, as an advocate of all species throughout the earth, the “protectionism” of the ESA has a two part association: 1) to stabilize the endangered or threatened species, and 2) to revitalize and reestablish its numbers and allow it prosper once more. This two-part proposal by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service goes to the very spirit of “stabilize and “revitalize” any endangered or threatened species that the ESA is meant to convey. The development of a nonessential experimental population of the North American Wolverine under Section 10(j) of the Endangered Species Act goes to the very core of what the ESA is about, which is providing a program to revitalize an endangered or threatened species community, while at the same time allowing them to integrate in the communities of other species, including humans. The Colorado high peaks and mountain ranges are a perfect habitat for the North American wolverine to establish a thriving community once again in the lower 48 United States. However, the proposal should explicitly state that any wolverines that travel into Colorado on its own will remain fully protected under the ESA unless and until an experimental population release occurs. The nonessential experimental population of the North American wolverine, as proposed under Section 10(j) of the Endangered Species Act is a great first step to bringing back this extraordinary survivor and goes to the very core of what the Endangered Species Act is all about.

Dear ESA People:
I want to lend my voice of approval for the proposal to designate re-introduced populations of wolverines in the Lower 48 States (Colorado) experimental non-essential. They can never become a sizeable population, but perhaps a viable one. There seems to be no substantial reason to not reintroduce wolverines. Rangeland domestic sheep activity in the high country has declined and a Defenders of Wildlife type program to compensate ranchers would be inexpensive. The summertime natural food base should be adequate in the animal's preferred alpine habitat. Winter food turn out to be winter-kill deer and elk with little competition with the reintroduced Canada lynx population. With the absence of fishers in Colorado there would not be that competition. Snowmobile recreation likely would be the greatest threat by providing compacted trails for coyotes to gaim access to high country in winter, in addition to direct human harassment. No doubt the wolverine team will have explored these points. This note primarily wants to thank the FWS for proceeding with its ESA mission.

Wolverines are threatened by climate change which is affecting the snow cover in their habitat. They do not need pressure from being trapped as well. In addition, trapping is cruel and inhumane. No animal should die in a trap.

In addition, federal protection will provide resources for monitoring the wolverine's progress and help to sustain them into the future.

Please grant the wolverine threatened status and protect them for the future!

In summary, ORV use in unprotected areas may be a limiting factor to the species range expansion in times of high population numbers. The long-term recovery of CPSD tiger beetles may be more dependent on environmental factors such as drought (see Factor E). Representing the 1100+ members of the SEWEE Association, the friends group for Cape Romain NWR, and the other two NWRefuges on the cast of South Carolina we would like to request that Bull Island be specifically identified as critical habitat for the Atlantic Loggerhead Sea Turtle. We feel this is essential given the threats associated with sea level rise and the serious erosion of Cape and Lighthouse Islands.... both of which are smaller than Bull Island. Cape Island in particular has already suffered extreme erosion breaking into three separate islands and has significantly reduced the beach area available  to females for egg laying. All  these islands are heavily used by loggerheads during the recruitment season, Specific identification of Bulls Island, which receives a great deal of public use, as critical habitat will enhance management efforts of that island.

As a concerned citizen, I thank you for the opportunity to express my support for immediate designation of critical habitat on U.S. nesting beaches that are important to threatened loggerhead sea turtles as required under the Endangered Species Act. I support permanent the critical habitat protections proposed for 739 miles of coastline that cover 84 percent of nesting areas from North Carolina to Florida to Mississippi.

In addition, I urge you to extend the critical habitat designation to all key Florida nesting beaches. Please do not exclude the three Florida counties covered by voluntary Habitat Conservation Plans (HCPs) as proposed by USFWS. These plans expire over time and are vulnerable to cut-backs and political agendas. Loggerheads live for decades so they need permanent habitat protections over hundreds of years. Listing procedures are criticized by landowners/developers alike because they feel the Act list species without “adequate scientific studies,” and by environmentalist for moving too slow to protect disappearing species. However, the ESA only protects those species that have been formally listed as endangered or threatened; the Act offers no help to animals such as deer, cardinals or dolphins because there is no threat of extinction. The loggerhead sea turtle is being threatened and human activity is a major contributor, by creating havoc for the life of the species. Untended fishing gear causes many loggerhead deaths, suffocation from being trapped in fishing trawls, as well as the loss of suitable nesting beaches and introduction of exotic predators all contribute to loggerhead population decline. A prudency determination is examined under Section 4(a)(3)(A) of the Act. Regulations are implemented under this section requiring that “to the maximum extent prudent and determinable.” In Natural Resources Defense Council v. United States Department of the Interior the court determined that Congress intended the imprudence exception to be a narrow one that is “clear from legislative history.” “The committee intends that in most situations the Secretary will… designate critical habitat at the same time that a species is listed as either endangered or threatened. It is only in rare circumstances where the specification of critical habitat concurrently with the listing would not be beneficial to the species.” Natural Resources Defense Council v. United States DOI, 113 F.3d 1121 (9th Cir. Cal. 1997). The identification of a critical habitat would be beneficial to the species to lessen the threat of extinction from human activity and other dangers to the loggerhead sea turtle. A critical habitat designation for the endangered loggerhead sea turtle is not only prudent but vital.

My name is Richard A. Lazar, president of Readiness Systems, LLC, and I have broad experience in AED program operations, risk management, law, and public policy. I submit the attached comment in opposition to the FDA’s proposed rule to reclassify AEDs as Class III medical devices.

According to the agency’s proposed rule, the primary purpose of reclassification is to reduce the perceived risk of death resulting from AED failures. Yet, a study relied upon by the agency finds that AEDs work as intended during rescue attempts greater than 99% of the time. AED failures during rescue attempts very, very rarely contribute to the probability of sudden cardiac death.

The FDA’s proposal to reclassify AEDs will require manufacturers to go through a time consuming and costly regulatory process thus stifling innovation and increasing AED cost. Further, the proposed rule does not address people problems that cause many AED failures at point of use. In addition, the rule will contribute to the AED shortage problem resulting in fewer AEDs being available to treat sudden cardiac arrest victims.

This is a clear example of the perfect as the enemy of the good driving a regulatory action that will cost lives and money with very little public health benefit. Data do not support the proposed rule on safety and effectiveness grounds and public health considerations further argue against adoption of this rule.

For reasons discussed in the attached comment, I urge the agency to continue regulating AEDs as Class II medical devices with the addition of special controls to address safety and quality concerns.

Respectfully submitted,

The Sudden Cardiac Arrest Foundation, a national nonprofit organization dedicated to raising awareness and saving lives threatened by sudden cardiac arrest, urges the FDA to reconsider its proposal to increase regulations for automated external defibrillators, and instead designate the safe and effective life-saving devices as class II medical devices with special controls.

To US Food & Drug Administration:
Early defibrillation is the definitive treatment for sudden cardiac arrest (SCA), which claims nearly 300,000 lives in the United States per year. Widespread distribution of automated external defibrillators (AEDs) is overwhelmingly advocated by the medical community and legislators as a strategy for achieving early defibrillation. Even with the growing availability of AEDs in the US and highly successful early defibrillation programs throughout the country, the current national SCA survival rate is less than 8% largely because without AEDs early defibrillation doesn’t happen in time. In order to improve the national survival rate and help restore more lives, we must continue to drive widespread access to AEDs.
I am writing to express my concern that the proposed reclassification of AEDs to class III requiring PMA will directly impact access to AEDs limit innovation, both highly negative results. Over several decades, hundreds of peer-reviewed studies have already demonstrated that AEDs are safe and effective and that early defibrillation saves lives. Additional regulation will not benefit public safety. To the contrary, these additional regulations will likely stifle innovation and new, improved technology will be delayed, or may not even be pursued in the US due to regulatory costs and time-to-market considerations under the PMA process.
Furthermore, AEDs will become more expensive as a direct result of expenses associated with increased regulatory requirements, further limiting access to these lifesaving devices. I urge FDA to consider alternative pathways that ensure the safety and effectiveness of AEDs, but at the same time continue to support efforts to drive widespread access to early defibrillation. For the hundreds of thousands of Americans who unexpectedly suffer an SCA each year, we cannot afford to further decrease the odds that an AED will be available when needed to help restore their lives.

We support the Sudden Cardiac Arrest Foundation's recommendation that the FDA reject its proposal to reclassify AEDs and related accessories as class III medical devices requiring pre-market approval or a notice of completion of a product development protocol. We agree that this classification change will result in reduced access to the life-saving devices and it will stifle innovation.
We recommend that the FDA regulate AEDs as class II medical devices with special controls, along with the more beneficial national recommendations to raise public awareness, increase CPR-AED training among laypersons, increase AED deployment and improve systems to ensure device readiness.
Our concern is for the greater public good and we will have a greater and more beneficial impact on public health through awareness, training and the availability of AEDs and early emergency response.
Sudden cardiac arrest strikes 1,000 people every day in the United States and only 10 percent of the vicitms survive.

Our friend's son was one of the lucky ones, saved by the deployment of an AED in a public building. Imagine the increase in survival rate with stronger initiatives to raise public awareness, bystander intervention and AED accessibility. Imagine how many lives can be saved each year! AEDs restore life for people who die suddenly. If the FDA designates AEDs as class III medical devices, it will reduce distribution and access.We urge the FDA to listen to the voices of those who understand first-hand the need to keep AEDs readily available for victims of sudden cardiac arrest.

THIS IS NOT ONLY ABOUT NARCOLEPSY. Many other sleep disorders have symptoms similar to narcolepsy. Many people with sleep disorders have multiple causes for their sleep issues, and are often diagnosed with several different disorders. In some disorders, for example delayed sleep phase disorder, there may be different underlying causes in different people. Also, people who are sleep deprived due to another disorder may be incorrectly diagnosed as having narcolepsy. And, of course, different medications work differently for different people.

All these reasons argue for having as many different treatment options as possible for these disorders. This includes medications to improve quality of sleep and sleep architecture, adjust timing of sleep and other circadian variables, and improve alertness and function when awake.

Medications need to be tested on patients with different underlying causes for their sleep dysfunction, and results categorized according to those underlying causes. This is needed because a medication may be effective for one underlying cause, but not for another.

Results need to document long term subjective improvements, not just improvements in related biomarkers. In the case of circadian disorders, this means to ascertain patient well-being, not just a change in dim light melatonin onset (DLMO). For a hypothetical narcolepsy drug, this means documenting an improvement in patient alertness, not just a change in hypocretin levels. It is also necessary to demonstrate that the desired effect persists in the long run.

CIRCADIAN SLEEP DISORDERS NETWORK (www.circadiansleepdisorders.org) believes that there is considerable overlap in some of the symptoms and potential drug treatments between circadian disorders and narcolepsy, and that research and development to aid narcolepsy will benefit circadian disorders as well.

There are an estimated 500,000 American adults suffering from Delayed Sleep Phase Syndrome (DSPS), and many more teenagers. Another 75,000, mostly blind, suffer from Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Disorder (Non-24).

For many of them, today's treatments for DSPS and Non-24 are only partially effective or not effective at all. The resulting sleep deficit severely inhibits critical cognitive functions and compromises education, employment, and personal lives. Many of these people are unable to work on a normal daytime schedule, and many cannot find jobs that can accommodate their unusual schedules. This is a particular problem for Non-24, since their schedule is not constant but varies, often unpredictably. These are people who could be productive citizens if better treatments were available.

To the US Food and Drug Administration:

This comment is a follow-up to a previous communication on the subject of re-classification of AEDs. I have reviewed, yet again, all of the available data pertaining to AED deployment in a wide variety of locations. I have medically-supervised the use of AEDs by police, fire-rescue and paramecics since 1988. Over this entire span of t ime I have observed only one device failure, and that dates back to 1990. This experience includes hundreds of uses and different manufacturers' devices. Reclassification, from my experience and data review, is both unneeded and potentially injurious to technologic advances. Extension of reclassification to ALS defibrillators that integrate AED technology, and also to accessories used by these devices, would be detrimental to their ongoing deployment and technologic advances in design amd operation, some of which I already anticipate as still more improvements in patient care. These are advances in device technology that should not be delayed by reclassification mandate. These are not patient safety issues at all, but rather immient changes that can advance patient care quickly.
I urge the FDA to not proceed with reclassification as class III medical devices and mandatory PMA for their acceptance.

Topic 1: Disease symptoms and daily impacts that matter most to patients:
1. Of all the symptoms that you experience because of your condition, which one to three symptoms have the most significant impact on your life? Hypnopompic hallucinations, excessive daytime sleepiness, automatic behavior.
2. Are there specific activities that are important to you but that you cannot do at all or as fully as you would like because of your condition? Extreme difficulty waking up in the morning. Feel nauseated if I did not sleep long enough. Difficulty with memory due to doing things while half asleep in automatic behavior. Limited endurance due to excessive daytime sleepiness.
3. How have your symptoms changed over time? My symptoms have been relatively stable over time, however, they have improved greatly with the use of xyrem.
3.1. Do your symptoms come and go? If so, do you know of anything that makes your symptoms better? Xyrem Worse? Stress sometimes makes things worse, as with most any chronic disease.

Topic 2: Patients' perspectives on current approaches to treating narcolepsy:
1. What are you currently doing to help treat your condition or its symptoms? Xyrem 2x nightly, Antidepressant daily, occasional use of stimulants as needed, such as for long drives.
1.1. What specific symptoms do your therapies address? Cataplexy (xyrem eliminates this almost completely), excessive daytime sleepiness, hypnopompic hallucinations, automatic behavior.
1.2. How has your treatment regimen changed over time, and why? Started on provigil (didn't work), then daily stimulants for about 18months, then xyrem, then weaned off of daily stimulants within 6 months and now use stimulants less than once per week.
2. How well does your current treatment regimen treat the most significant symptoms of your disease? Extremely well. With xyrem, I feel like I function almost like a person without narcolepsy. I can't imagine what I would do without it...I'd be unable to work or drive.
2.1. How well do these therapies improve your ability to do specific activities that are important to you in your daily life? With xyrem, my symptoms are about 90% improved.
2.2. How well have these therapies worked for you as your condition has changed over time? I've been on the xyrem for over 4 years...it has worked consistently for me.
3. What are the most significant downsides to your current therapies, and how do they affect your daily life? Biggest downside to xyrem is that I can't eat after 7:30PM, can't have any alcohol in the evening (not one drop!), have to be on a low salt diet, and have annoying jaw clenching. However, it's all worth it to be able to stay awake all day long. Cost is a bit absurd, but my insurance covers it.
4. Assuming there is no complete cure for your condition, what specific things would you look for in an ideal therapy for your condition? Xyrem without the nasty taste and salt restrictions would be nice. I could also live without the jaw clenching side effect, but my doctor is going to try a new treatment for the jaw clenching in a couple of weeks so perhaps that will resolve. It has been great to get away from the daily stimulants, so I am very grateful for that.

The source of the quality and control problems involving AEDs is not the sole fault of the AED manufacturers; they are not the “bad apples.” Rather, the problems and errors are an organizational system problem with responsibility shared by many stakeholders including manufacturers, distributors, professional societies who authorize and govern training, and those who acquire an individual AED or are responsible for placement at an organization.

The proposed changes which respond to adverse event data may be intended to solve the problem of errors or failures. But we believe that focusing specifically on manufacturers without also involving interactions with other sources of error can have unintended and undesirable consequences. We argue that FDA should examine other options that would protect the public interests in terms of safety and prevention of harm, and that would increase the probability that an AED will be available and used correctly for its primary function when sudden cardiac arrest occurs in the community.

We argue that FDA should delay its decision to change its policy until additional opportunities can be considered. These include working with other stakeholder groups such as the American Heart Association; distribution channels such as online department stores or supply houses; and occupational - medical communities such as the American College of Occupational and Environmental Medicine in order to design a solution that would change not only the manufacturing processes but also the user processes to ensure that the overall design of the “manufacturing – distributing – training – using system” are integrated and aligned. ZOLL Medical Corporation (ZOLL) appreciates this opportunity to submit comments in response to the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) Proposed Order regarding Effective Date of Requirement for Premarket Approval for Automated External Defibrillator Systems (AEDs). The FDA is proposing to require the filing of a premarket approval application (PMA) or a notice of completion of a product development protocol (PDP) for all AEDs, including, not only the AED system itself, but each of its accessories and components, such as pad electrodes, batteries, and adapters.

ZOLL remains committed to bringing and maintaining safe and effective medical devices under appropriate FDA oversight so as to provide the U.S. public health system the best and most innovative lifesaving medical devices in a timely fashion. This letter is to support the Orbital ATK request to extend the simulator certification period for the L-1011 simulator. I am a professional pilot, instructor and evaluator and have been since 1974. My background on the L-1011 (and numerous other types) is as pilot, instructor, proficiency check pilot, line check pilot and Director of Academics for Delta Air Lines. I have over 3 decades of experience training and evaluating pilots using both simulation and aircraft.
The advantages to simulation are well documented in the industry. Comprehensive training programs designed to train pilots in all areas of the flight envelope, weather conditions, abnormal and emergency procedures cannot be reproduced to the same fidelity, and in many cases ( e.g. windshear, CFIT, low visibility, critical abnormals, emergency procedures, etc.) cannot be duplicated in the actual aircraft. Abnormals which can be reproduced in a heavy aircraft require a level of caution which detracts from an instructors ability to train at the limit of performance.
Threat and Error Management (TEM)situations where startle factors and crew coordination are critical can only be trained (or talked about) to a limited extent due to safety concerns for the aircraft, crew and public. Simulation is the correct tool to properly train, practice and validate critical TEM skills.
The L-1011 systems are managed and monitored by a Flight Engineer (F/E). Simulation capability is critical to the training, maintenance and evaluation of both F/E technical and TEM skills and our ability to correctly assess and validate both independent and crew F/E proficiency.
As both an instructor and evaluator for Delta Air Lines I have used this simulator to train and evaluate hundreds of line pilots; more importantly, this simulator provides the best environment to identify and correct deficiencies in L-1011 pilot (or F/E) performance. Without the capabilities afforded by simulation, in my opinion as a professional, the level of pilot performance cannot be maintained at its highest levels.
Worldwide, to the best of my knowledge, there are no other L-1011 simulation options available. In my opinion the ability to training and evaluate L-1011 (complex heavy jet) pilots utilizing the full capabilities of simulation provides a higher level of pilot & F/E proficiency versus aircraft only training.

The alternative to using this simulator for required pilot flight checks is to accomplish them in the aircraft in flight.
The kinds of maneuvers required for pilot proficiency checks in heavy widebody aircraft was transitioned to simulators long ago for obvious economic, safety, and environmental reasons.
Having been a flight check airman, for this type aircraft, in those long ago days, it is my considered opinion that flight safety in the congested airspace of Southern California would be best served by returning this resource to service.

To: USCG
From: Randy Henry, Oregon State Marine Board, Oregon Boating Law Administrator
Subject: NPRM PFD Labeling Standards
Date: Oct 11, 2013

OSMB Comments on Proposed Labeling

The Oregon State Marine Board appreciates the opportunity to comment on proposals to update PFD labeling. We have reviewed the proposed federal language as well as our current Oregon statute and rule and note that it will take time to bring Oregon law in line with new labeling. We agree that updated labeling is important and support consistency across the US and Canada. Here are specific comments related to the NPRM.

The current “Type 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5” is confusing and not well understood by recreational boaters. We support the change to “wearable” and “throwable.” Without differentiating type, though, Oregon will need to rewrite rules to relate to the specific attributes that make one type of PFD appropriate for a certain activity. For example, with the Type II designation gone, having clear labeling attributes to reference will be essential as currently Type II PFDs are not allowed for use in Class III and greater whitewater.

There should be clear visual differentiation between “intended use”, “approved use” and “non-approved use.” In fact, complete removal of “intended use” from the PFD label would reduce confusion with “approved use.” For example, a PFD labeled with “Intended Use: Paddling & Sailing” may imply suitability for kayak use, with kayaks often used on whitewater rivers. The PFD may not, in fact, be suitable for use in white water.

In certain situations and for certain individuals, additional flotation may be preferred. Explicit labeling of flotation would clarify this. It would be beneficial to note the pounds of flotation on the label.

Current labels are inconsistently formatted, making comparisons between different brands and styles difficult. Consistency within the label will help the consumer locate key information and determine which PFD is best.

The clearest current example of labeling is on inflatable PFDs because "approved" and "non-approved" uses are explicitly noted, and there is no reference to "intended" use.

In Oregon, one of our primary issues is helping consumer and law enforcement understand what PFDs are suitable or approved for whitewater. Labeling which helps clarify will be useful.

When boaters use their vessels in both Canadian and American waters, life jacket labeling should be such that owners of vessels know that they are satisfying the regulations of both countries.

As a vessel examiner I have found it is confusing to explain some of the labeling to owners, especially the inflatable life jackets.

Re: USCG-2013-0263
Personal Flotation Devices Labeling and Standards, 33 CFR Part 175, 46 CFR Parts 160/169

To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on proposed changes to Personal Flotation Devices (PFD) labeling and standards.
The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission supports the Coast Guard’s proposal to remove references to type codes in its federal regulations on the carriage and labeling of Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, and take steps toward harmonization of US regulations with PFD requirements in Canada and other countries. When fully enacted, this standardization will more effectively convey safety information to the consumer, resulting in improved consumer awareness of appropriate PFD selection and use, greater compliance with PFD regulations and enhanced enforcement by law enforcement professionals.

The Commission's comments on specific sections of the proposed rulemaking and analysis are below:

• Rulemaking
o The Commission must undertake rulemaking action to remove PFD type code references from its regulations. Depending on the extent of the amendments, the rulemaking process may take from four months to 1 year. Based on our current understanding of the federal proposal, we anticipate the changes to be fairly straightforward and handled as administrative changes taking the minimum amount of time.

• Updates to Publications and Materials
o The Commission has already begun to update its publications, website and boating safety education materials to remove PFD type codes and reflect the definitions included in the proposed rulemaking. Based on current inventories of publications and the uncertainty of the federal rulemaking timeline, this will be an on-going effort. The Commission requests that the Coast Guard to establish a phase-in period sufficient to allow time for states to allocate the necessary effort and funding to complete this comprehensive task.

• Associated Training and Outreach
o It is anticipated that the Commission will need to undertake training, both internally with its staff and externally with its in-state partners, to ensure a common understanding of the new PFD labeling when it is finalized by the USCG. This would most likely include, but is not limited to additional training sessions or briefings for agency education and law enforcement staff, course providers and volunteer instructors such as Commission-trained instructors, USCG Auxiliary and US Power Squadrons members. Public outreach will require the development of press releases, fact sheets, website FAQs and informative social media campaigns. Training and outreach on this topic will require staff effort and funding, possibly at the expense of other timely in-state boating safety issues.

• Additional Impacts
o The Commission administers a nationally recognized water rescue program for emergency response personnel in close partnership with several key state and federal partners. Because of these partnerships and the standards to which the water rescue program is aligned, the Commission is aware that the following organizations or programs may also be affected by the removal of PFD type codes and should be consulted regarding its impacts: the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 1670 standards, FEMA's National Incident Management System requirements for funding, American Society for Testing and Materials voluntary technical standards, and the National Board on Fire Service Professional Qualifications (ProBoard) accreditation standards. It is also important to note that the Commission will need to expend significant effort and funding to update its water rescue materials and provide training briefings to its instructors.

Despite the challenges involved in the impacts of the removal of PFD type codes from federal regulations, the Commission is supportive of the change. As the Coast Guard has noted, labeling of PFDs is an important safety matter and is the primary means by which the consumer can know how to select and appropriately use the correct PFD for the activities in which they engage. Due to the significance of this effort, the Commission again encourages the Coast Guard to establish a phase-in period sufficient to allow time for states to allocate the necessary effort and funding to accommodate the impacts of this effort.

The Commission also encourages the Coast Guard to continue to closely coordinate its efforts with the National Association of State Boating Law Administrators (NASBLA) and other partner organizations. These organizations can assist with identifying other potential complications in implementing these changes and to ensure consistent communication of the changes as they are enacted.

Sincerely,

Laurel L. Anders
Director, Bureau of Boating & Outreach
Pennsylvania Fish & Boat Commission

I suggest changing from a 90 day wait to 3 months. Everyone always assume they are the same but they are not. 90 days, literally means 90 days. Problems occur when months have more or less than 30 days. Employers miscount the 90 day period which results in enrollments requested too early, or worse, too late. First of the month following 3 months is much easier for employers and employees to calculate when they are to be effective, thus reducing enrollment problems.
Examples assuming first of the month effective date after 90 days vs 3 months. Date of hire counts as the first day.

Hire date January 1
90 day wait - Effective date is April 1
3 month wait - Effective date is April 1
(no problem exists)

Hire date of February 1
90 day wait - Effective date is June 1
3 month wait - Effective date is May 1
(because february is a short month, the actual 90 days does not occur until May 2. Therefore, the 90 day wait won't be effective until first of the following month.)

Hire date of March 3
90 day wait - effective date June 1
3 month wait - effective date july 1
(Even though the employee was hired after the first of the month, the 90 day wait was reached on June 1 because March and May both of 31 days, and april has 30 Most employers would think the effective date would be the next month. If the application is not submitted until sometime in the month of July, the 30 day open enrollment period would have ended on July 1and carriers could decline the application since it was not submitted timely)

I know it isn't a huge difference but the 3 month versus 90 days results is less problems determining the correct effective dates for employers.

common than jellyfish in South Puget Sound.

markedly degraded areas are still proposed for designation as critical habitat (e.g.,
Sinclair Inlet, Commencement Bay, and Elliott Bay). While this follows the
precedent set in other critical habitat designations and the capacity of these areas to
support the Endangered Species Act (ESA) listed rockfish species may have existed
historically, designating them as critical habitat in their current condition should be
accompanied by pollution data for these areas and an acknowledgement that
restoration is needed before they can be fully used by listed rockfish. Critical habitat
designation in those areas should be used as a mechanism to encourage agencies to

Monitoring plans for Department of Defence (DOD) waters
• Section 4(a) of the ESA exempts li sting military lands as critical habitat where the land is
covered by an Integrated Management Plan that the Secretary has found, in writing, will
benefit the listed species.
o The Department recommends that the Integrated Management Plans for all such
facilities in Puget Sound provide greater detail on how listed rockfish species will
benefit. The Department was unable to find direct evidence that supported how DOD
sites in Puget Sound will sufficiently benefit listed rockfish. Additionally, levels of
various industrial toxic chemicals at some DOD (i.e., U.S. Navy) facilities are
substantially above levels elsewhere in the Sound, and these sites likely serve as point

Current and hi storic fi sheries

Net fisheries for bottom fi sh include set nets and otter trawls. A forage fish purseseine
fishery targets surf smelt, and the Puget Sound lam para herring fishery nets
are similar to purse seine nets. Beam trawls are used in shrimp fi sheries. Pelagic
trawls have been used to target Pacific hake and pollock. Non-net fisheries include
long-lines (also tenned set lines) targeting halibut or shark, and pot fisheries for
bottom fish, Dungeness crab, and shrimp (WDFW 2010a).

Since 2010, fishing rules have changed and currently only limited fisheries exist. These
limited fi sheries (i.e., salmon, crab, and shrimp harvest, and the resultant derelict gear
from these fisheries) are what should, therefore, be evaluated for future fishery impacts.
Set net, otter trawl, beam trawl, pelagic trawl, and longline/setline fisheries for marine
fish have been closed in Puget Sound since 2010. While forage fish drag seines and
lam para nets are still used, there is no record of any of these methods ever catching one
of the three ESA-listed rockfish species. Monitoring of shrimp beam trawl fisheries have
occurred in recent years due to concerns about ESA-listed eulachon, and no catch of
ESA-listed rockfish has been documented. Also, Hood Canal fisheries are listed as a
concern, but these have been entirely closed to bottomfishing since 2004.
Low-level research impacts
• Research activities are called out as a special consideration for conservation and
management and the Departmenf s bottom trawling activities are mentioned by name.

further, occurring under multiple Section 10 incidental take permits ( 15848 for bottom

current activity levels. Consider the following:
o Since 2008, the Department's annual bottomfish stock assessment surveys have
occurred on fixed index sites in all major sub-basins of the Sound. While localized
habitat disturbance within these sites certainly occurs, trawls occur in previously
trawled (i.e., already disturbed) locations, are short in duration, and target low-relief,
soft-bottom habitats where hang-ups are unlikely.

not represent a removal of resources from the ecosystem.
o Since 1996 the Department has captured and killed a total of23 of the three listed
species (18 yelloweye and 5 canary rockfish) in the entirety of the Distinct Population
Segment, with the last fi sh killed in 2007.
o In an eff01t to further reduce the biological and habitat impacts from trawling, the
Department began using a remotely operated vehicle (ROY) to assess groundfish
abundance and distribution in 2003, and prior to that time used tethered drop cameras
as a supplement to trawling.
Model improvements
• The methods described for modeling rockfish habitat result in selection of areas that are
not rockfish habitat. For example, many of the steep slopes included in the proposed
designation lack the substrate composition and/or complexity (i .e., rugosity)
characteristic of rockfish habitat. Consequently, the Department recommends refining
the habitat suitability model with field verification through ROY surveys, both pre- and
post-designation of critical habitat.

application of the designation method. The Department recommends further refining

• The Department believes that high resolution bathymetry across the habitat range,
along with sonar-derived substrate, is the most important data layer for defining
rockfish habitat. There is a multi-agency working group that is inventorying high

calculating rugosity tends to include all steep slopes, but it is known that many of
these slopes in the Distinct Population Segment outside of the San Juan Islands
are not suitable rockfish substrate -- as determined with drop-camera and ROY

distribution data for listed species to detennine the suite and range of BTM
metrics, including rugosity, to calibrate a BTM, depth and substrate based habitat
suitability model, as an approach, instead of the less accurate a priori assumption
that all rugosity > 1.005 is suitable habitat.

effectively resolve features that are 90m or larger, or that exhibit rugosity at that
scale. Features and substrates that appear flat and 'simple' at 90m could have
finer scale structure that is used by fish. As a general rule, one can generate the
finest scale rugosity at a scale three times the bathymetry resolution, and delineate

From Sibyl Bogardus, Frances Horn, and Dennis Fiszer, Regional Chief Compliance Officers, HUB International

We submit the following comments on proposed regulations published December 24, 2013, “Amendments to Excepted Benefits.”

1.The rules are unworkable in the real world. For example, the 15% exception for supplemental benefits -- used as a condition in these newest proposed rules -- has not proven to be viable since its introduction in 2007.
2.The rules are is too “condition-based.” In the future when drafting regulations, rather than ask what conditions will be imposed for an exception to apply, it would be helpful to instead first ask, “How can we make this as simple as possible?” Each condition creates a growing burden. Each layer of complexity increases the likelihood of employers dropping benefits, counter to the intent of the law. It is hard to envision an arrangement that complies with all conditions in these recent regulations. Moreover, employers in general do not wish to circumvent the law; their ask, “How do we comply?” When compliance is impossible or next to impossible, their reaction is to drop the program.
3.The rules send employers right down the path of not offering affordable minimum value coverage. Many employers will not be eager to offer wraparounds because of the $3,000 penalty. However, these programs (if offered) should eventually result in employers in high cost areas dropping group health insurance. Over time, more employees will move to the exchanges as more employers offer unaffordable group health plans coverage right up to the percentage you allow, even if it means paying the $3,000 per person penalty presumably on a reduced full-time workforce. That is one step away from dropping coverage overall, more likely after the Cadillac tax takes effect in 2018.
4.Prior regulations and agency interpretations forbid standalone HRAs, or health reimbursement accounts, to offset what employees pay out of pocket. Yet, these proposed rules allow an employer to offer exactly such a program for what is likely to be a small percentage of its workforce, provided the individual waives the employer coverage and goes to the insurance exchange, often with taxpayer subsidies. This regulation continues non-systematic dismantling of the employer-sponsored system in favor of public exchanges and increases the federal cost in a manner Congress didn't anticipate and the Congressional Budget Office hasn't reviewed, to our knowledge.
5.A simple dollar amount safe harbor is always more workable. Health reform has undermined employer-sponsored plans. If the agencies are trying to reconstruct what has been destroyed by supporting an employer-sponsored supplement, isn’t it simpler to state, “An employer can reimburse up to $___ for each employee’s out of pocket expenses if that employee elects exchange coverage because the employer plan is not affordable to him or her” or some similar simple rule?
6.The regulations further fragment the system of health care coverage. Employers likely will not design the wraparound programs; rather, insurance carriers will, and they will include a cost factor for a sales force, a profit margin, etc.
7.The proposed rules undermine health reform’s goal of system-wide cost containment. Reform promotes cost containment by a return to managed care, narrower networks, and similar restrictions. It is against the public policy underlying reform for this regulation to encourage individuals to seek care at out-of-network providers, but that is what the wraparound regulations support by allowing repayment of those out of pocket amounts. Moreover, the reimbursements further undermine underwriting assumptions used in carrier pricing – that individuals are being steered to in-network providers.
8.These regulations will further increase carrier premium costs. Federal regulations and the many other non-regulatory modifications to health reform law create uncertainty by undermining carrier pricing. So, now insurance carrier premium pricing must take into account the risk of changes by agencies and other branches of government. If the risk is great, while the ability to charge higher premiums is restricted, the likely result is insurance carrier exits from market segments -- not a desired or intended result of the law as enacted.
9.The new proposed EAP rules increase the likelihood of employers dropping their programs, on top of disruption in the benefit design itself. If you simply say that EAPs are exempt, we can all move on. Employers offer these programs to provide more of a benefit to all workers and to address significant issues like workplace and personal stress – not to circumvent health plan regulations. Recognition of that intent and the positive results achieved by these programs could be handled by a simple exemption and a simple statement indicating EAP coverage does not result in subsidy disqualification.
