Dredged Material Management Program’s Comments and Suggested Edits to Proposed
Designation of Critical Habitat for the Distinct
Population Segments of Yelloweye Rockfish, Canary Rockfish, and Bocaccio
November 4, 2013
A. Draft Biological Report
1. Page 5: “There is little information regarding the habitat requirements of rockfish larvae,
though other marine fish larvae are vulnerable to low dissolved oxygen levels and elevated
suspended sediment levels that can alter feeding rates and cause abrasion to gills.”
DMMP Comments: This and other text in the report (page 18) imply that low dissolved
oxygen is incontrovertibly associated with suspended sediment and, by association, with
dredged material disposal at the DMMP’s designated open-water sites. We agree that
anaerobic sediments create an oxygen demand when suspended in the water column which
decreases dissolved oxygen (DO) levels. However, given the rapid descent of material
dredged by a clamshell dredge and the generally well-mixed nature of waters overlying the
DMMP sites, disposal activities are not likely to lead to appreciable reductions in dissolved
oxygen in the mid and upper portions of the water column. At the non-dispersive disposal
sites, any reductions in dissolved oxygen levels would be expected to occur in the lower
portion of the water column. However, monitoring of experimental disposal sites in Elliott Bay
during and up to 9 months after disposal showed no significant long-term impacts to water
quality (PSDDA/FEIS 1988). At the dispersive sites, oxygen-demanding materials would be
rapidly diluted and any decrease in dissolved oxygen content in the water would be un-
measurable.
2. Page 18: “At the non-dispersive sites disposed materials are generally released in areas
with unconsolidated sand and mud substrates and relatively flat bathymetry (Army Corps of
Engineers 2010). However, sediment plumes within the water column may disrupt the ability
of rockfish to pursue prey, may temporarily reduce dissolved oxygen levels, and may obscure
and homogenize depressions used by adult fish.”
DMMP Comments: Near-bottom sediment plumes associated with unconfined aquatic
disposal of dredged sediments at the DMMP’s designated sites occur intermittently, are
short-term in their duration, and are unlikely to reduce DO levels (see #1 above).
All of the DMMP’s designated sites are located in relatively deep waters characterized by
sand and mud with flat bathymetry. The extent to which critical habitat (CH) for rockfish is
mapped within any of the DMMP’s disposal site boundaries reflects the site’s proximity to
rugose/complex habitat rather than the presence of such habitat on the disposal site itself.
The disposal sites may serve as transit areas between rugose locations but it would appear
very unlikely that they represent critical habitat for rockfish. While there may have been
depressions in the bottom bathymetry at the non-dispersive disposal sites at the beginning of
the program 25 years ago, those depressions have long since been eliminated as a result of
site use.
For the record, The DMMP agencies’ position is that our designated open-water disposal
sites do not exhibit the complex/rugose characteristics of rockfish critical habitat and
disposal of dredged material at the sites is unlikely to adversely affect the physical and
biological features of rockfish critical habitat. We believe that continued use of the DMMP
sites should not be considered an activity that potentially threatens the listed rockfish
species. The remainder of our comments and suggested text revisions, however, assume that
NOAA will retain dredged material disposal as an activity requiring special management
considerations for protection of rockfish critical habitat.
3. Pages 17 & 18: “SPECIAL MANAGEMENT CONSIDERATIONS OR PROTECTION…We
identified a number of activities that may affect the physical and biological features essential
to yelloweye rockfish, canary rockfish, and bocaccio such that special management
considerations or protection may be required. Major categories of such activities include…(2)
dredging and disposal of dredged material….”
DMMP comment: This text doesn’t clearly distinguish between the activities and issues
related to dredging (and sediment quality) and those related to open-water disposal.
Insufficient info is provided on the testing and suitability determination process and monitoring
that are the keystones of the DMMP program. Readers could easily conclude that
contaminated sediment is being disposed at open-water sites. Lumping the issues
associated with a nearshore activity like “dredging” together with those from “open-water
disposal” in deep water is confusing.
Suggested text revision: “Dredging” and “dredged material disposal” should be presented as
separate activities with separate management considerations. The following reflects our
revisions to Section (2) of the Special Management Considerations (page 18) and would serve
as the text for “dredged material disposal”:
The Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) leads the administration of the Dredged Material
Management Program (DMMP). The DMMP consists of four agencies that work
collaboratively to manage and regulate the disposal of dredged material from dredging
projects in Puget Sound. The other three agencies in the DMMP are the U.S. Environmental
Protection Agency, Region 10 (EPA); the Washington Department of Ecology (Ecology); and
the Washington State Department of Natural Resources (DNR). The DMMP manages
material dredged to maintain navigational waterways and berth depths when those areas are
filled in by natural sediment deposition. The DMMP does not manage contaminated sediment
cleanups--those are managed by cleanup programs within Ecology and EPA. The DMMP
agencies determine what material can be disposed of at open water disposal sites (managed
by DNR) based on review of an extensive suite of chemical and biological testing performed
specifically to determine dredged material suitability. Only material that passes this testing is
allowed to go to open water disposal sites; material that fails cannot be disposed of at an
unconfined open water disposal site. As manager of state-owned aquatic lands, DNR
manages the disposal sites and is responsible for environmental monitoring of all non-
dispersive disposal sites. Twenty-four years of site monitoring at and around non-dispersive
sites has verified that the material disposed stays on-site and the program’s disposal site
management objectives (protecting benthic resources and compliance with WA SMS
standards) are being met both on-site and off.
Of the eight open water disposal sites in Puget Sound, seven are within the area considered
for critical habitat designation; 5 of these are considered non-dispersive because they are
located in
areas where currents are slow enough that dredged material is deposited on the disposal site
and remains there. The other two are dispersive sites that have higher current velocities, so
dredged material does not accumulate at the disposal site and settles on benthic
environments elsewhere. At the non-dispersive sites, disposed materials are generally
released in areas with unconsolidated sand and mud substrates and relatively flat bathymetry
(Army Corps of Engineers 2010). However, temporary sediment plumes within the water
column associated with disposal at both dispersive and non-dispersive sites may disrupt the
ability of rockfish to pursue prey.
The following reflects our revisions to Section (2) of the Special Management Considerations
(page 18) and would serve as the text for “dredging”:
Dredging projects require multiple permits which may include a permit from the Army Corps of
Engineers per Section 404 of the Clean Water Act, Washington State Department of Ecology
401 Water Quality Certification, Washington State Fish and Wildlife Hydraulic Project
Approval, and Washington State Department of Natural Resources State Owned Aquatic
Land Use Authorization. Dredging also occurs as part of state and federal cleanup programs.
Dredging activities may affect benthic habitats and short-term water quality, particularly when
it occurs in areas with contaminated sediments (Appendix B). Contaminants can include
metals, organometallic compounds, chlorinated hydrocarbons, phenols,
pesticides/polychlorinated biphenyls, polybrominated diphenyl ethers, and polycyclic
aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) (Army Corps of Engineers 2010). These contaminants can be
released into the water column by the dredging process and may be taken up by
phytoplankton, zooplankton, benthic invertebrates, demersal fish, forage fish, and other fishes
(Army Corps of Engineers 2010). Those contaminants can then be bioaccumulated by long-
lived predators such as rockfish and may disrupt behavior and immune system function (West
et al. 2001; Palsson et al. 2009). Dredging can also alter wave patterns and sediment
transport mechanisms near the dredge site as well as cause physical changes to the seafloor
geomorphology (e.g., substrate type and composition, surface texture) that can affect water
circulation and nutrient distribution and cause sedimentation of rocky substrate.
4. Page 18: “SPECIAL MANAGEMENT CONSIDERATIONS OR PROTECTION…Possible
modifications to dredging and disposal to prevent adversely modifying or destroying critical
habitat include placing restrictions on the spatial and temporal extent of dredging activities
and the deposition of dredge spoils, and to require some dredge spoil to be placed in
approved upland disposal sites.”
DMMP Comment: The DMMP’s position is that there is no current information to support the
further restriction of disposal windows at existing open water disposal sites. There is no
evidence that disposal at these sites is adversely affecting any of the listed rockfish species.
At this point in the 25 year history of this program, nondispersive disposal is simply adding
additional layers of the same type of substrate, not modifying or destroying critical habitat.
Furthermore, any restrictions to the spatial or temporal extent of dredged material disposal
would result in more material being disposed upland. Some areas of Puget Sound already
have very limited timeframes on dredging windows (15 – 45 days per year) due to restrictions
of the HPA and Corps’ permitting. Disposal restrictions could result in an effective ban on in-
water disposal, creating a significant economic impact (see also comment #7)
Suggested text revision: The following modifications reflect separating the dredging and
disposal activities (see #3) and edits to correct terms and clarify text:
“Possible modifications to dredged material disposal to prevent adversely modifying or
destroying critical habitat include placing restrictions on the spatial and temporal extent of
deposition of dredged material.. A consequence may be that some dredged material will need
to be taken to an approved upland disposal site.”
5. Page 31: “SPECIFIC AREAS WITHIN THE GEOGRAPHIC AREA OCCUPIED BY THE
SPECIES – The San Juan/Strait of Juan de Fuca Basin…Two open-water dredge disposal
sites are located in the basin, one in Rosario Strait and the other northwest of Port
Townsend. These are termed dispersive sites because they have higher current velocities;
thus, dredged material does not accumulate at the disposal site and settles on benthic
environments over a broad area (Army Corps of Engineers 2010). Sediment disposal activities
in this specific area may temporarily alter dissolved oxygen levels and alter the ability of
juvenile rockfish to seek out prey.”
DMMP Comment: See #1. The DMMP does not agree that disposal of sediments at
dispersive sites will temporarily alter DO levels in the vicinity of the sites given the depth of
the water column and strong currents that characterize these locations.
B. Federal Register Notice
All comments on the draft Biological Report (#1-5 above) apply to the Federal Register
Notice.
6. Page 47641: “Delineating and Mapping Areas of Complex Bathymetry Deeper than 30
Meters Containing Features Essential to the Conservation of Adult Canary, Yelloweye, and
Bocaccio Rockfish and Juvenile Yelloweye - The BTM also provides a ‘‘rugosity’’ value, which
is a measurement of variations or amplitude in the height of a surface—in this case, the
seafloor (Kvitek et al., 2003; Dunn and Halpin, 2009). Rugosity values range from 0 (i.e., flat
habitat) to 5.7 (very complex habitat). We refer to benthic areas with rugosity values of 1.005
or higher as ‘‘high rugosity.’’ We selected a rugosity value of 1.005 and higher as representing
the presence of this essential feature because the spatial area mapped as proposed critical
habitat at that level of rugosity encompassed the vast majority of the documented
occurrences with precise spatial data of yelloweye rockfish (90%), canary rockfish (86%), and
boccacio (92%) within the DPS.”
DMMP Comment: More explanation needed as to why benthic areas with rugosity values of
1.005 (on a scale from 0 – 5.7) would be considered “high rugosity” especially given that the
selection of 1.005 as a cut-off value appears to be related to presence/absence (and not
density) information alone.
7. Page 47657: “Public Comments Solicited – We are particularly interested in comments
and information in the following areas…(5)current or planned activities in the areas proposed
as critical habitat and costs of potential modifications to those activities due to critical habitat
designation; and (6) any foreseeable economic, national security, or other relevant impact
resulting from the proposed designations”
DMMP Comment: Any restrictions to the spatial or temporal extent of dredged material
disposal at existing open water sites would result in more material being disposed upland.
Since upland disposal is substantially more costly than in-water disposal, this will have a
large impact on the cost of maintenance dredging in the Pacific Northwest, which is essential
to the maritime economy of the region. Therefore, dismissal of further economic analysis (See
exhibit 3-4 in the Draft Economic Analysis) is unacceptable.

In particular, MWA will focus its comments on the proposed creation of “wraparound coverage” (Wrap Plan) as a limited excepted benefit. The proposed amendment sets out five requirements which must be met in order for a health plan to qualify as a Wrap Plan within the limited excepted benefits category, only two of which are the subject of this comment:
2) The benefits of the Wrap Plan must be designed to provide coverage beyond the “essential health benefits” (EHB) or provide coverage for non-network providers or both. The benefits may provide coverage for out-of-pocket costs, but this cannot be the primary benefit;
4) The total cost of the Wrap Plan cannot exceed 15% of the cost of the Primary Health Plan of the same employer that meets the minimum value (MV) requirements; and

The proposed regulations provide limitations for a health plan to meet the definition of an excepted benefit under the limited excepted benefit category for two stated purposes: 1) to prevent the encouragement of the employer cancelling minimum value coverage and replacing it with a Wrap Plan; and 2) to prevent lower income workers from receiving a lesser benefit than the employer’s higher income workers.

MWA asserts that the second and fourth requirements not only do not promote the two stated goals of the amendment, but actually impede the attainment of those goals. MWA further asserts that the second stated goal, i.e., preventing lower income workers from receiving a lesser benefit than the employer’s higher income workers, is a misstated goal. The goal of the amended regulations should be to provide each eligible worker with complete coverage for all Essential Health Benefits (EHB) and to eliminate as much as possible, all out of pocket expenses for EHB.

The second requirement for a Wrap Plan to qualify as a limited excepted benefit mandates that a Wrap Plan cover non-essential health benefits and provide out of network coverage. The EHB were established to define what a qualified health plan under ACA should provide in benefits. Low income employees will generally not have the money to pay up-front costs for EHB and therefore, will eventually be discouraged from purchasing coverage. If the Wrap Plan’s primary purpose was to decrease or even eliminate the out-of-pocket costs associated with the silver and bronze level plans, the employee would see a much greater benefit where they need it the most. They do not need non-EHB coverage or out of network coverage.

Thus, MWA recommends changing the primary reason for the Wrap Plan to providing coverage for EHB which eliminates or nearly eliminates front end out-of-pocket costs for low income earners as opposed to making it focused on non-EHB or Out-of-Network benefits.

The fourth stated requirement in order for coverage to qualify as a Wrap Plan, and therefore a limited excepted benefit, is that the Wrap Plan cannot cost more than 15% of the cost of the employer’s major medical coverage (MV) which is offered to the employee. A Wrap Plan will supplement a product purchased from the exchange, not the employer’s MV plan. Therefore, requiring a Wrap Plan to maintain a cost less than 15% of the cost of the MV is really not relevant. There is no correlation between the costs of the Wrap Plan versus the cost of the MV plan.

In states with high healthcare costs, the MV plan will have a higher cost, and therefore, the Wrap Plan can charge more and still be within the 15% threshold. By contrast, in states with lower healthcare costs, the Wrap Plans will have to charge substantially less or offer substantially less in benefits in order to meet the 15% threshold. Typically, Wrap Plan coverage is priced on the level of benefits provided, limited by an annual dollar amount for each covered person. The geographic healthcare costs are not a factor in the Wrap Plan pricing, again evincing the lack of relevance between the cost of the employer’s plan and the cost of the Wrap Plan.

The 15% threshold means a Wrap Plan could fall out of the 15% range simply because a major medical plan has a cost decrease. Likewise, if the Wrap Plan has a cost increase based on experience, the increase could cause the plan to fall outside the 15% range.

The 15% rule in the proposed regulation does not support the purposes stated in the regulation: 1) the 15% rule does not prevent the employer from cancelling MV coverage and replacing it with a Wrap Plan. The requirement that an employer can only offer a Wrap plan as an option to a MV plan, together with the ACA tax requirements, more than adequately protect the first stated goal of the amended regulation; and 2) the 15% rule could prevent, not assist, low income earners in receiving high quality and important EHB.

Full comments are attached.

We are a public Employee Assistance Program operated by State of Vermont’s Agency of Human Services. We are concerned that the proposed criterion B3 on Federal Register Page 77640, which states that benefits under the employee assistance program must not be financed by another group health plan, will have the unintended consequence of curtailing EAP for hundreds of thousands of public employees.

All Vermont public schools are currently members of VEHI, an Intermunicipal Insurance Association or public entity pool regulated under Vermont law, which provides health benefit programs for member schools. For over 25 years, public entity health benefits pools have performed the essential government function of providing high value health benefits to public employees at the lowest cost to local governments and their taxpayers. Many pools, including VEHI, invest in research-based wellness and prevention services designed to improve employee health and lower medical claims. As part of their wellness program, VEHI contracts with our EAP to provide services to all school employees.

The EAPs offered by health benefits pools have been effective in helping employees identify and resolve personal and work concerns that affect job performance and general well-being. EAPs are typically offered as separate programs at no charge to employees, regardless of whether they have enrolled in their employer's health benefit plans. To encourage EAP employee participation, no contributions or co-payments of any kind are required.

A typical EAP addresses a wide range of personal issues impacting employees and their spouses, including, but not limited to, eldercare, childcare, marital concerns, financial issues, stress management, parenting, and substance abuse. EAP counselors offer basic support, financial and legal help, problem resolution, resources and the like. While psychologists on occasion also help EAP participants, EAP participants requiring mental health services are referred out under their health plan. As such, these EAPs do not provide significant benefits in the nature of medical care.

The cost of EAPs is often funded by the annual contributions paid by each health benefit pool's participating employers, contributions that also fund their health benefit plans. As such, those employers are not charged a separate fee for the EAPs, in part because the cost of those programs represent a small percentage of their annual contributions (< 1 % of total pool costs), but mainly because those employers are often unlikely to retain the EAPs if they had to pay a separate fee. It is thus common practice for those employers, including public employer pool participants, to offer EAPs as a "value-add" for employees with program costs funded by the annual contributions paid by those employers to their health benefits pools.

The proposed requirement that EAP benefits must ''not be financed by another group health plan' is of grave concern. As noted, the costs of these programs - which have proven to be both highly effective and very popular - are often funded by the annual contributions paid by the pools' public employer participants. To charge a separate fee for EAPs will surely spell their demise, to the great detriment of the many thousands of public employees who depend on them.

Our concerns can be addressed if the final rules do not include the health plan financing prohibition. So long as EAPs are separate from health plans and do not provide "significant benefits in the nature of medical care" and also meet the other criteria in the proposed rules, the principal concerns noted in the preamble at 78 Fed. Reg. 77,636 to 77,637 should be fully addressed. Allowing such an EAP to be financed directly or indirectly by an ACA-compliant health plan would certainly not encourage employers to offer an EAP as a covert substitute for "minimum essential coverage''.

Our recommendation is consistent with the position adopted by the Departments in IRS Notice 2013-54 regarding health flexible spending arrangements ("FSAs") and health reimbursement arrangements ("HRAs"). To prevent employers from offering them as a substitute for ACA-compliant health plans, HRAs must be limited to employees who are actually enrolled in a group health plan, and FSAs can only be offered to employees who are eligible to participate in medical plans that are not limited to excepted benefits. Once these requirements are met, HRAs and FSAs qualify as bona fide excepted benefits. Allowing EAPs to be financed directly or indirectly by an ACA-compliant health plan will serve the same purpose by encouraging employers to offer both EAPs and health plans to their employees, even though their participation in the EAP is not contingent on their enrollment in their employers' health plans. It will also not encourage employer abuse or evasion of the mental health parity requirements adopted by the Departments.

Thank you for your consideration and attention to this matter.

The proposed rule defining excepted benefits to include Employee Assistance Programs contains the following:
"The second criterion for an EAP to constitute excepted benefits is that its benefits cannot be coordinated with benefits under another group health plan. The Departments propose three conditions to meet this standard..... Lastly, benefits under the EAP must not be financed by another group health plan."

The last of the three criteria is problematic. Many EAPs are provided by or through health plans. The EAP may be offerred by a health plan as a separate product that is purchased specifically by an employer or union. The health plan may offer other benefits that can be purchased separately, e.g., dental, vision, disability, medical or behavioral health. A literal reading of the proposed rule may prohibit this common practice. Another common industry practice is for EAP products to be offerred by health plans as an add-on benefit to other health, behavioral or disability products. The EAP product may be offerred at reduced or no cost to employers or unions as an incentive to purchase the health or other products. Again, a literal reading of the proposed rule would prevent this common practice, disrupting a very large number contracts. Many of the largest health insurers employ this model covering many thousands of EAP contracts. Many union and multiple employer welfare associations and Taft-Hartley Trusts provide EAP products that are supported through the MEWA or trust, as well as other health and welfare benefits. The third proposed criterion might require these union EAPs to be considered health benefits.

The other two criteria in the proposed rule will prevent the coordination of benefits between EAP and health insurance products. The third criterion is not only unnecessary, it would disrupt thousands of contracts between employers, unions and EAPs. I strongly recommend the third criterion be eliminated.

Alliance Work Partners (AWP),one of the largest non-profit, freestanding EAPs in the US, respectfully offers the following comments on ACA proposed regulations regarding EAP as an excepted benefit:
Criterion 1 – EA Program does not provide significant benefits in the nature of medical care.
The discipline of EAP is uniquely specialized and EAPS are, at their core, defined as workplace productivity tools that offer a broad array of services. As specified in the Employee Assistance Professionals Association (EAPA) EAP Standards, “An EAP is a workplace program designed to assist: (1) work organizations in addressing productivity issues, and (2) "employee clients" in identifying and resolving personal concerns, including health, marital, family, financial, alcohol, drug, legal, emotional, stress, or other personal issues that may affect job performance. EAP is short-term and solution focused. Medical issues are referred out of the EAP to medical professionals. EAP core technology represents the essential components of the employee assistance (EA) profession. These components combine to create a unique approach to addressing work-organization productivity issues and "employee client" personal concerns affecting job performance.”

•In specific response to whether EAP offer significant benefits in the nature of medical care, “Significant” could include the following which EAPs do not provide
oDSM-5 or ICD-9 diagnoses
oCare provided by MDs
oLong-term or intensive services
oInpatient, partial or outpatient treatment in a medical facility
oDocumentation for services provided on official healthcare forms (HCFA)
•Session limits are not ideal for defining “significant” relative to EAP as sessions can be used for non-medical services such as services not provided by physicians, work life services which help with issues like legal, financial, eldercare, childcare, college, school and adoption concerns. In addition, allotted sessions may be divided among varied problem categories such as, parenting, marital, stress management or used in multiple episodes of care within a contract year.

Criterion 2 – EAP benefits cannot be coordinated with benefits under another group health plan
•Participants in a separate group plan must not be required to exhaust benefits under the EAP before an individual is eligible for benefits under the other health plan
oWe endorse this proposed regulation as written. It reinforces the requirements under MHPAEA, gives employees freedom to choose amongst services and ensures that employees will not be required to complete work life services or other training programs before being able to access care through the health plan
•Participant eligibility for benefits under the EAP must not be dependent on participation in another group health plan.
oWe endorse this proposed regulation as written. EAP is a workplace focused service and the bulk of our services would not be effective if not available to the entire workforce. This professional focus for the EAP being on the discipline of workplace productivity improvement, is one reason EAP services need to be differentiated from the group health plan.
•We agree that benefits under the EAP must not be financed by another group health plan.
•Evidence proves an EAP is incorporated into a Health Plan can become limited in scope. The focus of the EAP can become strictly limited to medical/insurance cases and not the broader needs of the entire workforce.
•Little or no regular promotion, which leads to utilization ceasing.
•Few or no utilization reports
•Critical incident response is unavailable except as a “buy-up” service.
•Little or no management consultations or referrals.
•intervention is often limited to telephonic or online assessments and referrals (referrals are not usually customized or specific to select providers).
•Face-to-face counseling is offered but rarely provided.
•Infrequent follow-up with clients, meaning there is no way to know whether employees have improved or received additional help.
•Requiring benefits under the EAP must not be financed by another group health plan has the greatest potential to improve the quality of EAP services provided in the current EAP market. What health plans call EAP often does not provide the minimum scope of EAP services or meet existing quality standards for EAP programs. No allowing health plan to finance their EAP product does not prohibit them from offering their product to customers. Therefore, claims of market disruption are exaggerated.

•Criterion 3 - No employee premiums or contributions are required to participate in the EAP.
oWe endorse this proposed regulation as written. Premiums and contributions are common structures of medical plans. Employee premiums and contributions have not been part of the structure of EAP.

•Criterion 4 - There is no cost sharing under the EAP
We endorse this proposed regulation.

My response to new proposed EAP Federal Rules is positioned as a stakeholder to treat EAP’s as excepted benefits for reasons similar to the arguments with respect to other specialized health plans including vision and dental.

Criterion 1 – The clearest way to clarify EAP with respect to the regulations would be to define what an Excepted EAP is rather than what it is not by using the industry definitions which illustrate the non-medical nature of EAP services.
The discipline of EAP is uniquely specialized and EAPS are, at their core, defined as workplace productivity tools that offer a broad array of services. A listing of core services illustrates that few of the services in the array would be considered medical. As specified in the Employee Assistance Professionals Association (EAPA) EAP Standards, “An EAP is a workplace program designed to assist: (1)work organizations in addressing productivity issues, and (2)"employee clients” in identifying and resolving personal concerns, including health, marital, family, financial, alcohol, drug, legal, emotional, stress, or other personal issues that may affect job performance. EAP is short-term and solution focused. Medical issues, when recognized, are referred out of the EAP to medical professionals as further identified in the EAP Standards. Employee assistance program core technology represents the essential components of the employee assistance (EA) profession. These components combine to create a unique approach to addressing work-organization productivity issues and "employee client" personal concerns affecting job performance.”

Criterion 2 –
A.Participants in a separate group plan must not be required to exhaust benefits under the EAP before an individual is eligible for benefits under the other health plan.
•I endorse this criterion

B.Participant eligibility for benefits under the EAP must not be dependent on participation in another group health plan.
•I endorse this criterion. EAPs should be independent of and not funded by any group health plans. All employees determined as eligible for benefits by their employer should have access to EAP services, without regard to their participation in a specific health plan. I have seen conflicts arise in employer groups where employees have elected to participate in their spouses’ health plans or where employers offer multiple health plans and not all of the plans offered include an EAP. In these cases, all employees would not necessarily have access to an EAP. Therefore, separation of the health plan and the EAP is essential.

C.Benefits under the EAP must not be financed by another group health plan.
I support this provision. When the EAP benefits are financed by the group health or disability plan, there are several negative results:
•Funding amount from the group health or disability plan for the EAP is minimal.
•EAP is hidden within the plan leading to low level of awareness by employees of the EAP benefit.
•Minimal EAP services are available. Counseling is provided through brief telephonic access only leading to few cases being resolved within the EAP itself.
•No organizational support available to triage for crisis response or for clinical consultations to assist the managers and/or HR professionals to help mitigate risks to the organization.
This leads to low utilization and low satisfaction among employees and the organization leaders in the time of need.

Criterion 3 - No employee premiums or contributions are required to participate in the EAP. I endorse this proposed regulation as written. Premiums and contributions are common structures of medical plans. EAP, as an employer paid benefit, is offered at no cost to the employees and their dependents as part of the plan.

Criterion 4 - There is no cost sharing under the EAP
I endorse this proposed regulation with respect to employees not being responsible for any cost sharing.

Criterion 1
In general, for each presenting participant an EAP does one of two things, neither of which constitute the provision of medical care: (1) assist the participant, within the EAP, with resolution of one or more of the above issues that could progress into a mental health or substance abuse diagnosis but, at the time of the service, has or have not yet been diagnosed as such (most of these models are 6 sessions or less), or (2) after brief screening and assessment, refer the participant to a health care specialist or treatment agency covered under the participant’s group health plan or to a community behavioral health resource when the participant does not have an appropriate group health plan benefit. According to the Internal Revenue Service, screening and other preventive care services such as these are to be disregarded for purposes of determining whether an EAP provides “significant benefits in the nature of medical care or treatment”. EAPs simply act as a referral source to mental health and substance abuse treatment services that are provided outside the EAP by health care practitioners qualified to provide such services. It is worth noting that EAPs provide these services to participants in order to assist employers with employee productivity issues that stem from employee’s unresolved personal problems. EAPs provide to employers valuable information regarding absenteeism, presenteeism, work engagement, life satisfaction, and workplace distress. This is the bedrock of what EAPs are historically all about, making the EAP field very different from the medical field. Should the Departments find it necessary to impose a general standard such as the one proposed here, CGP offers the following comments:

The quantitative limitation of 10 outpatient visits or less “for mental health or substance abuse disorder counseling” is reasonable. However, it is important that the Departments make clear whether the limitation on the number of visits applies per calendar year or per presenting issue. The quantitative limitation should be defined as “no more than 10 outpatient visits per presenting problem in a calendar year”.

The phrase “diabetes counseling” is ambiguous and should be clarified further. Diabetes counseling is really a subset of “disease management”, which aims to prevent the worsening of several health concerns including diabetes and the possible onset of disease states, as well as training and education on a variety of disease-related topics.

Criterion 2
(a)We support this condition.
(b)We support this condition.
(c)Many EAPs are provided by or through a group health plan and therefore financed by the group health plan. The group health plan may provide the EAP either through its own service arm utilizing its own staff and network affiliates or through a third party EAP. The EAP may be offered to employers as an add-on benefit, similar to dental, vision, or disability benefits, and may be offered at reduced or no cost to employers as an incentive to purchase the group health plan or other products. This proposed condition would be inconsistent with this widespread industry practice. For those group health plans that offer this type of embedded product in an effort to ensure continuity of care and better quality care, we do not support this condition. However, some of these embedded EAPs are plagued with extremely low or no utilization activity and the group health plan therefore pays its EAP vendors very little with this expectation in mind. These so-called “free” or “sleeping” EAPs have been promoted by certain group health plans as “loss leaders”, meaning if an employer purchases another higher margin product from the group health plan, the group health plan will offer the EAP for free. Many observers in the field view this practice as degrading the quality and impact of a more comprehensive offering. For these types of offerings, we support this condition. Accordingly, this condition should be further refined so as not to disqualify EAPs that coordinate services with a group health plan in order to provide participants with more effective benefits.

I am writing in response to the invitation for public comments on the proposed rule entitled, Amendments to Excepted Benefits in the December 23, 2014, Federal Register and issued jointly by the U.S. Departments of Labor, Treasury, and Health and Human Services (the Departments). The proposed rule amends the current regulations to establish a new limited wraparound excepted benefit category and conditions to achieve equity in coverage between certain health benefits offered to full-time employees and part-time employees.

These comments outline significant concerns with respect to the authority of the Departments to establish this new type of wraparound excepted benefit coverage under the existing limited benefit category of excepted benefits. In addition, there are other important concerns including the application of the excise tax on high cost employer-sponsored health coverage, and the need for additional conditions in order to achieve the intended equity in coverage with respect to employer contributions and the proposed sunset date.

1) Consider adding a requirement that carriers must state that they meet these specific requirements in the form and rate filings, so that state regulators are aware of these requirements (which in practice, are rarely encountered).

2) Due to frequent changes to the AV calculator on the primary plan, EHB on the primary plan, and BHP designs, consider requiring annual approval, to ensure that designs supplement the individual market and BHP plans appropriately.

3) These rules should state the extent to which riders can be used. For example, can a rider be used to provide the meaningful additional benefit, or must the meaningful additional benefit be part of the main policy and not at the option of the person to purchase? Can riders be used to exceed the maximum (FSA limit which is $2500 in 2014) through parsing out supplementation of a certain EHB category from the main policy and relegating that EHB category to a rider? Should riders be disallowed entirely from these plans? Riders are problematic in this particular excepted product, at least in terms of supplementation of the meaningful benefit as well as an EHB category.

4) The pilot program / sunset date as proposed may cause issues in states that have statutes that favor consumer protections, such as guarantee renewability.

5) The carrier should have to clearly state what benefit is intended to qualify as the additional meaningful benefit. The rule should provide more guidance on "meaningful" - is this in terms of actuarial value? At what level is the benefit meaningful?

6) The regulations should clarify how the carrier is expected to ensure and document that the employer met the requirements that allow the product to be sold. Record retention would be helpful as well on this important topic to assist with regulators' market conduct activity.

7) The proposed rule should state whether all EHB member costs categories must be supplemented on equal/similar terms. Right now, this is vague: a carrier might propose a) excluding major or minor categories from supplementation, such as office visits, or imaging, or pharmacy, or mental health, or even 2) copays altogether (versus deductible, coinsurance). Such exclusions or tiering of payments or coverages make such supplemental plans less transparent and the plans less valuable. Consider requiring that all EHBs and all member costs be supplemented on equal terms up to the policies' overall limit.

8) Due to the low loss ratios that supplemental products are typically allowed to have (50-60% in many states, without retrospective corrections) - meaning high margins for insurers - as well as the high degree of administrative costs in supplementing plans - the three agencies should consider alternatives that better help low income workers, such as allowing employers to support individual's premiums, or individual's out of pocket costs, at least for workers at certain levels of FPL. The higher retrospective loss ratios required on the individual market will assure a higher degree of employers' support is used to support workers, versus insurers.

It is important to note that Minnesota runs a Basic Health Plan (BHP) - MinnesotaCare. Minnesota is the only state currently offering a BHP. Many Minnesotans who would normally qualify for federal benefit and premium subsidies in the individual market are instead triaged to the BHP, such that Minnesota has no enrollment in the 87% and 94% CSR plans in the individual market. We have difficulty in understanding how the spirit and intent of this rule should coordinate with Minnesota's atypical situation, given that the benefits available under the BHP are generous already; there is little left to supplement. As such, products will have difficulty justifying that the premiums are not excessive in relation to the claims incurred for many of the people this rule is intended to assist. At a minimum, for states with a BHP, consider requiring multiple fixed supplement forms that coordinate with the multiple fixed BHP designs, and that the meaningful additional benefit provided be a benefit that is not available through the individual market nor the BHP.

Going back to the inception of Red Snapper IFQ program there has been the question of what to do with inactive/never activated accounts. I am not sure what percent of the quota presently falls into this category but I seem to recall that it used to be around 3 percent. Presumably the statement "allow NOAA Fisheries IFQ Customer Service staff to close an IFQ account if no landing transactions or IFQ transfers have been completed by the IFQ account holder in at least a year" addresses this issue. I think a year is a ridiculously short period of time to apply to this serious of a situation. If a shareholder had been an active participant for years and all of a sudden becomes "inactive" it is likely due to death, illness or some other catastrophic event. At such times a year is certainly an insufficient period of time for family members to determine the proper course of action in regard to disposition of assets. In addition what is meant by "close an IFQ account"? Does this mean a shareholder loses their shares and they are redistributed to current shareholders? It would seem to me that a statute of limitations would apply to this situation and surely it would be well in excess of 1 year. In regard to late landings I would be in favor of 1 hour vs 30 minutes.

I do not see why anyone should need more than 72 hrs to offload.

NOTIFICATION WINDOW-
24 hours will be a huge improvement to the notification window, giving fishermen every opportunity to report known itineraries as soon as they are negotiated.

LANDING WINDOW
-A 30 Min window is way too short. A 90 minute window will provide an allowance for weather and extreme situations. Most estimates will fall within this window, and not necessitate further modifications.
Keep in mind that a typical trip home from the fishing grounds is ten hours long. Half an hour is only 5 % of that total. Weather changes quickly. A ten knot breeze from the southwest can quickly change to a twenty knot wind from the northwest. This is a 100 % change. Two to four foot seas can quickly change to six to eight foot seas, severely impeding safe travel speeds. Weather often changes on the way home from the fishing grounds, after notifications have been made.
It is entirely likely that changing weather can delay a 100 mile offshore journey by more than 30 minutes. A 90 minute window would be more appropriate.
.
ADDITIONAL DELAYS CAUSED BY ONEROUS REGULATION
After amending the landing notification ONE time, it sounds punitive that a second amendment would trigger an additional 3 hour delay. The whole idea is to update law enforcement with current information. What is the rationale to cause more delay, delay imposed only by regulation? If a captain is compelled to remain on the water simply because of regulation, something is wrong. This is a safety issue. Law enforcement should accommodate captains as they communicate changes in itineraries for the purpose of mutual consideration. The current rules have no allowance for weather deterioration and the attendant delays in travel time from the fishing grounds. We should address this first, and then determine if there really is a problem with too many revisions, before we codify onerous delays in three hour blocs.
PLEASE REMOVE THIS PROPOSAL.
At a bare minimum, consider a one hour delay, and then only on the third update.

LANDING PRIOR TO THE NOTIFICATION –
Should read that an officer is present or has authorized the landing. This would require that the authorization is accompanied by a confirmation number. OLE already has catch estimates. Suspicious activity should be noted and the available resources would be more effective if they were targeted to the outliers instead of the whole fleet, who are well aware that violations have severe economic consequences for IFQ shareholders. Additionally, the officer always has the option to deny the request. Allowing fishery enforcement officer’s room to exercise judgment might promote relationship building among Law enforcement and industry.

TIMEFRAME FOR COMPLETING OFFLOAD-
72 hours is too short to codify into law. If there needs to be a time specified, then 96 hours would be an improvement.
Additionally, and perhaps more importantly, the rule should read that offloading should occur within X hours of the current notification, not the landing itself. Glutted markets sometimes require small-scale independent fishermen to store fish onboard until a proper bargain with dealers can be struck. Forcing economic activity into regulatory timeframes is a slippery slope, and should be avoided in a market economy.

TIMEFRAME FOR SUBMITTING LANDING TRANSACTION -
Please consider amending the proposed language by removing ‘the same day’, and replacing it with ‘to within 24 hours’, or ‘no later than midnight the next day’. Many offloads occur later in the day, and are conducted by laborers who weigh, haul, and repack fish well after the office staff, that submit the online reporting, have gone home for the day. An allowance for this normal and customary aspect of business is reasonable.

ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES –
The first line item reads “Only accounts without shares or allocation or dealer accounts who have paid all cost recovery fees can close their account. “ This should apply in conjunction with the third line item that reads “The rule would also allow NMFS IFQ Customer Service staff to close an IFQ account if no landing transactions or IFQ transfers have been completed by the IFQ account holder in at least 1 year.”

I’m writing in regards to the proposed rule changes to the red snapper and grouper-tilefish IFQ programs.

Vessel Accounts: The proposed rule that allows allocation to be held in either a vessel or the linked shareholders account at the time of landing is much needed.

Notification Window: Extending the notification reporting window to 24 hours is needed for flexibility.

Landing Window: The landing window needs extended to 1 hour minimum. Many commercial fishing vessels only make way at about only 6-8 knots and there are times when vessels begin to enter the pass and the outgoing tide slows them down substantially. It’s not like they can just push the throttle down and make up the difference in speed. If you don’t get into cell phone range until your 3 hours out you have very little margin for error. There could be issues like other vessels obstructing the course, no wake zones with the addition of tide burden changes or even increased seasonal summer time traffic. Inclement weather could be a factor too. Even normal waterway traffic such as narrow channel and commercial traffic ahead moving very slow ahead of fishing vessel can lead to window lapse. Perhaps for safety reasons the window merits the time be extended to even 2 hours. For all these reason I think extending the window to minimum of 1 hours has plenty rationalization.

Changes to a Landing Notification: As long as the vessel is not required to wait an additional 3 hours to land when the landing time is later than the previous notification.

Landing Prior to the Notification Time: Perhaps add designated crew member in the event of emergency that affect both the vessel owner and or operator. There are times that family emergencies or other unknown issues develop.

Time Restrictions of Offloading: I think allowing the unloaded to continue even after 6:00 p.m. even with or without an officer being present should be allowed as long as the unloading began before 6:00 p.m. The summer days are much longer in all regions (time zones) and there is still ample daylight up until 8:00 p.m. and given the severity of enforcement and penalties subject to violation there is little reason to think there would be issues.

Time frame for completing offload: I strongly think that 96 hours is more appropriate than 72 hours because of so many issues that might arise. Those issues include but not limited to market gluts, emergencies, issue with dealer or crew member, weather (hurricane), weekends, holidays, ice machine or cooler problems and mechanical issue for either vessel or even the fish house truck.

Prohibit Deduction of Ice and Water Weight: I think it would be extremely erroneous not allow for at least 2% ice & water weight deduction. Ice and water weigh deduction is a reality and not allowing for that is just unreasonable. If you've ever unloaded fish before you would understand the sum of ice and water weight. If worried about the 1-3% recovery fees why not implement a “use it lose it” clause in the red snapper IFQ that’s not harvested so that could be redistributed to the shareholders to maximize the benefit. The Red Snapper Ad Hoc panel that developed the profiles for IFQ had asked for a “use it or lose it” but the Gulf Council removed it from the original plan. That manifested the lost recovery fees mentioned.

Time frame for Submitting Landings Transaction: I would think 24 hours or longer is more reasonable than the same day transaction. Sometimes you just have to put yourself in similar circumstances to understand the need.

Also, I would like to add that I don’t think it’s fair to allow other dealers to view the specific transactions of other dealers and vessels. It would think that information should be private. Why do other dealers need a specific access of any other vessel or fish dealer’s commerce? This seems like a conflict and unfair to both the fishing vessel and the dealers by allowing others to have open access to your personal business records.

Close Account Form: What happens to the shares in the closed accounts? I assume the shares from closed accounts would be re-distributed to each shareholders based on percentage.

One hour leeway would be more desirable that 30 minutes for the following reasons.

1)Many boats cruise slowly
2) Tide and weather are significant factors as to the accuracy of landing times

The proposed 30 minute landing time for IFQ Fisheries will be too restrictive in my opinion. I feel that a one to two hour time frame would be a more realistic time window for the commercial fisherman.

I would also suggest that you provide an editable 3 hour notice such that adjusted arrival times, etc. can be entered and resubmitted by simply clicking a check box and/or other options without having to create a whole new notice.

Some of the proposed changes to the grouper snapper IFQ program are not well thought out and will cause difficulty to an already difficult business. Specifically I see problems in the following.

Requirement that a vessel must land within 30 minutes after the time given, this sounds good on paper but there are many many reasons that a boat will run late, most are out of the control of the fishermen these include, weather, boat traffic, currents, mechanical problems, communication problems, and many more unavoidable situations, it would be much more reasonable to have a 6 hour window as long as it is after the time given. If law enforcement officers need to know where a vessel is that was supposed to land they do have the option to track them with the required VMS. How hard is that? Please remember that even commercial air liners often land at different times than they are scheduled and they and their operators are much more sophisticated than fishermen.

Not allowing the deduction of water and ice makes dealers report incorrect weights, thus making the information unusable. Is the intent to product lower quality fish or to cost the seafood industry some percentage of current landings. If law enforcement on the scene feels that too much weight was deducted from a load of fish they can ask the dealer to rinse and de-ice the fish and re weigh them. Additionally there is a built in safe guard in that the fishermen will not let the dealer take off too much weight from their catch because they get paid biased on the weight of their catch. Due to the fact that this is a weight based business transaction between fishermen and dealer it is self regulating.

Additionally it should be taken into account that not all dealers are located on the water, I have felt and continue to feel that all the laws in regards to unloading are very unfair to land locked dealers. Firstly I'd like to commend the Fisheries Service for many of the new proposals regarding Gulf IFQ landing protocols that will enable and increase flexibility for fishermen/shareholders and dealers that participate in this program. The 24 hour window for landings notification will be of great benefit to industry and is a good example.

However, there are several proposed changes that need further review.

Allowing only a half hour or even 1 hour window from the notified time to actual landing is prohibitive and punitive and simply does not make common sense. Most vessels in the commercial snapper/grouper complex are “slow” boats, only making 5-7 knots at sea, and this is EXTREMELY subject to inclement weather, tides and currents, or boardings by enforcement. If a vessel is 120 nautical miles from port....(very common) being able to predict landing within a half hour in a 20 hour trip is difficult at best. *** I discussed this with Andy Strelcheck, and he informed me that in the body of the rule (not in the original notification) there is a provision for a ONE TIME ammendment PER LANDING notification to change the landing time without the penalty of waiting an additional three hours***** Affording fisherman this tool at least makes a ONE HOUR window livable....I would advocate for at least 1.5 hours if not 2. Currently we have 12 hours to land from the time of landing notification, despite the fact that this window was unintended. Nonetheless it is how industry has operated since the inception of these programs. Yet, because many VMS units don't report very well...IF AT ALL.... having to rely on these antiquated dinosaurs of technology to comply with a hard and fast time window puts a fisherman in jeopardy of a violation. In addition many cell phone services only work within 6 miles of the “beach”. So again, if a fisherman is running late they may not be able to “update” a “tardy” notification until it's too late.

The idea of prohibiting the “tare” of ice and water weight during the weighing process would upset ALL THE LANDING DATA that stock assessments have used since day ONE! Since we started recording landings the subtraction of ice and water weight has been part and parcel of the DATA....So then lets add the weight back into the model and suddenly gag are no longer under going overfishing!!!!. this proposal could be improved providing a limitation on the “value” assigned to the “tare” i.e.: 1 or 2 % Some dealers, like myself weigh fish in “totes” or “lugs” that hold up to 130 lbs. After recording the weight of a tote, the fish are then removed and placed in whatever shipping container is designated. But guess what...for every hundred lbs of fish removed there is approximately .3 to 1 lb of ice and water left over in the tote. We “tare” that amount or subtract it from the overall landing. How could anyone find it reasonable to charge a fisherman's IFQ account for something that clearly is NOT A FISH...or any part of a fish? As a dealer I can't sell THAT! How can you expect me to pay the fisherman for something I can't sell?

If this proposed modification is implemented as written, we will have a sudden imbalance in the data stream for stock assessment that has been the status quo since Fred Flinstone.

Thie following provision: Allow NOAA Fisheries IFQ Customer Service staff to close an IFQ account if no landing transactions or IFQ transfers have been completed by the IFQ account holder in at least 1 year... This provision is too broad, has no checks and balances within it, and may disenfranchise shareholders that have every intention of staying in the fishery but for whatever reason did not do so in a 12 month period. My suggestion is that the rule would include language that makes NOAA Fisheries accountable for due diligence as in sending a certified letter with a 30 day response window. Shareholders should have the opportunity to respond to such a drastic action

Thanks for trying to make the IFQ program more usuable.

Martin Fisher

My name is Tess Hayden and I am a second year graduate student at Alaska Pacific University in Anchorage, Alaska, currently finishing up my master’s in environmental science. I strongly urge you to reconsider this supplemental draft EIS for two main reasons.

First, there is a serious lack of scientific data showing the impacts of drilling on marine mammals. In particular, there is not enough evidence proving that the noise from drilling activities will have a negligible impact on these mammals. Until you can prove that drilling will not negatively impact these mammals and their breeding, feeding, and migration habitats, then you should not be in a position to issues permits.

In order to fix this lack of data, you need to incorporate new acoustic information into your EIS. You can then use this information to create a noise budget. Creating a noise budget for drilling activities will further ensure the protection and continued health of the marine mammals that inhabit the Arctic Ocean.

Second, this draft does not incorporate enough information about protecting biologically significant areas. With both increased drilling and shipping, certain areas need to be protected for both migration patterns and for subsistence use by the Alaska native populations. This draft is lacking information when it comes to protecting those areas. With the changing climate and increased activity in the arctic, it is important that the species inhabiting this area are able to live in a healthy environment. There must be strict guidelines for human activities in the arctic so that those species are not driven towards extinction.

I hope that you take these items of interest into consideration. These are very important issues that were not given enough attention in supplemental draft. Please consider collecting more scientific data before allowing drilling activities in the arctic.

Thank you for taking the time to read over my comments.

Tess Hayden

This is a comment from a local resident that neither opposes nor endorses any of the progressive alternatives but is submitted to request additional analysis in regards to seismic exploration.
The issue is that pinnepeds in the arctic do not react predictably to seismic procedures that are designed to mitigate incidents of harassment of whales. Additionally, a hypothesis has not been disproven by research that seal mortality has increased due to seismic exploration activity in 2010-11.
Necropsies performed on recovered skin-lesioned seals dying on the Arctic coastline in late summer of 2011 following a high level noise, (120 db at 130000 meters), seismic operation by Statoil far offshore in deeper waters near the ice shelf, indicated organ damage in form of spotted scarring on liver, kidneys, lungs.
As substantiated by US Dept of Navy research on Very Low Frequency High Amplitude Sonar, marine mammals, especially young and inexperienced animals, are susceptible to nitrogen narcossis resulting from sudden surfacing from depths when startled. Although they have biologic capability to mitigate embolism formation in muscle tissue, organs are more susceptible.
There is no conclusion to this hypothesis because research on seal response to noise has not been successfully conducted in the arctic. In fact, scientists know very little about seals in the arctic because they have been unable to capture and tag but a few, and none of these have been studied for their response to seismic exploration procedure.
This is a request for more research on this subject before finalizing this EIS.

It is flawed because it’s built on remarkably poor and outdated science. And it fails to consider the cumulative negative effects of industrial noise on wildlife. You need to shelve your current study about protecting Arctic marine mammals from noise-related impacts of offshore oil and gas development.

Please protect one of America’s treasures, the Arctic's pristine waters and its marine life, from industrial noise.

Thank you for your consideration on these matters.

Dear NOAA and BOEM,

The Ocean Protection Coalition is a 35 year-old community based organization that is dedicated to the health and vitality of the world's oceans.

We strongly oppose the proposed continuation and expansion of offshore oil exploration in the Alaskan Arctic.  American citizens, and people all over the world, have clearly stated their concerns over the extremely unwise and unsafe practice of drilling for oil or natural gas in a harsh and frozen marine environment. A spill there will be impossible to control or contain.  Spills, leaks and accidents are inevitable in oil operations, even in the best of conditions. In the Arctic, these occurrences will have long term and irreversible effects on many species of whales, seals, sea lions, birds and fish.  We know this already, so why continue on a path we know to be harmful, by exploring for oil in areas we know to be too hazardous to drill?

Since we already know that offshore drilling in the Arctic will inevitably lead to disaster, it makes no sense to engage in exploration activities, such as seismic testing.  The underwater explosions for proposed seismic testing in Arctic waters will deafen, harm and kill thousands of whales and other marine mammals.  Why do this, to advance activities we know will lead to catastrophe for these struggling species?

For these glaring and inescapable reasons, the OPC strongly recommends you adopt Alternative 1, the no action alternative, and cease further oil exploration activities in unsafe offshore areas of Alaska and the Arctic.

Signed,

The Steering Committee and Members OPC,
and the citizens of Northern California

My name is Jeff Lackey. I manage two vessels out of Newport. Both participate in the whiting fishery and one (F/V Miss Sue) participates in the bottom trawl fishery in the catch shares program. I support the proposed rule to modify the trawl RCA boundaries that has been analyzed and twice approved by the council. The new rule will provide our vessel opportunities seaward of the RCA’s to catch target species, primarily Dover Sole.

The proposed rule is in line with the MSA: The MSA at its core has two main components: The first is conservation of the resource and the second is utilization of the resource. Sometimes we don’t talk enough about the utilization component of the MSA.

There are three important points relative to Conservation for the proposed rule:
1st) significant reduction in catch of rebuilding groundfish species in the almost three year history of the catch shares program (detailed in the EA section 3.4.2.1) demonstrates the effectiveness of individual accountability
2nd) habitat / species in these areas are not likely to incur any significant impacts under the proposed rule (according to EA section 4.3.2)
3rd) Analysis for risk of extreme catch events in EA (section 4.4.2.1) leads to the conclusion that the proposed rule “should provide additional fishing opportunity for valuable target species, with little conservation risk to rebuilding stocks of groundfish.”

Relative to Utilization, the EA (section 5.1) demonstrates the proposed rule is consistent with National Standards 5, 7, & 8 which state that conservation and management measures shall “consider efficiency in the utilization of the fishery resources”, “minimize costs”, & “take into account the importance of fishery resources to fishing communities”

The proposed rule provides increased harvest opportunities, and that translates to increased efficiencies, which is so crucial to our vessel and other vessels dependent upon bottom trawl fishery.

Some people may be concerned about lifting a small portion of the RCA restrictions. We are all in the process of getting past the mindset that restrictions only come in the form of geographical lines or gear regulations. The catch shares program itself is a huge restriction and the data on catch of rebuilding groundfish species clearly shows the restriction is working.

Over 90% of the area analyzed under the proposed rule is soft substrate. The biggest area of hard or mixed substrate off the coast of central Oregon where we fish is “Daisy Bank” and there is already a protected EFH area there. Even if there were not an EFH area there, our vessel would not go there because the captain will avoid hard bottom / high relief areas, just like he now does in such areas outside of the RCA’s. It is also worth noting EA section 5.2 notes that “The proposed action is not anticipated to result in substantial adverse effects to groundfish EFH and is not anticipated to affect EFH designated for other species.”

To Whom It May Concern:
I urge NOAA to reconsider Amendment 45 to the Fishery Management Plan for the Crab FMP. I am an undergraduate student at Dartmouth College with an interest in public policy in general and fishing policy in particular. I agree with the fundamental goal of the Magnuson Stevens Act: to prevent overfishing while achieving the optimum yield of our fish stocks. Adopting Amendment 45 will be counterproductive to achieving this goal because I doubt the ability of fishing operations to self-regulate. Self-regulation will fail because the industry will likely fail to reach an agreement to sustainably fish. If the industry does reach an agreement initially, it is unlikely all operators will permanently adhere to it. Even if all operators do live up to the agreement, it will likely be inadequate to prevent overfishing.
Amendment 45 fails to provide adequate measures to ensure that fisheries will have to develop a sustainable fishing strategy in the absence of sideboard limits. The Amendment tries to promote effective self-regulation by requiring each operation to consent to eliminating sideboard limits. Each operation has an economic incentive to fish sustainably in order to preserve the stock for future use. The operations would therefore only consent to eliminating sideboard limits if they believed they had alternative strategy to ensure sustainable fishing. However, this logic is flawed because some fishing operations may agree to eliminate sideboard limits without a guarantee of effective self-regulation. A firm that is operating at a loss because of sideboard limits will agree to eliminate sideboard limits regardless of whether it believes self-regulation would guarantee sustainable fishing. This is because the continued existence of a financially struggling firm is more threatened by short-term financial loss than by the long-term threat of overfishing. It is therefore possible for firms to agree to eliminate sideboard limits without actually having any intention of engaging in effective self-regulation.
Even if the firms did manage to agree on effective self-regulation, Amendment 45 lacks measures that would ensure self-regulation would continue to be effective after the initial required consent. Firms may agree to self-regulation initially, but change their mind as circumstances change. This could happen in two ways. First, if a firms financial situation changed for the worse, it might be driven to overfish in order to stay profitable. This would happen for the same reasons as described above. Second, if communication and trust between the independent operators deteriorated, the stock would be subject to a race for fish. If one firm stops playing by the rules established by the industry, or if the other firms suspect that one firm is cheating, then trust between the various firms would deteriorate. In this case, an individual firm would know that even if it restrained from overfishing, the stock might still deplete because other firms are not fishing sustainably. The individual firm would then lose its incentive to fish responsibly. All of the firms would make this same calculation if trust deteriorated, which would lead to overfishing.
Even if we assumed that trust between the fishing operators did not deteriorate, self-regulation would still lead to overfishing because the industry would not adopt adequate measures to ensure sustainable fishing. This would occur for two reasons. First, the fishing operations likely lack the resources necessary to determine if the stock is healthy or not. While the NMFS has access to teams of scientists and years of case studies to calculate the health of a stock, most independent firms lack these resources. This is especially true of hook and line vessels, which tend to be owned by small firms. This means any effort to establish sustainable fishing practices by the industry itself will likely not be grounded in scientific evidence, which exposes the stock to overfishing. Second, even if the firms had access to scientific evidence, there would still be an economic incentive to use less conservative estimates for what constitutes overfishing. One of the most common critiques the fishing lobby has of NOAAs fishing regulations is that it relies on science that too conservatively estimates what a healthy stock looks like. If catch limits are eliminated, it is therefore unlikely that firms will adopt a standard of sustainable fishing that lives up to the scientific standard currently used by NOAA.
Self-regulation of sustainable fishing by the fishing industry, even when allowed on a small scale, will inevitably lead to overfishing. Though Amendment 45 only affects eight vessels, overfishing by those vessels will have compounding effects on the pacific cod stock over time as each year more fish will be removed than is sustainable. I therefore strongly oppose the adoption of Amendment 45.

Riley Collins
Dartmouth College Class of 2018

listing the dusky shark under the Endangered Species Act is based on the best available
science. The dusky shark was once relatively common in the coastal waters of the Northwest
Atlantic. But decades of fishing has driven the population to small fraction of their
historical abundance. In February, the Natural Resources Defense Council submitted a
petition to your agency requesting that the Northwest Atlantic population of the dusky
shark be listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act. This unique and important
species needs the protections provided by the Act if it is to survive. The National
Marine Fisheries Service has taken the first step in saving the dusky shark by making a
positive 90-day determination on NRDC's petition, as well as on a similar petition made by
WildEarth Guardians. The agency should now move forward as quickly as possible to conduct
a full scientific review of the requested listing and to designate critical habitat. This
review should rely on the best available science.

1. The Navy grossly underestimates the effects of its activities and this alone should warrant the denial of this permit (DoN, 2013). On page 4 of Navy’s supplemental document about strandings (DoN, 2013) under anthropogenic causes of strandings two extremely important causes are missing: acute stress reactions and behavioral avoidance reactions. Navy fails to mention well known peculiarity of marine mammals response to acute stress, namely “alarm reaction” that leads to irreversible physiological changes and results in imminent death.

Cowan & Curry (2008, p.24) write: “the reflex response of an odontocete to any major perceived threat (the ‘‘alarm reaction’’) is to activate the physiological
adaptations to diving or escape to an extreme or pathological level, resulting, if greatly prolonged, in widespread ischemic injury to tissues”. Furthermore stranded cetaceans often demonstrate these abnormalities and at this point it is impossible to state for sure what happened prior to the stranding and what happened as a result of the stranding (Sacchini et al., 2011). RE: Regulatory Amendment 19 to the Fishery Management Plan for the Snapper Grouper Fishery of the South Atlantic Region - Increases to Black Sea Bass Annual Catch Limits and a Seasonal Closure of the Pot Sector

July 31, 2013

Dear Rick,

On behalf of the Georgia Conservancy, we appreciate the opportunity to offer public comments on the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council’s (SAFMC’s) Regulatory Amendment 19.

The Georgia Conservancy is a statewide conservation organization that works to develop solutions to protect Georgia’s environment through advocacy and collaboration on water, air, land and growth management issues. Founded in 1967, we have a rich history of advocating for coastal conservation.

Through our Coastal Policy, we advocate for conserving our coastal resources including our fisheries. We support management measures that lead to self sustaining populations in order to address growing demands for our coastal resources. A sustainable coastal ecosystem is vital to Georgia’s prosperity.

We reviewed the proposal which would shorten the required 10-year black sea bass recovery, as outlined in the Magnuson-Stevens Act, to 7 years. We feel that anytime an amendment to a sound conservation law is proposed, there must be a good reason. Plus, the science must support it.

The 2013 update to the stock assessment shows that the black sea bass population is no longer overfished or undergoing overfishing and has been rebuilt. Observations from anglers and oceanographers match what the science shows.

We understand that black sea bass have a relatively shorter life span of up to 10 years enabling the depleted stocks to recover at a faster rate. We consulted various experts including Susan Shipman. She shared that when the current recovery schedule was proposed for final action at a SAFMC meeting, Dr. Roy Crabtree predicted that the recovery would be sooner than 10 years, based on black sea bass life history and fishing mortality restrictions being implemented.

With black sea bass populations at their best levels in 20 years, it is important to consider other fish and creatures that compete for food and habitat in the ocean ecosystem. Keeping a good balance is an important aspect of active management.

For these reasons, the Georgia Conservancy supports the Council’s proposal to shorten the recovery period to 7 years while proceeding with caution.

As an advocate for protecting North Atlantic Right Whales, the Georgia Conservancy also supports the proposed measures prohibiting the use of pots to commercially harvest black sea bass from November 1st through April 30th, the implementation of a program to limit the number of participants, and the requirement of bringing the pots back to shore after each trip.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

Clay MobleyPierre Howard
Coastal DirectorPresident
