Eliminating the 4(c) exemption from the BCA would be the most effective course of agency action from a conservation standpoint. While the new regulations offered by the BCA impose greater restraints than existing regulations, the 4(c) exemption of the BCA allows for the sale of billfish caught by U.S. vessels and landed in the nation’s only commercial fishery for billfish. As such, 4(c) keeps open what is likely the country’s largest market for the sale of billfish so long as the billfish are not caught in the Atlantic, by non-U.S. vessels, or outside of Hawaii and surrounding Pacific Insular Areas.
Another possible restriction NMFS could impose on the transportation and sale of billfish caught by U.S. vessels and landed in Hawaii or the Pacific Insular Areas could be to limit the total number of billfish allowed for sale per vessel per year in the fishery. An example would be to allow each U.S. vessel selling billfish to sell only 40 billfish (caught meeting BCA regulation requirements) per year. The limit could be adjusted according to its effectiveness each year.
Another possible restriction could be to limit the sale of billfish caught by U.S. vessels and landed in Hawaii or the Pacific and Insular Areas to certain months of the year. This would likely not be as effective as a limit on the total number of billfish allowed for sale per year, but would be more effective than no further restriction at all.
A final possible restriction may be to limit the sale of billfish caught by U.S. vessels and landed in Hawaii or the Pacific and Insular Areas to certain size requirements. Please see the attached letter from Dr. Donald McIsaac, Executive Director of the Pacific Fishery Management Council (PFMC), regarding PFMC comments on alternative harvest control rules analyzed in a Management Strategy Evaluation for Sacramento River winter Chinook.  Should you have any questions, please contact Mr. Mike Burner at  503-820-2414 or toll-free at 1-866-806-7204.

Dear NMFS Decision maker c/o Heidi Taylor



Our salmon seasons have been constrained recently because of the poor state of the winter-run Chinook.

The ocean salmon fishery isn't what ails winter-run; the water projects on the Sacramento River and in the Sacramento San Joaquin Delta are the problem. We were totally shut down from fishing in 2008 and 2009 and didn't take a single winter run and yet their numbers didn't suddenly bounce back. Conversely, in response to the wet winter of 2010/2011 we got an increase in winter run numbers, clearly demonstrating that more water is what's needed to revive them, not less fishing. The fisheries catch a handful of these fish every year while the Delta pumps and water projects can take thousands annually.

The current control rule requires that fishing be closed when the population drops below a certain level, rather than continually decreasing the number of days and areas open to ocean salmon fishing proportional to a shrinking winter run population.

Control Rule 4 would exchange the current rule's potential ban on fishing for proportional restrictions on ocean fishery impact. Recreational and commercial anglers, and the businesses that support them, strongly prefer this approach. It permits continued access to non-listed salmon stocks rather than eliminating the fishery altogether. Control Rule 4 offers the winter-run essentially the same level of protection from extinction as the current control rule without the devastating socio-economic costs of unnecessary fishery closures. Bottom line, Control Rule 4 would be gentler on the fishery without presenting any incremental risk to the winter-run which is why I'm writing to support it.

Dear Heidi Taylor

The Golden Gate Salmon Association (GGSA) appreciates this opportunity to comment on the Management Strategy Evaluation review that NMFS is now undertaking regarding protective measures for the endangered Sacramento River winter-run Chinook salmon.

The Golden Gate Salmon Association (www.goldengatesalmon.org) is a coalition of salmon advocates that includes commercial and recreational salmon fishermen, a Native American tribe, businesses, restaurants, fishing guides, environmentalists, families and communities that rely on salmon. GGSA’s mission is to protect and restore California’s largest salmon producing habitat comprised of the Central Valley rivers that feed the Bay-Delta ecosystem and the communities that rely on salmon.

Our salmon seasons have been constrained recently because of the poor state of the winter-run Chinook. Currently, federal fishery managers are guided by a "control rule" that requires the fisheries to reduce interaction, or incidental take, of winter run as the winter-run population drops.

Fair enough, but the current control rule requires that fishing be closed when the population drops below a certain level, rather than continually decreasing the number of days and areas open to ocean salmon fishing proportional to a shrinking winter run population.

Control Rule 4 would exchange the current rule's potential ban on fishing for proportional restrictions on ocean fishery impact. Recreational and commercial anglers and the businesses that support them strongly prefer this approach that would permit continued access to non-listed salmon stocks rather than eliminating the fishery altogether. According to the Management Strategy Evaluation (MSE) Report (Winship et al., 2012), Control Rule 4 offers the winter-run Chinook essentially the same level of protection from extinction as the current control rule. There is no material benefit from the current control rule, which carries with it the devastating socio-economic costs of unnecessary fishery closures. Bottom line, Control Rule 4 would be gentler on the fishery without presenting any incremental risk to the winter-run.

GGSA is especially concerned because returning adult winter run salmon will likely be far fewer in 2015 and 2016 due to the effects of drought, excessive Delta pumping in 2014, and the refusal of the Livingston Stone winter run hatchery to truck or barge their brood around the hostile, drought-stricken Sacramento River and Delta. There is a very real likelihood that the three year average for winter run will fall in 2015 and 2016. Under the current control rule, such a decline could be enough to severely restrict the ocean sport and commercial salmon fishery, even though fishing is not the cause.

Exceeding the OMR and I/E Delta pumping restrictions built into the 2009 Salmon biological opinion this year has likely killed some of the few juvenile winter run that survived the migration down the river. Salmon-dependent communities find it a bitter pill to accept NMFS constraining our ocean fishery because of winter run impacts while simultaneously signing off on increased pumping that’s sucking them in and killing them!

Currently, California’s salmon industry is valued at $1.4 billion in economic activity annually and about half that much in economic activity again in Oregon. The industry employs tens of thousands of people from Santa Barbara to northern Oregon. This is a huge economic bloc made up of commercial fishing men and women, recreational anglers (fresh and salt water), fish processors, marinas, coastal communities, fishing guides, equipment manufacturers, the hotel and food industry, tribes, and the salmon fishing industry at large.

The ocean salmon fishery did not contribute to the listing of the winter-run, whose survival challenges result from water projects on the Sacramento River and in the Sacramento San Joaquin Delta. Indeed, season closures in 2008 and 2009 did nothing to resurrect the winter-run, whose decline can be traced directly to excessive fresh water diversions and exports from the Sacramento River. Conversely, in response to the wet winter of 2010/2011 we got an increase in winter run numbers, clearly demonstrating that more water is what's needed to revive them, not less fishing. The fisheries catch a handful of these fish every year while the Delta pumps are known to take thousands annually.

However blameless, California's sport and commercial salmon fishermen recognize that they must not exacerbate the problem. It does not follow, however, that ocean salmon fishing ought to be banned rather than restricted in a proportional manner. For this reason, GGSA is urging NMFS to replace the current approach with Control Rule 4.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely
John McManus
Executive Director
Golden Gate Salmon Association

Our salmon seasons have been constrained recently because of the poor state of the winter-run Chinook.



The ocean salmon fishery isn't what ails winter-run; the water projects on the Sacramento River and in the Sacramento San Joaquin Delta are the problem. We were totally shut down from fishing in 2008 and 2009 and didn't take a single winter run and yet their numbers didn't suddenly bounce back. Conversely, in response to the wet winter of 2010/2011 we got an increase in winter run numbers, clearly demonstrating that more water is what's needed to revive them, not less fishing. The fisheries catch a handful of these fish every year while the Delta pumps and water projects can take thousands annually.



The current control rule requires that fishing be closed when the population drops below a certain level, rather than continually decreasing the number of days and areas open to ocean salmon fishing proportional to a shrinking winter run population.

Control Rule 4 would exchange the current rule's potential ban on fishing for proportional restrictions on ocean fishery impact. Recreational and commercial anglers, and the businesses that support them, strongly prefer this approach. It permits continued access to non-listed salmon stocks rather than eliminating the fishery altogether. Control Rule 4 offers the winter-run essentially the same level of protection from extinction as the current control rule without the devastating socio-economic costs of unnecessary fishery closures. Bottom line, Control Rule 4 would be gentler on the fishery without presenting any incremental risk to the winter-run which is why I'm writing to support it.



There is a very real likelihood that the three year average for winter run will fall in 2015, 2016, and 2017. Under the current control rule, such a decline could be enough to severely restrict the ocean sport and commercial salmon fishery, even though fishing is not the cause.



In addition, NMFS is constraining our ocean fishery because of winter run impacts while simultaneously allowing more Delta pumping this year that's sucking winter run in and killing them!



For this reason, I urge NMFS to replace the current winter run control rule with Control Rule 4.



Thank you for your consideration.



Sincerely
Patrick

As one of America’s 60 million anglers, I am submitting comments regarding changes currently under consideration for Atlantic HMS Amendment 7. The options that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is considering have the potential to significantly improve not only bluefin tuna stocks but also many other highly prized sportfish including marlin, sailfish and swordfish in the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico. Catch-and-release fishing for tunas, billfish and swordfish has proven to be hugely popular when stocks of these fish are healthy and allocated in a manner that makes economic sense and conservation sense.

Offshore recreational fishing for species like bluefin tuna has a significant economic impact on many coastal communities throughout the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico coasts, but these opportunities are dependent on healthy and abundant fisheries. You have the opportunity to improve the sustainability of many important large pelagic fish stocks and I urge you to seize the opportunity by strengthening and in some cases modifying the actions you are considering.

Allocating fish from the angling sector to the longlining sector does not make sense and is not supported by any socio-economic analysis. It is completely unfair and nonsensical to punish recreational anglers for the bycatch offenses committed by longliners.
I support the creation of the new seasonal longlining restricted areas in the Gulf of Mexico and in the Atlantic off the North Carolina coast, but these areas should be substantially larger than what is proposed. To meet the bycatch reduction targets needed to protect bluefin tuna when they are spawning, the closure should include the entire Gulf of Mexico and the length of time for these closures must be increased to include March through May.
Do not reopen areas in the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico currently closed to longlining. The benefits of these conservation zones are well documented.
An annual bluefin catch cap should absolutely be instituted and the improved at-sea monitoring under consideration should be implemented.
NOAA has a major opportunity before it to change management of bluefin and by extension other highly prized sportfish. Please consider my perspective in your final decisions.

I am supporting the measures proposed in Amendment 7 to the Highly Migratory Species Fishery Management Plan.

My concern is that something must be done rebuild Atlantic bluefin tuna populations and to protect endangered sea turtles injured or killed as bycatch.

I would like a final rule prohibiting all pelagic longline fishing in the entire Gulf of Mexico Exclusive Economic Zone during the entire bluefin spawning period.

Thank you..

Dear Mr. Warren:

Populations of bluefin tuna have declined precipitously: at least 64% for Atlantic bluefins and an incredible 96% for Pacific bluefins.

Bluefin tuna are top ocean predators and therefore critical to preserving healthy, diverse ocean ecosystems. However, because they're top predators, they also concentrate toxins like mercury in their muscles, which are highly prized food. So we shouldn't be eating them, but we should be doing everything we can to rebuild their populations.

Please implement the March through May Gulf of Mexico Exclusive Economic Zone Pelagic Longline Gear Restricted Area and the Cape Hatteras Gear Restricted Area that prevents all pelagic longline fishing from December through April.

I also want to see a cap set on bluefin catch and it is critical to monitor the populations and the catch. We need this information in order to restore bluefin populations..

Thank you for considering my comments.

Comments on Amendment 7 to the HMS FMP

I encourage the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) to adopt strong measures in proposed Amendment 7 to the Highly Migratory Species Fishery Management Plan in order to conserve and rebuild Atlantic bluefin tuna, as well as protect the many other species of fish and wildlife that are injured or killed by encounters with pelagic longline gear.

Atlantic bluefin tuna have been fished to dangerously low levels. Strong measures are necessary to end overfishing of bluefin tuna and put the species on the path to recovery. Protecting spawning grounds and other areas where bluefin congregate is critical to achieving these requirements. Therefore, I request that NMFS adopt a final rule prohibiting all pelagic longline fishing in the entire Gulf of Mexico Exclusive Economic Zone during the entire bluefin spawning period, and in the Cape Hatteras Restricted Gear Area from December through April.

Past experience has shown that time-area closures are highly effective in protecting bluefin, billfish, and other incidentally caught species. I oppose NMFS's proposal to open Charleston Bump, DeSoto Canyon, and the Florida East Coast to pelagic longlining. NMFS may not move forward with this proposal without conducting a thorough analysis of the impacts of reintroducing pelagic longlining to closed areas on bluefin, billfish, sharks, marine mammals, and threatened and endangered species. The analysis NMFS has offered to support its proposal falls far short of meeting the agency's obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act, or Marine Mammal Protection Act.

The pelagic longline sector of the HMS fishery kills and discards more bluefin tuna than any other sector of the fishery, and regularly exceeds its annual bluefin tuna quota. Last year, dead discards caused by the pelagic longline sector accounted for one quarter of the entire U.S. Atlantic bluefin quota. NMFS's proposal to take quota from other sectors of the fishery and reallocate it to the pelagic longline sector -- increasing pelagic longline quota by over 85% -- unfairly penalizes cleaner sectors of the fishery and unlawfully facilitates continued high rates of bycatch and dead discards by the pelagic longline sector. I request that NMFS instead adopt a final rule that requires the pelagic longline sector to account for its own dead discards within its own, fairly allocated portion of the overall bluefin quota.

There are several aspects of NMFS's rule that I strongly support. The proposed strict annual cap for bluefin catch, implemented via an individual bluefin quota system for active longline vessels, increases accountability and encourages fishermen to adopt more selective practices. Similarly, requiring vessels to retain all dead bluefin tuna instead of discarding them will reduce waste of bluefin and foster more accurate accounting of fishing mortality.

Finally, NMFS should adopt measures requiring enhance at-sea monitoring to help enforce the cap on bluefin catch and better track interactions with other marine life, including measures requiring electronic monitoring and increased observer coverage.

NMFS now has a valuable opportunity to rebuild bluefin tuna and protect numerous other marine species by implementing measures to increase accountability within the pelagic longline sector and foster transitions to more selective fishing gear. Please take this opportunity by strengthening the proposed rule in the ways described above. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Re:Amendment 7 – Public Comment – NOAA-NMFS-2013-0101

Dear Mr. Warren,

Regarding Amendment 7, I am in favor of:
•Strictly maintaining the longline allocation for bluefin at 8.1% of the total US quota.
•Establishing a time-area closure in the Gulf of Mexico that closes this important area to longline fishing when bluefin tuna are present.
•Increasing the size and number of time-area closures in the Atlantic, preventing longliners from fishing in areas where they incur bycatch of bluefin.
•Establishing an annual bluefin bycatch “cap” for every single longliner in the US Gulf and Atlantic, the total of which not to exceed their 8.1% allocation.
•Maintaining the existing spatial and temporal framework of bluefin quota allocation for the recreational and commercial handgear categories.
•Establishing 100%, industry-funded observer or electronic coverage of every longline vessel in the US Gulf and Atlantic to ensure compliance.
•Effectively address the issue of “latent permits” in the longline fishery by eliminating the ability to re-activate these permits.
•Effectively addressing the ongoing requirement of discarding all juvenile bluefin caught in the longline fishery, a problem that would continue under proposed Amendment 7.

I oppose any attempt to give any of the Recreational and Commercial handgear quota to the longliners.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on Amendment 7.

I support any and all restrictions which might positively impact the excessive and unessicary depletion of blue fin tuna stocks committed by commercial fishing interests, in both national and international waters.

“...The best way to fight racism is with solidarity.”

— Bobby Seale

I first met Silas Sconiers on Sept. 10 at Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore’s Park Training Room. Members of the Miller, Porter County and Diana chapters of the Izaak Walton League of America, Perch America, Northwest Indiana Steelheaders, Lake County Fish & Wildlife and Friends of the Kankakee were there in support of Sconiers.

As a last resort, after years of being ignored, Sconiers has filed a civil rights complaint regarding the fact there is no public access on Gary’s lakeshore for anglers.

Also on hand were Sloan Farrell from the U.S. Department of the Interior’s Office of Civil Rights and Rose Pruitt and Ken Brodie of the National Park Service. Pruitt is chief, Office of Equal Opportunity Programs, and Brodie is Environmental Justice Coordinator for the park service.

Sconiers, 62, lives in the Midtown neighborhood of Gary. He is a retired employee of EJ&E Railroad who served in the National Guard for 12 years.

And, he’s a man on a mission.

***

“I was born in a house on 25th Avenue and Jackson Street,” Sconiers began. “When I was about 6, we moved to Gary Small Farms. I broke a lot of records as a hurdler at Calumet High School.”

As a kid, did you like to fish?

“Did I like to fish? We lived out on the Small Farms — we were river rats!”

Brother, I resemble that remark.

“We had homemade boats. We stayed up and down that river (Little Calumet). We swam at Lake Etta and Lake Sandy Jo. If you didn’t know how to swim across Lake Sandy Jo you were a punk. You had to be able to swim across Lake Sandy Jo to be a man.”

Fishing the Big Lake?

“Dad used to take us out to Buffington Harbor all the time. We used to go out there every Sunday so we could get out of going to church with Ma. We’d catch so many perch — jumbo perch.

“You could catch ‘em with a naked hook. We used to make our own lures with a pair of split shots and an old house key. We’d shake it up and down and the perch would grab it. Those perch were ravenous.”

When was the last time you were able to fish off the pier at Buffington Harbor?

“Probably around 1967. I went to several government agencies, from the governor’s office to the (Environmental Protection Agency). More than one governor or mayor has turned a blind eye on the situation.”

Explain your complaint.

“I want an equal opportunity for the citizens of Gary. The city of Gary is the only city in the United States and Canada on the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway system without a public access fishing spot.

“The city of Gary has 22 miles of lakefront. It makes no sense that we don’t have access. Gary is comprised of 93 percent minorities. And we don’t have a place to fish. Something is wrong here. We just want the same opportunity as everyone else.

“They say the beaches are open to us. That’s a joke. The first time some sunbather gets a hook in his or her foot there will be hell to pay. A grown man can cast as far as he possibly can from the shore and still be in only a foot of water. And there’s no structure — just sand. When you fish off a pier, you’re fishing in 15 to 30 feet of water. That’s where the game fish are.”

Silas, with all the negative headlines you see, you’d think City Hall would welcome the opportunity of opening up Lake Michigan’s piers to sports fishermen. It’s a good, clean outdoors activity.

“If the kids had a place to go fishing maybe they wouldn’t be getting into trouble. Kids need something to do. It’s a way to keep their minds occupied and get fresh air. When they sit around listless, they get into trouble.”

Would getting access be an expensive endeavor?

“We have piers, break walls and wharves already in place in the city of Gary. All we need is access. The city doesn’t have to spend one dime. The fishing clubs would gladly buy life preservers. We would gladly empty the garbage cans ourselves.

“It’s a shame. You go out to Marquette Park and look at what they done. All they did was shuffle the sand around and plant stickerbugs.”

Stickerbugs?

“It’s an African-American term for briars.”

***

For more than a century in the Steel City, it has always been about the Carnegies, the Judge Garys, the fat cats of the Tolleston Gun Club, the Donald Trumps, the politicians and the yachts.

And for a kid from Gary not be allowed to toss a line off a pier into Lake Michigan is as pitiful as it was for a kid living next to old Chicago Stadium and never once getting the chance to see his beloved Bulls play live.

As one of America’s 60 million anglers, I am submitting comments regarding changes currently under consideration for Atlantic HMS Amendment 7. The options that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is considering have the potential to significantly improve not only bluefin tuna stocks but also many other highly prized sportfish including marlin, sailfish and swordfish in the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico. Catch-and-release fishing for tunas, billfish and swordfish has proven to be hugely popular when stocks of these fish are healthy and allocated in a manner that makes economic sense and conservation sense.

Offshore recreational fishing for species like bluefin tuna has a significant economic impact on many coastal communities throughout the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico coasts, but these opportunities are dependent on healthy and abundant fisheries. You have the opportunity to improve the sustainability of many important large pelagic fish stocks and I urge you to seize the opportunity by strengthening and in some cases modifying the actions you are considering.

•Allocating fish from the angling sector to the longlining sector does not make sense and is not supported by any socio-economic analysis. It is completely unfair and nonsensical to punish recreational anglers for the bycatch offenses committed by longliners.
•I support the creation of the new seasonal longlining restricted areas in the Gulf of Mexico and in the Atlantic off the North Carolina coast, but these areas should be substantially larger than what is proposed. To meet the bycatch reduction targets needed to protect bluefin tuna when they are spawning, the closure should include the entire Gulf of Mexico and the length of time for these closures must be increased to include March through May.
•Do not reopen areas in the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico currently closed to longlining. The benefits of these conservation zones are well documented.
•An annual bluefin catch cap should absolutely be instituted and the improved at-sea monitoring under consideration should be implemented.

NOAA has a major opportunity before it to change management of bluefin and by extension other highly prized sportfish. Please consider my perspective in your final decisions.

I oppose the proposed NOAA rule that the 2014 Atlantic Shark Commercial Fishing Season open on January 1 because of its negative effect on the regional lemon shark aggregation off the coast of Jupiter, Florida. To relieve fishing pressure on a highly vulnerable, breeding population of lemon sharks, I request the fishing season revert to the original opening date of July 1st, after the completion of the annual birth cycle and when the seasonal distribution of lemon sharks is less concentrated geographically.

The socioeconomic benefit of the Jupiter lemon shark aggregation is significant to regional Florida economy because the SCUBA diving industry markets the natural aggregation for dives, seasonally. This aggregation has gained worldwide attention -- considered one of the best opportunities to dive with and photograph sharks in their natural environment, however, declines in lemon shark sightings that are already underway and are reflected in anecdotal reports by the recreational diving community and industry.

There is scientific evidence that the aggregating lemon shark population, off of Jupiter, Florida, is experiencing declines. Current data analysis suggests the existing population has crashed. While NOAA suggests that they have moved, there is no evidence to support that conclusion. Further, there is no evidence from tagging and tracking studies that lemon sharks have not tried to return to Jupiter. Indeed some were followed remotely from the Carolinas to Jupiter in 2013. Now, since the change of the January seasonal opening date, researchers and dive operators have been alarmed by the extremely low numbers of lemon sharks found off Jupiter, and fear that this aggregation, which is believed to represent a substantial proportion of the breeding population of the eastern seaboard lemon shark population, has already been severely depleted.

Data courtesy of Bimini Biological Field Station - Shark Lab.

I oppose the proposed rule that the 2014 Atlantic Shark Commercial Fishing Season open on January 1 and recommend changing back to the original opening date of July 1.

Many elasmobranch populations are threatened worldwide primarily by high rates of directed fishing and by-catch mortality in global fisheries, but also by marine pollution and habitat destruction. As such, dramatic declines in abundance have been reported from many parts of the world’s oceans and there is an urgent need for the collection of biological information on many shark species. Exacerbating this decline for sharks is their inherent vulnerability due to relatively slow growth and reproductive rates, and propensity to migrate long distances crossing international boundaries making stock assessments and effective management difficult. Furthermore, some species (i.e. lemon sharks, Negaprion brevirostris) are at even greater risk due to their propensity to form large aggregations, at particular times of year and in specific locations. For commercial fishers such concentrations of animals are easy to target and capture.

For lemon sharks, aggregations have been documented to form during the winter months (December - April) in Florida with mature male and female animals present (see Dr. Steven Kessel acoustic tagging data, as well as numerous photographic evidence from recreational divers). Thus with the commercial fishing season opening on January 1st these sharks become an easy target for fishers. This seasons acoustic tagging data has shown large reductions in tag re-detections, real evidence that such targeting has already occurred and is reducing the lemon shark population.

Currently, the Bimini Biological Field Station and colleagues are working on a number of manuscripts that document significant detection reductions and spatio-temporal movements of over 100 adult lemon sharks (2007-2013). I urge you to consider the information submitted by my colleagues Dr. Kessel and Dr. Gruber relating to the proposed rule. This will ensure that the lemon sharks during their most vulnerable time remain protected.

Thank you for your consideration.

I oppose the proposed rule that the 2014 Atlantic Shark Commercial Fishing Season open on January 1 based on its negative effect on the regional lemon shark aggregation off the coast of Jupiter, Florida. To relieve fishing pressure on a vulnerable population, we recommend the fishing season open on the July 1 date, when the seasonal distribution of lemon sharks is not as concentrated.

· Although the opening season criteria used by the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) includes “variation in seasonal distribution, abundance, or migratory patterns of the different species or management groups based on scientific and fishery information” we are concerned that significant negative effect that this opening date could have on the well-documented aggregation has not been considered or adequately addressed.

· Lemon sharks (Negaprion brevirostris) are biologically vulnerable to overfishing considering their conservative life history strategy.

· Lemon sharks demonstrate specific behavioral ecology resulting in a predictable annual aggregation. The aggregation is well-documented and highly publicized among the public. This characteristic means that the sharks, during this season, are extremely vulnerable to being easily targeted to quickly fill quotas because of the density of the aggregation.

· This specific aggregation of lemon sharks is extremely valuable to the regional SCUBA diving industry that markets the natural aggregation for recreational dives. This aggregation has gained wide attention and is considered one of the best opportunities to dive, view, and photograph sharks in their natural environment. The socioeconomic benefit of the aggregation is significant to this region of Florida’s economy. The declines that are already underway have been reflected in anecdotal evidence by the recreational diving community. Diving professionals who have witnessed the aggregation first-hand for several years have reported much smaller numbers of lemon sharks or difficulty in finding the aggregation at all.

· Regulatory measures implemented in 2006 to protect sandbar sharks have increased pressures on other large coastal species, including lemon sharks. The current data suggest the population of aggregating lemon sharks is experiencing declines. On average, there has been a 10-15% decline in redetection rates per year since 2007, indicating harvest rates are too high for the population to ever recover, even under maximum recovery rates for this species.

To whom it may concern,
My name is Joe Ludwig. I have been involved in the directed shark fishery for the better part of 30 years now here in Florida as either a crew member, capt, and finally a permitted boat owner/operator since 1995. My permit number is SKD-13. The name of my current boat is F/V Sea Dancer Too.
In the 1980's there was a wide open, full throttle fishery with little regulation. By the 1990's came the bi-annual season with "reasonable"trip limits and fairly robust quotas. In the late 1990's and into the 2000's we endured fairly large quota cuts and declaration of several "prohibited" species. Then in 2007 our fishery was pretty much destroyed with the prohibition of an "open" sandbar fishery to all permitholders with the creation of a "research" fishery only open to a select few. That coupled with a paultry 33 fish trip limit of non-sandbar and other prohibited species has made things for fishermen like me quite difficult at best.
To my knowlege, the sandbar research fishery has yet to produce more than 30% of its quota in any season, leaving 70% of this valuable quota unfished every season. Why is it that these fish are not released to the rest of the legitimate, directed permitholders so as to allow the quota to be realised even if only under a strictly limited bycatch allowance in the open LCS fishery? I can't help feel that these fish are being "stolen" from everyone including the fishermen and the public.

With regard to the 2014 season or any years season opening date: Having nearly 30 years experience as a sharkfisher, I think that any proposed date prior to 5/1 does not make sense from a conservationist standpoint. If conservation is our ultimate goal, why is it that it should be allowed to harvest these fish when they are at or near full term gestation. They should be allowed to have their litters so as to insure future generations. Why kill 5-8 fish only to realise 1. It simply does not make sense.
With regard to the "choke" species ie; blacknose in the SCS and now I see hammerhead in the LCS fishery:
I believe these species need to be "prohibited" so as not to cause even more damage to the fishermen whereby we cannot have a chance to fish the qoutas to 100% leaving tens or hundreds of thousands of pounds uncaught each year causing even more financial hardship.
I for one am all for regulations but I fear that we are at the point of over regulation!
Thank you for your time and consideration on these important to us all issues,
Joe Ludwig Owner/operator F/V Sea Dancer Too, Sea Dancer Inc.

We oppose the proposed rule that the 2014 Atlantic Shark Commercial Fishing Season open on January 1  and recommend changing back to the original opening date of July 1 fir the following reasons:  Large coastal sharks congregate at the narrow shelf off West Palm Beach to Jupiter between December and April. I oppose the proposed rule that the 2014 Atlantic Shark Commercial Fishing Season open on January 1 based on its negative effect on the regional lemon shark aggregation off the coast of Jupiter, Florida. To relieve fishing pressure on a highly vulnerable, breeding population of lemon sharks, I request the fishing season revert to the original opening date of July 1st, after the completion of the annual birth cycle and when the seasonal distribution of lemon sharks is less concentrated geographically.

Lemon sharks demonstrate specific migration patterns resulting in a predictable annual aggregation at a predictable time and place. The Jupiter lemon shark aggregation is well documented and highly publicized among the public. This means that the sharks, during the January-April season, are even more vulnerable than usual and are easily targeted by fishermen who can quickly fill their quota due to the density of the aggregation. Theoretically and actually commercial targeting of this aggregation can completely wipe out these sharks, locally, in a matter of days to weeks.

Please change the date to July 1 2014 instead of Jan 1 2014.
Thank you.

Instead we kept getting calls from FDA rep's who were not attorneys in an attempt to hassle us into settling! We finally talked to an attorney during a settlement conference that was held by a neutral agency called civil remedies division of the departmental appeals board. And guess what? This attorney was not an attorney with FDA. This is a settlement attorney to help us to understand what is going on. We could not get this help from FDA.

FDA also proposes that "FDA have determined that, with certain limitations and controls, non-attorney staff outside OCC can carry out the function of reviewing the evidence and signing the tobacco retailer CMP complaints in appropriate circumstances.

We strongly contest this rule. What exactly is an "appropriate circumstance"? FDA hardly gave us any evidence that the "alleged allegations" even happened. They gave us a picture of a carton of cigarettes that the person "allegedly" purchased and a picture of the front of our own store. I fully support the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council revising the commercial/recreational allocation for red snapper and developing an allocation mechanism that would be more fair and equitable for the recreational fishing community. I believe this action is necessary for several reasons.

First, the commercial red snapper fishery is under an individual fishing quota or IFQ system which affords permit holders exclusive rights to a public resource. As the red snapper stock has rebuilt, commercial fishermen land their quota quicker, with less effort and in the absence of competition. They are realizing huge or even excessive economic benefits from the red snapper rebuilding success.

Since they have exclusive ownership of the commercial component of the resource they actually need less fish to make the same amount of money. Furthermore, it is not good public policy to support a management approach that encourages a concentration of ownership by a few at the expense of the general public.

Secondly, a rebuilding red snapper population will not benefit the recreational sector unless the current allocation is revised. As more red snapper become available to recreational anglers, the quota will be caught quicker resulting in shorter seasons. This ultimately reduces recreational opportunities, decreasing the socioeconomic output of the recreational red snapper fishery and basically defeating the entire desire to rebuild fish stocks. Most people will agree that a management approach that disadvantages the recreational sector as a stock rebuilds is not fair and lacks basic common sense.

For these reasons, I fully support efforts by the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council to move forward with an allocation mechanism that provides at minimum 90% of any red snapper quota above 9.12 million pounds to the recreational sector.

The recreational sector should be given equal opportunity to enjoy the benefits of a rebuilt fish stock, and I would encourage the Gulf Council to allocate the majority of red snapper quota over 9.12 million pounds to the recreational fishing community.

As a recreational angler, I support the alternative proposals outlined in Reef Fish Amendment 28 to shift up to 100% of any total combined commercial and recreational quota in excess of 9.12 million pounds of red snapper to the recreational sector in the Gulf of Mexico.

There has been plenty of debate between the commercial and recreational fishing sectors regarding Gulf of Mexico red snapper, with those holding the greater 51% allocation claiming “it’s fair as it is” while those granted 2% less left asking for sensible relief from burdensome restrictions.

The concept of “fairness” was memorialized in the 1980’s when the commercial sector was gifted the additional percentage of quota. However, a lot has changed in the past 30 years, including a reduction in the number of commercial license holders, while the total number of recreational anglers has increased throughout the Gulf.

A total allowable catch (TAC) for Gulf of Mexico red snapper harvest at the 9.12-million-pound mark represents the highest allowable harvest of red snapper since the original allocation was set by managers. With fewer commercial fishermen fishing today - and now doing so under an individual fishing quota (IFQ) system aimed at capacity reduction - the 51% of the 9.12 million pounds provides a reasonable and economical harvest of 4.65 million pounds to the commercial sector.

But while 4.65 million pounds of commercial red snapper harvest represents the highest commercial quota in more than three decades, the recreational fishing sector has gone from a 195-day fishing season with a four fish per angler bag limit, to less than 45 days on the water with just a two fish per angler bag limit. While a 51 to 49 allocation percentage may seem fair on paper, the overall reduction in available fishing days for the recreational fishing community since 2007 and the grave impact this has had on our coastal tourism economy is neither fair nor reasonable to the public resource users.

Based on the alternative proposals outlined in Reef Fish Amendment 28 calling for an increase in the recreational red snapper quota only if the total snapper quota is greater than 9.12 million pounds, I would personally support adjusting the allocation percentage of any additional red snapper quota to a minimum of 90% for the recreational sector and 10% for the commercial sector, until a point at which fisheries managers determine that anglers can return to the original 195-day fishing season and four fish bag limit.

This limited adjustment to dealing with additional quota above the 9.12-million-pound is truly the fair approach, in that it provides both sectors with a return to sensible harvest numbers previously enjoyed by both sectors at the start of the red snapper rebuilding period.

Successful rebuilding of the Gulf of Mexico red snapper fishery has most recently afforded a 9.3-million pound quota for both the commercial and recreational sectors under the original 51%-49% allocation scheme. While the angling community remains saddled with draconian allowable fishing season of between 25 and 45 days, there have been numerous statements made on-record by commercial representatives before the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council about the drop in market price for red snapper when the commercial quota exceeds 5 million pounds.

Considering the 51/49 allocation and the market loss experienced by the commercial fishing industry when more than 5 million pounds of red snapper floods the consumer market, perhaps it would be in the best interest of the entire fishery if the commercial sector be capped at the 5-million pound mark. That could best be accommodated by this type of two-tiered allocation approach which allows the commercial/recreational allocation to gradually and reasonably shift toward the recreational sector as the stock rebuilds.

Such an approach would protect the commercial sector from potential overages in the recreational sector while providing a mechanism that will address the growing concern about increased availability causing ever decreasing recreational red snapper seasons.

I would encourage the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council to move forward with an allocation plan that provides at minimum 90% of any red snapper quota above 9.12 million pounds to the recreational sector until the recreational sector landings are brought back to 2007 levels, a time when the public was allowed a more reasonable bag limit and 195 days of recreational fishing.

DIA is a neutral, nonprofit, global, professional association of 18,000 members who work or have interest in every facet of the discovery, development and life cycle management of pharmaceuticals, biologics, medical devices and related products. DIA members are from industry, regulatory agencies, academia, health care organizations, and patient organizations and share DIA’s mission to foster innovation to improve health and well-being.

In September 2013, Therapeutic Innovation and Regulatory Science (TIRS), the peer-reviewed journal of DIA, published an article by Dr. Lode Dewulf describing a lack of data on medication use during pregnancy to support health care decision-making in and around pregnancy. That article is attached for your reference. Subsequently, DIA held multi-stakeholder discussion forums at the DIA Euromeeting and the DIA Annual Meeting to explore the breadth of this issue. Participants identified the dearth of such data as a significant public health issue that negatively affects the quality of care for pregnant women.

Additional discussions and literature searches after the 2013 forums resulted in a second article on the challenges of gathering data on the outcomes of medication use during pregnancy, various approaches to such data collection, strengths and weaknesses of each approach, and strategies for increasing data collection. The article was published in the March 2014 issue of Therapeutic Innovation and Regulatory Science (TIRS), the peer-reviewed journal of DIA. It has been attached to these comments.

Forum participants also concluded that communication is key to improving the availability of data for informed decision-making on medication use in pregnancy by women and their health care providers in order to:
•Address ethical, cultural, and legal issues that impede appropriate study of medication use during pregnancy, and
•Establish a reliable network of communication so that learnings can be shared to support women, families, and health care providers in informed decision-making.

While a number of efforts are underway to address the unavailability of data for medication-related decision making by pregnant women, they are fragmented and thus are not making the necessary impact to resolve the problem. Approaches to addressing this complex problem are discussed in a third peer-reviewed article published in the March 2014 issue of TIRS and attached to these comments.

DIA has the ability to convene the necessary stakeholders in a neutral forum and stands ready to assist with this effort.

“Study Approaches and Methods to Evaluate the Safety of Drugs and Biological Products During Pregnancy in the Post-Approval Setting”

Regarding Day Two presentations and panel comments on the use of automated databases and electronic medical records as data sources to evaluate post-marketing drug safety in pregnancy:

I am an epidemiologist with over 20 years of research and programmatic experience in global maternal-child health and medication safety in pregnancy. My experience has been gained through positions and leadership roles in academia, government, and consulting. As an early developer of large-linked database pregnancy methodology and an early adopter/promoter of the concept of large automated databases to evaluate medication/vaccine safety in pregnancy and adverse outcomes, I applaud the work presented during this meeting.

I want to express some thoughts about context and future interpretation of these and other such data sources. We are experiencing great change and challenges in healthcare delivery in the USA. Increasingly, healthcare practitioners’ decision-making is influenced by outside sources such as insurers and by patients themselves. This impact may be seen in tests, procedures, prescribing, and even diagnoses. This in turn can impact encoded data in large data sources and, therefore, the interpretation of summarized data. I’m not clear how this impact can be meaningfully measured or analytically modeled.

Arguably, this impact may have existed previously. However, the US is likely experiencing a heightened impact on data due to the current extent of influence on practitioner decision-making. This may also impact smaller scale studies and registries. Perhaps with these designs, there is greater opportunity to explore the degree of impact at the individual record level.

I believe this concern further highlights the importance of employing multiple designs and multiple data sources in evaluating post-marketing drug/vaccine safety in pregnancy, both in terms of signal generation and hypothesis testing.
I offer these comments to stimulate reflection and discussion.

Thank you,
Janet R. Hardy, PhD, MPH, MSc
Managing Principal,
The ECC Population Health Group LLC
global maternal-child health and pharmacoepidemiology consulting

Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Affiliate

1. Section 8.2.2. There is a third type of data quality that is particularly applicable to pooled data, and that is whether the studies in the pool used the same data handling rules. The data in each study may be perfectly fine internally, but when pooled with other studies that used different rules, the pooled data are no longer valid for analysis. E.g., one study can start capturing AEs and SAEs at Informed Consent, and another study can start at Day 1. Nothing in the data indicates that the baseline period does not contain all AEs. 1. Section 2.2 Study Data Reviewer's Guide:

It's good to see a specific request for this type of information, and especially some guidance as to what should be included. The listed items are excellent from the perspective of orienting the reviewers to the study and the conformance of the data to whatever standards were used.

The information currently listed appears to describe the SDTM define.xml files - is this the intent? Should it include the ADaM define.xml as well, or will that be addressed in a separate guidance?

Is the expectation/desire to see the study design section in a diagrammatic form (as seen in the SDTM IG) or in a more machine readable form (SDTM Trial Design datasets)?

2. In the same section, there is an opportunity to include information about how the data were handled and what quality rules were followed, i.e., the business rules applied to the data. This significantly impacts the quality of the data, its usability, and the ability of the agency to judge if it has been used appropriately given the design and handling rules. This is particularly true when pooled studies used different business rules for the same data. E.g., one study can start capturing AEs and SAEs at Informed Consent, and another study can start at Day 1. Nothing in the data indicates that the baseline period does not contain all AEs. Another example would be if one study instructed sites to capture symptoms and another instructed them to capture diagnoses. The AE profiles of the 2 studies could look different while in fact being the same. While the first example could be found in the protocol (assuming someone thought to look for it), the second might not. There are many many additional examples of this. While submitting the data management plans for each study is probably not feasible for now, the Reviewer's Guide could at least contain a list of the rules that differed among studies.

3. Section 3.3.5.1. The first sentence appears to contradict the rest of the paragraph. Suggest adding "unless size constraints prevent this." at the end of the first sentence.

4. Section 4: most of the references to SDTM should be changed to SDTM IG. SDTM is the underlying model for the SDTM Implementation Guide (for Human Clinical Trials) as well as for SEND and the Medical Device IG. SDTM defines the generic variables (e.g,. - - TERM) that the IG uses for implented domains (e.g., AETERM). The guidance references including the appropriate required, expected and permissible variables, but these characteristics are defined in the IG, and not in the model.

5. Section 4.1.2. Section states that all variables for which data were collected should be submitted. There are variables in CDASH used for administrative or data cleaning purposes (e.g., AEYN, CMONGO) or for deriving variables in SDTM (e.g., date variables) that are not generally submitted in SDTM. It would be helpful for the guidance to indicate that this is acceptable. Perhaps a statement such as " administrative variables and those used to derive SDTM variables (that are not needed for summarization or analysis) may or may not be submitted, at the sponsor's discretion. These should be appropriately marked on the annotated CRF submitted with the data."

6. Section 4.1.6.1. The definition of SDTM is too limited. First, SDTM is the model, and the SDTM IG is the implementation for human clinical trials. Secondly, the SDTMIG provides much more that the structure - it also defines many rules for handling the data, some derivation rules, etc.

7. Section 4.1.6.2. Reference to CDASH is very appropriate - encouraging the implementation of the same data structures from the beginning will greatly enhance the quality of the data.

8. Section 4.1.6.3. Disposition domain: out of curiosity, how many types of death are there?

9. Section 4.1 7.5. "All variables that contain coded data should be accompanied by a variable that provides the decoded information." This appears to be a bit backwards, as the standard SDTM variables contain the decoded data, and it's the coded variables that may be added. As stated, it appears that it is the coded values that are expected.

10. Section 4.1.10.2. Consider shortening "not entered in database" to "not entered" and "not entered in the tabulation dataset" to "not submitted." Space is often constrained on CRFs and a shorter note is easier to fit on the form without obscuring as much of the underlying form.

11. Section 6.3.1.1. While the benefits of having coded data in the SDTM datasets may be real, please take into account the value of having the data remain as "stand-alone" as possible, i.e., understandable with a minimum of external reference required.

Dear Sir or Madam:

The Industry Discussion Group of the Pharmaceutical Users Software Exchange (PhUSE), Computational Science Symposium, Non-Clinical Road-map and Impacts on Implementation Working Group is pleased to have the opportunity to offer comments on these guidance documents regarding electronic submissions. General Comments:

In general, the guide is well written, but note that clarification or changes in some areas would be beneficial prior to implementation of the Study Data Technical Conformance Guide.

The guide is clinically focused making it difficult to ascertain what applies to nonclinical data versus what applies only to clinical data. We suggest specifying where possible.

Specific Comments:

Please view the associated uploaded file for a full list of specific comments on the Study Data Techincial Conformance Guide.

The section “3.3.5.2 Column Length” of the draft Study Data Technical Conformance Guide states the following:
“For all datasets, the allotted character length for each column should be set to the maximum length of the variable used.”
This statement will become clearer when discussed in relation to the length attribute of define.xml which would represent a ‘potential’ length. Confusion may arise in a scenario like this (which I believe could occur very often).

Assume in a certain study that a CRF expects four possible values for the SEX attribute; F(Female), M(Male), U(Unknown), UN(Undifferentiated). As described in the section “3.5 Controlled Terminology” of “CDISC Study Data Tabulation Model Metadata Submission Guidelines”, all of the four ‘potential’ values should be included in the codelist section of the define.xml. The define.xml 2.0.0 specification also says the length attribute represents ‘maximum expected variable length’, and therefore the length value of the SEX variable would be ‘2’, whether or not the ‘UN’ value is actually used. On the other hand the length of the variable in the SAS V5 XPORT would be ‘1’ when the 'UN' value is not used.

The current statement in the draft guide indicates the rule might also be applied to the define.xml, in which case a sponsor needs to scan all the data before finalizing define.xml, which requires considerable amount of effort. It is therefore proposed that the draft guide clarifies that the define.xml length should be minimum designed/potential length and could be different from the SAS length.

United Parcel Service (UPS) would like to submit the following comment in response to Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) Docket No. FAA-2014-0780; Directorate Identifier: 2014-NM-168-AD, which proposes a new Airworthiness Directive (AD) for Boeing Model 747 series airplanes that requires revising the airplane flight manual with limitations that preclude the carriage of intermodal containers nominally measuring 8 feet wide, 20 feet long, and 8.5 feet tall in an offset manner.

The proposed AD, as written, precludes not only the intermodal container loading configuration described above, but also precludes the carriage of any 20 feet length by 8.0 feet wide by 8.5 feet tall intermodal container loaded in an offset method, even if the cargo and pallet combination is secured directly to the airplane utilizing FAA-approved cargo tie down procedures as prescribed in the Boeing WBM for Boeing Model 747 series aircraft. Cargo loads secured directly to the aircraft in accordance with the existing FAA approved OEM WBM procedures and limitations should not be prohibited as these cargo loading configurations have not been shown to produce an unsafe condition through testing.

In addition, the Discussion section of the subject docket includes the following statement:

The Weight and Balance Manual is part of the Operating Limitations section of the Airplane Flight Manual (AFM). In accordance with 14 CFR 21.41, the Operating Limitations are part of the airplane type certificate and, therefore, can be modified only by changing that certificate; that is, by obtaining an amended or supplemental type certificate. Revisions to the AFM are approved as AFM supplements, and the approval is based on a finding that, with the AFM revisions, the airplane continues to meet the applicable airworthiness standards. Operators are required to comply with the Operating Limitations by 14 CFR 91.9(a).

The above statement infers that the WBM in its entirety is part of the Operating Limitations section of the AFM. This statement is not accurate as the Operating Limitations section of the AFM contains those sections from the WBM concerning the Certified Weight and Center of Gravity Limits, Airplane Gross Weight Versus Fuel Density Limitations, and Fuel Loading Limitations. The sections of the WBM concerning which types of cargo may be carried, where the cargo is located, and how cargo is restrained is not part of the Operating Limitations sections of the WBM, but are operating procedures. Operating procedures are provided in order to allow the operator to plan and distribute payloads so the Operating Limitations sections of the WBM and AFM are satisfied.

Prior to publishing final airworthiness directive, UPS recommends revising the sentence of the above referenced paragraph to the following:

Sections of the Weight and Balance Manual contain Operational Limitations in order to comply with the performance and operational limitations of the Federal Aviation Regulations (FARs), such as the certified weight and center of gravity limits. These sections are part of the Operating Limitations section of the Airplane Flight Manual (AFM).

Additionally, throughout the supplementary information section of the subject docket, reference is made to TSO-C90D pallet. Revision D is the latest issue of TSO-C90, and per the WBM applicable to the Boeing Model 747 series airplanes, approved ULDs for carriage may conform to the TSO-C90 revision to which they were certified. UPS recommends revising the discussion section to remove the revision level when TSO-C90 is referenced.

To Whom It May Concern:
We are writing in support of the Petition for Exemption, Docket Number FAA-2014-0107, wherein the Petitioner, Everts Air, seeks relief from certain requirements of inter alia §121.436 of Title 14, Code of Federal Regulations. The recently enacted regulation requires co-pilots (second in command) hired or promoted to that position after 31 July 2013 to be certified as captains (pilot in command) with respect to the aircraft type rating. This regulation will also require all pilots serving as second in command to be certified in this manner after 01 January 2016.
The petitioner, Tatonduk Outfitters, Ltd., d/b/a Everts Air provides essential services in a unique environment. There are no simulator training devices for several of the aircraft they operate, including the DC-6 and C-46. Thus, all training must be conducted in the airplanes, in flight. It is noteworthy that Everts Air does not seek relief from the requirement that all pilots must possess airline transport licenses.
This mandate will not result in an increased level of safety, rather a lower standard of safety as the more critical and technically demanding captain’s maneuvers will now be required of the second in command candidate. Historically, training in aircraft rather than simulators has proven dangerous, particularly in training lesser experienced pilots in emergency and abnormal procedures and maneuvers. This element represents an increased risk.
When this rule was promulgated by Congress, there was an assumption made that all airline training was accomplished in a simulator. The simulator represents a safe and relatively low cost training environment. The cost of training a pilot in a flight simulator is on the order of $14,000.00. The cost of training the same pilot for the type rating course in the airplane is nearly ten times that, and represents a cost that Everts Air will have to pass along to us as the customer.
We are deeply concerned that this cost will drive the petitioner to withdraw from several markets, leaving non-certificated and/or fewer safe operators. Their alternative is to increase the cost, making arctic operations impractical for industry, including aviation, thus increasing the cost of living in rural communities.
The §121 air carrier has proven to be the safest supply chain for business, industry and residential needs in outlying areas. We agree with the petitioner’s position that training to the level that was in place before the enactment of 14 CFR 121.436 represents continued service at the highest standard of safety.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the U.S. Coast Guards submission of an Information Collection Request (ICR) regarding OMB Control Number: 1625-NEW. It is important that the States being required to comply with this collection of information have an opportunity to comment on its utility and suggest ways to minimize the burden of providing the required information. As a State that numbers vessels, administers recreational boating safety funds and is a member of the National Association of State Boating Law Administrators (NASBLA), please find my comments below.

The ICR should be granted since the information sought is used for the purpose of normalizing recreational boating fatality rates across the nation and is necessary for the Department of Treasurys calculations regarding tax revenues and distributions of the Sport Fish Restoration and Boating Trust Fund. As a point of clarification, the Coast Guards tabulation of State numbered vessels as a result of this ICR cannot be used to measure risk as stated in the supplemental Paperwork Reduction Act Submission that accompanies this ICR, especially since there are numerous recreational boating accidents and fatalities that occur in vessels not required to be numbered and not reflected in this collection of information.

As noted in the Federal Register, in accordance with 33 CFR 174.123, each State that has an approved numbering system must prepare and submit Coast Guard Form CGHQ-3923, Report of Certificates of Number Issued to Boats, to the Coast Guard. Although OMB No. 1625-NEW reflects the revised vessel type terminology resulting from the Coast Guards 2012 issuance of the Final Rule on Changes to Standard Numbering System, Vessel Identification System, and Boating Accident Report Database (Docket No. USCG-2003-14963), it does not accurately reflect the CFRs terminology in its title or instructions (i.e., all references to the approved numbering system, state numbered boats and certificates of number have been replaced with registration and registered).

Also of concern is the fact that OMB No. 1625-NEW is dated 6/2014 inferring that is already in use (or may be required for use). Because States are currently in various stages of implementation of the Final Rule (with final implementation required by 1/1/2017), States cannot be compelled to begin using OMB No. 1625-NEW prior to 1/1/2017. Any required deviation from the use of CGHQ-3923 prior to 1/1/2017 will result in additional (and in some cases, significant) burden and cost to the States.

Again, thank you for the opportunity to comment on this collection of information request.

As a frequent visitor to the Grand Canyon National Park (GCNP) Backcountry I urge you, please, DO NOT approve this proposal without key modifications. Aircraft-caused noise pollution in Grand Canyon is a significant problem, it is getting worse, and this proposal will increase the amount of noise pollution within the park. Grand Canyon visitors deserve natural quiet and should not have the quality of their visit compromised in order to serve the interests of the air-tour industry. For the following three reasons, I believe that the proposed incentives are completely unnecessary:

1 The proposed adoption of an average annual noise metric is a serious step backward designed specifically to favor the Air-Tour industry and allow for an increase in noise within the park. The court supported Daily Noise Standard should be the law of the land.

2 The proposal defines success based on noise rather than quiet. Noise should be treated as the pollutant, where its propagation within the Park is monitored for a full day on the peak operating day and includes all low-altitude flights of any type. This is the method that was applied to assessments during the NPOAG Working Group process (and was supported by all participants). Then, if the quiet zone, or its duration, increases, then the program is effective, otherwise it is not.

3 The proposal allows Air-Tours to accumulate Quiet Technology (QT) credits on off-season QT flights, but then allows air-tours to use those credits with non-QT flights during peak periods. This allowance fails to achieve the goal of incentivizing the conversion to QT during peak (maximum noise pollution) times. While the number of flights should be reduced, all flights should be required to use QT aircraft 100% of the time.

The monitoring of the Daily Noise Standard within in the GCNP should be funded through a fee on the Air-Tours themselves. That way, those that are polluting the environment, and profiting from the act, are themselves playing a role in minimizing the negative impact of their behavior. The burden falls on them to reduce noise pollution within the park.

Thank you for your serious reconsideration of this proposal,

Ned Bryant

Dear Superintendent Uberuaga,

Since 2002, River Runners for Wilderness (RRFW) represents a broad spectrum of river runners, wilderness lovers and American citizens who care about the wilderness river resources in the Colorado River watershed. Our members, now numbering over two thousand with outreach to over 10,000 whitewater enthusiasts, continue to have a deep concern for the future of the wilderness values of the Colorado River watershed and the management of these national treasures. These values include the preservation of Natural Quiet. River runners spend up to thirty days a year in Grand Canyon, 24 hours a day. They, and the ecological resources in Grand Canyon through which they travel, are now impacted adversely by incessant aircraft noise.

River Runners for Wilderness is pleased to provide comments for the Grand Canyon National Park Quiet Aircraft Technology Incentive: Seasonal Relief from Allocations in the Dragon and Zuni Point Corridors.

Grand Canyon National Park has a long history of attempting to grapple with the issue of preserving Natural Quiet from destruction by aircraft. Impairment of the Grand Canyons natural quiet was identified in 1975, when the Grand Canyon Enlargement Act noted overflights were causing a significant adverse effect on the natural quiet and experience of the park. Attempts to preserve the Grand Canyon soundscape made headway with passage of the National Parks Overflights Act in 1987. We regret that since the 1970s, aircraft noise over Grand Canyon has greatly increased.

Additional aircraft flights over Grand Canyon include over 100,000 flights per year in the western areas of Grand Canyon. New tour flights occur over Marble Canyon, and transportation flights have been removed from the noise modeling. Both the new west and east end flights occur from dawn to dusk in the spring, summer and fall. Natural Quiet has been all but destroyed in these areas by these flights.

Additional degradation occurred when all aircraft over 18,000 feet above sea level were exempt from being counted in the parks noise modeling. During the 2007 Grand Canyon National Park Overflights Working Group meetings, the Federal Aviation Administration assured meeting participants that the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen) would eliminate many commercial aviation flights from the skies over Grand Canyon. In a November, 2014, hearing in Washington, DC, three members of Congress expressed serious concern that the NextGen program was stalled, broken and not going to materialize any time soon. Implementation was to occur by 2020, and now appears as though it will never be implemented.

In 2012, the definition of Substantial Restoration of Natural Quiet was re-written by a special interest rider, known as MAP-21. The original definition of Substantial Restoration was weak at the start, where 50 percent or more of the park would be naturally quiet at least 75 percent of the time. MAP-21 stripped or more and at least from this definition. We request that this definition be reinstated. At present, this definition does not substantially restore natural quiet.

MAP-21 requires the FAA and Grand Canyon National Park to provide the air-tour industry with incentives to convert to quiet technology aircraft. Two incentives have already been identified and provided to the industry. These include decreased fees paid to the National Park by industry to operate over Grand Canyon National Park, and the use of previously unused allocations. Given these two incentives have already been provided, and given that MAP-21 did not identify how many incentives were needed, we do not support any additional incentives.

It is unclear to us how a year-round noise level of 58 decibels in the Dragon and Zuni corridor, the same as a sound level of continuous light traffic, is acceptable. It is our understanding that this sound level will be achieved by allowing unlimited quiet technology flights in the winter with nearly 4,000 new aircraft flights in the Dragon and Zuni corridors in the summer. We oppose both the level of acceptable noise and the level of new flights. The aircraft industry over Grand Canyon has received incentives enough, and these proposed incentives would continue to destroy Natural Quiet in Grand Canyon. Grand Canyon National Park should not deviate from using a peak sound level per-day as a threshold for the preservation and restoration of Natural Quiet.

As it is, the air-tour industry has excess allocations they are not using in the Dragon and Zuni corridor. We request that the maximum allowed flights be fixed at the 2012 level of 41,000 flights.

This is a comment on the proposed Grand Canyon National Park Quiet Aircraft Technology Incentive: Seasonal Relief From Allocations in the Dragon and Zuni Point Corridors ([Federal Register Volume 79, Number 217 -- Docket No. FAA-2014-0782).

The effort to achieve soundscape improvements originates from the National Parks Overflights Act of 1987. This effort has continued despite a series of lawsuits by the air-tour industry, and various political efforts to undermine the Act. From 2005 through 2009, I participated in the Grand Canyon Overflights Working Group as representing recreational interests, specifically hikers. Despite the failure to reach an agreement, I learned a great deal about the technical aspects of the Grand Canyon soundscape, and about the political, economic, and agency dynamics.

One of the things I learned is that Quiet Technology (QT) qualified helicopters now increasingly in service with the air-tour operators are actually effective in reducing the aircraft noise footprint, and I favor converting all operating aircraft at Grand Canyon to this standard.

But I am dismayed by this new proposal, and I find three serious flaws in the proposed plan, each serious enough alone to call implementation into question.

Firstly, the proposed adoption of an average annual noise metric is a serious step backward. This specific application was originally given by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in contrast to the natural quiet definition established by the National Park Service (NPS), and offered as a metric to favor air-tours. In litigation resolved in Federal Court in 2002 the NPS standard of each and every day was upheld and ruled appropriate. It is shocking that NPS would now accept this metric which embodies statistical quiet not actual quiet, and is an invalidated standard. The test of whether any QT program is effective must be based on a metric founded on the each and every day standard which remains the appropriate and legal soundscape definition at Grand Canyon National Park.

Secondly, the proposal for the Dragon and Zuni flight corridors defines success based on noise not quiet. A noise-based metric restricted to scheduled air-tour operations has no valid statistical correlation to quiet in Grand Canyon as a whole. The appropriate standard would measure the noise propagation in the Park for a full day on the peak operating day and including all low-altitude flights of any type -- the same method that was applied to assessments during the NPOAG Working Group process (and was supported by all participants). This modeling would measure quiet periods in areas surrounding the flight corridor. If the quiet zone or duration is increased the program is effective, otherwise not. Such a metric need not wait for the elapsed program duration either. If the peak operating day of the program fails the test the program would be (should be) immediately terminated.

Thirdly, the proposal allows air-tours to accumulate QT allocation credits on off-season QT flights, but then allows air-tours to expend those credits with non QT flights during peak periods. Not only does this clearly go against the each and every day standard by allowing more flights on peak days, but also fails to achieve the objective of giving an incentive for conversion to QT equipment, by giving an economic incentive to retain and operate nosier helicopters at a lower cost-basis. For any effective incentive program all flights must require QT aircraft for every operation under the program, or fail to meet this basic test.

All operational air-tour aircraft at Grand Canyon should be required to meet QT qualifications as well as being more compliant (less noisy) than the aircraft they replace. And incentives may aid in attaining this objective. But this requirement alone cannot deliver soundscape controls without rational and appropriate NPS regulatory management. This incentive proposal should not be implemented and any future incentive proposal must make a realistic effort to offer results that would overcome the deficiencies in this proposal.
