Mandatory equipment changes have occurred for snow machines in Yellowstone and 4-stroke motors in Grand Canyon for river tours. Airplanes are expensive, but so is the proportional weight of their impact to natural quiet.
If you check out the regulations (14 CFR 93xx), the definition of QT for any aircraft is based on cryptic equations whose variables center on numbers of db. QT for my 4-seat Cessna is 69 db. Who knows what that is? A good deal of actual aircraft noise is based on the flying habits of the pilot.
Even if a company can demonstrate they theoretically comply with QT, being able to expend their normal allocation AND operate without limit during free for all periods sounds to me like the potential for a tremendous INCREASE in overall noise in the canyon and a decrease in noiseless periods, because the number of flights per operator is increasing (even with QT). This is troublesome.
I encourage NPS and FAA to consider how this proposal will be implemented. How will aircraft be validated for QT? Who will enforce the compliance and how? And I believe that, for the privilege of being able to fly thousands of missions over the heart of GC at only 500 feet above the rim (!!), they should absolutely be required to convert to QT as a condition of operation. I do NOT support a freebie time period that allows operators to increase their usage while dodging the normal allocation.

I have rafted the Grand Canyon four times now and hiked a few times. Aircraft-caused noise pollution is a serious detriment to the enjoyment of Grand Canyon National Park. Under the guise of restoring natural quiet, I fear this proposal will actually increase the amount of noise experienced by visitors. The number of flights in the Dragon and Zuni corridors should be capped at 2012 levels.
Thank you for rejecting this incentive and instead really protecting the natural quiet.

As a yearly backpacker in the Grand Canyon, I have found that the air tours completely disrupt the solitude I expect to find deep in the canyon.  I cannot readily determine the effect of the proposal here, but I would point out that these exemptions are planned--at least in part--for the time of year when backpacking and hiking is most comfortable in the canyon area north of Desert View.  In other words, if the proposal increases flights and noise during the cooler months of the year, you will be doing the most harm possible to those within the canyon.

I do not support an increase in Grand Canyon overflights. I do not support reducing the fees paid by each flight. Entry fees at the gate are going up: why are entry fees for flights being reduced? Let the air tour operators replace their fleet with quiet aircraft without these incentives. They may enough of a profit to do so.

It is true that most flights are in remote areas of the Canyon, however those of us who are in those areas find the overflights to be more intrusive.

It is interesting that at Pima Point on the South Rim there is a display on "natural quiet" which encourages the visitor to listen for the sounds of nature. At this point, mostly the sounds of nature are the helicopters buzzing merrily over Hermit Basin.

I find it hard to believe anyone would advocate for additional flights over the Grand Canyon. The solitude and tranquility is ruined enough by existing endless lines of helicopters flying out and back over the Dragon area. That there is a process to put MORE flights in that path makes no sense.
As an avid backpacker and visitor of the Grand Canyon, I beg all those that make these decisions to please, not allow any more flights. Please spend one morning or afternoon in the Hermit, Yuma Point, or Boucher area before you decide, and I guarantee you will agree it makes no sense to add any more flights, or give any more incentives to those who fly.

As a river guide in Grand Canyon I feel that the excess of aircraft is an obtrusion, a distraction from the wilderness experience. It's something that many of the clients I take down the river ask about. When we see a continuous line of helicopters, one after the other, maybe 25 helicopters in a row people stop and stare. While running the river at the bottom of the Grand Canyon in one of the most scenic landscapes in the world, it seems odd that instead of people asking me about geology, human/ natural history, people ask why the Park Service allows this kind of air traffic.

Making the process "less noisy" isn't a reasonable compromise for a wilderness seeker who goes to our National Parks to experience wilderness with solitude. The sound still attracts the stare.

Any decision to increase the number of flights, or to extend the the hours of flight time is simply against the law. According to the 1987 National Parks Overflights Act, the natural soundscape would be protected from unacceptable impacts. The aircraft should already be as quiet as possible based on the latest technology.

Based on the law, and preserving the wilderness experience the number of flights allowed needs to decrease, along with the hours of the day that flights are allowed.

I have backpacked in the Grand Canyon for almost 30 years now and have more than 35 trips of experience in the canyon. I have noticed a continued increase in aircraft flyover noise through those years, even though flights below the rim were discontinued. The flyover noise over the Nankoweep area seems to be almost continuous and extremely excessive. While I do agree that tourist air flights are a benefit for those that can not see the canyon by other means and are a good economic benefit for the canyon area, I STRONGLY feel that the canyon has hit a threshold of excessive noise caused by these flights. This noise should not be increased in any way and strong efforts should be taken to reduce the noise in all areas where flights are presently allowed.
I STRONGLY hope you will consider NOT allowing any additional fly over traffic than what has been allowed previously (2012 regulations)/
I STRONGLY hope you will consider NOT allowing any additional or new fly over locations than what has been allowed previously.
I STRONGLY feel that there should be some seasonal times created when NO FLIGHTS are allowed over the park OR that an increased flight altitude restriction be created that would significantly minimize noise during late fall through mid-spring timeframes.
I would also urge you to consider REDUCING flight traffic over more remote areas of the canyon such as the Nankoweep Basin area.
Finally I would request that you create more regulations and a fee structure to incentivize the Tourist Flight Operators to ONLY use low noise aircraft over the canyon and PREVENT them from using any other than low noise aircraft for this purpose. People who use these flight services can afford the fees charged by these operators. The fees charged by the Park to these flight operators should DEFINITELY NOT be reduced in any way. FEES SHOULD BE INCREASED for any flight operator using high noise aircraft.
Thank you for soliciting comments on this subject and for your review of mine.

I hike and backpack regularly. While on many trails, it is common to hear air traffic noise. If I am hiking in a small park, I accept that, knowing that the trails may certainly fall along a flight path. But, if I am in a large park, wilderness area, etc., I expect to not be disturbed by air traffic noise. By the time an aircraft is over these areas, it should be high enough to go unnoticed as it continues its flight. There are some areas that I've hike where I have not seen a single aircraft for days, let alone hear one.

The Grand Canyon is one of the most spectacular places to hike and backpack. New trails bring new vistas, while hiking previously explored trails never gets old due to the stunning beauty all around. It is absolutely unacceptable that air traffic noise is allowed in the Park area. No one should have their experience compromised by the drone of aircraft. The Park does a remarkable job of providing access to the vistas for people who can not access the trails. Flying overhead does not increase anyone's appreciation of the views and instead disrupts those who are on the ground enjoying the experience. Even if a visitor is not on the trails, I am sure that that having air noise is not acceptable. If I am sitting at a vista along the Rim, watching the changing views, enjoying the elk grazing around the woods, enjoying my peaceful experience, air noise is not welcome. As an Arizona resident and long time, frequent visitor to both Rims, I desperately encourage you to do all that is possible to end the air noise in all of Grand Canyon and Supai.

Dear Sir,
I think I'm in a unique position to comment as I'm a professional pilot with over 17,000 hours of jet time, as a fighter pilot & a Southwest Airlines Captain. I am also a Grand Canyon Field Institute instructor, leading multi-day hikes below the Rim.
There are very few places frequented by us humans where we can enjoy Natural Quiet. It is a precious & increasingly rare commodity. From my personal experience of having taken many clients into the Canyon, they universally comment on the solitude & quiet that they've never experienced to the degree they do in the Canyon.
Please act in the interest of preserving the Natural Quiet in the Grand Canyon.

I have been going to the canyon for over twenty five years. I have stood on the rim,raft the river, and hiked many miles. The last thing the place needs is more aircraft. Quiet means Quiet.
Thank you.

My name is John Gintert. I have been a resident of Arizona since 2011. In September 2014 I visited the back country of the Grand Canyon National Park on a backpacking trip with my mother and sister. We hiked from Hermit's Rest and camped at Hermit Creek the first night, Boucher Creek the second night, and below Yuma Point on the third night. The Grand Canyon is an awesome experience! The sheer scale of the landscape and the expansive views are mind blowing. From the time we left Hermit Creek until we came to Yuma Point a day and a half later, the only other people we saw were some rafters when we got down to the Colorado River at the end of Boucher Creek. That was only 30 minutes after we got a glimpse of a longhorn sheep. It would have been an almost perfect solitude if it weren't for the constant reminder of the commercialization of the canyon due to tour flights passing overhead.

In our experience, the helicopters flying over the canyon started at 8AM, and by 10AM there was an almost constant drone of aircraft passing overhead. The helicopters can usually be heard flying southward from the north rim minutes before they can be seen. The sound of their rotors beating the air travels for miles, echoing off the sides of the canyon and destroying the natural peacefulness. Typically, by the time a flight disappears over the south rim and its noise starts to diminish, another flight can be heard approaching from the north. The tours keep going until 6PM during the summer, so for 10 hours there was barely a minute in which I couldn't hear an aircraft coming or going. It was a great annoyance to be so far into the wilderness only to have the quietness spoiled by commercial tour flight operations.

Reducing the decibel level of flights is a good strategy to reduce the overall noise due to these operations, and I think creating incentives for the operators to implement quiet technology is a good idea. However, the threshold classifying "quiet" technology in the CFR is 80 decibels, which is still plenty loud enough to be heard throughout the canyon. Additionally, the proposed incentive has the potential to increase the number of commercial tour flights by 33% next year. I fear that the effect may be the opposite of that intended; that the increased number of flights actually increases overall noise levels.

In my opinion, the proper way to create an incentive is to penalize the operators who do not adopt more quiet technology with an additional fee for every noisy flyover. I also propose that all non-quiet flights should be banned. It seems reasonable to require all operators to abide by the noise limit of 80 dB within two years or pay additional penalties.

Our trip to the GCNP was enjoyable, but I was distracted by the commercial tour flight operations. I may return someday, but with so many destinations in Arizona that offer more solitude, I cannot say that I will make this a regular hiking destination.

My three trips floating through the Grand Canyon have all been negatively impacted by planes/helicopters flying over the river. The worse case was military overflights. Aircraft should be banned from the entire area.

Quiet technology isn't really quiet -- just less noisy.
Simply adding more seats to an aircraft should not qualify it for the quiet technology incentives. Operators should be maximizing their passengers per flight anyway.
Switching to quiet technology should be the cost of doing business in Grand Canyon, and a strict requirement integral to operating responsibly in one of the natural wonders of the world.
Adding more flights when we already fail to meet the standard of the "substantial restoration of natural quiet" in Grand Canyon National Park is counter-productive and unacceptable. It doesn't matter if aircraft are "quieter" -- if you add more flights, it's noisier, plain and simple.
The suggested incentives raise a lot of questions: How can the public be assured that noise won't increase? In this time of diminishing budgets, does Grand Canyon National Park have funds and personnel sufficient to monitor this? Will there be transparency and accountability? Once you give "seasonal relief from allocations," will it ever be possible to take it away? How will these changes be enforced and monitored?
In 2012, the very definition of the Substantial Restoration of Natural Quiet was re-written by a congressional special interest rider inserted into a must-pass spending bill. Substantial Restoration had previously been defined as: 50 percent or more of the park would be naturally quiet at least 75 percent of the time. The wording or more and at least were removed from this definition in a political move just as the National Park Service was preparing to issue final recommendations on reducing airtour noise over Grand Canyon. Under the new degraded definition, half the park can be loud all of the day, and the other half noisy up to 25 percent of the day. We do not support allowing unlimited quiet technology flights in the winter season, and up to 3,700 new airtours in the Dragon and Zuni corridors in the summer. These increases would adversely affect the visitor experience in the backcountry and along the river corridor.

The Grand Canyon is too spectacular and special to be inundated with noise from aircraft, no matter WHICH trail you are on. It should be kept as quiet and wild as possible. I have backpacked from the North Rim down to Phantom and up to the South Rim and dearly hope to be able to backpack there again.  Thank you for keeping the Grand Canyon quiet.

Our National Parks were set aside to provide a place for peace and sanctuary. How the NPS can allow any flights over the Grand Canyon is beyond me, let alone increase the number of flights. All airplane and helicopter flights should be completely eliminated. How the hell can you work for the National Park Service, where your mission in to preserve the parks for future generations, and yet allow those obnoxious helicopter flights to take off every 5 minutes and completely eliminate peace and solitude??? Step up to the plate and do the right thing.

Don't allow any more flights no matter what technology is used to quiet them. Keep whatever fights are currently allowed over the corridor traills where people don't have an expectation of quite. Flights over remote areas detract from the experience and beauty of the canyon. No  matter how quiet they are, they are unnatural and unwanted.

I am definiely NOT in favor of this proposal.  I believe it is so important to keep places pristine and without the intrusions of helicopters, both visually and audiby.  The Grand Canyon is one of the finest places to experience solitude and we owe it not only to ourselves, but to future generations to protect this beautiful place!

Please reduce noise in the Grand Canyon, do not keep it the same or increase it.
I am a frequent backpacker in remote areas of the Canyon, and it's best feature is the solitude and quiet.
The overflights in the Boucher area are SO ANNOYING!!! Constant noise all day long. As a Viet Nam Veteran,I DO NOT like the sounds of helicopters anyway, much less in the Canyon.

snwcmpr

I backpacked some of the primitive trails (the Boucher) this past May with my two grown children. It was an amazing experience that I'd like to do again on a regular basis. The only downside were the incessant helicopters that began flying overhead around 8 AM and ran every 15 minutes ALL DAY long. I've backpacked in the Adirondacks, the Great Smoky Mountains and the White Mountains and the helicopter activity in the GC was a real detraction. I understand that the FAA and the NPS are trying to encourage Quiet aircraft Technology but I think a stick would be better than a carrot in this case. More flights are not better even if they're quieter. This proposal seems like a very bad thing to me. I agree with and repeat another commenters words:

"As a backpacker and avid Grand Canyon lover, the increase in aircraft will destroy the quiet serenity that prevails in the canyon. It appears the increase will harm, not improve the natural quiet in the Canyon. No matter how "quiet" the aircraft are, increasing the number of aircraft allowed in the airspace above the Canyon will not help make it more quiet. Please reconsider this proposal and limit the number of aircraft allowed in the airspace over the Canyon.
This is one of the few places left in our country that is truly "wilderness." Where quiet time to be among the incredible beauty of the Canyon is not interrupted by the sounds of the modern world. Where you can truly feel like you're all alone and in another time. It is a place where cell phones don't work, where there is no TV to distract us, where we can truly escape and be a part of nature. More aircraft will further destroy the serenity found in the Canyon. Please do not allow this to happen."

"To whom it may concern,

This is a comment on the proposed Grand Canyon National Park Quiet Aircraft Technology Incentive: Seasonal Relief from Allocations in the Dragon and Zuni Point Corridors ([Federal Register Volume 79, Number 217 -- Docket No. FAA-2014-0782).

As a frequent visitor to the Grand Canyon National Park (GCNP) Backcountry I urge you, please, DO NOT approve this proposal without key modifications. Aircraft-caused noise pollution in Grand Canyon is a significant problem, it is getting worse, and this proposal will increase the amount of noise pollution within the park. Grand Canyon visitors deserve natural quiet and should not have the quality of their visit compromised in order to serve the interests of the air-tour industry. For the following three reasons, I believe that the proposed incentives are completely unnecessary:

1 The proposed adoption of an average annual noise metric is a serious step backward designed specifically to favor the Air-Tour industry and allow for an increase in noise within the park. The court supported Daily Noise Standard should be the law of the land.

2 The proposal defines success based on noise rather than quiet. Noise should be treated as the pollutant, where its propagation within the Park is monitored for a full day on the peak operating day and includes all low-altitude flights of any type. This is the method that was applied to assessments during the NPOAG Working Group process (and was supported by all participants). Then, if the quiet zone, or its duration, increases, then the program is effective, otherwise it is not.

3 The proposal allows Air-Tours to accumulate Quiet Technology (QT) credits on off-season QT flights, but then allows air-tours to use those credits with non-QT flights during peak periods. This allowance fails to achieve the goal of incentivizing the conversion to QT during peak (maximum noise pollution) times. While the number of flights should be reduced, all flights should be required to use QT aircraft 100% of the time.

The monitoring of the Daily Noise Standard within in the GCNP should be funded through a fee on the Air-Tours themselves. That way, those that are polluting the environment, and profiting from the act, are themselves playing a role in minimizing the negative impact of their behavior. The burden falls on them to reduce noise pollution within the park.

Thank you for your serious reconsideration of this proposal,

Aircraft-caused noise pollution is a serious detriment to the enjoyment of Grand Canyon National Park. Under the guise of restoring natural quiet, the present proposal will actually increase the amount of noise experienced by visitors to the Parks backcountry areas. Therefore we propose:
The number of flights in the Dragon and Zuni corridors should be capped at 2012 levels.
One-hour air tours should be eliminated.
No additional incentives, such as those proposed here, are required nor appropriate.

I've been complaining about aircraft noise in remote Grand Canyon areas for almost 25 years. The only way to solve this problem is to eliminate overflights completely. Anything else you do might help some, but please don't try to convince me that you are restoring natural quite. I know first-hand that all the changes made in the last 25 years have done essentially nothing to restore natural quiet. Quieter aircraft does reduce noise somewhat, but it does not restore natural quiet. Natural quiet means no aircraft noise (aircraft are not natural). So by allowing QT aircraft to operate more flights is counter-productive. In addition to requiring QT aircraft, the number of flights need to be reduced too!

You talk about giving "relief" to air tour operators -- what about backpackers and hikers who are there to enjoy the natural beauty (and quite) of the Canyon. Quit coddling the aircraft operators.

Please don't do this. It's probably useless to make these comment's. Money is speech, and corporations are people. And, I'm 62 years old, and I'm not rich. But, The Canyon is a special place, quiet is a special resource. I've personally witnesses planes breaking the rules while camped near Shiva Temple in The Canyon. Relaxing the rules even more will lead to the detriment of the experience of being in The Canyon. They don't follow the rules that are now in place. There are some things, some experiences, and some places that need to be protected. Please, don't expand the regions where someone is supposed to monitor when there are no resources to monitor what is already in place. I just read the information below, and see there is a place for "submitting for a third party". Oh, year, helps you notice if it's coming from a generous person/corporation beig represented by a great lobbyist. Please, protect The Canyon,

The Grand Canyon needs to have fewer air tours, not more, even if the aircraft have "quiet" technology. Air tours destroy the natural sounds and atmosphere of a large portion of the park. You do not have to be an extreme adventurer to be subject to the noise from air tours. The noise from air tours can be heard from many view points and trail heads. There is a misconception that air tours only affect the "hard-core" hikers that venture far away from the main visitor areas. Nothing can be further from the truth. Air tours can be plainly heard from Hermits Rest, which is so popular that it is part of the parks shuttle bus system.

And yes, if one is on an overnight hiking trip underneath an air tour corridor, the non-stop noise drastically distracts from the experience. People come from all over the world to hike in the Grand Canyon, and for many it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. The onslaught from the tours only exacerbates the image of the US as a land of "cheap thrills" and that money rules. US National Parks are our ambassadors to the rest of the world. We want them to send a good message.

The economic impact of air tours is negligible. The air tour companies only serve to profit a handful of individuals who then use their profits to influence legislation that continues to allow their air tours. For every breathtaking view a visitor gets from an air tour, they are ruining the experience of dozens if not hundreds of others. Privatize the profit and socialize the costs.

There are numerous ways for everyone to experience the awesomeness and grandeur of the Grand Canyon without air tours. Handicap accessible viewpoints, mule rides, paved walkways and greenways, numerous paved roads to various viewpoints throughout the park. These are examples of the ways that the "less adventurous" can experience the canyon. And from the sheer numbers of people hiking the Bright Angel trail, it is obvious that one need not be an elite athlete, or an athlete of any kind, to be able to experience the inner canyon.

Obviously I am against air tours of any kind. Rocky Mountain National Park successfully put an end to its air tour operations a long time ago, with no adverse affects on its local economy. But the policies being considered here are absolutely out of line with anything except making air tours easier and more profitable for the air tour industry.

Our National Parks do not exists as entrepreneurial avenues for companies to pursue profit. Please do not increase the number of air tours even though they have the "quiet" technology.

Sincerely,
Mark Hyams
Albuquerque, NM

I visit the Grand Canyon every year (sometimes multiple times a year), and this proposal truly bothers me. As a backpacker and avid Grand Canyon lover, the increase in aircraft will destroy the quiet serenity that prevails in the canyon. It appears the increase will harm, not improve the natural quiet in the Canyon. No matter how "quiet" the aircraft are, increasing the number of aircraft allowed in the airspace above the Canyon will not help make it more quiet. Please reconsider this proposal and limit the number of aircraft allowed in the airspace over the Canyon.
This is one of the few places left in our country that is truly "wilderness." Where quiet time to be among the incredible beauty of the Canyon is not interrupted by the sounds of the modern world. Where you can truly feel like you're all alone and in another time. It is a place where cell phones don't work, where there is no TV to distract us, where we can truly escape and be a part of nature. More aircraft will destroy the serenity found in the Canyon. Please do not allow this to happen.

I have been hiking, backpacking, and river running in the Grand Canyon for over thirty years. During the past decade, I have spent over 250 days and nights below the rim enjoying one of the world's greatest wild places. I have also experienced the annoyance and destruction of wilderness experience that often attends the constant passage of both fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters. Depending on the location of a hike, it can be a blissful experience of nature or can be frequently interrupted by unnatural aircraft noise.

I oppose the proposal in this docket for "seasonal relief" in the Dragon and Zuni Point corridors.

This action is disguised as an effort to encourage the adoption of "quiet" aircraft technology by INCREASING the total number of air tour flights. So-called "quiet" flights in the winter will be offset by more flights in the summer. The park service has publicly admitted that even though the goal is to restore natural quiet, this proposal does the opposite.

Rather than increasing the number of air-tour flights, the number of flights in the Dragon and Zuni corridors should be capped at 2012 levels.

No incentive scheme such as that proposed here, which results in an increased number of overflights, is required, and none is appropriate. Any such increase will destroy, not improve, natural quiet. The park cannot be made more quiet by flying more planes over it, no matter how "quiet" each plane is.

Previous incentives for "quiet" technology are sufficient. Operators have had their fees reduced from $25 per flight to $20 per flight as an inducement to use quieter aircraft.

It is particularly ironic that lower fees have been introduced as a part of the QT program, since at this moment, the Park has proposed to increase fees enter the park from $25 per vehicle to $30 per vehicle. First we granted a $5 lower fee for airplanes to fly over the Grand Canyon, now we propose a $5 higher fee to visit the canyon on foot. I'm sure it wasn't intended but the resulting incentives favor flying over the Canyon rather than visiting it -- and experiencing it fully -- in person.

Grand Canyon is meant to be a wilderness area, and aircraft noise is counter to this designation.   I believe that this proposal will in fact increase noise, despite wording that makes claims to the contrary.  So I urge rejection of the proposal.  In fact, I believe that air tours over Grand Canyon should be decreased further, if not eliminated entirely.

To whom it may concern,

This is a comment on the proposed Grand Canyon National Park Quiet Aircraft Technology Incentive: Seasonal Relief from Allocations in the Dragon and Zuni Point Corridors ([Federal Register Volume 79, Number 217 -- Docket No. FAA-2014-0782).

As a frequent Grand Canyon backcountry hiker and rafter Id like to share my experiences with air tours within the park boundaries. Id also like to strongly voice my opposition to the proposed incentive to air tour operators because as written the incentive will result in increased flights over the canyon and no reduction in noise or visual pollution.
I have hiked and camped in the areas under the Dragon and Zuni point corridors. The north side of the river in this region is somewhat difficult for hikers to gain access. Those who do hike there are expecting a wilderness experience that is not subject to the constant racket of from air tours. While hiking up Crystal and Dragon drainages the noise from the helicopters is incessant with nearly a helicopter every five minutes from an hour after sunrise to an hour before sunset. A comparable amount of noise pollution can be experienced by hikers and rafter from Cape Solitude to Nankoweap Canyon. One has to wonder why the recreational experiences of a select few are allowed to negatively impact outdoor enthusiasts along broad swathes of the canyon who are attempting to enjoy experiences with nature on the ground.

Good stewardship by the park service should result in helicopter traffic being carefully reduced over time with the goal being the eventual elimination of helicopter tours altogether. As currently written the incentive will increase, not reduce, helicopter traffic in the park and does little if anything that will result in the reduction of the current levels of noise pollution. Furthermore, the proposed incentive allows air tour companies to acquire quiet technology (QT) credits during the off-season that can then be spent on non-QT flights during the peak periods. How does this reduce air tour-related noise pollution over the long run and how does it incentivize the air tours to go to QT? If acquiring QT is the goal of the park perhaps the park should require it. Isnt flying in the park privilege enough that does not require incentives?

I am hopeful that the National Park Service will consider the protection of the resource first, rather than the money to be made from commercial interests. The sound and visual qualities of a natural environment are central to the experiences of the majority of park visitors and the constant noise from overflights associated with an elite few are not consistent with the majority enjoying a natural experience above and below the rims of the canyon.

Thank you for your consideration.

Scott C. Marley

I have spent much time backpacking in the park and can assure you that more overflights + more seats = much more noise.  The area around Nankoweap, Crystal, and Boucher already sounds like a war zone.  Even though much in that area is Wilderness, it is NOT a wilderness experience.  GCNP has closed so many roads to access Wilderness areas, but noisy tour aircraft decimates the Wilderness of that area.  The noise pollution affects all living creatures in GC and certainly effects those of us visiting.  Share the noise with this in the Corridor viewing the Canyon from the rims, and THEN see what the public reaction is.  Companies making money off of everyone's land should not get a price break while user fees go up for those of us who drive and walk in.

The proposal is absurd and undermines the natural quiet of Grand Canyon National Park. Despite the claims that it will encourage quiet technology, it will increase the noise levels in the national park by allowing additional flights that are not required to use quiet technology and increased flights on already noisy busy days. As a frequent hiker in areas beneath the Zuni corridor, I can attest that the current noise levels are already offensive and unbearable. Allowing increased flights during the already busy summer season will only make this worse.

Flights should be capped at existing levels (or reduced) and quiet technology should be required of those flights.

The annual noise standard is a flawed method of measuring noise, as a daily standard has been upheld in federal court.

Any proposal to increase flights should also include monitoring to measure the effects.

Bottom line though is that the resources of Grand Canyon are being impaired by overflights. The law and the courts have agreed. Increasing flights is not the answer. Even if you can now legally do whatever you want--it doesn't mean you should.

Grand Canyon National Park is a wonderful and special place, and its resources and being damaged and visitors' experiences are being ruined by the few who can afford expensive air tours and by the companies who profit from them.
We travel every year from NY to AZ to experience the serenity of the Grand Canyon. Please don't let this natural serenity be poisoned by overflights.

Here are my comments...

Decreasing the fees paid to the National Park by the airtour industry to operate over the park, and to allow the use of previously unused allocations are incentive enough when all Americans nationwide are being asked to pay more to enter their National Parks.

The effort to achieve soundscape improvements originates from the National Parks Overflights Act of 1987. This effort has continued despite a series of lawsuits by the air-tour industry, and various political efforts to undermine the Act.

Quiet Technology (QT) qualified helicopters now increasingly in service with the air-tour operators are actually effective in reducing the aircraft noise footprint, and I favor converting all operating aircraft at Grand Canyon to this standard.

But I am dismayed by this new proposal, and I find three serious flaws in the proposed plan, each serious enough alone to call implementation into question.

Firstly, the proposed adoption of an average annual noise metric is a serious step backward. This specific application was originally given by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in contrast to the natural quiet definition established by the National Park Service (NPS), and offered as a metric to favor air-tours. In litigation resolved in Federal Court in 2002 the NPS standard of each and every day was upheld and ruled appropriate. It is shocking that NPS would now accept this metric which embodies statistical quiet not actual quiet, and is an invalidated standard. The test of whether any QT program is effective must be based on a metric founded on the each and every day standard which remains the appropriate and legal soundscape definition at Grand Canyon National Park.

Secondly, the proposal for the Dragon and Zuni flight corridors defines success based on noise not quiet. A noise-based metric restricted to scheduled air-tour operations has no valid statistical correlation to quiet in Grand Canyon as a whole. The appropriate standard would measure the noise propagation in the Park for a full day on the peak operating day and including all low-altitude flights of any type -- the same method that was applied to assessments during the NPOAG Working Group process (and was supported by all participants). This modeling would measure quiet periods in areas surrounding the flight corridor. If the quiet zone or duration is increased the program is effective, otherwise not. Such a metric need not wait for the elapsed program duration either. If the peak operating day of the program fails the test the program would be (should be) immediately terminated.

Thirdly, the proposal allows air-tours to accumulate QT allocation credits on off-season QT flights, but then allows air-tours to expend those credits with non QT flights during peak periods. Not only does this clearly go against the each and every day standard by allowing more flights on peak days, but also fails to achieve the objective of giving an incentive for conversion to QT equipment, by giving an economic incentive to retain and operate nosier helicopters at a lower cost-basis. For any effective incentive program all flights must require QT aircraft for every operation under the program, or fail to meet this basic test.

All operational air-tour aircraft at Grand Canyon should be required to meet QT qualifications as well as being more compliant (less noisy) than the aircraft they replace. And incentives may aid in attaining this objective. But this requirement alone cannot deliver soundscape controls without rational and appropriate NPS regulatory management. This incentive proposal should not be implemented and any future incentive proposal must make a realistic effort to offer results that would overcome the deficiencies in this proposal.

It is our understanding that the noise modeling in Grand Canyon National Park is based on data collected in 2005. We suggest the fees paid by the air-tour industry for each helicopter flight over Grand Canyon be used to fund yearly noise modeling. Modeling and real-time data must be made available to the public on a monthly basis, year by year. This data must have percent time audible measurements. Aviation accounts for 11 percent of all carbon dioxide emissions in the United States transportation sector. Each hour long helicopter flight over Grand Canyon creates over 350 pounds of carbon dioxide emissions. I respectfully submit the following comments on the Grand Canyon National Park Quiet Aircraft Technology Incentive: Seasonal Relief from Allocations in the Dragon and Zuni Point Corridors.

I have been a commercial river guide and trip leader for 15 years on the Colorado River in Grand Canyon National Park and all over the western U.S. for 5 years previous. I also conduct ecological research in the river corridor and work for a local non-profit focused on conservation in the Grand Canyon ecoregion. I have spent over 250 days/year in the wilds of the Grand Canyon ecoregion for the past decade and can speak first-hand to the increased impact that overflights have on people enjoying natural quiet in this part of the U.S. I also represent the public... we own these lands and we value natural quiet and suggest limiting air access when the risks and negative impacts outweigh the positive. I participate in getting over 30,000 people per year down the river, and millions of people access the South and North Rim every year. Why do we continually fight the air industry to provide more and more access to a place that is already significantly impacted by overflight corridors over some of the otherwise quietest areas in Grand Canyon?

When Congress passed the 1987 National Parks Overflights Act, it challenged the National Park Service (NPS) to substantially restore natural quiet to Grand Canyon National Park. Twenty-seven years after it was enacted, barely 50 percent of the park is free from aircraft noise 75 percent of the time. Nearly half of the parks silence, one of the qualities that distinguish Grand Canyon from ordinary places, has been sacrificed to air tour noise. That is why Congress enacted restrictions to dial down the noise in 1987 and why in Section 4.9 of NPS Management Policies, the agency said that it will restore to the natural condition wherever possible those park soundscapes that have become degraded by unnatural sounds (noise), and will protect natural soundscapes from unacceptable impacts.

Despite these commitments, noise from air tours continues to impair a substantial area of Grand Canyon National Park.

With respect to the current proposal, please consider the following points:

Quiet technology isn't really quiet -- just less noisy than the obtrusive and disturbing current technology.
Simply adding more seats to an aircraft should not qualify it for the quiet technology incentives. Operators should be maximizing their passengers per flight anyway.
Switching to quiet technology should be the cost of doing business in Grand Canyon, and a strict requirement integral to operating responsibly in one of the natural wonders of the world.
Adding more flights when we already fail to meet the standard of the "substantial restoration of natural quiet" in Grand Canyon National Park is counter-productive and unacceptable. It doesn't matter if aircraft are "quieter" -- if you add more flights, it's noisier, plain and simple.
The suggested incentives raise a lot of questions: How can the public be assured that noise won't increase? In this time of diminishing budgets, does Grand Canyon National Park have funds and personnel sufficient to monitor this? Will there be transparency and accountability? Once you give "seasonal relief from allocations," will it ever be possible to take it away? How will these changes be enforced and monitored?
In 2012, the very definition of the Substantial Restoration of Natural Quiet was re-written by a congressional special interest rider inserted into a must-pass spending bill. Substantial Restoration had previously been defined as: 50 percent or more of the park would be naturally quiet at least 75 percent of the time. The wording or more and at least were removed from this definition in a political move just as the National Park Service was preparing to issue final recommendations on reducing airtour noise over Grand Canyon. Under the new degraded definition, half the park can be loud all of the day, and the other half noisy up to 25 percent of the day. We do not support allowing unlimited quiet technology flights in the winter season, and up to 3,700 new airtours in the Dragon and Zuni corridors in the summer. These increases would adversely affect the visitor experience in the backcountry and along the river corridor.

I oppose any additional incentives beyond those that are already in place (i.e., decreasing the fees paid to the National Park by the air tour industry to operate over the park and allowing the use of previously unused allocations). The natural soundscapes in Grand Canyon are a threatened park value which we will continue to defend.
Thank you very much for your consideration of our views.

I have been rafting and backpacking in the Grand Canyon for over 17 years. There is nothing that takes me away from the immediacy of the canyon and all its delights than seeing contrails overhead and hearing the man-made noise of aircraft. I understand the need for tourism, but the desire for more will ruin what is one of the only places to truly escape from the outside world. I urge you to refrain from increasing the total number of air flights in the Grand Canyon. Lets keep this natural wonder the Grand Canyon that it is.

To Whom it May Concern,

I have been out to some of the remote areas that are subject to overflights. The wilderness quality of the area was severely degraded by seemingly incessant overflights. It seemed that rather than being in one of the crown jewels of the National Park system I had wandered near an Army airfield. Without a doubt it changes the character of the Park.

1 The proposed adoption of an average annual noise metric is a serious step backward designed specifically to favor the Air-Tour industry and allow for an increase in noise within the park. The court supported Daily Noise Standard should be the law of the land.

2 The proposal defines success based on noise rather than quiet. Noise should be treated as the pollutant, where its propagation within the Park is monitored for a full day on the peak operating day and includes all low-altitude flights of any type. This is the method that was applied to assessments during the NPOAG Working Group process (and was supported by all participants). Then, if the quiet zone, or its duration, increases, then the program is effective, otherwise it is not.

3 The proposal allows Air-Tours to accumulate Quiet Technology (QT) credits on off-season QT flights, but then allows air-tours to use those credits with non-QT flights during peak periods. This allowance fails to achieve the goal of incentivizing the conversion to QT during peak (maximum noise pollution) times. While the number of flights should be reduced, all flights should be required to use QT aircraft 100% of the time.

The monitoring of the Daily Noise Standard within in the GCNP should be funded through a fee on the Air-Tours themselves. That way, those that are polluting the environment, and profiting from the act, are themselves playing a role in minimizing the negative impact of their behavior. The burden falls on them to reduce noise pollution within the park. The fees they pay the park should be increased to cover this. The burden of proving that the actual amount of quiet is increasing should be on them.

Thank you for your serious reconsideration of this proposal,

Peter Zinsli

I have hiked and backpacked in the Grand Canyon several times over the last 2 decades. The helicopter flights over the canyon have always disturbed me. The serenity and beauty of the canyon experience is rudely interrupted by the noisy intrusions. Please do not increase the amount of flights. The National Park has done a great job of managing human access and enjoyment of the Grand Canyon via land and water.
But I was horrified when, as a private boater expected to haul out every crumb of waste I brought into the canyon, I turned a bend in the river and faced helicopters polluting the airspace of the canyon in a most invasive and abusive way.
Why is this third element, the air, so violently mismanaged?
Is it merely capitalism winning in the war of greed over public rights? Or is this merely terrible management?
Please register one vote for 'no helicopters at all, ever.'

Moab, Utah

As a mariner and member of many local and regional non profits from the New York Harbor area we would like to see some of our successful initiatives funded and taken national. Our success in New York could easily be scaled up and adapted for many ports across the country. We have dedicated groups focussed on educational projects which help reduce risk between commercial and recreational vessels. Safe boating in the Port environment is very different from inland lakes and rivers and the safe interaction is critical. Education is at the forefront of this safety initiative.

The first and most prominent is the www.thesafeharbor.us project. It is an educational platform which is a comprehensive one stop shop for all information regarding safety and safe boating in the Port of NY & NJ. A web site is the main portal and contains a few key components. First, the web site itself has links to all critical information such as tides, currents, charts, weather and boater safety education classes. The web site is easy to navigate and offers a built in tracking component to measure success.

Second is a video series filmed in documentary style speaking the each user group in the port and their experience operating in the port. The documentary style tells a compelling story first hand of how things "really are" in the crowded waterway. There are 2 PSA's for the USCG and a full 28 minute film is produced combining all the chapters into one beautifully narrated story.

Third and most important is the marketing and distribution. This is a useful tool but needs to get into the hands of boaters. Our direct to consumer outreach at power boat shows, paddle shows and sailing shows reaches all aspects of recreational boaters. Hands on speaks to boaters to share stories, clarify misinformation and create a relationship with the boater and the web site. Outreach comes in the form of press outreach and earned media as well as inexpensive online promotions through social media and web advertising. This is targeted and trackable outreach.

Since the creation of this project we were nominated for the National Harbor Ops of the year award at the National Ports conference in Pittsburgh and subsequently we have spoken to Admiral Servidio and Neffenger about this project. We have also spoken to the Port of Boston, Chicago, Houston, Hawaii and Los Angeles who are all very interested in this platform for their port but are having trouble finding funds to bring it to their Port.

Our team would take the raw elements of this platform and customize a solution, based on our success and what we learned, for each port based on their individual wants and needs. Each port is different and has subtleties which need to be captured to provide authenticity and real value for the greater boating community. We would partner with similar boating non profits and clubs locally in each port to help execute and distribute the product to the community. We would develop a plan to hand over the product to each port community to manage long term so it stays in the hands of locals who "know best" what that port needs.

Our funding requirements would be roughly $450,000 per port for the full platform which includes a developed, created, distributed product and handed over for long term maintenance to the port. We would want to roll this out over a 3 to 5 year plan so we would want a annual renewing grant to be able to execute this for each port. We would want funding for the Ports who have expressed interest and they are again the Port of Boston, Chicago, Houston, Hawaii and Los Angeles. The funding would have a huge complimentary in kind component as we would partner with the port members such as USCG Aux, US Power Squadron, Pilots, and the USCG in each area. The project in New York had over $250,000 in "in kind" contributions. There is real value in this project and it is a strong community builder. We are a group of local small businesses and partner with local and regional non profit partners so the requirements of being a national non profit may need to be waived to execute this plan.

Lastly, the single biggest outcome of this project are the lines of communications it opened during the development, creation and execution. It is a project ALL port partners see value in and can support. Opening the lines of communications have lasting impact on the overall safety and security of the port. It places names and faces with operators both commercial and recreational and allows for dialogue. When peoples voices are heard they feel welcome and understood and this level of understanding promotes greater cooperation and cohabitation is our crowded waterways. This dialogue is the key to long term safety and security in our ports.

1. This idea would be appropriate for Southern states such as Florida, etc. however, here in Maryland where boating is seasonal, a year round campaign would not be beneficial. We have a limited number of boaters in the late fall and winter months and these usually consist of commercial watermen and more experienced boat owners. It is important that all stakeholders in the National RBS Program have a unified message to use regarding various boating safety topics. It is important that outreach programs that receive any funding in support of this priority must focus on creating a national standardized boating safety message(s), idea(s) and program(s) that support what the states need to focus on as a direct result of what they are trying to minimize due to boat accident data.

3. Standardizing the administration of accident reports, boater education and life jacket wear requirements is a good idea and should be reciprocal/compatible with what other states are doing as well. 4. We support the idea of the Grantee providing Accident Investigation Seminars however, it seems difficult that the Coast Guard would be required to approve the various locations. The Maryland Natural Resources Police has taken great benefit from the ability to send members of the agency to the NASBLA accident investigation training for the basic and advanced course. This training provides for the backbone of what our specialized boat accident investigators receive as part of their training.

5. Maryland supports this area of interest. However it is time for an innovative approach to help support this priority. There are annual studies each year on life jacket wear rates, and not much seems to change. The past traditional surveys seem to bring about the same results each year. An innovative way needs to be supported in an effort to track and evaluate life jacket wear rates.

6. We support this area of interest. Maryland fully supports the development of technical standards for building boats. Maryland fully supports education and training all marine patrol officers in the state in the use of the seated Standardized Field Sobriety Tests (SFST). Perhaps of all the priorities mentioned here to comment on, this may have the greatest impact now and in the future for funding. Additional work needs to be done in enforcement and outreach for BUI. One great example that should continue to grow is the national BUI awareness and enforcement campaign, Operation Dry Water. In line with this Area of Interest (Year-Round Safe Boating Campaign), SPIN - STOP Propeller Injuries Now!) will present at the NBSAC meeting on Nov 6th a study of media in California and examples from a few other states to demonstrate that we have missed developing a better partnership with media. . Such media messages could be further developed by NASBLA for instance. The various safe boating venues and websites have become very sophisticated over the years. Reporters are not going to work that hard. We need to make this easy for them We need them as a partner to provide the clear, concise and pointed messages on safe boating practices that we so urgently need to get out to the public.

Marion IrvingdeCruz for Stop Propeller Injuries Now! www.propellersafety.com/spin

Federal Data Act Pushes Grant Transparency
By Zach Halper - April 30, 2014
Grant management for recipients of federal funds figures to become more streamlined. Congress has passed the Digital Accountability and Transparency (DATA) Act, bringing government-wide standards for grant reporting that is expected to result in easier reporting processes for nonprofits.

In conjunction with the Senates unanimous approval on April 10, the House of Representatives passage of the DATA Act which now awaits President Barack Obamas signature will shine light on federal spending data that was previously hidden behind different systems and formats. For grant managers who receive funding from federal agencies, the law will bring a great deal of change to reporting standards.

According to information published by StreamLink Software, a grants software company in Cleveland, Ohio, the federal Treasury Department and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) will begin creating the data standards necessary to regiment grantee and contractor reporting, and enable the online publishing of data after the bill is signed by the President. After a one-year review of what is currently being reported, agencies will have two years to implement the data standards into the information they report to the Treasury, White House, and government-wide grant and contract databases.

We applaud the legislations intent to provide greater transparency into federal spending and appreciate the work of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and House Oversight and Government Reform Committee to address many of the concerns industry had with previous versions of the legislation, said Mark Hettinger, senior vice president of public sector and government affairs at TechAmerica. The DATA Act is a step in the right direction for federal transparency and accountability.

TechAmerica, a technology advocacy organization in Washington, D.C., did have concerns about potential national security risks but, according to Hettinger, those concerns were eased with the current version of the bill allowing Department of Defense the option to extend implementation of the bills requirements to enable better protection of data from damaging disclosure.

The changes to what organizations will need to report from their federal grant spending will be determined during the two-year pilot program period, according to Matt Rumsey, policy associate at the Sunlight Foundation. This program will determine what reporting needs to be consolidated and what, if anything, needs to be added.

On the outset, [the DATA Act] will affect nonprofits that receive federal funding, said Rumsey. In the long run, it will help nonprofits looking to get federal funding because it will be easier to follow the money.

Adam Roth, president and CEO of StreamLink Software, anticipates that nonprofits will have a few more items they will have to report to the federal government but that the reporting process will be easier. Ultimately this will result in a much more streamlined process for nonprofits, explained Roth, who noted that current reporting requirements are all over the place. He also said that organizations should be prepared to show the outcome of the dollars they receive.

Rumsey said the Sunlight Foundation, as well as other transparency advocacy organizations, have been pushing for something like the DATA Act for several years. While the changes will have the most impact on nonprofits receiving federal funding, Rumsey did note that it could have some impact on the philanthropic sector as a whole. Roth, meanwhile, believed the changes on the federal level came as a result of culture change, noting that many states had already moved to enact similar processes.

There had also been some movement prior to the DATA Act on the federal level, with Roth specifically mentioning recent changes by the OMB that place more importance on performance rather than compliance for grant recipients.

I think this is a culture change, said Roth. The federal changes are a signal of the change in how business is being done.

While Rumsey is pleased the legislation has passed, he stressed that the DATA Act is only the beginning. For the law to be as effective as it needs to be, he said, the law needs to be implemented correctly.

This is a big step, but its not the last step, said Rumsey. We need to make sure the law is implemented strongly and that the government puts its energy behind it.

A sign of how well the law is being implemented will be whether those agencies that are allocating dollars are following the guidelines set by the law, said Roth. He added that it is the responsibility of those in charge of implementing the law to ensure that the new standards are being followed across all agencies.

Here is a portion of the Act:

This act requires the following:

Public Law (05/09/2014)
(This measure has not been amended since it was passed by the Senate on April 10, 2014. The summary of that version is repeated here.)
Digital Accountability and Transparency Act of 2014 or the DATA Act - (Sec. 2) States as the purposes of this Act to:
expand the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006 by disclosing direct federal agency expenditures and linking federal contract, loan, and grant spending information to federal programs to enable taxpayers and policy makers to track federal spending more effectively;
establish government-wide data standards for financial data and provide consistent, reliable, and searchable government-wide spending data that is displayed accurately for taxpayers and policy makers on USASpending.gov;
simplify reporting for entities receiving federal funds by streamlining reporting requirements and reducing compliance costs while improving transparency;
improve the quality of data submitted to USASpending.gov by holding federal agencies accountable for the completeness and accuracy of the data submitted; and
apply approaches developed by the Recovery Accountability and Transparency Board to spending across the federal government.
(Sec. 3) Amends the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006 to define "federal agency," for purposes of such Act, to mean an executive department, a government corporation, or an independent establishment.
Directs the Secretary of the Treasury, not later than three years after the enactment of this Act and monthly, when practicable, but not less than quarterly thereafter, to ensure that information on funds made available to or expended by a federal agency is posted online, in a searchable, downloadable format.

We do not see where additional work to promote the NPR USCG 2009-0206 Lanyard Cut Off Switch fits into this suggested list of Areas of Interest for the FY2015 non profit grants.

In 1994, while on their wedding anniversary outing, Mr. and Mrs. Kopytko and the experienced operator-guide were thrown from the boat. The boat was equipped with a lanyard but it was not in use by the operator. The boat circled and the open propeller struck and killed the guide immediately. It circled again and struck Mr. Kopytko who died on the dock before medical attention could save him. It circled again and struck Phyllis Kopytko. Phyllis is an amputee and survivor of forty operations but alive and writes here to voice her total disillusionment after 20 years of speaking out to prevent propeller strikes. How many other prop strikes have occurred in this circle of death during the past 20 years? There is a study for you to conduct.

You may remember when the USCG was called to Congress for a committee hearing on the death of two young boys from CO poisoning in Colorado. Phyllis was there. SPIN was even introduced and our issue of the propeller guard was brought up. Congressman Lo Biondo turned to the USCG representatives and asked where they were on solving this problem or, was this a Mission to Mars? We have always remembered that because we have landed on Mars but we still do not have a guard on the recreational boat. Injuries and fatalities continue. The prop guard attempt has 20 years of resistance and failure. However, one of the ways to prevent prop strikes is to have all boats equipped with safety lanyard cut-off switches (kill switches) and to require that the operator use it while underway. The Coast Guard issued USCG-2009-0206 now five years ago. It is stuck in the system. We need your oversight. Do we need another study? Another grant? Whatever will make this happen, let us get on with it.

While the history of the propeller guard regulatory failure dates back 20 years, this new initiative to require kill switches (safety lanyard cut-off switches, to be politically correct) is stalled since 2009. This regulation would prevent many deaths and injuries in man-overboard scenarios where an operator, tethered to the ignition by this kill switch would shut the engine off, stopping the boat, before it circled around (in what is known as the circle of death) to strike, injure or kill.We all seem to concur as the efficacy of this technology which is supported by virtually all stakeholders.

The Coast Guard has all partners on board in support of the NPR:
National Sate Boating Law Administrators
National Boating Advisory Council
ABYC standards
All the members of the Safe Boating Council and their affiliate organizations

The general public, especially survivors where death and injury were prevented for voluntary use where their boat happened to be so equipped.

Even the major marine manufacturers have standardly equipped their boats in recent years

All major reports and studies have been done to support the need.

The cost benefit has been calculated in favor of saving lives and limbs.

.
There is absolutely no reason the USCG can give for why this proposed rule is being held up in the department. WE assume they mean some level above them in Homeland Security. Homeland Security made the decision to move all of the USCG missions under their wing recreational and military. Since 2003, we have noticed less and less formalization of projects on the recreational side other than a few housekeeping initiatives. It makes us wonder if HS is just too focused on the terrorist threat. They are making a mistake by ignoring the recreational side. A universal identity card for everyone using our national and state waterways would be a security check and, just maybe, have a uniform mandatory education requirement attached a requirement to standardize reciprocity between states as well.

Is there anything with this grant system that might promote and push to a successful conclusion USCG-2009-0206 ? If so, please proceed.If it needs yet another study, so be it; but let us implement this obvious solution and get on with more complicated matters.

Phyllis Kopytko and Marion IrvingdeCruz, Stop Propeller Injuries Now!

From: Randy Henry, Boating Law Administrator, Oregon State Marine Board,
Subject: Comments regarding Docket No. USCG-2014-0911 Recreational Boating Safety Grants for Nonprofit Organizations
Date: 10/24/2014

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the "Recreational Boating Safety Grants for Nonprofit Organizations. We appreciate very much the transparency of opening the grant language for public review. We will address each area of interest in our comments below.

1. Year-Round Safe Boating Campaign - The Oregon State Marine Board supports this initiative as written.

2. Outreach and Awareness - If using a conference to focus on topics discussed regarding the year-round safe boating campaign, we believe the conference should be the annual meeting of the National Association of State Boating Law Administrators that occurs each October. This is the only conference that focuses on recreational boating, covers all 56 states and provinces, and has broad attendance and participation from key program managers and leaders from the US Coast Guard, state boating agencies and industry. Further, the conference timing would allow reports to be provided at the end of the fiscal year, providing a full review of grant recipient actions and activities.

3. Standardize Statutes and Regulations - Oregon law requires boating education courses to be approved by the National Association of State Boating Law Administrators. I believe many other states that have implemented mandatory boater education also have the NASBLA standard written into law. This robust development and review process is the national standard for recreational boating education and is done in close association with the US Coast Guard. While #3 in general is desirable, creating a secondary approval category will be confusing to recreational boaters. This should require a NASBLA approved boater education program.

4. Accident Investigation Seminars - We wholly support this area of interest as written.

5. Life Jacket Wear - We support data collection to provide baseline life jacket wear, but conducting the study annually is wasteful given the minor changes in use over time. These funds should be saved and used for other benefit. Oregon collects boat-use data on a triennial basis which provides adequate information for trends analysis while saving significant dollars. If moving to a three-year survey, then some of the savings could be applied to a more robust sample size to provide statistically valid state-specific wear rates.

6. Voluntary Standards Development - We support this area of interest but recommend additional labeling to not just deal with fly-bridge capacity, but capacity, built-in flotation and other physical characteristics and limitations, especially for boats 20-26' long. The number of boats in this size range are very common now and the public is unclear about these factors.

7. Safety Training for Urban Youth - We have concerns about this area of interest. Certainly there is need for this, but it does not fit within the RBS mission. Many boating safety programs and curriculums contain elements beneficial to promoting general water safety. However, creating programs that focus solely on non-boating water safety removes important and limited resources from boating safety accident prevention and education efforts.

8. "Boating Under the Influence" (BUI) Detection and Enforcement - We wholly support this area of interest.

Again, thank you for this opportunity to comment on RBS Grants for Nonprofit Organizations.

Randy Henry
Oregon State Marine Board

The National Safe Boating Council (NSBC) Board appreciates the opportunity to provide comments regarding the U.S. Coast Guard proposed areas of interest for which fiscal year 2015 national nonprofit organization grants could be awarded as described in 79 FR 60486, docket number USCG-2014-0911, and respectfully submits the following feedback. The NSBC has extensively reviewed all eight proposed possible areas of interest outlined in the Federal Register and fully supports each with the noted exceptions:

5. Life Jacket Wear. Upon review of awarded grant programs on www.USCGBoating.org, this area of interest has been awarded to one organization annually since 1999. While we feel that a valid measurement on life jacket wear nationwide is needed, we would like to submit that it may be worthwhile to consider offering this funding every three to five years, rather than every year, as has been the practice. Upon reviewing the data, the study has been using the same methodology, and has reported similar results each year since its beginning. We suggest a review of sampling methodology used may be due in order to validate the accuracy of the reported results and to ensure the study is being conducted in the most efficient manner possible. For example, state agency analysis in Pennsylvania and New York has shown that recreational boaters may be more likely to wear life jackets during colder weather months and during times of perceived risk. We submit that funds may be better used to support outreach and education campaigns that are also responsible for providing statistically valid measurement to the Coast Guard. Based on supporting measurements of success, we believe that awareness campaigns do influence boaters behaviors and a focused survey in locations or during times where voluntary or mandatory wear programs are instituted might better measure the change in behavior and provide insight into what programs are increasing life jacket wear.

7. Safety Training for Urban Youth. The Coast Guards proposed possible area of interest titled, item #7, Safety Training for Urban Youth does not seem to be fully aligned with objectives of the National Recreational Boating Safety Program (NRBSP) to reduce accidents, injuries, and death upon our waterways and facilitate safe boating. Based upon an NSBC review of the data referenced by the Center For Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for this potential program, the statistics and reference support are deeply rooted in drowning deaths that occurred in swimming pools due to a basic lack of swimming skills or other causal factors, and not related to accidents associated with recreational boating. The NSBC questions why the Coast Guard used CDC data and statistics, rather than the annual Recreational Boating Safety Statistics. In the past three years, out of the 1,969 recreational boating deaths, the Recreational Boating Safety Statistics data suggests 61 or .03% have been youth under the age of thirteen. This statistic incorporates data from all bodies of water, including those in found urban, suburban, and rural settings.

In addition, each national nonprofit organization is tasked with aligning their grant proposals with the 2012 2016 National Recreational Boating Safety Strategic Plan. While there are loose implications that Safety Training for Urban Youth may relate to Objective 2 and Objective 3, there is no explicit mention for safety training for urban youth or training for any youth, outlined in the Strategic Plan. With that in mind, we believe that there is not enough evidentiary support to provide grant funding for Safety Training for Urban Youth and we would support this program be removed from the list of areas to be potentially funded by the already limited grant money available under the NRBSP.

Again, we appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed areas of interest outlined in federal register as earlier noted. I can be reached at rjohnson@safeboatingcouncil.org or by phone at (703) 361-4294.
