The USCG is investing in, and encouraging the development of high quality, innovative and effective boating safety education. More educated boaters lead to safer waterways, happier boaters and a more vibrant recreational boating community and industry. Education has expanded from the classroom to the water, where hands on training has proven to been extremely effective in raising the skill and knowledge level of boaters. One way of making boaters' learning experience in the classroom and on the water even more effective is to insure they are properly prepared with basic knowledge and understanding prior to engaging with an instructor, or have access to materials and ongoing learning in addition to the traditional methods. The internet and online learning has proven to be an effective and economical way of delivering meaningful and productive education in countless industries and to a broad range of constituents. From university settings to professional and technical continuing education, online learning has become a critical component of modern education strategies.

We would encourage the USCG to consider expanding the area of interests relating to boating safety education to include opportunities to enhance current initiatives with online learning elements. This approach has the potential to deliver effective education to a far broader audience and in a manner that takes advantage of the shifting behavior and culture of the 21st century consumer (boater). It will make boating safety education accessible to a far wider audience.

Item # 1. Year-Round Safe Boating Campaign- It is very important to my state to have safe boating campaigns that target different activities and user groups throughout the year. With such diversity among all the states, having a focused national campaign will provide the greatest message getting to all individuals, nationwide.

Item # 2. Outreach and Awareness Conference- This item is important to my state, yet not at the expense of Item #1. More individuals will be reached using a year round campaign then focusing on a single event where fewer participants hear the message. Using Item #1 and Item #2 together is a well balanced mix.

Item #3. Standardize Statutes and Regulations- This item is important to my state because having reciprocity amongst all states provides the public with more opportunities to recreate nationwide.

Item #4. Accident Investigation Seminars- This item is very important to my state. The training of our law enforcement officers to investigate and evaluate boating incidents is vital for getting proper data and statistics. Advanced training should be located in an area that can support the accident investigation seminars.

Item # 5. Life Jacket Wear- This item should not continued year after year. For the last 15 years the study has been conducted and spent $3,625,00 to realize that the life jacket wear rate has increased 1%. This information does not help my state in finding solutions for changing the behavior. A better use of the funding would be to focus on getting the boating public to voluntarily wear life jackets.

Item #6. Voluntary Standards Development- My state has no concerns regarding this item.

Item #7. Safety Training for Urban Youth- This item should not be a part of the RBS Program non-profit organization grant solicitation. In the provided material from the CDC, water-based fatalities are "non-boating related" yet the RBS program grant money is clearly for boating safety.

Item # 8. "Boating Under the Influence" BUI Detection and Enforcement- This item is important to my state for training officers to use the Standardized Field Sobriety Tests (SFST). Including a public outreach portion to this item about the dangers of boating and drinking would also be beneficial to Iowans. Having support for the validation of the seated SFST is vital as the BUI cases continue to go through the legal process.

- A year-round safe boating campaign is important to my state because being a coastal state the boating season never truly ends. It does slow some in the winter, but there are still boaters on the water. This is especially true during cold weather months when the air temperature may be warm but the water is dangerously cold.

- An outreach and awareness conference is important to my state. While, it is appropriate that a compilation of each grant abstract and an explanation of the accomplishments of each be provided to NBSAC members, state Boating Law Administrators, and attendees of both the outreach and awareness conference identified in this proposed area of interest and the NASBLA conference. I dont believe that it is necessary to have grantees giving presentations and wasting valuable time of the attendees. This is especially true when presentations are mandated. I would offer that a Return On Investment (ROI) study be done (not with grant funds) to determine the man-hour cost of everyone in attendance over a 4-hour period, factor in the hotel cost, and the cost of the conference room. I would offer that the ROI wouldnt recover the difference in the grant funding lost to do the presentations. I would rather see a report that is compiled regarding the grant projects, the amounts awarded, and the decision matrix behind why the award was granted to a specific project or organization.

- Standardize statutes and regulations are important for my state and for full nationwide reciprocity for persons completing a NASBLA-approved basic boating safety course is important to my state and those who visit from other states. The NASBLA standard has been the standard to follow and the one that is codified in state codes and regulations. To suddenly remove this in lieu of a national standard is haphazard and not forward thinking. Why derail the National Education Standard set forth by NASBLA when it is accepted, vetted, codified by states, and works. Additionally, the National Standard is not only standard but also the ANSI standard for boating safety education. It would not be cost effective for states to waste boating money to argue against current code sections at our respective legislative bodies to remove NASBLA approval as the standard when this has been the accepted standard for so long.

- Accident investigation seminars are important. An area of emphasis should include an effort to gain widespread consistency around the country in the documentation of alcohol involvement in recreational boating accidents. Online training could satisfy this need, and it should be provided to all marine law enforcement officers around the country as a fully grant-funded project, with no additional cost to the individual officers or their agency. If the Coast Guard expects states to report accidents in a standard manner then training in a standard manner should be provided especially when those same funds may be called into jeopardy when a report is late or missing information.

- Life jacket wear is important; however, and annual survey is a waste of grant dollars especially when the trend change is so small. I doubt that we will find the Holy Grail of lifejacket wear through this annual study/survey. If it is to be done on an annual basis, there are much more cost effective ways to do it. Finally, it would be more appropriate that this project be conducted preferably at 5-year intervals much like the Fish and Wildlife survey.

- Voluntary standards development is important to my state to ensure boat manufacturing and equipment problems are corrected. This is especially true when boats are being manufactured all over the place and some with issues that cause a major safety risk to recreational boaters.

- Safety training for urban youth should not be included in the solicitation for RBS Program non-profit organization grants and is not a priority for the RBS program within my state. Its a commendable idea, but how many urban children actually boat? How many adults in true urban areas have boats or would even entertain the idea of owning a boat? I would find that data through other means first and then address boating safety if and only if it is true concrete issue.

- Boating under the influence detection and enforcement is important to my state. The proposed areas of interest do not include a public outreach initiative focused on informing the boating public of the dangers of operating while impaired by alcohol or other drugs, such as Operation Dry Water. This area of interest should either be amended to include a BUI outreach initiative or a new area of interest should be created to cover this topic. There should be an emphasis on further training BUI instructors, maintaining currency, enhancing their accountability and reporting of training effort, and providing updates and refresher training for instructors and marine law enforcement officers.

The American Canoe Association (ACA), appreciates the opportunity to provide comments regarding the U.S. Coast Guard proposed areas of interest for the 2015 national nonprofit organization grants as described in docket number USCG-2014-0911 and announced in the Federal Register, Volume 79, No. 194 on Tuesday, October 7, 2014. 1. Year-Round Safe Boating Campaign - We feel this is an appropriate Area of Interest.

Due to the current challenges of budgeting travel for individuals and organizations, a series of coordinated regional conferences should be considered in order to diversify and increase the conference participation numbers. Reporting on the USCG funded nonprofit grant projects at this/these conferences is a positive way to increase transparency and promote the projects for use and replication by other organizations.

3. Standardize Statutes and Regulations We feel this is an appropriate Area of Interest.

4. Accident Investigation Seminars We realize that this topic relates to the National Recreational Boating Safety Strategic Plan, but we are unsure of how this specifically will reduce boating related deaths and accidents. It will assist with increased accuracy of reporting, but funding amounts for this interest area should be proportional to the potential for this Area of Interest to actually lower the overall casualty numbers.

5. Life Jacket Wear - It is our understanding that this area of interest has been awarded to one organization annually for well over a decade at a cumulative cost of over $4,000,000. While we feel that a valid measurement on life jacket wear nationwide is needed, we would like to suggest that this type of study be offered for funding every three to five years. Upon annually reviewing the data, the study has been using the same methodology, and has reported similar results each year since its beginning. We suggest a review of sampling methodology used may be due in order to validate the accuracy of the reported results and to ensure the study is being conducted in the most efficient manner possible. Once again, funding amounts for this interest area should be proportional to the potential for this Area of Interest to actually lower the overall casualty numbers.

6. Voluntary Standards Development We feel this is an appropriate Area of Interest.

7. Safety Training for Urban Youth This would be a great program to offer; however, due to the lack of overall casualties of urban youth in recreational boating, we do not feel that this has the potential to make a significant impact on reducing deaths and accidents. It is our understanding that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) youth data and statistics primarily includes drowning while swimming in pools and other bodies of water. RE: Lower Cook Inlet Oil & Gas Lease Sale 244

The most striking new substantial information that must be taken into account is research associated with ocean acidification and climate change. These two are intertwined, and new research regarding the dramatic effects of ocean acidification around the world is alarming. There is no longer any doubt among scientists that our fossil fuel use is having a dramatic and drastic effect on our oceans. The U.S. must suspend its leasing program and do thorough analyses of the new information and how it relates to the cumulative effects of further oil and gas development, both off shore and onshore as proposed in the current 2014 Cook Inlet Ois and Gas Lease Sale 244. The most effective way to combat ocean acidification is to reduce carbon dioxide emissions, which means moving to renewable energies. We must do this if we are to slow the demise of our marine environment.

Homer is a fishing and tourism community. We have adopted a climate action plan, and this Lease Sale is forcing industrial oil and gas development into this region despite this communitys continued desires to develop in a sustainable way in concert with our efforts to reduce our carbon footprint.

This new lease sale will push more oil and gas development into Lower Cook Inlet across the mouth of Kachemak Bay all the way to Seldovia, an area that has different current patterns than the upper inlet. The three gyrs in the Lower Inlet just outside Kachemak Bay and just inside are critical nursery areas for marine life, especially fish and shellfish. Oil development in this area is potentially very hazardous to these nursery gyrs. An oil spill could likely end up cycling into these gyrs, killing the young marine animals developing there. What studies have been done of the potential effects that oil and gas development in this part of the Inlet would have on these important areas? Discharge overboard from oil and gas drilling rigs is so much closer to these gyrs that it is unconscienable that zero discharge would not be required.

Other resources our community wants protected is the wild habitat surrounding Kachemak Bay. Oil and gas development is not compatible with our fisheries or our tourism. Homer has spent years building its reputation as a place of quiet beauty and it is renowned worldwide. In communities Outside where tourism is big, some of the local governments have passed legislation to keep their area free of oil and gas development because that is not what their economy depends on. People do not come to see oil rigs and industrial development. The same is true here in Homer, and this lease sale is imposing an industry that has never been here. The impacts will likely affect our reputation and the visitor industry.

This lease sale threatens the Kachemak Bay Critical Habitat Area, an area important as well for threatened beluga whales. It does not appear that this lease sale is considering that drilling adjacent to critical habitat areas threatens the waters of these important areas if there is a spill. Winter storms would leave no time to react if the worst case scenario happens.

Homer has also passed a Climate Action Plan that is a pathway toward reducing the our communitys carbon footprint. Oil and gas development does not move the Homer area in the right direction. This plan has not been considered in decisions to lease areas near Homer but should be considered because of the cumulative effects that a sale will have on this area. Homer is interested in exploring tidal energy and is working with the Kachemak Bay Research Reserve to gather data about the best areas in Cook Inlet and Kachemak Bay to experiment with tidal generation. The Federal government could install tidal generators and have a perpetual energy producer that would bring money into the Federal treasury without threatening local resources.

In conclusion, I am requesting several things:
1. Cancel this lease sale.
2. At the very least, remove areas that will dramatically affect marine life, particularly in the gyrs in Lower Cook Inlet. The lease line should be moved substantially northward.
3. Remove all lease areas in the Kachemak Bay Watershed.
4. Require toward zero discharge for all new drilling in Cook Inlet.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

Nina Faust

To Bureau of Ocean Energy & Management:

I am writing in opposition to the opening of oil and gas lease sales in lower Cook Inlet, Alaska. The lower Cook Inlet area is too rich a biological ecosystem to risk any negative effects from oil or gas leaks or spills. Aside from the biodiversity of the area (which should be good enough reason to prevent lease sales) the economies of towns and the livelihood of local residents are dependent upon a heathy ecosystem in Cook Inlet.

No amount of spill risk is acceptable in the Lower Cook Inlet region!!! Oil spill response technology remains inadequate to address a spill in the rough and unforgiving waters of Lower Cook Inlet, and dispersants will cause long term ecological harm to fisheries that support valuable commercial, sport and subsistence harvests. The last time leases were considered in this area, the risk of a major oil spill was estimated at 74% (Minerals Management Service lease sale 149 in 1995). BOEM must accurately evaluate the spill risk and explain how the 74% level, or ANY level of spill risk is acceptable for the lower Cook Inlet region.

History and projected spill risk estimates indicate that spills occur reliably during oil exploration and production. Lease approvals cite spill prevention and response protocols that companies should practice regularly. The history of oil production in Alaska shows that oil companies ignore these protocols and spills occur and responses are slow as a result. Among numerous examples is British Petroleum's record on the North Slope in 2006 and 2008 in which neglect of maintenance protocols resulted in the largest spill in North Slope drilling history (267,000 gallons). History shows that spills also occur during the transportation phase of Oil production (Exxon Valdez incident).

There are places other than Lower Cook Inlet for oil and gas exploration. The risk of permanent negative impacts on the rich biodiversity of this region and on those people who rely on this region for their livelihood is too great to be ignored or bargained away. I oppose Area Lease Sale 244.

Sincerely,

Wendy B. Anderson
Homer, AK

I own a small oyster farm in Jakolof Bay, and request that the EIS include consideration of potential impacts to the shellfish industry in Kachemak Bay. It is a nascent industry now, but the Alaska Mariculture Initiative (receiving state and federal funding), has a vision to grow mariculture in Alaska to a $1 billion industry. So the potential future impacts should be included along with the impacts to existing farms.

The eastern border of the lease area covers nearly the entire entrance to Kachemak bay. The majority of tidally-influenced water entering Kachemak Bay must pass through this lease area first. This puts the bay at risk if any spill were to occur in the lease area. While the lease sale states that specific areas in Kachemak are "excluded" there is in fact no practical way to exclude the movement of water (and any pollutants it transports) through the lease area and into Kachemak Bay. Any spill would impact the adjacent "excluded" areas. It is clear from the straight lines drawn across water bodies, that currents and gyres critical to the health of Kachemak Bay, were not considered in the area identification process.

In a recent incident in Jakolof Bay - where an estimated 50 gallons of diesel were spilled on a flat calm winter day (December 2012) - spill response teams told us that due to tidal flows, booming the area would be ineffective, as a result no boom was deployed. The AK Department of Environmental Conservation closed our harvesting operation for 3 months from this very minor incident. The risk from oil-industry pollution to the oyster farming industry in Kachemak Bay is significant.

If an EIS is an unavoidable next step, it should also include a study of potential impacts to plankton, and phytoplankton cysts (in hibernation on the ocean floor). Plankton is the very bottom of the food chain for marine life. A wide variety of plankton species are critical to the health of shellfish and all marine life. Plankton are extremely sensitive to chemical pollutants and need to be considered in any assessment (including the risk of dispersant use in the event of a spill).

An EPA waiver in Cook Inlet permits toxic discharge prohibited elsewhere in the United States. These federally allowed toxic discharges would be flowing into our approved shellfish growing area with every tide. These impacts must also be considered along with the spill risks.

A 1995 EIS for this same area estimated a 74% chance of a spill. Since then spill response technologies have not advanced, seismic activity for this area has not decreased, tanker traffic here has increased, and tankers here are not required to have tug assists. There is a long list of incidents, accidents and near accidents in Cook Inlet from Seabulk Pride to Kolluk, that remind us how treacherous conditions in the vicinity can become. Very minor changes in tide, temperature, wind direction, wind speed, or wave height can transform a minor incident into a major catastrophe. When locals say Cook Inlet is unforgiving, they speak from experience. If an EIS could include a scientific scale for unforgiving, Cook Inlet would get the highest marks. It should not take yet another EIS to restate that fact.

I'd like to also request an extension of the comment period, notification of Lease Sale 244 has not been widely distributed, and we have not had time to coordinate with other farmers, as well as subsistence and recreational harvesters, to develop comments from shellfish harvesters and the mariculture industry as a whole.

My interests can not stop this initial "investigative" phase already underway and the expenses already being incurred for something that was already rejected through a similarly lengthy and expensive process. The same concerned citizens that have spoken out against lease sales in this zone in the past, remain concerned, conditions have not improved here. No Lease Sale is the best alternative in this sensitive area, given the risks and dangers.

(1) This project is essential to establishing a balanced energy portfolio for Virginia and the nation. The RAP is a comprehensive plan that addresses the potential environmental impacts that need to be considered. We recommend approval by the BOEM. A key, follow-on issue will be the timeliness with which DMME/Dominion undertakes and completes the necessary tasks and assessments.

(2) Major goals of the project include: (a) identifying how best to move from test-scale to fully operational scale (b) identifying safe, efficient, and economic approaches appropriate to this offshore environment and (c) developing a strong working relationship with BOEM during the research phase and over the course of the project. Achievement of these goals will contribute substantially to the success of the research project and likely shorten development time for the full-scale project.

(3) The 12-megawatt test project is an important step that we support. However, DMME/Dominion should commit to bringing more than 2,000 megawatts of offshore wind online in the more immediate future, with the build-out underway by 2020. Fully developing this resource will create thousands of new jobs, decrease the threats our communities and economy face from climate disruption, and help Dominion meet the new limits on carbon pollution that the US EPA is proposing.

(4) Monitoring of the test project should include (a) interim reports by DMME/Dominion on technical and scientific results (b) reports by BOEM on the progress of the site evaluations and progress toward installation of facilities (c) early indicators of any issues that could jeopardize movement from test-scale to full scale (d) transparency of DMME/Dominion’s evaluation of the economic viability of the project.

(5) Project management should interact with other offshore wind projects in the Atlantic lease areas to ensure that design and implementation along the U.S. East Coast are optimized, i.e., knowledge about the environment, the challenges, and best practices are shared. This will ensure that the American public benefit from a robust, resilient system along the Eastern seaboard.

(6) The RAP discusses impacts to marine mammals including the endangered North Atlantic right whale, and potential mitigation measures. BOEM should incorporate strong right whale protection mitigation requirements in the EA and approval of the Research Activities Plan (RAP). On December 12, 2012, several wind power developers and eight leading conservation organizations (including NRDC, NWF, Oceana, SELC, and Sierra Club) submitted to BOEM an agreement for additional mitigation measures for right whales for site assessment and characterization activities in the Mid-Atlantic Wind Energy Areas. See the two attachments. The right whale experts involved in developing this landmark mitigation agreement have extensive expertise on right whales. Scott Kraus, Ph.D., Vice President of Research, New England Aquarium, was among those fully involved in developing the requirements. Keep Big Oil Out of the Arctic!

Dear Acting Director Cruickshank,

While I applaud your agency for seeking public input, I strongly oppose your plans to lease the Beaufort Sea, one of the two Polar Bear Seas, for oil and gas exploration.

The pristine Beaufort is home to many threatened animals, including polar bears and humpback whales, as well as walruses, belugas and numerous other marine mammals. It is adjacent to the extraordinary Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, which is home to the Alaskan polar bear's favorite onshore denning area. And its coastal shelf is blanketed by Globally Important Bird Areas, home to king eiders, yellow-billed loons and many other species.

It is also extremely vulnerable. Climate change is already wreaking havoc in the Arctic. The region is warming twice as fast as the rest of the globe, as average temperatures have risen two-and-a-half degrees over the past 60 years. Storms are becoming more violent, the coastline is eroding and pack ice is shrinking with terrifying speed.

Your own analysis says that oil development comes with a 40 percent chance of a major spill. That would be an unthinkable disaster. Conventional spill response technology has never been successfully tested in the harsh Arctic environment, with its high winds and currents and long dark winters. Shell Oil's series of failures while trying to drill in the Chukchi, the second of the Polar Bear Seas, tells us all we need to know about the risks.

Again, I urge you in the strongest possible terms to keep the Arctic Ocean off-limits to oil and gas exploration.

Thank you very much for your time and all you do,

Caleb Laieski

Dear U.S. Bureau of Ocean Energy Management,

I'm concerned about the potential impacts of oil and gas drilling in the Arctic Ocean. Arctic waters provide vital habitat for iconic wildlife such as walruses, seals, bowhead whales, polar bears, and migratory birds. Residents of the region's coastal communities depend on a healthy ocean to support their way of life. The Arctic is already under stress from climate warming, which is occurring at twice the rate of lower latitudes. The extent of summer sea ice, upon which many Arctic species depend, is in steep decline.

Allowing oil drilling and development in America's Arctic Ocean would only add to these burdens. It's a risky and unnecessary venture that would introduce significant noise, pollution, and traffic into these fragile and remote waters. Shell's blundering attempts to drill in the Arctic Ocean in 2012 and the recent National Academy of Sciences report on the limits of oil spill response in the Arctic both clearly show that the risks of drilling in the Arctic Ocean are too high. And as the 2010 Deepwater Horizon incident in the Gulf of Mexico demonstrated, there is always the risk of a major oil spill, which would be difficult if not impossible to contain and clean up in the Arctic Ocean. Such a spill would devastate endangered marine wildlife, and severely affect the Native subsistence communities that have thrived in this remote region for thousands of years.

The rush to allow oil drilling in the Arctic Ocean also moves us away from a clean energy future that doesn't rely on dirty fossil fuels. Even if oil is discovered there, we can't afford to burn it without risking further climate calamity.

You now have several opportunities to take a step back and reassess whether to open the Arctic Ocean to oil drilling.

* You have started to develop a schedule for future offshore lease sales between 2017 and 2022. I urge you not to include any new oil and gas lease sales in Arctic waters in this upcoming five-year program.
* You have started to collect information for potential lease sales in the Beaufort and Chukchi seas in 2017 and 2016, respectively. I urge you not to hold those lease sales.
* The Ninth Circuit Court has sent back the Bush-era decision to offer oil leases in the Chukchi Sea. You should engage in meaningful reconsideration of that decision, and I hope that after careful consideration of the effects and risks of opening the area to oil drilling, you will agree the leases should not stand.
* Shell Oil continues to press its case to drill in the Chukchi Sea. After its calamitous outing in 2012, I urge you not to allow the company to return for more risky drilling.

The evidence against opening the Arctic Ocean to risky drilling for dirty oil is overwhelming. You have a golden opportunity to chart a better course for the region and for the planet. Please don't squander that opportunity.

Thank you very much for your time and all you do,

Caleb Laieski

Prohibiting Discrimination Based on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity by Contractors and Subcontractors.

The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (OFCCP) has enacted a Regulation implementing the Executive Order 11246 in accordance with the Executive Order 13672, Further Amendments to Executive Order 11478, Equal Employment Opportunity in the Federal Government, and Executive Order 11246, Equal Employment Opportunity, which was signed by President Barack Obama on July 21, 2014. These Regulations will be effective from April 8, 2015 and it will apply to Federal contractors who hold contracts entered into or modified on or after that date. Pursuant to the rule-making process, the Regulation which Prohibit Discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity by Federal Contractors is a final rule.

Previously, the Executive Order 11246 explicitly stated on Section 202 that all qualified applicants will receive consideration for employment without regard to race, color, religion, sex or national origin and it required them to take affirmative measures to prevent discrimination on those bases. More specifically the new Regulation will substitute sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, or national origin for sex or national origin.

The sexual orientation refers to an enduring pattern of emotional, romantic and/or sexual attractions to men, woman or both sexes and it also refers to a persons sense of identity based on those attractions, related behaviors and membership in a community of others who share those attractions. Sexual orientation is usually discussed in terms of three categories (heterosexual, homosexual and bisexual) and is defined in terms of relationship with others. Thus, it is closely tied to the intimate personal relationship.
The gender identity of an individual refers to ones internal sense of being male, female or something else and it should be distinguished from transsexuality. Indeed the term transsexual usually refers to people whose gender identity is different from their assigned sex.
Understanding that sexual orientation and gender identity, since they are both a intimate manifestation of personal feelings to the society, may be a reason of discrimination, especially within the work environment. The researches demonstrate that many people in the last decades had been discriminated for their sexual orientation or gender identity, so the intent of the Regulations promoted by Office of Federal Contract Compliance Program perfectly satisfy an important necessity of the society.

In 1964 the Civil Right was aimed at attaching discrimination in nearly every aspect of the society referring to sex, race, color, national origin and religion. Anyway the continuos changes in the last years created the need of an implementation of the general regulation, especially in work field. It appears that there was not one particular accident but a series of events that gave rise to this rule.

This new Regulations could be compared to the Italian law, which differently provides a general prohibition of sexual orientation and gender identity discrimination in every field of the work environment. Initially the law (D.Lgs n. 216/2003) provided an exception for the military service and the police, but after an infraction procedure begun against Italy from the European Commission, this exception has been abrogated. Thus, now in the Italy and , in general, in the European Union no discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is admitted.

I was drawn to study this rule because I strongly believe that nobody should be singles out and harmed because they are different. For some people sexual orientation and gender identity discrimination has taken over their life and affected their freedom to attend work and other public places. I believe that it is an important goal both for these people and the United States, so I look forward to see the difference it makes once it takes effect in the community.

Dolphins and whales are acoustic animals that live in their world of auditory images. Blasting them with powerful sounds in their hearing spectra, like sonar and air guns, will greatly disrupt their ability to forage and communicate over short and long distances. These sounds can travel huge distances, even across the largest ocean basins. For example, seismic blasts from the North Slope have been detected by the hydrophone arrays on both sides of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, even South of the Equator, and at the Navy range in the Bahamas, known as the Tongue Of The Ocean (TOTO). I am a marine biologist with many years of experience in the field of marine mammal acoustics, not a tree- and whale-hugger.

To Whom It May Concern:

The permit for Geological and Geophysical Activities in Mid-Atlantic and South Atlantic Planning Areas will result in catastrophic consequences for marine mammals that inhabit these areas. In 2013 we have recorded at least 202 live stranding events worldwide that involved 819 live stranded cetaceans. Our data is most likely underestimation of the real numbers. 45 % of all stranded whales, 57% of all stranded dolphins and 72% of all mass strandings happened in the vicinity of seismic surveys, naval exercise or both. We are not aware of any extensive investigation that carefully studied any of these cases/events and the connection most likely will not be made not because it is not there but because no one has been investigating anything. Our data also shows that 70% of all live stranded whales were deep diving whales including Kogia spp., sperm whales and beaked whales. This year alone we already recorded 7 events (single and mass live strandings) that happened in the vicinity of seismic surveys. None of these events are being investigated as far as we know.

The US Atlantic Coast traditionally sees more live strandings that the West Coast and the reasons for that are being currently debated. The rescue response in inadequate and the majority of stranded animals either die or are euthanized. For example, in 2013 in the US at least 23 whales stranded alive (according to our records), the majority of them were Kogia spp. Only one whale was rescued, while the rest was euthanized or died. The East Coast already has extensive naval exercises activities and any additional anthropogenic activities will put extra stress on the populations that inhabit these waters. Any anthropogenic activities along the East Coast will result in more live strandings and more deaths as the stranding network in its current condition cannot even deal with what they currently get. Kogia spp. are among the most frequently stranded whales on the East Coast and NOAA lists their population levels as data deficient. Any additional stress could easily push this species to the brink of extinction.

BOEM permit application completely ignores severe and far reaching consequences of live strandings. For example, a study by Wade et al. (2012) indicated how removal of key individuals can affect the entire populations. They key individuals often die during mass or single strandings and their death affects the entire population because these individuals are either leaders, or important for mating and reproduction or important for knowledge transfer that takes place in species like sperm whales, pilot whales and potentially many other species. Hence, BOEM does not make the accurate estimation of actual damage their activities will result in.

Some areas of the East Coast like Cape Cod for example, are naturally dangerous for marine mammals because they can act as traps. Any anthropogenic activities near these areas will make cetaceans especially vulnerable to strandings and death that overwise could be avoided.

The impact of Geological and Geophysical Activities in Mid-Atlantic and South Atlantic Planning Areas will have profound and potentially irreversible impact on marine mammals and affect populations including those that are either endangered (Northern Right Whales) or data deficient (Kogia spp).

We have very little hope that BOEM will decide to reject this permit as it looks like a done deal, but we hope that everyone understands the profoundly negative effect these activities will have on marine mammals along the East Coast. There will be a lot of strandings, a lot of deaths and numerous populations will be affected. Seismic surveys have been linked to strandings in the past and our data shows that there are more potential cases that are not counted simply because no one investigates them. Because of that we feel that BOEM does not provide the accurate impact assessment and most likely grossly underestimates the actual impact Geological and Geophysical Activities in Mid-Atlantic and South Atlantic Planning Areas will have.

References:

Paul R. Wade, Randall R. Reeves, and Sarah L. Mesnick, “Social and Behavioural Factors in Cetacean Responses to Overexploitation: Are Odontocetes Less “Resilient” Than Mysticetes?,” Journal of Marine Biology, vol. 2012, Article ID 567276, 15 pages, 2012. doi:10.1155/2012/567276

Prohibiting Federal contractors from discriminating against employees who inquire about, discuss, or disclose their compensation to other employees is a step in the right direction for pay equality. However, we believe that allowing informal discussions among employees might result in consequences not considered by the OFCCP in its executive summary, namely the dissemination of false or misleading information. To offset these potential consequences, the OFCCP should require that, in addition to the proposed amendment, Federal contractors keep a publicly accessible file containing each employees pay rate and job responsibilities. This not only promotes the same goals advocated for by the OFCCP, but also minimizes the potential negative effects of uninformed and misleading discussions between employees.

The disclosure of compensation information, in theory, promotes long term pay equality only if the information being disclosed is accurate. Pay secrecy, after all, can be defined on a continuum, its effects depending on the level of restrictions imposed on the information employees are provided about what others are being paid. See Adrienne Colella, et al., Exposing Pay Secrecy, Academy of Management Review 2007, Vol. 32, No. 1, 5571.

If an employee is asked about his or her wage and is untruthful, co-workers may begin to believe that their employer compensates its employees arbitrarily or unfairly, even if untrue. The potential impact of perceived unfairness is that an employee performing at a high level may reduce his performance to that of lower performers who he believes to be receiving the same pay. William F. Muhs, D.B.A, Pay SecrecyHelp or Hindrance? (1985).

Studies show that disclosing compensation in circumstances where employees perceive their employer as being unfair lead[s] to significantly lower effort relative to a setting where co-workers wages are kept secret. Daniele Nosenzo, Pay Secrecy and Effort Provision 19 (Centre for Decision Research & Experimental Economics, 2012), available at http://www.nottingham.ac.uk/cedex/documents/papers/cedexdiscussionpaper201213.pdf. Thus, OFCCPs prediction that additional openness about compensation could . . . save both the contractor and the government time and money relies heavily upon the assumption that the information being disseminated is accurate.

In order to facilitate accurate communications between employees, we recommend the OFCCP amend the rule to require Federal contracts to keep on file and make available each employees compensation information, along with other non-sensitive information, such as job responsibilities and justifications for pay increases. The benefit of requiring contractors to maintain this information is two-fold.

First, it promotes the accurate dissemination of compensation information by employees. For example, an employee asked about his or her compensation is more likely to be truthful is he or she knows that an official file exists that can be used to verify his or her response.

Second, it allows employees to have more constructive conversations with their employer about pay increases since the employee could cite information on file rather than word of mouth. Requiring a paper trail may also have the effect of encouraging employers to make more informed decisions regarding fair compensation which will also help accelerate progress towards pay equality.

We acknowledge that the administrative costs associated with implementing such an amendment might be higher than those currently proposed. However, in the long run, we think the marginal benefit of dollars spent creating an accurate source of compensation information will be significantly higher than the current proposed amendment.

For all of the foregoing reasons, we suggest the OFCCP amend the proposed rule to require Federal contractors to maintain an official file with compensation information for each employee. If pay equality is the OFCCPs goal, it should strive for promoting accurate communications between employees, not just communications.

According to the National Committee on Pay Equity, women in 1973 earned 56.6% of what men earned. By 2010, the gap had narrowed somewhat. Women then earned 77.4% of mens earnings. Still women in the U.S. have a long way to go for full wage parity. Economist Evelyn Murphy, President of The Wage Project, estimates that over a working lifetime of 47 years, the current wage gap amounts to a loss in wages for a woman of $700,000 for a high school graduate, $1.2 million for a college graduate, and $2 million for a professional school graduate. These are staggering figures.

Why should men care whether women receive equal pay? Why should American businesses care? All Americans should care because, not only is it good for women, it is good for the U.S. economy. According to a study conducted by Women Certified, a womens consumer advocacy organization, 41% of women are their families sole source of income and women contribute 83% of the U.S. gross national product. So pay inequity hurts not only businesses, but families. The AFL-CIO study shows that the average 25-year-old woman who works full-time, year-round until she retires at age 65 will earn $523,000 less than the average working man. And at the current rate of change, working women in the U.S. will not achieve equal pay until after the year 2050.

Only if U.S. women take action to remedy unequal pay, both on behalf of themselves and their female colleagues, can meaningful equality of compensation be a reality. But many employers have implemented pay secrecy policies, which limit a female employees ability to know that she is being paid less than her male co-worker, and therefore to take appropriate action to end the inequity.

In 2007, the U.S. Supreme Court put another obstacle in the path of womens pay equality. Lilly Ledbetter had sued her employer, Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co., under the Equal Pay Act, when she learned that she had been paid less than her male counterparts for many years. The Supreme Court held in Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co., 550 U.S. 618 (2007), that, since the employers initial pay decision had been taken years before Ms. Ledbetter discovered the pay inequity, she could not sue her employer under the Equal Pay Act because the decision had not been made within the 180 day statute of limitations before she filed her complaint.

Fortunately, Congress overrode this unjust Supreme Court opinion and passed the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009. Pub. L. 111-2. The Act provides that each discriminatory paycheck, not just the employers first decision to pay the woman unequally, resets the time to file a pay discrimination claim. The Ledbetter Act made it easier for female workers to file pay claims, even if they discover the unequal pay years after it began.

Ms. Ledbetter and many other women workers would have learned more quickly that they were being paid less than their male counterparts if most employers had not implemented pay secrecy policies. Many employers forbid their employees to discuss their pay with one another and punish those who do. This roadblock often prevents women workers from discovering that they are not being paid as well as the men who work beside them.
Employers who implement these policies often punish employees who reveal their pay to their co-workers. Punishment for the violation of its pay secrecy policy often takes the form of demotions, pay cuts and termination of employment in retaliation for revealing compensation information.

I have lived and worked in the South Hampton Roads region of Virginia for 32 years. I have also lived in other coastal areas including southern Rhode Island, Long Island New York and San Francisco. My comments and recommendations are based on my strong interest in sustaining life on this planet for future generation by ensuring our natural resources such as the subaquatic lands in question here, will be preserved.

My concerns focus on the impacts of potential exploration and leasing of all three Outer Continental Shelf areas of this process: the Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, Central Gulf of Mexico, Western Gulf of Mexico, Beaufort Sea and the Chukchi Sea.

The resources I think need to be most considered are as follows:

1. Wildlife: I anticipate the activity of leasing for oil and gas exploration will result in irreversible negative impacts on wildlife that are sensitive to changes in their environment. Some of this wildlife includes fisheries that we depend on for our food supply.

2. Shoreline Habitats: These areas are bordered by wetlands and estuaries that are critical to sensitive ecosystems, sustain bottom life that supports our food supplies, and buffers our lands from storms and ever rising seas due to climate change.

3. Accidents: No matter how careful any leasing, exploration and drilling activity is planned, the risk will be too great. Human error, as well as the tendency to make poor decisions for financial gain, will likely, at some point, result in both minor ongoing and catastrophic accidents that will result in spills of oil and other residues that will negatively impact our shorelines and other natural and human habitats.

Alternatives to leasing these lands for oil and gas exploration and mining:

A. Wind and tidal power generation: Our economy is currently in a period of evolution toward using more renewable resources for our energy needs. The technologies for harvesting power from wind, solar and waves are proven and available now. These alternatives should be explored as equally important as the opportunity to extract non renewable fossil fuels from these Outer Continental Shelves.

B. Improve and support Energy Efficiency in existing buildings: U.S. buildings use 36% of total energy use, 65% of electricity consumption and emit 30% of greenhouse gas emissions. Also, US DOE studies in 2005 show that an estimated 40% of that energy is lost and escapes from buildings due to air leaks in building envelopes. This represents 16% of the US total energy use. I suggest that as an alternative to exploiting these Outer Continental Shelves for minerals to generate energy, just as much emphasis and study should be put into improving the energy efficiency of our buildings.

Other considerations I consider important:
For almost 30 years there has been a ban on drilling in the Atlantic and for good reason. Some places are far too special to risk with offshore drilling and the Atlantic ocean and Virginia's coast is such a special and fragile place. Our sensitive coastal environment and our lucrative coastal economy (tourism and fishing in Virginia being $ billion industries) depend on clean beaches and healthy ocean waters. These treasures are put at risk with offshore drilling.

I support the efforts of the Surfrider Foundation and the Southern Environmental Law Center to defend the NC coastline and submit the following comments on the 20172022 OCS Oil & Gas Leasing Program.

Please protect the coast of the Carolinas from any oil & gas lease sales in the 2017 2022 OCS Oil & Gas Program.
The expansion of offshore drilling in U.S. waters would cause enormous impacts to our nations coastal and marine ecosystems. Oil and gas development in new areas would require seismic surveys, drilling operations, oil transport by tankers, and the installation of platforms, pipelines, and other infrastructure. Collectively these activities would significantly damage both the environment and related economies and ways of life. Such offshore drilling expansion would also expose
new regions of the country to the risk of a catastrophic oil spill. A recent report by the National Ocean Economics Program concluded that recreation, coastal tourism, and commercial fishing sectors that rely directly on the health of ocean ecosystems generate billions of dollars for coastal states such as Florida, North Carolina, New Jersey, Massachusetts, California, Oregon, and Washington. Additional studies by the Surfrider Foundation and its partners to inform ocean planning efforts in Oregon and Mid-Atlantic have documented the extensive public participation and economic impacts of non-consumptive ocean and coastal recreation. These uses depend on clean beaches and waters, abundant wildlife, and scenic viewsheds all of which could be compromised by the expansion of offshore drilling.

We understand that it is likely that applications to conduct seismic testing will be approved in 2015. Not only are the air gun blasts used in seismic testing harmful to marine life such as the critically endangered North American right whale, allowing seismic testing opens the door to risky oil drillingunder the same lax assessments of risks and precautions that led to the BP Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico.

Accordingly, we urge you to protect regions of the U.S. that have not been exposed to offshore oil and gas development, specifically the area off the coast of North Carolina. The development of the Five-Year Plan must include a comprehensive review and analysis of potential impacts to both the environment and coastal communities from drilling operations and large oil spills. This analysis should incorporate a cradle to grave assessment of the environmental impacts resulting from exploration, development, production, transportation, and end use of offshore oil and gas. Fully understanding the range of potential impacts of offshore oil and gas development is essential to making informed decisions concerning the future of our ocean and coastal ecosystems.

Finally, I concur with the Surfrider Foundation's assertion that the 20172022 OCS Oil and Gas Program must substantively consider the role that renewable energy and conservation can play meeting our nations future energy needs. Even under the best-case scenario, Americas offshore oil reserves would provide us only 18 months supply of oil at our current rate of consumption, underscoring the fact that we simply cannot drill our way to energy independence. For this reason, as well as the environmental and economic risks discussed above, our nation must seek a comprehensive and environmentally sustainable energy plan that prioritizes conservation and support for renewable energy technologies.
In summary, when preparing the 20172022 OCS Oil and Gas Program, we ask that you protect the Atlantic Coast from any oil and gas exploration and development activities. We also ask that you undertake a robust analysis that adequately analyzes the cumulative impacts to both the environment and coastal communities from drilling operations and large oil spills, and considers alternatives to offshore drilling.

I stand in solidarity with the Surfrider Foundation as well as the Southern Environmental Law Foundation in opposing this short-sighted, economically and environmentally risky proposal, and appreciate the opportunity to provide comments here.

My comments are concerning the Scoping for EIS development for the 2017-2022 Oil and Gas Leasing Program.

My concerns primarily are in terms of costs and benefits. The ability to issue leases for gas and oil doesn't necessarily mean that leases will be procured. However, it is already known that the energy and dollar benefits of extracting gas an oil off the South Atlantic Bight are likely to be rather insignificant. However, the potential impacts could be far more costly and last much longer than any benefits achieved.

Even if there is no actual removal of oil or gas from the South Atlantic Bight region, merely exploring will pose significant risks. Exploration for gas and oil typically involves seismic testing. Current seismic testing by the U.S. Navy in the South Atlantic Bight is already widely perceived to be very harmful to sea life (http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/energy/2014/02/140228-atlantic-seismic-whales-mammals/), including endangered northern right whales who migrate through this area twice a year to go to and from their calving grounds off Georgia and Florida. There are other large marine mammals that could be impacted, as well.

There is an assumption that exploration will lead to extraction should it be possible to make a profit off the resources. There are many reasons why offshore oil and gas extraction is bad for the environment, not the least of which is potential loss of ocean habitat. Placement of offshore equipment, if not very closely regulated into using only hard or muddy bottom, could damage deep sea, as well as near shore corals and the other fauna that depend on them. Our country has come so far in terms of restoring fish stocks, by stopping overfishing. However, a number of deepwater species remain overfished (http://www.nmfs.noaa.gov/sfa/fisheries_eco/status_of_fisheries/). Any damage to habitat could further imperil overfished stocks. Granted, in the shallower waters of the Gulf of Mexico, oil rigs have actually created artificial reefs used by recreational fishermen. But the waters of the Gulf are shallower than those of the Atlantic and there is no guarantee of increased fishing opportunities.

Should extraction be allowed, visible offshore equipment would likely have a negative economic effect to the coastal communities near the equipment in terms of property values and income from tourism.

Most people worry about the unthinkable - a Deepwater Horizon-type of oil spill. Such an oil spill off the South Atlantic Bight has the potential to be even more devastating than the Deepwater Horizon. The gyre in the Gulf of Mexico which circulates the water not only is slower moving, it sometimes doesn't even move at all. The Gulf Stream in the South Atlantic is much faster moving and is constant. While the overall chances of a spill are low, the devastation from an oil spill could be terrible.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Please do not allow leases to be available off the South Atlantic Bight.

The Atlantic G&G FEIS and ROD hands the Atlantic over to the surveyors who will pound heavily for the next two years so that when 2017 rolls around they will have a lot of data to sell to the lease prospects. It takes a few years to drill exploratory wells and set up the production infrastructure, but these new technology efforts are not the same as setting up derricks and drilling into reservoirs, they are significantly more complex and extensive and are more rapidly deployed.

Drilling now happens from mobile platforms drill ships, semisubmersible production units, and FPSOs. These things dont just bob around in the water, they are stabilized (Dynamically Positioned = DP) with four to eight thrusters typically driven by 3000-4000hp engines (24,000- 32,000hp) running high-thrust (read NOISY) props all of the time. This is akin to having four cargo ships driving into each other 24 hours a day from the moment this equipment is put in service until the end of their service life.

Then there is the seafloor processing equipment which separates the wanted product from brine, solids, gases, re-injects process water, gas, muds, and solids back into the earth, and pumps the wanted product up to the surface. In deep water this all happens under enormous pressures and consequent enormous noise.

An while some of the servicing equipment that connects hoses, adjusts collars and fixtures, turns valve controls etc. are controlled from tethered ROVs, increasingly the subsea equipment is controlled and tended by AUVs that are controlled through acoustical modems on multi-nodal communications nets operating in the 25kHz 90kHz range. This frequency range overlaps the bio-sonar range of dolphins, beaked whales, and porpoises as well as the predator-alert hearing range of herring, shad, and other bait fish.

So by 2022 the once comparably bucolic Atlantic Soundscape interrupted only by the dulcet sounds of cargo ships and fishing boats will become a huge industrial oil refinery roaring from 5Hz 100kHz. And nobody is saying anything about this. Unless we can throw some sticks into the spokes there will be airguns in the water by July.
