This energy exploration and proposed extraction will result in the loss of our fishing and tourism economies thereby destroying a rich historical and financial way of life for a large number of North Carolinians.

I feel like I make a comment on a new five year plan every couple months. I support development of the Outer Continental Shelf in Alaska, and encourage the Bureau to proceed with lease sales and development without delay.
In the 50+ years of oil development in Alaska, we've proven time and again our ability to responsibly develop these assets with minimal environmental impact, and with huge benefits to our population. Alaskans have indeed proven that, through our daily activities, we are a living example of conservation; wise, responsible, sustainable development of our natural resources.
Providing leases on federal OCS units in Cook Inlet, the Chukchi, and the Beaufort will help the wheels of commerce continue to spin in Alaska. In the short term, these leases will provide funds to the government and jobs for environmental scientists, logisticians, engineers, purchasers (and, inevitably, droves of environmental activists and their lawyers). Longer term, development in Alaska provides the bulk of our economy - jobs, revenues, infrastructures, down to the heat that keeps our homes warm.
For these, and many other reasons, I encourage lease sale in Alaska and further request a smooth and expedited road to development.

We have four oceans surrounding our nation, three have been drilled for oil/gas extensively. Three have had catastrophic oil spills that have devastated the marine life and local economies. Yes, there is oil in the Atlantic, it will create jobs, but at what cost?

We already have healthy industries on the east coast that produce millions of jobs: tourism and fishing. Seismic testing and drilling could have horrible consequences. Oceana has done study that showed more new jobs would be created from offshore wind jobs; and more power would be produced as well. These jobs would not be subject to the whims of the price of oil, and the wind will never stop blowing.

Current estimates from your agency are that there are 3.3 billion barrels in the Atlantic. Based on current consumption of 19.9 million per day, this is 165 day supply.

Oil is a 20th century fuel. Let's find a 21st century solution to our energy needs.

I am against oil exploration and/or drilling in the Atlantic ocean. Oil drilling would be a direct threat to our regions economy as well as our ecosystem. The risks are too great for the small payout.

I am in complete agreement with seismic testing for oil reserves and with drilling and recovering oil from the east coast of the US.

The environmental impact is minimal with appropriate monitoring of testing, drilling and recovering oil.

The economic impact on the region is positive and will bring jobs, industry and income.

Please continue with the seismic testing, exploration, drilling and recovery of oil offshore in the Atlantic Ocean.

Both our east and west coasts are very important for recreation and fishing. Offshore drilling for oil and/or gas should be totally prohibited. Development of offshore wind energy should be allowed and encouraged.

We're you folks out to lunch during the last gulf oil spill? Please remove the arctic and the Atlantic Ocean from the 5 year drilling plan. As a life long resident of the east coast of florida, the risk to our environment and economy is not worth it!!

Offshore drilling is unhealthy and short sighted.  Unhealthy for our tourist and natural resource economy, unhealthy for environmental health and unhealthy for public health.  We have alternatives that would serve long term.  Let's implement them now and relinquish the antiquity of petroleum dependency.

Please know that I am well aware of the need for petroleum to maintain our complex way of life. The issue addressed in this posting is the proposed testing and possible extraction of oil off the coast of S.Carolina and other Eastern Shores of the Atlantic.The pros and cons of this issue will fill reams and volumes of documentation. My comments are both ethically motivated, economic, and brief. I have a B.S. in Biology and post graduate degrees in religion. My objection to the initial phase which will include using seismic testing is that it may do irreversible damage to marine life and subsequently to the environment as well. If oil is found, the infrastructure needed to extract both oil and gas will further damage the fragile coastal ecosystem of this area.
Finally, there seems to be a great deal of misinformation as to who will reap the benefits of potential profits from off shore drilling. It certainly won't be the sate of S.C. Oil leases and profits will not go the the states. As to potential jobs... after the initial exploration is complete and if enough oil is found to merit extraction, the jobs created locally will be minimal. There is plenty of research available and it is well documented, that jobs created in the petroleum industry are specialized and will be available only in small numbers to highly qualified individuals. Finally, isn't it about time we begin to take seriously the long term impact of fossil fuels on our planet. Isn't it time to get serous about climate change and the need to explore more viable alternative energy sources that will both create the jobs of the future and assure a clean and eco-friendly planet for future generation.

Let's use our coastal waters for clean energy - wind power is the way to go.  Oil & gas leasing off the coast should not be allowed. Our tourist dollars are to valuable to our state & our environment is too important.  It is time to move forward with clean energy choices.  I invested in solar & have a solar passive house with a solar hot water system & solar PV panels to generate electricity.
As business owners on the MD coast, we vehemently oppose any offshore drilling. The repercussions of an imminent catastrophic leakage would destroy our community and way of life.

I support opening up the entire Alaskan OCS, including the Beaufort, Chukchi, North Aleutian Basin, and Cook Inlet to oil and gas leasing, exploration, and development.  All of these areas should be included in regular (annual or biennial) lease sales.  Upon leasing, the winning leaseholders should be allowed to explore and drill on these leases and shouldn't be stopped by incessant ENGO litigation. . .if you're going to lease it in the first place, successful oil companies should be allowed to do what oil companies do. . .drill!  Nobody has a stronger environmental ethic than Alaskans do and if we don't choose to responsibly develop our offshore resources, rest assured they will be developed in other jurisdictions where they don't have equivalent versions of the Clean Air/Water acts, where safety isn't a priority, etc.  We need to think globally and develop locally!  The economic impact of Alaskan OCS development would be profound and is desperately needed to keep TAPS full.  In addition, assurances must be given to the winning leaseholders that they will be allowed to build the needed infrastructure to bring their projects to fruition, such as guarantees of pipelines across NPR-A and other associated access requirements.  Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

More scientific study is needed to evaluate the impact of oil and gas exploration off the N.C. coast, especially in regards to an assessment of the marine ecology of N.C.'s Outer Continental Shelf. It's not fully understood what species of fish and wildlife live within potential drilling areas and how this might impact the ecosystem. Of particular concern are species associated with Sargassum habitat including sea birds, sea turtles and marine mammals. These animals are federally protected and the same rules protecting them should apply to ALL industries. Chronic and acute impacts of discharges from drilling operations needs to be studied, as well as if drilling equipment will interfere with animals migration patterns or food sources. Even an eighth grade school student knows if one link of a food chain is negatively impacted, the entire system could collapse. With over half of the air we breathe being provided by some of the smallest organisms in the ocean (phytoplankton) this is a habitat that great risks should be taken for it's protection and management.

I Strongly believe that the region has a thriving tourism industry that have been creating thousands of jobs every year. There are statistics available that back my belief. These jobs are real and the tourism industry as a whole is growing in this region. I think Oil business is crucial and I do understand the value of it. However, Think about all the hurricanes that this region have experienced in the past and will still experience in the future. Now imagine a scenario where you have oil rigs all over North Carolina's coastal region and think about the consequences when nature strikes. It will be with no doubt a natural disaster that will cost the state tons of money, maybe more money that they were hoping to gain from this deal. Why risk the well being of this beautiful region that attracts visitors from all over the eastern part of the country and an industry that employs thousands of people and bring millions of dollars with an industry that brings high risks and unknown benefits.
I say NO to drilling of of the shores on the Eastern coast of North Carolina, And the whole eastern sea board. All spill's, Leaks, Cargo Frate is not worth the risk of this venture. So no drilling.

Please don't conduct seismic testing on our beautiful East Coast! Here in Charleston, our tourism industry relies on clean, sparkling, peaceful beaches to attract visitors. Charleston is the #1 tourist city in the US! Don't destroy our pristine coast!

Please do not approve the opening up of the Atlantic Coast/ Southeast US to seismic testing for oil and/or potential oil drilling. It will majorly negatively impact our small unique community of Sullivans Island SC, and adjacent city of Charleston,SC. Sullivans Island and Charleston are unique in their historic significance. Charleston is a world class travel destination (Conde Nast rated us as number one). Our greatest community assets are tourism and our precious coastal environment. Our building and structures have dated back to the prerevolutionary period. Oil spills, which do happen, would destroy our beaches affecting our economy for many years to come. It would potentially destroy our ecosystem, which is a very delicate marsh environment. Our historic buildings including forts and batteries would potentially be destroyed. Our estuaries and wetlands are unique. We have many commercial fisherman. Their livelihoods would be ruined.
I am making a desperate plea to NOT approve the opening up of the SE Atlantic US Coast for seismic testing and/or oil drilling!
Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely,
Rochelle Rutledge, MD
Sullivans Island , SC

SC depends on CLEAN beaches for the major industry - TOURISM.  An oil spill off the shores of SC will have devastating affects on the economy of SC and on the income of so many residents of SC, that it seems to me that there are NO benefits to drilling for oil for SC.  Put up wind farms - they won't spoil the beaches, pollute the marshes and destroy the economy.  And a wind farm can be installed far enough out in the ocean that the views will not be affected.

No no no. The jersey shore is all we have. It's been there and has been enjoyed forever. Leave it be. There are many undisturbed cannisters of mustard gas from ww2 which cannot be removed along the shoreline and beyond.  We cherish the jersey shore and will put up a hell of a fight. Find somewhere else.

I recently moved to the Outer Banks of North Carolina. Part of the reason for the move from Raleigh was to enjoy the pristine ecological environment. I enjoy learning more about wildlife, and have a special place in my heart for the ocean and the creatures in it. I am distressed that this fragile ecosystem is being placed further in jeopardy by even entertaining the idea of offshore drilling. I do not feel that it will be good economically for the Outer Bankstoo many people rely on commercial fishing for their livelihood. And it will affect property values herejust because the proposed platforms will not be able to be seen from the shore does not mean that folks will not be aware of them. And there is precedent in the Gulf of Mexico for serious problems due to oil spills. Please do not bring offshore drilling to the Eastern seaboardnot just the Outer Banks, but the entire coastline. I don't want my government involved in mining a finite resource from the earth when there are so many other forms of alternative energy to explore that are safer for the environment, such as wind power and solar power.
Petroleum may be the cheapest option short-term but we cannot sustain this limited resource long-term and it presents a mutlitide of public health risks.

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing in regard to the potential threat of seismic testing and oil and gas exploration off the Atlantic Ocean. I am a life-long resident of the Lowcountry and am proud to call the Charleston my home.

I am writing to tell you about the countless summers spent in the sand and surf, learning life lessons from watching the tide rise and fall, watching friends and family gather together to enjoy the splendor that is our coast line, and creating memories with my partner that are sure to last a life-time. I have enjoyed the early morning, rising to harvest oysters with my father, brother, and nephew, creating times of bonding and love that could never be replicated. I have seen shrimpers, fishers, and oystermen and women provide for their families from provision this water gives us. I am grateful for the pristine coast and the way it sustains our economy, brings us joy, and creates memories. The threat of being unable creating similar memories with my children is chilling and terrifying.

I am writing to voice my opposition to the proposal for leases to explore these waters. The risk of what may transpire, drastically outweighs the reward, putting all of the memories, economy, and lively-hood in peril for the chance at a ver small amount of non-renewable fossil fuel.

I am writing this not for myself, but for the children, the grandchildren, and the great grandchildren. I am writing in the hope of passing along to them the clean, healthy seas that make life here so beautiful.

With kind regards,

Matthew B. Lewellyn
For the love of God leave us with some bit of nature undisturbed. Leave our coast alone

I am concerned about the proposed opening of the North Carolina coast to offshore oil drilling. I am opposed for these reasons:

1. I lived in Louisiana and saw their beaches first hand. Granted, their beaches are more silt than sand but their beaches were not tourist hot spots due to the evidence of off-shore oil--there were pipes coming on shore and globs of oil on the beaches. Our beaches are visited by millions, millions who want clean beaches.

2. NC coasts are not like other places that have oil exploration--our currents are stronger, hurricanes regularly brush our shores. We are called the graveyard of the Atlantic for a reason--a reason that does not bode well for vessels used to service the rigs.

3. Not enough is known about the ecology of the shores, of the continental shelf, of deeper ecology. More studies need to be done to help us know what is being impacted.

Please rethink this proposal--it will not work for the NC coast for too many reasons!

The sun, the tides, the wind. Endless supplies of energy. Where is the intelligence? To be found is a significant lack of balance in priorities, and lack of will to venture forth with renewable energies which are waiting to be tapped into.

I am a lifelong South Carolina coastal resident. I am opposed to any offshore oil or gas exploration or extraction.
We, as a nation, have the capacity to develop long term sustainable energy such as solar, wind etc. and should get away from fossil fuels altogether. Fossil fuels are ruining the planet.

I highly recommend the BOEM to advance the cause of opening up more of our outer continental shelf for exploration so that the US can continue to be competitive with other oil-producing nations.  This step will ensure our energy independence, create more highly skilled jobs for US employees, and add to our GDP.  BOEM and similar agencies should both conduct comprehensive studies and advise our representative leaders but should also  consolidate this process in an efficient manner for companies to drill.

There is no point in President Obama's stand against the XL pipeline, which is basically a symbolic stand against pipelines that already crisscross our country, if we then allow drilling off the East Coast.  There is really not even a question of what will happen 'if' there is a spill, only a question of what will happen 'when' there is a spill.
I'm a resident of SC and am in favor of SC off-shore oil and gas exploration!  We need as many of these initiatives as possible to help lead us to energy independence for the USA!

This effort is a move in the wrong direction. We need to look forward to renewable resources, clean air, clean water, and certainly protect our environment. Offshore drilling is dangerous to all, whether you are the ones left to clean up the mess or an unknowing consumer who shops for local seafood trusting that it is not contaminated. And for what? The return for this amount of risk is negligible. The benefit to those who live along the beautiful South Carolina coast is miniscule - far outweighed by the probability of damages to our environment - spills, toxic waste in our fresh and salt water, damages from trucks and heavy equipment to our roads and bridges (which are already in a poor state). Beautiful Places and Smiling Faces - will this still be our motto in 20 years?

Please do not allow further expansion of offshore drilling. We need to focus on renewable non-carbon based energy, not more of the same. Increasing oil availability and consumption will further exacerbate global warming.
Stop the madness.
Thank you,

Joel Isackson MD
Assistant Professor of Medicine
David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA

Seismic testing to begin the process of offshore drilling off the coast of the North Slope has already been proven to have a negative effect on the Bowhead whale an already struggling species. This specific species has an incredibly complex system of communication through high frequency calls. Seismic testing is proven to separate pods and send them into abnormal migration patterns. These whales are not only a vital unit in the Arctic ecosystem they play a crucial role in day to day life for the Iupiat people who's ancient traditions are completely integrated with the timeless migration patterns of this whale. If BOEM does not protect this area they will be effecting all species negatively including our own.

Also it almost goes without saying that off shore oil and gas drilling and production will continue humanities dependence on fossil fuels. If we do not stop using this type of energy we will face a 2 degree rise in climate. We cannot afford to loose these 2 degrees if sea levels rise even more we could loose the coastal areas we are trying to protect, not to mention major cities and billions of dollars.

As a Coastal homeowner and an animal conservationist, I have deep reservation on the proposed Mid-Atlantic Leasing of the Outer continental shelf.

North Carolina has many unique environmental qualities (excerpted from Bob Geary - Indy Weekly):

The North Carolina coast, because of an unusual confluence of coastal flows along with the Gulf Stream, is a unique habitat for fish, shellfish, birds and marine animals to feed and breed in bountiful numbers.

The diversity of species, including 30 whales and an amazing variety of birds, is unmatched in the U.S.

Not enough is known about the impact of oil and other pollutants on our coastal ecosystem.

Not enough is known about the direction of ocean currents at different times.

A major oil spill, from a deepwater well or tanker at sea, could be devastating to the ecosystem.

A major spill, if it comes ashore, would be catastrophic for the commercial and recreational fishing industries and for tourism.

Having watched the impact of Deep Horizon in 2010 and the oil spills on the Alaskan Coast, I do not want that here on our NC coast. The potential benefits will never out weight the cost in natural resources, marine life and tourism.

Regards,

please,do not endanger our, or anymore  coastline...... this is the common property of the people, and not big oil. i was in Galveston, TX. in July after the Deep Water Horizon disaster, and it was heartbreaking to see the enormous  impact on the  earth. With oil surplus  know storage available now is the time to look at better  solutions. I have lived on the Outer Banks My whole life, My children and grandchildren should have the same clean healthy earth as the people before them. Thank you for  holding this meeting

The North Carolina coast draws thousands of tourists to its pristine beaches and deep sea fishing opportunities, not to mention the ocean mammals and other wildlife in the area.  It is simply too dangerous to allow offshore drilling. There is no existing technology that can guarantee a completely safe operation; we just have to remember the disasters of the past and their impacts on local wildlife and economies.  We should be putting our money into renewable energy resources; relying on fossil fuels is an old, outdated technology.  We have to protect the planet and the diversity of wildlife that makes our earth a beautiful place to live.

Please, say,"No," to offshore drilling.  This is the worst thing that could happen to our community on Hilton Head Island.  I vote with my Town Council who voted last evening not to support offshore drilling.

The certain environmental damage from seismic testing and subsequent oil drilling, as well as oil drillings risk of catastrophic damage to irreplaceable natural resources, means that costs of those activities far outweigh their meager economic potential.   Please remove South Carolina from the Proposed Five-Year Program.

I am a resident of Kure Beach, NC. My comments are going to be qualitative in nature as this is a matter that is dear to my heart.  I am also an alumnus of Louisiana State University and while attending there I soon learned that "no one" plans a vacation to the Louisiana shore.  Why would you not?  Because a long time ago, LA gave up tourism to their shoreline in the name of gas and oil exploration.  Not that it hasn't been lucrative for the right people and companies (my mother holds natural gas leases), but at what cost?  I am here today to say that I do not believe that the risk to our beaches, our wildlife or the way of life that has been here for so very long is worth ANY amount of oil that can be extracted from our ocean.  My husband and I recently moved back to this area and had plans to retire in the SE North Carolina area and do not want to have to deal with any risk that a potential oil spill would have. I have not seen proof of any direct economic impact that again is worth the risk that seismic testing or eventual drilling would prove worthy.  To me, what it boils down to is that the environmental risk(especially what we don't know when it comes to sonar and testing in our oceans), are just not worth it!  Please do not test or drill on our beaches!!

The oil and gas industry is composed of producers, refiners, marketers, suppliers, and other businesses that depend on regulatory certainty and predictability. The industry is accustomed to adapting to changes in market forces, including changes in oil prices, material costs, and labor costs. However, changing regulations or rules that are too stringent and cost prohibitive excludes certain business from the opportunity to compete. The final 5 year program should provide predictable and stable, thought out, rules that allow for flexibility and innovation to be utilized. Withdrawing areas from consideration will only hamper productivity and predictability by industry.

The proposed 5 year plan by the Bush Administration included 5 lease sales within the Alaska Exclusive Economic Zone: two in the Beaufort Sea, two in the Chukchi Sea, and one in the Cook Inlet. All 5 lease sales were cancelled/or delayed. The Cook Inlet sale was cancelled because of a lack of industry interest. Why was industry not interested in Cook Inlet? While industry has been active in state lease sales in the Inlet, federal lease sales have not been as successful. I hope you take lessons learned from these previous experiences because unless exploration and production companies receive some measure of success with their existing leases, there won't be any industry interest in future lease sales. With over $2 billion derived in one bonus bid in the Arctic, it is clear that billions more could be derived from future leasing in the Arctic. Therefore, I support leasing to occur in all areas of the Arctic Outer Continental Shelf, including the pending sales in 2016 and 2017.

Alaska and the federal government will receive much needed revenue from increased activity in the Arctic, as well as tens of thousands of jobs. While the federal government exceeds $18 trillion in debt, the State of Alaska is running $3.6 billion in the red on an annual basis. Revenue derived from bonus bids, rental payments, and production royalties are sorely needed. All areas of the Arctic OCS should be included in the proposed 5 year plan in the early years, not the out years. As an Alaskan, I absolutely support oil and gas development and production onshore and offshore, Dozens of studies have been conducted in the Arctic on oil spill cleanup in ice and lessons have been learned. Industry can and will develop in the Arctic in a responsible manner as has been done in other Arctic nations. Don't drive industry interest to Canada, Russia, and other Arctic nations. Allow for development to occur in U.S. waters within Alaska's EEZ.

I would like to comment that you should pay close attention to the detail of seismic activity around the drilling. I had asked a few members of BOEM about how this may affect the drilling process and nobody seemed to have answers about it. This is something of great importance due to the fact that seismic occurrences can affect drilling into the ocean floor. Just 3 or 4 years ago there was a large earth quake on the east coast which if there had been drilling could have caused serious issues. The level of seismic activity in the Gulf of Mexico may be limited but the activity on the East and West coasts should be taken quite seriously. A price cannot be put on the health of our oceans, which is why we need to pay close attention to each detail in a proposed drilling option. Even if the possibility of seismic activity is low there needs to be a plan in place and the equipment to be engineered to sustain the most severe form of activity. Please take care of our great blue marble!!

I am totally opposed to offshore oil/gas exploration and drilling. Seismic prospecting is extremely hazardous to marine life, especially whales and dolphins. Offshore drilling is dangerous - BP's gulf tragedy and resulting ruination over 5 years ago will never be eradicated. The Exxon Valdez oil spill in Alaskan waters in 1989 (nearly 30 years ago!) continues to negatively affect marine and wild life in Prince William Sound - there is no cure for oil poisoning! Crude oil poisons water, air and land - oil wells leak and often explode - there is no cure. We cannot heal Earth by continuing to invade her via mining, drilling, fracking, despoiling waters, darkening the skies with poisonous fumes. The time will come when our children's children's children ask "what is oil and gas", "why did they destroy our air, land and water?"  "Was there ever wildlife here?"

I do NOT want ANY oil drilling in our precious oceans.  Period.  Besides being for energy solutions that are forward-thinking and away from fossil fuels, I mainly am concerned with the oceans risk.  This is wrong, and should not be allowed to happen.

Thank you for the briefing and information provided. As Chairman of the Wrightsville Beach NC Chamber of Commerce we are alarmed at the aspect of drilling off the coast of NC. Our beach community and 167 businesses on our communications list are dependent on the tourism in the area. Regardless of the form of exploration and development it will have a negative impact on our community. The very discussion of testing brings a chill to those who come to our beaches.

The experiences of the Gulf Coast are an example and in viewing their exclusion from further exploration it is clear that the threat is understood by the states along the gulf who have opted out of the package.

While there is recognition of the need for energy independence the potential hazards from drilling would over shadow the small potential from carbon fuels off our coast . Wind is a possibility but we are not exploring solar or wind sufficiently.

Please relay to congress that more discussion must be held about the balance of the fuels before we unleash the drilling and carbon industry.

We and our members would be happy to participate in further discussions either in state or in congress. We are open to contact at the location recorded.

As a resident of Wilmington, NC, I am concerned that controls need to be effected that will protect the environment and wild life.  I am a proponent of the oil and gas leasing program with strong reservations.  The companies that will be allowed to bid on leases must be controlled to protect our national defense and public safety.  Strong inspection processes must be implemented to control spill events.  Seismic investigation has been noted as harmful to whales and fish and I am concerned that it may change the ecology of our coastal area.  With this being said, I aupport the oil and gas leasing program if properly controlled.

When I was graduate student at UNC, the sometime head of Geology, Roy Ingram, was a consultant to the oil companies that were exploring off this coast. They found no oil, but plenty of gas. Why do the whole mess over again? It's been damned near 50 years and they should still have the data. It wasn't financially profitable then and probably isn't now.

Let's not screw up the environment any more. North Carolina has a very poor record on environment and secondary education, and the legislature is now starting to dictate to the Universities...

North Carolina's tourism and fishing industries are economic engines that would be threatened by fossil fuel drilling off our coast.  It's a matter of when -- not if -- spills will affect these industries. This very real economic threat far outweighs any possible economic benefits from offshore drilling.

The amount of usable resources this drilling could encounter, and the high cost of delivering the required apparatus and machinery to the drilling locations makes drilling for oil on the Atlantic coast an absurd proposal for solving any of America's energy concerns, let alone those of the rest of the world. Instead of spending the time and funding on exploiting this frankly useless oil reserve, it would be better to spend our resources on renewable energy projects that could provide for us for decades to come.

I am a resident of Kitty Hawk, NC and I oppose the leasing of the waters off the coast of the Outer Banks and the Mid-Atlantic in general. My livliehood and that of my family and all of my local friends' is dependent on the billion dollar tourism industry. We manage a property rental and own restaurants, that are directly tied to the tourism. Without the tourists we would not be able to live here. I am for alternative means of energy  (wind and solar) as the cost (risk) is too great for the Oil & Gas industry to start here. As President George Bush once said, we are addicted to oil. We need to invest in alternative energy. We need to be global leaders in this trend of developing sustainable alternative energy development and sources.

This seismic survey plan is a betrayal of science, reason, and basic human decency. Blasting the Atlantic Ocean with weaponized sound is an immoral act. Doing so to get more oil to kill the climate faster is insane. This so called "balanced" policy is ludicrous. And who speaks for the millions of marine mammals that inhabit our oceans? These waters are their homes, we are intruders. And what about the impact on local communities in terms of tourism, fishing and infrastructure?

And just exactly where is the wisdom of extracting more oil from the Earth and burning it into the atmosphere? It seems as though that issue itself is unquestionable. The assumption seems to be that more oil is always better. This is clearly not the case -- think Exxon Valdez, Deep Horizon, etc.

If the "southern governors" want to bring new jobs to their states, why don't they ask the Obama administration to fund environmentally friendly solar or wind plants? There are ways to do this that don't kill or injure local animals and plants, but no one seems to want to take the trouble to fund clean alternate energy that won't continue to line the pockets of current 1%ers.

I live on the SC coast and I am very much against any oil/gas exploration.

I would hate to see North Carolina's coast opened to offshore drilling. The people here DON'T WANT IT. Come up with a proposal for offshore wind, and when the tourists come, they'll want to come back to this progressive, growing town, not be disappointed with tar balls washing up on our crystal coast.

BOEM I do not support seismic testing and offshore drilling off our coast.
We must grow hemp and run this country on it like we did when we first started. Like how the Constitution was written on Hemp paper and the President at the time made a car that would run on Hemp so get with it and stop playing games with us

Drilling for oil and/or gas off the SC coast is opening up this pristine, breathtaking landscape to the pollution and monumental risk this type of exploration requires.  Millions of jobs in the tourist, wildlife and fishing industries are at risk.  Please do not let Big Oil overtake and devastate our incredible shoreline.  The seismic testing required to determine feasibility will also have long-lasting effects on the sea wildlife--it could disrupt their habitats for years to come.

I have spent at least a month every summer of my life on the coast. In 2007 we purchased a home on the waterway overlooking Bear Inlet and Bear Island. Bear Island is a pristine, unspoiled island,Hammocks Beach State Park. This island is home to rare birds and is a major nesting site for sea turtles. It is also a prime fishing and shellfish area and home to dolphins and other sea life. Bear Island and the Outer Banks and all of our beautiful NC coast is priceless and irreplaceable. Please do not do any seismic studies that will harm our wildlife and possibly destabilize the ocean floor.

The risks are too high to even consider any offshore drilling. There is so much to lose for the chance of a small gain. If drilling is done, there will be a spill. It is just a matter of when and where. Protect all of our coastline. Spend the research dollars figuring out the best place for wind farms. Solar and wind are in abundance on our coastline. Please invest in clean renewable energy instead of drilling for fossil fuels. the search is damaging and then use of the fuel pollutes. It is more important to develop sustainable energy rather than fossil fuels. Lowering the price of gas is a temporary thing controlled by many outside factors.
The cost to our environment can never be repaired.

Sherry Eason
910-750-2605

Please save our Atlantic shores as fish are safe there. I can not buy any fish from the Pacific coast as radiation is all over that ocean. NC is a beautiful state and the coast must be saved from greedy oil corporations who rarely build safe ships or oil drilling platforms. With global warming affecting everything it is time to stop pursuing gas and oil and protect what is left of our environment for the generations to come!

My name is Karen Lebing, P.O. Box 462, Waves, NC 27982, Ph. 252-987-1268. I live on the Outer Banks and I am very very concerned about the proposed drilling off our coast. Oil spills happen, plain and simple, and it becomes an environmental nightmare! Please, do not allow our beautiful beaches to become ruined with oil.

COMMENTS IN SUPPORT OF DOCKET NO. FAA-2015-5041
PETITION FOR SPECIAL FEDERAL AVIATION REGULATION (SFAR) FOR
LOS ANGELES COUNTY - HELICOPTER MINIMUM ALTITUDES

The comments below are filed by Homeowners of Encino, a California
non-profit corporation duly organized and existing under the laws of the State of California. Homeowners of Encino is a public benefit association organized for the purpose of promoting social welfare. This corporation seeks to protect the residential character of its neighborhoods and to enhance the quality of life for its members and the community. All of its members reside within Los Angeles County and are heavily impacted by helicopter noise.

The requested FAA Rule Change Petition to establish a 2,000 ft. AGL minimum altitude for helicopters in Los Angeles County is long overdue. Helicopter noise has become a very serious problem in urban and suburban environments. In some areas, helicopter noise energy approaches more than 50 percent of all external noise penetration into residential and recreational areas. This is particularly true for in-route helicopter air traffic, as helicopters reach maximum altitude very their near departure points.

By establishing a 2,000 ft. AGL minimum altitude for helicopters operating in Los Angeles County, the FAA will be taking an important step in recognizing the problem created by unrestrained helicopter operations. The FAA should not be persuaded by the argument that slower helicopters are going to be forced into general aviation airspace, creating an increased crash hazard potential. Helicopter operators have freely chosen to operate in congested airspace. Ultimately, safety is the responsibility of the operator.

Helicopter noise in Los Angeles County has been a concern to residents for many years. Voluntary measures by helicopter pilots to avoid noise-sensitive areas in Los Angeles County have been ineffective. Cooperative efforts between the FAA, aviation associations, airport managers and aircraft operators have failed to satisfactory address helicopter noise problems. This has created the need for Special Federal Aviation Regulations SFARs for Los Angeles County.

We believe that establishing a 2,000 ft. AGL minimum altitude for helicopters operating in Los Angeles County is in the public interest and will increase the safety of helicopter operations by reducing hazards from helicopters flying at low altitudes which does not allow time for recovery or forced landing preparation in the event of a power failure. An SFAR will provide the Federal Aviation Administration greater authority to enforce minimum safe altitude regulations similar to the provisions for all other aircraft. It will not unduly burden helicopter operators with increased costs or loss of efficiency. It will minimize the intrusion of helicopters in the community by reducing noise pollution in residential areas, near schools, parks and other noise sensitive areas.

On behalf of the thousands of members of this association, we fully support the proposed SFAR and ask that the FAA issue a Notice of Proposed Rule Making (NPRM) and take prompt action to implement the proposed Rule Change.

Cordially yours,

Gerald A. Silver
President, Homeowners of Encino

Eighty-five unique helicopter flights along the general Hollywood Sign / Observatory / Griffith Park sight-seeing helicopter tour route were documented at AGLs ranging from 200 feet to 900 feet, all within a single day, Saturday, February 13, 2016. The entire dataset was documented and submitted as complaints on FAA's ACS WebTrak which displays the actual AGLs.

Griffith Park terrain is rugged. The typical habitat includes varying mixes of chaparral, oak woodland and riparian plant communities. Trails and fire roads generally run through deep canyons and traverse slopes. No road or trail along this tour route in Griffith Park is sufficient for an emergency landing. An R-44's blade tip to tip is 33 feet, a level area is necessary, and skidding upon impact usually occurs upon auto rotation landings. Several flat areas are present, but only on flattened peaks, most often at an elevation equal or above regular tour flight paths.

Pilots should have contingency plans to execute emergency landings. However, there are several reasons why this in not possible over this terrain: 1) the helicopters are not flying high enough to effectively execute controlled auto rotation, and 2) there are usually no areas flat enough to safely land. In an emergency situation, pilots may be able to maneuver to lower terrain to the south, but this would put them over hillside residential homes.

There is no safety in flying over rugged terrain at such low altitudes. Besides the safety of pilot and passengers, these helicopters pose a serious brush fire threat to Griffith Park's large and vulnerable habitat and wildlife.

A nearby helicopter route over the Hollywood Freeway (the chart-recommended route) provides a much higher level of safety. On this route helicopters can fly at least 1500-2,000 AGL, and can take advantage of numerous large parking lots all along the Freeway for contingency planning.

We cite the following Griffith Park crash incident to illustrate that emergency landing sites are not available in Griffith Park, as this R-44 landed on the side of a ridgeline. This was a very lucky crash, as the four occupants suffered only injuries.

June 6, 2013 (Helicopter Makes Emergency Landing in Griffith Park | KTLA).
http://ktla.com/2013/06/06/helicopter-crashes-in-griffith-park-at-least-3-onboard/

I support the 2000' height restrictions in this petition, but I would like the final regulations to be based on decibels rather than height, since noise is the key issue. Often the noise and vibrations are so loud that the windows rattle and glasses in my kitchen cabinet clink together. There have been earthquakes in our area that do not result in that kind of shaking!

The problem is noise, and the FAA should make regulations that establish a decibel limit for the impact that helicopters make on the communities they fly over. If 2000' is high enough to reduce the decibels to an acceptable degree, the great. If not, the height limit should be raised further. Or if 1500' is sufficient to reduce noise to an acceptable limit, or if new helicopters come to market that are quieter, that's fine too. But height restrictions without a decibel threshold might not be enough: a static hovering helicopter can be much louder than a passing one at the same altitude. I care less about height than about noise. It's the noise pollution that is wrecking our quality of life and disrupting neighborhoods. The success of the regulations should be measured in decibels, not just feet. The threshold should be set at a level such that helicopter noise does not disrupt normal conversations inside residential structures in the Los Angeles area.

I would gladly pay for a noise monitoring device to be placed on my rooftop so that offending helicopter activities could be automatically reported.

Finally, I would like the FAA to retract its conclusion in the January 16, 2015 Significant Progress Report and move forward the the congressional mandate to issue regulations for helicopter noise. I have not experienced any reduction in helicopter noise since January 2015 or since the implementation of the web tracking system in April of 2015. Voluntary measures are not working, and in fact there is no evidence that the voluntary measures even exist or have been agreed to in any formal way. The January 2015 significant progress report stated "FAA anticipates that a memorandum of understanding among stakeholders, including the FAA, will be signed, and the initial set of voluntary measures will be finalized and implemented this year." It is now March of 2016, and to my knowledge, no such MOA exists. I follow this issue closely, and I have not even seen a draft of the text of such an MOA. It is not on the FAA website, and it s not on the website of local advocacy groups either. Clearly, then, the FAA's finding of "significant progress" was based on faulty assumptions, and they should reverse their conclusions. The finding of significant progress should be retracted so that the regulatory process can move forward as mandated in the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2014, Pub. L. No. 113-76 (Jan 3, 2014). Furthermore, any future findings of "progress" on this issue must be measured in units, such as decibels, that are directly related to the noise impacts that are the problem here. The numbers of meetings attended, advisory notices issued, pamphlets distributed, and even a fancy website tracking system--all cited as supposed "achievements" in the significant progress report--have not resulted in any reduction of helicopter noise in the community. Therefore, they cannot be considered "significant progress" on this issue, and the FAA should be considered legally bound to move forward with issuing regulations for helicopter noise in the Los Angeles area as mandated by the 2014 law.

I am a City Councilman for the City of Lomita where I have lived since 1977. I have served our City in various official capacities, including Traffic and Safety Commission, Planning Commission, and most recently City Councilman for the last five years. I am also a Board member for the Los Angeles Area Helicopter Noise Coalition where I have participated in numerous collaborative meetings with the helicopter operators and the FAA over the past two years. As an elected official for the City and a long-time resident of Lomita, I believe the FAA needs to seriously consider this proposed regulation.

Most of the flights over our city are from the Robinson Helicopter Co., based at Torrance Airport. They have grown to become the largest manufacturer of civil helicopters in the world. They test fly their new aircraft using uncharted and unpublished helicopter routes along the Pacific Coast Highway corridor, located in Torrance and Lomita. The vast majority of these flights are conducted well below the 2,000 foot altitude recommended by the FAA and hence, are very disruptive to our residents. Nearly all of these flights, as well as other training flights from nearby flight schools, create unacceptable noise-levels for our residents who live in the highly populated areas below the test routes. Residents complain, and I agree, that the excessive noise levels have created a serious "quality of life" issue that needs to be rectified by raising flight altitudes and creating routes that have less impact on our communities.

The City of Lomita, population of approximately 20,000, as well as other surrounding cities in the South Bay area are strongly supportive of this petition, as evidenced by the attached Lomita City Council Resolution and letter of support from the South Bay Cities Council of Governments. Lomita's residents have lived with this nuisance for far too long, and it is time for the FAA to take action.

Sincerely,
Michael Savidan
Councilmember, City of Lomita

RE: COMMENTS IN SUPPORT OF DOCKET NO. FAA-2015-5041
PETITION FOR SPECIAL FEDERAL AVIATION REGULATION (SFAR) FOR
LOS ANGELES COUNTY - HELICOPTER MINIMUM ALTITUDES

Friends of Griffith Park is a non-profit 501(c)(3) advocacy and support organization for Griffith Park. At 4320 acres, the park is the largest urban park in the nation. It is a respite for all classes of Angelinos and also a surprisingly healthy and biodiverse ecosystem.

Griffith Park is plagued with helicopter noise. High on the list of offending helicopters are the tour helicopters which fly next to the historic Griffith Observatory and the world-famous Hollywood Sign. Helicopters here fly mostly at 1600-1900 feet MSL. With Griffith Park's high peaks of 1800 feet and many ridgelines running all directions at 1100 to 1700 feet elevation, many helicopters fly well below 1,000 feet AGL, often even at 400-600 feet AGL.

We fear that sight-seeing helicopter pilots have a tendency to make their paying customers happy by getting as close as possible to these landmarks. While a voluntary charted helicopters route is clearly specified on the Los Angeles Helicopter Route Chart just to the south of the two landmarks, few helicopters follow it. They go right over the park's rugged terrain, instead.

The routine flow of helicopters negatively impacts the peace and quiet of park users, including hikers and runners. Studies have shown that the noise "annoyance level" for hikers is generally "dose-related", and one gets a large dose here. Equestrians have also complained that loud noises overhead expose them to risks of their horse being spooked, a serious safety issue.

Helicopters have crashed or crashed-landed in Griffith Park at least three times in the last decade. The risk of causing a brush fire is heightened by the fact that most of helicopters operating here are Robinson R-44 models, an aircraft with a history of problems. A minimum altitude requirement will provide a safer margin for landing, in case of mechanical failure.

A loud and disruptive open space environment may have global implications on otherwise healthy ecosystems, as the species comprising the system experience changes in their reproductive success and energy efficiencies, such as foraging behavior and anti-predatory behavior. Balances, densities and animal community structure may be jeopardized.

Griffith Park is becoming a highly impacted open space area with new streams of tour helicopters. The rich and biodiverse wildland, in the middle of a sprawling city, supports many bobcats, deer, gray foxes, an abundance of birds, and for four years, an adult mountain lion.

In 2000, the National Park Service showed its concern about acoustical environment by establishing "Soundscape Policies." Now, some National Parks have protections from helicopter noise. Unless general altitude limitations can be enacted for Los Angeles County, it will become necessary to forward measures more specifically to protect these wildlands from noise impacts. It is clear that FAA has the "authority to preserve, protect, and enhance the environment by minimizing, mitigating, or preventing the adverse effects of aircraft."

The requested FAA Rule Change Petition to establish a 2,000 ft. AGL minimum altitude for helicopters in Los Angeles County is long overdue. Helicopter operators have chosen to operate at their own free will and at their own discretion as to what is safe, against an increasingly angered population of people below them.

We believe that establishing a 2,000 ft. AGL minimum altitude for helicopters operating in Los Angeles County is in the public interest and will increase the safety of helicopter operations by reducing hazards from helicopters flying at low altitudes.

We are in full support the proposed SFAR and hope the FAA will act promptly to take action by implementing this rule change.

Sincerely,

Gerry Hans
President
Friends of Griffith Park
www.friendsofgriffithpark.org

To: Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs

Subject: Notice of Proposed Requirement to Report Summary Data on Employee Compensation

I submit this comment from the perspective of a construction general contractor holding Federal contracts.

Specific criteria stated in the Presidential Memorandum directed the DOL to develop a compensation data collection proposal that would minimize, to the extent feasible, the burden on Federal contractors and subcontractors. The Memorandum also encouraged the Department to develop a proposal that relies on existing reporting requirements and frameworks to the extent feasible. Said criteria are paramount as existing regulatory requirements for federal construction contractors are massive. Regarding only recent employment-related regulations, the construction industry is still digesting the new/revised requirements of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, the Vietnam Era Veterans Readjustment Assistance Act and the Rehabilitation Act.

Federal construction contractors should be exempted from the proposed rule as there are existing employee compensation regulations and reporting requirements:

Per the DOLs website: Davis-Bacon Act and Related Act contractors and subcontractors must pay their laborers and mechanics employed under the contract no less than the locally prevailing wages and fringe benefits [as determined by the DOL] for corresponding work on similar projects in the area. The Davis-Bacon Act effectively prohibits compensation discrimination in construction.

The Davis-Bacon Act also requires compensation data collection and reporting. Construction employers are required to sign and submit, under penalty of perjury, weekly certified payrolls (on Form WH-347) listing each of their workers, their job classifications, hours worked and rates of pay.

In response to the request for comment on an alternative reporting framework to ensure that the costs and burdens of this rule are minimized, I offer the following alternative for construction contractors:

Most of the information the OFCCP is seeking (i.e., compensation, job category, hours worked, number of employees) is already reported on contractors Form WH-347 filings.

If reporting categories for sex and race were added to Form WH-347, all of the sought information would be reported without redundancy and the costs and burdens of the proposed rule would be substantially minimized.

In conclusion, for the reasons stated herein, I respectfully request that Federal construction contractors be exempted from the proposed rule.

Marc Porter
Executive Vice President
The Law Company, Inc.

When the M/V Gasconade gets iced in in its home port it is not usable when there are conditions south of Omaha that allow industry to operate outside of the releases for the navigation season. In addition low flows at its home port early on in a typical year frequently find the M/V Gasconade setting on the river bottom, immobile.

Its current home port in Omaha it quite a distance away from areas of the Missouri River with heavier use and longer navigation season. Its remote location causes delays during times of urgency and it is located too far north to cover for the M/V Cheyenne when it is out of service for maintenance.

We believe relocating this important navigation asset to a port in Kansas City will still allow the USCG to assist navigation north of Kansas City and allow greater efficiency of USCG resources.

BACKGROUND:

The major contaminants usually encountered in milk and milk products include pesticide residues, heavy metals, and aflatoxin M1 (AFM1). Primarily, milk get contaminated before milching, from the cattle feed, from sources/materials used during the processing of milk as well as improper handling of the milk during the pre- and postprocessing period.
OBJECTIVE:

The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of household practices on milk contaminants.
MATERIALS AND METHODS:

Samples of pasteurized as well as unpasteurized milk (Vendor's milk) were analyzed for AFM1, pesticide residues, and heavy metals. Simulating the household practices, the impact of boiling on these contaminants was assessed.
RESULTS:

The contaminant Aflatoxin M1 (AFM1) was detected at a concentration ranging from 0.071-0.075 ppb in unpasteurized as well as pasteurized milk samples analyzed during the course of study. Moreover, boiling had no impact on the quantity of AFM1 present in the milk. Pesticides and heavy metal contents were found to be within acceptable limits in all the milk samples tested.
CONCLUSION:

Mycotoxins especially aflatoxins in cattle feed and their consequential presence in milk and milk products is a serious concern world over as they are reported carcinogens. These fungal toxins are resistant to high temperatures and may lead to various health hazards. Preventive steps must be taken at each stage to ensure good quality of milk and milk products free from these contaminants. Awareness programs and education for the dairy farmers and milk processors may be helpful in this regard.

I would like to evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility but first, I would like to question the purpose of the statute. In the purpose section, it merely states what the statute does rather than the reason someone felt it necessary to remove the requirement to obtain court approval prior to the collection of money for non-tax-related debts. I don't understand how this would satisfy the due process requirement, despite the indications within the statute that it does. The collection of the information as needed to satisfy the debt process doesn't appear to include anything that would normally be related to the information that one would need to present to a court. Wouldn't it be pertinent, since we would be saving the additional step of obtaining a court signature, to collect the information which would give one the authority to do so? I think this is missing from the information needed to be collected. Also, is this process subject to an appeal? I did not see this action within the statute. Instead, the regulation appears to be designed for the federal government to collect its non-tax-related debt without oversight. I couldn't disagree more with this idea.

The specific section I refer to is 20.206 (f), as it relates to the burden of proof. This sections places the burden on the debtor to dispute the amount of the debt when all the department must do is produce a "document that establishes the existence of the debt and the amount of debt." Id. There is nothing in this section about what the requirements for this document are. That appears as if the department is creating its own rules without regard for a true due process acknowledgement. Formerly, by presenting these facts to a judge, the department would be required to show proof on at least a probable cause standard that the debt was owed, the amount of the debt and the need to collect it via garnishment.

In our current economic climate, wouldn't this regulation be counterproductive to the actual repayment of debts? Historically, fear of immediate garnishment has not motivated people to pay their debt. This can be evidenced by the amount of people incarcerated for not paying child support and their subsequent refusal to work. In my very limited life experience, threats do not work as motivation.

Removing judicial protection and oversight of the wage garnishment process is reprehensible.  I understand that sometimes it is necessary to garnish wages, but it is not a process that should be used easily or lightly.

I disagree with this proposed rule to eliminate the requirement of a court's approval prior to garnishing one's disposable income for non-tax delinquent debt. My reason being is that it eliminates the requirement for due process. I don't think that it's fair because everyone's circumstances are different and stripping one's right to have their case viewed by another set of eyes before undergoing wage garnishment is only right. The court act as an unbiased party to evaluate the situation from an outside perspective so that the most reasonable outcome is reached.

For example, in the case of student loan debt, in today's economy it is extremely tough to score a high paying job directly out of college, generally people begin at entry level jobs barely making $40,000 a year. This is barely enough money for a single person to survive on their own let alone if they have a family to take care of. In this case it would be best to let the court decide if wage garnishments are appropriate at that time or even looking at lowering the amount that is being requested for approval as an option

I also understand that the Department is trying to account for fairness by explaining the debtor's rights in Section 20.205, which indeed all do seem fair, and again in section Section 20.209 when it describes the limits on the percentage an agency can garnish at one time. However, I just don't think it's fair to eliminate the party's right to procedural due process.
I disagree with the recommendation and view this as an extension of the government to further control the public.

Workplace drug testing must be highly reliable and accurate, especially in transportation industries. False negative results may endanger public safety. False positive results cause innocent workers to lose their jobs.

Urine testing has been demonstrated to be highly accurate when performed properly by qualified personnel. The HHS laboratory certification program, while not perfect, is generally effective. The blind testing requirements usually prevent unqualified laboratories from obtaining certification and detect when qualified labs' quality standards decline.

Hair testing has not been shown to be accurate. While there have been published claims that hair testing is accurate, they do not come from independent research subject to peer review. Most such publications have come from parties with financial ties to the hair testing industry.

There might be some justification for using an unreliable testing technology if if were the only one available. But allowing the use of an unreliable technology when an accurate technology is already in use can only cause harm to employers, employees, and the public.

HHS should use its resources to improve the areas in which urine testing is less than perfect. The scientists at SAMHSA have demonstrated their ability to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of new testing technologies. They should be permitted to continue doing their jobs objectively, without political pressure.

Lewis Maltby
President
National Workrights Institute

I have worked in the Occupational Health field for 25 years as a client services manager. If I had to choose a replacement to urine, which is easily adulterated without detection at times, I would choose Saliva Oral Fluid over Hair. Saliva Oral Fluid is FDA approved, based upon the manufacturer, and has been utilized in the private sector for 10+ years; it is an observed collection. Since it is an observed collection, and there are no issues concerning hydration, dilution, substitution, I feel that an employer is getting what they paid for regarding the price of a drug screen. Currently with urine, an employer doesn't know if the drug screen is valid since it is easy to adulterate. In the clinic, and for the employer, saliva oral fluid is more time efficient and the donor is away from the job site for less time. The cost of a drug screen for an employer is not only about the lab processing fee; it's also about the donor's loss of productivity and a financial loss for each donor that must be detained in the clinic waiting to produce a valid urine specimen. For that reason, saliva oral fluid is a cost effective solution. Hair is also an effective solution, but it is more expense for lab processing fees. On both the up and downside, hair has a 90-day look back or longer, but some donors make it difficult to collect a hair specimen due to shaving. In a perfect world, hair and saliva oral fluid would be a perfect match as it would reveal if the donor abused historically over 3-months, and within the last 3 days. However, the cost for both tests would be a challenge for employers regarding affordability. For the above reasons, I don't believe a hair test is a viable option for both the employer and public safety. For reasons of validity, public safety, productivity, and conducting a test that produces the greatest result for public safety, Saliva Oral Fluid is the best choice, in my opinion, .

As a trained collector who has performed thousands of urine specimen collections and the Contracting Officer's Representative for over five years for two contracts that enable Executive Branch Agencies to perform over 50,000 urine collections in a Fiscal Year, I submit the following comments.

The science that has been presented through the Drug Testing Advisory Board (DTAB) has proven that hair testing is not an adequate specimen for federal collections at this time. Repeated information has been presented at DTAB meetings that there is a racial bias in hair testing and that the science is not as solid as urine and oral fluid. The drug detection times are longer than urine and oral fluid; counter intuitive to the Federal program which is trying to detect recent usage.

Hair specimen collections would be met with resistance from the donors. Both urine and saliva are less invasive and divisive than hair. The hair care industry is a multi million dollar industry in the United States. Infant's first haircuts are documented and hair clippings are saved. People's lives are documented by their changing hair styles. Hair can be washed, cut, styled, colored, braided, weaved, accessorized, lost, and shaved. None of these efforts are put into urine or saliva. People put a lot of effort into their hair, trying to take even a small portion of it for testing, would be met with resistance. Collecting a hair specimen from the body would result in fewer trained collectors willing to obtain such a specimen.

With oral fluids being added as an alternate specimen, SAMHSA and DTAB should wait to see the trial/error/issues that arise with this new specimen before considering another specimen type.

On May 29, 2015, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) published a notice in the Federal Register requesting information on specific aspects of the regulatory policies and standards on hair specimens that may be applied to the Mandatory Guidelines for the Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs. The notice solicits comments on twenty questions that involve hair specimen, specimen preparation, analytes/cutoffs, specimen validity, and testing. As the largest national organization representing motor carriers, American Trucking Associations (ATA) is vitally interested in making changes to Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs. ATA strongly supports SAMHSAs increased attention in developing hair testing standards and believes that the inclusion on hair specimens into the Mandatory Guidelines for the Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs is a giant leap forward in modernizing transportation drug testing

ATAs mission is to advocate for highway safety measures on behalf of its members. Highways are the motor carriers and drivers workplace. As such, ATA and its motor carrier members have a responsibility to ensure that their professional truck drivers operate in a safe workplace. Truck drivers represent 97% of those subject to Federally required drug tests. As required by current law, the Department of Transportation (DOT) is only allowed to make scientific or technical changes to DOTs drug program when SAMHSA makes improvements to the Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs. So SAMHSAs role is important. Hair specimen testing, particularly for pre-employment and random testing for safety sensitive employees, is a step in the right direction to ensuring that drug users are not placed in positions where they could cause harm to themselves or others.

Hair specimen testing has grown in popularity within the trucking industry. In the United States more than 40 trucking companies, employing tens of thousands of truck drivers conduct pre-employment and random drug tests using hair, in addition to DOT-mandated urine tests. Companies that have adopted pre-employment and random hair testing have found that it provides many benefits. Hair specimen testings long detection window and observed collection process has helped many of these companies identify thousands of drug users who might not otherwise be recognized as such. These companies have found that preventing individuals who use illegal drugs from joining their fleets from the outset has caused significant drops in post-accident and random drug test positive rates.

Since hair testing is not an accepted DOT testing method, companies that conduct hair tests are prohibited from sharing these test results with other employers. As a result, drivers who fail pre-employment hair tests can simply seek employment with other carriers where they can more easily pass a pre-employment urine drug test, without fear that their positive hair test results will follow them. In other words, many of the drivers that have tested positive on hair tests are still on the road, but driving for other companies and not receiving drug rehabilitation that they so desperately need.

It is important to point out that all drug testing samples have benefits and weaknesses. For instance, the limitations of urine have been well documented by stakeholders and Federal watchdogs, like the Government Accountability Office (GAO) . SAMHSAs proposed oral fluid testing standards is a step to improving drug testing collection for post-incident/accident, reasonable suspicion, and some random testing. Although, oral fluid will be limited by its very short detection window for identifying most drug users. In other words, oral fluid testing can detect very recent drug use, but is hindered in its ability to detect individuals who abstain from drug use just before testing.

Conversely, hair specimen testing is much better at identifying life style users during pre-employment testing. Also, given its long detection window, it is an effective deterrent against use and useful as a random testing tool. Of course, since the intent of random testing is to deter use, a test that captures a long window of time will be especially effective. Finally, hair tests are less difficult to subvert.

Experts will be quick to point out that hair is not as effective as some other samples at detecting recent use or current intoxication. However, ATA encourages SAMHSA to consider these and other criticisms of hair testing in the context of the known limitations of other specimens. Moreover, if SAMHSA is to require a standard of perfection with respect to any sample, that same standard should be applied to all specimens. **Comments continue in the attached document**

Re: RIN: 1290-AA29, "Equal Treatment in Department of Labor Programs for Faith-Based and Community Organizations; Protection of Religious Liberty of Department of Labor Social Service Providers and Beneficiaries"
---------------------------------------------

The following comments to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) "Equal Treatment in Department of Labor Programs for Faith-Based and Community Organizations; Protection of Religious Liberty of Department of Labor Social Service Providers and Beneficiaries" are submitted by the American Jewish Committee (AJC).

We are pleased that Department of Labor (DOL) has published this NPRM, which is an important step toward implementing Executive Order 13559. We welcome these proposed regulations as an advancement that increases beneficiary protections and clarifies the roles and responsibilities of both the faith-based provider and the Agency when they partner to provide vital and necessary social services.

Although these proposed regulations are a vast improvement over the current ones, we believe they can be further strengthened in several areas:

Clarifying prohibited uses of direct federal financial assistance;
Assuring the religious liberty rights of the clients and beneficiaries of federally funded programs by strengthening appropriate protections;
Stating more clearly the distinction between "direct" and "indirect" aid;
Improving monitoring of constitutional, statutory, and regulatory requirements that accompany federal social service funds; and
Ending taxpayer-funded employment discrimination.

Toward that end, we join in, and incorporate by reference, the comments on the proposed rule to be filed by the Coalition Against Religious Discrimination (CARD), except that we do not join in the subsection under the heading "1. Prohibiting Providers from Discriminating Against Beneficiaries" (the section begins with the words "[a]s stated" and ends with the words "still applies").

We thank you for your work on these important regulations and your attention to our comments. AJC strongly believes that it is entirely possible for the government to partner with faith-based organizations in their charitable works and provision of services to communities in need while maintaining strong religious liberty and civil rights protections. We provide comments on the proposed rule in order to further that principle. If you should have questions about our comments, please contact Richard Foltin at foltinr@ajc.org or 202-785-5463.

RE: Proposed rule on Federal Register for suggested changes to Equal Treatment for Faith-Based and Community Organizations
Catholic Relief Services - United States Conference of Catholic Bishops (CRS) is pleased to have the opportunity to review and provide comment on the above reference federal register notice for the proposed changes to 29 CFR Part 2 "Equal Treatment in Department of Labor Programs for Faith-Based and Community Organizations; Protection of Religious Liberty of Department of Labor Social Service Providers and Beneficiaries". The intent and language of the proposed changes is reasonable and acceptable to CRS, however we have one recommendation that we feel is imperative to include for organizations like CRS who are implementing federally funded program overseas. CRS recommends that the Department of Labor includes language that specifically states that the written notice and referral requirements are applicable only to domestic programs.
In the Interagency Working Group on Faith-Based and Other Neighborhood Partnerships report to the President (April 2012), the authors acknowledged that the model set of regulations and guidance for agencies to adopt focuses largely on domestic considerations. The report also states that there are additional implications that Federal Agencies must consider when applying this guidance to programs operating in foreign countries (Interagency Working Group on Faith-Based and Other Neighborhood Partnerships report to the President (April 2012), pg. 5). Mapping the requirements back to Executive Order 13279, it is apparent from how this E.O. defined "social service program" that in 2002 the regulations largely focused on domestic considerations.
CRS implements programs with Federal Assistance in over 80 foreign countries. The operational, physical, cultural, regulatory environments in which CRS operates is significantly different than the context which domestic Faith-Based and Neighborhood Organization function. CRS implements programs in areas that are remote, have limited to no formally structured social service programs so there are often no alternative programs that a beneficiary can be referred, must operate within the bounds of local structures and regulations, and the majority of our beneficiaries are illiterate or pre-literate.
Given the above, CRS strongly recommends the Department of Labor take the foreign context into consideration for the requirements to provide written notice and referral to alternative providers found in 2.34 and 2.35. CRS recommends that the Department of Labor specifically state that the written notification and referral requirements in this section are applicable only to domestic programs.

Re: Comments on Regulations (FAR Case 2014-025) and Guidance (ZRIN-1290-ZA02) Implementing the Fair Pay and Safe Workplaces Executive Order

Dear Ms. Jones and Ms. Flowers:

Thank you for this opportunity to register our support for the proposed regulations and guidance to implement the Fair Pay and Safe Workplaces Executive Order (E.O. 13673). Implementation of these provisions will help ensure that federal contractors respect their workers and comply with workplace laws. Because the federal government contracts hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of goods and services every year, it is critical to ensure that the government only contract with responsible companies with a satisfactory record of integrity and ethics. However, because the federal procurement system does not effectively review the responsibility records of companies before awarding contracts, or impose conditions on violators to encourage them to clean up their acts, we encourage more stringent oversight.

As a result, contractors that violate workplace laws have little incentive to come into compliance, and companies with the most egregious violations of these laws continue to receive federal contracts. For example, according to a 2013 report from the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, the government awarded $81 billion in federal contracts in a single year to companies with the most egregious violations of wage and workplace safety laws.
This not only harms workers, but also taxpayers. A recent report from the Center for American Progress Action Fund shows that contracting with companies that have the worst records of workplace violations also frequently results in poor contract performance.

Executive Order 13673 promises to protect workers, ensure taxpayers receive good value and help law abiding businesses compete on an even playing field by creating a fair contractor responsibility review process.
The draft regulations and guidance put forth by the administration will allow contracting agencies to partner with the Department of Labor to evaluate bidders' records of compliance with workplace laws and, when necessary, work with companies to ensure that they come into compliance before receiving any new contracts.

We applaud the FAR Council and the Department of Labor for offering robust draft regulations and guidance. Moreover, we encourage the FAR Council and the Department of Labor to strengthen the final regulations and guidance even further by creating a substantive process for stakeholder involvement; strengthening remedies to ensure that companies do not fall out of compliance; boosting disclosure requirements to the government and to the public and upholding a thorough review process for subcontracting companies.

We urge the administration to act swiftly to implement final regulations in order to help ensure that the federal government upholds its commitment to only contract with companies with a satisfactory record of integrity and ethics.

Sincerely,
Jayne Vellinga
Executive Director
Chicago Women in Trades
