With regard to the supporting documentation for Department of Justice proposed uniform language for testimony and reports for the forensic examination of serology I would like to address section B. Confirmatory tests used to identify body fluids.

In this section it states "These tests are used to achieve the level of specificity needed to identify blood or semen to the exclusion of all other substances." It goes on to state the practice that may be utilized to accomplish this ... "The process of confirming that a body fluid is present on evidence can either be done using a single identifying test or by coupling multiple screening tests. It is a scientifically acceptable practice to use two screening techniques that are based on different chemical principles to confirm the presence of a body fluid if the limitations of one test are not subject to the same limitations as the other."

I believe the statement that two presumptive tests can equal a positive identification of a body fluid is unsupported by any scientific evidence. The 10 year old citation referencing this claim, however, is not a document I am able to retrieve. I believe such a breakthrough in scientific findings should be thoroughly documented. This document states that a confirmatory test is "used to achieve the level of specificity needed to identify blood or semen to the exclusion of all other substances." I agree. To say that a positive AP test and a positive p30 test will positively identify semen is not supported by the scientific literature or common sense.

It has been scientifically demonstrated that P-30 is not tissue specific, nor gender specific. ,
Additionally, it has been reported that as little as 2 ng/ml of P-30 can yield a positive reaction with the ABAcard P-30 test. , Detection levels below the level stated by the manufacturer for the Seratec PSA test have also been reported . The manufacturers of these tests also state in their own literature that that male urine will yield a positive result with their test kits. ,
The arguments presented that the dilution of unknown stains will avoid false positives with urine, necessarily presumes that much is known of the nature of the unknown stain. The concentration, history and the presence of any other unknown body fluids or chemical substances must be known. The concentration of the unknown stain is requisite if you assume a dilution will avoid the false positive that can occur. The fact that other body fluids that contain PSA could also be present and add to the level of PSA present necessarily would have to be accounted for. The fact that no other screening tests are performed, such as a presumptive test for urine, that would at least alert the examiner that a potential for a false positive exists, further reduces the potential for a positive identification of semen.
The arguments that two presumptive tests can rise to the level of a positive identification are simply nonsensical and are not documented by any peer reviewed scientific research. It is this type of testimony and forensic examination reports that continue to reflect on the forensic sciences as voodoo science.
It is unfortunate that these "proposed" guidelines are clearly already in use by some laboratories that cite the documentation present in this report and the training they have received that they believe validates these proposed conclusions.

Respectfully,
John T. Wilson

I agree that fingerprint experts can knowledgeably testify that the mark from a crime scene and the ten-print from a suspect share a spatially identified list of characteristics. Such a finding reduces the set of people who might have left the mark. However there is no scientific basis to estimate the size of that set and no scientific criteria about when that set can be reduced to a single person.
"Identification" is justified by the supporting document released by the Justice Department with three arguments: 1) persistence and uniqueness: Persistence is documented but uniqueness is a hypothesis. Uniqueness of 10-prints does not establish uniqueness of a mark from a crime scene, however. 2)Population studies of the frequency of features:these do not establish the joint frequency of the several characteristics common to a mark and a 10-print. Unlike DNA, where independence is justified by Mendelian genetics, there is no reason to assume that the presence of one minutiae is independent of the presence of another. 3)"As more reliable features are found in agreement, it becomes less likely to find the same arrangement of features in another source". While true, this statement does not address the issue of the size of the set, nor its reduction to s single person.
The Department of Justice's proposed guidelines would permit fingerprint reports and testimony that goes beyond what science can now support. They should be limited to reporting what similarities (and differences, if any) are found.

Proposed Uniform Language Discipline Reviewed: Forensic Geology
Reviewer Name: Andrew M. Bowen (on behalf of OSAC GEO Subcommittee)
Reviewer Organization: OSAC Geological Materials Subcommittee
Reviewer Email: AMBowen@uspis.gov

General Comment on the Document:
The OSAC GEO Subcommittee is currently working on creating the standards that will guide the strength of the conclusions and the interpretation of the results (i.e. the phrasing of the opinions). It is felt that the statements in this document are ahead of the state of the group at this time, and we recommend waiting until consensus standards exist that can be adopted by the Department of Justice.

Comment on Statements Approved for Use in Forensic Geology Testimony and/or Laboratory Reports:
Many laboratories use a "strength of association" scale of some type, and we recommend that the possibility of using a "strength of association" scale be included in the approved statements.

The GEO Subcommittee members are concerned about the statement regarding "mixing" in item 3 of this document. Some types of mixing do not preclude a conclusion from being reached. However, this document implies that no conclusion can be reached in cases where "mixing" has occurred. The term "mixing" needs to be clarified, or consider removing this language.

The GEO Subcommittee members are concerned about the language "no mixing is indicated" in item 4 of this document. As discussed above, some types of mixing do not preclude a conclusion of elimination from being reached. As stated above, the term "mixing" needs to be clarified, or consider removing this language.

Comment on Statements Not Approved for Use in Forensic Geology Testimony and/or Laboratory Reports:
The GEO Subcommittee members are confused about the intent of statement 3 in this portion of the document. The boundaries of some geological materials are clearly defined and well known. Geological materials are rarely "homogeneous", so as written this statement would apply to few geological materials (if any). From a scientific standpoint, virtually nothing can be predicted with "absolute certainty". The GEO Subcommittee recommends either removing this statement, or re-wording it to clarify its intended meaning.

I am a forensic scientist at a state laboratory with 15 years of experience in microscopical hair analysis and comparison. There are two sections of this proposal that I would like to comment on:
1.The proposal limits the analyst to classifying a hair to two growth phases: anagen and telogen. While only a small percentage of hairs on an individual's head may be in the catagen root phase, catagen roots do occur in casework, and to disregard this classification may force the analyst into an inaccurate description of the hair root. Hair roots in the catagen growth phase may or may not yield a nuclear DNA profile, but recognition of the potential of a catagen root for this type of analysis during a hair exam is important. An analyst should not be locked into describing a hair root as either "anagen" or "telogen" when it is neither.
2.The use of the term "exclusion" is problematic. Hair is not a manufactured product like glass, paint, or fibers, with an expectation (to some extent) of homogeneity, and therefore should not be treated as such. Barry Gaudette's article, "Strong Negative Conclusions in Hair ComparisonA Rare Event," (in the Canadian Society of Forensic Science Journal, 17, 1985, pp. 32-37) should be considered, and the word "exclusion" should be used in narrow terms in microscopical hair analysis; a better term would perhaps be "Non-association." In regard to a conclusion of dissimilarity, consider that the proposed wording should use the word "standard" in place of "sample," since the analyst needs to make an assumption it is adequate (both quantitatively and qualitatively) for analysis, and the phrase "and assuming the standard is representative" should be included. An analyst should not be required to make a conclusion that could be inaccurate based upon a "sample" that may or may not be representative. This is especially true since, unlike other areas of trace analysis, the analyst is not likely to be performing his/her own sampling of the source.

Component Recognition versus Identification.

Plain language
The language used in the document should be simplified. There are many instances where the use of plain language would make the document easier to understand.
For example on p2-3 under the Explosives and Hazardous Devices Examination Process heading: "There are different methodologies and processes for conducting a forensic explosives and hazardous devices examination. This sentence could be rephrased as "The following steps are useful for a forensic explosives and hazardous devices examination but do not represent the only way to conduct such examination."
In this example if the current language is retained, "Department" should be clarified by replacing it with "Department of Justice" or "DOJ" (or whichever Department this refers to).

Non-public document

FACT SHEET ON HR. 1786/ S.928, WHAT IS THE GOAL OF THE REOPENED SEPTEMBER 11TH VICTIM COMPENSATION FUND (VCF)
What is the goal of the reopened September 11th Victim Compensation Fund (VCF)

Whatever the award amount, every award does nothing more than provide financial assistance for documented and provable financial losses including lost income, out of pocket medical expenses, etc. resulting from the rescue and recovery at the World Trade Center.

Here are some examples of economic loss awards:

- A volunteer fireman from a small town in the Midwest who travelled to New York to assist in the rescue effort leaving behind his private contracting business. He became disabled at age 47 by WTC related pulmonary fibrosis (which will ultimately kill him according to his doctors), asthma, chronic bronchitis and steroid induced diabetes. He is oxygen dependent. He earned about $31,500 per year before he became ill. He was awarded $1,050,632 reduced by offsets of 652,628 for an award of $398,003

- An FDNY Lieutenant who became disabled from working by severe WTC related pulmonary conditions at age 52. He was earning about $100,000 per year at the time of his disability. His VCF award was $1,012,392 reduced by offsets for a pension and prior lawsuit of $404,833, for a total award of $607,558.

- An EMT trained volunteer who showed up on September 11 to try to help. He became disabled at age 35 by chronic lower respiratory disorder, asthma, RADS and chronic upper respiratory disorders. He was earning $30,000 per year and did not qualify for Social Security Disability insurance. He was awarded $1,179,933 with an offset of $104,560, which was a lump sum workers compensation payment from the New York Volunteer Fund which he accepted because he was near destitute. His total award is $1,075,373, which represents about 30 years of earnings loss.

VCF economic loss awards are dependent on the injured 9/11 responder's or survivor's age at disability, pre-disability earnings and the offsets. While some awards may seem large, in the examples above, the injured 9/11 responder or survivor awards are based on what they lost. The award replaces any retirement benefits that the claimant would have accrued but for their disability. The award simply replaces what he and his family lost.

In fact, when analyzed, the awards being made by are modest, are consistent with the law as embodied in the statute that created it in 2001, and, most importantly, reflect injury severity and the losses suffered by the injured 9/11 responder or survivors.

For the last 8 years I have been a volunteer advocate working towards data-driven reform the Virginia Sex Offender Registry.

In Virginia we publicly list juveniles (as young as 14 years old) who have been convicted of some sexual crimes. We allow judges to decide if the juvenile must register or not, sadly for the crimes that give them this option the too often select public registration because our State Legislator decides what judges are reappointed or not and rulings on sex crime cases are held up during that decision.

Once listed the juvenile is dumped into our two-level conviction-based classification (Non-Violent or Violent) system as a Violent Offender with NO opportunity to ever petition for removal. It's life without parole for children.

Any failure to register on time results in a felony conviction and as a juvenile they must depend on an adult to take them in during business hours for the quarterly re-registrations plus any changes in residence, phone, email, etc. An arbitrary additional felony is the penalty that they face when they have no control over getting their information in in-person and on time.

If you Google the name Edgar Coker Jr you will read about a case in Virginia that was a false accusation of rape and the juvenile male was mandated to register as a public Violent Sex Offender and all the obstacles not only that Edgar face because of the public stigma but that his family faced. Only because the UVA Innocence Project invested more than 6 years into getting his conviction overturned was he finally freed of that label. Now 3 years since being removed from the VSP Registry he still hasn't been able to overcome the shame and the damage that that public label did to his young life.

Every year in the Virginia Legislature some Delegate or Senator will incorrectly tell a Committee who is hearing a Bill to expand juvenile registration or adding employment and college details online that if the Committee doesn't approve the Bill then our State will loose funding and if I was not there to stand up and correct the Patron of what SORNA actually does require then another myth-based, knee-jerk piece of legislation would probably have sailed through our Legislature without anyone taking the time to actually look into what SORNA does and doesn't require.

There is plenty of research out there against juvenile registration; juveniles are NOT small-adults there are children whose brains are not fully developed.

Juveniles should not have to register as Sex Offenders in America whether it's online or even on a private list.

Please direct the 50 States, D.C., and the Territories to create a process to remove all their Registered Sex Offenders (RSO's) whose convictions were when they were a juvenile from every registry (private or public) by January 2018 and to stop adding new juveniles immediately.

Thank you

After examining the proposed Supplemental Guidelines, I have the following thoughts:

First Thoughts:

1.I appreciate that changes begin to recognize there is value in juvenile justice and SOR statues that are not one-size-fits all (even for offenders adjudicated for a serious sexual offense statute).

2.I appreciate that this change recognizes there are other methods that may serve to meet SORNA's ends (methods which may do so even better than SORNA, and possibly with even less chance of iatrogenesis).

Other Thoughts:

I realize that the SMART Office is charged with carrying out the will of the legislature, and while this may have been well intended policy, we have to be honest about the fact that it was misguided--particularly as it relates to juvenile offenders. As I read the guidelines, I had some concerns, which I've noted below. That said, I think the changes are definitely an improvement to the SOR.

1.It sounds as though implementing SORNA for juveniles is being done simply for the sake of implementing it-- because that's what legislators passed, so that's what has to be done, but unfortunately not because we have proof that it is an effective means of preventing sexual abuse. The goal seems to be more about implementation than actual sexual abuse prevention.

2.A number of statements in the Supplemental Guidelines (and SORNA) continue to be premised on the assumption that juveniles will sexually reoffend--an assumption that is not supported by research (Batastini, Hunt, Present-Koller, & DeMatteo, 2011; Caldwell,2007; Caldwell, 2010; Caldwell & Dickinson, 2009; Caldwell, Ziemke, & Vitacco, 2008; Carpentier & Proulx, 2011; Carpentier, Silovsky, & Chaffin, 2006; Kemper and Kristner, 2007; Letourneau & Armstrong, 2008; Letourneau, Bandyopadhyay, Armstrong, & Sinha, 2010; Letourneau, Bandyopadhyay, Sinha, & Armstrong, 2009b; Parks and Bard, 2006; Rajlic, & Gretton, 2010; Reitzel & Carbonell, 2006; Schmidt, Campbell, & Houlding, 2011; Spice, Viljoen, Latzman, Scalora, & Ullman, 2013; Waite, et al., 2005; Worling, Litteljohn,& Bookalam, 2010). Findings support the exclusion of juvenile offenders from registration. Only in extremely rare cases, after careful judicial review of numerous factors, should a juvenile offender be required to register as a sex offender.

3.There's more concern for behavior when a juvenile committed an offense, than where they are now in life; whether they have been treated, rehabilitated, or how likely they are to commit a subsequent sexual offense. Focus is on a prior serious sexual offense--not whether they are likely to commit a future serious sexual offense. The statement, "juveniles at least 14 years old who are adjudicated delinquent for particularly serious sex offenses", is not synonymous with re-offense, as the guidelines imply.

Technical Suggestion:

The definition of "sexual act" should be included in the background information, right after the term is used. The DOJ has defined a "sexual act" as any degree of genital or anal penetration, and any oral-genital or oral-anal contact.


All in all, I think the changes are a positive step in the right direction. However, I strongly encourage the exploration of other methods of sexual abuse prevention that 1) have less likelihood of iatrogenesis for juvenile offenders, and 2) are focused on only those juvenile offenders that have been determined after careful judicial review (not offense statues) to be a risk to the public.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the changes to the guidelines. Your thoughtful consideration of my concerns is appreciated.

Sharon E. Denniston, Ph.D. PPA
Juvenile Advocate
Illumine Research, Analysis, and Consulting
sdenniston@illumineRAC.com

General Comment On June 7, 2006, then-DEA Mid-Atlantic Lab Director Richard Fox filed a sworn affidavit under penalty of perjury which stated, in part, that: "Neither the analyst in this case, nor any other DEA analyst, has ever misidentified marijuana. "As such, the uncertainty measurement associated with the conclusions reached by the analyst resulting in the identification of marijuana is zero." Fox told me that he had worked in over 1,000 marijuana cases and testified in hundreds in his career at DEA. I asked Dr. Walter Rowe to comment on Fox's statement that the D-L, TLC, and microscopic exam screening tests were infallible marijuana identification tests with a zero uncertainty or error rate. He responded that: "I don't have an issue with his statements. Fox's statement is in agreement with the drug analysis guidelines set out by ASTM Committee e30." Rowe who is himself a member of the ASTME30 committee was referring to E2329-10 which does state that it is possible to obtain zero uncertainty with the analystical scheme used to identify marijuana. This standard, according to former SWGDRUG Core Member Jack Maio, was created by the DEA and provided to ASTM Committee 30, whose members included Mario and Rowe. ASTM accepted E2329 verbatim and published it as ASTM E2329 Practice for Identification of Seized Drugs. Since Rowe approved E2329, I asked him about its claim that the three screening tests for marijuana comprise an infallible identification test, I asked Rowe for a single reference. He replied: "I don't have time to educate you on the nature of the tests. Neither TLC or a microscopic examination of suspected marihuana is a screening test." I concluded with asking Rowe to comment on Fox's statement that no DEA analyst "has ever misidentified marijuana "? Rowe responded: "Do you have contrary evidence?" I also sent Fox's infallibility affidavit to Barry Fisher, former president of the American Academy of Forensic Scientists who responded that: "Fox's statements are correct." In late 2014, E2329 was unanimously approved by the Seized Drugs Subcommittee of the Organization of Scientic Area Committees (OSAC) which is chaired by Dr Sandra-Rodriguez Cruz of the DEA. and published by ASTM as the Standard Practice for Identification of Seized Drugs. According to the 2009 NAS report, the claim that the 3-part analytical scheme was an identification test for marijuana was the result of a discussion by SWGDRUG members including Dr Joseph Siegel and then-DEA lab director Joseph Bono. According to Siegel, who wrote the drug section of the 2009 NAS report: "With respect to marihuana, I was a charter member of SWGDRUG . . . We extensively discussed the analysis of marihuana; . . We concluded . . . that the protocol of the Duquenois-Levine test, thin layer (or gas) chromatography and a microscopic visualization, is sufficient to identify marihuana scientifically and conclusively without needing GCMS or another confirmatory test." So in 1997, Joseph Bono declares that the 3-part analytical scheme is an identification test for marijuana. In 1999, he proclaimed that it was infallible as well. In a sworn affidavit under penalty of perjury he proclaimed, in part, that "the analyses are incapable of producing a false positive. In other words, even if the test results are inaccurate, the results will not indicate the presence of a controlled substance when none is present in the unknown sample." But the Academy Award for infallibility goes to DEA analyst Heather Hartshorne who testified that in "isolation" the three tests were only presumptive, but in "concert" they were an "error-free" identification test as was her performance. Hartshorne held her ground calmly despite being told by Judge Ryan that her testimony was "ridiculous on its face" and proved the tests and her performance were "flawed." Less than six months after Judge Ryan excoriated what he called Hartshorne's "infallibilty," her supervisor James V. Malone testified to infallibility in the following exchange. Prosecutor (P): To your knowledge, while you've been at the lab, has the laboratory ever misidentified a controlled substance? James Malone (JM): No. . . . We have not misidentified anything. P: . . . If I used a reagent that wasn't working anymore and tried to run a Duquenois-Levine with that reagent, what would happen? JM: You wouldn't get a false positive, no. Malone was also asked whether he had any issues historically or otherwise with Heather Hartshorne. I asked DEA spokesperson Lawrence Payne whether the infallibility testimonies of Richard Fox, Joseph Bono, Heather Hartshorne and James Malone were true. This requirement will place an unnecessary burden on individuals, companies, and government agencies to allocate already constrained funding to fix a problem that doesn't exist. Forensic examination of media has been on-going for over three decades. The accreditation system already in place is sufficient, the American court system. I don't think subordinating accreditation of American forensic service providers to an international body is beneficial or productive to a system that already works.

Laboratories use many different forensic hardware and software solutions providing a competitive necessity in keeping costs down for forensic labs. This would likely end up producing a "certification or accreditation" standard for equipment allowing commercial vendors to increase price points of equipment, again, unnecessarily. It could also produce a standard that many smaller providers cannot afford, essentially shutting them down.

The second and third order effects of this requirement on agencies outside of DOJ, but which interact with DOJ have not been fully flushed out. By restricting DOJ grants to only those who are accredited, you essentially cut out any other group attempting to better standards, technology, or procedures, but are not accredited.

Finally, there are 9 challenges listed. There is no plan to address these challenges other than to recommend engagement or further study. These challenges are wide-ranging and need to be solved before implementing an accreditation system.

Probably most worrisome is the fact that the challenges are biased toward larger labs and likely contract vendors that are able to create labs that meet certification and accreditation standards by running smaller government law enforcement labs out of business. It creates an incentive to take law enforcement information to outside vendors, outside the control of the investigating agency. It will create a cost to the smaller entities and increase the backlog and timelines in a process that already takes too long.

Another requirement did catch my attention, not because of the mis-punctuation, but because it stated, "The Attorney General should require that federal prosecutors, in cases in which they are in a position to request forensic testing, contract with accredited Digital and Multimedia FSSPs.. This provision does not apply to analyses conducted prior to the involvement of a federal prosecutor." Most, if not all, federal prosecutors want to be brought in at the beginning of a case. This oversight is very valuable to law enforcement. By implementing this standard, the Attorney General is undermining the relationship between federal prosecutors and non-accredited labs. In addition, if the prosecutor is constrained by the fact the law enforcement agency has an unaccredited lab, does this mean the agency has to contract that requirement out or request assistance of another agency...that also has a backlog for which the requesting agency is not a priority?

Bottom line, most federal agencies have guidelines in place to certify capable forensic analysts. If they are meeting the needs of the criminal justice system, leave it alone. Certification means that prospective examiners have to meet a minimum qualification criteria designed to ensure quality in analytical products. Agencies already monitor best practices and because of the forensic tools already in existence, standardization is built into the process. The author asserts that this will improve, "he quality of services provided by the FSSPs nationally" with no citations to back that up. The determination of "quality" of a service is subjective anyway, so its unknown how the ILAC accreditation standards will automatically equate to quality output better than what is being seen today.

Overall, I came away with the notion that all research conducted was academic with limited scope, limited interaction with the larger law enforcement forensic community, and that this is merely an attempt to gain control of a group of individuals in an inherently decentralized community to benefit an international group and a larger group of big business companies that will pick up the slack from all the entities that are put out of business as a result of implementation.

National Commission on Forensic Science - Recommendation for the Accreditation of Digital and Multimedia Forensic Science Service Providers

Georgia Bureau of Investigation Director Vernon Keenan and Digital Forensic Investigator Manager Beth Messick have reviewed the above document and have the following comments.

Overview -
The document states that accreditation will improve the Digital and Multimedia FSSP's ongoing compliance with industry best practices, promote standardization, and improve the quality of services provided by the FSSPs nationally. This digital forensic practitioner does see a need for these items to be addressed. However, the items are difficult to address in an accreditation environment where digital media is very fluid and significant changes are being developed at a rapid pace. It is believed that the time it would take to develop standards for new technologies would quickly fall behind the need for the new technology to be used in the criminal justice system. If the accreditation process is not properly written with flexibility, it could become out dated with no relevance to current technology being used in criminal proceedings. Even criminal statues are not current with technology and often times are not tested until cases are appealed to higher courts. It is only at this time that some standards are recognized.

Recommendation -
The recommendation section addresses actions for the Attorney General to take and are directed more to control of FSSPs with a DOJ nexus. There are means to force FSSPs with a DOJ nexus to comply or at least be directed to comply. However, FSSPs without a DOJ nexus are only encouraged by the Attorney General by all means possible with any available enforcement. It is possible that available enforcement will not be sufficient to have the non-DOJ FSSPs participate in the assessment. This could result in DOJ FSSPs working under stringent circumstances that could possibly lead to stifling of creative problem solving and additional work backlog for these FSSPs with the DOJ nexus.

Challenges to Achieving Accreditation -
This forensic practitioner fully agrees with all statements in this section. A key statement is "To improve the overall quality of forensic science, all entities performing forensic science testing, even on a part-time basis, must be included in universal accreditation." There is a possibility that digital and multimedia forensics have advanced past the point of a universal accreditation. This forensic practitioner agrees with all nine challenges recognized in the document and believes it will be difficult to overcome these challenges.

Appendix A: Examples of Digital and Multimedia Forensic Science Service Providers -
The examples of functions that would be excluded from the accreditation appear vague and confusing. If these items are not properly written with more detail explanations, they could be left to individual interpretations.

Appendix B: Certification vs. Accreditation -
Professional certification could be considered as a realistic and obtainable alternative to accreditation. The certification could be administered through an independent body and include training, practical experience and adherence to a code of ethics.

In conclusion, this forensic practitioner is in favor of developing best practices, standardization and improving the quality of services by FSSPs. If accreditation is used as a means to achieve these goals, the process needs to be properly written with flexibility so that it does not negatively impact FSSPs. Flexibility would need to account for rapidly changing technology. Professional certification could be considered as an alternative means to achieve these goals.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on your Initial Draft Recommendation for the Accreditation of Digital and Multimedia Forensic Science Service Providers (FSSP), docket ID DOJ-LA-2016-0002-0002.

After reviewing the document, we have the following comments:
-Currently, there exist no standards which are wholly applicable or appropriate to forensic labs. There are more appropriate and less burdensome methods for quality assurance in digital forensics, which differ from traditional 'wet' forensic labs.
-The proposed standards may present barriers to agencies. For example, the content of ISO/IEC standards is not publicly available; agencies must pay for access. Additionally, costs associated with establishing and maintaining accreditation may divert resources from mission critical operations.
-The pace of technology evolves much more quickly than traditional 'wet' forensics. As such, labs are forced to develop creative solutions to meet these novel technical challenges. Burdensome accreditation requirements would restrict the ability to respond in a timely, agile, and efficient manner.
-Unlike many 'wet' lab forensic techniques which necessitate the destruction of an evidence sample rendering it unavailable for re-examination, the nature of digital forensics is such that in most cases evidence is neither destroyed nor modified through analysis, making the analysis repeatable.

We have worked with and reviewed the products of both accredited and non-accredited labs and our experience finds no positive correlation between accreditation and quality of products from a Digital FSSP. In contrast, evaluation against public, community-developed, common sense standards specific to the digital forensic discipline, coupled with an objective, transparent peer review process provides a reasonable assurance of the technical quality and soundness of the work while imposing minimal additional costs, overhead, and restrictions.

I feel the effort to require "labs" to be accredited is misguided and an over reach of Federal authority. I have worked in the digital forensics field for 20 years, mostly as a State Law Enforcement Officer. I began my studies at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center, Glynco, Ga. Over the years I attended SCERS, multiple courses of instruction from software companies in the use of their products and multiple conferences and events in the discipline. I worked as an examiner for my agency, as part of the Computer Crime Unit, but in a remote office location, providing support to my fellow officers, Federal, State and Local. I conducted searches, performed exams and prepared reports used in successful prosecutions in State and Federal Courts.

The prospects of having to apply for (and pay for) accreditation in the future would prevent me from being about to pursue this field in the future.

Especially in criminal/legal matters, my work is always subject to examination by opposing counsel. If I follow accepted standards, my work will speak for itself. If I'm working as an independent examiner or consultant, I also assume the liability for my actions. An expensively obtained "accreditation" is not going to insure I do my job correctly. The only thing that will insure that is my personal integrity, training and experience.

Please accept the attached document of comments for review.  The opinions expressed within are my personal comments as a long standing practitioner, and do not necessarily reflect the views of my employers, past or present.

As a sole proprietor owner that is already very well accredited through the self regulated systems in place, a DOJ mandated accreditation will no doubt be an undue financial burden to my company. I am concerned about attorneys who do not know there is an underlying file at the laboratory and even if they received a copy of the underlying file, they would not understand it. Comment from the Digital Evidence Virtual Centre of Excellence CIC (http://www.devce.org/).

We agree with the concept of the use of accreditation or certification to provide evidence that bodies and practitioners providing evidence for criminal justice purposes are competent, proficient and use methods which are fit for purpose, but have concerns about the use of ISO 17025 as the standard.

This is a very broad standard and leaves many issues open to interpretation. In particular, the concept of validation is poorly understood, even in those countries (such as the UK), where the process of adopting this standard for digital and multimedia evidence has been ongoing for several years. The UK's Forensic Science Regulator has had to allow deadlines for compliance to "slip" several times, and there is minimal evidence to suggest that the majority of laboratories have made significant progress towards achieving accreditation - mainly because of the problems around validation.

There is confusion about whether processes or tools should be validated - and then that confusion is overcome, the terminology around verification causes further confusion as it conflicts with normal software development and testing concepts. We suggest that the term "verification" (and similar terms), as used in ILAC G19, should be replaced with "confirmation".

We would suggest that, in addition to the ILAC G19 guidance the DoJ should consider including ISO/IEC standards 27037,27041 and 27042 as part of the accreditation and/or certification scheme as these have been written to align with ISO 17025, but have been produced specifically to address the needs of practitioners in digital domains, and to provide clearer guidance on how ISO 17025 type quality systems can be applied to digital investigations.

We also recommend that consideration is given to exploring how bodies which have achieved certification to the 270xx standards can be allowed to provide evidence - i.e. to show how compliance with the 270xx model provides evidence of a 17025 compatible scientific regime.

This recommendation for FSSP accreditation will significantly hamper investigation collection processes.  While LE usually is in the first responder category.  The true first responder is the customer/individual and how much critical volatile data will be lost because the team collecting the data did not meet the FSSP accreditation and becomes non-admissible? While an accreditation process will ensure LE officials maintain a standard process for digital collection and analysis.  It locks personnel into a restrictive way of recovering and discovering that limits finding new ways to analyze and collect artifacts.

Digital forensics is the application of science and engineering to the recovery of digital evidence in a legally acceptable method. It is forensics. There are successful programs that operate under 17025 such as the FBI's RCFL and the USPIS.

The weakness that I see is that there really isn't one certification that really qualifies the DE examiner. An examiner should have a science degree and at least several computer forensic competency certificates (industry standard that appear rigorous but are very expensive) and be proficiency tested. In my opinion, this would be the gold standard.

I fully support the standardization of the digital forensics discipline and believe if implemented properly, this can be step in the right direction of providing more rigor to this science. The lack of requirements for digital forensic practitioners to be certified in their discipline, be accountable to industry best practices and standards, or work out of accredited laboratories places the credibility of this forensic science in jeopardy.

Although digital forensics has been recognized as a legitimate forensic science and has been utilized in the criminal justice system for the same length of time that DNA has, the discipline is anything but disciplined. Within the United States, any law enforcement agency, business, or individual can open a forensic "laboratory" and begin providing services without having to demonstrate even foundational knowledge, skills, or abilities. To further evidence this, within the law enforcement community alone there are only 67 digital forensic laboratories accredited to the ISO 17025:2005 standards for the nearly 18,000 law enforcement agencies in the country.

This entire topic was the basis for my Master's thesis. I was the laboratory director for a law enforcement digital forensics lab that started as non-accredited (2 people working in the lab) and when I left it was ASCLD/LAB accredited with 9 people. I was able to debunk the myth that accreditation was only for federal agencies or large laboratories and that it was too onerous for a small agency to comply with. I now oversee cybersecurity (including forensics) for a federal agency focusing on national security.

If you are interested, my thesis paper (attached) titled, "Disheveled Digital Forensics: The Impact of Inconsistent Standards, Certifications, and Accreditation", lays out real cases that are indicative of the problem of a lack of accreditation and certification as well as a path forward for meeting ISO and/or ASCLD standards.

As a nearly 20 year digital forensics practitioner, I strongly recommend against this course of action. The large majority of the work of a digital forensic examiner is analytical in nature, not "forensic," regardless of the name. We largely testify as expert witnesses in court, and under the Federal Rules of Evidence to do so, nearly all practitioners meet the standard required to testify as such.

Accreditation adds an undue burden to smaller forensic organizations and sole-proprietorships, of which there are many in our field. This biases work toward larger companies who can afford time away from performing casework to study accreditation and testing materials, achieve those certifications, and maintain them. One constant that I've seen in my time in the field is that those with strings of certifications after their names were often the worst practitioners of the craft; instead of spending time performing actual case work, they chased certifications to inflate their curriculum vitae. To most hiring managers and long term practitioners in the field, large numbers of certifications are seen as a negative, not a positive.

SWG-DE has been overly prescriptive in its methodologies for more than a decade, attempting to pull digital forensics to the level of "add three drops of this, two drops of that, and mix" methodology. Our work is anything but routine and rote, and to look at each case through such rigid procedures ensures only that critical case elements will be missed as they were "not part of the accredited SOP."

Approval of this regulation will serve only to dumb-down the abilities of the seasoned examiners who serve the greater justice.

I agree that this views document is important and necessary. However, I do not believe it should be limited to "test methods" which may not for example include practices for disciplines involving pattern impression evidence.
This recommendation in its current form  is not sustainable or scalable meet the current demand and work load for digital forensics.

Clarification is needed on whether those that provide Digital Forensic Services in the private sector for the private sector entity are required to meet this accreditation. At various points, this seems to apply to those seeking DOJ funding or to contract with the DOJ within the private sector must meet be accredited. However, there is not enough to distinguish between private sector not working with the DOJ.

Within this publication by the DOJ, https://www.justice.gov/ncfs/file/451341/download, it states: "The recommendation that forensic science service providers be accredited is a policy one, meant to ensure an increase in overall quality and quality assurance. It is not meant to be used as a criterion for a threshold admissibility determination for a particular expert or conclusion. Those types of decisions are made pursuant to judicial standards applying the criteria enunciated in Daubert, Frye, FRE 702, and/or various state laws." Reading this, it would seem to be pertinent to Private Sector, that providing those services within the scope of non-DOJ related work, that accreditation is not mandatory.

For those providing services to the Private Sector, this must be clarified.

Thank you.
Attached is a synopsis of my views regarding this draft proposal on FSSP Accreditation.  I am less than enthusiastic at this point for reasons given in my response.

Should Digital and Multimedia be required to be accredited? This all comes down to two words: Credibility and Expense. I will use the socratic method, so you can come to your own conclusion.

Credibility - What can we do to bolster the public's/court's belief in digital evidence, and that we know what we are doing?Is this a forensic science? One commenter said the only part that is forensic is the acquisition. The commenter says the presentation and interpretation is not. Is that true? I think the interpretation is the most opinionated thing that an examiner can do? Has the examiner spent countless hours of study understanding operating systems, and the artifact that they leave behind; documented their findings, and published them for peer review? ...Or have they attended a three day vender course telling them where things can be found , but not explaining how they get there and what they mean. In your heart do you believe that every person who takes a 3 day class, calls themselves examiner is truly an expert in digital media?

What will accreditation do? Require that if a Bachelors degree is offered in this discipline that the examiner must have one, or the equivalent. It will require that your lab have rules, and that you follow your rules. It will require that you secure the evidence, and have a chain of custody. It will require that if you make a mistake; you document it and put in place procedures so that it will not happen again. .... Oh yeah you must wipe your drives , and use a uncontaminated computers to do your exams... You know... just like what's generally accepted in the SCIENCE.

Expense - This is an expensive business. Running a law enforcement agency is expensive. Do you require police officers to go through an academy? Do you require them to go through Field Training under the direction of a specially selected and trained officer? If an officer from another state shows up; do you require any training, or just let them go to work? Most examiner have less hours of digital media training than a hours of training a police officer received in an academy. Some with as little as 24 hours of training on the use of a forensic tool. Barbers have more training and regulations. Expense is no excuse.

What would you consider to be the minimum requirements for a digital evidence forensic examiner?
College (no, school's for fools) (Yes, at least four years in digital evidence. Would you let someone perform surgery on you if they had not been to medical school? What if they told you how they know so much about surgery, and they were one of the best in the business?)
House of training (100 hours of classroom instruction) (if not how many?)
FTO Program (no, to much work) (at least six months working under a specially selected and trained examiner)
Peer review work, publish research... anything else?
Work in an accredited laboratory. (No, too much work... and to expensive) (Yes, the people deserve the very best)

ALL LABORATORIES SHOULD BE ACCREDITED

This is my opinion, and does not reflect the opinion of my agency. This is being made anonymously, because I am not authorized to comment.

Those of us who are sole proprietor businesses serving as expert witnesses and independent digital evidence examiners will be forced out of business.  My examinations take place in a home office, or at a hosting LE agency.  Certification of a laboratory will not happen.  I am one of the only examiners in my area who will do work for various public defender offices (including federal) and these badly needed services will be priced out of their reach.

While certifications are important, this looks like someone is trying to turn this into a massive money making government controlled field.  As a forensic examiner, I train yearly in my field and have been qualified as an expert in my field by federal and state courts.  As a forensic community, we need to set the standard and we need to be the ones who says which certifications are needed.  We are the ones in the trenches every day doing the work and testing new methods, not the federal government.

I have been performing digital investigations for 18 years and have experience in both the government and private sectors. I have taken numerous training courses and have earned digital forensic certifications from SANS, and vendors such as Access Data and Guidance Software. I have also trained both law enforcement officials and private sector forensic examiners on digital forensics. I currently work for a large defense contractor and manage their digital forensics support team.

While forcing accreditation of forensics processes and procedures makes sense for law enforcement agencies and government organizations, I do not think it makes sense to attempt to force this same structure on private industry. In fact, I reviewed the ASCLD accreditation and went through an ASCLD training course that made it abundantly clear that it was far too stringent for what we in private industry do on a day-to-day basis. In most cases, we are simply collecting and analyzing data while following best practices within the field. This doesn't require the stringent restrictions and requirements that analysis in support of a criminal act would. We are simply trying to provide decision makers with enough information to make a disciplinary decision and often need the flexibility to do things in a different way when collecting or analyzing data - taking the same steps every single time may not make sense in those instances. When a criminal issue in involved, we do not continue to perform our work - we simply hand off the analysis tasks to law enforcement and they collect and follow their processes as they would in any other criminal issue. Again, if you want to force accreditation then force it on government and law enforcement agencies and don't paint broadly over everyone with the same brush.

I, like others, believe the current proposal is flawed and will cause significant harm to the practice of digital forensics. It also must be noted the conflict of interest of having members of the sub-committee that work for organizations that have a financial interest in a centralized accreditation. I've seen this before when working with the largest organization - they simply did not care about the underlying reasons to get or not get an accreditation. It's not for everyone, but this doesn't take the reasons into account.

I have yet to see a decent reason for this - there has not been an issue with digital evidence not being allowed into court due to lack of accreditation. The evidence in many cases, including ones I've been involved in, has not been an issue as long as industry best practices have been followed as best as possible. In some situations that means gathering the best available evidence and being flexible. I don't see the ability to be flexible with this attempted move.

I agree with another commenter, when he stated "The ISO standards referenced by the study are not relevant to digital forensics. ISO itself accepts this on its website where it states "Prior to the release of ISO/IEC 27037, there were no globally-accepted standards on acquiring digital evidence, the first step in the process." In addition, the underlying standards and inspection criteria proposed by the Commission are not available publically without charge. All relevant information should be provided to the public as a fundamental principal of open government and transparency."

I have been performing digital investigations for 16 years and have experience in the federal, military and civilian sectors. I have taken numerous training courses and have earned digital forensic certifications from the Defense Cyber Crime Center, SANS, and vendors such as Access Data and Guidance Software. I conduct cyber investigations and provide digital forensic support to a medium-sized federal law enforcement agency.
I support the certification of digital forensic practitioners and the accreditation of digital forensic processes and procedures. However, I believe the current proposal is flawed and will cause significant harm to the practice of digital forensics and ultimately prove unworkable. It also must be noted the conflict of interest of having members of the sub-committee that work for organizations that have a financial interest in a centralized accreditation mandate creates the appearance of impropriety.
The Commission has yet to adequately provide a rationale for proposed approach. In the other sciences there was a body of legal casework tying back to poor science or poor quality control. There have been no such widespread systemic failures in the digital analysis world. I am not aware of any case where digital evidence was suppressed simply because it was not done in an accredited lab.
The scope of the draft document is so broad as to encompass virtually any review of digital data in any criminal, civil, regulatory or administrative matter issue before any government agency or court. In addition, no impact analysis has been done to determine how this will affect the administration of the criminal or civil litigation.
The ISO standards referenced by the study are not relevant to digital forensics. ISO itself accepts this on its website where it states "Prior to the release of ISO/IEC 27037, there were no globally-accepted standards on acquiring digital evidence, the first step in the process." In addition, the underlying standards and inspection criteria proposed by the Commission are not available publically without charge. All relevant information should be provided to the public as a fundamental principal of open government and transparency.
To paraphrase the United States Special Operations Command, the focus should be "people not processes." Regardless of the accreditation methodology, people will be performing the digital forensic examinations. Therefore, it is critical that digital forensic practitioners be trained and certified in their discipline. It should be noted there are numerous, well respected digital and cyber investigative certifying organizations today.
The Council of Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency (CIGIE) has adopted a peer review methodology that focuses on training, proficiency testing and certification to verify and evaluate the conduct of digital forensics. This approach offers an alternative to the one size fits all, vendor-driven solution currently presented.

I disagree with this proposal. Requiring everyone to work in an accredited lab is simply unreasonable. This will increase the cost of a digital forensics exam and increase the backlog of cases currently faced by the law enforcement community by creating an artificial shortage of qualified forensic examiners.

This sounds like an effort to plug a round hole with a square peg that will result in putting out of business a great number of small business that are doing quality work for the forensics community. We already have a need for more quality forensics folks, and this should effectively do away with a great number of those who would otherwise contribute to the community.

Here are some problems I see with lab accreditation being forced on digital forensics:

1) it costs too much and is too great a burden for the very limited benefit in this context
2) It doesn't address the core competencies of quality computer forensic examiners
3) It doesn't apply well across everyone doing a form of digital forensics
4) It is already being addressed in the form of the adversarial legal system. If someone disagrees with what a forensic examiner claims, they can freely dispute it and attack the examiner on their own or using another examiner.
5) lab issues are among the least of my concerns when I have problems with what another forensic examiner has done in a case.

This whole idea is a lot like when private investigation boards have taken ownership and control of regulating computer forensic examiners. the standards to become a PI, the test to achieve PI status, and the ongoing requirements have almost absolutely nothing to do with the work I do as a computer forensic examiner. I am also a lawyer, so I could understand how the legal questions and the lack of technical forensic questions were not related to what is required of a competent computer forensic examiner.

Please do not try to impose a blanket standard or accreditation obligation on the computer forensic community. It will hurt the industry and our economy, and probably only end up benefiting the organization collecting fees to accredit those examiners willing and able to pay the fee and suffer the burden to continue.

Page 2 Directs recommendations at the Attorney General and DOJ, however there as many or more labs that fall under other Departments of the Federal Government that should also be addressed, for example DHS runs the USSS labs.

I support this document and agree with the comments made here. There have been documented instances of individuals who have met the legal standard of "an expert" under FRE 702, but would not be recognized as an expert in the particular field for which they are offering the opinion. It's hard enough for experienced jurists to tell the difference between good and bad science. Assuming that a jury would be able to understand that declaration of expert status is a legal formality and not a stamp of approval is a risk that can easily be eliminated by choosing our words more carefully in the qualification process.

It is not practical for smaller agencies, operating with the proper industry certifications, to go through the lengthy process of becoming accredited. The threat of "no federal funding" or "encouraging federal prosecutors" not to use such agencies is ridiculous. First of all, Federal Funding dried up for these agencies years ago, we have seen no federal funds in years. Second, to encourage federal prosecutors not to use labs that are staffed with qualified people, who have been in the field for years, and have the proper training and certifications, is a poor solution which only creates division in an industry that relies on multi-jurisdictional cooperation.

With that in mind, the better approach to ensure labs maintain a minimum standard to operate is to encourage cooperation and collaboration between federal, state and local FSSP operations. Joint training, task forces and working groups such as we have done under the direction of the Massachusetts Attorney General is a model the rest of the country should consider. Rather than them dictate the way the process should work, they work with state and local agencies, and they don't threaten consequences.

I completely understand the cause for concern, but shutting out smaller law enforcement is not the solution, working with them is.

I have been doing digital forensics for 10 years. My lab is NOT accredited.
This new requirement is ridiculous.
For many reasons;
A lack of resources will inundate the labs that do have accreditation, exacerbating an already ridiculous case load.
Only the most serious of crimes would be investigated. (many children will suffer)
As long as an analyst's procedures are sound, repeatable, and generally accepted by the forensic community, there should be no issues.
Who going to pay for this wide spread accreditation?
Some, if not all, of the finest analysts I have ever seen did not work in accredited labs.
I don't care what anyone says, digital forensics is as much an art as a science.
It's very difficult to place the same type of standards on evidence that is fundamentally different that any other.
Bad move if this passes.

This appears to be another form of the American Society of Crime Lab Directors (ASCLD) certification being forced on the independent practitioners of computer forensics and digital forensics. This is a function that is already performed de facto by the expert witness validation process in our judicial system. Adding another layer (especially one as potentially expensive as this) serves no purpose other than inserting additional bureaucratic procedures that will serve to stifle innovation in the digital forensics field, drastically increase overhead costs in the private sector and reduce the pool of available digital forensic practitioners to support civil and criminal defendants.

I would ask that the committee examine the harsh realities and effects on the capability and costs that have been associated with accreditation efforts within the U.S. Government prior to imposing such accreditations on the private sector. Having worked in a government computer forensic lab that went down the ASCLD accreditation route, I can tell you that over 50% of the daily workload today is supporting bloated policies and procedures that have nothing to do with actually performing digital forensics or operating in a manner that is/was in accordance with sound digital forensics principles. This workload is dedicated to supporting the accreditation of the lab. The backlog of cases ballooned and the ability to effectively analyze digital evidence has been significantly impaired. One of the net results of the accreditation procedures is the limitation of the tools that government examiners were able to utilize in support of our investigations. This accreditation impact is manifested in the decline of the capabilities and reputation that the FBI Computer Analysis and Response Team (CART). When I entered the digital forensics field in 1996, CART was seen as the best of the best. Now their reputation among expert witnesses in the field is that of 'push button' examiners that are using outdated tools and don't have the experience or digital acumen to handle any case of substance. The FBI itself recognized this deteriorating capability when the bureau created the Investigative Analysis Unit (IAU) to handle the higher end computer forensic and network intrusion cases. The IAU has a stellar reputation for excellence in the digital forensic field. Why the difference? CART bought into the accreditation fallacy and quickly became obsolete as they could not change their tools or procedures to meet the ever changing digital forensic landscape challenges.

The committee should also recognize that by it's very nature, a government entity accrediting private digital forensic laboratories that represent the opposition to the government prosecutors on regulatory, criminal and civil matters is opening the door for an extreme abuse of power. How can an entity that relies on the government to accredit it's digital forensic facilities ever be sure that acts of retribution will not be carried out and that very same accreditation be revoked following a case? Intimidation in this matter, either real or perceived, can erode the very basis of our legal system. There is a significant stigma associated with a digital forensics examiner testifying for the defense in a criminal matter today. Sad, but true. Imagine the impact of allowing those very same purveyors of this stigma to have the ability to revoke an accreditation following a particularly vigorous and successful defense? We can not allow this to happen.

This proposal of FSSP accreditation is flawed and should NOT be considered for the following reasons:

1)
Digital FSSP work, as it relates to digital evidence, does not stop with local, state or federal agencies. Any eDiscovery service provider and law firm provides digital evidence in today's legal proceedings. It is unreasonable to require accreditation for any and all participants within the legal system that handle digital evidence or provide testimony.

2)
New advances in the technology being investigated by FSSPs to solve crimes will far surpass the capabilities of tool sets approved by accredited labs procedures. The investigators will be required to use outdated toolsets which are dictated by the accredited lab procedures and therefore putting the investigation at risk to miss crucial digital evidence.

3)
The investigation of digital evidence is dynamic and diverse in nature. There cannot and should not be a fixed process that must be followed for all digital investigations. Each investigation is unique and trying to have a one-process-fits-all approach is not only inappropriate, it is setting the FSSPs up for failure.

Other highly trained digital forensic investigators have already voice their opinions as to why this recommendation is flawed and should not be considered.

If adopted, it would truly mean a significant setback for law enforcement as well as private sector FSSPs.

Vote "NO" on this recommendation and allow FSSPs across all segments of law enforcement and private sectors continue their efforts in fighting digital crimes.

Will the event data recorders listed in HR 22 be considered digital evidence ? When the data is imaged from the EDR and then interpreted to form conclusions in vehicle homicide cases would that be covered under this proposal ?
Are we next going to recommend the mandatory universal ISO accreditation of "Forensic Accountants", "Forensic Psychologists", "Forensic Interviewers"...
I agree that there should be standardization in this profession. What are the requirements for a "lab" if someone owns a independent private practice firm?

Who are the particular people that proposed this mess? What are their backgrounds in digital forensics? What are their true intentions, or are they just ill informed?

Let's be very clear here - this kind of government involvement is like a poisonous fungus - once gaining a foothold its growth cannot be stopped. It's nice that the members of this committee found something they could spend their time on, but this thing should be stopped now.

I believe that adopting the accreditation recommendation harms small providers and does not necessarily guarantee better results. This will only reduce the number of professional resources, and will greatly favor large FSSPs.

I don't believe that my ability to perform digital forensic analysis is necessarily enhanced by working out of an accredited lab. I am quite able to meet high standards regardless of what lab I work out of.

I have over 15 years of experience in digital forensics.  I hold five different digital forensic certifications. My agency cannot afford FSSP accreditation and to be quite honest I do not think it's needed. The National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers (NACDL) is the preeminent organization advancing the mission of the criminal defense bar to ensure justice and due process for persons accused of crime or wrongdoing. A professional bar association founded in 1958, NACDL's approximately 9,000 direct members in 28 countries - and 90 state, provincial, and local affiliate organizations totaling up to 40,000 attorneys - include private criminal defense lawyers, public defenders, military defense counsel, law professors, and judges committed to preserving fairness and promoting a rational and humane criminal justice system.

After reviewing the "Recommendations to the Attorney General Regarding the Use of the Term 'Reasonable Scientific Certainty'" (Recommendations), the NACDL wholly agrees with and supports all three recommendations of the subcommittee which, taken together, would end the use of the terms "to a reasonable degree of scientific certainty" or "to a reasonable degree of (discipline) certainty" by those employed and appearing on behalf of the Department of Justice.

Science demands accuracy and lucidity in the reporting of results. In 2009, the National Research Council of the National Academies published "Strengthening Forensic Science in the United States: A Path Forward" (NAS Report). That report noted that in many of the scientific disciplines, no consensus had been reached on the meaning of commonly used terms in forensic testimony ascribed to results such as "match," "consistent with," "identical," "similar in all respects tested," and "cannot be excluded as the source of." Such terms were then, and are now, still being utilized to describe the findings and conclusions of examiners and the degrees of association between the evidentiary material and particular individuals or
objects. The NAS Report called for raised standards of reporting and testifying about the results of examinations.

The primary cause for the confusion cited by the NAS Report was engendered by a paucity of research in the forensic sciences and corresponding limitations in interpreting forensic analyses results. Both before and after the NAS Report's issuance, testimonial and reporting confusion was magnified by the use of the generic term "reasonable scientific certainty." As the Recommendations clearly denote, the reasonable scientific certainty terminology has no scientific meaning, and even worse may mislead triers of the fact as to the objectivity involved, the degree of scientific reliability and any limitations being asserted, as well as the ability of the analysis to reach an individualized conclusion.

In the courtroom, the presentation of a scientific conclusion has an outsized impact on the presentation of the evidence, and its magnified effect results in shifting aside concomitant evidence that the jury should consider in reaching a conclusion as to guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Even more egregious is that testimony presented as "probably" or "possibly" linked to a particular source when coupled with the term "reasonable scientific certainty" has the effect of completely confusing a jury as to what value, if any, such evidence has in the trial context, a result which can be equally damaging to both the prosecution and the defense. The confusion taken as a whole can cause the jury to assign an aura of infallibility to science that is not deserved under current standards.

By eliminating the term "reasonable scientific certainty," testimony as to forensic conclusions will be expressed in more accurate terms. This term is not routinely used by medical professionals or other scientists in expressing conclusions. Neither the Frye and Daubert tests nor case law across the nation require the use of the term "reasonable scientific certainty."

The prohibition against the use of this term by attorneys appearing on behalf of the government as well as by forensic science service providers and forensic medical providers will result in more accurate courtroom testimony if the recommendations are adopted by the Commission and subsequently by the Attorney General. It will also serve as a benchmark by which the states can emulate the same standard as they seek to achieve the same clarity in proceedings across the nation.

I commend this document. As a small improvement, I respectfully suggest replacing "an individualized conclusion " with "a conclusion." I do not understand how the term "reasonable scientific certainty" would mislead factfinders about analysts' ability to reach "conclusions of individualization" (which I assume is what is meant by the phrase "individualized conclusion"), in particular, as opposed to any other conclusions.

While I agree with the overall reasoning put into this recommendation, I would strongly caution against implementing the "ban" of this term in the absence of further information as to what will or should replace it in a discipline-specific manner. This is akin to the whole "there is no scientific basis for a minimum number of points" that was brought from on high with no further direction or explanation. The void that created was felt broadly for the following decades. In the interests of justice, please don't put the cart before the horse yet again.

While I recognize that the term "Reasonable Scientific Certainty" is far from perfect, I feel it is unwise to abandon this term and potentially undermine widely accepted precedents without endorsing a set of standards (or even guidelines) for the forensic community to utilize going forward. As a practitioner, I have learned and accepted this terminology to mean that we are as certain as we can be within the current limits of our respective disciplines and that appropriate measures to reduce potential error have been employed.


Furthermore, it is my understanding that the OSACs are currently working on updated standards to address this issue, and thus, I feel that it would be appropriate to refrain from finalizing this document until the OSACs put forth an alternative means of clear communication for the factfinders. In the meantime, the "Reasonable Scientific Certainty" phrase communicates to the factfinders that the opinions put forth are grounded in scientific principles while acknowledging that we can no longer claim to have 100% certainty.

If the term reasonable scientific certainty conveys to a layperson that all of the rigors of a particular scientific principle, analytic test, or process have been followed and the result or opinion is within the acceptable limitations and error for said test. Jurors are too often asked to interpret the validity of a scientific standard or test, and the weight of the results on the guilt or innocence. Their job should be to weigh only the results, without having to consider the validity of the testing methods, provided they are an adopted standard. I am in favor of retaining the term reasonable degree of certainty, however a standard definition of what that means in court testimony would represent a compromise to lawyers and practitioners. It appears this is exactly what has been requested of the OSAC.

We respectfully submit our comments for your consideration. However, we strongly disagree with the proposed rule. We think that the "release to one is a release to all" presumption is "release to one [requester] is a release to all [requesters]." In our opinion, that is exactly what the courts meant in Favish and Reporters Committee.

The above cases dealt with "the identity of the requesting party has no bearing on the merits of his or her FOIA request" and "disclosure does not depend on the identity of the requester." In our humble opinion, the proposed rule is a distortion of the maxim, as we understand it (to treat all requesters fairly by disclosing the same requested records to all who request them). To now interpret or presume that the maxim means that for every first request we respond that the next logical step is to "post" those responsive records online for all, in our humble opinion, actually goes against the FOIA. We do not think this proposed rule would equate to more transparency. It would be more like a library section filled with dusty, un-opened books. Thus, at least 95% of these proposed postings would be a waste of our resources and essentially useless to the general public/masses.

We currently have a proactive disclosure mechanism that, if used as it should be, satisfies your interpretation of the maxim. If we also use the turbo version of the proactive disclosure that instructs us to post FOIA-responsive records that we anticipate others will also request, that is indeed a significant improvement to the proactive disclosure procedure. However, if this proposed rule is accepted, there will no longer be any need for proactive disclosures, among many other processes firmly established within the FOIA and thusly in the FOIA regulations.

Our office very rarely receives more than two requests for the same records. How can we conclude that even one more member of the public will be interested in and want to access the records that we post online when only one party previously requested the records? A suggested alternative to this proposed rule would be to change the minimum amount of requests received from three to two for the proactive disclosure rule.

Posting vs. releasing via the FOIA process would risk exposing the public and the Government to inconsistent and erroneous releases and withholdings, redundancies, takedowns, re-posts, not to mention possibly taking away the right to appeal.

The spirit of the FOIA, as well as U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder's memorandum, is transparency in disclosure. When one submits a FOIA request to obtain certain records and records are disclosed to the requester(s) with as much openness and transparency as possible within the nine exemptions, this-is-transparency. We do not think the intention of the FOIA was to create an online public warehouse for records requested by just one individual, which the "general public" might, but more like not, have any interest. Remember, in responding to some requests, we must make sure that the "general public" criteria are met. In addition, we already publish many, many records on our public websites that do not require a FOIA request.

Again, although we use the proactive disclosure mechanism now in place, we very rarely see the machine at work. In other words, we do not often receive three requests for the same records. Therefore, how does it make sense to post online records responsive to just one request?

The DOJ FOIA regulation is the parent of our DOI FOIA regulation, so we will use what we are comfortable with, the DOI FOIA regulation, in making our additional argument against the proposed rule.

If you approve the proposed ruling, it may all but eviscerate FOIA regulations. For instance, all the sections of the regulation that pertain to fee categories, fees, and fee waivers will be a moot discussion, unless they will pertain only to the first requester.

This proposal generates so many questions that we know we have not thought of a fraction of them. Moreover, we do not think there are any satisfactory answers to go forward with this proposal. Again, we think that if you approve this proposed ruling, it will be neither efficient nor provide sincere transparency.

Thank you for your consideration of our comments.
