Demand Progress appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed guidance implementing "Release to One is a Release to All," docket number DOJ-LA-2016-0024-0001. Our comments focus on timing of posting and section 508 compliance.

TIMING OF POSTING

We support option 1, that agencies should post documents online as soon as administratively feasible following a release
to a requester. While we are sympathetic to a request for delay, especially one made by some journalists, we believe that an "exclusivity" delay is unworkable and contrary for the provisions of the statute.

For example, imagine a circumstance where a particular record is of widespread interest to the media. Under a simultaneous online release policy, it's likely that fewer journalists would file FOIA requests for the same record, knowing that someone has requested it and it will become available online to all at once. But, in a circumstance where the requester is given exclusive access (with an online publication delay), more journalists would feel compelled to file. This defeats the regulation's purpose, which is to diminish multiple requests and provide timely access to all.

Similarly, once a journalist has written about a record, if it is not publicly available from an authoritative source, other journalists likely will file and ask for a copy themselves. In other words, the online publication delay may prompt additional FOIA requests.

In addition, the concept of exclusive access described in the proposed regulation is a misnomer. Imagine that an office receives requests from two requesters for same documents received one day apart -- one on March 1, the other on March 2nd. If the purpose of the online publication delay is exclusivity to the first requester, it would be undermined by processing the request from the second requester. Either the response to the second requester would have to be held for a period of days to guarantee exclusivity, a position not supported by the law and unwise from a policy perspective, or the record would be provided to the second requester on a timely basis, undermining the idea of exclusive access.

In effect, what you describe is exclusive _authoritative_ online publication, but the original recipient may publish an (unofficial) version online or additional requesters may receive an authoritative copy prior to the end of the exclusivity period. Either way, this does not serve either the goal of exclusivity or the idea of timely access for everyone.

Finally, to whom should this policy of exclusive authoritative access apply? Presumably it should not be everyone, as there are many instances where corporations use FOIA to access information about the government -- information that can move financial markets and the exclusive access to which would unsettle markets and create information asymmetries. FOIA requests could be weaponized, in fact, as a way of _preventing_ rivals from accessing particular information in a timely fashion. There should not be a race to file FOIA requests.

Similarly, if we assume this should only apply to journalists, we go down the bumpy road of trying to determine who constitutes a journalist for the purpose of triggering the delay. As the application of who counts as a journalist can vary from request to request, and agency to agency, I loathe to think about the litigation that likely would ensue here where exclusive access is predicated upon this kind of determination. This is a thicket that agencies would be best to avoid.

It may be true that some journalists may forgo filing FOIA requests in an effort to "free ride" off of others who make the requests. Although it seems more likely that a delay in online access will cause multiple journalists to file the same request, creating a drain on government sources. Regardless, FOIA is not intended as a journalist access law; it is intended as a public access law, with information available to all. Furthermore, concerns that providing online access to all journalists will create a feeding frenzy with the concomitant result of less substantive coverage describes the world we live in now; it is difficult to see how that will appreciably change or be an issue that DOJ should address.

SECTION 508 compliance

The section of the guidance focused on Section 508 compliance seems underdeveloped. As the recent meeting of the FOIA Advisory Committee illustrated, there is a lack of clarity about what 508 requires, especially circumstances where its undue burden exemption can be invoked. I would suggest that the purposes of this guidance will be severely undermined if online publication requires first the re-creation of records in a 508 compliant format, which may itself be a violation of the new FOIA statute. In the online context, the ability to request records be available in a 508 compliant format, and not a requirement that records be published in that format, may be more appropriate.

Thank you for this opportunity to comment.

We welcome the opportunity to comment upon the Department's proposed "release-to-one, release-to-all" policy for fulfilling requests made under the Freedom of Information Act. The Sunlight Foundation strongly supports the proposal overall, with some specific concerns regarding individual components in the draft regarding overly broad exemptions and exceptions.

As a decade-old nonpartisan, nonprofit organization dedicated to using journalism, advocacy and technology to improving the transparency and accountability of our politics and government, we see great potential for this approach to improve public knowledge of the operations of government, reduce the costs of administering one of the core sunshine laws of the nation, and reduce asynchronies in the disclosure of government data that are providing an unintended subsidy to industry.

As we have argued in the past, this policy represents a significant change in the nation's information disclosure policies that would not only complement recent updates to how the federal government protects, structures and publishes public records but could, in the long run, increase public knowledge of what is being done in our name. Governments everywhere should use the demand signal of FOIA requests to prioritize proactive disclosures online.

Structuring and publishing the datasets that commercial interests repeatedly, frequently request should increase the capacity of FOIA officers to respond to more complex public interest requests. We hope that agency CIOs will work directly with the nation's FOIA officers to apply Project Open Data's resources to proactive disclosure of records online in machine-readable format.

Should the proactive disclosure of records as open government data be directly tied to the demand expressed by inbound FOIA requests in 2017, we expect to see significant improvements in government transparency and accountability to not only occur in the U.S. federal government but secondary effects in other states and countries that learn from our example.

Lab accreditation for digital forensics would certainly achieve greater uniformity across the country however, without funding for every identifiable "lab" to achieve accreditation, this is unworkable.  The reality of digital forensics is that we rely upon the credentials of the examiners that they obtain through third party vendors, or in California, the California Department of Justice.  Once the examiner is sufficiently credentialed to conduct examinations with the particular vendor's product and testify in court as an expert witness, they have met the requisite burden.  Most vendors require re-certification on some recurring basis to maintain their certification.  Virtually every law enforcement agency in the United States has some device or capability that would arguably fall within the definition of a digital forensics lab, i.e. every agency with a Cellebrite for mobile device data extraction.  While they may have the resources to have some of their agents certified by Cellebrite, not every agency has the funding to establish an accredited "lab."  In order to establish the uniformity in accreditation that this recommendation suggests, there must be funding for law enforcement agencies to comply.  Another consideration that isn't discussed within the proposal is whether the accreditation would pre-suppose or require the use of a particular vendor's tools.  For instance, the FBI led RCFL's use, certify and train on Access Data products exclusively.  There are other competitors in the field who have superior products in many aspects.  Would the entity underwriting the accreditation test every forensic solution in existence and whitelist the ones it felt were most appropriate?  If a law enforcement agency couldn't afford to migrate to a whitelisted product, would that invalidate their lab?  In the alternative, would the entity be vendor neutral and rely upon the certifications of the examiners to establish a baseline.  In which case, it seems that accreditation would be unneeded, which is practically speaking where we collectively are now.

I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the National Commission on Forensic Science (NCFS), Subcommittee on Accreditation and Proficiency Testing recommendation (Draft 2 after Public Comment) to the Attorney General for the accreditation of digital and multimedia evidence (DME) forensic science service providers (FSSPs).

As previously stated in my correspondence dated April 5, 2016, the Department of Education Office of Inspector General (Education OIG) strongly supports the quality of forensic sciences. This office was in fact a key player in the effort of the Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency (CIGIE) to enact Quality Standards for Digital Forensics (QSDF) for the Inspector General community.

Although the second draft is a good step forward, we continue to have significant concerns with the emphasis on ISO 17025 as the de-facto standard to address digital analysis. Although ISO 17025 is currently used as the standard to accredit forensic labs (primarily traditional wet-labs), we believe that the use of standards more directly related to the type of work done in digital forensics would not only enhance quality, but would be more efficient than applying the predominantly "testing and calibration" centric standards as reflected in ISO 17025. While the appropriate standard is being developed, we do agree that the "Views of the Commission Regarding Critical Steps to Accreditation" document outlines useful quality steps. We note that with minor enhancements, CIGIE's QSDF addresses those quality steps.

Additionally, we point out that the subcommittee's recommendation that Federal prosecutors should be required to contract with accredited DME FSSPs excluding "analyses conducted prior to the involvement of a Federal prosecutor" fails to fully appreciate the investigation and prosecutorial process. It is the norm for investigative agencies, including Education OIG, to contact a prosecutor early in the process; in fact, the Inspector General Act of 1978, as amended, requires us to "report expeditiously" to the Department of Justice "whenever the Inspector General has reasonable grounds to believe there has been a violation of Federal criminal law." We also note that Federal prosecutors generally do not contract with FSSPs; instead, they rely on the digital forensic analyses performed by the investigatory agencies, including Offices of Inspectors General.

Lastly, I would continue to encourage a longer term, more collaborative approach where Federal, state, and local agencies conducting digital analysis would formulate, adopt, and implement standards that are realistic, practicable, and meet the original purposes of the subcommittee's recommendations. A rushed decision to require accreditation using only the ISO 17025 standards could have significant impact on agencies statutory responsibilities and negative repercussions on the administration of justice. The Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence (SWGDE) is currently an organization that exists to bring "together organizations actively engaged in the field of digital and multimedia evidence to foster communication and cooperation as well as to ensure quality and consistency within the forensic community." Federal agencies (such as ours) participate in SWGDE as an avenue to discuss such issues as the ones the subcommittee is considering.

Thank you for taking the time to review and consider our concerns. We look forward to working with the NCFS as it continues its important work.

I am not providing my contact information because I fear retaliation from the Department of Justice and, more specifically DOJ OSC, against me and my business, if I do provide that information. This NPRM proposes a vast expansion of OSC powers. I oppose portions of the NPRM as an unlawful, ultra vires, expansion of DOJ OSC power, and suggest that they should not be implemented as written. To be specific:

(1) Providing the public with only a 30-day comment period is contrary to the intent and express language of E.O. 12866, and is merely a politically motivated attempt to complete this rule as a "midnight regulation" before the end of the Obama Administration. OIRA has testified that it will not permit these types of regulations, and requested that agencies submit their proposed rules early to avoid this type of last-minute rulemaking activity. As such, OIRA should, at a minimum, require DOJ to extend the comment period related to this proposed rule to permit the public to have a full and fair opportunity to comment.

(2) With respect to the new definition at 44.101(f): 8 USC 1324b(a)(6) says "for purposes of satisfying the requirements of section 1324a(b)." This is not ambiguous. It refers directly to the I-9 process and not to "any" other employment eligibility verification process. The E-Verify law does not cite 1324a(b), and using E-Verify does not "satisfy the requirements of 1324a(b). Other types of employment processes, like state processes (see Colorado and West Virginia) vaccination law compliance, tax law compliance, and criminal background checks, are not covered by 1324b(a)(6), but under this rule OSC could investigate and charge an employer for alleged misuse of any of these "efforts to verify an individual's employment eligibility." This language is much more broad than the Mar-Jac language. Mar-Jac did not include "other" employment eligibility process like drug testing and tax compliance under 1324b(6). Mar-Jac relied on the E-Verify MOA, under which DOJ may request information from USCIS on E-Verify use to support DOJ investigations into document abuse in 1324a(b) processes. That MOA cannot expand 1324b(6) jurisdiction to "any" other process. The proposed definition needs to more appropriately define the reach of 1324b(6) to only employment eligibility verification processes that include those processes associated with actually satisfying the requirements of 1324a(b), i.e., the Form I-9, and maybe E-Verify but not other processes.

(3) The intent definition at 44.101(e) is overly broad. In a strange twist, that definition would actually apply to employers who intentionally treat individuals differently even if they want to help them through the employment eligibility process. This can't be what DOJ means, but it is what it says. Would an employer be violating your regulation if they hired a sign language interpreter to help a person fill out form I-9? The employer treated the person differently in that case. What if they permitted a friend or family member to help translate the form? Again, treating the person different. Although this is not a logical reason to charge an employer, it does seem that under your regulation, and a different Administration, some employers could be charged for actually helping legal immigrants obtain jobs (perhaps to the exclusion of citizens). Congress wanted this law to apply to employers who intentionally discriminate out of ill will or a some other bad motive. Your definition needs to reflect that Congressional intent.

There are undoubtedly more problems with your regulation, but I do not have time to do more research under your 30-day time deadline. But I will mention that in INA 274b(c) the law requires the President to appoint a Special Counsel for "Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices," not the more broad all-encompassing "Employee Rights" you suggest for your name. Your proposed name change is thus not in line with the statute. It is possible that the Special Counsel provided in the statute would not have legal authority to oversee "Employee Rights" cases in this new, broader office.

Dear Attorney General Lynch,

MBG Marketing submits these comments on the Department of Justice's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking - Standards and Procedures for the Enforcement of the Immigration and Nationality Act. 81 Fed. Reg. 53965 (Aug. 15, 2016) ("NPRM" or "Proposed Rule"). We are a grower-owned blueberry marketing cooperative with growers in eight states. MBG's member-owners are employers that will bear the added burden and uncertainty created by this Notice of Proposed Rulemaking.

The Proposed Rule threatens to impose penalties on employers far beyond what Congress ever intended or how the underlying statute has ever been applied. The current rule, in place for nearly 30 years, requires two things to find a violation and impose penalties against an employer: (1) a discriminatory intent or purpose on the part of an employer; and (2) proof that the charging party was harmed. This is supported by judicial decisions and consistent with established Title VII law. The proposed rule would erase those two requirements and establish a strict liability rule.

For small and seasonal businesses, particularly those in agriculture, workers are hired quickly at the beginning of the growing or working season, and there is often high turnover during the season. A small family-owned business might have only a handful of year-round employees but may hire dozens or even hundreds of seasonal workers during a season to replace those who leave after a few weeks or even a few days. A limited staff, often the owner or a family member, must complete a Form I-9 for each of those workers, in a workforce that is often comprised of non-citizens and workers with little or no proficiency in speaking or reading English. If a lawful permanent resident presents a "green card" to complete the I-9 process but a U.S. citizen provides a driver's license and Social Security card, without any prompting by the employer and where both are hired and begin work immediately, there is no intent to discriminate, no act of discrimination by the employer, and no harm to either employee. Still, such a situation could trigger sizable penalties under this new rule.

This is a highly technical rule dealing with nuanced arguments about the degree of intent or purpose behind an action, but it carries a very real possibility of injuring small and seasonal employers, particularly those in agriculture. The burden of this rule on the employer community will also be far greater than the estimate provided in the NPRM. The rule, as proposed, represents a costly, dangerous, and radical departure from longstanding substantive and procedural law on this subject and should be changed or abandoned by the Department of Justice.

The fundamental problem with this proposed rule is that it seeks to eliminate the knowledge and intent requirements included in the statute, lowering the bar for Special Counsel prosecutions and abandoning longstanding Title VII jurisprudence. This flies in the face of Congressional intent and three decades of practice and interpretation. Additionally, the NPRM has a significant impact as defined by the RFA and Executive Order 12866. We oppose the regulation as proposed and urge its withdrawal. We appreciate your consideration of our comments.

Sincerely,

MBG Marketing

These types of entities are automatically considered "other than small business" because SBA cannot determine their business size standards and they are not eligible for socioeconomic categories. The System for Award Management (SAM) displays these types of foreign entities as "other than small", even though many would normally be considered small. Therefore Contracting Officers/Contract Specialists/Purchasing Agents report foreign entities in Federal Procurement Data System (FPDS) as "other than small" upon reporting contract awards because that's what the information in SAM shows.

The data used to support this FAR proposed rule change is largely based on data from SAM and FPDS on contract award for performance overseas, but the data by default shows all foreign entities as "other than small".

I'm also curious as to how this would impact the DoD requirement at DFARS 219.201. Would DoD agencies outside of the U.S. have to start using DD Form 2579 - Small Business Coordination Record? There's a lot that is unclear in these proposed rule changes and much more detail is needed. The changes seem to really only benefit U.S. owned small businesses and it would absolutely create confusion for government agencies overseas. These changes would also drive up prices and negatively impact the U.S. taxpayer. Foreign owned entities will almost always have better pricing for contracts which performance is overseas versus U.S. owned small businesses. The proposed change to FAR 19.000(b) is not clear. Specifically, it is not clear what you mean by a contracting officer "applying" FAR part 19 inside/outside the United States and its outlying areas. Does "application" of a part take place where the contracting officer is physically located or where contract performance will take place? If the answer is where contract performance takes place, then how does a contracting officer determine where a supply contract takes place prior to issuing a solicitation? Is it where delivery is required? There are six potential scenarios, only two of which seem clear.

1. Contracting officer located in US/outlying areas, service contract with place of performance in US/outlying areas, contracting officer shall apply FAR part 19.

2. Contracting officer located in US/outlying areas, supply contract requiring delivery to US/outlying areas, contracting officer shall apply FAR part 19.

3. Contracting officer located in US/outlying areas, service contract with place of performance outside US/outlying areas, unclear whether application of FAR part 19 mandatory or optional.

4. Contracting officer located in US/outlying areas, supply contract requiring delivery outside US/outlying areas, unclear whether application of FAR part 19 mandatory or optional.

5. Contracting officer located outside US/outlying areas, service contract with place of performance in US/outlying areas, unclear whether application of FAR part 19 mandatory or optional.

6. Contracting officer located outside US/outlying areas, supply contract requiring delivery to US/outlying areas, unclear whether application of FAR part 19 mandatory or optional.

It would be clearer if FAR 19.000(b) stated that contracting officers shall/may apply FAR part 19 to contracts performed inside/outside the US/outlying areas. Then, either add a definition or explanatory paragraph that says for service contracts a contract is performed where the services take place and for supply contracts a contract is performed where delivery takes place (if that is your intention).

I think that this rule is a great idea. Set-aside rules should equally apply to CONUS and OCONUS contracts. A plethora of small businesses exist which can benefit the US Government in the international arena. There are many times when a small business will be more capable than a large business in fulfilling overseas contracts. I am glad that the law will reflect this fact.

As an EDWOSB owner who works in national security, I FULLY support this rule. I routinely deal with contracting officers at overseas DoD HQs who have no idea whether or not small business procurement rules apply overseas, and sadly, are not motivated or do not know where to reach out to find a definitive answer. So, contracting officials end up erring on the side of caution and assume they are NOT allowed to do small business set asides or sole sourcing for OCONUS service contracts. This has happened to our business on at least five occasions. The current ambiguity of FAR regs has not only resulted in my small business losing contracts, but has cost the govt significantly more time and money to go through full and open competitions and still end up NOT with the vendor they wanted in the first place. The proposed rule is critical to clear up confusion among contracting officials, save govt resources, and ensure the spirit of the FAR, NDAA and SBA is fully realized: to promote US small business opportunities in federal contracting, which is good for the US economy. Where services are performed should be irrelevant to advancing this goal.

Small business contractors have shown they are not capable of managing the significant risks involved in overseas construction. I have personally managed almost $90 million in small business federal construction contracts. All contractors have had difficulties with supply chain management, meeting specified staffing requirements, understanding local market conditions, and managing local subcontractors and material suppliers. One of the companies requested and was granted a waiver of the performance and payment bonds and another did not have the capital to obtain full bonding and required supplemental funds from the USG to finalize, exposing the USG to unneeded risk. Performing construction overseas requires a robust and mature team of construction professionals who can utilize established supply chains, experienced security facility officers, and a depth of company veterans versed in overseas federal construction requirements. Small businesses often rely on temporary workers and contract employees, AKA hired guns, brought in for specific assignments. All projects I have been involved with are significantly over budget, delayed, of average quality, and encumbered by significant claims. Small business contractors should mature their companies in the domestic market, develop a bench strength of experienced professionals, and establish a track record of successful federal government performance before taking on the monumental challenges and complexities of work in the foreign environment. The USG is doing a disservice to these companies by setting them up to fail while needlessly exposing its mission to unneeded risk, schedule delays, and cost overruns in environments where failure is not an option.

We are a Small Business, and we are not in favor of this change, even though it appears to be a done deal already.
The SBA is really the United States Small Business Administration, not the NATO SBA or the USMCA SBA or the UN SBA or the UK SBA, in other words, if the small business is not a United States owned run and located small business then why are expecting US Taxpayers to sponsor, support, solicit and allow non US small businesses, become benefactors of the US Federal Procurement regulations? US Federal contracts awarded in CONUS and performed OCONUS are different than whats being discussed here. Those are already allowed and should be.
The US DoD agencies already, largely ignore, the existing Federal set aside regulations, and interpret them in ways that do not impede the agencies ability to expeditiously award to large businesses. Instead of trying to fictitiously bolster the SBA set aside numbers, which is the only real reason for this exercise, why not force compliance with existing set aside regulations?
Here is a start, if the solicitation was not set aside then the agency should not get credit for the award in the post award state. Meaning, if the form 2579 was not signed off, in the positive, and the solicitation was set aside, but it was left as a fully open and competitive with no set aside, then even if a small wins the award, there should be zero credit for the small winning the award because neither the SBO or the SBA had anything to do with its award to a small. If the SBO or the SBA, does not do their job in making solicitations set aside for smalls, and not forcing the smalls to compete against the larges, then why do they get credit for non-compliance?
The other topic would be large companies now getting credit for small business sub-contracting, all the way through the entire supply chain, which they neither control or work directly with. Here is another thought, force large business subcontracting compliance, at the prime level only, or cancel the contracts if they dont comply. But the answer, instead of compliance, appears to be, lets expand who the United States approves as a CONUS small business, to now include foreign located, foreign owned, foreign controlled OCONUS companies. The Unites States Small Business Administration used to have a Federal regulation that unless the small business was owned and located in the United States, then it was not a small business which could benefit from the United States procurement regulations, and that should be the law of the land.
Regardless, this policy shift is absolutely nothing more than the allowing the SBA and the agency level SBOs, permission to take credit for additional small business awards in the post award state. Our position was and continues to be, force the US Federal agencies to comply with the set aside regulations already in place by the US Code and no longer allow credit towards goals, which neither the SBA or SBO had any hand in assisting, IE: form 2579s, and no more credit for post awards numbers, if it wasnt set aside at the solicitation level, than its not a set aside contract. Our US SBA regulations should be for US small business owned controlled and operated companies only.

Disclaimer: I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule captioned above. I have worked with Government acquisitions for more than 17 years, but I am commenting in my personal capacity. My comments do not represent the views of the Department of the Army or any federal agency.

The proposed rule does not account for the long held positions of the Department of Defense:

a)It has been the legal position of the Department of Defense (DoD) that the Small Business Act does not apply outside of the United States and its outlying areas. Since at least 1971, the Armed Services Procurement Regulation (ASPR) has included a provision that only made applicable the Small Business Act inside the United States and it territories. See e.g. To Mr. Secretary, B-172888, July 15, 1971, 1971 U.S. Comp. Gen. LEXIS 2406 (discussing ASPR 1-700 which provides that the Small Business Act is not to be applied to contracts which are awarded and are to be performed in foreign countries.) Absent a statement of Congressional intent, GAO has deferred to DoDs interpretation of the Small Business Act embodied in FAR 19.000(b), This part, except for Subpart 19.6, applies only in the United States or its outlying areas. Subpart 19.6 applies worldwide. See Matter of: Latvian Connection Gen. Trading & Constr. LLC, B-408633, 2013 CPD 224, September 8, 2013.

b)GAOs deference to DoDs interpretation embodied in the FAR is an example of Chevron deference. Chevron deference does not give agencies license to follow statutes to the extent they deem desirable; instead, it is deference to an agencys permissible interpretation of an ambiguous statute. Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837, 842-43 (1984).

Disclaimer: I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule captioned above. I have worked with Government acquisitions for more than 17 years, but I am commenting in my personal capacity. My comments do not represent the views of the Department of the Army or any federal agency.

1.This proposed rule overreaches Congressional intent.

a)The U.S. Supreme Court holdings provide that a statute must show affirmative intent to apply overseas and reconcile conflicts of law. See EEOC v. Arabian Am. Oil Co., 499 U.S. 244, 111 S. Ct. 1227, 1991 U.S. LEXIS 1855 (1991); Foley Bros., Inc. v. Filardo, 336 U.S. 281, 69 S. Ct. 575, 1949 U.S. LEXIS 2929 (1949). As addressed in the 2013 GAO Latvian decision, B-408633, Section 15 of the Small Business Act is silent in regard to its application overseas. Latvian Connection Gen. Trading & Constr. LLC, B-408633, 2013 CPD 224, September 8, 2013. It is a well settled canon of statutory construction that unless a contrary intent appears, legislation of Congress is meant to apply only within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States. Foley Bros., 336 U.S. 281, supra, (The canon of construction which teaches that legislation of Congress, unless a contrary intent appears, is meant to apply only within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States [citation omitted] is a valid approach whereby unexpressed congressional intent may be ascertained. It is based on the assumption that Congress is primarily concerned with domestic conditions. For example, in Arabian, supra, the Court examined whether Title VII applied extraterritorially. 499 U.S. 244 (1991). The Court wrote that we look to see whether language in the [relevant Act] gives any indication of a congressional purpose to extend its coverage beyond places over which the United States has sovereignty or has some measure of legislative control. Id. at 248, citing Foley Bros. 336 U.S. at 285, supra. Unless there is the affirmative intention of the Congress clearly expressed, we must presume it is primarily concerned with domestic conditions. Id.

b)The proposed change to FAR 19.000 to state that contracting officers may apply all of the provisions of FAR Part 19 outside the United States and its outlying areas has the weakness of not being a plausible interpretation of any statute. The problem with the rule where set-asides MAY be performed outside the United States is that no law, other than this proposed rule, permits set-asides outside the United States nor accounts for or reconciles the numerous conflicts with international agreements or foreign laws. Since the Small Business Act did not specify that it applied overseas nor account for conflicts with international agreements and foreign law, the controlling case law on federal statutory construction would conclude that it does not. There is nothing stated or expressed in the Small Business Act that demonstrates any intent by Congress to make the Act apply outside the United States. Therefore, it would be inconsistent with U.S. Supreme Court precedent to attempt to stretch its application beyond what was clearly intended by Congress. This proposed rule purports to extend the application of the Small Business Act beyond what was intended by Congress.

Disclaimer: I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule captioned above. I have worked with Government acquisitions for more than 17 years, but I am commenting in my personal capacity. My comments do not represent the views of the Department of the Army or any federal agency.

a)In accordance with the FAR part 2 definition of bundling, bundling is a subset of consolidation. In addition, bundling involves combining requirements for supplies or services such that it is likely to be unsuitable for award to small business; the definition currently excludes contracts that will be awarded and performed entirely outside the United States. The proposed rule change would remove language stating that bundling does not apply to contracts that will be awarded and performed entirely outside the United States.

b)FAR 7.107-2, Consolidation, notes that because of the potential impact on small business participation, before conducting an acquisition that is a consolidation of requirements with an estimated total dollar value exceeding $2 million, the senior procurement executive or chief acquisition officer shall make a written determination that the consolidation is necessary and justified in accordance with 15 U.S.C. 657q . . . . FAR 7.107-3, Bundling, notes that because of the potential impact on small business participation, before conducting an acquisition strategy that involves bundling, the agency shall make a written determination that the bundling is necessary and justified in accordance with 15 U.S.C. 644(e).

c)The proposed rule change would now put contracts to be awarded and performed overseas within the FAR bundling definition. The result would be that overseas contracting offices would be subject to bundling and consolidation requirements. This is despite the proposed rule language that purports to make the decision to set aside discretionary outside the United States. The two principles are inherently conflicting. If a set-aside is discretionary outside the United States, this proposed rule purports to make bundling and consolidation justifications mandatory. The proposed rule requires clarity on these matters.

d)The application of the restrictions on bundling to overseas procurement would make it significantly more difficult to use indefinite delivery indefinite quantity contracts and other contract vehicles to fulfill agency requirements, will have negative effects overseas. This would impose heavy burdens and delays in the procurement process and in effect potentially require a Contracting Officer to justify not applying FAR part 19 when the application is supposed to be discretionary under the rule. The extension of FAR 7.107-3 and 7.107-4 would have the effect of making overseas procurement actions involving bundling extremely burdensome and time consuming and unlikely to occur, but the rule fails to provide clarity as to whether the bundling justification would be required despite the set aside determination being discretionary.

e)One reason why making bundling is problematic is that it can be, and often is, inconsistent with international agreements, Foreign Military Sales (FMS) letters of offer and acceptance, and other arrangements with foreign partners that are funding acquisitions. With regard to FMS, a foreign purchaser has the right to direct limitations on competition, and, in practice, this extends to directing the procurement approach to a certain extent, subject to acceptance by the implementing agency. Simply, if foreign purchasers perceive efficiencies or other benefits from bundling requirements that the U.S. government has previously fulfilled in smaller procurements and procuring agencies are not able to follow their reasonable directions readily, agencies, and consequently U.S. companies, may lose FMS business. In addition, the proposed change will prohibit the implementation of acquisition approaches and source restrictions that the U.S. government has already agreed to in international agreements and other arrangements with foreign partners. Failure to honor these agreements may result in legal liability and diplomatic repercussions.

f)In addition, bundling is an important tool for agencies regularly procuring services overseas outside of the context of an arrangement with a foreign partner. Finding vendors that are willing and able to fulfill government requirements well and promptly can be difficult in various foreign areas. Agency experience often drives the development of bundled procurements for use in these foreign areas in order to provide capable prospective offerors with the prospect of enough work to induce them to enter markets, develop their capabilities, and compete in procurements when adequate capabilities are not otherwise available.

Disclaimer: I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule captioned above. I have worked with Government acquisitions for more than 17 years, but I am commenting in my personal capacity. My comments do not represent the views of the Department of the Army or any federal agency.

The proposed rule provides no guidance to the Contracting Officer regarding parameters or requirements to follow in exercising discretion.

a)The proposed change to FAR 19.000 gives no guidance whatsoever as to how contracting officers should decide whether or not to set procurements outside of the United States and is outlying areas aside for small business, yet it vests the discretion to set otherwise qualifying procurements aside or not in Contracting Officers. Whether or not a procurement is suitable for a small business set aside depends upon a wide variety of factors, including international agreement obligations, as well as other factors, some quite technical, with respect to both the work being procured and economic theory and conditions. Furthermore, the challenges that can make it difficult for small businesses to succeed and survive in international dealings, especially projects of extended duration overseas, are numerous, vary by region and country, and change over time. In addition, the determination of the factors to be considered as to any particular procurement, as well as applying and weighing them, is inherently subjective and is likely to become controversial among members of the acquisition workforce. Determining whether or not overseas procurements should be set aside would place an unnecessary burden on Contracting Officers and their advisors, and thus on the acquisition process.

b)Moreover, the subjectivity inherent in the discretion to set-aside overseas procurements or not introduces a prime opportunity for prospective offerors that perceive they would benefit from set asides, or from full and open competition, to seek to influence government personnel involved in overseas acquisitions in corrupt and other improper ways. This is particularly so since, in many foreign countries, there will likely be very few U.S. small businesses that are capable of fulfilling any particular type of complicated government requirement.

c)Outside of FAR Part 19, the FAR in Part 25, Foreign Acquisition, is problematic when attempting to reconcile it with this proposed rule. FAR Subpart 25.802 and DFARS Subpart 225.7401 both require the Contracting Officer to conduct the necessary advance acquisition planning and to incorporate relevant requirements of international agreements into the solicitation and the contract, when contracts are to be performed overseas. Accordingly, consideration of agreements for any operational contracting in the Department of Defense and the Army is mandatory at the planning stage of an acquisition, as well. Department of Defense Instruction (DODI) 3020.41, Encl. 2, p. 11 (1.h. and 1.i) (2011) and Army Regulation (AR) 7159, 2-1(d) and AR 700-137, para. 3-6.

This proposed rule fails to provide direction to a Contracting Officer or require the Contracting Officer to document the decision as to how to account for requirements of international agreements when making discretionary set aside determinations.

Disclaimer: I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule captioned above. I have worked with Government acquisitions for more than 17 years, but I am commenting in my personal capacity. My comments do not represent the views of the Department of the Army or any federal agency.

a)An exception to the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA), 10 U.S.C. 2304(b)(2), allows agencies to exclude all but small businesses in furtherance of section 9 and 15 of the Small Business Act. However, another of these exceptions to full and open competition, 10 U.S.C. 2304(c)(4), states Full and open competition need not be provided for when precluded by the terms of an international agreement or a treaty between the United States and a foreign government or international organization, or the written directions of a foreign government reimbursing the agency for the cost of the acquisition of the supplies or services for such government. In other words, when work is contracted outside the United States, CICA requires full and open competition unless a treaty or international agreement separately requires the use of noncompetitive procedures. Therefore, CICA explains how it was intended by Congress to apply extraterritorially. The Small Business Act fails to do the same and the proposed rule equally fails to reconcile treaty obligations of the United States vis a vis the Small Business Act.

b)Contrary to the plain language in the proposed rule, the Contracting Officer may not have the discretion to apply FAR part 19 to most construction and services contracts to be performed in a foreign overseas location due to international treaty obligations or other applicable international agreements or local laws. Treaties and international agreements are treated as paramount and are recognized as authorized restrictions on competition outside the United States. If a relevant agreement exists, the federal Contracting Officer would be precluded from soliciting any other source of contractors than specified in the Agreement, including U.S. small or disadvantaged businesses.

c)The proposed rule states that Contracting Officers will have discretion as to whether to apply FAR part 19 procedures overseas: [t]his proposed rule will clarify that Contracting Officers are allowed, but not required, to use set-aside and sole source procedures of FAR part 19 for overseas procurements. The language of the proposed rule could generate confusion among Contracting Officers and the SBA, possibly misleading them to think that Contracting Officers are allowed to set-aside procurements for contracts to be performed overseas without restriction. The proposition that Contracting Officers have discretion to apply FAR part 19 to overseas procurements is inaccurate in many cases.

d)There are countless Defense agreements that restrict competition to local contractors. For example, there are multiple countries that have technical and responsibility-type pre-qualification procedures in place such that only pre-qualified offerors may be solicited. In some cases, the host nation or a joint committee consisting of U.S. and host nation members must approve the offerors and awardees. Other countries utilize an indirect contracting system, where the host nation contracts for and administers the U.S. requirement under its laws and regulations. Some international agreements mandate direct solicitation of local offerors and require either the award be made only to a local contractor or that a local contractor receive the award if they are the best value. At a minimum, the U.S. Government has agreed that it will ensure that local contractors are affirmatively provided the opportunity to compete for contracts in their country. The proposed rule fails to account for these treaty obligations of the United States.

e)The relationship with the host nation could be damaged with resulting political fallout if the U.S. does not honor its international agreement obligations; note also that proposed changes to the bilateral relationship generally go through a SOFA Joint Committee and the host nation would have input and would have to concur with any proposed change to the relationship. Any argument that we now must award construction and services contracts for performance to U.S. small businesses instead of local sources due to a change in U.S. law would not be well received by the host nation.

Disclaimer: I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule. I have worked with Government acquisitions for more than 17 years, but I am commenting in my personal capacity.

Another problem with awarding contracts for performance overseas to U.S. small businesses is that they will likely have difficulty meeting mandatory self-performance requirements overseas. While large businesses that establish operations in foreign countries hire local employees and are able to re-assign employees overseas, small businesses will usually lack the necessary on-site personnel to meet requirements that prime contractors perform percentages of on-site work (typically 20 % to 35 % in construction). These self-performance requirements are important because they help to ensure that the government obtains the primes expertise that it bargained for and that the prime monitors compliance with contract requirements and takes responsibility for what it delivers.

Additionally, if a small business is required to self-perform at least 50% of services with its own employees, and incur at least 50% of manufacturing costs, currently required by FAR 19.508(e) and 19.811-3(e), it would be difficult to meet the requirements of host nation labor laws on the sovereign territory of another country. The DOD is required to apply host nation labor laws overseas. DFARS 222.7201. Labor laws that apply inside the US, such as the Service Contract Act and the Davis Bacon, do not apply outside the US. See FAR 22.1003-2 and FAR 22.403-1. The proposed rule does not provide direction to the Contracting Officer as to how to apply and administer the SBA self-performance requirements, yet also meet the host nation labor laws which require use of local labor in country, especially for construction projects. A foreign person, such as a US national, would need a legal work permit to work in that foreign country. For construction projects, the work is performed on the foreign territory so the labor to fulfill the contract will generally be local. Moreover, most foreign countries are not as flexible as the US is in ability to hire labor as at will employees or as independent contractors. In general, they would have to execute long term employment contracts with full benefits or import third country national labor and obtain extensive knowledge of the host nations immigration laws, and labor and employment laws. It is unlikely that a US small business will have these capabilities or expertise and offer those services at a fair and reasonable price.

Another unintended consequence is the cost of Value Added Taxes (VAT) on materials and supplies and services purchased in the foreign country, averaging approximately 20%. According to many international agreements, the contractors are exempt from paying VAT for work performed on behalf of the US Government, but generally the contractor must pay VAT at the initial point of sale and seek a refund from the foreign government. It generally takes 6 months to more than a year to obtain a refund in many countries. Small Businesses must have the capital and resources to finance 20% of a contract for a year or more before they are reimbursed.

U.S. small businesses, in most cases, are better off supplying their expertise in relation to specific aspects of the work under overseas acquisitions as subcontractors to prime contractors that are able to undertake, and may even have previously undertaken, the necessary preparations to perform the governments overall requirements. An additional unintended consequence of awarding more contracts for performance overseas to U.S. small businesses that can have only limited operations in the foreign countries concerned would be incurrence of excessive overhead charges in cost-type situations. A small business doing a limited amount of work in a foreign country will not have the large and diversified cost pools for home office/international operations and country office overhead that a large business typically does. When a cost-based expense arises under a fixed-price government contract, such as when there is a user-directed change or a termination for convenience, a small business performing overseas will, thus, legitimately charge the government significantly more overhead costs from above the site or project level than a large business, whose home office-type costs, including those for its in-country operations, would be distributed over more work than those of a small business.

Because exactly what preparations are required to succeed in a foreign market is very difficult to determine and varies with circumstances, the proposed change in FAR 19.000 is likely to result in financial hardships of U.S. small businesses that were not prepared to undertake the work they bid for, and consequent failures and delays of agencies procurements, as well as hardships for the US employees, customers, and suppliers that depended upon those small businesses.

Regulation is and has been clear that the "only" does not allow FAR 19 to be applied to performance outside the U.S. This is a established, well-known fact, and has been educated accordingly by institutions such as the Defense Acquisition University for well over a decade.
Non-U.S. businesses cannot classify as a small business, regardless of size. As a result, applying small business size standards outside the U.S. serves to limit competition to U.S. companies only, excluding foreign entities, and is contrary to CICA.
The end result would be a form of trade protectionism (U.S. businesses only) and socialist policy (subsidizing businesses that are otherwise too inefficient to compete without a government handout).
Small businesses, by their very nature, are ill-equipped to perform services and construction in non-neighboring foreign countries. In some countries, such as throughout the Middle East, foreign entities also cannot operate without sponsorship, meaning the employment of all its staff performing there by a foreign entity. The result of a small business set-aside in such a situation, for a service, for example, would necessitate that the U.S. small business subcontract all of the performing personnel to the foreign entity. The end result would be merely higher prices, higher liabilities, ignorance about the market and environment, and less control over the work. In other words, a waste of taxpayer dollars.
If used at all, this rule should exclude construction and services.

Disclaimer: I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule captioned above. I have worked with Government acquisitions for more than 17 years, but I am commenting in my personal capacity. My comments do not represent the views of the Department of the Army or any federal agency.

The proposed rule, if adopted, should be revised to indicate that overseas Contracting Officers will NOT have discretion to apply FAR part 19 when international treaties or international agreements require solicitation or award to host nation sources. Further, if the proposed rule is adopted, FAR part 19 should be revised to exclude overseas construction contracts from FAR part 19 coverage. If the proposed rule is not rescinded, FAR 19.000, Scope of part, (b) instead of being revised to simply state that FAR part 19 may apply overseas, should be revised as below:

(b) This part, except for subpart 19.6, applies only in the United States or its outlying areas, unless the Contracting Officer decides to apply FAR part 19 to a particular overseas procurement. However, Contracting Officers shall not apply FAR part 19, except for subpart 19.6, to (1) construction contracts that will be performed outside of the United States; and (2) contracts that will be performed outside of the United States that must be solicited or awarded to a host nation source due to international treaty obligations or international agreements. Subpart 19.6 applies worldwide.

FAR 19.309, Solicitation provisions and contract clauses, would need corresponding revisions to show when FAR part 19 related contract clauses need to be added to a solicitation.

Disclaimer: I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule captioned above. I have worked with Government acquisitions for more than 17 years, but I am commenting in my personal capacity. My comments do not represent the views of the Department of the Army or any federal agency.

Numerous patent conflicts exist within the FAR and DFARS that are not reconciled by the proposed rule.

a)A contractor is also not entitled to represent itself nor can it claim small business status outside the United States. The standard representation and certification clauses utilized in every FAR procurement, 52.204-8 -- Annual Representations and Certifications, and the companion clause for commercial item solicitations, 52.212-3, Offeror Representations and Certifications -- Commercial Items, explicitly provide in paragraphs (c)(ix) and (c), respectively, that small business representations only apply when the resulting contract is to be performed in the United States or its outlying areas. The proposed rule is unclear as to permitting a contractor to certify to such status under a FAR contract to be performed outside the U.S. or its outlying areas. The proposed rule is also unclear as to how a Contracting Officer could utilize that certification in his/her decision-making, based on the current language of these mandatory clauses.

b)It is also important to note that small business subcontracting plans are explicitly NOT required for any contract performed outside the United States or its outlying areas. 15 U.S.C. 637(d)(2)(B), FAR Subpart 19.702(b)(3) and Subpart 19.708. It would be illogical for an Agency to set-aside a prime contract overseas when that same agency is not permitted by law to regulate or require small business subcontracting when the contract work is performed entirely outside the United States and its outlying areas. In fact, in the Department of Defense, DFARS clause 252.225-7002(b), Qualifying Country Sources as Subcontractors, prohibits DoD contractors from precluding qualifying country sources or U.S. sources from competing for subcontracts under overseas contracts.

c)Other areas of conflict between this proposed rule and foreign acquisition include the Buy American Act provisions that apply only inside the United States which generally require only U.S. materials and end products. The Balance of Payments regulations, however, apply outside the United States. DFARS Subpart 225.75. Balance of Payments regulations prohibit discriminatory treatment of certain foreign materials and products depending on thresholds and other determinations. It is left unexplained how Balance of Payments requirements would be reconciled with small business self-performance requirements, FAR clause 52.219-14, especially in the area of supply manufacturing. In addition, the World Trade Organization signatories Agreement on Government Procurement states, inter alia, that: In respect of the procurement covered by the Agreement, Parties to the Agreement are required to accord to the products, services and suppliers of any other Party to the Agreement treatment no less favourable than they give to their domestic products, services and suppliers (Article III:1(a)) Further Parties may not discriminate among goods, services and suppliers of other Parties (Article III:1(b)) In addition, each Party is required to ensure that its entities do not treat domestic suppliers differently on the basis of a greater or lesser degree of foreign affiliation or ownership as well as to ensure that its entities do not discriminate against domestic suppliers because their good or service is produced in the territory of another Party (Article III:2).

These provisions are just a small sampling of the patent conflicts between foreign acquisition requirements and the proposed rule does not provide guidance and clarity of what a Contracting Officer must consider in determining whether to set aside a procurement.

Adoption of this rule will only add time, without corresponding value, to the acquisition of supplies and services for OCONUS requirements. Nothing precludes Small Businesses from competing for these requirements at present, but requiring Contracting Officers to consider SB Goals and set asides in addition to the more complex sourcing of overseas requirements will only add acquisition lead time without any improvement in the acquisition outcome. As a result, this rule should not be adopted as it does not offer any value, yet increases costs.

Disclaimer: I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule captioned above. I have worked with Government acquisitions for more than 17 years, but I am commenting in my personal capacity. My comments do not represent the views of the Department of the Army or any federal agency.

The bundling and consolidation procedures are designed to protect U.S. small businesses. Thus, when award is intended for a host nation source, as is the case with most contracts to be performed in a foreign country, the Contracting Officer should be allowed to consolidate and/or bundle requirements with a view to the local market without going through consolidation or bundling procedures intended to protect U.S. small businesses authorized by the Small Business Act only. In addition, if set asides are discretionary outside the United States, then it does not make logicial sense to make Small Business Act requirements intended to protect US small businesses such as consolidation and bundling, mandatory on these discretionary set-asides.

If the proposed rule is not rescinded or substantially revised, the paragraph (3) of the FAR subpart 2.1 bundling definition should be revised as below, to ensure bundling would come into play only AFTER a Contracting Officer decides to set aside a requirement for small businesses outside the United States:

(3) This definition does not apply to a contract that will be awarded and performed entirely outside of the United States, unless the Contracting Officer decides to apply FAR part 19 to a particular overseas procurement. Further the FAR subpart 2.1 definition of consolidation or consolidated requirement should have a paragraph (3) added: (3) This definition does not apply to a contract that will be awarded and performed entirely outside of the United States, unless the Contracting Officer decides to apply FAR part 19 to a particular overseas procurement.

Disclaimer: I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule captioned above. I have worked with Government acquisitions for more than 17 years, but I am commenting in my personal capacity. My comments do not represent the views of the Department of the Army or any federal agency.

a)As a practical matter, overseas construction contracts especially are inherently local in nature in that they are tied to local labor and trades and generally require detailed knowledge of host nation building standards, local subcontracting rules, local permitting and licensing requirements, as well as host nation laws on labor, safety, and environmental matters. Overseas construction contracts in highly developed countries generally are not suitable for U.S. small businesses nor can U.S. small businesses offer a fair and reasonable price in comparison with local sources.

b)U.S. companies that are not large and sophisticated, with financial depth and local expertise, are unlikely to be successful in attempts to fulfill a wide variety of requirements overseas. A business operating outside of the context of its home legal and regulatory system, as well as the social and market conditions in which it developed, and with which its personnel are most familiar, is certain to encounter a wide variety of unforeseen impediments and costs in addition to almost all of those it would encounter when performing in its home country. It is simply not possible for a Contracting Officer in determining whether or not to set-aside a procurement, or for the SBA in implementing its Certificate of Competency process, to model these impediments and costs or to determine what their impacts would be in a particular country in a particular procurement. The Contracting Officer will not be able to operate as the business advisor of a U.S. small business attempting the difficult task of setting up operations and performing in a foreign country. The risks involved in setting up operations and performing outside the United States are high and U.S. small businesses may end up suffering substantial losses that they cannot absorb. As a result, despite Contracting Officers best intentions, small business set asides of procurements for performance overseas would result in higher rates of default, delay, and claims than those encountered under unrestricted competitions or inclusion of host nation firms.

c)Large businesses, in general, because of their financial and personnel depth, as well as expectations that they will be able to establish continuing and substantial operations in foreign countries, go through processes to establish operations in specific foreign countries. These processes include retaining local lawyers, accountants, and consultants, assigning personnel to learn how to operate within local business norms, and establishing reliable sources of supply in the local economy. Attempting to establish business operations can be complex and resource consuming due to many factors, such as navigating host-nation legal/regulatory systems, including taxes, immigration, subcontracting rules, and licenses/permits, including the time consuming process of attempting to establish business connections and supply/subcontractor sources within the host nation. A small business is unlikely to be capable of making the necessary capital outlay, assigning the necessary personnel, or offering local partners sufficient expectation of future work to make the same kinds of preparations effectively.

d)Architect-Engineer (AE) contracts in Japan, Korea, and NATO countries are also highly complex as they generally involve designing a project to local host nation technical standards and some U.S. standards, as well as determining whether additional host nation standards should be considered as acceptable alternatives to U.S. standards in order to make the project affordable to build and economical to maintain. Attempting to design a project in Japan or a NATO country usually requires some amount of coordination and consultation with host nation subcontractors. Particularly for life, health, and safety design features, conflicts of law issues can develop that may lead to project delays and increased costs; in some cases the AE could be liable for such increased costs. Further, in designing the project due consideration for host nation environmental procedures should generally be considered. AE contracts outside the United States are complex and high risk, they are not appropriate for U.S. small businesses.

e)In sum, for the small amount of contracts to be performed outside the United States that could go to U.S. sources (generally this is highly specialized work, either of a classified or secure nature or otherwise too specialized for local sources), the risk and complexities involved in such work within a foreign environment typically would make such work unsuitable for U.S. small businesses with limited ability to absorb losses.

In the event that the proposed changes to the FAR are adopted despite the concerns advanced in these comments, the delays and waste of labor associated with protests of decisions, at least, should be mitigated. Since the proposed change, if implemented, would express the opinion of the agencies that use the FAR that complying with the Small Business Act overseas is optional, they should be able to exempt complaints about noncompliance overseas from adjudication.

Thus, it is proposed that contracting officers decisions to set-aside, and not to set-aside, procurements outside of the United States and its outlying areas for small business, and advertisements of procurements alleged to represent bundling of requirements for performance outside of the United States and its outlying areas, be excluded from available grounds for protest.

This could be done with an additional sentence in each of FAR 19.000 and FAR 7.107-3 to state, A contracting officers determination to set-aside, or not to set aside, a procurement for performance outside of the United States and its outlying areas, for small business shall not be grounds for protest[,] and A contracting officers determination that a solicitation for performance overseas does not represent bundling shall not be grounds for protest.
See attachment.  Summary: references to $150K need to be updated to $250K to reflect the increase in the SAT.

The background section of the proposed rule states: "The SBA rule also clarified that the limitations on subcontracting and the nonmanufacturer rule do not apply to small business set-aside contracts valued at or below $150,000,..."

That is not true. The limitations on subcontracting and the nonmanufacturer do not apply at or below the "simplified acquisition threshold (SAT)" as that term is defined at FAR 2.101. The SBA regulation (13 CFR 121.406(d)) states:

"The performance requirements (limitations on subcontracting) and the nonmanufacturer rule do not apply to small business set-aside acquisitions with an estimated value between the micro-purchase threshold and the simplified acquisition threshold (as both terms are defined in the FAR at 48 CFR 2.101)."

The SAT can be as low as $250,000 or as high as $1.5 million, depending on the circumstances. As such, the figure "$150,000" should be replaced with "the simplified acquisition threshold" at proposed FAR 19.103(a)(1), 19.508(e), 19.508(g)(1)(i), 52.204-8(a)(3), 52.212-1(a), 52.219-1(b)(3), and 52.219-28(d).

It appears the adjustment for the administrative cost was based on a static analysis. Most contracting offices use some for of automation such as electronic contract writing systems and many seamlessly interface with IAE/SAM. This process automation coupled with productivity gains may more than offset the inflationary adjustment.

The proposed language at FAR 13.003(b)(1), 19.203(b), and 19.502-2(a) is inconsistent with 13 CFR 125.2(f)(1) and, consequently, creates a gap in coverage for emergency acquisitions in "outlying areas" as defined at FAR 2.101.

13 CFR 125.2(f)(1) states:

"The contracting officer shall set aside any acquisition with an anticipated dollar value exceeding the Micro-purchase Threshold but not exceeding the Simplified Acquisition Threshold (defined in the FAR at 48 CFR 2.101) for small business concerns when there is a reasonable expectation that offers will be obtained from at least two small business concerns that are competitive in terms of quality and delivery and award will be made at fair market prices."

However, proposed FAR 13.003(b)(1), 19.203(b), and 19.502-2(a) state actual dollar thresholds instead of just using the terms "micro-purchase threshold" and "simplified acquisition threshold."

FAR 13.003(b)(1) states:

"Acquisitions of supplies or services that have an anticipated dollar value exceeding $3,500 ($20,000 for acquisitions as described in 13.201(g)(1)) but not exceeding $150,000 ($750,000 for acquisitions described in paragraph (1)(i) of the simplified acquisition threshold definition at 2.101) are reserved exclusively for small business concerns and shall be set aside (see 19.000, 19.203, and subpart 19.5)."

FAR 19.203(b):

"For acquisitions of supplies or services that have an anticipated dollar value exceeding $3,500 ($20,000 for acquisitions as described in13.201(g)(1)), but not exceeding $150,000 ($750,000 for acquisitions described in paragraph (1)(i) of the simplified acquisition threshold definition at 2.101)..."

FAR 19.502-2(a):

"Each acquisition of supplies or services that has an anticipated dollar value exceeding $3,500 ($20,000 for acquisitions as described in 13.201(g)(1)), but not over $150,000 ($750,000 for acquisitions described in paragraph (1) of the Simplified Acquisition Threshold definition at 2.101),..."

The problem with the FAR language is that it doesn't recognize that the automatic reservation for small business would apply up to the threshold in paragraph (2) of the Simplified Acquisition Threshold definition at FAR 2.101 in the case of an emergency acquisition in an outlying area. This is because the applicable definition of "United States" at FAR 2.101 includes only "the 50 states and the District of Columbia". Thus, an outlying area would be outside the United States when applying the definitions of "micro-purchase threshold" and "simplified acquisition threshold". Note that FAR part 19 applies, with the exception of FAR subpart 19.6, "within the United States and its outlying areas" (FAR 19.000(b)).

Thus, there will be a gap in FAR coverage for emergency acquisitions in outlying areas valued above $750,000 but less than $1.5 million. These acquisitions are automatically reserved for small business pursuant to 13 CFR 125.2(f)(1), but not the FAR.

The hazardous waste industry needs to be exempt from this ruling, due to the unique challenges of transporting and disposing of hazardous waste.  The cost of owning and operating tractor trailers and Transfer, Storage and Disposal Facilities (TSDF's) are a major barrier for small business concerns.  The application of this rule in the hazardous waste industry would eliminate the ability of small business concerns to participate in Hazardous Waste Contracting.  It is a similar situation to the manufacturing and construction industries, for which special provisions were made.  Please consider making similar provisions for Hazardous Waste Contracting.

We understand the intent of the proposed rule. It appears, however, that the very specific world of hazardous waste contractors was not considered in this rule making. Small and disadvantaged hazardous waste contractors are a specialized group --only perhaps a few dozen across the US-- who are involved in managing hazardous waste for military installations for the Defense Logistics Agency. Defense Logistics has had a robust small business and diversity program .

These small business firms perform all site work and RCRA regulatory compliance work for the bases. The work also includes the transportation and disposal of the hazardous waste. The way the Deviation reads, 50% of the dollars must be retained by the small business. There are no small businesses that own RCRA disposal facilities. That means that right off the bat, approximately 50%-60% of the government dollars received go to a large business to cover those disposal fees. Often transportation of the waste from the base to the disposal site is also performed by large businesses. Easily, in most situations, 70-75% of government dollars go to large businesses on these contracts.

The new Deviation would effectively halt the small business program at Defense Logistics and any other agency that uses small businesses to perform the site work, but also to manage all of the disposal.

This comment is from a contracting officer/former cost analyst attempting to prepare an acquisition strategy for an actual FY19 award of services in the 8(a) program affected by the Proposed Rule. It is concerning the application of the Proposed Rule to the unique sole-source authority for awards to 8(a) Alaska Native Corporations (ANCs) and Indian Tribes. (As background, FAR 6.302-5 authorizes contract awards directly to ANCs and Indian Tribes in amounts up to $22M without making available to the public a justification and approval supporting circumstances other than full and open competition.)

The Proposed Rule's changes are silent about the intersection between the newly proposed FAR 52.219-14 allowance for subcontracting to similarly situated entities and the existing FAR 19.808-1(e) prohibition against a follow-on contract being awarded on a sole-source basis to an ANC or Indian Tribe if the predecessor contract was performed by another 8(a) participant owned by the same ANC or Indian Tribe. Under the current regulations, my acquisition strategy in response to this prohibition should be to conduct an 8(a) competition for the follow-on services contract because FAR 19.808-1(e) prohibits the incumbent from receiving an 8(a) sole-source award. Sometimes, the strategy will instead be that a different ANC or Indian Tribe is given the 8(a) sole-source award, and the service employees then either re-badge at newly competed labor rates or a subcontract is awarded to the incumbent for performance without competition. In that case, the existing limitations on subcontracting control the amount of that subcontract. With the Proposed Rule's allowance for similarly situated entities to perform all of the work, however, another strategy is made possible, whereby a different ANC or Indian Tribe will receive an 8(a) sole-source award and then subcontract all of the work out to the incumbent without competing it, resulting in increased costs. In effect it is a loophole that renders the FAR 19.808-1(e) prohibition meaningless.

The Councils should therefore consider a change to the Proposed Rule that will exclude certain entities from the new similarly situated entity allowance, as follows: A) Add the following to the end of Proposed Rule's FAR 52.219-14(e)(1), (2), (3), and (4) subparagraphs "If the Offeror/Contractor is awarded a sole-source contract under FAR 19.8, then for purposes of this clause any Alaska Native Corporation, Indian Tribe, Native Hawaiian Organization, or Community Development Corporation that is similarly situated to the Offeror/Contractor shall be not treated as a similarly situated entity (see FAR 19.808-1(e))." Then, B) Add the following to FAR 19.808-1(e): "In addition, acquisition planners shall ensure no more than 50 percent (85 percent for general construction, 75 percent for construction by special trade contractors) of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance, excluding the cost of materials, is planned to be subcontracted to the incumbent that would otherwise be subject to this prohibition at the prime contract level.

GAO has reported for at least a decade (e.g. see GAO-16-113, GAO-12-84) on the waste occurring in sole-source 8(a) contracts to ANCs and Indian Tribes, and this Proposed Rule is forming a loophole that may just add to that waste. Specifically because of the higher dollar amounts authorized and the lack of public posting required under this 8(a) sole-source authority, allowing for only up to 50 percent to be subcontracted back to the incumbent strikes a better balance between obtaining fair and reasonable prices and ensuring mission success, while still furthering the American economy for disadvantaged businesspeople in the spirit of the 8(a) program.

This regulation change is long overdue to level the playing field for small business. The resell is a small business but approximately 88% of the award goes to large businesses (AWS/AZURE).
