Resolution 2016-05

Whereas, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was enacted when the Internet was still in its infancy; and

Whereas, an array of court decisions continues to make application of the ADA to online-only places of public accommodation uncertain; and

Whereas, on the 20th anniversary of the ADA in 2010, the Obama Administration publically acknowledged the need for clarifying regulations in this area but has consistently thwarted efforts by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) to make progress on this critical regulatory agenda; and

Whereas, most recently, the Obama Administration scuttled plans to release a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) on the ADAs application to state and local government Internet accessibility obligations; and

Whereas, while bringing some further attention to state and local governmental entities Internet accessibility obligations is always in order, organizations of and for people who are blind or visually impaired have rather been demanding action on the obligations of public accommodations operating exclusively online and not on state and local governments for which Internet accessibility obligations have never been in doubt; and

Whereas, in a vain attempt to portray regulatory progress regarding Internet accessibility, the DOJ has most recently issued a so-called supplemental advanced notice of proposed rulemaking (SANPRM) concerning state and local governments which asks many of the same insulting questions DOJ posed for public comment in previous proceedings demanding evidence of the relative costs and benefits of Internet accessibility; and

Whereas, no civil right whether started at Seneca Falls, Selma or Stonewall, or sought in Silicon Valley or cyberspace no civil right should ever be sold at auction;

Now, therefore, be it resolved by the American Council of the Blind in convention assembled on the 8th day of July, 2016, at the Hyatt Regency Hotel, Minneapolis, Minnesota, that this organization express its profound frustration and disappointment with the Obama Administration for its failure to be responsive to Americans with vision loss who, for more than a decade, have been calling for much-needed regulatory clarification of the Americans with Disabilities Acts application to online-only places of public accommodation; and

Be it further resolved that this organization reach out to the major party candidates for President of the United States to communicate our demand that, within the first six months of the new presidency, issuance of regulations clarifying that online-only places of public accommodation are nevertheless ADA-covered entities with Internet accessibility obligations must be achieved.

Adopted.

Ray Campbell, Secretary

Dear Ms. Bond:

My name is Anthony Lanzilotti. I live in Brigantine, New Jersey, and I am a blind student pursuing a bachelor's degree so that I may accomplish my long-term goal of attending law school and becoming an attorney.

In order to read websites, I use JAWS, a screen access software. This type of software renders text into speech, allowing me to read, write, conduct research, and complete my coursework independently. However, this software does not work with websites that are not built accessibly, in accordance to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.0 AA issued by the W3C. When websites are not built to these guidelines, the effectiveness of my screen access software is undermined, and I am unable to read and access information that is essential to my participation in the programs, services, and benefits offered through public websites.

Lack of website accessibility has been a constant obstacle in my academic endeavors. For instance, when I was pursuing my associate's degree in a publicly supported community college, the WebAdvisor system that we used to manage our accounts, access class schedules and selections, add and drop courses, and review our transcripts was not accessible and did not comply with WCAG 2.0 AA. As a result, I could not perform any of these activities independently. I was forced to ask others for assistance with WebAdvisor, and in doing so was forced to reveal private information, such as my academic records, to a stranger.

Only after I engaged in an extensive legal negotiation with my community college, it agreed to make accessible the WebAdvisor System and other web-based materials in accordance to WCAG 2.0 AA. The resulting agreement can be found at
https://nfb.org/images/nfb/documents/pdf/higher-ed-toolkit/atlantic_cape_consent_decree_.pdf
Had the WebAdvisor System been accessible, I would have used JAWS to privately and independently review my transcripts and to access the information posted there without needing legal intervention.

I strongly urge the U.S. government to establish technical standards for public websites in accordance with WCAG 2.0 AA and to stop the disability discrimination that occurs when blind students cannot participate in their campuses' online programs, services, and benefits.

Sincerely,

Anthony Lanzilotti
Brigantine, New Jersey

Performance Plan-1300.11(d)
-Must have data driven countermeasures, the States use the Countermeasures that Work for proven data-driven countermeasures. There are still no proven data related countermeasures for Traffic Records. The State of Mississippi has had struggles with acceptable countermeasures that are data driven and can be used to create programs. There are no suggestions or ideas on acceptable traffic records programs. The State of Mississippi recommended during the comment time for the latest addition of Countermeasures that Work, that a traffic records section or data section be created to help the States. This addition was not added into the latest edition.
Performance Plan-1300.11(d)(5)
-The States must have an evidenced based performance plan, but there are no clear directions on what this plan "must" have and there are no examples given by NHTSA on what exactly is to be included. The MOHS was requested to provide a copy of the EBE with the submission of the HSP. There needs to be more guidance of what the EBE must contain to make sure that the States are in compliance. There is also a requirement that the EBE must be cross referenced in the HSP and 405, why do both?
1300.14 Review and approval procedures
-Failure to respond promptly. The MOHS was given "5" days to respond the questions of the 405 application. During those days, the MOHS was involved in our State wide conference and did answer the questions within the 5 days. There are some cases when the "promptly" makes it very difficult. NHTSA had out application for 30+ days to review, but gave the states 5 days to answer and could create a penalty. With the application submission due within the Summer with vacation, conference, etc., this could penalize the State if the administrator or even the secondary person is out on leave or away from the office on business. This needs to be reconsidered and not a penalty.
1300.21- Maintenance of Effort
-Need more clarification on the Maintenance of Effort. This has been difficult to the States. Also, the years of 2014 &2015 are listed as the years that MOE will be used, will these years be in effect for the length of the FAST Act?
1300.21(d)(3) Child restraint inspection stations
What is considered "active"? Please define and is this necessary. The requirement is to include stations and the populations for the areas. This is burdensome to the states and to determine the CPS technicians. Many agencies, fire departments, etc. have activities, but may not be reported to the HSO and this would be extremely difficult to know about, if they are not funded agencies.
1300.21(d)(4) Child Passenger Technicians
What is a "sufficient" number of technicians? Some States, such as Mississippi have a hard to acquiring and retaining CPS technicians, there needs to some guidance on this and not punitive. Why have in the HSP, if it is in the 405 application. This is duplicative.
1300.21 (d)(5) Seatbelt Enforcement
The MOHS has struggled with this question time and time again and each year providing more information to the reviewers. Why does the number have to be 70%? In some rural state, participation lacks not due to the HSO trying to work with agencies. In the case of the State of Mississippi, in the areas that have low participation, the Mississippi Highway Patrol steps in, they are state wide and cover 100% of the State and focus on certain areas that the MOHS provides data for, so that areas are covered. This can be problematic for a State, if there is low activity.
1300.22 Traffic Records
This area is extremely burdensome for the States, especially with difficulties with data collection. This area has been a struggle for the MOHS since MAP-21 created it.
1300.22(b)(3) Quantifiable and Measureable Progress
Very difficult, no examples given, no suggestions, no data strategies given, very burdensome. It is suggested to submit to NHTSA for review, but they are going to give feedback. We submitted our measure and got no feedback and had major questions on it during the review process. The States, especially the MOHS with guidance on this section.
1300.26 Graduated Driver License
This is EXTREMELY hard for a small state to qualify for with the legislative challenges that the state faces. We would like to see a step-in program like the distracted driving program.
1300.27 Non-Motorized
The MOHS would like to have additional criteria or options available for applying for this money, besides the 15% of total fatalities. Rural states will have a hard time reaching this measure. The MOHS has had a 20% increase in just pedestrian fatalities, this needs to be considered as a criteria and not just 15% of the total. This would be a combination of over 100 fatalities per year, we are now at 60+. This makes it difficult to focus on a problem, when the MOHS knows there is an issues, but can't get the funding needed to help.

Question 6: What are the availability and the cost of hiring and using trained professionals who could provide captions for live-audio content in synchronized media? What are the additional costs associated with producing captions for live-audio content in synchronized media, such as the technological components to ensuring that the captions are visible on the Web site and are synchronized with the live-audio content?

Response: According to SCAN NATOA, the hourly cost for a typical captioning service can range from $150 - $275 per hour. Captioning live-audio content would be closer to the higher end of that estimate, as it requires the captioner to be working concurrently with the broadcast of the content. For a medium-sized city like Lakewood, a typical City Council meeting lasts about 2 hours. At 26 meetings per year, the estimated cost is $14,300 per year. Prior to initiating a live-caption service, a closed captioning encoder would need to be installed so that the captions appear onscreen, and this one-time cost is $9,000. There are additional costs for streaming content from our channel to the website, and that is $4,200 per year (this cost is necessary whether or not captioning is ultimately required).

However, if the SANPRM requires that all programming on our channel be closed captioned, the cost would be $1,500 per month to lease a hardware/software system to caption audio. This equates to $18,000 per year and would encompass all live and pre-recorded video (no need for a live person to caption). As above, a closed captioning encoder is required and would cost $9,000.

Question 7: Should the Department consider a shorter or longer effective date for the captioning of live-audio content in synchronized media requirement, or defer this requirement until effective and efficient technology is available?

The City of Lakewood believes that this requirement should be deferred until effective and efficient technology is available. Technology is improving, and in several years automatic captioning systems will be just as good or even better than live human captioning. While there are systems already available today, there are still some issues with it, including accuracy and the high costs. As the technology becomes more widespread, costs will decrease.

This SANPRM should also reconcile with the FCC's current captioning requirements on TV providers. Lakewood's video programming originates from our TV operations, which are then made available on our web site. Section 79.1 (d) exempts local governments from closed captioning their TV content, and if this SANPRM is adopted in its current version, that exemption would conflict with the requirements to close caption audio content on video content on web sites.

Washington State has reviewed the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Uniform Procedures for State Highway Safety Grant Programs Interim final rule. Docket No. NHTSA-2016-057. Additionally, GHSA and NHTSA need to continue to streamline the process by reducing administrative burdens on states. We need to spend our time and resources ministering not administering, so any consideration to help get funds out to save lives is beneficial and appreciated.

The following are considerations by section:

1300.3 - Definitions
Washington States Strategic Highway Safety Plan outlines the data, priorities, objectives, and countermeasures listed as proven, recommended, or unknown. We have some objectives with no CMTW and in some of our rural and tribal areas they need to create or modify these to meet local needs. We have encouraged our partners to consider creating a proposal with an evaluation to assist in identifying potentially new CMTW. The definition seems to limit this to "proven effective", which gives a false impression that these can only be used and that there are no new CMTW to consider. This section seems to contradict 1300.11(d)(4) and Administrative Rosekind's discussion with the states about new ideas and innovative strategies in traffic safety. The Washington Traffic Safety Commission and Department of Licensing work closely on motorcycle training and education, despite these being important elements to a rounded safety program NHTSA needs to allow more funding for motorcycle enforcement if we are going to make a difference in reducing motorcycle fatalities.

Thank you for providing the opportunity to submit comments related to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Interim Final Rule (IFR) Docket No. NHTSA-2016-0057. Most of the comments provided herein relate to the grant for the 24/7 Sobriety Program as that is where our expertise lies.

Page 19. This page discusses the need for data-driven measures to be used in the context of 23 CFR 1300.11(d): Highway Safety Program Area Problem Identification, Countermeasure Strategies, Projects and Funding. We believe that data-driven measures should be used more broadly and this requirement should also extend to the approved 24/7 Sobriety Programs, by requiring them to be data driven in terms of testing methodologies, and sanctions and rewards in 23 CFR 1300.23 Impaired Driving Countermeasures Grants.

Pages 43-44. These pages of the executive summary in the IFR provide: "The agency acknowledges that the effectiveness of such [24/7 sobriety] programs is likely associated with their alignment with traditional principles of deterrence: swift and certain [sanctions]. 24-7 sobriety programs typically approach this deterrence model by focusing on the most high-risk offenders, requiring abstinence from alcohol or illegal drugs, testing compliance multiple times per day, and swiftly delivering defined consequences for noncompliance." Intoximeters agrees that immediate sanctions for violations is one of the hallmarks of a 24/7 sobriety program. However, this portion of the executive summary refers to ( 23 CFR 1300.23(h) ) makes no mention at all of swift and certain sanctions and the preference therefore. We suggest making revisions to this rule to provide preference for programs that clearly provide for and define what qualifies as a swift and certain sanction. Without this clarity, statewide programs merely monitoring for drug or alcohol use using twice a day testing, transdermal testing or another method approved by the Secretary could qualify for grant funding, even if they do not employ the swift and certain sanctioning methods, could qualify for grant funding.

Additionally, States should be encouraged to define the timing and process to achieve swift and certain sanctions for each testing methodology utilized in its 24/7 sobriety program. Behavioral research would suggest that the methods that apply the consequence should do so as close to the time the compliant or non-compliant behavior occurred. Testing methods that facilitate this should be preferable as they have the greatest impact on long term behavior change.

Page 46. Here, requirements covering types and periods of testing that should be used in 24/7 sobriety programs to ensure swift sanctions are specifically called for. Peer reviewed research of the 24/7 sobriety program provides for support that the primary testing methodology should be twice per day in person breath testing in approximate 12 hour intervals. The Rand Corporation found that when at least 85% of the 24/7 participants were on this testing regime, it produced a 12% reduction in driving under the influence arrests. Kilmer, PhD, Beau; Nicosia, PhD, Nancy; Heaton, PhD, Paul; and Midgette, MPP, Greg, Efficacy of Frequent Monitoring with Swift, Certain, and Modest Sanctions for Violations: Insights from South Dakota's 24/7 Sobriety Project, American Journal of Public Health, Vol. 103, No. 1, p. e37 (Jan. 2013). Twice per day in person breath testing provides the ability to sanction an individual the in the shortest period of time because the individual has appeared at the test site to submit to the test before law enforcement, or its designee. Other types of testing method such as transdermal alcohol monitoring bracelets or remote breath testing devices, by their nature cannot provide sanctions as swiftly. There is no person to person positive reinforcement for compliant events with each successful test and the data from these devices requires a third party to track down and apply sanctions for non-compliant behavior.

Page 149. This portion of 23 CFR 1300.23(j)(x) provides that grant monies may be used to fund the "costs associated with a 24-7 sobriety program." Given that many 24/7 programs are offender pay and could potentially be income producing for a testing agency, perhaps some additional guidance would be helpful as to what costs may qualify. Would costs for 24/7 program coordinators as well as computer or breath testing, transdermal testing equipment qualify for use of grant funds? Are there limitations on the use of these funds to purchase equipment or services that are used to generate income and potentially profits?

Again, thank you for your consideration of Intoximeters' comments on NHTSA-2016-0057 interim final rule. Should you have questions or require further information, please do not hesitate to contact us.

Intoximeters, Inc.

Mr Giuseppe:

I am submitting the following comments in regards to the notice which appeared published in the Federal Register on December 28, 2016 [Docket No. NHTSA-2016-0116; Notice 1] pertaining to the Ford Motor Company's Petition for Decision of Inconsequential Noncompliance.

I am compelled to comment on this petition because I feel the rationale for some of the arguments that Ford advances as to why the noncompliance is inconsequential are in one instance flawed and in the others incomplete or irrelevant.

In its first point, Ford contends that the front row seats in the subject vehicles are not "bench seats" in the traditional sense. Ford states "The ability for an occupant to position or mis-position themselves in the outboard seat is the same for trucks with or without the center dsp because the seat contours and seat belt anchorage locations are the same. The seats are identical and interchangeable but the head restraint width requirement is different"

This argument lacks merit and does not hold up under even a medium amount of scrutiny. While it maybe true for the cases where there are just two occupants riding in the front row, in cases when the center seating position is occupied, it is very likely that both the driver and the right front outboard passenger's heads will NOT be centered on their respective head restraints. The subject vehicles are equipped with a "40-20-40" bench seat. Hence, of the 62,5 inches of hip room, approximately 20%, or 12.5 inches is allotted to the center occupant [the hip room for the 5th% female specified in FMVSS 208 is 12.8 inches] In large part, the subject vehicles are work trucks with a large percentage of them owned businesses and fleets. It is common to see 3 large or medium sized occupants in the front row of a full-size pickup truck traveling to and from work sites (construction workers, road crews, landscapers, etc.). When the center position is occupied, both the driver and the right front passenger will almost certainly shift themselves outboard. Drivers needs to shift in order to keep their right hand comfortably on the steering wheel and their right elbow off the center occupant's ribs. The right outboard passenger will likely need to shift even more off center than the driver because it would be too uncomfortable for the center occupants to keep both feet on the floor directly in front of them given the raised floor tunnel for the transmission. ( the CAD study on page 18 of Ford's petition shows a 45 degree thigh angle for the one-legged manikin in the center position versus 15 degrees for the outboard occupants). Center occupants will likely put their left foot on the tunnel area and right foot off the tunnel into the space in front of the right outboard side passenger.

Moving on, I am puzzled that no where in the petition do I find Ford state what is the minimum width for the non-compliant head restraints. Ford reports an average width for a random sample of 15 trucks (multiple model years and trim levels) of 239 mm. When considering whether a noncompliance is inconsequential wouldn't it be important to know what the minimum width is? Even if the average width was more than 254 mm, any vehicle equipped head restraints below the minimum width would be non-compliant. Also, why is the sample composed different trims levels? Shouldn't the leather and cloth versions been treated as different populations? Ford says that another sample of just the current Lariat trim was 249mm, so might not the non-Lariat versions have and average of 229 mm?

As to Ford's 2nd point ("Seating reference point measurements demonstrate head restraints provide required width protection and intended level of safety"), Ford states in it's conclusion that it meets the required width at 635 mm above the SgRP, but it does not state what the measured value was? I think it would be more persuasive and relevant to know what the width is at 685 mm above the SgRP since that corresponds to 65mm below the new increased minimum restraint height of 750mm in FMVSS 202a.

As to Ford's 3rd point (Exemplar measurements demonstrate that the subject head restraints provide required width protection and intended level of safety for all occupants), Ford states that "based on a survey of 15 trucks the highest point on the head restraint that meets the 254 mm width requirement ranged from 674mm to 721 mm above the SgRP with the head restraint in the full down position". Therefore, one can conclude that some head restraints did not meet the minimum width at 685 mm above the SgRP. Also, are these 15 trucks from the Lariat Population (249 mm avg width) or the population of multiple trim levels (239 mm avg width)?

As to Ford's 4th point, I believe the reference to the IIHS testing is irrelevant since it does not account for anything involving the presence of a front center DSP.

I believe that the safety regulations exist for a reason, and as an automotive technician I've seen countless failures because of minor differences in specifications.  Ford Motor Company needs to be held accountable for defects in engineering and craftsmanship, no matter how "inconsequential" the infraction may seem.  Is this infraction similar to the VW scandal of EPA cheating with diesels?  I would say not, but do not budge on safety.  Its the only thing that keeps us alive.  Thank you

First and foremost, I would like to thank the National Highway Safety Administration (NHTSA) for taking this opportunity to release the Enforcement Guidance Bulletin, with the possibility of discussing various aspects of driver safety related to verifying automotive safety technologies.

For the last century within the automotive industry, there has been an evolution of technological advancements which introduced varying levels of vehicle safety systems. These systems progressed from within the vehicle compartment to controlling outside vehicle scenarios; in doing so, vehicle computerized input is required for vehicle system activation.

Currently, various research testing facilities and automotive manufacturers are conducting safety testing to introduce a baseline of vehicle comportment and guidelines related to these systems such as NCAP testing procedures. Moreover, NHTSA has introduced and is developing operational guidance for deployment of vehicle safety systems and has given some exemptions to manufactures to enable and increase automotive safety testing and research.

As these changes occur, so are required regulatory changes to current Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) under The National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act, 49 U.S.C. 30101. Currently, these standards could be adapted to incorporate assisted and shared driving task, but some concerns are that the autonomous vehicle technology could not necessary be controlled properly by adapting current vehicle safety standards as the basis of these standards are based on traditional vehicle design.

New vehicle design and technological advancements in safety design will require the commitment of multiple manufacturers working together and standardizing programming and vehicle communication coding. This can be seen in the push of standardization of Autonomous Emergency Braking (AEB) where vehicle manufactures have joined forces in a push towards the standardization of automatic braking systems.

NHTSA, currently has various enforcement authority to address safety changes such as ordering manufactures to conduct a recall, 49, U.S.C. 30118(b) and requesting performance record of a vehicle or component, without root-cause analysis.

But as can be seen with recent and major manufacturer safety equipment recalls, performance records of specific defective component in question could help increase the signaling a larger manufacturing defect. This response time is due to the obligation of the manufacturer in notification of a known or possible suspected defect (49 CFR part 573). As new safety systems are introduced, the relationship between various manufactures system could themselves introduce a type of "relationship-defect". These relationship defects would not apply to individual manufacture nor the equipment manufacture (CFR part 573.5(a-b)) and without constant monitoring and reporting of these defects there would be no efficient root cause or data analysis (49 U.S.C. 30118(b-c)) to properly report failures.

Furthermore, it could be possible for manufacturer safety systems to show no sign of known defect, therefore without active monitoring and a significant reduction in defect and non-compliance reporting time (CRF part 573.6) the outcome and severity of these defects could be hard to interpret or solve especially between manufactures. The control and determination of these defects could be raised if regulations were introduced to implement vehicle warning indicators with a compulsory performance record with and without so called "known defect" and the event be submitted into a live database, thus gathering information from all manufactures, and significantly reducing the delay in response of suspected "relationship-defect".

Sincerely,
Jason Gagnon

After losing my 2 youngest daughters, AnnaLeah (17) and Mary (13), due to a truck underride crash on May 4, 2013, I have been calling for a National Vision Zero Goal (along with over 20,000 Vision Zero Petition Signers).

So, I watched the recent Driving Behavioral Change in Traffic Safety conference with a great deal of interest--knowing full well that the path to moving toward zero crash deaths and serious injuries would require many changes in attitude and action, not either/or but both/and, and, and. . .

I asked myself: What will it take to make a significant reduction in the number of people who die on our roads?

It will take all of us working together.

It will take facing the problem head on.

It will take acknowledging that there is a problem-and the full extent of it.

It will take recognizing that we are all a part of the problem.

It will take talking about it openly.

It will take understanding that crash deaths are not just an expected risk of driving on the road but are to a great extent preventable.

It will take accepting that risky driver behavior is not a personal right but a violation of other people's right to be protected from reckless behavior.

It will take calling risky driver behavior what it is: RECKLESS.

It will take classifying a vehicle as a weapon and reckless driver behavior as an act of violence.

It will takeenacting laws that prohibit a full range of reckless driving behaviors and then enforcing those laws with stiff consequences.

It will take understanding that changing personal behavior is not the only way to reduce crash deaths and learning how to work with others who are addressing vehicle and environment risk factors.

It will take recognizing and embracing that preventing crashes from happening is not the only thing which needs to be addressed butthat we can also reduce the severity of those crashes so that death is not the end result.

It will take manufacturers and employers and consumers and law enforcement and engineers and countless others to recognize how their individual decisions and actions contribute to not just crash statistics but to the unnatural ending (or saving) of life for people with names and faces and hopes and dreams and other people who care about them whose lives will be changed forever.And it will take us all realizing that someday soon one of those names and faces could very well be ourselves or someone whom we love and will miss dreadfully. And that it could have been prevented.

It will take listeningto the hundreds of thousands of families who have lost loved ones due to traffic crashes and apologizing, as a society, for letting them down-for not addressing it as the priority it should be. Bringing healing and hope that their frustrations and anger and grief are being heard and that their petitions for change are being taken seriously. Giving them a voice and channeling their zealous energy in positive ways which can in fact be a powerful tool for changing the future and moving us more surely Toward Zero Crash Deaths, Serious Injuries, and Fear of Traffic.

And beyond that, I firmly believe that, in order to move as a nation Toward a Vision of Zero Crash Deaths,it will take take a commitment to a National Vision Zero Goal and a coordinated endeavorof government, private industry, workers of every skill imaginable, and informed citizens. Anything short of thiswill be disjointed and less effective, whichtranslates into not simply unmet project goals but people dying.It is not an impossible dream but it willrequire sacrifice and will be well worth the effort.

The other thing which I just wanted to mention is the idea of a nationwide network ofVision Zero Traffic Safety Community Action Groups. I have observed through my involvement in social media safety advocacy that there are a multitude of individuals and organizations attempting to impact the traffic safety problem. Unfortunately, with a likewise multitude of specific issues upon which they are focusing, efforts to address the problem are fragmented and scattered. It seems to me that if we all come together, at least on some level, we could be more effective.

I kept writing down ideas as they came to me during the various presentations and discussions and emailing them to the event coordinator. I did not hear my specific questionsbeing addressed. But I recorded them (in their raw intensity) in the attached document. Please take the time to open it up, consider what I have to say, and act upon it, in a way that only you can do, to make a meaningful difference.

Thank you.

In memory of AnnaLeah (forever 17) and Mary (forever 13) along with countless others whose lives were cut far too short,
Marianne Karth

The National Association of Emergency Medical Technicians (NAEMT) sincerely appreciates the opportunity to offer comment to a proposed new EMS agenda for the future. This initiative can be a helpful exercise to continue educating and aligning all EMS stakeholders around a shared vision and common goals, and can provide valuable background and insights to help leaders make informed decisions.

Our comment has been uploaded as a file.

Emergency Medical Services, the care provided to a victim of sudden illness or injury, provided by an agency of a ruling
authority, must be differentiated from the mobile health services provided by private companies, hospitals and entrepreneurs,
for persons requiring transportation beyond the capabilities of an automobile, bus or train. Even more so, that differentiation
must be distinguished between EMS and Mobile Integrated Health programs aimed at cost containment for healthcare systems.

EMS is by definition an "emergency service", and must be recognized as such if it is to retain resiliency. As EMS veterans
near the end of their careers, they face the complete lack of support provided the law enforcement and fire communities with
whom they work. Police and fire systems realized that a persons reasonable life span must be defined with an end point
recognizing the physical and mental limitations of age. LEO and firefighters career paths sunset in 20-25 years because it is
accepted that one cannot have a cop running around at 65 trying to chase a 20 year old, or a firefighter carrying someone
down a ladder at 70. However, the expectation that a paramedic should be able to carry a litter down a flight of stairs until they
reach 72 is perfectly acceptable.

So much effort has been made to align EMS with the healthcare industry, which faces none of the unique challenges facing
EMS, yet little to nothing has been done to equate EMS with the other emergency services. Medicine is but one facet of EMS.
To have a physician, who has never set foot on an ambulance, dictate operational policy is unwise and unsafe.

In order for EMS to survive, the people providing the service must be the primary focus. The logistical, financial and humanistic
aspects of a true third service must be addressed. The claim that issues such as these aren't within the scope of the project is
not reasonable. The future of the service cannot ignore the people providing it. When current providers advise recruits to seek
a career in another discipline primarily due to the lack of "career path". there is a fundamental flaw.

A mandate for municipalities to provide EMS is essential. When mandates exist to protect valuables (LEO) and property (fire)
but nothing to protect the life of the owners, what good are those protections. The fallback of :there simply isn't any money" is
no longer acceptable. First and foremost fee-for-service must be eliminated. CMS should no longer reimburse "emergency"
medical service. Like police and fire, funding for EMS must come from the taxpayer. EMS operations must be coordinated by
veteran providers intimately familiar with the industry; Not cops, nor fireman, nor physicians.

Vehicle design and safety considerations must be mandated universally, regardless of cost. It is just a senseless to expect a
transport ambulance to carry all the equipment of an EMS unit, as it is to say an EMS vehicle should be built like a recreational
vehicle. Injury is the leading cause of people leaving and refusing to consider the industry. EMS personnel are disposable to
most agencies, and shame on this effort if it chooses to ignore this.

As you may have guessed the author is a 35+ year veteran, still providing service as 60 approaches. Sadly the distance to
retirement is just as long as is was when the journey began. The firefighters and police officers from the hay-day are all retired,
but perpetuity is the only future here. It is the goal of this old-man is to provide a future for the young men and women coming
through the door. The opportunity now exists to influence that end, don't squander it.

The EMS Agenda for the Future has been an overlooked document by those who would be able to necessitate it's implementation. This is because the prior document has failed to lead to worthwhile funding reforms to promote sustainable EMS agencies. Without this sustainability, all other points become moot.

A worthwhile look at the future of EMS needs to emphasize a path forward for sustainable reimbursements. Medicare is funding EMS on average 17% below cost of service, Medicaid throughout various states is below that. Insurers are seeking to control costs by withholding direct payment in some states or requiring EMS agencies to take payments at a network rate. This causes many services to bleed money, rely on local tax bases, or simply go out of business. Others push high bills on to patients.

The funding gap is causing EMS agencies to make fiscal decisions that has lead to low pay for EMS workers, outdated equipment or practices due to an inability to fund change, non-interoperable data systems due to high costs to implement or upgrade, and a weak position for EMS for the future.

In order to promote the data driven vision that seems to be the goal, EMS must be reimbursed better. Federal mandates to payors may help with this, otherwise with a lack of sustainability the agenda will continue to be delayed.

As the current President of the Air and Surface Transport Nurses Association (ASTNA) www.astna.org I wish to add our voice to the process of planning for the Future Agenda of EMS in the USA. Nurses need to be included as a vital and essential profession within EMS, in both clinical as well as administrative and research capacities. Education of all EMS providers should be at a Baccalaureate Degree level and there should be consistency in the curriculum across the nation. There is too much variance in the educational standards and levels presently both at national levels, as well as at State and local/ county levels. For EMS providers to be relied upon and be recognized as a profession, University degreed education is essential.
There is also great variance in scope of practice across the nation, within states and even between counties. This variance should be eliminated and uniformity and consistency should be encouraged.
EMS systems should become extensions of healthcare systems, nationwide and not be isolated to the 'public protection role'.
It is essential that EMS be regarded as a specialty service on its own. Having Fire Departments control EMS does not contribute to meaningful , positive outcomes and practice as the focus is not EMS, it is fighting fires.
There should be greater regulation of Ambulance companies standards and quality/ performance metrics should be utilized on each and every interaction to ensure that patient's are getting the best standards of care. With regards to helicopter Air Ambulances, the federal government needs to step in and regulate this 'industry' which has changed from one designed to care for and transport the most critically ill and injured in need of such a costly and specialized resource , to one that only exists to make money , and lots of it, off the back of patients who have NO say in which provider transports them. New operations open practically every month , sometimes mere yards away from already established transport providers base of operations. Competition for "calls" is at its worst now, often placing undue pressure on clinicians to ignore bad weather and sound judgement to just do the call so that they can bill an insurance company. My speciality has lost and continues to lose nurses each and every year due to undue competition that synonymous with Helicopter EMS programs in the USA. It is a fact too that anyone can run a helicopter operation , there are no federal standards in terms of what is required for safe operations, personnel experience and training , and the vehicles that clinicians operate in. On one hand you have a twin engine helicopter, staffed with a highly experienced pilot with IFR competencies and a medical crew who are board certified and degreed with a great deal of additional training and skill and state of the art equipment and capability then on the other hand, you have a single engine, basic, cheap aircraft, which is small and does not allow full access to the patient, is staffed by a pilot with bare minimum experience and flight hours, no current IFR experience, medical crew with a bare minimum in terms of education (formal) and training , and exceptionally limited experience ,taking care of patients with older, basic equipment. Yet both these models are able to bill for and be paid the same . This is a non-sustainable model and is not based on patient outcomes and quality metrics. EMS needs to be made a more attractive career option for students and others, and the benefits and remuneration should be such that it retains it's experienced and skilled practitioners, rather than encouraging them to change careers and do something completely different in order to make ends meet financially. ASTNA is more than willing to be part of this discussion in terms of formulating our future and role in the EMS of tomorrow. We feel we have much to contribute , being the pioneers of Flight medical transport in the USA and indeed modern EMS.

I would like to see the agenda for the future contain a mechanism for using Military Medic training, off shore medic training, and critical care Paramedic training as a medium to start a training package to develop a pre hospital paramedic practitioner. This would require Paramedics, military medics, with degrees and years of experience to take an advanced program of instruction at the post graduate level, and these individuals would serve as the go between for the emergency rooms and patients doctors as well as EMS services to treat individuals in the pre hospital setting and transport these patients to the correct level of care, clinics, doctors offices, or maybe leave them at home with special instructions and prescriptions called in and not just transport them to emergency rooms.

The key here would be to start the process of outlining what this education and the associated responsibilities should be.

This comment is my own opinion and in no way or form is does it pertain to my employer or associates. They have their own set of beliefs and opinion that may not align with mine.
I believe in a system that is uniform no matter the size or geographical location. A system that any EMT or Paramedic can go from one state to another and pick up right where he/she left off. Although some may think its a form of micro-management, I believe that every single truck and resource should be set up the same in every state. There is currently an equipment list of required items however, this leaves room for extra items and one system may have certain medical equipment in different locations as another system. This can make it hard to just jump in a truck and go to a call risking time and efforts just locating items. I also believe that if we as an up and coming industry are to develop as big as we can, we should dress the part. There are some requirements but I think there should be strict rules including dress code for all different facets and recourses including badges and proper identification. Maybe there should be 1 uniform federal ID badge that every person should be issued and required to wear in plain view including name, employee number, service level and department, and federal ID number. There are some companies that make us all look like we deserve $10 an hour and that is not a joke it really is hurts us.
Training. I am a strong believer in proper training. I was never in the military nor was my immediate family. However, I believe anyone can do anything with the proper training. I believe that trainers should be held to a certain criteria as well as trainees should be held to a certain criteria and they should need to have a training packet filled out and signed off on every item and that packet needs to be the Training and education directors immediate responsibility to ensure no oversight and that we are allowing the right people to perform such daunting tasks just like doctors perform in controlled settings. Right now there are some requirements but it seems very cavalier. Then the director should have to send the packet to a federal level where each persons federal file of employment and performance is kept and updated. I believe that a lot of us get into this field for the 911. I also believe that good things take time. there should be a federal requirement unless there are reasons for hardship, requiring a person to have a certain amount of training and patient contacts in a certain amount of time in order to work directly in a 911 system. There should also be requirements to work as a secondary recourse or cover recourse similar to the requirements that need to be met for directly working the 911 system. Maybe I am way off and out of line for writing and commenting like this so please forgive me for my passions. Thanks for taking the time to read all of my suggestions. It may seem insignificant in comparison to other goals, but I think the direction we are headed comes from the ground level and up metaphorically.

How could the revised EMS Agenda contribute to improved EMS education systems at the local, State, and national levels?

I think the answer is the same for both. EMS education could be improved by encouraging the input of attorneys, ideally those knowledgeable in the legal issues involving EMS and/or who are also practicing EMS providers and state EMS officials in revising and enhancing the current educational curriculum to better address the current laws and regulations relating to EMS practice in each respective state. The Dec. 4, 2014 letter from NEMSAC to Dr. Brinsfield listed the recommendations to FICEMS regarding the strategic objectives.

I suggest placing higher priority on the Objectives that currently have lower priority status for example Objective 5.5, those that promote the use of detection equipment, training, and personal protective equipment known to enhance the safety of EMS Personnel. Promote a culture of safety among EMS personnel, agencies and organizations by letting them know what the best tools are. The EMS agenda should include a system for testing and evaluating training & equipment.

Another example is Ojective 5.2 - (Low priority/long term goal/recommended implemented concurrently with other objectives). Evaluate factors within EMS practices that contribute to medical errors or threaten patient safety.

One area for improving patient outcomes is by studying all currently available triage tagging tools. There are many studies that compare triage methods (SALT, START, etc...) but I have found only one study that compared only two initial field triage tagging tools. The study compared START triage paper tags & chemical light sticks. The study concluded when you incorporate a light in your adverse condition initial field triage procedure that you reduce patient collection times by over 30% & you reduce patient collection errors from 4 errors down to 1 error. Those are significant numbers. Here is a link to the study, http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17334196 . The study took one day to conduct. One obvious shortcoming to the study is that only two initial field triage tagging tools were compared and they were only compared under good weather conditions. The outcome may have been very different if the study was done in freezing weather conditions. In those conditions the chemical lights sticks would have not worked properly or at all. The study did not consider other styles of paper triage cards, triage paper bands, triage slap bands, triage colored cloth pins, triage tape, triage ribbon, single colored battery powered chemical light stick alternatives, triage lights, or paper tags with RFID.

A recent article in JEMS, titled "Responders from the Berkeley Balcony Collapse Reflect on Incident Challenges" mentions a lesson learned regarding the use of triage colored tape. The article states, "The department had recently issued new MCI bags to each apparatus. These bags had colored tape to assist with the visual identification of patient priorities. However, it was difficult to identify the tape on such a dimly lit scene, especially if the patient was wearing dark clothing. The color of the tape was also hard to distinguish." Here is the link to the entire article, http://www.jems.com/articles/print/volume-41/issue-5/features/responders-from-the-berkeley-balcony-collapse-reflect-on-incident-challenges.html?cmpid=jemsnowenl05102016&eid=288539289&bid=1400865

The topic of conducting a study on all currently available initial field triage tagging tools tied for 2nd place posting at DHS's, Science & Technology's, National Conversation website regarding the "Responder of the Future". The question, "Are we 24/7 field triage prepared?" tied for 1st place ranking. This is a good example how easily a concept could contribute to improved coordination for mass casualty incident preparedness and response. Here is the link to the conversations and voting results, http://scitech.ideascale.com/a/ideas/top/campaign-filter/byids/campaigns/60591

The study & articles I referred to above demonstrates that by simply using paper triage tags or tape in adverse condition initial field triage that you contribute towards increased patient collections times & increased patient collection errors, yet they are what is most commonly used. Examples of MCI's that may have been better responded to are the nighttime Paris attacks & more recently the nighttime attack in Orlando, Fl. You need to see who & where survivors are! But these lessons remain localized. Inform the EMS community & other responder community's decision makers, as to which tools contribute to medical errors & threaten patient safety.

Your office did a great job regarding the topic of using "Tourniquets and Hemostatic Dressings: The New Evidence-based Guideline". More of this, is what I am referring to. Now that the use of tourniquets is supported, all currently available tourniquets should be evaluated or those that are evaluated should be identified in some manner. I recall reading a news story that a Police Department had purchased some lower cost foreign made tourniquets and that when they used them that they broke.

In closing, revise the EMS agenda for the future in a manner that puts precedence to those everyday field topics that can be easily studied and test the equipment that is being used. These studies will contribute vital information on everyday matters that occur in the field. Thank you for your time and consideration.

EMS systems in rural areas face significant challenges that must be addressed in any updated EMS Agenda for the Future. These challenges include a lack of funding, difficulty recruiting and retaining volunteer personnel, a declining population and tax base, and inadequate access to training and certification services.

The root of the challenges that rural EMS systems face are financial. Because rural EMS systems operate in sparsely populated areas, they have fewer patients to transport and so collect fewer fees. They are also supported by a relatively small tax base, if they receive any tax support at all. In many areas, EMS receives little or no local tax support because EMS is not considered an essential service. This means there is less funding to pay for operations and readiness, which is a major reason that so many rural EMS agencies depend on volunteer staffing and rely on private donations to fill in budget gaps.

On top of this, in recent years many rural areas have experienced population loss as young people increasingly relocate to suburban and urban areas to find work, leaving the area largely populated by older residents. In addition to further reducing the tax-base of a community, this trend also leaves the local EMS agency with fewer people available to recruit and retain to make up the next generation of volunteer EMTs. At the same time, serving an older population puts pressure on EMS agencies by creating an increased workload.

Finally, over the years the training and certification requirements to become an EMT have increased. This means more time, effort and expense for volunteer EMTs and volunteer EMS departments, especially if personnel have to travel long distances to obtain training and/or take certification tests. Additionally, maintaining competency in systems with ultra-low call volumes is challenging. All of this puts more pressure on volunteer EMS leaders to actively recruit and retain personnel.

None of these challenges on their own are insurmountable, but taken collectively they are daunting. This is particularly true when you consider that most of the EMS leaders dealing with these issues are volunteers with full time jobs and lives outside of public safety. I dont think there are any silver bullets for addressing these issues, but here are some ideas to consider:

Lack of Funding: Increasing Medicare and/or Medicaid reimbursement rates for ambulance transport in rural and super-rural areas would help. Allowing EMS agencies to bill for services other than ambulance transport would also be beneficial. Ultimately, EMS needs to have access to a basic level of funding to support readiness, regardless of the number of calls responded to. EMS is an essential service that requires dedicated tax support. The Agenda should articulate this and suggest how it can be accomplished. Alternate funding should also be considered. Partnering with insurance companies who could allocate cost savings from wellness programs to EMS could assist in the development of out-of-hospital funding for community paramedic programs in rural EMS systems. Additionally, exploration of corporate assistance programs such as a small surcharge per product sold earmarked for EMS could greatly assist in funding for agencies challenged by low reimbursement rates.

Recruitment and Retention: As the population base in rural communities decline and the amount of time that it takes to become an EMT increases, rural EMS agencies are struggling to develop formal recruitment and retention programs. Recruiting and retaining volunteer personnel is a leadership activity that should be recognized and supported in the Agenda. The agenda should also address how government at the local, state and federal level can assist with volunteer recruitment and retention, including providing incentives to individual volunteers.

Training and Certification: Volunteer EMTs need to be able to access training and certification opportunities without having to incur significant costs or travel long distances. This includes access to skills and knowledge maintenance for responders who may only respond to a small number of calls each year. For instance, cost-effective online continuing education would be very helpful in allowing volunteer responders to obtain required CEHs at home and minimizing the time away from family for recertification requirements. The harder that we make it for volunteers to obtain training/certification, the more difficult it becomes for agencies to recruit and retain personnel.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the revision of the EMS Agenda for the Future. On behalf of the New England Region EMS for Children (EMSC) State Partnership Program Managers we would to submit the following suggestions and considerations.

How could the revised EMS Agenda contribute to enhanced emergency medical services for children?
The EMS Agenda for the Future was a document that examined the previous 30 years of EMS and then looked to creating a vision for EMS. Unfortunately, pediatric emergency care was not addressed in any meaningful way: gaps were not identified; substantial suggestions for improvement were not made; and innovative ideas for the future were limited. Pediatric emergency care was not address adequately in the original document and in the past 20 years, the challenge of pediatric emergency care has grown significantly. Pediatrics must be woven into all aspects of the revised Future Agenda. If there is an effort to continue to improve a national standard of EMS in all aspects, it is critical children are not siloed or left behind. Without this inclusion, the Future Agenda of EMS will not meet the needs of our future adults.

Pediatrics should not be considered a special population they are an age segment of our patient population that represents approximately 22% of the population. Placing children into a special type of category gives way to excuses not to devote the same resources to them as devoted to adults. For example, the excuse usually is kids are special and only a few of our calls involve children; thus we dont need to expend the same amount of funding for pediatric equipment and education. When in reality, this age group is encountered as frequently as a full cardiac arrest or an amputation. We dont excuse a service/agency from not having a defibrillator or a tourniquet. Why should we excuse a service that does not have a pediatric sized resuscitation mask, BVM and endotracheal tube? EMS should have education and training, evidence based protocols, and equipment for every age range in the patient spectrum.

Sir, I respect your background and your beliefs, but I must question your statement that "Having Fire Departments control EMS does not contribute to meaningful, positive outcomes and practice as the focus is not EMS, it is fighting fires."
As the Health and Medical Coordinator of a metropolitan fire department, I would like to invite you to come and spend some time with us and truly learn what our mission and focus is in today's public safety arena. Fire departments in Arizona realize that over 80% of all emergency calls to 9-1-1 involve EMS and not fire suppression. As such, funding for training and equipment does place emphasis on the needs for delivering high quality and effective EMS to the population served. Due to the quality of fire prevention activities and building codes that support a safer environment for our citizens and our firefighters, we do see a marked decrease in the number of structure fires and the resulting savings in both dollars and lives.
EMS is an essential component of the public services provided in the United States. The Federal EMS Act of 1973 defined an EMS system as "an entity that provides for the arrangement of personnel, facilities, and equipment for the effective and coordinated delivery of health care services under emergency conditions in an appropriate geographic
area" (EMS Act 1973, (P.L. 93-154)). Fire services have historically demonstrated their capability to provide this crucial system to serve the needs of their areas' citizens without regard for a citizen's ability to pay for their response and services. Of the 200 largest cities in the United States, 97% have fire service-based prehospital 9-1-1 emergency medical response (JEMS 200-City Survey, 2009) and the fire service provides advanced life support (ALS) response and care in 90% of the 30 most populated U.S. jurisdictions (cities and counties) (IAFF/IAFC files, 2013).
The origin of the relationship between fire departments and patient care (emergency medicine) can be dated back to much earlier than the 1960's when firefighters were assisting physicians with resuscitation techniques and equipment. (Henderson, JAMA 1928) Firefighters today are regarded as all-hazards responders whose focus is on the protection of life and property, not just people running around with fire hoses putting out flames! Fire agencies and their EMS services have become the health system safety net, especially for the poor and underinsured members of our society..
You may even be surprised by the number of EMS studies and research that are done through the cooperation of fire departments across the United States due to the ability to collect meaningful and consistent data from these agencies. The development of cardiocerebral resuscitation, now known as "hands only CPR" came from studies conducted with Tucson Fire paramedics and EMTs in conjunction with the Sarver Heart Center and the University of Arizona.
So, sir, before you disparage fire-based EMS in future musings, I suggest and encourage you to spend some time with these dedicated personnel. I believe you will learn a lot about the quality and caliber of service they provide and realize the value they bring to the delivery of EMS in today's society.

Hospitals and EMS must work together as a team to ensure a smooth transition of care for the patient. Most hospitals have an EMS Coordinator that acts as a liaison between the hospital and EMS. They provide EMS training, feedback to life squads, and promote an effective working relations between the two. Effective communications between hospitals and life squads is imperative to providing the best possible pre-hospital patient care. The largest hospital network in the United States is the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) with 152 hospitals in the U.S. Not one of the VA hospitals employee an EMS Coordinator to liaison between the VA Medical Center and the EMS community. I propose that you approach the VHA and encourage them to become more active in the EMS community. Request that they establish the position of EMS Coordinator in VA Emergency Departments. Life squads bring hundreds of patients to VA Emergency Departments daily. A partnership of this magnitude would improve Veteran patient outcomes and benefit the EMS community with support and collaboration.

Request for Comment on "Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) No. 150: Vehicle-To-Vehicle (V2V) Communication Technology for Light Vehicles;" Docket No. NHTSA-2016-0126

Dear Executive Director Danielson:

The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) is pleased to comment on the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's (NHTSA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) for "FMVSS No. 150: Vehicle-To-Vehicle Communication Technology for Light Vehicles." This addition to FMVSS requires all light vehicles to be equipped with vehicle to vehicle (V2V) technologies that will enable them to send and receive Basic Safety Messages (BSM) to other vehicles. IIHS has reviewed the NPRM for FMVSS No. 150 and previously submitted comments for the "Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM); Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards: V2V Communications" on October 20, 2014 (IIHS 2014a).

IIHS supports FMVSS No. 150 and its phase-in schedule to make V2V communication standard on all light vehicles by 2023. This mandate will be beneficial as its timing closely corresponds with the automotive manufacturers' commitment to make autonomous emergency braking (AEB) standard on all vehicles by 2022 (IIHS 2016a). The Highway Loss Data Institute (HLDI) has repeatedly shown that current AEB systems are effective at reducing insurance claims (HLDI, 2011, 2012a, 2012b, 2013, 2014b). IIHS agrees that adding V2V technologies has the potential to make AEB systems with resident-only sensors even more effective by expanding detection range and accounting for other crash scenarios such as intersections. Resident-only systems have limited capability in preventing intersection crashes, and adding V2V has the potential to help mitigate the 8,446 deaths that occurred in intersection crashes during 2015 (IIHS 2016b).

Fleet penetration research done by IIHS estimates that it takes about 30 years after a mandate for safety features to penetrate 95 percent of all registered light vehicles (HLDI, 2014c). Based on these estimates, the proposed mandate would lead to nearly full fleet penetration of V2V-capable light vehicles by 2053. However, the proposal only requires vehicles to be able to send and receive the BSMs without any requirement on how those messages should be used. IIHS believes rulemaking which outlines specific uses for the BSMs should quickly follow this NPRM to enable the full benefits of V2V to be reached as soon as possible.

IIHS is appreciative of the NHTSA's continued efforts to require essential technologies to enable and enhance crash avoidance systems and lead to further reductions of losses on our nation's roads.

Sincerely,

David Aylor
Manager of Active Safety Testing

Without appropriate levels of national support, however, EMS systems will continue to be impetuous in their use of emergency transport assets, while non-transport units will be under-utilized and under-recognized. On behalf of the members of the Alliance of Automobile Manufacturers, Inc. (Alliance), this responds to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA or agency) Federal Register notice referenced above which initiates rulemaking to create a new Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS), FMVSS No. 150, to mandate vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communications for new light vehicles produced on or after a date to be determined by the final rule date and to standardize the message and format of V2V transmissions.

Section 30111 of title 49 of the United States Code requires that each FMVSS, "shall be practicable, meet the need for motor vehicle safety, and be stated in objective terms." In order for the proposed rule to be practicable, the final rule must clearly state and assure that (1) the 75 MHz of spectrum in the 5.9 GHz radio frequency band remains available for Dedicated Short Range Communications (DSRC) and is kept free from harmful interference, and (2) the Security Credentials Management System (SCMS) is operational before the effective date of the final rule for testing and verification purposes. The Alliance also notes that, as described herein, certain portions of the proposed rule's requirements are not stated in objective terms. To meet the statutory requirement, this must be remedied prior to a final rule.

Sufficient lead-time is essential in ensuring that the criteria are met thoughtfully and effectively. The proposed 2-year lead time with a 3-year phase-in period is more aggressive than recent rulemaking activities with much less complexity and NHTSA should consider a longer time period. Added time is necessary to enable "ground up" design for all vehicle architectures. The Alliance suggests a 3-year lead time with a 4-year phase-in period (as described in Attachment B) to ensure the necessary electronics can be designed thoughtfully, effectively, and less costly than proposed. Industry has been developing innovative technologies and networks that will enable V2V communications and some vehicle manufacturers may elect to implement systems that meet the proposed criteria in advance of any required phase-in schedule. Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Department of Transportation's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking ("NPRM") for Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards establishing new Vehicle-to-Vehicle ("V2V") communication protocols for autonomous vehicles. As a concerned citizen, I appreciate and respect the great lengths to which the Department of Transportation and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration ("NHTSA") have gone to ensure a smooth transition to this exciting new technology. Specifically, NHTSA's September 2015 Model Deployment, the pending 2018 Readiness Reports, and the numerous Driver Clinics inspire great confidence in the DOT's attentiveness and responsiveness to driver needs. I write to address a blind spot within DOT's otherwise comprehensive analysis. Despite its thorough treatment of feasibility and cybersecurity, the NPRM fails to address the market effects of a federally mandated technology standard for V2V communications. The rigidity and inflexibility of a government mandate is ill-suited to the rapid fluidity of this emergent technology. I am deeply concerned that such a mandate will cripple this fledgling technology and stifle the imagination of software developers across the industry.
Section 5(A)(I) of the NPRM discusses "Proposed Channel Usage," and allocates a specific frequency (the 10MHz channel within the 5.9GHz radio band) for V2V communications based on the Federal Communication Commission's ("FCC") assessment of available and appropriate channels. Such an important public goal as transportation safety should not subsist on the scraps left over from other uses of our broadband communication channels. As contemplated in NHTSA's 2015 "DSRC-Unlicensed Device Test Plan," the DOT should re-open joint research with the FCC and the National Telecommunication and Information Administration (NTIA) to further examine channel sharing and re-channelization. Developers across the industry have great plans in mind for this emergent V2V technology, and the DOT's hesitance to lobby the FCC and the NTIA for greater bandwidth will undercut this technology's promise before it even comes to market.
The bandwidth and data transmission abilities of the proposed 10MHz standard may meet the needs of the industry's future as imagined by the DOT, but it substantially impedes further development by private industry. Section 5(B)(I) of the NPRM proposes a bitrate requirement of six megabits per second (6 MBps) with a maximum transmission range of three hundred meters (300m). 6 MBps suffices for transmission of basic geopositioning and directional data, but falls far short of transmitting real-time data such as diagnostic information, emergency broadcasts, or other more imaginative uses of V2V communication such as video uplinks or photo streams. Further, the proposed channelization confines the V2V data transmission to a range of only 300m. This substantially curtails V2V's ability to manage traffic and congestion flows within a city. V2V was originally conceptualized as much more than crash avoidance: it has the potential to re-route and manage traffic throughout an urban area. None of the NPRM's three considered alternatives discuss this limitation, instead, they all center on packet loss, reliability, and bitrate. The NPRM does not provide a reason for prioritizing frequency and size of transmissions over the distance of transmissions.
An alternative considered in the NPRM would rely on a "Voluntary Consensus Standard" determined by an industry consortium, rather than a unilateral federal mandate (NPRM 5(D)(2)). Without federal prompting, private industry has already established two industry groups within the well-respected Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers ("IEEE"), and the Society of Automotive Engineers ("SAE"). These groups independently settled on a proforma 802.11p standard for communications within the 5.9GHz frequency and have made great progress in innovating with future expansion in mind. DOT paternalism in this area needlessly overrides industry consensus and introduces unnecessary rigidity and inflexibility into the rapidly changing tech world.
The NPRM itself expresses uncertainty as to the sufficiency of the limited bandwidth it provides: "we are unsure given the lack of real-world testing whether altering the bitrate and channel bandwidth is necessary." NPRM 5(B)(I). Where DOT itself is unsure as to whether it has allowed sufficient latitude to software developers, it should tread with caution and not prematurely stifle the industry. Prior to implementing a binding technology standard, the DOT should conduct further research to determine whether the proposed 10 MHz standard will restrict automotive innovation by limiting the range and amount of data transmitted by V2V communication.

This comment is in response to RIN 2127-AL55, Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards establishing 49 C.F.R. Part 571 for the purpose of implementing vehicle to vehicle (V2V) communications authorized by 49 U.S.C. 30101.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) have implemented several policies that reduced the number of automobile deaths and automobile accidents since the inception of NHTSA. See Seat Belts, Nat'l Highway Traffic Safety Admin., https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/seat-belts (last visited Mar. 10, 2017). In advancing NHTSA's mission to "save lives, prevent, and reduce vehicle-related crashes" NHTSA have proposed implantation of Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication technology (V2V). II.Manufacturer Liability
The primary concern from vehicle manufacturers is manufacturers accountability to a products liability "failure to warn" claim. Under a "failure to warn" claim, a manufacturer may be liable for a consumer injury if the manufacturer failed to warn consumers of any dangerous characteristics in its product which the consumer would not have ordinarily discovered. 8 Am. Jur. Proof of Facts 3d 547 (Originally published in 1990). To avoid liability for a "failure to warn" claim, a product's instructions or warnings must sufficiently alert the user to the possibility of danger. Id. NHTSA has countered manufacturers' "failure to warn" litigation concerns in the text of this proposed rule, however, NHTSA's solution is not relevant to V2V technology. NHTSA claims that because V2V does not engage in actual vehicle control but instead only produces a warning sound, synonymous to current warning technologies, potential liability will be limited by lack of causation due to the driver's role in failing to avoid crashes. Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards: V2V Communications, 82 Fed. Reg. 3854 (proposed Jan. 12, 2017) (to be codified at 49 C.F.R. pt. 571).
NHTSA's solution, however, is easier said than done. What NHTSA fails to acknowledge is V2V safety warnings are nothing like the current safety warning technologies in vehicles. Current safety warning technologies generate a safety warning by utilizing information only available to the driver's vehicle. For example, the parking censor feature in most vehicles produce an audible tone that increases in frequency the closer an object gets to the rear or front of the vehicle. Active park assist, Ford, https://owner.ford.com/how-tos/vehicle-features/convenience-and-comfort/active-park-assist.html. (last visited Mar. 10, 2017). Any potential defect with the product can be identified because it can be attributed to the manufacturer of the vehicle. Conversely, V2V warnings are not solely reliant on the manufacturer's vehicle. Instead, V2V relies on information coming and going from the driver's vehicle to other vehicles on the road. Vehicle-to-Vehicle Communications, Nat'l Highway Traffic Safety Admin., https://icsw.nhtsa.gov/safercar/v2v/ (last visited Mar. 10, 2017). Therefore, the driver's vehicle does not have any control over the quality, durability, or maintenance of another driver's V2V technology. Additionally, the environment and surrounding topography can also affect the performance of a consumer's V2V system. Fabian de Ponte Muller, Survey on Ranging Sensors and Cooperative Techniques for Relative Positioning of Vehicles, 17 Sensors 271, 276 (2017). These unknowns increase the overall complexity of a failure to warn claim and therefore increases litigation.
III.Cost on Consumer
Furthermore, increased liability and litigation on the manufacturer will have an adverse effect on the consumer by increasing vehicle cost. Sam Batkins, The Consumer Price of Regulation, American Action Forum (May 27, 2014), https://www.americanactionforum.org/research/the-consumer-price-of-regulation/. Over the last decade, several regulations on vehicle manufactures have forced manufacturers to push cost onto consumers. For example, greenhouse gas regulations have increased consumer prices over $3,000. Id. Additionally, automobile regulations on rear view visibility and chassis construction have increased the cost of vehicles to the consumer an additional $500. Id. I urge NHTSA to address the potential liability issue facing the automobile manufacturers due to the forced inclusion of V2V technology in order to keep consumer cost down.

"Different groups in a population may have differences in their ability to tolerate a particular NIR (non-ionizing radiation) exposure. For example, children, the elderly, and some chronically ill people might have a lower tolerance for one or more forms of NIR exposure than the rest of the population. Under such circumstances, it may be useful or necessary to develop separate guideline levels for different groups within the general population, but it may be more effective to adjust the guidelines for the general population to include such groups. Some guidelines may still not provide adequate protection for certain sensitive individuals nor for normal individuals exposed concomitantly to other agents, which may exacerbate the effect of the NIR exposure, an example being individuals with photosensitivity." from ICNIRP STATEMENT, GENERAL APPROACH TO PROTECTION AGAINST NON-IONIZING RADIATION PROTECTION, (HEALTH PHYSICS 82(4):540-548; 2002) https://www.icnirp.org/documents/philosophy.pdf

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration needs to ignore the mere convenience of such technology provides and focus their attention on the more important matter of protecting the health of the occupants of the car.
