Dear Members of the FDA,

Our great country was founded on the principle of opportunity. Opportunities are really what make our country special on the world stage. We are so lucky as Americans to have so many opportunities before us. Unfortunately, individuals with rare diseases do not have many. In 2014 when our son, Connor was diagnosed with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy we were told to love our child as much as possible (as if we didn't already) because there was 'nothing' for him. PTC Therapeutics has worked tirelessly for almost two decades researching, developing, and testing a great opportunity for my son and other boys with the Nonsense Mutation form of Duchenne called Ataluren. This experimental drug could potentially give my son the opportunity to remain ambulant longer, aid in lung function, and give him the childhood that is slipping away from him.

Will Ataluren single-handedly 'cure' his Duchenne? No. We know that. However, it has the potential to greatly improve his quality of life. Our son, unfortunately, was unable to participate in the Ataluren trial. We are, however, currently in another drug trial for an antimyostatin drug. We singlehandedly know the stress and hardship patients and families go through as individuals in a clinical trial. We also understand the stress impressed upon doctor teams and drug companies in the process of testing and filing for approval. The data PTC Therapeutics has supplied you shows a drug that has the potential to make significant gains in young men with Duchenne. It is thought that combining therapies such as Ataluren with other drugs will one day significantly improve the effects of Duchenne, making it a condition that is chronic, but not terminal. Please know that Ataluren will be a key factor in our son's survival and our son's future.

Connor is a happy, smart, caring 10 years old. As a baby and toddler, Connor reached all milestones on time, and we never had any reason to believe that he was ill except for the fact that he could never jump. As you can imagine, we were beyond shocked and devastated when we got his unexpected diagnosis shortly before his 7th birthday. Connnor loves to cook, eat adventurously, dreams of becoming a chef, and loves to play video games. He also loves to run around and DREAMS of doing this endlessly with his friends. He does well in school, is a loyal friend, amazing son, and loving older brother to his little sister, Marissa. Connor is on his way to becoming a smart, engaged and opportunistic teenager. Connor patiently waits for them to stop by our house to visit, and they do for quite some time, but I see the look of pain on his face when he realizes they are off on another adventure on bikes without him. Each boy who lost his life to Duchenne was someone's child, brother, grandson, cousin, nephew, friend, student, godson, neighbor. And they are greatly missed. Every. Single. Day.

The Barshay Family

I would like, as part of the process in which the FDA will evaluate approval of Ataluren, to submit a written statements to the committee to consider about our center positive clinical experiences with Ataluren in nmDMD.
I belong a Neuromuscular clinical group that have been working for many years to get the best treatments and clinical care for neuromuscular patients and their families.
I consider that Ataluren's role in the management of nmDMD patients, based on the scientific data available and in our personal experience, is important given its effectiveness and the positive benefit/risk ratio profile observed. We have 4 nmDMD patients, 9-12 years of age, which have been on Ataluren for the last two years. We have been following them closely and we have observed a positive benefit of the treatment in three of them, with either a decreased in the disease progression or stabilization of the disease, reflected in the 6MWT and the TFTs performed. Only one patient (who started treatment on the edge of the lost of deambulation) hasnt showed a clear positive response. It is also important to note that the clinical program with Ataluren have increased our knowledge of the natural history of the disease, which will definitively benefit these patientss management and outcomes.
Although we still need more data on the long-term effect of the treatment and in other groups of patients (such as the non-ambulant nmDMD patients), the results and the positive benefit/risk ratio profile observed so far support Ataluren as a useful drug for this group of patients, being effective and well tolerated.
In several areas, and especially in rare Duchenne muscular dystrophy, real-life findings from individual cases are important as they present practical information concerning standard clinical management of the disease. Although our cases cannot directly be extrapolated to make assumptions about the overall efficacy or safety, we consider they are important as they provide useful information based on standard clinical practice.

Night splints, orthotics, PT and OT were part of my life ever since I can remember. After walking or standing for 10 minutes, my muscles would get so tight that I'd have to collapse into a chair with my legs straight, unable to bend. By 6th grade I was crawling up the stairs to my bedroom and my parents made a new room for me on the first floor of our house.

The Translarna trial has changed my life in profound ways. When I was in 9th grade I was accepted into the phase 2b trial and I began taking Translarna three times a day. My life has not been the same since.

Halfway through high school, I stopped using my motorized scooter. I began slowly gaining strength and endurance and by my senior year I had learned to drive. Looking at me now, you may not even realize that I have muscular dystrophy. I owe much of my endurance and strength to Translarna for transforming me into who I am today. I have suffered no ill side effects, and I see no reason why this drug should not be approved to help other people like me.

I am writing in support of approval of ataluren. My son, Elijah, has Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. His mutation is not amenable to treatment from this drug, however I know that approximately 13% of patients with this diagnosis are.

Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy has always been a part of my life. I was born into a family that had two boys pass away when they were still young teenagers. My cousin also had the disease. When I was 8 years old my younger brother David, who was 4 at the time, was diagnosed with it. As the years passed, I watched my brother slowly lose muscle strength. Full time wheelchair use came by age 9, then later the ability to raise his arms without the help of his other hand, and eventually the ability to feed himself. I assisted with his total care as his body deteriorated in front of my very eyes. I awoke one morning to find that he wasn't breathing, and he was gone. Losing a teen sibling is pain that unless someone personally experiences, can be never be imagined.

As I had known I was a carrier; I never intended to have children. However, blessings do have a way of happening. My pregnancy resulted in both excitement and trepidation. Five years later, our worst nightmare happened. Due to physical development concerns, we found ourselves in a neurologist's office with Elijah. As soon as I mentioned my family history, the neurologist checked a few things, and promptly sent us for blood work. We received the results right before Christmas: Elijah had Duchenne. Ten years since my brother succumbed to Duchenne, and STILL no treatment existed for his body's inability to produce dystrophin! Today in boys on ataluren with Duchenne who have nonsense mutations, dystrophin is being produced. There is hope! What I would give to have this hope for my own son.

Elijah is now almost 13 years old. As the disease progresses, he progressively needs more assistance with all areas of daily living. Every day he needs assistance with brushing his teeth, bathing, dressing, cleaning himself after using the restroom, and getting into and out of bed. I know that without a treatment, I my son will die of this disease as I watched my brother. As a parent, it is gut wrenching to know that your child will likely not live to see his 25th birthday. Dealing with this fact is dealing with heart break and grief daily. Ataluren changes the course of the disease, and gives the opportunity for a longer life, and more functional ability. Any treatment that can help change the course, and give those with Duchenne a fighting chance to live longer, fuller lives needs to be an approved drug. My son's specific mutation cannot be treated by ataluren, however for those that can be helped, the drug needs to be accessible.

Sincerely,
Amy Aikins

I have been using Ataluren ( Translarna) in 4 patients with DMD associated with a nonsense mutation, initially through a compassionate funding programme and since August 2016 via the NHS England managed access programme.
We follow standard of care protocols and have closely monitored our patients with clinical and physiotherapy assessments as part of the Northstar protocol which guides steroid use and monitoring in the UK. Our son Adam was in the original cohort of 26 boys for the one month PTC safety and efficacy trial that started in 2006. He was 9 years old at the time. He's now 21 years old and continues to be in Ataluren trials. He is a senior at the University of Vermont, living independently in the dorms, with the assist of personal care attendants for nighttime and morning routines.

When Adam was diagnosed with DMD in 1999 at the age of 3, we were told he wouldn't survive to see his high school graduation. Eighteen years later, he is a vibrant, intelligent, hard-working, fun-loving college student. He currently is working on his Honor's College thesis, is an editor at Headwaters Magazine (a UVM publication) and attends courses toward degrees in Environmental Studies and Green Building Design. He enjoys music, and hanging out with friends and family. It's our position that Ataluren provides Adam the stamina he needs to be productive and to achieve his goals.

In 2006, we participated at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP). There were before and after biopsies, blood work and lots of physical testing. And then we waited. Finally in August 2008, the 2b extension trial began and we traveled to CHOP from northern Vermont on several occasions per the trial protocol. He was put on what was believed to be the therapeutic dose (high dose). There would be 2 additional biopsies, bloodwork, and 6MWT's, along with frequent travel from Burlington Vermont to Philadelphia. In early 2010, now 13 years old, Adam was still walking independently. He would play wall-ball at school, ride a modified bicycle, and enjoy numerous Boy Scout activities. He had a motorized scooter to help prevent fatigue with long distances. He was rarely ill. My husband and I believed strongly that Ataluren was keeping Adam stable, including his heart and lungs. The slowing of progression of this devastating disease gave us great hope. Then abruptly on March 3, 2010 we were ordered to stop drug immediately. The trial was over. We were devastated.

During the time Adam was off the drug (about a year) my husband and I noted more significant decline. We noticed Adam was less stable on his feet. He was wobbly and he tripped and fell more frequently. The falls were always frightening, and we worried about fractures and trips to the Emergency Room. We started the process of ordering a power wheelchair. Once back on drug at the actual therapeutic dose, we saw his function stabilize. He was now 14, and then 15 years old, and mostly managing all of his activities of daily living independently. He continued to walk, could wipe his own bum, was a talented drummer and artist. He loved school and enjoyed camp on Martha's Vineyard.

In March 2012, we were transferred to Boston Children's Hospital for our clinical site. That June, at age 16, Adam had a fall from his wheelchair and broke his femur. He wouldn't walk again. The following year he had scoliosis surgery. Just prior, a bipap machine for nighttime assist was ordered. Even with these major insults to his body, he recovered really well and continued to be independent in most all activities of daily living. In 2014, he graduated high school with high honors, continued to play the drums, and achieved the rank of Eagle Scout. Later that year, he moved from home into the Honors College dormitories at University of Vermont, where he would begin his college career. He was living independently with modest support from personal care attendants. He was living his life on his terms. As a family, we celebrated his successes.

In December 2016 Adam had a tragic wheelchair accident. He went head over first with his chair landing on top of him. He banged his head, broke both femurs and developed fat embolism syndrome. The emboli quickly flooded his lungs and brain and he was placed on life support. We thought we would lose him. Yet within 5 weeks time, he was ready to move back into the dorms. His spirit was dampened slightly, but we all agreed he needed to keep on his path and pursue his goals. His recovery was remarkable. In all our heart we believe Ataluren kept him strong in mind and body, aiding in his health recovery. To this day, he continues to live independently with the assist of overnight aides. He feeds himself, works on his computer, gets to all his classes, and use a portable urinal independently. We consider these great successes for a 21 year old with DMD.

As a family we have given close to 12 years toward the advancement of this therapy. We were the first to have an option to try and we gave it our all. There were many starts and stops, and of course fibrosis and damage had already been done. We can only imagine, what his life would be if he was on the right dose from a very early age without interruption. Please approve this drug, so we and all the families who follow can have an opportunity at living a full satisfying life.

We have been prescribing Translarna since 2015 at the Neuromuscular Center at the University of Padova. To date, we have treated 6 patients, all of whom were ambulatory nmDMD patients aged 5 years or older, as per EMA official indications.
We have had a positive experience with Translarna in our patients, and overall, our "real life" clinical experience was consistent with the results described in clinical trials. There were no safety issues that caused any concern. Mild triglyceride elevation in one patient was followed up and resolved spontaneously without any symptom, and without the need to modify the treatment regime. A slight reduction of appetite in one or two patients did not cause concern; on the contrary, as these patients were also on glucocorticoids and at risk of excessive weight gain, this "side effect" made the clinical management of the patients easier. All families were compliant with the proposed treatment, and the drug was always taken at the recommended doses.
As for efficacy, it is obviously difficult, in single patients or in small numbers, to compare the observed trajectory of motor function with what "would have happened", had the drug not been taken. However, our clinical impression was that Translarna stabilized motor function more than glucocorticoid treatment alone in our older patients (> 7 years), and that the young patients' (below 7 years) improvements in motor function were more marked than with glucocorticoids alone. We would be in favour of prolonging treatment in our patients as long as possible, also in the hope that ataluren might benefit respiratory and cardiac function in the long term - an outcome that is very hard, if not impossible to explore in randomized clinical trials.

Alzheimer's Disease

Cannabis slows the progression of Alzheimer's disease by slowing the production of beta-amyloid proteins, considered the key contributor to the disease's progression (Iuvone, et al., 2004). It also protects brain cells from the deleterious effects of amyloid-beta, reduces inflammation, and supports the brain's repair process by enhancing the birth of new cells (Campbell & Gowran, 2007).

Dystonia

Cannabis reduces the involuntary muscle contractions associated with dystonia (Consroe, Sandyk & Snider, 1986).

Epilepsy

CBD has been shown to effectively and significantly decrease the frequency of seizures and in some cases has even shown to produce complete seizure freedom (Blair, Deshpande & DeLorenzo, 2015).

Fibromyalgia

Studies have found that cannabis is effective at improving sleep disruption, pain, depression, joint stiffness, anxiety, physical function and quality of life in individuals with fibromyalgia (de Souza Nascimento, et al., 2013) (Russo, 2004).

Lupus

Cannabis reduces inflammation, thus potentially offering therapeutic benefit to those with lupus, and can reduce pain associated with the disorder (Nagarkatti, et al., 2009) (Clayton, Marshall, Bountra & O'Shaughnessy, 2002).

Migraines

Through activation of the cannabinoid receptors, cannabis inhibits the pain response caused by migraines (Akerman, Holland, Lasalandra & Goardsby, 2013) (Baron, 2015) (Greco, et al., 2014).

Multiple Sclerosis

Cannabis reduces pain and muscle spasms associated with multiple sclerosis and helps slow the disease's progression (Lakhan & Rowland, 2009) (Pacher, Batkai & Kunos, 2006). One animal study found that cannabinoids reduced damage to myelin caused from inflammation, thereby providing neuroprotection (Pryce, et al., 2003).

Parkinson's Disease

Cannabis' neuroprotective effects and ability to encourage cell health reduces the progression of Parkinson's disease (More & Choi, 2015). It has also shown to help manage the tremors, rigidity, bradykinesia, motor disability and impairments, sleep problems and pain associated with the disorder (Lotan, Treves, Roditi & Djaldetti, 2014).

Tourette Syndrome

Cannabis safely reduces the frequency of tics caused by Tourette syndrome (Muller-Vahl, 2013).

States That Have Approved Medical Marijuana for Central Nervous System Disorders
No states include central nervous system disorders on their list of approved conditions for medical marijuana. However, many do allow medical marijuana for the treatment of specific central nervous system disorders.

For example, Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Mississippi, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas, Utah, Virginia, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming have approved medical marijuana for the treatment of either epilepsy or seizure disorders. California and Illinois have specifically approved medical marijuana for the treatment of migraines. Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Michigan, North Dakota, New Hampshire, Oregon, and Rhode Island have approved medical marijuana for Alzheimer's disease. Arkansas, Illinois and North Dakota have approved medical marijuana specifically for the treatment of fibromyalgia. Illinois and New Mexico has approved medical marijuana for the treatment of dystonia. Illinois and New Hampshire have approved medical marijuana specifically for the treatment of lupus. Arkansas, Illinois and Minnesota have approved medical marijuana specifically for the treatment of Tourette syndrome. Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Mexico, New York, and West Virginia have approved medical marijuana for the treatment of Parkinson's disease. Alaska, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Vermont, and West Virginia allow medical marijuana for the treatment of multiple sclerosis.

In addition, in Washington D.C., any condition can be approved for medical marijuana as long as a DC-licensed physician recommends the treatment. Plus, various other states will consider allowing medical marijuana to be used for the treatment of central nervous system disorders with the recommendation from a physician. These states include: California (any debilitating illness where the medical use of marijuana has been recommended by a physician), Connecticut (other medical conditions may be approved by the Department of Consumer Protection), Massachusetts (other conditions as determined in writing by a qualifying patient's physician), Nevada (other conditions subject to approval), Oregon (other conditions subject to approval), Rhode Island (other conditions subject to approval), and Washington (any "terminal or debilitating condition").

At the Department Neuroscience of Federico II University of Naples, three children are treated with Ataluren (40 mg/kg/day) for nonsense mutation in DMD gene.
The first boy is an 11-year-old with nonsense mutation (c.2077T> C, exon 1). His medical history started at the age of 5 years with increased transaminases. After the diagnosis a steroid treatment was introduced, but it was stopped for agitation and sleep alterations. At the age of 10 years the treatment Ataluren was started. At the baseline 6MWT distances between >300 <400 m. During the following year motor performances remained stable. Other measures of functional performance such as the timed 10 m walk/run, timed 4-stair ascent and descent, and the time to stand from the supine position also confirmed the clinical stability.
The second boy is 8-year-old with the c.3242C> A, exon 24 nonsense mutation. At the time of diagnosis, 5 years of age, he presented with poor language ability and mild cognitive impairment. Steroid treatment with deflazacort was started, but the patient developed early Achilles tendon retraction. The treatment with Ataluren was started at the age 8 years when the motor involvement was severe (6MWT about 75 m). Over the course of the 12-month treatment period the 6MWT distance almost doubled and the patient could walk/run 10 m in a much faster time than before.
The third patient is a 5-year-old boy with nonsense mutation c.7471C>T, exon 51. At last neurological examination he showed attention difficulties and a waddling gait and hyperlordosis. He also had a positive Gowers sign and pseudohypertrophy of the quadriceps and gastrocnemius muscles. Ataluren treatment was started and measures relating to mobility improved during the 12-month treatment period, in particular the 6MWT distance was 320 m at baseline and 400 m after 12 m.
During the course of follow-up none of the children exhibited cardiac or respiratory involvement. Periodic echocardiograms, electrocardiograms and spirometry check-ups were all normal. All patients received regular sessions of physiokinesitherapy and psychomotor testing.
For each of the three cases described above the caregivers also reported during the treatment less fatigue and a reduction in the number of falls/month. In addition, all the three children achieved better school performance ratings, were more participative and spent more time involved in fun activities. Ataluren was generally well tolerated, with none of the patients showing significant side effects.
From our experience in these three cases we found that Ataluren was relatively straightforward to administer with no compliance issues, and it was generally very well tolerated, with no side effects reported. Moreover we had note that when the treatment was started early may lead to a better therapeutic outcome, probably because we prevent muscle degeneration. Finally the improvement that we observed for case 2 highlights that some positive results may still be achieved in patients with a more severe muscle involvement.

Central nervous system disorders are a group of diseases and conditions that affect the health and functioning of the spinal cord and brain. Studies have shown cannabis can limit the progression of many central nervous system disorders and help manage symptoms like pain, seizures and spasms.

Overview of Central Nervous System Disorders
Central nervous system disorders are a broad category of conditions or diseases that affect the spinal cord or brain. There are many different types of central nervous system disorders, some of which include epilepsy, migraine, Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Tourette syndrome, dystonia, multiple sclerosis, meningitis, lupus, fibromyalgia, and bipolar disorder. While central nervous system disorders can vary greatly from each other, all the disorders cause a loss of sufficient, intact nervous system circuits that orchestrate particular functions.

The damage that leads to or causes central nervous system disorders can include trauma, infections, degeneration, congenital problems, structural defects, tumors, blood flow disruption and autoimmune disorders.

Symptoms associated with central nervous system disorders vary depending on the specific condition, but can include headaches, tingling or loss of feeling, muscle weakness, muscle wasting, loss of sight or double vision, memory loss, impaired mental ability, lack or coordination, tremors and seizures, muscle rigidity, and back pain.

Most central nervous system disorders cannot be cured, but medications, therapy, surgery and other treatment options can help limit their progression and manage associated symptoms.

Findings: Effects of Cannabis on Central Nervous System Disorders
Studies have shown that cannabis has neuroprotective effects, and in turn supports the health of the brain and spinal cord and helps in the treatment of a variety of central nervous system disorders. The cannabinoids found in cannabis, including cannabidiol (CBD) and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), have shown they effectively protect neurons and astrocytes from damage, modulate inflammatory reaction and assist in neuroregeneration (Lafuente, et al., 2011) (Kubajewska & Constantinescu, 2010) (Croxford, et al., 2008).

CBD and THC activate the cannabinoid receptors (CB1 and CB2) of the endocannabinoid system, which plays a significant regulatory role in health and disease (Pacher, Batkai & Kunos, 2006) (Di Marzo, Bifulco & De Petrocellis, 2004). The upregulation of the endocannabinoid system has shown to reduce the severity of symptoms like neuropathic pain and muscle spasms and slow the progression of central nervous system disorders like multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and others (Di Marzo, Bifulco & De Petrocellis, 2004) (Pertwee, 2006) (Pacher, Batkai & Kunos, 2006). Studies also show that cannabinoids reduce the debilitating seizures caused by epilepsy and reduce spasms experienced by those with multiple sclerosis, and minimize the neurological damage caused by spinal cord and traumatic brain injuries (Iuvone, et al., 2004) (More & Choi, 2015) (Blair, Deshpande & DeLorenzo, 2015) (Lakhan & Rowland, 2009).

My younger brother has muscular dystrophy. For me, what this means has evolved over time. Before entering 2nd grade, we moved to a new home with more rooms on the ground floor, anticipating that he would soon be unable to climb stairs. When his legs grew so weak that he began needing to crawl up the stairs, we relocated his bedroom downstairs. He began using a motorized scooter in school. We limited our family vacations to activities that he could participate in--no more hikes or sports. My parents, who had educated themselves thoroughly and joined support groups, told us that he would continue to decline, his skeletal muscles atrophying until he became chairbound, his diaphragm weakening until he lost the strength to breathe. Clearly, for him more than anyone else, the burden of this disease was enormous, but even as a sibling, I observed that this was one of the focal points of our family life. It shaped where we could live, what we could do, and how we thought about our future.

Several years ago, my brother began taking ataluren as a part of the experimental trial. The changes were not immediate; in fact, it was sometimes difficult to convince him to take the medicine, as he saw little initial benefit. But over several years, he began to regain his strength. He stopped using his scooter; he moved back to his upstairs bedroom. Currently, at 24, he is finishing a degree in accounting, living independently several hours from our parents' home. Two years ago, he completed a 5K race--a feat that would have previously been far beyond his reach. To say that ataluren has been transformative feels like an understatement. It has literally reshaped his possibilities in life.

Dear Janet Woodcock, MD and all FDA Advisory Committee members,

In 2014 my son Connor was diagnosed with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. To reiterate and innumerate the physical, psychological, emotional and financial tolls that this disorder takes on our son and our family on a regular basis would likely be redundant at this point.

A little over a year ago Connor was enrolled in the third leg of a clinical trial for an anti-myostatin drug through Kennedy Krieger Institute in Baltimore. This trial, per the FDA requirements is a "randomized, placebo controlled, double-blind, ascending dose" study.

While we have been undeniably provided with an extremely high-level of care and compassion throughout the trial, we have also willingly subjected our son to dozens of painful blood draws, hundreds of abdominal injections, MRI's, ECHOS, Dexa scans, PT sessions and seemingly endless 300 mile trips to and from Baltimore, knowing full-well that for the first six months of said trial Connor may have been receiving the placebo.

We subjected him to all of this also knowing that there's a very real possibility, that at the end of this trial, he and other boys like him may be denied access to this particular drug, even though there is already a mountain of evidence pointing to the fact that it is effective.

While we do not necessarily agree with all of the terms, processes and protocols dictated by the FDA, we do accept them. We accept these terms because there is no alternative, and there IS a chance. There is a chance this drug, and this extremely taxing process, will improve the quality of life for our son and for many other boys. We accept these terms because there's a chance it will work. We also accept these terms knowing that there's a chance it will not work. In the case of DMD, every BODY is different.

It's worth reiterating that Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy affects primarily young boys, and is a degenerative disease. There is currently no cure and few treatment options. Time is the enemy.

Today's physicians may not technically be bound by the Hippocratic Oath, but when you choose to practice medicine, you are entering into an unwritten social contract to "DO NO HARM". Ensuring new drugs are safe, and keeping the pharmaceutical industry in check by ensuring the efficacy of those drugs is a noble public service.
Unfortunately, from the perspective of the parent of a child with Duchenne, the process and protocols for achieving these ends feel inherently broken.

The bottom line is that it is unreasonable to subject all drugs to the same process of evaluation, and, in certain situations, absolutely unethical to hold all drugs to the same standards of efficacy.

In the case of DMD, we are discussing a rare disease that affects young people. You are talking about a small potential patient population from the start. Within that already limited group, an even smaller group will meet all of the markers in terms of physical requirements, age requirements, and extremely specific genetic criteria to qualify for current potential clinical trials.

The researchers, scientists and doctors behind the development and testing of Ataluren have jumped through countless hoops and hurdles attempting to make this drug available to a wider population of those afflicted with DMD. The safety of this compound was established long ago, as was the efficacy.

Consider the evidence before you, but more importantly, consider the patient base we're talking about. We are asking for a chance. This is a common sense decision. No harm will come from allowing DMD patients access to this drug. Great harm could potentially come if you continue to deny access.

DO NO HARM.

Respectfully Yours,
Ethan Barshay

My name is Klair Bayley, Excutive Officer Of Clinical Care and Advocacy, and my submission is on behalf of Save Our Sons Duchenne Foundation, the peak body for Duchenne in Australia.
Prior to this review, the Duchenne community across Australia would like the FDA to know more about Duchenne, its natural history and its devastation on those with the condition and their families.
Duchenne is a progressive degenerative muscle wasting condition that devastates individuals with Duchenne and their families. It affects 1:3500 - 1:5000 boys and in very rare cases 1:50,000,000 girls. Those with Duchenne commonly have a delay in their motor milestones, and commonly have learning delays. They gain the ability to crawl, walk and run, usually slower than their peers, and then Duchenne takes it all away. With loss of strength in their pelvic girdle and leg muscles boys increasingly fall, and then lose ambulation commonly between 10-14 years, and as their peers are gaining independence into their teens, those with Duchenne are losing their independence. The muscles of the upper body also begin to decline, they lose the ability to lift their arms and eventually have minimal function in the hands and fingers. Also the muscles in the heart, lungs, diaphragm and smooth muscle, are affected, causing increasing deterioration such as cardiac and respiratory failure and eventually, in the absence of an effective treatment, a premature death. Life expectancy is mid to late 20's.
The impact on families is incredibly high, with psychological, physical, social and financial implications associated with having a child, or children with an incurable, degenerative muscle wasting condition. Duchenne affects the entire family, with a cyclical grieving process as the child gradually loses function, families explaining the process as 'watching your child fade away, and not being able to do anything about it'. Thinking of a future where you have hopes and dreams as a parent for your child and then knowing that they will not be able to achieve these. Family dynamics change, with the affects cascading on to siblings. There are a lot of sad moments as children reach milestones and a parent looking on knows that this will be short lived and the progressive nature of Duchenne will rob them of their independence. They see the daily frustrations as there child try's to keep up with their peers only to fatigue and then fall.
As a community we live in hope for an effective therapy that will change the terminal diagnosis of Duchenne into one of a treatable chronic condition, one that changes the natural history of Duchenne and sees our children become men and hopefully old men. There is certainly hope on the horizon with clinical trials for Duchenne. Members of our community in Australia and New Zealand have been part of the clinical trials for Ataluren for several years. The community both of the parents and the clinicians have reported that during the clinical trials, there has been a good safety profile with no reported side effects and the families have reported that their sons have tolerated Ataluren well.
The observations we have had reported to us and that we have seen are a stabilisation in a population with a progressive, degenerative condition. There are activities of daily living that become harder as the disease progresses, but that we have had reported by families with a child on Ataluren such as grooming, feeding themselves and toileting independently, that have been maintained and that the families have not noted a decline. Their have been reports of the boys regaining some motor function and strength in completing tasks and also reduced fatigue. These observations have been reported from both the close family and extended family as well as teachers, who have noticed improvements or not reported decline when we would expect to see decline as the child get older. Maintaing function and motor skills improves the child's quality of life and their independence.
Having hope is imperative within a community that the clinical trials and emerging therapies will be available as quickly as possible, and accessible, equitably to all, in order to maintain motor function, but also to ensure that the other muscular systems such as the heart and lung muscles do not deteriorate. Safe and efficacious therapies are certainly welcomed by the Duchenne community. Quality of life is paramount and maintaing function and independence needs to be taken into serious consideration.
There is no time to waste. We hope that our submission can assist with the FDA in their decision making process, but better understanding the condition, its impact and the individuals whose lives this decision will change. We thank you for your time.

To the members of the Peripheral and Central Nervous System Drugs Advisory Committee:

In 1983, my older brother Michael was diagnosed with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. Doctors were confident that there would be a cure to this disease in his lifetime. In 1995, my cousin Adam was diagnosed. Again doctors were confident that there would most certainly be a cure in his lifetime. Both young men passed away, my brother in 2003 and my cousin in 2015, sadly before any cure or treatment was available.

As a carrier of Duchenne, I was relieved to find out that I'd be bringing triplet daughters into this world. My daughters, Sarah, Megan, and Anna were born prematurely in 2009. Sarah and Megan were developing very slowly and doctors told us this was common with preemies. However, the girls weren't catching up. In fact, they were demonstrating Duchenne-like characteristics in the way they walked, stood up, and the shape of their bodies. I asked their doctor about the possibility of Duchenne and was told, "of course not, girls don't get Duchenne." I went to a second doctor who told me the same thing but referred my daughters to a third doctor to treat them for what she'd assumed was cerebral palsy due to prematurity. After a year with this third doctor he finally agreed to conduct a blood test and then a muscle biopsy.

The tests confirmed our worst nightmare, that Sarah and Megan, identical twins, have a nonsense DMD mutation and a disabling lack of dystrophin in their muscles. My daughters were diagnosed as manifesting carriers of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.

Our entire extended family was rocked by this revelation, another generation that has to live with this horrible disease. But today there is more hope than there was in 1983 or in 1995. There are so many drugs being developed and so many trials going on. Unfortunately, because my daughters have some amount of dystrophin in their muscles, they have not been able to qualify for any trials.

I implore you to recommend approval for Ataluren, not just for boys but also for the female manifesting carriers that often experience the same symptoms as the boys but don't have access to this or any of the many drugs in trial.

Ataluren is not a cure for Duchenne, but it can treat it. It can lessen the symptoms. It can give the kids more time. It may not work for everybody, but if it can work for one person, if it can extend one life, that should be enough to grant approval.

And maybe, with the help of Ataluren, today's generation will live to see a cure.

Sincerely,

Deb Jenssen
Madison, Alabama

Hello, my name is Cinnamon Martz and my son Brandon Martz is 19 years old and has DMD. Brandon took part in the Phase 2B safety and efficacy study of ataluren in 2008 at age 9.

About a month of Brandon being on the drug he jumped for the first time in his life. My husband and I asked Brandon "What was that sound?" to which he replied as if he had been doing it his whole life "I jumped off the bottom step." Once Brandon took this first jump he just continued to do it over and over again. Brandon was able to jump off of the bottom step of any flight of stairs and he would nail the landing, perfect no wobbling, losing balance, a boy who was not supposed to be able to jump was jumping.

The next thing I noticed was he started preferring to use stairs versus ramps that he had gotten accustomed to using. At the house we lived in we had a deck that led to the back yard. We had a ramp built into the design, we also had stairs built in, two different sets of stairs since the deck was two levels. One day just like the jump I looked out the window and here comes Brandon inside using the stairs instead of the ramp with no effort alternating his feet while taking the stairs. Before Brandon started the drug he avoided stairs, at the age of 9 he was not able to use them. Well not until he started taking ataluren.

We continued to see improvements like this. Things Brandon could never do he would just start doing them as if he had always done them. Brandon no longer used the Gower maneuver to get off of the floor. With Brandon being able to get down and up off the floor that was something he really enjoyed because Brandon's friends would come for sleep overs and throw their sleeping bags on the floor and Brandon would always sleep on the couch. At 9 years old Brandon got his first sleeping bag and he started sleeping on the floor with his friends. This was a big deal for Brandon.

Brandon's new-found abilities were proof that ataluren does work. I found that with these new improvements I needed to have talks with Brandon that I never thought I would be having. One was about the danger of running. Brandon, my son whom I had never had to tell not to run out into the street, or not to run off began running. What a wonderful gift I was given to need to talk to my 9-year-old son with DMD about the dangers of running off.

There are so many stories I could tell you about how ataluren has impacted Brandon's life for the better. I think though that the most important take away I could give you is ataluren gave my son back the abilities that DMD took away from him or never allowed him to experience in the first place. Ataluren has given Brandon a better quality of life than what we were told his life would look like. Brandon has been on the drug for almost 11 years with zero safety problems. Brandon has spent this last almost 11 years living his life fully, traveling, joining clubs, working summer jobs, going to Baseball games, Football games, Concerts, his Senior Prom. Ataluren has given Brandon a lot more endurance and strength than he had before taking the drug.

At 19 ataluren has made it possible for Brandon to be very independent. Brandon does not use a ventilator. He does use a BiPAP machine when he sleeps at night but that is all that is needed and he did not start using that until he was 17.

Brandon does also use a wheelchair when he was 15 he got into a horrible accident and broke his leg severely. Within 8 weeks of the break, and with intensive Physical Therapy he was back up walking again. We could hardly believe it and celebrated with a trip to an amusement water park. Unfortunately, he did end up breaking the same leg again, had another surgery, more PT and Brandon was able to get back up a second time and walk using a walker but by then we were all too concerned that this could not happen again so Brandon made the choice to start using a wheelchair. At the age of 19, Brandon can open the fridge and make his own food, he does not need assistance feeding himself. He uses a computer, his phone, he plays video games, he sketches.

I am thankful that ataluren has slowed the progression of DMD in Brandon's body. I am grateful for this in so many ways but in one specific way that I think about, is when/if Brandon faces losses of progression he will be older with the intellectual/emotional maturity that comes with age to better deal with them.

I am asking you to please approve ataluren, Brandon has had zero safety issues with the drug, he has only received benefit from taking ataluren. At age 19 I can tell you with certainty that Brandon has experienced a life well lived, and he is not done yet. Thank you for taking the time to read my comment and for your consideration.

I am writing on behalf of my son, Thomas Parzymieso, age 9, who has Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. Just after his second birthday, it was confirmed that Thomas has a nonsense mutation at exon 21. To date, he has been unable to participate in any of the U.S. clinical trials for Ataluren due the unfortunate date of his birth.

The first clinical trial to open enrollment after his diagnosis came when he was five years old, in 2013. It was announced that the trial would be inclusive of boys between the ages of 7 and 10. Before he could reach his seventh birthday, that trial reached its full enrollment and closed. Around the same time, PTC opened up a second Ataluren trial for boys aged 5 and under. Thomas was already 6. Next, came access to all siblings of boys enrolled in the trials. Thomas has only one sister. Concurrently, Europe saw the conditional approval of Ataluren, opening up access to hundreds of other boys around the world. Consideration was even requested for compassionate use, but that plea was denied.

Still, my son waits. He waits for access to a drug that, although not a cure, has shown in the clinical data, and in the voices and experiences of those families who have been involved in the trials, that it has real benefit -- whether it be delayed progression, increased energy, or healthier than expected cardiopulmonary function.

While my son waits, he has lost function. He now uses a scooter out in public. He cannot participate in summer camps with his friends because they are too physically aggressive. He doesn't have the stamina or strength to participate in sports - his one true passion in life.

Over the years, we have tried to get Thomas included in other clinical trials, but due to age considerations and other health issues, he has been denied access. As a result, my son has no other options available to him but to watch his disease press on.

Now that Thomas is 9 years old, he is starting to be more aware of the world around him. He is realizing that he is different than his peers and why. He sees the older boys with Duchenne and notices that they are all in wheelchairs. He hasn't yet come to realize the inevitable. He still dreams of becoming a professional NFL or NHL player, and is planning on selecting his college based on who has the better football team, where he will be the backup quarterback. But, he is curious about why he takes steroids, Vitamin D supplements and heart medications; and asks thoughtful questions about his body.

We know that Ataluren will not enable Tommy to ever play competitive sports. Our hope is that Ataluren will, however, buy his legs time to keep him standing and as independent as possible through high school - a goal that we have seen accomplished by many of the young men who have been fortunate enough to be included in the Ataluren trials.
We accept that Duchenne has changed Thomas's and our lives forever. What we cannot accept is a life without options. Access to Ataluren is the option that we have been waiting on for seven years. We haven't another moment to spare.

Thank you in advance for your consideration.

In the "Discussion" part of the NPRM and AD (e) "Reason" it is stated that following the incorrect data from the flight management system could result in loss of control.
Pilatus requests the FAA to reconsider the final statement "loss of control", since in our opinion this may be misleading.
The autopilot fails to follow the correctly indicated nominal vertical flight path. If the pilot does not observe the indicated vertical deviation, which is his primary duty during IMC final approach, it could result in the pilot losing situational awareness.
In the worst case, the aircraft would descent towards terrain and ultimately, if no attention is given to TAWS call outs, collide with the terrain - potential CFIT.

Pilatus therefore proposes to change the last part of the (e) Reason sentence to read:
"We are issuing this AD to prevent the pilot from following incorrect data from the flight management system, which could result in the loss of situational awareness."

1) The UAV should have a safety buzzer onboard that blares in case of falls or emergency landing. This notifies the immediate environment of impending dangers.

2) Another safety measure is to have heat sensor that shows realtime temperature of the transmission lines. This is to guard against fire hazard.

The inability to track a drone in flight is one of the biggest threats to all other aircraft and the flying public as a whole.  Drones should be required to have a device that transmits a signal to notify other aircraft and/or ATC towers within a certain radius that the drone is in flight, it's overall dimensions, and it's flight capacity.

With only 110 lbs of payload it is difficult to trade payload/endurance for safety. However, it has been demonstrated on a similar rotary wing drone that the autonomous flight control system can be programmed to auto-rotate the aircraft in the event of an engine failure. This software adds no additional weight penalty. The ability to select a suitable emergency landing site has also been demonstrated. It is neither large nor heavy (order of 1 pound additional weight). In this manner, the aircraft knows its total energy (altitude and airspeed) and can continuously calculate suitable emergency landing points within the "total energy" constraints at the moment of an engine or gearbox malfunction. Typically, these things are done in a manned rotary wing aircraft by the pilot. These functions can be performed via automation which significantly enhances the safety of people and things on the ground.

From a sense-and-avoid standpoint, there are demonstrated systems that will enhance overall safety whether in an emergency condition or not. The fundamental concept is to not fly into something, whether that something is another aircraft, a building, a tower, etc. This is not difficult to implement, however the published information on the "airworthiness" operations do not include such a system. Considering the aircraft is intended to be flown beyond visual sight, more serious consideration to some form of sense-and-avoid should be mandated.

Information on the control link from the ground operator to the aircraft is lacking in detail. Has a lost-link procedure been implemented? Has a "captured-link" (link control by third party) been considered and mitigated? How can the public ensure the aircraft operating in an autonomous mode, beyond line of sight of the control operator(s) will not "wander off" into more populated areas or into airways (ala, the navy's rotary wing drone in southern Maryland several years ago).

Finally, what is the certification basis of the rotary wing aircraft design and fabrication and the method of compliance with that certification basis? Is it the same as manned aircraft (Robinson R-22 for example) or is it a Special airworthiness certification standard of some form? Assuming it is Experimental (and not Restricted), then it is imperative that the public knows the aircraft will not deviate from its limited operating area defined by the FAA. The information provided in the public announcement does not provide a sufficient level of confidence that the rotary wing drone aircraft will not stray out of its intended operating area.

Page 22 of "Airworthiness Criteria for the FlightScan Camcopter S" states, "A means to alert the crew in the event of a failure must be provided when an unsafe system operating condition exists and to enable them to take corrective action."  For a UAS experiencing a lost command and control link, this requirement would be impossible to meet since the flight crew is remote.  The requirement should take into account this possibility and state that automatic means of recovery in light of failure is also acceptable.

As identified by the FAA, we too believe that UAS Command and Control communications link security criteria need to be defined urgently.
In order to sufficiently do so, encryption, authentication and authenticity have to be provided. Securing data cannot be achieved by merely integrating AES encryption, as this prevents other parties to read the content, but does not protect against replay and/or man-in-the-middle attacks. Even with AES encryption, commands can be recorded and replayed, making the drone vulnerable to hijacking and other harmful communication inputs. Henceforth, we recommend to implement encryption, authentication, as well as authenticity (making sure that each data package that is received comes from the trustworthy source) to truly secure communication links.
Furthermore, as the UAS will be operated BVLOS, redundant communication links are strongly recommended to protect the system, mission and bystanders. Drone operators are frequently faced with interference issues and loss of communication due to unstable signals. This needs to be anticipated by utilizing more than one link. We recommend to have a variety of different datalinks available that will be used according to signal quality, ideally through dynamic switching. This means that a redundant communication link should not merely act as 'back-up' once the primary link is lost, instead the system should be able to switch dynamically between the links that provide the best quality at any point in time.

Based on the published information, there appears to be no consideration for the following items:
1. Will the rotary wing aircraft operate on or near an airport; if so, does the airport have a control tower. Regardless, what agreement is there with others operating at the airport/heliport?
2. What is the lost-communications procedure? Is the rotary wing aircraft to operate in the autonomous mode and the radio link only exercised if a change in mission is required or the aircraft shows signs of autonomous failures. How does the rotary wing aircraft notify "other interested parties" such as tower operators, other aircraft in the vicinity and the like that it is executing some form of pre-programmed lost comm/lost control link procedure.
3. Since a rotary wing aircraft has the ability to auto-rotate in the event of an engine failure, is this capability included in the autonomous commands, only effected by the control operator, or there is no auto-rotation capability at all. If there is an auto rotation capability, how does the aircraft select an appropriate landing point? How does the aircraft know when to "pull collective" at the appropriate point in the flight path (radar altimeter for example)?
4. Since the most likely FCC approved control frequencies are VHF/UHF/SHF/ EHF which are all line-of-sight electromagnetic wave propagation, then how will the rotary wing aircraft be operated beyond line of sight but still be in control by the control operator via the ground station (non-satellite relay solution)?
5. What are the communication requirements of the various personnel identified in the notice during flight operations. That is, are they co-located and in verbal communications or are they in radio contact with one another but in different physical locations.
6. Is there any other means of controlling the aircraft that is not described?
7. What are the aircraft control link security methods implemented that preclude another station (intruder) taking control of the aircraft. What is the aircraft's ability to detect either an intrusion or jamming of the control circuits? Does it then follow lost comm procedures or continue on its autonomous flight?

1) The UAV should have a safety buzzer onboard that blares in case of falls or emergency landing. This notifies the immediate environment of impending dangers.

2) Another measure is to have heat sensor that shows realtime temperature of the transmission lines. This is to guard against fire hazard.

In lieu of a very costly certification program such as Part 23, the basic criteria the FAA should apply is the concept of redundancy (or fail safe). It is the least expensive way to assure safety. The DoD 2005 UAS Roadmap report shows a very poor UAS record compared to GA statistics. Read Appendix H-1.The RQ-7 Shadow had a record of 380 mishaps per 100,000 hours when the experience with the system was 4,000 hours and went down to 191 when the experience was 30,000 hours. This compares with about 7 fatal accidents per 100,000 hours with General Aviation aircraft. That's about 30 times more likely for a mishap to happen. If you now consider that we are talking about a helicopter whose mechanical complexity is several times more than that of a fixed wing, you are definitely unwillingly allowing many accidents we will all regret. The same study shows that in the US military experience about 38% of the causes are engine malfunctions (you will need either 2 independent engines or 1 certified engine), 19% are due to control failures (you will need to install dual control systems or a single certified system), 14% are due to comm link failures (you will need a 100% autonomous autopilots) and 12% are crew [coordination] related (a 100% autonomous system can take care of that too). If the Schiebel or any other UAV platform has been flown for more than, say, 1,000 hours with say, 300 takeoff and landings and demonstrated no crashes or, say, flown 10,000 hours and experienced, say, just 2 crashes or less (equal to 20 crashes per 100,000 hours, which would be about 3 times more than GA) , then I would say that is a reasonable level of safety for flying around public places. Otherwise my suggestion is that any unproven design should be restricted to the same rules as any experimental aircraft. A fail safe design is the key concept until reliable statistics say otherwise.

See attachComment 1: With regard to the Risk Classes defined on page 2 of the supporting information "Airworthiness Criteria for the FlightScan Camcopter S", currently proposed as:

b) Risk Class 2: 530 to 24,999 Ft-Lb
c) Risk Class 3: 25,000 to 799,999 Ft-Lb

We non-concur and propose the following instead:

Rationale:
1)The Federal Register states that "To facilitate the establishment of an initial risk class for UAS, the FAA proposes a scale of risk based on kinetic energy. These proposed risk classes are based on logical break points between data clusters that parallel the existing classes of aircraft defined in AC 23.1309-1E, the size boundaries for Light-Sport Aircraft, and the size boundaries in 14 CFR part 107." It is unclear how rotorcraft kinetic energy is to be calculated for the purposes of risk classification. The reference to fixed-wing aircraft in the Federal Register indicates that these risk classes may not be tailored for rotorcraft.
2)Mass or weight is the traditional means of specifying classes of aircraft for airworthiness purposes. It is unclear why UAS would be different.
3)In the part 23 rewrite, number of passengers and performance were used to classify airworthiness. Again, it is unclear why UAS would be different.
4)Making a velocity assumption for KE calculation is somewhat arbitrary.
5)The proposed 3-level classification level is simpler, and traces to established limits for the Part 107, Light Sport Aircraft, and Part 23.

Putting a 3 hour curfew on the opening of the SR 401 bridge in Port Canaveral places, in my opinion, an unnecessary harsh imposition on recreational boaters traversing this waterway.

Most people work during the week and cannot use their boats on many occasions other than the weekend. We are one of those families. By closing the bridge for the middle of the day makes it nearly impossible for us to get out from our marina on Merritt Island into the Atlantic for a daysail on Saturdays. Due to having to go through the lock as well, which can take up to an hour, we need to leave the marina at 08:00 in the morning if we want to get through the bridge before it closes. This means that we have to get up at daybreak and then rush to be able to get the "relaxing" day on the water for which we moved to Florida for in the first place.

If we wait until the bridge opens again it means that we only have a few hours on the water before we have to return and in the summer afternoon thunderstorms makes it dangerous to be out much after 15:30 or 16:00. So, if we don't get up early in the day and rush to the marina and then out to the port we basically cannot sail our boat (on which we paid large sums of tax) on a Saturday anymore. We go to church on Sunday so not opening the bridge between 11:00 and 14:00 on Saturday has made it basically impossible for us to sail out of port Canaveral anymore.

With regard to the inclusion of 27.1309 in the "Airworthiness Criteria for the FlightScan Camcopter S", it is unclear what the definitions of "catastrophic", "extremely improbable", "minor", and "probable" would be for the S-100. The Advisory Circular to Part 27, AC 27-1B Change 4 dated 01 May 2014 defines "extremely improbable" as "...a probability of 1E-9 or less...". Furthermore, the AC does away with the term "probable" and replaces with "frequent" and "reasonably probable". The AC27-1B references the RTCA DO-178C definition for "catastrophic" - "failure conditions that would prevent continued safe flight and landing" and "minor" - "failure conditions that would not significantly reduce aircraft safety, and would involve crew actions that are well within their capabilities." It seems that this definition could be tailored for the S-100 as it is unmanned. We recommend that the FAA provide tailored definitions of these terms as part of the "Airworthiness Criteria for the FlightScan Camcopter S". As currently written, it seems that holding the S-100 to definitions associated with Part 25 aircraft is not a risk-based airworthiness approach and will drive cost and weight. Under our proposed 3-tier Risk Classification, we would recommend that a value of 1E-4 be used for "extremely improbable" for Risk Class I.

A message for those opposed to this race:

I am a self-labeled conservationist. I hold a B.S. in both biology and marine science from Jacksonville University and I am currently working on my masters of Fisheries and Aquatic Science from UF. I have 10 years of experience working with marine natural resources and species. I have worked as a VOLUNTEER marine observer for this organization for over two years. This organization hosts races in many other coastal cities in Florida. There is a lot of foresight and coordination between multiple agencies prior to these races. Prior to each race, the boaters must attend a mandatory educational meeting with the lead observer. During this meeting, they are educated about the specifics on the race area, including any sensitive habitat the animals that that inhabit the area. They are informed of the protocols to follow in the event an animal is sighted. Each race has a team of marine observers, some on boats, some on land, some on balconies, and one or two in the air (helicopter). These observers are all volunteers that have either degrees, experience, or training to qualify them as a marine observer through FWC criteria. They are not employees of P1 nor do they receive compensation. Most of these observers have worked together for many races and they have a system that works. If an animal is observed, it is tracked by the observers. If it comes within a certain distance of the race course, the race gets temporarily shut down until the animal is out of the course. Observers also monitor for an hour before the races start, and 30 minutes after the races end as an extra precaution and to make sure no animals were injured. During most races, local Police Departments, FWC and Coast Guard boats also help to patrol the race area to ensure compliance with environmental and race regulations. In addition to all of this, this organization is raising funds to start an environmental non-profit to travel with the races and provide environmental education to children, help educate locals about the measure taken to protect wildlife during these races, clean-up the beaches after races, and to recruit new volunteer observers. I too was concerned about the thought of a high-speed race in a shallow marine environment. However, after participating I can honestly say that the race organizers and the observer team are advocates of the wildlife, and work to keep both wildlife and boaters safe. A boat strike could hurt man, animal and boat. We don't want that. Another thing to note is that these races usually only occur once a year in a given city, it's an annual sort of thing most of the time.

I can respect everyone's right to have an opinion about this race/area. I just want to provide you with a little more insight about the measures that are taken to protect the resources you are concerned about.

I am opposed to the powerboat race. It is not appropriate in the Marine Stadium Basin.

ENVIRONMENT
It may have been considered appropriate in a time, 60 years ago when the Marine Stadium was built, when people were less concerned or knowledgeable about the environment and the harm that powerboats and jet skis can do to an ecologically fragile area and wildlife preserve. The race planners appear to have taken some precautions to protect manatees, but there is an abundance of other wildlife in the water, on land and in the air that will be disturbed if not harmed.

PUBLIC INPUT
The Virginia Key Advisory Board was formed to oversee all activities on the key. This race was just brought to their attention well after arrangements were finalized. Public input was denied during the application process.

DISRUPTION OF PUBLIC USE
The basin is used year round on a regular basis by many non-motorized water sport athletes and enthusiasts. The hours for the race will deny regular users and paying club members use of the basin in the morning and afternoon.

INAPPROPRIATE USE
A race of this nature, fast, loud and water churning is inappropriate for a small basin in a public park appreciated and used for its calm, flat waters. A high impact event such as this race indicates that the basin is available for additional high impact activities - a direct conflict with current use and activities.

I do not believe that EIS supplied is sufficient, and therefore leases should not be sold.

Statements like this are a serious cause for concern: "Due to the distance of deep water from shore, the possibility of a spill from a deepwater blowout reaching coastal wetlands with the toxicity to significantly impact the coastal wetlands is low because of the response procedures implemented during a catastrophic spill".

There is nothing in the report to indicate that this is 100% achievable, and sufficient consideration is not given to how foul weather will effect the environmental impacts, spread of oil, and clean up efforts in the event of a spill. An effective EIS should not only rely on "best case" scenarios, and yet it does throughout.

"Studies indicate that periods as long as hundreds of years are required to reestablish a seep community once it has disappeared (depending on the community type) (Powell, 1995; Fisher, 1995). There is evidence that substantial impacts on these communities could permanently prevent reestablishment (Fisher, 1995), particularly if hard substrate required for recolonization is buried by resuspended sediments from a loss of well control. Because widely scattered, high-density chemosynthetic communities would typically be located at more than 2,000 ft (610 m) away from a loss of well control event due to mitigating measures, potential accidental impacts from the CPA proposed action are expected to cause little damage to ecological or biological function of these communities."

I see nothing in the report to indicate that 2,000 ft is a magically safe distance for such delicate communities. This is once again a "best case" scenario, even wishful thinking.

The EIS also seems to ignore the cumulative effects of multiple oil drills/spills in a region, and acts as if the area in question in isolated. There should be a discussion on what happens if multiple spills happen in the gulf at the same time, both minor and major. The economic consequences of an oil spill are more far reaching then the EIS implies.

The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management's (BOEM) analysis of threats to the environment is inadequate. BOEM's oil spill analysis, for example, vastly understates the damage to the environment and wildlife and risk of oil spills. It ignores the reality that transporting oil and gas is inherently dangerous and spills occur routinely in offshore oil and gas operations from both tankers and pipelines. In particular, the Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) is not comprehensive in its risk analysis of catastrophic oil spills, which increase in probability as drilling is forced into deeper reserves, and which are subject to climate change effects (e.g. fiercer storms, rising sea levels) that increase the risk of damage to infrastructure and catastrophic spills

Additionally, the feds have failed to adopt reforms that address the safety and environmental risks since the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. A 2016 General Accounting Office report found that the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) "has not fully addressed deficiencies in its investigative, environmental compliance, and enforcement capabilities identified by investigations after the Deepwater Horizon incident" and that BSEE is still using "pre-Deepwater Horizon policies and procedures." Among other things, this means that our environment and offshore workers are still facing significant, unacceptable dangers.

Another issue is that BOEM fails to adequately disclose the amount of hydraulic fracturing and other unconventional well stimulation will take place under the lease sale, and it entirely fails to evaluate the impact of discharging wastewater, including toxic fracking chemicals, into the Gulf of Mexico.

BOEM's proposal lacks meaningful mitigation of the harms that it discloses such as coastal erosion, harms to birds, and noise impacts on marine mammals.

BOEM improperly dismisses air pollution that resulting from the proposed lease on Gulf communities because there is already significant Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) - related infrastructure in Gulf States. This approach undercuts the entire purpose of a cumulative impacts analysis and efforts to inform and engage environmental justice communities, in violation of NEPA.

The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) requires a "detailed statement" of "alternatives to the proposed action," which is considered "the heart of the environmental impact statement." But BOEM's alternatives analysis is seriously lacking. For example, BOEM failed to consider an alternative that would prohibit drilling in certain biologically sensitive areas, such as critical habitat for imperiled loggerhead sea turtles; an alternative that would restrict the number of wells to be drilled; or an alternative that would end all new offshore oil and gas leasing pending a plan to limit warming to 1.5 or 2C.

In general, the EIS is not comprehensive enough regarding alternatives. As the BOEM currently manages renewable resources, it is reasonable for them to consider using the OCS land for projects other than fossil fuel extraction. The required "no-action" alternative is not rigorous; to suggest that "no-action" on one particular lease sale will have the same effect as some foreseeable future sale fails to consider that the "no-action" alternative will be selected in the future, and also fails to appraise the reduction of cumulative and indirect effects as required by NEPA. Lastly, BOEM failed to look outside their jurisdiction for alternatives for the lease sale.

BOEM's analysis states that more drilling won't have an impact on fossil fuel emissions because if no drilling takes place in expanded areas, it will take place in other areas to make up for it. How realistic is this scenario given the Paris Agreement and strong global efforts to promote renewable alternatives?
Offshore wind is a viable source of renewable energy in the Gulf of Mexico. What are BOEM's estimates as far as delaying the development of renewable energy from the GOM by promoting more fossil fuel infrastructure at this point?
New fossil fuel leasing in the Gulf of Mexico could ultimately contribute nearly 33 billion tons of carbon dioxide equivalent to global warming as much greenhouse gas pollution as 9,500 coal-fired power plants operating for a year. To what extent will the lease sales deepen our climate crisis?

There are many compelling reasons why Alternative E of the 2018 Gulf of Mexico OCS Lease Sale Draft SEIS is the only reasonable action for the Department of the Interior to take.

Taken together with respect to the lack of critical data corresponding to lingering human and environmental health stressors from OCS petrochemical mineral extraction, transport, and refining, risk management best practice would suggest implementation of the precautionary principle as exercised in Alternative E is the socially responsible course of action among all available alternatives, although not necessarily for the reasons cited by BOEM staff.

What Gulf residents deserve is a sober quantification of the potential impacts from the refining of OCS minerals in Gulf refineries. An analysis of this nature should include particulate matter, heavy metals, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons quantification in addition to photochemical smog components. It is impossible to even being to properly consider the environmental justice and human health impacts without this elementary data. Also included in this data should be the amount of hazardous vapors released in routine storage and transport of product with an OCS origin.

Data related to the amount of petrochemical mineral stock processed at Gulf refiners or stored at Gulf transport facilities from OCS leased properties should be tracked not just to monitor environmental justice and human health impacts but also account for how much, if any, product is being exported abroad.

BOEM's pending offshore renewables study offers yet another compelling reason to accept Alternative E for 2018. Much of the available literature on renewable use in Europe suggests in comparison that the Gulf of Mexico is not only windier and sunnier but that it also has very good tidal energy potential, as well. The fact that there is such a dearth of parity in renewable energy and fossil fuel exploitation in the Gulf is itself a glaringly compelling reason to do more renewables and less OCS drilling.

While OCS drilling activities contributes significantly to the federal revenue stream, it's true that recent lease sales haven't proven to be huge contributors. Taking Alternative E would not significantly diminish federal revenue.

Also, given the glut oil market we are in where petrochemical export options are being actively explored, Alternative E would not significantly deprive the market of a supply to meet its short-term demands.

There are additionally many unanswered questions about the effectiveness of industry's preferred Gulf of Mexico marine mammal impact mitigation techniques. Thorough vetting and duplication of these policies and procedures to reduce impacts from such activities like ultrasound mapping has yet to be undertaken appropriately.

These points taken in consideration with outstanding concerns surrounding the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement's implementation and oversight protocols by the Government Accounting Office paint a picture of Alternative E that isn't just attractive to sloganeering activists, but suggests sound policy consideration and defensible precautionary principle bona fides.

I hope BOEM and its leadership within the Department of Interior take these and the concerns of others seriously enough to understand the very positive encouragement available from among impacted communities all along our Gulf for a concerted effort to thoroughly reconsider Gulf of Mexico OCS drilling priorities that adopting Alternative E of the 2018 Gulf of Mexico OCS Lease Sale Draft SEIS could represent.

Sincerely,
Ramsey Sprague
