I am writing as a pilot who own a small business and has flown drones since 2012 and has accrued over a thousand hours of flights time both commercially and for recreation.

I have a concerns with the sUAS Critical System Design requirements which, if imposed, would dramatically increase the cost of utilizing sUAS as part of my business. They would require back up systems, quad rotors would require additional rotors, GPS etc which all would increase the cost of doing business. I am worried this requirements will dramatically increase the the cost of a sUAS to a point that small businesses might not be able to afford them. I understand there are safety concerns involved, however I would also point to out that I have operated drones since 2013, I fly regularly and have accrued hundreds of hours of flight time. During these operations there was not a single accident that caused bodily harm or damages to property or people at any point in time. After flying hundreds or times, and having zero accidents I think its important for the FAA to acknowledge that there are many professional operators like myself who have a perfect safety record even though we fly drones almost every single day as part of our job.

The FAAs proposed rules for flight over people and at night are measured and based on the remarkable safety record demonstrated by 14 CFR Part 107 certificated remote pilots over the last two-plus years.

I urge the FAA to increase the threshold for the proposed Category 1 from .55 pounds to .99 pounds. The slightly higher threshold of less than one pound would allow for more innovation while not compromising public safety.

Advances in sUAS design have created examples such as the DJI Mavic Air with a gross weight of .95 pounds. Despite its weight of less than one pound, the Mavic Air has many on-board safety features such as automated collision avoidance.

I also urge the FAA to reconsider the prohibition on flight over moving vehicles/people in moving vehicles. It is very difficult to operate in urban and suburban environments without transiting over moving vehicles. While the sUAS is always within line of sight, there are often vehicles transiting under the sUAS out of sight of the remote pilot and/or observer without any way for the pilot to avoid intermittent or sustained flight over a moving vehicle (which is subject to the drivers discretionary maneuvering on the ground).

Additionally, there is no threat the safety of the occupants inside a covered moving vehicle from a direct strike from a sUAS. The only danger would be one of distraction to the driver, particularly from sUAS weighing on the lower end of the weight spectrum. Greater distraction would be created by a low-flying sUAS laterally from the unwitting driver of a moving vehicle in their line of sight -- rather than a sUAS hovering or transiting directly above a moving vehicle.

Thank you for considering these new regulations with a focus on common-sense regulation that maintains or enhances safe operation by professional sUAS remote pilots.

Sincerely,

Julian Tryba
Boston MA

I would love for restrictions on night time and flying over people to be lifted (with the proper training). For some of us Drone pilots we have very limited places to fly. Of course maintaining safe operation of utmost importance, so I wouldn't mind taking required actions for the privileges.

As a relatively beginner drone pilot I am happy to share my comments regarding this proposed changes which I find interesting, necessary, and exciting.

Regarding flights over people, it is great that the FAA is revising this section because there is a lot of potential in this area. It is also great an important the Administration is taking the necessary steps to make this kind of flights safe, but I think the rules can be improved.

Drones that are eligible to be Category 1 are those 0.55 pounds or less, but I think that limit is too low. One of the drones I fly is a DJI Spark which is one of the smallest prosumer drones available and it weighs 0.66 on take-off, therefore according to the proposal it would qualify as a Category 2 drone, but it is so small I dont think it would create serious damage or harm.
I think it would be better to increase the limit from 0.55 to 1 pound. Drones with this weight are usually very small, and while I have not conducted any test and I dont plan on crashing onto people, I dont think they pose a greater risk.
This change can even be extended to registration, drones weighing 1 pound or more need to be registered, while those weighing less are exempted, as it happens right now with those weighing less than 0.55 pounds.

On marking the drones category, I dont really understand why. I get why the registration number has to be visible and of easy access not only in drones but in any aircraft; in case of an accident, it is helpful to trace the owner and other helpful information for an investigation. But whats the purpose of marking the category? If there is a purpose Im not seeing, I would like it to be explained, otherwise I personally would prefer not to add additional markings to the drone.

About the categories, Ive read that the FAA has explained that the kinetic energy numbers used for the categories requirements are the same as those set for debris and shrapnel impacts from a commercial space launch operation, guided and unguided missiles, missile intercepts and space reentry vehicles. I share the opinion that these numbers are appropriate, outdated, and should not be used for small drones standards as no aircraft of this type has the characteristics of rocket shrapnel.
In this case the FAA should conduct new studies utilizing impact measurements, standards, and injury severity tests more appropriate to this kind of aircrafts.

One section I disagree with is the prohibition of flying over moving vehicles.
Current Part 107 regulations allow flying over people inside non-moving vehicles because they are protected. What is the difference then, on a moving vehicle? Persons are still protected inside the vehicle by the roof and structure, and in any case if a drone fails or falls, by the time it reaches the ground the vehicle may no longer be in that place.
Instead of completely prohibiting flying over moving vehicles new regulations should be put in place requiring us (pilots in command) to determine the safety of the operation over moving vehicles, consider flight variables and of course traffic conditions.
Here, concerns about distracted drivers are not credible given how many other moving things, including pedestrians, manned aircraft, and birds are typically within a drivers view. So its worth revising this section and lift the prohibition.

Other section with which I do not completely agree with is in the pilot knowledge requirement. I strongly support training and taking the certification test, flying a drone is not something that should be taken lightly. Us as pilots must be prepared and have sufficient knowledge to fly at night, and of course the current test has to be updated to cover these situations; but for current Part 107 pilots it should be provided online instead of having to pay and take again the test. In my case, Ive only had my certification for a couple months and Id prefer no to pay again so soon to take the exam again. And I know Im not the only person in this case.

Summarizing the changes I suggest:
1. Increase the 0.55 pounds limit for Category 1 drones, and maybe registration requirement.
2. Explain why drones have to be marked with its corresponding category, or eliminate this requirement.
3. Conduct new studies utilizing impact measurements, standards, and injury severity tests more appropriate for category assignment.
4. Do not prohibit operations over moving vehicles.
5. Make updated night-operations section as a separate test and make it available online for current Part 107 pilots.

Thanks for reading my comments and I hope they prove useful.

We support the FAAs creation of Category 1, which allows
any drone below 0.55 pounds to be operated over people without any special
modifications or testing. However, the 0.55 pound weight limit is too low. That was a
number chosen in 2015 to quickly implement drone registration, rather than to set the
future limits of operational limitations. Scientific research by the FAAs ASSURE center
of excellence makes clear that heavier drones, such as those weighing two or three
pounds, already pose an extremely small risk of injury to people below, without any
special design. The Category 1 weight should at least be doubled, to about one pound,
posing a negligible increase in risk, and providing an easy way to implement a minimally
useful category for flight over people. Because Category 1 imposes negligible risk, and is
likely to also be excluded from Remote ID requirements, it should be finalized and
implemented before the future Remote ID requirements are in place, in order to expand
the benefits of small drones sooner.

We disagree with the FAAs prohibition of operations over persons in moving vehicles. Because such vehicles are moving, in the event of a malfunction of a drone over it, the vehicle will no longer be directly under the drone by the time the drone impacts the ground. Additionally, persons inside the vehicle are protected from injury by the vehicles roof and structure. Concerns about distracted drivers are not credible given how many other moving things, including pedestrians, manned aircraft, and birds, are typically within a drivers view, and the fact that such distraction is more likely when a drone flies next to, not directly over, a moving vehicle. We are unaware of a drone distraction causing any reported motor vehicle accident, despite millions of drones in operation in the U.S. for the past few years, so this FAA limit seems arbitrary. The appropriate regulation for vehicle overflight would be to require the remote pilot to determine the safety of the operation over moving vehicles, accounting for variables such as aircraft altitude, overflight duration, vehicle speed, and traffic conditions.

Flight at night will be useful in expanding beneficial, and in some cases life-saving, operations across industries. We support the FAAs effort to expand Part 107 operations, and to do so safely. It is essential that the FAAs requirements for night operation are reasonably designed to address safety risks without being impracticable or overly burdensome.
Lighting Requirement: We support the FAAs requirement of an anti-collision light that is visible for 3 statute miles, without imposing any specific certification rules or standards, because this mitigates the risk of collision while preserving flexibility in the equipment that is used. No specific color or type of lighting should be required, as none has been required for night waivers under Part 107, which have now been conducted safely for over two years. Position lighting should not be specifically required, because in many circumstances the remote pilot has the ability to determine the position, direction and orientation of the drone in other ways at night, such as area illumination by flood lamps, or by the use of technology features.
Pilot Knowledge Requirement: We support ensuring that drone pilots operating at night have sufficient knowledge about night physiology and night illusions. The FAA should focus its knowledge testing narrowly on these principles as they relate to the reality of operating a drone from the ground, not a manned aircraft from a cockpit. Also, this testing should be available separately from Part 107, and made available online, so that the many existing Part 107 pilots may add night operations without having to return to a test center, pay, and take the entire test again.

Recreational Communities: Recreational participants in community-based organizations should be permitted to continue operating at night pursuant to their own safety guidelines. Many model aircraft have been operating at night safely for decades using their own approaches to aircraft lighting. Although the three-mile collision light will work well for any operating environment in the United States, it is likely more than required to avoid collisions in many airspace environments, or at the very low altitudes often used in certain model aircraft operations. (For example, drone racing involves operations only a few feet off the ground and near illuminated fixed obstacles, a location that precludes any possibility of collision with a manned aircraft.) It would be burdensome for such operators to be required to seek waivers, and difficult for FAA to make case-by-case determinations across such a variety of operations.

Classifying me with a Hollywood production crew is grossly unfair.

The general approach proposed by FAA is reasonable. I suggest minor changes as follows:
1. weight of drone under 2 lb should be in the unrestricted category
2. in addition to licensed drone pilots, others with adequate recreational experience should be included as eligible to conduct flights at altitude above people and/or at night. Manufacturers' software identifies pilots with high flight hours and high total flights, and that software can be adapted to deny or permit experienced pilots greater flexibility without 107.

I'm a certified NASAR volunteer with a local search and rescue organization and we are growing in many areas, including the sUAS operations. The FAA regulations make it very difficult to carry out very important operations during time critical missions where the lives of people may hang in the balance. There are 3 distinct areas of concern that I sincerely hope the FAA considers changing in the proposed regulations FAA-2018-1087.

1. Operations at night. The regulations proposed look very accommodating for first responders, LEO and SAR organizations and I'm very happy to see this is being considered. As outlined in the information, only 1200 waivers have been granted to fly at night since part 107 took effect. The sUAS is very effective in SAR missions and especially when outfitted with night vision cameras and lights. This is critical for disaster areas where normal landmarks may no longer be visible as well.

2. Flight over people. This is also addressed in the proposed regulations and specifically addressed for the need in terms of SAR or law enforcement terms as well. Please consider urgency in the regulations as well. There is always risk when flying over people with any type of aircraft, however in the wake of a disaster when everything is time critical, the presence of a sUAS in the hands of trained professionals can certainly save lives which should drastically outweigh the risk of possibly injuring someone in the event of a crash. The provisions for flight over people seem to be very strict so I request a bit more leniency if there is a life saving operation at hand.

3. VLOS operations. Search and Rescue operations many times depends on being able to quickly survey an area after a disaster to take pictures and overlay those pictures on satellite images for Incident Command. Disaster areas may be very difficult on the ground to survey and find directions without this and the mapping capabilities of sUAS make it very suitable for this task. It may be very difficult to dependent on visibility, objects, location, etc to fly these critical missions where VLOS is required. Relaxing the regulations specifically for SAR, Law enforcement, Fire Departments, etc.. would greatly aid in ensuring that the critical tasks at hand can be accomplished. Proper mapping, planning and executing a plan based on this information is very time critical and the importance cannot be understated.

Thank you for looking into these changes in the regulations. It will transform the way organizations utilize this technology moving forward!

Thank you for reading through my comments I hope they help in any way possible.

Levi Young

I write to ask that you clarify the application of proposed Treasury Regulation section 301.6222-1(c) in the situation described below.

Proposed Treasury Regulation section 301.6222-1(a)(1) provides, in part, that the treatment of partnership-related items on a partner's return must be consistent with the treatment of such items on the partnership return in all respects, including the amount, timing, and characterization of such items. Proposed Treasury Regulation section 301.6222-1(b)(1) provides, in part, that, if a partner fails to satisfy the requirements of section 301.6222-1(a), then, unless the partner provides notice in accordance with section 301.6222-1(c), the IRS may adjust the inconsistently reported partnership-related item on the partner's return to make it consistent with the treatment of such item on the partnership return and determine the underpayment of tax that results from that adjustment.

Section 301.6222-1(c)(1) provides, in part, that section 301.6222-1(a) and section 301.6222-1(b) do not apply to partnership-related items identified as inconsistent in a statement that the partner provides to the IRS according to the forms, instructions, and other guidance prescribed by the IRS, and that, instead, the procedures in section 301.6222-1(c)(3) [sic] apply.

Section 301.6222-1(c)(4)(i) provides that, if a partner notifies the IRS of the inconsistent treatment of a partnership-related item in accordance with section 301.6222-1(c)(1), and the IRS disagrees with the inconsistent treatment, the IRS may adjust the identified, inconsistently reported item in a proceeding with respect to the partner, but that nothing in section 301.6222-1(c)(4)(i) precludes the IRS from also conducting a proceeding with respect to the partnership.

Section 301.6222-1(c)(4)(ii) contains rules that apply in the case of a proceeding with respect to a partner described in section 301.6222-1(c)(4)(i), and section 301-6222-1(c)(5), Example 2, illustrates those rules. However, no portion of section 301.6222-1(c) contains any further guidance regarding what happens if the IRS chooses to conduct a proceeding with respect to the partnership.

Consider the case of Partnership that is composed of General Partner and Limited Partner. Partnership's ordinary income for the year is $10,000, which is allocated on Partnership's return, prepared at the direction of General Partner, $5,000 to General Partner and $5,000 to Limited Partner. Partnership's return also designates General Partner as Partnership's partnership representative.

Limited Partner believes that the allocation of income was incorrectly computed, and that $6,000 of income should have been allocated to General Partner and only $4,000 of income should have been allocated to Limited Partner. Limited Partner accordingly reports only $4,000 of Partnership income and notifies the IRS of the inconsistent treatment in accordance with section 301.6222-1(c).

The IRS chooses to conduct a proceeding with respect to Partnership. During the course of the IRS's examination, the partnership representative takes the position that the Partnership return was correct as filed, and, the IRS, at the conclusion of its examination, mails an FPA accepting Partnership's return as filed. As Limited Partner is not the partnership representative, Limited Partner cannot cause Partnership to file a petition for readjustment under Internal Revenue Code section 6234.

Assume in the alternative that Partnership does or does not elect under proposed Treasury Regulation 301.6226-1 the alternative to the payment by Partnership of an imputed underpayment determined under Internal Revenue Code section 6225 and the Regulations thereunder.

No provision of the proposed Treasury Regulations appears to address what procedures apply for collection of an imputed underpayment from Partnership or for collection of tax from Limited Partner. This matter should be clarified by the addition of operative rules and/or an appropriate Example.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I recommend that the 2018-2019 Priority Guidance Plan include published administrative guidance regarding nonprofit limited liability companies (LLCs), namely, LLCs operating as 501(c)(3) exempt entities. Relatively speaking, the LLC entity form is rather new (compared to, e.g., corporations). However, by now, the LLC form is well-understood and commonly used in for-profit endeavors.

LLCs have been used less in the non-profit area, even though this is becoming more possible. For example, Ohio allows an LLC to be formed for a profit or nonprofit purpose. See Ohio Rev. Code 1705.02. As is well-known in the for-profit area, one benfit of LLCs (even aside from the pass-through tax treatment) is the flexibility of the LLC's internal structure and governance, which is why many for-profit endeavors are now registered as LLCs rather than corporations, and even why some corporations are converting into LLCs. This LLC flexibility would also be beneficial in the nonprofit/tax-exempt area, and at least some states (e.g., Ohio) would permit this.

The concern comes from the IRS's treatment of nonprofit LLCs. As far as I know, the best IRS guidance on tax-exempt LLCs comes from its continuing professional education articles (2000 EO CPE Topic H and 2001 EO CPE Topic B). There are also the "Limited Liability Company Reference Guide Sheet" and its Instructions. Perhaps a more-formalized publication would be more helpful in this area.

I have one additional comment in this area (nonprofit LLCs). The above-mentioned guidance states that an LLC can be considered tax-exempt only if all of its members are also exempt entities. I suggest that the IRS revisit this issue and perhaps modify its interpretation to allow a nonprofit to be exempt even if its members are individuals. I understand that a nonprofit corporation, unincorporated association, or trust can qualify for exempt status, even though the corporation or unincorporated association has individuals as members. I understand that the LLC is disregarded as an entity, but that just seems to make it similar to an unincorporated association, which can qualify for exempt status. So I encourage the IRS to revisit this issue and allow nonprofit LLCs to qualify for exempt status even if its members are individuals, as long as the other requirements are met (like for unincorporated associations).

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sergey Vernyuk

This proposed rule should be rejected, because it extends the effective period of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act ('TCJA') in a way contrary to the plain statutory language, and clear legislative intent. Additionally, the language of the proposed rule is based on flawed premises and assumptions.

The 2018 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act temporarily increased the Basic Exclusion Amount from $5 Million to $10 Million. According to the plain text of the statute, the BEA increase was intended to be temporary. The TCJA specifically included a "sunset" provision (expiration date) for many of its provisions. The BEA increase explicitly included a sunset provision of January 1, 2026.

This was not an arbitrary date, or a mere technicality. The TCJA was passed under reconciliation rules in Congress. Under these rules, including the "Byrd Rule," the TCJA could not increase the national deficit after the budget window under consideration in the reconciliation instructions. In order to comply with these rules, Congress included sunset provisions.

The proposed rule, as written, would increase the impact on the deficit beyond 2026. This cannot possibly have been the intent of the legislature, as such an effect would have violated the reconciliation rules in effect. In short, the proposed rule attempts to do by administrative fiat what could not have been done legally by Congress at the time Congress passed the law.

It is settled law that under the Chevron Rule, if Congress has "directly spoken" on an issue, "the law must speak for itself" and the matter is settled. An administrative agency does not have any authority to contravene plain statutory text or the clear legislative intent of Congress.

Further, the language of the proposed rule is based on flawed assumptions. Consider the following language from the Proposed Rule document V(1):

"Given the cumulative nature of the gift and estate tax computations and the differing manner in which the credit is applied against these two taxes, commenters have raised two questions regarding a potential for inconsistent tax treatment or double taxation of transfers resulting from the temporary nature of the increased BEA. First, in cases in which a taxpayer exhausted his or her BEA and paid gift tax on a pre-2018 gift, and then either makes an additional gift or dies during the increased BEA period, will the increased BEA be absorbed by the pre-2018 gift on which gift tax was paid so as to deny the taxpayer the full benefit of the increased BEA during the increased BEA period? Second, in cases in which a taxpayer made a gift during the increased BEA period that was fully sheltered from gift tax by the increased BEA but makes a gift or dies after the increased BEA period has ended, will the gift that was exempt from gift tax when made during the increased BEA period have the effect of increasing the gift or estate tax on the later transfer (in effect, subjecting the earlier gift to tax even though it was exempt from gift tax when made)?"

For one, just because two taxes are "cumulative" does not mean there is any "inconsistent tax treatment" or that "double taxation" is improper. The gift tax and estate tax are two separate taxes. While the calculation of one has an effect on the other, they are in effect separate taxes. Taxing a gift once, and then the same property again when transferred via an estate is indeed double taxation-- because there are two taxes. That is not "inconsistent."

For example, an individual is taxed on dividends received, even though corporate profits are already taxed. While it is "double" taxation, it is appropriate and consistent "double taxation," as there are two transfers, and two different taxes. It would be arbitrary and capricious for a administrative agency to "re-interpret" the tax code to make dividends tax exempt because of the mere existence of corporate taxes. The propose rule here is no different. If Congress had intended for double taxation to be avoided, they would have consolidated the gift tax and the estate tax into one tax, not maintained two separate taxes.

Further, there is nothing "inconsistent" nor is there any "problem" in the two scenarios identified in the highlighted text. In example 1, the prior gift was made under a different tax structure. If Congress had intended the TCJA to be retroactive, they could have done so. Likewise, in example 2, there is no problem or inconsistency. The latter transfer was made under a different tax regime, after the BEA increase expired, as explicitly intended by Congress. As discussed above, Congress did not and could not have intended otherwise.

In short, the proposed rule illegally and unconstitutional usurps the will and intent of Congress, as contained in explicit statutory language. The proposed rule attempts to create "problems" or "inconsistencies where there are none. TCJA is not ambiguous. The perceived "inconsistencies" and problems" are features-- not bugs.

Base broadening (i.e. the elimination of unproductive tax preferences) was an essential part of tax reform. However, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did not go nearly far enough in trimming the fat from our wasteful tax code.

To this point, I would like to focus my comments on a particularly egregious provision, I.R.C. 409, which has been abused since its codification by businesses seeking to unscrupulously wipe away their tax liability.

Effective for years beginning after December 31, 1997, the Internal Revenue Code was amended to allow employee stock ownership plans (ESOP) to be shareholders in S corporations and to exempt the flow-through earnings to the ESOP from the unrelated business income tax. As such, beginning in 1998, the income of an S corporation could pass through to an ESOP, and, because an ESOP is tax exempt, no tax is paid on the income until it is distributed to the ESOP participant.

ESOPs are, ostensibly, an effective means of boosting workers retirement savings, which at the same time offer them a literal stake in the company. Starbucks is a perfect example of how they can be legitimately deployed -- as a publicly-traded corporation, the company gains little to no tax advantage by offering an ESOP to its employees, but does so anyway to ensure workers are rewarded in retirement for their years of service to the company.

However, for the majority of businesses with an ESOP, the motivation behind establishing their plan is not a sense of altruism or concern for their employees welfare, but rather sheer greed. These companies cunningly utilize their status as a pass-through entity and pair it with an ESOP to exploit an enormous tax loophole, ultimately avoiding payment of taxes altogether. These firms wrap themselves in the flag of boosting retirement savings; employee-ownership; and giving their employees a piece of the rock (along with myriad other trite phrases), but fail to mention that they are ultimately shifting their tax burden from the business entity level to their own employees.

The loophole works like this: a pass-through company (generally an S Corporation, whose income is taxed at the individual, rather than corporate, rate) will create an ESOP. The ESOP is actually a tax-exempt trust, which in the case of an S corporation means that every penny of a firms income is passed through to the trust, allowing the company to pay no tax altogether. Employees become shareholders of the trust, and when it comes time to retire must bank on the fact that the company will buy them out of their shares (and still exist altogether).

Special interest groups like The ESOP Association and the Employee-owned S Corporation Association (ESCA) like to argue that the tax is eventually paid, and in this regard theyre at least partially correct. What they conveniently leave out, though, is that the tax is paid by employees, rather than the business itself. When employees cash out, and their employer buys back their shares in the tax-exempt trust, they face 100 percent of the tax burden. In other words, while their competitors are facing effective tax rates of over 50 percent (when state and local taxes are tallied up), S Corporation ESOPs enjoy tax-free status by making their workers bear the full brunt of the tax burden, and putting it squarely on their shoulders.

Beyond the inherent unfairness of granting a few select businesses the privilege of not having to pay any tax whatsoever, S Corporation ESOPs carry serious risks that cannot be ignored. There is nothing quite as ugly in the employee benefits world as an ESOP gone bad. Many companies with an ESOP do not even consider the future repurchase obligation, mentioned above, that makes the whole retirement ecosystem function properly. This creates a situation where employees place all their retirement eggs in one basket; if the company is unable or unwilling to buy back their shares when it comes time to exit the workforce, that employee will have no way to access the funds they thought they would be entitled to.

Lastly, it is important to note that this tax avoidance carries with it a substantial cost. The Tax Foundation estimates that Special ESOP rules cost taxpayers more than $22 billion over a decade . (The organization could only find a handful of corporate tax expenditures which are more costly.) That means that ordinary, hard-working employees and businesses who pay more than their fair share in tax are subsidizing the tax-exempt status of a handful of companies. This is the anthesis of a fairer, simpler tax code.

The employee stock ownership plan is the epitome of bad tax policy. In particular, 100 percent employee-owned S Corporation ESOPs are an example of an egregious tax loophole that needs to be closed. Members of Congress owe it to their constituents to not use taxpayer money to prop up a small cadre of businesses who, ironically, are the ones who have the resources and ability to exploit this loophole.

I am writing to request that the Service leave intact, with respect to Form 1042-S, the non-aggregation rule in 301.6011-2(c)(1)(iii) and associated provisions. The desired result is to entirely exclude Form 1042-S from the types of returns covered by the proposed regulations. I also ask that the effective dates be clarified.

AGGREGATION: Since the implementation of reporting requirements for Tax Year (TY) 2014 to accommodate FATCA, Form 1042-S has undergone voluminous complex and ongoing changes. No other covered information return has been subjected to such extreme treatment. Among those changes are the creation, re-labeling, and discontinuance of income and recipient/payer status codes, including for TY 2018 reporting and possibly beyond. For software providers, these constant changes create great difficulties, especially with respect to re-mapping and cross-referencing when an existing code is changed or eliminated in a subsequent year. In some cases, this has affected the same code multiple times. For example, for TY 2013, income code 50 was used for Other income. For TY 2014, income code 50 was given the new descriptor Income previously reported under escrow procedure; 51 was added to denote Other income; and a new, never-clarified income code 20 (Gross income other) was also added. Then, for TY 2015, 51 was re-labeled as Interest paid on certain actively traded or publicly offered securities, and income code 54 was created to denote Other income. Additionally, income code 20 was re-assigned the descriptor Compensation during studying and training, and the previous descriptor of Gross income other was assigned a new income code of 23 (which was itself subsequently re-labeled Gross income). The re-mapping difficulties caused by changes such as this, particularly the extensive income code changes introduced for TY 2015 reporting (which also involved incrementing by one digit a series of 5 consecutive income codes that had been in place for decades), are numerous and complex from a development point of view, and extremely confusing for our clients and their payees, particularly in cases where the IRS Copy A is submitted electronically in compliance with Publication 1187, while recipient paper copies must follow the paper 1042-S instructions, which differ from Pub. 1187 in several respects.

Since Martinsburg does not run parallel systems to accommodate multiple years and the attendant different codes specific to each year, withholding agents submitting Forms 1042-S electronically must use the most recent electronic format and codes that are in production (see Publication 1187) at the time the submission is made. An overlooked original TY 2014 1042-S reporting Other income submitted electronically in 2018 would have to be submitted under income code 54 (the current Other income code); but the information pages for the 2014 1042-S as issued by IRS (and not updated to reflect 2018 codes) do not contain income code 54 at all; it did not exist in 2014. For 2014, Other income was denoted by code 51. A taxpayer receiving paper Copies B, C and D of a 2014 1042-S for income code 54 would have no idea how to handle that income on their amended 2014 tax return, so for practical purposes, the withholding agent would have to reflect income code 51 on the recipient copies, but income code 54 on the electronic submission (Copy A) to IRS. That in turn sets up a potential conflict on the tax return processing side, where a processor attempting to implement data matching to ensure that no attempted fraud was being committed would find a mismatch between the recipients copies and the withholding agents electronic submission of Copy A to IRS.

The ability to continue filing both original and, perhaps more significantly, amended Forms 1042-S on paper under the existing non-aggregation rule would greatly reduce the need for many of our clients who currently are NOT required to file the form electronically due to a low volume of nonresident payees, to apply to the Service for a waiver of the electronic filing requirement, and would help the Service avoid spending valuable time processing the requests.

EFFECTIVE DATES: On Page 24950 of the 5/31/18 Federal Register, the proposed regs use the phrase "...returns REQUIRED TO BE FILED after December 31, 2018" with respect to both 301.60112(b)(4) and 301.67211. But for 301.60112(b)(5) they say only "...returns FILED after..." Is this discrepancy intentional? Required to be filed after December 31, 2018 seems to imply that perhaps the provisions associated with that phrase are only intended to apply to information returns specific to TY 2018 or later, whereas the simpler filed after December 31, 2018 could be interpreted as applying to any corrected returns actually filed after that date, without regard to the tax year for which they are issued. It would be extremely helpful if the Service could clarify this language and its intent.

The National Foreign Trade Council is pleased to submit the attached comments to the proposed regulations under Internal Revenue Section 7602(a) (REG-132434-17).  The NFTC requests the opportunity to present our views at the July 31 hearing on this matter.

As the attached, lengthier document explains in greater detail, while National Taxpayers Union (NTU) commends the Treasury and the IRS for recognizing the overly broad nature of T.D. 9778, and offering modifications through the proposed rule, we recommend complete withdrawal of the original rule and its successor.

National Taxpayers Union (NTU) has long maintained a vital interest in the issue of non-IRS employees having access under IRC Sections 7602 and 6103(n) to taxpayer returns and information. While we commend the Treasury and the IRS for recognizing the overly broad nature of T.D. 9778, and offering modifications through the proposed rule, NTU continues to recommend complete withdrawal of T.D. 9778, for the following reasons.

1) Government Efficiency Must be Balanced with Taxpayer Rights. NTU stands second to none among organizations supporting private-sector contracts to perform certain public services, when the primary goal is to deliver such services more efficiently and effectively. Yet, even the IRS concedes that contracting non-IRS employees in examinations and legal proceedings is a level well above traditional outsourcing.

In NTUs decades-long history, one overriding theme we have encountered in questions of tax administration is, does the policy at hand undermine or enhance public confidence in the impartiality of the rights and remedies afforded them? There are few more blunt ways for undermining such confidence than creating additional, artificial advantages by which government can disproportionately enforce its position against a taxpayer. Allowing the IRS to marshal often highly-compensated private sector attorneys in the pursuit of other private sector actors however carefully deployed should therefore be avoided.

Taxpayers rights to privacy likewise remain at stake with this proposal. Indeed, one could argue that despite narrowing the scope of individuals permitted access to taxpayer information, as the proposed rule attempts to do, the risk to confidentiality may not be significantly affected. The specialists in non-federal tax law or other areas of law may have little experience with information-privacy safeguards developed to shield sensitive taxpayer data from being compromised.

2) Continuing Even Some Policies in T.D. 9778 Could Contribute to Public Skepticism over the Dispute Resolution System. REG-132434-17 helpfully stipulates that it would not permit IRS to hire an attorney for non-substantive specialized knowledge, such as civil litigation skills. On the other hand, the regulation document also notes that the agency may hire a contractor who may happen to be an attorney, but who is hired for knowledge, skills, or abilities other than providing legal services as an attorney. Taxpayers may be forgiven for wondering how this duality will be reconciled at the field level. Would it, for example, permit the hiring of consultants who would not otherwise act as attorneys on the particular factual issues of an examination, but who could provide analysis of the impact if the government prevailed in a given scenario? Such professional advice is available to a taxpayer only at a significant and often prohibitive cost.

Some would contend that even in light of the IRSs standard operating procedures, the Service is not immune to prioritizing its own resources and that REG-132434-17 is written mostly with Large Business and International Division cases in mind. After all, would the agency really consider spending millions of dollars on outside contractors to help pursue a small business examination involving tax issues worth perhaps thousands of dollars? In most circumstances, the answer would be no. In certain cases, however, relating to potentially precedential issues, emerging industries with highly specialized functions, or complex questions involving minor financial amounts immediately at stake, the IRS could very well opt to do so.

3) Congress Is Heavily Scrutinizing and Acting to Limit the Activities Envisioned in the Proposed Rule. Based on events in Congress this year, it is increasingly likely the door could not only be closed, but also locked, on the approach of T.D. 9778. Aside from the three hearings in which NTU participated (in each instance scrutinizing T.D. 9778), as well as the high-profile introductions of H.R. 3167, S. 2809, and H.R. 3220, just two months ago the House of Representatives unanimously voted to pass H.R. 5444. Section 308 of this legislation effectively nullifies the substance of T.D. 9778, as well as REG-132434-17. Key Members of both parties on the Senate Finance Committee have voiced interest in a cooperative legislative package that would build upon the momentum the House has given to H.R. 5444. We believe the IRSs constructive deference to previous and pending Congressional actions that aim to excise T.D. 9778 would be the wisest course.

Clarification is requested whether these proposed regulations would allow the hiring and participation in a Federal tax audit of certified public accountants or other non-attorneys specializing in the application of Federal tax law, such as enrolled agents or faculty teaching Federal tax law at colleges and universities, to provide the IRS assistance in the application and interpretation of Federal tax law.

The proposed regulations provide examples of the allowable use of persons with specialized expertise in certain substantive areas. The proposed regulations mention foreign, state or local area as an example of a substantive area for which a contractor with specialized expertise may be hired. Although the proposed regulations do not list Federal tax law as an example of a substantive area for which a contractor with specialized expertise may be hired, the proposed regulations indicate the list provided is "non-exclusive", which thus leaves open the possibility that an expert in Federal tax law may be hired to provide specialized expertise.

The proposed regulations then provide special limitations on the hiring of non-governmental attorneys by indicating that non-governmental attorneys can be hired only for their expertise certain specified areas, including foreign, state or local tax law. The exclusion of Federal tax law thus means non-governmental attorneys can't be hired as specialist to provide expert assistance in the application of Federal tax law.

In the United States, certified public accountants and enrolled agents, along with attorneys, can be qualified to provide tax advice in the application of Federal tax law and have the ability to practice before the Internal Revenue Service. Additionally, non-practicing attorneys and accountants may specialize in Federal tax law and teach this topic at universities and colleges throughout the United States, including at law schools and graduate and undergraduate business schools. As drafted, the proposed regulations would not preclude the IRS from hiring these individuals as experts to provide guidance in the course of an audit on the application and interpretation of Federal tax law.

The preamble to the proposed regulations indicate one reason for barring the use of attorneys with specialized knowledge of Federal tax law to provide expert assistance in the application of Federal tax law is that the Internal Revenue Services possesses the requisite expertise in the application of Federal tax law. Thus, it is not necessary for the IRS to seek expert assistance from a non-governmental attorney to provide expert assistance in the interpretation of Federal tax law. The same rationale applies to other non-attorney experts in the field of Federal tax law, such as certified public accountants, enrolled agents and faculty professors. The proposed regulations should clarify that the IRS will not seek the assistance of any individuals, whether an attorney or a non-attorney, with expertise in the application of Federal tax law to provide assistance in the application of Federal tax law.

I believe that flexibility in the regulations on Qualified Opportunity Zones issued on October 19, 2018 regarding ESOPs (Employee Stock Ownership Plans) would make it possible for employees within these zones to benefit from equity participation in addition to wages. Suggested change to proposed regulations under Code section 1400Z-2:

Add to the definition of qualified opportunity zone stock in 1.1400Z-2(d)-1(c)(2) a provision that the term qualified opportunity zone stock includes any interest constituting synthetic equity within the meaning of section 409(p)(6)(C) and the regulations thereunder, in the case of an S corporation the stock of which is owned by an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP), as defined in section 4975(e)(7).

Explanation. The full tax benefits of an ESOP are available only if all of the stock of an S corporation is held by the ESOP. Accordingly, outside investors in ESOP-owned S corporations typically acquire their equity by investing in hybrid securities of the S corporation which do not fall within the meaning of stock under section 1361. Such securities include convertible debt and subordinated debt with warrants attached, among others. This issue was confronted by Congress in enacting the ESOP anti-abuse provision of section 409(p), which creates the concept of synthetic equity to describe the hybrid securities representing this kind of non-stock equity. The concept is equally applicable here, to ensure that the purpose of the opportunity zone tax provisions is carried out by enabling the use of ESOPs in appropriate situations.

1) Introduction NTU has a longstanding interest in sound tax administration that balances the Services tax collection mission with the protection of taxpayer rights and remedies. We have advocated for legislation to help achieve this balance more fully, including the Taxpayer First Act, and have commented on numerous IRS rulemakings. (1 Minute)

2) The need for public confidence in the balance of the examination process between the government and the taxpayer recommends full withdrawal of T.D. 9778. The Service wisely acknowledges that the use of outside counsel in examinations should only be under limited circumstances. REG-132434-17 is a commendable step, but leaves unresolved the issue of how such a rule would be put into practice in the field and how it could still potentially disadvantage and intimidate taxpayers, undermining their confidence in an examination process that has already been weakened by recent jurisprudence and policymaking with little public input. 3) The precedent set by the rule could still be problematic for taxpayers. NTU has seen past instances where relatively narrowly crafted rules, guidance, and other IRS policymaking initiatives have been expanded or applied to areas that were unintended or unexpected. A mechanism for a developer to sequentially substantially rehabilitate multiple buildings in qualified opportunity zones should be available, and not precluded because the building was substantially renovated with the intention of selling after renovation rather than renting the property.

Outline of topics to be discussed by Jacqueline Coolidge at a Public Hearing scheduled for July 31, 2018 10:00 a.m. re
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking REG-132434-17 (Certain Non-Government Attorneys Not Authorized to Participate in Examinations of Books and Witnesses as a Section 6103(n) contractor)
The proposed regulation would prevent the IRS from getting the help of outside counsel when it is up against multinational corporations in complex tax cases involving a summons. While the rationale for the proposed change is to contribute to a reduction in regulatory burdens, the great majority of tax-related regulations, including in countries where the revenue service uses risk-based audit, impinge overwhelmingly on small and medium enterprises, but constitute only a miniscule fraction of a percent for large businesses. The current regulation proposed for reform is relevant almost exclusively for large multinational corporations, so the proposed change would not yield a significant improvement, but would almost certainly hamper the ability of the IRS to enforce the law.
The proposed regulation makes an artificial distinction between substance expertise (primarily specialists in foreign, state, or local law, including tax law, or in non-tax substantive law that is relevant to an issue in the examination) and providing legal services as an attorney. This distinction creates more confusion and complexity than the current, existing regulation.
The net effect appears to be the hobbling of the IRS in cases where it may be examining complex transactions including international transfer pricing, where both US tax law and one or more foreign tax laws or regulations are involved. Such cases may involve many millions of dollars of potential tax liability, where multinational corporations have ready access to armies of tax lawyers, while the US IRS, already budget-constrained (and suffering from many years of budget cuts), would be further reduced to fighting such cases with only its in-house resources.
While it is always a good practice to periodically review, streamline, and update regulations, there does not appear to be merit behind the proposal to restrict the IRS to in-house resources while the taxpayers it may need to examine or audit have full access to any and all resources they can afford. Tilting the playing field against the IRS would make it much more likely that multinational corporations could get away with more aggressive and potentially abusive international tax maneuvers involving a combination of US tax laws and foreign tax laws. Since questions related to US tax laws would inevitably be involved, the IRS could face litigation for hiring outside counsel that considered both US tax laws and the relevant foreign ones.
It may be beneficial to further clarify that outside counsel must be under the full control of IRS staff or even possibly to ensure that only IRS staff are allowed to question witnesses under oath. It makes no sense to bar the IRS from hiring outside counsel to review documents, develop examination and/or litigation strategy, draft interrogatories, or prepare memoranda and briefs. Hobbling the IRS would most likely result in yet more successful tax avoidance (and even evasion) on the part of large multinational corporations, leaving the remainder of US taxpayers to bear the burden of under-resourced public services.

Dear IRS / Dept. of the Treasury,

I am writing with comments and concerns about the proposed OPPORTUNITY ZONE (OZ) rules and regulations.

While the program, in theory, sounds good, the proposed rules, as is, are blatantly unfair to investors who do not have capital gains to shelter and, more importantly, to the low income communities the program is designed to serve, uplift and I would hope protect. The present rules will almost certainly lead to clear not in the public interest results.

As such, I hope the following comments will be received, noted and constructive changes made.

For purposes of this document I have broken the two (2) core tax incentives provided by the OZ program into PART A and PART B as follows:

***PART A the tax incentives applied to realized but untaxed capital gains when invested into an OZ within 180 days of their realization, principally the reduction of capital gains by 15% on the untaxed capital gains when sheltered within an OZ; and

***PART B the tax incentives applied to the appreciated value of an investment in an OZ, principally the zero capital gains tax rate applied to the appreciated value of an OZ investment when held for 10 years or longer.

***Concern 1 -- It would appear that the PART B incentive is available ONLY to those who have PART A untaxed capital gains to shelter within the PART A incentive of the OZ program.

This is highly prejudiced against investors whom have not capital gains to shelter in PART A and creates a highly anti-competitive marketplace whereby investors who have unrealized capital gains to shelter within an OZ will be willing to generally bid more for any given property within an OZ to capture and secure the PART B incentive of the OZ program. The PART A incentive in fact will act as a forward financing element driving up the initial cost of an OZ property and driving investors who do not have capital gains to shelter, including the communities living within it, out of the market.

***Concern 2 -- As alluded to in Concern 1, by limiting the PART B incentive only to those who have capital gains to shelter in PART A, the overwhelming majority of tax payers living within an OZ (I estimate over 99%+ of tax payers within any given OZ) will find themselves in competition with OZ program investors and have not a hair of a chance in winning bids due to the unbalanced and unfair marriage of the PART A and PART B incentives within the program.

That the overwhelming majority of residents within the OZs are low income and minorities I will not go in depth on, except to say it conjures up images of a modern day homestead program only for those who have capital gains to shelter in Part A of whom, in our country, are mostly white, deeply educated and/or extremely lucky.

Given these less than desirable beginnings, I urge your department to unwed the PART A and PART B incentives from each other. Simply put, ANY INVESTOR should be able to access the PART B incentives as long as they follow the otherwise good guidelines proposed about investing in and fixing up properties they have acquired or businesses they have financed within an OZ.

Without this minor but significant change, I believe the OZ program will become a political football no one foresaw and in fact jeopardize the program's longevity and stability. This would be a shame given a simple separating of PART A from PART B will not only alleviate the above concerns, but further increase demand for properties within any given OZ zone on a fair and level playing field for all.

Thank you for your time and consideration of this review.

Sincerely yours,
Robert R. Khan
Perrysburg, OH

Section 1400Z-2(e)(1)(B) - subsections (a), (b), and (c) shall only apply to the investment described in subparagraph (A)(i).

Congress intent with this legislation was to incentivize investment in QOZs, and arbitrarily limiting any incentives to capital gains but not fresh capital, when a clearer reading of the text is available, frustrates Congress very purpose.

The opening line of summary text of H.R. 828 states that the bill to provide tax incentives for investments in the zones, including deferring the recognition of capital gains that are reinvested in the zones. Capital gains, while an interest piquing headline, were not the exclusive focus of the incentives.

The text of H.R. 828 1400Z-2(a)(1) and (2) specifically focus on capital gains as these provisions only logically apply to capital gains and the deferral of their tax. However, (a)(3) never suggests an application meant to be limited to capital gains. (3) EXCLUSION OF GAIN ON QUALIFIED OPPORTUNITY ZONE PROPERTY HELD FOR AT LEAST 10 YEARS.Except as provided in paragraph (2), in the case of the sale or exchange of qualified opportunity zone property, or an investment in a qualified opportunity fund, held for at least 10 years, gross income for the taxable year shall not include any gain from the sale or exchange of such property or investment. The Senate bill mirrors this language.

Congress did not appear to intend to limit this program by only providing tax incentives for investments of capital gains, and to provide no incentive whatsoever for investment of previously taxed assets. The notion that 1400Z-2(a)(3) would only apply to capital gains timely reinvested seems to simply be due to the order in which this provision appears after capital gains specific incentives.

Congress sought to incentivize investment in distressed areas through Qualified Opportunity Funds. Deferral of tax on timely reinvested capital gains is one carrot to achieve that end. Another is the permanent step-up in basis on gains in QOF investments held for over 10 years. There is no reason in logic, or the text, that Congress intended to limit that second incentive to reinvestment of capital gains.

I write to recommend flexibility in the regulations regarding Qualified Opportunity Zones (REG-115420-18) issued on October 19, 2018. I would like to recommend language that would encourage the use of Employee Stock Ownership Plans (ESOPs) for private companies operating within these zones. The State of Illinois has designated several tracts throughout Cook County as opportunity zones. I believe that it is essential to permit every possible means under the law to expand ESOP investments in Qualified Opportunity Zones.

The specific proposed revision to Qualified Opportunity Zone regulations would make it easier to create ESOPs in Qualified Opportunity Zones by allowing the ESOP to be designed using structured equity.

To that end, we propose that the following change to proposed regulations under Code section 1400Z-2:

Add to the definition of qualified opportunity zone stock in 1.1400Z-2(d)-1(c)(2) a provision that the term qualified opportunity zone stock includes any interest constituting synthetic equity within the meaning of section 409(p)(6)(C) and the regulations thereunder, in the case of an S corporation the stock of which is owned by an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP), as defined in section 4975(e)(7).

The full tax benefits of an ESOP are available only if all of the stock of an S corporation is held by the ESOP. Accordingly, outside investors in ESOP-owned S corporations typically acquire their equity by investing in hybrid securities of the S corporation which do not fall within the meaning of stock under section 1361. Such securities include convertible debt and subordinated debt with warrants attached, among others. This issue was confronted by Congress in enacting the ESOP anti-abuse provision of section 409(p), which creates the concept of synthetic equity to describe the hybrid securities representing this kind of non-stock equity. The concept is equally applicable here, to ensure that the purpose of the opportunity zone tax provisions is carried out by enabling the use of ESOPs in appropriate situations.

I am aware that the City of Newark, New Jersey has made a similar submittal on this topic of ESOPs and Opportunity Zones and I am glad to join them in pursuing this policy goal.

Thank you for your consideration,

Alma E. Anaya
Cook County Commissioner, 7th District

1. Gross Income Requirement for Qualified Opportunity Zone Businesses

The City of Houston is concerned that the proposed regulations describe the gross income requirement for qualified opportunity zone businesses in a way that may be difficult to satisfy for enterprises and industries that could serve as major employers in the Houston area, but that have a broad domestic or global customer base.

The requirement in Prop. Treas. Reg. 1.1400Z-2(d)-1(d)(5)(i) that for each taxable year at least 50 percent of the gross income of a qualified opportunity zone business [must be] derived from the active conduct of a trade or business in the qualified opportunity zone suggests that the business income must largely come from the opportunity zone.

Recommendation:

We recommend that Treasury revise the gross income requirement in the proposed rules to be more like the gross income requirement in the New Markets Tax Credit regime (found in Treas. Reg. 1.45D-1(d)(4)(i)(A)). This would give businesses a clear standard for how they can satisfy the 50-percent gross income test in a manner that is divorced from customer location, but rather is focused on either where the qualified opportunity zone businesss tangible property is used or where the qualified opportunity zone businesss employees are performing services. Specifically, a business should be deemed to have satisfied the 50-percent gross income requirement for qualified opportunity zone businesses (in Section 1400Z-2(d)(3)(A)(ii) that incorporates Section 1397C(b)(2)) if:

(1)at least 50 percent of the use of the tangible property of such entity (whether owned or leased) is within a qualified opportunity zone, or
(2)at least 50 percent of the services performed by such entity by its employees are performed in a qualified opportunity zone.

2. Qualification of Residential Real Property Rental Businesses

The City of Houston wants to ensure that a residential rental property business located in a qualified opportunity zone is eligible to be a qualified opportunity zone business. Although there is nothing in the statute or the proposed regulations that would indicate that such a business could not qualify if it met the other necessary requirements of the law, we would like confirmation that residential rental property is an eligible opportunity zone business given that such businesses are not qualifying under either the New Markets Tax Credit regime or the Enterprise Zone Business regime.

Investment by a qualified opportunity fund could provide necessary capital to execute much needed multifamily and clustered single-family development.
Recommendation:

We recommend that Treasury confirm that residential real property rental businesses are eligible to be qualified opportunity zone businesses so that the opportunity zone provision can be leveraged to spur the development or substantial rehabilitation of affordable rental housing.

3. Extension of Working Capital Safe Harbor Period in Case of Covered Disasters

Natural disasters including hurricanes, tropical storms, other flooding events and fires are occurring at increasing frequency throughout the country, and the impacts on development projects could range from short-term construction delays to the need to completely rebuild buildings and infrastructure that have been substantially or completely destroyed.

While the working-capital safe harbor provides relief necessary to ensure that a qualified opportunity zone business has up to 31 months to hold cash or cash equivalents as it works to construct or rehabilitate tangible business property, such relief could prove inadequate if a catastrophic event impacts a qualified opportunity zone during the period.

Recommendation

We recommend that Treasury expand the safe harbor for reasonable amount of working capital in Prop. Treas. Reg. 1.1400Z-2(d)-1(d)(5)(iv) to extend the 31-month period (and provide for a revision and flexibility with respect to the written schedule) in cases where the tangible property (related to the working capital assets subject to the safe harbor) is located in a qualified opportunity zone contained in an area:

(1)that President declared a major disaster (under Section 401 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, 42 U.S.C. 5170);
(2)for which a Federal Emergency Management Agency Notice of a Presidential declaration of a major disaster is issued in the Federal Register;
(3)that constitutes a covered disaster area for purposes of Treas. Reg. 301.7508A-1(d)(2); or for which a mandatory evacuation order is in effect at some time during the 31-month period

To Whom It May Concern:

We write as a broad coalition of stakeholders to provide comments in response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Investing in Qualified Opportunity Funds, issued October 29, 2018 (NPRM). We are grateful for the work of staff at the Department of the Treasury and Internal Revenue Service (Service) to produce the NPRM and prioritize guidance that will facilitate the use of the Qualified Opportunity Zone (QOZ) tax incentives to the benefit of designated low-income communities nationwide.

We applaud the approach that Treasury has taken on a number of key issues. For example, the proposed 31-month safe harbor at the QOZ Business level will help many QOF investors to structure investments and time the acceptance of capital. Additionally, we strongly support the proposed definition of substantially all pertaining to the amount of a QOZ Businesss tangible assets located in a QOZ. The proposed 70-percent threshold achieves the right balance to ensure that Qualified Opportunity Funds (QOFs) will not be discouraged from investing in QOZ operating businesses as Congress intended. Both of these rules should be finalized and, as detailed in the attached comments, Treasury should consider whether additional guidance in these areas is needed.

The proposed regulations address a range of other issues, including that all capital gains are eligible for the incentive; that partners may invest and defer partnership level gains in QOFs if the partnership does not; that debt of a QOF taxed as a partnership is not treated as an additional investment by the partners; and that QOF investors may hold their interests in QOFs and make the basis step-up election until 2047. Final regulations should include all of these proposed rules.

Looking beyond the scope of the current NPRM, the lack of clarity on several other key issues is preventing many QOFs from forming and significantly limiting the nature and extent of new investment in designated communities. As detailed in the attached comments, guidance is urgently needed in the following areas:

Final regulations should remove barriers that prevent multi-asset QOFs from forming so that capital can flow to QOZ communities. Guidance providing a reasonable period of time for QOFs to invest and reinvest funds, as well as clarity that investors tax benefits will not be compromised when a QOF sells and reinvests in qualifying investments, will allow QOFs to form and invest as Congress intended.

Final regulations should interpret the statute in ways that encourage and enable QOF investments in operating businesses, as well as real estate projects. Clarity is needed regarding how operating businesses can meet the gross income test to qualify as a QOZ Business, and how their property can meet the substantial improvement test to be considered QOZ Business Property.

Additional guidance is welcome on a host of other important issues, a few of which we touch on in the attached comments. However, without adequate guidance in the three key areas noted above, the QOZ tax incentive will fail to achieve the impact Congress intended. The attached comments make recommendations for the content of final regulations, but we urge Treasury to move quickly on these critical issues and, if more expedient, to do so in subregulatory guidance.

I am a U.S. tax preparer located in Switzerland and also a business owner affected by Section 965. My company prepares around 1,000 U.S. tax returns each year. The transition year tax has been an unbelievable burden to many of the 30 - 40 clients I have that are foreign business owners.

In every growing business there must remain some income in the company to fund working capital, seasonal fluctuations in cash flow and the purchase of assets. Most of us living and working overseas who have our own businesses have service companies where the level of depreciable fixed assets might be relatively low compared to the cash needs of the company. My own company has monthly payroll that is equal to the amount of net fixed assets I have. There is no way I can manage the company to earn just 10% of my fixed assets. I wouldn't have enough cash at year end to pay January payroll. And now going forward I and my clients will be double taxed on the income retained by our foreign companies. The foreign country will tax the income and the US will tax anything that exceeds 10% of our measly assets (we are not allowed a foreign tax credit on this income!). This is forcing me and my clients to take drastic steps to protect our companies and avoid double taxation such as renouncing citizenship or giving away our businesses to a nonresident alien so it is no longer a controlled foreign company. If we don't take these steps the only other alternative to avoid double taxation is to take almost all the profits as salary leaving our businesses strangled for funds which can cause cash flow problems and restrict our growth.

The IRS is taxing the business income as deferred income to the owners. Obviously the people that created this rule have never run a business and don't understand that all successful companies have retained earnings that are usually well above the amount of cash on their books. That's because it takes income to grow and operate a successful business. That income will never be paid to the owners except perhaps a small amount as dividends. And those dividends are taxed by the U.S. already. Business owners know that the salary we draw is our income, not the retained earning sitting in our company's books. We are not big global companies that are shifting income to lower tax countries. We live and work in one place and are now penalized by the IRS for our American entrepreneurship. And the more successful we are, the more earnings our companies need to grow or to fund the company's cash flow, the more we're penalized for it because of GILTI and Sec 965.

How can the IRS justify going backwards and taxing earnings since 1986? Can any governing body decide to retroactively change any rule and go after people or companies who were compliant under the old rules but now are considered not compliant because of the retroactive change. This is a fundamental violation of our rights and a perversion of every tax deadline and effective date that was ever set. If we can go backwards and change rules, then deadlines and dates no longer have any meaning. And now we live in fear that what is legal now may be changed in the future.

As a tax professional, I understand the new territorial regime and the desire for America to benefit from the foreign success of the American multi-national companies. But caught in this web of regulations are small, single location foreign businesses with entrepreneurial American owners. The taxation of these company's retained and annual earnings is onerous and unfair. The value that remains in these companies in the form of retained earnings is NOT income to the owners. If and when the company is sold, the sale price will reflect the amount of actual assets that remain in the company and any capital gain will become taxable at that time to the owner. But until that time, our businesses are a 3rd party investment and should NOT be taxable to the owner until a taxable event occurs, such as sale of the owner's share in the company or death of the owner (and potential wealth tax if the value of the company is high enough).

Here is a simplified Flow through model to add these German Taxes: from 100 Euro that I collect (100-19)% x (100-31)% x (100-26,5)% = 81% x 69% x 73.5% = 41 Euro is left over. So I pay 59% in Taxes! In respect of Section 1.965(c)(1)(i), we feel this ruling will cause hardship for individual taxpayers. Assume that an individual shareholder has a CFC in treaty country with NON-Subpart F income. Prior to the enactment of Section 965, U.S. tax was only paid when the taxpayer received a distribution. As the corporation was situated in a country with which the U.S. has an income tax treaty, the dividend was considered a qualified dividend subject to a 15/20% rate of tax. As taxes in the foreign country are approximately 24%, no U.S. tax was generally payable on this dividend.

As the corporation has accumulated E&P, the 965 inclusion will cause this income to be currently taxable at 15.5% (actually slightly more). This results in a rate higher than that of the qualified dividend. To offset this tax, the shareholder will be required to pay dividends of PTI in order to create foreign tax to use for foreign tax credit purposes. The inability to use .557 of the foreign tax causes a large amount of U.S. tax to pay as the foreign taxes eligible for credit will only amount to 10.6% (24% less .557).

This causes hardship for U.S. citizens residing outside of the United States that are operating active businesses through a corporation. In many cases, these corporations are used for tax & retirement planning purposes within the foreign country. First, we are forced to distribute the earnings we are saving for our retirement to pay the second tier of tax in the foreign country to create foreign tax for credit against the 965 tax and second, that we are denied credit for these taxes and must now pay U.S. tax on these earnings.

We do not believe that this was the intent of the legislation and accordingly are requesting review of the rules.

Regarding the federal public notice (released on December 13, 2018) for the Navys request to establish a danger zone in the waters adjacent to the Finegayan Small Arms Range, I have several concerns:

In-depth research does not seem to have been conducted on the identified affected area (892 acres), as preliminary determination was mentioned several times throughout the public notice.

No specific days and times are provided for the people of Guam regarding the restricted access to the proposed danger zone area. Intermittently is used but means irregular and not continuous and does not state when restrictions will apply.

In terms of when the range is in use, the notice states that a red flag from a conspicuous and easily-seen location along the nearby shore will be displayed during the day. Should the range be used at night, a strobe light will be displayed. But what if the red flag or the strobe light is not clearly visible to commercial, public, or private vessels? What if the strobe light malfunctions? What then of the safety of the people on board those vessels?

The notice identifies endangered species that may live within the proposed danger zone area, including the green sea turtle, the hawksbill sea turtle, and three species of coral, all of which are ESA-listed. Yet, the Navy admits that there is no designated critical habitat for listed species in the action area. What specific impacts will this proposed danger zone have on our endangered aquatic life? What are the long-term ramifications for not protecting our aquatic life and not providing them with a designated critical habitat?

Regarding the Essential Fish Habitat, a complete consultation process must be executed, and further research must be conducted, as the proposed danger zone may adversely affect [this] EFH. Fish is one of our local food sources, and if our fish are harmed or contaminated by the proposed surface danger zone, a vital food resource will be removed for the people of Guam.

There was not ample time provided for the community to respond. We were given only one month to submit comments. During this month, it was the holiday season, a time many of us were spending with our families. Further, the deadline for comments was January 14, which is around the first week of school, when many students and parents are busy with preparing for the new semester. We need more time to read about and provide comments for the possible long-term damaging effects this proposed danger zone may have on our environment, aquatic life, and overall health. We deserve this right.

Moreover, I am asking the following of the US Navy and the US Army Corps. of Engineers:
That more in-depth research be done and that our community be provided with substantial evidence from and related to Guam;
That concerns with safety be addressed (e.g., the red flag and strobe light);
That there is a public hearing so that the concerns and voices of the people of Guam can be heard and recorded; and
That other options be considered, particularly the option of not having a danger zone in the Finegayan area (inclusive of the ocean area).

The people of Guam have the right to ask for more in-depth research to be conducted for this proposed danger zone in Finegayan. We have a right to more information. We have a right to a public hearing so that we may vocalize our concerns. We have a right to answers for our questions. All of these things must happen before the Navy is permitted to move forward with this proposed danger zone. It is imperative for the health and safety of our environment, our people, and our aquatic life. It is imperative because our vital food source and CHamoru cultural values and practices are being jeopardized.

This proposed danger zone shows the continued disrespect for CHamoru lands, waters, and values, as well as the lack of concern for the health of the people and aquatic life on Guam. But we are of the land and of the sea; we have been for over 4,000 years. Thus, we must have an integral role in the decision-making of this danger zone and all other US military-related projects.

We do not have enough information about this proposed danger zones and restrictions, we should have a public hearing or hearings for more information regarding these plans for Finegayan. Despite the claims that these danger zones and restricted areas will "not have have a significant impact on the quality of the human environment and, therefore, preparation of an environmental impact statement will not be required" (procedural requirement C), there remains a need for an environmental impact statement to be prepared so that the community can fully understand the plans regarding the arms range and its danger zone. While environment assessments are important--preparing one after the public notice period and comments conclude is not sufficient. We have an obligation to protect the our tsi, tno', and the Chamoru way of life--our culture, oceanic environment, and health depend on it. We have a right to obtain answers to our questions regarding these proposed restricted areas and the small arms range impacts and plans that will impact us and our future generations.
