I have to be honest: Im not fully versed in every detail of the recent changes to tax law, and Im not familiar with the intricacies of the tax code regarding commuter benefits and how those should be included or excluded in income. However, to me, the intent of Congress was clear: the cost of providing parking to employees was meant to be taxed. And providing large exclusions to companies that own their own lots would defeat the spirit of the tax law. Moreover, it would amount to the IRS deciding to favor commuting by personal automobile over transit: the IRS should not make that decision for Americans, and must instead treat them equally, as the law intended.

I practice medicine. I work at a hospital. I do surgery, including emergency surgery. Recently, all of the "clinician" parking that was reserved specifically for physicians and those who practice medicine were taken away because we were told they were now a "tax benefit." So now any person can park anywhere near the hospital. There is no longer any designated parking.

So let me paint this scenario for you...Your 17 year old son is in a terrible car accident and has been rushed to the hospital. He needs surgery immediately to stop internal hemorrhage (bleeding) and every second counts. A body can bleed out completely in less than 7 minutes. I am the on-call surgeon. I live only 3 minutes from the hospital. I get to the hospital in less than 6 minutes...but guess what...there is no place for me to park. It takes an additional 10 minutes for me to find a place to park after winding around several lots and side streets. I eventually end up parking at the McDonald's across the street just because there is nothing within a 1-mile vicinity. Now I run as fast as I can across a 6-lane busy road to get to where I'm needed and to save a life (now short of breath from running, and grumpy from frustration).

Who in God's name thought this "parking spot tax thing" was a good idea? None of our hospital employees pay for a spot, so it's not like the nurses and other personnel have to pay and the doctors don't. It's all free, but the doctors and clinicians have "designated parking" closer to the door for that very specific reason (see scenario above).

So, the next time you have a medical emergency and you're waiting for the on-call doctor to arrive to save a life, you can thank the IRS for taking that additional 10 minutes.

Free parking is by far the largest commuting benefit in the United States, with an annual cost estimated by the U.S. Treasury as triple that of mass transit benefits. The core IRS values of transparency, fairness, integrity and efficiency demand that the IRS tax parking fairly and employers pay the same tax rate on parking benefits under section 274(a)(4) as they would on any other commuting benefits.

As with all IRS actions, this has significant effects on the functions of our economy and society. A distortionary tax on commuting benefits that ignores the costs of parking would harm the nation.

As parking effectively takes away room from other beneficial uses for human capital, it's important to minimize the subsidy we have given it.

Because parking is a capital-intensive benefit often provided directly by the employer, while transit service is a labor-intensive benefit typically provided by a third party, treating these benefits equally requires a distinct approach to each.

1) The proposed "primary use test" is arbitrary and should be eliminated. There is no empirical basis or support in the law for such a broad exemption that affects so many large employers.

Instead, all employers should calculate the actual number of employees using free lots at peak employee occupancy. ("Any reasonable method" for estimating parking use provides employers too much latitude and too little guidance.) If they choose not to perform an actual count, employers should be able to use an alternative ratio based on national drive-to-work averages: for example, 87 percent of peak employee count.

If a "primary use test" must be used, it should trigger when 10 percent of unrestricted parking spaces are used by employees, not 50 percent. Also, any employers being arbitrarily exempted from all parking-related taxes due to the primary use test should be equally exempt from taxes on other commuting benefits.

2) The capital costs of on-site parking are too large to ignore. Real estate and construction costs are by far the largest cost of many parking benefits. For third-party parking providers, these costs are built into their prices, and will be taxed appropriately under the IRS's draft guidance. But providers of on-site free employee parking would evade taxes on these costs. They should not be -- such outlays should be taxed either in the year of expenditure or as a depreciating asset. If employers choose not to calculate the capital costs of their parking benefits, the IRS should provide an estimated figure for capital parking costs per space per day (to be added to the expense of parking lot operation and maintenance).

3) The IRS should provide guidance to tenants whose free employee parking is bundled with a building lease. The tax code shouldn't encourage bundled parking leases over separate ones. The IRS must offer some guidance for estimating the cost of bundled parking spaces.

Employers should have the right to offer commuting benefits, including parking benefits, to their employees. But the public shouldn't put its thumb on the scale of that decision by exempting some parking benefits from taxation -- especially if the same tax is falling fully on employers' other commuting benefits.

Taxing parking also has the additional benefit of correcting a distorted market sector (the provision of parking in new developments). Many cities are considering reductions in or outright eliminations of the minimum parking requirements which allows developers and business owners to decide for themselves how much parking they may or may not need to provide. While this is an excellent first step, there are many subsidies and incentives in place throughout our countries various legal, financial and regulatory systems that encourage people to drive cars and cities to build infrastructure to support that driving. This model of 'drive everywhere' is a net loss system when the long term costs of infrastructure are fully amortized and compared to same-period tax revenues generated by development supported thereby, in other words it operates in the red. Taxing parking properly would be one more step to help correct this distortion in the market and encourage citizens and governments to make better transportation choices that would positively benefit our economies both local, state, and national.

As a provider of community services to people intellectual and development disabilities funded by Medicaid, I am very concerned about the new implementation of Section 274 of the Internal Revenue Code and its impact on UBTI, particularly on parking and mass transit expenses. Below I outline several concerns and recommendations for forthcoming regulations:

* Our services are reliant on state and federal government structuring of our payments - ultimately we cannot afford additional taxation without government action to increase our rates for services. Therefore I support the widely supported push for your use of inherent administrative authority to delay of implementation until at least one year after final regulations are promulgated to allow for that funding to be allocated and for our service field to understand the impact of these new rules. I also support a delay in furnishing any regulations as Congress continues to actively pursue repeal of this section.
* Our services are staff and transportation heavy - it is our job to get people with significant disabilities in the community to jobs, community events, and daily skills training. Parking and transportation is essential for our staff and the individuals they serve. As you pursue any finite regulations around section 274, I would urge the agency to consider the decimation of lifeline services upon overtaxation and encourage thoughtful calculations around how parking and transit is considered in our line of work.
* In terms of parking and transit benefits, I believe strongly that the application of the unrelated business income tax on employee compensation reduction agreements is in error and that employers should not be taxed on pay that is withheld to apply to transportation benefits.
* For parking guidance in general, there is no clarity of application and it seems to be overly broad in its interpretation - which for our services that occur throughout the community in a variety of settings will not work at all. I urge the IRS to conduct listening sessions on this particular component before pursuing any further regulatory action to fully understand the impact of various interpretations.
* Finally, for any forthcoming regulations, I would request the precedence of a delay of implementation specific to providers of intellectual and developmental disability supports that are funded by the Medicaid program (the Department of Labor has applied this standard in major rulemaking and we would request it be considered here as well)

Please feel free to reach out to me directly for more information or to my national trade association, the American Network of Community Options and Resources (ANCOR), who shares in my concern.

Thank you for consideration of my input.

I am writing as a professional working in the area of transportation demand management and employee transportation benefits. I have previously published research on the topic of employee parking benefits, their tax implications, and the ancillary effects on employee behavior.

Parking policy is more influential on the travel habits of Americans than nearly any other transportation policy or benefit, and as such, seemingly minor changes can have massive impacts. I am of the opinion that the U.S. broadly suffers from an incoherent approach towards parking and other transportation policies. Broadly speaking, providing free or cheap parking worsens traffic congestion a significant degree, reduces carpooling, reduces transit use, and undermines many other federal, state, and local efforts to improve our overall transportation system. Whatever we save workers by giving them free or low cost parking, we reimpose on them through increased congestion, longer travel times, and a host of other co-morbidities.

For this reason, it is imperative that the IRS interpret the 2017 tax law changes on this sector of the economy to be highly restrictive on companies who would otherwise prefer to offer free or reduced cost parking to employees.

A few key issues to focus on:

Municipal employers who are currently offering on-street parking or municipal parking lot parking, and assigning zero value to those benefits: This area is much more significant than it might first seem, though recent attention in New York city on "placard abuse" is an indication of the severity and dysfunction that offering free parking to municipal employees breeds. While municipalities are a different class than for-profit and non-profit employers, the IRS should be creative and relentless in finding a policy that correctly accounts for the value of this benefit. First, a methodology for correctly appraising the value of on-street or municipal lot parking should be developed, and second, a method of applying that value towards the income of the recipient (since the employer is exempt in this case) should be a priority of the IRS.

Value of parking spaces generally: There is an ongoing discussion of how to properly value and subdivide a parking lot or structure to correctly apportion cost to an employer or employee for the purposes of taxation. It is imperative that the IRS include any and all improvements, original capital cost, ongoing operations and maintenance cost of the parking lot as part of the value calculation for a parking lot. Appraisals, comparable properties, present-day construction costs, and other tools can be used to estimate a parking lot or structure's value when original capital cost is not available. For on-street spaces, comparable meter rates, or alternate-use permit rates (vending permit, construction permit, etc.) should be used to estimate a value for the purposes of taxation.

Shared-use parking lots: Where customers and employees share the same parking lot, a business' tax liability for the employee-used portion of the lot should be calculated off the percentage of the lot used by employees. The parking lot's entire value should be calculated, with the employee percentage applied to that as a method of estimating tax obligations.

De-minimus parking lots / space rates: For the simplicity of users with small parking footprints (10 or fewer spaces), a standard cost should be available so they can calculate the value of their parking and it's attendant tax implications. The standard value of a parking space should be at least $2,500 per year, which accounts for the 200 SF of land used, improvements, and maintenance.

As a provider of community services to people intellectual and development disabilities funded by Medicaid, I am very concerned about the new implementation of Section 274 of the Internal Revenue Code and its impact on UBTI, particularly on parking and mass transit expenses. I urge the IRS to conduct listening sessions on this particular component before pursuing any further regulatory action to fully understand the impact of various interpretations.

This is an excellent change.  Parking is an expensive amenity, often supplied in surplus, which can have significant negative impacts on the surrounding community.  Space consumed by excess parking also deprives the community of alternate uses for land which would provide higher value and greater local taxable value.  Taxation of parking as an amenity provides a positive price signal to employers to use land in the most beneficial way available.

As a provider of community services to people intellectual and development disabilities funded by Medicaid, I am very concerned about the new implementation of Section 274 of the Internal Revenue Code and its impact on UBTI, particularly on parking and mass transit expenses. Below I outline several concerns and recommendations for forthcoming regulations:

* Our services are reliant on state and federal government structuring of our payments - ultimately we cannot afford additional taxation without government action to increase our rates for services. Therefore I support the widely supported push for your use of inherent administrative authority to delay of implementation until at least one year after final regulations are promulgated to allow for that funding to be allocated and for our service field to understand the impact of these new rules. I also support a delay in furnishing any regulations as Congress continues to actively pursue repeal of this section.
* Our services are staff and transportation heavy - it is our job to get people with significant disabilities in the community to jobs, community events, and daily skills training. Parking and transportation is essential for our staff and the individuals they serve. As you pursue any finite regulations around section 274, I would urge the agency to consider the decimation of lifeline services upon overtaxation and encourage thoughtful calculations around how parking and transit is considered in our line of work.
* In terms of parking and transit benefits, I believe strongly that the application of the unrelated business income tax on employee compensation reduction agreements is in error and that employers should not be taxed on pay that is withheld to apply to transportation benefits.
* For parking guidance in general, there is no clarity of application and it seems to be overly broad in its interpretation - which for our services that occur throughout the community in a variety of settings will not work at all. I urge the IRS to conduct listening sessions on this particular component before pursuing any further regulatory action to fully understand the impact of various interpretations.
* Finally, for any forthcoming regulations, I would request the precedence of a delay of implementation specific to providers of intellectual and developmental disability supports that are funded by the Medicaid program (the Department of Labor has applied this standard in major rulemaking and we would request it be considered here as well)

Please feel free to reach out to me directly for more information or to my national trade association, the American Network of Community Options and Resources (ANCOR), who shares in my concern.

Thank you for consideration of my input.

This is a great start towards realizing the value of parking as an asset.  Where I live the market rate is $300 a month per space to park during the weekday.  Property owners should absolutely be taxed on this valuable asset.  The problem I see is with the exemptions where the parking is provided for both employees and the public.  This exemption would mean that the worst offenders (malls and big-box stores with huge sprawling lots) would pay the least.  This is the opposite of what should be happening.  Cheap and free parking has been plaguing us for decades and this new regulation has a chance of reining in some of that abuse and making property owners start paying for the social and environmental damage they're doing.  Please do not exempt these large mixed use parking lots.

It's unfair to exempt parking from this tax while leaving transit benefits subject to the tax. This component of the tax bill was intended to offset cuts to the corporate tax rate and on that basis alone it should not be undermined.

Even more importantly, exempting parking from this tax -- under almost any circumstance -- serves as a subsidy for driving at the expense of more affordable, healthy, and sustainable modes of travel like walking and transit. The IRS should not be in the business of propping up driving at the expense of other modes of travel that are more societally beneficial.

The tax bill lowered corporate tax rates in an effort to boost the economy, and one small way it paid for this effort was adding a tax to a facet of the economy -- parking -- that has a variety of negative externalities. This was a smart policy, taxing a thing that should not be subsidized to support a stronger economy overall.

Please don't undermine that effort with policies that exempt anyone from this parking tax. In places where parking is expensive this tax exemption will be very costly and promote driving in places where congestion is already worst, and in places where parking is inexpensive the impact will be relatively small.

Thank you for your consideration.
Please tax parking fairly. It is not appropriate to tax transit passes while considering removal of a parking tax. Employers and employees should be rewarded, not punished, for utilizing transit.

It is imperative that the IRS tax parking equitably and that employers pay the same tax rate on parking benefits under section 274(a)(4) as they would on any other commuting benefits.

Because parking is a capital-intensive benefit often provided directly by the employer, while transit service is a labor-intensive benefit typically provided by a third party, treating these benefits equally requires a distinct approach to each.

1) The proposed "primary use test" is arbitrary and should be eliminated. There is no empirical basis or support in the law for such a broad exemption that affects so many large employers.

Instead, all employers should calculate the actual number of employees using free lots at peak employee occupancy. ("Any reasonable method" for estimating parking use provides employers too much latitude and too little guidance.) If they choose not to perform an actual count, employers should be able to use an alternative ratio based on national drive-to-work averages: for example, 87 percent of peak employee count.

If a "primary use test" must be used, it should trigger when 10 percent of unrestricted parking spaces are used by employees, not 50 percent. Also, any employers being arbitrarily exempted from all parking-related taxes due to the primary use test should be equally exempt from taxes on other commuting benefits.

2) The capital costs of on-site parking are too large to ignore. Real estate and construction costs are by far the largest cost of many parking benefits. For third-party parking providers, these costs are built into their prices, and will be taxed appropriately under the IRS's draft guidance. But providers of on-site free employee parking would evade taxes on these costs. They should not be -- such outlays should be taxed either in the year of expenditure or as a depreciating asset. If employers choose not to calculate the capital costs of their parking benefits, the IRS should provide an estimated figure for capital parking costs per space per day (to be added to the expense of parking lot operation and maintenance).

3) The IRS should provide guidance to tenants whose free employee parking is bundled with a building lease. The tax code shouldn't encourage bundled parking leases over separate ones. The IRS must offer some guidance for estimating the cost of bundled parking spaces.

Employers should have the right to offer commuting benefits, including parking benefits, to their employees. But the public shouldn't put its thumb on the scale of that decision by exempting some parking benefits from taxation -- especially if the same tax is falling fully on employers' other commuting benefits.

Encouraged amendments:

Eliminate the primary use test or reduce the threshold to 10 or fewer.

Ensure that entities exempt from parking taxes also be exempt from taxes on all other forms of transportation benefits.

Require entities / employers to actually count on-site parking space use or default to national standard of 86% parking space use vs. inaccurate estimates.

Recognize land and development costs associated with cost of a parking space by creating a daily rate per slot, similar to vehicular mileage costs.

Free parking is just as much a subsidy to employees as alternative transit benefits (such as a public transit pass). The core IRS values of transparency, fairness, integrity and efficiency demand that the IRS tax parking fairly and employers pay the same tax rate on parking benefits under section 274(a)(4) as they would on any other commuting benefits.

Taxing alternative commuter benefits more than parking creates a perverse incentive for employers to expand free parking while eliminating benefits for alternative forms of transportation. This would likely exacerbate dependence on single occupancy cars, increasing pollution and disproportionately disadvantage workers who can't afford cars.

Because parking is a capital-intensive benefit often provided directly by the employer, while transit service is a labor-intensive benefit typically provided by a third party, treating these benefits equally requires a distinct approach to each.

1. The proposed "primary use test" is arbitrary and should be eliminated, or at the very least dramatically limited to exempt fewer employers. There is no empirical basis or support in the law for such a broad exemption that affects so many large employers.

Instead, all employers should calculate the actual number of employees using free lots at peak employee occupancy. ("Any reasonable method" for estimating parking use provides employers too much latitude and too little guidance.) If they choose not to perform an actual count, employers should be able to use an alternative ratio based on national drive-to-work averages: for example, 87 percent of peak employee count.

If a "primary use test" must be used, it should trigger when 10 percent of unrestricted parking spaces are used by employees, not 50 percent. Also, any employers being arbitrarily exempted from all parking-related taxes due to the primary use test should be equally exempt from taxes on other commuting benefits.

2. The capital costs of on-site parking are too large to ignore. Real estate and construction costs are by far the largest cost of many parking benefits. For third-party parking providers, these costs are built into their prices, and will be taxed appropriately under the IRS's draft guidance. But providers of on-site free employee parking would evade taxes on these costs. They should not be -- such outlays should be taxed either in the year of expenditure or as a depreciating asset. If employers choose not to calculate the capital costs of their parking benefits, the IRS should provide an estimated figure for capital parking costs per space per day (to be added to the expense of parking lot operation and maintenance).

3. The IRS should provide guidance to tenants whose free employee parking is bundled with a building lease. The tax code shouldn't encourage bundled parking leases over separate ones. The IRS must offer some guidance for estimating the cost of bundled parking spaces.

4. The IRS should also clarify and mitigate the impact of these policies on tax-exempt nonprofits.

Employers should have the right to offer commuting benefits, including parking benefits, to their employees. But the public shouldn't put its thumb on the scale of that decision by exempting some parking benefits from taxation -- especially if the same tax is falling fully on employers' other commuting benefits.

Thank you for your consideration.

Please tax parking! Offering tax exemptions to employers for parking but not for bus passes encourages MORE DRIVING, MORE greenhouse gas emissions, MORE fossil fuel consumption, and LESS active transportation such as walking, taking the bus and riding a bicycle. Driving costs communities more in road maintenance, traffic accidents, deaths, and space consumption. Driving is really the most expensive and least healthy way for humans to travel. If anything, public transit passes should be tax exempt for employers to provide to employees, and parking should be taxed at a maximum level. Thank you for considering the social, environmental AND financial costs of tax dedutions and their long term implications. Check out the Netherlands for an equitable and ideal transportation model.

Part of the purpose of taxation is to generate revenue, and part is to drive behavior.

Taxing transit passes but not taxing parking will generate almost no revenue because transit passes are uncommon benefits, and will be even less common with this and drive the wrong behavior. We need more focus on transit, less on cars.

This also makes local economies less sustainable, because it will drive users to use transit less, thus making them less financially viable.

This is bad policy, bad taxation policy, and bad interpretation.

I strongly support taxing the parking provided at work sites. This "free" parking is subsided by me any everyone else who chooses, or is not able, to drive to work. It also supports very inefficient use of valuable land and adds to congestion.

I just received an explanation of this new guideline from our accounting firm.  I respectfully ask the IRS to reconsider this ridiculous new taxation.  Businesses already pay real estate taxes on all property,  and pay income taxes on income, which is defined as revenue less expenses.  Businesses incur costs on parking areas for customers and employees similar to any other real property like stores, office buildings, etc., all of which are normal and expected costs for running a business.  To disallow such expenses from the taxable income calculation is not logical, and a threat to business. Please reconsider the issued guidance and rescind it to the preexisting understanding of such necessary expenses.  Thank you.

This will lead to a much more accurate accounting of employers cost of providing parking.

I urge the IRS to reconsider the guidelines that exempt them from paying taxes related to parking. The "reasonable use year" is totally ridiculous, and all businesses should be required to pay the same taxes on 100 employee's parking, whether they are part of a dedicated lot or a lot allowing 100 other users to park there. Otherwise it is disproportionately harmful to small businesses and gives extra benefits to national chain stores. The business should also be required to either directly count the number of employees parking, or base this number on  national average percentage of people driving to work, instead of allowing loopholes in "guesstimation" which again disproportionately helps large businesses. This tax makes all the sense in the works to be kept, overall, but it needs a few changes for it to be effective and not allow loopholes

Because parking is a capital-intensive benefit often provided directly by the employer, while transit service is a labor-intensive benefit typically provided by a third party, treating these benefits equally requires a distinct approach to each.

1) The proposed "primary use test" is arbitrary and should be eliminated. There is no empirical basis or support in the law for such a broad exemption that affects so many large employers.

Instead, all employers should calculate the actual number of employees using free lots at peak employee occupancy. ("Any reasonable method" for estimating parking use provides employers too much latitude and too little guidance.) If they choose not to perform an actual count, employers should be able to use an alternative ratio based on national drive-to-work averages: for example, 87 percent of peak employee count.

If a "primary use test" must be used, it should trigger when 10 percent of unrestricted parking spaces are used by employees, not 50 percent. Also, any employers being arbitrarily exempted from all parking-related taxes due to the primary use test should be equally exempt from taxes on other commuting benefits.

2) The capital costs of on-site parking are too large to ignore. Real estate and construction costs are by far the largest cost of many parking benefits. For third-party parking providers, these costs are built into their prices, and will be taxed appropriately under the IRS's draft guidance. But providers of on-site free employee parking would evade taxes on these costs. They should not be -- such outlays should be taxed either in the year of expenditure or as a depreciating asset. If employers choose not to calculate the capital costs of their parking benefits, the IRS should provide an estimated figure for capital parking costs per space per day (to be added to the expense of parking lot operation and maintenance).

3) The IRS should provide guidance to tenants whose free employee parking is bundled with a building lease. The tax code shouldn't encourage bundled parking leases over separate ones. The IRS must offer some guidance for estimating the cost of bundled parking spaces.

Employers should have the right to offer commuting benefits, including parking benefits, to their employees. But the public shouldn't put its thumb on the scale of that decision by exempting some parking benefits from taxation -- especially if the same tax is falling fully on employers' other commuting benefits.
Please enforce the tax code as written. Subsidized parking is harmful to cities. Cars are already subsidized far too much.

RE: Notice 2018-99, Parking Expenses for Qualified Transportation Fringes Under 274(a)(4) and 512(a)(7) of the Internal Revenue Code

Dear Acting Commissioner Kautter,

We write to offer our comments regarding Internal Revenue Service Notice 2018-99: Parking Expenses for Qualified Transportation Fringes Under 274(a)(4) and 512(a)(7) of the Internal Revenue Code.

Section 13304 of Public Law 115-97 eliminates employers ability to deduct the expenses of:

[Q]ualified transportation fringes. . . [and] . . . any expense incurred for providing any transportation, or any payment or reimbursement, to an employee of the taxpayer in connection with travel between the employees residence and place of employment, except as necessary for ensuring the safety of the employee.

However, the guidance outlined by Notice 2018-99, specifically regarding the primary use test in step 2 on page 9, creates a policy not authorized by this legislation. As written, we are concerned that that the guidance may produce unintended consequences by promoting the development of unused parking in order to avoid additional tax liability. Not only could this lead to harmful and inefficient land use policy by incentivizing the creation of empty parking spaces, it also has disparate impacts on small businesses that may have fewer overall available parking spots.

To that end, we recommend that the primary use test and the any reasonable method of counting cars be eliminated from final guidance. Similar to the primary use test, the recommendation to use any reasonable method to determine how many employees park should be replaced with a requirement that employers actually have to identify the number of people who park. If employers do not wish to make this calculation, they should have the option to assume that 86% (the national average) of their employees drive and then park at work.

While Notice 2018-99 is sufficient in detailing the parking expenses that employers should consider when calculating tax liability, we are concerned about the lack of guidance for situations where a business parking is bundled into a lease. Employers and property managers need guidance on how to calculate the cost of parking-only in the lease and equitably divide that cost between tenants.

As a provider of community services to people intellectual and development disabilities funded by Medicaid, I am very concerned about the new implementation of Section 274 of the Internal Revenue Code and its impact on UBTI, particularly on parking and mass transit expenses. Below I outline several concerns and recommendations for forthcoming regulations:

* Our services are reliant on state and federal government structuring of our payments - ultimately we cannot afford additional taxation without government action to increase our rates for services. Therefore I support the widely supported push for your use of inherent administrative authority to delay of implementation until at least one year after final regulations are promulgated to allow for that funding to be allocated and for our service field to understand the impact of these new rules. I also support a delay in furnishing any regulations as Congress continues to actively pursue repeal of this section.
* Our services are staff and transportation heavy - it is our job to get people with significant disabilities in the community to jobs, community events, and daily skills training. Parking and transportation is essential for our staff and the individuals they serve. As you pursue any finite regulations around section 274, I would urge the agency to consider the decimation of lifeline services upon overtaxation and encourage thoughtful calculations around how parking and transit is considered in our line of work.
* In terms of parking and transit benefits, I believe strongly that the application of the unrelated business income tax on employee compensation reduction agreements is in error and that employers should not be taxed on pay that is withheld to apply to transportation benefits.
* For parking guidance in general, there is no clarity of application and it seems to be overly broad in its interpretation - which for our services that occur throughout the community in a variety of settings will not work at all. I urge the IRS to conduct listening sessions on this particular component before pursuing any further regulatory action to fully understand the impact of various interpretations.
* Finally, for any forthcoming regulations, I would request the precedence of a delay of implementation specific to providers of intellectual and developmental disability supports that are funded by the Medicaid program (the Department of Labor has applied this standard in major rulemaking and we would request it be considered here as well)

Please feel free to reach out to me directly for more information or to my national trade association, the American Network of Community Options and Resources (ANCOR), who shares in my concern.

Thank you for consideration of my input.

IRS Notice 2018-99

While the examples provided in Notice 2018-99 are helpful, the law itself is very confusing, complex, and creates an administrative/accounting burden.

In addition, the notice does not address the issue of employees paying for parking via payroll deduction. Would the examples provided in the notice change if the employees use payroll deduction to pay for parking in the employers parking facilities? Tax policy related to commuter benefits has been the subject of several recent congressional actions and is a matter of great public consequence. Recent research has documented the negative impacts of the current tax exclusion for qualified transportation fringe benefits on traffic conditions in our most congested cities, as well as its cost to the public purse.

In the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (P.L 115-97), Congress sent a clear directive to end the tax deductibility of employer expenses related to the provision of qualified transportation fringes. The act stipulates:

No deduction shall be allowed under this chapter for the expense of any qualified transportation fringe (as defined in section 132(f)) provided to an employee of the taxpayer

Qualified transportation fringe benefits include parking provided by employers to their commuting workers. However, the IRSs interim guidance for implementing the law with regard to employer-provided parking fails to execute the will of Congress that no deduction be allowed for any expenditure related to a qualified fringe benefit. Specifically, the primary use test described in the guidance would allow many employers to deduct expenses for providing a qualified transportation fringe benefit (commuter parking) to their workers in contradiction of the clear will of Congress.

Any further guidance or permanent regulations must correct this problem to ensure that the will of Congress is fully implemented and that all employers are treated equitably. Fully implementing this provision can also be done in such as a way as to ensure a reasonable compliance burden for businesses.

Primary Use Test Is Inequitable and Unjustified
The IRSs interim guidance enables employers to continue to deduct the cost of providing unreserved parking used by their commuting employees, so long as the total share of the spots used by commuting employees in a parking lot owned by the employer and open to the general public is less than 50%. The calculation of the number of spaces open to the general public includes surplus parking spots that may not regularly be used by anyone.

Allowing employers to continue to deduct the cost of providing commuter parking in lots open to the general public does not reflect the will of Congress. It is also inequitable, privileging employers who own large parking lots with unused parking over those with smaller lots or those who purchase or lease parking spaces for their commuting employees from third parties.

The primary use test is also unjustified as an effort to reduce taxpayers compliance burden. There are numerous reasonable methods the IRS could recommend for employers to estimate the number of spots in a parking lot used for commuter parking from hard counts of employee parking usage to calculation methods based on the size of an employers workforce and an assumed share of workers commuting by car. If compliance burden is a concern, employers could simply calculate the number of spots used by employees by multiplying the number of workers by 90%.

Guidance Creates Ambiguity, Hampers Enforcement
In addition, the provision allowing employers to use any reasonable method to determine the average actual or estimated usage of a parking facility with varied utilization creates opportunities for taxpayers to choose the method that best justifies definining the facility as primarily for use by the general public and, therefore, tax deductible. This provision has the potential to make it even more difficult for the IRS to clearly enforce the will of Congress that expenses related to the provision of employer parking not be deductible.

I urge the IRS, in future guidance and regulations on this topic, to establish consistency and clarity in the treatment of workplace parking by requiring the cost of all commuter parking regardless of the type of lot used to provide it to be quantified and excluded from tax deductibility. I also urge you to establish clear and reasonable methods for calculating the share of parking occupied by commuting employees in order to create certainty for taxpayers and ensure that the will of Congress in this regard be enforced.

Dear Mr. Clinton,

I write regarding IRS notice 2018-99 regarding Parking Expenses for Qualified Transportation Fringes Under 274(a)(4) and 512(a)(7) of the Internal Revenue Code.

Section 13304 of Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (P.L 115-97) stipulates

No deduction shall be allowed under this chapter for the expense of any qualified transportation fringe (as defined in section 132(f)) provided to an employee of the taxpayer

It goes on to further stipulate,

No deduction shall be allowed under this chapter for any expense incurred for providing any transportation, or any payment or reimbursement, to an employee of the taxpayer in connection with travel between the employees residence and place of employment, except as necessary for ensuring the safety of the employee.

Primary Use Test (Page 9)
The guidance outlined by notice 2018-99, specifically regarding the primary use test outlined by step 2 on page 9 creates an unauthorized policy not intended by the legislation. Specifically, we are concerned that the guidance promotes development of unused parking as a way of avoiding additional tax liability. Additionally, the policy would be an unfair burden on small business owners.

Under the general use test, a small business that uses 6 of its available 10 parking spaces for employees would be subject to the added tax liability whereby an employer with 10,000 available parking spots of which only 4,000 are used by employees would not have to pay taxes on parking expenses.

The primary use test is a loophole that was not intended by Congress. Further, as written, it disproportionally impacts small businesses. Finally, allowing for unused parking spaces to count towards the total parking spaces available creates a land-use policy that supports the creation of empty parking spaces.
Any Means Necessary (Page 11)
Additionally, we have concerns regarding the Any Means Necessary method of calculating the number of parking spaces used by employees. The process outlined in step 2 and step 4 allows for great opportunity for fraud and abuse. Many facilities have no need for public parking and the sole purpose of a parking lot is for employees. Because parking is easily available and plentiful, there is no need to reserve employee parking. The IRS should require employers who provide free parking, but do not reserve it to assume that 90% of employees drive to work alone. Employers should be given the option to fully evaluate the percentage of employees who park and if that number is below 90% then they may use that number in generating the additional tax liability.

Bundling of Parking into a Lease (Page 7)
Finally, we are pleased with the way in which the guidance clearly spells out expenses which are to be considered a part of the calculation. However, the IRS needs to provide additional guidance as to how parking that is bundled into a lease should be considered. Across the nation a significant amount of parking is bundled into the cost of an office lease. While the guidance is correct in requiring parking expenses to be unbundled, it does little to offer solutions to employers or property managers on how to unbundle those costs and equitably divide them between multiple tenants.

Summary of Recommendations
Eliminate the Primary Use Test The 50% primary use test threshold creates an unintended loophole and should be eliminated as it is policy that is not authorized by Congress. We understand the need to accurately account for the percentage of parking expenses that should be attributed to employee parking, but a 50% primary use test Is an arbitrary number that is based upon a percentage of spaces used rather than additional tax liability. If the IRS believes that a primary use test is the best policy mechanism moving forward then we advise reducing the percentage to 10%.

Establish a De Minimus Threshold Like other portions of tax law, establishing a de minimus threshold would be beneficial to small businesses.

Eliminate Any Means Necessary method of counting cars The Any Means Necessary method to determine how many employees park should be replaced, and the additional tax liability should be determined by requiring employers to identify the actual number of people who park. If an employer does not wish to make this calculation, then they should be given the option to assume that 90% of their employees park at work. Calculating the number of employees who park is not burdensome and many employers already track these figures.

Create Clear Guidance on Bundled Parking: Create guidance that offers property managers and employers a better understanding of how to unbundle parking expenses from leases that include parking.

Thank you
Cole Smith
398 Milledge Avenue SE
Atlanta, GA 30312

Please do tax parking lots! But if you don't tax them, it would be completely unfair to tax transit/bike commuter benefits. Parking lots take up gobs of space, causing our cities and towns to sprawl to the point that walking, biking and taking transit are much more difficult, if not impossible. Why on earth should employers be incentivized to pave more parking lots and provide these free spots to their employees? Nope, tax them so they consider moving in the other direction, with employers instead providing benefits to encourage people to commute without gross, expensive, polluting, dangerous vehicles.

This has the potential to vastly improve our communities across the US and help us achieve a healthier and more equitable society. The simplest way to improve the IRS proposal would be to reduce the number of employers it completely exempts from parking taxes. This would mean reducing the ratio for what the IRS calls the primary use test. The IRS has proposed a trigger of 50 percent: that is, if a companys employees take up more than half the spaces in its general-purpose parking lot, the company must pay taxes on the costs of the lot, prorated to the amount filled by employees. But if employees take up less than half the lot, the company gets taxed as if it had zero auto commuters.

Theres no reason for such a high threshold. Eliminating the primary use test or cutting it to (for example) 10 percent employee parking would sharply reduce the number of taxpayer-subsidized parking spaces across the United States. Another option: if an employer is exempt from parking taxes, then its other transportation benefits shouldnt be taxable, either.

Another important fix would be to require employers to count how many workers actually park on-site, rather than using any reasonable method to guess. If an employer doesnt want to count, they should have the option to use a standard national average like 86 percent.

A bigger, broader improvement would be for the IRS to recognize land and development costs as contributors to the cost of a parking space. Because this IRS deduction must be based on measurable cost to the employer, not value to the employee, its hard to quantify this true cost. Most of the cost is incurred up front, on the day a company buys its land or builds a parking garage. (In its proposal, the IRS declares that depreciation of an existing parking structure doesnt count as a parking costa simple decision worth many billions of dollars to employers that own some of the nations trillions of dollars worth of parking structures.) Still, the IRS could offer two cost-estimate methods, one a thorough accounting, the other a set per-slot daily rate of perhaps $5, similar to the agencys approach to vehicle mileage costs.

The bottom line, though, is that the IRS has proposed regulations that would ignore something like half the cost of many employers parking benefits. Transit benefits and third-party parking, meanwhile, must fully pay their way.

That decision would violate the plain language of the new US tax code. Its up to the IRS to come up with regulations that implement the actual law.

Free parking is by far the largest commuting benefit in the United States, with an annual cost estimated by the U.S. Treasury as triple that of mass transit benefits. The core IRS values of transparency, fairness, integrity and efficiency demand that the IRS tax parking fairly and employers pay the same tax rate on parking benefits under section 274(a)(4) as they would on any other commuting benefits.

As with all IRS actions, this has significant effects on the functions of our economy and society. A distortionary tax on commuting benefits that ignores the costs of parking would harm the nation.

It's only fair that employers pay the same tax rate on parking as on other commuting benefits. Car driving should not have special treatment or consideration. Walking, scooters, biking, public transit, and ride shares are all equally valid option for getting to and from work.

Because parking is a capital-intensive benefit often provided directly by the employer, while transit service is a labor-intensive benefit typically provided by a third party, treating these benefits equally requires a distinct approach to each.

1) The proposed "primary use test" is arbitrary and should be eliminated. There is no empirical basis or support in the law for such a broad exemption that affects so many large employers.

Instead, all employers should calculate the actual number of employees using free lots at peak employee occupancy. ("Any reasonable method" for estimating parking use provides employers too much latitude and too little guidance.) If they choose not to perform an actual count, employers should be able to use an alternative ratio based on national drive-to-work averages: for example, 87 percent of peak employee count.

If a "primary use test" must be used, it should trigger when 10 percent of unrestricted parking spaces are used by employees, not 50 percent. Also, any employers being arbitrarily exempted from all parking-related taxes due to the primary use test should be equally exempt from taxes on other commuting benefits.

2) The capital costs of on-site parking are too large to ignore. Real estate and construction costs are by far the largest cost of many parking benefits. For third-party parking providers, these costs are built into their prices, and will be taxed appropriately under the IRS's draft guidance. But providers of on-site free employee parking would evade taxes on these costs. They should not be -- such outlays should be taxed either in the year of expenditure or as a depreciating asset. If employers choose not to calculate the capital costs of their parking benefits, the IRS should provide an estimated figure for capital parking costs per space per day (to be added to the expense of parking lot operation and maintenance).

3) The IRS should provide guidance to tenants whose free employee parking is bundled with a building lease. The tax code shouldn't encourage bundled parking leases over separate ones. The IRS must offer some guidance for estimating the cost of bundled parking spaces.

Employers should have the right to offer commuting benefits, including parking benefits, to their employees. But the public shouldn't put its thumb on the scale of that decision by exempting some parking benefits from taxation -- especially if the same tax is falling fully on employers' other commuting benefits.

As a provider of community services to people intellectual and development disabilities funded by Medicaid, I am very concerned about the new implementation of Section 274 of the Internal Revenue Code and its impact on UBTI, particularly on parking and mass transit expenses. Below I outline several concerns and recommendations for forthcoming regulations:

* Our services are reliant on state and federal government structuring of our payments - ultimately we cannot afford additional taxation without government action to increase our rates for services. Therefore I support the widely supported push for your use of inherent administrative authority to delay of implementation until at least one year after final regulations are promulgated to allow for that funding to be allocated and for our service field to understand the impact of these new rules. I also support a delay in furnishing any regulations as Congress continues to actively pursue repeal of this section.
* Our services are staff and transportation heavy - it is our job to get people with significant disabilities in the community to jobs, community events, and daily skills training. Parking and transportation is essential for our staff and the individuals they serve. As you pursue any finite regulations around section 274, I would urge the agency to consider the decimation of lifeline services upon overtaxation and encourage thoughtful calculations around how parking and transit is considered in our line of work.
* In terms of parking and transit benefits, I believe strongly that the application of the unrelated business income tax on employee compensation reduction agreements is in error and that employers should not be taxed on pay that is withheld to apply to transportation benefits.
* For parking guidance in general, there is no clarity of application and it seems to be overly broad in its interpretation - which for our services that occur throughout the community in a variety of settings will not work at all. I urge the IRS to conduct listening sessions on this particular component before pursuing any further regulatory action to fully understand the impact of various interpretations.
* Finally, for any forthcoming regulations, I would request the precedence of a delay of implementation specific to providers of intellectual and developmental disability supports that are funded by the Medicaid program (the Department of Labor has applied this standard in major rulemaking and we would request it be considered here as well)

Please feel free to reach out to me directly for more information or to my national trade association, the American Network of Community Options and Resources (ANCOR), who shares in my concern.

Thank you for consideration of my input.

I encourage the IRS to account for the full cost of providing parking to employees, which means capital costs not just maintenance and operating costs. The cost of parking is huge, from an economic, environmental, and public health perspective. It is time for the government to stop subsidizing single-occupant vehicle travel through cheap parking.

I am an employee of Citizens National Bank of Meridian, a $1.4 billion asset community bank in Meridian, MS. I write today because I am very concerned about the impact of the proposed regulation under Section 199A of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on my bank and Subchapter S banks nationwide.

Approximately 1900 banks nationwide, or a third of all banks, have elected Subchapter S tax status. These tend to be smaller banks with assets of $200 million to $250 million that specialize in small business, agricultural, and consumer lending. While they serve all market types, they disproportionately serve rural markets. Subchapter S community banks offer a variety of services in their communities to complement their core lending services. These typically include trust and fiduciary services, insurance and securities brokerage, and wealth management. Without community banks, many rural communities would not have local access to these services.

Treasury's proposed rule effectively punishes community banks that offer these types of services at more than an unreasonably low de minimus level. It would force Subchapter S banks to choose between providing the full range of banking services needed in their communities and taking full advantage of the 199A deduction. This tax relief is critical to continued community bank independence.

The proposed rule's de minimum thresholds for revenues derived from specified service trades or businesses (SSTBs) are unreasonably low and will trip up hundreds of community banks in their ability to use the tax relief as intended as intended by Congress. Banks that do not exceed the thresholds today may well exceed them in the future as they evolve to meet the needs of their markets. Moreover, revenue from SSTBs is highly variable from year to year. Asset and revenue growth will shift many banks from the 10 percent to the 5 percent threshold. The proposed rule would have a chilling effect on a bank's ability to raise capital as investors want to whether the deduction will be available now and in the future.

Bank activities are already strictly limited by the Bank Holding Company Act. This effectively serves as a guardrail against abuse of the tax deduction. At a minimum, the definition of SSTBs should be more narrowly drawn and should exclude critical community bank services such as trust or fiduciary services, securities brokerage, and the origination and sale of mortgages and loans guaranteed by the Small Business Administration and U.S. Department of Agriculture. Loan sales allow community banks to increase lending in their communities while preserving their capital and liquidity. This too is a critical part of the community bank business model. Finally, it would be a draconian penalty for a Subchapter S bank that exceeds the de minimus thresholds to lose the deduction for all of the income earned by the bank. We urge you to clarify that this is not the intent of the proposal.

Thank you for considering my perspective as a community banker working to promote economic growth in our community. I urge you to ensure that the final rule under Section 199A strengthens Subchapter S community banks so that they can remain competitive and independent.
Sincerely,

The Private Practice Section (PPS) of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) is a national organization of 4,211 physical therapists who own, operate, or work in private practice community-based settings, most of which are small businesses. Private practice physical therapists are healthcare providers who use their expertise to restore function, improve mobility, relieve pain, and prevent or limit permanent physical disabilities in patients of all ages. PPS is interested in policies that recognize our members as valuable economic engines as well as healthcare providers.

The proposed rule would shift physical therapists from the QTB category into the exemptions parameters by including physical therapists in the health category of Specified Service Trade or Business (SSTB).

PPS Recommendations
1.PPS is concerned that adding physical therapists to the list of SSTBs goes beyond Congress legislative intent.
2.PPS urges the Departments of Treasury to maintain the current definition of services performed in the field of health as defined under Treasury Regulation 1.448-1T(e)(4)(ii).
3.Should the Department proceed to incorporate physical therapists in the SSTB definition, this could decrease the number of small business owners who are able to utilize the pass-through tax deduction; PPS urges the IRS to not proceed with the proposed changes and retain the existing SSTB definition.

The purpose of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) was to deliver real tax relief to Americans across the countryespecially low- and middle-income Americans. As with any legislative proposal, lawmakers undoubtedly took the existing Treasury Regulation 1.448-1T(e)(4)(ii) into consideration when drafting the legislative language to create this tax deduction. The IRS proposed regulationwith its expanded list of providers under the SSTB health categorywould result in the deduction being available to fewer taxpayers, not more. PPS is concerned that the IRS efforts to change the regulation after the law was passed would result in a policy impact that is counter to the intent of the legislation. Therefore, instead of adding physical therapists to the SSTB health category, PPS recommends that the IRS maintain the current, more narrow definition in order to ensure the deduction is available to most number of people, particularly those who are small business owners. Doing so would support the economic vitality and value to a community that small businesses provide; physical therapists who operate small businesses should be assured full access to this pass-through deduction.

The lawmakers choice to grant the qualified business income deduction to QTB with two exceptions shows the purposeful decision to include specific types of businesses while excluding others. The SSTB section under section 199A limits the extent to which taxpayers who provide specific types professional services would qualify for the qualified business income tax deduction. The Departments proposal to add physical therapists and others to the definition which currently only specifically references physicians, nurses, and dentists takes liberties beyond the parameters and structure provided by the statute. Should the Department proceed to incorporate physical therapists in the SSTB definition, this could decrease the number of small business owners who are able to utilize the pass-through tax deduction. PPS urges the Department of Treasury to maintain the current definition of services performed in the field of health as defined under Treasury Regulation 1.448-1T(e)(4)(ii).

Furthermore, while the Department of Treasury may deem it appropriate to identify physicians, nurses, dentists, and physical therapists as all belonging to single category of individuals who furnish services in the field of health, it is imperative that IRS recognize the inherent differences of these trades. Furthermore, Congress treats these occupations very differently. For example, physicians, nurses, and dentists have long been included in federal programs such as the Electronic Health Record Incentive Program and the National Health Service Corps student loan program to name a few. In contrast, physical therapists are not eligible to participate in these programs. Therefore, it is evermore appropriate for the IRS to maintain the current narrow definition of services furnished in the health field of SSTBs.

PPS thanks the IRS for the opportunity to comment on the Qualified Business Income Deduction proposed rule. The TCJA was heralded as an effort to maximize tax cuts and benefit small businesses which would in turn support job growth across the country. PPS encourages the IRS to reconsider its proposal and retain the current definition of QTB in order to ensure the deduction is available to the most individuals and entities because doing so would achieve the goals of the law and the impact it was intended to have on the engine of the economysmall business owners.

To Whom it May Concern:

On behalf of Wisconsins for-profit, tax-paying skilled nursing and assisted living providers, the Wisconsin Health Care Association and Wisconsin Center for Assisted Living (WHCA/WiCAL) requests the IRS reconsider proposed rule REG-107892-18. In order to assure Congressional intent is satisfied, IRS must amend the rule to clarify agency interpretation of the statutory definition of specified service trade or business to allow a broader tax cut available to job creators, including long-term care facilities.

The rule as written takes a strict view of the language included in the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, and would likely deny skilled nursing facilities and perhaps some assisted living facilities the intended tax relief provided by the Act.

IRS states in its explanation of provisions that the definition of a specified service trade or business for purposes of Sec. 199A includes:

any trade or business involving the performance of services in the fields of health, law, accounting, actuarial science, performing arts, consulting, athletics, financial services, brokerage services, or any trade or business where the principal asset of such trade or business is the reputation or skill of one or more of its employees or owners.

WHCA/WiCAL requests that the final rule be clarified so that skilled nursing and assisted living communities are not defined as a specified service trade or business.

Long-term care providers in Wisconsin are currently in the midst of an unprecedented workforce crisis, and facilities struggle to attract and retain facility staff. Since 2016, 18 skilled nursing facilities and more than 150 assisted living facilities have had to close in Wisconsin, costing local communities economic activity and hemorrhaging critical jobs. In many rural communities, long-term care facilities are often the largest employer, and the threat of closure could devastate workers and local economies.

According to a report on our states Long-Term Care Workforce Crisis that WHCA/WiCAL was involved in coordinating, 1 in 5 positions currently remain vacant because we do not have the resources to compete with big-box retailers, convenience stores, and gas stations for labor because our facilities are underfunded through the state and federal reimbursement system for long-term care facilities.

This tax relief would allow our facilities to reinvest in our workforce, and be more competitive in the labor market. Many of the frontline positions in our facilities including dietary, housekeeping, and maintenance workers have nothing to do with health care, but rather deal with operational elements designed to ensure that businesses are able to keep the lights on.

The long-term care provider community supported the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act because it offered the promise of much-needed tax relief to our businesses. Such relief would result in a more sustainable business model and would allow facilities to invest in a more robust workforce.

This proposed rule must comply with Congressional intent to offer relief to job creators and local economic drivers. We encourage the IRS to consider the direct and substantial local economic impact and workforce contributions provided by long-term care facilities in communities across Wisconsin and throughout the country.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,



JOHN VANDER MEER
President & CEO
WHCA/WiCAL

Gentlemen:

Comments in reference to nursing homes being included as a specified service trade of business; defined by the by Internal Revenue as: Any trade or business involving the performance of services in the fields of health, law, accounting, actuarial science, performing arts, consulting, athletics, financial services, brokerage services, or any trade or business where the principal asset of such trade or business is the reputation or skill of one or more of its employees or owners.

In the case of a nursing home, it is not the skills of one or more of its employees or owners; in matter of fact, the skill sets rendered by the nursing staff is limited to full filling the orders issued by a physician. The physician is independent of the nursing home, operates as an independent contractor, not employees, and is paid for his services either from Medicaid, Medicare, insurance or private pay directly from the patient. Nursing homes require a large capital investment in bricks and mortar to provide housing for the residents including meals provided from commercial kitchens, laundry facilities, security, socialization programs and many other activities. Housing is one of the largest and most expensive cost centers of resident care.

The primary intent of Congress was to keep practicing physicians, lawyers, accountants and other similar professionals from reorganizing their business entities to enable them to take advantage of the 20% deduction rule. However, the legislative support staff took the broad brush approach and use the terms services in the fields of health and did not zero-in on Congressional intent. Congressional intent was to help businesses with significant numbers of employees and capital needs. As you can see, the legislation was intended to provide tax relief for people like us so that we could have additional funds to help employees and/or put additional dollars to work in the economy. An additional benefit provided by the tax relief would be to reduce our ever increasing medical cost. Less taxes equals less consumer cost.

We respectfully request that you to make it clear, in the final regulations, that a nursing home is not considered to be a Specified Service Trade or Businesses under the health care portion of these proposed regulations.

I am an employee/shareholder of Glenview State Bank, a $1.2 billion asset community bank in Glenview, Illinois. I write today because I am very concerned about the impact of the proposed regulation under Section 199A of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on my bank and Subchapter S banks nationwide.

Approximately 1900 banks nationwide, or a third of all banks, have elected Subchapter S tax status. These tend to be smaller banksthat specialize in small business, and consumer lending. Subchapter S community banks offer a variety of services in their communities to complement their core lending services. These typically include trust and fiduciary services, insurance and securities brokerage, and wealth management. Without community banks, many communities would not have local access to these services.

Treasury's proposed rule effectively punishes community banks that offer these types of services at more than an unreasonably low de minimus level. It would force Subchapter S banks to choose between providing the full range of banking services needed in their communities and taking full advantage of the 199A deduction. This tax relief is critical to continued community bank independence.

The proposed rule's de minimum thresholds for revenues derived from specified service trades or businesses (SSTBs) are unreasonably low and will trip up hundreds of community banks in their ability to use the tax relief as intended as intended by Congress. Banks that do not exceed the thresholds today may well exceed them in the future as they evolve to meet the needs of their markets. Moreover, revenue from SSTBs is highly variable from year to year. Asset and revenue growth will shift many banks from the 10 percent to the 5 percent threshold. The proposed rule would have a chilling effect on a bank's ability to raise capital as investors want to whether the deduction will be available now and in the future.

Bank activities are already strictly limited by the Bank Holding Company Act. This effectively serves as a guardrail against abuse of the tax deduction. At a minimum, the definition of SSTBs should be more narrowly drawn and should exclude critical community bank services such as trust or fiduciary services, securities brokerage, and the origination and sale of mortgages and loans guaranteed by the Small Business Administration and U.S. Department of Agriculture. Loan sales allow community banks to increase lending in their communities while preserving their capital and liquidity. This too is a critical part of the community bank business model. Finally, it would be a draconian penalty for a Subchapter S bank that exceeds the de minimus thresholds to lose the deduction for all of the income earned by the bank. We urge you to clarify that this is not the intent of the proposal.

Glenview State Bank has been serving its local community for almost 100 years (since 1921).

Base broadening (i.e. the elimination of unproductive tax preferences) was an essential part of tax reform. However, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did not go nearly far enough in trimming the fat from our wasteful tax code.

To this point, I would like to focus my comments on a particularly egregious provision, I.R.C. 409, which has been abused since its codification by businesses seeking to unscrupulously wipe away their tax liability.

Effective for years beginning after December 31, 1997, the Internal Revenue Code was amended to allow employee stock ownership plans (ESOP) to be shareholders in S corporations and to exempt the flow-through earnings to the ESOP from the unrelated business income tax. As such, beginning in 1998, the income of an S corporation could pass through to an ESOP, and, because an ESOP is tax exempt, no tax is paid on the income until it is distributed to the ESOP participant.

ESOPs are, ostensibly, an effective means of boosting workers retirement savings, which at the same time offer them a literal stake in the company. Starbucks is a perfect example of how they can be legitimately deployed -- as a publicly-traded corporation, the company gains little to no tax advantage by offering an ESOP to its employees, but does so anyway to ensure workers are rewarded in retirement for their years of service to the company.

However, for the majority of businesses with an ESOP, the motivation behind establishing their plan is not a sense of altruism or concern for their employees welfare, but rather sheer greed. These companies cunningly utilize their status as a pass-through entity and pair it with an ESOP to exploit an enormous tax loophole, ultimately avoiding payment of taxes altogether. These firms wrap themselves in the flag of boosting retirement savings; employee-ownership; and giving their employees a piece of the rock (along with myriad other trite phrases), but fail to mention that they are ultimately shifting their tax burden from the business entity level to their own employees.

The loophole works like this: a pass-through company (generally an S Corporation, whose income is taxed at the individual, rather than corporate, rate) will create an ESOP. The ESOP is actually a tax-exempt trust, which in the case of an S corporation means that every penny of a firms income is passed through to the trust, allowing the company to pay no tax altogether. Employees become shareholders of the trust, and when it comes time to retire must bank on the fact that the company will buy them out of their shares (and still exist altogether).

Special interest groups like The ESOP Association and the Employee-owned S Corporation Association (ESCA) like to argue that the tax is eventually paid, and in this regard theyre at least partially correct. What they conveniently leave out, though, is that the tax is paid by employees, rather than the business itself. When employees cash out, and their employer buys back their shares in the tax-exempt trust, they face 100 percent of the tax burden. In other words, while their competitors are facing effective tax rates of over 50 percent (when state and local taxes are tallied up), S Corporation ESOPs enjoy tax-free status by making their workers bear the full brunt of the tax burden, and putting it squarely on their shoulders.

Beyond the inherent unfairness of granting a few select businesses the privilege of not having to pay any tax whatsoever, S Corporation ESOPs carry serious risks that cannot be ignored. There is nothing quite as ugly in the employee benefits world as an ESOP gone bad. Many companies with an ESOP do not even consider the future repurchase obligation, mentioned above, that makes the whole retirement ecosystem function properly. This creates a situation where employees place all their retirement eggs in one basket; if the company is unable or unwilling to buy back their shares when it comes time to exit the workforce, that employee will have no way to access the funds they thought they would be entitled to.

Lastly, it is important to note that this tax avoidance carries with it a substantial cost. The Tax Foundation estimates that Special ESOP rules cost taxpayers more than $22 billion over a decade . (The organization could only find a handful of corporate tax expenditures which are more costly.) That means that ordinary, hard-working employees and businesses who pay more than their fair share in tax are subsidizing the tax-exempt status of a handful of companies. This is the anthesis of a fairer, simpler tax code.

The employee stock ownership plan is the epitome of bad tax policy. In particular, 100 percent employee-owned S Corporation ESOPs are an example of an egregious tax loophole that needs to be closed. Members of Congress owe it to their constituents to not use taxpayer money to prop up a small cadre of businesses who, ironically, are the ones who have the resources and ability to exploit this loophole.

I am the CFO of a small ($500 million) community bank with offices in North Dakota and Minnesota. I am very concerned that the proposed 199A regulations could disqualify our bank and many other community banks from the QBI deduction. The proposal clearly affirms that Sub S banks are entitled to the 20% qualified business income deduction in order to equal the playing field between C corps and S Corps.
With the current clarifications, our bank will not qualify for the deduction because of two common bank services:
1. We sell our 30 year residential real estate loans on the secondary market for interest rate risk management purposes. We have no way to put 30 year deposits on the books, so the easy way to manage is to sell the loans on the secondary market to avoid that risk. By doing that, we receive a servicing fee. The current proposal classifies us as a broker of loans because of this.
2. We advise our clients on all aspects of their financials, which includes helping them with retirement investments and 529 college savings plans. This investment income is also proposed to be deemed SSTB revenue.
According to my calculations it is likely that revenue from these two sources would cause us to exceed the de minimis threshold of 5% and we would not be eligible for the entire QBI deduction.
This puts us at a competitive disadvantage with our peers, and I can't believe this was the intent when this bill was passed. The idea of trying to separate these products into separate business entities is very inefficient and not practical. The end result is that this proposal is unfair to Sub S banks and not what congress intended. I urge you to make changes to rectify this. Thank you, Dean McCleary, CFO American Federal Bank, Fargo ND
