I am a previous poster and I am going to right some wrongs. I had said things that were insulting to the actuaries, for that I apologize, they were doing their jobs. What I think happened was that they were not given the proper data to form their analysis. This is Section Eight of the application I am referring to, the claim of $1.2 to $1.3 million a year from employer contributions from a present base of 200 or so active employees. I for one would love to see an accounting of that number active workers. The 701 pension fund that's in question here is the 'A' Plan, which was always made up of the freight employees. Drivers and truck terminal dock workers in General Freight, I had previously stated that in the mid seventies there were a over 150 companies doing this work, now maybe 10. Of those 10 only 2 I believe come under the 701 jurisdiction, YRC (Yellow Roadway Company) and ABF (Now ArcBest Freight). Now both companies have a few hundred workers in New Jersey, but only a hand full come under the 701 pension plan. Let me explain in the 1990's and early 2000's quite a few Union truck companies folded or were taken over by other trucking outfits or merged. When this started happening workers had to try to go with the work, in the case of ABF, Carolina Freight was dissolved into ABF. Now a lot of the Carolina employees had been working there for decades and going to ABF meant they had to change union locals. In this case they had to go to #560 from #701. It was decided that the Carolina people could go to 560, but could maintain their pension seniority at 701. The same went for YRC, When Yellow Freight took over Roadway Express, (I believe it was later declared a merge). Once again the gaining local was 560 and pensions were continued at 701 for any Roadway personnel. ABF just signed a new labor contract with the International Teamsters in May of 2018 and all the locals votes were published. I find it very interesting, that in New Jersey they listed both locals results: Local 560, cast 107 votes; Local 701, cast 7 votes! Now I'm sure there are some office people also under 701's pension umbrella, but that still leaves me wondering. There are not really any other Locals involved, 560 has the north end of the state and the southern end is controlled by Philadelphia Locals. YRC doesn't have a contract due until next year (2019), it was originally due for this year but they got an extension in 2014. Last year the Teamster International Freight division headed by Ernie Soehl, (who also happens to be Local 701's president), gave YRC permission to set up pay scales regionally instead of nationally. This is on top of the 15% give back still in effect from 2009, and also the $1.42 per hour employer contribution for pension and welfare whereas ABF is paying about $10 and hour. They are not a healthy company and I personally don't know how the fund can say they will get over a million a year. Last year there was a lockout at Shore Point Distributors because the company had a contract due and wanted to set up a 401 system for their workers and leave 701's pension fund. 701 wouldn't talk about it, so the lockout. Six weeks later, contract signed and company out of pension fund, They were 'B' plan but you see what I mean.
The dispute over the pension plan isn't unique. The percentage of private-sector workers who have what's known as defined-benefit plans, such as pensions, fell from 28 percent in 1979 to 2 percent in 2013, according to the Employee Benefit Research Institute.
I have more to say but it will wait a little longer. Mull this over for a while.

As I understand it the purpose of The Treasury Department is to assess the validity of the application as to whether or not it will keep the 701 Fund insolvency at bay. I intend to make an argument that this plan will not work as it stands. My problem is with the employer contributions being not even close to a reasonable figure.
According to my research there are only 2 companies left in the 701 Pension 'A' Plan, YRC and ABF. These are the jobs that account for the 250 or so remaining working members. Let's take a look at ABF first, good company, financially stable, and they just ratified a national contract with the Teamsters this past May. I have the results of that vote count by each individual local. Under NJ/NY you see 3 locals listed, #445 and #707 are NY locals and #560 is a NJ local below as is local #701.
The total votes cast by #560, the only other NJ local add up to 107 members while the votes for #701 add up to 7, seven. That is a total of 7 members under 701's Pension and Welfare umbrella.
[ http://www.tdu.org/abf_vote_count_may_2018 ]
So that leaves approximately 242 that must be at YRC. Yes, there are many more members at YRC. YRC has 2 terminals in New Jersey that are represented by 701, South Plainfield and Trenton. I wasn't able to come up with any hard numbers of employees working for YRC, so I got inventive. This past Monday, which is the busiest day of the week for trucking companies since freight comes in over the weekend and they want it out fast. I took a ride to both terminals. When I got there I counted cars, at one o'clock in the afternoon there were 40 cars at Trenton and one hour later there were 31 at South Plainfield. Not all those 71 cars can be Union workers. There has to be managers and dispatchers, Salespeople, and they both have large garages so there will be mechanics, and office personnel. It's possible some of the office people under the Office manager could be union people, but I found nothing to verify. Figuring very conservatively, and strictly a guess, I will say 4 managers, 2 dispatchers, 1 office manager, 2 mechanics and 4 office personnel. That's 13 per terminal, 26 non union people. 71 now becomes 45 union workers, Not done yet, both terminals have night shifts working that use quite a few casual workers, (non-list or even non union). The union workers at night might be 20 for both terminals. That brings us to 65 plus the 7 from ABF for a grand total of 72. That seems hardly enough to insure a yearly pension contribution of $1.2 to $1.4 million. ABF will stand by their contract and pay the negotiated pension contribution of around $12/13 dollars per member. Maybe not with YRC!
YRC has not paid it's full contribution since 2009 when it signed a new 4 year contract with an employee giveback of 15% and shortly thereafter stopped all pension payments for 23 months. This was done with the Unions help in order to keep the company in business. In 2011 YRC came back and amended the contract to make pension payments but at 25% of the rate agreed upon in 2009. With this they also extended the 15% giveback and the life of the contract another 5 years, again to keep the company in business.
[ http://www.myadvan.com/IPI%20Safety.../ipi_series_1.htm ]
Again in 2014 the company came back and with the Union help rewrote the contract that still had 2 years to go for the good of the company. The 15% continues and the contract states 'Pension will be paid at 25% of the 2009 rate. This was another 5 year contract that should come due in 2019.

D. Benefit Improvements Section 432(e)(9)(E) sets forth rules relating to benefit improvements made while a suspension of benefits is in effect. Under this provision, a benefit improvement is defined as a resumption of suspended benefits, an increase in benefits, an increase in the rate at which benefits accrue, or an increase in the rate at which benefits become nonforfeitable under the plan. The statute provides that a plan sponsor may, in its sole discretion, provide benefit improvements while a suspension of benefits is in effect. However, a plan sponsor may not increase plan liabilities by reason of any benefit improvement for any participant or beneficiary who is not in pay status (in other words, those who are not yet receiving benefits, such as active employees or deferred vested employees) unless (1) the benefit improvement is accompanied by an
equitable distribution of benefit improvements for those who have begun to receive benefits (typically, retirees), and (2) the plan actuary certifies that, after taking the benefit improvement into account, the plan is projected to avoid insolvency indefinitely. Whether an individual is in pay status for this purpose is generally based on whether the individuals benefits began before the first day of the plan year for which the benefit improvement would take effect

Re:Docket No. OLP 168; Comment in response to Arizonas Opt-in Application and Supplemental Information

I am submitting this comment on behalf of my client Dwandarrius Jamar Robinson. Mr. Robinson was sentenced to death by an Arizona state court on May 21, 2018, and is currently appealing his conviction and sentence. I represent him in his direct appeal proceedings. If necessary, Mr. Robinson intends to pursue relief in state post-conviction and federal habeas proceedings.

On Mr. Robinsons behalf, I oppose Arizonas application for opt-in certification under 28 U.S.C. 2265(a). Certification of Arizonas ineffective mechanism would put Mr. Robinsons ability to seek and obtain remedies in federal habeas proceedings at serious risk. If Arizonas mechanism is certified and Mr. Robinson pursues in federal habeas relief, he would have to litigate whether the opt-in provisions apply in his particular case and make difficult decisions regarding the development and presentation of his claims for relief in both state and federal appellate and post-conviction proceedings.

Arizona should not be certified under 28 U.S.C. 2265(a) as it does not have an adequate mechanism for the appointment of post-conviction counsel. Specifically, it does not appear to guarantee the timely appointment of competent post-conviction counsel and does not guarantee adequate compensation or funding. The United States Attorney General should not certify such a mechanism.

For these reasons, and the reasons identified in the comments opposing certification submitted during the initial comment period, Mr. Robinson opposes Arizonas application for certification as an opt-in state.

Respectfully,

Consuelo M. Ohanesian
Deputy Legal Advocate
Office of the Legal Advocate
Attorney for Dwandarrius Jamar Robinson

Insider threat detection may require collating information from a variety of sources, including relatives or others having information exchanges with a subject of an insider threat investigation. The proposed regulations should include exemptions from disclosure of investigations or surveillance of relatives of any subject or any other person who may be engaged in information or data exchanges with the subject of an insider threat investigation. Otherwise, FOIA or other requests for information from a related third party could have the same consequence as revealing the insider threat investigation or surveillance to the subject, ie giving the subject information about the insider threat investigation and the ability to avoid or impede the investigation. For example, if data is being transmitted outside an agency, it may be necessary to monitor and investigate persons who are recipients of such data from remote devices, computers, storage devices, cell phones, etc.
Such monitoring of recipients or information exchangers must also be protected from disclosure during an insider threat
investigation, or the whole investigation could be revealed to the subject, whether by a family member or other person.

See The Future of Insider Threats from Forbes

Time to preempt insider threats is most vital to mitigate potential corporate harm. Given the diversity of behavior for every single user, it can take months to collect data comprehensive enough to identify a baseline of normal activity, to recognize which data are most vulnerable, important, or sensitiveand therefore might need added protection or restrictions on accessand to detect anomalous behavior or determine what additional indicators could strengthen the system. Additionally, educating employees on how to spot social engineering attacks often takes significant time, and can require a significant culture shift. To help companies prepare for, prevent, detect, respond to and recover from insider threats, security companies are developing solutions that combine comprehensive visibility of corporate data, advanced analytic tools and automated incident-response.

Comprehensive data collection and analysis can help to establish the behavior baselines necessary to detect and mitigate the insider threat. Companies have traditionally relied heavily upon single-transaction log data, such as monitoring outgoing email rates, website visits or changes in network permissions. Alone, these are weak signals. In the case of Edward Snowden, such analysis failed to raise suspicion because he took small amounts of data over a long period of time, and his various transactions were considered benign in a system designed to capture only individual events rather than alert potentially-connected malicious actions over time. While these weak signals alone are generally insufficient to detect an insider threat, collecting large quantities of data from a wide variety of sources over time can be useful to help companies identify correlations and detect anomalies confidently. This means amplifying weak signals with data loss prevention that detects users sending sensitive information outside of the company network; endpoint data collected from remote devices connected to the company network, such as laptops, cellphones or remote desktops; address resolution protocol (ARP) monitoring to track the physical origin of network traffic; or data on application usage, logins and logouts, or permission changes.

The rule proposal referenced in this notice would provide the FBI, and soon the DOJ, a broad exemption from portions of the Act, and only requires the DOJ to adhere to the Act if the DOJ determines they should adhere to it (CPCLO Order No. 002-2017, 2017, p. 25752). To help the DOJ determine if those specific portions of the Act apply to the DOJ, the DOJ has briefly stated it will apply the Act if, "[the] DOJ determines compliance would not appear to interfere with or adversely affect the purpose of this system to detect, deter, and/or mitigate insider threats" (CPCLO Order No. 002-2017, 2017, p. 25752). The guideline provided by the DOJ does not specify what it would consider as interference or as adversely affecting it (CPCLO Order No. 002-2017, 2017). Nonetheless, if the DOJ were to find that releasing the information would not "interfere with or adversely affect" it, the DOJ is not requiring that it release the information (CPCLO Order No. 002-2017, 2017, p. 25752). Instead, the DOJ "may" release the information and retains "sole discretion" of applying the Act to itself (CPCLO Order No. 002-2017, 2017, p. 25752).
The scope of the proposed rule was rather large when limited to the FBI, but is only more expansive if applied to the entire DOJ. The broad way in which the rule proposal language applies the exemption would essentially allow the DOJ to never determine that they should adhere to the Act. In its defense, the DOJ states the proposed rule prevents subjects of investigation from being tipped off, it prevents exposure of classified information, and protects the lives of those investigating (CPCLO Order No. 002-2017, 2017).
While it is true that subjects of investigation may be tipped off, there are constitutional protections and rights afforded to all those residing in the US (Electronic Privacy Information Center, 2016). The proposed rule does not provide for any guaranteed disclosure if constitutional rights to be at risk of violation, or already violated. Without any way to ensure that information collected and stored would ever be disclosed, the DOJ is asking for a blank check to conduct investigations, and data storage, of individuals without their knowledge or any protections to potential abuse by the DOJ or participating entities. Secondly, classified information can always be redacted to eliminate, or at least minimize, the release of information concerning the nation's security. But again, this rule proposes to allow the DOJ to determine for themselves what information they should or should not release. Finally, it is important to protect the lives of law enforcement personnel, but information that may lead to the identification of that personnel can and should be redacted and not used as a reason to keep a secret database.
Though it was not mentioned previously, there is a large privacy concern with a secret government database that could store sensitive information about people (Electronic Privacy Information Center, 2016). Recently, the US government has experienced several "[c]yber-based intrusions and attacks on federal systems" (Electronic Privacy Information Center, 2016, p. 6). The government has demonstrated that they are not able to protect sensitive data from intruders (Electronic Privacy Information Center, 2016). What is a person to do if their confidential information is stored on DOJ databases, that data is breached by an intruder, and the only people aware are under no obligation to tell inform that person?
The DOJ rescinded their proposed rule change is a great idea. The DOJ wanting to expand it beyond the FBI is not. Law enforcement and collaborating agencies must not be allowed to operate in secret and with disregard of constitutional safeguards. Therefore, neither a "FBI Insider Threat Program Records" rule or "DOJ Insider Threat Program Records" rule should be adopted (CPCLO Order No. 002-2017, 2017).

Department of Justice's website states that policy objectives for the Privacy Act of 1974 are as follows:
1.To restrict disclosure of personally identifiable records maintained by agencies.
2.To grant individuals increased rights of access to agency records maintained on themselves.
3.To grant individuals the right to seek amendment of agency records maintained on themselves upon a showing that the records are not accurate, relevant, timely, or complete.
4.To establish a code of "fair information practices" that requires agencies to comply with statutory norms for collection, maintenance, and dissemination of records.

Many of the requested exemptions concern all of these points, but the 3rd and 4th points seem to have targeted. Although the Privacy Act of 1974 has its flaws, particularly when it comes to its imprecise language in some areas, I believe that parts of it are used for the greater good. For the Department of Justice to ask to be exempt from some very necessary aspects of the act is concerning to me. While I agree that insider threats are a danger to this nation, I do not understand why our intelligence gathering agencies are no longer capable of dealing with them. For over 40 years this rule has been in effect and in 40 years I am certain that we have had countless insider threats. My primary concern with and objection to this request for exemption has to do with its timing: why ask for these exemptions now and not 10, 20 or 30 years ago? I'm sure during the worst parts of the War on Terror during the Bush administration there was a great deal of concern for insider threats. In the view of many people, this country was blindsided by the events of September 11th, 2001 and the threat very well could have come from the inside.

I doubt that there would've been a great deal of objection to a request for exemption then. But this is now 2017 and there's a massive spotlight shining on a scandal that could eclipse the illegal acts committed during the Watergate scandal. On one hand, if this exemption request is preparation for the in-depth probe that one would need to investigate Russia's involvement with the 2016 election, I am interested in who exactly will be investigated and how they might be defined as being potential insider threats. On the other hand, if this exemption request has been put in place as a part of a new anti-terrorism plan, I worry that this will expand the DoJ's net for gathering useless information. I understand the necessity of keeping aspects of an investigation private but I also understand that providing additional privacy can get investigations off track. This newfound freedom in investigating whomever without concern that they will ask why could stop agencies from focusing only on the individuals that it is necessary to investigate. In conclusion, unless this exemption request comes as a response to a series of very recent events that require a swift response from the Department of Justice, I have a great deal of concern about how useful these exemptions really will be in the course of investigations. The country and this administration is currently under a great deal of scrutiny for the seemingly illegal acts people who have been entrusted the country have seemingly taken part of. Requests for further freedom under a cloak of "necessary" privacy does not help one make the case that nothing strange is going on. In troubling times such as these transparency, honesty and adherence to the rules is what will put the minds of the American people at ease. Asking to be made the exception to a very necessary rule does not win trust.

Dear Special Master Rupa Bhattacharyya:

Sullivan Papain Block McGrath & Cannavo PC (Sullivan Papain) hereby submits the following comments to the Notice of Inquiry, Docket No. Civ. 154. Sullivan Papain represents approximately 2,600 claimants, most of whom are first responders, in the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund. Sullivan Papain has been General Counsel to the Uniformed Firefighters Association for more than 35 years. We also represented 384 firefighters in the original VCF during the 2002-2004 years. We represented 675 seriously injured first responders in the World Trade Center Disaster Site Litigation, which settled in 2010-2011.

Currently, we represent primarily first responders, as well as office workers, residents, business owners, and students in the Ground Zero area. Our clients come from all walks of life: firefighters, fire officers, police officers, sanitation workers, state and federal court personnel, financial services workers, school teachers, students, administrators, restaurant owners, apartment dwellers, volunteers, and others.

Based on our daily conversations with those who have been affected by the WTC toxic exposure, we object, in general, to the practical consequences of the proposals suggested in the Notice of Inquiry. Specifically, (1) we object to the de facto formation of a post-February 1, 2019 class of claimants; (2) we object to the closing of the VCF on December 18, 2020; and (3) we object to the current level of funding of the VCF which is woefully inadequate to fully and justly compensate all those who qualify.

We recognize that the VCF is a creation of the United States Congress, and thus, our comments are also directed towards the legislative branch of government.

We preface our comments with the following self-evident facts: victims of toxic injuries do not choose when they become sick, or when they become disabled. The formation of a post-February 1, 2019 class of claimants would mean these later-filed claimants would not be treated the same way as the earlier-filed claimants. The post-February 1, 2019 claimants should not receive lesser awards simply because they received diagnoses and/or disability determinations at a later date.

The only acceptable solutions should be addressed by the United States Congress: (a) the amount of available funding must be increased to provide full and just compensation; and (b) the deadline for filing claims must be extended beyond December 18, 2020.

The VCF, at its current level of funding and expiration date, cannot do its work in a fair and equitable way.

We are in agreement with the Special Masters statement in the Notice of Inquiry that existing claimants are becoming sicker and are amending their claims, whether they received awards or are awaiting first-time awards.

Claimants are dying at a high rate, resulting in families filing death claims.

Meanwhile, at this late date, we continue to receive daily inquiries from new toxic exposure victims, who are learning of the WTC Health Program and the VCF for the first time.

Finally, people who are very sick do not control how long they will be under intensive medical treatment; they may have trouble getting certification from the WTC Health Program, which is known for its delays due to understaffing and oversubscription in giving non-first responders necessary medical appointments.

We all also know the latency period for many cancers and asbestos-related diseases can be extremely long: up to ten to thirty years, if not longer.

It is fundamentally unjust that a claimant who files a VCF claim after February 1, 2019 will be treated differently from those who filed earlier.

A.Aircraft Requested for the Exemption

Make / modelRegistrationSerial No.Remarks

1.The Bell UH-1 and Bell AH-1 are “historically significant.” The U.S. Army and Marine Corps operated the UH-1 Huey and AH-1 Cobra. Although a UH-1 variant remains in service with the U.S. Marine Corps (the UH-1Y Venom), the UH-1Y Venom is a significantly different twin-engine aircraft. The AH-1 Cobra and the UH-1 Huey are no longer in U.S. military service.
2.The Bell UH-1 and Bell AH-1 meet the test for “fragility.” According to the FAA registry database, 5500 UH-1D/H models were built, and only 491 remain registered, representing less than 9% of the original fleet remaining. Even fewer of those registered remain operational. Additionally, only 18 registered AH-1 Cobras remain on the FAA registry today. Because of the small percentage of UH-1D/H aircraft registered and operational today and the significant public interest in these historical aircraft, these aircraft meet the criteria for fragility.
3.The UH-1 and AH-1 are “over 50 years old.” The U.S. military first utilized them in the 1960s. Although the Bell 204/205 is a similar civilian aircraft, the UH-1 Huey is not eligible for the Bell 204/205 standard type certificate; therefore, no standard category civilian model is available. Likewise, the AH-1 has no standard category civilian counterpart available.

Subject: Docket No. FAA-2019-0485; Product Identifier 2019-NM-064-AD

References:
/A/ Airbus Service Bulletin (SB) A330-78-3023
/B/ Rolls-Royce Service Bulletin (SB) RB211-78-AH677 and Safran SB 78-AH677
/C/ Rolls-Royce Service Bulletin (SB) RB211-78-J078 and Safran SB 78-J078

The proposed subject rule requires compliance with actions specified and in accordance with EASA AD 2018-0148R1. The EASA AD requires actions in accordance with the Ref. /A/ Airbus SB, which requires inspection in accordance with the Ref. /B/ Rolls-Royce and Safran SB which also contains conditional requirements as provided in the Ref. /C/ Rolls-Royce and Safran SB.

American Airlines has reviewed the subject proposed rule and has the following comments:

1.Ref /C/ SB (on-condition actions applied dependent on ref /B/ findings) reinstalls or replaces (if damaged) Item 23 washer AN960C10L. This washer part number is obsolete; and per Air Force Navy Aeronautical Standard AN960 REV 21 cancellation notice 2, NAS1149 part numbers supersede the AN960 part numbers. This is confirmed by OEM Safran.
Therefore, AAL requests the allowance for use of NAS1149 series washers in lieu of AN960 washers (where called out in applicable service documentation including Ref /C/) be addressed by the AD.

2.Ref /C/ SB (on-condition actions applied dependent on ref /B/ findings) reinstalls or replaces (if damaged) Item 22 bolt NAS6303U04. This bolt part number is a typo of NAS6303U4; per National Aerospace Standard spec NAS6303 THRU NAS6320, the correct part number of bolt is NAS6303U4. This is confirmed by OEM Safran.
Therefore, AAL requests the allowance for use of NAS6303U4 in lieu of nonexistent NAS6303U04 bolts (where called out in applicable service documentation including Ref /C/) be addressed by the AD.

3.Ref /C/ SB (on-condition actions applied dependent on ref /B/ findings) identifies item 4 of bush repair kit 91H119-00 as NAS5050-4C; this part number does not exist as there is no NAS5050 spec, and is a typo of part number NSA5050-4C. This is confirmed by OEM Safran.
Therefore, AAL requests the allowance for use of NSA5050-4C nuts in lieu of nonexistent NAS5050-4C (where called out in applicable service documentation including Ref /C/) be addressed by the AD.

4.Ref /B/ SB references Rolls-Royce nacelle SRM 54-02-04 for paint restoration, but the paints in this section do not exist. The Airbus SRM 51-75 provides instructions for paint restoration that are applicable to these locations. This is confirmed by OEM Safran.
Therefore, AAL requests the allowance for use of Airbus SRM 51-75 as an alternate to Rolls Royce SRM 54-02-04 (where called out in applicable service documentation including Ref /B/) be addressed by the AD.

This is confirmed by OEM Safran.
Therefore, AAL requests the allowance for use of CMM 78-30-20 Figure 39 Graphic 78-30-20-991-839-A01 for the RH thrust reverser (where called out in applicable service documentation including Ref /B/) be addressed by the AD.

6.Ref /B/ SB includes instructions to de-energize the ground service network with reference to AMM 24-42-00 before closing the fan cowl doors. I support the legislation, which will ultimately make the plane safer, and decreases the chance of accidents or crashes on the plane by requiring that a one time leak-test is run on the wing struts of the aircraft. To start, the firewall is a flameproof bulkhead that separates the engine compartment from the rest of the aircraft, meaning it is a vital part of the aircraft, because if a part of the engine is damaged, the plane and it's passengers are in grave danger (aopa.org). The other part of the plane that needs to be checked and tested are the wing struts. The wing struts are formed in joined wing designs where the horizontal tail sweeps forward and joins the main wing, forming a strut. The tail is then in compression, reducing wing bending moments (quora.com). This part of the plane has an impact on the planes capability of dealing with the elements, in this case wind, which is constantly at work against an aircraft. The Boeing 787 seats 242 to 330 passengers in typical two-class seating configurations, meaning that each flight has a potential risk of putting a large amount of lives at risk due to malfunctions (wikipedia.org). This can and should be eliminated as keeping the passengers safe is the number one priority, and this can be done through the test. Because of a lack of precaution and safety concern in regards to these parts of the plane, a plane had a bolt on the 737-800's right wing slat that had pierced the fuel tank creating a 2-3cm hole. The fuel leaking from the tank then ignited creating a fire that completely destroyed the aircraft (flightglobal.com). These precautions need to be taken in order to ensure extra safety of passengers on the plane, and this single test could help decrease the risk of an accident like that again.

I own a Cessna CJ2 (C525A) in which the Tamarack (ATLAS) winglets were installed last July. Obviously, this aircraft is now grounded per the issuance of the AD. We have completed the recent Service Bulletins issued by Tamarack that address the faulty control box and the operating installation of the centering strips on the winglet control surfaces themselves.

I do have a number of concerns that remain:

1. Has there been any testing of the impact of the centering strips in the event there is a fault that causes a fully deflected ATLAS control surface? We have not witnessed any information regarding performance or handling from Tamarack/Cranbrook.

2. In regards to the concept of using speed tape to neutralize the winglets control surfaces. These devices and the associated systems are required to avoid over-stressing of the wing spar itself. If they are neutralized, how is the wing spar going to be protected from being over-stressed in flight? I dont see this as a solution.

3. In regards to removing the winglets and returning the aircraft to its original configuration. There is no guidance to maintenance organizations regarding the process and FAA requirements to achieve this goal. We have talked to all the major aircraft maintenance organizations in the U.S., including Cessna/Textron, regarding this option. We need to have some guidance in this requirement independent of Tamarack/Cranbrook in order to remove these devices if chosen.

4. Finally, the issue of aircrew training. Similar to the 737 Maxx situation, there is a larger aircrew training and knowledge gap relating to these winglets and their potential uncommanded control inputs and their affect on the aircraft in various phases of flight. The fact is that theres is no functional training available to aircrews on what is going to occur and how to counter a uncommanded deflection of an ATLAS flight control surface in-flight. This is simply incorrect if not ignorant. I spent 20 years as an Air Force fighter pilot and tactical training instructor and have managed to experience many unplanned and highly unusual aircraft upsets and attitudes during that time. I recovered the aircraft in each of these instances due to the academic and in-flight training I experienced as part of the qualification process to be certified to fly each aircraft prior to their occurrence. I find it unbelievable that the only training that exists for these devices is an addition to the emergency checklist that directs aircrews to immediately slow the aircraft to an indicated airspeed below 160 KIAS. While this may be an adequate end result, there is no knowledge or training available to aircrews in what is going to happen and/or the control inputs required to safely control the aircraft from the time of the occurrence of a fully deflected winglet control surface and 160 KIAS. In effect, all aircrews are rapidly put into a situation of being Test Pilots in the event of this occurrences should it happen. There needs to be a requirement, or at a minimum the opportunity, for aircrews to witness and experience this abnormal situation if and when it occurs. I would also mention that the addition of these devices shouldnt change the single pilot certification of these aircraft. More pilots dont replace adequate knowledge and training, especially when there is none available in the first place. If there is no training that either is required by the FAA or is provided optionally to aircrews by the manufacturer, I will direct the removal of these devices on my aircraft. Civilian pilots shouldnt be involuntarily be placed in the position of Test Pilot in the event a simple fault occurs in this system and our passengers should not be put at undue risk due to the unavailability of adequate knowledge and training of our aircrews.

In closing, I spent nearly $250,000 in modifying our CJ2 with the ATLAS winglet system. It has provided a substantial improvement to the aircraft in many ways and would like to have them remain on the aircraft in an unrestricted manner. I have not seen a negative element of this modification until these recent events and resulting SBs and the AD. I believe the ultimate solution and sunsequent retraction of the recent AD has two primary elements. The first being the reasonable correction of the aircraft systems that could cause the problem and the assurance that the aircraft is controllable through all phases of the normal flight envelope. The second being aircrew training to safely fly the aircraft from the onset of the abnormality to either landing or until the abnormality is alleviated through the normal flight envelope of the aircraft.

Thoughts on FAA Airworthiness Directive 2019-08-13:

This AD seems to have been issued in a rash and unjustified fashion based on an opinion rather than analysis. Component failures happen regularly in the field and are addressed with maintenance actions that are often not reported to the FAA. With the understanding that flight control malfunctions must be reported, it seems hardly justified to address a malfunction or this crash any differently than one that occurred due to an unreported failure of a radar altimeter for instance (this is a hypothetical example only).

The FAA has published AD 2019-08-13 and grounded 76 (potentially) revenue generating aircraft.

The FAA (in their AD) did not perform causal or probability analysis to show that deactivating the winglets is an unsatisfactory method of preventing further accidents; an analysis that could easily be performed by reviewing a wiring diagram and requesting Tamarack's analysis of the ability of aerodynamic force to center the winglet when power has been removed. If this analysis really was performed (but not publicized), it is questionable whether the FAA reviewed the ability of the winglets to center after being modified in accordance with the Tamarack Service Bulletin that adds trailing edge strips and replaces the electronic controller.

The FAA (in their AD) did not utilize the extremely abundant amount of data supporting the use of speed tape (a product that has been in use for decades) to analyze the effectiveness of speed tape at holding the winglets flush; again an analysis that should be very easy to perform using Tamarack force analysis and flight test data.

The FAA (in their AD) did not consider the number of fleet hours and the ability to overcome malfunctions of the winglet system using the ailerons.

As a pilot, I have flown with these winglets more than 150 hours and not experienced a single malfunction of the active load alleviating system. The most significant of happenings was a minor unexpected roll caused by deflection of the load alleviating aileron on departure. To elaborate on this, the aircraft was slow during the climb and the wing was loaded in a climbing turn. The unexpected roll was caused by thermal turbulence and was momentary in nature. It was EASILY overcome by the ailerons and the load alleviating system was behaving exactly as it was designed to behave. I am fully confident that (A) The condition could have been resolved not only by the momentary nature of the event, but also by unloading the wing, increasing forward speed, selecting the reset button, pulling the winglet circuit breakers or ANY combination of these. And I am confident that (B) nearly all reported instances of uncommanded roll were very likely the result of pilots who did not understand how the active load alleviation system works in order to resolve the event. For this reason, perhaps required additional training from the manufacturer may be the required resolution to these findings?

In conclusion, I feel that there are better ways to resolve this than grounding 76 airplanes. Please work diligently with Tamarack to get our airplanes flying again so that they do not sit and potentially develop further maintenance squawks. Please include AOG time in your cost analysis of any resolution.

Thank You and Kind Regards.

In regards to FAA Airworthiness Directive 2019-08-1:

It was disappointing to learn that the FAA would be submitting this AD. I was disappointed to learn that when the FAA considered the pilots report of the latest failure (in Europe) as carrying greater weight on the discussion over the metrics and detailed performance data removed from systems onboard the aircraft in question. These two reports (pilots vs recorded data) appear to be opposed in describing the facts of the incident. To learn that the FAA ignored digital data which refutes the pilots report seems to imply bias on the part of the FAA.

Both of these AD's (from EASA and the FAA) have imposed an enormous financial toll on the owners of these aircraft. I can speak from personal experience when I say that the stress of canceling trips, stranding passengers and failing to meet the needs of the users of the aircraft has caused a great deal of stress, not to mention the financial impact it has had on operations and businesses that rely on these aircraft. Comment From: James P Plettner MD owner and pilot N6UB
Citation CJ 525-0127

Comment to:
FAA AD 2019-08-13
EASA AD No.: 2019-0086-E
Tamarack SB1467
Tamarack SB1475

Since the AD is already in effect, I will focus my comments on the decision making and science behind an appropriate resolution of the AD.
I have been flying since age 15. I am also a surgeon. I have been the director of a surgical residency program and participated in research at various institutions including the National Cancer Institute. My whole life has been about analysis of risk and benefit and trying to make the best decision possible given the data available.
As pilots we train for engine failures, thrust reverser deployment in flight, landing gear malfunctions, and loss of pressurization to name but a few examples. If we were not willing to accept any risk we would never fly, have the benefit of thrust reversers, retractable gear, or have pressurization. The question to be addressed is if the Tamarack active winglet system has an acceptable degree of risk given the benefits.
Anecdotal experiences of flying without a problem do not mean that no problem exists. Conversely, being overly cautious due to current external pressures will unnecessarily penalize both owners and a truly innovative and very responsible company. Tamarack has developed a product that allows the safety and performance increases of winglets to be available to legacy aircraft without a total redesign of the wing spar. This is huge step a forward and has applicability to many aircraft. I wont elaborate on the performance enhancements but will describe what I have experienced as the safety benefits of the ATLAS system in my CJ.
1.Much lower angle of attack in cruise at altitude and a much quicker attainment of that AOA after level off. This gives a much greater margin from stall AOA and the plane is much more stable at altitude.
2.Significant improvement in rate of climb.
a.Dramatic increase in fuel reserves on my typical mission
b.Less time in the potentially dangerous condition of higher angle of attack and lower altitude on initial climb out.
3.Flying final approach using the angle of attack indicator as a reference for Vref results in a much lower landing speed and thus a significant safety margin for runway overrun accidents.

With any system there is a failure risk and I will summarize what has been documented about that risk for failure of the Tamarack ATLAS system.
1.Extensive flight testing has shown that by following the prescribed emergency response to an asymmetrical deployment, the aircraft is controllable without extraordinary measures. This data is well documented and has been reviewed by EASA. In fact, none of the documented system failures has resulted in an accident. All aircraft were able to return to stable flight and the analysis of the flight data from the European incident that initiated the AD correlates with the Tamarack flight test data.
2.No aircraft that has complied with the initial mandatory service bulletin has had an incident.
3.Flight test data supports that the addition of the more recent service bulletin installing centering strips is an effective means of returning the active control surface to the trailing position should another unanticipated malfunction occur.
In evaluating this data, it appears that the AD should be lifted providing that the service bulletins are complied with.
Finally, and most importantly, since all the information has been well documented and reviewed by EASA, I respectfully request that the FAA participate in the EASA management safety review that is scheduled this upcoming week. Please do not underestimate the cost of delaying a further US decision.
As an owner, I can only tolerate the ongoing expense of maintenance of my aircraft and the cost of replacement aircraft for so long before I will be forced to remove the winglets.
As a company, the longer the AD remains in effect the greater the chance that Tamarack will be unable to recover. It is precisely because of innovators like Tamarack that the safety of flight progresses. While first and foremost the FAA mission is safety, we need to also be sensitive to the fact that the longer the AD remains in place the lower the likelihood of a successful outcome for this innovative and valuable technology.
If indeed a successful resolution is forthcoming in the near future from EASA, it would make sense that the FAA would be able to benefit from the European analysis and expeditiously provide conditions for the satisfaction of the US AD.
James P. Plettner MD

I own and operate a Citation CJ2 with the Tamarack winglets, as modified by SB 1467 and SB 1475. This Airworthiness Directive grounds airworthy aircraft and it is not supported by sound engineering effort. It appears that the FAA has not taken the time to analyze the data from the incident flight nor the original certification.

There was plenty of time for the FAA to perform its own analysis in the long period between the issuance of the EASA AD and the FAA AD. It does appear that the FAA performed some analysis to determine that the mitigation (securing the flight control surfaces), which was already approved by EASA, was not sufficient for USA registered aircraft. The use of Speed Tape is well-known in the industry, but more importantly, it was already approved by the foreign aviation authority.

What we do know:

1) The uncommanded deflection of the ATLAS control surface was caused by a loose fastener. This problem is corrected by SB1467, which should, in and of itself, be a terminating action for the AD.

2) SB1475 modifies the control surface to prevent full deflection in the event of a uncommanded deflection. This mitigates the problem with the loose fastener and should, in and of itself, be a terminating action for the AD.

3) The data extracted from the incident-aircraft that reported a roll disagrees with the pilots claim of an aggressive roll rate. This data was available during the six week period between the issuance of the EASA AD and the FAA AD and does not support the claim that the aircraft is unsafe.

4) During certification, the aircraft was tested with dual, asymmetrical, deflections and found to be controllable by a pilot of normal skill and strength through the flight regime. The fastener migration problem was not a totally unforeseeable problem like the departure of a wing from an aircraft. It was a reasonably foreseeable problem which was addressed during the original certification of the winglets AND THE WINGLETS WERE DETERMINED TO BE SAFE EVEN IN THE FACE OF AN UNCOMMANDED DEFLECTION. Indeed, it is extremely unlikely that the problem simultaneously occurs on both winglets, so the expected roll rate would be half that of what was tested during certification.

We dispute some of the FAAs determinations supporting the A.D.:

The malfunction of the ATLAS may reduce the pilot's ability to control the airplane. Yes, it *may* *reduce* the pilots ability to control the aircraft, but, as already stated, the reduction is minor and was demonstrated safe during the original certification.

The service information provided by the STC holder does not contain adequate instructions to mitigate the unsafe condition. Incorrect, SB1467 and SB1475 from the STC holder completely mitigate the unsafe condition.

The severity of the risk warrants compliance before further flight. Perhaps, but if it does, it is clear that the A.D. should be modified so that SB1467 and SB1475 are acceptable compliance.

The claim that the NTSBs investigation of a fatal accident linked to the ATLAS is unsupported. The NTSB has neither completed their investigation, nor even involved Tamarack in the investigation. If the NTSB had cause to implicate the Tamarack winglets, they would have involved Tamarack in the investigation. The reference to this accident in the A.D. can only incite hysteria and is not supported by fact.

The aircraft could be made safer by adding one additional line item to the ABNORMAL/EMERGENCY section in the Tamarack Winglet AFM Supplement to indicate that, in the circuit breaker should be pulled. Interrupting power to the control surface, in conjunction with SB1475, will cause the control surface to blow in-trail and stop any rolling moment.

ATLAS CIRCUIT BREAKER - PULLED (in the event of TACS RUNAWAY).

A proper risk analysis of the Tamarack Winglets needs to include the benefits from having them in place. There is increased runway performance both for takeoff and landing that, although they are not certified as such, they are still present, and provide additional margin-of-safety over the book performance numbers. The aircraft climbs better, and is able to attain FL450 at higher weights and temperatures, providing additional margin-of-safety in bad weather. The aircraft uses less fuel, providing additional range and safety over a fuel exhaustion accident. Runway LOC - Weather - Fuel Exhaustion are the trifecta of fatal aircraft accidents.

We request that this AD be modified, to, within the next 30 days or 10 hours in service, require compliance with SB1467 and SB1475, and modify the AFMS to include the ATLAS BREAKER step. Furthermore, the modification to the AFMS should be something that an owner/operator holding at least a Private Pilot certificate can perform themselves.

I would estimate the cost of this grounding to us as a single operator at $100,000/month direct (replacement aircraft costs) and $10,000 month indirect costs.

In the very first sentence of the proposed rule, EPA states that the rule would create "a new, time-limited alternative dispute resolution process (ADR process) as a precondition to judicial review."

But then EPA states: "This proposed procedural rule would not regulate any person or entity outside EPA."

How can these two statements both be true? If failure to comply with ADR requirements of the proposed rule would result in a failure to exhaust administrative remedies and a binding bar on stakeholders seeking judicial review, then the rule would, in fact, "regulate persons or entities outside EPA," and directly affect the rights of the public. As such, the Proposed Rule appears to be legislative, and EPA's statement that it is "not subject to the notice and comment requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act" is legally flawed.

Here, EPA has unfortunately ("voluntarily") provided only 30 days for public notice and comment, and has even more unfortunately scheduled the notice and comment period to fall over the Christmas and New Year holidays, with the comment deadline on January 2, 2020, the day after New Year's Day. EPA should immediately extend the notice and comment period for this proposed rule by at least 30 days. I note that pursuant to Executive Order 12866, "each agency should afford the public a meaningful opportunity to comment on any proposed regulation, which in most cases should include a comment period of not less than 60 days." Id. sec. 6(a), available at https://www.archives.gov/files/federal-register/executive-orders/pdf/12866.pdf

Respectfully submitted,

Daniel E. Estrin

This past November, the overall unemployment rate hit a 50-year low of 3.5 percent. In the black community, the past three years have seen six instances in which their unemployment rate reached new all-time recorded lows.

After years of stagnant economic recovery under the pro-regulation agenda of the previous administration, the American economy has roared back to life. It's important to keep this recovery rolling - both for the economic well-being of our nation as a whole as well as bringing the American melting pot from an angry boil to a more perfect and balanced racial union.

That is why, as the leadership of the Project 21 black leadership network, we have a keen interest in efforts to streamline the regulatory processes of the government so they are more accommodating to job creation and increasing the prospects of everyone participating in the American economy.

The proposed rule seeks to improve the environmental permitting process to resolve delays that currently stop planned projects for years at the cost of jobs, access to products and services and increased innovation and opportunity.

The proposed rule reins in the power of the Environmental Protection Agency's Environmental Appeals Board (EAB) by requiring a unanimous agreement of the parties on its use, a clear definition and focusing of its powers, the elimination of third-party intervention and a 60-day deadline for issuing a ruling. These reforms speed up determinations and give clear recourse to aggrieved parties in a permit-review process where slow-moving challenges have often become a de facto denial of their ability to proceed.

It is not our intent to allow any protection found in the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Safe Drinking Water Act or Resources Conservation and Recovery Act to be circumvented. Rather, we support the rule because it brings clarity to a process that has been mismanaged by an entity created within the bureaucracy and abused by special interests in a manner that effectively throws a wrench into America's economic engine.

It's often overlooked that Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.'s famous "I Have a Dream" speech was delivered at an event focused on job creation - the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. While Jim Crow was buried generations ago, high black unemployment has often been more than double that for white Americans and was commonplace until just recently. A lack of employment options brings with it a downward spiral of depressed wages, lack of job portability and the misery of an addiction to the welfare state that we saw with the failure of the Great Society initiatives that flourished after Dr. King's March.

The past three years have seen a dramatic record-breaking drop in black unemployment. In 2009, the difference in the black-white unemployment rate was 14.8% to 8.5%. In November of 2019, that disparity fell to 5.5% to 3.2%. Average black household income in 2018 exceed what it was in 2007 before the Great Recession.

It would be a shame to allow this trend to be stalled or reversed. That is why EAB reform is important.

In 2011, Shell was forced to postpone exploratory drilling for oil and gas in Alaska due to Clean Air Act complaints brought against it through the EAB by the Alaska Eskimo Whaling Commission. This caused a reported loss of 800 jobs. Shell later reduced its operations in 2012 before finally abandoning its efforts in the Chukchi Sea altogether in 2015. With an expedited appeals process, which also gives parties the ability to be heard in a federal court, jobs might not have been lost, energy independence may be more of a reality today and investment not wasted.

The EAB process has become even more complicated because the previous administration chose to expand the ability to challenge permits on the basis of their potential effect on climate change.

In 2017, the average salary for a black employee in oil and gas extraction was over $109,000.

In its "Blueprint for a Better Deal for Black America," Project 21 noted "[e]xcessive regulation stifles economic growth and has a disproportionate effect on small businesses." Noting black entrepreneurs are heavily invested in small firms of 50 or fewer employees, we demanded a "better deal" that included reining in government agencies operating to a political agenda and requiring a "Minority Impact Assessment" to ensure new regulation does not unnecessarily impact job growth, wages, homeownership, the cost of living and other factors in minority communities.

Through the proposed rule, this administration seeks "faster resolution of issues and more creative, satisfying and enduring solutions" at the Environmental Appeals Board. More permits mean more jobs. More jobs mean more opportunity. More opportunity means an America where economic prosperity is bringing about the equality Dr. King and the supporters of the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom wanted.

Horace Cooper
Council Nedd II
Stacy Washington
Project 21

This comment addresses the Environmental Protection Agency's proposed Environmental Appeals Board (EAB) Reforms, Docket ID EPA-HQ-OGC-2019-0406. The National Center for Public Policy Research, a Washington, DC-based educational foundation, welcomes EPA's proposed reforms to the EAB.  Specifically, streamlining the process through which parties may challenge EPA permit decisions, allowing them to go directly to federal court rather than having to go through the EAB first, is a step in the right direction.  Members of the EAB function as "judges," but are judges in name only.  Many are simply career employees who lack both the legal training and the issue-specific expertise to render an informed opinion.  While reducing the amount of time judges are allowed to serve on the EAB to 12 years is welcome, it would be better to further cut the time to six years at most, so that fresh perspectives can be brought into the process.  In general, the environmental permitting process in the United States is is characterized by expensive and time-consuming litigation that undermines economic activity, often with no environmental or social benefit.  Projects that are held up by permitting disputes are projects that often never come to fruition.  This is an opportunity lost for people seeking improvements in their lives.  Additionally, by eliminating the EAB's authority to review Regional permit decisions on its own initiative in the absence of an appeal brought by an interested party, EPA is properly reining in the EAB and striking a blow against administrative regulatory abuse.  Thank you very much.  Bonner R. Cohen, Ph. D., Senior Fellow, National Center for Public Policy Research, December 29, 2019

The Hawaii Department of Health's Hazardous Waste Program (a state program authorized under 40 CFR part 271) provides the following comment in response to EPA's request for comment on how to conform 40 CFR 270.42(f) and 270.155 with the proposed revisions to 40 CFR part 124 (p. 66091). We are not commenting on whether the proposed changes to 40 CFR 124 should be adopted as proposed.

If changes are made to 40 CFR part 124, we recommend that EPA conform 40 CFR 270.42(f) and 270.155 by retaining the existing practice of cross-referencing the appropriate section(s) of part 124. For states that adopt federal hazardous waste regulations by reference, which we understand is one third to one half the states, including Hawaii, retention of the current practice of cross-referencing will be much easier than handling "separate regulatory text that would create an identical ADR exhaustion process" within 40 CFR part 270.

Since the proposed changes to 40 CFR part 124 would not affect hazardous waste permits issued by authorized state programs, the federal language will not be adopted by states, and therefore in the case of incorporation of the federal rules by reference, will (continue to) need to be excluded from incorporation. States can more easily continue to exclude the proposed language from their incorporation of the federal rules if the appeal procedures continue to be located only in 40 CFR part 124 and cross-referenced in 40 CFR part 270.

If EPA chooses to add "separate regulatory text that would create an identical ADR exhaustion process" within program-specific rule chapters such as 40 CFR part 270, those proposed changes should be set out and noticed for public comment. 40 CFR part 270 was not listed in the heading or List of Subjects in this proposed rule notice as an affected CFR part, and therefore this notice may not have reached all parties interested in potential changes to 40 CFR part 270, including authorized state hazardous waste programs.

Additionally, there is a typographical error in the proposed regulatory language indicating revision of 124.20 twice (pp. 66094 and 66096), so it is not clear whether or not the deletion of the current 124.21 "Effective date of part 124" and its replacement with the current 124.20 "Computation of time" is intended.

4330 East-West Highway
Bethesda, MD 20814

Re:Docket Number: CPSC-2019-20008

Dear Commissioners:

The National Council of Textile Organization (NCTO) is pleased to respond to the Consumer Product Safety Commissions (CPSC) request for information about expanding the exemptions for flammability testing and other ways to reduce the burdens associated with the Commissions Standard for the Flammability of Clothing Textiles, 16 CFR Part 1610.
NCTO, headquartered in Washington, DC, is the national trade association representing the entire spectrum of the U.S. textile sector. The U.S. textile industry is one of the most innovative and scientifically advanced industries in the world providing products to the home furnishings, automotive, aerospace, military, medical, and apparel industries.
The textile industry is proud of its long history of working with CPSC on 16 CFR Part 1610 and other flammability requirements for textile products, and continues to strongly support the Standard for the Flammability of Clothing Textiles to reduce the risk of injury or death by prohibiting the use of dangerously flammable clothing.
Possible Exemption of Spandex from Textile Requirements
The Federal Trade Commission is responsible for generic names and definitions for manufactured fibers. At 16 CFR 303.7, Spandex is defined as:
A manufactured fiber in which the fiber-forming substance is a long chain synthetic polymer comprised of at least 85 percent of a segmented polyurethane.
Small amounts of Spandex fibers can be added to some fabrics to provide stretch characteristic in the fabrics and end products. Often, the amount of Spandex blended into a fabric is relatively small as a percentage of the overall fabric weight.
NCTO has no test data on 16 CFR Part 1610 flammability testing of 100% Spandex or fabrics containing various levels of Spandex blended with other exempted fibers, i.e., polyester, nylon, olefin, acrylic, modacrylic or wool.
Since the CPSCs Standard for the Flammability of Clothing Textiles has been very successful in screening our dangerously flammable general wearing apparel fabrics, we would not be supportive of any changes in the General Wearing Apparel Standard that would reduce the level of fire safety that currently benefits the American public. NCTO would be supportive of possible exemptions from testing for plain surface fabrics or raised surface fabrics only where definitive and convincing test data are available that support a testing exemption for Spandex.
Availability and Specifications of Stop Thread
Paragraph 1610.2(p) of the Standard for the Flammability of Clothing Textiles (16 CFR Part 1610), defines stop thread as:
Stop thread supply means No. 50, white, mercerized, 100% cotton sewing thread.

The thread industry converted its size numbering system several years ago from Ticket Sizes to Tex Sizes. The General Services Administration authorized the use of Tex sizes and lists the companion Ticket sizes in commercial item description A-A52094A dated March 30, 2007 and a copy is attached.

Identifying the stop cord thread as a Tex size 40 would update the regulation using the current terminology adopted by the thread industry and would require the same thread as originally cited in the regulation.

Test Result Codes

We agree that the standard reporting codes in 16 CFR Part 1610, paragraph 1610.8(b)(2) for raised surface fabrics may be confusing. The code for SFpoi is defined as, Surface flash, at point of impingement only (equivalent to did not ignite for plain surfaces). However, this code is also used for specimens when no surface flash is created simply because there is no other code that clearly defines a specimen that does not ignite WITHOUT exhibiting a surface flash.

Perhaps the addition of one more code would be appropriate for raised surface fabrics that do not create a surface flash and do not ignite. When this occurs, the code Did Not Ignite (DNI) would be appropriate and the SFpoi code could be used only when a surface flash occurs without fabric ignition.

We hope you find our comments to be useful as the Commission evaluates the limited areas in 16 CFR Part 1610 that are under review.


Sincerely,
Donald Vavala
dvavala@ncto.org

I think that adding a pictorial-only warning label for lawn mowers are a good idea. Many times, when it is all words, people will overlook the warning label and not even read it. Pictures will stand out and may catch the eye of someone who may not normally look at the warning label. I think having words along with the pictures will be a good idea, to explain a picture that could come off as confusing.

This rule for the CPSC would be beneficial to provide a more universal way of providing warning labels so that everyone, regardless of language, will be able to be safe. A picture can be understood by all people and will allow the warning to thus be more effective. The commission should definitely adopt this rule for walk-behind power lawn mowers as they are very dangerous and need proper safety warnings.

I think that the modification to change the labeling on lawn mowers is an important public safety concern. I believe that the switch from having warning labels written with words to pictorial representations of the risks of a lawn mower will be affective in achieving its purpose. The pictorial representation of the risks would send a more clear message to whoever is operating the equipment that it is in fact dangerous. I sense the biggest benefits of this are for people who do not read well and children, seeing a representation of the dangers are a better deterrent to errant use than a strongly-worded label.

It is concerning that the CPSC is considering a rule that would manipulate the warning information stickers on the back of lawn mowers. While a picture-only reference would be easier to read and understand for the majority of users, there should still be explicit safety/warning information on the back of these lawn mowers. Accidents are bound to happen. The label should include a picture, but this should not mean removing the warning labels associated with the product.

It is both absurd and asinine that emissions from gasoline powered mowers are not regulated. This is serious a consumer health risk, and far more significantly a public health danger. Pollutants from gasoline combustion, notably benzene, acrolein, formaldehyde, carbon monoxide, and sulfur dioxide are significantly harmful to human health, even in very small exposures (with the exception of carbon monoxide, which is not permanently damaging unless high exposures are found). Beyond the direct damage to human health, there are far more profound implications, such as our ability to sustain life on this planet. The unregulated pollution from a mower produces an average of 25 times more pollution than that of a typical car per hour, and that is certainly a threat to our existance (by which I mean the existance of people who are now children, and will still rely on our atmosphere for life 50 years from now).

I believe that this is a very sound and reasonable proposed rule. Please find attached the Air-Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute's Comments in response to CPSC Proposed Safety Standard for Residential Gas Furnaces and Boilers. AHRI's Final Comments include Attachment 1 and Attachment 2.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed safety standard for residential gas furnaces and boilers. We the undersigned health, consumer, community and environmental justice organizations support the proposed standards and strongly encourage the Consumer Product Safety Commission to strengthen them further.

The new standard limits the maximum amount of carbon monoxide allowed to be produced and leaked by residential gas furnaces and boilers. CO is a highly toxic gas, produced by devices that burn carbon-based fuels such as methane gas.

CO is only detectable with an electronic sensor – it cannot be seen, smelled, or heard. CO in the air rapidly enters all parts of the body, including blood, brain, heart, and muscles. As CO has a 200 times stronger bind to hemoglobin than oxygen in the bloodstream, CO not only starves the body and all of its systems of oxygen, it also causes cellular damage to all vital organs.

Because CO is undetectable by humans and poisoning is extremely difficult to medically diagnose due to the vagueness of symptoms and narrow diagnostic window, it has been dubbed the “silent killer.” Health effects of poisoning are determined by several factors including the amount and duration of exposure, previous exposure, age, body size, pre-existing conditions, and oxygen metabolism rate. Symptoms are varied even among family members and range from mild symptoms such as fatigue, dizziness, headache, confusion, and nausea to more severe symptoms such as disorientation, unconsciousness, long-term neurological disabilities, coma, cardiorespiratory failure, and death.

CO poisoning can be acute or chronic. Acute poisoning occurs by breathing large amounts of CO over a short period of time. Chronic poisoning occurs by breathing small amounts of CO over an extended period of time. Victims of chronic CO poisoning will often face long-term health issues, often unexplained or misdiagnosed. One of the most common long-term health issues associated with chronic CO poisoning is neurological damage and associated cognitive impairment that is often mistaken for Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, or dementia.

Most CO alarms sold in the US are designed in accordance with the voluntary standard UL 2034. These alarms, if maintained and working properly, only require a warning prior to CO levels becoming so high that it may cause a loss of one’s ability to react to the immediate danger. These levels are significantly higher than the World Health Organization’s health guidelines which recommend a CO exposure limit of 3.5 ppm (4 mg/m3) sustained for 24 hours. Additionally, any displays on the alarms are required to display 0 ppm until CO concentrations reach 30 ppm. In a CPSC survey from 2020, 85% of respondents believed that their alarm would alert them if carbon monoxide were present. Carbon monoxide alarms do not warn consumers when there is low-level but injurious carbon monoxide exposure, and consumers are mostly unaware. Due to this, protective measures for carbon monoxide at injury-causing levels are still needed.

Environmental justice communities face disproportionate exposure to CO. Low-income renters often live in older buildings with smaller units and inadequate ventilation which can contribute to elevated pollutant concentrations inside the household. Large multifamily buildings that utilize gas boilers in the lower levels or basement for building-wide heating can expose tenants living near the boiler to higher CO concentrations inside their apartments. Further, communities of color are more likely to suffer from preexisting medical conditions that increase susceptibility to the health impacts of CO exposure.

For these reasons, it is crucial that the CPSC ensures residential furnaces and boilers sold in the US are as safe as possible by implementing a rule that not only prevents death, but also injury. Thus, we urge the CPSC to strengthen the proposed safety standard for residential gas furnaces and boilers. To strengthen the proposed standard we recommend incorporating the following safeguards:

Shutdown/Modulation Thresholds: Lower shutdown/modulation threshold to account for established U.S. health guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), which states that an elevated level of 2% COHb for non-smokers “strongly supports a diagnosis of CO poisoning.”
Tamper Resistance: Add requirements to prevent tampering with or deactivating of the CO shut-off device.
Restart: Extend the time period before restart is allowed during a sensor failure event to at least 30 minutes, as the current time is not protective enough if a CO incident occurs.

Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on the proposed safety standard for residentials furnaces and boilers. After finalizing this standard, we encourage the CPSC to consider similar safety standards for all residential natural gas, methane, liquefied petroleum, and propane gas-burning appliances.
Attached are comments from WM Technologies.  Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments for this important topic.

- Who am I?

I am Jonathan Kane, Company Director of KANE USA Inc & Kane International Ltd (KANE), owned by KANE Group Ltd, UK 2nd gen family biz I run with my brother, Michael Kane. President & CEO of KANE USA.

- What does KANE do?

We design, make, sell & service portable test equipment for heating & hot water contractors worldwide testing safe appliance installation & service such as those typically sold by AHRI & HHIC, the UK equivalent industry association.

- Who else does KANE support?

KANE is a member of both the US association AHRI & its UK equivalent, HHIC.

KANE is also a long standing supporter of CO victim support with long associations with NCOAA USA & CO-Gas Safety UK - www.co-gassafety.co.uk - their web site has much CO related information.

- What do we think of this proposal?

KANE believes CPSC will find it almost impossible to reduce CO poisoning incidents in a timely manner by requiring appliance mfrs to install CO sensors because:

1. CO sensors are as yet unproven for typical US appliances regarding cost, reliability, life & accuracy such as to avoid false alarms or false negatives

2. Meeting 18th month deadline will be impossible for most or all appliance mfrs

3. This only addresses new appliances - critical market penetration will take over 10 years

4. There are other ways for appliance mfrs to address these issues.

- What has KANE learnt from the UK?

The UK experienced these issues and developed 3 successful solutions, alongside the widespread availability of residential CO alarms to EN50291:

1. HHIC Benchmark Log Book

HHIC, UK AHRI equivalent - www.hhic.org.uk - introduced the generic "Benchmark" branded log book for contractors to complete after install or service.

Its introduction directly correlates with falling CO deaths, especially after requiring contractors to add emissions results from appropriate portable test equipment - all UK appliance mfrs supply logbooks for free so contractors can use for existing and new installs.

2. Appliance testing after install & service

The UK requires appliance testing after install or service to confirm operation to manufacturer instructions - this alone has dramatically reduced the number of incidents, given most causes of CO poisoning are due to faulty install or service.

UK simple test procedures ensure contractors use approved test equipment (for example to ANSI & AHRI standard 1260) to confirm & record appliance & room CO migration.

These tests are detailed in British Standard BS 7967 & UK CMDDA1 procedure for testing

3. Emergency responders

UK gas emergency 1st responders visits now identify if CO is present and locate its source (appliance, neighbour, etc). This allows residents to show their doctor or emergency health care providers they were poisoned.

- Conclusion

Failure to ignore these examples of UK best practice will ensure CPSC's plan will take longer to implement than expected, will add new costs to consumer appliances. It will be decades before CPSC sees a meaningful difference in CO death or injury reduction.

I would be happy to provide more detail when required or facilitate meetings with UK association HHIC and CO-Gas Safety victim support charity.

I look forward to hearing from you

Jonathan Kane

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed safety standard for residential gas furnaces and boilers. We the undersigned emergency response and HVACR professionals support the proposed standards and strongly encourage the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) to strengthen them further.

Carbon monoxide is a highly toxic gas, produced any time carbon-based fuels such as methane gas are burned. The new standard is intended to limit the amount of (CO) produced by and leaking from furnaces and boilers. Reducing any amount of ambient CO in residences is important to protecting the health of consumers and those who maintain and repair these appliances, as CO poses a real and tangible threat to health.

HVACR professionals are frequently near CO-producing appliances due to the nature of their work. They regularly perform routine maintenance and emergency appliance repair, often multiple times a day. Emergency responders are also exposed to CO regularly. According to the International Association of Firefighters, “essentially all firefighting environments can be expected to contain high levels of carbon monoxide,” and “an actively exercising firefighter in a high CO environment may suffer collapse and sudden death without any warning symptoms.”

Severe health threats from CO exposure

CO poisoning and CO exposure are often misdiagnosed and wrongly attributed. CO’s harm is due to oxygen displacement and causes widespread tissue damage across all body systems. CO poisoning damages cardiac, nerve, and/or brain tissue. Even when a person survives a CO poisoning event, they may not know it despite widespread damage to both brain tissue and nerve tissue throughout the body.

Prolonged exposure to moderate to high concentrations of CO causes reduced brain function, impaired vision and coordination, headaches, dizziness, confusion, and nausea. Even at low concentrations, CO exposure can cause acute fatigue in healthy people and chest pain in people with heart disease. Chronic low-level CO concentration exposure is associated with adverse cardiovascular, central nervous system and fetal development effects such as heart attacks, congestive heart failure, ischemic heart disease, sensory-motor deficits, emotional changes, congenital defects, and low birthweight.

NCOAA and the undersigned emergency response and HVACR professionals strongly urge the CPSC to implement the new safety standard for residential furnaces and boilers protecting consumers, emergency responders, and HVACR professionals from this “silent killer” that is CO.
To strengthen the proposed standard we recommend incorporating the following safeguards:

Shutdown/Modulation Thresholds: Lower shutdown/modulation threshold to account for established U.S. health guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), which states that an elevated level of 2% COHb for non-smokers “strongly supports a diagnosis of CO poisoning.”
Tamper Resistance: Add requirements to prevent tampering with or deactivating of the CO shut-off device.
Restart: Extend the time period before restart is allowed during a sensor failure event to at least 30 minutes, as the current time is not protective enough if a CO incident occurs.
