Good Afternoon,

We are writing to request safe harbor from co-pays for our Chronic Care Management patients. Since 2016, we have partnered with over 150 independent healthcare practices to provide Chronic Care Management services to their eligible patient population. In the past 24 months, we have completed over 250,000 chronic care management visits, touching nearly 15,000 patient lives in the process. Were proud to say that patient engagement in the program has made a difference; Wellbox patients have a noted 2-3x increase in preventative services and a noted 60% decrease in emergency room visits within the population of the practices we serve. As a direct result, a third-party study on outcomes we recently commissioned found that our CCM program has decreased total cost of care by 5.6% in the populations we serve.

We can see that CCM helps people living with chronic diseases, and yet, we still struggle to increase adoption and engagement at both a provider and a patient level. Financial vulnerability in medically vulnerable populations is a large reason for this.

Medicare patients are, more often than not, on fixed incomes. They cannot always afford secondary insurance and when they can the coverage of CCM is variable. The risk of having a co-pay deters a lot of people from enrolling in the program. Approximately 20% of people cite the co-pay as their reason for not joining the program during our enrollment campaigns. This percentage is even higher in low-income areas where people do not have secondary insurance at all and a co-pay is guaranteed. Unfortunately, these are also the people who have the most limited access to healthcare and need the program the most.

Once enrolled in the program, 12% of those who leave specifically cite the co-pay as their reason. Nearly 60% told us that they would have remained on the program if there was no cost. Anecdotally, we suspect that financial vulnerability actually accounts for a much larger segment of our unenrollment however pride prevents people from admitting that is why they have chosen to leave. Needless to say, the correlation between people receiving a bill and becoming disinterested in the program is strong.

We believe strongly in the purpose of chronic care management and the good that it can do within high-risk, high-cost populations and urge the current administration to offer safe harbor to eligible Medicare patients, eliminating the co-pay and thereby allowing increased adoption, engagement, and savings.

Thank you for your considerations,

The Patient Experience and Customer Success Teams at Wellbox

The physician practice can provide ongoing support to the patient; positive feedback, intervention where necessary, and deeper analysis of patient trends for improved outcomes. The tools are there for effective population management.

Copay is a significant hindrance to this vision. Many patients won't see the value and therefore be resistant to spending more for a future unknown benefit. Actions taken by the OIG that reduce the copay burden will assist.

For a patient to be effectively monitored and managed, patient generating data tools or devices are necessary. And the devices must work in concert with the software platform the practice is using. It's an integrated system. This includes a system of diabetes monitoring devices, disposable testing strips and the software platform on which they would operate. In most cases, these devices may not be readily available to the patient outside the practice. And importantly, these devices won't have much value or utility outside of this setting and therefore the opportunity of them being an "inducement" is very limited.

Again, actions taken by the OIG in allowing practices "safe harbor" in providing these devices will further help the vision of improved outcomes for diabetes patients.

From: Karen Olsen Bruhns, Professor Emerita of Anthropology, San Francisco State University; archaeologist working in El Salvador since 1975
Re: Renewal of MOU with El Salvador

I strongly support the extension of the Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of El Salvador Concerning the Imposition of Import Restrictions on Certain Categories of Archaeological Material from Pre-Hispanic Cultures of the Republic of El Salvador.

El Salvador was the first Central American republic to gain some degree of protection from the rapacity of the antiquities US market in 1987, when the looting of the site of Cara Sucia became an international scandal (not coincidentally some 80-90% of the looted Cara Sucia materials, by my best estimate, decorates US museum and private collections). This agreement has been extended, amended and enlarged and became a Memorandum of Understanding in 1995. The MOU is currently up for extension and it is essential, not just for the sake of El Salvadors cultural heritage, but for that of Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica, that this MOU be renewed.

It is true that the government of El Salvador has not moved as swiftly as it might to enforce registration of national (private) collections and to prosecute looters and traffickers in antiquities. In part this has been because of internal social and economic problems needing focused attention, in part because the laws pertaining to the protection of cultural patrimony need to be entirely rewritten. With the establishment of a Secretary of Culture (recently recast as a ministry), serious work is (slowly, alas) being done to reform and modernize the Ley del Patrimonio Cultural and to regulate collecting and trafficking in antiquities. The government, universities and FUNDAR (www.fundar.org.sv) have cooperated in public education, site protection, and publicity of the need for the preservation of the Prehispanic (and Colonial) heritage. As a parenthesis, it is noteworthy that El Salvador has had national laws prohibiting the export of archaeological pieces since 1903, the earliest of Central American republics to enact such legal protection.

Today, more than ever, it is important to help El Salvador protect its archaeological heritage. Despite increased enforcement of anti-looting and anti-trafficking laws and agreements in the Americas in general, the US market for illicitly obtained antiquities keeps expanding. Prices escalate as access to looted materials becomes more limited. With regards to Salvadoran antiquities, prices in the US market have gone from a few hundred dollars to many thousands. Galleries such as Barakat in Beverley Hills, California, Griffin Gallery in Boca Raton, Florida or William Seigal in Santa Fe, New Mexico are among the many antiquities businesses parading their looted goodies online, including large collections of Salvadoran materials. One doubts that all this material has been in the United States since 1987. Prices on archaeological styles such as Copador, Salua, and Campana polychrome ceramics have increased sharply in the past dozen years as has the demand for Preclassic figurines, jade ornaments, and similar small items. A horrifying extension of this business of looting the past for the interior decoration of the foreign present is the intensifying sacking of colonial churches, again for US based collectors and museums. It is evident that there is an ever-growing demand in the United States for destroying other countries heritage for our own interior decoration. Despite educational campaigns by professional archaeological associations, and despite the publicized (and too occasional) seizures of Precolumbian materials at ports of entry, the market for stolen antiquities continues to grow.

Of equal concern is that, should El Salvador not have an MOU with the United States, it is certain that US based traffickers, smugglers, thieves, and antiquities galleries/museum personnel would begin to funnel materials from the other countries with attractive archaeological remains, especially the Maya culture areas of Guatemala, Honduras, Belize, and Mexico, through El Salvador. Identification labels in antiquities galleries (and museums, for that matter) virtually never state the true provenance of a piece, but I would predict that there would be a several thousand percent increase in the number of pieces said to have been legally exported from El Salvador. The heritage of many countries would be increasingly threatened were El Salvador not to have an MOU with the United States.

For these reasons I most strongly support the extension of the MOU.

Thank you.
Karen Olsen Bruhns, PhD.
Professor Emerita of Anthropology
San Francisco State University
Research Associate, California Academy of Sciences
Director, Cihuatn/Las Maras Archaeological Projects, Fundacin Nacional de Arqueologa de El Salvador (FUNDAR)

From:
Paul Amaroli
Archaeologist conducting research and conservation projects in El Salvador since 1978.
With Salvadoran colleagues, prepared base documents for the 1987 Emergency agreement for import restrictions from the Cara Sucia region, and the 1995 MOU for archaeological materials from El Salvador.
Currently staff archaeologist with FUNDAR (Fundacin Nacional de Arqueologa de El Salvador), www.fundar.org.sv
Recently completed two sequential conservation projects at El Salvadors largest archaeological park, Cihuatn, sponsored by the Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (2014-2018).

To:
Cultural Property Advisory Committee

I am writing to express my support for extension of the Memorandum of Understanding Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of El Salvador Concerning the Imposition of Import Restrictions on Certain Categories of Archaeological Material from the Prehispanic Cultures of the Republic of El Salvador.

Through long experience in Salvadoran archaeology, I can attest without a doubt that the MOU has been an effective deterrent to the traffic of prehispanic artifacts from El Salvador to the United States. Before its existence, the only obstacles to such export of artifacts were the infrequent actions by Salvadoran customs to detain suspect shipments, usually done only at the bequest of cultural officials acting on tips. Coyotes (as traffickers are known) have remarked that the MOU has been an impediment to their activites.

Much needs to be done in El Salvador to improve the protection of cultural heritage. But there have been advances over recent years, and it is highly significant that more archaeologists than ever are now employed by the governmental cultural organ.

Looting continues to be a major problem. And as noted in the past, it is increasingly a habitual associate with the construction of subdivisions and other development projects. As bulldozers level the landscape for buildings and roadways, workers scramble to collect pots and other artifacts (usually associated with burials). More traditional looting at completely rural sites still continues as well, as illustrated by the San Andrs site (Attachment 1), where crews of looters, armed with pistols, have rapaciously excavated up to the very fence line of the San Andrs Archaeological Park.

While the MOU has been an effective deterrent, artifacts looted from El Salvador are still making their way to the United States. Internet sales make some of this traffic easily visible, as may be seen by googling Copador, one of the most salient and saleable polychrome ceramics of the territory of El Salvador (its distribution weakly includes neighboring areas of Guatemala and Honduras).

Clear goals which should be established by the government of El Salvador include the following. Known archaeological sites need to be periodically monitored by government archaeologists, minimally every two months, and a long-term project of systematic survey should be conducted with a national strategy since the majority of sites here are still unrecorded, and many of those nominally registered have very sparse and dated information. The very dated and loophole-filled cultural heritage law needs to be replaced by modern and strong legislation (it is called the Ley Especial de Proteccin al Patrimonio Cultural de El Salvador); drafting a new law would greatly benefit from input from other countries with effective cultural heritage laws. And the new law should include workable mechanisms to encourage the construction community to report finds, rather than loot and destroy them.

I urge the Committee to extend the MOU for another 5 years.

Thank you.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Department of States (DOS)s interim final rule, Visas: Ineligibility Based on Public Charge Grounds. The Los Angeles Regional Food Bank strongly opposes this rule. The rule is unjustified, departs from over a hundred years of law and policy, is not supported by available research, and will make immigrants and citizens in their families afraid to seek critical programs and services. We urge the Department to withdraw the rule in its entirety, and to ensure that the long-standing principles clarified in the 1999 field guidance and State Department guidance issued at that time remain in effect.

Last year, our organization submitted the attached comments on a proposed public charge rule from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). We understand that the DOS Interim Final Rulemaking is intended to align the Department's standards with those of DHS. Because the DOS rule is intended to mirror the DHS rule, our objections to the DHS rule are relevant and applicable. We request that the Department read and consider the attached comments as part of the administrative record.

As you are aware, three federal courts, in New York, Washington, and Maryland, have issued nationwide preliminary injunctions against the DHS rule, finding it likely that the plaintiffs will succeed on the merits of their cases. Two additional courts in California and Illinois also found the plaintiffs cases compelling and issued geographically-limited injunctions against the rule. All five courts explained in detail why changes finalized by DHS are contrary to law and/or are arbitrary and capricious. DOS should not rely on the enjoined DHS regulation to justify its actions, when multiple courts have found that its interpretation is likely unlawful. So long as the DHS rule is enjoined, the Departments principal justification for issuing the interim final rule fails. Moving forward with implementation would conflict with the Departments stated goal of alignment with DHS.
Withdrawing the interim final rule alone is an insufficient remedy. Any change in policy which differs from the May 1999 public charge Field guidance will result in one policy being applied to applications processed by consular offices abroad and a different policy to applications processed in the U.S. The State Departments abrupt changes to longstanding standards for evaluating public charge in the January 2018 revisions to the Foreign Affairs Manual (FAM) radically redefined the criteria for admissibility to the United States. Whether or not the DHS rule remains enjoined, any departure of the FAM from the principles articulated in the 1999 guidance will cause chaos and confusion in an already complex legal immigration system, and will cause further harm to immigrants and citizens in their families.

We urge the Department of State to withdraw this Interim Final Rule and the January 2018 FAM instructions. Reinstating longstanding public charge policy as articulated in the 1999 guidance will reduce confusion and support the well-being and long-term success of immigrants and their families.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Department of States (DOS)s interim final rule, Visas: Ineligibility Based on Public Charge Grounds. The rule is unjustified, departs from over a hundred years of law and policy, is not supported by available research, and will make immigrants and citizens in their families afraid to seek critical programs and services. Last year, our organization submitted the attached comments on a proposed public charge rule from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). We understand that the DOS Interim Final Rulemaking is intended to align the Department's standards with those of DHS. Because the DOS rule is intended to mirror the DHS rule, our objections to the DHS rule are relevant and applicable. We request that the Department read and consider the attached comments as part of the administrative record.

As you are aware, five federal courts have found that the DHS rule violates the Administrative Procedures Act and is contrary to law. The district courts in New York, Washington, and Maryland have issued nationwide preliminary injunctions against the DHS rule, while courts in California and Illinois issued geographically-limited injunctions against the rule. DOS should not rely on the enjoined DHS regulation to justify its actions, when multiple courts have found that its interpretation is likely unlawful. So long as the DHS rule is enjoined, the Departments principal justification for issuing the interim final rule fails. Moving forward with implementation would conflict with the Departments stated goal of alignment with DHS.

Withdrawing the interim final rule alone is an insufficient remedy. Family immigration is the primary basis for legal immigration to the United States. Today, family visas account for approximately 65% of legal immigration each year. Over the years, the U.S. and its communities have reaped the extensive benefits of family-based immigration policies as family immigration drives small business creation, fuels innovation, promotes integration, and ensures the maintenance of strong family support systems, strengthening our nation.

This Rule parallels the DHS rule stayed by several federal judges on Oct. 11. In fact, that is its justification, listed in both the Rule's Summary and the section titled "Why is the Department promulgating this rule?" Because the Rule has been stayed indefinitely, the Department of State need not worry about the rules stated purpose; preventing visas being issued to foreign nationals who would then arrive at the U.S. border and be found inadmissible under a stricter DHS definition of "public charge". While the orders from the SDNY and ED of Wash. are technically temporary, they required that plaintiffs show that they are likely to ultimately prevail on the merits. The federal judicial orders together found that DHS's new definition of "public charge" was unconstitutional and violated the APA in several ways. There is no reason to believe that the new State Department definition of "public charge" is not also unconstitutional and in violation of the APA. It is very unlikely that three federal judges would reach very similar conclussions of law, pertaining the constitutionality of the DHS Rule and also hold that it violates the APA and turn out to be wrong.

The Rule was promulgated inappropriately under the Good Cause exception of the APA. It should have been promulgated under standard notice-and-comment rulemaking. If it did ever qualify for the exception, it now does not. There is no urgency to match the DHS standard, which DHS has been enjoined from implementing by Judge Daniels.

The Rule lacks a rational basis.

The Rule is unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause of the Constitution because it discriminates against non-English speakers, without tying English language ability to avoid becoming primarily dependent on public benefits.

This Rule violates the Rehabilitation Act by discriminating on the basis of disability in the adjudication of an application for a federal benefit.

This Rule is arbitrary and capricious under the APA. Similarly trained consular officials could reach separate conclusions based on very similar fact patterns because the rule is so arbitrary.

The Department of State exceeded its authority by redefining "public charge" in a way that Congress has considered and declined several times to enact.

The Rule will negatively affect federal tax revenue by withholding visas from skilled foreign nationals.

The Rule should, therefore, be immediately rescinded. The Department should return to using the prior definition of public charge, based on primary dependence, rather than being merely "likely" to use federal benefits. The Department should not attempt to reintroduce the Rule, because its definition of "public charge" is unconstitutional, violates the APA, and violates the Rehabilitation Act.

I request that the Department of States interim final rule, which codifies changes to 22 CFR 40.41 regarding definition of public charge, be withdrawn. I am a professional in U.S. international education. My institution welcomes and orients thousands of international students and scholars to the U.S., most of whom are in nonimmigrant visa status through our institutional sponsorship. In addition, our international students and scholars are often accompanied by their immediate dependent family members. The services we provide allow talented students and scholars from around the world to seek an education, engage in cutting-edge research, and participate in meaningful intercultural exchange.
This interim rule would negatively impact our community of non-immigrant students and scholars. A number of our students and scholars receive sponsorship from their home country governments or funding from our institution in order to pursue their education in the U.S. Often, these individuals do not hail from affluent families.
Though health insurance is provided by our institution and is required for all international students, the rule as written would give adjudicators the discretion to deem students with limited family resources ineligible for U.S. visas based on the conjecture that they might need public health benefits in the future. Our institutional interest is to bring in the best and the brightest from around the world. If this rule restricts us to bringing in only the wealthiest, it will deny us the opportunity to invite talented people we might otherwise bring into our classrooms, our research labs, and our academic faculty.
Additionally, this interim rule has the potential to impact the broader health and financial stability of our international graduate students and visiting scholars with U.S. citizen children. In these families, the children are eligible for Medicaid by virtue of their U.S. Citizenship but their parents are not. Though the proposed rule specifically states that in such circumstances, an eligible childs use of Medicaid will not be considered a negative eligibility factor for the nonimmigrant parent, the broad discretion given to the adjudicators to project potential future benefits use could still allow for a parents immigration petition to be endangered by their childs use of the Medicaid program.
In response to the proposed DHS rule on public charge, there has been a chilling effect whereby individuals who qualify for certain benefits (or whose children qualify for certain benefits) disenroll from these benefits for fear that they will endanger future immigration benefits. We have already seen several families disenroll their U.S. Citizen children from Medicaid for this very reason. These children are part of our university community, part of the surrounding community, and part of our citizenry - their health outcomes can and will impact the health outcomes for all of us. The proposed rule harms these U.S. Citizen children and if enacted, will inflict further harm on them, on their families, and on our communities. Considering the aforementioned points, we urge you to withdraw the interim final rule.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Department of States (DOS)s interim final rule, Visas: Ineligibility Based on Public Charge Grounds. The AIDS Foundation of Chicago (AFC) strongly opposes this rule as it departs from over a hundred years of law and policy, is not supported by available research, and will make immigrants and citizens in their families afraid to seek critical programs and services. We urge the Department to withdraw the rule in its entirety and ensure that the long standing principles clarified in the 1999 field guidance and State Department guidance issued at that time remain in effect.

Last year, AFC submitted the attached comments on a proposed public charge rule from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). (See attached letter dated December 6, 2018 re. DHS Docket No. USCIS-2010-0012, RIN 1615-AA22, Comments in Response to Proposed Rulemaking: Inadmissibility on Public Charge Grounds). We understand that the DOS Interim Final Rulemaking is intended to align the Department's standards with those of DHS. Because the DOS rule is intended to mirror the DHS rule, our objections to the DHS rule are relevant and applicable. We request that the Department read and consider the attached comments as part of the administrative record.

DOS should not rely on the enjoined DHS regulation to justify its actions, when multiple courts have found that its interpretation is likely unlawful. Five federal courts have found that the DHS rule violates the Administrative Procedures Act and is contrary to law. The district courts in New York, Washington, and Maryland have issued nationwide preliminary injunctions against the DHS rule, while courts in California and Illinois issued geographically-limited injunctions against the rule. So long as the DHS rule is enjoined, the Departments principal justification for issuing the interim final rule fails. Moving forward with implementation would conflict with the Departments stated goal of alignment with DHS.

Whether or not the DHS rule remains enjoined, any departure of the FAM from the principles articulated in the 1999 guidance will cause chaos and confusion in an already complex legal immigration system and will cause further harm to immigrants and citizens in their families.

We urge the Department of State to withdraw this Interim Final Rule and the January 2018 FAM instructions. Reinstating longstanding public charge policy as articulated in the 1999 guidance will reduce confusion and support the well-being and long-term success of immigrants and their families.

Dear CPAC, Ive already written separately on behalf of IAPN and PNG. Please also consider these additional personal comments.

1. The ANS kindly provided me a forum to detail my own views about import restrictions on coins and their detrimental impact on legitimate collecting, the appreciation, study and preservation of historical coinage and the people to people contacts coin collecting brings. See http://numismatics.org/wikiuploads/DigitalPublications/WitschonkeTompaFinal.pdf

2. Since that article has been published, collecting has even become more challenging given a rush of new import restrictions, most significantly ones of highly collected coins from Italy, Greece, Bulgaria, and Egypt.

3. These restrictions are highly problematic because the way are applied. My reading of the CPIA is that import restrictions are meant to only apply prospectively to items illicitly exported from the country for which import restrictions were granted after the effective date of the governing regulations. The problem is that they are instead applied far more broadly as an embargo on all items on designated lists imported into the US after the effective date of applicable regulations. The one federal court that has been asked to look at the issue refused to get involved, claiming that it was a foreign policy issue.

4. If restrictions were applied as contemplated by Congress, the impact on trade between the US and fellow collectors in Europe would be limited. However, embargoes make it impossible to legally import coins of types on designated lists because most coins simply lack sufficient information as far as Customs is concerned to import under the CPIAs safe harbor provisions.

5. Let me provide an example. I purchased a Himyarite coin from Spink, a UK seller, back in 2009 for $70. It has wonderful old collection toning so was likely in a collection in the UK for many years before it was purchased. However, Spink did not provide me with any collection history for the coin, probably because they had none. It simply was not thought important to retain for coins at the time, and there still is no legal requirement that documentation is retained for such items. Moreover, even when it is retained, it is quite easy for it to be lost over time. For more, see https://culturalpropertynews.org/the-international-art-market-as-cultural-bogeyman-part-1/. I know I must have an invoice for my coin somewhere, but it is not easily at hand. Moreover, there was no reason for me to think I would need to keep an invoice when I purchased the coin. And, in any case, the invoice would not have an image on it so it is quite possible a customs official would not accept it as conclusive proof I purchased this coin in 2009 anyway.

6. Such restrictions only harm honest collectors and dealers because as should be apparent from the attached pictures, such coins are so small that they may easily be smuggled. This makes CPIA import restrictions as applied by Customs the epitome of a poor regulatory scheme one that only punishes honest people importing coins from legitimate source in Europe, and which does nothing really to deter smugglers of such small items from todays war torn Yemen.

7. Over time, the ever increasing number of embargoes placed on all sorts of coins has really harmed ancient coin collecting which provides most, if not all, support for the scholarly study of coins (Numismatics).

8. A great example of how collecting supports academic study is the Caravan Kingdoms book written by a German collector of coins from the area along with an ANS academic, and published at the ANS. The ANS, and its publications are collector and dealer supported. The ANA, the other major center for the study of coins in the US, is also collector and dealer supported. In contrast, the Smithsonian, though it has a large collection, does little or no academic work and recently even discharged collectors helping to catalogue the collection as part of a Smithsonian wide move limiting the activity of volunteers.

9. Without a strong collecting base, there will no longer be the necessary level of support for the ANS, the ANA and the study of numismatics in the US. So, although import restrictions have been pitched in the past as necessary to promote academic study of archaeological objects, that simply is not the case with respect to coins. In fact, if anything, over time import restrictions will have the opposite effect on Numismatic study in the US.

Sincerely,

Peter Tompa

The Cultural Property Advisory Committee at the U.S. Department of State has been signing Memorandums of Understanding (MOU) agreements with foreign governments that blockade the entry of cultural property to the USA and deny Jews and Christians from Arab countries the rights to their historic heritage. Through the MOU process, our government is transferring ownership of confiscated Jewish property to various Arab governments that expelled or forced their Jewish populations to flee antisemitic persecution under duress. Despite the protestations of Jewish communal organizations, including; ADL: The Anti-Defamation League, Conference of Presidents of Major Jewish Organizations, Bnai Brith International, Simon Wiesenthal Center, World Jewish Congress of North America, and many others, MOU agreements have been signed with Algeria, Libya, Egypt and Syria.

The signing of the MOUs is done under the auspices of The Cultural Property Implementation Act (CPIA). This law provides for the US to enter into agreements with foreign nations to temporarily restrict the import of significant cultural items as part of a multi-nation effort to deter looting of ancient archeological sites. Over time the State Department has broadened the scope of the law to provide for near permanent bans on the import of ALL cultural items to the present time. The MOUs recognize those nations claims and seizures of all cultural property, including the personal property of individuals and the communal property of religious and ethnic groups.

The MOUs are based on a flawed premise that Jewish cultural property constitutes the national heritage of Arab governments. In fact, under the color of law, Jewish cultural property in Arab countries was expropriated from private homes, schools, and synagogues. It is the heritage and patrimony of the Jewish people. Arab governments have done little to preserve the remnants or memory of Jewish history in the countries and verified reports describe Jewish synagogues, pilgrimage sites, homes, and cemeteries being looted and destroyed. Jewish holy sites throughout the Middle East and North Africa have been appropriated and many demolished.

As set forth in more detail in our submissions:

1. The short time frames given to comment and lack of information provided make informed comment impossible;

2. CPAC should table both requests given the lack of information;

3. The Yemeni government and its Saudi allies have "unclean hands" given their intentional targeting of cultural sites, and should not be awarded with a MOU;

4. To the extent CPAC goes forward, it should at most recommend protections for objects associated with Yemen's World Heritage sites;

5. There should be no restrictions on all coins that either were made or circulated in Morocco or Yemen. One cannot assume given their wide circulation in ancient times as currency and more recently as collectibles that all undocumented coins for sale in legitimate markets in Europe had find spots in either Morocco or Yemen; and

6. To the extent restrictions are nonetheless recommended, they should be limited to coins stolen from museums or those illicitly removed from Morocco and Yemen after the effective date of any governing regulations. CPAC should oppose embargoes on undocumented coins. Such embargoes only damage legitimate trade, the appreciation and study of other cultures, and the people to people contacts collecting brings.

Attached please find my letter, on behalf of the Lawyers' Committee for Cultural Heritage Preservation, in support of the Memorandum of Understanding between the United States and the Republic of Yemen and the Memorandum of Understanding between the United States and the Kingdom of Morocco.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this matter.

Respectfully yours,

Katherine Kaplan
Executive Director
Lawyers' Committee for Cultural Heritage Preservation

I think it is a grave mistake to return ownership of Jewish cultural artifacts to Yemen and Morocco. These artifacts were confiscated or flat out stolen from Jewish communities who were forced to flee under duress, and frankly, they do not belong in Yemeni or Moroccan custody. These objects are a part of the Moroccan and Yemeni Jewish legacy, and should be kept there. Signing MOU's like the ones proposed perpetuate the false notion that Jewish cultural property constitutes the national heritage of Arab governments.

It is well established fact that Arab governments forced Jews to leave over the 20th and 21st century, and they have done little to nothing to preserve the remnants or memory of Jewish history in the countries. Additionally, there are verified reports describing Jewish synagogues, pilgrimage sites, homes, and cemeteries being looted and destroyed.Jewish holy sites throughout the Middle East and North Africa have also been appropriated and many demolished. Knowing this, it is beyond offensive to allow these two countries to expropriate a cultural heritage they actively expelled. and will likely not take care of. Major Jewish institutional leaders have decried these MOU's, and I encourage the committee to heed their recommendation to not change ownership.

Moreover, I would like to draw the committee's attention to the Jewish holiday calendar. I hope the committee is aware they have scheduled public comment smack dab in the middle of the High Holidays, making it very difficult for the Jewish community to adequately respond to the committee's call for comment. In the future, to ensure that all parties' needs are represented and accounted for, please check with Jewish leaders for a more appropriate time to set meetings and comment periods. Thank you.

It's a terrible idea to return Jewish property to Yemen.  These scrolls and artifacts were stolen from the Yemen Jewish community!  To give them to Yemen, where Jews are not safe and not welcome, is an anathema.  They belong with the Yeminite Jewish community - which is no longer in Yemen.

As someone of Jewish heritage this is an outrage to my culture!!! How can this country even think its ok to give to another country artifacts from my people?! These countries have oppressed my people and have done whatever they could to bring nothing but harm and hate! Then to give the Jewish people a very small window of time to write in and give opinions in which a large chunk of that time is the Holiest part of our calendar is another outrage!
Please do not allow these sacred items be placed in the hands of a country that hates my people and allow them to destroy my heritage and the heritage of my children and then their children!

It is appalling that Jewish items would wind up in the hands of those that have oppressed Jews.
Please do not allow this to happen.

The State Department has accelerated the timeline for action to minimize the opportunity for the Jewish community and others to oppose this action. The call for public comment was made during the Jewish High Holidays.
MOUs with Arab governments are based on a flawed premise that Jewish cultural property constitutes the national heritage of Arab countries. In fact, Jewish cultural property in Arab countries was expropriated from private homes, schools, and synagogues.
MOUs claim to be about looting, but their broad scope and limited evidence of success suggests their real impact is providing a legal vehicle to legitimize foreign confiscations and wrongful ownership claims of confiscated Jewish property. Legitimate efforts to curb looting are essential, but they must be targeted to preserve archaeological resources, and not to disguise the brazen cultural property confiscations of Jewish and Christian communities throughout the region.
We ask that the State Departments Bureau of Education and Cultural Heritage adheres to the limitations set by Congress under the Cultural Property Implementation Act by denying broad, excessive import restrictions to nations that have neither valued nor cherished the ancient heritage of Jewish, Christian, and other minority peoples.
MOUs from the Middle East should include provisions that list and name specific Jewish and Christian items to be excluded from the restricted list of items.
The proposed MOUs would legitimize Arab governments confiscation of Jewish Communal Property. A Red List from Yemen outlines the cultural property the government seeks to take ownership of and it includes Torah scrolls.
MOUs demand that the governments themselves show they are taking measures to preserve and protect the heritage in their own countries and the Yemeni government is complicit in the bombing and shelling of cultural sites, including museums.
Yemen should be asked to present an inventory of remaining Jewish moveable and non-movable patrimony and an account of what they are actively doing with respect to the care of synagogues, cemeteries and other sites and items of Jewish and Christian heritage.
U.S. imports from Yemen indicate that the U.S. is not a destination for looted or stolen material. Proponents of import restrictions point to looting of museums, but such material is already subject to detention and seizure under the National Stolen Property Act.
Article 17 of the U.N Declaration of Human Rights states that no individual or community should be arbitrarily deprived of their property. Therefore, the United States should not enter into any agreement, and should withdraw from any existing agreements, with a foreign state that either condones, supports or promotes any Article 17 violation by that state.

The current humanitarian crisis in Yemen is atrocious. The horrific events are compounded by the losses of our collective human history, as the cultural memory of a nation is sold (and likely laundered) through illicit networks. The desire to remember, and be remembered, is a basic human need that should be a human right. Be it a national or international stage, the looting and illicit trade of human history damages society on every level. But complex situations, like the humanitarian and cultural crisis in Yemen, cannot be solved with narrow tools like the UNESCO Convention (1970).
UNESCO 1970 attempts to regulate the antiquities trade by absolutizing a "Source Country's" right to cultural material found within its modern borders (without proper import/export documentation). It's a noble goal, but too narrow for something as complex as cultural heritage in Yemen. Yes, let's assist Yemen to align with UNESCO 1970, but Yemen must also recognize the property rights of Yemen's former Jewish communities. We should work with Yemen to return the thousands of Torah scrolls, manuscripts, books, and judaica to the communities now in Israel.
To quote Michael R. Fischbach's Jewish Property Claims Against Arab Countries regarding "Operation Magic Carpet" (pages 50-51):
"Of particular concern to the emigrants was what little moveable property they carried with them, especially communal religious articles such as Torah scrolls and books. ... The Jews were required to leave Torah scrolls and other religious items in Aden before boarding the planes. ... A major problem for Adeni Jews was that a great deal of their property had been destroyed two years earlier during anti-Jewish disturbances in December 1947..."
It is a complex situation, but in the spirit of protecting human history, Yemen is holding a lot of Jewish heritage and should send it all to Israel. Just as the United States acted to protect the sacred heritage of a mistreated people within its national borders (see the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, 1990), Yemen should act to protect the heritage of a people that is no longer represented within its national borders (i.e. Jewish communities and their heritage left in Yemen).

I have personally supported MOUs on almost every occasion that they have been considered.  That support, however, was and is with the understanding that any agreement would comply with the letter and intent of the Cultural Property Implementation Act (CPIA) which is the underlying authority for CPAC.  Unfortunately, the administration of MOUs has not reflected those basic elements of CPIA that protect the rights of private collectors by clearly defining what objects can and should be prohibited. An MOU should clearly spell out the criteria for detention of seizure of objects being imported to the U.S. and that clarity should reflect the elements of law to be considered. In the case of coins and other portable antiquities import restrictions should be limited to coins stolen from museums or those illicitly removed from Morocco and Yemen after the effective date of any governing regulations. These objects have been international trade items for two millenia or more and do not qualify in the widest of interpretations as national patrimony.  If an MOU is adopted in this case, I would hope that the rule of law prevails and that is clearly defined in CPIA.

As an archaeologist with research interests in the effects of collecting and the antiquities market, I would urge the CPAC to support the request of the Republic of Yemen for US import restrictions on poorly-papered archaeological and ethnological material. The unauthorized removal of such material from Yemen strips local citizens of the opportunity to enjoy the rich and mixed cultural heritage of the land they inhabit but also prevents scholarly research on the material in context.

The war that has beleaguered this country since March 2015 has caused much damage to its heritage, both immovable and portable, severely damaging its cultural patrimony. It is evident from what we see surfacing on the US and global antiquities market that there is currently no lack there of apparently freshly-surfaced archaeological and ethnographic material from Yemen. The USA is a major and voracious consumer of these artefacts, whether or not it has paperwork evidencing legal export. It is telling how many US dealers and collectors of dugup antiquities time and time again attempt to oppose any attempt under the CCPIA to keep such material off the US market. In particular we note the trade in Torah scrolls of stated Yemeni provenance, the trade in which the US is implicitly involved. These are often cut up by dealers to make them more suitable as trophy collectables.

When the relatively new Dhamar Regional Museum was bombed in the first few weeks of the war, the ruins were relatively quickly looted of the loose artefacts, many of which have so far not yet surfaced. There have been a number of cases of people being caught at the borders attempting to smuggle artefacts, but objects of types originating (sometimes exclusively) in Yemen are prevalent on the antiquities market showing not all illicit imports can be detected in a war-torn country.

Quite clearly, doing all possible to prevent illicit material passing onto any major market is going to be of substantial benefit in deterring the development of a serious situation of depletion of this resource. There is no need to see anything drastic about keeping illicit artefacts (or those not complying with the liberal measures of the CCPIA) off the US market.

Quite clearly, and in particular in the current situation, the restriction of antiquities originating in Yemen through applying the measures of the CCPIA is not only utterly consistent with but imperative in the general interest of the international community in the interchange of cultural property among nations for cultural, scientific and educational purposes.

Most other countries which are party to the 1970 UNESCO Convention on the Means of Prohibiting and Preventing the Illicit Import, Export and Transfer of Ownership of Cultural Property apply it to the cultural property of all other member states, irrespective, the Convention is after all intended to foster international collaboration and build peace in the minds of men. The US is one of the few countries which applies it selectively, on a country-by-country basis, dividing international partners into better and worse, If the US applies restrictions on imports of artefacts exported from Yemen to only those properly documented, it would only be joining the rest of the international community in implementing the Convention. The US should be a leader in such a concerted effort, not a reluctant tagalong especially given the size and nature of the no-questions-asked US antiquities market and the appetites of those involved in it.

But the 1970 Convention was created not as a means to protect property, but as one of a number of measures intended to bolster the process of bolstering the building of peace in peoples minds. Far more important than soft-diplomatically and demonstratively saving things, Id like to see the State Department and the government of the USA help stop this war, and not abet the antagonists by selling them arms. People are more important than pots.

I write to you today, to voice my support for the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) proposed changes to the rebate system. The proposed rule will not only provide much-needed transparency in the drug pricing system, but it will ensure savings generated by those rebates directly benefit patients with high drug costs instead of middlemen. This will significantly improve access and affordability for seniors and other patients with chronic conditions, leading to better health outcomes and reduced long-term medical spending. I am pleased to see the Administration advancing out-of-pocket cost saving solutions like this one that puts seniors over middlemen {PBMs/Insurers} and I urge you to implement this proposal.

Under section 1001, paragraph (cc) subsections ii and iii, your proposed wording creates a new loophole that pharmacy benefit managers can use to impose fees to providers that do not decrease the overall cost of the drug on the health plan or the consumer. I would suggest adding phasing after chargeback or series of chargebacks to the pharmaceutical manufacturer in paragraph ii.

Under subparagraph iii, this sentence should be re-written to state as follows. "The out-of-pocket price at the point of sale should reflect any reduction in price received from the pharmaceutical manufacturer and health plan sponsor should receive the full value of any reduction in price obtained through chargebacks or a series of chargebacks obtained from the pharamceutical manufacturer."

I would also propose that a rebate safe harbor be put in place to all for the use of manufacturer copayment discount cards for medicare members to reduce their out-of-pocket expenditures provided that the value of the benefit received from these cards is disclosed to the health plan sponsor by the beneficiary for the purposes of adjusting TrOOP. In pharmacy practice it is difficult to explain why medicare member cannot use copay rebate cards in the same manner as other members of the general public.

By allowing the use of copayment cards at the point of sale to medicare members and enforcing a TrOOP adjustment provision, the Medicare plans would still continue to save money by reducing the amount of time members spend in catastrophic coverage. Enforcement of failure to make a TrOOP disclosure already exists under the Federal False Claims Act and would then be subject to penalties under that act.

To do less is a moral disgrace. The proposed MOUs would legitimize Arab governments confiscation of Jewish Communal Property and should not be agreed to or implemented.

If I am understanding the current practice between pharmacy benefit managers (PBM) and manufacturers correctly regarding drug prices, they are hidden and complex, with rebates given and the amount determined between the two. The consumer is left to pay a set price of which they know nothing of initial cost, mark-ups, or backdoor deals. Pharmaceutical prices have risen dramatically over the last few decades, leaving consumers to choose at times between medication and paying for food or rent. It does seem that the PBMs benefit from the lack of transparency. Revision to the Safe Harbor Regulation would help increase clarity and pass along the discount from the manufacturer to the PBM as well as the consumer. It would prevent side price reductions from manufacturers to the PBM and force them to be operating truthfully and not profiting by overcharging consumers. The Pharmaceutical companies fear by eliminating rebates, drug prices will increase however, they have been increasing for so long with no change anywayonly the PBM has been profiting. I am not an economics major but that statement seems to be a threat rather than a concern.

In a prime example, the cost of insulin for diabetic management has doubled in the last decade (Dorsey, 2018). What used to cost $100 to $200 has now gone up to $400 to $500 (Dorsey, 2018). There are no generic substitutes for insulin, and while it is expensive to produce, no groundbreaking revelations have surfaced in a newer, better type of insulin other than what is already available (Campbell, 2018). The three current manufacturers of insulin Sanofi, Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk fully control the manufacturing and price setting of their product because of the patent and legal control (Campbell, 2018). I can see where raising the sticker price and giving PBMs a hidden discount would substantially increase their profits, while unethically leaving the consumer to choose between their medication and living conditions

Drug prices are a significant issue in the American health care system; as the push is for a more value-based system where better to start than holding the multi-million dollar companies accountable for their ethical decisions in under the table deals and price gouging. I think a better name for our countrys health care system would be: The Affordable and Accountable Care Act.

References
Campbell, K. (2018). Insulin costs are skyrocketing. This is why. Retrieved from https://health.usnews.com/health-care/for-better/articles/2018-06-29/whats-behind-the-rising-costs-of-insulin

Dorsey, J. (2018). Cost of diabetes insurance, insulin prices, and complications. Retrieved from https://www.healthedeals.com/blog/save/diabetes-costs/

The complete removal of Safe Harbor provisions for pharmaceuticals, permitting rebates and kickbacks to pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) as well as group purchasing organizations (GPOs), is long overdue. These safe harbors serve no purpose other than to funnel money from health care consumers to PBMs. In so doing they increase US health costs by an estimated $100 billion annually; destroy competition in the prescription drug industry; and thereby reduce 1) the availability of medications, 2) access of consumers to medications, 3) the quality of medications, and 4) patient freedom of choice regarding medications.

As pointed out in the rationale for the proposed rule as well as both Governmental and non-government research, existing PBM rebates in no way fall under the stated purposes for safe harbors, and in contrast have the opposite effect of stifling competition and excluding manufacturers from the marketplace.

As a health care consumer, and therefore a victim of both rising pharmaceutical costs and drug shortages attributed directly to the existing PBM rebates, I would urge broad-based repeal of the existing safe harbors for rebates to PBMs Involving prescription pharmaceuticals.

Dear CPAC Members:

I am writing on behalf of the American Numismatic Association to oppose recent requests to have the United States impose import restrictions on numismatic antiquities originating from Turkish and Tunisian soil. These proposed Memoranda of Understanding would unjustifiably restrict the importation of coins struck in ancient and medieval times in Greek, Roman provincial, Byzantine and later mints.

The ANA is a nonprofit, educational organization chartered by the United States Congress to promote the study and collection of money and related items for research, interpretation and preservation of history from ancient times to the present. The ANA has 25,000 active members, but also represents thousands of collectors in the greater hobby community, many of whom collect and preserve world and ancient coins.

The ANA is deeply concerned that the application of import restrictions on numismatics, such as those already imposed in Italian, Cypriot and Chinese MOUs, adversely impact the long-standing legitimate trade and collection of numismatic items. Most coins do not carry any provenance with them. Thus, a legitimate holder of numismatic material may not be able to establish the necessary historic ownership of legally purchased materials to avoid forfeiture under the contemplated import restrictions in the Turkish and Tunisian MOUs.

Any enforcement would be further complicated by the nature of ancient coins which, unlike archaeological material, were distributed in large numbers through commerce over wide areas beyond those in which they were produced. Thus, ancient coins from Turkey or Tunisia could be found anywhere in Europe or within the boundaries of the former Greek and Roman empires.

U.S. citizens have enjoyed coin collecting - from ancients to moderns - since the American Revolution. President John Quincy Adams was a serious collector of ancient Greek and Roman coins. Other Presidents such as Thomas Jefferson and Theodore Roosevelt appreciated owning the very types of coinage that would be restricted under the proposed Turkish restrictions. The ANA trusts that the Cultural Property Advisory Committee will consider the legitimate interests of coin collectors, coin dealers and all Americans interested in private ownership of ancient, medieval and world money in addressing this issue.

Coins are an important part of our knowledge of the past - produced in tens and hundreds of thousands or more, they are much more common than almost any other historical artifacts, while their size and composition make them much more durable, with the result that ancient and medieval coins survive in large numbers. They are also much more accessible than most artifacts due to their imagery and inscriptions which make them important historical documents for those who can interpret them. Thus, they are an ideal medium for education - and enough have survived to allow coins to be privately owned and collected without depriving academic and museum institutions or endangering our knowledge of the past. As history that can be held in your hands, coins are an excellent gateway for interest in our past - as anyone that has held a 2000-year-old coin can attest.

Continuing efforts to impose import restrictions on coins and related numismatic materials - whether from Turkey, Tunisia, Italy, Greece or any other country - have an adverse impact on the ANA and its educational goals. Import restrictions have the potential to limit and/or eliminate an interest in collecting and learning from ancient numismatic material, as they could be deemed illegal to own and disappear from public awareness. They have already resulted in unwarranted seizures and have caused a reluctance among numismatic collectors to display, travel with or ship their legitimately acquired coins for educational purposes at ANA Summer Seminars. Likewise, researchers and scholars knowledgeable in ancient numismatics are less likely to participate in educational programming in the United States for fear of subjecting their valuable collections to forfeiture, thus depriving American audiences of their knowledge and expertise and access to an important part of our cultural heritage.

On behalf of the ANA, its members and hundreds of thousands of coin collectors and hobbyists throughout the U.S., I hope that you will recommend against import restrictions on numismatic materials from Turkey or Tunisia. Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me.

Sincerely,

Kim Kiick
Executive Director
American Numismatic Association

I wish to state my opposition to the inclusion of ancient coinage in any MOU involving the important of cultural property from Turkey. While it is important to prevent looting and damage to the archaeological record, including preventing the illegal exportation of unique or significant cultural property, most ancient coinages were produced in and survive in great quantities. Unless an item can be directly tied to illegal activity, it should not be the onus of the importer or collector to prove that their property is legitimate.

It also needs to be remembered that many cultural and ethnic groups have occupied the territories now claimed by Turkey. It would be false to claim that the government of Turkey is the legitimate successor to all of these peoples; in particular, to assert their ownership of Armenian cultural property, since the United States Congress has formally recognized the genocide against the Armenian people perpetrated by the Ottoman Empire, the direct predecessor to the Turkish state. Considering the present state of relations between the Turkish government and the Armenian people, allowing them to claim control over Armenian cultural property may endanger those objects.

Lastly, it must be pointed out that some of the most important research on ancient coinage has been done by collectors working outside of traditional academic structures. Many collections of ancient coinage are poorly available, lacking catalogues or any form of digitization, and even academics interested in the subject are often forced to rely on auction catalogues as a major source of data. To exclude insignificant (in the sense of existing in large numbers or being commonly found) items originating in the territories claimed by Turkey from the market would endanger further research on these materials.

I am writing you in opposition of import restrictions on cultural property from Tunisia and Turkey. The entire point of UNESCO was at the outset cultural exchange not the reinforcement of Nationalism through the hoarding of items of cultural property. This is most especially true of common items such as coins which exist in abundance and offer no real scientific value in and of themselves. One could argue their location / find spot may be of value but to aid in reporting and recording this the countries in question could easily copy something like the Portable Antiquities scheme. But for coins and most movable ethnological material private collectors are both better stewards and better embody the spirit of cultural exchange than a Nation State. Also worrisome is that most Nation States have suppressed minorities and one is hard pressed to picture the current Turkish State as the best caretaker of Kurdish ethnological material. Lastly, I have yet to see any published evidence that any of previous MOUs have impacted alleged looting. This is probably because there is no hard evidence linking looting and collecting not are there any serious efforts by countries requesting MOUs to tackle the underlying problem.

I'm writing to oppose the inclusion of ancient coins into MOUs with Turkey and Tunisia.

Money made anciently was mass produced, traveled far beyond their original mint cities, and have been collected and studied for their history, culture, and mythology for over 500 years.

Mass produced money was exchanged beyond the boundaries of the ancient civilizations that produced them. Most coins produced in lands that the current countries Turkey and Tunisia and not found within borders of the ancient civilization that produced them. Imagine a dollar bill that was used to buy goods in Canada and 2000 years later the dollar bill is found in Canada. Should that dollar bill be repatriated to the United States since it was produced there even though it was used to buy goods in Canada and found there? Another example, should the Statue of Liberty be repatriated to France since it was first produced there? Or should olive oil amphoras from Athens that are found in Turkey be given back to Greece? The only fair-minded approach is to make the governing statues for coins is to target the coins FOUND in Turkey and Tunisia and not coins ORIGINATING from Turkey and Tunisia. The MOU unfairly focuses on the ORIGIN of coins from Turkey and Tunisia.

Millions of ancient coins survive to our day. These coins have been found, displayed, appreciated and collected for over 500 years by scholars, European royalty, American Presidents, immigrants from their home countries, and regular collectors like me. They create a tangible link to our shared tradition and classical past. Generally, these coins are not even found in archaeologically sensitive sites. Due to their economic nature they were not viewed as luxury item or display items but rather as a medium of exchange and thus were traded away or hidden away in small pots (hoards) away from buildings and subsequently forgotten. Coins are a special case ancient antiquities due to their common nature and long history of scholarship that warrant a special case exclusion from any MOU.

Finally, the governing statute requires that less drastic remedies be tried before import restrictions. But neither Turkey nor Tunisia has tried systems akin the UK Treasure Act and Portable Antiquities Scheme before seeking restrictions from the United States. In a misguided attempt they are hoping the MOU can provide the remedy they do not.

When considering the MOUs with Turkey and Tunisia please leave ancient coins out of the agreement.

I am opposed to the proposed MOU with Tunisia and Turkey. I am a collector of ancient coins specializing in the Eastern Roman Empire ( Byzantine ). This agreement if passed will hurt the study of ancient coins of all time periods.
