As founder of the nonprofit Ancient Coin Collectors Guild (ACCG), I am obviously opposed to import restrictions on ancient coins. In spite of that, The ACCG has routinely supported MOUs in the past as long as they conform to the letter and intent of the Convention on Cultural Property Implementation Act (CCPIA). Of course, they never havethough Courts and Congress have never performed the oversight required to ensure that import restrictions only apply as contemplated in the CCPIA.

The requests from both Turkey and Tunisia for the U.S. to impose import restrictions on archaeological and ethnological material raise a multitude of concerns about the scope, purpose and administrative process under which the Cultural Property Advisory Committee operates. The legislation adopted in 1983, after more than a decade of careful and serious deliberation by Congress, is today a sham and the guidance to administrators that was so prudently and deliberately included within the legislation is all but ignored today by those charged with serving the public need and interests. Congress understood very well that the rights of private citizens to enjoy the benefits of cultural property as an educational medium and form of social enrichment are every bit as Important as the mandate of national governing bodies to protect their national patrimony. Both can, and should, be treated with respect. Sadly, the past two decades have seen the hard work of legislative committees destroyed. The law that we all are bound to observe (CCPIA) is routinely ignored or perverted by the very administrators who are charged with its enforcement. The advisory committee that was empaneled to assure that a balance of views is maintained has become essentially useless and powerlesssimply a shill for the self-serving bureaucratic machine. Yes, these are harsh criticisms but they are well founded and echoed by a number of past members of CPAC who faced that agonizing reality.

The simple fact is that international trade in cultural property is legal. It has been going on for thousands of years and will continue as long as humans exist on this globe. The reason is just as simple as the fact. Will the myriad array of objects flowing into this country from China today become, at some mystical point in time, the rightful property of China again? People buy, sell and trade the things that they make. Once an object legally leaves the land in which it was made, it becomes the property of all the world. Import restrictions were intended for monumental objects of specific national importance, not for the trinkets of society or the common household items found in every home nationwide. Certainly not for the billions of coins that people have exchanged across borders and oceans every day since the 7th century BC.

As for illegal traffic in objects designated as national patrimony, that is a matter of serious concern and is appropriately dealt with by the laws of every country in which it is an issue. That illegal activity is not what CPAC was established to control. In fact, it cannot be controlled by the normal import/export processes. Criminal acts are best addressed by law enforcement officials. Applying repressive restrictions to legitimate trade is not going to hinder illicit transactions. In fact, it encourages illicit transactions by repressing a timeless market for objects that were never intended to be controlled by CCPIA. Collectors will inevitably buy from the market available. It is better that they buy from a licit market than an illicit market.

As for Turkey in particular, I implore every member of CPAC to carefully read the comments submitted by Dr. Alan Walker in this forum. The Turkish government is the least deserving polity in the world to present a claim to the cultural heritage of the lands they conquered and occupy. They certainly did conquer and exterminate the indigenous peoples of Anatolia, but they did not inherit their culture any more than Americans have inherited the culture of the indigenous peoples who were displaced here. The Turks did not make the objects that they claim the right to remove from trade and in fact they have never treated those objects as part of their national heritage.

Under their Standard Operating Procedures, the State Department and Customs would likely impose wide-sweeping restrictions as a matter of policy. It is time for CPAC to stand firm against this sort of blatant disregard for the protections embodied in CCPIA. If there ever was a place to draw a line in the sand it is over the MOU with Turkey.
Please see the attached comment of Dr. Alan Walker regarding the proposed MOU with Turkey.

Turkey has no legitimate moral claim to cultural artifacts that predate its violent invasion into Asia Minor. Please do not include any Paleolithic, Neolithic, Bronze Age, Iron Age, Greek, Roman, Jewish, or Byzantine objects in this MoU.

I am writing to voice my opposition to the proposed MOU with Tunisia and Turkey.  I am a collector of ancient coins specializing in the Roman provinces of Asia Minor.  My study is already made difficult by the existing Turkish laws and inaccessibility to private and public collections, this would make my research even more difficult.  I believe the MOU is unnecessary and inhibits the lawful collection and study of antiquities.

The governing statute requires that restrictions only be applied on artifacts "first discovered in Turkey or Tunisia. But hoard evidence demonstrates that many Greek and Carthaginian coins circulated extensively outside the confines of those modern nation states. The State Department and U.S. Customs have already recognized this fact for higher denomination Greek coins struck in Greece. To be consistent, any restrictions should not touch higher denomination coins from Turkey or Tunisia, including Roman didrachms, tetradrachms, and gold coins.. At a minimum, this finding should be preserved.
The governing statute requires restrictions only be placed on artifacts of "cultural significance." But coins -- which exist in many multiples-- do not meet that particular criteria.
The governing statute requires that less drastic remedies be tried before import restrictions. But neither Turkey nor Tunisia has tried systems akin the UK Treasure Act and Portable Antiquities Scheme before seeking restrictions.
The governing statute requires that restrictions be consistent with the interests of the international community in cultural exchanges. But restrictions diminish the ability of American collectors (particularly Turkish or Tunisian Americans) to appreciate the cultural heritage of these countries and greatly limit people to people contacts with other collectors in Europe.
Much of what Turkey would be allowed to claw back if a MOU is granted are cultural artifacts of displaced Greek, Armenian and Jewish populations. That simply should not be allowed to happen as it would only reward Turkey for its harsh policies to ethnic and religious minorities.

Please do not include ancient coins in any MOU. I strongly oppose the proposed MOU's with Tunisia and Turkey. They cover coins that have no cultural connection with their present-day governments and they cover coins that may have left the country legally long ago. Inevitably the enforcement expands to objects of no cultural significance. Ancient coin types exist in many multiples so individual coins are rarely of any cultural significance. Turkey and Tunisia already have far more unstudied coins than they know what to do with and the US does not need the hassle of judging what is and what is not covered.

Collecting is good for scholarship, not bad as MOU's seem to suggest. The "scholarly" reasons to include them do not hold up under scrutiny. It may be that those governments think they have value (they do) and want to confiscate coins. There are many instances of local officials, including museum curators, illicitly selling coins they were supposedly responsible for. Outlawing traffic means criminals take it over (It doesn't go away). Collectors are far better custodians of ancient coins than those governments. Let coins come into the US where any information they contain will have a much better chance of becoming public.

I have been told I am the most-cited scholar in the area of ancient coins. I am an elected Fellow of The American Numismatic Society. My interest was kindled by collecting and my contributions would not have occurred without collecting. Furthermore, my area of speciality (die-study statistics) relies on numerous published examples of coins, the great majority of which were published by dealers for collectors. Without easy access to ancient coins on the market, I venture to say more than half the Ph.D.s in ancient numismatics could not have been written! A substantial percentage of the scholarly works on ancient-coins were written by amateurs who became experts because of their collections. (I actively consult with collector/scholars.)

I suspect the proposal is being promoted by those sympathetic to the arguments of the archaeological community who oppose collecting. But those arguments are wrong and misguided and MOU's will not have the consequences they hope for. If the objective is to preserve archaeological information then suppressing collecting is a misguided approach that will inevitably fail. Furthermore, it will have negative unintended consequences that will far outweigh the potential (but illusory) positives. After paying attention to this for a long time I still wonder why very intelligent people in the archaeological information game remain PC and don't risk saying the obvious "This approach won't work!"

We, in the US, would like to think that a person is who he is, which is not determined by his fore-bearers. The creators of ancient coins are long gone. Cultural patrimony belongs, not to the state happening to occupy certain territory (often of an unrelated culture), but to the world. Recall that Turkey claims Greek coins found on its soil, and Greece claimed an EID MAR Roman denarius arguably found on its soil. Claims of cultural patrimony are hypocritical. Governments regard coins as having value and are as greedy as any collector.

I could go on and on rebutting arguments for including ancient coins in MOU's, but I won't. Please contact me if you want relevant facts.

I hope if you disregard my advice and include ancient coins that the US gets something substantial in return.

In summary, *Please do not include ancient coins in any MOU.*

I am a firm believer that heritage of a country should remain in wherever it was unearthed. It is much more meaningful and valuable this way. It gives the museum visitor a better perspective because he/she will be able to connect the artifact with the city/country that he/she is visiting.

The continued addition of ancient coins into MOUs is frustrating and upsetting for me. I am a collector and also work in the business. While the market is changing to try to attach pedigrees to coins the reality is that there are so many coins that have been circulating around for years and yet fall under the restrictions for the US. The thought behind the MOUs was to protect cultural property and hopefully to stop unnecessary looting of sites. The reality is that when the US agrees without nations that dont have fair rights for their citizens regarding discovery of coins or antiquities it results only in a larger black market. Research done to prove that coins have contributed to the rise in terrorism has been dispelled. Oil is likely the bigger issue. Countries need to create powerful programs like Englands treasure act and PAS. This incentives people to report findings and then get reimbursed for their discoveries. It also then allows important find data to be supported. Creating further MOUs does NOT stop looting it only promotes illegal activities. Please do not do continue this trend that services to hurt collectors and small businesses.

I would please request that numismatic items, such as coins be excluded from this and any other MOU. I request this as an active researcher and owner of numismatic items, most of which are extremely common and low value, but as a whole are vital to my research. I routinely acquire ancient coins today to aid in my research. These coins are almost never worthy of inclusion in museum collections. I'm very concerned about my ability to transport these out of and into the United States. Considering the large number of ancient coins legally imported into the United States today, it is difficult to imagine how specific numismatic items covered by this MOU could possibly be distinguished except by numismatic experts in customs.
This is an absolute cash grab by a government that has no connection not right to pull off this heist. And this should be stopped.

To whom it may concern:

I would like to voice my opposition to the inclusion of coins in any import restrictions under an MOU with the Turkish government. I would ask that the following points be taken into consideration:

1. All ancient coins circulated widely in their time. It is therefore not uncommon to find coins minted in Asia Minor outside the confines of the modern nation state of Turkey. Clearly the current Turkish government would have no right to request restrictions on items not found within their borders. However, it is impossible to distinguish a coins found in Turkey from a coin found in another country.
2. Ancient coins were produced in mass quantities, for use by the populace. While interesting, generally they do not rise to the standard of being an artifact of cultural significance.
3. It is not clear that the Turkish government has attempted other remedies to address looting before turning to import restrictions. There are innovative strategies such as the UK Treasure Act that seek to find a balance between preserving cultural heritage and the recognition of personal property rights.
4. Collecting ancient coins acts as an important gateway for individuals to develop an interest and understanding of both general history and ancient cultures around the world.
5. Ancient coins are not the subject of import restrictions in the majority of the world. On what basis should special restrictions be placed on American citizens?

I appreciate your consideration of the interests of American ancient coin collectors in the evaluation of an MOU with the Turkish government.

Sincerely,

Michael Wells

For generations, people from all walks of life have enjoyed the hobby of coin collecting. It's a thought provoking hobby that teaches an appreciation for our history and heritage as a western culture. Much of our country's culture and thought is based on ideas handed down through the millennia by Greek and Roman cultures. Our Founding Fathers were well read in the area of ancient literature and governance, and at least one of our presidents, John Quincy Adams, collected ancient coins. At nearly 60 years old, I am a long-time collector of ancient coins, starting at age 17. I walk in these same footsteps and find great satisfaction in teaching myself, my children, and my grandchildren about history through my collection.

There has lately been a movement to try and include coins in the concept of cultural heritage belonging only to a country of origin. Coins have always been minted in very large quantities, quantities large enough to facilitate all levels of daily commerce for entire civilizations that stretched from the Atlantic Ocean to the East China Sea. They are not rare and are only used by archeologists to date sites. They are too small to effectively be shown in museums, and yet they are loved and cherished in the hands of collectors.
A good example would be bronze coins struck by Constantine the Great. These coins bearing his name and likeness were struck over a 30 year period by 19 different mints scattered across the entire Roman world, from London to Thessalonica. The number of these coins still in existence is staggering as they provided for the daily purchase of consumer goods for the entire Roman Empire. These coins could be considered as the Lincoln cents of the day and you can buy a clear example for less than $3 on eBay.

In closing, I would ask you to consider coins for what they are, a common piece of history that belongs to the world, not just the country in which they were struck.

I am opposed to the proposed MOU which would restrict importation of "cultural" objects from Turkey.  In the recent past, the Turkish government has claimed ownership of objects, notably rare coins, that have absolutely no connection with Turkish culture.  I refer specifically to the so-called Elmali hoard of ancient and archaic coins, all inscribed in Greek, which was claimed as integral to Turkish cultural heritage because the hoard was allegedly unearthed on Turkish territory.  In fact, the MOU would also apply to objects of Jewish and Armenian heritage as well.  Much of what Turkey would be allowed to "claw back" if a MOU is granted are cultural artifacts of displaced Greek, Armenian and Jewish populations.  (The Turks have a proven history of genocidal attacks on these peoples, now confirmed by resolutions passed by the US Senate and House of Representatives).. That simply should not be allowed to happen as it would only reward Turkey for its harsh policies to ethnic and religious minorities.

CPAC should deny or limit any import restrictions contemplated under proposed new MOUs in docket DOS-2019-0043. The request from Turkey and Tunisia are a gross overreach and are an unwarranted and unnecessary restraint on scholarship, property, and trade. This is a case of cultural misappropriation under the guise of cultural protection.

In the rise and fall of empires, coinage was minted and circulated across vast spaces far beyond the national borders of today's Turkey and Tunisia. To subject all that coinage to restrictions is a huge distortion of historical borders.

The huge mass of coinage considered does not warrant the tag 'cultural significance.' Coinage is overwhelmingly common. Just check your pocket. Would you accept the restrictions being requested in the MOUs for them? Set too low a bar and the 'law' of unintended consequences looms large.

Even where cultural significance can be proved -and this is rare- U.S. statutes mandate less drastic measures should be deployed before attempting import restrictions.

After all that, any restrictions should be narrowly construed, and avoid impacting Roman, Byzantine, Carthaginian, and Islamic coins, and well as the coins used in cross-border trade, namely silver and gold coinage.

Please consider the issues carefully and thoughtfully, and do not implement unwarranted restrictions.

I'm sorry, but this is a terrible proposal as far as coins are concerned. Unlike Roman statues and Greek vases, these are mass-produced items that survive in millions, with just a very few culturally or historically significant rarities among them. Collectors in North America and Europe study and catalogue them, providing a service for which museums don't have the resources and supporting and underpinning the work of the professional numismatiic scholars. It's a fantasy that museum staff and scholars in countries like Turkey or Tunisia will be able to handle all this material. The best that can be hoped is that at least they won't sell the coins off to local criminals, who will then "export" them to the West - a flourishing practice that makes a mockery of all the high-flown rhetoric about "protecting the national heritage". The heritage will end up rotting in museum cellars, or on the booming international black market in antiquities.
Wouldn't it be better to look for intelligent, nuanced, win-win solutions here?
The first thing to do would be to ensure the security of all archeological sites in these countries. Pretty hopeless, that, at least until you eradicate corruption in the police and local authorities and arrest the middlemen who buy from the grave-robbers. Unfortunately, the middlemen are often rich and powerful men with important friends.
The second thing would be to give museums the right to review all finds and buy those that are of significance (like the British treasure trove legislation). Yes, buy them - not confiscate them and throw them in the cellar or sell them to a friend or relative. This right could be extended internationally, so that Country X, when it spots an item of "national interest" on sale in a U.S. auction or dealer's catalogue, could claim it back, though only after (1) justifying its importance and (2) compensating the owner. (The U.S. Government could help here with generous funding support if it so wished.)

I write to you today, to voice my support for the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) proposed changes to the rebate system. The proposed rule will not only provide much-needed transparency in the drug pricing system, but it will ensure savings generated by those rebates directly benefit patients with high drug costs instead of middlemen. This will significantly improve access and affordability for seniors and other patients with chronic conditions, leading to better health outcomes and reduced long-term medical spending. I am pleased to see the Administration advancing out-of-pocket cost saving solutions like this one that puts seniors over middlemen {PBMs/Insurers} and I urge you to implement this proposal.

I strongly oppose the proposed regulation in its current form. I agree that unique sculptures and artifacts should have proper provenance and may represent cultural property, coins were intended to circulate and are therefore not the property of any individual country.

The Portable Antiquities Scheme in the UK is a great example of how to document finds and should be mirrored in Turkey and other nations. Limiting any export would be a massive loss for academia and the scholarship of coinage.

As an archaeologist, I am a firm believer that artifacts should remain in their country of origin unless one has received explicit permission to export the object. By making sure that one receives permission to export any item of cultural heritage, one ensures that the artifact is properly obtained and maintained.
It is extremely important to act to protect cultural heritage anywhere in the world. In this case, Turkish efforts/indifference is not enough, so the US must be proactive.

Please exclude most or all coins from the MOU with the Republic of Turkey.

I am writing as an American collector of ancient coins. I collect ancient Greek coins. I import ten or 20 coins minted in Greek from dealers and auction houses in Germany and the UK. Some of these coins have paperwork dating back to the 1960s, but sometimes there is no paperwork because the coins entered Western European collections during the Ottoman period during which time there were no records or the records have been lost.

There are hundreds of thousands of collectable coins without paperwork. Restricting their entry into the United States will create a "grey market" allowing black market items to enter disguised as "orphaned" legal coins when customers are confused. Please work instead with the Republic of Turkey to create a framework for a legal trade, especially in Greek and early Christian items.

Many of the coins minted on the territory of the Republic of Turkey were created by Greek and Armenian people. Turkey does not do a great job highlighting the culture of the peoples who inhabited the land before the Seljuk Turks arrived in the 11th century.

Please harmonize any agreements so that Americans have the same restrictions that EU citizens have. We should not be the first nation to prohibit imports of early coins. American collectors should have the same rights and responsibilities as British and German collectors when it comes to Greek and Roman artifacts from the region of Turkey.

Many of my comments also apply to coins of Tunisia. Please consider exempting coins from any MOUs with that country.

Please find attached my letter concerning the proposed MOU with Turkey.

Omur Harmansah
Associate Professor of Art History
School of Art and Art History
University of Illinois at Chicago

RE: Proposed MOU with Republic of Turkey

I am writing on behalf of the International Association of Professional Numismatists ("IAPN") concerning the Cultural Property Advisory Committee's ("CPAC's") review of a proposed Memorandum of Understanding ("MOU") with the Republic of Turkey. The small businesses of the numismatic trade ask this Committee to pay close attention to the statutory requirements found in the Cultural Property Implementation Act, 19 U.S.C. 2601-2613 ("CPIA") before approving what will certainly be a controversial MOU that would recognize Turkish government rights to the cultural goods of displaced Greek, Armenian and Assyrian-Syriac minority populations. Indeed, the very idea that the U.S. Government would recognize the rights of the modern Turkish State to the material remains of these groups should give great pause not only to the members of CPAC, but to the entire U.S. State Department leadership, particularly its political appointees responsible for the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs and Public Diplomacy.

Of course, IAPN is particularly interested in how CPAC addresses the issue of historical coins, which are probably amongst the most common ancient artifacts. The "public summary" of the Turkish request is silent about whether import restrictions on coins are contemplated, but if history is any guide, proponents of this MOU will seek import restrictions on all types of cultural goods, including coins created by the ancestors of displaced Greek and Armenian minorities. Leaving aside whether coins that exist in many multiples can be restricted under the CPIA's "cultural significance" test, or whether there are alternatives to import restrictions, such as the establishment of a Portable Antiquity Scheme, the critical issue is whether it is proper to assume coins of types struck or sometimes found in Turkey were in fact "first discovered" there so that they would be subject to Turkish "export control." 19 U.S.C. 2601. Indeed, this is particularly true for the imperial mints at Greek speaking ancient Antioch and Byzantium/Constantinople. Those mints issued huge numbers of coins for Alexander the Great and his Hellenistic successors, the Romans, and the Byzantines. Such imperial issues that were struck there and elsewhere in what is today Turkey were never intended to circulate only within the confines of modern-day Turkish nation state. Indeed, scholarly evidence demonstrates that ancient "Turkish" coinswith the possible exception of some local bronze civic issues -- are often found outside of the confines of modern day "Turkey," which would make any restrictions imposed upon them solely predicated on where they were made or are sometimes found contrary to the CPIA's statutory intent. Ancient Coin Collectors Guild v. U.S. Customs and Border Protection ("ACCG v. CBP"), 801 F. Supp. 2d 383, 407 n. 25 (D. Md. 2011) ("Congress only authorized the imposition of import restrictions on objects that were 'first discovered within, and [are] subject to the export control by the State Party.").

To the extent CPAC nonetheless approves of restrictions, CPAC should provide explicit direction to U.S. Customs and Border Protection ("CBP"), the U.S. Government enforcement agency, to ensure coins are not repatriated to the modern Turkish nation state merely because they are of types found on some designated list. In particular, any import restrictions on imperial types that circulated throughout the Empires of Alexander and his Hellenistic successors, the Romans, and the Byzantines and which, therefore, cannot be assumed to be found in Turkey must be framed explicitly to ensure that they only apply to coins actually found in Turkeyand hence which are also subject to the export control of Turkish authorities. 19 U.S.C. 2601, 2604. Furthermore, any such restrictions should also be conditioned on allowing historical coins to leave Turkey with export permits, an assumption found both in the UNESCO Convention and the CPIA. 1970 UNESCO Convention, Art. 6; 19 U.S.C. 2606. Allowing U.S. coin collectors to purchase and legally import such coins would only help stimulate tourism which is essential to the local Turkish economy, and would further honor the CPIA's injunction that less drastic remedies be considered. 19 U.S.C. 2602 (a) (C) (ii).

Our complete comments and research about the circulation of Turkish mint coins in international commerce are attached.

Dear Chairperson and Members of the Cultural Property Advisory Committee,

I write to you on behalf of a dozen maritime and nautical archaeologists affiliated with the non-profit 501(c)3 Institute of Nautical Archaeology (INA) who have been conducting archaeological excavation and research in Turkey for more than five decades.

In 1960, a young archaeologist at the University of Pennsylvania pioneered the first scientific underwater excavation of an ancient shipwreck. That man was Dr. George F. Bass, known today as the Father of Underwater Archaeology, and the site was the Late Bronze Age shipwreck at Cape Gelidonya, Turkey (ca. 1200 B.C.).

Following the 1960 excavation, the Turkish Ministry of Culture granted Bass permission to exhibit the Cape Gelidonya artifacts in Bodrum, and gradually the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology was realized. Over the next five decades, the Turkish Ministry of Culture granted INA archaeologists official permission to excavate, conserve, research, and study well over a dozen ancient shipwrecks in Turkish waters:

Byzantine shipwreck at Yassada (626 A.D.): 1961-1964
Late Roman shipwreck at Yassada (4th century A.D.): 1969-1974
Ottoman shipwreck at Yassada (16th century A.D.): 1969-1974
Hellenistic shipwreck at Sere Liman (275 B.C.): 1977-1979
Medieval glass wreck at Sere Liman (1025 A.D.): 1977-1979
Late Bronze Age shipwreck at Uluburun(1305 B.C.): 1984-1994
Byzantine shipwreck at Bozburun (880 A.D.): 1995-1998
Classical Greek shipwreck at Tekta Burnu (425 B.C.): 1999-2001
Archaic Greek shipwreck at Pabu Burnu (530 B.C.): 2002-2003
Late Hellenistic column wreck at Kzlburun (1st century B.C.): 2005-2011
(8) Byzantine shipwrecks at Yenikap (7th-10th centuries A.D.): 2004-2013

In 1976, INA affiliated with Texas A&M University, and the graduate Nautical Archaeology Program (NAP) was established as an independent academic unit. Over the past 40 years, dozens of NAP graduate students pursuing Master's or doctoral degrees have received (and continue to receive) archaeological field training on INA shipwreck excavations in Turkey.

Current NAP students and INA Research Associates working in Turkey utilize INA's Bodrum Research Center (BRC), which features artifact and wood conservation laboratories, an archaeological research library, and a 20-person residence hall and kitchen. The BRC is also home to INA's Turkish-flagged archaeological research vessel and two-person submersible, as well as a wide variety of survey, excavation, and safety equipment.

The BRC is staffed by 20 individuals including a team of conservators who work closely with the staff of the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology, where artifacts and hull remains from INA-excavated shipwrecks are on public display in exhibits that educate visitors about the importance of our shared maritime past.

With this letter I wish to express, on behalf of INA researchers conducting archaeological survey and excavation in Turkey for the past 50 years, our collective support for the Government of Turkey's request for import restrictions on Turkish archaeological and ethnological materials from the prehistoric to the Ottoman era. It is paramount that the U.S. make a good-faith effort to prevent Turkey's cultural patrimony from entering our country illegally. A Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the U.S. and Turkey will absolutely be advantageous in terms of enhancing the protection of cultural heritage, nurturing the collaborative spirit that has characterized underwater archaeology in Turkey since the 1960s, and encouraging the international exchange of cultural material.

In 2008, with official permission of the Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism, 75 objects from the Late Bronze Age shipwreck at Uluburun traveled from the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology to the Metropolitan Museum in New York City, as part of a stunning exhibit entitled Beyond Babylon: Art, Trade, and Diplomacy in the Second Millennium B.C.

Turkey is the birthplace of scientific underwater archaeology in the Mediterranean. In 2020, as we mark the 60th anniversary of Bass' pioneering fieldwork at Cape Gelidonya, Turkey remains at the forefront of our discipline in large part because of the Turkish Government's commitment to scientific excavation and conservation of underwater cultural heritage.

On behalf of all INA archaeologists who have dedicated their careers to the excavation, conservation, preservation, and publication of the physical remains of our shared maritime past, please support the Turkish Government's request for import restrictions on archaeological and ethnological material from Turkey's prehistoric through Ottoman era.

Respectfully,

Deborah N. Carlson, Ph.D.
President, Institute of Nautical Archaeology
Associate Professor, Nautical Archaeology Program
Sara W. and George O. Yamini Professor of Nautical Archaeology
Texas A&M University
College Station, TX 77843-4352

The Tunisian request is overly broad and does not define Tunisia's cultural patrimony. According to the US State Department web site, Tunisia seeks U.S. import restrictions on archaeological and ethnological material representing Tunisia's cultural patrimony. Tunisia gained independence from France in 1957, 63 years ago. The coins that passed through (not struck in) what is now Tunisia is vast. The number of coins certainly exceeds many millions. The risk of approving Tunisia's request without more specificity is that it could sweep in NEARLY ALL COINS STRUCK IN THE WORLD in the past 2600 years. I request that the State Department delay approval and request further refinement from Tunisia as well as additional public comment.

Coins are portable trade units that are often decommissioned and/or demonetized. My neighbor unearthed an early 19th century swedish copper coin while gardening in Northeast Minneapolis. Minnesota was a magnet for scandinavians. Though numismatically worthless, it was fun and meaningful to him and his children. As a tangible item, it only tells a common old story. Sort of like this, 'it was minted, it was used, dispersed, buried and then found'. Soon it will be lost again.
The vast majority of coins do not tell any particular story. They were practically always produced in vast numbers to facilitate forever 'new' types of trade. Most stayed local and were lost, buried, melted, saved . . . whatever. Their mass production specifically for trade uses, renders this 'category of human artifact' unlike virtually anything else that may be under legal consideration to conserve and preserve geographically and culturally imperiled narratives.
I oppose this MOU, especially the inclusion of coins, for the reasons so cogently detailed by Alan Walker, Randolph J. Myers, and Wayne Sayles.

As noted by most in every other MOU, coins should not be included in these restrictions. Coins by their nature were minted in the hundreds of thousands if not millions and were intended by their nature.

Identifying coins as the property of heritage the modern state that exists on the soil where the coin was minted has always been ludicrous. It is even worse in the case of Turkey where Greek heritage is now evidently the property of Turkey rather than the world.

As noted above coins have always traveled. Ancient coin hoards time and again have shown coins that were minted hundreds if not thousands of miles away. The fact that the Kingdom of Saba would imitate coins of Athens makes it clear that the celators in Southern Yemen knew what an Athenian owl was. Likewise these influences are evident on the coins found in Turkey and Tunisia.

And yet, time and time again the State department imposes restrictions on coins which make no sense. And this is positively harmful to our study of the past since it has been private numismatists who have conducted research and provided the bulk of of our historical knowledge gleaned from coins. But the state department seems committed to killing an ancient hobby just so that countries can arbitrarily claim ownership of coins from states whose borders may not even correspond to its own.

Under the logic of the state department in these MOUs, coins of the Byzantine Empire minted in Constantinopole which reflect Greek culture and influenced money across the world are arbitrarily the property of Turkey. Coins of ancient greek city states which reflect Hellenistic culture that spread from the Pillars of Hercules to India arbitrarily belong to Turkey. The same warped logic is applied to coins Carthage, the Vandals, the Exharchate of Carthage etc even though Modern Tunisia does not even come close to encompassing these states. This is frankly insane.

Please stop hurting education and the pursuit of knowledge with these MOUs

RE: Proposed MOU with Tunisia

I am writing on behalf of the International Association of Professional Numismatists ("IAPN") concerning the Cultural Property Advisory Committee's ("CPAC's") review of a proposed Memorandum of Understanding ("MOU") with the Republic of Tunisia. The small businesses of the numismatic trade ask this Committee to pay close attention to the statutory requirements found in the Cultural Property Implementation Act, 19 U.S.C. 2601-2613 ("CPIA") before approving yet another MOU on behalf of yet another MENA government with a long history of authoritarianism. The fact that Tunisia recently held free elections and is on a path to Democracy, is, if anything, more of a reason for CPAC to ensure that its recommendations reflect the rule of law, rather than simply a way to provide the Tunisian cultural bureaucracy with the same exceptionally broad import restrictions recently provided to other authoritarian MENA Governments, most recently nearby Algeria.

Few official details have emerged to justify any MOU with Tunisia. Even a "public summary" that recently appeared on the Cultural Heritage Center website provides little more than fragmentary information about the request. Given the paucity of information provided, CPAC should question whether the patrimony of Tunisia really is in danger from the pillage of archaeological or ethnological material, or whether this is yet another situation where the U.S. Government is in effect being asked to enforce confiscatory local laws promulgated when Tunisia was a dictatorship that will do far more to "claw back" "undocumented" material that left Tunisia during a long era of political and economic engagement with France, a colonial power, than address current looting.

Of course, IAPN is particularly interested in how CPAC addresses the issue of historical coins, which are probably amongst the most common ancient artifacts. Leaving aside whether coins that exist in many multiples can be restricted under the CPIA's "cultural significance" test, or whether there are alternatives to import restrictions, such as the establishment of a Portable Antiquity Scheme, the critical issue is whether it is proper to assume coins of types struck or sometimes found in Tunisia were in fact "first discovered" there so that they would be subject to Tunisian "export control." 19 U.S.C. 2601. Indeed, this is particularly true for the imperial mint at Carthage. That mint (or mints) issued huge numbers of coins for the Carthaginians, the Romans, the Vandals, and the Byzantines. Such imperial issues were never intended to circulate only within the confines of modern-day Tunisia. Indeed, scholarly evidence demonstrates that recorded hoards of ancient "Tunisian" coins are found far more often outside Tunisia than within its borders. That factual reality would make any restrictions imposed upon Carthage mint coins solely predicated on where they were made or are sometimes found contrary to the CPIA's statutory intent. Ancient Coin Collectors Guild v. U.S. Customs and Border Protection ("ACCG v. CBP"), 801 F. Supp. 2d 383, 407 n. 25 (D. Md. 2011) ("Congress only authorized the imposition of import restrictions on objects that were 'first discovered within, and [are] subject to the export control by the State Party.").

To the extent CPAC nonetheless approves of restrictions, CPAC should provide explicit direction to U.S. Customs and Border Protection ("CBP"), the U.S. Government enforcement agency, to ensure violence is not done to statutory intent. In particular, any import restrictions on imperial types that circulated throughout the Empires of the Carthaginians, Romans, Vandals and Islamic Dynasties cannot be assumed to be found in Tunisia, and must, therefore, be framed explicitly to make clear that they only apply to coins actually found in Tunisiaand hence which are subject to the export control of Tunisian authorities. 19 U.S.C. 2601, 2604. Furthermore, any such restrictions should also be conditioned on allowing historical coins to leave Tunisia with export permits, an assumption found both in the UNESCO Convention and the CPIA. 1970 UNESCO Convention, Art. 6; 19 U.S.C. 2606. Allowing U.S. coin collectors to purchase and legally import such coins would only help stimulate tourism which is essential to the local Tunisian economy.

Please see our full comments and research about the circulation of Carthage mint coins attached.

As an archaeologist who has been working in Turkey for over 35 years, I write in strong support of Turkey's request for a cultural property agreement with the United States. I support with request for two reasons: the extraordinary richness of Turkey's endangered cultural and ethnological heritage, and the great value of the study and research opportunities available for American students and scholars working in Turkey.

I first traveled to Turkey as a college student in 1980 in order to participate in Harvard University's archaeological excavations at Sardis. I continued to work at Sardis until 1992, rising to the position of Assistant Director after completing the Ph.D. at the University of California at Berkeley. In 1993, I joined the faculty of New York University, and served as Co-Director of the NYU-sponsored excavations at Aphrodisias in Turkey until 2006. From 2005 to 2009, I also directed an archaeological survey of the region around Aphrodisias. I joined the faculty of the University of Michigan in 2006. In 2014, in cooperation with colleagues from Brown University and Union College, I started a new research project in Turkey at the ancient city of Notion. This project received a three-year NEH grant in 2018.

My special expertise is in Greek and Roman civilization, and the importance of Turkey's archaeological heritage for ancient history cannot be overestimated, from the time of the Trojan War, which was fought on Turkish soil in ca. 1200 BC, to the establishment of Constantinople, modern Istanbul, as the new capital of the Roman empire in the early 4th century AD. Foreign archaeologists have been working in Turkey for 150 years, and the promotion of archaeological research has been a significant concern of governmental authorities since the early days of the Republic of Turkey.

In spite of the well-coordinated efforts of the Ministry of Culture, however, looting of archaeological sites remains a major problem, often stimulated by the demands of the international illegal antiquities market, as I can attest from personal experience. When we arrived at Aphrodisias in the summer of 1993, we found that thieves had broken into our storage facilities, and chiseled the head off an important Roman sculpture. Upon our return to the US that fall, my colleague Bert Smith happened to notice that very head in the window of an antiquities dealer on Madison Avenue in New York. He immediately altered the FBI, and fortunately that head was returned to Turkey, where it has now been reattached to its body and put on display in the Aphrodisias Museum. But such happy endings are rare, and it is surely the case that many more such stolen antiquities go unrecovered.

A new agreement to impose import restrictions on cultural and ethnological materials from Turkey to the US would certainly hinder the international traffic in illegally excavated antiquities - and it is important to emphasize that the damage done by antiquities thieves in Turkey is not limited to the specific monuments they steal. Incalculable harm is done to archaeological sites throughout the country by looters in search of treasure even where none is found. Every year when we return to Notion we find new evidence of illegal excavation on the site, even though we work closely with the local police (gendarmerie) and the staff of the archaeological museum in nearby Ephesus to hinder looters.

The agreement requested by the government of Turkey would also support continued good relations between Turkey and American colleges, universities, museums, and other cultural institutions carrying out research and teaching programs in Turkey - with beneficial results for all parties. More rather than less involvement by American and other foreign researchers in Turkey would surely help to secure the country's cultural and ethnological heritage, while also providing invaluable study and research opportunities to non-Turkish students and scholars.

Finally, to respond briefly to the comments submitted by collectors opposing the MOU with Turkey, let me say as a former Museum Director that while I have great respect for the role that collectors have played in the history of classical archaeology, and while I believe that there is considerable common ground between collectors and research scholars, I also believe strongly that the collecting community should limit its activities to legal markets, i.e., to materials not prohibited by the 1970 UNESCO convention on cultural property. I would also add that in my experience as an expert consultant, ICE investigates cases of potentially illegal importation of cultural materials fairly and judiciously.

Let me conclude by reiterating my strong support for the proposed agreement between Turkey and the United States, which will provide Turkey with a valuable tool in securing its rich cultural heritage, and promote cooperative relations to the benefit of both parties, including American students and scholars.

Dear US Department of State officials,

Any regulations related to the importation of ancient coinage from Turkey will raise serious challenges related to applicability, namely in relation to the determination of what is a Turkish coin. Such challenges call for careful expert study.

The most clear example of this challenges is related to coinage of the Roman era.

During the "late Roman" period of the Roman Empire - generally taken as meaning the late third through to fifth centuries AD - Roman coinage was struck at a series of approximately 15 mints scattered across the territory of the Empire. Five of these mints were on the territory of the modern state of Turkey - Heraclea, Constantinople, Nicomedia, Cyzicus and Antioch.

Coinage struck at these Imperial-controlled mints was then distributed throughout the Roman Empire and beyond. This distribution began immediately after striking and continued, due to normal coin circulation, throughout the duration of the Roman Empire.

As an example of this distribution, figures from the UK's PAS (Portable Antiquities Scheme) website (finds.org.uk), which records only local finds made by the public in England and Wales and voluntarily reported, registered (as of January 07, 2020) the following coins struck at these mints:

Heraclea: 105 examples
Constantinople: 1,054 examples
Nicomedia: 112 examples
Cyzicus: 181 examples
Antioch: 309 examples

Thus we have 1,761 coins struck on the territory of modern Turkey, reported as found by members of the UK public in recent years. We can assume that such finds almost entirely represent coins which appeared in the UK in ancient times - over a millennia and half before the creation of the modern state of Turkey.

This distribution pattern of Roman coinage can be found in countries across north, west, east and south Europe as well as the Middle east and North Africa - in other words through the extent of the Roman Empire.

How does one determine what coins fall under the aegis of such an agreement? The argumentation that any coin struck in the territory of modern Turkey is a Turkish coin is ridiculous. Can a coin struck by Roman Imperial authorities in Constantinople (modern Istanbul) in the 320s AD, but found by a detectorist in England (where it had lain in the ground for approximately 16 1/2 centuries) be considered a Turkish coin? Of course not. What then is the implication for such an MOU on the many thousands of such coins on the market today?

These same issues also apply to "Greek" coinage - much of which was struck in Turkey, as well as Byzantine and early Islamic.

Based on the above facts, I would advise the responsible authorities to take the time to investigate this matter carefully and take the results of such an investigation into consideration when developing or implementing any policy decisions. Any professional numismatist can provide an extensive list of sources that delve into these matters in much more detail.

Thank you for your consideration.

Dear Members of the Cultural Property Advisory Committee,

I write as an archaeologist who has lived and worked in Turkey. I am also a former federal program officer, now retired, at the National Endowment for the Humanities, where I served on the NEH task force that designed and implemented the agency's grant program for the preservation of cultural heritage materials in Iraq following the beginning of the war in 2003.

I offer my strongest support for approving the request made by the Government of Turkey to the Government of the United States in re Article 9 of the 1970 UNESCO Convention on the Means of Prohibiting and Preventing the Illicit Import, Export, and Transfer of Ownership of Cultural Property. This request seeks U.S. import restrictions on archaeological and cultural materials representing cultures from the Paleolithic to the Ottoman period, a heritage that spans over 12,000 years.

Turkey's support for the import restrictions is fully justified, and these efforts serve the interest of the United States and the global community, as well. The country holds a unique set of previously discovered and not yet revealed (and therefore potentially vulnerable) resources reflecting the broadest possible range of human development. These include evidence for some of the earliest manifestations of religion (at the pre-agricultural site of Gobleki Tepe), early agricultural communities such as atal Hyk, sites that embody some of the key participants in the second millennium BCE Biblical history of the eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East (Boazky, the capital of the Hittite empire), the first instances of engagement by Near Eastern monarchies in the religious centers of ancient Greece in the following millennium (Gordion, where the 8th century BCE king was reported to have dedicated his throne to Apollo's shrine at Delphi), sites that play critical roles in the earlies masterpieces of Western literature (Hissarlik/Troy in the Homeric epics), and sites playing a key role in Roman imperial and early modern Middle Eastern history (Ephesus and the settlements of Galatia in the New Testament and Constantinople/Istanbul and other sites of the later Roman Imperial era through the Ottoman Empire).

I can also assure the committee of the deep interest and pride that the Turkish populace takes in its archaeological and cultural heritage. It is particularly noteworthy that this pride extends back to pre-Islamic times and includes an interest in non-Muslim as well as Muslim remains. In other words, the country's legal support for cultural heritage preservation is fully matched by popular support for that effort. The proposed U.S. import restrictions would therefore support Turkey's national commitment to its heritage while supporting the preservation of a heritage that is directly aligned with our own country's sense of its global heritage.

The size of Turkey and the richness and extent of its archaeological and ethnographical heritage mean that Turkey continually works to maintain control over its heritage, especially in light of demands from unscrupulous collectors for "fresh" materials for their private use. Putting import restrictions in place and thereby reducing the market for these looted heritage materials will be an important step in ensuring the preservation of this heritage.

Finally, let me respond to what I anticipate will be a request from the coin collector community to be exempted from the proposed import restrictions. In the past and for other MoUs, this community has argued that ancient coins constitute a special case: the coins are supposedly found in isolation and therefore their recovery through non-scientific excavations, in other words looting, does not adversely affect the archaeological and historic record. Nothing could be further from the truth. Coins and coin hoards are integral components of the archaeological record. Gordion, in central Turkey which was the focus of my doctoral dissertation, and Sardis, in western Turkey, another Turkish site where I conducted research, are archaeological sites that have been excavated by U.S. teams since the middle of the last century, and both have produced multiple coin hoards that have yielded significant information for their histories. The same can be said of other sites where I have excavated, including Caesarea Maritima in Israel and Corinth in Greece. There is no justification for exempting ancient coinage from the proposed import restrictions.

In conclusion, by restricting the import of archaeological materials from the Paleolithic to the Ottoman period, and ethnographical materials from the first century CE to 1923, the U.S. helps in an important way to bolster Turkey's cultural heritage preservation efforts, to the benefit of us all. For this reason, I urge the committee to support putting in place the MoU import restrictions for Turkey.

The Committee for Cultural Policy and Global Heritage Alliance jointly submit this testimony on the Proposed Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for the imposition of import restrictions between the United States and the Republic of Turkey.

The 1983 Cultural Property Implementation Act (CPIA) was intended to balance U.S. interests in free trade and access to art with source county claims to heritage and the need to protect archaeological sites from looting. In the CPIA, Congress reserved judgment on the scope of import restrictions to the U.S. Instead, the law allowed targeted export restrictions on materials currently threatened by looting and required that important market nations act together to similarly block imports.

The Cultural Property Advisory Committee (CPAC) provides recommendations under the CPIA. In order to recommend import restrictions, CPAC must find that the request satisfies all four requirements set forth under the law. The requirements are:
The cultural patrimony of the State Party is in jeopardy from the pillage of archaeological or ethnological materials of the State Party.
The State Party has taken measures to protect its cultural patrimony.
The application of the requested import restriction would be applied at the same time by other nations with a significant import trade in the restricted objects, and would have a substantial effect in deterring a serious situation of pillage - - and other remedies are not available.
The application of the import restrictions is consistent with the general interest of the international community in the interchange of cultural property among nations for scientific, cultural, and educational purposes.

The legal criteria are not met. The factual basis for the Turkish request is absent. So is any practical argument for an MOU having any positive effect. What we do know is that religious minority communities both in Turkey and in the United States will suffer from the gratuitous granting of import restrictions to a repressive and abusive regime that already claims rights over minority heritage beyond what are allowed under Turkish law.

We ask that the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs and the Cultural Property Advisory Committee follow the criteria under U.S. law, and reject the request from the Republic of Turkey for unnecessary, over-reaching, and legally unjustified import restrictions.

Despite the dedicated efforts of the Institut National du Patrimoine to protect Tunisian cultural heritage sites and collections, there is ample evidence that illicit excavation and sales of Tunisian cultural property continues. Given the demonstrated market for such material in the United States, the request from the Government of the Republic of Tunisia for import restrictions on archaeological and ethnological material is sensible and should be honored. In fact, the documented instances of looting in regions of Tunisia such as Kasserine have more than doubled since the revolution of 2011 (Foroudi, 2019), so from the perspective of authorities seeking to protect Tunisian patrimony, such restrictions are overdue.

Over the past five years, Tunisia has lost more than a fifth of its GDP (World Bank, 2018). While the tourism sector shows signs of recovery, growth remains tepid and unemployment rates remain high (Bobin, 2019). This ongoing economic pressure combined with the perception of diminished rule of law appears to be the main driver for the ongoing looting, and diggers have created a thriving online marketplace in Tunisia to pass their finds onto brokers who can seek higher prices abroad. Using Facebook pages with names like "Specialists in Digging Treasures and Burials," this marketplace has continued to grow, despite ongoing reports to the INP from concerned citizens identifying looters' pits in their own backyards (Barakat, 2019).

For the past decade, I have worked closely with colleagues in the INP and Libyan Department of Antiquities struggling to stop the looting of archaeological sites and the illicit trafficking of antiquities across their mutual border. I have heard from them directly that the resources of their departments and those of allied law enforcement do not permit them to adequately investigate and prosecute such crimes, and they readily admit that their borders remain porous enough for this material to be smuggled abroad. During this time of prolonged regional instability, American import restrictions to further constrain this illicit market is a prudent step that should be pursued.

I am writing on behalf of the Ancient Coin Collectors Guild. The Ancient Coin Collectors Guild (ACCG) is a nonprofit advocacy organization. It has 22 affiliate member organizations and advocates for the interests of thousands of ancient coin collectors and hundreds of small businesses of the numismatic trade. Its website may be found at http://www.accg.us/home.aspx (last visited March 19, 2019).

This latest proposal, if enacted, will further damage legitimate coin collecting, given the way U.S. Customs enforces import restrictions. The Cultural Property Implementation Act only authorizes detention, seizure and forfeiture of types of objects on designated lists illicitly exported from the country for which restrictions are granted after the effective date of government regulations. 19 USC Section 2606. U.S. Customs instead, however, has detained and seized coins of types on designated lists imported into the United States after the effective date of the applicable regulations, i.e., an embargo of all coins of restricted types rather than targeted, prospective import restrictions that do not impact the purchase of coins from the legitimate marketplace abroad, mostly within Europe.

For most of its history, Jordan was a small part of much greater Empires. For that reason, most Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Islamic coins that circulated in Jordan were made elsewhere and circulated outside of Jordan in much greater quantities than those that circulated within Jordan's modern borders. Moreover, even coins struck by the Nabataeans in Petra circulated regionally within their Empire that includes parts of modern day Jordan, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Palestine and Israel.

In light of the above, we would request that CPAC follow the precedent set by earlier Committees which recommended against import restrictions on Cypriot and Italian coins. If CPAC instead wishes to recommend restrictions, we request that any such recommendation be made contingent on Customs limiting them to coins proven to be illicitly exported from Jordan after the effective date of any regulations.

I am writing to you today in support of the proposed MOU between the USA and Chile concerning import restrictions for certain archaeological and palaeontological material. I believe that import restrictions on Chilean cultural and palaeontological objects will serve as an important point of defence against the illicit and illegal trafficking of such items and will help protect all of our cultural and natural heritage.

I have spoken to the committee in person during the last two renewals of the US/Bolivia MOU. During both occasions I stressed that ancient borders do not match modern borders, and that ancient cultural objects from one Andean country can easily appear to be from another Andean country. Thus to prevent an illicit Bolivian antiquity from being improperly imported into the United States simply by having the possessor declare it to be Chilean, we must restrict the movement of Chilean antiquities as well. By having such restrictions through the whole region we prevent all Andean antiquities from being laundered.

The possibility of restricted Bolivian antiquities being presented as or implied to be Chilean on the American market is something that has come up in my research. During my master's dissertation completed in 2006 I located a number of antiquities on the market being presented as "coastal Tiwanaku". Tiwanaku is in Bolivia and Bolivia certainly has no coast; the implication, then, was that these Tiwanaku-style objects were not from Bolivia which had an MOU with the USA, but rather from one of the few Tiwanaku-period sites on the Chilean coast, and thus not subject to import restrictions. It is precisely because we have no way to be sure which country a looted object like that came from that we need import restrictions on ALL such objects.

I would also like to say that I am glad to see that palaeontological material will also be included with the proposed MOU, in line with Chile's cultural property law. While my research on the topic of fossil trafficking in Latin America is in its early stages (but will be supported by a large European Commission grant starting in January of 2020 and lasting for 5 years), my research team and I have already identified northern Chile as a fieldwork location due to the sensitive nature and marketability of paleontological remains from there. We have also identified the US as the primary market point for said remains after having conducted preliminary work on the topic in US-based fossil and gem shows. While I do not yet have mature results of this research, I can safely assert that the problem exists and that import restrictions would be helpful.

I have worked in Jordan since 1996 as an excavator, surveyor, GIS specialist, and remote sensing specialist. As a former NEH/ACOR Senior Fellow, Director of the Moab Archaeological Resource Survey in west-central Jordan, and developer of the Digital Archaeological Atlas of the Holy Land (DAAHL -- an online GIS databases for archaeological sites in the Near East), I wish to register my wholehearted support for the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan's request for a Memorandum of Understanding with the Government of the United States of America Concerning the Imposition of Import Restrictions on Archaeological Material from Jordan from the Paleolithic through the Ottoman Periods.

Looting of archaeological sites has been a long term problem throughout the Near East, and sites in Jordan have been seriously impacted. The DAAHL database currently contains records of more than 440 archaeological sites with reported looting or illegal excavations. Materials recovered from these illicit diggings find their way to the black market and sometimes support efforts of regional groups to destabilize governments and U.S. initiatives in the Near East. I have attached a Google Earth image that shows the impacted sites. They are scattered throughout the country, but mostly are located in the more populated areas in the west.

The DAAHL database contains about 11,200 archaeological sites from Jordan, and the 443 looted sites represent about 4% of the total inventory known to me. But there are currently many more sites in Jordan than are currently in the DAAHL database. Many have not been monitored or visited by professional archaeologists for years, so it is quite possible that the looting problem is much more extensive than these figures and map illustrate.

I am also the developer of the TerraWatchers web application (terrawatchers.org); it is a crowd-sourced method of monitoring and reporting damage to archaeological sites in the Near East. We have recently finished a mission to examine nearly 11,000 sites in Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq for damage caused by the ongoing conflict. We are planning a mission in cooperation with ACOR and several universities and community groups in Jordan to digitally visit and report current damage to all the sites in the Department of Antiquities of Jordan site database. The observations that this new project records will provide the first comprehensive examination of looting across the entire country. It's results will be greatly enhanced if a strong MOU with the United States can be developed, as that will dis-incentivize future looting activity and hopefully provide information that can lead to the apprehension of those who are responsible for it.

Nobody denies our history should be protected and studied. The question is how best to achieve this. Another question that must be addressed whether the modern nation state automatically owns everything that happened to be be produced in its borders thousands of years ago. The boundaries of modern nation states do not neatly overlap the boundaries of ancient kingdoms and empires and many modern courtries were created with lines drawn on a map 100 years ago at Versailles.

The question becomes even more pressing when it comes to ancient coins. Coins by their nature were meant to circulate. Ancient roman coins have been found in India, they were imitated in Sri Lanka and found under a castle in Japan. Islamic coins have been found in Scandinavia and famously the Merican King Offa minted a gold coin which copied the text from an Abbasid Dinar...up side down.

Yet time and time again the State Department has been coming up with silly and arbitrary restrictions on the import of ancient coins pretending that they did not circulate beyond the borders of the modern nation state and for some reason are the property of the current political entity that now exists there.

This approach has been extremely harmful to our ability to study the past. Almost everything we have learned from ancient coins has come from private collectors who have the time and interest in learning more about these little bits of metal. Museums notoriously do not have the inclination to display these and often have no idea of the coins in their collections. They also notoriously do not make these easily available to researchers for study. Governments hoarding these are even worse. Yet there has been a concentrated attempt to destroy the hobby of coin collecting which has been invaluable in our understanding of the past.

The Kingdom of Jordan it appears will be the latest modern country attempting to joins the list. The territory of the modern state of Jordan includes many ancient coins of the Decapolis, the Kingdom of Petra, Islamic coins etc. none of whose borders were contiguous with the modern country and overlap other countries. To arbitrarily give Jordan ownership of these coins because a mint that may have issued these coins (which again circulated freely through the ages) is ridiculous. Yet the State Department time and again indulges in these silly games which impose burdens on American collectors that do not exist on other collectors in Europe etc. This is extremely harmful to the study of the past where collectors have contributed so much and continue to do so.

Please do not include coins in the restrictions sought by the Kingdom of Jordan

March 21, 2019

This responds to object to the proposed MOU and associated import restrictions with the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, that is being considered by U.S. Cultural Property Advisory Committee, found at Docket ID: DOS-2019-0004. As detailed below, I believe the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordans request failed to offer proof of their existing relevant laws, regulations, or decrees for violation of import or export controls on cultural properties, that they have failed to engage in credible enforcement efforts, and because the request is excessively broad, unwarranted and illegal because of its implicit inclusion of all ancient coins whether or not they were minted or found in modern-day Jordan.

According to the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs, found at https://eca.state.gov/cultural-heritage-center/cultural-property-advisory-committee/foreign-government-requests, a Foreign Governments request for cultural property protection must include a statement of facts that addresses the matters on which the Department makes the determinations specified in the Convention on Cultural Property Implementation Act, 19 U.S.C. 2602(a)(1). These determinations include 2. that the State Party has taken measures consistent with the 1970 UNESCO Convention to protect its cultural patrimony. And measures consistent with the 1970 UNESCO Convention includes: 2. Imposition of penalties or administrative sanctions for violation of import or export controls on cultural property, documentary evidence of which should include copies of the relevant laws, regulations, or decrees. As well as 4. Credible enforcement efforts, including monitoring for compliance and appropriate sanctions, documentary evidence of which should include data of sufficient duration and scope to provide the information necessary for a reliable determination.

But the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordans request, found at https://eca.state.gov/files/bureau/jordan_public_summary.pdf, other than citing the rather draconian cultural patrimony laws that goes back to 1934, failed to provide relevant laws, regulations, or decrees for violation of import or export controls on cultural properties. They also failed to show they engaged in credible enforcement efforts including providing data of sufficient duration and scope to provide the information necessary for a reliable determination. Instead, Jordan essentially concedes these omissions in their statement: In May 2017, the then head of the Director General of Department of Antiquities, Munther Jamhawi, announced that the Department was in the process of drafting a new law to fill the gaps in the existing law and to improve measures to combat the illegal excavation and trafficking of antiquities and increase penalties for trafficking crimes. The Department is consulting with UNESCO on drafting the new law (emphasis added).
Besides failing to provide the necessary relevant laws, regulations, or decrees and failing to have engaged in credible enforcement efforts, the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordans request is excessively broad and unwarranted by its implicit inclusion of ancient coins. Over the course of history the area of modern-day Jordan was part of much larger Kingdoms and Empires. For example, the coins of the Nabataean Kingdom, which controlled much of the trade routes of the region, would have circulated throughout their kingdom, included parts of modern-day Jordan, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Palestine and Israel. The Greek Imperial coins of the Decapolis also likely circulated not only in areas which is now modern-day Jordan but also Israel and Syria. Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Islamic coins minted elsewhere circulated in areas which is now modern-day Jordan, but no one can assume all such coins -- or even a substantial percentage of them -- were found there.

Finally, as more fully detailed in Peter Tompas letter to Dr. Jeremy Sabloff, Chair
Cultural Property Advisory Committee dated March 20, 2019: For coin collectors, there is a real question whether import restrictions can lawfully be placed on coins solely based on whether they were minted in the confines of modern day Jordan. Scholarly evidence demonstrates that Jordanian coinswith the possible exception of some local bronze city issues -- are typically found outside of the confines of modern day Jordan, which would make any restrictions placed upon them by place of minting alone contrary to governing law. Ancient Coin Collectors Guild v. U.S. Customs and Border Protection, 801 F. Supp. 2d 383, 407 n. 25 (D. Md. 2011)(Congress only authorized the imposition of import restrictions on objects that were first discovered within, and [are] subject to the export control by the State Party.).

Respectfully submitted,
Randolph J. Myers
GISAID Submission to Notice and Request for Comments on the Implications of Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) Regimes on Global Health and Biomedical Research, DOS Notification 10789

And it is extremely difficult for tourists to visit many of the rooms and courtyards featured on the Umm el-Jimal tour on signage, brochures, hand-held app and the website."

Providing adequate site security at Umm el-Jimal has been an ongoing frustration, despite repeated assurances from the Ministry of Tourism that the situation would be remedied. We now have a newly hired site steward, a resident in the village (funded by the USAID-SCHEP program) who is monitoring and reporting the damage being done to the site. I have been working on Nabataean coins for many years as both a collector and scholar. Hence I appreciate both the interest of Jordan to protect its cultural heritage, and the responsibility of dealers and collectors to respect applicable laws as well as to treat the coins as objects of cultural and historical significance. Since it is difficult to serve all and everybody's legitimate interests in a debate that is often characterized by a strong bias of any of the involved parties (Governments, archaeologists, collectors, dealers), it may be helpful to also consider the following in moving the debate forward:

- The Nabataean kingdom covered, at different times, various parts of what is now Jordan, Israel, Palestine, Syria, Saudi Arabia and Egypt. Nabataean coins are found in all of these countries. Hence, it is neither possible to equate "Nabataea" with "Jordan", nor to attribute (or re-patriate) a non-provenanced Nabataean coin legally to Jordan. This situation is further compounded by the obvious fact that, as with any ancient or modern coinage, coins were produced for circulation and may therefore be found on the territory of another modern state (e.g., Israel) than that where it was minted (e.-g., Jordan);

- The various countries mentioned above are governed by different legislations regarding the ownership, sale of, or export of coins from their territory. Israel, for example, is fairly liberal in granting export permissions;

- Nabataean coins are an extremely important source of Nabataean history. It is therefore imperative to ensure that any studies undertaken in this field are scientifically reliable and available to the larger interested public (historians, numismatists, and collectors). Until now, the bulk of relevant publications on Nabataean numismatics has been produced by non-Jordanians. While it is, of course, desirable, to have more Jordanian expertise and scholarship in this field, it also means that any Jordanian institution holding Nabataean coins should ideally mke these holdings freely available to interested scholars.

This MOU is based on the false premise that all ancient coins found in Jordan fall into a similar category and therefore can be regulated in the same  way. The truth of the matter is that they originate from many different eras and cultures, principally pagan Greece and Rome with some of the later issues being of the Christian era. This is typical of the Mediterranean area in general and has no special significance for the modern country of Jordan. These types of coins are readily available to collectors from many regions and Jordan can in no way claim exclusivity in this regard. This proposal would undoubtedly negativity impact ancient coin collecting and would hamper numismatic and historical research in this important field.
