The site of Tall el-Hammam in the S Jordan Valley is one of the largest archaeological sites in Jordan, with ruins dating from the Chalcolithic Period, Bronze Age, Iron Age, and Roman/Byzantine Period. The land occupied by the site is privately owned and is used for agricultural purposes, particularly the lower tall. The upper tall is virtually inaccessible to agriculture, and is, therefore, in a better state of preservation than the lower tall. Of the 26-hectare footprint of the fortified Bronze Age city, two-thirds is severely damaged by heavy agriculture (mainly bananas). The balance of the site is also in constant danger of looting by locals who have, at times, even gone so far as to use powered equipment like backhoes to dig for artifacts. Since the Jordan Department of Antiquities has no ownership of the site, protecting it is problematic. The Tall el-Hammam Excavation Project has managed to work well with the local clan/landowners in order to protect the excavated sectors of Tall el-Hammam, and has constructed fences and employed an influential local family to serve as site-guards. This has been effective for the now-14-season duration of the Tall el-Hammam Excavation Project. However, the site is so large that monitoring it comprehensively is impossible under the current situation. Looter holes continue to appear across the site, which are being dug by locals who are (likely) not members of the major controlling clan with which we work. The budget of the DoA has not allowed it to purchase any of the land occupied by this important archaeological site. Beyond its historical importance, the site also has significant tourism potential, now that it is located on a major highway (newly constructed) connecting the Baptism Site (Jordan River) to Amman, Mt. Nebo, and Madaba. The tall proper is also surrounded by hundreds of megalithic features (like dolmens and standing stones), which are systematically being destroyed by residential, military, and highway construction projects, as well as vandalism. The Tall el-Hammam Excavation Project has managed to help preserve sections of the site, and continues to do so. Without this, the site would be severely impacted by agriculture and looting. The only way that the site can be properly preserved is for it to be purchased by the Jordan DoA and managed in cooperation with the local landowners. I encourage Jordan to seek help from the USA and other potential partners to purchase and secure this and other nearby sites in the S Jordan Valley. The financial investment of TeHEP at the site for excavation on an annual basis for the past fourteen years has helped keep the site protected to a certain extent, and the local clan has partnered with us successfully in this regard. But as we all know, looters are tenacious, and do damage even to the most protected archaeological sites in Jordan. It will take a coordinated effort to address the looting issue properly, and I encourage whatever financial support that US agencies can provide in helping the DoA address this critical issue. The investment surely must include educational programs for locals and local schools to create appreciation for this and other elements of Jordan's cultural heritage. [The contributor of these comments is Director and Chief Archaeologist of the Tall el-Hammam Excavation Project.]

Dear CPAC,
As an archaeologist with a special interest in the damage done to archaeological sites and assemblages through the collection of and trade in archaeological artefacts, I am writing to express my full support of the request from the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan for a cultural property agreement and MOU with the United States in order to help in stopping the illicit trade of artefacts from Jordan.

Jordan has taken many measures consistent with the Convention to protect its cultural patrimony, most notably in the maintenance of a state body, the Jordanian Department of Antiquities tasked with this care. This was established in 1923 and its work includes inventorying, monitoring, and managing Jordan's vast number of archaeological sites. This task is now aided by a comprehensive public geographic information system and database of archaeological sites in the country (developed in cooperation with US specialists - http://www.getty.edu/conservation/our_projects/field_projects/jordan/). The DoA deserves all the help we can give it to achieve the task of managing and securing the regions archaeological heritage and ensuring that future generations will also benefit from the wealth of the past. The reported involvement of local communities in the protection of the heritage (again currently supported by US aid - https://tinyurl.com/y6f9ketk) is also indicative of the importance it holds to many citizens.

In recent years, there has been increasing pressure on the cultural patrimony of the country, including from pillage of archaeological material. Clandestine looting has been documented in the field on a number of sites (most notably by the groundbreaking "Follow the Pots" project, headed by Morag Kersel, DePaul University in Chicago - - http://followthepotsproject.org/). Material of types known to occur in the Jordanian archaeological record, apparently freshly surfaced, is turning up right now on eBay and in venues such as the US-based V-Coins portal. It is in the unstable situation existing in the Middle East today that the cultural heritage is at most jeopardy and requires care to keep freshly smuggled illicit artefacts off the major markets.

Of those markets, that of the US is undoubtedly among the most voracious. It is telling how many US dealers and collectors of dugup antiquities time and time again attempt to oppose any attempt under the CCPIA to clean up the US trade and keep undocumented examples of such material off the US market.

In Jordan, there have been initiatives to train local agents of law enforcement in how to counter trafficking of cultural objects, and to raise awareness and of the threats arising from trafficking of cultural objects. An example of this was the five-day National Training on Countering Illicit Trafficking of Cultural Heritage session held in Amman in February 2018 (made possible thanks to the funds received from the Norwegian Government - https://tinyurl.com/y5hhztwr). But to stop it, the chain of supply and demand for illicit antiquities obviously needs to be tackled at both ends, in the market countries as well as the victimized source countries.

Most other countries that are party to the 1970 UNESCO Convention on the Means of Prohibiting and Preventing the Illicit Import, Export and Transfer of Ownership of Cultural Property apply it to the cultural property of all other member states without discrimination, the Convention is after all intended to foster international collaboration and build peace in the minds of men. The US is one of the few countries that apply it selectively, on a country-by-country basis, dividing international partners into better and worse. If the US applies restrictions on imports of artefacts exported from Jordan to only those properly documented, it would only be joining the rest of the international community in implementing the Convention. The US, surely, should be a leader in such a concerted effort, not a reluctant tagalong especially given the size and nature of the no-questions-asked US antiquities market and the appetites and attitudes of those involved in it. Doing all possible to prevent illicit material passing onto any major market is obviously going to be of substantial benefit in deterring the development of a serious situation of pillage in Jordan. There is no need to see anything drastic about keeping illicit artefacts (or those not complying with the liberal measures of the CCPIA) off the US market. On the contrary.

Quite clearly, and in particular in the current situation, the restriction of antiquities originating in Jordan through applying the measures of the CCPIA is not only completely consistent with, but also imperative in, the general interest of the international community in the interchange of cultural property among nations for cultural, scientific and educational purposes.

I strongly oppose the inclusion of ancient coins in the Jordanian MOU. I collect ancient Roman, Byzantine and Greek coins. Ancient Jordan was part of much larger Empires. Greek, Roman, and Byzantine coins minted elsewhere circulated in Jordan, and one cannot assume that many of such coins were found there. How can Jordan exert control over coins that were minted elsewhere and MAY have had a small chance of being used there or found there?

Even more "local issues" circulated regionally outside of Jordan. For example, the coins of the Nabatean Kings would have circulated throughout their kingdom, which included parts of modern day Jordan, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Palestine and Israel. Moreover, later Greek Imperial coins of the Decapolis also likely circulated throughout the area, which included Israel and Syria. Again, how can Jordan exert control over coins that may have never circulated in Jordan?

Lastly, these coins were mass produced are found all over Jordan (and the Middle East) and outside of any registered historic site. They are not ancient rarities.

Ancient coins were mass-produced in huge quantities, and designed to cross borders, both ancient and modern. They did so in almost equally large numbers, and may be found in places far beyond the place in which they were made, again without respect to borders ancient or modern.

There can be no doubt that the effect of this and other similar MOUs is that they are a direct attack on the legal collecting community, the same community that is ultimately responsible for a huge amount of study and research, as well as the undeniable fact that private collectors and their collections were often the direct founders and foundations of many of the major institutions throughout the modern world, including the British Museum, the Smithsonian institutions, the Mnzkabinett Berlin, and untold others.

These MOU do nothing to stop the alleged looting of sites, they only punish those carrying out a perfectly legal and admirable avocation (often called the 'Hobby of Kings, and the King of Hobbies'). Removing corrupt officials, enacting better and more reasonable local laws - such as that of the PAS in the UK, and educating the people closest to the so-called 'source' is but a start to creating a far better global system toward the furtherance of archaeological goals than any regressive MOU.

Looting is opposed by all collectors, and is actively condemned by them in equal measure. It is the looting and destruction of sites that should be being addressed, and not the legal pastime of collecting (the alleged links to which have proved tenuous, grossly exaggerated, or in some cases demonstrably false). It has even been claimed, with supporting evidence, that there are more items being destroyed by neglect, indifference, ignorance and carelessness in the "basements" of museums and government storage places than by the actions and participation in the hobby of any legal collector.

I fully support better and proper local laws that deal explicitly with looting and the destruction of archaeological sites. These MOU do nothing, or at best almost imperceptibly little, to address these far more pressing concerns.

Additionally, there has to be an unambiguous definition of what is "cultural", and also a clear definition as to whose 'culture' that may refer to given the vast changes in borders and territories over the intervening centuries and millennia, and over the vast areas in question.

Dear Committee Members,

As a concerned US citizen, I ask that you support the request by the Government of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan seeking import restrictions on archaeological material.

Jordan has a rich cultural heritage and is home to archaeological sites dating from prehistory through the Ottoman Empire. Visitors and Jordanians may wander through ancient Roman and Nabatean cities, view Byzantine mosaics in situ, marvel at the monumental gateway of an Umayyad palace, and walk through the narrow streets of an Ottoman-era administrative center during a single weekend (or a very long day, for the ambitious). Those seeking to better understand the region's history may also visit the excellent Jordan Museum in Amman, attend lectures at the American Center of Oriental Research, take a virtual site tour online, or arrange a guided visit offered by one of the country's many tour operators.

Unfortunately, both well-documented archaeological sites and those still under exploration are vulnerable to looting. Looting destroys sites and removes artifacts from their historical (or prehistorical) context and from the public sphere. Looting also deprives Jordan of opportunities to further develop the country's travel and tourism industries.

There is no reason for the US to allow unrestricted import of Jordanian archaeological materials. Unrestricted import is of no benefit to US scientists, institutions of higher learning, or the general public. Instead, Jordan allows US archaeologists to obtain permits for excavation and research, organizes scholarly conferences, and makes archaeological materials available for study by US, Jordanian, and other scientists. Jordan also participates in public awareness and education programs to ensure that Jordanian citizens and visitors alike are able to experience Jordan's rich history.

Jordan is actively engaged in efforts to combat looting and trafficking in antiquities and to preserve cultural heritage. The antiquities trade is illegal within Jordan. The US can and should support Jordan by using import restrictions to prevent pillaged good from entering the US market.

Sincerely,
Katherine Yun, MD MHS

This information collection effort is an abuse of the consular processing system and our administrative government structure. To issue a proclamation on October 4, 2019 set to go into effect on November 3 is already a capricious and careless way to approach people who have been engaging in the consular process for years. To then open a comment period at around ~11:00am on October 30 and set it to close at 11:59pm on October 31 is a clear obstruction of a respected process to engage the voices of the people in government policies and procedures. This agency has provided less than 24 hours for individuals to submit comments on this proposal. In addition to disapproving the content of this proposal, I would also like to register my disappointment at this deficient public comment process.

Substantively, this proposal is yet another arbitrary and capricious "policy of exclusion in search of a justification" (Daniels, J.), a gross violation of the Administrative Procedures Act (APA) by an administration fixed on a racist immigration policy which aims to keep people of color and people without enormous financial means out of the United States. This change is arbitrary and capricious, as there is no rational justification provided for a rule that stands to cut migration to the U.S. by up to 65%. This information collection effort and the underlying rule change are also clearly unconcerned with ensuring that hospitals and care providers get paid. While evidence of so-called "junk plans" (high-cost, low coverage temporary plans) is being accepted, full coverage free healthcare is not, meaning the main beneficiaries of this proclamation will be unscrupulous insurance agencies, not hard-working healthcare professionals.

Further, the proposal is in violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), in addition to its clear violations of the APA. This document informs us that consular officers will consider as "reasonably foreseeable medical expenses. . .expenses related to existing medical conditions, relating to health issues existing at the time of visa adjudication," heightening barriers to entry for individuals with ongoing health challenges, in addition to those without the resources to obtain health insurance upon arrival. Rendering eligible individuals inadmissible by virtue of their health needs is clear discrimination on the basis of ability.

While I would say that this government should know better, I believe that the clear outcomes of a policy change like this one are the goals of such change. Discrimination against individuals without money, discrimination on the basis of race, and discrimination on the basis of physical ability are not mere side effects of this administrations concerted efforts to limit migration to the U.S., they are central tenets of administrative policy. Because of the foregoing information, and so many other intended impacts of this racist bureaucratic agenda, I firmly register my disapproval of this proposal to collect information about migrants health insurance coverage, and all associated and underlying policies and procedures.

I will comment briefly. First, a two day notice period for comment on something as complex as providing evidence of health insurance is unconscionable. As you well know, the immigrant visa process is a lengthy complicated process where families may spend months gathering documents and satisfying the myriad requirements of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). To obtain a certificate of insurance or insurance coverage before a family member has entered the United States may be very difficult as not all employers or insurance contracts automatically allow the addition of dependents. Moreover, some insurers may require identification information such as a social security number. An immigrant cannot obtain a social security number until he or she has successfully completed the immigration process (unless she or he was already authorized to study or work within the United States). Asking an immigrant to orally certify compliance when the insurance industry is unlikely to be prepared is not appropriate and will generate lengthy and unnecessary stress and delays for both the agencies and the individuals in the process.

Second, the assessment that this collection will only take ten minutes is patently misleading. While it is possible a DOS interviewer might complete a form in ten minutes, it would take me hours to explain all of the options in health care coverage to a well educated person and one already conversant with U.S. customs and business practice. The alternative of proving wealth as adequate to cover health coverage is too vague and too subjective. The process articulated invites arbitrary and inconsistent treatment of immigrants across consulates. This is not a fair or orderly process. Third, I do not mean to waive other meaningful objections about the fundamental legal authority to make this requirement of insurance before immigration or other legal objections. We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this new draft guidance. Overall, we were very encouraged to see that a modern psychometric perspective underlies the document. We hope to see this framework spread throughout the relevant parts of FDA. Below are some more specific comments.

1.On p.3 of the document (line 67), the phrase "reliable PRO instruments" is used. In the psychometric framework, reliability is a property of scores, not scales/instruments. This occurs several other places in the draft (line 115 & line 241) . It is an often overlooked point, but it has some important consequences. For example, it encourages researchers to appreciate that there are multiple ways to score any given scale and that each such approach may have a different result when it comes to reliability (or validity). It is all to easy for researchers to forget that a thoughtful approach to scoring is key to good measurement.
2.On p.3 (lines 74-77), we really appreciated the efforts to tie existing FDA ideas around validity with the modern psychometric framework. A potentially useful resource in this endeavor is Edwards, Slagle, Rubright, & Wirth (2018), which examines the different perspectives and discusses integration.
3.On p.7 (line 204), it states that different uses of a PRO may necessitate "different validity evidence." Did this mean different types of evidence, different amounts of evidence, or both? This seems like an excellent place to highlight the notion present in modern validity theory that the stakes of an inference have a direct effect on the amount of evidence that is desirable (i.e., higher stakes decisions/inferences require greater evidence).
4.On p.7 (lines 215-216) the document states "the amount of change measured by the PRO instrument that is clinically meaningful." We agree this is incredibly important, but as currently stated we feel it glosses over the fact that there is tremendous uncertainty about how best to go about this. Despite the prevalence and historical acceptability of some options, there does not seem to be a scientifically defensible gold standard and this is an active area of research.

This SEIS is significantly inadequate in multiple ways. First and foremost, this analysis does not properly account for the costs to our climate associated with the Keystone XL pipeline (KXL). It assumes future oil prices that are in no way certain. We have seen the price of oil fluctuate dramatically in the many years that TC Energy (formerly TransCanada) has been seeking to construct this project on United States soil. Given the extreme risk and disruption to United States property - both private and pubic, including essential public infrastructure and the seizure of personal property through imminent domain - the business interests of TC Energy and global oil markets should be properly accounted for. Currently, they are not.

Tar sands oil, or bitumen, (the dangerous material proposed to be carried by KXL) is extremely energy intensive to produce, making its carbon footprint exceptionally high. We all pay the cost for this carbon pollution in the form of infrastructure damage, personal property damage, agricultural disruption, loss of human life (due to both climate-fueled natural disasters as well as immediate health risks due to respiratory complications, heat strokes, etc.), and increased insurance premiums and taxes due to all of the aforementioned. Due to these issues, we have seen a decline in fossil fuel use globally, and we have also seen global efforts to create a carbon tax or "cap and trade" carbon market. Given that tar sands oil is more expensive to produce due to the extra complications of refining bitumen AND because it emits so much carbon pollution in its production, it is very plausible to consider that tar sands oil will not be economically profitable within the proposed lifetime of KXL. In essence, we would be sacrificing United States private and public interests for a foreign corporation's project that might prove itself to be economically failing in due time. KXL is not in the national interest of the United States.

Even removing the long-term economic viability of KXL, the Keystone XL pipeline is not the United States' interest due to the extreme risk it portends to United States land and water. Even during this comment period, we saw a 383,000 gallon spill by TC Energy's existing Keystone pipeline in North Dakota. This spill occurred in sensitive wetlands. Numerous other spills have occurred over the years with TC Energy's pipelines on U.S. property.

The current KXL route threatens the Missouri River and threatens the drinking and irrigating water intakes for the Fort Peck Indian Reservation in northeast Montana. The proposed siting of this pipeline sits just downstream from the Fort Peck Dam spillway, which is very dangerous. The volume and velocity of water discharge can lead to scour erosion of the riverbed, exposing the pipe and making a spill all but inevitable over time. The SEIS does not account for "lateral migration" of the river whereby natural movement of the river can lead to a buried pipe being closer to the surface of the land than intended if a river moves. For instance, consider a pipe buried 25 feet below the river but only 5 feet deep under land. At some point, the pipeline must bend to reach that 25 foot depth. If the river moves sideways over time, it will eventually reach that bend resulting in diminished depth and greater risk of pipe exposure due to scour erosion.

Another problem with this SEIS is it improperly calculates the risks of small pipeline leaks. KXL's leak detection system only "kicks in" when 2-5% of the flow is diminished. Given that KXL transports 830.000 gallons per day, even a "pinhole leak" of 1% would result in 8,300 barrels leaking undetected per day.

Lastly, this SEIS process has seemed designed to diminish public input. No hearings whatsoever were held. Instead, a single "public meeting" was arranged in only one state. Having only one meeting in the entire nation and a complete lack of a hearing does not allow the public dialogue needed for such a significant issue. Tribal consultation with the Fort Peck Indian Reservation was also lacking in this process. They are one of the communities most impacted by this potential pipeline and have tribal sovereignty which was not respected.

Issue:
3.1 Specific Aims, Page 39, lines 13-16: The Protocol states, “The assessment will attempt to derive separate toxicity values for individual vanadium compounds or oxidation states (V+5, V+4) and an overall toxicity value for vanadium, as supported by the available data.”

Comment: The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection (WVDEP) agrees that it should be the goal to develop toxicity values for the different vanadium species and oxidation states and these values should be applied when such species and oxidation states are known. WVDEP also has concerns about the limited technical and financial ability to measure the relative proportions of the various vanadium species and oxidation states at Brownfield and Voluntary Remediation Program sites given the ubiquitous nature of this metal. Therefore, WVDEP recommends that these toxicity values for specific oxidation states and species be used when such information is known. However, the overall toxicity values for vanadium to be used when species and oxidation states are unknown should be based on using the most conservative toxicity estimates from the various vanadium compounds as surrogates for vanadium in general. For example, if the chronic RfD for Sodium metavanadate ends up being 0.0005 mg/kg-day and the chronic RfD for Vanadium pentoxide results in 0.03 mg/kg-day, and these are the only viable RfD values, then the RfD for Sodium metavanadate would be chosen as the surrogate for overall vanadium since it would result in the highest noncancer hazard quotients. In this way, the overall vanadium toxicity estimates would be protective of human receptors in the absence of knowledge of speciation and oxidation states, and those parties who challenge this determination can assess the species and oxidation states as an option. This conservative surrogate approach is greatly preferred over the molecular weight adjustment used in the EPA Regional Screening Levels since there was no evidence supporting the assumption that vanadium pentoxide (V2O5) toxicity was based purely on the molecular weight of vanadium and we know that oxygen can generate toxic effects through oxidative stress caused by the production of free radicals.

With the establishment of the Clean Air Act of 1970 under the Nixon Administration the United States created a standard for the regulation of air pollution. After the initial passing of this act in 1970 there have been two major amendments one in 1977, the next in 1970. The first amendment in 1977 enabled the National Ambient Air Quality Standards to address the concern of limiting air pollution in “non-attainment areas”, areas which don’t meet one or more of the federal quality air standards. The next set of amendments to the Clean Air Act occurred in 1990, which provided the National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollution with more jurisdiction in the management of air pollutants. They did so by authorizing programs that aimed to limit the effects of acid rain and targeted urban air pollution, toxic air emissions and ozone depletion. Under the Clean Air Act the EPA is required to set “national ambient air quality standards” or NAAQS for nitrogen oxide and other pollutants that are considered to be harmful to human and environmental health. (https://www.epa.gov/clean-air-act-overview/clean-air-act-text).

NOx pollution is commonly emitted by automobiles, trucks and other “non-road” vehicles such as construction equipment and boats, as well as industrial sources including power plants, industrial boilers and turbines. In terms of human health, an article written by Jennifer Peel et al, discusses how the emissions of nitrogen oxides and other pollutants can cause premature death and variety of other serious health effects including decreased lung function and cardiovascular mortality. From an environmental perspective, nitrous oxide is a particularly potent greenhouse gas known to be highly effective in terms of trapping heat as well as destroying the ozone layer. We also have to consider the bigger picture of climate change, and how the changes in temperature and weather patterns are expected to not only lengthen the ozone season but also intensify “high ozone episodes” in certain areas. This is important in terms of New York’s proposal for the use of simple cycle and regenerative turbines, specifically during periods of “peak electricity demand”. These simple cycle combustion turbines are known as peakers, and typically operate during periods of higher temperatures when electric demand increases Results from a study done by scientists at the University of Minnesota concluded that as the world becomes “warmer and wetter”, nitrous oxide production will be enhanced. So, these turbines would be beneficial when it comes to lowering nitrous oxide emissions during the warmer periods, and ozone seasons.

With that being said I think that implementing the use of these turbines during the ozone season to lower the allowable amount of NOx emissions will help to ensure the health and safety of New York residents, and if the Environmental Protection Agency were to go through with their approval of these revisions I would support it.

EPA cannot approve this limited maintenance plan because Pennsylvania identifies no actual contingency measures. In its proposed rulemaking EPA says, in the event of the 4th highest reading exceeds the standard for two consecutive years, “ PADEP will evaluate whether additional local emission control measures should be implemented that may prevent a violation of the NAAQS.” Simply waiting to see if an exceedance occurs in order to begin evaluating whether measures should be implemented, followed by determining what those measures should be, is not a valid contingency measure and should not be approved by EPA. A contingency measure is supposed to be a known measure that can be quickly implemented by a state in order to prevent a violation of the NAAQS. By approving this limited maintenance plan, EPA is allowing states to say, yeah OK we’ll think of something if and when our readings get too high. Simply promising to develop a contingency measure at some point in the future is not an adequate contingency measure in and of itself. EPA must require an actual measure be held on the sidelines in order to prevent another exceedance.

Second, the problem is further exacerbated by PADEP’s known history of failing to meet its CAA requirements in a timely manner. Just look at the Oil and Gas CTG, it was released in 2016 with a due date in 2018, but here we are three years after the deadline and PADEP has yet to finalize regulations for this requirement. In fact, EPA recently announced that PA may be put on a FIP due to their failure to submit this plan. There are many similar examples where PADEP has missed CAA deadlines and EPA is well aware of PADEP’s regular tardiness. EPA is also aware of the fact that it takes over two years for PADEP to implement a new regulation! Imagine that, PADEP exceeds the NAAQS for the 2nd time in two years and their “contingency measure” is to 1) study the cause of the exceedances, (presumably after ozone season is over? Or maybe when ozone data becomes certified in May of the following year?), 2) figure out if measures are needed and what measures should be implemented to prevent a 3rd exceedance and thus a violation of the NAAQS, and then 3) propose, finalize, and implement such a new measure. Step 3 by itself would take two years! Even if Step 3 was somehow abbreviated it is hard to imagine PADEP would be able to implement a new, unknown measure before ozone season begins for the 3rd year and potential exceedances can begin. EPA may try to argue that PADEP does not have to use the 2-year regulatory process and that it has other means to implement a contingency measure, for instance via emergency orders or through a source specific permit process. But therein lies the point! Without actually identifying a contingency measure NOW, at this stage of the process, EPA has no idea how PADEP could potentially meet the “as expeditiously as practical” standard because it does not know what the contingency measure is!

In summary, EPA must disapprove this limited maintenance plan on the grounds that planning to develop future measures is not an adequate contingency measure. It must also disapprove this plan because EPA is well aware that PADEP cannot meet the “as expeditiously as practical” standard in developing a new measure in the future. Please be aware that these comments will be forwarded to the litigants involved in the Sierra Club v EPA/Texas/TCEQ case recently decided on Jan. 29, 2021 due to the potential contravention of the DC Circuit’s ruling regarding contingency measures. Thank you.

Thank you for this opportunity to provide comments on the allocation formula for the Sewer Overflow and Stomwater Reuse Grants (OSG). I believe that this can be a meaningful grant program capable of providing much needed financial assistance to municipalities and supporting the overall improvement of water quality. On behalf of the WI Department of Natural Resources’ State Revolving Fund (SRF) loan program, I offer a few comments for consideration during the development of this program:
The Background section in the Notice indicates that financial assistance would be provided to municipalities in the form of a grant. My understanding is that, in many states, the OSG program may be run through, or in conjunction with, the SRF programs. The WI SRF, and the majority of our counterparts in other states, awards additional subsidization in the form of principal forgiveness to municipalities. Principal forgiveness is functionally different from a grant in that grant recipients are responsible for federal reporting which can be burdensome and serve as a barrier to participation (especially for smaller municipalities that could benefit the most from the program). By awarding principal forgiveness, the WI SRF takes on much of the reporting burden which would otherwise be the responsibility of the municipality. Changing the language from “grant” to “additional subsidization” would provide greater flexibility at the state and municipal level and would be more consistent with SRF programs.
Annual Average Precipitation: the intensity/flashiness of rainfall is often a greater contributor to overflows than the average volume of rainfall. Similarly, states with high annual average precipitation likely have infrastructure in place designed to accommodate that volume. Perhaps there are other metrics available that could identify the frequency of storm events that are likely to lead to an overflow.
Urban Population: we agree that urban centers will typically have higher concentrations of impervious surfaces and they will likely have more stormwater infrastructure in place. For your consideration, we have noticed that in Wisconsin, some smaller, rural communities struggle more with inflow and infiltration and overflows because they lack the economies of scale to televise and rehabilitate sewers on as regular of a basis.
Thank you for your efforts to develop the OSG program and for your consideration of these comments.

Prior to issuance of E.O. 14005, FAR 25.103(b)(2)(i) authorized the head of the contracting activity to make an individual determination of nonavailability without having to publicly share the rationale for the determination or the nature of the market research conducted. The agency simply reported to the Federal Procurement Data System if a nonavailability waiver was used on a particular acquisition. In addition, a written determination of nonavailability was not required if the acquisition was conducted using full and open competition, synopsized, and no offer for a domestic source was received. This process made it challenging for an existing Government contractor or potential new entrant to become aware if its capabilities were being overlooked. Further, if the contracting officer considered that the nonavailability of an article was likely to affect future acquisitions over a period of time, FAR 25.103(b)(2)(ii) authorized the contracting officer to submit a copy of the determination and supporting documentation to the appropriate regulatory council identified in FAR 1.201-1 ( i.e., the Defense Acquisition Regulations Council or the Civilian Agency Acquisition Council), in accordance with agency procedures, to consider inclusion on the list of nonavailable articles at FAR 25.104(a). Inclusion of the article on the nonavailability list reduces the level of public outreach even further in light of the presumption of nonavailability.

E.O. 14005 makes a number of changes to tighten the waiver process and strengthen efforts to increase reliance on domestic sourcing. First, with respect to individual waivers (see FAR 25.103(b)(2)(i)), the E.O. updates, centralizes, and provides transparency to the process for their issuance. Section 4 of the E.O. established the Made in America Office (MIAO) in the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to manage a centralized process for reviewing proposed agency nonavailability waivers for individual and multiple procurements. Agencies can no longer simply rely on the absence of domestic offers in a competition to justify a nonavailability waiver. OMB Memorandum M-21-26, Increasing Opportunities for Domestic Sourcing and Reducing the Need for Waivers from Made in America Laws, and guidance issued jointly by MIAO and the Office of Federal Procurement Policy (OFPP), Improving the Transparency of Made in America Waivers (October 26, 2021), provided direction to agencies for the development, coordination, and posting of waivers. In particular, the guidance instructs agencies to describe steps the agency has taken to understand market capabilities and capacity to help potential interested sources and supply chain experts identify where opportunities might have been missed and could be pursued when future needs arise. The guidance provides that waivers will cover individual transactions but allows agencies to pursue multi-procurement waivers for repetitive needs where market research indicates that domestic capability may be lacking for a period of time, provided the waiver is time limited. The guidance states that agencies should continually study the market and reflect recent analysis in their proposed waivers and not assume that there is no qualifying product simply because one was not found in a prior year. The guidance further directs that proposed waivers must be posted on the MadeinAmerica.gov website so that interested sellers can have a better understanding of where agencies are having trouble finding U.S.-made products. The guidance explains that greater transparency should lead to a more responsive supplier base and help agencies build diversity by pulling new entrants into the Federal marketplace. HMS thanks OMB for developing draft guidance for regulation of artificial intelligence applications. Attached are HMS' brief comments to the draft.

Regulation is going to get stuck. Because of how AI works, accuracy and fairness compete. An AI will be racist or sexist or unfair simply as a natural by-product of optimizing for accuracy or profit. It won't deliver "fair" or "trust" or "non-discriminatory" on its own. What makes AI regulation so difficult is that, although in theory, many existing laws can work just fine for AI, in practice there's a missing piece.

AI outpaces humans. It takes time for people to see that damage has been done and it's not possible to see the harm as it's happening. Reactive regulation will be ineffective because it leaves regulators without any technical way to regulate. All they have are organizational and human responses - oversight committees and corporate processes.

The regulation needs to be proactive. Here are two ways that can happen.

Real-time monitoring

We need humans to be able to understand what machines are doing, even if they can't match their speed and scale, or understand the deep complexity of the algorithms, data, and models. The financial industry has largely solved this problem. FINRA, the industry's self-regulatory agency has direct access to highly granular trading data with sensors placed directly into data feeds.

In a recent Brookings article, the authors of The Ethical Algorithm, explain how the financial industry uses technology to monitor technology. The solution is to monitor selectively; placing sensors where the most important algorithmic decisions are made and knowing what to looking for. This same idea could be applied to big tech AI - the science is understood, the measures are known and the techniques are available. Monitoring could theoretically be run completely from the outside, perhaps using composite systems or only at specified times. It could be built off to the side and never deployed in production. It could, in short, be non-intrusive.

Fairness by design

The behavior of an AI system relies to some extent on its post-design experience. In AI design, more effort has to go in upfront to define intent, anticipate consequences and uncover sources of bias. Fairness has to be designed in from the beginning.

Today, the problem is that it's an afterthought, if at all. Fairness slows down development. Most engineers and project managers have no experience with AI design and don't think about fairness. Many companies avoid fairness design and testing because of the legal liability of discovering that their AI is, in fact, unfair. Discovering discrimination leaves the company in a worse position.

Privacy-by-design is the precedent for fairness-by-design. Privacy-by-design was first thought of in the 1970s and was then incorporated in the 1990s into the data protection directives. Privacy-by-design principles are fundamental to GDPR and, although, in need of a refurb for the age of AI, they have had a meaningful impact in advancing better regulation.

In AI we need fairness-by-design in regulation because it's probably one of the best ways to have people think about the unique requirements of AI design. A mindset where speed and MVP (minimum viable product) is more important than fairness and MVD (minimum viable data) is a tough mindset to break. The market rewards the former and there are no guard rails to argue for the latter. No mal-intent is required for AI to be unfair.

We need regulation because we need people to start thinking more about what goes into AI; the people, the data, the design. In much the same way as regulation of food safety includes employees' hygiene ("employees must wash their hands before returning to work") we need regulations in AI that focus on the quality of the inputs.

We need to take a proactive rather than a reactive approach. Machines are too fast, are too big and do too much damage before anyone notices. Don't believe the story that AI regulation is a tweak on what we have in telecoms or utilities or media. We know the underlying science, which tells us how we can make use of intentional design principles and real-time monitoring in market-oriented ways so that we do not reveal proprietary intellectual property or stifle innovation.

At a time when delivery robots block the sidewalks, leaving wheelchair users stuck, when navigation apps create neighborhood traffic nightmares, when department stores secretly track customers' movements and sell the data, and when angry residents throw rocks at autonomous cars and throw scooters into the sea, it's tempting for Washington to override state and local laws on AI. In fact, the White House's draft memo on Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications seems designed to preempt state action. But the administration's statements about over-regulation suggest this is a call, not for a federal answer to these problems, but for the destruction of local solutions.

That would be a mistake.

In the absence of federal action, U.S. cities and states have been regulating facial recognition, autonomous vehicles, rideshare companies, and consumer data collection and sale, offering their residents additional protections and creating environments to test new ideas. As quickly changing technology creates new models and markets, local action offers a natural way to experiment with regulatory environments on a smaller scale before national policies are finalized.

However, even the biggest cities and states cannot do what the federal government can.

The federal government is in the best position to identify and address some kinds of AI risk, including those which come from cumulative or widespread use or which are threats to or through national infrastructure and networks. It can implement solutions that require significant financial resources, political power, collaboration across governments or with industry, or which might require rethinking common regulatory frameworks or creating national standards. It can take a broader view, offering protection across the U.S. and far beyond.

Congress and the White House should use local and international experience to help inform U.S. federal AI policy, provide protection for all residents by creating minimum national standards, and make limited use of federal preemption, at least for now. They should also work to build deep AI technical and policy capacity across all levels and sectors of government.

It's hard for governments to compete with AI industry salaries and there are great inefficiencies in each city or state or even each country separately building technical capacity and trying to think through all the societal implications of artificial intelligence and its applications. Many don't have the internal resources to do it well or even at all, leaving industry, academia and nonprofits filling the void: convening city and state leaders, providing tech education for policymakers and building and deploying AI and algorithms for city, state and federal services. Those organizations should all continue to contribute their expertise, but governments should not have to rely on it.

The federal government should create a national AI research and policy office, as a resource for local and federal agencies and policymakers, recruiting top talent and encouraging collaboration across all levels of government and across all sectors, providing a cost efficient way to develop, access and share unbiased AI technical and policy expertise. It should be done very quickly, this year. It might only be needed for a limited period, less than 20 years, but there's a pressing need right now.

The substantive work could be undertaken in collaboration with existing agencies or national research labs including the United States Digital Service, the Office of Science and Technology Policy, the national transportation lab Volpe, and the DOE's new Office of Artificial Intelligence. Each holds some of the resources that are needed, but none holds the mandate.

Governments across the world are trying to figure out what the benefits and risks of AI are, what safeguards should be in place and how high-level principles about trustworthy, responsible, or ethical AI or international human rights should translate to specific action or law about AI. We don't know how AI's unprecedented ability to autonomously pull together data, find patterns and make inferences online and in the physical world, cheaply, quickly and at a massive scale is affecting and will affect societies globally. We don't know how we want it to, or how to get there.

The administration's hands off approach to regulation won't answer these questions. Neither will regulations, not on their own.

Answering these questions will require significant investments in research and development, collaboration, negotiation, and experimentation, deep and careful thought across many fields, and leadership at all levels, across and between governments. But we can't wait until we have perfect answers to start to respond to the risks we see now.

The U.S. federal government is well positioned to lead, but if it won't, it should at least stay out of the way.

I recommend two classifications of artificial intelligence applications:
1) applications that guide the operation of machinery to reduce error and increase efficiency, and
2) applications that are intended to support or replace human decision making.

Examples of type 1 are AI that supports automated steering in vehicles, packing in factories, and storage/retrieval in warehouses. Examples of type 2 are AI that powers policy advice (e.g. financial or medical) or human surveillance.

Type 1 applications should require less strict regulation than type 2, as the success parameters are easier to measure and the symptoms and consequences of application failure are generally clear. In contrast, type 2 applications are more prone to have hidden complications and major negative social side effects that are hard to foresee. The testing and approval processes for type 2 AI applications should therefore be more deliberate and more rigorous.

Transparency in these discussions is indispensable. In this regard, we appreciate the OMBs recommendations for such multi-stakeholder consultation.

In the course of discussions with stakeholders from various standpoints, we believe it is important to develop and implement policies to improve AI literacy of each citizen in order to promote the relationship with the public mentioned in the principles 1. Public Trust in AI and 2. Public Participation of the Draft Memorandum.
In addition, it is important to enhance social acceptability of AI. When considering 5. Benefits and Costs, we believe that principles 6. Flexibility, 7. Fairness and Non-Discrimination, 8. Disclosure and Transparency, and 9. Safety and Security of the Draft Memorandum should be fully taken into consideration.

Finally, we expect that the policies to be developed in accordance with the Draft Memorandum will be consistent with the international policy guidelines on the subject such as the OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence.

Request for Comments on a Draft Memorandum to the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, "Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications," (Federal Register Doc. 2020-00261)

Dear Mr. Ray:

The U.S. Council for International Business (USCIB) is pleased to participate in this call for public comments concerning the Office of Management and Budget's draft "Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications." USCIB is a U.S.-based business association composed of U.S. multinational companies, law firms, and trade associations from every sector of the economy. Importantly, our membership includes a cross-section of leading global companies in the information and communications technology (ICT) sector as well as a diverse array of leader users of ICT technologies and emerging innovations, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI). We appreciate the opportunity to offer both a cross-sectoral and tech-informed perspective on proposed policies or regulations related to AI applications.

As the sole U.S. affiliate of Business at OECD, USCIB members played leading roles shaping the OECD's landmark AI Principles and subsequent OECD Council Recommendation on Artificial Intelligence. USCIB member experts from leading AI innovators such as IBM, Microsoft, Google, and Facebook were tapped to advise development of these principles, which the G20 Trade and Digital Economy Ministers subsequently endorsed at the June 8-9, 2019 meeting in Tsukuba, Japan. Although OMB's proposed AI regulatory guidance is outlined a bit differently from the OECD principles, USCIB members note with favor the high degree to which the OMB proposal aligns substantively with the OECD principles. This constitutes a solid foundation to build upon in considering appropriate policies and regulations for ever-evolving technology.

Key Alignments between OMB Proposed Guidance and OECD AI Principles

We would like to highlight elements of the OMB proposed guidance that are closely aligned with what we developed in the OECD and would like to see implemented in the United States.

Discouraging Premature Regulation - USCIB agrees that pre-emptive regulation risks hampering innovation that ultimately could contribute to economic development, commercial and employment opportunities, and societal well-being. We feel there is great potential for the application of AI in healthcare, "smart city" applications, optimizing and securing telecommunications networks, fraud prevention, financial services, transportation, agriculture, and enabling disabled individuals to become active participants in the digital economy, to name a few. We further concur that a "light touch" approach to regulation of AI is preferable until we develop a clear understanding through further research of how it may be applied beneficially to a variety of use cases, while at the same time addressing privacy, security, and other challenges.

Flexibility - We note that OECD AI Principle 2.3 urges development of a policy environment for AI that supports an "agile transition" from R&D to deployment. OMB's call for performance-based flexible frameworks when developing regulatory and non-regulatory approaches that can adapt to rapid changes and updates to AI applications is in the same spirit.

Safety and Security - USCIB commends OMB for highlighting the need for public trust in AI by designating this as the first principle. We share OMB's view concerning the importance of safety and security issues throughout the AI design, development and operation lifecycle.

Risk Assessment - USCIB strongly agrees that policy and regulatory approaches to AI should be based on consistent application of risk assessment and risk management practices. This concept is the cornerstone of the OECD's 2015 Digital Security Risk Management for Economic and Social Prosperity, which USCIB members also actively shaped as Expert Group participants.

Public Participation - OMB's proposed principles underscore the importance of the public comment process throughout the rulemaking process. They also urge agencies to inform the public and promote awareness of AI standards through the creation of informative documents. This is consistent with OECD's emphasis on initiating public dialogue to enhance understanding of AI and to debate AI-related opportunities and challenges for the economy, society, and the workplace to inform policymakers.

Please see the attached PDF for our comprehensive comments.

Sincerely yours,


Barbara P. Wanner

On behalf of Amnesty International and our more than seven million members and supporters worldwide, we hereby submit this statement in response to the request for information on the "Draft Memorandum to the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Application" (henceforth "AI Memorandum"). Amnesty International ("Amnesty") is an international human rights organization with national Sections in more than 70 countries, including the United States (U.S.)
AMNESTY'S ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ("AI") AND HUMAN RIGHTS INITIATIVE
Amnesty's Artificial Intelligence ("AI") and Human Rights Initiative tackles human rights challenges posed by AI technologies. A core part of the initiative is the enforcement of human rights law to ensure that the development and use of AI does not undermine human rights standards, and instead strengthens such standards where possible.

OVERVIEW
1.AI has the potential to bring positive change for human rights. As noted in the Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications, the deployment of AI technology "holds the promise to improve safety, fairness, welfare, transparency and other social goals." However, Amnesty believes there are key issues with AI systems that urgently need to be addressed to respect human rights.
2.Global innovation and development of AI technology is being substantially driven by major U.S.-based companies in Silicon Valley. The U.S. is one of a handful of countries that has experienced significant economic gain linked to the development of AI. The U.S. Government therefore has a critical role to play in adopting robust regulatory measures and accountability mechanisms to ensure that AI advances rather than undermines human rights. For the purpose of this paper, Amnesty adopts the definition of artificial intelligence as codified in Section 238(g) of the John S. McCain National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019, Pub. L. No. 115-232, 132 Stat. 1636, 1695 (August 13, 2018), and also understands that the scope of the potential regulation covered by these regulations applies to "narrow" AI.
3.Amnesty's chief concerns with current AI systems are that:
AI technology is predicted to fuel significant changes to employment in the U.S., particularly through automation of jobs, which will require governmental action to protect U.S. workers' rights.
AI systems collecting and processing vast amounts of personal data create new threats to human rights, notably to the right to privacy on both an individual and societal level.
A growing body of research demonstrates that AI systems are already contributing to discrimination - for example, in policing and criminal justice systems in the U.S. The Toronto Declaration underscores the risks to the right to equality and non- discrimination that are inherent to machine learning, and outlines means of protecting and promoting this right.
The impact of AI on policing and conflict could have extremely dangerous and irreversible implications on international human rights and humanitarian law.
A lack of transparency and accountability in current systems denies those harmed by AI-informed decisions adequate visibility of harms and access to effective remedy.
Innovation in AI technology is being led by powerful corporate actors and has rapidly advanced before appropriate state-based regulatory safeguards have been put in place.

I am writing to offer very strong support to the provisions allowing component level testing for children's products. We are a small manufacturer (but larger than the small batch exemption) producing wooden toys. To be sustainable we have a very broad product line of about 1000 products covered under the CPSIA. Our initial estimate, in 2008, was that third party testing would cost us $1 million per testing cycle. There is no way for us to afford that. At that time we saw our only opportunity to be component testing and ultimately the CPSC agreed that that was allowable.

We completely manage our own production in our own domestic facility. As such, we use a specific assortment of finishes and inks across our entire product line so it makes sense to test the coatings once and not, for example, every time we use the same red paint on a another product.

A great many of our products are physically built exactly the same, for instance, a truck body that will go on to be decorated as a school bus, fire truck, or dump truck, etc.

Simply put, for each product, we can match up the relevant chemical tests with the respective physical tests to economically provide evidence of compliance on our certificates. We have been fortunate to find testing labs willing support this approach and our lab costs are a much more affordable $50,000 per testing cycle.

To further illustrate how important this is to us, a significant number of our products sell at volumes of under 100 per year. A "full range" test on a single product could cost $2,000. Component testing brings that cost down by 90% or more. Another benefit is the ability to make custom versions of our products on the fly - taking a standard product base and adding a completely custom decoration.

Getting retailers to understand and accept a certificate of compliance based on component testing can be a challenge, especially if they need to see the tests that back it up. We are currently in a major problem with Amazon because they did not build their new compliance system to understand component level testing. They are also expecting to see third party certification on matters that do not require it (flammability and bag thickness - which we do ourselves).

We have had to go back to the regulations numerous times lately to cite the rules that allow us to do things the way we do them. It would help if there was clearer guidance to inform retailers, and others, what is acceptable with procedures and formats.

The CPSIA testing rules have forced changes in our product line over the last decade. We have discontinued many products that were low volume and design outliers, not for safety reasons but for testing costs, even using component testing. Most new product development now looks toward add-ons to existing product platforms to take advantage of shared testing costs. We get the impression that component testing is not a common practice, yet it is core to our continued existence.

As a representative for an industry leading mattress manufacturing company, I have several concerns with this proposed amendment.

First, let me state the company I represent completely supports regulations which protect our customers. We take pride creating products that keep our customers safe. This proposed amendment does not seem to be one of those regulations in my opinion. Here are the reasons why I feel like this amendment is not needed:

1 – At the moment, all US mattresses must pass 16 CFR testing for parts 1632 & 1633 in order to be considered compliant with fire mitigation standards. Both tests accomplish the same purpose which is to ensure mattresses can self-extinguish in the event they come in contact with fire. Out of the 2 tests, the cigarette smolder test (part 1632) exposes the mattresses to a significantly lower amount of heat when compared to the open flame test (part 1633). I personally believe that part 1632 is outdated and unnecessary due to the strict requirements of part 1633 which is a much more intense and scrutinized test. Based on the test results of our company with these tests, it is very uncommon for a mattress to pass part 1633 and fail part 1632. In fact, we have never passed part 1633 and failed part 1632. For that reason, I do not think it is worth anyone's time or money to revise the cigarette requirements for 16 CFR testing for parts 1632. I think a better amendment would be to abolish part 1632 altogether.

2 - We should not need to increase the flammability standard for CFR 1632 if the cigarette industry is continually making lower risk products. The fact that products very similar to the cigarettes used for SRM 1196 are no longer available (such as the cigarette R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Company previously created) tells me that the cigarette industry has transitioned to become Fire Standard Compliant (FSC) which lowers the risk of cigarettes fires. If smokers are no longer using these higher heat cigarettes it does not make sense that the mattress industry should go out of its way to create them and use them for testing.

3 - The cost increase associated with SRM 1196a is substantially larger than the current SRM 1196. This additional cost will ultimately be passed along to consumers increasing the cost of mattresses nationwide. The mattress industry is currently experiencing a period of unprecedented increased costs due to supply shortages and supply chain disruptions caused by the COVID 19 pandemic, and the trade war. I personally do not believe it is fair to the American consumer to pass along any additional costs due to a seemingly unnecessary precaution with this amendment.

4 - With a 74% increase in cost for the new cigarettes, it is clear that the NIST has a financial incentive to pass this amendment. I do not believe it is fair to the mattress industry to be statutorily obligated to purchase this expensive cigarette produced by the NIST at a 74% cost increase when compared to SRM 1196; Especially if there are not comparative products on the open market.

Thank you for your consideration

I am writing to express my opinion that ultrasound contrast agents should be regulated as devices rather than drugs. An ultrasound contrast agent does not achieve its primary intended purposes through chemical action within or on the body. An ultrasound contrast agent is not dependent upon being metabolized for the achievement of its primary intended purposes. Furthermore, an ultrasound contrast agent is only active when an ultrasound machine is used. I am supportive of the FDA’s position that “going forward, in accordance with Genus, FDA intends to regulate products that meet both the device and drug definition as devices.”

Given the Genus decision, I agree that the FDA should “re-examine whether individual imaging agents meet the device definition, including whether they achieve their primary intended purposes through chemical action within or on the body or are dependent upon being metabolized for the achievement of their primary intended purposes.”

I am the original developer/inventor of Definity, an FDA approved ultrasound imaging contrast agent. The first FDA approved ultrasound contrast agent was Albunex (air filled albumin microspheres), developed by Molecular Biosystems (MBI) which was regulated as a Device. Subsequently, MBI developed Optison (albumin coated perfluoropropane microspheres) via the device pathway. Sonus, and my company, ImaRx Pharmaceutical (partnered with DuPont) were also developing ultrasound contrast agents, but were regulated as drugs by the FDA. This led to a lawsuit, as different requirements were being made for similar agents. The FDA approved Optison as a drug, but accepted the clinical and other studies that had been performed while Optison was developed under the device pathway. Ultimately, Sonus product was not approve by the FDA, but the other approved agents, Definity and Lumason had to do more extensive and time-consuming studies than were required for Optison.

I am a radiologist and am familiar with the different imaging modalities. Ultrasound is one of the most common imaging exams, used in echocardiography, radiology ultrasound, gynecology and other studies. Ultrasound is relatively inexpensive and does not use ionizing radiation, has advantages of portability and ease of use. Ultrasound contrast agents improve the sensitivity and accuracy of diagnostic ultrasound. Iodinated contrast media for CT scanning, and gadolinium agents for MRI have been implicated in renal toxicity. Ultrasound contrast agents are not nephrotoxic. I believe that ultrasound contrast agents are safe and, in general safer that X-ray or MR contrast agents. I believe that ultrasound should be used as frontline imaging instead of CT or MRI, whenever ultrasound is adequate for diagnosis.

The time-consuming and expensive studies required for development of ultrasound contrast agents as drugs has hindered innovation. Ultrasound contrast agents fulfill the criteria as established by Genus and merit regulation as devices.

I am currently developing a new ultrasound contrast agent, MVT-100, which is very similar to Definity, except that one of the three lipids (critical excipients) is changed in MVT-100 to a more biocompatible and stable lipid. We had guidance from the FDA that the 505(b)(2) pathway should be used for this new contrast agent. The API, particle count, particle size and gas concentration in MVT-100 are essentially identical to Definity. I believe that MVT-100 should be regulated as a device and given the extensive experience with Definity, and essentially identical characteristics (except substitution of 1 lipid)* that MVT-100 should be regulated via the de-novo 510K pathway.

I appreciate the chance to voice my opinion and would be happy to provide additional information if this would be helpful to the FDA. Regulation of ultrasound contrast agents as devices, rather than drugs, will spur innovations and lead to improvements in patient care.

Sincerely

Evan Unger, MD, FACR
Executive Chairman
Microvascular Therapeutics
1635 East 18th Street
Tucson, AZ 85719
www.mvtpharma.com
eunger@mvtpharma.com

*The API in Definity and MVT-100 is octafluoropropane. The microbubbles are stabilized by a lipid blend of three lipids, total lipid concentration = 0.75 mg/ml. The lipids are the same except that in MVT-100, phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) is substituted for phosphatidic acid (PA), which is present in Definity. PE is the second most common lipid in the human body. PA is not normally present in the body and is seen in inflammation. PA is the most hydrolytically unstable lipid in the lipid blend. PE is more stable to hydrolysis, affording the potential of MVT-100 for room temperature storage versus refrigerated storage for Definity.

I ask FDA to consider reclassification of most cathartic products for colonoscopy preparation to a device category. Following the Genus v. FDA decision, products that could be considered as a drug or a device shall be regulated as a device. Specifically, barium sulfate in the Genus product fulfills the following FDA requirements for a device:

“…(2) does not achieve its primary intended purposes through chemical action within or on the body, and (3) is not dependent upon being metabolized for the achievement of its primary intended purposes.”

The class of marketed products such as GoLYTELY (TM), MoviPrep (TM), SUPREP (TM), and SUTAB (TM) exert their intended effect on the GI tract purely through the osmotic effects of their components including PEG-3350, sulfate salts, and ascorbate salts. Under the FDA definition of chemical action, none of these products achieves its intended effect through a chemical action. Further, none of these products is metabolized to achieve its primary purpose. Despite the FDA precedent to regulate these products as drugs for the last 30-plus years, they have analogous features to barium sulfate products and should be regulated as devices under this new schema.

Consequently, I ask also that cathartic products for colonoscopy preparation in development, such as our own novel pill colonoscopy prep, DCL-101, be classified by FDA as a device. DCL-101 is compositionally identical to iso-osmotic GoLYTELY (TM) but has encapsulated the salt components to render the product taste-free.

As an Investigational Drug Service pharmacist at a major pediatric hospital in the US, I am concerned about the lack of consistency and harmonization of information provided on labels for all investigational product (IP) dosage forms, overwraps, shipping containers, and storage containers provided to study sites by the study sponsors. These concerns are shared with my fellow pharmacists, pharmacy technicians, managers, and department leadership and extends to other disciplinaries that are closely involved with research activities, including nursing, informatics, and research administration.

The majority of IP received at our sites have some form of improper, incomplete, or unclear labeling that often poses an increased risk of a medication error from occurring and/or the compromise of study integrity, which is vital to carrying out a successful research study or clinical trial. Any deviation from expected labeling requirements (which largely follows FDA labeling regulations and laws for commercial products) often requires substantial energy and time from our staff to investigate the discrepancies, reconcile inventories, and ensure proper supply and data integrity. Any issues with labeling deficiencies provided by the manufacturer, study sponsor, or other repacking intermediary fall on our team as the end users of the IP immediately prior to dispensing or administration to the patient.

This administrative burden can translate to clinical error, which would potentially cause patient harm or compromise the study. It seems rather unfair that there is a lack of regulatory standards placed on study sponsors in the labeling of IP at the point of production and distribution and it is up to IDS or research staff to find and mitigate these problems. In the attached document, I highlight several real and possible issues with IP. Many of these images were discussed and shared during the public meeting and only serve to highlight the concerns that I have.

Our hope is that a consensus can be reached as to which pieces of information must be on IP labeling and to hear a clear regulatory pathway to implement and enforce these standards.

As a Master of Public Health student at a national university, I have some concerns for the public’s safety with the inconsistent and harmful labeling of medications in response to docket number FDA-2021-N-0127. Many medication errors are due to the confusing, inconsistent, and missing information on medication bottles, including investigational new drugs. Drug labels need to be health literate for everyone who uses the medicine; such labels should include vital information in a legible font and size. To reduce the rate of error associated with drug labels, there needs to be a consistent format that describes what to include on labels and how to include the information to avoid adverse effects on a patient’s health.

The vital information that should be on every prescription label, even those of investigational new drugs, should be universal across the health care system because 33% of medication errors are due to packaging and labeling.1 Some of the error is due to a lack of explicit dosage and interval information.1 On labels there needs to be how much of the medication to take and when to take it. In addition to dosage, each dosage of the same medication should be easily differentiated to reduce more errors. The FDA is looking at using color coded labels for different dosages of the same drugs such as 5 mg would be a blue label while 10 mg would be green.2 Using a color-coded system would just reinforce that the company, pharmacists, doctors, nurses, and patients are using the correct dosage to avoid over- or under-dosing. This is especially important with investigational new drugs to know the side effects of too little or too much of a dose. Dosage should be clear on every medication label to help avoid health complications.

Another source of vital information that needs to be provided on investigational new drugs are storage requirements. Investigational new drugs are being studied to make sure they are safe and healthy for patients, and to ensure that the studies are being consistent these medications should be stored in the same way. Storing the drugs consistently ensures that the medication is not being modified from heat, cold, or humidity, which can change the effectiveness of the medication. Incorrect storage can cause a medication to expire earlier than labeled by weakening the medicine.3 To ensure investigational new drugs are effective and safe to use the labeling needs to include proper storage information.

Health literacy is one of the major issues in the US healthcare system that contributes to medication errors. Labels should include easy to understand language and symbols that communicate information between the pharmacist, physician, and patient. This easily understood language would be on individual bottles and stock supply bottles. This would help eliminate the confusion with medications and their uses, which would result in a reduction of medication error. This would standardize the labeling system because everything would be in an easy-to-understand language, and there would be little to no confusion regarding prescriptions. In a science, technology, engineering, and mathematics workshop, the label was found to be a defense mechanism for errors, but if it is hard to understand for patients and between specialties then the risk of error increases.4 Using health literate labels ensure that every party who utilizes and works with the drug can understand the risks, benefits, and uses.

Investigational new drugs are closely monitored by the FDA and other agencies to ensure effectiveness and patient safety. To reduce the errors associated with these drugs and to save time and energy for the investigators, labels should contain universal information including but not limited to dosage, interval, and storage. Labels should be at a health literacy level appropriate for the intended population to ensure proper use and to eliminate the risk of any errors. Investigational new drugs are at a higher risk of error because they are new to the market and still being studied, but errors can be reduced with informative, appropriate labels. In agreement with docket number FDA-2021-N-0127, new investigational drug container labels are a cause of medication error, but these errors can be significantly reduced using a universal, health literate, and easily communicated language on the labels.
