The 2 day presentation regarding investigational drugs and labeling was well structured and brought to light some important considerations with end users of the packaging and safety considerations for patients and for those dispensing the products.

I wanted to bring closed system transfer devices (CSTDs) to your attention as well. If needed, the final investigational product and commercial product should take this into consideration as well.

Per USP 800, each institution must maintain their own hazardous drug list, and many use CSTDs with antineoplastic monoclonal antibodies. To minimize error in preparation of antineoplastics and to maintain the same process and workflow for all “chemotherapy” and investigational products, we had chosen to use CSTDs with all antineoplastics (unless incompatible).

One trial is insisting on no CSTDs for a checkpoint inhibitor and refusing to do compatibility testing, though they have compatibility with other CSTDs outside of the one my facility uses. This is an agent which is commercially available. Other institutions are using CSTDs with commercially approved antineoplastic monoclonal antibodies, yet the FDA has not issued safety concerns in using CSTDs with any of these agents. There is nothing in the labeling which specifies incompatibility with CSTDs with such agents. Of note, I received a report from another facility who observed a silicone particulate in the vial of a commercial monoclonal antibody using an CSTD the trial sponsor approved of (this was not part of the trial, but a colleague’s reporting).

Outside of research, there may be unfamiliarity with therapeutic agents requiring BSL-2 or greater precautions in preparation and administration. For example, whenever possible, a CSTD is incorporated into the handling process to reduce exposure to viruses. However, investigational agents are not always provided in a packaging consistent for use with CSTDs. While larger institutions are preparing such agents in separate BSCs, this workflow is not possible for smaller institutions and will be prepared in the same area as other intravenous medications. These are clean room environments which, as you know, require sterility and no microbial growth. The NIH Guidelines for Research Involving Recombinant or Synthetic Nucleic Acid Molecules (NIH Guidelines) detail safety practices and containment procedures for basic and clinical research involving recombinant or synthetic nucleic acid molecules, including the creation and use of organisms and viruses containing recombinant or synthetic nucleic acid molecules. Using infectious agents for therapeutic purposes introduces the possibility of contamination in a sterile environment which can be reduced with CSTDs.

There is a disconnect between product labeling, USP 800, and the NIOSH list. There are “drugs” now which need to be handled as infectious agents, which are biohazards, but not hazardous drugs in the traditional sense. As I’m sure you are aware, the drafted updates to the NIOSH list have removed BCG.

Agents which are classified as BSL-1 only require preparation on a benchtop. Disposal goes the way of many infectious agents (e.g. red trash which is either autoclaved and sent to landfill or incinerated) and cleaning with appropriate agents (e.g. bleach) is recommended. Isolation precautions and procedures for people involved in the care of patients with various infections differ, and the same is true of agents with different biosafety levels. Some agents require more containment based on infectious and genotoxic risk. As pharmacy is often involved in the preparation of such agents, a biosafety assessment regarding workflow for preparation and administration is left up to individual Institutional Biosafety Committees, and there are differences between individual institutions. Standardization of this biosafety assessment with considerations for CSTDs and USP 800, would be appreciated for the end user, particularly because these agents can become commercially available and there are inherent differences between institutions and assessments. The workflow in a laboratory setting on a benchtop or in a BSC is very different from the pharmacy workflow where multiple products are being prepared for multiple patients.

In addition to minimum labeling requirements, we should also ask for a minimum biosafety evaluation for preparation and administration with incorporation of CSTDs and considerations for USP where appropriate

I believe changing the airspace around Fulton Airport would greatly increase safety. It allows for better aircraft separation between the class echo airspace and class golf airspace. If the airspace remains as it is currently, aircraft doing pattern work and aircraft coming into land while in instrument meteorological conditions could get dangerously close. Expansion of Risk Assessment:
While the FAA specifically notes that only a marginal 4% of US-registered aircraft are affected by this legislation, the underlying issue remains that the vast majority of general aviation fixed-wing aircraft have been in service for over twenty and even thirty years. It would be beneficial to the safety of general aviation to expand the evaluation to include other aircraft types with similar CB switch installations. Reducing the need for future rule-making as the aviation industry continues to advance in technology, thereby causing previous generations of aircraft to fall further behind modern safety standards.

Anomalies Reporting Mandate:
The NPRM references “smoke and burning odors” as primary reports of dysfunctional CB switches. However, there is no specification of future reporting requirements to demonstrate the necessity of maintenance and inspection. Meditation operator reporting of anomalies before and after corrective activities would enable the FAA to monitor the success of this legislation and properly identify any trends between aircraft, flight usage, and region. Allowing future issues to be expected and prepared for prior to their occurrence. As well as identifying specific aircraft models/types with potential CB switch issues.

Comment on Alaska SIP/EPA's Approval from Central Boiler and WoodMaster
Central Boiler, Inc. and WoodMaster, Inc. object to the Alaska SIP and EPA’s approval of parts of the State of Alaska’s SIP to address Clean Air Act requirements. Central Boiler, Inc. and WoodMaster, Inc. manufacture EPA-certified, clean, and efficient outdoor wood-burning hydronic heaters. In addition to agreeing with HPBA’s comments, we also object that cord wood outdoor hydronic heaters are excluded in Fairbanks North Star Borough, Alaska and not given consideration based on emissions or performance like other wood heating appliances.

I work in the wood stove manufacturing industry. On a personal level, I would like to say that members of the wood stove industry have great disdain for wood smoke pollution. As an industry, excessive wood smoke is seen as unnecessary, wasteful, and unhealthy. There is no question that the level of pollution in Fairbanks requires action. Unfortunately looking closely at what is proposed, I do not believe that it will have the desired effect and is extremely flawed if the true goal is to clean the air in Fairbanks.
Wood stoves use different types of technology to burn cleanly. Certain types of technology are more likely to be affected by the 6g/hr one hour filter requirement than others. That does not make them bad technology. Wood stoves today were built to burn cleanly over the entire burn cycle, rather than to focus on the first hour. This is simply because that’s how they’re used in the real world and also the way they are certified.
For example, non-catalytic stoves are more likely to be rejected under this rule because they require more heat to burn cleanly. In the first hour, it can take a while to heat up and start burning cleanly. At first glance, it may seem that catalytic stoves are better, but non-catalytic stoves are more user friendly. They do not require any action on the part of the user to burn cleanly. Unlike catalytic models which must actively be monitored and engaged to achieve low emissions. Catalysts also require replacement over time, and if they are not replaced, will result in increased emissions. Why limit access to one technology when both provide similar total emissions over the entire burn cycle? The average emissions from catalytic vs. non-catalytic stoves is nearly identical.
Implementing a 6g/hr limit on the one hour filter does nothing to fix a user that is burning improper fuel or not using their appliance correctly. Alaska needs wood as a fuel source. Education will reduce more emissions than this limit ever could. Even an EPA stove with low emissions on the one hour filter can burn dirty in the hands of the wrong user. In the hands of the right user, a stove that had a bad run on the one hour filter can burn exceptionally cleanly.
In 1988 EPA standards required 7.5g/hr, which was approximately 85% cleaner than uncertified stoves. Then, in 2020 EPA Step 2 removed nearly all those appliances and replaced them with units that cut the emission by another 70%. In that period, appliances have gone from 50-60 g/hr to 2.5 g/hr or less.
This has resulted in only exceptionally clean appliances being certified. The list of available stoves has been severely restricted in the past year alone. Today, the difference between the best and worst performing wood burning units is tiny (not much more than 1 g/hr). It is a difference so small that it could be achieved by leaving the door open too long while reloading. The only effect this requirement would have is to limit customers choice, not improve air quality.
If the 6g/hr one hour filter requirement is adopted, it could cause increases in emissions in other territories. No doubt other jurisdictions could look upon this requirement and (with good but misguided intentions) adopt it as well. That would limit access to clean, inexpensive stoves in a variety of styles. They may choose to hold on to their old uncertified stove rather than upgrade. The implications of this requirement go beyond Fairbanks.
Due to the unpredictability of fire, fuel, operator knowledge, and weather, measuring emissions based on the average burn cycle makes sense. There are simply too many variables in the burn cycle to say that a one hour filter will result in a cleaner burning appliance. This criteria is critically flawed and unscientific when compared to how these products are used and certified in the real world. Two wood stoves that are certified with 1.5g/hr of emissions will emit approximately the same quantity of emissions over the course of a day (if fuel, operator, etc. are equal).
Limiting emissions on the one hour filter is not part of the wood stove design criteria, nor part of the NSPS certification requirement. These stoves were designed to pass tests and satisfy customers. They have already been certified to a stringent standard at great expense. You can’t simply start applying other arbitrary criteria to their certification, particularly flawed ones such as this. It opens too many doors. Where does it end? Successful appliance development is a long term, often multi year process that balances multiple factors to achieve the desired result. To arbitrarily eliminate an exceptionally clean burning, very recently certified appliance which a small manufacturer developed over a period of years, at great cost, is unconscionable.

We are a manufacturer of EPA certified wood stoves; and have been since before EPA’s initial wood emissions standards were promulgated over 30 years ago. As wood related environmental regulations have evolved over the years we have responded - by developing new technologies and appliances that have exceeded every new challenge as it came along.

The foundation of our company is engineering. Our R & D department is staffed with some of the most highly qualified, experienced, and innovative technicians and engineers in the industry. You do not need to take our word for that, feel free to ask people at the EPA, the HPBA, the safety and emissions labs, even people in the know at NESCAUM. We know our stuff.

It turns out that Alaska’s new requirements will most likely benefit our company financially. From what will turn out to be a very short list of qualifying appliances we already build three excellent units. Please bear that in mind when you consider our comments below.

We recognize that Fairbanks is a serious non-attainment area and ADEC is obligated to present a mitigation plan to the EPA. That is their justification for the new requirement that the first hour filter catch must not exceed 6 grams. We have no doubt that Alaska is genuinely attempting to use this requirement to ensure that only the very best performing appliances will be installed. We do not however believe the requirement makes much technical sense and, for the following reasons, are doubtful it will be even minimally effective at achieving the intended result:

Simply put a certification test is conducted by burning a rigidly prescribed wood load in the stove in a rigidly prescribed manner on a test stand which continuously weighs the wood load as it burns. At the same time samples of the stove’s emissions are collected on filters. When a test is completed the filters are weighed which enables the calculation of the emissions in, grams/hour, over the entire test. The test is then repeated at a variety of burn rates with corresponding emissions calculated for each test. These tests are then averaged to determine the stove’s official emissions, in grams/hour.

This seems simple enough, but different stoves burn, not surprisingly, differently. Some stoves start more quickly than others, some burn longer than others, some burn cleanest when burned more quickly, some when burned more slowly. And so on. In the end the testing process does a simple thing. It measures the total amount of emissions produced by the stove over a burn cycle, from start to finish, at a variety of specified burn rates.

Anybody who has ever burned a woodstove knows that a stove takes some time to heat up and burn well so absolutely nobody will be surprised that emissions tend to be worst in the first hour. The Step2 Standard approximates how stoves get operated in a home. Nobody lights a stove and burns it for just one hour, it is practically impossible to do so in a home. So, if two different stoves produce the same total emissions over the course of a day (meaning one produced more emissions in the first hour but less later) their contribution to the airshed will be the same.

Which is what is wrong with Fairbanks’ arbitrarily selected 6 gram of emissions over the first hour requirement. It does nothing to improve air quality and is simply not a relevant selection criterion for determining a “better” appliance.

The current list of EPA Step2 certified appliances is already short. These certified products are the cleanest burning stoves ever produced in commercial quantities and represent the best commercially viable appliances our industry can offer at this time. The differences between them from an air quality standpoint, are not significant. We do not believe that any further whittling down of the list is necessary or justified.

Further comments regarding Alaska’s decision not to accept stoves tested to the ASTM cordwood standard, even though they are currently accepted by the EPA:

Everyone agrees that testing stoves with cordwood more accurately reflects real world operation and should become the default emissions testing protocol. Unfortunately developing a test standard which effectively measures the emissions from a stove burning cordwood is a complex process. Standards development is almost always long and difficult, this one more than most.

After having participated in the ASTM process and conducted considerable internal R & D we are confident that it is a very credible test as it stands. It is different than the current NSPS, but not easier to pass. It produces consistent and reliable emissions values. Although we are confident that our newest stove would pass the current NSPS we have chosen to certify it to the ASTM cordwood Standard. Our certification choice will help move the bar forward towards better testing down road as more data, and criticism, accumulates. Rejecting the process out of hand does the opposite.

The proposed North Star Borough plan includes the following provision:

"(i) 40 C.F.R. Part 60, Appendix A-3, Method 5G or 5H, revised as of July 1, 2017, and adopted by reference; and
(ii) after September 1, 2020, with either a tapered element oscillating microbalance (TEOM) or 1-hour filter data from the EPA certification report for the device; TEOM data must be obtained following the procedures set out in the Northeast States for Coordinated Air Use Management (NESCAUM) Standard Operating Procedures for use of Thermo 1405 TEOM for use in a dilution tunnel using Option 2 in Section 6 and excluding Section 7, revised as of May 17, 2019, and adopted by reference; if using TEOM data, the department may approve devices only if the TEOM data indicates that no rolling 60-minute period exceeds 4.0 grams per hour; if using the 1-hour filter data, the department may approve devices only if no reported valid test run measurement exceeds 6.0 grams per hour;"

My comments on this provision are as follows:

1. I have used a TEOM extensively for wood stove development, generally for getting a quick "snapshot" of real-time of stove performance. I would have grave reservations about including the use of a TEOM for measurements that would lead to formal approval or certification. The EPA has a substantial database of woodstove performance using other methods of collection and measurement. I know of no definitive study that correlates results captured with a TEOM to results from Method 28, for example. Furthermore, the whole PROCESS for such an alternative approval process is described in the proposed plan in a single sentence, without reference to what entity would be approved to do the testing; the format(s) the tests would be reported in, and so on. This strikes me as being very ad hoc.

2. My company makes one stove with a weighted average emissions of 0.5 grams/hour (Model 211, Absolute Steel Hybrid) and HHV efficiency of 77%. This stove is in the top 5 wood stoves for emissions out of all 2020 wood stoves approved and listed on the EPA website. The test fuel for this stove was cribs. This stove had one test run with emissions of over 6.0 g/hr; but the run was not counted in the EPA weighted average because it was replaced with 2 other runs under EPA's test provisions. The run containing the >6.0 gm/hr filter catch was reported, because all test runs are required to be reported, even if the run was not included in the final calculations.

The provision that any stove with a REPORTED test run of over 6.0 g/hr strikes me as arbitrary. We could theoretically do a test (tests?)with a TEOM to prove that the stove was indeed clean burning, but we have already done this by replacing the offending test with 2 additional tests, under the EPA's current provisions. The automatic disqualification after getting 6.0 gm/hr in the first hour is arbitrary; and the remedy of an additional test using a TEOM (when the result has already been discarded by EPA) seems unnecessary. I understand the general thought behind this provision: "If stoves emit more on start-up, let's measure the first hour and eliminate stoves that emit more than _________X". It's not clear to me how 6 gm/hr was chosen. Is there science behind this number? Why would Alaska disqualify on the basis of a run that was reported, but not counted, in the EPA weighted average? Is >6 gm in one hour, on one test, a better predictor of performance than the weighted average of multiple runs? Will this particular requirement produce better results than just lowering the emissions limit from 2.0 gm/hr to 1.5 gm/hr for Fairbanks?

3. There are 3 radical changes happening at once in this plan: 1) changing the test equipment (to include using a TEOM) and 2) changing the metric used to measure and determine the desired result (from weighted average to a weighted average PLUS a one hour emissions cap) and 3) changing the test fuel (from cribs to cordwood). I'm not sure this will get cleaner air in Fairbanks. I am, however, pretty sure that an experiment with this many variables will produce some unexpected results. If the results are not an improvment in air quality, there are enough players to spread the blame around far and wide.

The proposed applications will cause more harm than good, both economically and ecologically. The short-term gains in pest control are unlikely to persist even over the course of an entire growing season due to nearby source populations, good dispersal, and potential multi-voltinism of BMSB in warmer micro-climates. The costs to pollinators, especially bees, which are known to be highly sensitive to dinotefuran, will be larger and more persistent. Production of early-flowering crops such as pomes and stone fruit is likely already pollinator-limited in many agricultural landscapes (Reilly et al, 2020) in the US. Pollination of these crops relies on short-lived solitary bee species which have one generation per year and low fecundity rates (Danforth, 2020), and are limited to orchards and forests. As a result, the reestablishment of already-crop-limiting pollinators in orchards after pesticide treatment is expected to take much longer than the reestablishment of BMSB.

I am a student at the University of Massachusetts Amherst writing about a potential change to the recently proposed rule regarding acifluorfen. The rule described this rule would allow for temporary permissions to be granted to various crop and livestock producers, as well as various pesticide and herbicide manufacturers. It would grant extra usage allowances to protect economic gain via the growth of beets and other crops. However, there are some concerns to be brought up about the nature of these allowances.
Firstly, the rule proposes allowing for the herbicide acifluorfen to be used in an amount of “0.1 parts per million (ppm).” This amount is stated to “ensure that there is a reasonable certainty that no harm will result to infants and children from aggregate exposure to the pesticide chemical residue.” However, while this does seem to indicate that the application of acifluorfen to crops would be safe for human consumption, the wording behind the reasoning is still somewhat vague. If a concerned citizen were to wonder by what metric the pesticide usage amount were deemed safe, finding out would seem to be incredibly difficult. Additionally, if a citizen were to question how the EPA were to go about enforcing this sudden change, there is seemingly no way to do so listed in the description of the rule. The crops grown while these herbicides are in use will eventually reach the dinner tables of American families, and they should have the right to know and access information about production very easily.

Generally speaking, the citizen population is more wary of pesticide and herbicide use than they are trusting. Paul Slovic, a professor and researcher of psychology at the University of Oregon, along with other colleagues, found that about 69% of the American population thought that pesticides and herbicides were highly risky. So, to provide more transparency to the wording and accessibility of information about how this rule would be implemented would be of great use to the American public.
Issues with pesticides and herbicides are still frequent and relevant to this day. A recent case regarding the broad-spectrum herbicide dicamba, and how it was misused, occurred only a few years ago. The topic is still something which worries many Americans. Allowing for transparency around this change in herbicide usage is only right.
The solution I am proposing is to add increased transparency about how the EPA came to the conclusion that this was a safe measure. It is shown that the American citizenry still maintain a distrust of pesticides and herbicides, and would likely gain increased comfort and satisfaction knowing about how those standards are created the way they are. Additionally, detailed descriptions of the enforcement of these pesticide limits are in order. Transparency in these actions is essential in ensuring that the American public feel safe about the foods they eat, so such a change would be greatly appreciated.
I hope for these aforementioned changes to be implemented within the rule in the near future.

I concur with the EPA’s decision to implement Indiana’s revisions to volatile organic compound (VOC) control in their SIP (Docket numbers EPA-R05-OAR-2021-0477; FRL-984-01-R5). Given the widespread nature of VOCs and the various impacts they can have on human health and the environment, staying on top of their regulation both in improving qualifying terms and offering more options to regulated parties is important for continued progress towards air quality standards. Furthermore, revising exemptions based on emissions amount may be an important step in a health focused approach to air quality.
Revisions to include VOC sources under 15 pounds per day in emissions is an important step in mitigating potential hazards, as it has been shown that VOCs in residential districts can disproportionately affect health despite only comprising a small portion of total emissions (Liu et al. 2023, p.9) As such, not exempting certain sources based on amount may be a better method of attaining air quality standards, reducing risks from exposure.
Offering cold cleaner degreasing operations alternative options given that the same or better standard is still met is a good decision. If current usage of low pressure solvents is causing secondary hazardous waste and unnecessary VOC emission from a need to hand clean machine parts, then alternative options should show an improvement overall.
I concur with the revisions to Indiana VOC control. Given that the revisions to Indiana VOC control are expected to maintain the same or better control in certain industries, and the removal of exemption for certain sources, I support the EPA’s proposal to approve these revisions.

From my understanding, with this rule the EPA seeks to maintain, remove, edit, and update certain crops “tolerance” of some of the listed pesticides. By maintaining the “tolerance” this means that the maximum amount of residues of said pesticide allowed in or on food - such as processed foods and feed for animals - will stay the same. I understand that the EPA periodically reviews the various registered pesticides as well as their tolerances, however, I wonder how often these tolerances change? Additionally, for every pesticide listed the ruling states that the “EPA concludes there is a reasonable certainty that no harm will result to the general population, or specifically to infants and children”; however, being the EPA, is the harm of other plant species or the surrounding environment ever considered? For example, with the pesticide ametryn, although the EPA found that no harm will come to the general population, specifically infants and children, they do not state its effect on other plants. In a fact sheet from the EPA, it states that ametryn risks are low to, however, levels of concern occur in mammals and birds that rely on grasses as well as broadleaf plants/insects for their diet. Furthermore, for use as an herbicide, the fact sheet states that “ametryn is toxic to plants, including dicots which are much more sensitive to ametryn than monocots” (EPAa 2004). Similarly on a different fact sheet, with benfluralin, the EPA noted that in “longer-term studies, benfluralin is toxic to the kidneys and liver, and is toxic to the thyroid at high dose levels” and classified it into the following category: “suggestive evidence of carcinogenicity, but not sufficient to assess human carcinogenic potential” (EPAb 2004). I wonder how the EPA assesses the risk of exposure to each of the pesticides listed in this ruling, for example, what sources are they getting their information from. Lastly, it is noted that under Executive Order 12898 (Federal Actions to Address Environmental Justice in Minority Populations and Low-Income Populations), the EPA found that the proposed actions “will not result in disproportionately high and adverse human health, environmental, climate-related, or other cumulative impacts on disadvantaged communities”. Again, how was this conclusion come to? One of the tasks the EPA was given to do is use the best available science in order to regulate pesticides to ensure they are safe to use. After Rachel Carson’s book “Silent Spring”, there was a distinct call to action. The story let it be known the long term environmental costs of increasing the use of unregulated pesticides, inspired the creation of the EPA, as well as began the legislative and regulatory framework on pesticides (S. EPA Office of Inspector General). Since then it seems as if the EPA has become a “timid regulator” that is unable or maybe refuses to keep up with other countries in order to protect the health of people and wildlife (Donley 2022). For example, two investigations by the EPA’s watchdog found many both scientific integrity and transparency issues (Donley 2022). We must do better by not just seeing pesticides as a tool in which growers cannot afford to lose but as something that may cause us to fall behind other leaders in global agriculture in terms of assessing the safety of pesticides. Thank you for your time.

Operationally, the Theory of Planned Behavior links students' beliefs to positive change in behavior through a mechanism involving the delivery of relevant, important, and meaningful topics and content, and the interaction and modeling by volunteers, while instilling the sense that they are capable of performing the activities aligned with financial responsibility that lead to positive outcomes.

OCC 2021 0014- Public Comment
After the 2008 financial crisis, our country became aware of the fundamental flaws in our banking and lending systems. In particular, we witnessed the predatory lending practices against low-income and communities of color. Community banking in these communities can be essential to bolstering investment in and creation of small businesses and economic capital. Thus, the emphasis by the OCC to invest in these communities through improvement of banking policies and practices is commendable. The goal of transparency and consistency in promulgated rules in furtherance of the CRA and limiting the burden on banks will certainly incentivize these entities’ investment in underinvested communities. Promoting the goals of the CRA is also important, especially as we see it as a necessary safeguard against future financial crises.
However, I raise concerns about rescinding and replacing the 2020 rule with the rule promulgated in 1995. Though the proposed reasoning (lack of confusion, undue burden on banks) makes sense in theory, this rule ignores the fact that the 1995 rule was promulgated before the financial crisis. 1995 was a time of deregulation and neoliberal economic policy that actively hurt low-income communities and communities of color. The government officials in charge of leading financial agencies, in my opinion, had outdated economic thinking that contributed to the financial crisis. As such, replacing this rule with a rule promulgated at a very distinct time in our history has the possibility of leading to regressive, not progressive, financial policies in low-income communities.
I propose rethinking potential shortcomings in the 1995 Rule, with hindsight as our guide. Instead of just replacing 2020 rule with the 1995 rule, I encourage OCC to approach the implementation and enforcement of CRA with the lessons we learned from the financial crisis and, instead, tailor it to the needs of these communities, soliciting feedback from those who will be most impacted by this change. Unfortunately, these voices are often silenced and ignored in these decisions. In particular, the specific comments that the OCC requests seem to be tailored towards soliciting the feedback of banks and corporate entities, instead of people who will be most impacted. Though it is important to encourage banks to come to the table, it is imperative that community members who will be served by the banks and savings associations have a voice and are highly encouraged to voice comment.

RE: OCC Docket ID OCC-2021-0014-0001

To whom it may concern:

I am pleased to see the notice of rescission of OCC Guidance that proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act and its Modernization. As a Banking professional who works with institutions subject to examinations from all regulators, I strongly believe that a unified front from joint regulators concerning the modernization is paramount to successful implementation of the changes. I believe all Banks want to service and have a positive impact on their communities and are making stronger efforts than ever before to succeed in doing so.
While I fully support the modernization of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), I would ask the following to be dutifully considered when the joint agencies come together to make their decisions:
1) Let's provide clarity and certainty around CRA-eligible activities. Currently it seems there is too much ambiguity in CRA compliance and too much need to document detailed compliance requirements. Different examiners and different agencies interpret the same rules differently. Subjective terminology often requires examiners to make determinations on a case-by-case basis, so institutions struggle to know what they have to do to comply. I've seen institutions serving the same communities, being examined very differently, when their customer outreach, product base, and demographics are all identical.
2) Currently I believe too much unnecessary documentation is often needed, overly complicating, and limiting the ability to reach underserved and low-to-moderate income populations. Performance Evaluation Methods are inconsistent, and the current regulatory framework is too complex, the asset thresholds for the performance tests and standards have not kept pace with bank asset sizes, and the standards are not applied transparently or consistently in performance evaluations.
3) It would be nice to be able to account for digital transformation and customer preference: Modernization efforts should consider the transformation in both technology and customer preference. It is important for both branch and non-branch channels to be given equal weight, and that institutions be able to demonstrate they are serving the needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income customers, by employing channels that fit their model and their market.
4) Let's consider and permit more flexibility to invest where there is need. The current CRA statute and regulations do not define "community." Instead, banks define their assessment area, which is often the de facto "community." I’ve seen this often leads to some confusion and limits what would qualify for CRA credit. Banks I work with have expressed concern that, in practice, the lack of clarity in the regulations and guidance limits banks’ willingness or ability to engage in CD activities outside of their assessment area(s). Modernization should allow CRA-eligible activity wherever it is needed, including areas identified as underserved, while continuing to ensure banks are helping to meet local community needs.
5) Provide optionality for business models and strategies: While clarity is needed, CRA modernization should also avoid an overly strict one-size-fits-all framework. Rules should take into consideration different banks’ unique business strategies, just as they consider the unique needs of each community that is being served.
I thank the agency(s) for their consideration and efforts made to increase the clarity of the Community Reinvestment Act and its provisions. I look forward to assisting institutions seeking to ease public access and provide necessary products, services, and solutions to their communities.

Regards,

Drew P. Young

To Whom it May Concern:

Revolve Asset Management, the fund manager for Entrepreneur Backed Assets (EBA) Fund, appreciates the opportunity to comment on the OCC’s proposed rules to rescind the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule issued in 2020 and replace it with rules adopted jointly by the Federal banking agencies in 1995, as amended.

Undoubtedly, CRA has led to significant improvements in access to capital for entrepreneurs in underserved markets. Since 1995, banks have issued almost $2 trillion in small business loans, community development loans, and investments in low-to-moderate income (LMI) communities. Furthermore, in cities across the country, CRA has motivated banks to provide loans to and investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) for economic development.

We agree that replacing the June 2020 Rule with rules based on the 1995 Rules would provide consistency among regulators and rely on a proven framework to help banks meet the needs of low to moderate income borrowers and businesses with under $1 million in Gross Annual Revenue. Furthermore, we are encouraged that all three agencies appear committed to developing a uniform revision of CRA and believe that replacing the June 2020 Rule with new rules based on the 1995 Rule will provide an adequate transition period pending a joint revision. We believe a joint revision is critical.
The OCC should not continue to provide consideration for activities that do not directly or indirectly serve either a bank’s assessment areas or the broader statewide or regional areas that include a bank’s assessment areas under the 2020 proposed rules. Given that the OCC had not completed much of the work necessary for banks to understand their revised performance thresholds in new areas, we believe banks attempting to claim credit for new activities only allowed under the 2020 rule would likely have done those activities regardless of the CRA consideration.
The OCC requested specific comment on whether the proposed plan to maintain strategic plans approved under the June 2020 Rule with target market assessment areas is a reasonable way of addressing this transition consideration. The OCC should only maintain strategic plans approved under the June 2020 Rule with target market assessment areas during the transition consideration if the strategic plan period has already begun.

The OCC specifically requested comment on whether three months is sufficient time for banks to make the changes necessary to comply with the public file content and availability requirements of the proposed rules. The OCC advised that during the transition period, examiners will consider all CD activities under the June 2020 Rule that are conducted on or after October 1, 2020. Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rulemaking.

Sincerely,

Revolve Asset Management

Comment of David Zaring, Professor, Department of Legal Studies and Business Ethics, The Wharton School, and Alex Gao and Francisco Torres, students at the University of Pennsylvania School of Law

On September 8, you proposed to rescind the rule revising the Community Reinvestment Act regulations issued by the federal banking regulators in 1995, at least as applied to the national banks regulated by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). The rescission of the rule would align the OCC's CRA rules with those of the other federal banking regulators.
The rule OCC proposes to rescind, reforming the agency's approach to the CTA, was controversial. It did, however, make some progress towards addressing the challenging problem of what to do with internet-based banks. The agency, along with the other banking regulators, should think flexibly about the CRA obligations of internet banks, and support the development of plans designed to ensure that low- and moderate-income (LMI) consumers receive access to banking services in ways that reflect the different geographical scope of these banks compared to their brick-and-mortar peers.

In particular, the OCC should relax the geographic assessment area requirement for banks that do most of their business, lending or otherwise, in cyberspace. Internet banks should be given a choice as to how to meet their CRA requirements. They could do so the traditional way: through an assessment area based largely on their headquarters. But they should be given the option of looking beyond the assessment area, a geographic standard that makes less sense for banks with limited geographic footprints. This would allow these banks to target the LMI borrowers that are meant to be the beneficiaries of the Act wherever they can be found. Alternatively, internet banks should be permitted, with the approval of their bank regulator, to direct their lending and service efforts to particularly underserved areas of the country. One member of the board of governors of the Federal Reserve has suggested that Indian Country might be such a location. Other parts of the country are “banking deserts,” with few branches and little choice for LMI borrowers; strategic plans by internet banks targeting these areas could be useful.

Permitting this sort of compliance would avoid problems that have hampered some of the goals of the act. Because internet banks are disproportionately located in certain cities, those cities have been overserved in the name of CRA compliance, while other jurisdictions have been underserved. It also would comply with the text and purpose of the CRA.

We need an accurate AIM baseline

By David Wojick

It is crucial that the AIM baselines developed by EPA be accurate, especially that EPA's estimates are not significantly lower than reality. The baselines determine the allocations and these must be adequate, lest there be a severe shortage of HFCs.

To take an extreme example, suppose the EPA consumption baseline is just half of what is needed for business as usual. In that case the initial, modest 10% reduction becomes a destructive 55% cut. If EPA is low by just 20%, the 10% reduction still balloons to 28%. Such a shortage of allowable HFCs could wreak havoc with certain industries, to the great embarrassment of EPA and the Administration.

There are three components to the baselines and each needs to be as accurate as possible. EPA recently called special attention to potential gaps in one component, namely the average annual production and consumption of regulated HFCs in 2011-13.
See https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/02/11/2021-02774/notice-of-data-availability-relevant-to-the-united-states-hydrofluorocarbon-baselines-and-mandatory.

EPA proposes to use those HFC quantities reported to its Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP) to estimate this component of the AIM baselines. The Agency notes, however, that there are two limitations to this approach, which it terms "gaps" in the needed data. These data gaps refer to cases of HFC consumption that are not reported. Note that under AIM consumption is defined as production plus importation of regulated HFCs.

The first type of gap is consumption that is not reported because the amount involved is less than the threshold for mandatory reporting. Because it is focused on major emissions of GHGs the GHGRP threshold is rather large, namely 25,000 metric tons (MT) of CO2 or its equivalent.

For GHGs other than CO2 this equivalence is determined by what is commonly called the global warming potential of the gas. In AIM this factor is called the exchange value (EV). Thus for example AIM gives HVC-132a, which was widely used in car AC systems, an EV of 1430. The threshold for GHGRP would thus be 25,000 MT divided by 1430 = 17.5 metric tons. Given that a car might only use 2 pounds of HVC-132a this is a large quantity, requiring almost 20,000 cars.

Moreover, some of the controlled HFCs have far lower EVs, as low as 53. The point is that there might be many instances where HFC consumption did not meet the GHGRP threshold. These numerous gaps could lead to significant underestimation of the baseline.

The second type of gap is one where the consumption did meet the reporting threshold but it was not reported. This is probably relatively unlikely to occur in domestic production, because the producers know they are making HFCs and that these are reportable GHGs. The case of importation however is quite different, especially where the HFCs are contained within imported equipment.

In these cases the importer may not even know that HFCs are present, or if they do that they need to be reported to EPA. To use the above example, someone might import tens of thousands of cars and not report the AC HFCs because they are a minor, hidden and highly technical component of the car. Note that almost half of the cars sold in America are imported, several million a year.

Imports may be especially problematic, in effect combining the gaps. That is HFCs might be produced in large quantities in another country but imported within equipment in many smaller batches. Obvious examples include air conditioners, ranging from window to large building units, fridges, freezers and coolers, as well as aerosol sprays, heat pumps and electricity transformers. The sprays are especially difficult to identify because the unit quantity is in ounces while the import numbers may be in billions.

In the NODA EPA lists those companies that reported importing AIM regulated HFCs during 2011-13. The number is small and includes just one car maker. Given that something like half the cars sold are imported, by many different makers, and all contain HFCs, this list is clearly inadequate for establishing an AIM baseline. An accurate number of importers handling HFCs is likely very large. For that matter, individual consumers buy online from foreign vendors in great numbers.

EPA also lists total reported quantities for both importation and domestic production (minus destruction) for each of the three baseline years. The import quantities are about 20% of production. Given the trillions of dollars spent on imports it is likely that these import numbers are very low compared to reality.

Clearly EPA must look beyond the GHGRP for baseline data. There are other chemical databases that should be useful, including EPA's own Chemical Data Reporting (CDR) system. In addition, many trade associations have statistics or knowledge of production and/or imports in their industry. Getting the AIM baselines right is in everyone's interest.

Economically destructive cap and trade for HFCs is here

By David Wojick

This is a bit complicated so bear with me. To begin with, Biden's avalanche of climate scare executive orders included one telling the State Department to prepare the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer for submission to the Senate, for ratification.

The Kigali Amendment has nothing to do with ozone depletion (a fanciful tale in itself), quite the contrary in fact. The 1987 Montreal Protocol mandated the phase out of CFCs, the primary refrigerant and aerosol propellant at the time. CFC were globally replaced with HFCs, at great expense and bother.

The 2015 Kigali Amendment now mandates the phase out of HFCs. I am not making this up.

HFCs do not threaten the ozone layer, so they have nothing to do with the Montreal Protocol. But the Protocol community decided to do what is called "mission creep". They crept over to global warming, where HFCs are considered a problem. They have what is called a high "global warming potential" or GWP, so they too have to go.

Reportedly Obama and Kerry played a big role in creeping the Protocol, but they never submitted it for Senate ratification, knowing it would never get past the Republicans.

But now, to steal a great line: A funny thing happened on the way to the Senate.

Remember the giant Omnibus Appropriations Act passed in February? It funded the federal government and the Covid stimulus to the tune of $2.3 trillion. It also, as usual, included some riders that probably could not pass by themselves.

Well on page 1074 we find the "American Innovation and Manufacturing Act" or AIM. Incredibly, AIM includes the entire Kigali Amendment. (Still not making it up.) Not by name, mind you, but all the HFC phaseout rules and time table, pretty much word for word. I wonder if the Senators that voted for this addition to the Omnibus knew they were letting Kigali in the back door?

Simply put, this is a cap and trade system for HFCs, with a cap that declines over time to the point where almost no HFCs are allowed in America.

So, for example, AIM and Kigali establish the same cap. Here it is almost funny. Kigali was formulated in 2015 so the cap is mostly based on how much HFC was made and imported in 2011-13. Back then this was recent supply data. AIM uses the same dates, even though the present HFC supply situation may be very different. The only explanation for AIM using 8 to 10 year old data to establish the cap today is that it is Kigali by the back door.

So the Senate will be asked to ratify something that is already law. I hope they refuse but maybe it is not worth the filibuster. To paraphrase another great line, the greens don't need no stinking Senate. They got Kigali in the back door already. Note that China, the world's biggest producer of HFCs, has not ratified Kigali or implemented it by law.

In any case we now have before us a looming declining-cap and trade system for HFCs. EPA is moving quickly and is expected to propose the regulations for this system shortly. There are some big potential problems.

Keep in mind that some of the many primary uses of HFCs, in vast quantities, are these:
Air conditioning in cars, homes and big buildings
Refrigerators, freezers and chillers
Aerosol sprays
Electric power transformers
Heat pumps
Structural foam
Fire suppression

Note too that the leading candidates for HFC replacement are HFOs, which presently have some serious problems. For example they can be flammable, and they do not last all that long. In fact one reason they do not have a high GWP is that they self destruct quickly in air.

By far the biggest problem with AIM is that outdated cap. Technically it is called a "baseline" which sounds friendlier than a cap. But the HFC allowances EPA will distribute, in ever decreasing amounts, are from the baseline, so it is the cap.

In fact there are two big problems here. First of all we really have very little information on HFC production and import 8 to 10 years ago. EPA recently acknowledged this, again in an almost funny way.

They issued what is called a "Notice of data availability" or NODA. Normally a agency issues a NODA to announce the availability of new data, hence the name. But EPA's NODA says they do not have good data about HFCs in 2011-13 and asks for suggestions. So this is really an EPA "Notice of data unavailability" or NODU.

Second it looks like HFC use today is much greater than it was 8-10 years ago. It is crucial that the AIM baseline developed by EPA be accurate, and especially that EPA's estimates are not significantly lower than reality. The baseline determines the allocations of allowances and these must be adequate, lest there be a severe shortage of HFCs.

Good afternoon,

On behalf of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, we respectfully submit these comments in response to the current EPA Proposed Rule: Phasedown of Hydrofluorocarbons: Establishing the Allowance Allocation and Trading Program Under the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act, EPA-HQ-OAR-2021-0044.

We appreciate the opportunity to provide feedback and insight in this particular area of interest.

Security Equipment Corporation uses Hydrofluorocarbons (HFC) in several of our SABRE Law Enforcement red pepper sprays and our FRONTIERSMAN bear attack deterrent. These products are used by law enforcement agencies and consumers who hike, camp and hunt in the great outdoors. Our products are used widely throughout the United States. HFC 134a is the non-flammable aerosol propellant in these products. It provides safety to law enforcement officers and consumers.

The purpose of the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2019 is to reduce the use of HFC’s and eventually ban them. We depend on HFC’s to provide safe products which in turn provide safety to law enforcement officers and consumers.

The recommended replacement for HFC-134a is HFO 1234ze. HFO 1234ze is being pushed by Honeywell to phase out HFC’s. Honeywell advertises HFO 1234ze as a drop-in replacement for HFC 134a. Through the course of testing HFO 1234ze compared to the HFC 134a, we have found three significant areas where HFO 1234ze is inferior to HFC 134a. These issues will cause the potential for great harm to law enforcement and consumers relying on our products for protection.

We have been petitioned previously about the ban of HFC’s. The EPA issued it’s SNAP Ruling in 2015. We began testing alternative propellants and formulas that time. The SNAP Ruling was overturned, however, we continued to test alternative formulas in order to comply with the eventual ban of HFCs. To date we have worked with Honeywell technical resources to develop a HFO 1234ze formula that is comparable to the current state. After several years of trying, we are no closer to success. We do not believe that regulations allowing more time to test will yield positive results. Buying more time will not solve the problem.

The major deficiencies of HFO 1234ze include 3 areas:

Issue #1: Vapor Pressure.
The Vapor pressure of HFC 134a is 71 psia @ 20 C.
The Vapor Pressure of HFO 1234ze is 56 psia @ 20 C.

At all temperatures, the vapor pressure of HFO-1234ze is substantially lower than that of HFC-134a. For aerosol products, this lower vapor pressure manifests as reduced product deployment distance. Our testing has shown on average a 35% reduction in deployment distance when formulated with HFO-1234ze versus of HFC-134a. The reduced distance constitutes much less protection to law enforcement and consumers. This is a huge safety concern. Law Enforcement will need to stand closer to a violent subject in order to use the red pepper spray products. Consumers using the bear deterrent will need to be closer to an attacking bear for the spray to reach the bear.

The greatest issue to human health is the limited range of law enforcement red pepper spray and bear spray containing HFO 1234ze. By reducing the distance of the spray, law enforcement officers are put at a greater risk for injury or death due to a combative subject. Consumers using our bear deterrent will have to be much closer to bears which could likely cause great bodily harm or death.

Issue #2: Boiling Point.
The Boiling Point of HFC 134a is -26.5 C.
The Boiling Point of HFO 1234ze is -19 C.

The boiling point is the temperature at which the liquid turns into a gas and pushes the liquid formula out of the canister. HFC 134a boils at -26.5 C. this is 7.5 degrees lower than 1234ze. HFC 134a is able to fire law enforcement red pepper and bear spray at colder temperatures than HFO 1234ze. This means law enforcement and consumers are able to have a product that works at a greater range of temperatures and provides a greater level of safety.

Issue #3: Flammability
HFO 1234ze is categorized as non-flammable. It is non-flammable when sprayed through a candle to test for aerosol flammability. However, when it is mixed in formulation and sprayed through a candle, there is significant flame extension. HFC 134a is also non-flammable. It does not project a flame when sprayed through a candle during an aerosol flammability test. It suppresses the flame and does not allow the inert ingredients, all of which are categorized as non-flammable, to ignite.

Flammability is a great concern to law enforcement. Law enforcement officers cannot use a flammable red pepper spray with a Taser. The Taser will ignite the red pepper spray and the subject who has been sprayed. This is a great risk to cause injury to a subject and a law enforcement officer.

Flammability is a great concern to bear spray users who work on oil and gas pipelines. It was the main concern we heard from users when we developed our non-flammable bear spray products. HFO 1234ze would create a significant flammability risk for consumers using bear spray who work on oil and gas pipelines.

++ Reverse capricious and unreasonable timing and waiver provisions: The oppressive and inflexible time limits and application of waiver provisions in the 2020 Rule make it impossible for many states and tribes to fulfill their statutory obligation to protect water quality, especially for complex projects such as fossil fuel pipelines which often cross hundreds of waterways. While Congress plainly intended to include reasonable time limits for Section 401 reviews, cases such as Hoopa Valley Tribe v. FERC have been grossly misinterpreted by EPA and other federal agencies to compel draconian and oppressive results inconsistent with plain Congressional intent.
++ Ensure that the public’s rights are protected: Members of the public, and particularly environmental justice and other underserved communities, regularly rely upon Section 401 by engaging in certification processes to protect their communities and waterways from pollution. By restricting states’ and tribes’ authority and time to complete their reviews as described above, the 2020 Rule also necessarily reduces the public’s rights. This is inconsistent with the statute and settled federal authority, including the very first section of the Clean Water Act, which commands that public participation “shall be provided for, encouraged, and assisted by the Administrator and the States.”
++ Undo the federal agency “power grab”: The 2020 Rule creates procedural “traps” to allow federal licensing agencies to “call foul” based on a purported procedural defect and then conclude that a state or tribe has waived its authority because there is no remaining time to cure the purported defect. This turns the intent of Section 401 on its head and plainly contradicts the statute, which requires that federal agencies “shall” respect state and tribal determinations regarding water quality impacts. Disputes regarding state Section 401 decisions, whether substantive or procedural, are the domain of the judiciary, not of the same federal agencies that are obligated to comply with Section 401’s mandatory duties.

Section 505 of the Clean Water Act also allows people to enforce any “effluent standard or limitation,” which explicitly includes “a certification under [Section 401].”

I implore you to do the right thing, to fulfill to the best of your capability EPA’s mission of protecting human health and the environment, and to reverse the unlawful giveaway to polluting industries that was plainly the intent and result of the 2020 Rule.

Respectfully submitted,
Tina Krauz

RE:Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2021–0302
Notice of Intention to Reconsider and Revise the
Clean Water Act Section 401 Certification Rule

Clean Water Act (CWA) Section 401 requires that any applicant for a Federal license or permit to conduct any activity which may result in any discharge into the navigable waters of the United States, shall provide the licensing or permitting agency a water quality certificate from the State agency with jurisdiction over water pollution control. In Puerto Rico, such agency is the Puerto Rico Department of Natural and Environmental Resources (DNER) pursuant to the provisions of Act No. 416-2004, as amended, Puerto Rico Public Environmental Policy Act and after enactment of the “Reorganizational Plan of the Department of Natural and Environmental Resources of 2018”, Act No. 171-2018.

Herein the DNER are submitting its comments regarding the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Intention to Reconsider and Revise the Clean Water Act Section 401 Rule.

Pre-filing Meeting Request (Part 121.4)

It is the DNER understanding that the pre-filing meeting is useful in the cases of new discharges, in order to allow that the applicant and the certifying authority could share information about the discharge and the certification process. The rule should provide some flexibility in the cases of renewal applications or when the applicant has multiple facilities with discharges of the same nature that require Federal permits. Part 121.4 should include some language that allow that the minimum 30-days timeframe to submit the certification request be shortened upon agreement between the applicant, the certifying authority, and the permitting agency.

Certification Request (Part 121.5)

Part 121.5 should include provisions to request the applicant to comply with any requirement established in the applicable State laws and regulations. For example, the certification request should include all the necessary information required by the State Water Quality Standards Regulation that allow the certifying authority to verify compliance with the Antidegration Policy or complete any procedure for the translation of water quality standards into effluent limitations using Waste Load Allocations, Mixing Zone or any other provision included in such regulation.

Reasonable Period of Time (Part 121.6)

When establishing the reasonable period of time, the Federal permitting agency should consider in addition to the factors listed in item (c) of Part 121.6, the timeframe of the certification process of the certifying authority. It has been our experience that in some cases a Federal agency, even in the knowledge that the state process does not allow the issuance of a water quality certification to be completed within the established “reasonable” period of time (60 days after receiving the certification request), have refused to establish a longer period of time and denied the extension of time requested under the provisions of Part 121.6(d). EPA should therefore consider revising Part 121.6 to prevent that a Federal agency from acting arbitrarily in determining the reasonable period of time, particularly in cases of certification request for general permit where the Federal agency is also the applicant. Furthermore, when establishing the reasonable period of time, the Federal agency must take into consideration the laws and regulations governing the certifying authority's administrative procedures. Therefore, Part 121 should include a subpart that address applicant right to request a reconsideration of a condition included in the certification or the denial of the certification, following the statutory procedures of the certifying authority.

In addition, Part 121.6 establishes that the reasonable period of time begins after receipt the certification request. According to Part 121.1(m) receipt means the date that a certification request is documented as received by a certifying authority in accordance with applicable submission procedures. It should be specified that the reasonable period of time begins after receipt a complete certification request. Also, the beginning of the reasonable period of time set forth in Part 121.6 is inconsistent with Part 124.53, which indicates that the State certification shall be granted or denied within a specified reasonable time not to exceed 60 days from the date the draft permit is mailed to the certifying State agency unless the Regional Administrator finds that unusual circumstances require a longer time. EPA should review the language of both rules to be consistent and avoid confusion when implementing the rules.

We appreciate the opportunity to provide our comments and feedback regarding EPA's intention to reconsider and revise the 2020 CWA Section 401 Certification Rule.

Cordially,

Ángel R. Meléndez-Aguilar
Manager
Water Quality Area

I oppose the merger of Huntington National Bank and TCF National Bank and I am requesting a public hearing in Detroit on this matter. Banks spend billions of dollars annually under the premise of supporting low-to-moderate income communities and individuals, yet we have astronomically high levels of poverty, Black and Latino Business owners cannot access capital and Black & Latino Developers cannot gain access to capital to build and strengthen their communities. Huntington has not proven to be any different. With each merger, they promise to commit millions/billions of dollars for low-to-moderate income communities, yet based on their most recent CRA Performance Evaluation, largely Black and Latino populated cities with high levels of low-to-moderate income census tracts show that Huntington Bank has received a POOR Lending Rating for Home Purchase, Refinance and Home Improvement as proven from this excerpt taken from Huntington Banks most recent performance CRA evaluation for the Detroit MD. (page 62-63)

Detroit MD Overall, the geographic distribution of home mortgage loans is poor. The overall geographic distribution of home purchases loans is poor. The percentage of loans in low-income geographies was well below the percentage of owner-occupied units in these geographies. The percentage of loans in moderate-income geographies was significantly below the percentage of owner-occupied units in these geographies. The bank's market share in low-income census tracts exceeded its overall market share for home purchase loans. The 62 Charter Number: 7745 bank's market share in moderate-income census tracts was significantly below its overall market share for home purchase loans. The overall geographic distribution of home improvement loans is poor, considering the limited volume, where a single loan can significant impact distributions. The percentage of loans in both low- and moderate-income geographies was significantly below the percentage of owner occupied units in those geographies. The bank's market share in low-income census tracts exceeded its overall market share for home improvement loans. The bank's market share in moderate-income census tracts was significantly below its overall market share for home improvement loans. The overall geographic distribution of home refinance loans is adequate when considering market share performance. The percentage of loans in both low- and moderate-income geographies was significantly below the percentage of owner-occupied units in those geographies. The bank's market share in both low- and moderate-income geographies exceeded its overall home refinance market share.

Yet, Huntington Bank received an Outstanding Rating which they like to boast about, when challenged by the communities they are supposed to serve. This type of performance is unacceptable.
Until Huntington Bank agrees to partner with local Black and Latino Leadership and decentralize their current community benefit plans, which do not work, this merger should not close.

Great Communities Now Coalition wholeheartedly stands behind the efforts of the Detroit Black and Latino Community CRA Leadership Council (DBLCCLC's). For much of history, Blacks and Latinos have been held accountable to accomplish results that are often unobtainable because we are often bound to an uneven and unequal playing field. As is well known, these practices have had long term impacts on African American success and lack thereof and its disturbing that such practices still continue to exist today. Over the years of inequities by unfair banking, poor lending practices, blocks to asset equity, limited or blocked access to capital have resulted in failure to thrive in our communities. Then when it is exercised, the cost often combined with higher interest rates, charges, and fees place many black and Latino borrowers in a further defeated position. Basically, long term and generations of negative economic impacts have been created for many many years. Supports and information provided to some are sorely lacking in the Black and Latino communities.

The proof is in the details. Let's have a focused review of the true and real banking practices. There definitely is a real and long standing need to put some extra soil under the concrete of our Black and Latino communities to level the playing field and allow those left behind to gain footing and momentum. The banking industry has historically (and it continues today) employed practices that marginalize blacks and Latinos causing unstable economic foundations. We are asking that the entities that be look closer at repairing/sealing the gaps. We need institutions that will boost African American communities and reach out to Huntington and other banks of the like to take a look at their practices and change the negative course of their actions! Until that is done, any efforts to boost Huntington Banks strength, that could likely foster further economic, community, social and psychological damages, should be wholly denied. Now is the time to fix these inequities!
Ms Jacqueline D. Perkins
Communities Now Coalition

I agree with the proposed rule to classify the Texas Kangaroo Rat as endangered and designate its critical habitat as there is overwhelming evidence in support of the rat. The United States Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) has identified a decrease in the Texas Kangaroo Rat’s population and has traced this decline to the increase in humans in the rat’s habitat (Texas Kangaroo Rat). Human growth in the rat’s habitat has led to increases in farming and development which interferes with the rat’s ability to survive, as the rat is known to live in short grasses and burrow within prairies which end up being cleared with human growth. The FWS also states that there is present evidence that climate change and human fire suppression will lead to the rat’s current habitat becoming a shrubland which would be detrimental to them (Texas Kangaroo Rat).

Focusing on the farming concerns specifically, the area around the rat’s habitat has become heavy on grain farming and livestock. Farming is detrimental to the rats as it destroys much of the short grass prairies the rats rely on. The increase in farming shows no signs of stopping as the National Agricultural Statistics Survey taken in 2017 displayed a 35 percent increase in farm acreage in Childress County and a 76 percent increase in Cottle County since 2012 both of which make up a large portion of the rat’s habitat (United States Department of Agriculture). This acts as an exhibit to show that without action, the habitat of the Texas Kangaroo Rat will only continue to decrease as time goes on, which is why it is essential that this rule moves forward and classifies them as endangered.

Critics against listing the rat as endangered may mention the fact that some evidence points towards cattle farming being beneficial for the species. This is because in the past the rat relied on bison and prairie dogs to maintain the short grass, keep the area low on shrubs, and leave sparse spaces for potential habitat and food. The issue with this, however, is pointed out again by the FWS who mention that the loss of habitat from the decades without bison has already dealt too much damage to the rat’s habitat and cattle grazing would not do enough to revitalize the population (Texas Kangaroo Rat). The common theme when analyzing the state of the Texas Kangaroo Rat is no matter how you look at it, human actions are harming their ability to survive.

Allowing the Texas Kangaroo Rat onto the endangered species list would allow for habitat protection of a species that desperately needs it. If expansion into the rat’s habitat were to stop, the rat would have a chance to rebound from the decades of population decline they have faced. The common denominator is that they need help.

In summary, it is essential that this rule is finalized and adds Texas Kangaroo Rat to the endangered species list. Adding the species to the list would provide protection of its habitat, which statistics on farm growth and climate concerns both show is degrading more and more without intervention. I urge this rule to be finalized after the commenting period.

I strongly agree with the proposed rule that the Texas Kangaroo Rat should be listed as an endangered species under the Endangered Species Act of 1973. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Endangered Species Act is in place to protect fish, wildlife, and plants that are considered endangered or threatened. It also serves the purpose of executing plans for the recovery of the species and their habitat (U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, n.d.). As reported by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, the Texas Kangaroo Rat is listed as a threatened species (Texas Parks and Wildlife, n.d.). The Endangered Species Act defines a threatened species as “any species which is likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future throughout all or a significant portion of its range” (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, 2019). The Texas Kangaroo Rat falls into the category of a threatened species as defined by the Endangered Species Act due to its decreasing availability of proper habitat, therefore should be a species listed under the act.

The Texas Kangaroo Rat can be found in Texas as well as other areas in the southwestern United States as well as northern areas of Mexico. The primary habitat of this species is areas with clay soils and short grasses, and the animal lives in dens underground near mesquite trees and bushes (Texas Parks and Wildlife, n.d.). However, it has been found in recent years that the Texas Kangaroo Rat’s habitat is dwindling due to the conversion of their prairieland habitat to roads, cities, and various farmlands. Additionally, speculations have risen as to whether climate change and the warmer temperatures have had a negative impact on the short grasslands in which the animal prefers to live (U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, 2023). Therefore, between the destruction of habitat and the over-utilization of this land for commercial and recreational purposes, this can be a portion of the basis for adding the Texas Kangaroo Rat to the list of endangered species.

Furthermore, the decrease in beneficial species to the Texas Kangaroo Rat such as bison and prairie dogs has also been detrimental to the species. Texas Kangaroo Rats benefitted from the grazing of bison as well as the colonization of prairie dogs to keep the habitat maintained with short grasses and areas to burrow. However, due to the decline in these species, human-made factors affecting the environment, climate change, and the ultimate destruction of critical habitats, the Texas Kangaroo Rat has become threatened. According to the Endangered Species Act, critical habitats are defined as “geographic areas containing features essential for the conservation of listed species, and which may require special management considerations or protection” (U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, 2023). If this proposed rule is put into place, then plans can begin to be implemented for the critical habitats of the Texas Kangaroo Rat to be restored and protected. According to the act, species can be listed if threatened due to destruction or modification of habitat, over-utilization for commercial purposes, or other human-made factors affecting the wellbeing and existence of a species (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, 2019). The Texas Kangaroo Rat should be protected under the Endangered Species Act because of the current known threats to its habitat and its ability to thrive in the environment.

The Texas Kangaroo Rat species is no stranger to the threat of extinction. Dipodomys elator was first found in the 1890s in the northern low plains of Texas. It has continued to inhabit this area and the counties that make it up, even though human development of the region since the boom of the westward expansion has critically endangered it multiple times. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, it was first listed as endangered in 1983. It has found its way on and off of being listed as endangered. Now in 2023, it not only finds itself to be endangered but it’s habitat has also been classified as critical habitat that is at risk of destruction due to factors such as human impact, climate change, and invasion of woody plants into the prairie biome.
Unfortunately, very little is known to us about the species’ behavior. They are incredibly elusive, which makes it difficult for researchers to present a concrete number of individuals that are left. At this point,there are thought to be less than 100 Dipodomys e. in its wild habitat, based on field research conducted by a group with LandPotential. This species of Kangaroo Rat is a forager and a primary consumer that feeds primarily on grain. It is reliant on the presence of the mesquite tree, Prosopis glandulosa, to build its complex system of burrows.
Besides its unique appearance that sets it apart from other kangaroo rats, the Texas Kangaroo Rat also is known to create extensive and elaborate burrows, with many food storage areas and chambers to help regulate temperature. Since it is a unique organism and a primary consumer, it holds a crucial place in the area’s food web, which could see cascading results if Dipodomys e. is lost. The relationship with the mesquite tree, as mentioned above, is also unique and is one of the reasons that it finds itself endangered due to agricultural plants crowding out and outcompeting mesquite trees. This kangaroo rat has been found to be compatible with living on lands that can be dedicated to livestock grazing. Conversion of agricultural fields into livestock grazing areas and limiting habitat fragmentation due to development may help to get population numbers up. I believe that it is important to list the Texas Kangaroo Rat to help save it because it is such a unique and rare species that we know too little about. It is worth dedicating time and resources to saving because it could cause issues within the food chain that we are unable to see at this time and may prove to be disastrous for Texas’ wildlife, biodiversity, and distinctive habitats.
