I agree with the proposed rule that the Texas Kangaroo Rat should be considered an endangered species. I also agree that its habitat must be protected. Measures must be taken to protect this species, however, to do it correctly we must analyze the cause of the species’ decline. Once fully understood, we can begin the steps toward recovery.

A study led by Russell S. Pfau, a professor at Tarleton State University, assessed genetic diversity patterns to see if they contributed to the decline. Tissue samples were taken from four locations across Texas. The study concluded that low levels of mtDNA variation were present throughout the species (Pfau et al., 2019). The low variation levels could have been caused by the scarcity of vegetation leading to a population bottleneck.

Another study led by Janet K. Braun from the University of Oklahoma attempted to determine the presence of the species in Oklahoma where it has previously been found. Surveys were conducted throughout various counties over three years. The results show that levels of the Texas Kangaroo Rat have been eliminated in the areas of Oklahoma where it was historically present (Braun et al., 2021). This could be attributed to human activities such as habitat fragmentation and various agricultural activities. It is because of these facts that I believe the Texas Kangaroo Rat should be listed as an endangered species and it is crucial that measures are taken to protect its habitat.

In regards to setting aside land for the preservation of the Louisiana Pine Snake I believe this is a good idea and necessary to prevent the extinction of these snakes. The diet of the Louisiana Pine Snake consists of mostly Bairds’ pocket gophers and occasionally other small rodents. Due to the diet specification of the Louisiana Pine Snake, the preservation of this species is more difficult. This is due to the habits of the Louisiana Pine Snake and the availability of these gophers in comparison with other small prey in the areas where these snakes reside. These snakes use the burrows of the gophers they eat to hunt their prey, to hide from other predators, primarily avians, and evade environmental pressures such as wildfires. The Louisiana Pine Snake is a constrictor snake and is non venomous which reduces the risk of harm to humans by these snakes. The Louisiana Pine Snake primarily resides in long leafed pine forests which have been reduced due to logging of these types of trees. Unfortunately the habitat of these snakes were reduced due to this along with logging companies replacing the long leafed pines with loblolly pines which grow faster than long leafed pines. However loblolly pines have denser canopies than long leafed pines which chokes out the undergrowth below the trees which change the forest floor and make the area unfit for the prey of these snakes. The other challenge with the preservation of these snakes is that they only produce three to five eggs per clutch which is much less than other snakes making repopulation more difficult to achieve. Therefore through setting aside land for the preservation of these snakes along with reestablishing long leafed pine forests throughout the areas in which these snakes reside, we can ensure that these snakes will continue to exist for future generations. When considering this issue the economic impact of such actions should be taken into consideration. Since the economic consideration is currently under peer review it is difficult to tell how much these actions could impact these regions.

Executive Summary
The proposed critical habitat designation for the Louisiana pinesnake is poorly tailored to address the threats to the species. By failing to adequately consider effects on private landowners, the Proposed Rule violates the Endangered Species Act (ESA), the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), and the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA).

First, the Proposed Rule radically underestimates the costs of designating critical habitat. Because critical habitat designations disproportionately impact private landowners, Congress required the Service to consider all economic impacts of designating critical habitat. Instead of following that mandate, the Service considered only the economic impacts solely attributable to the critical habitat designation. The Service also failed to measure how the critical habitat designation will reduce the values of private lands affected by the designation. As a result, although the Service expects that the designation will have little measurable effect on the species’ conservation, it still proposes to designate 72,925 acres of private land as critical habitat.

Second, the proposed critical habitat designation does not include the analyses required by NEPA and the RFA, despite the rulemaking record reflecting many impacts on the human environment and on small entities.

For these reasons, as discussed in the comments below, Pacific Legal Foundation urges the Service to correct these errors prior to finalizing the proposed critical habitat designation for the Louisiana pinesnake.

Neonics are a modern class of insecticides that have been widely adopted to manage some of the most destructive insect pests on crops. These products are being used in place of older insecticides because of their effectiveness against pest management programs and favorable environmental profile and mammalian safety.

Neonics are used on many crops such as soybeans, wheat, cotton, sorghum, and canola. They are also used on many smaller-acreage horticultural crops, ornamental plants, lawns and even on pets for flea control. These pesticide products are extremely valuable for America's agricultural industry because of their use in integrated pest management (IPM) programs. Neonic insecticides help ensure beneficial insects remain available to keep other potential pests in check due to their selective control of target pests. If farmers were potentially forced to rely on older classes of chemistry it could result in reduced yields, more frequent sprays, higher costs, and less selective on types of pests impacted.

Pesticides are highly regulated products in commercial use, with over 120 different baseline studies required for new EPA registrations. These studies assess safety to humans, wildlife, and the environment. On average it takes around 11 years for a new product to be registered, sold and used in the U.S. marketplace. All pesticides, including neonics, are required to undergo periodic evaluation to ensure they continue to meet the highest standards of safety necessary to protect human health and the environment.

One of the most common uses for neonics is part of seed treatment technologies to protect vulnerable seeds from threats of insects and diseases that exist in the soil during early developmental stages. Agricultural retailers provide seed treatment services for their farmer customers to deliver a very precise pesticide application that ensures the plant has a greater opportunity to grow a strong root system which is the foundation of a healthy, productive plant. Seed treatments also reduce the environmental impact on the crop production process by decreasing the necessary number of pesticide applications during the planting season and lessening potential exposures to non-target species, including humans and pollinators. Agricultural retailers, their farmer customers and other key segments of the industry are constantly evolving to improve seed treatment processes.

My main concerns are regarding additional PPE requirements, reductions in seasonal application rates, crop growth stage restrictions, and proposed spray drift and runoff mitigations. EPA has proposed that applicators wear a respirator and gloves for certain uses of clothianidin and thiamethoxam including for treating corn and seed. While safety is of the highest importance, any additional PPE requirements should be based on confirmed risks so to maximize employee compliance and not overburden our members with unnecessary costs.

I am concerned that the proposed reduced application rates will result in fewer total soil and foliar application availability for all neonics. For some crops, these reductions would have minimal impact but for others it would be more significant. Since these restrictions are based on maximum pounds of active ingredient per acre per year, they may harm industries where multiple crops are grown per year on the same site. In this case, the restriction would not account for the need of applications across multiple crop growing seasons. Compared to other insecticides, neonotinoids are more selective, allowing for the preservation of beneficial insects, which are a key element of IPM programs. Neonicotinoid products are very effective against certain types of insects and would be replaced with older, less selective products that would negatively affect beneficial insects, reduce yields, and lead to more frequent and costly applications of insecticide products.

In an effort to reduce harm to pollinators, EPA has proposed changes in appendix B that would broadly eliminate needed bloom applications for crops where previous exemptions were made. The main crop groups affected include fruiting vegetables, tree fruit and nut crops. I am also concerned by the language proposing applicators be required to use a "medium or coarser droplet size." This wording is problematic because it makes compliance unlikely and open to litigation. My industry has been able to achieve these goals without such strict language.

EPA needs to make risk decisions and benefit assessments based on actual data and real-world situations that can be properly peer-reviewed. I trust EPA will refine, as necessary, based on sound science and field data and think through IPM and resistance management requirements as the agency continues the registration review process.

The State of Utah (State) has reviewed the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (Service) advance notice of proposed rulemaking published in the Federal Register July 27, 2022, which addresses regulatory standards and criteria for compensatory mitigation mechanisms consistent with the Endangered Species Act (“ESA”) and its implementing regulations. The State supports consistency, transparency, and predictability for project proponents and mitigation providers as the conservation banking program continues to grow. However, the State submits the following additional comments for your consideration.

1.Cooperation and Coordination with the State.

The ESA protects species of wildlife and/or plants that have been “listed” as endangered or threatened. Once a species is listed, it is then afforded certain protections under federal law, in accordance with the ESA. However, the ESA carves out a role for the states to assist in achieving the ESA’s protective purposes by providing that, in carrying out the statute, the Service “shall cooperate to the maximum extent practicable with the States.” Congress therefore recognized the expertise of state agencies and required the Service to solicit and consider information provided by the states, such as preparing rules related to species conservation banking. This is highly relevant to the proposed rule, as the Service has expressly adopted policies to work with the states in the implementation of the ESA, stating specifically that “[s]tates possess broad trustee and police powers over fish, wildlife and plants and their habitats within their borders. Unless preempted by Federal authority, states possess primary authority and responsibility for protection and management of fish, wildlife and plants and their habitats.”

The express recognition of state authority and the need for cooperation and collaboration is of critical importance when considering compensatory mitigation mechanisms, as implementation will undoubtedly have a profound impact on the management of wildlife within the State, whether listed or not, and the habitat upon which such wildlife depends. Utah’s Division of Wildlife Resources (“DWR”) currently manages mitigation processes for wildlife within the State and seeks sustainability and diversity of wildlife throughout the State. Mitigation processes that fail to fully consider state input and/or fail to ensure coordination between the Service and DWR will undoubtedly interfere with the DWR’s role as trustee and guardian of the State’s protected wildlife and all associated management. Thus, any actions taken pursuant to the proposed rule and all proposed changes to the mitigation mechanisms should be done in consultation and coordination with appropriate state fish and wildlife agencies.

The Southern Beaufort Sea population is the most imperiled polar bear population in the world. With only about 900 bears remaining, scientists have determined that the survival of every individual bear is vital to the survival and recovery of the population.

The heavy equipment used in seismic exploration and drilling activities can crush polar bears in their dens or scare polar bears out of their dens too early, leaving cubs to die of exposure or abandonment by their mothers. The noise generated by routine operations can disturb essential polar bear behavior and increase their energy output.

Walruses are also incredibly sensitive to human disturbance. Without summer sea ice for resting, walrus mothers and calves have been forced to come ashore, where they are vulnerable to being trampled to death in stampedes when startled by noise.

In addition to seismic exploration, the rule covers construction and operation of roads, pipelines, runways, and other support facilities. It also covers well drilling, drill rig transport, truck and helicopter traffic, and other activities.

The Marine Mammal Protection Act generally prohibits killing, harming or harassing a marine mammal. The statute allows the federal government to authorize certain industrial activities to harm and harass marine mammals, provided such activities will take only a “small number” of animals and have no more than a “negligible impact” on the population.

The proposed rule covers existing and planned activities across a wide swath of Alaska’s Arctic, including 7.9 million acres in the Beaufort Sea, and onshore activities from Point Barrow to the western boundary of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. It includes the Willow development project that the Center and allies have challenged in court, and which the Biden administration this week submitted a brief defending.

Please accept the following comments regarding Docket No. FWS-R7-ES-2021-0037, from the Alaska Support Industry Alliance on behalf of their 500 member companies:

As the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has correctly concluded, oil and gas activities covered by the proposal will:

• Affect only “small numbers” of polar bears and walruses,
• Have no more than a “negligible impact” on those populations, and
• NOT lead to an unmitigable adverse impact on the availability of these populations for subsistence uses by Alaska Native communities.

These findings are well-supported by data collected for decades on the North Slope, and are consistent with similar findings that have been made by FWS in numerous ITRs going back to the 1990s for both the Beaufort Sea and Chukchi Sea. Legal challenges to past ITRs have resulted in the ITRs being fully upheld by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals. Clearly, the Fish and Wildlife Services conclusion that oil and gas activities on the North Slope will not have significant impacts to the polar bear population is consistent with decades of data and observations.

For decades, North Slope operators have implemented mitigation and monitoring measures that have proven to be highly effective in limiting marine mammal impacts to no more than a negligible level. This conclusion has been evaluated and confirmed in multiple public documents and decisions under multiple federal administrations.

Like the current and past ITRs, the proposed ITR authorizes only “Level B harassment” of polar bears and walruses. This type of take involves only temporary behavioral disturbance of small numbers of polar bears and walruses. The proposed ITR does not authorize the injury or killing of any animals, nor has any other ITR issued over the decades in which this MMPA regulatory framework has been implemented for North Slope activities.

The proposed ITR should be finalized as soon as possible, as doing so will preserve a long-term regulatory framework that gives certainty to the regulated industry and continues the system of successful mitigation measures that have proven benefits for polar bears. The proposed ITR, and the ITRs before it, demonstrate that the various conservation measures taken by the oil and gas industry on the North Slope result in negligible impacts to the environment, wildlife, and subsistence harvest by local communities. This regulatory framework is also reflective of a productive scientific collaboration between government and industry that has generated an unprecedented.

Thank you for your consideration -

Rebecca Logan
CEO
The Alaska Support Industry Alliance

That next spring of 2019, I observed no insects on the mature, heavily blooming kale and collard plants on my daily inspections of my garden beds. Regulators must not let financial institutions gamble with our future. We need you to push banks to take the urgent steps necessary to address the dangers they face from climate change, and stop their short-term business decisions from endangering our economy and communities.

I support the proposed guidance’s recommendations to banks that they:

Incorporate climate-related risk management into every level of business;

Plan for climate change over a long time horizon, and update models as additional data becomes available;

Develop clear definitions of possible climate-related risk exposures, and metrics for setting limits;

And make sure that their internal strategies are consistent with their public-facing climate commitments.

The OCC must ensure that banks’ actions match their commitments to zeroing out their net carbon emissions. Banks’ management of climate risk should be factored into their supervisory ratings, too.

It is in the best interest of both the public and banks themselves to act now to minimize climate risk. The OCC must use the full extent of its authority to issue strong final guidance to banks on climate risk, continue to protect against unsafe and unsound bank practices, and require remedies from banks where appropriate.

Banks' continued investments in fossil fuels are driving climate change – a crisis that puts our financial system, people of color and low-income communities, and our planet at risk.

Regulators must not let financial institutions gamble with our future. We need you to push banks to take the urgent steps necessary to address the dangers they face from climate change, and stop their short-term business decisions from endangering our economy and communities.

I support the proposed guidance’s recommendations to banks that they:

Incorporate climate-related risk management into every level of business;

Plan for climate change over a long time horizon, and update models as additional data becomes available;

Develop clear definitions of possible climate-related risk exposures, and metrics for setting limits;

And make sure that their internal strategies are consistent with their public-facing climate commitments.

The OCC must ensure that banks’ actions match their commitments to zeroing out their net carbon emissions. Banks’ management of climate risk should be factored into their supervisory ratings, too.

It is in the best interest of both the public and banks themselves to act now to minimize climate risk. The OCC must use the full extent of its authority to issue strong final guidance to banks on climate risk, continue to protect against unsafe and unsound bank practices, and require remedies from banks where appropriate.

Social accountability is not part of the banks philosophy. They must be forced to abide by ethical and moral standards.

I vehemently urge the USFWS to follow through with their proposal to list the tricolored bat as Endangered under the Endangered Species Act of 1973. The tricolored bat serves as a crucial component of their various ecosystems throughout the United States by devouring potentially harmful or disease-carrying insects like mosquitos. They preserve balance in their ecosystems by keeping insect populations in check. The service that they provide to farmers alone is enough to argue for the preservation of the species with some resources estimating that bats may save US farmers roughly $23 billion each year by reducing crop-damaging insects and reducing the need for pesticides (Bat Conservation International n.d.). Other estimates put the global economic benefit of insect-eating bats between $54 billion and $1 trillion (Kunz et al. 2011). However, ESA listing decisions should be made based on the best available science and information and not on the economic and ecological benefit they provide. Bats have been present on our planet for roughly 54 million years but their populations are currently declining at an unprecedented rate. Habitat loss and modification due to human impacts and climate change along with a disease called white nose syndrome are some of the main factors causing these declines. According to Leob and Winters (2022), white nose syndrome caused a 90.3% decline in surveyed tricolored bat populations during just the first three years after the arrival of white nose syndrome to those populations. Some scientists in Canada have estimated that the species has become extirpated from certain parts of its norther-most range because of white nose syndrome (Vanderwolf and McAlpine 2021). These factors have the potential to be exaggerated by climate change and warming temperatures, especially given new research from Leob and Winters (2022) that suggests that colder hibernating temperatures tend to slow the development of the white nose fungus on bats. A behavioral change was witnessed in surveyed populations in which bats moved closer to the openings of dwellings due to the colder temperatures and the effect those temperatures had on their survival rate through hibernation with white nose syndrome.

Listing the tricolored bat as Endangered will free up important federal funding to be utilized for the conservation of the species and can help facilitate further research into the white nose syndrome epidemic that is affecting many bat species throughout the country. It will also help raise much-needed public awareness surrounding the declining population of bats around the country and hopefully mobilize more conservation groups and local governments to take action. Most research cites the white nose syndrome to be the predominant reason for the sharp decline in tricolored bat populations. For this reason, most of the funds, resources, and conservation action plan should focus on a cure or mitigation strategy for white nose syndrome and an assessment of how climate change will impact the survival of the species in the future. Recent research that was mentioned above has shown behavioral shifts in tricolored bats that indicate a potential mitigation strategy. Further research into subjects like this could assist in the future preservation of the species. An evaluation of relevant and recent research clearly shows that the listing of the tricolored bat as endangered is warranted. It is a crucial step in the protection of the individual species and the overall protection of biodiversity in the United States. Thank you for your time and consideration.

We support the USFWS’ proposal to list the tricolored bat Perimyotis subflavus as an Endangered species. White-nose syndrome (WNS) has significantly impacted P. subflavus populations throughout Missouri. Hibernacula counts performed throughout Missouri indicated that P. subflavus populations in caves experienced a 53.2% decline between 2012 and 2017 (Colatskie, 2017). This significant population loss resulted in very few observations during summer maternity surveys proceeding the hibernacula survey. Pittsburg State University conducted a study between 2018 – 2020 to evaluate the post-WNS roosting ecology of P. subflavus in the Missouri counties of Shannon, Reynolds, and Carter. Our research objectives included identifying the habitat characteristics associated with maternity roost trees, assessing population health, and monitoring the species with acoustic detectors. Pre-WNS historical records provided by the Missouri Natural Heritage database indicated that the species frequently occurred throughout the study area. Unfortunately, during our research, we found that the species was extremely rare in southern Missouri. During the study, we captured two P. subflavus individuals (one male, one female) across 47 mist-net night attempts (235 survey hours; Hammesfahr et al. 2022; Hammesfahr et al., Accepted). Additionally, acoustic detections of P. subflavus were minimal. Out of 40 acoustic survey nights, we collected a total of 65 bat passes over the three-year study (Hammesfahr et al., Accepted). Given the poor success rate of both capture and acoustic detection in our study and the low documentation of the species within Missouri cave hibernacula, we strongly recommend that P. subflavus be classified as an Endangered species.

White-nose syndrome has been documented in 12 bat species — almost half of all hibernating species in North America — with tricolored bats among the hardest hit. It has spread across the bats’ entire 39-state range, as well as seven Canadian provinces. With no known cure, it’s critical we do everything we can to help these delicate and beneficial creatures survive the epidemic.

Bats save farmers an estimated $3.7 billion through their pest-control services by eating insects — without creating dangerous pesticide pollution. Tricolored bats, the smallest bats in the East and Midwest, can consume up to 1 million insects per year.

Listing them as endangered and designating critical habitat will acknowledge the dire situation they face and ensure they get the help they need.

I am commenting on the proposed rule "Endangered and Threatened Species: Status for Tricolored Bat," docket number FWS-R5-ES-2021-0163, posted by the Fish and Wildlife Service on September 13, 2022. I am commenting on my own behalf.

I support the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and the conservation of our nation's biodiversity, and therefore invested in the conservation of the tricolored bat. I support the conclusion of the FWS that the tricolored bat is at serious risk of extinction and therefore should be listed under the ESA as an endangered species. This is a good start at conservation of this species as it opens up funding for government agencies and partners, and it also brings awareness of threats to this species.

However, I do not agree with this proposed rule's decision to not designate critical habitat. The proposed rule states that "identifying wintering habitat (hibernacula) as critical habitat on published maps for the tricolored bat would likely increase the threat from human entry." I find this to be an insufficient argument, and ask that FWS provide further explanation to why this is a likely scenario. It does not make sense to me that designating critical habitat for some endangered species would deter human entry or disturbance, but that for other species (such as the tricolored bat), it would encourage human entry. I find the example of the rock gnome lichen in the Critical Habitat Exclusions section of the FWS's Critcal Habitat webpage to not be congruent with that of the tricolored bat. The rock gnome lichen exists in a very small range. The tricolored bat's range is much more spread out (across several countries and many states). Additionally, the Wisconsin DNR has published on its website several maps detailing the natural communities in the state that are associated with the tricolored bat. The tricolored bat is identified as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need and listed as threatened under Wisconsin law. There have been no reports in Wisconsin of these maps causing an increase in human interaction with tricolored bat hibernacula.

An additional argument I have regarding the decision to not designate critical habitat is that the proposed rule identifies that habitat loss is a threat to the species, but then later states that a factor in the decision not to designate critical habitat is that "forested habitat loss is not a major driver of the species' status." This argument does not line up with the earlier statement "There are a variety of causes of habitat loss and disturbance that affect the tricolored bat such as (but not limited to) forest removal or conversion."

While I agree that designating critical habitat is not a fix-all solution to the endangerment of the tricolored bat, I do believe it is important to identify and protect (to the extent that the ESA can) critical habitat for the species. I am optimistic that such a designation would raise awareness for the species and better focus the conservation actions of government agencies and partners in saving this species.

I support the listing of the tricolored bat as an endangered species under the ESA. I have hope that the additional funding this will open up can help in the search for a solution to WNS and help find ways to decrease the impacts of climate change, habitat loss, and human disturbances to the species. I do, however, strongly urge FWS to reconsider the decision to not designate critical habitat.

The Suwannee Alligator Snapping Turtle (M. suwanniensis) needs to be listed as threatened to avoid further population depletion and extinction. Protecting the species to me means establishing a critical habitat in which activities (i.e. fishing) are limited and clarifying measures under Section 4(d) of the ESA, including captive breeding programs for conservation efforts and incidental take. While approaching this issue, it is important to consider public perception and information made public about the species as illegal harvesting is a concern.

I support the establishment of critical habitat for the species. While it is stated that no area meets the definition of a critical habitat, I think the species would benefit from this designation and it should be investigated further. The establishment of critical habitat for a threatened species is vital and is a key step to recovering a population (Martin et al. 2017). Time is a limited resource when it comes to conservation and each day we loose more habitats that could have been determined "critical". While this would not constitute "hasty decisions", it should put more weight on the choice to define a critical habitat for the species in order to prevent further impacts due to habitat degradation. However, a major concern is further exposure to illegal harvesting, so I propose enforcement for the area as necessary (i.e. nesting times). This would require resources and costs that may not be available, but this scenario could provide further insight on illegal harvesting and other human-related impacts. The establishment of a critical habitat would also mean restrictions on recreational use, which could benefit the population due to reduced risk of bycatch and hook and line ingestion.

Under the section 4(d) rule, I support exempting incidental take as long as such practices are under compliance and the requirement that injured or dead turtles need to be reported. This will ensure that the public feels more empowered than threatened to protect the species and encourage reporting. The information gathered from rescued and deceased turtles could also be useful in the future for species protection. I think the provision on captive breeding should be revised to approve for captive breeding, but only for preexisting captive turtles and should not allow for further taking. Captive breeding programs are a strong tool for species conservation, but they can be challenging, especially with reptiles. From a few reviews on preexisting endangered turtle breeding programs, "the potential for avoiding extinction in the short term is often challenged by unclear or negative outcomes in the long term" (Canessa et al. 2016). The monitoring of reintroduced turtles could be difficult, providing more challenges for long term species protection. Breeding should be practiced in order to promote genetic diversity, but otherwise resources should go towards protecting habitats. For example, M. suwanniensis could be a key species in protecting certain areas which could also protect other species like birds or even manatees. In Mississippi, the protection of turtle populations has proven useful in wetland restoration, including the ﻿Alligator Snapping Turtle (Macrochelys temminckii), as they tend to adapt well to restored wetlands and have ecological importance to these areas (Nickerson, Mitchell, and Glorioso 2019).

The proposal to list the bracted twistflower as a threatened species and designate critical habitat under the Endangered Species Act of 1973 is necessary to protect the species. Since 1989, The bracted twistflower has only been spotted in five counties in Texas. 11 of the 17 original sites in those counties where the flower grew remain intact. Many of these counties are seeing an increasing amount of urban sprawl. Particularly in areas like Austin and San Antonio, which are highly populated and fast-growing cities. It’s been estimated that “33% of the species habitats have been lost to urban and residential development over the last 30 years.”

As these urban areas continue to grow and expand their development, it is likely that the bracted twistflower will suffer further habitat loss without intervention. The primary goal of the Endangered Species Act of 1973 was to halt and prevent the rapid loss of animal and plant species and to conserve the ecosystems upon which endangered and threatened species depend. This proposed rule coincides with the purpose of the Endangered Species Act by working to preserve the population of the bracted twistflower. Protecting species like the bracted twistflower can help ensure that the ecosystems in which the bracted twistflower are found remain healthy, even as urban sprawl continues.

Regarding the "Covered Period". This interim rule removed the Alternative Covered Period which will have "unintended consequences" for borrowers and will have a significant negative effect on the amount that may be forgiven. The Covered Period has been Amended to conform to the section 306 of Economic Aid Act change to definition of covered period. The option to elect an alternative covered period has been removed because the Economic Aid Act provided borrowers flexibility to choose the end of their covered period. Under the previous rules, borrowers that were unable to immediately hire their employees back due to state/government COVID restrictions, were eligible for the Alternative covered period. The Alternative covered period began the date of borrowers first payroll period after loan disbursement, and ended 24 weeks after, no later than December 31, 2020. For example- if a borrower received funding May 1st, but did not have their first payroll period September 1st, under the Alternative Covered Period- the covered period would begin September 1st and end on December 31st. Under your new rules whereas you deleted the Alternative Covered Period, borrowers that had previously qualified for the Alternative Covered Period will now be forced to have an expiration date that is 24 weeks after up to 8 weeks of the loan disbursement date, regardless of when their first payroll was.  For example, the borrower that's loan was disbursed on May 1st but did not begin payroll until September 1st, although they could then chose the flexible covered period of 8 weeks after loan disbursement- which would be June 26th. This borrower did not begin using funds until their first payroll of September 1st- which means 10 weeks will be lost in the forgiveness "covered period". The new rules need to continue to have the Alternative Covered Period, alongside the Flexible covered period. Otherwise, borrowers that had previously been told they were ok under the Alternative Covered Period will suffer greatly.

Hello,



I am writing to comment on the SBA IFR document pertaining to second draw PPP loans (Docket No. SBA-2021-0002), specifically, the removal of the alternative size standard for businesses that do not have an NAICS code beginning with "72".



During the first round of PPP in 2020, per question #2 on the SBA's "Paycheck Protection Program Loans Frequently Asked Questions" document, most recently updated on 12/9/2020, businesses with more than 500 "employees" were permitted to apply and obtain PPP loans if they met the alternative size standard such that the business did not have more than $15M tangible net assets and an average net income of $5M for the two years prior to loan application. This standard makes sense as it recognizes that a business concern with several part-time employees (causing it to go over the then 500-employee threshold) does not necessarily mean that it is flush with cash and thus not in need of a PPP loan.



For example and in regards to the second draw of PPP rules (which now has a 300-employee threshold in order to qualify), a hypothetical business with 299 full time employees working 40+ hours per week would qualify for a second draw PPP loan in regards to this criteria, but a business with 301 "employees", 90% of which are part time and may work as little as 5 hours per week would not qualify for a second PPP loan. This criteria does not make sense, because a business with 299 full time salaried employees would require a massively larger cash flow to support payroll costs, whereas the business with 301 (mostly part-time) employees is left out of the loan opportunity. In reality, the business with 301 employees is much more representative of a "small business concern" as opposed to the company with 299 full time employees.



To extrapolate on the logic above, the company with 301 employees may have suffered a much more significant reduction in revenue due to the government mandates forcing closures upon it as opposed to the company with 299 employees, making it much more relevant to the purpose of the PPP to help businesses survive the pandemic.



Many businesses with an NAICS code other than "72" have been drastically impacted by the pandemic, in many cases worse than companies that have an NAICS code of "72".



Unfortunately, this exact scenario has impacted myself personally and the fantastic business that employs me. In 2020, our business averaged 404 "employees" (head count, not full time equivalent) making us ineligible for the second draw of PPP as our NAICS code begins with "71" and not "72". However, 90% of those 404 employees are part time workers, in many cases 16-20 year olds working their first job and learning valuable life and business skills. While 404 employees may sound like a lot on face value, the full time equivalent of this roster is significantly below 300.



In addition, this business does not have more than $15M in tangible net assets and has not averaged $5M in net income over the last two years. In fact, the 2020 revenues for this business decreased 50% for the entire year compared to all of 2019. As you can see, the impact of the pandemic on this business has been drastic, and it experienced a significantly higher reduction in revenue for the entire year than the IFR requires of second time borrowers (only a 25% reduction for a single quarter compared to 2019).



Without the application of the alternative size standard on the first draw of the PPP, this business would not have qualified and likely would have made incredibly difficult decisions to evaluate the viability of the business with such significant drops in revenue.



Please consider the re-implementation of the alternative size standard for businesses to have the opportunity of a second draw PPP loan to expand to companies that do not have an NAICS code of "72".



Thank you for your time and consideration.

Hello,

I am writing to comment on the SBA IFR document pertaining to second draw PPP loans (Docket No. SBA-2021-0002), specifically, the removal of the alternative size standard for businesses that do not have an NAICS code beginning with "72".

During the first round of PPP in 2020, on the SBA's "Paycheck Protection Program Loans Frequently Asked Questions" document, most recently updated on 12/9/2020, businesses with more than 500 "employees" were permitted to apply and obtain PPP loans if they met the alternative size standard such that the business did not have more than $15M tangible net assets and an average net income of $5M for the two years prior to loan application. This standard makes sense as it recognizes that a business concern with several part-time employees does not necessarily mean that it is flush with cash and thus not in need of a PPP loan.

For example and in regards to the second draw of PPP rules (which now has a 300-employee threshold in order to qualify), a hypothetical business with 299 full time employees working 40+ hours per week would qualify for a second draw PPP loan in regards to this criteria, but a business with 301 "employees", 90% of which are part time and may work as little as 5 hours per week would not qualify for a second PPP loan. This criteria does not make sense, because a business with 299 full time salaried employees would require a massively larger cash flow to support payroll costs, whereas the business with 301 (mostly part-time) employees is left out of the loan opportunity. In reality, the business with 301 employees is much more representative of a "small business concern" as opposed to the company with 299 full time employees.

To extrapolate on the logic above, the company with 301 employees may have suffered a much more significant reduction in revenue due to the government mandates forcing closures upon it as opposed to the company with 299 employees, making it much more relevant to the purpose of the PPP to help businesses survive the pandemic.
Many businesses with an NAICS code other than "72" have been drastically impacted by the pandemic, in many cases worse than companies that have an NAICS code of "72"

Unfortunately, this exact scenario has impacted me personally and the fantastic business that employs me. In 2020, our business averaged 404 "employees" (head count, not full time equivalent) making us ineligible for the second draw of PPP as our NAICS code begins with "71" and not "72". However, 90% of those 404 employees are part time workers, in many cases 16-20 year olds working their first job and learning valuable life and business skills. While 404 employees may sound like a lot on face value, the full time equivalent of this roster is significantly below 300.
In addition, this business does not have more than $15M in tangible net assets and has not averaged $5M in net income over the last two years. In fact, the 2020 revenues for this business decreased 50% for the entire year compared to all of 2019. As you can see, the impact of the pandemic on this business has been drastic, and it experienced a significantly higher reduction in revenue for the entire year than the IFR requires of second time borrowers (only a 25% reduction for a single quarter compared to 2019).
Without the application of the alternative size standard on the first draw of the PPP, this business would not have qualified and likely would have made incredibly difficult decisions to evaluate the viability of the business with such significant drops in revenue.

Please consider the re-implementation of the alternative size standard for businesses to have the opportunity of a second draw PPP loan to expand to companies that do not have an NAICS code of "72".

Thank you for your time and consideration.

I was encouraged by my regional SBA director to submit a comment regarding how the gross receipts definition has impacted our eligibility for the 2nd draw PPP loan. I am specifically referring to paragraph 2 in this regulation on using SBA's size definition for calculating gross receipts.

In this definition gross receipts includes grant spend when accounted for on a accrual basis. This means that if a certain period was low on sales revenue, a company will spend more grants as a proportion of their cash needs. This will show up as an increase in grants in the gross receipts calculation when following recommended accounting procedures for grants. This is not an increase in the amount of grants awarded, just an increase in spend.

I do not have data on other companies in a similar situation, but this definition has ruled us out for PPP funding that is needed. Due to Covid, revenue and capital investments from private sources are both lower for our business than last year. Because of this, we are spending more on grants to keep our employees paid. We did not receive more grants than last year, we are simply using them as a larger supplement for covering expenses.

If grants were not considered gross receipts based on the SBA definition, we would be eligible to apply for the PPP and get cash flow assistance. This rule change would still require businesses to demonstrate a decrease in revenue to be eligible for a loan.

From a pro/con standpoint, I understand that increased requirements were put in place to ensure that businesses that need the funding are getting it. Changing this rule might open the gate for more companies that don't need the PPP, but it would prevent companies (like mine) that need it from being excluded. This comment is being submitted anonymously, as revealing this information might have an adverse impact on our customers, competitors, and potential investors.

Question: Section 1102 of the CARES Act provides that PPP loans are available only to applicants that were "in operation on February 15, 2020." Is a business that was in operation on February 15, 2020 but had a change in ownership after February 15, 2020 eligible for a PPP loan?
Answer: Yes. As long as the business was in operation on February 15, 2020, if it meets the other eligibility criteria, the business is eligible to apply for a PPP loan regardless of the change in ownership. In addition, where there is a change in ownership effectuated through a purchase of substantially all assets of a business that was in operation on February 15, the business acquiring the assets will be eligible to apply for a PPP loan even if the change in ownership results in the assignment of a new tax ID number and even if the acquiring business was not in operation until after February 15, 2020. If the acquiring business has maintained the operations of the pre-sale business, the acquiring business may rely on the historic payroll costs and headcount of the pre-sale business for the purposes of its PPP application, except where the pre-sale business had applied for and received a PPP loan. The Administrator, in consultation with the Secretary, has determined that the requirement that a business "was in operation on February 15, 2020" should be applied based on the economic realities of the business's operations.

I think it would be appropriate for seasonal employers to choose gross receipts from any 12 week period of 2020 compared to the same 12 week period in 2019 to demonstrate the 25% reduction in gross receipts as required to be eligible for the PPP Second Draw Loan.  The Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) has helped many small businesses survive the pandemic of 2020 and 2021.  Each business has its own unique considerations with respect to how it has been impacted by the pandemic, and the SBA has identified "Seasonal Employers" as one category of unique types of businesses.  The SBA understands that Seasonal Employers can be disproportionately impacted in a negative manner depending on which months the business suffers reductions in revenue.  The SBA has allowed Seasonal employers to choose any 12 week period for purposes of calculating "Average Monthly Payroll" to ensure flexibility in the calculation for businesses that make most of their income during relatively short periods of the year.  The "Second Draw PPP Loan" application has a requirement to demonstrate a loss in revenues of 25% or greater during any calendar quarter of 2020 compared to the same quarter of 2019 to be eligible for this second draw.  I think it would be appropriate for seasonal employers to choose any 12 week period of 2020 compared to the same 12 week period in 2019 to demonstrate this 25% reduction in gross receipts.  The measure of gross receipts being limited to only 4 periods of time throughout the year will likely prohibit seasonal employers from participating in this program even if they have truly suffered significant revenue losses due to the pandemic.

The Interim Final Rule on Second Draw PPP Loans defines seasonal businesses as "meaning an employer that does not operate for more than 7 months in any calendar year or that during the preceding calendar year, had gross receipts for any 6 months of that year that were not more than 33.33 percent of the gross receipts of the employer for the other 6 months of that year".

This definition creates a steep cliff in determining the eligible loan amount. Using our organization as an example, we have gross receipts for any 6 months of 2019 that were 37% percent of the gross receipts for the other 6 months of that year. Due to 6 months of gross receipts exceeding the 33.33 percent threshold, and therefore being required to use the average monthly payroll for the entire year of 2019 or 2020 in determining the loan amount, the calculation for the eligible loan amount for our organization is reduced by 42%. This difference dramatically reduces our ability to retain and/or hire staff.

We believe this will affect many small businesses that certainly behave in a seasonal manner but fail the strict seasonal definition of the IFR and encourage a more phased approach in determining eligible loan amounts for seasonal businesses.

The SBA's Paycheck Protection Program Affiliation Rules as of January 19, 2021 (paragraph on page two) as they pertain to revenue reduction requires clarification.

"Gross receipts of a borrower's affiliates (unless a waiver of affiliation applies) are calculated by adding the gross receipts of the business concern with the gross receipts of each affiliate."

The affiliation rules as they apply to the paycheck protection program gross receipts should be:

"Gross receipts of a borrower's affiliates (unless a waiver of affiliation applies) are calculated by adding the gross receipts of the business concern with the gross receipts of each affiliate with employees."

The PPP second draw was intended to target business concerns that qualified for the first draw that experienced a 25% reduction in gross receipts. Under this interpretation, the gross receipt rule has the potential to "bring in" gross receipts of affiliated entities that had no employees and was in no way included in the first round draw and qualify a business concern that would not otherwise qualify.

Affiliated companies without employees should not be included in affiliation rules for the purpose of qualifying business concerns for the second draw.

In determining the 25% reduction threshold, must it be a quarter defined by the calendar months (1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th), or can I use any 3 sequential months?  For example, can I use the months of May, June and July?

I urge you to consider requirements other than a 25% reduction in revenue in 2020 compared to 2019. This rule is satisfactory for businesses who did not expand or change operations going into 2020. Businesses, especially restaurants, cafes and those who supply such impacted businesses are greatly impacted by restrictions due to the pandemic.

Our business is a cafe and coffee roasting busines. We sell coffee wholesale to other cafes, restaurants, grocery outlets as well as at retail. We expanded and relocated and had a major change in operations at the end of 2019. We increased our number of employees from 7 to 19 and our operating expenses increased dramatically. We are operating with a much higher revenue requirement that we are not able to meet due to the restrictions on our business due to Covid-19 emergency orders. Our revenue is not less that 2019 due to our expansion and change in operation, but we face the same restrictions and revenue reduction as those operating at status quo in 2020 compared to 2019. Yet we do not qualify for a second draw because we expanded right before the pandemic and have more income than 2019.

We drastically need the PPP second draw loans as do other small businesses who expanded going into 2020. Please consider implementing a requirement change that does not penalize those businesses who are not static.

My concern is specifically with the requirement to show a quarterly loss of 25% or more (from 2020 compared to 2019).  Our business does have a 3 consecutive month period where our gross receipts are down more than 25% when compared to the same 3 month period as 2019. The problem is that the 3 month period does not fall into a typical business quarter; it falls across May, June and July. We want to be able to use this 3 consecutive month period to meet the requirement of showing a reduction in gross receipts.

If we are not allowed to use a 3 consecutive month period that is not a typical business quarter, it is, in effect, an arbitrary penalty for us (and the many other businesses that are in the same situation as our business) just because our period of loss doesn’t happen to fit into a typical business quarter. A 3 consecutive month period of loss takes the same toll on a business, whether it fits in 1 business quarter or 3 consecutive months that spread across 2 quarters (i.e. May, June and July). In other words, when it comes to meeting the reduction in gross receipts requirement, I don’t believe there should be a difference between having the 3 months fit into 1 business quarter or it being 3 consecutive months. (Note: When I say 3 months that are not in one business quarter, I am not saying any 3 months through the year; I am saying 3 consecutive months).

I ask that the SBA to change their guidelines on the revenue reduction requirement for the second draw PPP to allow for any 3 consecutive month period (the same 3 consecutive months for 2020 when compared to 2019) to show a reduction in gross receipts. I know of several other small businesses that fall into this same situation, and so allowing for a quarter to mean any 3 consecutive month period will help many struggling small businesses, that otherwise would not receive the help they need.

I believe it would serve small businesses much better to pro-rate available PPP loan forgiveness based on % loss 2019 versus 2020.  Minimum or maximum amounts would need to be considered but for many small businesses that lost 20-24.9% in one or more quarters and therefore can't get any loan, it makes it extremely difficult during these times.

This is long overdue; any new startup will attend a training session by SBA and many small business offices with all the departments and agencies. At these sessions we are all told as a startup you need to gain experience as a subcontractor with a larger firm to have past performance to cite in your future proposals as a prime bidder.

Many a new start up will only discover a few years later those large primes have corporate policies that prohibit their providing any past performance response to a contracting officer for a subcontractor, no matter how great the subcontractor may be. Large firms have received from their corporate legal departments guidance that to respond may open the corporation to legal liability if the subcontractor should fail as a prime on the new contract.

Large primes may just continue to ignore this new rule, unless there is a real penalty if they fail to comply. What will SBA do if large primes fail to comply? Should enforcement fall to the small business it may be cost prohibitive to complete.

Timing: The proposed 15-day response time for a request seems reasonable and would allow a small business to get a past performance for a short-turnaround proposal. Our question arises is how long after the past performance is issued would it be accepted by the government? In the instance where a small subcontractor requested an evaluation at the end of Year 1 (of a 5 Year contract) would the government only accept it for a new proposal for 3-5 years from the issuance date (depending on the Past Performance requirement of the new contract) or would that evaluation be good for 3-5 years from the contract close date?

Should a prime contractor past performance of a first-tier subcontractor be only good from the issuance date it is conceivable that a first-tier sub would want at a minimum a past performance at the end of years 1, 3, and 5 to bid new work. The final past performance (at the end of the contract) would then be valid for 3-5 years in the future. A suggested plan would be that the prime contractor issue past performance for up to 6 months past the end date of a contract, otherwise every first-tier subcontractor would want a past performance within two weeks of the contract end to achieve the greatest serviceability length for future submissions.

Would it be possible to have first-tier subcontract past performances be filed annually as part of the CPARS process? A prime would file with the government as part of the contract execution this information. While the burden shifts for the prime to responding to individual requests to a legal filing it then allows the government to enforce the work by reflecting non-filing of information as part of the CPAR review and scoring. With the government as the holder of the information, it would not be subject to modification by unscrupulous parties.

We welcome the upcoming changes and appreciate the SBA recognizing how this one element gives the buyer (the US Government) better information and provides recognition to sellers for the work they do.

We are strongly in favor of requiring a prime contractor to complete a timely, formal Past Performance for work performed for them by either a Joint Venture or a 1st Tier Subcontractor. As a person who worked as a wildlife biologist, I agree reptiles being collected from the wild are threatening many species. I also know that captive breeding is saving many species through creating "assurance colonies" that can replenish the wild populations and enlarge limited gene pools. We must set up more assurance colonies, allowing licensed commercial reptile breeders to replenish the pet trade as well as the wild populations. In that way, captive breeders can continue adding to the economy of the pet trade, by saving, rather than depleting populations. Breeders should be licensed, and their animals for legitimate sale, and the ones to be kept in their assurance colonies, can be chipped. Any animals found in the pet trade without those chips can then easily be identified as illegally have been obtained from the wild.

Concerning the ban on trade in rhino horn.
For some 40+ years, all this ban has achieved are:
- 1000s of dead, poached rhino, especially in Southern Africa;
- 100s if not 1000s of dead rangers and other rhino protectors;
- 100s if not 1000s of dead and/or incarcerated poachers;

While the enormous loss of rhinos is an unparalleled tragedy, there is another overlooked tragedy rarely if ever spotlighted. In Southern Africa, most adult indigenous African men have 2-5 wives, and each of those wives have 3-7 children. The death or incarceration of an African male breadwinner places all his wives and children, lets say approx. 20 people per man, into deeper poverty than may have been the case previously. How many 1000s if not 10,000s rural village African women and children have suffered this fate?

So, by any measure, this ban has produced an awful toll not simple on Black and White rhino in Africa, but also on the poor rural communities which are home to the rangers and poachers. Surely it has to be time to rethink this ban, especially since rhino horn can be harvested without killing the animal.

Here's hoping good sense will come to play in the US CITES COP delegation, and within CITES itself. Failing this, it will come as no surprise if the Southern African nations opt out of CITES sooner or later.

The United States cultivated ginseng industry urges FWS to put forward the recommendation to CoP19 to amend the Appendix II listing for American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius) to include the annotation:
“Specimens marked and identified as artificially propagated Panax quinquefolius grown under artificial shade are not subject to the provisions of the Convention.”

This proposal is limited to artificially propagated American Ginseng grown under artificial shade and the intention is to further protect the sustainability of wild American Ginseng. There is a clear, distinct difference between wild and cultivated ginseng. Artificially propagated species do not need trade controls because, by virtue of being artificially propagated, there is no risk of extinction or threat to the survival of the species. Field-cultivated American ginseng is recognized as artificially propagated, and there is precedent in CITES Appendix II for GBW’s proposed amendment. As referenced in GBW’s original proposal, the spurges, cacti, cyclamens, Himalayan yew, and orchid listings all contain exemptions for artificially propagated plants.

The purpose of the Convention is not to control artificially propagated species. The proposal i) advances the aim of the Convention, ii) protects the survival of the American Ginseng species, and iii) removes trade barriers that have been inadvertently applied to non-wild flora (artificially propagated American Ginseng). I am submitting comments related to proposals and amendments for CITES CoP19 on behalf of Dallas Safari Club and DSC Foundation.

Fundamental consideration
Stakeholder interests must be fully considered and we respectfully encourage and request that the USFWS seek and ask the needs of those that live with and daily manage habitat and thus the species that are being considered in all proposals. Specifically, we acknowledge the responsibility of custodianship of countries that make the daily decisions on how to manage species, habitat, human:wildlife conflict, etc. and the need for all to seek their guidance on how to best support them in managing their species.

Secondary consideration
We believe that the proponents of a proposal must be heavily considered, especially when the proponents do not have nor manage the species they are proposing Uplisting. Specifically, counties like Mali, Senegal, Gabon, Togo, and Niger continue to propose amendments or Uplistings for species that they do not have and against the needs and desires of the countries that have stable or increasing populations and bear the responsibility of managing those species.

Proposal 1
Hippopotamus amphibius (Hippopotamus)
Proposal: Transfer from Appendix II to Appendix I
Conclusions: As also assessed by the CITES Secretariat, the criteria for inclusion in Appendix I set forth in Resolution Conf 9.24 (Rev. CoP17) are NOT MET because a) there is no marked decline nor observed or ongoing and b) trade is substantially decreasing and is not a cause of any decline.

Proposal 2
Ceratotherium simum simum (population of Namibia) (White rhinoceros)
Proposal: Transfer from Appendix I to Appendix II with the following annotation: For the exclusive purpose of allowing international trade in:
a) live animals for in-situ conservation only; and
b) hunting trophies.
All other specimens shall be deemed to be specimens of species included in Appendix I and the trade in them shall be regulated accordingly.
Conclusion: As also assessed by the CITES Secretariat, Namibia’s wild population of C. s. simum does not meet the biological criteria for inclusion in Appendix I. The precautionary measures proposed in the form of an annotation are satisfactory and proportionate to the anticipated risks to the species and effective enforcement controls appear to be in place. Thus, should be transferred from Appendix I to Appendix II.

Proposal 5
Loxodonta africana (populations of Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe) (African elephant)
Proposal: Transfer from Appendix II to Appendix I
Conclusion: As also assessed by the CITES Secretariat, there are no data that demonstrate that any of the four African elephant populations that are the subject of this proposal underwent marked declines in their populations in the wild. The populations in Botswana, Zimbabwe, Namibia, and South Africa are robust, and the area of distribution of the species in the four range States is not restricted. Thus, Criteria A, B or C in Annex 1 of Resolution Conf. 9.24 (Rev. CoP17) are NOT MET given the populations of African elephants from these four range States.

My name is Justin Gosnell. I live in South Carolina and have been interested in reptiles for my entire life. The timber rattlesnake is native to my state. To USFWS Director Martha Williams and USFWS Policy and Regulations Branch Chief Madonna Baucum:

Wildlife exploitation, including trade, is one of the greatest drivers of extinction. In the face of an unprecedented biodiversity crisis, U.S. leadership in championing wildlife protections will be more necessary than ever at the 19th CITES Conference of the Parties (CoP19) in Panama this November.

"A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community. It is wrong when it tends otherwise."
-- Aldo Leopold

There are proposals to open trade in elephant ivory and rhino horn, which could mean game over for these cherished animals. Another would alter listing and voting criteria to interject socioeconomics into a treaty focused on science and imperiled species in need of protection from human demand.

I also urge you to vote to curb trade in hippos, sharks, guitarfish and aquarium fish. Species such as leopards, pangolins, saiga antelope, lions, aquarium fish, rhinos and jaguars all require urgent action in November and beyond.

Dear US FWS Director and Staff,

The Executive Committee of the IUCN SSC Tortoise and Freshwater Turtle Specialist Group (TFTSG) submitted a letter dated April 28, 2021 to the Federal Register advocating for the inclusion of all non-CITES-listed freshwater turtles in *at least* CITES Appendix II.

Specifically, we argued that this would extend the benefits of CITES trade regulation to all groups of freshwater turtle species that are not currently included In the CITES Appendices, but clearly meet the criteria of CITES Resolution Conf. 9.24 to qualify for inclusion. We are pleased to learn from your Notice of April 26th, 2022, that the Service is seriously considering this recommendation, and would like to provide the following additional information:

In our submission, we specifically mentioned the Familly Kinosternidae - the genera Claudius and Staurotypus, and several species of Kinosternon. For further clarification, we believe that of the 22 species in the genus Kinosternon 20 species warrant inclusion in Appendix II while 2 species - K. cora and K. vogti - warrant inclusion in Appendix I. Both these species have suffered a decline in the area and quality of habitat; have very small (sub)populations; a majority of individuals are concentrated geographically in small ranges in Mexico; and both have a high vulnerability to either intrinsic or extrinsic factors; specifically, the targeted collection for the international pet trade that took off as soon as these species were described in 2020 and 2018, respectively. For these reasons these two species of Kinosternon clearly meet the biological criteria for inclusion in Appendix I and should be considered for this inclusion.

We appreciate that the list of species recommended for inclusion in or transfer between the CITES Appendices, as presented in your Notice, is substantive and implies a huge amount of preparatory work, which we recognize may not all be possible to carry out in time for the CoP19 deadline. We therefore strongly encourage the Service to support and where possible co-propose Proposals prepared by like-minded Parties to include in Appendix II those freshwater turtle species which are currently not included in the CITES Appendices, or which are currently listed in Appendix III. A wide range of evidence, including population modeling and population viability analyses, declared trade volumes, reported seizure volumes from illegal trade, and most convincingly the empirically documented depletion and collapse of freshwater turtle populations subject to unregulated or poorly-regulated exploitation for food, pets and other uses, has made it clear that non-detrimental utilization and trade of turtles is only possible under the monitoring and evaluating mechanisms inherent in CITES Appendix II listing. If this can not happen for all freshwater turtle species at CoP19, we urge the Service to prepare for this to be proposed at CoP20. We look forward to supporting your efforts wherever possible.

Yours truly,
Peter Paul van Dijk, Ph.D.
Deputy Chair, IUCN/SSC Tortoise & Freshwater Turtle Specialist Group

If original lender refuses to go through the hassle of an increase, the borrower is left without recourse.

Sir or Madame:

I am honored to be able to respond to your Final Interim Regulations regarding the Paycheck Protection Act, First Draw Program under the Economic Aid Act. Thank you for publishing them. I am a consultant for an SBA Small Business Development Center but my comments are all my own and not those of the SBA or the SBDC.

At this time I have only two comments.

First, the requirement to spend 60 percent of the Paycheck Protection Loan for the first draw loans on "Payroll Costs" is contrary to Congressional Intent. This requirement is included in the law for second draw loans but was excluded from first draw loans.

Second, please provide some clarification on the definition of "compensation" under the program. Under the IFR it appears that compensation only includes salaries, wages and commissions. Then the IFR includes paid leave, such as vacation, sick and other leave as separate items in the definition of Payroll Costs. This is most important when applying the calculation of "state and local taxes on compensation." Most typically paid leave is included in salaries and wages and these are the bases for paying state and local taxes such as unemployment taxes. So the addition of paid leave items seem to be redundant and so creates an ambiguity. This issue also impacts on the second draw regulations that adopt the same definition of Payroll Costs as the first draw loans.

Thank you so much for your consideration on these comments and please stay healthy.

The proposed change reverses longstanding Small Business Administration regulations guaranteeing the separation of religion and government. The rationale behind the longstanding practice is to prevent taxpayer funds from being awarded to religious organizations, which could easily misuse the funds for religious purposes.

This rule was set aside for the Paycheck Protection Program, and the result was fraud and special privileges for religious organizations.

I believe this rule is absolutely essential in effort to support the sustainability of our small business while in this pandemic. COVID-19 has detrimentally impacted our economy and these new circumstances brought by the virus has resulted in financial   hardships amongst small business throughout our country. The vulnerability of small business can result in decreased sales, unemployment, and bankruptcy; all potential threats that can be subsided by this proposed rule. We should be doing everything possible to provide economic relief and loan forgiveness for these business that are a vital asset to our economy.

1. In context to a seasonal employer using payroll from any 12-week period to determine the average total monthly payments... Why is it only seasonal employers get this benefit and not all seasonal business? I run a small seasonal business as a sole proprietor. Even though I operate less than six months a year, and make 75% of my income in just a few months. I don't qualify because I have no employee and/or payroll. I must use the standard calculation that does not represent a seasonal business fairly.

I appreciate you taking your time to read this.

-Ryan

Business Loan Program Temporary Changes; Paycheck Protection Program as Amended by Economic Aid Act
Stated on printed page 3701 under supplemental information Under section d i.
It states the following:
"Step 1: Find your 2019 or 2020 IRS Form 1040 Schedule F line 9 gross income (if you are using 2020 and you have not yet filed a 2020 return, fill it out and compute the value). If this amount is over $100,000, reduce it to $100,000. If this amount is zero or less, you are not eligible for a PPP loan.
ii. Step 2: Divide the amount from Step 1 by 12.
iii. Step 3: Multiply the average monthly gross income amount from Step 2 by 2.5.
iv. Step 4: Add the outstanding amount of any Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) made between January 31, 2020 and ending on April 3, 2020 that you seek to refinance. Do not include the amount of any advance under an EIDL COVID-19 loan (because it does not have to be repaid).

You must provide the 2019 or 2020 (whichever you used to calculate loan amount) Form 1040 Schedule F with your PPP loan application to substantiate the applied-for PPP loan amount and a 2019 or 2020 (whichever you used to calculate loan amount) IRS Form 1099-MISC detailing nonemployee compensation received (box 7), invoice, bank statement, or book of record that establishes you are self-employed. You must provide a 2020 invoice, bank statement, or book of record to establish you were in operation on or around February 15, 2020."

I am taking issue with the gross number for farmers. As an Agricultural lender, I find that number unfairly high. Essentially a sole proprietor farmer with no employees, who farms full time can show a negative net number or loss in the farming operation, and claim that he takes out 100,000 per year in income and receive a PPP loan for 20,833. The special exception for Farmers is unjust to all the schedule C businesses given that Net farm income, a broad measure of profits, is forecast to increase $36.0 billion (43.1 percent) from 2019 to $119.6 billion in 2020. Net cash farm income is forecast to increase $24.7 billion (22.6 percent) to $134.1 billion. In inflation-adjusted 2020 dollars, net farm income is forecast to increase $35.0 billion (41.3 percent) and net cash farm income is forecast to increase $23.4 billion (21.1 percent). If realized, both income measures would be well above their historical average across 2000-19 when adjusted for inflation and at their highest levels since 2013 and 2014, respectively. According to the USDA economic research Service.

As a tax payer and farm lender who understands farming operations it would be much more fair to use following formula. Take the Schedule F line 34 (net farm profit or loss) + Schedule F line 14 (depreciations and section 179 expense) + Schedule F line 15 (employee benefits program) + Schedule F line 22 (Labor hired). If you continued to cap it at 100,000 per employee this calculation could be used for a farmer who has no employees or has employees and would be much fairer.

I seek clarification to submit an application for increased loan amount on my first draw PPP. We are a seasonal business and did not obtain the full amount of our first draw loan due to ongoing modifications to the seasonal employer loan amount calculation. The interim rule on page 75 says that my seasonal business may apply for an increased loan amount. It contains no language that the loan must not be forgiven. This would be quite punitive in nature were this to be the case.We followed the law, sought loan forgiveness and now because of a true ongoing "glitch" we are being told we cannot seek a loan increase on first draw PPP. Clarification is sought that seasonal businesses are exempt from the forgiveness criterion to seek increase on the first draw PPP loan. Any other interpretation than this would neither make legal nor factual sense.Thank you.

All small businesses should be able to apply for PPP funding based on the same set of rules, no matter which date they submit the application. Yet now the SBA has changed the rules for new applicants (under the auspices of correcting previous guideline errors and with a goal of opening up funding to the smallest, most vulnerable businesses among us), while simultaneously penalizing those of us who were proactive and quick to submit our PPP applications when each round of funding was first announced.

How can the SBA not create a path for previous applicants to reapply/readjust loan amounts based on the amended rules? The new guidelines apply the new calculation rules to only NEW applicants rather than ALL, thus ensuring many who are most in need end up with far less funding than our counterparts who waited weeks and months later to apply.

The new PPP rules need to be amended such that ALL Schedule C sole proprietors can access PPP funds based on the same set of guidelines determining qualification and loan amount. No one should be left out just because we applied for and had our loans were funded before Biden changed the calculation rules.

2020 was catastrophic for many of us and the PPP funds have proven vital to our survival. But in many cases the final loan amount provided was still only a drop in the bucket for what we need. The difference between gross and net in the calculation can be huge when it comes to the amount of assistance one receives, and could easily be the difference between survival and closure during this difficult period. Please do the right thing and fix this error. The SBA made the same change for Schedule F filers in January (after the Dec rule changes). This is no different. Small businesses across the country are anxiously awaiting the SBA to remedy this flaw so that we can reapply/resubmit for equal access to this additional assistance. Please don't let us down.

Given the Paycheck Protection Program's intended users, the eligibility requirements for those seeking financial assistance need to be increased.
