No where in the rulings has the guaranteed payments for service (K-1, box 4a) been addressed. This is guaranteed payments for running the day-to-day operations. Without this individual the business would not exit. This is different from "general partners', who receive their compensation on (K-1, box 14).

I am asking that K-1, Box 4a be allowed to be included in the "Maximum Loan Calculation".

If in fact you determine this should be the case. I am hoping those businesses that have already received their Round 2 PPP Loan will have the opportunity to increase the loan for the new calculation.

Thank you for your time and consideration

I enjoy recreating on public lands and believe recreation is a valuable experience that needs to be protected for all Americans. Access to public lands is crucial for mental and physical health and any actions that would limit recreation access needs to be taken under the strongest of considerations.

Many studies show that the yellow-legged frog spends its winters at the bottom of frozen lakes and ponds. Therefore, human impact during winter months does not have a notable effect on the species. Dams were an identified threat to the species however, dams provide for lakes and ponds creating an expanded range for the species.

One of the main identified threats to the species is wildfire. Mismanaged forests are the largest cause of wildfire in Oregon and California. Roads not only provide access for management treatments but also act as a natural fire barriers. By mitigating fire risk roads will ultimately help protect the yellow-legged frog. The species also needs water sources to survive therefore vegetation treatments in Oregon and California will further protect the species. These types of projects have historically been blocked by environmental groups that claim they are trying to protect wildlife and habitat when in actuality if land agencies were able to properly manage the land these species would not need the restrictive protections of the Endangered Species Act. Furthermore, ESA protections might act as an additional obstruction for management projects that would benefit the species.

I also believe more information in separating clades needs to be collected before any such decisions can be made. "Information is currently lacking for the precise boundary separating the North Coast clade and the North Feather clade, and the Central Coast clade from the South Coast clade." Under current conditions, none of the analysis units had a "high" risk of decline. If land agencies are able to take a more proactive management approach on public lands even the 4 of 6 units listed as a "medium" risk for decline have a good chance of changing to "low" along with the North Sierra and North Coast Oregon units.

In conclusion I believe any decline in the yellow-legged frog species has come from lack of proper management. There is not sufficient evidence showing the potential threats warrant listing the species as endangered or threatened.

The latest temporary changes issued adversely affects all 501c4 organizations and 501c4 (s) that are also a destination marketing organization. The travel and tourism industry, like many other industries, has suffered great financial loss. Many organizations believed the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 responded to our plea for help to gain financial stability in such a trying time. SEC. 5001. MODIFICATIONS TO PAYCHECK PROTECTION PROGRAM.
(a) ELIGIBILITY OF CERTAIN NONPROFIT ENTITIES FOR COVERED LOANS UNDER THE PAYCHECK PROTECTION PROGRAM.—
(1) IN GENERAL.—Section 7(a)(36) of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 636(a)(36)), as amended by the Economic Aid to Hard-Hit Small Businesses, Nonprofits, and Venues Act (title III of division N of Public Law 116–260), is amended—
(A) in subparagraph (A)—
(i) in clause (xv), by striking “and” at the end;
(ii) in clause (xvi), by striking the period in the end and inserting “; and”; and
(iii) by adding at the end the following:
“(xvii) the term ‘additional covered nonprofit entity’—
“(I) means an organization described in any paragraph of section 501(c) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, other than paragraph (3), (4), (6), or (19), and exempt from tax under section 501(a) of such Code; and
“(II) does not include any entity that, if the entity were a business concern, would be described in section 120.110 of title 13, Code of Federal Regulations (or in any successor regulation or other related guidance or rule that may be issued by the Administrator) other than a business concern described in paragraph (a) or (k) of such section.”; and
(B) in subparagraph (D)—
(i) in clause (iii), by adding at the end the following:
“(III) ELIGIBILITY OF CERTAIN ORGANIZATIONS.—Subject to the provisions in this subparagraph, during the covered period—
“(aa) a nonprofit organization shall be eligible to receive a covered loan if the nonprofit organization employs not more than 500 employees per physical location of the organization; and
“(bb) an additional covered nonprofit entity and an organization that, but for subclauses (I)(dd) and (II)(dd) of clause (vii), would be eligible for a covered loan under clause (vii) shall be eligible to receive a covered loan if the entity or organization employs not more than 300 employees per physical location of the entity or organization.”; and
(ii) by adding at the end the following:
“(ix) ELIGIBILITY OF ADDITIONAL COVERED NONPROFIT ENTITIES.—An additional covered nonprofit entity shall be eligible to receive a covered loan if—
“(I) the additional covered nonprofit entity does not receive more than 15 percent of its receipts from lobbying activities;
“(II) the lobbying activities of the additional covered nonprofit entity do not comprise more than 15 percent of the total activities of the organization;
“(III) the cost of the lobbying activities of the additional covered nonprofit entity did not exceed $1,000,000 during the most recent tax year of the additional covered nonprofit entity that ended prior to February 15, 2020; and
“(IV) the additional covered nonprofit entity employs not more than 300 employees.”.
(2) ELIGIBILITY FOR SECOND DRAW LOANS.—Paragraph (37)(A)(i) of section 7(a) of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 636(a)), as added by the Economic Aid to Hard-Hit Small Businesses, Nonprofits, and Venues Act (title III of division N of Public Law 116–260), is amended by inserting “ ‘additional covered nonprofit entity’,” after “the terms”.

The Sierra NF conducted Visual Encounter Surveys for foothill yellow-legged frog and western pond turtle in all known occupied FYLF habitat in the Jose and Mill Creek basin during July 27-August 19, 2021. These surveys were the first herp surveys conducted by Sierra NF biologists post Creek fire (379,000 acres, Sept-Dec 2020). The Jose basin area was severely impacted by the Creek fire with most of the basin burning at moderate and high severity. FYLF were detected in only one survey reach of Mill Creek, where 17 FYLF tadpoles were observed. WPT, bullfrog, and green sunfish were found in many other survey reaches. Attached is a summary of the basin survey with maps, results and photos. A more detailed survey record for Mill Creek is also attached since this is the only reach where FYLF were detected. Full survey records for all reaches in the basin are available upon request and are on file at the High Sierra Ranger District, Sierra National Forest.

We encourage the US Fish & Wildlife Service (FWS) to objectively weigh all points of impact from this proposed listing – not only impact on the FYLF, but also, impact on:
- Other species of flora and fauna that reside in the same habitat as the FYLF
- The general health and resilience of public lands where FYLF reside
- The real and impending increased risk of catastrophic wildfire if additional restrictions on human activity are imposed on FYLF habitat as a result of approving this proposed rule
- The social and economic welfare of humans who reside, conduct commerce, and recreate within the range of habitat occupied by the FYLF

We encourage FWS to exercise caution in advancing a decision to list these four population segments of the FYLF as threatened or endangered. We strongly advocate against any decision to advance each listing without first analyzing the full scope of impact for each bulleted item noted above, as well as each item noted within the contents of the attached letter. While the health and welfare of the FYLF is indeed important, the health and welfare of all life that shares FYLF habitat is equally important. The stated mission of the FWS is: "Working with others to conserve, protect, and enhance fish, wildlife, plants and their habitats for the continuing benefit of the American people." With emphasis on ensuring “continuing benefit of the American people,” we strongly urge FWS to make decisions and take action for this proposed rule in full alignment with the FWS mission.

The Center for Biological Diversity supports the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service proposal to list the South Sierra and South Coast distinct population segments (DPSs) of the foothill yellow-legged frog (Rana boylii) as endangered and the North Feather DPS of Rana boylii as threatened under the Endangered Species Act. The status of these populations and the rationale for listing are well-supported by the Service's 2021 Species Status Assessment (SSA) and December 28, 2021 proposed rule in the Federal Register.

The Center disagrees with the Service proposal to list the Central Coast DPS as threatened rather than endangered. The Central Coast DPS should be listed as endangered, and was given endangered status under the California Endangered Species Act (CESA) by the California Fish and Game Commission in 2019. The Center also disagrees with the Service’s conclusion that the North Sierra DPS is not warranted for listing. The North Sierra DPS should be listed as threatened, and was given threatened status under CESA by the California Fish and Game Commission in 2019.

Subject: Protect All Populations of Yellow-Legged Frogs -- Endangered and Threatened Species: Foothill Yellow-Legged Frog; Threatened Status with Section 4(d) Rule for Two Distinct Population Segments and Endangered Status for Two Distinct Population Segments (Document ID: FWS-R8-ES-2021-0108-0027)

To U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Martha Williams:

Nearly one-third of the world’s amphibians are in danger of extinction—among them California's foothill yellow-legged frogs. Most of the state's populations of these frogs are in severe decline or heading toward extinction.

I strongly support the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposal to list the South Sierra and South Coast populations of the foothill yellow-legged frog as endangered and the North Feather River population as threatened under the Endangered Species Act. The dire status of these populations and the rationale for listing are well supported by the 2021 Species Status Assessment and December 28, 2021, proposed rule in the Federal Register.

Further, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to protect the Central Coast population as endangered rather than threatened. The species has already been eliminated from most of its historical habitats around San Francisco Bay and faces increasing threats from water diversions and wildfire frequency and intensity due to climate change.

And please protect the North Sierra population as threatened—it inhabits a relatively small area, with the frogs' habitat fragmented into many isolated populations. This population faces significant threats, including the operation of many hydropower dams and reduced snowpack and stream flows due to climate change. The state of California has determined that the Central Coast population warrants endangered status and the North Sierra population warrants threatened status.

"A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community. It is wrong when it tends otherwise."
-- Aldo Leopold

Several years ago during a meeting with Forest Service employees this frog was mentioned. I knew the meadow about which the employee was talking. His comments made absolutely no sense to me, and I do consider myself an environmentalist.
The FS employee stated that the rancher, who was running cattle in the area, would no longer be allowed to use the meadow because 'frogs' were found in the hoof prints made by cattle during wet weather. I thought that a very hypocritical statement, as the hoof prints were where the eggs were laid from the female frog. IF you take the cattle out of the meadow, no hoof prints for frog eggs, IE: NO FROGS, to begin with. The FS then should be responsible for creating an area in which the frogs can't breed, NOT be concerned about the amount of frogs being possibly stepped on by cattle.

Dams were an identified threat to the species however, dams provide for lakes and ponds creating an expanded range for the species.

One of the main identified threats to the species is wildfire. Mismanaged forests are the largest cause of wildfire in Oregon and California. Roads not only provide access for management treatments but also act as a natural fire barriers. By mitigating fire risk roads will ultimately help protect the yellow-legged frog. The species also needs water sources to survive therefore vegetation treatments in Oregon and California will further protect the species. These types of projects have historically been blocked by environmental groups that claim they are trying to protect wildlife and habitat when in actuality if land agencies were able to properly manage the land these species would not need the restrictive protections of the Endangered Species Act. Furthermore, ESA protections might act as an additional obstruction for management projects that would benefit the species.

I also believe more information in separating clades needs to be collected before any such decisions can be made. "Information is currently lacking for the precise boundary separating the North Coast clade and the North Feather clade, and the Central Coast clade from the South Coast clade." Under current conditions, none of the analysis units had a "high" risk of decline. If land agencies are able to take a more proactive management approach on public lands even the 4 of 6 units listed as a "medium" risk for decline have a good chance of changing to "low" along with the North Sierra and North Coast Oregon units.

In conclusion I believe any decline in the yellow-legged frog species has come from lack of proper management. There is not sufficient evidence showing the potential threats warrant listing the species as endangered or threatened.
Sincerely a recreational AND FS volunteer to at least two National Forests, as well as a registered voter.
See Ya,
Doug

The text regarding PPP loan forgiveness also references small business organized as C-corp or S-corp. Please clarify if small S-corps with only employee owners may use the new method for calculating the PPP loan amount. For example, someone renting out a property as their business was likely severely impacted by the pandemic. Rental businesses - due to mandatory depreciation - often run at limited profit or at a loss. If the business owner organized as sole proprietor, they can now draw a loan to make up for lost income, but if the same owner organized as S-corp, they cannot under the current wording, simply based on the business form they chose.

Additionally, please clarify footnotes referring to tax years used in the calculations of loan forgiveness to match the conditions for the loan application, i.e. include the option to use the same 12 month period that was allowed for the loan application for the certifications in the loan forgiveness applications. For S-corps, this affects footnotes 38 and 40. THe following is an excerpt from the FAQ used for early PPP loan applications:

Question: What time period should borrowers use to determine their number of employees and payroll costs to calculate their maximum loan amounts?
Answer: In general, borrowers can calculate their aggregate payroll costs using data either from the previous 12 months or from calendar year 2019. For seasonal businesses, the applicant may use average monthly payroll for the period between February 15, 2019, or March 1, 2019, and June 30, 2019. An applicant that was not in business from February 15, 2019 to June 30, 2019 may use the average monthly payroll costs for the period January 1, 2020 through February 29, 2020.
Borrowers may use their average employment over the same time periods to determine their number of employees, for the purposes of applying an employee-based size standard. Alternatively, borrowers may elect to use SBA’s usual calculation: the average number of employees per pay period in the 12 completed calendar months prior to the date of the loan application (or the average number of employees for each of the pay periods that the business has been operational, if it has not been operational for 12 months).

For businesses with changes at the beginning of 2020, eligible amounts were already reduced to a maximum 3/12 of the actual monthly cost due to the calculation method. Under the current wording, they may now not even receive forgiveness for this amount that they paid in good faith to employee owners. Example: if a small business owners used to be covered under their spouse's health insurance in 2019, but had to purchase their own health insurance in 2020, when using the 12 month prior to the loan application they may have been able to include 3/12 of the annual health care cost (before averaging, so the included amount would have been 3/12*2.5 of the actual annual health care cost), but for loan forgiveness for S-corp owners, this amount appears to be excluded. So not only was the actual monthly cost not addressed in the loan amount, additionally now the S-corp owners have to pay back this portion of the loan amount plus interest when they made good faith payments with the expectation of full forgiveness. Similarly, if a new employee owner began work beginning of 2020, 3/12 of their salary may have been eligible for inclusion in the calculation to determine the PPP loan amount, but that amount would not be eligible when only 2019 data is applied to employee owner caps. Again, the loan will have only covered 3/12 of the monthly income of a new employee owner instead of the 100% that should have been covered, but additionally this amount will now have to be returned with interest even if 100% of the proceeds were used to continue payroll from the first 3 months of 2020. This creates a hardship, especially for S-corp owners.

Hi Thanks for continuing to update ppp. I appreciate the gross receipts allowance. This was a GREAT advance in reducing racial and gender disparities. Whoever finally realized this, should get lots of stars. However, one thing that has been overlooked is the reality of racial disparities in health and all areas, and how this has caused some people to have had a bad year in 2019. A true picture of "pre-Covid income" in one's business would have allowed an option to average 3 - 5 years of prior gross receipts in the event that 2019 was not a typical year for one's business.

A one-person business is completely affected by any event of serious illness - like cancer and surgeries that take months to recover from OR attending graduate school for a year to update skills in the dislocated worker program, or a seriously ill dependent or Elder. There is no one to take over when you are a one-person business. Any personal crises means no work for periods of time, and in the case of cancer and serious illnesses, it may mean a whole year or several months with no in come. You could have been in business 20 years, but if this happened in 2019, the person did not get PPP, and they would have been our most vulnerable folks. 2020 would have been a terrible year again, so again, they are seriously left out of PPP. I believe this was an oversight of SBA, based on middle and upper class privilege which caused a blind spot to these realities. These are common realities of being low-income and a small business owner woman and/or Indigenous/Black/Person of Color business owner facing the current disparities in health and in all areas. Giving the option to allow a 3-5 yr. averaging of gross receipts for sole proprietors would spread out the bad year. If I had been allowed to do this, I would have received a $7,500 loan. As it is, I will be lucky to get $1,900. That's a huge difference for a person that is very low-income.

Using a three to five year average of past income would also use existing data instead of slowing down the process with trying to figure out a new schedule C for 2020 when taxes are not done - which for low-income folks is the case in March. We use volunteers. Especially with Covid, there are very few appointments available, as the assistance is given by people usually over 65 - most affected by Covid. So, appointments are over the phone and the system for providing assistance is all messed up due to not being able to meet in person. It's very hard to get a volunteer tax appointment as a self-employed sole proprietor. Last year, my 2019 tax appointment was in September after the April deadline - for a late submission - I waited 9 months for that appointment. When you make less than 22,000 per year - you don't have enough for food and bills, and you have to use debt to fill the gaps - therefore, there is definitely no sense in paying an accountant. That is a privilege for middle and upper class folks. Reality. We use volunteer agencies like Prepare and Prosper with IRS trained folks. This means we do not have our taxes done in early March usually and you are asking for a Schedule C. The first appointments don't even begin until March. During Covid, this is even worse. There is a huge backup and there are currently NO appointments available - so people are struggling to figure out how to do their taxes on their own for the first time ever. I anticipate more errors than usual because of this. If you focus on previous years rather than 2020, you have evidence to support the calculations already in place. Giving the option to use an average of 2019, 2018, 2017 previous schedule Cs to average gross receipts for businesses in business for at least 5 - 10 years, would be smart. In fact, if people went this route, using previous 3-5 year averages - the federal gov could have figured out the loans on their own and just given them. You have this data in your system.

Another comment is that you have not updated the seasonal business computation dates to establish a 12-week period during 2020 that is more fair to folks that don't have income for large parts of the year, which was especially true in 2020. Guess when and how poor people got paid in 2020 for contracted work? Reality for low-income folks - crises hits - So, bills are not paid - My consulting project was with a Tribe. Tribe closes its Casinos. Client consulting business is told project is on hold or cancelled and to submit an invoice for all work so far. Invoice is submitted. I, as subcontractor already submitted an invoice to contractor that I'm waiting for payment on. Guess when I got paid for a February invoice? July - because she had to wait for her PPP loan. So, during third quarter is when poor people finally got paid for things when the PPP loans went through. So zero income in all other quarters and third quarter income was from first quarter work! How does this 2020 income represent gross receipts pre-Covid? Averaging pas years would be better.

To Whom It May Concern,

While I applaud the changes in calculating the amount of PPP funds that a sole proprietor or independent contractor may receive via this IFR, it is absolutely asinine to not apply these changes retroactively for folks who had received money earlier this round (oftentimes only days before these rules went into place). Many sole props and independent contractors could not sit patiently to the side with hopes that a change such as this would magically appear. As such, they applied early out of necessity. As it now stands, sole props and independent contractors who waited to apply until now but had a net loss, stand to receive more money than folks who had a positive net income and paid taxes on said income. This is a double whammy for these latter folks. It is folly to assume that women and other minorities had not already received funds when this new rule rolled out. I am literally an example as I am a woman. If I would have waited to apply, I would have received nearly 20k in PPP funds but instead I only qualified for just over 8k. That is a HUGE difference for a small business and a difference that is compounded by the fact that I also paid additional monies on my positive net income in 2019. 

Additionally, I think it's important to understand why other sole proprietors or independent contractors may not have applied initially. Surely a big reason for this is because these folks may be on PUA. When PPP was calculated based on net income, PUA was often more money, or only marginally less, so many folks opted to remain on PUA instead of going through the hassle of PPP. Now that PPP is being calculated based on gross income, many of these same folks are leaving PUA behind for 2.5 months, taking PPP, and then going immediately back to PUA. This means that it may *seem* like there is a dramatic increase in folks who received PPP funds who are sole props or independent contractors. While technically this is true, those folks were still receiving money in another fashion via PUA and only made the switch when it benefited them. 

I'd also like to remind you even after this IFR came out, many banks still did not allow sole props and independent contractors to apply with these new rules. As the owner of a small business with 4 full time employees, I was pleased to receive a 2nd Draw PPP loan shortly after the program opened on January 13, 2021. Both the first PPP loan and the 2nd Draw loan enabled me to maintain my staffing levels and without reducing hours or firing employees during the rough patches of the pandemic.

When the 2nd Draw program was opened, I immediately applied since my bank had all the existing information from the 1st PPP Loan. My loan was approved on 1/25/21 and disbursed on 2/8/2021.

When the interim final rule (“Business Loan Program Temporary Changes; Paycheck Protection Program—Revisions to Loan Amount Calculation and Eligibility”) was released March 8, 2021, I was in favor of the decision made by the SBA and Treasury Department stating,
“that a Schedule C filer may elect to calculate the owner compensation share of its payroll costs—that is, the share of its payroll costs that represents compensation of the owner—based on either (i) net profit or (ii) gross income.” [Further]
““Previously, PPP rules defined payroll costs for individuals who file an IRS Form 1040, Schedule C as payroll costs (if employees exist) plus net profits, which is net earnings from self-employment. SBA is aware of significant concerns with this definition, because it does not take into account fixed and other business expenses that a small business must cover to stay in operation and therefore keep the owner employed. Thus, the support for employment for sole proprietors includes covering business expenses as well as net profits. This change would affect many sole proprietors who have been effectively excluded from the PPP, especially those with very little or negative net profit, many of which are located in underserved communities.” [Further]
“under the prior rules, many of these borrowers may not have received meaningful amounts from the PPP to support their own employment due to having small net profits.”

This was certainly my case in that while the PPP loan enabled me, as an employer, to secure my staff’s economic stability, it did nothing to help me as a member of the labor force to secure my own economic stability since my business had little net income the prior year.

After reading more, I was then infuriated when I read the following:
“SBA is implementing this change with respect to PPP loans that are approved after the effective date of this rule. A borrower whose PPP loan has already been approved as of the effective date of this rule cannot increase its PPP loan amount based on the new calculation methodology.”

Without a stipulation that a PPP 2nd Draw loan that has already been approved and disbursed can be increased retroactively given this new, unforeseen guidance regarding how the original loan value should have been calculated, the result is that this decision unfairly penalizes borrowers who were prepared to file for their 2nd Draw loans as soon as the program opened. These same early filers, like me, are also likely the most in need of immediate economic assistance which contradicts the statement earlier in the ruling which reads,
“Given the urgent need to provide borrowers with timely relief and the short period of time before the program ends…”

I reference the precedent set in the April 2, 2020 interim final rule (“Business Loan Program Temporary Changes: Paycheck Protection Program-Loan Increases”) which states,
“On April 28, 2020, the Department of the Treasury posted an interim final rule that provided an alternative criterion for calculating the maximum loan amount for PPP loans issued to seasonal employers (85 FR 23917)."
"Some PPP loans were approved to partnerships or seasonal employers before the additional guidance was issued and, as a result, those businesses may not have received PPP loans in the maximum amount for which they are eligible."
"In addition, although the interim final rule on disbursements posted on April 28, 2020, requires PPP loans to be disbursed in a single disbursement, if a PPP loan that is increased has already been disbursed, this interim final rule authorizes the lender to make an additional disbursement of the increased loan proceeds prior to submission of the initial SBA Form 1502 that includes that loan. SBA Form 1502 is required to be submitted within 20 calendar days after a PPP loan is approved or, for loans approved before availability of the updated SBA Form 1502 reporting process, by May 22, 2020.”

I vigorously urge the SBA and Treasury Department to issue a similar additional ruling which would make these rule changes retroactive for loans made since the program opened on January 13, 2021. It is unfair to penalize business owners who are doing their best to keep their staff fully employed and their business from closing by not applying these new loan calculations retroactively to loans approved prior to the new, random effective date.
Thank you for your consideration.

Please see attached comments regarding the interim final rule regarding debt refinance within the SBA 504 program.

RE:RIN: 3245-AH78
Interim Final Rule
Debt Refinancing in the 504 Loan Program

Dear Ms. Reilly:

AmPac Tri-State CDC, Inc. (“CDC”), submits these comments in response to the U.S. Small Business Administration’s (SBAs) interim final rule (“IFR”) titled, “Debt Refinancing in the 504 Loan Program,” (RIN: 3245-AH78). CDC appreciates the opportunity to comment on these crucial changes to SBAs 504 loan program. It has always been our belief that 504 regulations should not only protect the integrity of the program, but also improve avenues for CDCs to promote economic development through job creation guided by the best interests of the small businesses we all serve. Our comments are based on this philosophy, which we know you share.

CDC’s comments focus on suggested changes to the Interim Final Rule and policy guidance, which we believe will simplify the program, making it more accessible and efficient without adding undue risk.

13 CFR 120.882(g)(3)
CDC has two specific recommendations in this section. First, CDC recommends that SBA not include in regulation any conditions or requirements that restrict or limit the ability to refinance a loan that is subject to a guarantee by a Federal agency or department since no such conditions or restrictions exist in statute. CDC recommends SBA use similar language the agency previously used in regulations for the 504 debt refinance with expansion program at 13 CFR 120.882(e)(3) – there, SBA simply states, “Existing 7(a) and 504 loans may be refinanced under this section in accordance with SBA policies or procedures.”

Second, CDC recommends removal from policy and procedure guidance the written verification of the existing 7(a) lender’s inability or unwillingness to modify the current payment schedule as a requirement to allowing the refinance of an existing 7(a) loan. CDC takes strong exception to the limitations that SBA is imposing on the CDCs ability to refinance an existing 7(a) loan.

13 CFR 120.882(g)(6)(i)
CDC recommends that SBA remove the restriction that if a Borrower’s application includes a request to finance Eligible Business Expenses, “the portion of the Refinancing Project provided by the 504 loan and the Third Party Loan may be no more than 85% of the fair market value of the fixed assets that will serve as collateral and the Borrower may receive no more than 20% of the fair market value of the Eligible Fixed Asset(s) securing the Qualified Debt for Eligible Business Expenses.” No such restrictions or limitations exist in statute – not in the original enabling legislation in Section 521 of Division E of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016 nor the revised statutory language in Division N, Title III, Section 328 of the Economic Aid Act. SBA implemented this limitation in regulation and policy guidance in part to address the original statutory requirement that the Debt Refinancing Program must operate at “zero cost,” which was eliminated in the Economic Aid Act.
.
13 CFR 120.882(g)(6)(ii)
CDC recommends that SBA broaden the definition of Eligible Business Expenses to include “or other obligations of the business.” CDC recommends broadening the definition of Eligible Business Expenses to also include any other debt of the business that is not Qualified Debt. The small business is unable to refinance this debt even though it is secured by Eligible Fixed Assets, removing the opportunity for the business to benefit from the consolidated debt for future growth.

13 CFR 120.882(g)(7)
CDC recommends SBA clarify in its policies and procedures that a partial refinance of any Qualified Debt is allowed, including a partial refinance of an existing government-guaranteed debt or conventional debt. It is clear from the regulatory language that SBA has historically allowed and continues to allow a partial refinance of a Qualified Debt. CDC recommends that SBA simply apply this same policy guidance to refinancing conventional debts in the 504 Debt Refinancing Program and allow partial refinances of all Qualified Debt.

13 CFR 120.882(e)(1) and definition of “Qualified Debt” in 13 CFR 120.882(g)(16)
CDC recommends that SBA modify its definition for debt eligible to refinance in the 504 loan program [for 504 debt refinance with expansion program at 13 CFR 120.882(e)(1) and for the 504 debt refinance without expansion program at 13 CFR 120.882(g)(16)] by lowering its “substantially all” (85% or more) standard to a “majority” standard (51% or more).

CDC recommends that SBA lower in regulation and policy the “substantially all” standard (85% or more) to a “majority” standard of 51% or more. We believe this change will promote increased access to and utilization of both 504 debt refinancing programs without adding undue risk to SBA while honoring the original intent of the law.

We appreciate the opportunity to provide these comments.

Sincerely,

Hilda Kennedy
Founder/President

African elephants are at serious risk of extinction. In addition to being listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act, African savanna elephants were recently classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature — and forest elephants were classified as critically endangered. So, while I appreciate your proposal to improve their protections by revising the 4(d) rule for African elephants under the Endangered Species Act, please go further. I’m urging you to implement a full ban on elephant trophy imports and live trade to ensure these cherished species are fully protected from extinction.

U.S. trophy hunters play an outsized role in killing African animals for sport. Zimbabwe reports that historically, U.S. hunters have made up half of its wildlife-hunting market. Banning imports of elephant trophies — such as heads, feet, tails, skins and ivory — would deter hunters and send a consistent message that the United States doesn't support killing these extraordinary, deeply intelligent animals.

Likewise, you must ban the trade in live elephants to the United States. These social and wide-ranging animals deserve to live in the wild — not to be ripped from their homes and sold into captivity. I urge you to ban this trade.

In addition, while you’re considering these changes to elephant protections, it is important to recognize the two species of elephants in Africa, savanna and forest, separately under the Endangered Species Act.

The devastating extinction crisis must be met with an extraordinary response. I urge you to act boldly to protect elephants from overexploitation. Please ban the trade in African elephant trophies and live animals and adopt a strong new rule to protect these majestic creatures.

revise the rule for the African elephant ( Loxodonta africana ) promulgated under section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (ESA). The intended purposes are threefold: To increase protection for African elephants in light of the recent rise in international trade of live African elephants by establishing ESA enhancement permit requirements for international trade in live elephants and specific enhancement requirements for the import of wild-sourced elephants, as well as requirements to ensure that proposed recipients of live African elephants are suitably equipped to house and care for them; to clarify the existing enhancement requirement during our evaluation of an application for a permit to import African elephant sport-hunted trophies; and to incorporate a Party's designation under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) National Legislation Project into the decision-making process for the import of live African elephants, African elephant sport-hunted trophies, and African elephant parts and products other than ivory and sport-hunted trophies. We anticipate these measures will affect implementation in foreign countries of management measures that enhance African elephant conservation.

The Intellistop pulsating brake light module will be an important tool to alert trailing drivers that the vehicle in front is slowing or braking heavily. I would like to comment on the Application for an Exemption From Intellistop, Inc. I am the VP of Safety for a major bulk tank truck carrier and first saw this product at the NTTC National Conference. After careful review of Intellistop and how it works and the ease of installation of this product, I feel it would be a great safety feature on the rear of any commercial vehicle to reduce the amount of rear-end collision due to inattentive drivers approaching from the rear. Our company is required to stop at all railroad crossing and have had multiple rear-end collisions in the past. Anything that our industry can do to bring awareness to drivers approaching from the rear that a CMV is slowing or stopping would be helpful in reducing rear-end collisions.

Intellistop requires no additional lights be mounted on the vehicle and in most case can be installed in less than a hour. If the Intellistop unit where to malfunction the cmv would still maintain proper lighting, just without the pulse.

I am and have been an avid motorcycle rider for the past 50 years and always worry about inattentive drivers approaching from the rear and not seeing that I am slowing or stopping. I installed Intellistop on my motorcycle in less than 15 minutes prior to a 1500 mile trip and notices that drivers approaching from the rear were more aware of my presents in front of them and did not get as close as they once did prior to me having the Intellistop installed.

So in closing, I feel it would be advantageous for FMCSA to grant an exemption to Intellistop to help our industry promote safety and reduce rear-end collisions.

I thin that this is a perfect product for semi-trailer and vehicle safety. with this product it alerts the following vehicle, with the flash of the lights and the solid on, just like a third brake light on cars and pick-ups. I see this as a great mile stone to keep vehicles from foing under the rear of the trailer.

I propose that Intellistop be provided an exemption for the purpose of enhancing the brake signaling on commercial trucks. The evidence is clear that a pulsing light commands more attention for the motorist, there by helping reduce the number of rear end collisions.

The proof of that is all around us: firetrucks, ambulances and police cars all equipped with some type of flashing lights. In fact even construction vehicles are equipped with flashing lights.

To take it a step further the FAA requires that all planes operate a strobe light as the enhances a pilots attention to the plane.

Again I am in support of the exeption>

This technology should be standard on all trailing equipment. This will allow the public to more easily identify trailers when braking, and as a result reduce the amount of rear end collisions with trailers. I have tested and reviewed this product, and I would like to be able to install these on our trailing fleet to help keep our drivers and the public safe on our roadways. Any device that can add to the safety of traffic should be accepted when possible, and this product does just that. I would highly recommend this be accepted.

The technology and operational principle used by Intellistop is proven to provide a definite enhancement to the visibility by trailing drivers when other vehicles in front of them begin a braking action.  The same technology has been applied in smaller (non-CMV) fleet units nationwide for many years.  In particular, utility companies and others who have vehicles who make frequent stops have been utilizing pulsing brake light systems for years.  The goal of all fleets should be to do all that is reasonable and prudent to reduce the potential of accidents, and the Intellistop system will most certainly help fleets reduce the potential of rear-end collisions caused by inattentive trailing drivers.  With the increase in rear-end collisions caused by distracted drivers (largely due to cell phones) over the past several years, I believe fleet owners and federal agencies alike should take all steps possible to reduce crash potential, and the Intellistop system, applied to CMV fleets, would be an absolute positive factor in that regard.  As a DOT compliance and fleet safety consultant, my mission is to assist my clients with reaching higher levels of fleet safety and compliance with the FMCSRs.  In that spirit, I believe this request for exemption from the "steady burning tail lamp" requirement should absolutely be granted in the name of increased safety efforts for CMV fleets.

Back in September 2020, I stared a pulsating brake light study as NTTC was looking at executing an exemption. During this long study period I was able to review public comments, NHTSA data studies and as prior law enforcement officer the effects of emergency flashing lights. I also attached my study to this public comment. I have reviewed many vendor applications for the pulsating brake light. After multiple reviews, I was able to seek out Intellistop which had a product I was looking for. I’m a 27 year veteran of law enforcement and early on in my career I served in the patrol division of my department. During that time our focus was not only enforcing laws, but also making sure the motoring public was safe during their travels on America’s roadways. This wasn’t always possible due to weather and inattentive driving being the main catalyst in the vehicle accidents we investigated.Numerous traffic accidents I worked were due to poor visibility and or drivers experiencing “Highway Hypnosis”. It’s of my opinion that the brake light “pulsing” that the Intellistop feature provides produces a better visibility due to the fact that the 4 “pulses” alerts drivers visually because they are aren’t just anticipating a solid red brake light, but rather the 4 quick “pulses” then the solid red brake light. Regarding Docket ID FMCSA-2021-0187, we support expanded options for warning devices required on commercial vehicles. While the existing permitted devices (triangles, liquid flares, fusees) have served the industry well for many decades, new devices provide additional features and safety enhancements. It is unlikely that anyone has used a liquid flare in decades. Fusee flares present harmful environmental impact, health hazards (fume inhalation) and fire danger, and triangles are low cost but of low safety value. It is likely that most, if not all, accidents where a vehicle struck a parked commercial vehicle or its driver occurred when a triangle or flare was deployed. No safety device is perfect, but this petition for exemption offers the opportunity to try something new.

Runway approach lamps flash in a sequential pattern to visually aid pilots to the threshold. Guiding lights that move in a pattern visually provide the driver with a low-light-intensity direction to follow. In this application the moving lights would steer the approaching traffic away from the disabled commercial vehicle.

We have examined, studied, and used a commercially available smart flare set. The visual impact is quite impressive. The guidance to approaching drivers is easily appreciated by watching these vehicles move away from the stalled apparatus on the road side. While the cost is higher, it is a one-time cost that potentially saves lives. In addition, there are commercially available devices that will notify Waze and Google Maps and place a warning on navigation maps. This is not available when fusees or triangles are deployed.

Our company sells safety devices into the tow truck and commercial vehicle market. Many customers have inquired about the availability of this technology. In the past we have advised that electronic flares are allowed but not as a substitute for mandated warning devices. This exemption, if permitted, would allow for economies for the fleet operators and they would not have to purchase triangles and moving-light flares. The smart flares would suffice. Of course, pricing might dictate that fleet operators continue to use triangles, but a choice allowing for a more modern and effective safety device would now be allowed.

Jeff Holland
SureEcosystem
Cars and Motorcycles already use this safety feature. Why not trucks?? Also why haven’t we required Day time Headlamps as well.

I have been associated with the transportation industry for approximately 17 years, and my previous role was the Director of Safety for a large LTL carrier. Intellistop offers innovative technology that can reduce rear end accidents. Safety departments across the entire United States are tasked with reducing rear end accidents, and Intellistop has an effective solution. This technology is much more visible than anything on the market, and it should be available to carriers. This will save lives!

Before these devices are allowed for carriage and use by CMV drivers, there are a few items that should be addressed.
1. How many would be required to be deployed, 6 or 3? The regs as written are unclear. 392.22(b) says 3 fusees/flares (which these are intended to replace) must be placed, yet 393.95 says “At least 6 fusees or 3 liquid-burning flares” “must be used”. Which is it for these intended replacements, 6 or 3? It seems to me 393.95 should address carriage requirements, not use/deployment. 392.22 addresses use. I now this won’t be addressed in response to this proposed regulation but perhaps it can be added to the regulatory correction list for consideration.
2. Has the manufacturer tested and provided test data for the longevity and useability of these devices under normal CMV carriage and use? Will these even work after they’re knocked around the interior/storage compartment of a truck for 5 years and will the batteries still be good? Because if we rely on the same driver that has an expired extinguisher to check and replace the batteries in these then we are placing our trust, and other driver's lives, in the wrong hands.
3. CMV emergency response equipment shouldn’t rely on batteries which regularly expire during storage. The frequency of use by a CMV operator is limited to instances of breakdown or crash. When needed, however infrequently, they must work. Replacing a low-tech triangle or fusee/fare with technology that requires maintenance and upkeep is ill-advised. See #2.
4. These would be good tools for first-responders who will take care of the equipment they use almost daily, but for truck drivers? No. The manufacturer's own brochure (attached) indicates use for emergency responders as they say; "We're here to guide drivers not just warn them. They're already warned when they come upon a scene but where are they to go?" So why are they requesting an exemption for a use they seemingly don’t intend? This is further bolstered by this statement from the same brochure: "with an unlimited number of deployments why would you still pay for a single use flare?" Clearly these are intended for first-responder uss unless there’s some really bad truck drivers out there that need the "unlimited" use these provide.
In conclusion, these devices, as designed and intended for first responder use, are practical and effective replacements, but as an intended replacement for a CMV operators emergency equipment, which is stored and forgotten about for extended periods of time, these are not well suited nor advisable.

Regarding comments pertaining to Docket (FMCSA-2021-0187), providing an electronic alternative to existing requirements under 393.95, conern was raised over:

1) Number of electronic flares to be required: The submitted documentation suggests an equivalency of a minimum of 6 electronic flares to match the requirements of 6 flame fusee flares as specified in 393.95. As with 393.95, more than 6 fusee flares are permitted and more than 6 electronic flares would be permitted at the fleet operator's discretion. Of course, the operator may choose more than 3 liquid oil flares (oil pots).

2) Long-term battery status of rarely-usesd electronic devices: While most electronic LED flare systems are available in both a recharageable or alkaline battery format, the recommended system for infrequent use would be to use alkaline batteries. Alkaline batteries enjoy a long, stable shelf-life. When not in use, the shelf-life of installed alkaline batteries (in the device) will exceed 5 years. The most frequent failure mode is alkaline battery leakage, which is most often associated with low-cost (generic) AA batteries. It is recommended that an annual review, at a minimum, of all safety equipment be undertaken. Flame flares suffer failure through dampness, for example. Triangles may be cracked from storage under a seat or in an equipment locker. So all safety devices shouuld undergo a periodic inspection.

3) Ruggedness and reliability: Quality electronic flares are designed to be run over by vehicles, sustain water and heat exposure, and rough handling in general. There are products available that enjoy independent laboratory testing including crush strength, IP certification (leakage), as well as warranty. Fusees, triangles, and oil pots are not tested to these same standards, yet are subject to breakage and failure.

4) Electronic warning technology and frequent use: That law enforcement, fire departments, utility CVs, state DOT maintenance vehicles use a safety device fequently should not deter from infrequent use. In fact, all of the aforementioned could choose to deploy a set of triangles or fusees, but ask for the option not to. Each of the currently specified warning devices suffer particular failure modes. That advertising literature for one such device describes guidance as well as warning speaks to the adjunctive features of sequential flashing LED flares. And there are independent studies supporting the safety benefit of marching (coordinated) warning lights.

In summary, comments suggesting that existing 393.95 warning devices have been adequate and that new technology introduces uncertainty are appropriate and welcome by the industry. Careful review, however, reveals that existing warning devices introduce their own uncertainty (e.g., triangles blow over, flares cause fires, and neither provide for future cloud connectivity). There are no perfect solutions, but all industries should strive for better. This petition for an exemption only asks that the operator be offered a new choice.

I am in support of the use of the Pi Variables sequential LED lights in place of the fusees or liquid-burning flares. Using these units will have at minimum 3 positive affects in the emergency situations as well as during service calls on vehicles. The LED lights provide greater visibility to the moving traffic, provides directional guidance as the units light in sequence and thirdly eliminate the hazard of having open flames on the side of the road which if used when vehicles that carry flammable materials and in areas that have dry vegetation which can result in fires. Many times the fusees are left on the road to burn out after the CMV has been moved from the location, creating another hazardous situation. The LED lights are also environmentally friendly and non hazardous to use.

Comment pertaining to docket number FMCSA 2021-018. As a manufacturer of autonomous commercial vehicles we are aware of the need to deploy FMCSA-approved warning devices as defined in section 393.95. Driverless deployment of triangles or flame flares is fraught with challenges. Autonomous deployment of an electronic sequential flashing flare is more effective (visually) and more reliable. 1st responders are deploying sequential flashing LED flares instead of flame flares for incident management. TuSimple is unaware of anyone using liquid oil pot flares.

Independent of the AV driverless deployment, triangles and flame flares have obvious shortcomings. Sequential flares are more effective in diverting traffic away from vehicles on the side of the road, and do not present a fire hazard. LED battery powered flares are not as effective on a bright sunny day, but they do not have to be since oncoming drivers are not encumbered by poor visibility, and depth of field and situational awareness are at their best during the daytime. However, on days with inclimate weather or during nighttime, sequential LED flares are superior to a poorly aimed reflective triangle or one that has blown over. Battery powered flashing LED devices are commonly found on portable traffic diversion "A" frame style barricades.

Independent drivers and fleet operators, under this petition, will continue to have the option to use triangles or flares. There are those in the industry, however, that seek the option of a more innovative technology. We support the addition of sequential flashing LED flares to section 393.95.

The description of the regulation misstates its scope to make it sound less extreme than it is. The description claims that current law makes certain organizations ineligible for loans simply because of their religious affiliation. This is not true. More accurately, the proposed regulation removes rules that make organizations ineligible to participate in loan programs if they are [p]rincipally engaged inor [their] principal activity isteaching, instructing, counseling or indoctrinating religion or religious beliefs, whether in a religious or secular setting. 13 CFR 109.400(b)(11), 120.110(k), 123.301(g), 123.502(n), 123.702(b)(6).

In other words, the regulation would put the taxpayers in the businesses of financially supporting organizations whose principal activity is religious propaganda. I believe that involves the government in the establishment of religion and that is totally inappropriate. I note that a religiously affiliated organization whose principal activity is NOT religious propaganda but, say, secular education, or addiction counseling, or providing wholesome after school care, or whatever, would not be ineligible for the loans merely because an incidental outcome of providing the public good is that it increased the good reputation of the religious organization. That is as it should be. The government should not be in the business of financing the indoctrination of, anyones religious beliefs.

As we move closer to a more digital world, the need for HHS is becoming more important than ever. While there are endless reasons for making the switch, a few of the most important ones (in my opinion) are:

- Paper invoices are costly to not only print and mail but also in terms of staff time. By automating the process, money is saved on printing, storing, and mailing, and staff members are also freed up to focus on more essential tasks for the good of the business. There will no longer be any need to send out reminders or deal with payment errors, significantly slashing labor costs. This will also minimize the need of storing and managing the bulk amount of data in hard copy format, which all lead to cost and resource savings.

- Electronic billing will create an automatic process that speeds up the billing process exponentially. Suppliers are, therefore, able to receive payments more quickly for a more manageable and predictable cash flow and patients/customers have the ability to pay their bills via the method of their choice, anytime, anywhere.

- Electronic billing creates a digital record of the information that allows for precise communication and easy traceability while also eliminating many of the frustrations associated with unnecessary redundancy and overpayments.
With recent advancements in encryption and dual-authentication, electronic billing is safer than ever.

- Electronic Billing will reduce the HSS’ environmental footprint as they would significantly cut down on paper usage and wastage.

- Better efficiency equates to faster approval cycles, which itself can create discount opportunities. When invoices are being processed more quickly, the HSS can offer customers payment discounts for settling up debts early.

- Similar to the above, as the HSS becomes more efficient and cost effective, they can increase their profits while also reducing the net costs absorbed by their patients/customers.

The Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) urges the Department of Health and Human Services to withdraw this proposed rule, as described in the attached comments.

We write in strong support of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) January 13, 2021 proposed rule titled Establishment of Safeguards and Program Integrity Requirements for Health and Human Services-Funded Extramural Research Involving Human Fetal Tissue. The proposed rule will improve the integrity of fetal tissue research by strengthening informed consent requirements and ensuring compliance with the statutory ban on profiting from fetal tissue.
Unfortunately, the United States has a long history of unethical experiments in the name of medical research involving human test subjects , aborted but still-living ex-utero infants , and recently aborted fetal body parts commonly referred to as fetal tissue. These experiments present serious ethical and legal challenges that harm the integrity of the research.
The proposed rule builds on suggestions from the medical research community and a comprehensive review HHS undertook of all HHS research involving human fetal tissue from elective abortion. The proposed safeguards will ensure consistency with the statutes and regulations governing fetal tissue research and help guarantee the adequacy of procedures and oversight of such research in light of the serious regulatory, moral, and ethical considerations involved.
The research and medical communities have recognized the importance of obtaining informed consent before engaging in human fetal tissue research. In June 2016, the American Medical Association (AMA) issued a Code of Medical Ethics Opinion discussing the number of ethical considerations involving the use of human fetal tissue research. Specifically the AMA was concerned about the possible financial benefit to those who are involved in the retrieval, storage, testing, preparation, and delivery of fetal tissues and the degree to which a womans decision to have an abortion might be influenced by the opportunity to donate fetal tissue. The AMA listed several steps a physician should take to protect the interests of pregnant women as well as the integrity of science and physicians who are involved in research that uses human fetal tissues, including obtaining the informed consent of the pregnant woman. Additionally, many states that allow fetal tissue research often require the consent of the pregnant woman for the fetal tissue donation. The informed consent protections in the proposed rule will ensure the donation of human fetal tissue from abortion is in fact voluntary and informed, and not motivated by any enticements, benefits, or financial considerations.
After disturbing reports surfaced of abortion providers altering procedures to maximize their profit off fetal tissue, Congress acted quickly to investigate these claims. The House Select Investigative Panel on Infant Lives revealed organizations involved in fetal tissue harvesting and research failed to maintain any safeguards for the use of fetal tissue and were profiteering from fetal tissue trafficking. These new safeguards will end any adverse incentives for a woman to have an abortion or an abortion provider to alter the abortion, possibly endangering the life of the mother.
The House Select Investigative Panel also revealed certain institutional review boards lacked records regarding their oversight of fetal tissue research and transplantation, and the committee was unable to obtain access to records that could determine whether fetal tissue was obtained for valuable consideration. The proposed rule would improve the integrity of the research conducted by grant recipients by ensuring they comply with all federal statutes and guidelines.
We urge the HHS to finalize the rule to implement strong safeguards for the use of fetal tissue funded at the taxpayers expense.

Sincerely,

Representative Blaine Luetkemeyer and Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, et. al., Congress of the United States

Medical Reserve Corps (MRC) units across the country support Local Public Health departments, local emergency management, and local public safety departments during public health emergencies. Never has it been so clear how impactful MRC units are during public health emergencies.

The University of Minnesota Medical Reserve Corps unit has been included in the University's Emergency Operations Plan as an integral component of health emergencies on campus. Since January of 2020, the U of MN MRC has deployed students, staff, and faculty to assist in the response to COVID-19.

The U of MN MRC's COVID Vaccination Team supported 22 campus vaccination clinics since the vaccination campaign began.
The team was deployed to 4 different vaccination sites, including Duluth!
240 MRC volunteers filled a total of 600 different shifts, for a total of 1,988 hours.
This team also supported vaccination efforts at Federally Qualified Health Care Centers, with hours closer to 2,000 and increasing every week.

Our response partners have mentioned that they would not have been able to respond to the COVID testing and vaccination needs without the assistance of U of MN MRC volunteers.

Visibility and funding for Medical Reserve Corps units directly impacts a communities ability to respond to large scale health emergencies.

Funding will strengthen MRC unit's ability to recruit, train, and deploy volunteers dedicated to being of service to their communities. Funds are needed, most critically, to support leadership positions within the MRC units.

I have witnessed several MRC units imbedded in Local Public Health departments, dwindle to a shell of what they were 10 years ago, when funding was at it's peak. Without a designated MRC leader, MRC program activities, drills, and training have nearly become obsolete.

Let's prepare our country for the next public health emergency by funding a program that allows local communities to support the needs of their citizens during small, medium, and large public health emergencies.

1. What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?

Strength: Units and infrastructure existed. Massachusetts supports MRC Units with a little money that has kept them alive, but not thriving. Every year is a funding struggle as inflation erodes salaries. When the State locked down in March, the MRCs were a critical resource that allowed local and regional groups to quickly and safely deploy certified and trained volunteers to support food distributions to school children and others. The MRC volunteers also distributed PPE and other resource. It also gave local jurisdictions a way to quickly and safety onboard the hundreds of volunteers who wanted to help with the response which helped control the surge of Spontaneous Unaffiliated Volunteers and help ensure that volunteers deployed to work with children and seniors CORI/SORI checks. It also gave us a way to quickly verify medical and other credentials.

2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?

Biggest Need: Full-time MRC Leaders: Finding and keeping professional, consistent MRC Leaders is essential to any emergency response. You cannot hire knowledgeable, trained people who can lead a response at the last minute. MRC Units need a sustainable funding stream for trained, effective, consistent leaders who can lead, grow and sustain the MRC Units throughout the years. These leaders must be adequately paid, full-time planners, trainers, and responders. They could be housed in local health departments or regional collaboratives/non-profits or even police or fire departments.

3. Do you have recommendations on the top short- and long-term priorities for the MRC? What operational capabilities, services, or competencies would you propose that the MRC focus on? Do you have recommendations on ways to strengthening the MRC's role as a federal disaster response asset?

Short Term: Provide qualified MRC Units with enough money to hire and keep full time Leaders. A condition of the funding could be that they cover a certain population of a certain number of jurisdictions if they do not meet the population requirement. MRC Units might have to share a leader to meet these standards. As a condition of funding when there isn’t an emergency, allow the MRC Units to take on community service projects that improve the health and safety of the region.
Long Term: Work to make qualified MRC Units federal disaster responder. Allow MRC Units to attend trainings at FEMA training sites to become qualified and to provide more resources for local responses.

4. Any additional topics you wish to provide input on.

Provide states the resources to provide and maintain the online systems to register, train, and deploy spontaneous volunteers or make existing MRC system more flexible to allow for volunteers who do not want to join and organization in order to help with an emergency.

I am Executive Director of MRC GEM, an all-volunteer 501(c)(3) nonprofit Medical Reserve Corps serving 1.2 million. Recruited by local public health 14 years ago to revive a moribund MRC, we’ve built it into a vital community asset, creating a sustainable nonprofit. With 655 members a year ago, we’ve grown to nearly 2,600 members. To date, we’ve provided over 16,000 hours of direct support to the COVID-19 response efforts of Gwinnett, Newton, & Rockdale County Health Depts (GNR Health) and continue to provide volunteer support each week. With no paid staff, this level of action has presented a major challenge. Solid volunteer management, and the community partnerships we’ve grown, allow us to accomplish this.

Our members reflect the exceptional diversity of our community, representing 82 languages and dialects and including students, retirees, and employed people from every walk of life. MRC GEM is explicitly included in the emergency response plans of GNR Health and local EMA. I believe we are the largest all-volunteer MRC unit, and surely one of the most active. In “normal” times, we hold monthly member trainings and participate in many activities in support of the community and the MRC program.

Our key mission sets include shelter support, POD setup/operation, and community reception center (CRC) setup/operation for radiation response. They are deployable on short notice and adaptable for other needs. Our CRC Startup Team appears in the EMAC database as an asset deployable anywhere in Georgia and adjoining states.

I’ve personally served over eight years on the NACCHO MRC Working Group and provided many hours of assistance to other MRC units. I provide this background to point out that I have a solid basis for my comments. I hope this view “from the trenches” will be taken seriously and in the spirit in which it is offered.

Top strength of MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new strengths?

The “superpower” of MRC is the volunteer heart all our members have in common. The greatest strength of the program is that units can be tailored to the unique needs of the populations they serve. Each unit can be custom-designed, based on local needs, representative of the community, and ready to step up to serve and protect our own families and neighbors.

Our GNR Health staff was never stretched as far and for as long as during this pandemic response. Their wonderful personnel would surely have been worn down and worn out without the support of MRC GEM’s “surge capacity”.

Top needs or resource gaps of MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs?

The pandemic reinforced our ongoing need for adequate, reliable funding to draw and retain volunteers, who are recruited primarily by existing enthusiastic volunteers. They’re retained by (1) providing regular relevant programming and (2) recognizing them for their participation. Our top resource gap is the lack of funding, particularly unrestricted funding, to meet these two needs.

Our dedicated volunteer management is stretched to the limit managing responses and providing programming. Seeking funding is an ongoing additional burden that distracts from the main mission. Not being the typical “women’s and children’s charity” eliminates the majority of potential funding sources. Ignorance of the MRC program makes it difficult to reach the rest. One of the few positive impacts of COVID-19: it HAS helped to illustrate to our community what MRC does. Hundreds of new volunteers discovered us when they came to get vaccinated and were so impressed that they joined us.

Increased membership brings the cost of outfitting and training new members, at least $77 each. Restrictions on some funding prevents it from being used to feed volunteers at trainings or callouts, recognize their achievements, or even to equip them. After 14 years of building this unit from the ground up, this can be disheartening.

Short- and long-term priorities for MRC? What operational capabilities, services, or competencies should MRC focus on? Ways to strengthen MRC’s role as a federal disaster response asset?

Short term:
•Increase public awareness of MRC through PSA’s, etc. With COVID-19 still in the national spotlight, it should also be possible to get national coverage of how MRC units have responded.
•Increased funding for units with significant recent growth to help them retain volunteers.
•National/ regional events where unit leaders can exchange best practices. This is how the most active unit leaders learned essential skills and how we can help others learn.

Long term: Continue the above.

Operational capabilities, service, or competencies to focus on: Survey LHD’s and local EMA’s for their top needs, provide standardized training to meet these.

The program office provides adequate coordination under existing funding levels. American Rescue Plan funds should be distributed among MRC units, where they will do the most good.

Keep national funding methodology transparent and fair; all MRC should receive some funds. Larger or more experienced MRC could be weighted for funding because of their demonstrated responses and contributions. This would aspire other MRC to improve and innovate and recruit.

1. What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?

•MRC supported a pandemic response that was unparalleled in modern times. We marshalled medical and non-medical volunteers that swarmed to help, trained them, and put them in the field to effectively support public health initiatives. The pandemic was a test of our capabilities and even where we were weakest, we still effectively supported the pandemic response effort. This shows that the heart of MRC is what drives its volunteer base. It is the administration’s job to support the volunteers so that instead of feeling worn-out and exhausted from this pandemic, they feel appreciated and ready to serve in the future.

2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?
•We need dedicated MRC coordinators in every district – not people who do MRC management when it’s convenient around other tasks. The MRC is critical infrastructure to disaster response, both small-scale and large-scale. The MRC provides vetted, educated, and trained volunteers who are ready to deploy at a moment’s notice. The MRC workforce is free.
•MRC needs a nationwide PR campaign and resources that can be used via social media.
•MRC should be a national network rather than a regional pop-up. The states and units that are already in existence should be supported, funded, and their software systems connected so everyone talks to everyone else and volunteers can be easily transferred.

3. Do you have recommendations on the top short- and long-term priorities for the MRC? What operational capabilities, services, or competencies would you propose that the MRC focus on? Do you have recommendations on ways to strengthening the MRC's role as a federal disaster response asset?
•The best way to strengthen MRC’s role as a federal disaster response asset is to provide long-term leadership – district and regional coordinators along with a state team to continue growing and maintaining the program and volunteers. To know now how many volunteers are out there ready to serve and for us to not be prepared to support that effort would be unimaginable. MRC is not a jobs program, rather this is a program that provides tens of millions of dollars of free workforce labor via highly educated, trained, and committed volunteers.

4. Any additional topics you wish to provide input on.
The information received will inform the planning for executing the American Rescue Plan funding.
•MRC will be 20 years old next year and we still don’t have adequate full-time leadership. In one MRC district we have over 1800 deployable volunteers and no dedicated MRC coordinator – we are not using our volunteer assets responsibly in cases like this. These volunteers have entrusted us with their time, education, and personal information and the least we can do is put an enthusiastic, dedicated coordinator in charge of them.
•Our volunteer management systems are antiquated at best. Most of us moved to using online subscription services (that we paid for) to create deployments and signups (Signup Genius, for example). With $100 million, we should easily be able to upgrade our software such that it works as we need it to work.
•There needs to be nationally standardized training requirements for Level 1, 2, and 3 volunteers.

There are several focus areas that should be funded:
1. It would be nice to fund applied research at the local level, including measuring the local impact of volunteer activities.
2. Pay for a survey subscription service that is easy to use (like Survey Monkey) for Unit Leaders to have free access to use and download the survey data on their volunteers.
3. Pay for something like Sign Up Genius for the units. It was very helpful during the pandemic.
4. Have a national portal for volunteers and units to purchase low cost attire, including uniforms and equipment at a discount.
5. Match local funds for full time volunteer unit coordinators at the county level.
6. Provide a mechanism to award volunteers with service awards via the unit coordinators but the logistics handled from a central national location.
7. Provide a strategic national resource supply for unit leaders to access without having too much bureaucracy.
8. Allow unit leaders to have access to a line of credit to provide refreshments for volunteers.
