1. What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?

One of the biggest strengths we saw in our local area was the number of volunteers. We more than doubled our member roster once the vaccine was available. While this increase did create additional challenges, we would not have been able to complete vaccination clinics at the rate we were able to in our local area.
Additionally, the messaging system on our ESAR-VHP is a helpful resource for getting the messages, updates, and requests for help out to members quickly. The messaging is excellent for last-minute changes or requests for additional volunteers. Since we used this consistently it has highlighted the need to ensure member profiles are up to date with their current contact information. This is a project we will review regularly now.

2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?

One of the regular obstacles we found during the COVID-19 response was onboarding a large number of new volunteers in a timely manner. At one point the Governor made a request for volunteers and the local units were flooded with new members daily. Having 30+ members a day to onboard was difficult to keep up with. We have also found background checks to be challenging to complete. Recently, we found out our system is just checking the sex offender list which is not thorough enough. We are evaluating the best way to accomplish background checks for our volunteers and have found the biggest challenge is funding.
Additionally, with the high request for volunteers, we struggled to find a good scheduling system. We tried multiple approaches to the scheduling aspect of volunteer management and have not yet found a suitable solution. Since many of the volunteers are older, retired I received many phone calls from frustrated or confused member who could not get the schedule to work. I would like to see a scheduling system that is quick and easy for coordinators to enter requests and is simple enough for volunteers to use and sign up for shifts, regardless of how tech-savvy they are.
It would be beneficial to have an awareness campaign as well. We had a lot of people interested in helping, but they had never heard of the MRC before. It would be excellent to have a national advertisement/marketing to help spread the word about MRC so more members of the community would join and be on boarded and trained before the incident.

1. What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?

The Medical Reserve Corps is a strong dedicated network of experienced leaders at the national, regional, state, and local levels with skilled medical and non-medical volunteers across the nation who share their time and expertise to strengthen Public Health and emergency response in disasters and blue skies. The National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO) is a great MRC partner, trainer, and grant manager.

The Sacramento MRC has proven its ability to strengthen emergency response by providing medical care for COVID-19, H1N1, and evacuees from Northern California wildfires, supporting warming and cooling centers in extreme weather as well as staffing events with a terrorism nexus including the Capitol Air Show and the California International Marathon.

COVID-19 has highlighted the Sacramento Medical Reserve Corps’ strength in supporting Sacramento County Public Health with the response effort for vaccination and testing clinics, COVID-19 Hotline and after-hours calls, case investigation and contact tracing and laboratory courier. The MRC has served as a bedrock against which all involved county departments, leaders and those in the community have come to lean upon.

Participation in the COVID-19 pandemic response effort has highlighted the MRC network’s ability to mobilize, expand to bring on board a broad spectrum of new members with skills needed for the response effort and stay flexible and engaged to assist in the response effort where and when needed by Public Health and our emergency response and community partners.

The Sacramento MRC quadrupled in membership size to 800 volunteers during the pandemic including an engaged cadre of Dentists who administer vaccines at COVID-19 vaccination clinics with other volunteer medical professionals.

2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?

The top needs and resource gaps of the Sacramento Medical Reserve Corps are staffing, an integrated database for volunteer management and deployment, and background checks of medical and non-medical MRC members. The Sacramento MRC is currently staffed by a Coordinator who is a 15 year veteran of the MRC and 2021 California Emergency Services Association Gold Award recipient for her leadership during the COVID-19 response effort. The Sacramento MRC needs multi-year funding for a Director, a Coordinator, and a full-time assistant to manage the program which has served 22,000 volunteer hours during COVID-19, valued at $967,616, the 3rd top performing MRC in California for the pandemic. Development of an integrated data base will greatly help streamline volunteer management and deployment. The large growth of the Sacramento MRC program, an increase of over 600 members, resulted in a challenge to get background checks for our new applicants. Due to the number of background checks requested of our law enforcement partner, our arrangement for free background checks may no longer be honored. Background checks are very important to ensure that members that are deployed are good citizens with clear records who can represent the MRC program in the community. Both medical and non-medical volunteers need to be checked since we have experienced failed background checks in both categories. If this gap in background checks could be filled for MRC’s across the nation to make background checks standardized and accessible for all that would be very helpful.

3. Do you have recommendations on the top short- and long-term priorities for the MRC? What operational capabilities, services, or competencies would you propose that the MRC focus on? Do you have recommendations on ways to strengthening the MRC's role as a federal disaster response asset?

Recommendations for short term priorities for the MRC include: Multi-year funding to expand MRC staffing at the local, state, regional, and national levels, provide or fund background checks, and support technology needs for integrated databases to streamline volunteer management and deployment.
Long term recommendations include: Training funds for first aid, CPR, and higher level medical training programs (Due to the increase in MRC membership due to COVID-19 it will be harder to fund the cost of these trainings for members), revitalize the national, regional and state MRC conferences that brought MRC leaders together to share best practices, and provide first aid kits and supplies to MRC’s across the nation for deployments.

Thank you for taking time to consider my comments.
I think the funding should be used to assist the local MRC units with staffing to help maintain and sustain their local volunteers. It should also be used to provide financial support to rebrand or reorder supplies for the numerous new volunteers they received since the initiation of the Pandemic.
Medical Reserve Corps (MRC) units across the country support Local Public Health Departments, local emergency management, and local public safety departments during public health emergencies. It has never been so clear how impactful MRC units are during public health emergencies.
The State of Illinois, particularly the Local Health Departments has deployed their local volunteers as well as the new volunteers that registered after our Governor requested that retired and all current health professionals register on our ESAR-VHP system to assist back in March of 2020. We went from an estimate of 5500 volunteers registered in our system to greater than 42,000 volunteers. With our current MRC administrator staff for their organization there was NO way that those administrators could keep up with the influx of NEW volunteers. The MRC program needs a dedicated administrator at a minimum 50% of their time to maintain a viable unit to maintain and sustain volunteers for a ready response.

Visibility from a Federal perspective and funding for Medical Reserve Corps units can directly impact a community’s ability to respond to large scale health emergencies. I would Love to see a commercial or PSA on a major news network describing the MRCs intended mission and accomplishments.

Funding will only strengthen the MRC unit's ability to recruit, train, and deploy volunteers dedicated to being of service to their communities. Funds are definitely needed, most critically, to support leadership positions within the MRC units.

Let's prepare our country for the next public health emergency by funding a program that allows local communities to support the needs of their citizens during small, medium, and large public health emergencies.

I believe the top three strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps are: Engaging the healthcare community to assist in their community outside of the walls of their hospital or facility especially during impactful events and incidents, they provide professionalism to the MRC program; Inspiring non-medical community to become more active in supporting the medical needs of their community to include advocacy, first aid within their family and neighborhoods, to gaining more information on personal preparedness and public health knowledge to prevent the contraction or spreading of highly infectious diseases; National MRC program serves as a great resource to gain perspectives on how to work to further supporting the healthcare and medical needs of the community, allows for the ease of transfer of members from unit to unit, allows members to feel a since of community that goes beyond their own team. The connection and comradery of the national MRC program provides inspiration, education, guidance, and encouragement in how we as a national program can continue to support the public health needs of the nation.
Funding, with no consistent avenue to receive funding MRC units are struggling to recruit and retain volunteers. Volunteerism is an ever evolving practice, it takes time, emergency, motivation, and inspiration to reach the heart strings of everyday people to give up time and put in effort in meeting the needs of any community while at the same time neglecting their own person or family needs during major incidents. Beyond having an understanding in what their community knows, MRC units must be able to community and market their programs in such a way that inspires someone to give their time to volunteering especially during impactful incident. The MRC program needs funds to better attract potential volunteers wherever they go. Education, the MRC program leans heavily on the medical knowledge of the medical professionals that serve as the primary target audience and members of most MRC units. This is great, but even those who work in the medical field are not always well versed in emergency preparedness, incident command, or local or national liability protections when volunteering. MRC’s for years have either served primarily as a standing list of medical people who want to be contacted during emergencies about volunteer opportunities to individual MRC units creating their training programs or requirements. I think that if MRC had a national standard curriculum that educated members to having the basic understanding of what we all have identified as important information such as HIPAA, ICS, Bloodborne Pathogens, etc.; Membership guidance, who should be members of a MRC unit can fluctuate from unit to unit based on where they are located in a community, and what their unit’s primary focus is on in supporting the public health needs of the community. What we lack in the program is more closely related to the human resources aspect of volunteer management. In most cases we see government and private entities requiring specific level of background checks or the adherence to ethical behaviors. These all can range in costs and levels of complexity. What I believe needs to be standardized is a baseline for when does an individual forfeit their right to be a member of a team, what’s is a reasonable statute of limitations on potential problematic situations the potential member as committed in the past or how much time without incident needs to pass before they are eligible to seek membership of an MRC unit.
Short-term goals of the MRC program should include increasing the awareness of and medical and non-medical topics covered within the TRAIN system. MRC program in the short term should continue to provide best practices, lessons learned, and templates for MRC units to utilize in advancing their own units strengths and capabilities in their communities. Long-term goals of the MRC program should be how to further include MRC units and volunteers in the national response framework, further influence the planning for the use of MRC units and members within regulatory and accreditation organizations such as CMS, Joint Commission, ACHC, FEMA EMG, HPP, etc. Additionally especially during incident in which FEMA or other government agencies are deployed to assist local jurisdictions, these agencies should specifically be encouraged to touch based conduct public information stories for media and public consumption on MRC programs that are actively supporting the incident as well. Lastly a long-term goal of the MRC program is to continue to find opportunities to provide funding for units nationally.

Significant funding needs to be used to reinvest in the local MRC units, which have consistently experienced funding cuts for the last 10 years. Funding should be made available for coordinators who are providing volunteer management, trainings, supplies, volunteer badging/shirts, and updated technology including MURS radios and tablets with the appropriate ICS forms preloaded. Also, a serious campaign is needed to promote MRC to the general public as to educate them of our multifunctional contribution to the community at large. As many MRC volunteers are retirees, there should be a push to attract and retain younger volunteers who can participate and lead in the future. Lastly, MRC should have the funding to avail its members to programs such as BLS, ACLS and Red Cross first aid certifications.

1. What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?
Strengths: The MRC is able to fill in the gaps for care by scaling up responses rapidly, having some (but not yet enough) resources to address community emergencies (which we have been through two of in this last year--wildfires and COVID), flexibility in addressing responses in ways that meet the community's situation and needs, and the policy of having few barriers for people to receive services. The lack of bureaucracy is one of its strengths, from my perspective as an MRC volunteer. Our (Santa Cruz, CA) MRC is well organized and very welcoming, with an emphasis on bicultural and bilingual services. COVID has highlighted some of these strengths.

Having enough financial resources comes to mind quickly. The MRC relies on volunteer labor, and that is not a problem for some MRC members (many of whom, at least here, are retired), but to meet our community's needs, others who can't afford to volunteer but who are crucial for an operation's success in Central California--particularly having a larger contingent of bicultural and bilingual members--will require being able to pay people a living wage to substitute for their regular employment so that they can participate.

I don't know enough about what is possible to have a useful answer to this, but I can see that we are going to have a lot more need for MRCs everywhere to respond to climate disasters. I'm a mental health professional, so I have a bit of a bias here, but having well-trained MRC psychotherapists and social workers for mass events would be useful. Getting some of us trained in emergency response takes a bit of funding and lead time.

Being part of the MRC has been a boon in my life. I would love to see these in every community in the US, and to have cultural competence (which our county is very strong at) be a major part of the training and recruitment.

1. What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?

Increased capacity – obviously, Public Health is not funded to the levels necessary to complete core public health services, especially during a public health disaster and emergency. When a PH agency is trying to address population wide issues, there is an increased demand for additional hands doing the work. The Pandemic highlighted this fact and made it abundantly clear that even more effort needs expended to ensure population wide goals are achieved.

2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?

Full-time, dedicated coordinators. Currently, a part-part-time (not a typo) is trying to organize, train, and engage MRC volunteers. This is extremely difficult considering the many other tasks and duties associated with preparedness and response. Having a dedicated staff member will allow for exponential returns with volunteer recruitment and response capacity. Again, this has been magnified with the Pandemic.

3. Do you have recommendations on the top short- and long-term priorities for the MRC? What operational capabilities, services, or competencies would you propose that the MRC focus on? Do you have recommendations on ways to strengthening the MRC's role as a federal disaster response asset?

Sustainable funding is at the top of the list of “must meet deliverables.” If funding is not sustainable, it’s a short-term investment that is wasted when the funds are depleted. Addressing the questions posed is for naught unless this issue is resolved. MRC competencies based on core public health services would be advantageous for recruitment and retention.

4. Any additional topics you wish to provide input on.

Funding needs to be broader. There is ZERO local funding for MRC which means there are gaps in needed supplies to ensure 100% effectiveness when utilizing MRC response capabilities.

One area of potentially untapped resources that became available during the Covid-19 pandemic were Schools of Nursing. A surprising number of faculty and Deans were unaware of the role that they and their students could play by belonging to local MRC chapters. The relationship has the potential to benefit the nursing students, the MRC staffing capabilities during disasters and the community.

As a result of the pandemic, many nursing students could not attend their normally scheduled clinical rotations in hospitals and agencies for their training. However, the wealth of exposure to public health and community health nursing and first hand experience in immunizations, disease transmission, and contact tracing were extremely rewarding for those who participated with the MRCs.

A key area identified during this pandemic was the public's need to trust at all levels. Many local citizens verbalized relief to see people they knew administering their vaccinations and answering their questions. They told us that it gave them faith in the system. Having nursing students from their own communities, possibly people they live near or work with could only strengthen this trust.

I would strongly suggest that a campaign to have all Schools of Nursing participating in the Medical Reserve Corps would be very beneficial to all involved.

1. What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?
The Medical Reserve Corps serves a crucial and unique role in the communities they are in. They are able to be called upon and are more than willing to help in any situation. I think these groups truly bring out the heroes in any community. It helps to highlight a specific group of stakeholders that want to go above and beyond for their community. Many of these people are involved in multiple community organizations on top of their full time jobs. They are committed to making our county a safe and beautiful place to live.
The COVID-19 pandemic has allowed for those people to shine. For our organization, they have been a crucial and irreplaceable part of our mass vaccination efforts. They truly made our large community clinics possible by volunteering countless hours of their time. When we asked for help, they didn’t bat an eye. I think that the pandemic has allowed for everyone to see just how valuable these groups are to the communities they are in, and how crucial they are in the future.
2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?
General recruitment and additional trainings would be extremely helpful. In our area, we lack participation from younger generations, which is vital to the continuation of the program itself. In addition, we see a need for more community outreach and general emergency preparedness that could be partially fulfilled through MRC leaders with health department coalition.
The COVID-19 pandemic has made clear how important emergency planning is and how crucial these people are in times of need. Improving trainings, being able to provide more training, and general resources for recruitment would ensure that they are growing as an organization and are ready for future emergencies. We also seek to build up our JR MRC program in order to ensure we have a group in the future.

Short and long term priorities on our end include more trainings and building up our chapter. I would suggest that we discuss and prepare for emergencies that are specific to the context of the area they are in. For example, we lack specific planning on some emergencies that could occur in our area. I think that a set of trainings that are mandatory to complete are crucial in ensuring that everyone is both ready for anything, and prepared with what their roles are. This is also applicable to strengthen MRC’s role as a federal disaster response asset. In order to truly be helpful in one of those situations, they need the training to be prepared to step into that role.

Docket named HHS–ASPR–2021–0013 to ‘‘Request for Information (RFI) from Non-Federal Stakeholders: Advancing the Medical Reserve Corps with the American Rescue Plan."
Comments:
Response specifically regarding questions #2 and #3 below

2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?

An inventory management database (software, hardware specifications) nationally standardized and deployed is needed. The inventory control, tracking, monitoring/recall system is required to minimize waste of inventory and human resources required to mobilize assets. Inventory control standardized systems are necessary for effective procurement and management of countermeasures, to include equipment and medications/biologics/vaccines (ventilators, PPE, refrigeration/freezers, other).
Specifically, countermeasures and equipment should be tracked for expiration and as assets near the end of the manufacturer posted expiration dating rotation of that inventory to the public health facilities supply chain should occur to mitigate millions/ billions of dollars of waste. Inventory rotation from state/federal supply locations to suggested public locations such as, hospitals including 340B, local public health clinics, Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHC), to other states or internationally as the law allows. Without such an inventory system as part of logistics planning and operations, countermeasures are wasted and must be destroyed in many cases at additional costs to states and the federal government.
Also, extended dating of critical assets such as the federal SLEP - Shelf Life Extension Program, should be part of the inventory program.
The use of an RFID tag system would be optimal.
Pharmacy countermeasures could utilize the NCPDP standard for database elements including an expiration dating element and an added data element for time for rotation of that inventory when the expiration date is within a defined time ( e.g. 3 months, 6 months, ...).
Interoperability of the inventory database to other databases, such as the Immunization Information Systems (IIS), Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP), pharmaceutical wholesalers and others that may apply is necessary.

3. Do you have recommendations on the top short- and long-term priorities for the MRC? What operational capabilities, services, or competencies would you propose that the MRC focus on? Do you have recommendations on ways to strengthening the MRC's role as a federal disaster response?
Operational capabilities, services and competencies must include a national standardized inventory control system for optimal disaster response and fiscal accountability as identified in #2 above.

Thank you for receiving my comment. I coordinate a Medical Reserve Corps unit in Norman, Oklahoma. This unit is one of the largest units in the state. I am the responsible for the Emergency Management Division for Norman. Norman is the third largest City in Oklahoma. Funding for these programs have allowed an immense value added asset to the response and recovery operations for the City. We have been able to fill the gap when the local emergency medical was over committed. Events like tornados, flood, COVID and community events all are areas where we bring equipment and talented volunteers to bear on these problems.  This unit leads the way in innovative approaches to local needs. Currently we are in a process of developing a relationship with a major university for interns in the field of social work and mental health. We are developing a process of how these vital skills fit in the response and recovery phases. Funding that is provided goes directly to enhance our unit capability and provide for future response and operational readiness. The capacity to build and grow is directly attributable to funding. In Oklahoma many communities are recovering not only from COVID but from natural disasters as well. Currently Norman is recovering from two federally declared disasters and have had three significant, non-declared, weather events that have significantly negatively impacted the financial standing of the City and the Community. Continued funding for this and other Citizens CORPS programs is paramount for opportunities that engage our Citizens in the health, welfare, and preparedness of this nation.

People volunteer because they want to be part of a group, help their community, learn new things, or to keep their professional skills active in retirement. Volunteer managers require financial help to fund volunteer recruitment, recognition, and retention. With no budget for recruitment giveaways, we often give out information in the form of pamphlets, booklets, and flyers that we can produce or purchase with existing funds. But pens, pads, or preparedness items branded with our logo and website are helpful for recruitment. We purchased them in the past, but funding is now more restricted.

The current ASPR funding will not cover uniform expenses for purchasing more shirts, hats, vests, or badge lanyards. Uniform shirts or vests are necessary at a large-scale Point of Dispensing to identify the volunteers as part of the response and not as clients. And, this form of branding has helped to promote MRC and recruit more volunteers.

Recognition activities may include awards, picnics, and thank-you gifts for volunteers. Our current funding does not allow for items such as food, water, and incentives to retain volunteers. We can print certificates, but not purchase frames or folios for presentation. We purchase water out of pocket. Last year, I purchased supplies from the dollar store and crafted thank-you items.

MRC of Southern Nevada has been an invaluable asset to the community over the last 14 months, contributing over 11,760 hours (and counting) to the pandemic response, mostly by medical professionals staffing isolation/quarantine units, specimen collections sites, vaccine PODs, and our Public Health Laboratory. Our MRC (and many others) keep their volunteers active year-round by serving the community at non-emergency events, such as blood pressure screenings, fairs and charity fundraisers (where we provide first aid and distribute preparedness information), and training meetings. These activities are essential to not only build and retain an active cadre, but to integrate MRC into the community as a viable resource that can be tapped during emergencies.

Our current ASPR funding does not cover replenishment of certain supplies. We purchased first aid bags and AEDs years ago with grant funds, and some of the supplies have exceeded their shelf life. For example, Benadryl, eye wash, and AED replacement pads. We use these supplies for first aid at community events and, during the COVID-19 response, at POD and testing sites. To maintain readiness, these supplies must be available and renewed.

If the program decides to invest large-scale at the federal level, a software system that works for local units and has portability across regional and state lines would be helpful to standardizing and branding MRC nationally. Ideally, it would facilitate the transfer of volunteers from state-to-state and integrate data into the new MRC website. Many units have no funding for software and use Excel sheets or pen-and-paper. Our current statewide ESAR-VHP recruitment and management website is a significant ongoing contract expense year-to-year and is frequently broken (Juvare Cores). For example, the hourly input feature broke in October 2020 and was not fixed until April 2021, which was one of the busiest times of the pandemic. It records hours but does not generate useful reports. We reverted to an Excel sheet, which is more reliable but still difficult to report hours for any specific volunteer, activity, or time period. A unified system would streamline MRC volunteer management by reducing the number of databases to maintain. We appreciate MRC is in process of updating/upgrading the national website. If that upgrade can be accomplished successfully, perhaps we can design a volunteer management system that can work for everyone.

Greetings and thank you for this opportunity to provide input.

1. Strengths:
a. The passion and devotion of MRC volunteers are most notable and commendable. Whether retired or continuing to work, each volunteer demonstrates a passion to help their community in times of need.
b. Having developed significant support structures for MRCs to communicate and unite with shared ideas and resource sharing.
c. Having gained recognition to be the recipient of funds from the American Rescue Plan.

2. Needs:
a. Consistent recognition from health department administrators as to the need and support for MRC programs that go beyond "checking a box" that "we have one" to fulfill some requirement.
b. Recognition for and support of active training and response inclusion of behavioral health professionals in MRC trainings and deployments to address both public/community behavioral health aspects of a current deployment focus AND the unique needs of other health department and MRC responders' behavioral reactions to current deployments.
c. Development of specific behavioral health MRC teams to focus on the unique mental health aspects of community crisis response capabilities and resources. Allowing the active utilization to address local issues proactively instead of after-the-fact. Encouraging their utilization in partnership with other responding organizations such as Red Cross, Salvation Army, VOAD, etc. to specifically address both the public/community and responder reactions to the activating event and subsequent reactions. This is most readily seen in recent events including COVID-19, political/civil unrest, active shooters, etc.

3. Short and Long-term Priorities:
Short-term: Immediate active inclusion of behavioral health professionals into MRC teams to actively address both public/community issues to local events and the responder-related (health department, MRC, and local emergency responders/care providers if no other support services are available such as EAP and/or CISM type services) issues to local events.
Long-term:
a. Recognition of the behavioral health reactions will continue within the public/community with future events.
b. To adequately address the complexities of responding to future events by including sociologists, cultural anthropologists, medical anthropologists, and theologians from various faith traditions.
c. To serve as subject matter experts to local EMAs and elected officials as to the behavioral health aspects of assessment, planning, response, and recovery from various events.

Helpful realizations:
a. Behavioral reactions from the public/community will continue despite the denial of their existence from EMAs and political leaders. Behavioral reactions and the resultant festering will continue to plague us until we actively recognize and address them as seen from both research and experiential evidence.
b. Community/Public behavioral health protocols exist to address relevant issues.
c. As we as societies grow, develop and evolve, we must also include the once called "soft sciences" into our Whole Community response.
d. Choosing to not address community/public behavioral health issues could make way for litigation based on damages incurred from deliberate indifference - where case law already exists.

Issue #1 - The major problem is most unit coordinators have other responsibilities to their agencies that detract and limit their available time for MRC attention. The reason the units have a low priority the coordinators primary grant deliverables take precedence over managing the MRC unit. The solution would be to use federal funding for a dedicated MRC coordinator contract. Good examples of this are units with dedicated coordinators are more active and have more active members. Units with dedicated coordinators are Orange County NY, Dutchess County NY, New York City. These units all have a larger number of active members than units without a dedicated MRC Coordinator.
Issue #2 - The problem is inability to recognize members activities which causes low morale, loss of interest, a feeling of not being appreciated leading to decreased membership. Most funding sources preclude purchasing non PPE uniform items, recognition items such as pins, plaques, certificates, recognition dinners. Additionally some funding will not allow for the purchase of food during non-deployment events. Solution would be allow a percentage of federal funding to be used for this purpose to increase morale which will increase recruitment and retention. No unit should have to become a non profit for the sole purpose of being able to collect donations to purchase and support the program because federal funding does not provide these needs.

One of the top resource gaps I see for the Medical Reserve Corps (MRC) to best use the American Rescue Plan funds is establishing a national volunteer database ESAR-VHP (Emergency System for Advance Registration of Volunteer Health Professionals) system. A single system with an activity calendar that health departments or states embed into their own webpages selecting which units they like to highlight. MRC members logged into the system can sign-up for activities directly on the calendar. Those hours completed at the activity are then directly folded into the MRC reporting requirements and keep record for each volunteer’s trainings and hours of service on an individual’s account profile. Professional licenses can be verified in this system, where states provide integration links from licensing authorities to this single system (this is already occurring at the state level for numerous states). MRC members can be alerted through the single system via email, phone, and test message. Currently, states and health departments each must negotiate with vendors for their own volunteer’s database, which can come up short addressing all mentioned needs and identifying a quality user-friendly system(s). The items mentioned would greatly reduce burden on unit coordinators and supporting health department staff. A single system would limit the need to have multiple accounts for different platforms that only accomplish a small portion of the entire puzzle to effectively administrate a MRC unit. As well as easily coordinate the transfer of MRC volunteer information between different units.

Another resource gap highlighted by COVID-19 is identifying, empowering, and retaining volunteer leaders and unit coordinators (that are not health department staff) to facilitate and lead projects. COVID-19 created an influx of new volunteer registrants and previous established members with project ideas of how to serve and promote public health early in the pandemic, but it was problematic finding individuals to lead in the organizing and coordinating of project ideas, while Health department staff was engulfed in the more direct response roles and needs. This is an issue that also occurs during blue sky times. Recommend using American Rescue Plan funds to create incentives or stipend programs for volunteers’ leaders (that are clear limiting labor law concerns by grant recipient funding agencies) and advertisement tools to attract unit coordinators.

Thirdly, a priority for the MRC needs to be strengthening and retaining volunteers for long-term care emergency support and vaccine operations as public health run COVID-19 vaccine sites decrease. Folks want their volunteer time to be impactful and COVID-19 vaccination have been one of the most impactful and rewarding times ever for medical professionals. Recommend creating priorities, incentives, and rewards that encourages health departments and healthcare organizations to prioritize using MRC volunteers for seasonal influenza, hepatitis, and continued COVID-19 immunizations. Health departments and healthcare organizations may have the paid staff resources to accomplish these tasks, but if they are not utilizing MRC to assist occasionally with these type efforts volunteer size will diminish and not be retained for the next health crisis.

The number one strength of the Medical Reserve Corps program is the ability to recruit, coordinate and mobilize passionate and dedicated community members to support public health. Virginia’s pandemic response efforts would not have been successful without the contributions of Virginia MRC volunteers. In non-emergencies, Virginia MRC volunteers are workforce multipliers in support of ongoing public health and community emergency preparedness initiatives.

The strength of Virginia’s MRC is due to the integration of the state and local MRC programs, Virginia’s ESAR-VHP system and the inclusion of MRC volunteers in daily public health operations and pandemic response plans. Virginia successfully mobilized over 13,500 volunteers and onboarded over 18,8000 new MRC volunteers during the COVID-19 pandemic. The current workforce savings for the hours contributed by Virginia MRC volunteers, thus far, during the COVID-19 pandemic is over 16.8 million dollars!

The MRC program needs federal leadership with hands-on experience in public health and emergency response. The program flourished and had significant visibility at the federal level when it was under the direction of the Office of the Surgeon General and led by USPHS officers. Without this leadership, the MRC national program does not have the capability to expand, allocate funding or take action on new initiatives. The structure, staffing and leadership of the MRC program needs to be reevaluated and strengthened.

The MRC program must be recognized and supported at the same level as the PHEP and HPP programs. The MRC program should have the same structure and utilize the same funding mechanisms as the HPP and PHEP programs. The Medical Reserve Corps program should be a state requirement like ESAR-VHP, not an option.

We need advocates both inside and outside of our national organization who can promote our programs among those with influence to support those programs. I recognize the national MRC office believes it shouldn’t initiate conversations with Congressional staff (why is that?), but we have a cooperative agreement with NACCHO which should be able to do that. And not just speaking to Congress. We need advocates who can help us in the White House, among our governors, and with our long lost partner programs, organizations and associations. Perhaps it’s time to reappoint an outreach coordinator to rebuild those old partnerships, build new partners, and educate Congress and the administration about the MRC. And now would be a good time to let the administration know that many MRC units are ready and willing to help build our public health workforce, so they can pull back on the AmeriCorps proposal. It wouldn’t hurt to reach out to “celebrities” such as the Dr. Sanjay Gupta’s of the world, or even the various news and talk show hosts to find MRC advocates who are already in the spotlight. I know from a COVID perspective, the MRC program must do a better job teaching medical professionals about our program, and teaching state and local health departments how to manage volunteers as opposed to managing paid employees. There is a difference.
Of course, the national MRC program office needs to know what our needs are. That’s what this exercise is all about. But this shouldn’t be the only device. In fact, this survey wouldn’t have been necessary if the national program office had maintained regular discussions with local leaders on these topics. The national program office should be involved in strategic planning, and this should include developing an ongoing dialog with local unit leaders to evaluate and continually assess the vision, purpose, and mission of the MRC program as a whole. That conversation should also include a continuous evaluation of the national program office and its roles and responsibilities. This should include re-establishing workgroups made up of local unit leaders. And it should include the return of national conferences and regional meetings, sponsored by the national program office, where local MRC leaders can gather, share ideas, discuss MRC-specific issues, and have an in-person conversation with the people who represent our programs at the national level.
This new influx of money from the American Rescue Plan can also help rebuild the national program staff, regional staff, enable vacant positions to be filled quickly, and perhaps fund state and local unit leaders. And rather than allowing AmeriCorps to duplicate what many MRC units have done, maybe some of the MRC funds could be used in a partnership with AmeriCorps to pay for the “stipends” that are provided to their volunteers when working for MRC programs.
Another perennial topic that has been around since the beginning is the need for legal protections. This includes firming up Federal Tort Claims Act and workers compensation protections for volunteers and volunteer organizations. I would also add the need to examine and improve methods of moving volunteers across state lines other than the existing EMAC (Emergency Management Assistance Compact). Look at the Uniform Emergency Volunteer Health Practitioners Act that many states failed to adopt. And at one time, select members of local MRC units were formed into a national deployment cadre. But legal issues prevented them from working alongside our Public Health Service counterparts. The national MRC program office could devote some resources to work on these issues.
Many of the problems I’ve described today emerged or have exacerbated since certain national program staff left and the office was moved from under the Office of the Surgeon General to the Assistant Secretary of Preparedness and Response. Let’s ask HHS to re-evaluate this move. A good healthy organization should always examine and re-evaluate the changes it has made to make sure they were right for the program.

1.What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?

Top Strengths:
a.Our MRC unit is community based. Volunteers are representative of all professions: (medical and non medical) and the cultures that make up our communities.
b.Volunteers complete required training before the event occurs allowing for faster deployments.
c.Volunteers are members of their neighborhoods, communities, and business’ resulting in a necessary component for any outreach activity – lots of voices.
d.Covid-19 highlighted a unit characteristic that does not exist in Public Health – Flexibility. Many of our deployments occurred quickly and were meeting gaps in service. Our own agency recognized this flexibility asset and used it well.

2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?

a.Volunteer Coordinators must become certified Train the Trainers. We are trainers in our daily skill set but we are never considered fully qualified I believe MRC Administration needs to offer MRC coordinators an on-line opportunity to be certified as Train the Trainers. Our communities and housing organizations often see the multiple roles and professions we are and this confuses them because they do not see our SPECIALIZATION. I find the community mor accepting of who we are because of our Stop the Bleed training outreach. Our unit’s credibility is directly tied to the specializations we offer the community: Warm Shelter Building, Cold Shelters, Stop the Bleed, CPR, etc. We need to be more visible in the community by offering these trainings. Our housing organizations needs to see us as professional volunteers and experts. We are missing the mark here.

b.Do you have recommendations on the top short- and long-term priorities for the MRC? What operational capabilities, services, or competencies would you propose that the MRC focus on? Do you have recommendations on ways to strengthening the MRC's role as a federal disaster response asset?
SHORT TERM Priorities:
Find out what other MRC units did across the country for Covid 19. To see if any would work for the unit. Set up a board – spreadsheet – meeting-where I can find out what others did and I can show others what I did. MRC problem solving on the local level rarely is recognized at the national level. Did you know that our volunteers set up a vaccine outreach team? Many other units did this but we ll did it differently – help me find out how they set theirs up.
Long Term Priorities:
Federal deployment: Instead of helping my Red Cross send my best volunteers to another state. I want them to travel with a federal MRC unit.

1. Individual units need funding. This is more important now than ever before. Many units in the last few years have disbanded and I would imagine funding was a major reason for their demise. Surviving units are now struggling because of their success. My three units, for example, have increased combined membership more than 200 percent since the beginning of this pandemic. Simply managing the increased number of volunteers will require a 200 percent increase in staff time and resources. The American Rescue Plan funds could help ensure that our local MRC programs are able to keep and continue to train our new volunteers beyond COVID. If we took $80 million and shared it with each of our 762 local units (let’s round that up to 800 units just to make this easier), that would give each unit $100,000 and leave $20 million for the national program office. Better yet, the funds could be distributed over the course of 5 years, giving each unit $20,000 a year. That would give local units time to stabilize their units and build a good foundation for eventual sustainability. Another suggestion is a tiered approach where more money is given the first year, then tapering off the next few years. As a reminder, the original demonstration projects that launched the MRC program nearly 20 years ago were $50,000 grants.
2. Since day one, local units have asked for help at the national level to promote the MRC program. But we didn’t have the funding. Now that funding is no longer an obstacle, the MRC program needs a nationwide promotion campaign. I would recommend partnering with the Ad Council and the National Association of Broadcasters, which could help extend the reach of our advertising budget. Of course, a national promotional campaign will fall short if we don’t have top-quality locations to send potential donors and volunteers. This would start with a truly professional and active website and social media presence at the national level, as well as funding earmarked specifically for the development of websites and social media at the state and local levels. Additionally, portals in each state need to be updated. For most states, this is our ESAR-VHP (Emergency System for the Advanced Registration of Volunteer Health Professionals). However, I haven’t heard much from the national ESAR-VHP in recent years. In fact, a quick Google search brought me to the program’s HHS website. The landing page made no reference to the MRC program. (I found the MRC listed under “more volunteer opportunities.”) Perhaps it’s time to rebuild that relationship between the MRC program and ESAR-VHP. And, it might be worth discussing the possibility of developing a standardized volunteer database funded at the federal level but administered and operated at the state and local levels. This, alone, could help facilitate another need that has been discussed time and time again since the beginning of our program: funding and standardization of background checks.
3. Running parallel with our need for a national promotion campaign is the need for recognition. This is necessary in so many forms, starting with a way to publicly recognize our tremendous volunteers. I’m not talking about paper certificates, and I’m tired of hearing that the national program office cannot provide challenge coins, plaques or other tangible tokens of our appreciation for their enormous contributions to the safety and health of this nation. (Other federal programs have found ways to do it. It’s time that our national program office finds ways to do it too.) Our volunteers not only deserve medals, but the President of the United States should personally recognize their efforts. At the very least, the Surgeon General of the United States should book time on every major network to praise their contributions. There was a time when the Surgeon General was one of our top advocates. In fact, there was a time when the MRC had an advocate in the White House by way of the USA Freedom Corps. But those days are long gone. We need leaders at the national level who can break down bureaucracy and build partnerships to better support our local programs.

1. What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?
One of the TOP strengths of the MRC is that we are able to assist with emergencies that require the use of medically credentialed professional volunteers. That stands MRC apart for other volunteer programs, however, not having the funds to provide professional liability and workers compensation often deters volunteers from assisting and housing organizations from utilizing medical volunteers. The COVID-19 pandemic created a high demand for younger medical professionals to assist in many areas during the pandemic. Now more than ever there needs to be a program that highlights using professional medical students! These were the type of volunteers that were willing and able to help. This pandemic has only highlighted the need to medical MRC volunteers in the future!

MRC units are only as good as the leader is. Focus on strengthening the leaders and motivating them to build a strong MRC focus within their state! Strong MRC units that are active only reflect back in a positive way on the national program.

MRC has not been funded in a long time. There continue to be so many capabilities for and asks of the MRC community without the funds that other programs receive to achieve the same goals or less.

Preble County Public Health serves a small, rural county and our funding is very limited to support volunteer management. We have a small MRC program, but it's a strong program. During the Montgomery County Ohio tornadoes in 2019, Preble County MRC sent volunteers to support our neighbors in their Family Assistance Center, as well as assisting the American Red Cross with canvassing an impacted area. We had created a Surge Team where volunteers were trained to support our stand-alone emergency department during a medical surge (Preble County does not have a full hospital, and support from their network is a minimum of 45 minutes away). Our county is working to create a team through our MRC to support families following a death by suicide. Our volunteers were also active throughout the entire COVID-19 pandemic with various activities including assisting in local food pantries, large food distribution events, temperature checks and screenings at our local court house, well check calls and meals on wheels for our council on aging, COVID testing at a long term care facility during an outbreak, as well as mailings for our office, our pop-up testing site, our Mission: Masks campaign, and then all of our COVID-19 vaccine clinics.

It is imperative to have funding to support existing volunteer programs and to assist with creating new programs that will increase the number volunteers we have. We also need funding to maintain interest during times when volunteers are not needed on a regular basis. Until 2015 we received $500 annually from NACCHO to support our volunteer program. Those funds were vital for our program. Our PHEP funding for emergency preparedness doesn't even cover salaries for those required to fulfill the grant, let alone our MRC. In order to maintain our volunteer management program, a small amount of funding goes a long way to support volunteer recruitment, training, and retention.

Our eight-county region conducts an annual training for all volunteers in the region (including MRC and CERT) and it's very hard for the small health departments to contribute monetarily to support this essential effort, even though it's very well attended by volunteers from our county.

PLEASE allocate funds for each volunteer organization to be used for retention and recruitment of volunteers, and additional funding to support those units who have specific teams and programs to support our communities, such as our surge team, and our crisis response team. It is vital to have funding to maintain the volunteers we have and to be able to financially support this program so can recruit volunteers to support our agencies when needed most.

1. What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?

The top strength of the Pierce County MRC is the infrastructure in place that allowed the unit to help aid in the COVID-19 response – contact tracing, testing site, vaccine distribution, etc. – by providing medical resources and trained volunteers. The Pierce County MRC was also able to recruit and onboard over 200 new volunteers from the community to help with the emergency response. The MRC provided verification of the volunteer’s training and credentials and helped develop a process to verify clinical volunteers with out-of-state or expired clinical licenses that were eligible to administer the COVID-19 vaccine under the PREP Act regulations.



Pierce County Medical Reserve Corps has the least obstructive joining mechanism for state recognized emergency/medical volunteering. Therefore, the MRC can rapidly respond to emergent response events.



Another strength of the Pierce County MRC is our community relationships. The PCMRC is a trusted agency in the community and has been able to team up with various community partners during the COVID-19 vaccine distribution.



2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?

The biggest need of our MRC unit during the COVID-19 pandemic has been creating a volunteer coordination team in order to adequately lead the volunteers in emergency response. The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the need for these volunteer coordinators. The Pierce County MRC unit needs the resources to continue funding a trained volunteer coordination team in order to maintain sustainable volunteer recruitment and engagement as COVID-19 vaccine distribution continues and preparations for the flu vaccine clinics begin.

Another important need for the Pierce County MRC is having funding to obtain and maintain a functional volunteer management system. A volunteer management system is essential to the unit’s success, especially give the rapid unit-growth in the past year.

Supplies to maintain mission readiness for the full scope of our mission, including disease outbreaks, and disasters or acute events. We need to be ready to respond to “all of the above”

Training and participation in joint exercises with other agencies.

State-led or federal-led initiatives, such as trainings, networking opportunities, coordination, problem-solving, and policymaking.

The pandemic has not highlighted new needs. If anything, it highlighted how desperate our program needs resources like staffing and funding to keep remain reliable and effective.

3. Do you have recommendations on the top short- and long-term priorities for the MRC? What operational capabilities, services, or competencies would you propose that the MRC focus on? Do you have recommendations on ways to strengthening the MRC's role as a federal disaster response asset?

Long-Term: The MRC’s role as a federal response asset can be strengthened by encouraging collaborations between neighboring MRC units, sustainable funding, institutional/uniform operating procedures and requirements across units to make mutual aid more realistic and effective.

Short-Term: The MRC units need funding to maintain a volunteer coordination team and volunteer management system that can lead the unit through the remainder of the COVID-19 emergency response.

2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?

MRC units need consistent financial support that they can plan on receiving for maintenance of the unit, without having to develop new projects or initiatives. It would be beneficial for money specified for MRC to be available to agencies that support MRC units with functions such as website databases, background checks, badging and uniforms, but don't receive money directly awarded the units. Units need to receive money that can be spent on identifiable uniforms for volunteers. The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted that MRC volunteers were ready to step in to help, but that the system to onboard and manage the surge of volunteers stressed the system.

1.Top strength of MRC units: The Pee Dee PHRC unit has been able to mobilize over 100 volunteers to respond to COVID – 19 during 2020/2021, resulting in over 5,000 hours of service to date. Examples of services provided included transportation of COVID specimens for testing, assembling supplies for COVID vaccination kits and support at COVID vaccination community clinics. The processes established and capacity building grants provided prior to this emergency were instrumental in preparing the unit volunteers for this unprecedented response.
2.Top needs or resources gaps –
a.Ability to onboard new volunteers rapidly and efficiently during a response.
b.Ability to train volunteers using a web based user friendly platform for both administrator and volunteers.
c.Ability to schedule and track volunteers during a high volume and prolonged response such as the pandemic.
d.Interoperable program to report activity to National platform, and to reduce duplicative reporting requirements.
e.Re-think and “right size” “training” requirements to better fit needs of the units to prepare volunteers for deployments during an emergency.

What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?

Strength: Having the national network with active MRC units to begin with was a strength. When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, there was an almost immediate need for PPE collection and distribution support and our volunteers came ready to go. The huge influx of volunteers did not happen just quite yet, but the ones that were already registered volunteers offered their time repeatedly.

2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?

Two top needs to be addressed: MRC Coordinators and a national website.
Our state MRC coordinator position was not filled by a full-time MRC staff member when the pandemic started. That person was assigned a logistic role for the response and statewide volunteer management/support was minimum at best for a while. Full time, MRC dedicated, coordinators at all levels can respond to an incident more quickly and efficiently. Persons assigned in this position can also continue to grow and sustain the units that now have upwards of 100% and greater more volunteers than were registered pre-pandemic. Sustainability is key to preparedness and the resiliency of a community an units to be maintained with dedicated personnel.

It would be nice to have a national website that all state systems can communicate with including hour tracking and trainings. This kind of data is useful and sought out from all levels of government, starting from LHDs right up through outside stakeholders/partners.

3. Do you have recommendations on the top short- and long-term priorities for the MRC? What operational capabilities, services, or competencies would you propose that the MRC focus on? Do you have recommendations on ways to strengthening the MRC's role as a federal disaster response asset?

Long Term: Create a training program that every volunteer should complete and add more training for the volunteers who like to go above and beyond what a responder volunteer would do. A standardized base level training program would benefit the jurisdictions that request the use of volunteers from a neighboring jurisdiction.

4. Any additional topics you wish to provide input on.

Often when volunteers do not feel appreciated for the work they have done; they look elsewhere for the feeling of satisfaction that one desires. If there is support for recognition events, whether funding an event or providing recognition items, more volunteers will really feel valued and that their volunteer time is well spent.
One other idea involves maintaining volunteer engagement when there is no pandemic: educating the volunteers. Offer conferences and pay for speaker support or even some room and board for volunteers who must travel a distance for a conference.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide input.

Thank you for this opportunity to recommend allocation of the $100M in funding for the national MRC program. As a 40-year EMT and an MRC unit leader since 2004, I'm eager to contrast the annual $6M subsistence funding for the entire program with an allocation equal to well over $100,000 per unit. My input is integrated into the questions from the RFI, at a boots-on-the-ground level:
1. What do you see as the top strengths of the Medical Reserve Corps? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different strengths of the MRC?
STRENGTH: The degree to which ordinary people from all backgrounds rose to the occasion was unprecedented. We had a surge of over new 100 members since January alone, all striving to be part of the solution. PANDEMIC: We sent our July newsletter (attached) to press this morning, which provides an up-to-the-minute view of our unit’s strengths, versatility, and wide range of activities to combat COVID across our region. Note the profound impact of our deployments at local, regional, state, New England, and national levels. Consider the breadth and depth of collaborations with response partners: FEMA, local hospitals, senior centers, and multi-agency interactions. MRC units are among the linchpins that keep area residents safe across a range of challenges.
2. What do you see as the top needs or resource gaps of the MRC? Has the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted new or different needs of the MRC?
The need for uniforms is HUGE! It’s so important that our members have MRC polo shirts as consistent ID, we’ve had to find creative ways to fund them – by NACCHO grants, corporate sponsors, and donations. This should be a top priority at a national level! The MRC is already the country’s best-kept secret. The lack of national brand awareness is a major obstacle in recruitment, with additional impact on retention. When hundreds of MRC volunteers serve at a mass-vax clinic or respond to a shelter, and media coverage shows them all in street clothes, it’s a colossally wasted opportunity! It matters when a group of responders (whom nobody’s even heard about) LOOKS capable and professional, which speaks well for the MRC program they represent. Also, we had to purchase COVID appreciation pins out of our limited unencumbered funds, which is sad. Some of these people volunteer up to 50 hours or more a month, and all we can do is hand them a certificate? (We’re also not allowed to use some of our limited funding for food, which requires us to work through affiliates to provide a few pizzas for a team of 20 members who’ve donated 4 hours to staffing flu clinics and such.)

The incessant demands of COVID stretched our ability to track data. Can’t we do better than the deeply flawed Juvare system? Apparently, a major overhaul is planned; is someone investing funds wisely to check the user interface, reliability, and functions? We could really use a database similar to the one the Red Cross uses, if it can be accessed by local unit leaders for their own volunteers. We need one-stop shopping: a user-friendly system that allows us to enter and update member data, log their training and hours served, compile service hours and activity records, and so forth. I’ve had to roll up our numbers manually while transitioning to MA Responds and working with Excel spreadsheets, which takes hours and risks human error.

3. Do you have recommendations on the top short- and long-term priorities for the MRC? What operational capabilities, services, or competencies would you propose that the MRC focus on? Do you have recommendations on ways to strengthening the MRC's role as a federal disaster response asset?
Per capabilities: No need to reinvent the wheel; NACCHO provided a great 2019 Deployment Readiness Guide. We need help funding and implementing those concepts, to build and drill those capabilities. It would help if we could hire someone to guide strategic planning sessions with members and affiliates. Or can the MRC program provide that expertise? We also need more opportunities to learn from other MRC leaders. We really miss those integrated conferences! It makes sense that the agency would want to "reimburse" itself for the money it spends on color additive certification, however, there does not seem to be a reason for the sudden want to increase the fees. This article covers the Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) proposal to change color additive restrictions by raising certification service prices. In 2005, the certification program's costs increased due to a "rising staff wage, rent, and building charges, as well as basic operating expenses such as equipment purchase and maintenance," which created a burden on the program. The FDA aims to increase fee regulation and use those fees to cover the cost of operating the FDA color certification program. The proposed rule seeks to increase prices for straight colors such as lakes from $0.10 per pound to $0.45, with the minimum fee increasing from $244 to $288, as well as similar increases in repackaging of approved color additives and additive mixes. The increase is from $35 to $45 per 100 pounds, and for over 1,000 pounds, the price would increase from $89 to $114.This proposed regulation by the FDA of the increase in fees will not be associated with changes in the FDA certification program and is not expected to provide any economic gains/costs; rather, it considers more of a transfer of funds from manufacturers to the government. The funds will go towards the costs of accounting, reviewing data, issuing certificates, conducting research, inspecting establishments, and purchasing and maintaining equipment. The proposed regulation would put economic limits on color additive manufacturers, with an estimated one-time cost of roughly $1,354 to $1,407 and recurring expenses of approximately $165 to $193 (Food and Drug Administration, 2022).

Increasing the fees to cover the cost of operations for the program will impact healthcare at a federal level through better public health outcomes and lessen the burden on hospitals and medical professionals. It might have an influence on the federal level in terms of resource allocation if the FDA fails to get operating funds, preventing them from evaluating color additives. It could impact the federal level through the allocation of resources if the FDA failed to acquire funds to operate, which could prevent them from testing color additives. For example, if consumers have health problems as a result of dangerous color additives, the federal government may need funds to develop cures and preventative measures. It can lead to financial difficulties for the healthcare system, with the federal government concerned about finding money to support their goals of discovering treatment. I do agree with the FDA's proposed rule to increase service fees for color additives to support the operation of the FDA certification program since it will benefit public health by ensuring that color additives in various consumer products comply with FDA regulations. I believe covering the operational costs will provide the FDA with more resources to test and evaluate color additives in consumer products, which could help protect public health. While increasing the fee could potentially impact consumers and manufacturers by raising product prices and reducing purchases, the impact of ensuring product safety and consumer health outweighs the economic effects to me. Furthermore, this will facilitate the reduction of exposure to dangerous color additives, which can help individuals avoid frequent trips to the hospital while also improving a person's overall well-being and quality of life. Finalizing the rule will allow the program to continue functioning and have the resources to undertake evaluations to limit exposure to hazardous color additives, resulting in fewer hospital visits and improved health outcomes.

The proposed rule by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) seeks to adjust fees for certification services related to color additives, in accordance with the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act). The primary objective is to ensure the sustainability and adequacy of the certification program, which is mandated by federal regulations. By increasing fees, the FDA aims to cover rising operational costs associated with maintaining the certification program, such as staff payroll, facility charges, and equipment maintenance. These adjustments in fees are designed to align with the program's expenses, ensuring its continued effectiveness in regulating color additives used in various products, including food, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices. While the proposal acknowledges the need for higher fees to meet operational demands, it also emphasizes the importance of balancing this with the potential impact on color additive manufacturers. The proposed fee increases are intended to be reasonable, ensuring that they do not unduly burden manufacturers or disrupt the availability and affordability of color additives in regulated products. The effect on healthcare at the federal level, the proposal is unlikely to directly influence healthcare practices or patient outcomes. Instead, it primarily pertains to regulatory operations within the FDA, focusing on the certification of color additives used in consumer products. Therefore, while the proposal plays a role in maintaining regulatory standards and ensuring product safety, its impact on broader healthcare delivery or quality at the federal level is minimal. The recognition of the necessity to adjust fees to sustain the certification program and uphold regulatory standards is important in which I agree. However, careful consideration must be given to the magnitude of the fee increases and their potential implications for manufacturers. It's essential to strike a balance between covering program costs and avoiding undue financial strain on manufacturers, which could inadvertently affect product availability and affordability. Therefore, while supporting the overarching goal of maintaining an effective certification program, it's crucial to assess the proposed fee adjustments critically and ensure they are reasonable and justified.

Red color additives from beets should completely replace red 40. The synthetic food dye, Red 40, causes DNA damage, causes colonic inflammation, and impacts the microbiome in mice. Its effect in humans over years remains largely unknown and thus it should be banned. The incidence of colorectal cancer (CRC) among young people has been on the rise for the past four decades and its underlying causes are only just starting to be uncovered. Recent studies suggest that consuming ultra-processed foods and pro-inflammatory diets may be contributing factors. The increase in the use of synthetic food colors in such foods over the past 40 years, including the common synthetic food dye Allura Red AC (Red 40), coincides with the rise of early-onset colorectal cancer (EOCRC). As these ultra-processed foods are particularly appealing to children, there is a growing concern about the impact of synthetic food dyes on the development of CRC. Our study aimed to investigate the effects of Red 40 on DNA damage, the microbiome, and colonic inflammation. Despite a lack of prior research, high levels of human exposure to pro-inflammatory foods containing Red 40 highlight the urgency of exploring this issue. Our results show that Red 40 damages DNA both in vitro and in vivo and that consumption of Red 40 in the presence of a high-fat diet for 10 months leads to dysbiosis and low-grade colonic inflammation in mice. This evidence supports the hypothesis that Red 40 is a dangerous compound that dysregulates key players involved in the development of EOCRC.

Diet plays a pivotal role in influencing the risk of colorectal cancer, a significant public health concern. Synthetic dyes are prevalent in the global food supply chain. Three dyes [Allura Red (a.k.a. “Red 40”), Tartrazine (“Yellow-5”), and Sunset Yellow (“Yellow-6”)] account for 90 % of all dyes used in food in the USA; and Red 40 is by far the most common. Alarmingly, 94 % of people over 2 years old in the USA consume Red 40. It is used extensively in processed foods as a coloring for beverages, frozen treats, powder mixes, gelatin products, candies, icings, jellies, spices, dressings, sauces, and baked goods. It is critical we better understand the interaction of Red 40 with players involved in carcinogenesis.

The lack of rigorous prior research combined with high levels of human exposure to westernized diets containing Red 40, underscores the importance of researching this subject with current technologies, platforms, and appropriate animal models. We posit that the synthetic dye Red 40, acting as a foreign substance, induces a subtle and low-grade inflammatory response specific to the colon and rectum. This chronic inflammation may contribute to the development of CRC, particularly in the distal colon and rectum. In vitro experiments were conducted to examine the impact of Red 40 on human HCT 116 colon cancer cells. To this, we carried out dose- and time-course experiments with physiologically relevant doses of Red 40. Fig. 1 shows that Red 40 causes DNA damage (determined by the comet assay) in a dose (Fig. 1A) and time (Fig. 1B) dependent manner. Consistent with these findings, Red 40 also causes a dose-dependent increase in the DNA damage markers, p53 and phosphorylated p53 (on serine 15) (Fig. 1C). It is important to mention that Red 40 does not have significant cytostatic or cytotoxic effect under these experimental conditions as the cell grows rate /count and viability (94–96 %, n = 3) for Red 40 treated cells have not changed in comparison to non-treated cells (viability of 96 %, n = 3). See https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10502305/

Regulations, particularly for food and cosmetic products are necessary to ensure the safety and well-being of Americans. Despite the vitality of these regulations, the process of obtaining these certifications is often circuitous and timely, particularly for the FDA. Before a synthetic color additive can be used by manufacturers, the FDA must examine a batch of each coloring and ensure that the additive is up to numerous standards. Synthetic colorings such as Red no. 40 are typically more vibrant, and even, and are more inexpensive than other dyes on the market. As the manufacturers are using a cheaper coloring alternative and will likely make a large markup from the products they are selling, I fully agree with the slight price increase in the FDA color certification programs. Not only would this aid funding of a federal agency, but it would take into account recent inflation. Further, the FDA explains that certification would only undergo a $0.10 increase per pound, a cost fully manageable by manufacturers, especially those which have high consumer demand.
