Is Red Dye 40 Safe? No. Please ban it. Do you notice your kiddo gets hyper after eating a cookie coated with bright red frosting and rainbow sprinkles? It’s natural to assume that sugar is the culprit, but research suggests some of the blame belongs to artificial food dyes like red dye 40.

So, what is red dye 40? Red dye 40, made from petroleum, is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in foods and drinks.

But some studies have linked artificial food dyes like red dye 40 to hyperactivity, including ADHD.

Some studies show a link between dyes and increased ADHD or hyperactivity in children. And other studies show an improvement in behavior and attention once the dyes were eliminated. Still, more research is needed.

Currently, the U.S. doesn’t ban any artificial food dyes. But some countries say there’s enough evidence to justify banning them.

Registered dietitian Julia Zumpano, RD, LD, highlights the possible risks associated with red dye 40 foods and how to minimize them. Potential side effects may include:

Hyperactivity, including ADHD.
Behavioral changes like irritability and depression.
Allergic reaction.
Hives and asthma.
Sneezing.
Watery eyes.
Skin irritation.
Migraines.
Red dye 40 contains benzene, a known cancer-causing substance.

“Researchers also found tumor growth in animals that consumed high doses of food dyes, though it can be hard to translate what this means for kids,” says Zumpano. “Some studies say the small amount of benzene in the dyes couldn’t pose a high risk.” But some do.

1)I feel the most critical priorities should be in the areas of surveillance/detection and control/prevention of vector-borne diseases. The impact of increased travel (the time during the pandemic not withstanding) and climate changes poses an increased risk of disease spread. As with West Nile virus in 1999, and more recently Zika virus in 2016, as well as spread of already introduced diseases such as dengue and Lyme disease, it is incredibly easy for existing vector-borne diseases to spread to new areas. Strong vector surveillance and detection efforts are the most reliable way that we can try to detect these pathogens prior to a major outbreak of human cases. Using human cases as a surveillance mechanism simply means that we will be detecting the cases after people start getting sick, not in advance of it. Updating surveillance with new technologies is critical.
In addition, control efforts need to be enhanced. Vector trapping and control remains one of the primary methods for preventing potential outbreaks, but many of these methods rely on techniques that haven’t changed for fifty years or more. Developing and applying new techniques for vector control, as well as verifying the impact of current technique (through concerns of factors like insecticide resistance and a lack of knowledge about the practical impact of vector control of disease spread) will be critical for mitigating potential spread of disease. New techniques such as genetically modified vectors need to be tested (and funded) on a large scale. Many areas that may be most impacted by vector-borne diseases lack local funds, or state/federal support, to implement robust surveillance and control efforts.
Lastly, research into basic biology of vectors is the best method to develop new ideas for control strategies. An increased understanding of vector biology (especially as it related to climate and local conditions) allows for developing more effective approaches to control, as well as optimizing current control efforts for local vector population. Populations of vectors in different areas of the country may respond differently to control efforts due to genetic, environmental, and physiological factors in the local populations. This focus on regional specialization is often overlooked – controlling a tick population in New Jersey may be very different from controlling on in Michigan or Texas.

2)I suggest goals of improving and enhancing current surveillance efforts through improving current techniques – the used of field collections, disease testing, and vector identification. Developing new surveillance techniques should be a goal as well. Monitoring vector population control efficacy is critical, as well as designing, testing, and implementing new control efforts. I think a concrete goal of improving existing surveillance and control infrastructure must be included.
New basic research into vector biology if also required, both to assess the efficacy of current control efforts as well as to develop new control strategies.
Lastly, incentivizing education in vector biology and vector-borne diseases is critical. Fundamental skills such as basic entomology, insect taxonomy, and other fields of basic biology critical need to be incentivized for undergraduate and graduate education, so qualified professionals will pursue careers in these fields.

3)I think bringing control and surveillance techniques “into the 21st century” should be a focus. As previously mentioned, many techniques (trapping, for example) rely on tools developed decades ago. Even if these tools are still the best ones to use, a concerted effort to verify the efficacy of these methods (and verify that they have a concrete effect of disease mitigation) should be attempted.
A focus on border regions is also especially critical. Many border regions along the border in CA, NM, AZ, and TX have limited funds or state support to implement and develop strong surveillance and control efforts. While academic partners may be present, they require funding as well. These areas are at increased risk of vector-borne diseases due to climate and immigration.

4)One critical component that plagues this area is the “boom/bust” cycles of funding. Funding increases during outbreaks, news stories, or public concern, then wanes after the news no longer makes headlines. However, the threat remains. In fact, if surveillance and control efforts are effective, then there will not be major outbreaks of disease cases present, which then causes people to question the need for continued funding. Sustained, long-term approaches and funding are needed for long-term success in these areas.

The US must invest in advancing technologies capable of enhancing vector surveillance program capabilities and building surveillance capacity. Precision control technologies such as genetically modified mosquitoes and sterile insect programs have shown much promise, but these technologies focus on targeting specific vector species of concern. Only a small percentage of mosquito species are capable of transmitting disease. As precision control technologies continue to be developed, efficient allocation of resources will be required to ensure the right control technologies are deployed at the right times and in regions of highest risk. This presents a significant hurdle to conventional surveillance program practices, which rely on labor intensive deployment of traps, collection of specimens, species identification, sorting, and downstream pathogen testing of vectors.
Vector control organizations throughout the US face the following specific needs:
(1) Enhancing entomological capabilities in public health labs. Smaller public health departments typically do not have a professional entomologist on staff. If equipped with tools capable of accurately identifying vector species, aggregating data, and guiding decision making, smaller public health districts could recognize high risk events and enhance the impact of their vector control programs.
(2) Building surveillance capacity in the field and the lab for conventional best practices. Larger public health departments, or independent vector control districts, have limited capacity in the surveillance workflow. Technologies that may decrease time required in the field or in the lab, and thus enable districts to generate faster, more accurate, and higher quantities of data would be highly beneficial to effective allocation of control resources.
(3) Modernization and standardization of surveillance data for historical and regional comparisons, reporting to state agencies, and research. Traditional data visualization programs still require data to be manually input or uploaded to each system. Poor centralization of data limits vector control district abilities to review and compare historical data, restricts the ability of state and federal agencies to understand local vector control needs, and hinders research insights.
(4) Development of tools capable of generating new variables or layers of resolution to precision surveillance data. Information such as life stage of specimen, aging, and detection of pathogens are largely limited to research practices, but would enhance effective vector control decision making.
Emerging technologies have the ability to address many of these challenges. Solutions utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) approaches can automate routine tasks in the vector surveillance workflow. For example, applied optics and image recognition have been developed to automate identification of mosquito species (Goodwin, 2020 and 2021). Such an approach is scalable across the diversity of arthropod vectors including mosquitoes, tick, sandflies, and various life stages. Several opportunities to build on this technology include development of remote sensing technologies, such as smart traps, that reduce the need to collect specimens from the field, while increasing frequency of data available to vector control decision makers. Robotics may be applied to vector surveillance laboratory workflows to automate identification, sorting, and preparation for pathogen testing. In this process, highly standardized data can be generated, digitized, and integrated with data visualization, documentation, and reporting platforms. Vectech, a small business developing these AI and ML technologies for the vector surveillance market, has made significant progress towards these kinds of solutions.
HHS should support translating promising technologies out of university labs and research centers and into US businesses capable of commercializing and bringing new vector surveillance tools to market. Efforts may include: additional support for small business innovation research (SBIR) proposals related to innovative vector surveillance technologies, an ongoing waiver for SBIR awards over statutory budget limitations from the small business administration (SBA), broad agency announcements (BAAs) focused on this topic that encourage private-public partnerships, and establishment of an innovation accelerator (similar to the KidneyX program) focused on vector surveillance and control technologies.
References:
Goodwin A, Glancey M, Ford T, Scavo L, Brey J, Heier C, Durr NJ, Acharya S. Development of a low-cost imaging system for remote mosquito surveillance. Biomedical Optics Express. 2020 May 1;11(5):2560-9.
Goodwin A, Padmanabhan S, Hira S, et al. Convolutional Neural Networks That Identify Mosquito Species and Know When They Do Not Know. Research Square; 2021. DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-275109/v1

I've had months of treatment with antibiotics during which my symptoms have improved, but the Lyme Disease symptoms eventually return after the antibiotics are stopped. 1. What do you recommend as the top priorities to address vector-borne diseases in the United States during the next five years? Why are these the most important priorities?
Alpha-gal syndrome should be a funding priority. Alpha-gal syndrome affects up to 3% of populations with high tick exposure, including large areas of the southeast, mid-south, Midwest and eastern United States. If you run the numbers, this translates into hundreds of thousands and possible over a million Americans. More than ten times this number--20-35% of the population of states like Virginia--are sensitized to alpha-gal but don't have obvious allergic symptoms. These folks tolerate alpha-gal in food but can have life-threatening reactions to drugs and medical products.
2. What goals, objectives, and strategies would you propose for each of your top priority areas?
AGS is massively under recognized, under diagnosed and poorly understood. Moreover, it represents a rare opportunity to learn about the mechanisms by which allergies and potentially autoimmune diseases develop and the likely under appreciated role the IgE immune responses to carbohydrates play in disease and human health, including cardiovascular health.
• Awareness needs to be raised within the medical community.
• More surveillance is needed to determine the scope of the epidemic.
• Research is on the pathogenesis and pathology of AGS is needed. Elucidating the mechanisms by which AGS is acquired would have far-reaching implications not just for patients with AGS, but by shedding light on fundamental questions on how allergies and autoimmune diseases develop, a much broader cross-section of the Americans.

3. Do you have recommendations on specific research or programmatic efforts to improve surveillance, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of vector-borne diseases?
See above. The AGS patients also desperately need:
• A federally funded database of drugs, vaccines, and other medical products and their alpha-gal content. We currently rely on a prolonged and inefficient process of contacting manufacturers about each and every drug and medical product we need, often with the help of part-time volunteers at the Robert Wood Johnson Hospital Drug Information Hotline. This takes days or even weeks. Surgery and other hospital-based procedures can be significantly delayed as each product that will be used is painstakingly researched. Note that it's not just people with AGS who can react to alpha-gal in drugs. People who are sensitized but not allergic to alpha-gal containing foods may react to products with especially high alpha-gal content, like cetuximab, gelatin-based volume expanders, and who knows what else--we don't know. This would be one of the most impactful and cost-effective measures to implement. The project could draw from databases and processes developed both by Robert Wood Johnson and the UNC, UVA, and Duke hospital pharmacies. The problem patients face now is that if you aren't a patient of one of the above hospitals, they usually won't share info from their databases, due to constraints imposed by their legal departments. Furthermore, each hospital has its own formulary, and while there is overlap, availability of products varies from hospital to hospital.
• Labeling laws. Pharmaceutical and drug companies should be required to declare alpha-gal content, or at least the presence of mammal-derived ingredients and carrageenan--on the drugs and medical products they produce. Obviously, this strategy cannot be implemented nearly as quickly or as inexpensively as the above database.
• Mandate that the major hospital, EMR software companies (there are 5 or less) update electronic medical record (EMR) software to allow for the clear, accurate, and easily implemented documentation of alpha-gal syndrome. Currently, there is no standardized way to enter this information. Patients often have Fabry disease added to their records, which has nothing to do with AGS. Some EMR software offers the option of entering galactose-α-1,3-galactose in the allergen database, but most patients and physicians are not familiar with this formal name for alpha-gal. As a result, "allergy to alpha-gal" tends to be entered manually, which means that a pharmacy alert isn't triggered and medical products aren't screened for alpha-gal. This is a separate issue from the creation of an ICD code, which is an important but unrelated issue.

4. Any additional topics you wish to provide input on.

The information received will inform the development of the National Strategy to address vector-borne diseases.

As a current law student and patient suffering from persistent Lyme disease, I thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment. Based on my personal experience and knowledge, I request that the Department of Health and Human Services fund research on accurate testing for tick-borne diseases and clinical trials for treating persistent Lyme disease.

I was diagnosed with Lyme disease at age 10 when I became too exhausted to attend soccer practice and went to sleep as soon as I got home from school. I was given 30 days of oral antibiotics and told I was cured. A year later, however, I again faced severe fatigue, but this time my memory began to fail and my grades plummeted. After a total of two months of oral antibiotics and one month of IV antibiotics, I was once again told I was cured.

Around age 21 I began having severe insomnia and by the time I reached 26, my health had deteriorated. I had extreme dizziness, fatigue, stabbing neck pain and uncontrollable chills. At night I struggled to breathe as I lay on the couch unable to sleep. I saw 8 doctors who refused to take my symptoms seriously even though my CDC approved blood test for Lyme was positive. They blamed my positive results on my childhood illness, and sent me home. Finally, I found a Lyme-literate medical doctor who prescribed IV antibiotics, and I gradually recovered.

Much of my suffering and the suffering of millions of other patients would be eased if there were a test which showed total disease eradication and a curative treatment for persistent Lyme, so that patients would recover and be able to return to school or work.

Accurate Testing

Without accurate tests for Lyme disease, it is impossible for doctors to know when their patients are cured. The current CDC approved blood test is only 60% accurate and is based on antibody testing (see Ex 1 Wormser), which cannot confirm whether the infection persists (see Diagnosis and Testing, CDC (Nov. 20, 2019), https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/diagnosistesting/index.html). In addition, because the test itself is based on a single European strain of borrelia and excludes antibodies more specific to Lyme (see PAMELA WEINTRAUB, CURE UNKNOWN: INSIDE THE LYME EPIDEMIC 10, 320 (rev. ed. 2013)), as many as 22% of patients in the early stage of the disease test negative and roughly half of patients with late-stage Lyme also test negative (See Ex 2 Maloney).

If there were a test using more accurate indicators of infection such as RNA, PCR, or T-cells, instead of antibodies, the medical debate of whether Lyme persists after antibiotic treatment would be resolved. We would finally have confirmation of persistent infection. This would be truly life changing for Lyme disease patients, like myself, who are cruelly ridiculed by hospitals, Infectious Disease doctors, and insurance companies who claim persistent infection does not exist.

Accurate testing is critical to providing early treatment for this progressive disease and ensuring that patients with persistent infection continue to receive treatment until they are cured.

Pharmaceutical Studies

There is overwhelming evidence of persistent infection as shown in the International Lyme and Associated Diseases Society compilation of over 700 peer-reviewed articles supporting evidence of persistent Lyme disease (See Ex 3 ILADS). In addition, the new ICD11 Codes from the World Health Organization list fifteen complications from Lyme disease, fourteen of which are applicable to persistent Lyme (see JENNA LUCHÉ-THAYER, $LYME: HOW MEDICAL CODES WOUND CORRUPTION AND SCIENTIFIC FRAUD 85 (2018)). Thus, we need to turn our attention towards healing patients who are currently suffering from persistent Lyme disease.

Pharmaceutical studies should begin by relying on two key strategies used in the early years of the AIDS epidemic: drug repurposing and non-placebo-based drug trials (See generally SARAH SCHULMAN, LET THE RECORD SHOW (2021)).

(1) We must start with drugs already on the market to quickly relieve the extreme suffering of those who currently have persistent Lyme disease. There are many off-label pharmaceuticals, such as Dapsone (See Ex 4 Horowitz) and Disulfiram (see Ex 5 Liegner) that have shown promise for treating persistent Lyme in small studies, but we need larger, government funded studies to confirm effectiveness.

(2) We cannot rely on placebo based double blind studies, because withholding treatment to the placebo group is unethical and counter to the health of patients who will get worse without treatment. Instead, we should establish a baseline treatment, such as IV antibiotics, so that patients who fall into the control group do not get worse. In addition, a prolonged study timeframe is needed to ensure patients do not relapse.

I ask HHS to focus your research on testing accuracy and treatment for persistent infection. Our health depends on it.

Sincerely,
Jennifer Barrett, MBA
JD Candidate 2022

TWIMC,
There are two basic data flow mechanisms for understanding public health in the United States. Explicit CDC reporting, and the administration of public health benefits of Medicare and Medicaid via CMS.

The former is highly focused, and serves to gather specific data about a particular problem. The later is general, and focuses on the ongoing healthcare picture of a person, based on their clinical-financial transactions. Ideally, these two systems should balance each other out, helping to form a comprehensive data picture that could help to address the limitations in each approach.

However, the medical claims data pipeline is crippled when considering any vector-borne disease, because it does not include lab results.

Medicare and Medicaid data, for instance, can tell when a test for Lyme disease is administered, but does not receive the results of the test. The CDC receives the lab results as part of its surveillance, but does not have the capacity to study events before and after the lab test to provide clinical context.

Essentially, you have a data silo problem here. The left hand does not know what the right hand is doing.

CMS should require labs to provide lab results to CMS when then they are paid for by Medicare/Medicaid by default. CMS should also allow patients to opt-out of this data collection for a small fee: perhaps $35 a year.

This will enable those who have legitimate privacy concerns to avoid exposing their data to either unfair or biased insurance practices, or to data breaches, etc etc. But at the same time, it would ensure that CMS claims data were contextualized by the results of labs. This could allow for broad analysis of vector-borne disease, in the context of other healthcare processes.

The lack of this data also cripples CMS claims analysis for the purposes of Diabetes and COVID, but vector-borne disease has the legislative justification already for a system-wide rethinking.

Everyone knows that this part of public health data pipeline is inadequate, but so far, inertia has won out. I am sure that there are regulatory issues that I am not aware of that might make this change difficult. These should be identified and overcome, rather than the current broken idea (that claims and surveillance can be entirely separate) to continue.

Regards,
-Fred Trotter
CareSet Journal

There are many misunderstood elements to all tick-borne infections, primarily: risk of infection, adequate and accurate diagnostics, and proper treatment for various stages of infection. The medical community and public health departments still consider and promote the notion that tick-borne infections are “hard to get, easy to treat and rarely fatal”. The growth of the tick population is exponential, they are everywhere (back and front yards, play grounds). The CDC, IDSA and local public health departments do not acknowledge the extent of this epidemic, resulting in a community of folks who are severely ill and some who lose their lives. Patients are often denied testing. In order to improve the standard of care several aspects of this problem need to be better understood:

1. Establish Risk of Infection. The risk of tick-borne infection due to attachment time is poorly understood. Physicians will often forgo testing of the patient (and testing of the tick) by indicating the tick would have needed to be attached for 24-72 hrs. In fact, a review of the literature (Ref: Cook, M. “Lyme borreliosis: a review of data on transmission times after tick attachment” Int J Gen Med 2015; 8:1-8) found that transmission time of <16 hrs is possible and not well understood. They could not find research on tick transmission from less than 16 hrs, therefore it is not known if ticks can transmit infection faster. It needs to be understood where infection can reside in the tick (e.g. saliva, gut) in relation to transmission.
2. Establish national plans for tick surveillance and control. A summary by Mader et al (Ref: “A Survey of Tick Surveillance and Control Practices in the United States” Journal of Medical Entomology June 17 2020) found that across the US there is no coordinated effort to effectively survey the depth of tick population, types of infection or execute population control. Private companies spray yards to reduce the tick population but this is not sufficient for the rate of tick growth. Effective and unique measures are needed to control the population. Specifically, a nationally funded and coordinated collection of ticks across the U.S with testing for viral, parasite and bacteria presence. A follow-up study every 2-3 years would indicate growth and migration patterns.
3. Define diagnostic tests to delineate between acute and late stages of tick-borne infections. An understanding of extent of infection is a critical factor in those who do not improve on antibiotic treatment. Testing should span the range of possible infections for proper treatment.
4. Document and define stages of illness such that diagnostics and treatment can be targeted. Types, length and depth of infection in bodily tissues/fluids and forms of infection need to be delineated to properly diagnose and treat patients. Determining the existence of persistent infection and/or organism debris and potential contributions to illness is critical.
5. Document and clearly define possible symptoms of Lyme disease and other tick-borne infections to be accepted by the medical community. Individuals infected with tick-borne infections have experienced a wide array of symptoms and have often provided testimony to these effects. My sister did not experience arthritic symptoms at first but rather GI disturbance and hormonal imbalances for several years.
6. Improve treatment protocols for targeted infections and/or manifestations of infection. There is a need to investigate antibiotics, herbal medicines and supportive supplements where a synergistic effect can be achieved to heal the body as a whole. While many patients are responsive to long term antibiotics, many others are not (Ref: Johnson, L. et al “Antibiotic Treatment Response in Chronic Lyme Disease: Why Do Some Patients Improve While Others Do Not” Healthcare 2020 8(4), 383) and it is not understood why. Further study of which antibiotics, what doses, and oral versus IV administration effectiveness in cases of chronic illness or if alternative therapies are needed. Lyme can enter the cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) and tissues. Studies have found antibiotics like doxycycline had concentrations of only 14% in blood serum. [Ref: Andersson, H., Alestig K. “The Penetration of Doxycycline into CSF” Scand J Infect Dis Suppl. 1976;(9):17-9 PMID: 1070143.] Given the strength of the blood brain barrier at preventing certain medications from being fully effective, more research is needed.

As a vector-borne disease, Lyme disease is the most frequently diagnosed and treated vector-borne disease in the US, with the CDC estimating nearly a half million cases per year (cdc.gov). Cases of Lyme disease far exceeds that of any other disease transmitted by all vectors, including mosquitoes. For this reason alone, Lyme disease should be considered a top research and public health priority by the federal government.
The exceptionally high number of cases of Lyme disease is not consistent with the prevailing opinion that no other routes of transmission of Borrelia burgdorferi (and other species of Borrelia) are possible in humans. Using the CDC estimate of 476,000 new cases per year (based on data from insurance databases), Lyme disease ranks third among nationally notifiable bacterial infections in humans – behind two sexually transmitted diseases (Chlamydia and gonorrhea). Surveillance shows that the ticks considered to be the sole vectors of Lyme disease are found in less than half the country, and the tick-borne disease model suggests that the ticks have to be attached and feeding for two days before there is any risk of disease. These observations are totally inconsistent with the data indicating that a half a million cases of Lyme disease occur each year. The infectious disease catch phrase that Lyme disease is “hard to catch and easy to cure” is clearly false.
Both the 2018 and 2020 HHS TBDWG Report to Congress include recommendations to investigate other routes of transmission of Borrelia, in particular maternal-fetal transmission. There is a significant body of research on both animal and human subjects demonstrating that Borrelia spirochetes are transmitted in utero, causing “adverse outcomes” in the fetus. The issue of maternal-fetal transmission of Borrelia and the potential for congenital Lyme disease be considered a public health priority, as it is for syphilis, especially when considering that the number of cases of Lyme disease EXCEEDS the number of cases of syphilis on an annual basis.
The pathobiology of infection and the immune system implications of Borrelia infection should be emphasized when considering where to focus research. NIH should build on the momentum of research being funded by patient organizations, to better understand how infection with Borrelia spp. is able to profoundly disrupt the human immune response to enable long term colonization. Notable differences between how men and women respond to infection have been shown, and this should be considered in the context of women’s health, who are less likely to produce antibodies detectable by current serological tests and are more likely to experience persistent symptoms of Lyme disease.
Health care providers often miss the diagnosis of Lyme disease during the earliest stages when the disease is most treatable, because the algorithm for diagnosis requires either an erythema migrans rash, or a positive serological test. Missing the diagnosis in the early stages of the infection leads to treatment-resistant chronic disease, and the huge health burden (on patients, employers, insurance providers, Medicare, etc.) that comes along with it. This is not a rare occurrence, as has been repeatedly shown in research studies. There is an urgent and as yet unmet need for a clinically accurate diagnostic test for Lyme disease, and in particular a test that would provide health care providers with a means to diagnose a patient early enough in the disease when antibiotic treatment is 80 – 90% effective in preventing long-term illness. This is the recommendation of the 2018 and 2020 TBDWG, noted in the 2018 NIH Strategic Plan, and is now a priority of the LymeX Innovation program – which should be fully funded on the federal side of the “public-private” partnership.
Make Lyme disease the public health and research priority that it should be. Strategies include establishment of an NIH Center for Lyme disease, to coordinate translational research and recruit new researchers to the field. A national patient registry should be established. The impact Lyme disease has on women and children’s health should be recognized and prioritized.

My name is Amy LeBoeuf, founder and director of Louisiana One Health In Action (501c3) and Chair of the US One Health Education Team under the One Health Commission (501c3). I am submitting comments from my perspective as a K12 Public Educator of over 20 years, a One Health advocate, and a mother of a child impacted by vector-borne disease in response to the RFI regarding the top priorities to address vector-borne diseases (VBD) in the US in the next five years. My full comments are attached via the document below and highlighted here.

Educational Goal- Broaden the K12 National Health Education Standards to include One Health Concepts and Topics relating to Zoonoses and VBD
I have searched for resources to help teach my students about preventing vector borne diseases, and realized that there isn’t much available; and then I figured out why. There is no mention of prevention strategies for vector borne or other zoonotic diseases in our K12 National Health Education Standards (NHES). According to the CDC, these standards were developed to establish, promote, and support health-enhancing behaviors for students in all grade levels— They provide a framework for teachers, administrators, and policy makers in designing or selecting curricula, allocating instructional resources, and assessing student achievement and progress.” But the current NHES do not take into account the profound increases in vector borne disease that we are currently experiencing which leaves our children incredibly vulnerable. Children are losing their childhoods. We absolutely MUST do better.

As Chair of the US One Health Education US Team, I strongly believe that students could and should receive a more comprehensive understanding of health. That could be accomplished by incorporating a One Health perspective into the National Health Education Standards. The current standards do not address student education about ticks and other vectors, vector borne disease prevention strategies, nor conceptual understandings of how our human choices can impact our environment in ways that can directly affect the geographical range of these disease carrying vectors. Yet education is the ‘key’ to preventing the tragic outcomes of vector borne diseases.

Objectives-
We want our students to become adults who think critically, who understand factors that increase health risks, and who are armed with disease prevention strategies for life in an ever-changing world. What children learn through K12 Health Education not only protects them now but establishes their attitudes and health habits as adults which they subsequently can instill within their own families. The One Health concept about our interconnectedness with animals and with the environment could easily be incorporated into the NHES and into classrooms around the country. Without this action we leave our most vulnerable population- our children- at risk.

Strategies-
I implore you to join us in addressing this vulnerability by including in your recommendations that One Health be incorporated into the National Health Education Standards to teach children about Zoonotic and Vector Borne Diseases including basic vector biology, vector borne disease prevention strategies, and a conceptual understanding of how human behaviors contribute to expanding vector terrains and subsequently more sick people. Arming students with this knowledge is a powerful way to prevent vector-borne diseases.

Recommendations on specific research or programmatic efforts-

Citizen Science at the K12 and University Level
A recommendation for a specific effort in relation to prevention and surveillance of VBD is involving K12 and University students in citizen science via STEM lessons and activities centered around VBD topics can be a powerful way to not only meet educational standards, but raise awareness of VBD and the need for prevention. It can also meet the needs of the manpower required for an expansive surveillance effort.

CDC Designed One Health Patient Intake Form to Aid Patients and Physicians
Another recommendation interim until there are concerted efforts to raise awareness among the general public about VBDs and a national One Health framework that allows for collaboration among health professionals to address issues like VBD, could be even a simple measure like a CDC designed patient intake form from a One Health perspective. It could help by prompting patients to recall potential exposures as well as guide physicians to better understand patient risks through environment, pets, occupations, and outdoor activities. Since many of these VBDs present with flu-like symptoms, there is no reliable testing, early treatment is most successful, and many VBDs are clinical diagnoses based on symptoms and exposure, a simple tool like this could help physicians and patients alike think more critically about their daily risks and exposures. It could help determine when flu-like symptoms may not be just the flu.

Public input on strengthening and improving the nation’s response to vector-borne diseases.

Top 5 priorities
We need improved testing for Lyme and all tick borne diseases. Current tests are very inaccurate and until we know how many people are infected we don’t even know the scope of the problem. Testing is also crucial to determine whether treatments are effective. If we can’t tell whether the pathogen is eliminated, how can we decide which treatments are appropriate? We need tests that can determine active infection, past infection, re-infection and possibly even reactivation of a dormant infection.
We need better treatments for Lyme and tick borne diseases. Many people with Lyme, Bartonella and Babesia have infections that are never truly treated. People become ill from Lyme disease or Bartonella and are never well again. Of the estimated 476,000 people diagnosed with Lyme and tick-borne diseases in the United States each year, 25% of those are kids. That’s a staggering 326 children diagnosed with these debilitating diseases each day! There are children that are infected at an early age who become completely disabled. They will never have a normal life until we learn how to treat these diseases.
We need to educate doctors how to recognize and treat Lyme disease. Have sent people to the doctor with clear bull’s eye rashes and they have been told it is not Lyme disease. Doctors are still prescribing a single dose of doxycycline to “treat” Lyme disease. This is inexcusable. A disease that when left untreated can kill you and doctors fail to recognize or treat it appropriately!
We need to decrease the tick population. The numbers of ticks are continuing to increase and the percentage of infected ticks is also increasing. We need to find ways to decrease transmission of disease and decrease the tick population.
Finally, we need to educate the public about the dangers of ticks and tick borne diseases. People need to learn about tick habitat and how to remove ticks, how to get ticks tested and when to seek treatment.

Goals for these priorities
Testing - There needs to be research to determine how accurate Lyme tests are and this information needs to be shared widely with the medical community. New tests need to be developed that do not rely on immune system function. Better PCR tests should be developed for Lyme and other diseases. Tests should also be developed that look for multiple Borrelia species. Borrelia Miyamotoi is becoming more common in the United States, but our testing does not check for this pathogen.
Treatment - New approaches to treatments must be investigated. There also need to be recognition and standards developed for treatment of chronic Lyme.
Educating doctors - The CDC should update its recommendations about Lyme disease treatment to reflect the recent research about persistence of Lyme. The government should create accurate CME programs for doctors. Doctors should be required to learn the basics about diagnosing Lyme disease and they need to be educated about the accuracy of the current Lyme tests. Doctors need to be educated about chronic Lyme; too many ill patients are sent home without an accurate diagnosis. People are dying or suffering years of disability due to inappropriate diagnosis and treatment.
Decreasing ticks and transmission - Effective, non-toxic tick repellants need to be developed. We need effective methods to decrease tick populations and to decrease transmission of all tick borne infections. Efforts should be made to decrease the vectors of Lyme and other tick borne disease.
Educating the public - There are lots of small Lyme organizations creating awareness programs. Investigate programs that are already available and provide grants or support for these organizations to expand their effectiveness. Examples from PA Lyme:
https://palyme.org/tick-check-challenge/
https://palyme.org/dare-materials/
https://palyme.org/dare-2b-tick-aware-program-overview/

Recommendations
Free tick testing in PA has improved surveillance for tick borne diseases. Ticks are being sent from areas around the state. This program should be expanded nationwide to create a better understanding of tick borne illness around the country.
Research should be done on the striae seen in Bartonella. Do these common markings carry bacteria or bacteria DNA that could be isolated to improve diagnosis?
There are reports of numerous animals that are resistant or immune to Lyme disease. Studies should be done to understand this immune process. Perhaps it can be mimicked by some medicine or a vaccine.
mRNA vaccines should be investigated to see if they can be manufactured to create a safe and effective Lyme vaccine.
I appreciate the opportunity to provide input.
Kathy Rubel, MPT
Secretary for PA Lyme
Administrator for PANS/PANDAS Parent’s of Pennsylvania
Parent of a child affected by tick borne diseases
Bartonella patient

As someone who has worked in mosquito control and vector-borne disease research in academia I would like to recommend the following priorities. (1) Current diagnostics for bacterial caused tick-borne diseases need improvement. Specifically for B. burgdorferi and Rickettsia testing. (2) Greater resources should be provided to US territories. The Caribbean tends to be the first region hit hard by mosquito borne diseases. Infrastructure to have mosquito control regularly is starting to become established but further funds should be given to maintain and continue growth. (3) Testing and screening of vector-borne diseases at vector control districts are not standardized. Many do not do regular testing to survey for bacteria or viral pathogens. A protocol and the tools to help districts in high risk areas should be implemented.

Lastly, I think the current workforce is divided into multiple research fields with little interdisciplinary training. I think future training programs should ensure students or staff have skills in epidemiology, entomology and public health. Additional training should include working with wildlife that maybe important for the enzootic transmission of vector-borne diseases.

When we process these requests, we do not require the patient to pay anything – they are provided as a courtesy to the patient and to the receiving health care facility.  We also process requests for medical records from commercial entities and these requestors do pay for our service.  This proposed rule would limit the fees that can be charged to these commercial requestors.  The rest of this rule supports the work that we do as a company and I support the other provisions in this proposed rule.  I am asking you to remove the language that indicates that third-party commercial requestors would be eligible for the cost-based rates that patients are eligible for.  I want to emphasize that our practice is to not charge patients anything – even a cost-based rate.  But if we must begin providing commercial entities records at cost-based rates we will have incentive to start charging patients also to make up this revenue difference.

As a social security practitioner for my entire career getting to help those far less fortunate than me is singlehandedly the greatest gratification and compensation I could ever hope for in my professional or personal life- the work I do changes (and many times saves) people’s lives for the better and it is an amazing feat to accomplish against a very harsh system that judges (and largely prejudges) people unfairly.  One of the greatest challenges I face everyday is the ongoing battle to obtain necessary electronic medical records for my clients to be able to prove their claims and get them their life sustaining disability benefits and because we are in a limbo period due to the previous federal court ruling in the infamous CIOX case (which in my humble opinion never should have occurred to begin with), many of my clients are suffering worse because they can’t obtain their records or direct them to my office as their appointed representative without paying ridiculously absurd amounts for electronic files that take no more than a minute to assemble and send yet the medical providers and unconscionable third party records facilitators and services that they use, like CIOX, profit astronomically off of people’s misfortunes and this needs to come to an end.  Patients/clients seeking to obtain life sustaining disability benefits through social security, when they have no means or source of income or support (which is why they file for these benefits in the first place), should not have the added burden of paying anything, let alone exorbitant fees and costs for electronic or even paper records of their treatment to help prove their claims, nor should their attorneys or counsel have to bear these costs as they are essentially working for them for free and can only get paid if they get their client’s claims approved and the approval results in a lump sum of past due benefits, which again is quite a hefty burden to meet these days, in many cases taking several years and numerous levels of complex appeals and hearings- and even when fees are received they are limited by statute and regulations so they don’t always sufficiently account for time and costs in each case.  Personally, over 16 years I have incurred tens of thousands of dollars in I reimbursed costs of electronic and paper records that probably cost the providers and their third party facilitators pennies to put together and send, and when the initial third party rule was enacted it largely saved my solo practice and made my ability to assist my clients that much easier and less stressful.  Now that I am facing the same old battles over records costs with so many providers and facilitators like CIOX it is hampering my ability to assist my clients as easily as before unless I’m willing and able to bear the burden of those costs for my clients, which of course I move heaven and earth to do because their interests are most important... but at the end of the day I should NOT have to do so, and neither should anyone else.  I wholeheartedly and strongly request and urge that your agency please enact the new rules to prohibit costs of medical records to indigent patients requesting their own records for social security disability benefit cases, to include HITECH requests that direct the records to third parties like attorneys or appointed representatives; alternatively, I urge that the maximum charge for such records when being requested or directed to third parties on behalf of patients be no more than the $6.50 maximum or actual cost of labor for preparing and sending such records, regardless of the format.  I remain eternally grateful to be able to do the important work I do everyday for my clients and want to continue to doing so for as long as I can- this will pave the way for me to do so much easier.  I thank you for your consideration.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Our firm represents injured clients, many of whom are injured in auto collisions or fall events. On behalf of those clients, we commonly request medical records. We do so not only because producing medical records is a requirement to substantiate their claim, but also because without a vehicle or with an injury, my clients are often unable to obtain their medical records on their own. Just attending doctor's appointments while trying to heal, care for their families, and still keep their jobs to put food on the table and keep the lights on is an immense struggle.
On average, my clients' medical records costs in a case total $500 on the low end, but commonly cost multiple thousands of dollars. In most cases, it takes many months to years to collect the record because of the immense delays caused by companies like Ciox and MRO. Additionally, it is not uncommon for hospitals to respond to a request for medical records from our office which specifies the exact dates of service we required with a records bill for thousands of pages of unrelated records, refusing to limit the retrieval to just the requested records and charging our clients hundreds of dollars per request for records they do not need.
I find this a severe miscarriage of justice. There is nothing so private as a person's medical records. And under HIPAA, medical records belong to the patient, NOT the medical providers or records departments. It is unconscionable that medical records collection should be allowed to become a for profit business. Patients should not be charged anything more than a mere copy fee for the exact records that they need for the precise reason that they already own what it is they are purchasing. Increased fees charged by companies like Ciox and MRO, exorbitant costs from hospitals for unnecessary or unrequested records, and lengthy delays put an immense burden on the patient.
From an attorney perspective, there is not a single penny to be made by our industry off of medical records collection. The costs expended to order medical bills and records is 100% passed on to the client. Whether the cost goes up or down, our fees are not changed. Only the amounts the client keeps from their much needed compensation awarded by a jury of their peers is affected. When a jury renders a verdict, they do not render a verdict to compensate them and the medical records department. Juries do not take into account the fact that plaintiffs owe thousands in medical records retrieval charges or that they paid a for-profit company like Ciox or MRO without choice just to obtain what it rightfully theirs. These companies should not be allowed under the laws of this nation to take a part of the compensation awarded to plaintiffs by juries for the actions of defendants. Medical retrieval companies and records departments should not have their hands in the pots of jury verdicts.

It is critically important to make changes to the HIPAA rules concerning mental health information shared with family members by mental health professionals.  My family experienced tremendous delays in the provision of vital care for our 18 year old son when he suffered psychosis and was hospitalized on an emergency basis.  It took years before we were able to get the information sharing established that was necessary in order to get our son proper treatment.  Allowing mental health professionals the discretion to share information with and freely accept information from family members will help those who need the help the most at the times when they are least able to make appropriate care decisions for themselves.  There must be a balance.  Right now, we are hurting those with mental health conditions by preventing the sharing of information.  Please fix this problem.

I am a Social Security Disability attorney with 13 years of experience representing people with disabilities in Social Security appeals and litigation. Our clients, many of whom are indigent and all of whom are disabled, have to bear the cost of paying for medical records copies to prove their disability cases.

Medical records needed for Social Security and SSI claims should be provided at no charge to the claimants and their appointed representatives, regardless of their format. Copies of medical records requested to support an application for, or appeal of, any claim under the Social Security Act should be provided free of charge when requested by the claimant or his/her appointed representative. HHS should adopt a rule like those of many states that prohibit medical providers from charging fees for copies of medical records when requested to advance a claim for Social Security benefits regardless of whether the records are requested by the claimant/patient or his/her representative. The right of access to direct the medical records to a third party should include both electronic and paper medical records. Alternatively, HHS’s proposed fee structure that would allow covered entities to charge a reasonable, cost-based fee should be applied to electronic and paper copies. If fees are to be charged, covered entities should provide advance notice of the approximate fees.If fees are to be charged, covered entities should not be able to deny requests for copies of medical records when the individual is unable to pay the fee. Many states offer such protection, particularly for claims for SSDI or SSI.The permitted response time to send the requested medical records should be no more than 15 calendar days with the opportunity for one 15-day extension. Representatives must submit relevant medical evidence no later than five business days before a hearing, so time is of the essence when requesting the records. I support recognizing an individual’s “clear, conspicuous, and specific” oral request for electronic copies of PHI in an EHR to be sent to a third party and prohibiting covered entities from imposing unreasonable identify verification measures on an individual exercising a right under the Privacy Rule.

The Social Security Act places responsibility for case development and submission of evidence on the claimant applying for Social Security disability benefits and requires appointed representatives to comply under the Act and regulations. The cost and time it takes ot obtain the records is vital to supporting disabiity claims.

I support the proposed revisions to the right of access provisions in the Privacy Rule to make clear that copies of medical records requested to support an application for, or appeal of, any claim under t he Social Security Act should be provided free of charge when requested by the claimant or appointed representative (III.A.9.bb). Most times it is necessary for appointed representatives to request records to effectively assist a client in the process. This process has grown more critical as representatives have been forced to undertake all medical development in preparation of evidence at hearing levels before the Office of Hearings Operations. The decision in CIox Health, LLC v. Azar, which vacated the extension of the patient rate for fees for copies of protected health information sent to third parties, makes this revision even more urgent and important.

I strongly believe that copies of medical records, whether electronic or non-electronic, should be provided free of charge to the Social Security disability claimants and their representatives, and that claimants and representatives should have the right of access to these records in any form they choose. I don't support the proposal (III.A.5.b) to limit right of access to transmission of electronic records.

Absent a rule providing for free access for Social Security disability claimants and their representatives, however, HHS should require that providers be limited to charging a reasonable, cost-based fee to furnish records supporting claims or appeals under the Act (III.A.6.b). Covered entities further should be required to provide advance notice of approximate fees for copies of PHI (III.A.7).

I support eliminating the current requirement that a request for an electronic copy of PHI be in writing and signed by the individual making the request. I support the proposed language requiring covered entities to comply with an oral or written request to provide PHI to a designated third party when the request is "clear, conspicuous, and specific" (III.B.2). I also support language to prohibit covered entities from imposing unreasonable indentity verification measures when individuals exercise their rights under the Privacy Rule. These proposed changes will be particularly helpful to individuals with disabilities applynig for Social Security disability benefits who wish to exercise their right of access under the Privacy Rule.

I support the HHS proposal to require covered entities provide copies of PHI no later than 15 calendar days, or less if another applicable federal or state law requires a shorter time period (III.A.3.b.ii). Delays in obtaining medical records all too often lead to denials of disability claims at the initial level, requiring the claimant to wait for an additional year or longer fore a hearing before an Administrative Law Judge. Prompt response to requests for PHI will allow more claims to be decided at the initial level, thus getting earned benefits to the claimant sooner and reducing the hearings backlog.

I also support prohibiting covered entities from denying requests for copies of PHI when the person is unable to pay the access fee, or owes other out standing fees (III.A.9.cc). Claimants for Supplemental Security Income payments should be deemed unable to pay. Many SSDI applicants are also unable to pay these fees. There are numerous State laws addressing this provision that could be used as a model, granting access without fee when appropriate. Lastly, I support prohibiting a covered entity from denying access or copies of records simply because the requesting individual owes fees fore any other service.

Thank you for allowing me to comment on the proposed modification of the HIPPA Privacy Rule.

I work in the legal industry, wherein it is imperative to request and receive the complete medical records file of our clients, in order to assist them. Before the HITECH Act, retrieving medical records was an expensive endeavor. Our clients (the patient) paid ridiculous fees out of their own pocket to their own providers and copy service subcontractors to have their records provided to our office. Sometimes, a client would offer to visit their providers to request and obtain their records to save money, but this was usually a frustrating and time sucking event. Then, when the HITECH Act kicked in, we started assisting our clients in sending out first party HITECH Act requests, listing our office as the designee. At first, the providers and copy subcontractors (CIOX) fought it tooth and nail. They were none too happy about the new structured reasonable cost-based fee, and they tried every dirty trick in the book. We were constantly being overcharged and filing complaints with DHHS. I actually had a provider tell me he used all the absorbent per page and administrative fees he charged, as his vacation fund (and the year before he had taken his wife and three kids to Hawaii for two weeks). As time went on, providers settled in and became familiar with the HITECH Act and the cost-based charges. It became easy, and the charges were predictable at $6.50 each (a charge my clients could afford). The providers also started providing the records faster than they ever had. It made it so easy. Then, the CIOX v. Azar decision occurred, and overnight we started receiving outlandish pre-payment requests from CIOX. A request that days earlier would have cost our client $6.50, was now going to cost $350.00 for records on a CD. How could this be?! These our medical records that belong to our own clients, and are just looking to have their records sent to their designee for convenience sake. But, because CIOX was being asked to send a CD containing records to an address other than the patient's, the cost went from $6.50 to hundreds and sometimes thousands of dollars. It was shocking. And, this all occurred overnight due to sheer greed and profiteering, from the same copying and distribution of patients medical records they had been doing days earlier. It's not right. There also seems to be a skewed view about a lawyers office requesting or receiving the records. I have heard many comments from both copy subcontractors (CIOX) and providers that "your lawyers, you can afford it" or "we charge attorneys more." It made absolutely no sense, as those expenses come right out of our clients' pockets, who happen to be patients of those providers. These are very same pockets that only have to pay $6.50, if the records are mailed to them. In the end, we need this process to be easy and affordable to our clients... as it was before the CIOX v. Azar decision. Giant companies, such as CIOX or even the smaller providers offices shouldn't be allowed to profit off healthcare records, it's shameful.
We ask that the proposed changes are put into affect as soon as possible. And that any additional underhanded tricks by the large copy companies are stopped. As of this week, I understand CIOX is now attempting to claim the time providers spend entering chart notes into any EHR system, is considered "labor." This is the next dirty trick they plan to initiate, in order increase their profits by increasing the cost-based mandated fees. Thereby the craziness will continue.
Thank you for your time.

I have represented Social Security disability claimants for the last 9 years. Our clients hire us with the expectation we will help them obtain evidence in their claim and make sure their case stays on track with Social Security. Clients need help because it is a long and confusing process and they often do not know where to begin or what is required to be successful in their claim. In order to find a claimant eligible for disability benefits, Social Security requires medical evidence to support the claim.

-The cost of paper or electronic medical records should be free when requested by a claimant/patient or a representative in a Social Security disability claim.
-Many states already have statutes in place that prohibit a provider from charging for medical records requested by a claimant or a claimant’s representative for use in a Social Security disability claim.
-HHS should adopt a similar rule prohibiting medical providers from charging fees for paper or electronic copies of medical records that will be used in a claim for Social Security disability benefits, regardless of whether the request comes from the claimant/patient or the representative.

Clients are not well equipped to deal with the time it takes to obtain medical records. We find that providers frequently do not respond to faxed or mailed requests, do not answer the phone when we call to follow-up on the request, claim they never received the request, or do not follow the required time frames to turn over medical records.

-Social Security expects representatives to submit evidence before the hearing to avoid delays. Therefore, providers should not have more than 15 days with an optional one time 15 day extension to provide medical records.

Delays in obtaining medical records and charges for medical records hurt Social Security disability claimants and their ability to adequately support their claim. Disability claimants (on their own or through their representative) deserve fair and timely access to their medical records in all forms (paper and electronic).

Dear Acting Director Frohboese,

I work with a number of small and medium-sized medical practices to assess, and improve and monitor compliance with HIPAA. I am writing on behalf of these practices to encourage OCR to establish clear guidance on the interaction between HIPAA, ONC's Cures Act requirements on information blocking, and recent changes to the laws on confidentiality of mental health and substance abuse disorders.

Providers must comply with a mosaic of administrative and technical requirements including Federal and State law, professional standards, insurance policy terms, and payor requirements. This creates an administrative burden that diverts resources away from patient case and, in my opinion, erodes provider confidence in healthcare law.

Patients are often alarmed or offended by documentation that is considered routine by providers. For example, providers document routine screening measures for drug-seeking behavior. State laws and malpractice insurance policies require providers to document concerns about the patient's compliance with a treatment plan, assessments of patient welfare, and any real or potential indicators of doctor shopping or malingering.

Providers are concerned these disclosure of these notes will result in complaints or lawsuits from patients who are not familiar with the regulatory requirements. This is a particular concern in the case of workers' compensation cases or disputes over guardianship.

A lack of clear guidance on how to evaluate these scenarios will discourage providers from documenting valid concerns. Notes that could be misunderstood, or those that require lengthy explanations, will simply not be documented.

While I agree with the spirit of the proposed HIPAA regulations and the ONC Cures Act, I strongly encourage you to postpone the implementation of any HIPAA revisions until HHS and ONC have agreed upon clear guidance for providers and their staff.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Family planning is important because it allows individuals to achieve desired birth spacing and family size, and contributes to improved health outcomes for infants, children, women, and families. Family planning services include: Contraceptive services, pregnancy testing and counseling, pregnancy–achieving services including preconception health services, basic infertility services ,sexually transmitted disease services, broader reproductive health services, including patient education and counseling, breast and pelvic examinations, breast and cervical cancer screening, sexually transmitted infection (STI) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) prevention education, and counseling, testing, and referral.

Because of the 2019 rules so many clinics have shut down leaving people especially low-income individuals and minorities without access to the family planning services they need. Again, I urge the immediate approval for the readoption of the 2000 regulations with your proposed modifications, which will be used for establishing standards for compliance by family planning services projects authorized by Title X of the Public Health Service Act by the Office of Population Affairs (OPA), and the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health.

Dear Office of Population Affairs,

MHIRJ wishes to inform the FAA that during a recent proof installation with Service Bulletin (SB) 601R-35-022 by one of our operators in the US, it was reported that the corrective action to relocate the lighting strip power harness through a new top panel penetration point has resulted in an unforeseen new potential fouling condition with existing bracket. As a result of this finding, MHIRJ is recommending that the Service Bulletin be temporarily halted until further notice. To this effect, MHIRJ issued an AOM 1774, dated April 1 2022 (copy attached) to inform our operators.
MHIRH is currently revising the SB to revision B with a target for release by end of April 2022. Aircraft that have completed the corrective action per SB rev NC or A, will require to go back and trim existing aluminum bracket to ensure clearance with the harness.

Furthermore, MHIRJ recommends that the FAA delay the release of the final rule so that the AD refers to SB revision B.

Subject: DOCKET No. FAA-2022-0989; Project Identifier AD-2022-00468-E, General Electric Company (GE) GE90-90B, GE90-94B, GE90-110B1 and GE90-115B Model Turbofan Engines

These are FedEx Express’s comments regarding NPRM Docket No. FAA-2022-0989; Project Identifier AD-2022-00468-E which proposes to adopt a new Airworthiness Directive (AD) that applies to General Electric Company (GE) GE90-90B, GE90-94B, GE90-110B1 and GE90-115B turbofan engines with an installed high-pressure turbine (HPT) stage 1 disk, HPT stage 2 disk, or stages 7-9 compressor rotor spool with a part number (P/N) and serial number (S/N) identified in Table 1 to paragraph (c) of the AD. The proposed AD would require the replacement of the affected components per specific required compliance times noted in GE90-100 SBs 72-0893 (R01), 72-0897, and 72-0899.
General: FedEx agrees with the intent of this NPRM.
Operational Impact: FedEx Express will not experience any on wing operational impact resulting from the issuance of an AD that this NPRM proposes. FedEx does not have any of the affected HPT stage 1 disks, HPT stage 2 disks, or the single affected HPC stage 7-9 spool in the FedEx fleet.
Economical Impact: FedEx does not have any of the affected components in the FedEx fleet therefore the proposed AD will not have an economic impact at FedEx.
Summary: FedEx does not have any of the components listed by specific serial numbers in the related GE90-100 SBs 72-0893 (R1), 72-0897, and 72-0899 therefore the issuance of an AD will have no impact on FedEx’s operation.
FedEx will issue a document to prevent the installation of the affected HPC 7-9 spool and the affected HPT stage 1 and 2 disks following issuance of the proposed AD.

I submit these comments in response to the FAA notice of rulemaking promulgated on July 29, 2022. These comments specifically address the FAA’s mischaracterization of the Town’s actions and the status of the litigation against the Town of East Hampton relating to the East Hampton Town Airport (the “Airport”).

First, the notice fails to mention the myriad initial issues raised by the Town’s arbitrary and capricious plan to close and reopen the HTO Airport. As made clear by Ms. Kennington-Gardiner, the Regional Administrator of the FAA, in her February 2, 2022 letter, the HTO Airport could not transform into a private-use airport with the Town’s planned noise and access restrictions overnight. Any mention of that letter or the FAA’s serious concerns with the initial process is conspicuously absent. Specifically, Ms. Kennington-Gardiner’s letter raised the issue of whether, despite the expiration of federal grant assurances, certain federal statutory obligations remained in effect and could not be ‘extinguished’ by the nominal closing and re-opening of the airport, including exclusive rights, revenue use, and civil rights obligations. That issue is the subject of a pending Part 16 proceeding before the FAA. After that letter from the FAA and three lawsuits seeking temporary injunctive relief were filed in February 2022, the Town postponed its deactivation-and-reactivation to May 17, 2022.

As the FAA correctly notes, the New York Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Baisley, J.S.C.) issued three temporary restraining orders on May 16, 2022—the day before the HTO Airport was scheduled to deactivate—in substance, precluding such deactivation. Five minutes before midnight on May 17, 2022, the Town filed another letter from Ms. Kennington-Gardiner. Although the Town insists that the FAA has deactivated the public-use “HTO” identifier and activated “JPX” as a private-use identifier, it is clear that the FAA’s May 17, 2022 letter alone does not evince transformation of the airport from public to private use, particularly in light of three court orders explicitly preventing that. Instead, Ms. Kennington-Gardiner merely concluded in her May 17 letter that it would be “more prudent to continue operating the airport under the JPX identifier after May 19, 2022.” Rather than converting the Airport from public to private use, the airport merely took on a new location identifier. Consequently, the statement that the Airport is now a private-use airport as a result of the FAA deactivation of HTO is false and contrary to the explicit order of the Supreme Court; orders which were upheld on appeal.

It is also not clear when the deactivation of the HTO identifier became irreversible. It seems that the Town could have stopped the deactivation process far earlier, despite its representation to the Court that continuing to take administrative steps after February 18, 2022 would not render the process irreversible.
Further, the statement that the Town took steps to effectuate the Court’s order is blatantly untrue. Rather, the Town intentionally disregarded the Court’s orders and has continued its crusade of imposing restrictions on the use of the Airport. Despite the Court’s orders, the “JPX” Airport is operating as a private-use airport. As explained in certain petitioners’ pending motion for contempt against the Town, the Town has instituted a variety of measures effectively privatizing the airport. Users of the “JPX” Airport are required to utilize special-use instrument procedures to operate at the Airport that are not available to the general public. The Town is requiring potential users of the special-use instrument procedures to submit an application and is either no longer or sporadically processing such applications with the added requirement of providing proof of insurance and indemnification. The Town further purports that FAA approval of each application is required. The FAA has not said that advanced written permission and indemnification is required; rather, to permit public access to the Airport, the Town should dispense with these requirements.

Finally, it is incorrect to state that the Airport’s operating status has “remained in flux.” The operating status of the Airport has been and remains public-use, which was solidified by the temporary restraining orders issued by the Supreme Court on May 16, 2022. The fact that the Town has blatantly violated the Court’s orders does not affect the fact that the Airport is a public-use facility.

As I write this at 3:27 PM on 8/27/2022, I hear the drone of a helicopter overhead in Wading River, NY and am also able to confirm its location on the website https://www.radarbox.com/@40.94991,-73.23514,z12
The aircraft is identified as a “Blocked” helicopter with no information regarding its flight plan or aircraft serial number. Originating in NJ, the flight pattern followed the North Shore of Long Island over the Long Island Sound until the helicopter turned at Wading River, crossed Long Island in a south-easterly direction, reached Smith Point and then traveled east along the South Shore of Long Island to its final destination, arriving at 3:40 PM at East Hampton Airport. This helicopter did not fly around Orient Point to its destination in East Hampton per the all-water North Shore Helicopter Route.

This is a daily occurrence that can be both heard and seen on the radarbox.com website along with the vibration that is felt when helicopters are flying lower than the required minimum altitude of 2,500 feet.

In 2008 The North Shore Helicopter Route was developed by the FAA with the East End Helicopter Group voluntarily agreeing to an all water route one mile off the North Shore of Long Island from Lloyd Harbor, NY to Orient Point, NY flying at a minimum altitude of 2500 feet. It was codified by the FAA as the final rule in subpart H of part 93 of title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) in 2012.

Ah….sorry for the interruption but the drone of another helicopter can be both heard and felt: Registration N****, Serial No. ******. It departed from Bridgeport, CT at 3:10 PM on 8/27/2022, crossed Long Island Sound and began its crossing over land at Sound Beach, NY at an altitude of 1,925 feet (lower than minimum altitude of 2,500 feet); crossed over Wading River, NY at 1,925 feet and continued in a south-easterly direction. It then reached the Shinnecock Tidal Wetlands, turned east and traveled along the South Shore of Long Island arriving at its final destination, East Hampton Airport. An example of another helicopter that did not fly the all-water North Shore Helicopter Route around Orient Point to East Hampton…which is actually the norm.

As was just evidenced, the “voluntary” agreement that was codified is not being followed. The pilots that do follow the all water North Shore Helicopter Route are few and far between...and I am grateful to them.

In the notice of extension (issued July 2022, footnote 10) “The FAA notes that operators voluntarily agreed to fly the all-water route around Orient Point, and it appears that many operators, while continuing to comply with the regulation, have ceased flying the all-water route.”

The fact that the FAA is acknowledging that the pilots are no longer “voluntarily” flying the all-water route around Orient Point indicates the need for a renewed agreement with the East End Helicopter Group, enforcement of the codified federal regulation and a commitment to the residents of the North Shore who are deserving of the right to a noise and air pollution free existence while the East Hampton Airport closure or non closure unfolds.

It seems convenient for the FAA to extend the operation of the North Shore Helicopter Route by claiming the extension will avoid disruption of the current operating environment...However, there doesn’t seem to be any consideration regarding the disruption to the lives of the residents of the North Shore.

The FAA rule has been extended three times without change. How many more years will the FAA continue to force extensions on the residents of Long Island claiming that it needs time to determine appropriate future actions for helicopter traffic? This four-year extension is an excessive amount of time to impose on the residents of the North Shore when no opportunity to voice concerns has been afforded to them.

It’s time to include the public in the equation.
