These are comments I spoke at the hearing today, with citations and references.
Mothers & Others For Clean Air strongly supports granting California the cleaner truck waivers that is has applied for. California has very serious problems with health-damaging air pollution, and needs these cleaner truck standards as soon as possible to protect public health. But not only do the waivers protect public health in California, they protect public health all over the country. Other states follow California standards, and California standards mean that more clean trucks are part of the mix on highways all over the country. Between the other states that follow California standards, and the fact that air pollution crosses state borders, the California standards improve health for people all over the country, including where I live in Georgia.

Trucks are a major contributor to air pollution in cities and the air pollution they create or increase formation of, includes nitrogen oxides, particulates, and ozone. This traffic-related air pollution is very damaging to health. Just this week the Health Effects Institute released a meta-analysis of traffic related air pollution, showing that it causes increased mortality for all-cause, circulatory, ischemic heart disease, and lung cancer, causes new onset asthma in children and adults, and lower respiratory tract infections in children.

Not only that, because of red-lining and other forms of environmental racism, communities of color have had more highways and trucking distribution centers built in or near them, and therefore have more exposure to health-damaging air pollution.

As a pediatrician, I know that air pollution is very harmful to children, and that children do not have equal exposure to air pollution. Children spend more time outside and breathe more air for their weight than adults. As stated earlier, traffic related air pollution is strongly linked to asthma in children. If you have ever had to give a breathing treatment to a child struggling to breathe during an asthma attack, it is not something you will ever forget.

Nitrogen oxides and particulate air pollution damage children’s lung growth through the teen years, so that their lungs end up smaller than normal. This sets them for a lifetime of lung problems when they are adults.

A recent Lung Association report found that transition to zero emissions energy and transportation, including trucks and other heavy-duty vehicles, would provide billions of dollars in health benefits and prevent tens of thousands of premature deaths.

And again, because exposure is so inequitable, communities of color would benefit more from the health benefits from reduced truck air pollution.

Mothers & Others For Clean thinks there is enough health harm from truck air pollution, that California and the EPA are well within their duties to regulate truck air pollution to protect health, especially the health of vulnerable populations such as children, pregnant women, and communities of color.

I urge EPA to quickly approve these waivers, which will protect public health, and prevent deaths, asthma, and lower respiratory infections.

Hispanic Access Foundation, a Latina-led and Latino-serving nonprofit, is writing in support of enabling the strongest possible rules that curb air pollution. We need to protect the health and safety of Latino and other disinvested communities who disproportionately bear the burden of health problems caused by pollution emissions. It is important for us and the communities that we serve, that the EPA create the strongest possible limits - and enable the creation of even stronger limits by individual states like California - on heavy duty vehicle pollution to protect public health and reduce the climate impacts that we and our future generations will face.

Rules that curb pollution such as this one are essential to protecting the well-being of our communities:

--Smog and soot air pollution caused by trucks and buses are among the greatest threats to public health for the more than 45 million people in the U.S. living within 300 feet of a major roadway or transportation facility. It’s even worse for the more than 56 million Latinos who live in the 15 worst urban areas for ground-level ozone pollution.
--Air pollution from vehicle emissions increases asthma risk and severity. Latinos are twice as likely to go to the emergency room for asthma, and Latino children are twice as likely to die from asthma as white children. Over 3.6 million Latinos suffer from asthma.
--Additionally, the virus that causes COVID-19 spreads more quickly in areas with more air pollution, which are disproportionately inhabited by Latinos and other communities of color. Studies have established a direct link between exposure to air pollution and COVID-19 mortality. Even during the brief shutdowns in 2020, when air pollution decreased in most urban areas, the pollutant nitrogen dioxide remained disproportionately higher in marginalized areas, likely due to continued industrial pollution and heavy-duty trucking.
--Latinos and other communities of color are disproportionately exposed to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) pollution. This type of pollution is the largest environmental cause of human mortality. Latinos are 165% more likely to live in counties with unhealthy levels of particulate matter pollution.

On behalf of the undersigned groups and the concerned Michigan residents that we represent, we urge the EPA to approve California’s three Clean Air Act waiver requests in full and without delay, allowing states to enforce more stringent heavy-duty vehicle standards that will protect public health and help alleviate local air pollution challenges.

Michigan is one of the 5 states that committed to accelerating medium- and heavy-duty vehicle electrification by signing the Regional Electric Vehicle Midwest Coalition Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). Our state has also set a goal of reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions 52% below 2005 levels by 2030 and transitioning the State’s fleet of medium- and heavy-duty vehicles to 100 percent zero-emission by 2045. Since the national medium- and heavy-duty vehicle emission standards are less stringent, states like Michigan must be allowed to act to adopt and enforce the stronger CA ACT Zero Emission and Heavy Duty Omnibus rules in order to meet the goals of the MOU, adhere to federal clean air requirements, and meet the state’s climate goals. Granting the waivers for these rules will protect public health, stimulate the economy, and enable states to mitigate the twin crises of air pollution and climate change.

The ACT and HDO regulations are crucial in the fight against toxic diesel pollution in Michigan that disproportionately harms frontline communities. Exhaust from diesel trucks and buses is a leading source of harmful air pollution that sends countless Michigan residents to the hospital every year. The transportation sector accounts for 32 percent of all greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from all on road vehicles annually. Communities located near major roads and highways suffer disproportionate burdens from traffic and transportation pollution. These neighborhoods are often communities of color due to decades of racist policies, and bear a burden of unsafe pedestrian conditions, higher rates of asthma, and unremitting noise pollution.

The human health and climate impacts of diesel pollution demonstrate the magnitude of this problem and why it is imperative that states have the ability to enforce stronger vehicle emission standards. The latest IPCC report says we are running out of time to take bold action on the climate crisis that impacts us all, and especially those in frontline communities. The Advanced Clean Trucks (ACT) rule and the Heavy-Duty Omnibus (HDO) Low NOx regulation are the best tools states currently have for slashing criteria and greenhouse gas emissions from the transportation sector.

The benefits of the ACT and HDO rules in Michigan are enormous. A recent Synapse report found that transitioning to clean medium- and heavy-duty vehicles would bring over $20 billion cumulative benefits of reduced GHG emissions to Michigan from 2021-2050. The report also found that in a scenario in which 24 percent of MDVs and HDVs are electric by 2035, cumulative motor vehicle CO2 emissions would be reduced by approximately 53 percent in 2035 and approximately 94 percent by 2050.

In addition to their substantial public health benefits, these rules are rooted in extensive research, analysis, and stakeholder outreach. Consequently, they are cost-effective and technologically-feasible, and do not rely on additional complementary policies to be successful.

It is critical to Michigan’s public health and economy that the EPA follow decades-long precedent and fully approve the waiver requests for California’s Heavy-Duty Program, specifically the three waiver requests for the Heavy-Duty Low NOx Omnibus Rule, the Advanced Clean Trucks, Zero Emission Airport Shuttle, and Zero-Emission Power Train Certification Regulations, and the Heavy-Duty Emission Warranty Regulation amendments. Granting a partial waiver would unnecessarily delay lifesaving emission reductions and have far reaching consequences. Therefore, we urge you to fully grant California’s current waiver requests as soon as possible.

The proposed changes in the above stated rule were brought to our attention in late January 2023 by a colleague at a product and materials testing laboratory. Few manufacturers have personnel assigned to watch for updates in the Federal Register.

HVAC related associations have been developing training materials for their members. They should be used for testing and certifying HVAC technicians. I also recommend a thorough vetting of the questions and answers.  The last test put together by the EPA contained answers specifically on refrigerant pressures that required me to make up a fake pressure temperature table for use on the test only so the correct answer could be obtained.

Using reclaimed hydrofluorocarbons for current units is a more sustainable way to reuse these chemicals in a more sustainable way. This could decrease emissions and waste of HFCs and the appliances that use them, if established effectively. HFCs have a much higher global warming potential than carbon dioxide, too (Certified Reclaimed HFC Refrigerants, Propellants, and Fire Suppressants, 2019). We must establish proper reclamation practices to make this effort successful.

An important aspect of reclaiming HFC’s is focusing on the supply chain. Throughout the life cycle of HFCs – creation, use, and waste. But now we know we do not have to dispose of them, they can be reused and repurified and be reinstalled into refrigerants. The circular supply chain must be deeply considered in this process. Having regional reclamation sites should be considered so that more emissions are not exuded from flying reclaimed HFC’s across the country. The largest category of use for HFCs is industrial cooling systems, like refrigerators and freezers. This makes up almost 50% of all HFC use. The next category is mobile air conditioning units make up about 25% of total HFC usage (Climate and Clean Air Coalition, 1970). Having a clear and detailed plan of sustainable and circular supply chain processes brought to these two main categories of HFC’s will aid greatly in the reclamation process. Regular disclosures of large owners of these 2 categories should be mandated to help the information gather process.

Incentives should be in place for owners of larger industrial coolers and freezers. Also take into consideration large trucking or car dealership organizations, which also contribute largely to HFC use. Without any incentive, there is nothing stopping these 2 sectors from carrying on as they usually do. A financial incentive would motivate them to join the reclamation market for HFCs. Slight tax breaks, rebates, or subsidies should be highly considered in offering to large HFC consumer markets. With a financial incentive the reclamation process would only become more widely used and more efficient.

Gasoline
Diesel
Solvents
Oil
Oxygen
Acetylene
MAPP

Most citizens and nearly all technicians are also familiar with household flammables such as:
Propane (RV, grille, torch - heavier than air)
Natural Gas (furnace, stove, cook-top - lighter than air)
Alcohols
Butane (lighter, torch, camp stove - much heavier than air)

I am an employee of an HVAC distribution franchise, Johnstone Supply. We have over 150 team members and serve over 9000 HVAC contractors, businesses and government organizations in Maryland, New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia. I am reaching out regarding the refrigerant management rule proposal.

We recognize and appreciate the role HVAC distributors play in the effort to curb climate change. Educating our contractors so the most energy efficient products are installed while utilizing environmentally friendly practices is imperative. We welcome practical legislation that will support this process without adding additional carbon footprint to the system. There are several key aspects in the EPA's refrigerant management rules will have negative supply chain outcomes or result in a larger carbon footprint.

One concerning rule requires OEMs to use reclaim in factory charges. We are moving to a new low GWP refrigerant in 2025 and the technology transition rule requires OEMs use reclaim for factory charges in 2028. To enable this rule to be followed, the following steps would need to occur. A large installed base must experience catastrophic leaks in 3 years, requiring contractors to evacuate refrigerant from the system, return to a distributor and in turn returned to a reclaimer for processing. New HVAC equipment installed by contractors does not experience system leaks at a high rate in the first 3 years after installation. As a result, a very minimal quantity of reclaimed low GWP refrigerant would be available between 2025 and 2028. The lack of available reclaimed refrigerant, paired with a requirement of OEMs to use reclaim for factory charges would conspire to create a shortage of new HVAC equipment. There is not enough time to reclaim a meaningful supply of refrigerant from the installed base to cover the demand and would result in severe shortage of available equipment.

Another concerning aspect of the rule is the requirement to send all disposable cylinders to a reclaimer to capture heel charges. Contractors pay a substantial sum for new refrigerant cylinders and have large incentives to use all available refrigerant in each cylinder. There may be a couple of ounces of refrigerant left in each cylinder, or .5% of the refrigerant.

Our organization has sold over 15,000 disposable refrigerant cylinders year to date. This rule would require we ship the product back to a reclaimer for processing. We would have to pick up cylinders from our contractors or have them returned, palletize and handle, and then ship them back to a reclaimer. Shipping empty disposable cylinders on tractor trailers is not an environmentally friendly activity. The carbon footprint generated this process would greatly exceed any benefit of reclaiming a couple of ounces of refrigerant. Another option would be to make the cylinders of recyclable material. We support rules that cost effectively reduce carbon footprint, but this will have the opposite effect.

We also oppose the rule requiring QR code tracking requirements for disposable refrigerant. This rule has already been struck down by a court as beyond the authority of the AIM act and should not be proposed under another subsection.

We would welcome the opportunity for further discussion. Please feel free to reach out with any questions.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency proposes a rule to develop an additional program for managing hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) in subsection (h), as stated in the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2020. The proposed rule is called the "Phasedown of Hydrofluorocarbons: Management of Certain Hydrofluorocarbons and Substitutes Under Subsection (h) of the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2020" (Docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2022-0606-0014). There needs to be more awareness about the environmental impacts for those who frequently work with HFC refrigerants and those who advocate for environmental justice.
Initially, Hydrofluorocarbons were manufactured because they were assumed to be less damaging to the ozone layer (Washington State Department of Ecology State, 2023). The HFC Phasedown Program states that by 2036, production and consumption will be reduced by 85% (Environmental Protection Agency, 2023) under the new regulations. These revised regulations would provide health benefits to the technicians and their consumers. There are also environmental benefits, as the program will encourage recycling HFCs to reduce greenhouse gas production rates.
Many citizens argue that more training in managing hydrofluorocarbons in flammable refrigerators serves no purpose. The reasoning is that several technicians do not believe they need to be trained or tested on this gas if they know the safety protocols for handling such products. However, only some have the same expertise, and the availability of training or recertification on current HFC trends and usages will be helpful to some people. It would be beneficial to have more technicians who are more knowledgeable on this subject as it will ensure the safety of themselves and their consumers.
In addition, the tracking system proposed by the rule is non-invasive. Requiring machine-readable tracking identifiers [e.g., quick-response (QR) codes or another type of identifier] on all containers of HFCs (Environmental Protection Agency, 2023) will not affect the work ethic of the people involved. It is simplistic, and it will provide much-needed data to support the movement of managing hydrofluorocarbons.
For the companies for this transition, states are providing incentive programs to help them adjust to the new standards proposed by the EPA. California and Delaware have programs to increase the use of refrigerants with low amounts of Global Warming Impacts (GWPs). For example, the "Delaware Cool Switch" program will provide a rate of $25 per ton of avoided CO2 equivalent emissions to businesses that work with refrigerants (Delaware Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control, 2023). This is a great way to show support for the proposed rule because it is evident that businesses will lose a significant portion of funding with the transition to eco-friendly refrigerants.
This proposed rule is a good starting point to start the conversation about how hydrofluorocarbons affect climate temperatures and overall greenhouse gas consumption. I wish the proposed rule had more data on the environmental and health impacts of not switching to friendlier HFCs instead of "briefly" discussing it, as it would have strengthened the argument. With the testing that this rule suggests, the data on HFCs can bring more perspective, and researchers from the Environmental Protection Agency can develop a prototype to serve the goal, which is to participate in reducing greenhouse gas consumption.

Works Cited

Delaware Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control. “Cool Switch Low Impact Refrigerant Program.” DNREC, 21 Apr. 2022, dnrec.delaware.gov/climate-coastal-energy/efficiency/cool-switch/.

United States Environmental Protection Agency. “Management of Certain Hydrofluorocarbons and Substitutes under Subsection (h) of the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act.” United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2023, www.epa.gov/climate-hfcs-reduction/management-certain-hydrofluorocarbons-and-substitutes-under-subsection-h.

The Sierra Club and Environmental Integrity Project's complete set of comments on this proposed rulemaking is attached as a PDF for your review.

SUMMARY:

A.Regulation 61–62.1, Section (II)(G)(6) (now Regulation 61-62.1, Section (II)(L))

In the 2015 SSM SIP Action, EPA issued a SIP call for S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 62.1, Section (II)(G)(6), because it impermissibly provides an affirmative defense for excess emissions during emergencies. In response to EPA’s SIP Call, South Carolina’s November 4, 2016, SIP submission seeks to remove the provision providing for this affirmative defense (originally set forth in Section (II)(G)(6), now in Section (II)(L)(2))—“An emergency constitutes an affirmative defense to an action brought for noncompliance with such technology-based emission limitations if the conditions in [Section II.L.3 below] are met.” The Sierra Club and EIP support the removal of this language from the South Carolina SIP and respectfully request that EPA act quickly to finalize this revision.

B.Regulation 61–62.5, Standard No. 1, Section (I)(C)

In the 2015 SSM SIP Action, EPA issued a SIP call for S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 61–62.5 Standard No. 1, Section (I)(C), because it impermissibly provides an exemption from opacity limits for excess emissions from fuel-burning operations that occur during startup or shutdown. South Carolina seeks to remove the first sentence of Regulation 61–62.5, Standard No. 1, Section (I)(C), that provides the exemption. The portion being removed states, “The opacity standards set forth above do not apply during startup or shutdown.” The Sierra Club and EIP support the removal of this sentence and respectfully request that EPA act quickly to finalize the removal of this language from Regulation 61–62.5, Standard No. 1, Section (I)(C), in the South Carolina SIP.

Along with removing the first sentence of Section (I)(C), EPA has also proposed to act on two other revisions to this SIP-called provision submitted by the state on July 18, 2011 and August 12, 2015. Specifically, South Carolina has amended the language in Regulation 61–62.5, Standard No. 1, Section (I)(C) to exclude natural gas-fired units and propane-fired units from the SIP requirement to maintain startup, shutdown, and maintenance records. EPA has proposed to adopt South Carolina’s revised Section (I)(C) into the SIP with the following additional change:

"Owners and operators shall, to the extent practicable, maintain and operate any source including associated air pollution control equipment in a manner consistent with good air pollution control practices for minimizing emissions. In addition, the owner or operator of fuel burning sources EXCEPT NATURAL GAS AND PROPANE FIRED UNITS, shall maintain a log of the time, magnitude, duration and any other pertinent information to determine periods of startup and shutdown and make available to the Department upon request."

Sierra Club and EIP disagree with this portion of the proposed revision to South Carolina’s SIP Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 1(C).

Although emissions from the burning of natural gas and propane fuels tend in general to result in fewer visible emissions than from coal-fired units, these sources still have the potential to emit elevated levels of particulate matter, sulfur oxides, nitrogen oxides, and other pollutants that contribute to opacity during SSM events. Because adequate recordkeeping of startup and shutdown events is essential for the Administrator and public to determine whether a source is in compliance with the CAA, South Carolina’s exemption of these two classes of fuel-burning sources from necessary recordkeeping requirements for periods of startup and shutdown not only undermines applicable emission limits found in South Carolina’s SIP—which apply at all times, including during startup and shutdown, but also frustrates federal CAA enforcement. Accordingly, EPA should—under CAA section 110(k)(4)—conditionally approve the revised Standard No. 1(C), provided that South Carolina removes the “except natural gas and propane fired units” language no later than one year after the date of EPA’s approval. Alternately, EPA could disapprove this portion of the revised Standard No. 1(C).

C.Regulation 61–62.5, Standard No. 4, Section (XI)(D)(4)

In the 2015 SSM SIP Action, EPA issued a SIP call for S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 61–62.5 Standard No. 4, Section (XI)(D)(4) because it impermissibly provides an exemption from sulfur limits for kraft pulp mills for excess emissions during SSM. South Carolina’s November 4, 2016, SIP submission seeks to remove Regulation 61–62.5, Standard No. 4, Section (XI)(D)(4) from the SIP, thereby eliminating the impermissible SSM exemption. The Sierra Club and EIP support this revision and respectfully request that EPA act quickly to finalize the removal of Section (XI)(D)(4) from the South Carolina SIP.

I am an owner of an HVAC distribution franchise, Johnstone Supply. We have over 150 employees and serve over 9000 HVAC contractors, businesses and government organizations in Maryland, New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia. I am reaching out regarding the refrigerant management rule proposal.
We recognize and appreciate the role HVAC distributors play in the effort to curb climate change. Educating our contractors so the most energy efficient products are installed while utilizing environmentally friendly practices is imperative. We welcome practical legislation that will support this process without adding additional carbon footprint to the system. There are several key aspects in the EPA's refrigerant management rules will have negative supply chain outcomes or result in a larger carbon footprint.
One concerning rule requires OEMs to use reclaim in factory charges. We are moving to a new low GWP refrigerant in 2025 and the technology transition rule requires OEMs use reclaim for factory charges in 2028. To enable this rule to be followed, the following steps would need to occur. A large installed base must experience catastrophic leaks in 3 years, requiring contractors to evacuate refrigerant from the system, return to a distributor and in turn returned to a reclaimer for processing. New HVAC equipment installed by contractors does not experience system leaks at a high rate in the first 3 years after installation. As a result, a very minimal quantity of reclaimed low GWP refrigerant would be available between 2025 and 2028. The lack of available reclaimed refrigerant, paired with a requirement of OEMs to use reclaim for factory charges would conspire to create a shortage of new HVAC equipment. There is not enough time to reclaim a meaningful supply of refrigerant from the installed base to cover the demand and would result in severe shortage of available equipment.
Another concerning aspect of the rule is the requirement to send all disposable cylinders to a reclaimer to capture heel charges. Contractors pay a substantial sum for new refrigerant cylinders and have large incentives to use all available refrigerant in each cylinder. There may be a couple of ounces of refrigerant left in each cylinder, or .5% of the refrigerant.
Our organization has sold over 15,000 disposable refrigerant cylinders year to date. This rule would require we ship the product back to a reclaimer for processing. We would have to pick up cylinders from our contractors or have them returned, palletize and handle, and then ship them back to a reclaimer. Shipping empty disposable cylinders on tractor trailers is not an environmentally friendly activity. The carbon footprint generated this process would greatly exceed any benefit of reclaiming a couple of ounces of refrigerant. Another option would be to make the cylinders of recyclable material. We support rules that cost effectively reduce carbon footprint, but this will have the opposite effect.
We also oppose the rule requiring QR code tracking requirements for disposable refrigerant. This rule has already been struck down by a court as beyond the authority of the AIM act and should not be proposed under another subsection.
We would welcome the opportunity for further discussion. Please feel free to reach out with any questions.

I am a junior Environmental Policy major at Loyola University Chicago in Chicago, IL. and have recently become interested in the “Significant New Use Rules on Certain Chemical Substances (22-2.5e)” regulation because I am in the process of researching the public health and environmental effects of ethylene oxide on the community of Institute, West Virginia. After significant research on the topic, I feel my knowledge on the long term effects of chemicals like ethylene oxide will allow me to really contribute to the analysis of this regulation.
When reviewing the proposed rule document, I noticed that under the Significant New Use Determination it states that if a chemical poses “an unreasonable risk of injury to human health … TSCA Order requires that potentially exposed employees wear specified respirators unless … concentrations of the PNM (premanufacture notice) substance are below a New Chemical Exposure Limit (NCEL)” (Environmental Protection Agency, 2022). This allowance runs the risk that exposure to chemical carcinogens at rates below the NCEL will lead to the development of different types of cancer such as breast and lymphatic (National Institute of Health, 2022). Due to the extreme effects of any exposure to chemical carcinogens, I believe that the EPA should consider extending the number of days that chemical manufacturers and processors have to notify the agency before any commencement occurs. For example, the standard of 90 days should be increased to 120 if the proposed significant new use of the PNM is a “known” carcinogen and has the potential to affect surrounding communities. In this case, I encourage the EPA to increase the required testing, regulatory restrictions, and perform an extensive review/background check of the neighborhoods and communities that surround the manufacturing plant/processing facility and use that information as a basis of determining whether or not the PNM submitter should find alternative chemicals or substantially limit exposure levels. As another form of precaution, I believe that if chemical substances known to be human carcinogens are being released at any capacity, whether above or below the NCEL, manufacturers or anyone in close contact should be required to wear a respirator. Even though most cases of cancer caused by chemical exposure occur over long periods of time at high exposure levels, some substances may lead to cancer after only a very small exposure (American Cancer Society, 2022). For example, chemicals like Benzene and Ethylene Oxide pose serious long term health effects like high risks of leukemia, lymphoma, and breast cancer that need to be addressed and explained to chemical plant workers and neighboring communities. The effects of these chemicals should not be taken lightly and is why the implementation of a longer time-frame for chemical testing/review and required respirator masks at all levels of chemical carcinogen exposure is crucial to keeping workers and communities safe.

I am a former government attorney with extensive litigation and policy experience. My area of concentration is employment discrimination, with a focus on the federal sector.

I write, initially, to note my alliance with those urging that the Cummings Act be broadly construed. I also write to note what I view as an unacknowledged "elephant in the room."

It is clear that the goal of the Cummings Act is to use transparency and accountability as tools to eradicate discrimination and retaliation in federal employment. It is equally clear, however, that this goal is materially hindered by a policy reflected in EEOC’s regulation at 29 CFR 1614.409, which EEOC interprets as mandating dismissal of an appeal if a complainant files in court for any reason relating to the underlying complaint. Dismissal is mandated even in cases where EEOC (at the appellate or hearing level) has rendered a “finding” with respect to a claim asserted in the complaint Subsection 409 thus codifies a policy that perversely operates to allow discriminating agencies to ESCAPE accountability in the administrative process.

I am on record as taking the position that EEOC exceeded its authority when it undertook to "authorize" itself to essentially "look the other way" in the face of proven discrimination (or retaliation). See Manhattan General Equip. Co. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 297 U.S. 129, 134 (1936) (a regulation “out of harmony” with a governing statute is a “legal nullity.”) Whether a complainant goes into court -- or not -- does not absolve EEOC of its responsibility to correct and remedy discrimination and retaliation when and wherever it is found.

There are instances where a complainant may be forced into court because of EEOC's DELAY in securing an agency’s compliance with a remedial order. See e.g. Neville v. Lipnic, No. 18-50438 (5th Cir. June 28, 2019) (mandamus action where EEOC successfully invoked 409 to justify abandoning efforts to hold the agency accountable for violating complainant’s rights). Plus, in cases involving systemic discrimination, 409 can operate to allow an agency’s discrimination to persist long after it could have been stopped.

Given the anomalous effect of subsection 409, regulations implementing the Cummings Act should facially reflect that the following practical concerns have been considered:

1. How should a "finding" be treated under the Act in cases where EEOC ceases all processing activity in a complaint or appeal after finding that an agency had discriminated or retaliated against an employee?

2. Should cases involving “findings” that EEOC will not enforce be tracked for the duration of a de novo court process (including appeal)? If so, how should the “findings” be treated under the Act if the complainant loses in court for any reason, including one that is technical in nature (e.g. deficient service of process, untimely filing, failure to exhaust, etc.)?

I don’t believe trying to accommodate 409 would be a worthy (or even useful) endeavor. It makes more sense to simply require EEOC to comply with its statutory duty to correct ALL discrimination and retaliation found to have harmed any federal employee. Full stop.

I. The Impact of the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s (EEOC) Revised Regulation at Section 1614.409:Effect of Filing A Civil Action
On January 1, 2021, Congress passed into law The Elijah Cummings Federal Employee Anti-discrimination Act. It is absolutely wrong to repeal 5 CFR 432.108(a), which prohibits "clean record agreements" and prevents an agency from altering or removing information in an employee’s official personnel record as part of a settlement agreement or for another reason.

In my capacity as a supervisor in a Federal agency for many years I saw a large amount of unethical destruction and altering of official personnel records. Doing so is fraudulent, unethical, and demoralizing to the workforce. 5 CFR 432.108(a) correctly prohibits such dishonesty and should be left standing.

The proper way to correct errors in records is to add a statement to the existing record explaining why it is in error and updating it, thus maintaining the correct history of the record. That is the standard to which my agency held those we regulated. To do otherwise violates the principles of contemporary quality control as well as ethics. Upholding this standard is the only way that "agencies [c]ould still adhere to the principles of promoting high standards of integrity and accountability within the Federal workforce", which the docket claims is its intent, and it would not impede the other reasons given for wanting to allow clean record agreements. There is thus every reason to implement the ethical standard and no legitimate reason to alter an official record. So in fact the corrective actions currently allowed in 5 CFR 432.108 (b) and (c) are too open-ended and should be amended to require a correct historical record.

The docket's discussion of Section 432.108 concludes by stating that agencies "have an obligation to speak truthfully ... with respect to the employee and may not agree to withhold information about the circumstances of an individual's departure from the agency." The clean record agreements I have seen were typically accompanied by muzzling supervisors and directing personnel to withhold or destroy information. This too should be explicitly prohibited in the regulation if OPM has any interest in truth and "promoting ... integrity and accountability".

For example, normally when an EEO complainant of mine was removed prior to the Executive Order in May 25 2018, when the employee had a choice to decide to  settle the EEO case or not, the employee would generally weigh the benefits of pursing an EEO complaint (which usually takes years to get to a hearing and arrive at a judgment) versus settling with a clean record and agreeing not to work ever again for that agency. Even when the complainant had a very strong EEO complaint, the complainants generally were willing to sacrifice and give up their complaint and settle with an agreement never to work for that agency again in return for getting their record cleaned. They seriously and urgently needed to quickly move on to find their next job without having to explain to their next prospective employer their discriminatory removal. Despite that many had very strong cases, they just really and practically needed to move on. Because the EEO process is so incredibly slow and literally takes usually takes years to get to judgment, this process allowed them to move on quickly and find their next pay check. After EO 13839, they often have to discuss their removal at interviews or in applications and most end up having serious complications getting jobs because of the removal and often become unemployed or underemployed, even if they have a very strong discrimination case. This is adds to the harm of the discrimination they suffered. This new EO resulted in a huge waste of time when the employee just urgently needs to move on. I have even witnessed a few agency attorneys and judges confide privately about the waste of time and backlog caused by this Order when the employee simply could easily offered to sacrifice and settle these claims just to get a clean record instead of clogging up the system, particularly when all parties simply would have preferred to move on with little interest in fighting this out the complaint in the courts.

Re: Probation on Initial Appointment to a Competitive Position, Performance-Based Reduction in Grade and Removal Actions and Adverse Actions; Section 432.108 Settlement Agreements; "clean record agreements":

As a GS-14 ADR professional in the federal government, I can testify first-hand that regardless of the type or severity of the matter in dispute, or the organizational levels of the relevant parties, the prohibition on “clean record” agreements has adversely impacted mission accomplishment by federal agencies and degraded the wellbeing of federal employees. The prohibition has severely limited opportunities for agencies to efficiently and cost-effectively manage employee disputes at the lowest possible level in that settlement officials have few, if any, alternatives to taxpayer funded monetary remedies and, consequently, have little incentive to resolve conflict early.

Re:
“In addition, agencies are advised that, in any such agreement, they have an obligation to speak truthfully to Federal investigators performing future background investigations with respect to the employee and may not agree to withhold information about the circumstances of an individual's departure from the agency.”

While removing this overly broad restriction is greatly appreciated by all in the dispute resolution field, and will have significant, measurable positive outcomes throughout the federal government, it seems inconsistent to withhold agency discretion when it comes to divulging the particulars of “clean record” separation agreements to future federal employers. If the agency is mandated to “adhere to the principles of promoting high standards of integrity and accountability within the Federal workforce,” then it should be the agency’s responsibility to balance that standard against the value of a conflict resolved.

No agency should expunge incidents from an employee’s record which would preclude future federal employment just to reach a resolution; and no employee who separates from one agency with a “clean record” agreement, then seeks employment with a different federal agency, should have to defend their record again for what was negotiated in “good faith” and with the approval of an agency’s general counsel. Only the resolving agency’s general counsel would have adequate knowledge of the circumstances which prompted a “clean record” agreement and the investigator will likely be adversely influenced by the revelation. This is a form of “backdoor” retaliation and can have a “chilling effect” for employees.

A middle ground would be to permit agencies to include language that stipulates what will be divulged and what will not to any future federal investigator. This will put agencies and employees on equal ground and require that agency to stand behind its commitment to “promoting high standards of integrity and accountability” while also allowing for reasonable “clean record” agreements. Even if this avenue isn’t widely used, it is a further negotiation point that will help parties reach resolution.

It’s costly, inefficient, and it causes unnecessary court congestion, unfair expense to employees and the agency, and backlogs cases affecting all subsequent cases.

As a committed career professional employee with an excellent and unblemished performance record and more than 30 years of federal service so far, my hard work has reflected high standards and professional accountability, and has benefitted American taxpayers who fund my salary. For the following reasons, I support OPM’s removal of the prohibition on so-called “clean-record agreements.”

I was personally unfortunate, but sadly not alone, in being assigned for a time to a mean-spirited and irrational supervisor who was allowed to misuse their authority to suspend me for “misconduct” that never actually occurred. While this supervisor then conveniently retired, escaping any accountability, I have continued to perform well and attempted unsuccessfully for several years to use established processes to clear my permanent record of this unfair action. While the Agency now agrees that reversing the personnel action is the logical fix, the existing rule against settlement agreements has, to date, prevented such resolution unless I would successfully take the case all the way through a federal court to obtain a court order.

As a result of a misleadingly marred record, and despite my continued good performance, I have been hampered in competing for professional advancement or even transferring to another Agency (as I would be forced to explain my record of supposed “misconduct" and thus speak against this former supervisor).

While I support OPM's proposal to remove of the prohibition against clean-record settlements, I also believe logically that the proposed rule should clearly allow such “clean-record agreements” to stipulate what will be divulged and what will not be divulged to any future federal investigator. For example, if a settlement agreement, legally approved by a federal judge, calls for permanent and irrevocable removal of a specific personnel action, that action should never be represented by either party as ever having legitimately occurred. “Clean” should truly mean “clean,” to preserve and avoid undermining the integrity of such agreements.

Comments Regarding Grants to Reduce Air Pollution at Ports (Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2022-0874)Renewable Juneau appreciates this opportunity to comment on the RFI for Grants to Reduce Air Pollution at Ports.  Renewable Juneau is a non-profit 501c3 organization with a mission to inform, educate, and promote beneficial electrification to reduce climate emissions and increase use of renewable energy in Juneau, Alaska's capital city (renewablejuneau.org).

Renewable Juneau has been a strong advocate for dock electrification for cruise ships in the Port of Juneau for more than five years.  We offer the following comments in support of a grant program for ports that can help meet community climate and renewable energy goals by improving air quality and reducing carbon emissions.

Hoteling of cruise ships at docks in downtown ports like Juneau creates substantial local and climate-altering emissions. We strongly encourage the EPA's grant program to specifically recognize and provide funding opportunities for carbon-free shore power for cruise ship ports. Existing related Department of Transportation grant programs leave major gaps in addressing federal air emission and carbon reduction goals. The RAISE grant program requires high ratings in a wide range of areas, such as safety, that are unrelated to air quality and carbon reduction, so that shore power proposals are uncompetitive. The PIDP program has been interpreted as being limited to freight ports, and not applying to cruise ships. We urge the EPA to explictly fill these gaps.

We also recommend that the program include consideration of community climate goals and action plans, and how proposed projects meet these goals. It should also consider the opportunities for spin-off benefits of creating broader regional demand for shore power facilities. Most cruise ships operating on the West Coast and Alaska are equipped to accept shore power, but they need ports to provide carbon-free electricity in order to contribute to improving air quality and reducing carbon emissions.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Margo Waring, President, on behalf of the Board of Renewable Juneau.

Fincantieri Marine Group is providing public comment on questions asked in EPA docket pertaining to Grants to Reduce Air Pollution at Ports [60102].
EPA question 1. How can EPA structure this program to reduce air pollution in port communities and accelerate long-term trends to decarbonize the nation’s ports?
Comment: We recommend EPA consider the eligibility of shore power projects at port marine services facilities such as shipyards. Shipyard facilities often have high occupancy rates for vessels requiring service. When at a shipyard, these vessels run their shipboard systems on vessel power, unless shore power is available. This creates air emissions, which impact both shipyard workers as well as residents of surrounding communities.

While some shipyards are located within the jurisdiction of a port authority, many are located at industrial sites outside of a formal port authority. We recommend EPA consider these facilities for eligibility even if they are outside of a formal port authority’s jurisdiction.

EPA Port Emission Reduction Grant funds will be instrumental in assisting shipyards to implement vessel shore power projects to reduce emissions from vessels.

EPA Question 2.How do you see the IRA ports program complementing other programs (e.g., at EPA and the Department of Transportation) that can support efforts to reduce emissions at ports? What funding gaps can this program fill (e.g., specific zero emissions technologies or related planning support)?
Comment: The EPA Port Emission Reduction Program can help incentivize shipyards to implement shore power projects, complementing other federal programs. For example, the EPA Diesel Emission Reduction Act (DERA) grant program is more geared toward replacement or upgrade of diesel engines, rather than providing electrical ‘plug-in’ infrastructure for vessels.

Further, the US Department of Transportation (USDOT) Maritime Administration’s Small Shipyard Grant Program can be a funding source for electrical upgrades at small shipyards (as defined by 46 USC §54101(h)), vessel shore power projects rarely are funded, as that grant program’s selection criteria are more focused on capital projects leading to efficiency improvements in the shipyard production processes. Additionally, the grant program total annual funding ($20 million in FY2023) is far less than the EPA program has available.

The USDOT Maritime Administration’s Marine Highway Program (46 USC § 55601) has been used to fund vessel emission reduction projects, but these are focused on vessel upgrades. Shore power projects have been funded only sporadically, but the total available funding for the program ($10 million in FY2023) limits this program’s utility for funding shore power projects.

Last, while the USDOT Maritime Administration’s Port Infrastructure Development Program can be used to fund resilience projects at ports, small shipyards are specifically prohibited from participating in that program (46 USC § 54301(a)(4)).

For these reasons, shipyard shore power projects should be eligible for the EPA Port Emission Reduction Program, so as to complement existing federal assistance programs.

Food safety messaging is weak in this plan. Education campaigns that incorporate and emphasize food safety as an integral part of reducing food waste are of utmost importance.

As a food safety regulator at the local level, I am particularly concerned with ensuring food safety specifically in the realm of food recovery and food donations. I routinely field inquiries from well-meaning people, retail food establishments, and/or community organizations about feeding the less fortunate. Sometimes the proposal includes actual dumpster-diving to obtain food to then serve to the unhoused. When told of the regulatory requirements of food safety and/or the steps towards obtaining licensure/inspection, the individuals, firms, and organizations are often unwilling to be in compliance. The food safety requirements are seen as barriers to be avoided. This lack of understanding of the importance of food safety puts vulnerable populations at an increased risk of foodborne illness.

Reducing risk of foodborne illness should always be of utmost priority for everyone in the food supply chain, especially when making decisions on whether food should be donated or if the risks to human health dictate that the food to be sent to the compost pile or landfill.

I implore you to build-in a greater emphasis on food safety throughout this plan.

From my journey as founder and CEO of Full Harvest - a business-to-business Produce Marketplace - I've learned the critical importance of addressing food waste at the source. The USDA's Draft National Strategy for Reducing Food Loss and Waste is a significant step forward nationally, yet it can benefit from a stronger focus on upstream strategies and the modernization of the supply chain that will reduce on-farm food loss. Within the produce industry, over 25% of edible produce does not leave the farm(Santa Clara Report & WWF Driven to Waste). On-farm food loss across all commodities was recently found by WWF’s Driven to Waste report to be over 50%(the largest portion) of the global food waste problem, which is now the #1 contributor to climate change(Project Drawdown).

One of the leading reasons for food loss in produce is the offline nature of the industry. Currently, up to 95% of produce is purchased offline via phone, email and fax. Farms looking to sell their surplus or the off-grade portion of their harvest rely on these manual and time-consuming channels to find buyers. Similarly, buyers rely on the same offline processes and tools to find available produce. This results in a lack of market transparency / data and a large gap between what is produced and what is consumed.

Reducing on-farm food loss in produce can be best solved by efficiently connecting a larger number of buyers and sellers via a digital marketplace. Full Harvest’s B2B Produce marketplace is an example of a solution that is digitizing our produce supply chain and making it more efficient and transparent. We connect a national network of farms to a national network of large produce buyers - food processes, CPG companies, and retailers - via an online marketplace. Our marketplace provides farms the means to sell their “full harvest” of produce, including surplus and off-grade which is often lost on the farm. This increases farm incomes and we have seen some farms increase profit by up to 12% more per acre by being able to sell their “full harvest”. For the buyers, the marketplace expands the availability of produce and allows them to save by buying surplus and off-grade produce, often saving 10-30%. Finally, the marketplace directly prevents food loss and conserves resources like water, which is critical considering that over 70% of our fresh water is used on agriculture and a third of all food produced that is never eaten.

Full Harvest's success to-date demonstrates the potential impact of digitizing our supply chain. The strategy should increase focus on how to digitize the produce and other food supply chains. By prioritizing investment in the development, adoption and use of technology solutions and innovative platforms, the USDA can facilitate a more direct connection between food production and market demand, reducing the gap where food waste occurs. A few specific opportunities for the Strategy to consider are:
Provide funding for developing and expanding technology solutions, such as Full Harvest, that increase market efficiency and transparency to reduce food loss
Design and implement incentives and policies that encourage publicly funded institutions to adopt efficient technology solutions to purchase produce and other agricultural products, helping digitize their supply chains.
Offer tax incentives for growers that sell surplus and imperfect produce. As well as buyers that purchase them. This will encourage the sale of more produce and “full harvests.”
Subsidize the produce industry similar to the meat and dairy industries so that farmers can use the money to develop innovation to capture “full harvests” on-farm.
Continue to fund produce box initiatives to support underserved families and food deserts that utilize surplus and off-grade produce from farms.

The National Strategy should not just be about point-in-time solutions to reducing waste and loss. The Strategy must provide a transformative method for rethinking our entire food supply chain, which remains up to 95% offline. By supporting and scaling initiatives, such as the Full Harvest Produce marketplace, the USDA, EPA, and FDA can significantly contribute to building a more sustainable agricultural ecosystem, reducing hunger, and mitigating climate change.

The reality is stark: if we are to make a meaningful impact on climate change, an efficient digital food supply chain is essential. At Full Harvest, we are dedicated to this cause, leveraging technology to address on-farm food loss effectively. Our vision is a world where 100% of harvests are used, contributing to a sustainable future for our planet and generations to come. Join us in this vital effort to reduce food waste and its environmental footprint.

For a comprehensive understanding of Full Harvest's initiatives and alignment with the USDA's strategy, please visit fullharvest.com

Christine Moseley
Founder and CEO
Full Harvest Technologies, Inc

Food waste reduction and composting is a commendable practice. $10 million in grants for a learning program is a start. But it also takes incredible amount of labor and supervision to oversee the sorting of food waste from student trays. Students only have about 10 minutes of eating time to consumer their meals. At the most 20 minutes. Most schools offer a variety of entrees, fresh fruits & vegetables and offer vs. serve so students may select what they want to eat. They do not have time to eat it. If the administration really wants schools to reduce waste, the first step is establishing a minimum for seat time for meals at public schools. This must come with the recognition that the speed of service can only be so fast. It takes time for students to select their items and make decisions. The schedules at schools must be reasonable for school meal programs. The reimbursement rate for meals is insufficient already to cover labor, food and supply costs. If school meal programs are expected to help sort food waste, extend meal periods, or increase multiple lines it takes more labor. I really think that some site visits to schools to see current processes and what the impact would be on the programs would be a good field trip. The practices in SNMCS are already in place and there is waste because of reimbursable meal components requirements and lack of time to eat.
Compostable plates/trays are 4 times the cost of a foam tray. When labor shortages and lack of infrastructure don't allow for reusable plates we use foam trays. In June due to a state law we must switch to compostable materials. This is a mandated expense that we can't afford and receive zero funding for this switch. In a perfect world, we would have at least 40 minutes for school meals, allow students to take only what they want and not have mandated components, be funded to adequately cover the cost of the program. At some point, we need to look at what is being asked of our meal programs and decide if what is being asked is reasonable within the funding provided by USDA or stop asking for more.

Apeel Sciences has developed and commercialized a sustainable, edible, plant-derived solution that doubles the quality and marketable shelf-life of many types of fruits and vegetables, including organic varieties. This technology works by creating a natural barrier that slows down water loss and oxidation–two key factors that cause spoilage.

Apeel is made of purified mono- and diglycerides, which are simple and safe FDA-approved compounds found in a wide variety of everyday foods, and which are derived from non-GMO plant oils. Our solution is particularly relevant for perishable produce, a significant contributor to food waste. By extending quality and shelf-life, Apeel addresses food loss and waste at the grower/shipper, retailer, and consumer levels.
Our technology reduces the environmental footprint of fresh produce across the supply chain by decreasing food loss and waste, conserving resources like water and energy, and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

Alignment with the National Strategy Objectives:

Objective 1 (Prevent the Loss of Food): Apeel’s technology directly contributes to reducing food loss during distribution, helping to maintain the quality and freshness of produce longer. By extending the shelf-life of produce, Apeel plays a critical role in mitigating the environmental impacts associated with food loss, including significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions and resource conservation (e.g., water use).

Objective 2 (Prevent the Waste of Food): By extending the longevity of fresh produce, Apeel helps diminish the amount of food discarded by retailers and consumers, thereby aiding in waste prevention and further contributing to sustainability efforts by reducing the carbon footprint and resource use associated with food production and disposal.

Objective 4 (Support Policies for Food Loss and Waste Prevention): Apeel’s technology not only prevents food loss and waste but also embodies the innovative spirit that Objective 4 seeks to encourage through policy support. By demonstrating the efficacy of our preservation technology, we can inspire policy frameworks that incentivize similar sustainable innovations. This supports a broader strategy of reducing food waste through advanced technologies and aligns with the Strategy's goal of promoting policies for a more sustainable and efficient food system.

Suggestions for Amending the National Strategy:

Explicit Recognition of Innovative Food Preservation Technologies: Recognize the role of innovative post-harvest food preservation technologies, such as Apeel's, in extending the shelf life of produce. This would highlight the critical part such technologies play in reducing food loss and waste, contributing to sustainability and climate change mitigation while inspiring continued innovation in this space.

Incentives for adoption of food waste reduction technologies: Provide tax or other financial incentives for suppliers to offset costs incurred from utilizing innovative methods to protect and preserve fresh produce.

Supply Chain Optimization: Promote initiatives that streamline or provide more flexibility (and thus more resilience) to supply chains, thus decreasing spoilage while emphasizing sustainable practices that minimize the environmental footprint.

Inclusion in Government Programs: Consider our technology in USDA, EPA, and FDA programs focused on reducing food loss and waste and promoting sustainability. Collaboration with Apeel could serve as a model for innovative public–private partnerships.

Demonstration Projects and Case Studies: Include demonstration projects or case studies within the Strategy that showcase the real-world impact of preservation technologies. Apeel is prepared to provide data and examples from our extensive work with retailers and producers in the U.S. and abroad.

Support for Policy and Regulatory Frameworks: Encourage the development of policies and regulatory frameworks that facilitate the adoption of food preservation technologies, potentially including financial incentives or streamlined regulatory pathways for such innovative solutions.

Actions for Equitable Outcomes:

Community-Focused Solutions: Develop programs that support community-led solutions to food waste, especially in underserved and food-insecure communities.

Access to Preservation Technology: Facilitate access to food preservation technologies for small-scale producers and retailers in underserved communities, enhancing the longevity and distribution of fresh produce.

Research Funding Recommendations:

Post-Harvest Technology Research: Fund research focusing on post-harvest technologies that extend the life of perishable foods while also reducing reliance on single use or plastic packaging.

Consumer Behavior Studies: Support studies on consumer behavior related to food purchasing, storage, and waste, to develop targeted waste reduction strategies.

I am writing to provide comments on the Draft National Strategy for Reducing Food Loss and Waste and Recycling Organics, published on 12/05/2023. My comments specifically focus on evaluating how the strategy may influence the valorization of domestic farm food loss, particularly agricultural wastes rich in fermentable carbon, for utilization in biotechnology and other cutting-edge industries. This practice holds the potential to serve as economic engines for future growth and innovation.

As the Director of Sustainability at C16 Biosciences, a company with extensive expertise in biotechnology, industry, and sustainability, I bring a unique perspective to these comments. C16 Biosciences is at the forefront of innovative solutions for sustainable agricultural alternatives, with a focus on utilizing advanced biotechnological processes. Our company is known for pioneering approaches in the development of high-value products, which when derived from agricultural waste, will contribute significantly to the paradigm shift towards a more sustainable and circular industrial landscape and one devoid of food waste.

The forthcoming National Strategy for Reducing Food Loss and Waste and Recycling Organics policy represents a critical opportunity to encourage the utilization of domestic farm food waste as a valuable resource for advanced biotechnological processes, including synthetic biology and precision fermentation. This approach to valorizing agricultural waste rich in fermentable carbon can contribute to the creation of high-value products such as biofuels, bioplastics, biocatalysts, and alternatives to non-domestic crops and commodities.

Notably, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimates that 30-40% of total food production is lost before it reaches the market. Therefore, it is crucial to include provisions in the National Strategy to incentivize farmers and processors to monetize their pre-consumer food loss through technical and financial support for acquiring new or upgraded food loss storage, conversion, and management equipment or through tax credits for investments in food waste and loss conversion. These provisions maximize the potential to increase the profitability of farming operations and support agricultural universities and researchers in developing efficient and cost-effective methods for utilizing agricultural waste as feedstock for biotech and precision fermentation. Furthermore, these incentives would reinforce domestic supply chains, reduce on-farm food loss, and address challenges such as storage limitations, labor shortages, weather impacts, pests, and uncertain market demand. By converting farm waste and loss into valuable feedstock, we can mitigate food waste, create innovative products, and enhance the overall profitability of farms nationwide.

In conclusion, I strongly recommend the inclusion of provisions in the National Strategy for Reducing Food Loss and Waste and Recycling Organics to incentivize farmers and processors to valorize their pre-consumer food loss, with a specific emphasis on agricultural wastes rich in fermentable carbon. This support, whether through technical and financial assistance or tax credits, will be instrumental in both reducing industrial food loss and promoting the development of raw materials for biotech derived products. By fostering the valorization of domestic farm food loss we can simultaneously create high-value products, support farmers, strengthen domestic supply chains, and reduce food waste and loss.

Thank you for considering these comments in the development of the National Strategy.

Re: Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OLEM–2022–0415 – NRDC Comments on Draft National Strategy for Reducing Food Loss and Waste and Recycling Organics

Dear Director Hoskinson and staff,

NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council) respectfully submits these comments in response to EPA’s request, Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OLEM-2022-0415 Draft National Strategy for Reducing Food Loss and Waste and Recycling Organics. We appreciate the opportunity to provide recommendations on ways that Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and other agencies can prevent food waste, redistribute surplus food, and recycle food scraps.

NRDC works to safeguard the Earth – its people, its plants, its animals, and the natural systems on which life depends – including addressing the environmental harms of managing waste. We particularly focus on wasted food – an often-ignored resource. Since 2015, NRDC has worked with more than twenty municipalities to implement cross-cutting food waste reduction strategies and in states like New York and California on their organic waste policies. Through our work, we have seen the economic and political challenges to improving and expanding food scrap recycling and waste prevention. Drawing from these experiences, we provide the following comments.

We congratulate EPA, USDA, and FDA on your work to support and invest in food waste reduction activities across numerous offices and programs. It is exciting to see this list of actions that are being proposed or already undertaken and we offer these comments to help strengthen the effort.

Overarching Feedback:
• Reporting progress: It is great to see a focus on measurement across the strategy, but it is unclear how often reporting will happen. We would like to see frequent public reports on progress and suggest that government entities and agencies should be required to measure and annually report on their progress on actions outlined in the strategy.
• Lead by example: Federal agencies and facilities have an incredible opportunity to take the lead on implementing food waste reduction measures and send a clear signal. For example, federal facilities should measure, prevent, and recycle organic waste, donate surplus food, and purchase finished compost products. We suggest you include specific commitments to lead by example within federal agencies to the National Strategy.
• Create a whole-of-government strategy: Many federal agencies engage in food service, and some in particular manage significant amounts of food and could make a big impact on food waste reduction, like the Department of Education and Department of Defense. Efforts should be made to include these agencies in the Federal Interagency Collaboration to Reduce Food Loss and Waste and to incorporate their commitments into the National Strategy.
• Prioritize actions: With limited funding and staff time within the federal government, we suggest this strategy should outline what specific metrics will be used to assess and help prioritize the many commitments laid out in this plan to make sure that we are focusing on the most effective actions to achieve our national goal and ensure that funding is allocated proportionally.
• Establish incentives under existing grants for applicants to develop and implement food waste plans: Agencies should require grant applicants to develop food waste reduction plans to receive grant funding or should offer bonus points to grant applicants that include food waste reduction plans.

Please see the attachment for a more detailed description of these points as well as additional recommendations for each objective.

Overall, we appreciate the work that went into creating this strategy and are glad to see the agencies taking necessary steps to achieve our national goal. We hope you will take these recommendations into consideration as you work to produce a strong final strategy.

Sincerely,
Nina Sevilla
Program Advocate, Food Waste and Food Systems
NRDC

The Council on Federal Procurement of Architectural and Engineering Services (COFPAES - www.cofpaes.org) is a coalition of the nation’s leading trade and professional associations in the design community.

We appreciate this opportunity to comment on the notice of proposed rulemaking on Nondisplacement of Qualified Workers Under Service Contracts, Regulatory Information Number (RIN) 1235-AA42.

We believe the rule needs to be clarified to expand upon the reference to “the same location where the predecessor contract was performed”. This is confusing inasmuch as the rule also states, "Such coverage exists regardless of the direct beneficiary of the services or the source of the funds from which the contractor is paid for the service and irrespective of whether the contractor performs the work in its own establishment, on a Federal Government installation, or elsewhere." See 29 CFR 4.133(a).

This rule may be logical and applicable to some service contracts, for example, such as to operate a cafeteria at a Federal building, or to provide a “body shop” of employees to performance computer data entry services, or to staff a call center, all on-site at a government facility, or to staff a government owned, contractor operated (COGO) facility.

However, if, for example, a firm is providing mapping services with its employees at its own facility and delivering mapping data to a Federal agency, or a firm is providing engineering design services for an agency and a deliverable of plans and specifications is prepared on the contractor’s site and delivered to the government, this rule is unworkable and impractical, and should be exempt.

Furthermore, with specific reference to architecture, engineering (A/E) and related services, we respectfully urge that the rule exempt such services.
A/E services (including surveying and mapping) are governed by the Brooks Act (40 USC 1101 et seq and FAR 36.6). The law requires selection based on the qualifications of competing firms and key employees who will work on the contract. In fact, firms compete by submitting a SF 330 (https://www.gsa.gov/cdnstatic/SF330-21.pdf?forceDownload=1) which requires resumes of the personnel.

The rule’s requirements that incumbent workers be given a right of first refusal to work on a successor’s contract is inconsistent with the Brooks Act. Given the law and FAR requirement that evaluation and selection of a firm for A/E services be based on “demonstrated competence and qualification” including award to the “most highly qualified” firm, switching the personnel on the submitted SF330 for those who are employees of the predecessor is impractical and contrary to the qualifications based selection (QBS) process inherent in the Brooks Act.

Again, we respectfully urge the exemption of A/E services from this rule.

CODSIA views this rule as a major change in how companies will do business with the Federal government and, in order to achieve the President’s goals in EO 14055, requires diligent review. The 30-day comment period provided for this proposed rule is insufficient for our member associations, and their member companies small and large, to review the proposed rule, analyze its impact, gather feedback, and submit written comments. The rule appears to make significant changes. The challenge in preparing comments on this proposed rule is compounded by the proposed rule’s broad impact on the marketplace.

In addition, this comment period is occurring during the last quarter of the federal fiscal year. The end of the federal fiscal year is often characterized by a surge in spending to avoid losing "use it or lose it" budgets. Studies of federal spending have shown that roughly a third of all federal contract dollars are awarded in the last quarter of the fiscal year, including one out of every nine dollars in the last week alone. Thus, this busy contracting period makes it especially challenging to gather feedback from the affected federal contractors and agency personnel.

For these reasons, we respectfully request the Department of Labor provide an additional 60 days for public comments on “Nondisplacement of Qualified Workers Under Service Contracts” 87 FR 47552, RIN 1235-AA42 extending the comment due date until 15 October 2022.

If you have any questions or need any additional information, please contact me either by email: codsia@codsia.org or by phone: +1.703.927.1116.
