2. Office of Management and Budget. The Budget of the United States Government: Budget for America's Future. February 2020.

For this rule to be effective, it must require federal Contracting Officers to include in Request for Quotes (RFQs) and in Request for Proposals (RFPs) information about the quantity of qualified incumbents in each labor category along with the date of hire for each individual so that bidders can calculate labor costs accurately.

In general, the longer an employee has been working in their position, the more they will cost for a successor contractor to employ. Without this critical data about the seniority of incumbent workers, bidders may not bid enough to cover the current wages and compensation of the qualified incumbents, so those workers will most likely refuse to work for the new contractor and find employment elsewhere, as nobody wants a pay cut. This, of course, obviates the benefit of the new rule entirely if qualified incumbent workers only face pay cuts and therefore depart whenever contracts change hands.

In recent years, Contracting Officers often claimed they were not allowed to release this type information to the public, so bidders were left blind and having to guess how much money it would cost to retain the existing labor assets. This is why it is important that the final rule directly and clearly instruct Contracting Officers to release this data about the qualified incumbent workforce to all bidders during every RFQ or RFP process.

Finally, it is important also to educate Contracting Officers about the difference between qualified and unqualified incumbent workers. Many Contracting Officers act as if they believe all incumbent workers will automatically be hired by the successor contracting company, no matter what. Therefore, Contracting Officers need ways to definitely sort and segment the "qualified" incumbent workers out from the "unqualified" ones, meaning the ones that consistently exhibit performance, safety, and/or attendance problems. Otherwise, federal programs will never improve, and each program will only ever be as good as their weakest staff members. There have to be definitive guidelines and objective criteria in place for how to properly determine which qualified workers will stay and which unqualified workers will be purged when a contract changes hands.

I am a DoD Contract Specialist. My concern with this rule is that it may require a new contractor to hire employees of the incumbent contractor even if the reason the contracting office has selected the new contractor over the incumbent during the source selection process is unsatisfactory performance on the part of the incumbent. Past performance is an evaluation factor on almost every service contract we award, and there definitely are times when we are choosing a new vendor over the incumbent precisely because the incumbent has not been performing satisfactorily. It would make little sense for the incoming contractor to be required to offer a right of first refusal to the very employees whose poor performance (and the company's failure to rectify it) was the reason that the incumbent did not get the new contract. It seems there should be a way for the contracting officer to waive the requirement if unsatisfactory performance on the part of the outgoing contractor was a substantial factor in source selection.
Please see the attached comment from the Economic Policy Institute regarding the Nondisplacement of Qualified Workers Under Service Contracts (RIN 1235-AA42).

INTRODUCTION
The federal procurement system is criticized for being too slow or too difficult to navigate to attract new contractors. This proposed rule will further these perceived shortcomings.

THE BENEFITS ARE QUESTIONABLE
The Notice admittingly “overestimates” that this rule will impact 1.4 million affected workers. (p. 42578) But many of those workers are already covered under collective bargaining agreements that ensures them continued employment. Additionally, contractors covered by the Javits-Wagner-O’Day Act and the Randolph Sheppard Act have already sought exemption from this rule. Considering that the Notice assumes that “[m]any successor contractors may already be keeping the predecessor contractor’s employees on the contract…” it beckons why does this practice need to be codified and how many actual workers will benefit from it.

The rule discounts that there are legitimate reasons why an SCA-covered employee may not join a succeeding contract. The awarding contractor might want to staff the SCA-covered work with a more diverse workforce than the predecessor contractor, utilize a differently trained staff, or use its own wage band. These possibilities are ignored by the new rule and its stated purpose.

The impetus for this rule is, in part, to “reduce disruption in the delivery of services during the period of transition between contractors…” (pp. 42552, 42555, 425561, 425562, 425565, 425582, 42585). There is no research offered to support this conclusion or the premise that disruption between different service contractors is a problem on federal contracts.

THE BURDEN ON FEDERAL EMPLOYEES WILL BE SUBSTANTIAL
Too much is asked of contracting officers already. Many federal agencies are having a hard time acquiring and retaining qualified contracting professionals. Yet, this new rule wants to make their job more complicated.

Contracting officers are not responsible for tracking how many SCA-workers are needed on a service contract. (Each contractor proposes different solutions to satisfy the agency's need). To minimize the harm and transactions costs, contracting officer are incentivized here, through this rule, to improperly award more service contracts to incumbent contractors in order to avoid the hassle of developing a certified list of SCA-employees or waiting for the predecessor SCA-employees to deliberate whether they will remain on the project.

THE TRUE COSTS FROM IMPLEMENTING THIS RULE IS UNKNOWN
The Notice estimates that this rule will cost $51 million in year one. (p. 42581) Not included in that figure, is how much it will cost the successor contractors to track down all of the predecessor SCA-employees. (Under this rule, the successor contractor will only receive a list of names, but no phone numbers, e-mail addresses, or mailing addresses will be included). Will the Federal Government fund those costs or will offerors need to artificially inflate their proposals to cover the unknown costs imposed by this rule? Similarly, no costs estimates are provided for the resources needed for contractors (and subcontractors) to onboard the predecessor’s SCA employees at the last minute—costs that will be passed on to the taxpayer. Whatever the total cost is for implementing this rule, it is greatly underrepresented in the Notice.

THE RULE IS NOT PRACTICAL
Sections 9.11 and 9.12 (a)(2) already contemplate that the contracting officer may not be able to produce the predecessor’s employee list in time, if at all. This notion makes sense because it is foolhardy to think that an unsuccessful incumbent is going to assemble a certified list to assist its competitor. Notwithstanding, section 9.12 still imposes the obligation on the successor contractor to offer jobs to predecessor contractor’s SCA-covered employees even if no list is provided. (How?) There is also no deadline for when this obligation may be extinguished. This position contradicts the rules underlying goal of “reducing disruption” during the transition period. Instead, this rule will prevent the successor contractor from being fully-staffed at the start of the period of performance while it tracks down the identity of the predecessor contractor’s SCA employees.

Moreover, section 9.12(a)(1) provides that SCA-employees are entitled to no fewer than 10 business days to consider offers of employment, which also will cause the successor contractor not to have a full staff of properly trained employees until after the contract has commenced. This rule will cause more disruption, not minimize it.

CONCLUSION
This rule will change how proposals for government contracts are structured, evaluated, performed and administered while not resolving any known problem with the federal acquisition system. There is no justification for rushing to make this burdensome and costly rule apply to all service contracts; there are just too many unknowns.

Opportunity Village and the people we serve are grateful for the opportunity to provide public comment on the proposed notice of rulemaking to implement Executive Order 14055, “Nondisplacement of Qualified Workers Under Service Contracts.” While we understand that this is an important step towards reducing worker displacement, we are concerned that people who have significant disabilities may be unnecessarily overlooked in the process.

Opportunity Village is a not-for-profit organization supporting people with disabilities to live, work, and thrive in our community. One of the ways we are able to support people in achieving their goals is as a contractor through the AbilityOne program. In following guidelines set forth by the Javits-Wagner-O’Day Act, contractors such as Opportunity Village must insure that 75% of the workforce on any given contract is a person with a medically documented disability. Unlike EO 13495 signed by President Barack Obama, EO 14055 does not include an explicit exclusion for contracts awarded for services provided by persons who are blind or have severe disabilities, including contracts awarded under the Javits-Wagner-O’Day Act (JWOD).

We believe that including in the rulemaking, an exclusion for contracts or subcontracts awarded pursuant to the Javits-Wagner-O’day Act, will help to advance the administration’s stated goal of promoting inclusion and equity in the workforce while also protecting people who have significant disabilities, and the nonprofits that support them, from inconsistent regulatory interpretations.

We propose that the rulemaking on Executive Order 14055 reflect the following under definitions pursuant to EO 13495 from January of 2009: sec. 3:

ADD to 14055: Exclusions. This order shall not apply to: contracts or subcontracts awarded pursuant to the Javits-Wagner-O’Day Act, 41 U.S.C 46-48c.

Sincerely,

Bob Brown
President & CEO

Davis-Bacon regulations have not been updated in forty years and these updates will ensure that construction workers are paid the most up-to-date and accurate locally prevailing wage rates when working on a construction project financed by the federal government. Every year, federal contractors routinely cheat thousands of workers by not paying them the legally required Davis-Bacon prevailing wages. I urge the Department of Labor to approve and implement the proposed updates.

I am an independent financial advisor. My small business provides financial planning and other services to numerous clients. As a member of the Financial Services Institute, I am writing to express my concern with the Department of Labor's (DOL) recently proposed Independent Contractor Rule (Proposed Rule), which would eliminate the DOL's 2021 Rule on the subject. Contrary to the DOL's claims, eliminating the 2021 Rule will restore the previous state of confusion and uncertainty surrounding worker classification and harm my business. I encourage the DOL to modify its proposal to ensure that legitimate independent contractors, like myself, are protected from misclassification as employees.

As an independent financial advisor, I help Main Street Americans plan for a secure financial future. I am a licensed professional who chose to operate my own business including building client relationships and developing a valuable professional reputation. This was not a decision I undertook lightly, nor one forced upon me, but I chose to be an independent contractor to build my own business and better serve my clients without input from a corporate parent. Simply put, as an independent financial advisor I am free to recommend the financial products and services that I believe are truly in my clients' best interests while building equity in my business.

While I am a self-employed independent contractor, I am affiliated with an Independent financial services firm. Because the financial services industry is heavily regulated in order to protect investors, the firm with which I am affiliated is required by state and federal law to supervise my activities to comply with regulatory requirements. This legally required supervisory structure should not be misconstrued as an employee-employer relationship. The 2021 Rule specified that requiring an individual to comply with legal or contractual obligations does not constitute control. Unfortunately, the Proposed Rule would not just eliminate this important clarification critical to our industry but would make it "indicative of control" and, thus, an employee-employer relationship.

Uncertainty surrounding my status as a legitimate independent contractor hurts my business. It decreases the value of the business that I have built (an investment of time and money, including hiring my own employees) and takes resources away from the core work of helping clients with financial planning to defend against inaccurate claims of misclassification. The 2021 Rule provided the framework for a consistent application of the economic realities test focusing on two "core factors." This offered the tens of thousands of financial advisors like me regulatory clarity that is critically important for us to operate our businesses and focus on serving our clients. The Proposed Rule would revert to an unweighted six factor totality of the circumstances test, which significantly complicates the analysis and allows for inconsistent application (as was frequently the case before the 2021 Rule became effective). On top of that, the proposal significantly alters how those six factors are defined and applied, tilting them against independent contractor status in numerous ways.

While I understand the desire to curtail or prevent abuses of worker classification laws, the relationship between independent broker-dealer firms and their affiliated financial advisors is different from other professions. I urge the DOL to keep the 2021 Rule in place in order to protect legitimate independent contractors, like myself, from misclassification as employees or, alternatively substantially modify this proposal as avoid damaging my business and harming the clients I serve.

I am opposed to any governmental interference in my employment as an independent contractor. I enjoy negotiating my own fees and setting my own schedule and working as I see fit. I do not want to be an employee or be attached to any sort of union or other group that will hinder my ability to have a flexible schedule and income.

While I am a self-employed independent contractor, I am affiliated with an Independent financial services firm. Because the financial services industry is heavily regulated in order to protect investors, the firm with which I am affiliated is required by state and federal law to supervise my activities to comply with regulatory requirements. This legally required supervisory structure should not be misconstrued as an employee-employer relationship. The 2021 Rule specified that requiring an individual to comply with legal or contractual obligations does not constitute control. Unfortunately, the Proposed Rule would not just eliminate this important clarification critical to our industry but would make it "indicative of control" and, thus, an employee-employer relationship.

Uncertainty surrounding my status as a legitimate independent contractor hurts my business. It decreases the value of the business that I have built (an investment of time and money, including hiring my own employees) and takes resources away from the core work of helping clients with financial planning to defend against inaccurate claims of misclassification. The 2021 Rule provided the framework for a consistent application of the economic realities test focusing on two "core factors." This offered the tens of thousands of financial advisors like me regulatory clarity that is critically important for us to operate our businesses and focus on serving our clients. The Proposed Rule would revert to an unweighted six factor totality of the circumstances test, which significantly complicates the analysis and allows for inconsistent application (as was frequently the case before the 2021 Rule became effective). On top of that, the proposal significantly alters how those six factors are defined and applied, tilting them against independent contractor status in numerous ways.

While I understand the desire to curtail or prevent abuses of worker classification laws, the relationship between independent broker-dealer firms and their affiliated financial advisors is different from other professions. I urge the DOL to keep the 2021 Rule in place in order to protect legitimate independent contractors, like myself, from misclassification as employees or, alternatively substantially modify this proposal as avoid damaging my business and harming the clients I serve.

It baffles me why there is a refusal to listen to independent contractors who CHOSE to be independent and do NOT want to be employees. I spent over 30 years in the corporate world and it almost killed me. I left to start my own business back in 2008. After a year, I moved in to care for my mother after my father died. I would not have been able to (or continue to) be a caregiver for my elderly mother without being an independent contractor. I lived in California for 20 + years and have seen the chaos AB5 created. There is no evidence that the law created any jobs. In fact, there is evidence that it destroyed established relationships between outlets and freelancers, removing opportunities for freelance work.

I want to be independent, running my own business. It allows me time and flexibility I need to take care of my aging mother, including taking her to doctors’ appointments and other necessary care. Without the flexibility of being an independent contractor, my mother would not be able to live out her golden years at home. She cannot afford assisted living, so my freelance lifestyle allows her to remain at home and still get the care she needs.

Under the PRO Act, if I were forced to be hired as a W2 employee, I would not have this freedom. It is a horrible policy and must not be made federal law.

Instead, please replace the ABC Test in the PRO Act with the IRS Test. The latter is inclusive of freelancers who make up a modern economy and who don’t want to be hired as employees. Please don’t destroy my business and my freedom with the PRO Act. Please listen to the millions of independent contractors who chose to be independent.

As a member of the National Court Reporters Association (NCRA), which represents approximately 12,000 highly skilled and educated members, I am in fierce opposition of the Department of Labor's prospective rulemaking, Employee or Independent Contractor Classification under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

Our members include court reporters, captioners, legal videographers, scopists, and associated legal professionals, many of whom currently work as independent contractors and who will be adversely affected by the proposed factors reclassifying independent contractor status. If adopted into a final rule, the Department of Labor's proposed rulemaking will detrimentally and negatively affect my livelihood, and the livelihood of my colleagues and our families. For instance, independent contractor reclassification will likely result in mass layoffs for myself and many of my freelance associates, as many small employer firms do not have the financial resources to afford to retain independent contractors as employees. Other consequences are equally far-reaching and destructive.

I contend that the Department's proposed independent contractor re-classification will substantially infringe upon U.S. fair business practices. Currently, my colleagues and myself have the option to choose to work as independent contractors or as employees in federal or state courthouses across the nation, as well as corporations. If the proposed re-classification is adopted, my ability to choose how and where I work will be eliminated as a result of unnecessary and disruptive governmental overreach with destructive results in the marketplace.

I am adamantly opposing the Department's proposed rulemaking on independent contractor reclassification and respectfully request that it refrain from final adoption for the following reasons: (1) the multitude of economic reality factors outlined in the rule is written too broadly that it will result in the unintentional misclassification of workers, including myself, and will inflict undue financial and economic harm to myself, my counterparts, and our families; (2) the rule will create increased costs for court reporting, captioning, and legal videography firms, which will further rampant inflation and disenfranchise workers; (3) the rule denies my colleagues and myself the flexibility to choose how we engage in the workplace; (4) the rule does not contain an exemption for my profession, such as court reporting, captioning, legal videography, and associated legal professionals; and (5) the Department should defer to Congress to enact narrow legislation that explicitly addresses independent contractor reclassification as it pertains to specific professions.

The Department of Labor’s proposed rule change under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) will have a profoundly negative impact on many small businesses. The proposal limits the ability of entrepreneurs to start and grow their businesses as independent contractors or use independent contractors. The description of this proposed rule change as a “clarification” of existing law is misleading when, in reality, it represents a radical departure from current standards that will harm millions of small businesses.

The proposed rule uses a needlessly complicated and subjective “multi-factor totality of the circumstances” test where the freedom for entrepreneurs to operate as independent contractors is significantly diminished. In other words, the standards for qualification of independent contractor status are extensive, often subjective, and much more difficult to meet. Independent contractor criteria should be clear and objective, without reliance on bureaucratic judgement calls and grey areas.

The current independent contractor standards have served our economy and workers well and have been the basis for many entrepreneurs starting their own businesses. Furthermore, limiting the instances where small businesses can use independent contractors will be detrimental to entrepreneurs already struggling to find employees.

I urge you to withdraw this harmful proposed rule change.

I am adamantly opposing the Department's proposed rulemaking on independent contractor reclassification and respectfully request that it refrain from final adoption for the following reasons: (1) the multitude of economic reality factors outlined in the rule is written too broadly that it will result in the unintentional misclassification of workers, including myself, and will inflict undue financial and economic harm to myself, my counterparts, and our families; (2) the rule will create increased costs for court reporting, captioning, and legal videography firms, which will further rampant inflation and disenfranchise workers; (3) the rule denies my colleagues and myself the flexibility to choose how we engage in the workplace; (4) the rule does not contain an exemption for my profession, such as court reporting, captioning, legal videography, and associated legal professionals; and (5) the Department should defer to Congress to enact narrow legislation that explicitly addresses independent contractor reclassification as it pertains to specific professions.

I am an independent financial advisor. My small business provides financial planning and other services to numerous clients. As a member of the Financial Services Institute, I am writing to express my concern with the Department of Labor's (DOL) recently proposed Independent Contractor Rule (Proposed Rule), which would eliminate the DOL's 2021 Rule on the subject. Contrary to the DOL's claims, eliminating the 2021 Rule will restore the previous state of confusion and uncertainty surrounding worker classification and harm my business. I encourage the DOL to modify its proposal to ensure that legitimate independent contractors, like myself, are protected from misclassification as employees.

As an independent financial advisor, I help Main Street Americans plan for a secure financial future. I am a licensed professional who chose to operate my own business including building client relationships and developing a valuable professional reputation. This was not a decision I undertook lightly, nor one forced upon me, but I chose to be an independent contractor to build my own business and better serve my clients without input from a corporate parent. Simply put, as an independent financial advisor I am free to recommend the financial products and services that I believe are truly in my clients' best interests while building equity in my business.

While I am a self-employed independent contractor, I am affiliated with an Independent financial services firm. Because the financial services industry is heavily regulated in order to protect investors, the firm with which I am affiliated is required by state and federal law to supervise my activities to comply with regulatory requirements. This legally required supervisory structure should not be misconstrued as an employee-employer relationship. The 2021 Rule specified that requiring an individual to comply with legal or contractual obligations does not constitute control. Unfortunately, the Proposed Rule would not just eliminate this important clarification critical to our industry but would make it "indicative of control" and, thus, an employee-employer relationship.

Uncertainty surrounding my status as a legitimate independent contractor hurts my business. It decreases the value of the business that I have built (an investment of time and money, including hiring my own employees) and takes resources away from the core work of helping clients with financial planning to defend against inaccurate claims of misclassification. The 2021 Rule provided the framework for a consistent application of the economic realities test focusing on two "core factors." This offered the tens of thousands of financial advisors like me regulatory clarity that is critically important for us to operate our businesses and focus on serving our clients. The Proposed Rule would revert to an unweighted six factor totality of the circumstances test, which significantly complicates the analysis and allows for inconsistent application (as was frequently the case before the 2021 Rule became effective). On top of that, the proposal significantly alters how those six factors are defined and applied, tilting them against independent contractor status in numerous ways.

While I understand the desire to curtail or prevent abuses of worker classification laws, the relationship between independent broker-dealer firms and their affiliated financial advisors is different from other professions. I urge the DOL to keep the 2021 Rule in place in order to protect legitimate independent contractors, like myself, from misclassification as employees or, alternatively substantially modify this proposal as avoid damaging my business and harming the clients I serve.

As an entrepreneur who owns a very small business, I am opposed to the Employee or Independent Contractor Classification Under the Fair Labor Standards Act as suggested by the Department of Labor. The current rules are easy to follow and understand, and allow me the freedom to hire independent contractors on the few occasions I might need them. I do not have enough work to support additional employees. Requiring me to follow the new and very subjective rules is wrong.

As an independent contractor myself, I also object. The rules are fine as they are, and I resent the possibility that my work opportunities may be limited because of rules that make doing business more difficult. The online tutoring company I am contracted to has actually stopped hiring tutors in states that amended their IC rules poorly. Now it's going to happen on a national scale? This is not good. It hurts women in particular who need the flexibility of an IC job.

Do not approve the proposed rules. They are bad for business and bad for the country.

The proposed rule by the Wage and Hour Division is bad for business and bad for the American economy.
Over 59million people work independent gigs. More costs, more paperwork, more time required to get a project completed, less freedom, and fewer qualified human resources.

Practically speaking, What you are proposing is that I hire an employee to wash my windows once a month. It takes 15 minutes to wash my store windows. 12months @ 15minutes= 3hours. If the FLSA Agency is fearful that employees are being abused, then go after those businesses that you believe are cheating the employee...since you must have evidence it is happening otherwise why would you propose this rule?
This proposed rule is destructive to our American economy and an economic nightmare looking for a place to happen.
I object to this proposed rule change.

This legally required supervisory structure should not be misconstrued as an employee-employer relationship. The 2021 Rule specified that requiring an individual to comply with legal or contractual obligations does not constitute control. Unfortunately, the Proposed Rule would not just eliminate this important clarification critical to our industry but would make it "indicative of control" and, thus, an employee-employer relationship.

Uncertainty surrounding my status as a legitimate independent contractor hurts my business. It decreases the value of the business that I have built (an investment of time and money, including hiring my own employees) and takes resources away from the core work of helping clients with financial planning to defend against inaccurate claims of misclassification. The 2021 Rule provided the framework for a consistent application of the economic realities test focusing on two "core factors." This offered the tens of thousands of financial advisors like me regulatory clarity that is critically important for us to operate our businesses and focus on serving our clients. The Proposed Rule would revert to an unweighted six factor totality of the circumstances test, which significantly complicates the analysis and allows for inconsistent application (as was frequently the case before the 2021 Rule became effective). On top of that, the proposal significantly alters how those six factors are defined and applied, tilting them against independent contractor status in numerous ways.

While I understand the desire to curtail or prevent abuses of worker classification laws, the relationship between independent broker-dealer firms and their affiliated financial advisors is different from other professions. I urge the DOL to keep the 2021 Rule in place in order to protect legitimate independent contractors, like myself, from misclassification as employees or, alternatively substantially modify this proposal as avoid damaging my business and harming the clients I serve.

Yet again, our federal government fixing problems that don't exist.  I am an independent contractor working as a court reporter.  The reason I freelance is so I can pick and choose who, when, where, and how I work.  I have no desire to be a company's employee as this would severely limit the amount and type of assignments I'm able to take.  In addition, this rule will, in essence, put small court reporting agencies out of business because they would be unable to compete with the larger agencies.  Stop infringing on my rights as a worker.  If I wanted to work for someone, I would be an official reporter.  I vehemently oppose this rule and will do everything in my power, both individually and collectively as a member of the National Court Reporter's Association, to elect members of Congress who will curtail the DOL's intrusion into my beloved career.

It seems simple to me... Let's close loopholes that allow businesses to treat labor that is absolutely essential to their ability to function as an organization as if they are not employees. People can say whatever they want to try and justify this, but there is an inherent difference between a contractor that you hire to remodel your kitchen, and a stylist working at a hair salon.

As a member of the National Court Reporters Association (NCRA), which represents approximately 12,000 highly skilled and educated members, I am in fierce opposition of the Department of Labor's prospective rulemaking, Employee or Independent Contractor Classification under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

Our members include court reporters, captioners, legal videographers, scopists, and associated legal professionals, many of whom currently work as independent contractors and who will be adversely affected by the proposed factors reclassifying independent contractor status. If adopted into a final rule, the Department of Labor's proposed rulemaking will detrimentally and negatively affect my livelihood, and the livelihood of my colleagues and our families. For instance, independent contractor reclassification will likely result in mass layoffs for myself and many of my freelance associates, as many small employer firms do not have the financial resources to afford to retain independent contractors as employees. Other consequences are equally far-reaching and destructive.

I contend that the Department's proposed independent contractor re-classification will substantially infringe upon U.S. fair business practices. Currently, my colleagues and myself have the option to choose to work as independent contractors or as employees in federal or state courthouses across the nation, as well as corporations. If the proposed re-classification is adopted, my ability to choose how and where I work will be eliminated as a result of unnecessary and disruptive governmental overreach with destructive results in the marketplace.

I am adamantly opposing the Department's proposed rulemaking on independent contractor reclassification and respectfully request that it refrain from final adoption for the following reasons: (1) the multitude of economic reality factors outlined in the rule is written too broadly that it will result in the unintentional misclassification of workers, including myself, and will inflict undue financial and economic harm to myself, my counterparts, and our families; (2) the rule will create increased costs for court reporting, captioning, and legal videography firms, which will further rampant inflation and disenfranchise workers; (3) the rule denies my colleagues and myself the flexibility to choose how we engage in the workplace; (4) the rule does not contain an exemption for my profession, such as court reporting, captioning, legal videography, and associated legal professionals; and (5) the Department should defer to Congress to enact narrow legislation that explicitly addresses independent contractor reclassification as it pertains to specific professions.

The Employee or Independent Contractor Classification Under the Fair Labor Standards Act proposal causes severe repercussions to not only large-scale employers of contractors but also small-scale employers and the contractors themselves. The business model which this act seems to target, in which contractors provide their services without the constraints which would normally affect full-time workers, makes for very free working conditions which draw in a large workforce. The entirety of many of the large corporations which benefit from contract labor primarily benefit from this large workforce: companies such as Lyft and Uber require drivers around every corner in order to keep travel times short. Requiring contractors to register as employees would diminish this key aspect of the business. Furthermore, this flexibility and freedom of labor is what brings contractors towards these services: being an employee removes this freedom. Finally, small contracting services would be in a bit of a gray area with this act. Small corporations fulfilling similar activities may not have the resources to provide all the employee benefits necessary, especially given the multitude of contractors that drive their business.

If the proposed re-classification is adopted, my ability to choose how and where I work will be eliminated as a result of unnecessary and disruptive governmental overreach with destructive results in the marketplace.

he Department of Labor’s proposed rule change under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) will have a profoundly negative impact on many small businesses. The proposal limits the ability of entrepreneurs to start and grow their businesses as independent contractors or use independent contractors. The description of this proposed rule change as a “clarification” of existing law is misleading when, in reality, it represents a radical departure from current standards that will harm millions of small businesses.

The proposed rule uses a needlessly complicated and subjective “multi-factor totality of the circumstances” test where the freedom for entrepreneurs to operate as independent contractors is significantly diminished. In other words, the standards for qualification of independent contractor status are extensive, often subjective, and much more difficult to meet. Independent contractor criteria should be clear and objective, without reliance on bureaucratic judgement calls and grey areas.

The current independent contractor standards have served our economy and workers well and have been the basis for many entrepreneurs starting their own businesses. Furthermore, limiting the instances where small businesses can use independent contractors will be detrimental to entrepreneurs already struggling to find employees.

I urge you to withdraw this harmful proposed rule change.

I am an independent financial advisor. My small business provides financial planning and other services to numerous clients. As a member of the Financial Services Institute, I am writing to express my concern with the Department of Labor's (DOL) recently proposed Independent Contractor Rule (Proposed Rule), which would eliminate the DOL's 2021 Rule on the subject. Contrary to the DOL's claims, eliminating the 2021 Rule will restore the previous state of confusion and uncertainty surrounding worker classification and harm my business. I encourage the DOL to modify its proposal to ensure that legitimate independent contractors, like myself, are protected from misclassification as employees.

As an independent financial advisor, I help Main Street Americans plan for a secure financial future. I am a licensed professional who chose to operate my own business including building client relationships and developing a valuable professional reputation. This was not a decision I undertook lightly, nor one forced upon me, but I chose to be an independent contractor to build my own business and better serve my clients without input from a corporate parent. Simply put, as an independent financial advisor I am free to recommend the financial products and services that I believe are truly in my clients' best interests while building equity in my business.

While I am a self-employed independent contractor, I am affiliated with an Independent financial services firm. Because the financial services industry is heavily regulated in order to protect investors, the firm with which I am affiliated is required by state and federal law to supervise my activities to comply with regulatory requirements. This legally required supervisory structure should not be misconstrued as an employee-employer relationship. The 2021 Rule specified that requiring an individual to comply with legal or contractual obligations does not constitute control. Unfortunately, the Proposed Rule would not just eliminate this important clarification critical to our industry but would make it "indicative of control" and, thus, an employee-employer relationship.

Uncertainty surrounding my status as a legitimate independent contractor hurts my business. It decreases the value of the business that I have built (an investment of time and money, including hiring my own employees) and takes resources away from the core work of helping clients with financial planning to defend against inaccurate claims of misclassification. The 2021 Rule provided the framework for a consistent application of the economic realities test focusing on two "core factors." This offered the tens of thousands of financial advisors like me regulatory clarity that is critically important for us to operate our businesses and focus on serving our clients. The Proposed Rule would revert to an unweighted six factor totality of the circumstances test, which significantly complicates the analysis and allows for inconsistent application (as was frequently the case before the 2021 Rule became effective). On top of that, the proposal significantly alters how those six factors are defined and applied, tilting them against independent contractor status in numerous ways.

While I understand the desire to curtail or prevent abuses of worker classification laws, the relationship between independent broker-dealer firms and their affiliated financial advisors is different from other professions. I urge the DOL to keep the 2021 Rule in place in order to protect legitimate independent contractors, like myself, from misclassification as employees or, alternatively substantially modify this proposal as avoid damaging my business and harming the clients I serve.

I am an attorney that represents many small businesses. The proposed Rule change will be harmful for small businesses as the rule by going from a two-factor test to a six-factor test invites uncertainty. This uncertainty leads to litigation which is often brought on a class wide basis that exposes the employer to the type of liability that often bankrupts companies causing the loss of many jobs.

Secondly, the very employees you seek to help often times simply do not want to be treated as employees. They prefer the flexibility to work the hours they chose, the lack of oversight and the freedom that the independent contractor status affords them.

Third, many of the factors in the "six-factor" test have no practical application to many businesses. For example, the worker's investment in equipment or materials required ignores that a lot of the independent contractors are talent based not tool based. This factor is a throw--back to a trade-based economy, for example many independent contractors work in creative activities that are not tool based.

Finally, often times trial court judges, who have limited business experience, provide opinions that are not based in reality. For example, in Reich, 890 F. Supp. 592 the court found that the Defendant advertising its business weighed against independent contractor status. Clearly that is not rational. Likewise, courts have found that not owning a part of the business is indicative of employee status. This is simply contrary to the normal independent contractor relationship where one owns a business and hires independent contractors to work on projects as needed.

The current two factor test is more practical and properly focus on two factors:(1) the nature and degree of control; and (2) the workers opportunity for profit or loss. This method allows for employers to understand the guardrails and allows independent contractors the freedom they seek.

I am an independent financial advisor. My small business provides financial planning and other services to numerous clients. As a member of the Financial Services Institute, I am writing to express my concern with the Department of Labor's (DOL) recently proposed Independent Contractor Rule (Proposed Rule), which would eliminate the DOL's 2021 Rule on the subject. Contrary to the DOL's claims, eliminating the 2021 Rule will restore the previous state of confusion and uncertainty surrounding worker classification and harm my business. I encourage the DOL to modify its proposal to ensure that legitimate independent contractors, like myself, are protected from misclassification as employees.

As an independent financial advisor, I help Main Street Americans plan for a secure financial future. I am a licensed professional who chose to operate my own business including building client relationships and developing a valuable professional reputation. This was not a decision I undertook lightly, nor one forced upon me, but I chose to be an independent contractor to build my own business and better serve my clients without input from a corporate parent. Simply put, as an independent financial advisor I am free to recommend the financial products and services that I believe are truly in my clients' best interests while building equity in my business.

While I am a self-employed independent contractor, I am affiliated with an Independent financial services firm. Because the financial services industry is heavily regulated in order to protect investors, the firm with which I am affiliated is required by state and federal law to supervise my activities to comply with regulatory requirements. This legally required supervisory structure should not be misconstrued as an employee-employer relationship. The 2021 Rule specified that requiring an individual to comply with legal or contractual obligations does not constitute control. Unfortunately, the Proposed Rule would not just eliminate this important clarification critical to our industry but would make it "indicative of control" and, thus, an employee-employer relationship.

Uncertainty surrounding my status as a legitimate independent contractor hurts my business. It decreases the value of the business that I have built (an investment of time and money, including hiring my own employees) and takes resources away from the core work of helping clients with financial planning to defend against inaccurate claims of misclassification. The 2021 Rule provided the framework for a consistent application of the economic realities test focusing on two "core factors." This offered the tens of thousands of financial advisors like me regulatory clarity that is critically important for us to operate our businesses and focus on serving our clients. The Proposed Rule would revert to an unweighted six factor totality of the circumstances test, which significantly complicates the analysis and allows for inconsistent application (as was frequently the case before the 2021 Rule became effective). On top of that, the proposal significantly alters how those six factors are defined and applied, tilting them against independent contractor status in numerous ways.

While I understand the desire to curtail or prevent abuses of worker classification laws, the relationship between independent broker-dealer firms and their affiliated financial advisors is different from other professions. I urge the DOL to keep the 2021 Rule in place in order to protect legitimate independent contractors, like myself, from misclassification as employees or, alternatively substantially modify this proposal as avoid damaging my business and harming the clients I serve.

We, the members of the Environmental Law Society at Indiana University Maurer School of Law, urge the Environmental Protection Agency to finalize the Consent Decree in the matter of Statewide Organizing for Community Empowerment v. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, No. 1:22–cv–2562– JDB (D.D.C.). Finalizing this consent decree would be the first step towards the revision of 40 CFR 257.50(d) and the inclusion of inactive coal combustion residual (CCR) landfills in CCR disposal regulations.

Here in Indiana, there are an estimated twenty-one unregulated CCR landfills across eight separate sites. According to a map of unregulated landfills created by Earthjustice, these landfills are concentrated along Indiana's major waterways: Lake Michigan, the Wabash River, The White River, and the Ohio River. The Michigan City Generating Station site, owned by the Northern Indiana Public Services Corporation (NIPSCO), is particularly concerning to us because this site is located on the banks of Lake Michigan and near Trail Creek.

As the climate continues to change, extreme weather events occur with greater regularity. A single extreme precipitation event could swell the banks of any of these watercourses, damage the containment of the coal ash, and release the toxic compounds they contain over a large area. An occurrence of this nature would permanently and detrimentally affect property values, ecology, and habitability in and around the contaminated area, and the cleanup would be immensely costly.

As residents of Indiana and future environmental attorneys, we care about this issue because these unregulated coal ash ponds are already responsible for leaching toxic compounds into waterways and groundwater in Indiana and across the nation. This problem must be solved before disaster strikes and finalizing this consent decree would be a strong first step in that direction.

We urge you to finalize this consent decree.

Sincerely,

Members of the Environmental Law Society at Indiana University Maurer School of Law

To Secretary Regan:

350 Wisconsin would like to thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule.

First, we fully support closing the loophole in EPA’s 2015 coal combustion residuals (CCR) rule 40 CFR 257.50, to now also apply to CCR sites that were inactive or stopped receiving waste before October 17, 2016. This is an important change.

However, we are opposed to the failure of the proposed rule to include coal ash, which contains mercury, cadmium and arsenic, as a hazardous waste, under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act’s list of hazardous wastes, in 40 CFR 261.4.Subtitle C of RCRA. This waste should be categorized as hazardous so that these dangerous discards can no longer be dumped in landfills that were intended only for household waste, and which are often located next to poor black and white individuals and families.

EPA has ignored the science and capitulated to coal industry lobbying to allow the disposal of substantively Subtitle C hazardous wastes in Subtitle D household waste landfills, notwithstanding the fact that the law prohibits hazardous wastes in household waste facilities, 42 USC 6924; 40 CFR 258.4(c)(2). This circumvention of the clear language of the statute was simply a contrivance that categorized CCR as so-called “special” wastes, 40 CFR 261.4(b)4(i), which is a fictitious no-man’s land that attempts to avoid having to declare CCR as either household or hazardous wastes by the creation of this whole new meaningless category. This is clearly contrary to the intention of the Federal 1984 Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments to RCRA.

Black and white individuals and families’ who live near the household waste landfills in Georgia that accepted the CCR toxic wastes are at special risk. In addition to the impacts to people living near these landfills, CCR also create additional environmental harm, for example, flue gas ash also contains calcium sulfite and calcium sulfate, which bacteria can use in the absence of oxygen to degrade organic waste and create hydrogen sulfide, as a byproduct, which is flammable and horrifically odorous. Also, the fine particles from power plant fly ash, when combined in household waste landfills, can clog leachate collection systems, which are necessary for landfill safety. Additionally, fly ash also produces heat, which is of even more concern when mixed with flammable constituents of household waste, because that may cause intractable subsurface fires, which are both impossible to control and also degrade and destroy critical safety systems.

EPA has stated its major commitment to environmental justice. It cannot both maintain that position and, at the same time, make decisions that risk lives in marginalized communities, such as those unfortunate enough to live near these landfills that were intended as household waste landfills but which are now accepting CCR. The agency can change its direction and designate CCR as hazardous wastes that may only be disposed of in Subtitle C landfills, in which case it can continue to claim its commitment to environmental justice. Otherwise it will be clear that this stated commitment is not authentic.

Thank you again for this opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,
John Greenler
Executive Director
350 Wisconsin

To the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or "Agency"):

I am a law student interested in environmental law, in particular its role and intersection with environmental justice. I chose to send a comment to remind the Agency of its delegated statutory commitment under 21 U.S.C. 346a. The language of the statute expressly states, "A tolerance for a pesticide chemical residue . . . shall not be established or modified by the Administrator unless the Administrator determines, after consultation with the Secretary, that there is a practical method for detecting and measuring the levels . . . ." One of these petitioners requesting modification utilizes L-glufosinate
Free Acid on a litany of produce and meats during the agriculture and manufacturing products. Though this petitioner concedes the use of HRAV–5A and BK/01/99 analytical methods to practically measure the levels of the herbicide, there is still cause for concern for a relaxed modification of this herbicide. In the United States, pesticides correlate strongly with race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, where often the impact of exposure and subsequent development of disease or illness disproportionately affects BIPOC communities and farmers of color. See Donley et al. BMC Public Health (2022) 22:708 https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-022-13057-4.

Moreover, there are studies to indicate that the ingestion of L-glufosinate is harmful and toxic to the health of humans even in smaller doses. See Park et al. J Korean Med Sci. 2013 Nov; 28(11): 1687–1689. Moreover, the petitioner utilizes this herbicide in a multitude of products, such as corn, soybeans, and potato, which are staples of the American diet. I am writing to emphasize the EPA's role in reasonably assessing its analysis of pesticide tolerances and its firm commitment to environmental justice, as indicated in its Proposed Rule, because safety and awareness of the disproportionate effects of agricultural production should still remain at the fore of the Agency's firm commitment towards environmental justice.

In response to the RFI covering Docket ID No. EPA—HQ-OW-2023-0396, please consider the following as it relates to BABA waivers:

Currently, there are no known producers of domestic manual gear actuators for waterworks valves. It is common industry practice to furnish larger waterworks valves with manual gear actuators aiding valve operation. These manual gear actuators are typically integral to the valves and shipped from the valve producer as a complete, combined unit. Valves with manual actuators are critical to US water infrastructure, and a waiver for manual actuators is necessary. The lack of a waiver for manual actuators is a burden on domestic valve manufacturers that the BABA legislation was intended to help. This waiver is unnecessary under AIS requirements because actuators are considered “Non-Construction Materials” and outside the scope of AIS products.

Should a domestic actuator producer be identified, it is expected that limited capacity would render a cost and lead time which is not in the public’s best interest. That said, if a suitable actuator producer were identified, valve producers would require time to integrate a new product into the existing valve designs. This process would entail sampling the product to verify actuator quality and updating product design as necessary. Currently offered integral gear actuators are custom designed for each valve producer offering and may have taken months or years of sampling iterations.

In summary, a waiver covering manual actuators is necessary, and it is expected this will be the case for many years.

To whom it may concern,

I am a process mechanical design engineer with 45 years of experience in the wastewater treatment industry. A large wastewater treatment plant project can include literally thousands of complex equipment components and subsystems, requiring thousands of pages of specifications. Many such products used in the industry today are the result of years of research, testing, trial and error in real world applications. The US is littered with numerous examples of treatment facilities that failed due to mis-application of treatment technologies, requiring extensive renovation and expensive equipment replacement. Many of these complex packaged treatment systems and components are manufactured domestically, but many are not. Implementation of BABA is putting design engineers in the position of determining compliance of numerous packaged treatment systems down to the smallest component, which is another magnitude of complexity that we are not presently getting paid for.

Another issue is the stress that will be placed on domestic manufacturers that do not have the production capacity, or may be forced to produce a product that is not functionally equivalent to a readily available non-domestic product. BABA is a double edged sword. You may find experienced designers and facility owners that believe in proven technology, regardless of origin, and may be reluctant to sacrifice system functionality at the risk of EPA Discharge Permit violations, fines, and enforcement actions as a result of implementing BABA.

First of all, please consider extending the RFI Comment period beyond the December 20 deadline. Equipment manufacturers appear to be largely unaware of BABA’s potential impact on wastewater standard practices, judging by their lack of participation in the November 21, 2023 RFI Webinar.

Please consider applying BABA to readily available domestic commodities only, and not to complex packaged equipment systems. Also, please consider allowing the decoupling of complex subsystem procurement from the overall project. If facilities are free to use local funding for separate, specialized non-domestic equipment procurement, while the remaining portion of a project complies with BABA for construction materials and commodities, then pursuing BABA encumbered funding may be more palatable. In my opinion, implementation of BABA to complex packaged equipment systems has failed to properly assess the full impact on the domestic wastewater treatment manufacturing industry.

Netafim could source 100% of Thinwall and Heavywall drip lines from Fresno, enabling a product that is 100% extruded in the USA. For Thinwall drip lines, volumes below 5 million feet could be accepted anytime. Volumes above 5 million feet would need a reasonable lead time commensurate with the volume required. BABA requirements state that "Manufactured products must be produced in the United States, meaning the final point of manufacturing must occur in the United States and the cost of the components of the manufactured product that are mined, produced, or manufactured in the United States is greater than 55 percent of the total cost of all components of the manufactured product." Aerzen is the American affiliate company of Aerzen GMBH, located in the town of Aerzen, Germany. The attached presentation shows our HQ, our product lines in the domestic water and wastewater market, and an overall view of our major competitors in the market. The attached PDF shows the sourcing of components by percent of the total cost, for each of our product lines.
Our standard Positive Displacement (PD) blowers can meet the 55% domestic content, with the only German component being the blower stage (or air-end) itself, and all other package components coming from US sources. Aerzen USA is familiar with domestic compliance, since our final package manufacturing plant is located in Coatesville, PA. Historically, we have needed to comply with the PA Steel Act, which continues today. The final percentage can vary, depending on the size of the machine, and the accessories that Aerzen would supply (for example, VFDs). We use the cost of the motor in our total, and in recent years, true domestic motors have waxed and waned. We have historically used Toshiba, but discontinued when their castings were sourced in Vietnam, and used Baldor, where the price increased threefold, and when Baldor discontinued domestic supply, we used a small company called Reuland. I don't know whether they have any substantiation for their domestic component content, other than their advertisement. Their efficiencies were questionable. Now we're back to using Toshiba for certain sizes, due to changes in their supply chain. If motors are removed from the domestic calculation, it will impact our total, depending on whether motors are considered 100% domestic, or to be subtracted from the total and the remainder is to be calculated without the motor.
The domestic components in what Aerzen estimates to be BABA compliant come from various shops. The quality issue is that the components must be up to Aerzen standards, which is not always the case. The pricing issue is that these suppliers only make a limited quantity, and we don't benefit from the economy of scale in sourcing from our usual suppliers in Europe. This increases our cost by an average of 30%.
Our standard PD blowers are the only product line where we can comply with BABA as we understand compliance. Our high efficiency turbo and low pressure screw blowers have limited US component availability. We share that issue with our major competitors. If Aerzen were to limit our blower product offerings to standard PD blowers rather than turbo or screw, the power consumption from each machine would be anywhere from 15% to 30% higher, which increases the carbon footprint of a wastewater treatment plant, where the blower energy is 50% to 60% of the power used in the plant.
Between lack of foundry capacity and the environmental impact of producing permanent magnet motors, moving production to the US is a daunting task. In my work with WWEMA, I have found that pump manufacturers that are currently compliant are also limited on product development due to available foundry capacity. Even if foundry capacity is developed, the quality issues that are at the heart of turbo or screw blowers cannot be easily outsourced. All of these transitions take time, and do not appear to fall within the time constraints of BABA. For those reasons, we request a waiver on blowers, to give the EPA time to evaluate available resources, to understand the level of engineering involved with these products, and to make informed decisions on how to determine compliance. The diagrams provided by EPA during past webinars gives us hope of a successful resolution. Aerzen USA will open its doors to EPA and their consultant to tour our facility in Coatesville, PA, so you can learn more about the blowers we provide to the US market.

Rulemaking Assignment: EPA-HQ-OLEM-2023-0320

I decided to research the reconditioning and management of used 55 gallon drums, since the consumption of oil is an issue right now, and also because I have worked in many different fast-food and restaurant environments where we have to properly dispose of grease and other residues in a standard 55-gallon drum.
The context for this proposed rule is coming up with solutions identified with the lifecycle of used drums containing “hazardous waste, chemicals, paints, resins, tars, adhesives, foods, oils, soaps, solvents, or related materials.” These drums are linked to causing environmental impacts at industrial facilities, hazardous waste generators, and transportation/receiving facilities for these toxic drums. Since this issue poses multiple environmental threats, I am in support of passing this rule.
According to the proposed rule, the cleaning and reconditioning of these drums is harming human health. This issue falls under the RCRA (Resource Conservation & Recovery Act), the CAA (Clean Air Act), and the CWA (Clean Water Act). This issue encompasses the preservation of residual materials, the conservation of metal used to make the drums, and the maintenance of clean air and water due to the utilization of combustion techniques. Since so many different facilities deal with the reconditioning of these drums the chance of polluting the environment is very high.
Currently, drums are cleaned with two different methods, the first being burning off residue from the metal drums, or washing them out with water and a caustic solution (a solution able to burn or corrode organic tissue by chemical action) to remove residue. The EPA is looking to “Require wastewaters from rinsing containers to be managed in tanks and containers instead of land-based units.” This would allow companies to conceal a much larger amount of runoff water.
Another issue with reconditioning the drums is the possibility of an explosion or a fire starting. A lot of the time, people responsible for cleaning the drums do not know the previous contents stored inside, which could be highly flammable (oil, gas, acetone, etc.) and dangerous for receiving and transportation services to handle. (Government N. T., 2023). I support the proposition to reduce the “one-inch” regulatory limit for defining RCRA empty containers as well as require rinsing all of the containers before they would be considered RCRA empty containers. Also, requiring empty drums to meet structural integrity requirements prior to shipment would increase the safety of transportation and cut down on costs for damages. I would also recommend that you can always educate the public and the workforce, which is one of the best ways of implementing environmental policy.

It is vital to understand the implications of industrial drum usage on the environment, specifically the importance of the process of adequately cleaning the drums as even the smallest amount of residue can cause significant damage to the environment the drum is disposed in. Industrial drums are used to dispose of many substances including oils, solvents, paints, resins, adhesives, and toxic chemicals and gases. According to existing RCRA regulations, hazardous waste residues are exempt from regulation as long as “All wastes have been removed that can be removed using the practices commonly employed to remove materials from that type of container, e.g., pouring, pumping, and aspirating, AND (2) no more than 2.5 centimeters (one inch) of residue remains or no more than 3% by weight remains if the container is less than or equal to 119 gallons or no more than 0.3% by weight remains if the container is more than 119 gallons.” (Used Drum Management and Reconditioning, 2023) If a 119-gallon drum was storing a hazardous substance like petrol (one liter of petrol weighs 0.737kg) then by RCRA regulations, 99.98kg of petrol can be left as residue and the drum would be considered “empty”. Without proper disposal of industrial drums and the hazardous materials stored inside them, the 99.98kg of petrol residue could seep into soil and groundwater or pollute the atmosphere if disposed of via burning. It is of the upmost importance that new technologies and regulations are put into place, like the one being proposed, to ensure that the environment and the people living in it are safe from the hazardous materials stored inside these industrial drums. We thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule. We have two areas of concern in regards to this ANPRM. Our first concern is in section III C, (pg. 54540) where it mentions “one possible approach to addressing this issue would be just eliminating the empty container provisions in RCRA.” While this rule speaks to used drum management and reconditioning, there is no definition of “drum” in the proposed rule. Eliminating the empty container provision in RCRA would have an significantly increase the volume of waste generated due to the sheer number of containers used to hold a hazardous material. At our facilities alone, there are thousands of single use vials, pipette tips, jars, bottles are used daily. Elimination of the empty container provision would require a hazardous waste determination on all these empty containers and would be unduly burdensome and costly without an environmental protection benefit. We would request that the current empty container provision be retained as written.
Our second concern is in Section V (pg. 54542) where it is suggested that one method to address the issue is to modify the empty container definition to require some rinsing of a drum that held non-acute hazardous waste, similar to the requirements for triple rinsing containers that held P-listed hazardous wastes. Again, there is no indication if this would be limited to just “drums” or any container type since this ANPRM does not provide a definition of “drum”. Without that definition, we feel the rules could be interpreted as requiring rinsing and collection of the rinsate from all containers that once held a hazardous material. This would greatly increase both the volume of hazardous waste and labor involved to manage containers that are currently allowed to be disposed of as solid waste without further processing, nor do we do not see a proportionate environmental benefit to this extra step.
If the intent of this rulemaking is to improve management of drums for reconditioning, then any language should be specific to those drums. This language would include a definition of “drum” (such as “containers with a volume >30 gallons) and any additional requirements, such as rinsing, should be limited to containers meeting the definition of “drums” that are sent for reconditioning.

ACC appreciates the opportunity to provide the following comments to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on its proposed Used Drum Management and Reconditioning Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking.  ACC appreciates EPA’s recognition that this ANPRM does not represent a proposal and as such, will not directly result in regulatory changes without adequate supporting analyses and proper notice-and-comment opportunities. ACC member companies are regulated under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act and engaged in the generation and management of used drums, including the treatment, storage, or transportation of these containers under applicable regulatory requirements addressing hazardous waste management at the state and federal levels. Our member company facilities are potentially affected parties by the actions outlined in ANPRM and as such, offer the following recommendations for EPA’s consideration.

The State of Oregon acknowledges the EPA's request for guidance regarding the handling and reconditioning of used drums. In our State, we've encountered significant hazardous waste violations at drum reconditioning facilities. These violations encompass issues such as the acceptance of hazardous waste disguised as "RCRA-empty" drums, improper screening of loads, inadequate on-site container management, improper pour-off practices, and a deficiency in hazardous waste determinations for both pour-off and process wastewater wastestreams associated with these businesses.

In response to these findings, Oregon supports a comprehensive regulatory approach that maintains the full application of RCRA requirements to drum reconditioners. However, proposing that drum reconditioners obtain RCRA permits is considered impractical. Given the resource-intensive nature of permitting for both regulatory authorities and permit holders, it is advisable to limit the number of facilities with RCRA permits. Additionally, creating a variance allowing drum reconditioners to establish designated "non-RCRA empty" container storage areas is not recommended.

A proposed action is to amend the existing definition of "RCRA empty" to decrease the allowable amount of material remaining in a drum when sent for reconditioning. Drum reconditioners should be obligated to reject non-RCRA empty drums unless they secure a hazardous waste Treatment, Storage, and Disposal Facility (TSDF) permit. If TSDF permits are not obtained, potential pre-treatment system permit requirements should be in place. This precaution is essential, as instances of rinsate being flushed into the POTW with minimal or no testing or treatment have been observed. In cases where a drum reconditioner mistakenly accepts a non-empty drum, immediate notification to the State (or EPA in the case of unauthorized States) should be mandatory.
Addressing the concern of stockpiling/abandonment of drums; in addition to mandating an inventory and inspections of containers, implementing an accumulation time limit is proposed. Upon receiving a "RCRA empty" container, reconditioners have 90 days to initiate the cleaning/reconditioning process (or send it to a TSDF as suggested).

Furthermore, it is recommended that reconditioners undergo Hazardous Waste Management training, even if they are solely accepting empty containers. This training ensures that employees are well-versed in potential hazards, particularly in the event they unintentionally accept a non-empty container or a container with hazardous residue. If feasible, reconditioners should be compelled to document their entire reconditioning process, including testing and certifying container integrity with methods meeting UN/DOT standards. This documentation ensures transparency and guarantees the compatibility of the container with any future wastes it may hold.

Oregon also supports requiring drum labeling or other documentation conveying the hazards posed by drum residues. Endorsement is given to implementing waste analysis plans for characterizing rinsate from RCRA empty containers. It is crucial to ensure that containers are genuinely empty (not just "RCRA empty") before acceptance at facilities. Additionally, standards for containers with any amount of hazardous residues (including crushed or shredded containers) should be imposed to meet hazardous debris alternative treatment standards before land disposal (as outlined in 40 CFR 268.45).

SUBJECT: Comment on Order No. 3407 - Department-Wide Approach to Reducing Plastic Pollution

Overview of the regulationThe General Services Administration (GSA) is proposing a regulation focused on reducing single-use plastic (SUP) waste in product packaging through the Federal Supply Schedules (FSS) program. The regulation encourages industry partners to provide SUP-free packaging for products awarded on FSS contracts. Key components include defining SUP-free packaging, updating GSAR Parts 502, 538, and 552 regulations, introducing new clauses and provisions, and implementing an online icon on GSA Advantage. The estimated one-time public cost is $25,146,016, with GSA incurring $61,936.

The causes and impact of single-use plastic packaging
The causes of the environmental challenge posed by single-use plastic packaging are rooted in the extensive use and disposal of these materials, contributing significantly to climate change. The production of single-use plastics relies on fossil fuels, contributing to greenhouse gas emissions and exacerbating global warming. Additionally, improper disposal and inadequate waste management systems release methane and other pollutants during the breakdown of plastics, further contributing to climate change. The impact of this issue is multifaceted, ranging from marine and terrestrial pollution to wildlife harm, ecosystem disruption, and resource depletion. Addressing single-use plastic packaging is integral to effective climate change policy as it involves mitigating carbon emissions from plastic production, minimizing the environmental consequences of plastic disposal, and promoting sustainable alternatives. Implementing policies prioritizing reduction, recycling, and adopting eco-friendly materials can significantly mitigate climate change and preserve ecosystems.

The proposed rule, focused on reducing single-use plastic packaging in government contracts, potentially impacts small businesses. While the rule allows flexibility for businesses to propose solutions for transitioning from plastic to single-use plastic (SUP)-free packaging, there are associated costs with compliance. Small businesses, constituting a significant portion of Federal Supply Schedule (FSS) contractors, may face initial challenges in familiarizing themselves with the regulatory changes and allocating resources for SUP-free packaging identification and availability. The estimated average cost per contractor for compliance is $1,796.14, encompassing regulatory familiarization, SUP-free packaging identification, and availability efforts. However, the voluntary nature of SUP-free packaging identification could give small businesses a competitive advantage, allowing them to showcase their environmentally responsible practices on GSA Advantage and their ESG reporting.
Regarding paperwork requirements, the proposed rule falls under the Paperwork Reduction Act, involving updates to the existing Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Control Number 3090–0303. An estimation is that 3,500 respondents will complete one response each, resulting in a total burden of 7,000 hours for both GSAR 552.238–XXX and GSAR 552.238–YYY.

Potential Recommendations
The proposed regulation to reduce single-use plastic packaging in government contracts aligns with positive climate change policy objectives for the following reasons:
•The initiative addresses a significant environmental issue by targeting the reduction of single-use plastic waste, known for its adverse impact on ecosystems, marine life, and overall ecological health. By encouraging Federal Supply Schedule (FSS) contractors to adopt single-use plastic (SUP)-free packaging, the policy promotes sustainable and eco-friendly practices within the business sector.
•The voluntary nature of SUP-free packaging identification provides flexibility for businesses, aligning with the principles of market-driven solutions to environmental challenges.
•The potential reduction in single-use plastic waste contributes to mitigating climate change by curbing the carbon footprint associated with plastic production, disposal, and the overall life cycle of these materials.
•The policy positions the federal government as a leader in promoting sustainable procurement practices, setting an example for public and private sectors to prioritize environmentally responsible packaging alternatives.
This regulation supports a broader climate change policy by fostering a more sustainable and resilient approach to material consumption and waste management.

Debby Mathebula
