Specifically, the rule proposes expansive new recordkeeping for employers and sponsors regarding employment decisions, apprenticeship agreements, records of apprentice performance and progress, wages and benefits and more. It introduces a new mandate and related paperwork burdens requiring employers to verify that all journeyworkers involved in upskilling/supervising apprentices are qualified to do so. The rule provides little clarity on what would qualify as sufficient evidence to meet this requirement. Regardless, this requirement will represent an onerous new burden on employers that are required to verify undefined qualifications of the many journeyworkers frequently involved in on-the-job training.

The proposal’s imposition of a new endpoint assessment requirement represents an unnecessarily prescriptive change to existing GRAPs, which are already free to implement such assessments if sponsors and employers determine they are needed. The DOL should remove this requirement to prevent increasing administrative/recordkeeping costs, preserve flexibility and avoid a new impediment to apprentice recruitment/retention in GRAPs.

The rule has a concerning new obligation for GRAP providers to request information from employers regarding past labor law violations. The provision imposes new civil/ criminal liability on employers and provides little clarity regarding the responsibility of sponsors to verify employer disclosures. The DOL should remove this overreaching requirement, and at a minimum provide additional clarity to sponsors.

The proposal reduces flexibility for sponsors and employers by eliminating competency-based and hybrid GRAPs, instead mandating rigid, multiyear, time-based standards. This change would shut out new sponsors and employers interested in these approaches, and may result in the deregistration of existing GRAPs utilizing these legitimate,tested models if sponsors and employers determine transitioning to a time-based model is not feasible.

Finally, while the construction industry is accommodating new technologies and innovations, the proposed rule instead makes the process of establishing new occupations as suitable for GRAPs more difficult through the new “suitability” test. I urge the DOL to lower paperwork requirements for suitability applications, shorten the approval timeline and enforce decision deadlines. The proposal’s emphasis on preventing “splintering” is unnecessary, and the DOL should instead let industry determine whether new GRAPs are needed.

As currently written, the proposed rule is a step backward for the GRAP system and will exacerbate the construction industry’s existing workforce development challenges. The DOL must withdraw this proposed rule immediately to reconsider aspects of the rule that will increase costs and reduce GRAP participation. To guarantee access to high-quality, well-compensated careers in construction for as many Americans as possible, the DOL must instead focus on streamlining and modernizing GRAP regulations to ensure as many sponsors, employers and apprentices participate as possible.

The current GRAP system is already unappealing to many construction industry stakeholders and is not attracting enough new apprentices or graduating enough skilled apprentices to meet industry workforce needs. This proposal will make the GRAP system even worse.

Specifically, the rule proposes expansive new recordkeeping for employers and sponsors regarding employment decisions, apprenticeship agreements, records of apprentice performance and progress, wages and benefits and more. It introduces a new mandate and related paperwork burdens requiring employers to verify that all journeyworkers involved in upskilling/supervising apprentices are qualified to do so. The rule provides little clarity on what would qualify as sufficient evidence to meet this requirement. Regardless, this requirement will represent an onerous new burden on employers that are required to verify undefined qualifications of the many journeyworkers frequently involved in on-the-job training.

The proposal’s imposition of a new endpoint assessment requirement represents an unnecessarily prescriptive change to existing GRAPs, which are already free to implement such assessments if sponsors and employers determine they are needed. The DOL should remove this requirement to prevent increasing administrative/recordkeeping costs, preserve flexibility and avoid a new impediment to apprentice recruitment/retention in GRAPs.

The rule has a concerning new obligation for GRAP providers to request information from employers regarding past labor law violations. The provision imposes new civil/ criminal liability on employers and provides little clarity regarding the responsibility of sponsors to verify employer disclosures. The DOL should remove this overreaching requirement, and at a minimum provide additional clarity to sponsors.

The proposal reduces flexibility for sponsors and employers by eliminating competency-based and hybrid GRAPs, instead mandating rigid, multiyear, time-based standards. This change would shut out new sponsors and employers interested in these approaches, and may result in the deregistration of existing GRAPs utilizing these legitimate,tested models if sponsors and employers determine transitioning to a time-based model is not feasible.

Finally, while the construction industry is accommodating new technologies and innovations, the proposed rule instead makes the process of establishing new occupations as suitable for GRAPs more difficult through the new “suitability” test. I urge the DOL to lower paperwork requirements for suitability applications, shorten the approval timeline and enforce decision deadlines. The proposal’s emphasis on preventing “splintering” is unnecessary, and the DOL should instead let industry determine whether new GRAPs are needed.

As currently written, the proposed rule is a step backward for the GRAP system and will exacerbate the construction industry’s existing workforce development challenges. The DOL must withdraw this proposed rule immediately to reconsider aspects of the rule that will increase costs and reduce GRAP participation. To guarantee access to high-quality, well-compensated careers in construction for as many Americans as possible, the DOL must instead focus on streamlining and modernizing GRAP regulations to ensure as many sponsors, employers and apprentices participate as possible.

Of note, DOL data suggests that, in FY2023, construction industry GRAPs had roughly 250,000 enrolled apprentices and graduated 45,000. The current GRAP system is already unappealing to many construction industry stakeholders and is not attracting enough new apprentices or graduating enough skilled apprentices to meet industry workforce needs. Specifically, the rule proposes expansive new recordkeeping for employers and sponsors regarding employment decisions, apprenticeship agreements, records of apprentice performance and progress, wages and benefits and more. The rule provides little clarity on what would qualify as sufficient evidence to meet this requirement. Employer Burdens
•The U.S. Department of Labor’s (USDOL) proposed rule is 779 pages long and would create new layers of burdens on employers that would have a chilling effect on participation in registered apprenticeships.
•Rather than eliminating requirements on employers, the proposed rule would not eliminate any employer requirements and would add new requirements on related technical instruction, equal employment reporting, financial reporting, and recordkeeping.
•What’s more, the proposed rule does not provide for the commensurate expansion of regulatory or programmatic funding to implement the rule as proposed at the state or federal levels.
•The proposed rule provides for an amorphous definition of “supportive services” that could be interpreted as imposing a requirement on apprenticeship sponsors to provide supportive services, which could limit the number of apprenticeship sponsors.
•The proposed rule would require apprenticeship sponsors to report all violations of workforce practices going back for an undefined amount of time, which could legally jeopardize many employers’ ability to participate in the registered apprenticeship system.
•The outright prohibition on non-compete agreements in the proposed rule would likewise limit the expansion of new sectors that rely on intellectual property.
•The requirement for on-the-job trainers (journey workers) to have training in assessment, communication, and other instructor-related competencies is overly burdensome. There is a shortage of journeyworkers. Finding people who are technically qualified and working in the field but are also qualified as if they were college instructors will throttle the number of apprentices an employer can have and will add costs to getting the additional training for their JWs.

Eliminating Sound Models In lieu of Untested Forms of Apprenticeship
•The rule would promote the use of apprenticeship models, such as the CTE Apprenticeship, that deviate from best practices (such as requiring postsecondary credit for all apprenticeships and using industry rather than occupational frameworks) and diminish the role of leveraging a variety of innovative approaches to registered apprenticeship.
•Requiring 2,000 hours of on-the-job training and 144 hours of required technical instruction for every apprenticeship would effectively eliminate the competency-based pathway and would create a one-size-fits all approach that would cause fewer employers and learners to enter into apprenticeships in fields that have traditionally not participated in registered apprenticeship, such as healthcare and information technology.
•Furthermore, the proposed rule would require the use of end-point assessments for all apprenticeships, rather than making end-point assessment voluntary as a means of vouchsafing the effectiveness of end-point assessments and evaluating the data. Moreover, the rule does not specify the processes by which end-point assessments would be developed and standardized.

Doubling Down on Supply-Side Occupational Standards
•Developing overlapping National Occupational Standards and National Apprenticeship Standards Guidelines will likely generate confusion among education and training providers, employers, and students and jobseekers. Rather than creating new standards, the Urban Institute’s work on apprenticestandards.org should be fostered and expanded to create a library of industry-validated apprenticeship standards templates.
•Rather than developing multiple sets of standards through government, demand-driven, employer developed competency frameworks aligned to occupations should be utilized.

Moving at the Speed of Government, Rather than at the Speed of Business
•The proposed rule contemplates a 90-day approval window for registration proposals, which is far too long. We oppose a one-size-fits all registration window.
•The requirements to submit a state apprenticeship plan and to reauthorize state apprenticeship agencies will cause states to waste time and resources complying with unnecessary federal rules, instead of devoting those resources to training. Requiring a state apprenticeship plan without markedly increasing state programmatic funds to states to support apprenticeship will cause states to abscond from the federal registered apprenticeship system in lieu of state-sanctioned apprenticeship with interstate reciprocity agreements.
•The proposed rule restricts the ability of SAAs to determine apprenticeship suitability and introduces a strict “anti-splintering” provision. Taken together, these changes will inhibit the state-level experiments that fuel the registered apprenticeship system.
•SAAs should at least be able to determine the suitability of apprenticeships for their own states; the OA Administrator could determine suitability for cross-state purposes.

As a construction industry stakeholder that would be impacted by this overhaul of government-registered apprenticeship programs, I write to the U.S. Department of Labor to comment on the proposed rule published on Jan. 17, 2024.

I support expanding access to GRAPs as part of an all-of-the-above approach to workforce development and appreciate the DOL’s stated goal of improving the government-registered apprenticeship system, as this would help meet the workforce needs of the construction industry.

However, I am deeply concerned that the rule as currently proposed undermines these critical goals. The rule would needlessly implement dozens of new burdensome and costly recordkeeping and reporting requirements on GRAP providers and employer participants, and eliminate flexible, competency-based GRAPs, among many other concerning provisions.

The proposal will discourage participation by construction industry employers and GRAP providers and likely reduce the number of apprentices enrolled and graduating from GRAPs. Of note, DOL data suggests that, in FY2023, construction industry GRAPs had roughly 250,000 enrolled apprentices and graduated 45,000. The current GRAP system is already unappealing to many construction industry stakeholders and is not attracting enough new apprentices or graduating enough skilled apprentices to meet industry workforce needs. The DOL should remove this overreaching requirement, and at a minimum provide additional clarity to sponsors.

The proposal reduces flexibility for sponsors and employers by eliminating competency-based and hybrid GRAPs, instead mandating rigid, multiyear, time-based standards. This change would shut out new sponsors and employers interested in these approaches, and may result in the deregistration of existing GRAPs utilizing these legitimate,tested models if sponsors and employers determine transitioning to a time-based model is not feasible.

The proposal’s emphasis on preventing “splintering” is unnecessary, and the DOL should instead let industry determine whether new GRAPs are needed.

As currently written, the proposed rule is a step backward for the GRAP system and will exacerbate the construction industry’s existing workforce development challenges. The DOL must withdraw this proposed rule immediately to reconsider aspects of the rule that will increase costs and reduce GRAP participation. To guarantee access to high-quality, well-compensated careers in construction for as many Americans as possible, the DOL must instead focus on streamlining and modernizing GRAP regulations to ensure as many sponsors, employers and apprentices participate as possible.

This proposal will make the GRAP system even worse.

Specifically, the rule proposes expansive new recordkeeping for employers and sponsors regarding employment decisions, apprenticeship agreements, records of apprentice performance and progress, wages and benefits and more. It introduces a new mandate and related paperwork burdens requiring employers to verify that all journeyworkers involved in upskilling/supervising apprentices are qualified to do so. The rule provides little clarity on what would qualify as sufficient evidence to meet this requirement. Regardless, this requirement will represent an onerous new burden on employers that are required to verify undefined qualifications of the many journeyworkers frequently involved in on-the-job training.

The proposal’s imposition of a new endpoint assessment requirement represents an unnecessarily prescriptive change to existing GRAPs, which are already free to implement such assessments if sponsors and employers determine they are needed. The DOL should remove this requirement to prevent increasing administrative/recordkeeping costs, preserve flexibility and avoid a new impediment to apprentice recruitment/retention in GRAPs.

The rule has a concerning new obligation for GRAP providers to request information from employers regarding past labor law violations. The provision imposes new civil/ criminal liability on employers and provides little clarity regarding the responsibility of sponsors to verify employer disclosures. The DOL should remove this overreaching requirement, and at a minimum provide additional clarity to sponsors.

The proposal reduces flexibility for sponsors and employers by eliminating competency-based and hybrid GRAPs, instead mandating rigid, multiyear, time-based standards. This change would shut out new sponsors and employers interested in these approaches, and may result in the deregistration of existing GRAPs utilizing these legitimate,tested models if sponsors and employers determine transitioning to a time-based model is not feasible.

Finally, while the construction industry is accommodating new technologies and innovations, the proposed rule instead makes the process of establishing new occupations as suitable for GRAPs more difficult through the new “suitability” test. I urge the DOL to lower paperwork requirements for suitability applications, shorten the approval timeline and enforce decision deadlines. The proposal’s emphasis on preventing “splintering” is unnecessary, and the DOL should instead let industry determine whether new GRAPs are needed.

As currently written, the proposed rule is a step backward for the GRAP system and will exacerbate the construction industry’s existing workforce development challenges. The DOL must withdraw this proposed rule immediately to reconsider aspects of the rule that will increase costs and reduce GRAP participation. To guarantee access to high-quality, well-compensated careers in construction for as many Americans as possible, the DOL must instead focus on streamlining and modernizing GRAP regulations to ensure as many sponsors, employers and apprentices participate as possible.

The current GRAP system is already unappealing to many construction industry stakeholders and is not attracting enough new apprentices or graduating enough skilled apprentices to meet industry workforce needs. This proposal will make the GRAP system even worse.

Specifically, the rule proposes expansive new recordkeeping for employers and sponsors regarding employment decisions, apprenticeship agreements, records of apprentice performance and progress, wages and benefits and more. It introduces a new mandate and related paperwork burdens requiring employers to verify that all journeyworkers involved in upskilling/supervising apprentices are qualified to do so. The rule provides little clarity on what would qualify as sufficient evidence to meet this requirement. Regardless, this requirement will represent an onerous new burden on employers that are required to verify undefined qualifications of the many journeyworkers frequently involved in on-the-job training.

The proposal’s imposition of a new endpoint assessment requirement represents an unnecessarily prescriptive change to existing GRAPs, which are already free to implement such assessments if sponsors and employers determine they are needed. The DOL should remove this requirement to prevent increasing administrative/recordkeeping costs, preserve flexibility and avoid a new impediment to apprentice recruitment/retention in GRAPs.

The rule has a concerning new obligation for GRAP providers to request information from employers regarding past labor law violations. The provision imposes new civil/ criminal liability on employers and provides little clarity regarding the responsibility of sponsors to verify employer disclosures. The DOL should remove this overreaching requirement, and at a minimum provide additional clarity to sponsors.

The proposal reduces flexibility for sponsors and employers by eliminating competency-based and hybrid GRAPs, instead mandating rigid, multiyear, time-based standards. This change would shut out new sponsors and employers interested in these approaches, and may result in the deregistration of existing GRAPs utilizing these legitimate,tested models if sponsors and employers determine transitioning to a time-based model is not feasible.

Finally, while the construction industry is accommodating new technologies and innovations, the proposed rule instead makes the process of establishing new occupations as suitable for GRAPs more difficult through the new “suitability” test. I urge the DOL to lower paperwork requirements for suitability applications, shorten the approval timeline and enforce decision deadlines. The proposal’s emphasis on preventing “splintering” is unnecessary, and the DOL should instead let industry determine whether new GRAPs are needed.

As currently written, the proposed rule is a step backward for the GRAP system and will exacerbate the construction industry’s existing workforce development challenges. The DOL must withdraw this proposed rule immediately to reconsider aspects of the rule that will increase costs and reduce GRAP participation. To guarantee access to high-quality, well-compensated careers in construction for as many Americans as possible, the DOL must instead focus on streamlining and modernizing GRAP regulations to ensure as many sponsors, employers and apprentices participate as possible.

Of note, DOL data suggests that, in FY2023, construction industry GRAPs had roughly 250,000 enrolled apprentices and graduated 45,000. The current GRAP system is already unappealing to many construction industry stakeholders and is not attracting enough new apprentices or graduating enough skilled apprentices to meet industry workforce needs. This proposal will make the GRAP system even worse.

Specifically, the rule proposes expansive new recordkeeping for employers and sponsors regarding employment decisions, apprenticeship agreements, records of apprentice performance and progress, wages and benefits and more. It introduces a new mandate and related paperwork burdens requiring employers to verify that all journeyworkers involved in upskilling/supervising apprentices are qualified to do so. The rule provides little clarity on what would qualify as sufficient evidence to meet this requirement. Regardless, this requirement will represent an onerous new burden on employers that are required to verify undefined qualifications of the many journeyworkers frequently involved in on-the-job training.

The proposal’s imposition of a new endpoint assessment requirement represents an unnecessarily prescriptive change to existing GRAPs, which are already free to implement such assessments if sponsors and employers determine they are needed. The DOL should remove this requirement to prevent increasing administrative/recordkeeping costs, preserve flexibility and avoid a new impediment to apprentice recruitment/retention in GRAPs.

The rule has a concerning new obligation for GRAP providers to request information from employers regarding past labor law violations. The provision imposes new civil/ criminal liability on employers and provides little clarity regarding the responsibility of sponsors to verify employer disclosures. The DOL should remove this overreaching requirement, and at a minimum provide additional clarity to sponsors.

The proposal reduces flexibility for sponsors and employers by eliminating competency-based and hybrid GRAPs, instead mandating rigid, multiyear, time-based standards. This change would shut out new sponsors and employers interested in these approaches, and may result in the deregistration of existing GRAPs utilizing these legitimate,tested models if sponsors and employers determine transitioning to a time-based model is not feasible.

Finally, while the construction industry is accommodating new technologies and innovations, the proposed rule instead makes the process of establishing new occupations as suitable for GRAPs more difficult through the new “suitability” test. I urge the DOL to lower paperwork requirements for suitability applications, shorten the approval timeline and enforce decision deadlines. The proposal’s emphasis on preventing “splintering” is unnecessary, and the DOL should instead let industry determine whether new GRAPs are needed.

As currently written, the proposed rule is a step backward for the GRAP system and will exacerbate the construction industry’s existing workforce development challenges. The DOL must withdraw this proposed rule immediately to reconsider aspects of the rule that will increase costs and reduce GRAP participation. To guarantee access to high-quality, well-compensated careers in construction for as many Americans as possible, the DOL must instead focus on streamlining and modernizing GRAP regulations to ensure as many sponsors, employers and apprentices participate as possible.

Of note, DOL data suggests that, in FY2023, construction industry GRAPs had roughly 250,000 enrolled apprentices and graduated 45,000. As currently written, the proposed rule is a step backward for the GRAP system and will exacerbate the construction industry’s existing workforce development challenges. The DOL must withdraw this proposed rule immediately to reconsider aspects of the rule that will increase costs and reduce GRAP participation. To guarantee access to high-quality, well-compensated careers in construction for as many Americans as possible, the DOL must instead focus on streamlining and modernizing GRAP regulations to ensure as many sponsors, employers and apprentices participate as possible.

To guarantee access to high-quality, well-compensated careers in construction for as many Americans as possible, the DOL must instead focus on streamlining and modernizing GRAP regulations to ensure as many sponsors, employers and apprentices participate as possible.

As a construction industry stakeholder that would be impacted by this overhaul of government-registered apprenticeship programs, I write to the U.S. Department of Labor to comment on the proposed rule published on Jan. 17, 2024.

The construction industry faces a critical workforce shortage, needing to hire over half a million additional workers on top of normal hiring in 2024 to meet labor demand. I support expanding access to GRAPs as part of an all-of-the-above approach to workforce development and appreciate the DOL’s stated goal of improving the government-registered apprenticeship system, as this would help meet the workforce needs of the construction industry.

However, I am deeply concerned that the rule as currently proposed undermines these critical goals. The rule would needlessly implement dozens of new burdensome and costly recordkeeping and reporting requirements on GRAP providers and employer participants, and eliminate flexible, competency-based GRAPs, among many other concerning provisions.

The proposal will discourage participation by construction industry employers and GRAP providers and likely reduce the number of apprentices enrolled and graduating from GRAPs. Of note, DOL data suggests that, in FY2023, construction industry GRAPs had roughly 250,000 enrolled apprentices and graduated 45,000. The current GRAP system is already unappealing to many construction industry stakeholders and is not attracting enough new apprentices or graduating enough skilled apprentices to meet industry workforce needs. This proposal will make the GRAP system even worse.

Specifically, the rule proposes expansive new recordkeeping for employers and sponsors regarding employment decisions, apprenticeship agreements, records of apprentice performance and progress, wages and benefits and more. It introduces a new mandate and related paperwork burdens requiring employers to verify that all journeyworkers involved in upskilling/supervising apprentices are qualified to do so. The rule provides little clarity on what would qualify as sufficient evidence to meet this requirement. Regardless, this requirement will represent an onerous new burden on employers that are required to verify undefined qualifications of the many journeyworkers frequently involved in on-the-job training.

The proposal’s imposition of a new endpoint assessment requirement represents an unnecessarily prescriptive change to existing GRAPs, which are already free to implement such assessments if sponsors and employers determine they are needed. The DOL should remove this requirement to prevent increasing administrative/recordkeeping costs, preserve flexibility and avoid a new impediment to apprentice recruitment/retention in GRAPs.

The rule has a concerning new obligation for GRAP providers to request information from employers regarding past labor law violations. The provision imposes new civil/ criminal liability on employers and provides little clarity regarding the responsibility of sponsors to verify employer disclosures. The DOL should remove this overreaching requirement, and at a minimum provide additional clarity to sponsors.

The proposal reduces flexibility for sponsors and employers by eliminating competency-based and hybrid GRAPs, instead mandating rigid, multiyear, time-based standards. This change would shut out new sponsors and employers interested in these approaches, and may result in the deregistration of existing GRAPs utilizing these legitimate,tested models if sponsors and employers determine transitioning to a time-based model is not feasible.

Finally, while the construction industry is accommodating new technologies and innovations, the proposed rule instead makes the process of establishing new occupations as suitable for GRAPs more difficult through the new “suitability” test. I urge the DOL to lower paperwork requirements for suitability applications, shorten the approval timeline and enforce decision deadlines. The proposal’s emphasis on preventing “splintering” is unnecessary, and the DOL should instead let industry determine whether new GRAPs are needed.

We propose the documentation for AI systems, including the datasets used to train them should include the following:
Documentation requirements
1. What are the data sources used to train the model? Is the information publicly available to all users (or under copyright)?
1a) Which groups were responsible for putting together the datasets? Who labeled the datasets?
1b) A link to other data sources’ documentation
1c) A literature review of sorts of the previous work that informed the formation of the datasets
1d) If the datasets were collected using surveys, what were the interview questions asked?
2. What steps were taken to weed out biases and data voids from the sourced data? How is the data reviewed? Is the review process clear of any biases?
2a) What biases might be present in the dataset?
3. The performance metrics of the model
3a) Were there any nonfunctional metrics (e.x. fairness) metrics used?
3b) How was the model validated to conform to these metrics?
4. The context of the model
4a) What is the goal of these algorithms?
4b) Why were previous models not selected for this?
5) A high level description of the model's architectures and features (e.x. inputs, outputs, broad techniques)
6) Which requests have been received to either remove, change, or access the data and by who?

• Submitting a work for consideration doesn't entitle a publisher, agent, or submission software developers to use it in the training of AI technologies. Publishers should make reasonable efforts to prevent third-party use of contracted works as training data for AI technologies.

COPYRIGHT
People who use AI for art or writing cannot, and should not, have their work copyright protected. Is it important that there be uniformity of AI accountability requirements and/or practices across the United States? Across global jurisdictions? If so, is it important only within a sector or across sectors? What is the best way to achieve it? Alternatively, is harmonization or interoperability sufficient and what is the best way to achieve that?
Yes, it is critical to establish consistent AI accountability regulations and policies across the United States and globally. This is due to the growing usage of AI in a variety of sectors and industries, and it is critical to ensure that AI systems are developed and used responsibly, ethically, and with accountability.
Uniform AI accountability criteria and procedures will aid in ensuring that AI systems are developed and used in a way that safeguards individuals' rights, privacy, and safety, as well as that AI systems are transparent, explainable, and fair. It will also aid in the promotion of trust in AI systems and the prevention of unforeseen outcomes or harm.
The demand for consistent AI accountability rules and practices extends beyond a single industry, since AI is used in a variety of industries, including healthcare, banking, and transportation. As a result, a comprehensive strategy to AI accountability across all sectors is critical. The creation of worldwide standards and guidelines is the most effective strategy to achieve consistent AI accountability criteria and practices. Collaborations between governments, international organizations, and industry players can help achieve this. These standards and recommendations can help foster interoperability and harmonization of AI accountability criteria and practices by serving as a foundation for the development and deployment of AI systems around the world.
Interoperability and harmonization are vital as well, but they should be viewed as supplements to standard criteria and procedures. Interoperability allows diverse AI systems to function together effortlessly, whereas harmonization allows for the uniform integration of various requirements and practices. The establishment of international standards and guidelines, as well as cooperation between governments and industry players, can all help to achieve interoperability and harmonization.

Among the many applications of AI-based tools are efforts to predict "risks" of bad outcomes in medical patients considered for treatment of severe pain by means of prescription opioid therapy. Desired characteristics of such tools include complete public transparency on the underlying mathematical models employed, the data used in training these tools, and all implicit but un-quantified assumptions of cause-and-effect that are in turn embedded in both the math models and the training data.

A specific AI-based tool now in wide use in chain pharmacies and State Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs meets none of these criteria of transparency. To wit, "NarxCare", a creation of Appriss (now Bamboo Health) has never been externally validated to establish the accuracy of its algorithms or the relevance of data sets used to "train" it. But NarxCare is employed by pharmacies every day to identify chronic pain patients who may be at elevated risk of opioid use disorder attributable to medically managed exposure to prescription opioid pain relievers.

Multiple reports have appeared in social media from patients who have been denied safe and effective opioid therapy solely because of receiving elevated risk scores generated by NarxCare. The tool appears incorrectly to "flag" female pain patients with a history of sexual abuse as high-risk patients. However, this may not be its only weakness.

In support of this Federal Register comment, I offer the following published references:

https://www.painnewsnetwork.org/stories/2018/5/19/what-every-patient-should-know-about-narxcare#.WwHzcT9P6Sc.facebook=

https://www.thedoctorpatientforum.com/resources/articles/312-did-appriss-now-bamboo-health-actually-externally-validate-narxcare

https://www.painnewsnetwork.org/stories/tag/NarxCare

Use of Narxcare to profile pain patients is particularly inappropriate in view of well established medical literature establishing that risks of opioid use disorder (aka "addiction" in popular vernacular) or overdose-related mortality are both rare and unpredictable. As only one example, the following is required reading:

Nora Volkow and A Thomas Mcmillan, “Opioid Abuse in Chronic Pain -- Misconceptions and Mitigation Strategies, ” New England Journal of Medicine, March 31, 2016 http://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMra1507771

A Key extract:

“Unlike tolerance and physical dependence, addiction is not a predictable result of opioid prescribing. Addiction occurs in only a small percentage of persons who are exposed to opioids — even among those with preexisting vulnerabilities (Table 3). Older medical texts and several versions of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) either overemphasized the role of tolerance and physical dependence in the definition of addiction or equated these processes (DSM-III and DSM-IV). However, more recent studies have shown that the molecular mechanisms underlying addiction are distinct from those responsible for tolerance and physical dependence, in that they evolve much more slowly, last much longer, and disrupt multiple brain processes...."

Likewise of import are recent papers suggesting that risk ratios commonly generated by profiling instruments are totally useless unless accompanied by actual numbers of patients affected. When cohorts of patients are relatively small, as they are in the medical literature of chronic pain, great caution is warranted in attempts to generalize policy. This caution is grossly violated by tools such as NarxCare.

See, for instance:

Richard A Lawhern, “How Misused Terminology and Biased Studies May Be Misguiding Our Understanding of Opioid Addiction and Mortality”, Kevin-MD – Medpage, May 23, 2023, https://www.kevinmd.com/2023/05/how-misused-terminology-and-biased-studies-may-be-misguiding-our-understanding-of-opioid-addiction-and-mortality.html

We believe the concrete goals that AI accountability objectives should target include: Transparency, Privacy, Protection of work, and Inclusivity and Bias. In regards to transparency and privacy, we need to incorporate what the sources of input data are, such as individuals, organizations, the means of collection, and how inclusive and diverse this process is. We also need to consider how the AIs’ output data is being used. For example, we need to maintain concrete knowledge of who will be able to see it, who will use it, and what exactly it will (or is allowed to be) used for. Some concerns and ways of going about how it’s used include the dictation of constraints by using legal contracts and implementing legal policy prohibiting certain usage clauses based on sources and the nature of training data. To address the protection of work, AI tools provide results based on data stored in the system without providing credits to the original producer. In order to make these goals a reality, there needs to be reinforcement by methods of risk assessment by researchers, and having government regulation, even on a global level to maintain consistency. Currently, the European Commission has an AI Act, which could potentially go global, if many countries’ governments agree to it, which hasn’t happened yet due to the extreme flexibility of the technological industry. A key component of this reinforcement is to continuously update relevant acts to reflect new technologies and the usage of models.

The key element of "AI" systems that are based upon machine learning (ML) is the training data set.

I have almost 20 years of experience in software development, so I am very familiar with new tech trends coming along and businesses adapting and building upon them. I have worked on several ML-based projects.

In responsible companies, every bit of data used in a training data set is sourced with written consent, or licensed from a vendor who has rights to the data. This is because a commercial product was being created, and companies wanted to maintain rights to the ML systems created from the training data. These companies could protect their intellectual property (IP) by showing they had rights to the data used.

I have observed in recent tech trends new ML techniques which are certainly promising and of great interest to tech companies. However, one limitation of all these ML systems is they cannot produce an output which was not represented in the training data, in whole or in part. If a new product or service based on these technologies generates an image or text, it must therefore be represented in the training data.

My understanding is that these new services charge money for access, and that some users of the service go on to sell the generated products. But they have also admitted to acquiring their training data without consent, license, or rights to the source works. This seems to mean they have stolen the works of the rightful artists.

Therefore, it seems necessary for any company or individual using ML technologies to prove they have license and rights to all their training data.

With stricter regulations on AI technology, we can further protect the rights of the individual and the artist alike. AI can be used for good — but first we need to slow its use as it can easily fall into the wrong hands.

I apologize for commenting anonymously, I am a pseudonymous independent artist and I usually keep my real life identity separate. I am aware this might impact the validity of my statements.

I want to speak purely on image based generative AI, as it's what I'm most familiar with, I believe these problems extend to all factors of machine learning that are growing in prevalence, however, as most of them function under the same machine learning rules: lots of data > patterns identified > those patterns interpolated together.

The current landscape for most generative image AI being pushed commercially was trained (see: copied) vast quantities of copyrighted and personal/private material (>5 billion images, all through LAION5B), and that trained machine learned tool was used as a basis for most of the visual training we're seeing today. Other algorithms developed such as MidJourney are almost definitely doing similar, even if not disclosed. As it is, the data that these algorithms are trained on puts their abilities in direct competition with the very required creators it needs to compete in the first place, as it learns how to recreate the images it was fed. What makes the "AI" process novel is that what it's learning is "how" to recreate, rather than merely copying the image itself, when it has countless images available to do this to, it can eventually interpolate all of these "learned" images together to create an amalgamation of those images, and weight them in specific ways after user input. This means that if prompted, someone could have it weight in a style or something protected under IP copyright law.

What makes this familiarity with the tool relevant to this comment is that this creates a parasitic relationship with the fuel that is used for AI; it creates an endless and easy to produce supply for the very fuel it consumed to function in any worthwhile manner artistic style, or other content. This ultimately devalues the work of it's origin data in a world where work needs to accommodate supply and demand to sell. With the awareness that it needs that very creator to exist in the first place to make content for it to copy and train on, this can only be described as a parasitic relationship with living humans who created this data in the first place through their labors that it runs on.

I believe the future can include AI in many fields with huge gains, but the current situation with them is unethical, grey area theft in my opinion, and ultimately devalues society, if society measures it's value by skilled laborers. Many other fields similar to this might encounter issues where personal data is accidentally recreated, or biases from learned patterns in data will be used unethically to make business and legal decisions, which I feel has already happened, but will only grow to starkly higher numbers if left without regulatory responsibilities placed on it.

The issues I face, having to face a shadow version of myself that can create an endless supply of 'art like mine', effectively destroying my livelihood through commission work and any sense of identity my art provides, can be mitigated to great efficacy through regulatory actions that force all use of AI to require it to be trained on explicitly and clearly defined opt-in only systems so that all data can be trusted to have been responsibly and ethically obtained with "creators" permissions. The current models out right now must be legally mandated for algorithmic disgorgement or other similar solutions, as they are profiting in vast amounts through the grey-area exploitation of our data at this very moment.

Many of these algorithms and their creators are likely relying heavily on the hope that they can continue to build on the previously ill-gotten gains of their data harvested AIs even post-regulation, because they've done the bulk of illicit collection they needed to already in order to create a "nest egg" that they can build on for the foreseeable future.

AI image, voice, and text generation methods are 100% built on the use of other individuals work, and there is no way to guarantee that such works are being used to train the programs with the consent of the artists, writers, and individuals who originally made said content. AI service providers must not only secure the express permission of the person and or persons whose work it intends to sample, but do express due diligence and provide a method for creators to check if their work is housed within their servers, as well as provide a convenient and expeditious means for such work to be removed. Additionally, users of AI services found to have uploaded work not their own and without consent of the creating party should face penalties, be it suspension or expulsion from AI services.

Ideally, a QR code watermark should be generated and added to any and all AI generated pieces, linking to a catalog of sampled reference used in the creation of the AI work; the AI program does such cataloging at the bringing of the process anyway through a tagging system, but as of right now there is an intentionally opaque handling of the presence of such references in AI. That being said, the incidental usage of a person’s likeness in the background of a reference is perhaps fine, but should someone go out in public with the intent to collect such ‘incidental’ reference, then, well, that’s no longer incidental, and should be considered an exploitation of public space and a harassment of the public. So long as intent can be proven, a judge and jury of peers could carry out a sentencing.

AI service providers should as well report upfront the high energy consumption of using their programs, including carbon generation and water used in the cooling of machines. Consumer awareness of the climate impact of services can be a deciding factor in utilizing said services or not; consumers deserve to be informed of the cost of their decisions.

Comment 1: Prohibit Unauthorized Surveillance and Directed Energy Use by UAS
The FAA must explicitly prohibit the use of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) for unauthorized surveillance, directed energy emissions, and acoustic harassment in residential and public spaces. These activities pose serious risks to public health, civil liberties, and constitutional protections.
Recommendations:
- Require onboard logging of all sensor activations (infrared, RF, acoustic, electromagnetic) with audit access for FAA and independent oversight bodies.
- Mandate geofencing and strict altitude restrictions near residential areas, unless a documented and publicly disclosed public-safety exemption is granted.
- Coordinate with the FCC and EPA to establish enforceable exposure limits for RF, microwave, and infrasound emissions from UAS platforms.

Introduction:

I am the adult daughter of a deaf parent who has struggled with obtaining information and applying for benefits from the Social Security Administration. Particularly, my mother struggled when attempting to access information in person or on the phone due to her disability.

Background Section:

I am commenting on the addition of a new routine use to permit disclosure to a proper applicant who submits a social security card application when the number holder is physically or mentally unable to file for a social security card and provides evidence of custody or legal relation to the number older.

My concern comes from recent experiences in helping my deaf mother communicate with the SSA. Specifically, when my mother’s husband passed away and we attempted to work with the SSA, it was very difficult. First, there were required phone calls which my mother could not participate in without assistance. Second, at the actual office, the glass partitions between the SSA employee and made it near impossible for her to understand what the employee was advising. Had I not been there to assist in every encounter with the SSA, my mother would not have been able to get the information she needed to apply for her late husband’s benefits.

Analysis:

I am in support of adding use 48 as described above to allow proper applicants to assist physically or mentally disabled peoples in applying for a social security card. I think it would be prudent to define what legal relationship is allowed. For example, is a child or parent or spouse or sibling allowed to assist, or is a power of attorney required? I suggest specifying that any parent, child sibling, or spouse or caregiver may apply for a disabled person.

In order to effectuate the purpose of assisting disabled persons in obtaining information as allowed in use 48, the record access procedures should also be updated accordingly, because as they are published in the proposed rule, they do not allow for other people to assist number holders in accessing records.

Additionally, I think it is important to add specific rules pertaining to the accessibility of in person SSA office visits for deaf and hard-of-hearing people, so that they do not need assistance from others. I understand that this may not the proper regulations for such rules but I do ask that the Administration consider adding such rules in the appropriate place. I believe such accommodations may in fact be required by the ADA, and that the current systems are not adequately allowing deaf people accessibility to SSA assistance. There needs to be some sort of system to all deaf people to communicate with SSA employees in person and on the phone without needing another person, and/or allowing another person to communicate in their stead, similar to the proposed regulations to assist holders who are disabled for such business. For example, text message services in lieu of phone calls, and display screens that show spoken or typed information to a deaf person.

Conclusion:

I applaud the efforts to allow proper persons to access records for disabled persons. I suggest more specific detail regarding who may help access records. I suggest that such persons be allowed to assist disabled persons in all business, not just applications for social security cards, and that this also be codified in the applicable regulations. Finally, I implore the SSA to update their systems to be accessible to deaf persons so that they do not need such assistance, and can conduct business with the SSA themselves, as they are capable of doing with assistive technology that is easily accessible and affordable.

To Whom It May Concern:

I strongly oppose the proposed rule, prompted by Executive Order 14168, that removes “gender” references in favor of “sex marker” at birth. This shift would force transgender individuals to use birth-assigned data, undermining both their dignity and existing legal protections.

Constitutional Violations

Equal Protection: By categorically reverting to birth sex, the rule discriminates against transgender people, contravening the Fifth Amendment’s promise of equal protection. Modern precedent recognizes that sex-based classifications targeting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.
Due Process: The forced mismatch between lived identity and official records burdens a protected liberty interest in personal autonomy, violating substantive due process.
Conflict with Federal Law and Precedent

Title VII and Bostock: Discrimination based on transgender status is a form of sex discrimination. This proposed rule is incompatible with the Supreme Court’s holding in Bostock v. Clayton County, which clarified that treating transgender individuals differently because of their identity is unlawful sex discrimination.
Administrative Procedure Act: Agencies must provide a rational, evidence-based reason for policy changes. No substantive justification supports this shift, making it arbitrary and capricious. The Social Security Administration also fails to address reliance interests of those who have already updated their gender markers.
Contrary to Medical Consensus and Human Dignity

Major medical authorities confirm that gender identity is intrinsic, and forcing birth-assigned labels harms transgender people’s health, safety, and mental well-being.
Official recognition of true identity fosters inclusion and prevents stigma. This rule’s requirement to contradict an individual’s actual identity fosters discrimination and intrusive “outing.”
Practical and Legal Concerns

Paperwork Reduction Act: Changing settled documentation places undue administrative and paperwork burdens on individuals and the SSA, contrary to the PRA’s goals.
Reliance Interests: Many have lawfully updated SSA records consistent with their gender identity. Reversing these updates disregards their reliance on established procedures.
Inconsistent Records: Forcing a birth sex marker creates interagency conflict, as passports, driver’s licenses, and other documents increasingly reflect affirmed gender. This leads to confusion and potential denial of services.
In conclusion, this proposal is legally, constitutionally, and ethically flawed. It contravenes established civil rights protections, medical standards, and efficient government recordkeeping. I urge the SSA to withdraw or revise the rule to maintain accurate, respectful, and nondiscriminatory documentation for all.

I am submitting these comments as a long-time disability advocate and attorney representative for Social Security disability claimants.

The agency’s decision to further extend the Temporary Final Rule (TFR) allowing flexibility in the “close proximity of time” standard through May 11, 2029, is laudable. However, we urge the agency to make this TFR permanent based on the sound and judicious reasons set forth herein.
The four-month period assumes that all disability applicants can successfully schedule and receive medical care and testing without interruption or delay. See 90 Fed. Reg. at 5583 (Jan. 17, 2025). Current trends in healthcare delivery make this best-case consecutive 4-month timeframe nearly impossible to meet for most disability applicants. This is not because the Listing-level impairments do not exist and are not documentable, but rather because the American healthcare system is simply not conducive to such swift assessment and treatment of orthopedic conditions. Ultimately, American medicine is categorically unable to meet the standard upon which the agency relied when creating the Listings’ criteria; as such, I submit that the agency should adjust its timeline to better match the realities of American healthcare.
It is first imperative to acknowledge the barriers to accessing healthcare in the United States, particularly specialty care for serious musculoskeletal impairments. The American healthcare system contains numerous and multifaceted barriers to accessing musculoskeletal medical care. These barriers are very frequently encountered in the population of disabled workers who seek out my services as a Social Security disability attorney.
Many disability benefits claimants rely on public health insurance, which further complicates the landscape of accessing specialty orthopedic care and compounds the underlying hurdles to accessing prompt orthopedic medical care as contemplated in the four-month time period articulated in the musculoskeletal Listings.
Indeed, it appears that medical practices, even those serving solely individuals with private health insurance, are not capable of scheduling patient visits quickly enough to accomplish the documentation required by the Listings. Even after successfully waiting more than a month to see a doctor, most claimants with musculoskeletal impairments will ultimately receive a referral to a specialist, thereby incurring another month’s long wait for the next doctor. While the first doctor may have properly documented some of the claimant’s signs and symptoms, if imaging is required, it could easily be another month before the imaging is complete. This lengthy process for proper treatment and medical documentation is commonly observed by our disability advocates, and this is assumes that our clients are even able to access such care in the face of the aforementioned barriers.
I commend the agency’s decision to extend the 12-month flexibility in evaluating close proximity of time until 2029. However, as the data forecasts, the U.S. healthcare system will not be able to meet the anticipated timeline standards anytime within the next decade. Should the agency revert to a 4-month standard without a properly accessible healthcare network in place, the Listings, which are already incredibly difficult to meet, will become absolutely impossible for almost all claimants to meet. Thus, the agency will waste valuable resources conducting further case development (at steps 4 and 5 of the sequential evaluation process) for individuals who do meet the requirements of the listing save for an inability to procure the required documentation quickly enough. As such, we urge the agency to consider making the 12-month standard permanent.

I am Gary Redenbacher and currently the Chairman of the Council for Children at the Children’s Advocacy Institute, University of San Diego School of Law (CAI). CAI’s mission is to give voice to children in need. We advocate in the legislature and the courts for children. The protection of foster children, in particular, has been a focus of CAI since they have more acute needs than virtually all other people in our society.
I am writing to urge the Social Security Administration (SSA) and the Administration for Children and Families (ACF) to take action to protect the property, Constitutional and due process rights of children in foster care, and to ensure benefits intended to address unmet current needs are properly administered or be conserved for future needs.

Both the SSA and ACF must enforce existing laws and regulations that govern state agencies' use of federal SSA survivor and disability benefits (SSA benefits) for foster youth, but are not doing so. It is critical that these federal agencies hold themselves, each other, and state agencies accountable for their handling of SSA benefits that can be vital to the wellbeing of foster children and youth, both while they are in foster care, when they return home, and after they leave the system.

Current law says that children’s SSA benefits must be used for their maintenance or their future needs. Current SSA rules help distinguish these options so that when a child’s maintenance costs are covered elsewhere, precisely as is the case for youth in foster care, their benefits should be saved for their futures, or used to meet their needs while in care that foster care agencies won’t pay for, like orthodontics, technology, educational goals, adaptive devices, or enrichment activities. When agencies intercept the benefits of foster youth who are disabled or have lost a parent, they are not following these rules, and instead only using the money to benefit themselves. Agencies have not been following or enforcing their own rules regarding protecting the rights of children, fulfilling their duties as representative payees, or making sure benefits are used in the best interests of the children. Many states across the country and the political spectrum are now trying to remedy this, but need guidance from federal agencies to do so with confidence and support.
I recommend that SSA issue regulations and clarify and expand guidance to child welfare agencies, articulating plans for oversight and enforcement of current rules, strongly encouraging conservation of SSA benefits, and supporting the use of tools such as ABLE accounts or special needs trusts to protect youth from exceeding SSI resource limits. New policies should prohibit the use of SSA benefits solely for revenue generation by agencies and instead ensure these funds support the real needs of foster youth that will improve their chances of returning home faster or aging out with greater independence and stability.
Foster youth face significant risks upon exiting care, including homelessness and financial instability. Ensuring fair information about and access to their SSA survivor and disability benefits can bridge the gap during vulnerable transitions. Agencies must uphold the intent of these benefits to support the best interests of children, not state fiscal departments.

Thank you for considering these reforms and for your commitment to improving the lives of foster youth.

In this comment, I will start with some questions generated based on the RFI for the team's consideration. Number 6 presents something of an overly simplistic summary of how the system might be advanced.

1. Are there ways the benefits qualification process can more fully inform case planning?

2. How might tighter integration of benefits qualification and case planning improve a caseworker’s ability to serve clients and the initial provisioning of services?

3. How might integrations of approved document management services (e.g., ID.me) ease applicant burden and smooth transitions out of the foster system?

4. Where can automated checks be implemented to harvest time savings across the caseworker population?

5. Is there a mechanism that helps payees track and manage expenditures?
If not, the SSA could invest in offering a system enabling payees to automatically import account information. The system would track expenditures, allow the upload of receipts, notify payees of suggested conservation periods, allow payees to upload expenditure rationale for approvals, and include caseworker client support tools. Caseworker time saved from digitization of workflows, automated data validation, and event-based/scheduled push notifications can be reinvested into the client experience.

6. The SSA may consider highlighting constructive opportunities to burn conserved funds in service to the child’s best interest. Highlights may be served to clients via the Foster Care Management Portal or otherwise.

The frequency of highlighted opportunities may be introduced to payees as a function of available conserved funds, % of max conserved funds, and run rate coefficients assigned to a payee account.  The SSA may identify high-impact touch points to make caregivers more aware of engaging learning experiences. For example, aggregated data from expenditure reports may offer categorical signals on how the child's needs are being provided and where opportunities exist for administrative bodies to promote well-rounded foster care experiences. In summary, this comment broadly promotes two actions: (i) the development of semi-custom technology to advance caseworker efficiency and ease of engagement for payees and (ii) the reinvestment of caseworker time savings into concierge services.

The Child’s Bureau may use appropriate information about the child (e.g., wellness reports) to identify and suggest conservation burn opportunities that expand exposure to life experiences and concentrated skills building.  Young people benefit tremendously from commitments that nurture connections to curiosity, exploration, play & sustained activity, and imagination — learning happens in so many contexts of life!

As a retired SSA employee, I worked frequently with children in Children's Division custody who received SSI or children's benefits. The biggest problem was when a child left care, for whatever reason, it frequently took up to six months (and sometimes more) to get the conserved funds to the new payee, or the beneficiary, if they were over 18. It was difficult to get in touch with anyone about this, and we had young adults/payees who were in dire financial need at that point. When a child moved to a different home, they often came with only the clothes on their backs. When that money was most needed, it was inaccessible.

It needs to be more automated, or to have a central person/unit to release the funds as soon as the new payee is named. Instead, it takes months. I can't tell you how many times I had new payees at my desk in tears because they couldn't afford to buy clothes or school supplies, for instance, when they had recently been appointed.

There also wasn't much accountability in the process. It was very common to get shuffled around from person to person when trying to get assistance. No one seemed to be able to answer the question, or to take action to release the necessary funds. That is simply unacceptable, when there is a child in need.

I know case workloads are staggering, and bureaucracy is real, but if there were a way to automate it, that would make it easier for everyone. The children are the ones suffering under the current system.

I am a guardian ad litem in the state of Indiana for transition age youth experiencing the foster care system. When a child is eligible or receiving SSI/SSDI/RSDI in the state of Indiana, these federal funds are used by the department of child services to support the needs of the youth while they are in care. The direct payee for these benefits (if the child is a minor) is elected to be the Indiana Department of Child Services. This results in the youth’s benefits going through multiple channels before being provided to the recipient of these benefits, if at all. I have had multiple older youth in foster care where I have had to advocate for the youth to be their own payee to avoid their federal benefits being used by the state to support their needs in foster care. It would be in the best interest of the foster youth in this country to have a voice in how their benefits are being used by the state as wards of the state. In my professional experience, child welfare agencies are not having the appropriate discussions with foster youth regarding the identified payee of their social security benefits, resulting in this lack of financial support that they could strongly benefit from as youth emerging from foster care as young adults. When a child turns 18, they have the opportunity to enter into the voluntary collaborative care program for extended foster care until they turn 21. When foster youth transition into collaborative care, the payee for these benefits should be the young adult, not their foster parent or DCS.

This is about teenagers in foster care, who are in school. These children are often very smart and capable. But have issues with their foster parents. As a school teacher, I often get the impression that the parents are well-meaning old-fashioned parents, who want the children to operate within those standards. This means sports, standard Sunday programs, and part-time employment,  in addition to school work. The child may prefer social studies and languages while the parents might want the child to go for Math, Computing, etc. Work Force Programs in combination with 2-Year College studies are a viable source of choosing electives. We are writing to urge the Social Security Administration (SSA) and the Administration for Children and Families (ACF) to take action to protect the public benefits of foster youth from being spent by state agencies while they are minors. Through our experience both in managing and advising housing and benefits advocacy programs, we have seen how critical it is that young adults aging out of the foster care system have access to income to support their independence.

Federal law and regulations require that foster youth’s Supplemental Security Income and Social Security Survivor’s benefits be used, with input from the child, to meet the individual unmet current needs of the child or saved for their future needs. Yet most foster care agencies routinely apply for and then take foster youth’s benefits to supplant their own fiscal obligations without any notice to or consultation with the child or the child’s legal representatives.

Title IV-E mandates that states shall make foster care maintenance payments on behalf of each child in foster care, regardless of their disability or benefit status. But SSA regulations explain that if a child’s benefits are “not needed for these purposes”, the funds must be conserved or invested on behalf of the child. A child’s benefits are not needed for their maintenance when they are provided for elsewhere, as is inarguably the case for all foster children under Title IV-E. Thus, under federal law and regulation, a foster child’s federal benefits may only be used for the child’s unmet current needs – beyond that which the state is required to cover under IV-E – or conserved for future use.

A comprehensive resolution of this issue will be a collaborative effort between SSA, ACF and Congress. With over half of states enacting or considering reforms, leadership and guidance by SSA and ACF is essential to support state action to preserve these vital benefits which can contribute to preventing removals and reentries into care, expedite reunification, and significantly improve transitional outcomes for youth. SSA and HHS must both issue guidance because when child welfare agencies apply for benefits and assume the role of representative payee, they must comply with rules and regulations from both agencies, and need assurance that actions under one set of rules will not bring them out of compliance with another set of rules.

As an attorney for children for the past two decades, I am writing to urge the Social Security Administration (SSA) and the Administration for Children and Families (ACF) to take action to protect the property, Constitutional and due process rights of children and youth in foster care, and to ensure benefits intended to address unmet current needs or be conserved for future needs are properly administered. Both the SSA and ACF must enforce existing laws and regulations that govern state agencies; use of federal SSA survivor and disability benefits (SSA benefits) for foster youth, but are not doing so. It is critical that these federal agencies hold themselves, each other, and state agencies accountable for their handling of SSA benefits that can be vital to the wellbeing of foster children and youth, both while they are in foster care, when they return home, and after they leave the system.

Current law says that children’s SSA benefits must be used for their maintenance or their future
needs. Current SSA rules help distinguish these options so that when a child’s maintenance costs are covered elsewhere, precisely as is the case for youth in foster care, their benefits should be saved for their futures, or used to meet their needs while in care that foster care agencies won’t pay for, like orthodontics, technology, educational goals, adaptive devices, or enrichment activities. When agencies intercept the benefits of foster youth who are disabled or have lost a parent, they are not following these rules, and instead only using the money to benefit themselves. Agencies have not been following or enforcing their own rules regarding protecting the rights of children, fulfilling their duties as representative payees, or making sure benefits are used in the best interests of the children. Many states across the country and the political spectrum are now trying to remedy this, but need guidance from federal agencies to do so with confidence and support.

I request that SSA issue regulations and clarify and expand guidance to child welfare
agencies, articulating plans for oversight and enforcement of current rules, strongly encouraging
conservation of SSA benefits, and supporting the use of tools such as ABLE accounts or special
needs trusts to protect youth from exceeding SSI resource limits. New policies should prohibit the use of SSA benefits solely for revenue generation by agencies and instead ensure these funds support the real needs of foster youth that will improve their chances of returning home faster or aging out with greater independence and stability.

Foster youth face significant risks upon exiting care, including homelessness and financial
instability. The majority of youth in San Diego leaving care are facing homelessness and food insecurity. Ensuring fair information about and access to their SSA survivor and disability
benefits can bridge the gap during vulnerable transitions when these youth need any and every dollar they can access . Agencies must uphold the intent of these benefits to support the best interests of children, not state fiscal departments.

Thank you for considering these reforms and for your commitment to improving the lives of
foster youth.

Carolyn Griesemer, Esq.

I am responding to Docket No. SSA-2024-0038, Request for Information: Use and Conservation of Social Security Benefits and Supplemental Security Income Payments that Representative Payees Receive for Beneficiaries Residing in Foster Care.

I am an economist at the University of Chicago. I have studied the outcomes of children receiving Supplemental Security Income for the past decade. Although I do not have a particular expertise in children receiving SSI who are in foster care, I have studied the transition to adulthood for children who receive SSI more generally.

In a paper with Michael Mueller-Smith (QJE 2022), I study the effect of removing children receiving SSI benefits on their employment and criminal justice involvement in adulthood. We find that being removed from SSI at age 18 increases the number of criminal charges over the next 20 years by 30%. The effects are particularly large for what we call “income-generating” charges, meaning charges associated with activities intended to generate income (theft, fraud/forgery, burglary, robbery, drug distribution, and prostitution). Being removed from SSI also increases the likelihood of incarceration. The effects of SSI removal on criminal charges and incarceration are highly persistent over the next 20 years and increase during economic recessions.

These results suggest that the resources available during the transition to adulthood are critical for the life outcomes of children who receive SSI benefits. Staying on SSI after age 18 (which means having the cash benefits and other benefits included in SSI) reduces long-term criminal justice involvement substantially for these young people. This finding relates to the question about conserving SSI benefits for children until they reach adulthood. The results of our paper suggest that making such resources available to children when they reach 18 could reduce their criminal justice involvement and improve their long-term outcomes. Of course, the benefits of conserving these resources and making them available to individuals in young adulthood must be weighed against the benefits to those individuals of using the resources to provide services to them in childhood.

As a federally licensed tax professional (Enrolled Agent - IRS) we are obligated under various rules such as GLBA and Section 7216 to safeguard even a client or potential client's name. We also much disclose and obtain consent in writing before entering even a client's contact information such as name, address, email etc. into any 3rd party software. Our interpretation is that includes widely used software such as android apps, intuit, Microsoft, google etc.

IN the spirit of these rules, FINCEN MUST protect the information it is gathering under the new BOI rules.

I believe that FINCEN should disclose to the applicants upfront a minimum upfront:
1- What type of parties are able to access the information under some legal basis without the affirmative consent in writing of the applicants.
2- All other releases MUST require affirmative written consent that can be granted AND RETRACTED by the applicants.

REGARDLESS, when ANY party is granted access under any rules, those releases should be able to be viewed by logging back into the FINCEN portal. Those entering BOI information should have BROAD TRANSPARENCY about ANYONE who has accessed their information.

While recognizing the purpose of the new law is to identify criminal activities that harm the Country's security, most of the beneficial owners are law abiding citizens which should have access easily to who can see and use their information.

In some instances small companies starting to do business in the US do not yet have a US address.  It would be beneficial to allow the business address of the Reporting Company to be the truthful address of the entity.  If a US address is necessary, it would be helpful to state that a Registered Agent address is allowed, since that is often the only US address available and the Registered Agent will have the ability to contact the Reporting Company.

The current BOI reporting requirement seems like a good idea at face value, but imposes a bureaucratic burden that leaves a lot of gaps in execution.

For example, what if an owner or manager is another legal entity, other than a natural person (such as a trust, another LLC, etc.) - there is no clarity on how to report those, and an LLC manager (or other responsible parting for reporting purposes) may not always have visibility into changes of ownership of underlying non-natural person entities.

Also, where is a portal where one can see all reports they have made in the past so he/she can quickly make updates/amends as needed? What if an entity ceases to exist, why keep records in perpetuity (or so it seems)? Why not make these reporting requirements (instead), including updates, something reportable at tax time (once a year)?

Also, for Series LLCs (where many states allow their creation without notifying the state), FinCEN still does not make it clear how such entities should report their BOI.

A lot is missing from the current process, and a lot needs to be clarified.
