I think there is a potentially huge risk of exploitation of the CTA by third-parties, data-mining companies, and any state/local/national agencies. People have a right to conduct their affairs with minimal intrusion from government agencies. In order for an agency or person to request data from a FINCEN report, there must be an absolutely pressing need that is in the national security interest or other extremely pressing reason. Mere convenience or curiosity can NEVER be the standard that would allow an agency or individual to obtain access to a FINCEN report. The terms must not be nebulous.

I should also add that millions of Americans still don't know about the FINCEN BOI report requirement. There has not been a concerted singular effort to get out the information from trusted sources. Instead, the burden seems to have fallen on third-party financial or regulatory companies (or law firms, CPAS, etc.) to educate their clients which is time consuming and often distracts from their actual work they seek to perform and serving their clients. What is going to occur is a patchwork of enforcement for the INVETIABLE millions and millions of law-abiding Americans who inadvertently have failed to comply. What will be the government response? It will likely be a patchwork of enforcement since the federal gov will be unable to keep up with the "violations." This will create further mistrust and ambiguity in the federal government.

Additionally, much of this information in a FINCEN BOI report is already available with tax returns which are ALREADY signed under penalty of perjury and subject to audit and not to mention state, DMV, local and other databases. The FINCEN BOI reports purpose is largely duplicative and will be costly to run and probably impossible for the federal government to enforce with tens of millions of entities in existence that are currently required to file. The risks are enormous...we have seen state and federal governments increasingly weaponize data, information, and access to US citizens based on things like race, gender, political beliefs, religion or other protected classes. This cannot be allowed to occur, and we'd be foolish to think that these same agencies wouldn't use FINCEN BOI data in a similar fashion if they are left unchecked. Many federal agencies are run by unelected, unknown, and seemingly unaccountable humans, who are not usually impartial and frequently make mistakes. We have seen how the Patriot Act, originally introduced as a counter-terrorism measure in the wake of 9/11 constantly expanded beyond its original intent to now grant ability to spy on ordinary Americans for myriad issues.

The road to hell is paved with good intentions and the FINCEN BOI reports cannot become another statistic regarding this. Unfortunately it seems that it is heading that way without significant changes to who/what/when/where/why information can be accessed and a dramatic relaxation of penalties for "violations."

I am an officer of a Pennsylvania HOA. We are nonprofit for Pennsylvania purposes, by default, and file the tax form 1120-H. The HOA does not require this information in order to serve on the board.  As board positions can change frequently, a form will need to be filed with the government every time a board position changes. This is a burden to the administration of the HOA and will quell a member's desire to serve, and result in empty positions for the board. Without proper board representation, the corporation could be operating outside of current regulations for nonprofit corporation governance. For an HOA corporation, this legal requirement is, well, ridiculous.

Please consider the following:
For "Person(s) associated with this Transferee" the reporting person should have the ability to select multiple "Person Type" categories in field 39. Under the existing FinCEN GTO's it is very common for a Beneficial Owner to also be the Signing Individual. Retyping the same individuals information into the associated fields for multiple "Person type" and very time consuming and leads to an increase in typographical errors. Allowing the reporting person to select multiple categories in filed 39 will significantly reduce the amount of time necessary for the completion of the report.

Homeowner’s Associations, Community Associations, and Condominium Associations should be considered Exempt Reporting Companies from the current BOIR reporting requirements.

I work for a nationwide home builder with communities in various stages of development across the country. Almost every single community has an HOA or a Condominium Association which we create pursuant to the recorded documents in each state. Until each community has sold and closed enough homes to transition the HOA to the homeowners, the Declarant/Developer appoints employees to serve as the officers for the Board of Directors. "The BSA authorizes the Secretary of the Treasury (Secretary) to, inter alia,

Side Note: the cited language from 31 USC s. 5311 used to include the term "high degree of usefulness". Since the AML Act of 2020, that term has been changed to "highly useful".

FinCEN attempts to determine the burden and cost of the rule being renewed, and comes up with a total cost of $18,500,000.

That cost (burden) needs to be weighed against the benefit(s) - whether this recordkeeping requirement provides highly useful information to law enforcement. There was nothing in the notice about the usefulness of this recordkeeping requirement. If it is not providing useful information, or the value of the information is less than the costs and burden, do not renew the rule - scrap it.

Excluding state IA and ERA's nullifies the purpose and effect of the rule change along with that of the BSA while obfuscating federalism. If IA as the entry point of foreign corrupt practices and agents, and the majority of entry points are located in states with either little oversight, inadequate technology or regulation, then as written this rule change will permit bad actors to use state IA to circumvent the 'reasonableness' standard financial institutions implement.
For example, I know of a IA and fund situated in Texas, opened by a Native American who illegitimately used a tribal entity's EIN etc. That fund has deposits in the Bank of India with PNC and Capital One, yet there is no oversight of that fund by the state because the individual falsely used a tribal entity's sovereignty to open it using a state IA. None of the financial institution's risk tools captured or even flagged the account because it met state regulations/law despite it being used unlawfully and for a corrupt purpose.

Some states may have inadequate oversight regulations (sometimes intentional) that will allow local banks to skirt more strict oversight.  Since these banks have access to wire transfer services this creates an attractive opportunity for local banks to be a jumping off point for international money laundering especially through private equity funds that frequently operate internationally. Re: Docket Number FINCEN–2024–0006 and RIN 1506–AB58 To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing in response to the notice of proposed rulemaking issued by FinCEN on February 15, 2024, wherein FinCEN proposes to expand the definition of a “financial institution” under the Bank Secrecy Act (“BSA”) to include certain investment advisers and to compel such investment advisers (“Covered IAs”) to abide by additional regulatory requirements in order to address illicit finance risks (the “Proposed Rule”).

The BSA is an important piece of legislation that helps to combat money laundering, the financing of terrorism, and other illicit financial activity. It is rightfully applicable to the very financial institutions that are responsible for the movement and custody of funds and securities, such as broker-dealers and banks. Historically, most investment advisers have been scoped out of the definition of a “financial institution” for good reason – imposing BSA requirements on investment advisers would be unnecessary and redundant, as their clients’ cash and securities transactions are processed through broker-dealers and banks that are already subject to the BSA.

In recent years, the amount of regulatory compliance obligations imposed upon investment advisers, and their associated resourcing requirements and costs, have increased substantially and shows no sign of abatement at the federal level. While there may be differences of opinion on how meritorious each of these regulatory obligations are within the industry, it is an undisputed fact that each adds on to the regulatory burden carried by the investment adviser.

As currently written, the Proposed Rule has no identifiable quantitative benefit yet would force investment advisers as a group to spend billions of dollars to be in compliance with its onerous rules.

It would be burdensome and unjustified to compel investment advisers to shoulder additional regulatory obligations that are unnecessary and duplicative in nature. The focus of the BSA should continue to be on the very financial institutions that are responsible for moving and processing clients’ cash and securities: broker-dealers and banks, as that is where the risk lies. Expanding the application to parties who merely provide investment advice is a wayward measure that will not address any real risk. For these reasons, the Proposed Rule should be shelved, just like its predecessors.

Making everyone report to the SEC is a positive change as it will allow as it allows some extra oversight into those who may be trying to act in bad faith. However, excluding state IAs and ERAs from having to register with the SEC defeats the purpose of the rule change and the Bank Secrecy Act by giving bad actors a loophole. This could be potentially solved by making every IA or ERA register and although that may increase costs it might be partly offset by taxes on money that may have been laundered.

First, you need to extend the comment period. The first quarter of the year is extremely busy for registered investment advisers that are required to update Form ADV, oversee audited financials and preparation of tax statements.

I also agree with some of the other commenters that have noted that investment advisers, especially those that manage private funds, are extremely overburdened with new regulations that the SEC has adopted or is in the process of adopting. Small firms are forced to pay a substantial amount in order to comply with the regulations that have implementation dates in 2024 and 2025. Adding another regulation will be overly burdensome to the small investment advisers.

I am extremely supportive of anti-money laundering regulation as I served as the Anti-Money Laundering Compliance Officer for two broker-dealers of a major insurance company for several years. That being said I disagree with FINCEN's position that hedge funds are risky for money laundering because some Russian oligarchs have invested in hedge funds. Our hedge fund has an administrator that is registered as a transfer agency with the SEC and is subject to AML regulation. They perform KYC and check OFAC and sanctions lists before admitting a new investor or paying a redemption. Redemptions can only be sent to the investor's bank account on file. They are required to report suspicious activities. Quite honestly, I fail to see how the investment adviser would provide more safeguards to this process.

FINCEN's other example of a Singapore national money laundering using private equity involved some of largest investment banks in the world. These investment banks were required and had implemented AML policies and procedures with vast resources. Focusing on tighter controls at these institutions would better serve preventing money laundering rather than overly burdening small investment advisers.

FINCEN also excluded investment advisers that sub-advise mutual funds. What about investment advisers that sub-advise European SICAV's? SICAVs are essentially non-US mutual funds. They are heavily regulated by EU anti-money laundering regulations that from my understanding appear to be more onerous than US anti-money laundering regulations.

As the BSA officer for a bank, I would like to voice that the requirement for the monetary cash log for cash transactions between $3000 and $10,000 is burdensome and irrelevant. There are many factors that say this is an antiquated process.
1. Wire transactions - Many people now wire funds versus purchasing a cashier's check or money order because of the speed of getting the receiver the funds.
2. Zelle - Person to person payments are becoming more popular.
3. The younger generations do not prefer paper items.
4. We create a CTR for anything over $10,000. An amount of $3000 to $10,000 is pocket change for many people. It is not an indicator of a transaction which BSA was designed to detect.

Thank you,

Please find attached the American Bankers Association's comments on the NPRM re: Anti-Money Laundering/Countering the Financing of Terrorism Program and Suspicious Activity Report Filing Requirements for Registered Investment Advisers and Exempt Reporting Advisers, Docket Number FINCEN–2024–0006 and RIN 1506–AB58.

Please find attached the Alternative Investment Management Association (AIMA) response to FINCEN–2024–0006 and RIN 1506–AB58. Anti-Money Laundering/Countering the Financing of Terrorism Program and Suspicious Activity Report Filing Requirements for Registered Investment Advisers and Exempt Reporting Advisers. Please let us know if you have any questions on our response.

Ladies and Gentlemen:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule (89 FR 12108).

A similar rule was proposed several years ago, and it included a provision that would have required investment advisers to have an independent examination of its anti-money laundering and anti-terrorism financing program, similar to the independent examinations to which registered banks and broker-dealers have been subject for over twenty years.

In the current proposed rule, that requirement appears to have been dropped, at least explicitly. However, it is not quite clear what is contemplated by FinCEN in stating that investment advisers would have to "fulfill other obligations applicable to financial institutions subject to the BSA and FinCEN’s implementing regulations" as noted in the FinCEN press release concerning the proposed rule. This vague language will lead to confusion. Indeed, some would argue that it is redolent with the potential for regulatory drift. If that requirement is being reintroduced, obliquely, the compliance costs would be significant.

More generally, there is a serious question about the need for the proposed rule. First, the Bank Secrecy Act and related statutes do not capture investment advisers in the definition of "financial institution." It is then reasonable to query whether Congress would need to act such that, as a matter of statute, investment advisers can be the subject of any FinCEN rulemaking. One commenter, Cooley LLP, addresses this point and notes: "While the statutory BSA provisions do not include investment advisers in the definition of a financial institution, FinCEN has the authority to add businesses that engage in any activity 'similar to, related to, or a substitute for' activities in which any of the enumerated financial institutions are authorized to engage. FinCEN states in the commentary to the proposed rule that the asset management services provided by investment advisers are similar to or a substitute for those offered by other financial institutions already covered under the BSA, including broker-dealers, banks and insurance companies."

This is a weak argument. The fact that broker-dealers and banks provide investment advisory services as part of their range of services is not apposite. It is their per se activities as broker-dealers and banks (as set forth in statutes) that give rise to their particular and important roles in the important global battle against money laundering and terrorism financing, not their other activities.

Investment advisers are, essentially, agents standing in for their principals in terms of investment decision-making, similar to (but not identical to) the manner in which an attorney-in-fact stands in for another pursuant to an instrument granting power of attorney. Is anyone acting in this way also to be the subject of the proposed rule? Trustees? Attorneys? Executors of estates? Receivers? We think that the proposed rule necessarily invites such questions and will leave those acting in those capacities without clear guidance as to the applicability of a rule that suggests their activities are a "substitute for" what bona fide (de jure) financials institutions do. Given that this may come with serious consequences, the applicability of the rule to such actors should be seriously considered.

Are investment advisory services really "similar to, related to, or a substitute for" services provided by financial institutions? If so, why did it take more than twenty years to realize this? The likely answer is that those services, though proximate, are not meaningfully and substantively similar. While it is certainly a good idea to do all that can be done to address money laundering, which is a global plague (including among state actors), it is not at all clear that the statutory authority has been granted to FinCEN such that it can capture investment advisers under the definition of "financial institution" without Congressional action. Further, investment advisers effect transactions only (or almost always) through statutorily-defined "financial institutions" that are already covered by anti-money laundering laws, so it is no more clear today than it was several years ago why it is the case that the proposed rule is needed. An investment adviser that opens an account for a client will have to run the gauntlet of AML-CDD-ATF-KYC reviews imposed by de jure financial institutions that will facilitate transactions for those clients and/or serve as custodians for client assets.

In our view, the raft of regulations with which advisers must already comply is onerous enough. The Investment Advisers Act and the various securities laws impose numerous obligations. Further, it may well be that the proposed rule, in its present form, is beyond the scope of FinCEN's authority (that is, is ultra vires).


Dr. David E. McClean
Principal
DMA Consulting Group

**REVISED COMMENT**

Ladies and Gentlemen:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule (89 FR 12108). A similar rule was proposed several years ago, and it included, inter alia, a provision that would have required investment advisers to have an independent examination of its anti-money laundering program, similar to the independent examinations to which registered banks and broker-dealers have been subject for over twenty years. We note that in the current proposed rule that requirement reappears (though it was omitted in the FinCEN press release). That particular requirement, should this rule be adopted as proposed, would impose significant costs on advisers, which run the gamut from small firms with less than ten employees, to large organizations with billions under management and/or advisement and hundreds of employees.

More generally, there is a serious question about the need for the proposed rule. First, the Bank Secrecy Act and related statutes do not capture investment advisers in the definition of "financial institution." It is then reasonable to query whether Congress would need to act such that, as a matter of statute, investment advisers can be the subject of the rather sweeping rulemaking proposed. One commenter, Cooley LLP, addresses this point, and notes: "While the statutory BSA provisions do not include investment advisers in the definition of a financial institution, FinCEN has the authority to add businesses that engage in any activity 'similar to, related to, or a substitute for' activities in which any of the enumerated financial institutions are authorized to engage. FinCEN states in the commentary to the proposed rule that the asset management services provided by investment advisers are similar to or a substitute for those offered by other financial institutions already covered under the BSA, including broker-dealers, banks and insurance companies."(https://www.cooley.com/news/insight/2024/2024-02-22-fincen-proposes-rule-requiring-investment-advisers-to-establish-anti-money-laundering-programs)

This is a weak argument. The fact that broker-dealers and banks provide investment advisory services as part of their range of services is not apposite. It is their per se activities as broker-dealers and banks (as set forth in statutes) that give rise to their particular and important roles in the global battle against money laundering and terrorism financing, not their other activities. Investment advisers, registered or not, are, essentially, agents standing in for their principals in terms of investment decision-making, similar to (but not identical to) the manner in which an attorney-in-fact stands in for another pursuant to an instrument granting power of attorney. Is anyone acting in this way also to be the subject of the proposed rule? Trustees? Attorneys? Executors of estates? Receivers? We think that the proposed rule necessarily invites such questions and will leave those acting in those capacities without clear guidance as to the applicability of a rule that suggests their activities are a "substitute for" what bona fide (de jure) financials institutions do. Given that this may come with serious consequences, the applicability of the rule to such actors should be seriously considered.

Are investment advisory services really "similar to, related to, or a substitute for" services provided by financial institutions? If so, why did it take more than twenty years to realize this? The likely answer is that those services, though proximate to banking and brokerage functions, are not meaningfully and substantively similar. While it is certainly a good idea to do all that can be done to address money laundering, which is a global plague (including among state actors), it is not at all clear that the statutory authority has been granted to FinCEN such that it can capture investment advisers under the definition of "financial institution" without Congressional action.

Further -- and this goes to the need for the proposed rule -- investment advisers effect transactions almost always through statutorily-defined "financial institutions" that are already covered by anti-money laundering laws, so it is no more clear today than it was several years ago why it is the case that the proposed rule is needed. An investment adviser that opens an account for a client will have to run the gauntlet of AML-CDD-ATF-KYC reviews imposed by de jure financial institutions that will facilitate transactions for those clients and/or serve as custodians for client assets. Adding a duplicative layer of regulations would seem to serve no good public purpose. It would almost surely burden many investment advisers with substantial compliance obligations and costs.

Dr. David E. McClean
Principal DMA Consulting Group
http://dmacgroup.net
and author-editor, Understanding and Combating Global Corruption: A Reader

I believe the $10,000.00 filing requirement needs to be raised to a higher amount, to adequately reflect the intended purpose of the Bank Secrecy Act, which is to track money laundering and suspicious activity. Far too often, as a BSA bank employee, my required daily findings rarely generate information which results in Suspicious Activity Report filing. With inflation devaluing the currency, the amount of CTR filings I believe needs to be analyzed and examined.

The existing Currency Transaction Reporting System (CTR) is antiquated and dysfunctional. The $10,000.00 threshold, established as part of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) under the Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act of 1970, is not reflective of the present economic landscape. Adjusting for inflation, $10,000.00 in 1970 is equivalent to approximately $50,000.00 in today's dollars. Therefore, it is proposed to update the threshold to $50,000.00 to better align with current financial realities, to eliminate the CTR system in its entirety.

Moreover, the requirement for a CTR should not be applicable to all transactions but rather limited to those deemed suspicious by banking and financial authorities. Many businesses still engage in cash transactions rather than relying solely on digital means, and recognizing this, adjustments to reporting thresholds should be made to save precious taxpayer funds.

Furthermore, considering that criminals have adopted more sophisticated means than currency, it is suggested that the CTR system, in its current form, is no longer effective and has harmed more innocent Americans than served a purpose. Therefore, there I propose to rescind and terminate the CTR system, deeming it unnecessary in the 21st century.

The legislative framework known as the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) comprises the Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act of 1970, amended by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001 and the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AML Act). The BSA is codified in various sections of U.S. Code and includes implementing regulations at 31 CFR chapter X.

These laws often overlap, creating a complex regulatory landscape that can be likened to a "paint yourself in a corner scenario," leading to inefficiencies and challenges in compliance.

To streamline processes and reduce bureaucratic burdens, the U.S. Government should consider raising the threshold for tracking currency transactions from $10,000 to $100,000. The current threshold, established over 30 years ago, has become outdated due to economic inflation.

Furthermore, the stringent monitoring and surveillance measures associated with the current threshold have raised concerns about potential violations of the Fourth Amendment rights of U.S. citizens. There have been numerous instances of government overreach and unlawful snooping, totaling over 100,000 violations.

A review of existing rules and regulations is necessary to eliminate redundancies and streamline compliance efforts. Such a review could yield substantial cost savings for taxpayers and reduce the burden of excessive paperwork and investigations that often lead to dead ends.

Ultimately, by implementing a more substantive and efficient process, the U.S. Government can safeguard the constitutional rights of its citizens while maintaining effective measures to combat financial crimes.

By increasing this reporting limit it would ease the burden and time spent when having to file the lower cash amounts as we are seeing customers purchasing or dealing a lot more with cash in the last couple of years. I also believe this limit change would be beneficial to FINCEN.

On behalf of the Board of Directors and the Management Team at Broadview Federal Credit Union, we would like to thank FinCEN for providing us with the opportunity to provide input regarding CTR filings at our credit union.

Broadview FCU is headquartered in Albany, NY, and serves over 506,000 members.

As the $10,000 CTR filing threshold has not been adjusted for nearly 55 years, we request that it be raised to $20,000 or $30,000. In fact, $10,000 in 1970 would be equivalent to over $75,000 in today's dollars so comparatively, a threshold of $20,000 or $30,000 would still be well below the reporting threshold set in 1970.

We also recommend that the reporting threshold be adjusted every five years to keep pace with inflation.

The following are reporting statistics relative to Broadview FCU:

-In 2023, Broadview FCU filed 4,973 CTRs.
-3,818 (77%) were between $10,000.01 and $19,999.99
-777 (16%) were between $20,000 and $29,999.99
-378 (7%) were more than $30,000

Simply by raising the reporting threshold to $20,000, our CTR reporting would have been reduced from 4,973 filings to 1,155 filings. By raising the reporting threshold to $30,000, our CTR reporting would drop to 378.

Should you have further questions, please feel free to reach out to our Director of Anti-Money Laundering Investigations, Tim Ortwein, at tortwein@BroadviwFCU.com.

Thank you,

Bob Bascom,
Director of Legal Support and Legislative Affairs

I had worked on filing DOEPs at one of my employers between 2017 and 2022 in which I was not only responsible for maintaining the Phase II Exemptions, but also doing the annual reviews for the appropriate customers where appropriate. There are two concerns that I have that may be worth reviewing.

In the past, I had been responsible for reviewing Phase II Exempt customers that primary do business during the summer season, but with the COVID-19 pandemic that unfolded in 2020, there was the possibility that because the primary funding that unfolded had some businesses close based on the eligibility that businesses would open, maintaining five CTRs was cutting it close and they nearly missed having its eligibility revoked. Perhaps something to consider in the future is a courtesy waiver to grant a business an extension despite missing the five CTRs in 12 months in the event of a global pandemic were to occur again, regardless if the entity is a seasonal business or one that operates 365 days a year.

A second suggestion I had is some cash-intensive businesses that regularly meet CTR thresholds. In my experience, gas stations I reviewed typically had on average one CTR a week as most relied on the gas station pumps, and even with some gas stations that had lottery services, the lottery seldom makes a dent at the 51 percent threshold. Two options can arise from this: either make the DOEP review a semiannual basis (five CTRs every six month period) or raise the amount of CTRs for the DOEP annual review (preferably 12 CTRs every 12 month period).

Although SAR filings are a normal course of operations, there is a reporting burden placed on credit unions to comply with these reporting requirements.

On average, it takes an additional one and a half to two hours to fully research and analyze a SAR. The additional time includes ancillary activities such as determining if the situation meets SAR thresholds/requirements, conducting the research of the member’s account activity, identifying if there are other individuals or accounts involved, researching the manner the suspicious activity occurred, analyzing the evidence and findings for each unique situation, and obtaining the necessary approval to file the SAR. As a result, it takes an average of three and a half to four hours to fully complete each SAR.

Pearl Riverkeeper appreciates the opportunity to comment on the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Civil Works Environmental Justice Strategic Plan and Vision. Pearl Riverkeeper is a grassroots Mississippi and Louisiana-based non-profit and licensed Water Alliance member whose mission is to protect the right to clean water.

In August 2024, Pearl Riverkeeper attended three separate USACE EJ meetings associated with the publication of the USACE Pearl River Basin, Mississippi Flood Risk Management Project Draft Environmental Impact Statement. The Corps expended significant resources on the Jackson, MS EJ public meetings. At least ten USACE specialists from Vicksburg and New Orleans were in attendance and available to answer questions. The Corps representatives were respectful, listened closely to community concerns, and encouraged the attendees to submit comment cards. The Corps did a good job strategically identifying meeting locations in the EJ community.

There were numerous opportunities for improvement noted at the three Jackson, MS EJ meetings that apply to the Corps’ EJ Strategic Plan and Vision, specifically Goal One:“Provide training and tools for staff on how to engage and communicate with Tribes and communities with environmental justice concerns in ways that foster mutual respect and trust, and in how to consider the information received during engagements in projects, decisions, and other Corps activities.” and Goal Four: “make it easier for affected communities to participate in the Corps processes that affect their built and natural environment.”

Corps communication and messaging to the EJ community in Jackson faced challenges starting in the planning stages. The Corps’ only meeting promotion was an email sent to some civic and neighborhood organizations late on a Friday afternoon six days prior to the event. As a result, the EJ community meetings were very sparsely attended. The Corps should provide more than 6 days’ notice of public meeting dates, particularly in the summer when many have vacation plans and childcare opportunities may be scarce. In addition, the Jackson, MS EJ community meetings were conducted after the end of the official public comment period. EJ meetings should be held during the official public comment period, giving the community members more of a voice in the project outcome.

The EJ meeting PowerPoint slides were extremely dense and presented information at a very high level. We recommend that presentations include as few technical/scientific/bureaucratic terms as possible and eliminate information that the audience does not need in order to make informed decisions or take desired actions. Many of the Corps slides contained paragraphs of text that were difficult to read from a distance. Two superfluous text-laden slides were dedicated to explaining EJ Executive Orders EO12898, 14008, 14096. One of the slides contained text riddled with acronyms such as NED, LPP, CTO, DEIS, NFI, and R-H.

We recommend that for future EJ meetings, the Corps engage a local community facilitator knowledgeable about the USACE project alternatives as well as each community's needs. The facilitator should be allowed to review and participate in the development of the PowerPoint presentation.

The Corps should encourage meeting attendees to ask questions during the presentation rather than wait until the end of the briefing. A local community facilitator could help with this process. Corps meetings can be intimidating for the community, and the content presented is very technical and challenging. Encouraging dialogue could improve information exchange. Community members benefit from hearing questions posed by their neighbors and Corps responses. Reducing the number and complexity of the presentation PowerPoint slides would allow more time for audience participation.

PowerPoint maps should have clear graphics that can be deciphered from a seat in the audience. Many of the Corps Jackson, MS PowerPoint maps had CEJST, Justice40, and EJScreen overlays on top of them. The EJ overlays obscured key, easily identifiable landmarks, rendering the maps impossible to interpret, particularly at a distance. Adding a “you are here” pinpoint on each map could help community members more easily identify where their meeting location is on the map. Utilizing an ArcGIS interactive map could greatly improve community comprehension.

PowerPoint slides and the presentation must align with the information in official USACE publicly released documents. Accuracy and consistency are vital to developing community trust. A Corps presentation to the community must be consistent with what is written in public documents. If the community is told conflicting information, they will lose faith in the public engagement process.

Corps EJ meetings should provide an option for an online comment portal.

We join other similarly situated companies in the financial services market in opposing FinCen’s requirement to start collecting a consumer/applicant’s full Social Security Number (SSN) as part of the proposed Customer Identification Program (CIP) Rule change.

We base our position on the following:

(i) Highly Sensitive Info: A consumer’s full SSN is a highly sensitive piece of personal information. Nowadays, consumers are wary of providing such information especially in an online setting. A good example of a consumer’s hesitancy to provide the full SSN can be seen in the data from our platform. In Q2 2024, we changed our platform by moving away from collecting the last 4 SSN to requiring the collection of the full SSN. Early stats are trending towards consumers abandoning the application process when prompted to enter the full SSN, which corresponds to fewer finalized loans. While these early stats are not wholly dispositive, they do however show that consumers are hesitant to divulge and share one of the most sensitive pieces of personal information on the world wide web. This small sample size should not be dismissed and must be considered in the wider scope of all online transactions when considering the CIP Rule change.

(ii) Better Alternatives Already Exist: Instead of moving towards collecting the full SSN, further consideration should be given to alternatives that currently exist (and are being used) to confirm a consumer's identity. Many online platforms, like ours, have collected CIP required information directly from consumers – Name, DOB, Address, last 4 of the SSN– and then used a reliable third party (usually credit bureaus) to confirm an individual's identity. There has been no strong showing that this approach does not work. Credit bureaus nowadays hold a lot of consumer information that the likelihood of being unable to confirm identity is low. Even in those edge cases where identity cannot be confirmed with certainty through a credit bureau, many fintech companies have established CIP Programs that add another layer of verification. These CIP Programs will require consumers to provide additional information (e.g. government issued picture identification) to ensure that the identity of the consumer is correctly verified. As such, consideration on how to potentially strengthen the existing alternatives or adding layers to CIP Programs may be warranted before making a rule change towards full SSN collection.

(iii) Not Geared At Preventing Fraud: The CIP Rule is not only meant to help confirm a consumer’s identity, but also as means to prevent fraud. However, requiring consumers to provide their full SSN will not achieve that goal. As mentioned, we started collecting the full SSN on its platform in Q2 of 2024. Since that change, the number of valid fraud complaints received has not resulted in a material statistical drop. In fact, when looking at the month before and after implementation of the full SSN, the number of valid fraud complaints received dropped by an insignificant number. While every fraud complaint is important (especially to the impacted consumer), it seems like making a change to the CIP Rule will not significantly curtail valid fraud complaints. Moreover, given the negligible change in valid fraud complaints, it appears that the existing alternatives to verifying identity is actually working.

For the foregoing reasons, we request that FinCen reconsider its proposed change to the CIP Rule.

Respectfully submitted.

It would be helpful to clarify whether FinCEN is speaking about the Annual BSA Risk Assessment or about more general risk assessment processes utilized by banks in relation to this proposed rule. BSA Programs have many different risk assessment processes in addition to the annual, company-wide BSA Risk Assessment. An Annual BSA Risk assessment is an all-encompassing document that requires correspondence with different departments outside of just BSA and requires a significant amount of time to complete. The Annual BSA Risk Assessment usually compares data and trends year over year in order to document deficiencies or areas of weakness in the BSA Program and to target resources to mitigate those weaknesses. Annual BSA Risk Assessments go through Senior Management and the Board of Directors for review and approval. Updating these documents as new risks arise may prove difficult based on their complexity and the time it takes to complete them. That is why banks utilize different risk assessment processes throughout the year rather than relying solely on an Annual Risk Assessment to document and act upon new risks. These risk assessment processes that occur throughout the year analyze and mitigate risks in a more dynamic fashion than the annual risk assessment. These processes can include new product reviews, new client reviews, investigations, high risk reviews of certain clients, etc. and can be reported up to the Board of Directors and Senior Management through Quarterly BSA Board Reports, BSA Committees, Policy Updates, or other means of communication outside of just an annual risk assessment.

In addition, it is difficult to ascertain how banks are to incorporate all of the AML Priorities into our BSA Programs in measurable, action ways. Risk Assessment processes are meant to analyze and mitigate risks by developing action items. They are meant to make our BSA Programs better. Some of these priorities; such as fraud, human trafficking and human smuggling, and cybercrime; are already top priorities for banks and have well-defined red flags. Many Fraud and BSA software providers have system alerts targeted for this type of activity. Other priorities; like drug trafficking organization activity, transnational criminal organization activity, and proliferation financing; do not have well defined red flags. There are no system alerts targeted for such priorities and the documentation thus far from FinCEN does not point to specific transactional red flags for such priorities. It is difficult to determine how these priorities are to turn into actionable items to improve the quality of our BSA Program outside of a general awareness that these crime typologies are on the rise. I worry that banks will incorporate the priorities into their programs not because they are actually improving the programs, but because we feel like we have to incorporate them somewhere. This will take time and resources away from defining and planning around our actionable risk items and could lead to exam and audit scrutiny.

First Harvest Credit Union appreciates this opportunity to comment on FinCEN’s notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) that aims to strengthen and modernize anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT). The NPRM requires financial institutions to implement and maintain risk-based AML/CFT programs, review government-wide AML/CFT priorities incorporating such priorities to compliance programs, update organizational structure with respect to the AML/CFT Officer, and increase staff training.

The NPRM presents grave concerns for future AML/CFT compliance efforts. The new rule makes compliance significantly more granular and expensive. In contrast, the NPRM lacks specifics regarding the relative value of these new compliance efforts for law enforcement or national security. Specifically, our concerns are: 1) acknowledgement that programs are risk based at the examination/enforcement level; 2) increased volume of risk assessments; 3) limited guidance on innovation; and 4) requirements for the AML/CFT Officer.

The notion of risk-based programs for Bank Secrecy Compliance is not new. In practice, we hope that review and enforcement pursuant to the new rule will respect that AML/CFT programs are risk based and will be respected. Our credit union incurs significant expense related to AML/CFT compliance. This consists of dollars spent on third-party vendors to assist with member identification, OFAC, and sanctions compliance, to name a few. Time and resources are consumed in training and executing the programs. With this in mind, the final rule should create a safe harbor. That is, where a credit union can demonstrate that it has adopted a reasonable compliance program with appropriate controls associated with use of its third-party vendor, the credit union should be deemed to be in compliance. Second guessing by prudential regulators as to whether a SAR should have been filed must end. Also, there should be clear criteria for assessing the parameters of the risk-based program. When the program has been evaluated pursuant to such criteria, that should end the inquiry.

We appreciate that a critical component of AML/CFT compliance is risk analysis. Risk analysis is inherent in the business of a credit union. The NPRM dramatically increases the “amount” of risk assessment necessary for executing a program. The requirement for financial institutions to monitor and incorporate AML/CFT priorities should be removed from the final rule.

The scope of risk assessments is too broad. For example, the NPRM requires a risk assessment for filing of reports. The decision to file reports is generated by the program, which is vetted by our staff and our third-party vendor. That process should decide the issue minus government scrutiny. The definition of “material changes” should be narrowed. For example, updating a risk assessment in response to adding a new membership group would put the AML/CFT in a constant state of change. Adding a critical vendor should not trigger an AML/CFT risk assessment. Critical vendors undergo significant due diligence pursuant to NCUA Rules and Regulations and guidance. The terms and conditions of the service with such a vendor offer additional protections.

As a general rule, our credit union strives for efficiency and scale. The member identification requirements, OFAC matching, and sanctions compliance require us to outsource those functions, rendering us reliant on third-party vendors. It would be beneficial for all concerned parties for FinCEN and AML/CFT compliance vendors to identify exactly what functions could be streamlined. We anticipate that artificial intelligence might provide a pathway for innovation. There should be a national conversation about the component pieces of innovation and whether new approaches will satisfy applicable law.

We are encouraged that a qualified group might meet the requirements for the AML/CFT Officer as set out in the NPRM. If the final rule would mandate that the AML/CFT Officer be performed by one person would dramatically alter our organizational structure including job descriptions and pay scale. That aspect of the rule truly appears to stretch FinCEN’s authority to interpret the Anti-Money Laundering Act.

A qualified group would be more manageable for a credit union of our size and complexity. Our AML/CFT compliance efforts depend on the joint participation of staff from retail, lending, compliance, and fraud/risk management. We have appropriate reporting channels to apprise executive management and the Board of Directors of AML/CFT risks and the need for updates. We maintain that the credit union could demonstrate the effectiveness of a qualified group and satisfy AML/CFT requirements.
Sincerely,
Mike Dinneen, CEO, First Harvest Credit Union (NJ)

The City of Bartlesville, Oklahoma, serves as a regional water provider for approximately 55,000 residents, including the communities of Bartlesville, Dewey, Ochelata, Ramona, and five rural water districts. Since the drought of 2001-2002, the City has been exploring affordable, long-term water supply options. One option identified through a 2007 study, conducted in collaboration with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) under the Planning Assistance to States program, involves purchasing water storage rights at Copan Lake.

Currently, the Town of Copan holds reserved storage rights at Copan Lake but has chosen not to pursue them due to the associated costs. Once storage rights are reserved through the USACE, federal legislation is required to allow the release of those rights. The 2022 Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) codified the Town of Copan’s ability to release its reserved storage rights, enabling Bartlesville to purchase these rights at no more than 110 percent of the initial project investment cost per acre-foot of storage.

In 2021, the City of Bartlesville secured a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Town of Copan for the release of these reserved storage rights. However, after the USACE issued its interpretation of the pricing component, the price of the reserved storage rights remained unaffordable, pausing the finalization of the agreement with the Town of Copan.

The 2024 WRDA legislation refined the cost language from the 2022 WRDA legislation, ensuring that the pricing would be affordable. Since the passage of the 2024 WRDA, the City of Bartlesville and the Town of Copan have been negotiating to finalize the agreement, allowing Bartlesville to purchase the released reserved storage rights at a cost not exceeding 110 percent of the rate in the most recent agreement.

The City of Bartlesville is advocating for an interpretation of the 2024 WRDA legislation to set the price of water at Copan Lake for the City of Bartlesville at $81.53 per acre-foot. This reflects a 110 percent increase from the City’s most recent contract with the USACE, where the City purchased water storage rights at Copan Lake for $74.12 per acre-foot (2020)

Strongly supported by the Oklahoma Congressional Delegation, the relevant provision contained within 2024 WRDA (Section 1360(a)) is meant to build upon language included in 2022 WRDA that COE determined was insufficient to effectively allow for the needed cost structure for Bartlesville as requested. This provision is directly purposed to provide for the needed cost structure.

In 2023, Lee County, Florida, received approximately 3 million visitors that generated an economic impact benefiting businesses as well as federal, state, and local governments. As documented by our Annual Visitor Profile, beaches consistently rank as the top attraction visited. Lee County’s beaches are critical to the federal, state, and local economy, but, importantly, they also serve as the first and best line of defense against coastal storm impacts and threats that come from the erosion those storms generate. And while they protect our infrastructure, beaches also provide critical habitat for a variety of plants and animals.
For these and myriad other reasons, Lee County and the State of Florida have consistently invested in projects to nourish and maintain the beaches of Lee County where needed. This has allowed us to make great strides to recover from the historic impacts of Hurricane Ian and the follow-up assaults from Hurricanes Helene and Milton. Most of our non-federal beaches have been restored, with the final segment under contract for repair this summer. The one beach that is lagging is the federal project on Gasparilla Island.

The beaches of Gasparilla have been federally authorized and restudied to confirm the federal interest. They were severely eroded by Hurricane Ian as documented by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Corps) Project Information Report. Flood Control and Coastal Emergencies (FCCE) funding was allocated, and we were anticipating the Corps to award a contract for nourishment in September 2025. However, progress has been stalled by ongoing real estate issues surrounding the extent and duration of construction easements.

Community vulnerability is exactly what Congress seeks to minimize through the coastal storm risk management authorizations and FCCE funding it provides to the Corps. Unfortunately, urgency does not seem to be a driving force behind operations of the Army Corps, as the “required” easement extent provided June 2024 by the Corps has been changed twice since then and we are still waiting for the updated requirements. This despite the fact that the project was successfully implemented in 2007 and had FCCE repairs completed in 2013 and 2019. Meanwhile, the community of Boca Grande remains vulnerable to the impending tropical storm season.

We are hopeful that the Corps will resolve this roadblock by recognizing and promptly implementing the clear direction and intent of Congress provided in Section 1145(d) of the Water Resources and Development Act of 2024 to move projects like the Gasparilla Island Segment of the Lee County, Florida Beach Erosion Control Project forward consistent with the previous funding practice. If necessary, Lee County is fully prepared and committed to paying 100% of the nourishment costs associated with private property that does not have an easement that covers the defined life of the project and provide for public access, just as was done in 2007.

Prompt disaster response and mitigation are essential to protecting the lives and infrastructure of our community, and it requires cooperation and commitment to be done efficiently and effectively. Unfortunately, we do not currently see a sense of urgency as the Jacksonville District is stuck waiting for guidance on how to interpret and implement Section 1145(d) of the Water Resources and Development Act of 2024. We believe WRDA ’24 needs minimal guidance, if any, to implement this section, and implore you to immediately affirm the clear Congressional direction to implement these vital projects and expedite the needed repair and rehabilitation. Mid-West Electric Consumers Association represents 314 consumer-owned utilities in the Upper Missouri River Basin. The consumer-owned utilities have long term contracts to purchase power generated by the USACE and marketed by WAPA. Power rates paid by consumer-owned utilities pay for the federal hydropower program and significant portions of many of the other authorized purposes. Congress recognized with the passage of the 1986 Dam Safety Act (Section 1203 WRDA 1986) that the cost of dam safety modifications deemed “state of the art” should be recovered from power customers at a more equitable level. Congress again directed the USACE to apply the reduced cost share for state of the art repairs in the 2024 WRDA. Section 1233 directs the Secretary to expedite the review of, and give due consideration to applying the 1986 Dam Safety Act at the Garrison and Oahe facilities. WAPA and the USACE District Command in Omaha have already determined that the 1986 Dam Safety Act applies and have provided this recommendation to the Secretary. Mid-West urges to Secretary to follow the direction of Congress and the recommendations of the power customers, WAPA, and the Omaha USACE Command in applying the reduced cost share to the dam safety modification projects at Garrison (ND) and Oahe (SD).

On behalf of the Martin County Board of County Commissioners, I write to encourage the Corps of Engineers to quickly develop Implementation Guidance for Section 1145, Easements for Hurricane and Storm Damage Reduction Projects of the Water Resources Development Act of 2024. This important section represents one of the first times that Congress has explicitly directed the Corps to construct critical coastal storm risk management projects irrespective of prior Corps interpretation of policy relating to easements.

Martin County has appreciated its longstanding relationship with the Corps, including for the Martin County coastal storm risk management project on Hutchinson Island that helps protect some four miles of beach along our coastline. The Corps has constructed the project numerous times, but our most recent planned nourishment has been delayed due to the Corps’ ongoing confusion related to easements.

For our project, we were authorized to secure both 50-year public easements and perpetual public easements at the time of initial construction. Since this became more of an issue over the past few years, we have worked to change all our easements to public perpetual, but it is not a quick process. In our case, we have 28 50-year easements that must be transitioned. Of those, 15 are held by the state of Florida, and the other 13 are privately held. We believe we can transition all the easements, but we request quick implementation of Section 1145, particularly as it relates to the FCCE construction of projects within the next two years utilizing monies Congress has already provided.

Furthermore, we encourage the Corps to continue its longstanding approach to support sand placement on private lands that do not provide public use if the non-federal sponsor agrees to pay 100% of the costs associated with those lands, particularly for de minimis segments. The Implementation Guidance should clarify that projects shall be certified by the Secretary when the non-federal sponsor provides written assurance to comply with conditions stipulated in a Report or Project Partnership Agreement for the placement of sand on privately owned lands.

Given the recent significant storms that have hit Florida over just the past few years, plus with another storm season looming, we encourage the Corps to quickly develop implementation guidance for Section 1134 that mirrors the sense and intent of Congress with respect to this issue.

Thank you for your consideration of our comments.

Manatee County Natural Resources Department is acting under authority of the Manatee County Board of County commissioners to manage the Anna Maria Shore Protection project as the non-federal sponsor. The Manatee County, Florida Shore Protection Project (SPP) was authorized under Section 201 of the Flood Control Act of 1965 (Public Law (PL) 89-298) dated 27 October 1965, as amended by Section 131 of the Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) of 1976 (PL 94-587). The agreement governing initial construction and periodic nourishment of this project is the Local Cooperation Agreement (LCA) between the Department of the Army and Manatee County, Florida for Construction of the Manatee County Florida Shore Protection Project, executed on 4 August 1992. The most recent agreement governing periodic nourishment of this project is the Project Partnership Agreement (PPA) executed on 22 November 2019. Article II of this agreement lists the obligations of the Government and local sponsor. The non-Federal sponsor, Manatee County, Florida, is responsible for land, easements, right-of-way, relocations, and disposal areas required for the Project. The acquisition of land is limited by guidance provided in the CESAD-PD Memorandum dated 30 January 2019 (USACE CESAD-PD, 2019), which indicates that the landward extent of the federal project coincides with the State of Florida’s erosion control line (ECL). The sponsor has fulfilled all non-Federal responsibilities to date in accordance with the LCA.
While Manatee County is compliant with the perpetual public access easement requirements. Many local sponsors have difficulty obtaining perpetual public access easements. In those circumstances our department would like to offer an alternative for ACOE consideration that may help satisfy non-Federal sponsor requirements for perpetual public access easements. Rather than require perpetual access easements which had met resistance from project private property owners, we suggest consideration to provide interpretation that allows substituting permanent (perpetual) construction access easements to meet the permanent access requirements for both CSRM and FCCE actions.
Perpetual construction access easements are a recognized land reservation tool familiar to many property owners who accept applicable construction access easement incumbrances for water, wastewater, electricity and storm water purposes. Permanent construction easements should provide ACOE with all the access real estate requirements to complete and maintain shore protection projects with the only difference negating public use over the easement area. We understand that Federal expenditures by law cannot be expended on private property which is the basis for perpetual public access real estate requirements, however if the non-Federal sponsor for Florida projects is willing to pay 100% of the construction cost over the project area between the perpetual public access requirements of Florida's ECL and the Federal project limits landward, federal expenditure requirements will still be met. 100% non-Federal payment for ACOE additional work required to construct and maintain shore protection projects is already authorized in section 103.D.of WRDA 1986.

A drawing prepared to explain how the application of local permanent construction easement with 100% local funding of any ACOE additional work in substitution for perpetual public easements is attached.

As a title and settlement industry professional, I urge FinCEN to eliminate reporting of duplicative information and information that is not normally collected in a real estate transaction.

Title and settlement professionals are independent third parties whose job is to close a transaction in accordance with all of the parties’ instructions. By requiring us to collect information that is not normally provided by the parties or necessary for the clearing of title or settlement, you are adding unnecessary costs to the transaction, estimated at almost $500 per closing. As the vast majority of title and settlement companies are extremely small businesses, we will not be able to absorb the costs of this proposed rule as currently drafted without significant detrimental impacts to the viability of our businesses.

I strongly urge FinCEN to eliminate the need to report beneficial ownership information on each transaction. In light of the requirements of the Corporate Transparency Act, asking settlement providers to duplicate this reporting will only add cost without aiding law enforcement. Additionally, I urge you to rethink requiring reporting for low-risk transactions like estate planning trusts and other gratuitous transfers.

Lastly, as we have learned implementing the Geographic Targeting Orders, customers are not always willing to cooperate in providing information. Providing guidance which allows us to report only the information we obtained after a good faith attempt to collect data is vital to easing the risk and burden for a small business. It is critical for the final rule to allow those being required to file reports to submit as much information as they can reasonably collect without being penalized for missing information they cannot locate or is not willingly provided.

I share the concerns about the use of residential real estate for money laundering. However, the compliance burden on small businesses must be minimized significantly for this effort to be successful.

Thank you for considering these comments and those filed by the American Land Title Association.

As you are aware, title companies are already under significant pressure to deliver quality services while operating within tight budget constraints.  The expectation of doing more work, without the ability to charge for these services, only adds to the strain on our resources.  The proposed changes may exacerbate the challenges we face, particularly in light of the current economic conditions of the housing market. We already are grappling with the responsibility of protecting consumers and clients from various risks, including wire fraud, deceptive sellers, fraudulent transactions, and ransomware attacks. I am a lifelong resident of Illinois, growing up in the St. Louis metropolitan area near the confluence of the Mississippi and Illinois rivers. These rivers have played a formative role in my life. As a child I remember riding with my parents as they drove through areas impacted by the great flood of 1993. We frequently drove the Great River Road and to this day I revel in seeing the river across the changing seasons. This love of the river led me to pursue a career in natural resources, and I am privileged to currently work as a fisheries biologist in Illinois. This position has given me greater appreciation for the fisheries and aquatic resources of the Upper Mississippi River and the value of long-term monitoring programs like the Upper Mississippi River Restoration program’s Long Term Resource Monitoring element (UMRR-LTRM).
In the Water Resources Development Act of 2024, Section 1354 amends Section 1103(e)(4) of the Water Resources Development Act of 1986 (33 U.S.C. 652(e)(4)) by increasing the funding authorization level of the Upper Mississippi River Restoration Long Term Resource Monitoring element to $25,000,000 beginning in fiscal year 2025. Since its authorization in 1986, the UMRR-LTRM program has proven its value in tracking trends in water quality, aquatic vegetation, fisheries, land cover change and many more resources on the Upper Mississippi River. Additionally, the data is made publicly available both as raw data and in summarized tools that aid managers and the public in understanding the aquatic resources of the Upper Mississippi River. While authorization doesn't guarantee funding, this increase in authorization in WRDA 2024 is a testament to the value of the UMRR program and its successful implementation for almost four decades.
Specific to the fisheries resources of the Upper Mississippi River, the UMRR program has been critical to tracking impacts of invasive species, like the invasive Silver and Bighead carps. In the program’s recent status and trends report (Houser 2022), invasive carp biomass was shown to eclipse the total biomass of all native fishes on the La Grange pool of the Illinois River and Pool 26 of the Mississippi River. Silver and Bighead carps negatively impact plankton food sources and have caused dramatic declines in plankton on the Illinois River (DeBoer et al. 2018). All fish depend on plankton as an early food source, and many important forage fish (e.g. Gizzard Shad) and commercial fish (e.g. Bigmouth Buffalo and American Paddlefish) feed on plankton their entire lives. Using LTRM data, Chick et al. (2020) linked declines in sportfish populations to invasive carp in invaded pools of the Upper Mississippi River when compared to uninvaded pools.
Fisheries data from the UMRR-LTRM program has also been used to show declines in migratory fish species in the upper pools of the Mississippi River (Anderson et al. 2017), likely impacted by navigational dams when compared to the lower pools (Pool 26 and the Open River Reach of the Mississippi River and the La Grange Pool of the Illinois River). Spear et al. (2024) indicated that backwater areas may serve as a refuge for fish from the impacts of navigational traffic and highlights the importance of restoration efforts that aim to restore access to these important habitats. The Upper Mississippi River supports a valuable commercial fishery and the LTRM program serves as an important source of fishery-independent data to monitor commercially important fisheries resources (Houser et al. 2022, Maxson et al. 2024).
The increase in authorization for the LTRM program in WRDA 2024 will greatly assist managers in the Upper Mississippi River states by informing management actions and impacts of invasive carps as they move further upriver, as well as the success of restoration efforts throughout the basin. In particular, increased funding for the LTRM program may aid in establishing additional monitoring stations in areas not currently covered by the program (e.g pools 14-25). This area is of particular import due to identified pinch points of invasive carp movement past navigational dams (e.g. L&D 15, 19), as well as native fish passage efforts currently planned for L&D 22.
The UMRR program has established itself as a world-class program in large river restoration and monitoring. The documented effects of invasive species and impacts of navigational traffic are only possible through long-term monitoring programs such as the UMRR-LTRM. The increased authorization level in WRDA 2024 is a clear recognition of the program’s success, and it will greatly aid in its further utility for monitoring changes in the aquatic resources of the Upper Mississippi River in response to the multitude of factors impacting these resources and the people who depend upon them.

As a title and settlement industry professional, I urge FinCEN to eliminate reporting of duplicative information and information that is not normally collected in a real estate transaction.

Title and settlement professionals are independent third parties whose job is to close a transaction in accordance with all of the parties’ instructions. By requiring us to collect information that is not normally provided by the parties or necessary for the clearing of title or settlement, you are adding unnecessary costs to the transaction, estimated at almost $500 per closing. As the vast majority of title and settlement companies are extremely small businesses, we will not be able to absorb the costs of this proposed rule as currently drafted without significant detrimental impacts to the viability of our businesses.

I strongly urge FinCEN to eliminate the need to report beneficial ownership information on each transaction. In light of the requirements of the Corporate Transparency Act, asking settlement providers to duplicate this reporting will only add cost without aiding law enforcement. Additionally, I urge you to rethink requiring reporting for low-risk transactions like estate planning trusts and other gratuitous transfers.

Lastly, as we have learned implementing the Geographic Targeting Orders, customers are not always willing to cooperate in providing information. Providing guidance which allows us to report only the information we obtained after a good faith attempt to collect data is vital to easing the risk and burden for a small business. It is critical for the final rule to allow those being required to file reports to submit as much information as they can reasonably collect without being penalized for missing information they cannot locate or is not willingly provided.

I share the concerns about the use of residential real estate for money laundering. However, the compliance burden on small businesses must be minimized significantly for this effort to be successful.

Thank you for considering these comments and those filed by the American Land Title Association.

I own a small real estate title company that caters mostly to investors. As investors they often purchase property with owner financing or using private lenders and on occasion for cash. As such, they will all fall under the proposed regulation concerning "non financed" transactions.

Almost all of these transactions are done through entities that have to comply with the Corporate Transparency Act. That being said much of the information the proposed rule would require would be duplicative of the information that had to be submitted under the CTA.

I believe you have vastly underestimated the number of closings, that are not cash sales, that will fall under the proposed rules. You have also vastly underestimated the additional costs that will be incurred in my company having to obtain this information.

Another question is what protections will there be for a title company using it's best "good faith efforts" to comply but the client doesn't want to give up the requested information.

The comments regarding the proposed rule refer to the current Geographic Targeting Orders and what success has been achieved with those. I would be more agreeable with the proposed rule if it adopted the same dollar limits as with the current GTO. This would go a long way to relieving some of the burden associated with the proposed rule.

One last comment regarding the financial information to be disclosed. In Louisiana we are required to accept "certified funds" at a closing, which almost always involves a bank wire or certified check. With the prevalence of wire fraud these days the certified or cashiers check has become the more common source of funds. The proposed rule asks for the bank information and account information for the funds received. When we receive a bank cashiers check the only account information is that of the bank's internal account, as that is where the funds are coming from. And the bank already has to comply with AML issues. So why put an added burden on the small business to provide information already available through banks and the CTA?

I would ask you to revaluate the whole rule with regards to where this information is already available and at least put a dollar limit on reportable transactions to justify the additional work and limit how intrusive this proposed rule would be on the type and amount of information we would be forced to obtain that have nothing to do with our main business of seeing that real estate transactions are done in a good and proper manner and that good title is passed from one property owner to another.

Thanks you for your consideration.

The proposed anti-money laundering regulations for residential real estate transfers are beyond the scope of title agents whose primary roles are to examine title for purposes of title insurance and closing services which are defined as follows in the Texas Basic Manual: Closing the Transaction - "The investigation made on behalf of a title insurance company, title insurance agent or direct operation before the actual issuance of the title policy to determine proper execution, acknowledgment and delivery of all conveyances, mortgage papers, and other title instruments which may be necessary to the consummation of the transaction and includes the determination that all delinquent taxes are paid, all current taxes, based on the latest available information, have been properly prorated between the purchaser and seller in the case of an Owner's Policy, the consideration has been passed, all proceeds have been properly disbursed, a final search of the title has been made, and all necessary papers have been filed for record." Currently, for purposes of complying with Section 1445 of the Internal Revenue Code, we do have a Non-Foreign Individual Affidavit signed by the Seller but citizenship information is not requested. The proposed regulation is putting a tremendous additional burden on title agent for which it is not properly staffed or is staff properly trained to take on. If the regulation was imposed on title agents it is not just an additional cost of $500 per transaction it is more staffing and those with the experience and qualified to handle the task. It cannot be delegated to an assistant whose pay level is not on par with someone who has higher responsibility. The title agent's role is to
uncover and address risks in order to issue its policies to insure the title to real estate. As a title and settlement industry professional, I urge FinCEN to eliminate reporting of duplicative information and information that is not normally collected in a real estate transaction.

Title and settlement professionals are independent third parties whose job is to close a transaction in accordance with all of the parties’ instructions. By requiring us to collect information that is not normally provided by the parties or necessary for the clearing of title or settlement, you are adding unnecessary costs to the transaction, estimated at almost $500 per closing. As the vast majority of title and settlement companies are extremely small businesses, we will not be able to absorb the costs of this proposed rule as currently drafted without significant detrimental impacts to the viability of our businesses.

I strongly urge FinCEN to eliminate the need to report beneficial ownership information on each transaction. In light of the requirements of the Corporate Transparency Act, asking settlement providers to duplicate this reporting will only add cost without aiding law enforcement. Additionally, I urge you to rethink requiring reporting for low-risk transactions like estate planning trusts and other gratuitous transfers.

Lastly, as we have learned implementing the Geographic Targeting Orders, customers are not always willing to cooperate in providing information. Providing guidance which allows us to report only the information we obtained after a good faith attempt to collect data is vital to easing the risk and burden for a small business. It is critical for the final rule to allow those being required to file reports to submit as much information as they can reasonably collect without being penalized for missing information they cannot locate or is not willingly provided.

I share the concerns about the use of residential real estate for money laundering. However, the compliance burden on small businesses must be minimized significantly for this effort to be successful.

Thank you for considering these comments and those filed by the American Land Title Association.

To the Treasury and FinCEN staff:

I am writing to voice my opposition to the latest rule under the CTA related to reporting Beneficial Ownership Information to FinCEN for residential real estate transactions and transfers.

The federal government of late seems unaware of the natural rights of Americans, as protected by the Constitution. While preventing financial crimes is a worthwhile endeavor, your means cannot do that in a way that infringes upon Americans’ natural rights or assumes that they are guilty without due process.

Asking real estate intermediaries to collect beneficial ownership information to report to an organization involved in financial crimes unfortunately does that. It is an invasion of privacy and it creates additional burdens on the real estate process that will undoubtedly result in more fees being paid by individuals.

If your organization has concerns about money laundering, cartel activity or otherwise, you should be using the courts to receive and be provided with information on those specific cases and entities. As it is unlikely that those who would engage in such activities would be forthcoming with the information you are seeking, all you are doing with these rules is unconstitutionally penalizing law abiding Americans and infringing on their rights.

If you are concerned about foreign entities, then the rule should only focus on foreign buyers or transferees.

And, once again, by exempting business transactions, you are targeting and penalizing individual Americans with a different standard and set of rules.

It is unacceptable as proposed, and, as all government regulation does, would have a precedent to be further expanded and create broader rights violations.

A federal district court has already found the CTA BOI rule directed at small business reporting to be unconstitutional, for the same rationale as above.

FinCEN is choosing to ignore this for everyone but the plaintiffs in that case, something that is unheard of. If it is unconstitutional, it is unconstitutional- period- and should be immediately shut down.

I am asking you to not move forward on this real estate rule and to overturn the small business data collection rule as well.

Given the state of the US’s financials right now, it seems that Treasury staff should be more concerned about working with Congress to curb deficits and secure our financial future than finding ways to unconstitutionally harass law abiding Americans en masse.

Thank you
