I am Senior Counsel with Allegiance Title Company, a majority owned subsidiary of Fidelity National Financial, Inc.
I wanted to speak to the incredible and disproportionate burden the title industry would experience due to the proposed Anti-Money Laundering Regulations for Residential Real Estate Transfers.
The Geographic Targeting Order (as it is: limited to six counties in Texas, not including trusts, and having a sales price floor of 300k), already takes up HOURS of my time every week just to ensure that we are catching and reporting the applicable transactions timely, and that’s just for our 19 offices and fewer than 150 employees. And you can add to that the additional time for the staff handling the transactions that are interacting with the parties to obtain the required information in a secure manner.
The new rule would multiply this burden exponentially- adding EVERY county, no price limit, and adding trusts (when the majority of trusts we encounter are revocable family trusts, where the names of the trustees are also the grantors and primary beneficiaries, and thus nothing is hidden in the property records as to who is behind the trust).
We regularly remind our staff about this issue, and we include a requirement regarding the GTO on commitments for the counties it applies to, and yet, we have found it necessary to perform time-intensive searches within our software at least once a week for applicable transactions, documenting spreadsheets distinguishing transactions where it applies from ones that show up in the search for residential transactions with entity purchasers where sales price is over 300k, but are exempt due to conventional financing, etc. The regular searches are necessary, not only because of quick closes where some cash transactions may try to close within a few days, but also because transactions are REGULARLY assigned from individuals to entities throughout the transaction, and we’re often informed of this only a day or two before closing. Also, we need to review what our staff has collected before closing to ensure that we have what we need for the report.
The absolute urgency to then obtain information before closing is stressful and often results in having to argue with owners or their counsel about why we are requesting the personal info. of non-signers to the transaction. Numerous closings have had to be delayed, infuriating sellers needing funds to complete their own purchase and move.
This also seems completely unnecessary given that every deed in the public record is already accessible to the government, and the fact that, as of 2024, companies are ALREADY required to report their beneficial ownership information. You will already have this information accessible to you and should not then make us bend over backwards and spend untold millions of dollars every year just to duplicate information you already have.
Putting this burden on the title industry is unfair, inefficient, and harmful to consumers. PLEASE reconsider this policy. Please remove trusts, and if you insist on us reporting all entity transactions in every county regardless of price directly to FinCEN, I would suggest a simple fill-in form entry into your portal stating the date, purchase price, name of the entity buyer, and state of formation of the entity. States have public information about the entities, and FinCEN will now have even the beneficial ownership information about the entities due to the Corporate Transparency Act.
This may be well-intentioned, but the unintended negative consequences for our industry and consumers do not justify it.

Title companies in Texas are burdened with enough reporting requirements as it is currently.  Doing the job of a federal agency should not be another burden that we are stuck with.  Not only that, but the federal government is trying to do away with loan title insurance premiums collected at closing already.  FinCen's own numbers show that this would increase the financial burden to the reporter of $500 per transaction.  Who is going to pay for that?  The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network?  I doubt it!  I work for a small title company in a small town and we would either have to pass that along to our law abiding clients or eat the cost, which is not feasible nor fair. The federal government receives enough money to do their own investigations.  Maybe they should spend it more wisely.

I share the concerns about the use of residential real estate for money laundering. However, the compliance burden on small businesses must be minimized significantly for this effort to be successful.

Thank you for considering these comments and those filed by the American Land Title Association.

To the Treasury and FinCEN staff:

I am writing to voice my opposition to the latest rule under the CTA related to reporting Beneficial Ownership Information to FinCEN for residential real estate transactions and transfers.

The federal government of late seems unaware of the natural rights of Americans, as protected by the Constitution. While preventing financial crimes is a worthwhile endeavor, your means cannot do that in a way that infringes upon Americans’ natural rights or assumes that they are guilty without due process.

Asking real estate intermediaries to collect beneficial ownership information to report to an organization involved in financial crimes unfortunately does that. It is an invasion of privacy and it creates additional burdens on the real estate process that will undoubtedly result in more fees being paid by individuals.

If your organization has concerns about money laundering, cartel activity or otherwise, you should be using the courts to receive and be provided with information on those specific cases and entities. As it is unlikely that those who would engage in such activities would be forthcoming with the information you are seeking, all you are doing with these rules is unconstitutionally penalizing law abiding Americans and infringing on their rights.

If you are concerned about foreign entities, then the rule should only focus on foreign buyers or transferees.

And, once again, by exempting business transactions, you are targeting and penalizing individual Americans with a different standard and set of rules.

It is unacceptable as proposed, and, as all government regulation does, would have a precedent to be further expanded and create broader rights violations.

A federal district court has already found the CTA BOI rule directed at small business reporting to be unconstitutional, for the same rationale as above.

FinCEN is choosing to ignore this for everyone but the plaintiffs in that case, something that is unheard of. If it is unconstitutional, it is unconstitutional- period- and should be immediately shut down.

I am asking you to not move forward on this real estate rule and to overturn the small business data collection rule as well.

Given the state of the US’s financials right now, it seems that Treasury staff should be more concerned about working with Congress to curb deficits and secure our financial future than finding ways to unconstitutionally harass law abiding Americans en masse.

Thank you.

As a title and settlement industry professional, I urge FinCEN to eliminate reporting of duplicative information and information that is not normally collected in a real estate transaction.

Title and settlement professionals are independent third parties whose job is to close a transaction in accordance with all of the parties’ instructions. By requiring us to collect information that is not normally provided by the parties or necessary for the clearing of title or settlement, you are adding unnecessary costs to the transaction, estimated at almost $500 per closing. As the vast majority of title and settlement companies are extremely small businesses, we will not be able to absorb the costs of this proposed rule as currently drafted without significant detrimental impacts to the viability of our businesses.

I strongly urge FinCEN to eliminate the need to report beneficial ownership information on each transaction. In light of the requirements of the Corporate Transparency Act, asking settlement providers to duplicate this reporting will only add cost without aiding law enforcement. Additionally, I urge you to rethink requiring reporting for low-risk transactions like estate planning trusts and other gratuitous transfers.

Lastly, as we have learned implementing the Geographic Targeting Orders, customers are not always willing to cooperate in providing information. Providing guidance which allows us to report only the information we obtained after a good faith attempt to collect data is vital to easing the risk and burden for a small business. It is critical for the final rule to allow those being required to file reports to submit as much information as they can reasonably collect without being penalized for missing information they cannot locate or is not willingly provided.

I share the concerns about the use of residential real estate for money laundering. However, the compliance burden on small businesses must be minimized significantly for this effort to be successful.

Thank you for considering these comments and those filed by the American Land Title Association.

I oppose the use of Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCen) Beneficial Ownership reporting requirement for all American citizens period.  This is a gross invasion of privacy and is unconstitutional.

As a title and settlement industry professional, I urge FinCEN to eliminate reporting of duplicative information and information that is not normally collected in a real estate transaction.

Title and settlement professionals are independent third parties whose job is to close a transaction in accordance with all of the parties’ instructions. By requiring us to collect information that is not normally provided by the parties or necessary for the clearing of title or settlement, you are adding unnecessary costs to the transaction, estimated at almost $500 per closing. As the vast majority of title and settlement companies are extremely small businesses, we will not be able to absorb the costs of this proposed rule as currently drafted without significant detrimental impacts to the viability of our businesses.

I strongly urge FinCEN to eliminate the need to report beneficial ownership information on each transaction. In light of the requirements of the Corporate Transparency Act, asking settlement providers to duplicate this reporting will only add cost without aiding law enforcement. Additionally, I urge you to rethink requiring reporting for low-risk transactions like estate planning trusts and other gratuitous transfers.

Lastly, as we have learned implementing the Geographic Targeting Orders, customers are not always willing to cooperate in providing information. Providing guidance which allows us to report only the information we obtained after a good faith attempt to collect data is vital to easing the risk and burden for a small business. It is critical for the final rule to allow those being required to file reports to submit as much information as they can reasonably collect without being penalized for missing information they cannot locate or is not willingly provided.

I share the concerns about the use of residential real estate for money laundering. However, the compliance burden on small businesses must be minimized significantly for this effort to be successful.

Thank you for considering these comments and those filed by the American Land Title Association.

Opposing the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network Anti-Money Laundering Regulations for Residential Real Estate Transfers under the CTA BOI rule

To the Treasury and FinCEN staff:

I am writing to voice my opposition to the latest rule under the CTA related to reporting Beneficial Ownership Information to FinCEN for residential real estate transactions and transfers.

The federal government of late seems unaware of the natural rights of Americans, as protected by the Constitution. While preventing financial crimes is a worthwhile endeavor, your means cannot do that in a way that infringes upon Americans’ natural rights or assumes that they are guilty without due process.

Asking real estate intermediaries to collect beneficial ownership information to report to an organization involved in financial crimes unfortunately does that. It is an invasion of privacy and it creates additional burdens on the real estate process that will undoubtedly result in more fees being paid by individuals.

If your organization has concerns about money laundering, cartel activity or otherwise, you should be using the courts to receive and be provided with information on those specific cases and entities. As it is unlikely that those who would engage in such activities would be forthcoming with the information you are seeking, all you are doing with these rules is unconstitutionally penalizing law abiding Americans and infringing on their rights.

If you are concerned about foreign entities, then the rule should only focus on foreign buyers or transferees.

And, once again, by exempting business transactions, you are targeting and penalizing individual Americans with a different standard and set of rules.

It is unacceptable as proposed, and, as all government regulation does, would have a precedent to be further expanded and create broader rights violations.

A federal district court has already found the CTA BOI rule directed at small business reporting to be unconstitutional, for the same rationale as above.

FinCEN is choosing to ignore this for everyone but the plaintiffs in that case, something that is unheard of. If it is unconstitutional, it is unconstitutional- period- and should be immediately shut down.

I am asking you to not move forward on this real estate rule and to overturn the small business data collection rule as well.

Given the state of the US’s financials right now, it seems that Treasury staff should be more concerned about working with Congress to curb deficits and secure our financial future than finding ways to unconstitutionally harass law abiding Americans en masse.

Thank you

Opposing the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network Anti-Money Laundering Regulations for Residential Real Estate Transfers under the CTA BOI rule

To the Treasury and FinCEN staff:

I am writing to voice my opposition to the latest rule related to reporting Beneficial Ownership Information to FinCEN for residential real estate transactions and transfers.

I agree with FinCEN’s ultimate goal to stop illegal activity. However, this regulation goes too far in pursuing that end. Constitutional issues aside, it is counterproductive for FinCEN cast such an expansive net across all real estate transactions.

For one reason, I believe this will not achieve your goal. The kind of bad actors that you are trying to identify will either not report the transaction, or give false information. They will find some way to avoid exposure, as they always do. Most of the reporting will come from honest people, the opposite of what you are looking for.

Second, how will you identify the dishonest people? I can imagine ways for FinCEN to verify if a transaction happened that should have been reported, but it would be complicated and resource-heavy.

Deeds are recorded at the county clerk’s office. Even in my state of Texas, not all county clerks record their deeds through the same electronic systems. It will be difficult to pull all deeds from all counties in the country. Then you will have to analyze the text in the PDFs to guess which transactions had financing or not. This will only be an initial piece of your investigation process. It will not be impossible, but it will be difficult and consume a lot of resources.
I believe that FinCEN has many smart people and that their talents should be optimized. The mountain of work that it will take to gather and analyze many millions of deeds from the whole country is probably not the best way for FinCEN investigators to locate a relatively small group of criminals.
You already use Geographic Targeting Orders to focus FinCEN’s limited resources on locations and transactions where illegal activity is more predictable. That is a smart use of resources. You should apply that same kind of creative thinking to devise some other approach that targets criminal activity more strategically.

Even if you don’t know a better approach today, you may think of a better approach later. If your people are drowning in millions of deeds at that time, it will be harder for them to pivot to the more efficient program.

Implementing this new rule will mean stretching your resources across the entire country. If it turns out that you do not have the resources to faithfully implement this rule, then that will only embolden the bad actors who have no intention to comply.

Can FinCEN tell us how many employees it currently has on March 22 (9 days before the first CTA filing deadlines)? How many more employees does it need to monitor the 5 million new entities that the FinCEN predicts will be formed this year, for CTA compliance? How many more employees will it need to review every deed filed in America for this new rule to be faithfully implemented? Finally, if FinCEN does not have enough people to faithfully track all of these transactions, what is your plan to address that deficiency?

Whether you will be able to identify enough bad actors to justify the extreme effort, is unclear. I am more confident that this will discourage law-abiding people from transferring properties as part of valid asset restructuring. Law-abiding citizens transfer properties into LLCs and trusts all the time for honest and legal reasons. This will have a chilling effect on real estate transactions, which will have a negative effect on the overall economy.

I believe that the goal of the entire federal government (FinCEN included) should be to encourage, incentivize, and support productive activities by Americans. This new regulation will have a chilling effect on legal activities in the real estate market. It will make it more expensive and burdensome for law-abiding citizens to follow the law.

On the other hand, criminals will continue to behave in the same way with the same motivations as before.

With respect for FinCEN’s noble intentions, and the talented people working there, I ask you to reconsider this new reporting rule.

Thank you.

As a current Master of Public Policy and Public Health student, I am very interested in the economic background that fuels public health decisions. Non-prescription drugs play an important role in helping people treat health conditions without a physician’s approval. This greatly reduces costs related to hospital visits, time, and insurance administration. I am commenting on the FDA’s request for information on my own behalf, focusing on economic considerations that can influence regulatory decisions that promote public health.

Since nonprescription drugs are self-administered and self-selected, the FDA requires evidence to ensure that they are safe and effective. This includes labeling of the drug and case studies of people using the drug. These requirements address concerns about misuse and negative outcomes, but also increase the fixed costs of bringing these drugs into the market. The costs might discourage drug manufacturers from participating in nonprescription drug routes, especially for those that people buy less of. If this is limited, then some drugs that technically are safe to use without a doctor's approval can only be prescription drugs. This limits consumer access and could increase healthcare costs for an ordinary person.

Information asymmetry is a central challenge in this case. Consumers have a limited ability to accurately diagnose themselves or understand their ailments. While labeling requirements are helpful here, overly complex information can reduce comprehension and diminish the effectiveness of nonprescription access. However, increased access to nonprescription drugs can also create moral hazard. Consumers may start to substitute self-medication for instances where clinical care intervention is needed. This reiterates the importance of effective labeling practices.

When drugs that could be used as nonprescription become accessible only with a prescription, it creates a deadweight loss for consumers who would have otherwise benefited from the drugs. Thus, overly restrictive classification for these drugs can prevent beneficial transactions that would have rewarded both the manufacturers and consumers.

In conclusion, incorporating economic concepts can help to inform a more balanced approach to nonprescription drug access. Information asymmetry and moral hazard are two main points that must be focused on in order to benefit all parties. Using these frameworks, the FDA can continue to carry out its public health mission and expand access to affordable nonprescription drugs.

As a nonpartisan advocacy organization focused advancing preventive health for all women and girls, the Alliance for Women’s Health and Prevention (AWHP) is invested in policies that expand access to safe nonprescription medications. As such, AWHP appreciates the opportunity to provide input in response to the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) Request for Information (RFI) on Increasing Access to Nonprescription Drugs (Docket No. FDA-2025-N-4731). We commend the FDA and administration for advancing self-care, a core component of empowering individual health, and for mobilizing around safe, accessible nonprescription medications as a core tenet of this agenda.

Nonprescription, over-the-counter (OTC) drugs are essential for Americans nationwide, every single day. That value was especially evident during three years of pandemic-driven disruptions, when consumers relied on OTC tools — even rapidly adopting OTC COVID-19, and later flu, diagnostics. For many women, nonprescription options remain a practical way to access timely care while balancing work, caregiving, and other responsibilities — particularly when cost and scheduling barriers delay routine visits.

Women are often the healthcare decision-makers for both themselves and their households, and they, among other Americans, are navigating risings costs and persistent barriers to timely care. Expanding access to safe and effective nonprescription options can help women manage common health needs earlier, more conveniently, and at lower cost. This benefit spills over to the broader healthcare system by reducing unnecessary utilization of higher-cost care settings.

The most direct way to expand access to nonprescription drugs is to ensure that appropriate, safe therapies can move efficiently from prescription status to nonprescription, OTC availability. The switch pathway has long been a proven mechanism for improving access, supporting self-care, and lowering healthcare costs. Though it has been available and used for years, its utilization has not kept pace with today’s healthcare needs and environment, as well as the broader shift to patient empowerment. A more transparent, predictable, and modernized switch pathway would help increase access to innovative nonprescription options — including for health needs that women manage across the lifespan for themselves and their families.

To that end, we’re pleased to share the appended white paper, “Empowering Consumers, Reducing Costs, Improving Health: Reforming the Prescription to Over-the-Counter Drug Pathway – A Patient Centric Approach.” Based on input from 16 patient organizations, this paper was created in collaboration with the Alliance for Aging Research and outlines practical steps that the FDA, industry, and patient advocates can all take to increase access to nonprescription drugs via a strengthened OTC switch pathway.

Our recommendations are grounded in the principle that access is not just about availability — it’s about safe, empowered decision-making for all Americans. Of note, the paper highlights where appropriate OTC switches could improve access and affordability for women specifically, including urinary and sexual health conditions.

Thank you for considering AWHP’s perspectives and taking the time to request input and meet later this year regarding such an important issue. We look forward to continued engagement with FDA on policies that expand safe access, strengthen consumer confidence, and ensure women can benefit from innovative nonprescription options.

On behalf of Everlywell, we appreciate the opportunity to submit comments regarding the identification of drug products that would offer transformative societal benefits if transitioned from prescription to nonprescription (OTC) status. We strongly support the inclusion of LDL-cholesterol-lowering treatments, specifically those utilizing tech-enabled, nonprescription models, as a priority for this initiative.

Uncontrolled LDL (Low-Density Lipoprotein) is both a health crisis and a significant financial burden on the American public. Elevated LDL cholesterol is a primary risk factor for cardiovascular disease, which remains the leading cause of death in the United States. Cardiovascular disease accounts for approximately one out of every five deaths in the U.S. and creates an economic strain exceeding $400 billion annually in healthcare services and lost productivity. CDC data indicates that over 25 million American adults have high cholesterol, yet existing barriers to access have prevented a large portion of this population from controlling their levels.

Despite the existence of effective treatments, only half of U.S. adults who could benefit from cholesterol medicine are currently taking it, leaving millions of individuals untreated or undertreated. That is because the traditional prescription model is inaccessible to many Americans, as it requires frequent clinical appointments and time away from work. These barriers disproportionately impact rural and underserved communities, exacerbating health inequities.

Transitioning LDL-cholesterol-lowering therapies to an OTC framework would offer profound societal benefits:
1. Expanded Health Equity: Removing the requirement for a physician’s visit for routine management allows individuals with limited healthcare access to obtain essential medication.
2. Proactive Population Health: Lowering the threshold for treatment encourages earlier intervention, shifting the healthcare paradigm from reactive acute care to proactive management, ultimately reducing the incidence of heart attacks and strokes.
3. Healthcare System Efficiency: Shifting the management of routine cholesterol maintenance to an OTC model allows clinical resources to be redirected.

We believe the modern regulatory environment is uniquely positioned to support this switch through tech-enabled approaches. Nonprescription models that integrate validated diagnostic testing and digital screening tools ensure that patients can accurately self-monitor their condition. A tech-forward OTC approach allows for rigorous clinical screening, but with the convenience and scalability required to address a public health crisis of this magnitude.

The FDA’s initiative to expand the OTC pipeline is a critical step toward democratizing healthcare. Prioritizing LDL cholesterol treatments for nonprescription status will empower Americans to take control of their heart health and significantly reduce the national burden of cardiovascular disease.

On behalf of the Alliance for Aging Research (the Alliance), we appreciate the opportunity to respond to the Food and Drug Administration’s Request for Information (RFI) on Increasing Access to Nonprescription Drugs (Docket No. FDA-2025-N-4731). Increasing access to nonprescription drugs depends not only on which products are available OTC, but also on whether the pathway to nonprescription status is modern, transparent, and predictable. Today, the pathway to switch prescription drugs to nonprescription status remains one of the most direct pathways to expand patient access for conditions that can be self-recognized and self-managed. As Americans enter a new age of embracing self-care and having greater autonomy over their health, now is the time to modernize this process in a way that both maintains strong safety standards and also reflects real-world patient needs. This is particularly important for older adults and caregivers, who often face transportation, scheduling, and cost barriers that can make obtaining timely access to prescription care difficult — even for conditions that can be managed safely and effectively with clear labeling, education, and apt safeguards.

•Increasing transparency and predictability in FDA’s switch process and decision-making;
•Integrating patient perspectives into the development, review, and evaluation of switch candidates;
•Leveraging appropriate use of modern tools as encouraged by the Additional Condition for Nonprescription Use (ACNU) framework to support safe self-selection and use; and
•Improving education for consumers, caregivers, and healthcare providers to promote safe and effective use.

Thank you for your attention to this matter. We look forward to seeing the public meeting come together later this year and the Alliance stands ready to be a resource to the FDA as it evaluates strategies to increase nonprescription drug access to keep America healthy.

DrFirst appreciates the opportunity to respond to the FDA's Request for Information regarding increasing access to nonprescription drugs. As a pioneer in medication management technology with integrations into hundreds of electronic health record (EHR) systems—touching approximately one in three prescriptions in America—DrFirst is uniquely positioned to comment on how technology can enable safe expansion of nonprescription drug access. We offer comments on Questions 3 and 6.
Response to Question 3:
DrFirst supports thoughtful expansion of nonprescription drug access when implemented with appropriate safeguards. These include pharmacist engagement, health information technology, and patient education platforms.
The Pharmacist as an Essential Partner
Pharmacists represent an underutilized resource in expanding medication access. The American Pharmacists Association has documented expanding pharmacist scope across all 50 states, including immunization administration (over 270 million COVID-19 vaccines through September 2022), smoking cessation counseling, and prescribing authority for hormonal contraceptives (37 states) and HIV PrEP/PEP (30 states).1,2 For nonprescription drug expansion, pharmacists can provide initial screening, drug interaction assessment, patient education, and ongoing surveillance for adverse events. The UK’s 2004 approval of low-dose simvastatin for OTC sale with pharmacist screening provides a viable model.3
Technology-Enabled Safe Self-Selection
A landmark 2024 study in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology by Nissen and colleagues demonstrated that a technology-assisted web application could enable appropriate consumer self-selection of nonprescription statin therapy.4 Consumers using a structured digital application accurately identiﬁed their cardiovascular risk status, understood contraindications, and achieved therapeutic outcomes comparable to traditional prescription pathways. This evidence that technology can bridge the gap between full prescription status and unrestricted OTC availability is further supported by multiple systematic reviews demonstrating that mobile health applications signiﬁcantly improve medication adherence (OR 2.12–2.37; Cohen’s d = 0.40).5˒6

Stakeholder Alignment
To achieve this advancement, alignment across stakeholders is essential. Drug developers should invest in consumer-facing digital tools guiding appropriate self-selection; providers should embrace collaborative practice models with pharmacists; retailers should implement point-of-sale technology facilitating pharmacist consultation; and payers should expand coverage for pharmacist consultations related to nonprescription drug selection.

Response to Question 6:
Prescription Engagement Platforms
Modern prescription engagement technology addresses the primary barriers to safe medication use: education, affordability, and adherence. A recent peer-reviewed study from our institution published in PLOS Digital Health demonstrated that patients with heart failure who engaged with SMS text-based medication reminders had 19% higher odds of ﬁlling their prescriptions and 6% lower odds of hospital readmission within 30 days.7 These ﬁndings align with broader evidence that digital interventions—including personalized reminders, educational content delivery, and copay assistance integration—can meaningfully improve medication adherence across chronic disease populations.8
Clinical Decision Support and Interoperability
For drugs transitioning under the FDA’s Additional Conditions for Nonprescription Use (ACNU) pathway, technology can provide real-time clinical decision support, including drug interaction screening against prescription drug monitoring programs, contraindication identiﬁcation, and structured self-assessment tools documenting the basis for appropriate selection.
Success depends on integration with the broader healthcare information ecosystem through established standards, including NCPDP SCRIPT for prescription messaging and HL7 FHIR APIs for bidirectional data exchange. Consumer self-treatment decisions should ﬂow into the patient’s complete medication record.9

Summary
We recommend FDA: (1) embrace the ACNU pathway with technology as a core component; (2) recognize pharmacists as essential partners in expanded access; (3) require interoperability for platforms supporting nonprescription drug selection; and (4) design technology platforms to support pharmacovigilance and outcomes research from inception. DrFirst welcomes participation in the planned 2026 public meeting.
Respectfully,

Colin Banas, MD, MHA Chief Medical Ofﬁcer, DrFirst

I am a commercial drug developer with nearly 30 years experience, primarily in developing prescription drugs, and more recently in developing a first-in-class nonprescription (OTC switch) product.
My experience with the nonprescription division has been very different from my experience with other divisions of FDA. On the prescription side, I have understood FDA’s role in the drug development process as an advisor. FDA reviewers provide guidance, advice, and feedback to sponsors during drug development through meetings and correspondence. The guidance is meant to help sponsors make more informed decisions about their development programs and improve the quality of our new drug applications (and supplemental new drug applications). I always understood that the Sponsors retain full responsibility for drug development decisions until the application is submitted. FDA reviewers provide input to inform those decisions, but sponsors must decide how to proceed.
My colleagues and I have been surprised to find that this is not the case in working with the nonprescription division. In the nonprescription division the FDA acts as the ultimate decision maker for all aspects of the nonprescription development process, mandating details of specific DFL and PDP labeling and protocol designs.
We have requested many meetings over the years and the majority of the FDA’s extensive advice has been useful and appreciated, though some of the advice has changed over the years, and some of the Division’s advice has been inconsistent with the judgement of extremely experienced experts on the sponsor’s team. Unlike our previous experience with other FDA divisions, almost all of the nonprescription division’s ‘advice' is not advice but mandated requirements enforced by repeatedly calling to attention any ‘advice’ that has not been accepted and stalling the program until the ‘advice' is adopted. Negotiations to allow the sponsor to make the case for evidence-based choices about our own program have been futile and have cost us years. Our team eventually had to change our approach to simply accepting nearly all FDA advice as ‘requirements' even when our experts considered some of the advice counterproductive for our development program, creating unnecessary confusion or barriers for consumers.
The additional conditions for nonprescription use (ACNU) regulations have presented additional challenges for commercial OTC developers as FDA’s advice around an ACNU changed multiple times between 2016 when they first spoke to us about the ACNU concepts and 2025 when the ACNU rule was formally adopted.
This more autocratic micromanagement approach to nonprescription drug development we understand is not limited to our program and is inhibiting industry motivation to initiate or continue new OTC switch programs. We have heard from industry colleagues that the over-regulated OTC switch process has become so protracted, complex, and expensive that making a decision to initiate a first-in-class OTC switch is less likely today.
We recommend a good hard look at regulatory creep in this Division and realignment with practices consistent with the intention of FDA policies and the benefits of OTC switch to reduce cost and improve public health.

Making more drugs available without a prescription could help close that gap.
At the same time, I recognize the importance of ensuring that any transition from prescription to nonprescription status includes clear labeling, multilingual packaging where possible, and public education so that consumers can use these medications safely. Expanding access should not come at the cost of safety.

Expanding access to nonprescription drugs is a necessary and evidence‑based measure to ensure that all people—regardless of income, geography, or insurance status—can meet their basic healthcare needs. Increasing nonprescription availability supports public health equity by reducing barriers for communities that face limited access to clinicians, transportation, or insurance coverage. It is also culturally appropriate, as many populations rely on self‑care practices, community‑based health knowledge, and over‑the‑counter treatments as their first line of care. Allowing broader nonprescription access aligns with these established patterns of care rather than forcing unnecessary clinical gatekeeping. Moreover, expanding nonprescription availability is both effective and cost‑efficient: it reduces avoidable clinic visits, lowers system‑wide healthcare spending, and enables earlier intervention for common conditions. FDA’s initiative recognizes that accessible self‑care is a core component of modern healthcare delivery, and strengthening nonprescription pathways will improve outcomes, reduce disparities, and support a more resilient and patient‑centered health system.

This proposal would require repetitive inspections and appropriate corrective actions designed to properly tackle the safety concerns.

I agree with this proposal, and I think it’s a step in the right direction. Recently plane crashes have been all over the news and while the reasons for said crashes are different depending on the case, these incidents seem to have made a substantial number of people distrustful of flying. For instance, I was part of a group of six students who had planned to take part in a Social Justice trip during Spring Break. It would be unfair to blame every single airplane crash or flight accident on cracks since other factors like the weather, human error, the pilot’s experience, etc., do play an important role in the likelihood of an accident happening, but that does not mean that they should be ignored completely (Chen et al. Identification of flight accidents causative factors base on Shello and improved entropy gray correlation method).

I would suggest that the inspectors should be from different institutions. One could be from Boeing, at least one from the FAA and the CAA and one from the aviation company that is using the plane. This team would have to work together to make sure that the plane was perfectly safe and that cracks would not be a concern during the flight. I would also suggest that all members of the inspection team would have to agree on the safety issue for the plane to be allowed to take off.

OFCCP-2025-0004
Complaint Involving Employment Discrimination By A Federal Contractor or Subcontractor
The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs collection is applicable and necessary based on discrimination on disabilities, disabled veterans or qualified workers who file discrimination complaints in such cases. The OFCCP is responsible for a prompt investigation for complaints received by a Federal contractor or Subcontractor. under this regulation, it will determine whether unlawful discrimination against protected veterans and their families has occurred and take the appropriate steps to prevent future discrimination violations.

On Necessity and Utility of the Collection

Comment: The collection of LS-570 data is necessary for safeguarding worker rights and ensuring employer compliance, especially for vulnerable maritime labor populations. However, the form should be periodically reviewed for relevance to evolving labor demographics and employer practices.

Supporting Evidence: Periodic review of worker data requirements helps address gaps in coverage and equity for marginalized maritime workers (Seafarers International Union, 2022, https://www.seafarers.org/news/seafarers-international-union-addresses-maritime-worker-rights/).

On Burden Estimates

Question: Has the agency independently validated the burden estimates with a representative sample of small employers and insurance carriers to ensure these figures reflect real-world administrative costs and time, especially for historically under-resourced employers?

Supporting Evidence: Studies reveal that government paperwork burden is disproportionately felt by smaller entities, requiring robust field validation (OMB, 2020, https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/information-collection-budget-2020.pdf).

On Methodology and Assumptions

Comment: The methodology for calculating annual burden hours and cost should be transparent and explicitly account for new reporting technologies, language accessibility, and accommodation for individuals with disabilities.

Supporting Evidence: Transparent cost-burden methodologies promote equitable access and reduce unintentional exclusion of limited English proficiency (LEP) or disabled stakeholders (GAO, 2021, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-21-104234).

On Enhancing Quality and Clarity

Comment: The form and instructions should be routinely tested for plain language comprehension and accessibility, particularly among non-native English speakers and people with disabilities.

Supporting Evidence: Plain language and accessibility testing are proven to reduce administrative error and increase compliance (Plain Language.gov, 2023, https://www.plainlanguage.gov/resources/articles/accessibility/).

On Technological Modernization

Comment: OWCP should prioritize a secure, user-friendly electronic submission portal with mobile compatibility, including real-time error checking and multilingual support.

Supporting Evidence: E-filing systems improve compliance rates, user satisfaction, and equity (U.S. Digital Service, 2023, https://digital.gov/resources/how-to-improve-public-benefit-application-experience/).

On Minimizing Burden

Question: Has OWCP considered options such as pre-populated forms or secure data-sharing agreements with other federal/state databases to reduce repetitive data entry for carriers, especially those serving multiple covered populations?

Supporting Evidence: Data-sharing and pre-population significantly lower administrative costs and error rates (Pew Charitable Trusts, 2022, https://www.pewtrusts.org/en/research-and-analysis/reports/2022/08/data-sharing-modernizes-government-services).

On Equity and Anti-Discrimination

Comment: All communications, portals, and materials associated with LS-570 should comply with Section 508 and Title VI requirements, ensuring no discrimination based on language, disability, or socioeconomic status.

Supporting Evidence: Equitable access is a legal and moral imperative in federal benefit programs (U.S. Department of Justice, 2022, https://www.justice.gov/crt/fcs/TitleVI).

On Data Security and Privacy

Question: What additional data security and privacy protections are in place for electronically submitted LS-570 forms, given the sensitivity of policyholder and employer information?

Supporting Evidence: Recent increases in public sector data breaches necessitate robust privacy-by-design practices (GAO, 2024, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-106229).

On Feedback Loop and Continuous Improvement

Comment: OWCP should publish annual user experience feedback summaries and solicit ongoing input from stakeholders, especially worker advocacy organizations, to identify emerging barriers and guide future improvements.

Supporting Evidence: Transparent feedback mechanisms foster trust and program improvement (National Academy of Public Administration, 2022, https://napawash.org/academy-studies/public-participation-and-engagement).

On Environmental and Paperless Practices

Comment: Encourage or require carriers to submit documentation electronically to further reduce paper consumption and the program’s carbon footprint, with exceptions for accessibility needs.

Supporting Evidence: Paperless government processes contribute meaningfully to sustainability and efficiency goals (EPA, 2023, https://www.epa.gov/smm/advancing-sustainable-materials-management-facts-and-figures).

Public Comment from BufferSprings, LLC

BufferSprings is a service-disabled veteran-owned small business that helps federal contractors build real systems to support veterans, military spouses, Guard and Reserve members, and individuals with disabilities. We see every day where the process works and where it fails.

We support OFCCP’s effort to give VEVRAA its own enforcement framework and to remove confusing cross-references. Veterans deserve a rulebook that is clear and enforceable.

Our main points:

- Keep self-identification. It is the only consistent way veterans are recognized in contractor systems. Many veterans also identify as individuals with disabilities, so alignment with Section 503 is essential.

- Make enforcement about results. Conciliation agreements should include measurable milestones and check-backs. Remedies must fix the real barrier, such as MOS translation training, resume filters, or mentorship, not just paperwork.

- Use barrier analysis as the standard tool. When benchmarks are missed or harm is found, contractors should be required to diagnose where the system is failing, recruitment, screening, accessibility, or retention, and act on it.

- Simplify categories. The multiple “protected veteran” categories confuse both veterans and employers. OFCCP should allow a plain-language consolidated self-ID option that still maps to the statutory classes for reporting.

- Coordinate with Section 503. Many veterans are also IWD. Align corrective actions and milestones where facts overlap so fixes are efficient and effective.

- Keep benchmarks meaningful. Missing the national benchmark should trigger a barrier analysis and a clear plan to improve outcomes.

Veterans do not need favors. They need fair access and accountability that works. Contractors do not need guesswork. They need clarity, tools, and enforcement that is consistent.

BufferSprings stands ready to support OFCCP in building guidance that turns these rules into results.

Rob Arndt
Chief Executive Officer

The rule retains the current benchmark method for measuring veteran hiring but does not specify how frequently the national benchmark will be updated—adding a mandatory annual or biennial recalculation requirement would ensure alignment with the most current veteran labor force data.
While the proposed text encourages outreach to veteran organizations, it does not outline measurable performance indicators for assessing outreach effectiveness—consider requiring contractors to track and report referral yields from targeted recruitment sources.
The recordkeeping requirements focus on applicant and hire data but do not explicitly require documentation of reasonable accommodation requests for disabled veterans—adding this would strengthen compliance monitoring and disability protections.
The rule allows for contractor self-identification data collection but remains unclear on whether such data must be collected pre-offer, post-offer, or both—clarifying the timing and form of self-identification could prevent procedural inconsistencies.
The compliance evaluation process grants the agency discretion in selecting contractors for review without specifying prioritization based on veteran underrepresentation or past violations—incorporating risk-based selection criteria could optimize enforcement impact.
There is no explicit articulation of how intersectional factors (e.g., veteran status combined with race, gender, or disability) will be considered in compliance reviews—adding language here would improve detection of compounded disadvantage.
While electronic data submission is permitted, the rule does not address specific federal cybersecurity compliance standards for transmitted veteran demographic and employment data—mandating alignment with NIST or FedRAMP protocols would mitigate confidentiality risks.

I oppose the reversal of the Section 508 voluntary self-identification form because it undermines the progress we’ve made toward disability inclusion and accessibility in the federal workforce. The form provides valuable data that helps ensure individuals with disabilities are represented and supported, in compliance with federal equal employment opportunity goals. Removing or reversing this process risks reducing transparency, accountability, and the ability to measure whether accessibility and inclusion commitments are truly being met. Maintaining the voluntary ID form reinforces the government’s leadership role in modeling inclusive employment practices.

I strongly oppose the Department of Labor’s proposed changes to Section 503 of the Rehabilitation Act that would eliminate the requirement to invite applicants and employees to voluntarily self-identify as a person with a disability, and that would rescind the 7% utilization goal for federal contractors.

These rollbacks would cause serious harm to equal employment opportunity for people with disabilities, including Deaf and Hard of Hearing individuals.
•Self-identification matters. Without a formal, voluntary self-ID process, many qualified candidates with disabilities will remain invisible in the hiring process. Employers will lose critical data on disability inclusion, making accountability nearly impossible.
•The 7% utilization goal matters. This benchmark is not a quota; it is a fair, flexible guideline that motivates contractors to recruit, hire, and retain people with disabilities. Removing it will weaken compliance and reduce workforce participation.
•Equal opportunity matters. Section 503 has been essential in moving beyond nondiscrimination to proactive inclusion. Rolling back these obligations reverses decades of progress and sends the harmful message that disability employment is optional rather than a civil rights priority.

As someone who is [Deaf / Hard of Hearing / connected to the Deaf community], I know firsthand how important strong Section 503 protections are. These rules help ensure that talented workers are given a fair chance to contribute their skills in federal contracting jobs.

I urge the Department of Labor to withdraw this proposal and instead strengthen enforcement of Section 503 so that people with disabilities, including Deaf and Hard of Hearing workers, can thrive in the American workforce.

Respectfully submitted,
Thomas Graziano
Queens, NY

BufferSprings submits this comment in strong support of OFCCP’s request to renew the VEVRAA information collection request (OMB Control No. 1250–0004).

BufferSprings is a Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business with more than ten years of direct experience working inside federal contractor compliance, recruiting, and workforce systems. We work with both employers subject to VEVRAA and veterans navigating those systems. The observations summarized here reflect long-term, first-hand experience across hundreds of contractor establishments.

VEVRAA is one of the only enforceable employment protections veterans have. While it has been law for decades, it has not been treated as a priority in practice. For years, VEVRAA was overshadowed by Executive Order 11246, and contractors focused compliance resources where enforcement pressure was strongest. Veterans were deprioritized as a result. Although EO 11246 has since been rescinded, the enforcement culture that neglected veteran outcomes has not corrected itself.

The information collection covered by this request is not administrative overhead. It is the infrastructure that makes enforcement possible. Without applicant flow data, hiring outcomes, outreach evaluations, benchmark analysis, and related records, VEVRAA cannot be enforced in any meaningful way. OFCCP’s supporting statement correctly notes that less frequent collection would compromise enforcement. We agree.

Decades of reporting show that most federal contractors are not meeting the national veteran hiring benchmark. This is not a marginal gap. In many organizations, veteran representation remains flat or declines year over year despite continuous reporting. This pattern has persisted across administrations, economic cycles, and regulatory updates. The problem is not paperwork. It is lack of accountability.

A central failure in VEVRAA implementation is that required data is collected but rarely used to drive change. Mandatory VETS-4212 filings are commonly treated as an annual paper exercise. Reports are prepared, submitted, and archived with minimal internal review. In many organizations, the data is not reviewed by talent leadership or senior management and does not inform recruiting strategy, advancement, or retention.

In some cases, VETS-4212 data reveals persistent occupational segregation, with veterans disproportionately concentrated in entry-level and blue-collar roles while being underrepresented in professional, technical, and leadership positions. These patterns are visible year over year, yet they frequently trigger no internal review, no corrective action, and no accountability. When filings do not prompt scrutiny, they reinforce the perception that veteran outcomes are monitored but not enforced.

Benchmarks that do not trigger diagnosis become meaningless. Reporting without consequence encourages performative compliance. When contractors miss the hiring benchmark for multiple plan years, the data should prompt barrier analysis and corrective action. These expectations do not require new regulations. They require consistent use of information contractors are already required to collect.

BufferSprings supports minimizing unnecessary burden through modernization and clarity, not by weakening oversight. Burden is reduced when contractors build systems that work. Allowing accountability to erode will not.

Renewing this information collection preserves OFCCP’s ability to enforce VEVRAA as a real protection rather than a symbolic one. Veterans do not need promises. They need enforceable protections and employers who are held accountable.

PROPOSAL 1 — Allow Any Subsistence‑Eligible Alaskan to Fish From Any Vessel

Regulation to Amend: 50 CFR § 300.65(g)

Proposed Regulatory Language

“Any individual eligible for the federal subsistence halibut program may fish from any vessel, regardless of ownership or family relationship.”

Full Justification

Allowing any subsistence‑eligible Alaskan to fish from any vessel is essential for fairness, safety, and food security. Subsistence is not based on boat ownership, it is based on eligibility, need, and traditional use. Many rural families do not own seaworthy vessels, and access to halibut should not depend on whether a household can afford a boat. This proposal ensures that all subsistence‑eligible Alaskans have equal access to the resource.

This change significantly improves safety. Weather windows in coastal Alaska are short, unpredictable, and often dangerous. Families must be able to fish during the safest conditions, on the safest vessel available, rather than being forced into unsafe boats simply because of ownership restrictions. Allowing multiple subsistence‑eligible individuals to fish from one vessel reduces the number of boats on the water, lowers risk, and supports safe harvest practices.

Fuel savings are a major benefit. Fuel prices in rural Alaska are among the highest in the nation, and many families cannot afford to run separate boats. Allowing multiple households to fish together on one vessel reduces fuel consumption, lowers costs, and supports rural economic survival. This is especially important for single parents, elders, disabled individuals, and low‑income households who cannot afford to operate their own vessels.

This proposal also supports food security. Alaska is one barge away from empty shelves, and many communities cannot rely on consistent grocery availability. Families must be able to harvest halibut when they have access to a boat, safe weather, and available time. Restricting vessel use to owners or immediate family members creates unnecessary barriers that prevent households from obtaining the food they need.

Traditional and customary practices strongly support this change. For generations, Alaska families have fished cooperatively, sharing boats, gear, labor, and harvest. Subsistence is a community‑based system, not an individual sport. Allowing any subsistence‑eligible person to fish from any vessel aligns with long‑standing cultural practices of cooperation, mutual aid, and shared responsibility for feeding households.

This proposal does not increase harvest pressure. The number of halibut allowed per subsistence‑eligible person does not change. Allowing people to share boats only changes how they access the fishery, not how much they harvest. It simply ensures that every eligible household can participate, regardless of boat ownership.

Enforcement remains simple and clear. Eligibility is already defined by the federal subsistence halibut program. Law enforcement only needs to verify that each person fishing is subsistence‑eligible. This proposal does not complicate enforcement or introduce new burdens for NOAA, OSM, or field officers.

For all these reasons , safety, fuel savings, fairness, traditional practices, food security, and enforcement clarity any subsistence‑eligible Alaskan should be allowed to fish from any vessel, regardless of ownership or family relationship.

Contractor requirements to take affirmative action for protected veterans holds contractors accountable to show non-discrimination so it's an important initiative to continue. Dear Members of the Federal Subsistence Board,

I have lived in Sitka, Alaska for 36 years, and during that time my family has relied on subsistence harvests to place high-value, nutritious foods on our table. In a community where store food prices are consistently high, subsistence is not recreational — it is a practical and essential component of household food security. Predictable and stable regulations are critical to our ability to plan, harvest, process, and preserve these foods responsibly.

For that reason, I respectfully urge the Board to maintain the current subsistence fishing regulations for the 2027–2029 cycle unless clear biological or statutory deficiencies are demonstrated.

The existing regulatory framework is functioning as intended. In the absence of documented conservation concerns, unmet escapement goals, or demonstrated inequities in access, regulatory stability should be preserved. Incremental changes to seasons, harvest limits, or methods and means — particularly when not supported by new biological data — can cumulatively erode meaningful subsistence opportunity.

Current regulations reflect established customary and traditional use determinations, rural determinations, and substantial Regional Advisory Council input. Revising these provisions without compelling new evidence risks undermining user confidence and administrative efficiency.

Subsistence management should remain grounded in conservation data. Where stocks are meeting sustainable thresholds and harvest levels remain within biological limits, regulatory change is not warranted. Maintaining effective regulations allows agencies to focus limited resources on monitoring, research, and emerging conservation concerns rather than unnecessary revision.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Board retain the current federal subsistence fishing regulations unless demonstrable conservation need or statutory conflict requires modification.

Thank you for your consideration.

PROPOSAL — Clarify the Vessel Possession Limit for Subsistence Halibut
Regulation to Amend: 50 CFR § 300.65(e)

---

Proposed Regulatory Language
“For clarity, the vessel possession limit for subsistence halibut is equal to the combined allowable harvest of all subsistence‑eligible individuals on board. Each eligible individual may retain their full daily harvest limit, and the vessel may possess the total of all such individual limits. All halibut retained must be for subsistence use only.”

---

Justification

The current federal subsistence halibut regulations establish individual daily harvest limits of 20 halibut per day for rural residents and 25 halibut per day for tribal members. The vessel possession limit is intended to be the sum of the daily limits of all subsistence‑eligible individuals on board. However, the regulation is written in a way that is frequently misunderstood by the public and sometimes inconsistently interpreted in the field.

Many subsistence users believe that a vessel is limited to 20 or 25 halibut per day regardless of how many eligible individuals are on board. This misunderstanding creates confusion, discourages cooperative fishing, and leads to unnecessary conflict between users and enforcement. A simple clarification will ensure that all parties understand that the vessel possession limit is based on the number of eligible individuals on board, not a flat vessel cap.

This clarification does not change the total allowable harvest for any individual. It simply restates the existing rule in clear, plain language so that families who fish together can understand their lawful possession limit. Cooperative fishing is a longstanding subsistence practice that improves safety, reduces fuel costs, and allows families to share labor and resources. Clear regulations support these traditional practices.

This proposal improves transparency, reduces confusion, and ensures consistent enforcement without altering the biological impact of the subsistence halibut fishery. It is a clarification only, not a change in harvest levels.

PROPOSAL 2 — Allow Subsistence‑Eligible Alaskans to Hire a Vessel Operator for Transportation and Safety

Regulation to Amend: 50 CFR § 300.65(g)

Proposed Regulatory Language

“Subsistence‑eligible individuals may hire a vessel operator for transportation and safety. Hiring an operator does not convert the activity into a charter, guided trip, or commercial service. All halibut harvested under this provision must be taken only by subsistence‑eligible individuals.”

Full Justification

Allowing subsistence‑eligible Alaskans to hire a vessel operator is essential for safety, fairness, and access. Many rural residents cannot safely operate a vessel due to age, disability, medical conditions, lack of training, or lack of experience in ocean conditions. Others may own a boat but cannot physically run it. Some households have no boat operator at all. Subsistence access should not depend on whether a family has a skilled boat driver, or owner.

This proposal improves safety. Coastal Alaska weather windows are short, unpredictable, and often dangerous. A trained or experienced operator can safely navigate conditions that would otherwise put families at risk. Allowing households to hire an operator reduces the number of inexperienced drivers on the water and ensures that elders, disabled individuals, and single parents can participate safely in the subsistence halibut fishery.

This proposal also supports food security. Many subsistence‑eligible Alaskans work long hours, are on call, or have caregiving responsibilities that prevent them from operating a vessel themselves. Hiring an operator allows families to access halibut during rare safe weather windows, rather than missing their opportunity due to work schedules or physical limitations. Subsistence halibut is a critical food source, and access should not be restricted by a household’s ability to operate a boat, or if they own a boat1.

Fuel efficiency is another major benefit. Rural fuel prices are extremely high, and many families cannot afford to run their own vessels. Hiring one operator to take multiple subsistence‑eligible individuals reduces fuel consumption, lowers costs, and supports rural economic survival. This is especially important for low‑income households, elders, and people without reliable transportation.

Traditional and customary practices support this change. Alaska communities have always relied on skilled boat operators to transport families, elders, and neighbors to fishing grounds. Hiring someone for transportation is consistent with long‑standing cultural practices of cooperation and shared labor. The harvest remains strictly non‑commercial because only subsistence‑eligible individuals may fish, and no halibut may be sold or bartered.

This proposal does not increase harvest pressure. The number of halibut allowed per subsistence‑eligible person does not change. Hiring an operator only changes how families access the fishery, not how much they harvest. It simply ensures that every eligible household can participate safely and fairly.

Enforcement remains simple. Officers only need to verify that:

the if the operator fishing, he is subsistence eligible

the people fishing are subsistence‑eligible, and

no commercial guiding or charter activity is occurring.

This proposal does not complicate enforcement or introduce new burdens for NOAA, OSM, or field officers.

For all these reasons — safety, fairness, fuel savings, traditional practices, food security, and enforcement clarity — subsistence‑eligible Alaskans should be allowed to hire a vessel operator for transportation and safety without being classified as charter or commercial activity.

PROPOSAL 3— Allow Each Subsistence‑Eligible Alaskan to Run Their Own 30‑Hook Longline

Regulation to Amend: 50 CFR § 300.65(f)

Proposed Regulatory Language

“Each individual eligible for the federal subsistence halibut program may deploy one subsistence longline with up to 30 hooks. Multiple subsistence‑eligible individuals aboard the same vessel may each deploy their own longline. Longlines must be marked in accordance with existing federal requirements.”

Full Justification

Allowing each subsistence‑eligible Alaskan to run their own 30‑hook longline is essential for fairness, access, and traditional harvest practices. Current interpretations restrict longline use to vessel owners or immediate family members, which unfairly limits participation for households that do not own boats or do not have a family member capable of operating one. Subsistence access should be based on eligibility, not vessel ownership.

This proposal restores traditional and customary practices. For generations, Alaska families and communities have fished cooperatively, with multiple individuals setting their own gear from the same vessel. Subsistence is a community‑based food system, and longline harvest has historically been shared among households working together. Allowing each eligible person to set their own longline aligns with these long‑standing cultural practices.

This change improves food security. Many rural households rely on halibut as a primary food source, and limiting longline use to vessel owners restricts access for elders, disabled individuals, single parents, low‑income families, and anyone without a boat. Allowing each eligible person to set their own longline ensures that every household can obtain the halibut they need, regardless of boat ownership.

Fuel savings are another major benefit. Rural fuel prices are extremely high, and allowing multiple eligible individuals to fish from the same vessel reduces the number of trips required. This lowers fuel consumption, reduces costs, and supports rural economic survival. It also reduces the number of vessels on the water, improving safety.

This proposal does not increase harvest pressure. The number of halibut allowed per subsistence‑eligible person does not change. Allowing each person to deploy their own longline only changes how they access the fishery, not how much they are allowed to harvest. The total allowable harvest remains the same; it is simply distributed more fairly.

Enforcement remains simple and clear. Officers only need to verify that:

each person deploying a longline is subsistence‑eligible,

each person is using only one longline, and

each longline is properly marked.

This proposal does not complicate enforcement or introduce new burdens for NOAA, OSM, or field officers.

For all these reasons — fairness, traditional practices, food security, fuel savings, and enforcement clarity — each subsistence‑eligible Alaskan should be allowed to deploy their own 30‑hook longline, even when fishing from the same vessel.

PROPOSAL — Establish a Multi‑Day Possession Formula for Subsistence HalibutRegulation to Amend: 50 CFR § 300.65(e)

Proposed Regulatory Language:“The possession limit for subsistence halibut is the allowable daily harvest limit for each subsistence‑eligible individual multiplied by the number of days spent fishing. Each eligible individual may retain their full multi‑day harvest, and the vessel may possess the combined multi‑day harvest of all eligible individuals on board. All halibut retained must be for subsistence use only.”

Justification:The current federal subsistence halibut regulations only allow possession of a single day’s harvest, regardless of how many days a family spends fishing. This system does not reflect the realities of subsistence life in Alaska, especially for inland families who must travel hundreds of miles to reach the coast. A household from Fairbanks, North Pole, Tok, Delta, or other Interior communities cannot make multiple trips to harvest 20 or 25 fish at a time. A multi‑day possession formula allows families to harvest safely and efficiently during limited weather windows.

This proposal ensures that each subsistence‑eligible individual may retain the lawful amount of halibut for each day they fish. For example, a person with a 20‑fish daily limit who fishes for three days may lawfully possess 60 halibut. This system allows families to meet their annual food needs in one safe trip rather than making repeated dangerous runs in unpredictable weather. Subsistence users must harvest during rare safe weather windows, and a one‑day possession limit forces repeated dangerous trips.

The multi‑day formula also supports conservation. Under the current daily limit, fishermen are pressured to keep the largest halibut to maximize meat per fish. However, the largest halibut are the most important breeders, producing exponentially more eggs than smaller fish. A multi‑day possession system allows families to keep smaller, more appropriate food‑sized halibut while releasing large breeders alive. This reduces release mortality and protects the spawning biomass. Historically, Alaska families harvested what they needed during multi‑day trips based on tides, weather, and opportunity, not daily limits.

This proposal does not increase the total number of halibut allowed per person; it only allows lawful harvest to be retained over multiple days. The biological impact remains unchanged, while safety, fairness, and food security improve significantly.

Enforcement remains straightforward. Officers only need to verify the number of subsistence‑eligible individuals on board, the number of days fished, and that the possession matches the formula. This proposal does not complicate enforcement or introduce new burdens for NOAA, OSM, or field officers.

For these reasons — safety, conservation, inland access, fuel savings, and traditional subsistence practices — a multi‑day possession formula should be adopted for the subsistence halibut fishery.

PROPOSAL — Establish a Clear Residency Eligibility Standard for the Federal Subsistence Halibut Program
Regulation to Amend: 50 CFR § 300.65(g) – Eligibility Requirements

Proposed Regulatory Language:
“To be eligible to harvest subsistence halibut, an individual must be a United States citizen or a lawful permanent resident and must have been a legal resident of the State of Alaska for at least one full year prior to participation. Eligible individuals must also be year‑round Alaska residents and may not be absent from the State of Alaska for more than 90 days in a calendar year, except when receiving documented medical treatment. Temporary residents, seasonal workers, visitors, and individuals who have not completed one full year of Alaska residency are not eligible.”

Justification:
The current eligibility system for the federal subsistence halibut program is based on “rural” designations and tribal membership, but it does not define residency, duration of residency, citizenship, or absence limits. This allows individuals with weak or temporary ties to Alaska to qualify, including seasonal workers, snowbirds, and people who live Outside for most of the year. A clear, enforceable residency rule is needed to ensure that subsistence halibut is reserved for true Alaska residents who rely on this resource for food security.

This proposal establishes a simple, objective standard: participants must be U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents who have lived in Alaska for at least one full year and who maintain year‑round residency. Limiting absences to no more than 90 days per year, except for medical treatment, ensures that only individuals who genuinely live in Alaska full‑time are eligible. This prevents abuse by people who spend only a few months in Alaska while maintaining primary residence in the Lower 48.

This proposal does not increase the number of eligible users; it only clarifies and strengthens residency integrity. The biological impact remains unchanged, while fairness, food security, and community stability improve significantly. Historically, Alaska subsistence systems have relied on year‑round residents who live within and contribute to their communities, not temporary or seasonal populations.

Enforcement becomes straightforward. Officers only need to verify:
- U.S. citizenship or lawful permanent residency,
- one full year of Alaska residency, and
- that the individual has not exceeded the 90‑day absence limit except for medical treatment.

This proposal improves fairness, strengthens residency integrity, and ensures that subsistence halibut remains available to full‑time Alaska residents rather than seasonal or temporary residents.

Housekeeping Policy: Statewide Rural Status for Subsistence Purposes
Docket: DOI‑2025‑0071
Policy Type: Definition Clarification / Housekeeping

I. Purpose
This housekeeping policy clarifies the meaning of “rural residents of Alaska” for subsistence purposes under ANILCA Title VIII; Congress did not define “rural,” and the statute refers to “the people of Alaska,” indicating broad intent rather than geographic limitation; this definition aligns federal practice with Alaska’s actual food‑security conditions, geographic isolation, and dependence on wild resources.

II. Findings

A. Alaska Cannot Sustain Its Population Without Wild Foods
Alaska lacks sufficient farm‑ready land, agricultural capacity, and infrastructure to produce the calories, grains, feed, or fats needed to sustain its population for a full year without wild fish and game.

B. Limited Food Storage and Single‑Port Dependence
Most communities—including Anchorage—maintain only a three‑day grocery supply; Alaska relies on a single major port and limited air corridors, with no overland access to U.S. food systems.

C. Historical Vulnerability
The 1964 earthquake demonstrated Alaska’s isolation; damaged ports and airfields delayed assistance for days.

D. Alaska Is Functionally Rural
Alaska’s lack of farm‑ready land, dependence on a single port, and demonstrated vulnerability show that Lower‑48 urban criteria do not apply; for subsistence purposes, Alaska is rural in its entirety.

ANILCA requires that commercial, sport, and personal‑use fisheries be restricted before subsistence; recognizing statewide rural status does not create additional federal subsistence closures.

G. Consistency With ANILCA
ANILCA’s reference to “the people of Alaska” supports a broad interpretation; Congress anticipated population growth and did not limit subsistence protections to specific communities.

This housekeeping definition does not restrict any non‑subsistence user beyond what ANILCA already requires; it merely clarifies eligibility under existing federal law.

III. Policy Statement
For purposes of subsistence management under ANILCA Title VIII, the entire State of Alaska shall be deemed rural; all Alaska residents shall be treated as “rural residents of Alaska” for subsistence priority and eligibility until one of the following conditions is met:

Condition A — Statewide Food Self‑Sufficiency
Alaska can produce enough food within its borders to sustain its population for one full year without wild fish and game.

Condition B — Overland Access to U.S. Food Systems
Alaska shares a land border with another U.S. state that allows uninterrupted road access for food transport and is capable of supplying the state’s needs within 24 hours under normal operating conditions.

Until Condition A or B is met, no Alaska community shall be classified as non‑rural, and no resident shall be denied subsistence priority based on residence in any so‑called urban area.
