Dear Ms. Moriarty,

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments during the review of the Federal Subsistence Management Program. My name is Annika Ord and I was born and raised in Juneau, where I live now. I grew up in a commercial fishing family and spent much of the year fishing on the family boat, living remotely, and harvesting from the land and sea to feed our family.

Subsistence is important to me. Subsistence is important to me because it allows Alaskans to live from the land and help ensure that future generations have the same ability to practice this way of life. Subsistence is an essential right for rural Alaskans. As an urban Alaskan, I feel strongly about protecting the rights of rural Alaskans to harvest from the lands and waters and be represented by community members on the Federal Subsistence Board.

Subsistence should be prioritized. Federal protections of rural subsistence rights are essential to ensure that Alaskans can continue this way of life and provide for their families. Federal protections help protect the rights of rural Alaskans to live from the land and put food on their tables. Commercial and sport harvests are important too, but it's essential we protect subsistence harvests first, because subsistence harvests allow communities to stay in place, practice their culture, and put food on the table. Subsistence harvests are essential to food security and affordability for rural Alaskans. We must ensure subsistence protections remain for rural Alaskans and that they are managed sustainably to ensure continued access for future generations.

Decisions about subsistence must include people who understand subsistence harvesting practices and use of resources. Maintain the 6, voting public board seats and the subsistence knowledge requirement for the regional advisory councils. Local knowledge is essential for sustainable management of our lands and waters. The 6 public seats helps ensure that community voices are heard and that local knowledge of the lands and waters is represented. Agency members bring important expertise to the board, but they do not have the same, detailed understanding of community needs and local harvest patterns, including when their are times of local depletion or over harvest. The public seats are essential to ensure that subsistence management supports the rural Alaskans who rely on it.

Narrowing or restricting rural designations could exclude communities and individuals who still rely deeply on subsistence for survival. There are many factors that should be considered. Subsistence rural designation is important to all communities across Alaska. While I am not a rural Alaskan myself, I work with folks from all across the state and know how essential rural subsistence rights are for communities. Grocery prices are exorbitant in rural Alaska, as is electricity and fuel. Jobs can be scarce. Subsistence allows rural Alaskans to provide for their families, it helps people stay in their community, and live by the land. Urban Alaskans have much more access to affordable groceries, utilities and resources than those living in villages. Ensuring that rural designation continues to represent rural Alaskans is essential. We need to protect rural designation of our smaller communities and ensure that the process for designation is flexible and community-based.

Thank you,
Annika Ord

Dear Ms. Moriarty,

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments during the review of the Federal Subsistence Management Program. My name is Blake Buotte, I'm born and raised in the small fishing community of Petersburg, AK going on 39 years.

Subsistence is important to me. Subsistence is important to me because if we didn't have subsistence rights to the area I live in, I would struggle to be able to provide food for my family. With the cost of groceries being so expensive being in a little town, I rely on being able to use subsistence programs for halibut and for harvesting deer. Without this program we would struggle to support and help feed our families because one deer isn't enough to support a family.

Subsistence should be prioritized. Federal protections of rural subsistence rights are important to me because it's what helps residents and myself be able to help support and provide food for our families. Without these subsistence rights families would struggle and could end up relocating out of the state. I feel subsistence rights should take priority over sport and commercial activities. The commercial activities are making it harder for hunters, and fishermen to harvest what they need to provide for their families.

Decisions about subsistence must include people who understand subsistence harvesting practices and use of resources. Maintain the 6, voting public board seats and the subsistence knowledge requirement for the regional advisory councils. It's important to have practical subsistence knowledge so that they can understand how important and vital these subsistence rights are to our community and our way of life.

Narrowing or restricting rural designations could exclude communities and individuals who still rely deeply on subsistence for survival. There are many factors that should be considered. It's very important because it helps us harvest more than one deer a year, and helps us have a chance to compete with the charter and commercial activities that continue to wipe out our resources around these small towns.

Thank you,
Blake Buotte

To whom it may concern,
My name is Eric Anslinger, I am a resident of Fairbanks, Alaska. I serve as the VP (interior) for the Alaska Outdoor Council and on the Board of Directors for the SCI chapter Northern Alaska. I am writing these comments in direct opposition of the Federal Subsistence Board and its overreach of state authority to manage wildlife and its DEI objectives of removing access to resources for Alaska residents. It is my belief that the Federal Subsistence Board (FSB) has been operating in violation of section (E) of the Alaska statehood act. Congress granted Alaska sole control of its fish and wildlife in this act. The FSB was created by administrative action in response to the 1988 McDowell court ruling, in which the Alaska Superior Court deemed that all Alaskans have equal rights to state resources as written in Article 8 of the Alaska State Constitution. This action was administrative in nature and not part of any law passed through congress. Title 8 of ANILCA is written in direct defiance of the Alaska Statehood Act and the Alaska State Constitution. The state of Alaska has an office of subsistence management and a Tier 1 and 2 system that allows for local harvest when population numbers do not allow for excessive harvest. While amending ANILCA is a separate issue, although it is the permanent fix to this dual management issue. My recommendation is for the Secretaries of Interior and Agriculture to remove the perceived allocation authority of the FSB. I would argue that the FSB should be dissolved completely (which can be done without congressional action) the FSB should be made to be only an advisory body which requestions action through ADFG. Not only is there an issue of unfair and unfounded hunting closures by the FSB, they aren’t managing for maximum sustainable yield. Federally qualified hunters are allowed to harvest sublegal Dall sheep rams and ewes, they have no antler restrictions on moose, and the federal land mangers do not support or participate in predator manage programs. The FSB has led to a large amount of racial tension across the state with organizations like AFN stoking the flames and pushing for native only priority. When President Carter hamstrung Alaska into getting on board with ANILCA by restricting hunting on all federal lands, he set the tone for the next 40 years of conflict. I urge the department of interior and agriculture to force the FSB out of a management roll and give the State back its rights granted at statehood and allow all residents of Alaska to be treated equally.

Dear Ms. Moriarty,

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments during the review of the Federal Subsistence Management Program. My name is Nick Goll, I live in Juneau. I am a hunter, fisherman and wild harvester.

I have the privilege of living in a place where food is readily accessibly and relatively cheap compared to other places in SE Alaska. I hunt, fish and harvest to try and live a healthier life, it is not a main source of food.

Most communities around SE Alaska do not have access to affordable food, I travel a lot to other communities regularly and see the prices people pay for basic food, 2-3 times or even more than what I pay in Juneau which is already higher than most other places in the US. Subsistence is not only a right that was given to the Native Alaskans when their land was bought out from under them but it is their way of life and how they preserved their language and culture when the boarding schools tried to take it away. This is also a right given to the non-native people living in these communities as a way to feed their families and live the life they want to live. No government should tell anyone they can not provide for their family. Sport and commercial should always come after subsistence. Sport and commercial bring in money but most of it leaves the state, subsistence directly and immediately benefits the people that live here and have stewarded this land for thousands of years.

Decisions about subsistence must include people who understand subsistence harvesting practices and use of resources. Nicholas Goll

I submit this comment in support of the petition filed by Safari Club International Safari Club International.

The petition raises an important question of statutory interpretation and constitutional balance that warrants review. At issue is not whether subsistence should be protected — it should — but whether the current scope of federal authority reflects what Congress actually enacted.

Congress resolved Alaska Native land claims through the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA), which expressly extinguished aboriginal hunting and fishing rights in exchange for land, financial compensation, and the creation of Native corporations. That framework was intended to replace race-based claims with a system grounded in equal opportunity, shared benefits, and participation within Alaska’s broader legal and economic structure.

Subsequently, the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) established a rural subsistence priority. The statute’s plain language reflects Congress’s intent to protect subsistence uses without creating a race-based entitlement or permanently displacing the State of Alaska’s traditional authority over fish and wildlife management.

Judicial expansion of federal control beyond the clear bounds of ANILCA has produced uncertainty, overlapping jurisdiction, and management outcomes that lack local accountability. In practice, this expansion has shifted broad regulatory authority to federal agencies and boards in ways that Congress did not clearly authorize and that conflict with foundational principles of state sovereignty and equal protection.

Granting the petition would allow the Court to clarify these statutory limits and restore the balance Congress intended — one that protects subsistence, respects Alaska’s constitutional framework, and ensures fair and consistent management of fish and wildlife resources for all rural residents.

For these reasons, the petition should be granted.

As a proud hunter, angler, conservationist, and Alaskan, I write to express my strong support for reforming and improving Alaska’s Federal subsistence management program. The reforms being considered by the U.S. Department of the Interior are essential to ensuring the Federal Subsistence Board operates in a way that is consistent with the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA). I support the rural subsistence priority created by ANILCA, but I also support holding the Board to its legal obligations and requiring its decisions to be based in science.
First, I support reducing the Federal Subsistence Board’s membership to the five federal agencies. That was ANILCA’s intent and how the Board originally operated.
Second, I believe the Regional Advisory Councils (RACs) should play a stronger and more representative role. While fully supporting the rural subsistence priority, I agree that RAC members should be nominated by local Alaskans and reflect the range of regional perspectives—subsistence, sport, and commercial—instead of by federal bureaucrats in Washington, DC. This will encourage better participation and ensure fair consideration of local concerns.
Third, I understand that the Federal Subsistence Board frequently makes decisions that conflict with the science presented by State biologists. Alaska’s State biologists and managers possess the most comprehensive data and long-term research, and their recommendations should meaningfully guide federal decisions. I strongly support reforms that would require the Board to place greater reliance on the State’s science and expertise.
Last, I understand that the Federal Subsistence Board has regularly closed hunting or fishing to all but local users based on “emergency” and “temporary” special actions. For example, in 2021, the Board approved a special action that resulted in the closure of 20 million acres to moose and caribou hunting by non-local users in GMUs 23 and 26A. I believe that these shortcuts conflict with federal law and practice, and support requiring the Board to act with full public participation.
Thank you for considering these important reforms. As an SCI member, I strongly believe these changes will help ensure the Federal subsistence management program is fair, transparent, and grounded in science—and that it serves the interests of the Alaskans who rely on our wildlife resources.
Sincerely,

I am a 50-year resident of Alaska, and I strongly support limiting the federal subsistence board’s control over fish and wildlife management in our state. The federal board should be required to include Alaska state biologists in all decision-making processes. Alaska has extensive scientific expertise and resources, and we must use all available state data to make sound, biologically based decisions for our fish and wildlife. Alaska residents should never be excluded from accessing state resources unless there is a clear biological necessity to protect the resource. If hunting or fishing closures are required, restrictions should begin with non-Alaska residents first, not the people who live here and depend on these resources year-round.

To Whom It May Concern,

I am submitting this comment in strong support of retaining the current structure and authorities of the Federal Subsistence Management Program (FSMP) and the Federal Subsistence Board (FSB).

Subsistence is not a hobby or a special interest in Alaska Native and rural communities—it is a way of life. It directly supports food security, cultural continuity, community health, and the intergenerational transfer of knowledge. For many families, subsistence harvesting is essential to putting food on the table and maintaining cultural identity tied to the land and waters.

The existing FSMP structure, established under ANILCA, appropriately recognizes the federal government’s responsibility to uphold a rural subsistence priority on federal public lands. The current makeup of the Federal Subsistence Board, including the five public member seats and the three Tribally nominated seats, ensures that decisions are informed by individuals who understand subsistence practices, seasonal realities, and regional conditions. Removing these seats would significantly weaken Alaska Native and rural representation in decisions that directly affect our lives.

I strongly oppose any changes that would require the Federal Subsistence Board to defer to the State of Alaska when setting subsistence regulations. The State cannot legally mandate a rural preference, and such deference would effectively eliminate the protections guaranteed under ANILCA. Federal subsistence management must remain independent and capable of acting in the best interest of rural subsistence users.

It is also critical to retain the current structure and authority of the Regional Advisory Councils and to preserve the ability of the Federal Subsistence Board to enact special actions when conditions require timely response. These tools are necessary to adapt to environmental change, shifting wildlife patterns, and community needs.

Finally, the Office of Subsistence Management should remain under the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Policy, Management and Budget to preserve its integrity, independence, and effectiveness.

I urge the agency to preserve the current FSMP framework in its entirety. Decisions about subsistence must continue to include Alaska Native voices and those with lived experience and knowledge of subsistence harvesting and stewardship.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for considering the perspectives of rural and Alaska Native communities.

As a proud hunter, angler, conservationist, and Alaskan, I write to express my strong support for reforming and improving Alaska’s Federal subsistence management program. The reforms being considered by the U.S. Department of the Interior are essential to ensuring the Federal Subsistence Board operates in a way that is consistent with the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA). I support the rural subsistence priority created by ANILCA, but I also support holding the Board to its legal obligations and requiring its decisions to be based in science.
First, I support reducing the Federal Subsistence Board’s membership to the five federal agencies. That was ANILCA’s intent and how the Board originally operated.
Second, I believe the Regional Advisory Councils (RACs) should play a stronger and more representative role. While fully supporting the rural subsistence priority, I agree that RAC members should be nominated by local Alaskans and reflect the range of regional perspectives—subsistence, sport, and commercial—instead of by federal bureaucrats in Washington, DC. This will encourage better participation and ensure fair consideration of local concerns.
Third, I understand that the Federal Subsistence Board frequently makes decisions that conflict with the science presented by State biologists. Alaska’s State biologists and managers possess the most comprehensive data and long-term research, and their recommendations should meaningfully guide federal decisions. I strongly support reforms that would require the Board to place greater reliance on the State’s science and expertise.
Last, I understand that the Federal Subsistence Board has regularly closed hunting or fishing to all but local users based on “emergency” and “temporary” special actions. For example, in 2021, the Board approved a special action that resulted in the closure of 20 million acres to moose and caribou hunting by non-local users in GMUs 23 and 26A. I believe that these shortcuts conflict with federal law and practice, and support requiring the Board to act with full public participation.
Thank you for considering these important reforms. As an SCI member, I strongly believe these changes will help ensure the Federal subsistence management program is fair, transparent, and grounded in science—and that it serves the interests of the Alaskans who rely on our wildlife resources.
Sincerely,

As a proud hunter, angler, conservationist, and Alaskan, I write to express my strong support for reforming and improving Alaska’s Federal subsistence management program. The reforms being considered by the U.S. Department of the Interior are essential to ensuring the Federal Subsistence Board operates in a way that is consistent with the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA). I support the rural subsistence priority created by ANILCA, but I also support holding the Board to its legal obligations and requiring its decisions to be based in science.
First, I support reducing the Federal Subsistence Board’s membership to the five federal agencies. That was ANILCA’s intent and how the Board originally operated.
Second, I believe the Regional Advisory Councils (RACs) should play a stronger and more representative role. While fully supporting the rural subsistence priority, I agree that RAC members should be nominated by local Alaskans and reflect the range of regional perspectives—subsistence, sport, and commercial—instead of by federal bureaucrats in Washington, DC. This will encourage better participation and ensure fair consideration of local concerns.
Third, I understand that the Federal Subsistence Board frequently makes decisions that conflict with the science presented by State biologists. Alaska’s State biologists and managers possess the most comprehensive data and long-term research, and their recommendations should meaningfully guide federal decisions. I strongly support reforms that would require the Board to place greater reliance on the State’s science and expertise.
Last, I understand that the Federal Subsistence Board has regularly closed hunting or fishing to all but local users based on “emergency” and “temporary” special actions. For example, in 2021, the Board approved a special action that resulted in the closure of 20 million acres to moose and caribou hunting by non-local users in GMUs 23 and 26A. I believe that these shortcuts conflict with federal law and practice, and support requiring the Board to act with full public participation.
Thank you for considering these important reforms. As an SCI member, I strongly believe these changes will help ensure the Federal subsistence management program is fair, transparent, and grounded in science—and that it serves the interests of the Alaskans who rely on our wildlife resources.
Sincerely,

I support FAA’s decision to prohibit dispatch under MMEL item 75-33-01 where engine operability is not substantiated. The final rule states that Rolls-Royce reported a lack of data supporting compressor stability, relight capability, surge recovery, and inclement-weather capability with an intermediate-pressure bleed valve inoperative, and FAA determined that the resulting condition could lead to loss of thrust control and loss of the airplane.
My concern is not the prohibition. It is the evidentiary history and transition logic around a dispatch relief that had already acquired operational standing.
The public FAA Boeing 787 MMEL Rev. 18 draft retains item 75-33-01 on a page last revised August 10, 2017. The item is Category B and permits one IP bleed valve to be inoperative on each engine with appropriate performance adjustments. The current AD now states that there is no data to substantiate critical operability characteristics for that dispatch state.
I recommend FAA address four questions in the final public record.
1. What changed in the evidentiary basis for MMEL 75-33-01?
Please state, to the extent releasable, whether the relief was originally supported by test or analysis that has since been invalidated or superseded; depended on assumptions or configurations that changed; or whether the required substantiation was later found to be absent. These are materially different safety-process outcomes. If technical details are proprietary, FAA can still identify the category of failure without disclosing protected data.
2. What is the safety basis for the 60-day compliance period?
FAA found good cause to adopt the AD immediately because the condition can cause loss of thrust control, including a possible dual-engine loss-of-thrust-control condition, and because a single affected engine can leave the airplane one failure from a catastrophic outcome. Yet paragraph (g) continues to permit the existing MEL dispatch relief until 60 days after the AD effective date.
I recognize that FAA has historically used roughly 60-day periods for implementing some MEL/MMEL changes. Administrative implementation time, however, is not itself the safety basis for continued operation. If FAA retains the 60-day period, please state why the existing relief provides an acceptable level of safety during that interval and whether any interim restriction is necessary, particularly for dispatch with an inoperative IPBV on both engines.
3. What evidence would restore this dispatch capability?
Paragraph (h) provides the normal AMOC path for an acceptable level of safety. Because the reason for the prohibition is specifically lack of substantiating evidence, FAA should identify whether restoration of this relief would occur through MMEL revision, AMOC, another approval path, or some combination, and what categories of evidence would be necessary to re-establish acceptable engine operability.
4. Has FAA screened related relief for the same evidentiary dependency?
If the missing substantiation is traceable to an assumption, analytical method, engine-operability model, or approval practice shared with other MMEL relief, FAA should state whether related items or configurations have been reviewed. If the issue is isolated to 75-33-01, saying so would close the question.
I am not asserting that the original MMEL relief was improperly approved, that the 60-day period is unsafe, or that other MMEL items are defective. The public record does not establish those conclusions. My request is narrower: when an operational capability is withdrawn because its evidentiary basis is insufficient, preserve enough of the decision history to distinguish what changed, why temporary continued operation remains acceptable, and what future evidence could justify restoration.

Special condition Section 33.7 requires the FAA to fix distinct horsepower, torque, r.p.m., gas-temperature, duration, and occurrence limits for two new engine states, rated ICR active maximum continuous power and rated ICR 2-minute power. The notice's Discussion section explains this is needed because the applicant requested a rating structure under which the engine in ICR will have different limits from the all-engines-operating (AEO) or one-engine-inoperative (OEI) conditions. Together the two sections treat idle-cruise regime (ICR) operation as a genuinely new regime requiring genuinely new numeric limits, not an extension of ratings already on the books.

The same reasoning that required Section 33.7 to fix new numeric limits does not carry through to Section 1.1, where the definition that actually bounds the regime is left open-ended. Rated ICR stand-by power is defined only as "the approved lowest engine rpm at which the engine can safely operate while in the ICR mode of operation." Neither "approved" nor "safely operate" is tied to a criterion, a test standard, or a party responsible for demonstrating it beyond the Administrator's unstructured finding. An applicant proposing a very low stand-by rpm to maximize the fuel savings the notice cites as the design's purpose has no published floor to design against, and a commenter has no way to evaluate whether a given stand-by rpm meets the standard, because the standard is circular: safe is whatever is approved, and approved is whatever the Administrator finds safe. Fixing this means replacing the phrase with a stated minimum-performance or margin criterion, written into the special condition itself, that a proposed stand-by rpm must satisfy.

That gap surfaces concretely in Section 33.68. The special condition substitutes "rated ICR stand-by power rotor speeds" for "minimum descent idle rotor speeds" in the induction system icing standard, without stating whether the two speeds coincide. Minimum descent idle speed exists to keep the rotor turning fast enough to avoid ice-loading stall during a descent; stand-by power is defined only as the lowest rpm at which the engine can operate, with no reference to icing performance. If stand-by rpm is lower than the icing-safe descent speed it replaces, an operator in icing conditions using ICR could face exactly the ice-loading risk Section 33.68 exists to prevent, with nothing in this notice showing the speeds were compared. The fix is a stated finding, in the special condition, that rated ICR stand-by power rotor speeds meet or exceed minimum descent idle rotor speeds under icing, or an explicit limitation excluding ICR operation in icing conditions until that showing is made.

Section 33.87's endurance test substitutes rated ICR active maximum continuous power and rated ICR 2-minute power for rated maximum continuous power and rated takeoff power across the twenty-five 6-hour test cycles and the cyclic-loading periods, without showing the substituted levels reproduce equivalent thermal and mechanical stress. If the ICR ratings sit below the ratings they replace, the test could under-stress the engine relative to the baseline standard, and fatigue or creep modes that surface only near takeoff-level stress could go undetected before certification closes. Placing that horsepower/temperature relationship in the docket record would let commenters assess whether the substitution holds the engine to an equivalent standard rather than a looser one.

The Section 1.1 definition of rated ICR 2-minute power states, as part of the definition itself: "There is no mandatory inspection or prescribed maintenance action required after reaching this power level." That is a maintenance-program conclusion stated as a defined term, without any test or fleet data in this notice to support it. Embedding the conclusion in a definition, rather than deriving it through the normal instructions-for-continued-airworthiness process, forecloses a maintenance requirement before in-service experience exists to justify or challenge it. Striking the maintenance-preemption clause and letting inspection intervals for this power level follow from the continued-airworthiness analysis, like any other rating, would close that gap without disturbing the rest of the definition.

None of this is a case for withholding these special conditions; the PW220A's fuel-saving rationale for ICR is a reasonable basis for the design, and FAA's own framework already requires case-by-case novel-feature review before any certificate issues. It is a case for closing the specific gaps identified above before this text becomes, as 14 CFR 21.101 allows, the template applied to the next manufacturer's ICR engine.

The FAA's proposed special condition fails to establish the legally mandated 'level of safety equivalent' under 14 CFR 21.16 because it replaces a quantifiable, objective standard (§ 27.143) with a circular, subjective definition of 'suitable' awareness. By relying on unquantified balancing tests and omitting fail-obvious redundancy for sole-source electronic cues, the special condition violates the Administrative Procedure Act's prohibition against arbitrary and capricious rulemaking. The FAA must establish measurable proximity thresholds and latency bounds and codify them in a publicly available Means of Compliance before locking in a precedent that will automatically govern future STCs under 14 CFR 21.101.

Docket No. FAA-2026-1585 responds to a real gap in the existing airworthiness standard: 14 CFR 27.143's controllability requirement assumes cockpit control position tracks rotor actuator position through a mechanical link, and Skyryse's SkyOS fly-by-wire system for the Robinson Model R66 removes that link entirely, along with the tactile cue pilots have relied on to sense proximity to control-authority limits. Proposing a substitute means of awareness, rather than certifying the aircraft under a standard that no longer describes how it actually works, follows directly from that mismatch.

That same substitute is defined only as making the flight crew "suitably aware" of approaching control-authority limits, where "suitable" means "an appropriate balance between nuisance and necessary operation" — a term defined by another undefined term. Nothing in the special condition sets a proximity threshold, a maximum interval between onset of the condition and a pilot-perceptible cue, or any bound on acceptable false-alert rate. That is a step down in specificity from the very standard this special condition is meant to replace: Sec. 27.143 already quantifies cyclic control margin at VNE and a 17-knot, all-azimuth wind envelope for the mechanical baseline. An FBW substitute for a safety-critical cue should be held to comparable numeric specificity, not a discretionary balancing test resolved case-by-case inside an unpublished FAA engineering finding. The fix is concrete: set a maximum permissible interval between onset of proximity to the control-authority limit and a pilot-perceptible cue, tied to a defined proximity threshold expressed as a percentage of remaining control authority.

A second gap follows from the same design change. Because the mechanical cue path no longer exists, the digital annunciation system is now the sole channel through which a pilot learns of approaching control-authority limits — a single point of failure the proposed text does not address. Nothing in the special condition requires the design to be fail-safe or fail-obvious if the sensor or annunciation path itself degrades or fails silently. A pilot relying on a cue that has quietly stopped functioning is in a worse position than one relying on the mechanical system this special condition supersedes, not an equivalent one. Adding an explicit fail-safe or fail-obvious requirement for the awareness system itself would close that gap without altering the underlying performance standard.

Third, the special condition's applicability is not limited to this one aircraft in practice: the notice itself states that if Skyryse or another applicant modifies any other model sharing this type certificate with the same fly-by-wire design feature, these special conditions attach automatically under 14 CFR 21.101, without a fresh comment period specific to that model. An undefined "suitable" standard adopted here becomes the template projected onto future applicants who never had the chance to comment on whether it was adequately met the first time. Publishing a means-of-compliance document — an Advisory Circular or equivalent specifying how "suitable" will be evaluated — before or alongside the final special conditions would let both this docket's commenters and future inheritors of the standard verify the actual technical bar rather than an applicant-specific finding that never becomes public.

One administrative note: the docket's own Notice No. field is printed as the literal placeholder "XX-XX-XX-SC" in the Federal Register text. Worth correcting before this becomes part of a binding type-certification basis referenced in later dockets.

None of this suggests special conditions are premature, or that FAA has misidentified the underlying problem — the mechanical-to-digital control-margin gap is real and needs a standard. The request here is that the replacement standard be as measurable as the one it replaces, before it becomes the template for every FBW helicopter modification that follows.

What this data exchange should reveal is the need for honest accounting in the student loan program and where to rein in lending - in terms of both borrowers and institutions. When a student owes over $60,000 and has attended several online institutions over several years without any payments made, that is one clue that more borrowing for subsequent degrees won’t lead to future full repayment. Another clue is when 70 plus percent of an institution’s students rely on loans, but fewer than 25 percent make the slightest dent in loan principal within 7 years of leaving, that is an institution you may want to impose some restrictions on (such as limit loans to direct cost [tuition and fees] only).

Right now, the department of education is building its accountability efforts around the earnings metric, or the do-no-harm rule as it is called. However, this rule barely scratches the surface in terms of cost of the loan program. Instead of reining in where the largest volume of unpaid loans is going, it only captures a handful of programs where a small sliver of borrowing is occurring.

Right now, we call a loan of any amount, whether $5000 or $200,000 loan receiving $10 or other de minimis monthly payments “current” and in good standing - due to generous income driven repayment (IDR) plans. This is despite the heavy taxpayer subsidy on the rest of it and the likelihood that most of it will end up on the taxpayer tab. Similarly, we allow borrowers unlimited forbearances, often for years on end, with no allowance as a doubtful account or any restriction on further borrowing.

The current accounting practice based largely on historical default rates captures only a sliver of the nonpayment and cost to taxpayers. As we know from looking at the entire portfolio, very few loans are being repaid in full at any given time and the more a student borrows, the more degrees they hold, the larger the liability they pose to taxpayers, due to their reliance on IDR subsidies and PSLF. Dear Treasury Privacy Office,

I am writing to flag serious Fourth‑ and Fifth‑Amendment concerns with the proposed DO .0197 system of records. While I applaud the agency’s desire to streamline oversight of vital assistance programs, the breadth of data collection and the expansive “routine‑use” disclosures raise constitutional red flags that deserve a hard look before the rule is finalized.

1. Fourth‑Amendment – Unreasonable Searches
The proposed database will house full names, Social Security numbers, bank accounts, income details, and even granular transaction histories for millions of individuals and entities. Under Carpenter v. United States (138 S.Ct. 2203, 2018), the Supreme Court held that the government’s acquisition of detailed location‑history data constitutes a search requiring a warrant.

DO .0197’s routine‑use clause (see § 552a(b)(3) of the Privacy Act) permits disclosure of these same data to a plethora of federal, state, local, and even private actors—including law‑enforcement, debt‑collection agencies, consumer‑reporting bureaus, and “security‑clearance” offices—without individualized judicial oversight. This blanket sharing effectively creates a de facto warrantless search of every participant’s private financial footprint.

If the Treasury wishes to use the data for fraud detection or compliance, it must at least adopt case‑by‑case, warrant‑supported queries or, at a minimum, a narrowly tailored “targeted‑use” protocol that satisfies the reasonable‑expectation‑of‑privacy test. Otherwise, the system risks being struck down as an unconstitutional fishing expedition.

2. Fifth‑Amendment – Due‑Process and Property Interests
Senior‑government‑employment jurisprudence (e.g., Cort v. Ash, 422 U.S. 268, 1975; Arnett v. Kennedy, 416 U.S. 134, 1974) recognizes a property interest in one’s personal data when the government maintains a comprehensive record that can affect eligibility for benefits, licensing, or employment.

DO .0197 aggregates data that will be used to determine eligibility, allocate funds, and even influence security‑clearance decisions. Yet the notice provides no procedural safeguards—no notice‑and‑opportunity to contest inaccuracies, no independent review mechanism, and no limitation on retroactive use of historic data. This omission denies affected individuals the due‑process “notice and hearing” that the Fifth Amendment demands before the government can materially affect their rights or interests.

3. Recommendations
Narrow the Routine‑Use Scope – Limit disclosures to (a) law‑enforcement investigations with a judicial warrant or subpoena, (b) audit functions directly tied to a specific program, and (c) statutory exceptions that are narrowly defined. Remove blanket categories such as “consumer‑reporting agencies” and “debt‑collection agencies” unless a court order is attached.

Implement a Robust Redress Mechanism – Adopt a formal “record‑access and correction” procedure consistent with 5 C.F.R. § 552a. § 552a(k) requires agencies to provide individuals a reasonable opportunity to contest the content of their records. Publish clear timelines, an independent appeals officer, and a transparent audit trail.

Data Minimization & Retention Limits – Collect only the data strictly necessary to administer each program. Apply a tiered retention schedule (e.g., 3‑year limit for eligibility data, longer only for audit‑required records) and destroy obsolete records in accordance with NARA guidance.

Encryption & Access Controls – While the notice mentions encryption, specify role‑based access, multi‑factor authentication, and regular penetration testing. Publish a summary of these technical safeguards to reassure the public that the data will not become a “digital pantry” for every agency.

Public‑Comment Transparency – Post a plain‑language FAQ summarizing the constitutional concerns and the agency’s response. This will help citizens understand the stakes and foster the progressive, accountable governance we all crave.

4. Closing Thought
In the age of big data, the Treasury’s ambition to “centralize” information is admirable—but centralization without constitutional guardrails is a recipe for overreach. As we strive for efficient, equitable assistance, let’s also protect the privacy and due‑process rights that form the bedrock of our democracy.

Thank you for considering these points. I look forward to a revised proposal that respects both the public interest and the Constitution.

Anonymous

The below files will address at length a new approach and consideration regarding education in entrepreneurial financial literacy, particularly addressing our value systems in finance, as well as providing a new means of achieving those goals.
Please see the attached document for my public comment submission. I appreciate the opportunity to provide input on the update to the National Strategy for Financial Literacy.

My name is Maia Scurry. I am a full-time MBA student at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, a participant in the UW-Milwaukee Startup Challenge, and the founder of a digital asset financial literacy platform.

I am submitting this comment to recommend that the updated National Strategy explicitly include digital asset financial literacy as a core component of modern financial education — starting as early as K-12 and extending through the workplace.

Financial literacy in 2026 should reflect the realities of today's economy. From a very young age, we teach children about money. We teach them to count coins, identify bills, understand savings, and learn the value of a dollar. As they grow older, they learn about gold, commodities, and traditional financial systems. These are foundational lessons — but the financial world has changed significantly, and our education has not kept pace.
Today, digital currencies, cryptocurrency, and stablecoins are no longer fringe concepts. They are expanding rapidly and becoming part of everyday financial conversation. Young people are encountering these topics online, through social media, and in their communities long before they have any formal education on what they are or how they work. That gap is dangerous.

A modern financial literacy strategy should begin introducing age-appropriate digital asset education at the K-12 level — not to encourage speculation, but to build foundational awareness the same way we build awareness around traditional money. Students should grow up understanding what digital currencies are, how blockchain works at a basic level, what the risks and volatility look like, and how to identify scams and fraud in this space.

Beyond K-12, I strongly believe that digital asset financial literacy should be a mandatory component of workplace financial wellness programs for all employees. The workplace is one of the most effective and underutilized channels for reaching everyday people with meaningful financial education. Most adults spend the majority of their waking hours at work — and yet financial literacy programs offered through employers remain largely focused on traditional topics like retirement contributions and health benefits.

Employers have both the reach and the responsibility to help close this gap. Mandatory digital asset literacy modules, interactive workshops, and presentations delivered through the workplace would ensure that everyday workers — regardless of their background, income level, or education — have access to balanced, trustworthy information about the financial tools that are already part of their world. This is not about pushing people toward investment decisions. It is about making sure they are informed enough to protect themselves and make confident choices.

This is especially important in the military. Every year, large numbers of young people — many of them 18 and 19 years old, entering the workforce for the first time — join the military with little to no financial education background. They are earning paychecks, making financial decisions, and being marketed to by digital asset platforms with no formal preparation. Military financial readiness programs already exist, but they do not currently address digital assets in any meaningful consumer education capacity. Mandatory digital asset literacy modules, delivered through existing military financial readiness infrastructure, would directly serve this population at exactly the right moment in their lives.

The delivery format matters too. Dry, text-heavy materials do not work for this generation. Effective financial literacy in this space should be interactive — engaging modules, short presentations, quizzes, and real-world scenarios that meet people where they are and reflect how they actually learn.
Through my work in this space, I have seen firsthand that everyday people — particularly those ages 18 to 40 — are actively seeking this kind of education but have nowhere credible to turn. The demand is real and the gap in accessible, unbiased digital asset literacy is significant.

The National Strategy has an opportunity to get ahead of this gap rather than respond to it after harm has already occurred. Just as we prepared generations of Americans to understand and navigate traditional financial systems, we have a responsibility to prepare the next generation for the financial system that actually exists today. That preparation should begin in school, continue through the workplace, and reach every corner of the workforce — including the men and women who serve this country.

I hope this recommendation is considered in the updated framework.

Respectfully submitted,
Maia Scurry
MBA Candidate, UWM Class of 2027

The SIFMA Foundation for Investor Education (SIFMA Foundation) respectfully submits this comment in response to the Department of the Treasury’s Request for Information regarding the Financial Literacy and Education Commission’s (FLEC) update to the National Strategy for Financial Literacy (“National Strategy”).

For nearly 50 years, the SIFMA Foundation has advanced financial capability through scalable, school-based programs grounded in experiential learning. The Foundation has reached nearly 24 million students nationwide, with approximately 750,000 students participating annually, primarily through public schools, including in underserved communities.

Based on this experience and supporting research, the Foundation recommends that the updated National Strategy place greater emphasis on the development of financial agency, defined as the ability to apply knowledge to real-world financial decision-making. Effective financial education requires not only access to information, but also structured opportunities—particularly for youth—to practice decision-making in realistic contexts.

Evidence demonstrates that experiential learning approaches, including simulation-based instruction, improve both financial knowledge and applied skills. These approaches enable participants to engage in research-based decision-making, evaluate financial information, manage risk, and develop long-term financial behaviors. Educator-supported implementation further strengthens these outcomes by reinforcing concepts and promoting sustained engagement.

Accordingly, the Foundation recommends that the National Strategy prioritize application, behavioral outcomes, and scalability. This includes elevating experiential financial learning, strengthening financial information resilience, reinforcing the distinction between investing and speculative behavior, and pairing access to financial tools with the education necessary to use them effectively.

The recommendations that follow are informed by decades of program implementation, cross-sector collaboration, industry and educator engagement, and research, and are intended to support a National Strategy that is evidence-based, inclusive, and designed to build enduring financial capability.

Financial literacy is one of the most important life skills for citizens in a modern economy. A prosperous and competitive financial system depends on individuals who understand saving investing risk management and responsible financial decision making. The next National Strategy should expand financial education beyond basic budgeting to include the principles of wealth creation long term investing and economic understanding.

For more than two decades the Global Academy of Finance and Management has worked with universities financial professionals and educators worldwide to advance standards in financial education, economics, literacy and wealth management. Our experience shows that effective financial literacy must teach both financial capability and capital formation.

Priority Areas

The current priorities basic financial capability military financial education postsecondary education housing counseling and retirement education remain valuable and should be retained. However the strategy should add several modern areas.

First wealth creation and capital formation. Citizens should understand how wealth is built through ownership of productive assets such as stocks bonds businesses and diversified investment portfolios.

Second investment literacy. Americans should understand compound interest diversification long term investing and retirement planning.

Third digital finance and financial technology. Education should include fintech tools cybersecurity awareness and digital financial systems that increasingly shape modern finance.

Fourth fraud prevention and scam awareness. Financial crime has increased significantly and consumers must be educated to recognize and avoid sophisticated fraud schemes.

Youth Financial Education

Investment vehicles such as youth investment accounts can be powerful teaching tools. Financial literacy improves when young people gain real world experience saving and investing. Programs that allow students to observe the long term growth of diversified portfolios can teach the powerful concept of compound growth and long term discipline. Experiential financial education where students actually save and invest is far more effective than theoretical instruction alone.

Best Practices

The best practices identified in the 2020 strategy remain appropriate. However several additional principles should be emphasized.

Financial education should teach the principles of wealth building including compound interest long term investing diversification and asset ownership. Citizens must also understand the importance of behavioral discipline, economics, risk, and investments in finance. Many financial mistakes arise not from lack of knowledge but from emotional decision making such as impulsive spending or panic selling during market volatility.

Programs should also incorporate basic economic literacy including inflation productivity and the relationship between economic growth and investment.

Another important practice is raising professional standards for financial educators. Financial education programs should increasingly rely on qualified professionals with recognized credentials and real world financial expertise.

Role of Government

The federal government should act as a coordinator and facilitator of financial education initiatives. The most effective programs often arise through partnerships among universities nonprofit organizations professional associations and financial institutions. Public private collaboration can significantly expand the reach and impact of financial education.

Research and Measurement

Future research should focus on the effectiveness of youth investment programs behavioral finance interventions and digital financial education tools. Evaluation should emphasize behavioral outcomes such as savings rates retirement participation long term investing behavior and reduction in fraud losses rather than knowledge tests alone.

Conclusion

Financial literacy is ultimately about empowering citizens to achieve financial independence and security. A national strategy that promotes long term saving investing and responsible financial decision making will strengthen both household prosperity and the broader economy. By encouraging capital ownership disciplined investing and greater understanding of economic and taxation/retirement strategies, the United States can cultivate a financially capable population prepared to thrive in a complex and evolving global economy.

Respectfully submitted

Dear Treasury and FLEC,
American students need more than textbooks and lectures to build financial security. They need early, hands-on experience with real money in real accounts—especially the new Trump Accounts created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
I recommend removing the 2020 National Strategy topic areas and replacing them with the following topic areas:

My response will focus on recommendations for “Youth Investment Strategies.”
Creating a Trump Account app should be a top priority in implementing this recommendation. A single, easy-to-use app would let American students practice, save, invest, and watch their money grow, no matter who they are or where they live. This approach is uniquely effective for hard-to-reach populations because it is mobile-first, works on any smartphone or computer, and reaches students exactly where they already spend their time — in classrooms, after-school programs, faith-based organizations, youth groups, and the games they play every day. It is fair and objective: any American child, anywhere, can use the same tool regardless of income, location, or background. It is the most direct and effective way to turn financial literacy from theory into lifelong success in achieving the American Dream.
How the App Would Work
Phase I: Standalone Brokerage App (like Robinhood, but built for students)
Treasury should form a tiger team. The team would include experts from brokerage apps and gaming companies, as well as real classroom teachers and student representatives.
The app would have two simple parts:
1. Simulation mode – Used in schools, faith-based organizations, youth clubs, and nonprofits. Teachers would guide students through picking assets, measuring risk, setting short- and long-term goals, and seeing instant results. Students practice investing their Trump Account money (gifts or earnings) without any risk.
2. Live transaction mode – Students work with parents or guardians at home to make actual purchases inside their real Trump Account.
The app would run on phones and in any web browser, so no one is left out.
Phase II: Bring Financial Skills Into the Games Kids Already Play
Treasury should partner with companies like Roblox, Xbox, EA Sports, Minecraft, Fortnite, and Call of Duty. Add real financial choices inside the games:
• Earn in-game money and pay for housing, food, insurance, cars, taxes, and medical care.
• Manage salary caps in sports games.
• Decide how to finance tools and resources in building or battle games.
This turns playtime into powerful, transferable skills that work in any future job market—even one changed by AI.
Phase III: Live Streaming and Celebrity Outreach
Partner with social media influencers and celebrities with children to host live streams showcasing the app and games in action on platforms like Twitch and Kick. Treasury officials could join some streams. Why This Beats the Current National Strategy
• It connects government policy directly to what kids enjoy and already do every day.
• It gives students ownership of their financial future right now, instead of waiting until “life hits.”
• It appeals to Gen Z and Gen A by focusing on wealth building, financial freedom, and flexible income—not just paying bills.
• It protects against AI-driven job changes by teaching skills that create assets, not just wages.
I purposely excluded academic research findings from my recommendations. After 27 years working as a federal banking regulator, I’ve learned that overreliance on academic research findings produces solutions that focus on policy rather than the people these policies are intended to serve. Instead, I used insights from my real-life experiences growing up in poverty, receiving public assistance, having low and moderate income, earning in the top 5% of US households, and being retired and living on a fixed income. Men’s Health Network appreciates the opportunity to provide input on the U.S. National Strategy for Financial Literacy. We strongly support national efforts to improve financial education as a core driver of long-term income security, family stability, and overall well-being.

Financial literacy is not simply an economic skillset. It is a protective factor. It influences mental health, family relationships, workforce participation, and retirement security. For men and boys in particular — who often internalize expectations around provision, financial independence, and economic success — financial knowledge can serve as both empowerment and prevention.

We respectfully offer the following considerations for strengthening the National Strategy.

1. Financial Literacy Must Address the Modern Digital Risk Environment

Today’s financial ecosystem is radically different from that of even a decade ago. Young people — especially adolescent boys and young men — are growing up in an environment saturated with online sports betting and gambling platforms, gamified investing and trading apps, cryptocurrency speculation, social media–driven financial advice, and instant digital payment systems. These systems are intentionally designed to be frictionless, engaging, and emotionally stimulating. Financial education must reflect this reality.

The National Strategy should explicitly incorporate probability education related to gambling and speculative risk, the psychology of risk-taking in digital environments, the long-term compounding effects of debt, and the financial consequences of impulsive digital transactions. This is not about discouraging ambition or innovation; it is about ensuring individuals understand how these systems function and how to navigate them responsibly.

2. Strengthen Education Around Financial Scams and Exploitation

Financial scams are increasing in both volume and sophistication. AI-generated impersonation scams, fraudulent investment schemes, phishing attacks, and high-pressure “opportunity” pitches disproportionately affect individuals who lack foundational financial knowledge. Men and boys may encounter investment-related fraud and online financial manipulation through sports, gaming, and digital communities.

We recommend that the National Strategy treat scam prevention as a core competency of financial literacy, integrate digital verification skills into curricula, include behavioral awareness around urgency and manipulation tactics, and emphasize practical, scenario-based learning. Prevention requires more than warnings; it requires applied education and critical thinking skills.

3. Integrate Financial Literacy into K–12 Curricula Nationwide

We strongly urge the Commission to prioritize mandatory, developmentally appropriate financial education within K–12 systems. Students should graduate high school with demonstrated competency in budgeting and savings fundamentals; credit, interest, and debt accumulation; insurance and risk management; taxes and payroll systems; retirement planning basics; gambling mathematics and financial risk; and scam identification and consumer protection.

Financial education should be explicit about consequences. Without understanding personal finance, individuals are more vulnerable to debt cycles, predatory systems, fraud, and long-term instability. For boys in particular, who may face cultural expectations around financial success and self-reliance, early financial education can reduce future stress and build long-term resilience.

4. Recognize Financial Literacy as a Health and Stability Issue

Financial stress is strongly associated with anxiety and depression, family strain, reduced healthcare engagement, and workplace instability. Because men are often less likely to seek help for financial or emotional distress, prevention through early education becomes even more critical.

We recommend that the National Strategy acknowledge financial literacy as part of a broader well-being framework that includes mental health, family resilience, and community stability. Financial literacy should be framed as a proactive support system that strengthens both economic security and overall health.

Conclusion

The modernization of the National Strategy for Financial Literacy presents an important opportunity to reflect the realities of today’s digital financial landscape and to ensure that education is preventative, practical, and protective. Financial literacy must be honest about risk, integrated early in education, responsive to evolving digital threats, supportive rather than punitive, and framed as empowerment rather than remediation.

Strengthening financial literacy for men and boys strengthens families, workplaces, and communities. We appreciate the opportunity to contribute to this review and stand ready to support continued national efforts to promote informed financial decision-making and long-term income security for all Americans.

Dear Financial Literacy and Education Commission:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the update to the U.S. National Strategy for Financial Literacy. Treasury’s notice states that comments are due by April 6, 2026, and seeks input on priority areas, best practices, support for practitioners, research gaps, evaluation, and outcomes. Regulations.gov also states that the written comment is the official comment and should include all points the commenter wishes to make.

I submit this comment as the founder of a new community-based financial literacy initiative serving metro Atlanta, including Rockdale, Henry, Clayton, DeKalb, and surrounding areas. My startup planning has focused on three primary access points: churches and faith-based institutions, adult-school and workforce settings, and youth-serving programs. Those inquiries consistently point to the same practical needs: budgeting, cash-flow stability, debt and credit, banking access, fraud prevention, and beginner investing. Although these inquiries are not a formal survey, they strongly suggest that financial education is most effective when it is trusted, local, modular, and tied to real-life decisions.

Public data confirms the need for this approach. FDIC data show that 14.2% of U.S. households were underbanked in 2023, and Georgia’s state profile shows 7.0% of households were unbanked, compared with 4.2% nationally. These figures show that many households still operate outside, or only partially within, the mainstream financial system.

Georgia has made important progress by requiring the Personal Finance and Economics course for high school graduation, but school-based exposure alone is not enough. Adults, families, entrepreneurs, and out-of-school populations still need practical, community-based financial education delivered in settings they trust.

For that reason, I recommend that FLEC retain the current priority areas but add four explicit areas. First, add financial resilience and cash-flow stability, including emergency savings, bill prioritization, debt management, and irregular-income planning. Second, add fraud, scams, and digital financial safety as a stand-alone priority, consistent with Treasury’s concern about increasingly sophisticated fraud schemes. Third, add youth financial capability through real-world practice, so students learn saving, risk, fees, fraud awareness, and long-term thinking. Fourth, add small business and self-employment financial capability, including recordkeeping, tax awareness, separation of personal and business finances, and retirement planning for self-employed workers. Treasury’s notice specifically invites comment on youth investing opportunities and fraud trends, and SBA guidance likewise recognizes financial literacy as critical for small business success.

I also recommend that the revised Strategy preserve the 2020 best practices while clarifying them. Financial education should be organized around decision points, not just topics: opening an account, comparing a loan, responding to a scam text, reading a pay stub, or starting retirement contributions. It should also emphasize trusted delivery channels such as churches, adult schools, workforce programs, libraries, and community organizations. Programs should be modular, easy to adapt, and paired with worksheets, checklists, scripts, and next-step tools so participants leave prepared to act, not merely informed.

The federal government can add the most value by serving as a standards-setter, content provider, and capacity builder. FLEC should maintain a shared set of core financial capability benchmarks, publish plain-language fraud-prevention resources that local providers can reuse, and support small and emerging providers with adaptable tools and implementation guidance. This is especially important because scams are growing and federal anti-scam efforts remain fragmented across agencies.

Finally, evaluation should focus on measurable behavior change, not attendance alone. Useful outcomes include whether participants open and use safe accounts, establish emergency savings, improve bill payment, reduce reliance on high-cost borrowing, take a protective action against scams, or begin retirement saving. A strong revised National Strategy should help local providers move consumers from awareness to action.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Respectfully submitted,
Dr. Monitta Williams
Founder, Royal Legacy Financial Advisors
Covington, Georgia

Over the past five years, one development that should be incorporated into the national strategy is the growing effectiveness of experimental and project-based financial education, particularly for youth and young adults. Traditional lecture-based financial education often struggles to maintain engagement among middle and high school students. However, programs that incorporate simulations, games, and real-world decision-making activities have a demonstrated stronger engagement and retention of financial concepts. Through my work with Flip That House The Board Game University, we have implemented a project-based financial education model that teaches real life concepts such as homeownership, budgeting, credit, investment risk and wealth building through interactive game play and structured team activities. Students participate in simulated property investment scenarios, evaluate financial choices and learn the long term impact of financial decisions in a controlled learning environment.
This experimental model has been well received by middle and high school students because it transforms financial literacy from an abstract concept into a practical and engaging experience. Docket No. TREAS-DO-2026-0001

I am an Accredited Financial Counselor (AFC) and work directly with individuals and employees through one-on-one coaching, corporate workshops, and Employee Assistance Program financial education. My clients span income levels, education backgrounds, and life stages. Many are managing debt, limited savings, student loans, fraud exposure, and ongoing financial stress.

Every day, I see that financial instability is rarely about lack of intelligence or effort. More often, it stems from gaps in practical financial education, multigenerational money habits, digital misinformation, and the absence of clear decision-making frameworks. Many people were simply never taught how to manage money in a structured and practical way.

Background
I am responding to the Commission’s request for input on updating the U.S. National Strategy for Financial Literacy, particularly the Priority Areas, Best Practices, Federal Role, and Research sections.

Since 2020, the financial landscape has changed significantly. Consumers now face Buy Now Pay Later products, rapid fintech expansion, social media driven investing trends, increasingly sophisticated fraud schemes, and widespread financial misinformation. The updated Strategy should reflect these modern challenges.

Analysis
In practice, knowledge alone does not change behavior. Clients often understand basic concepts but struggle with implementation, especially under stress. Behavioral patterns, emotional money experiences, and digital influences shape financial outcomes as much as information does.

Fraud has also become a daily risk. I regularly speak with clients who have encountered imposter scams, cryptocurrency fraud, employment scams, romance scams, and identity theft. Financial literacy must include practical financial self-defense skills.

Finally, financial education is often delivered at a single life stage, such as high school or college. However, financial decisions occur throughout life. Without reinforcement at key transitions, knowledge fades and risk increases.

Recommendations
I respectfully suggest the updated National Strategy:

1. Retain existing core priorities while expanding Basic Financial Capability to include practical budgeting systems, updated credit literacy, digital financial safety, fintech evaluation, and financial misinformation awareness.

2. Add stand-alone priority areas for:
•Fraud Prevention and Digital Financial Safety
•Behavioral Finance and Financial Decision-Making
•Workplace Financial Wellbeing
•Lifespan-Based Financial Education, reinforced from childhood through retirement

3. Pair youth investment accounts with structured, age-appropriate education that emphasizes diversification, long-term investing, and clear distinctions between investing and speculation.

4. Strengthen transparency standards for financial educators, including disclosure of credentials, compensation structure, product affiliations, and fiduciary status.

5. Evaluate programs based on measurable outcomes such as emergency savings accumulation, reduction in high-interest debt, retirement plan participation, fraud victimization rates, and financial stress reduction.

6. Establish national benchmarks that promote household resilience, including increasing the percentage of households with emergency savings and reducing reliance on high-interest revolving credit.

7. Integrate behavioral design principles that make positive financial actions easier by default, including simplification, automation, and accountability structures.

Conclusion
Many Americans were never given a clear financial foundation. Practical, respectful, behavior-focused education builds confidence and long-term stability.
This update presents an opportunity to align financial literacy efforts with today’s realities and to create a national framework that supports financial resilience across the lifespan.

To the Financial Literacy and Education Commission:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide input on the update to the U.S. National Strategy for Financial Literacy.

The Center for Excellence, Equity, and Education (C4E3) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that delivers financial literacy programming to underserved communities through curriculum-based education, train-the-trainer models, and in-person workshops. We have served over 300 organizations and partnered with TRIO programs, workforce development boards, and community-based organizations to bring structured financial education to populations that need it most.

We respectfully submit the following recommendations for the Commission's consideration:

1. Prioritize facilitated, structured financial education over self-paced digital tools.

While digital resources like FDIC Money Smart and the CFPB's Your Money, Your Goals toolkit are valuable, they are most effective when delivered within a facilitated learning environment. Research consistently shows that financial behaviors change more durably through guided instruction, peer discussion, and coached application than through passive content consumption. The national strategy should incentivize organizations to invest in facilitated delivery models, including train-the-trainer programs that build internal capacity within the organizations serving vulnerable populations.

2. Recognize that financial uncertainty is personal, not just systemic.

The current strategy focuses heavily on systemic barriers to financial wellness: access to banking, predatory lending, income inequality. These are critical. But the strategy should also address the personal dimensions of financial uncertainty. Individuals navigating grief, family transitions, health challenges, housing instability, and reentry from incarceration carry those pressures into every financial decision they make. Effective financial literacy programming must account for the whole person, not just their balance sheet.

3. Strengthen the pipeline between WIOA workforce programs and financial literacy delivery.

Financial literacy is one of 14 required youth program elements under WIOA, yet implementation is inconsistent across the 590+ local workforce development boards. Some boards deliver robust programming through qualified vendors. Others satisfy the requirement through passive referrals to free online resources. The national strategy should establish minimum standards for what constitutes meaningful financial literacy delivery under WIOA, and should provide guidance on procurement pathways that enable boards to contract with qualified curriculum providers.

4. Expand financial literacy requirements in reentry programming.

The Second Chance Act authorizes financial education as an allowable activity, but does not mandate it. Given that returning citizens face immediate financial decisions upon release (housing, employment, banking, debt) with limited financial infrastructure, the national strategy should recommend that all federally funded reentry programs include a structured financial literacy component as a condition of funding.

5. Support train-the-trainer models to scale financial education sustainably.

Many community-based organizations, housing authorities, and workforce programs lack the staff expertise to deliver financial literacy in-house. Train-the-trainer models enable these organizations to build internal capacity, reduce dependency on external providers, and sustain programming beyond the grant cycle. The national strategy should highlight train-the-trainer as a best practice and should encourage funders to invest in capacity-building alongside direct service delivery.

We appreciate the Commission's commitment to updating the national strategy and welcome the opportunity to contribute to this important work. C4E3 stands ready to serve as a resource, thought partner, or pilot site for any initiatives that emerge from this process.

I appreciate the opportunity to provide input on the update to the U.S. National Strategy for Financial Literacy. My perspective is informed by both academic work in economics education and practical experience leading statewide financial education initiatives serving K–12 students and educators.

1. Priority Areas and Emerging Needs
The current priority areas remain important; however, the National Strategy should more explicitly emphasize early financial education and experiential learning. Financial habits begin forming in elementary school, and programs that provide hands-on experiences—such as in-school savings programs—are especially effective.

In Nebraska, in-school savings programs operate in 90 schools statewide, allowing students to actively practice saving behaviors. These programs move beyond knowledge acquisition to behavior formation and should be elevated within the National Strategy.

The Strategy should also strengthen its focus on fraud prevention and digital financial literacy, equipping consumers with practical tools to recognize and respond to increasingly sophisticated risks.

2. Best Practices for Financial Education Programs
The existing best practices remain strong. I recommend emphasizing:

Experiential learning through real or simulated financial decision-making
Early and continuous exposure across grade levels
Partnership-based delivery across schools, financial institutions, and community organizations
A focus on measurable behavior change

Programs such as the Stock Market Game demonstrate the effectiveness of experiential learning at scale, allowing students to engage directly with investing concepts in a classroom setting. In Nebraska, this program is paired with teacher professional development to ensure effective implementation.

Embedding financial education within existing curricula and using engaging, story-based content can further increase effectiveness and adoption.

3. Role of the Federal Government
The federal government plays a critical role in supporting financial education through coordination, research, and resource development. Continued investment in high-quality instructional materials and professional development is essential.

At the center of effective financial education is a well-prepared teacher. The highest return on investment in education is the teacher, and federal efforts should prioritize supporting educators through training, resources, and ongoing support.

Sustained financial support for state and local implementation is also critical. Local organizations are best positioned to deliver relevant and impactful programming, but scaling these efforts requires dedicated funding. Federal investment in state and local partners can expand reach, improve quality, and ensure long-term impact.

4. Research and Evaluation
More research is needed on long-term behavioral outcomes, particularly for early interventions. Evaluations should prioritize changes in saving behavior, financial decision-making, and confidence. Combining quantitative and qualitative measures provides a more complete picture of effectiveness.

5. Additional Considerations
Strengthening connections between federal strategy and state and local implementation will be essential. Providing both strategic guidance and financial support will help achieve meaningful and lasting improvements in financial literacy nationwide.

Thank you for the opportunity to contribute to this important work.
