The Utah Tobacco Free Alliance (UTFA) respectfully submits this comment in strong support of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) requests for Office of Management and Budget (OMB) approval to continue the collection of data for the National Quitline Data Warehouse (NQDW). These data collection efforts are critical to sustaining effective, evidence-based tobacco control programs and advancing cessation outcomes at the national, state, and community levels. This system provides essential infrastructure for understanding and improving tobacco cessation services.
Specifically, NQDW data enable state and local programs to:
•Monitor quitline reach, utilization, and long-term cessation outcomes.
•Identify disparities in access to cessation services among specific demographics.
•Improve program performance, optimize service delivery channels, and guide resource allocation.
•Benchmark across states and track trends over time.
In Utah, cessation services are a comprehensive, multi-channel operation. The state provides not only traditional telephonic counseling, but also digital coaching via text and online platforms. Furthermore, Utah directly funds evidence-based cessation aids, including Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT) and prescription medications such as bupropion.
Managing a multi-tiered service model requires sophisticated, comparative data. Access to high-quality, standardized data through the NQDW allows Utah partners to evaluate the specific return on investment for each of these interventions. Without it, the state would face significant barriers in determining which combinations of services—such as pairing text coaching with NRT versus telephone coaching with bupropion—are the most cost-effective, drive the highest successful quit rates, and best meet the evolving demands of Utah tobacco users who are ready to quit.
Discontinuing or reducing this national data collection would significantly impair the ability of states and partner organizations to evaluate local program effectiveness, ensure fiscal accountability for state-funded medications and services, and agilely respond to emerging nicotine use trends.
Tobacco use continues to be a leading preventable cause of disease and death. Maintaining robust, coordinated data systems efforts is essential to sustain reductions in tobacco use, address evolving product landscapes, including emerging nicotine products, and strengthen coordination across federal, state, and community partners.
The continued collection of these data supports a comprehensive public health approach grounded in evidence and accountability.
With respect,
Utah Tobacco Free Alliance (UTFA)

My name is Mercy, and I am a registered nurse currently training to become an Advanced Practice Registered Nurse (APRN). My clinical experience in acute care gives me a first-hand look at the real-time challenges frontline staff face regarding Emergency Department (ED) safety, community violence, and rapid decision-making. I am writing to express my strong support for the CDC’s proposed data collection renewal for the AVERT program.

This comment addresses Docket No. CDC-2026-0827 regarding the Paperwork Reduction Act renewal for the Advancing Violence Epidemiology in Real-Time (AVERT) project. AVERT collects near-real-time ED data on violence-related injuries and acute mental health conditions using the National Syndromic Surveillance Program (NSSP) BioSense Platform.

As a future APRN, I know how vital it is to translate public health data quickly into clinical safety and community support. Relying on lagging mortality databases delays critical intervention by months or years. AVERT fixes this by delivering near-real-time data, allowing local health systems to deploy hospital-based violence intervention programs (HVIPs) and crisis teams the moment surges happen. Real-time tracking is also essential for protecting healthcare staff. Research by Oztermeli et al. (2023) highlights just how pervasive ED violence is globally, showing that physicians and nurses are the primary targets, accounting for over 75% of severe reported violent incidents in the ED (55.2% directed at physicians and 21.3% at nurses). Furthermore, violent events overwhelmingly cluster in high-volume zones like examination rooms (58.2%), observation areas (24.1%), and triage units (11.3%), with verbal violence comprising 98.6% of cases as a primary indicator of escalating tension. By monitoring ED visits in real time, AVERT helps hospital leadership spot high-risk trends in specific units or shifts, allowing them to adjust staffing, security, and de-escalation protocols before a situation turns dangerous. Additionally, the CDC correctly calculated the minimal burden of this project; reducing it to just 18 total annual hours through automated NSSP scripts is a smart, efficient use of federal resources.

To make AVERT data even more useful on the ground, I recommend that the CDC develop bi-directional feedback dashboards to ensure health departments share automated, aggregate AVERT data directly back with local ED leadership and clinical staff to guide real-time staffing and safety decisions. Furthermore, the CDC should encourage health departments to cross-reference AVERT syndromic data with local social vulnerability metrics to address the root socioeconomic causes of community violence.

Renewing AVERT is a low-cost, high-impact decision that strengthens public health surveillance while keeping frontline workers and patients safe. To recap, the CDC should create direct feedback loops for local ED teams and integrate social vulnerability metrics into reporting. I strongly urge OMB and the CDC to approve this extension.

Sincerely,
Mercy Tefera, MN, RN
NNP Student
Emory University

The irony is the WTCHP did NOT inform members via email or USPS about this opportunity. I am a WTCHP member, yet I learned about this proposed feedback collection only because I found the notice on the WTCHP website. A program seeking approval for a new system to improve stakeholder feedback should have directly informed its members that they had an opportunity to comment on how that system will be designed.

I support collecting timely feedback from members and providers, but the proposal leaves serious questions unanswered. The Federal Register notice estimates surveys of 12,000 members annually, yet it does not explain how members will be selected or how WTCHP will ensure the experiences of members struggling to obtain healthcare are adequately represented.

The proposal specifically contemplates surveys following interactions such as enrollment and certification. WTCHP must also intentionally seek feedback from members experiencing treatment delays, difficulty locating providers, authorization problems, administrative failures, communication problems, billing issues and other barriers to receiving care. A feedback system that primarily reaches members after routine or successful interactions risks producing a misleading picture of member experience.

NPN members must be separately represented and analyzed. The healthcare experience of an NPN member can be very different from that of a member receiving care through a CCE. Combining these populations could conceal problems unique to the NPN. WTCHP should establish a meaningful NPN sample and separately report NPN results.

The notice states that information collected will support "contractor oversight," but it does not explain how. Members should be able to identify whether their experience involved a WTCHP contractor, and contractor-related feedback should be separately tracked and analyzed. If recurring problems involving a contractor are identified, there should be a defined process for investigation, corrective action and follow-up.

Transparency is also missing from this proposal. The notice does not commit WTCHP to publicly releasing survey results, focus group findings, methodology, NPN-specific findings, contractor-related findings or actions taken in response. Asking members and providers for feedback without showing them what was learned or what changed risks turning this into another information-gathering exercise rather than an accountability tool.

The proposed focus groups also raise questions about representation. Only 80 member focus group participants are estimated annually. WTCHP should explain how participants will be selected to ensure representation across responder and survivor populations, geographic areas, CCEs and the NPN, including members who have experienced significant difficulty accessing care.

Most importantly, WTCHP should establish a clear feedback-to-action process. The proposal says information will support Program management, contractor oversight, stakeholder engagement and operational decision-making, but it does not explain what happens when feedback reveals a systemic problem. Members deserve to know who reviews those findings, what triggers investigation or corrective action, who is responsible for addressing identified problems and whether WTCHP will report back to members.

I am also concerned by the statement that results "will not be used for regulatory purposes or as the principal basis for significant policy decisions." If thousands of members and providers identify serious or recurring failures, their experiences should carry meaningful weight. WTCHP should explain how significant findings will influence decisions and improvements.

Before this collection is approved, WTCHP should strengthen it by requiring representative sampling, separate NPN analysis, intentional outreach to members experiencing barriers to care, meaningful contractor accountability, public reporting of results and a documented process showing how member and provider feedback produces corrective action.

WTCHP members have spent years providing feedback about their healthcare experiences. If WTCHP is going to create another mechanism for collecting that information, members deserve more than another survey. We deserve a transparent system that demonstrates our feedback is heard, identifies systemic failures and results in measurable action.

Before WTCHP creates another feedback collection that will require additional federal resources and impose additional administrative costs, it should explain why existing GAO findings and recommendations have not been fully implemented.

GAO identified significant deficiencies in WTCHP quality assurance in 2017. Five years later, GAO again identified serious deficiencies in its 2022 report, "World Trade Center Health Program: Quality Assurance Program Should Include Monitoring of Access to Health Services."

The 2022 findings are particularly troubling for NPN members. GAO found that the WTCHP Quality Assurance Committee had not assessed whether members had timely access to healthcare through the NPN because quality assurance metrics for timely access did not exist. GAO also reported that information previously collected by the NPN contractor indicated potential problems with timely access.

GAO warned that without prioritizing timely access, establishing metrics and reviewing the resulting data, "there is increased risk that reported delays in some members' access to NPN-provided health services may continue and negatively affect those members' morbidity, mortality, and quality of life."

GAO made three recommendations: make timely access to healthcare a WTCHP strategic priority, establish quality assurance metrics for timely access through the NPN and CCEs, and require the Quality Assurance Committee to review those metrics at least annually and address needed improvements.

These recommendations were issued in July 2022. According to GAO's recommendation tracker, years later all three remain open. Two are listed as "Open," and the first is listed as "Open, Partially Addressed."

That raises a fundamental question about this proposed information collection: Why should WTCHP spend additional resources collecting more information from members and providers when the government has already identified serious deficiencies, recommended specific corrective actions, and those recommendations have still not been fully implemented?

The problem does not appear to be a lack of information. GAO already documented the problem. Members have reported delays. The NPN contractor had information indicating potential problems with timely access. GAO identified what WTCHP needed to do. Yet years later, GAO is still waiting for full implementation.

I am not opposed to meaningful member feedback. I am opposed to creating another administrative process that collects information without first demonstrating that WTCHP acts on information it already possesses.

Before OMB approves this new collection, WTCHP should be required to explain the status of the outstanding 2017 and 2022 GAO recommendations, why implementation has taken years, what remains unfinished, when each recommendation will be fully implemented, and what resources this new feedback collection will consume.

WTCHP should also explain why those resources would be better spent collecting additional feedback rather than completing quality assurance systems already recommended by GAO.

Responders and survivors do not need another mechanism that simply documents problems. We need WTCHP to correct problems that have already been documented.

Before collecting more data, implement what GAO has already told you needs to be fixed.

Public Comment on CDC Docket No. CDC-2026-0463: CDC’s Milestone Tracker App User Surveys

To the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on CDC Docket No. CDC-2026-0463. I support CDC’s continued evaluation of the Milestone Tracker mobile application as part of the Learn the Signs. Act Early. program.

I am a medical doctor with experience in autism diagnostic pathways and developmental disability support. I do not view the Milestone Tracker app as a diagnostic tool. The surveys should reinforce its role as a developmental monitoring and communication tool, not as a substitute for formal screening, clinical evaluation, or diagnosis.

The proposed collection already includes important domains: user satisfaction, usage patterns and actions taken after a missed developmental milestone or developmental concern. However, the surveys would be more useful if they captured the full follow-up pathway more clearly: concern recognition, caregiver understanding, communication with professionals, referral, barriers, evaluation and access to support.

First, CDC should measure caregiver actions after a missed milestone or developmental concern in a more structured way. It is useful to know whether caregivers discussed concerns with a doctor, early childhood educator, early intervention program, or other professional. It would be even more useful to distinguish between stages of follow-up: contacted a provider, scheduled an appointment, attended the appointment, received developmental screening, received a referral, completed an evaluation, was placed on a waiting list, or began receiving services. This would show where families may be lost in the pathway.

Second, the surveys should include structured questions about barriers to follow-up and referral. A caregiver may recognize a concern and still be unable to act because of long waiting times, cost or insurance barriers, transportation problems, lack of nearby specialists, limited early intervention availability, language barriers, low health literacy, work or childcare constraints, uncertainty about where to go, stigma, or prior reassurance that delayed follow-up. A concise checklist of common barriers would produce more actionable data than free-text alone.

Third, CDC should assess whether users understand the app’s intended role. The surveys should include a brief comprehension item confirming that users understand the app does not diagnose autism, developmental delay, or any other condition, and that concerns should be discussed with qualified professionals. This would help reduce both false reassurance and unnecessary anxiety.

Fourth, the surveys should ask specifically whether caregivers share app-generated information with professionals. A broad question about sharing concerns is useful, but it does not show whether caregivers use the app’s milestone summary during real-world encounters. CDC could ask whether users showed, emailed, printed, or otherwise shared the app’s milestone summary with a physician, nurse, early intervention provider, childcare provider, teacher, therapist, or other professional. If not, the survey could ask why: lack of awareness, no appointment, uncertainty about whom to contact, difficulty using the summary, privacy concerns, or concern that the professional would not review it.

Fifth, the surveys should evaluate whether the app helps families connect to referral, early intervention, and support. It would be valuable to know whether the app helped caregivers understand whom to contact, what information to bring to an appointment, what “early intervention” means, and what steps may follow a developmental concern. The key outcome should not only be satisfaction, but whether the app improves the caregiver’s ability to navigate the next step.

Sixth, CDC should strengthen equity-related measurement. The surveys should capture, in a voluntary and privacy-preserving way, whether users experienced difficulty related to language, reading level, digital access, rural or underserved location, lack of specialists, culturally appropriate support, or knowledge of local referral systems.

I recognize the need to minimize respondent burden. These additions could be implemented through skip logic, brief multiple-choice items, and optional free-text responses in the parent survey after a missed milestone or developmental concern.

In summary, I support CDC’s continued collection of voluntary, anonymous survey data through the Milestone Tracker app. I recommend refining the surveys so they measure not only satisfaction and app use, but also referral pathway completion, barriers to care, understanding of the app’s non-diagnostic role, sharing of app-generated summaries with professionals, connection to early intervention and support, and equity-related access issues.

Thank you for the opportunity. I believe there are many important areas that firefighter safety and health can be addressed or evaluated. Among them, here are my "top three":

Additionally, statistics show that for every firefighter injured, 3 or more members of our community who are not responders are injured. NIOSH can most effectively improve firefighter safety and long-term health by prioritizing strategies that materially reduce toxic exposure, cumulative carcinogen load, and time spent in immediately dangerous to life or health environments. Establishing clear performance standards, validation protocols, and exposure-reduction benchmarks for these technologies, in coordination with IAFC, NFPA, USFA, and the relevant technology and standards working groups, would accelerate responsible adoption across the fire service. Boulder Crest Foundation Public Comment — NIOSH Center for Firefighter Safety, Health and Well-Being Portfolio RFI (CDC-2026-0133, NIOSH-356)

Boulder Crest Foundation is a nationally recognized nonprofit organization serving veterans, military personnel, first responders, and their families, with the mission of building a world where all people can thrive in the aftermath of trauma. Through prevention-focused, Posttraumatic Growth (PTG)-based training and partnerships with first responder agencies, Boulder Crest equips firefighters and other responders with the skills they need to navigate stressful and traumatic work in a healthy and constructive fashion. This supports health, readiness, and long-term well-being. Boulder Crest Foundation (BCF) welcomes the opportunity to partner with NIOSH to inform, pilot, and evaluate scalable approaches that strengthen firefighter well-being as a core component of safety.

NIOSH can best leverage its priority topics by explicitly shifting the field’s center of gravity from reactive intervention to proactive prevention, and from a narrow focus on “resilience” to a broader, evidence-informed approach that incorporates how the work affects the whole person and the culture in which firefighters operate. Many existing mental health supports activate only after a crisis or severe impairment, when recovery is harder and outcomes are poorer; stigma and cultural barriers further suppress utilization. In BCF’s experience, treatment and clinical care remain essential for those who need it, but they are not sufficient as a stand-alone strategy for a workforce routinely exposed to trauma and chronic stress. NIOSH can address this challenge by embedding well-being prevention into the same safety infrastructure as PPE, exposure reduction, and fatality prevention, supporting department-ready training models that normalize struggle, reduce stigma, and increase early engagement before problems become crises. This aligns with NIOSH’s intent to identify emerging hazards and prevent harm earlier and faster.

NIOSH priorities, research areas, and service activities could be expanded by strengthening implementation pathways and building the evidence base for prevention-oriented training that improves readiness and safety-related outcomes. Specifically, NIOSH should expand (1) implementation science that tests what drives adoption and sustainment of exposure reduction, PPE practices, sleep and fatigue countermeasures, and other safety behaviors in real station conditions (including volunteer/combination departments); (2) research and guidance that treats psychological health as an upstream risk and protective-factor domain (e.g., peer connection, leadership engagement, recovery practices) rather than only a downstream clinical outcome; and (3) evaluations of training-focused models, distinct from treatment, that aim to improve intermediate outcomes linked to safety (sleep, decision-making under stress, willingness to seek help, peer support, retention, near-miss reporting). PTG provides a science-based framework for this broader approach and complements clinical care by helping individuals harness inner strength, connect with others, and identify new possibilities and meaning after adversity.

NIOSH can best partner with fire service organizations and related stakeholders by co-designing interventions with the field, piloting them through a national learning network of diverse departments, and scaling what works through national associations and state training systems. This partnership model should prioritize (a) practical dissemination products that chiefs and training officers can implement immediately (“what to do, how to train it, how to measure it”) and (b) rigorous evaluation that identifies which components work best in which contexts. BCF can support NIOSH as a partner in this effort by contributing prevention-focused expertise and helping co-develop, pilot, and evaluate PTG-informed training components designed to reduce stigma, expand the range of effective supports beyond resilience-only approaches, and strengthen culture as a determinant of safety and health. Boulder Crest’s Struggle Well Training emphasizes expanding the narrative beyond dysfunction and toward growth, normalizing struggle to reduce stigma, integrating wellness into training, and institutionalizing wellness across a responder’s career. These are principles that can strengthen NIOSH’s efforts to improve firefighter safety, health, and well-being.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide input. Boulder Crest Foundation stands ready to partner with NIOSH to advance firefighter safety, health, and well-being by strengthening prevention approaches, accelerating translation into practice, and expanding the evidence base for responder-specific strategies that protect both firefighters and the communities they serve.

National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
Docket No. CDC-2026-0133 / NIOSH-356

The American Board of First Responder Behavioral Healthcare (FRBH) appreciates the opportunity to provide input regarding priorities for the Center for Firefighter Safety, Health, and Well-Being.

FRBH is a national nonprofit standards-setting and accreditation body focused on workforce behavioral health protection in trauma-exposed public safety environments. Our work is grounded in a core occupational safety principle: where hazard exposure is predictable and inherent to the work, protection should be embedded within organizational systems and activated based on exposure conditions—not dependent on individual self-disclosure or voluntary help-seeking.

In trauma-exposed public safety work, occupational psychological hazard exposure is predictable, cumulative, and inherent to the mission—not incidental to it.

Firefighters operate in environments defined not only by physical and chemical hazards, but also by repeated exposure to trauma, severe injury, death, and human suffering. These exposures are inherent to the occupation and should be recognized as part of the firefighter hazard environment. As such, behavioral health protection should be addressed within the same occupational safety framework used to manage other job-related hazards.

Current approaches to firefighter well-being remain largely service-oriented and reactive, often centered on access to support following critical incidents. While these resources remain important, they are not sufficient as a primary occupational safety strategy. Models that rely primarily on individual help-seeking or post-incident recognition are not aligned with established approaches to occupational risk management.

FRBH recommends that NIOSH expand its research and service priorities to include exposure-informed, system-activated, and governance-embedded models of workforce behavioral health protection.

Specifically, NIOSH should consider advancing the following areas:

•Exposure Recognition and Threshold Definition: Establish research and guidance supporting how fire service organizations define qualifying exposure events and operational thresholds that initiate protective actions.
•Automatic Organizational Activation: Examine models in which defined exposures trigger timely, standardized organizational safeguards without requiring individual self-identification.
•Cumulative Exposure Oversight: Advance research on repeated and accumulated occupational psychological hazard exposure across a firefighter’s career and corresponding organizational response mechanisms.
•Embedded and Confidential Access Pathways: Promote structured, protected access to support resources that are integrated into organizational systems and accessible without stigma or procedural barriers.
•Leadership and Supervisory Accountability: Define the role of leadership in ensuring exposure-based protections are consistently activated, documented, and sustained.
•Continuity of Protection: Support approaches that ensure behavioral health protection extends across assignments, operational roles, and transition out of service.

These elements can be structured, evaluated, and verified as part of an organizational protection framework.

NIOSH’s focus on emerging hazards and the interaction between acute events and chronic risk presents a critical opportunity to strengthen how firefighter behavioral health is operationalized. Incorporating an exposure-based organizational protection framework would align behavioral health with established occupational safety principles and improve the consistency and reliability of protective measures.

Firefighter behavioral health protection should be governed as an occupational safety function—embedded in systems, activated by exposure, and sustained through organizational accountability. In trauma-exposed work environments, exposure—not disclosure—should determine when protection begins.

FRBH appreciates the opportunity to provide input and would welcome continued engagement as NIOSH advances its priorities in this area.

I urge you to rescind the proposed Commercial Leasing for Outer Continental Shelf Minerals Offshore the Commonwealth of Virginia (BOEM-2026-0100-0001), because of the extensive multifaceted harms deep sea mining causes as well as that it is unnecessary, unproven and financially risky.
We already have sufficient supplies of the metals needed for the renewable energy transition because of newer, safer battery chemistry. Demand for land-based mining can be reduced through intensive recycling and reuse (more than 3 million tons of e-waste go unrecycled in America every year), and making it easier to repair our technology so we can use it longer instead of throwing it away. Together these are expected to meet demand for critical minerals like nickel, cobalt, manganese, lithium and copper.
We don’t need deep sea mining to get the critical minerals like cobalt, nickel, lithium and copper that we need. More than 3 million tons of e-waste go unrecycled in America every year. By recycling and reusing the minerals we have, and making it easier to repair our technology so we can use it longer instead of throwing it away, we can meet our mineral needs
It is also harder to extract metals from the seabed than on land – five hundred to 2,000 times more area of the seafloor would need to be mined to yield the same amount as the thick, denser veins of terrestrial mines.
Deep-sea mining would not reduce or provide an “ethical” substitute for land-based mining. There is no evidence that deep-sea mining will have any impact on the volume, location, or social impacts of terrestrial mining.
Deep sea mining technology is expensive and unproven. A project by Nautilus Minerals off Papua New Guinea ended with the mining company declaring bankruptcy and liquidating its assets, allegedly leaving Papua New Guinea with losses of over a hundred million dollars.
A new techno-economic assessment of deep sea mining shows that the approaches of two leading companies seeking to mine U.S. waters are plagued by fatally flawed financial models, wildly underestimated costs, and critically immature technology.
Deep sea mining will not provide the benefits promised, just destruction. Commercial leases allowing deep sea mining must be withdrawn and rules that ban it be enacted instead.
Thank you

In support of BOEM’s planning process to determine whether to offer a lease for commercial OCS mineral development offshore the Commonwealth of Virginia, McQuilling Renewables suggests a maritime traffic assessment on commercial and recreational marine uses in and around the Virginia Request for Information Area.

Drawing on the skills, experience and global shipping supply chain network of McQuilling Partners, McQuilling Renewables, based in Garden City, NY, brings individually crafted marine supply chain solutions to US offshore industries.

McQuilling Renewables conducted a similar assessment of marine activity in an Area of Analysis (AoA) beyond the 60-meter depth contour for the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) with the purpose of supporting BOEM’s decisions on future lease sites for the offshore energy industry. The study paints a picture of marine traffic in deep water off New York State and characterizes marine uses by their persistence, density, navigational flexibility, maneuverability, economic effect, regulatory oversight, and purpose. The report was published in early 2025 and is available at https://www.nyserda.ny.gov/About/Publications/Offshore-Wind-Plans-for-New-York-State under 25-14 Offshore Wind Planning in the New York Bight: Maritime Assessment–Commercial and Recreational Uses Study [PDF].

A similar assessment for the OCS acreage in and around the RFI Area would illustrate the types and density of existing marine traffic so that offshore mining developers can assess logistical challenges in the area, including utilization days and busy seasons, and plan accordingly to prevent conflict. In turn, traffic developed from mineral exploration and development would inform coastal users and fisheries of the potential impacts of work in this area. Additionally, potential hazards on the seabed (unexploded ordinances) or underwater military uses (submarine channels) in and around the RFI Area should be assessed.

In the report for NYSERDA, McQuilling Renewables analyzed ocean uses through various visual data portals, including the Mid-Atlantic Regional Council on the Ocean (MARCO) Data Portal, Marine Cadastre, New York Geographic Information Gateway (NYGIS) and the Northeast Ocean Data Portal.

Investigative methods used in this report included gathering, analyzing and reporting on data from: regional online portals; historical vessel traffic positions and projections; boating statistics; offshore weather/sea state buoys; economic assessments and projections; previous NYSERDA studies; domestic and international regulatory guidance; marine safety considerations; U.S. Gulf oil and gas experience; publicly available online research; scholarly sources; and project based information from an offshore energy site being constructed in US waters. Projections of offshore marine traffic growth were incorporated based on an analysis of existing and projected projects. Non-offshore energy related marine traffic growth was also estimated using economic models and trade statistics in the region. The types of vessel traffic analyzed included all types of commercial, government, and private/recreational vessels.


This Maritime Assessment introduced a number of novel concepts across a range of topics, namely:
•Established seven criteria to classify marine uses as commercial or recreational

•Introduced the concept of marine transit traffic as compared to marine destinational traffic as a way to further classify uses, including establishing methodology to assess impact of activities

•Produced commercial marine traffic growth forecasts from 2024-2040 based on 2017-2022 AIS data trend line analysis from a grid of aliquots

•Produced commercial marine traffic growth forecasts from 2024-2040 based on GDP versus cargo movements using econometric modeling

•Used weather, sea state ocean metadata as conditioners for inferring presence and persistence of recreational vessels in/around area of analysis (AoA) where vessel position AIS data was lacking

•Employed discretionary use from recreational USCG boating statistics, along with National Weather Service advisories and met-ocean data as conditioners for presence and persistence of recreational vessels in/around AoA where vessel position AIS data was lacking

Based on this previous work, McQuilling is uniquely positioned to assess multiple use conflicts related to offshore mining in the Virginia Request for Information Area, enabling BOEM and mining companies to consider ways to eliminate, mitigate, and monitor for impacts related to this offshore industry development.

CDC says the redesigned survey can still add new topics. I urge CDC to include ME(CFS) and Long Covid questions – especially on post-exertional malaise; keep questions on fatigue; and keep the disability questions which are currently proposed for removal.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Jessica Johnson

I am writing as a caregiver for my wife, who suffers from severe Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS). I am deeply concerned that the proposed 2028 redesign of the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) leaves out ME/CFS and Long Covid.

The NHIS provides essential national data on these illnesses. It showed that approximately 1.3% of U.S. adults were living with ME/CFS in 2021–2022 and tracked Long Covid from 2022 through 2025. The proposed 2028 survey asks about other chronic conditions but excludes ME/CFS and Long Covid. It also eliminates questions about fatigue. The remaining disability questions fail to capture one of the most debilitating aspects of these illnesses: post-exertional malaise, where even minimal physical, mental, or emotional activity can cause a severe worsening of symptoms.

As a full-time caregiver for my wife, I see the devastating impact of severe ME/CFS every day. My wife requires care and support 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Her illness has dramatically changed our lives, limiting her independence, mobility, and ability to participate in everyday activities. I have taken on the responsibility of providing her constant care and support. ME/CFS affects not only those suffering from the illness but also their spouses, families, and caregivers. The physical, emotional, and financial consequences are profound.

Being counted matters. Without accurate national data, it becomes harder to understand how many people are affected, measure changes over time, recognize the severity of these illnesses, and justify urgently needed investments in research, treatment, and medical care.

The CDC has indicated that the redesigned survey still has room for additional topics. I strongly urge the CDC to retain or reinstate questions specifically addressing ME/CFS and Long Covid, include questions about post-exertional malaise, preserve questions about fatigue, and retain the disability questions currently proposed for removal.

People living with severe ME/CFS are often among the least visible members of our society because they are too ill to leave their homes, work, or advocate for themselves. Removing these illnesses from national health surveillance would make an already overlooked population even more invisible.

My wife and millions of others living with these debilitating conditions deserve to be recognized, counted, and represented in our national health data.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,

Jan-Eric Meinecke
Husband and full-time caregiver for a person living with severe ME/CFS

I am firmly against the deep-sea mining proposal on Virginia's outer continental shelf, responding to RFI (BOEM-2026-0100). This speculative exploitation is risky, unnecessary, and benefits a few at the cost of ocean health crucial for everyone.

Seabed mining threatens irreversible damage to marine ecosystems and those who depend on them. The RFI Area's marine life supports vital species for coastal communities along the Atlantic, provides a significant portion of the U.S. seafood supply, offers thousands of jobs, and contributes over $1 billion to Virginia's economy. These species, including marine mammals migrating through the mid-Atlantic, rely on a healthy environment, which seabed mining jeopardizes, especially given the ambitious scope outlined in the RFI.

Dredging for heavy mineral sands and phosphorites involves large-scale equipment disrupting vast seafloor areas, risking pollutant release into coastal waters across 2,764 square miles—an ocean expanse larger than Delaware.

Please deny this lease request and protect Virginia's coast from harmful seabed mining.

Re: Docket CDC-2026-1387 — Proposed 2028 NHIS Adult Questionnaire

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the redesigned National Health Interview Survey. I hold an MPH in Epidemiology and am a doctoral student in Pharmaceutical Outcomes and Policy at the University of Florida, with a focus on pharmacoepidemiology. My research interests include medication affordability, behavioral health, and access to and continuity of medication treatment for opioid use disorder.

I submit these comments in my individual capacity. These views do not represent the University of Florida or any other organization with which I am affiliated.

I support efforts to shorten the questionnaire while preserving measures needed to identify financial and practical barriers to medication access. My recommendations concern Sections B, F, and H of the August 2026 adult questionnaire draft.

1. Preserve the distinct medication affordability measures in F5–F7.

F5–F7 capture different responses to medication costs: taking less medication or skipping doses, delaying prescription fills, and not obtaining needed medication. Retaining these distinctions would help researchers understand how affordability barriers affect medication use.

I particularly support the F4 instruction directing respondents who did not take prescription medication to F7. This pathway can capture people whose inability to afford medication may have prevented any use. Please preserve it in both paper and electronic versions.

2. Add a brief follow-up identifying the treatment category affected.

B27–B29 identify current medication use for anxiety, depression, and other mental health conditions. However, these questions cannot establish whether an affordability barrier reported in F5–F7 affected those medications or medication for another condition. Their reference periods also differ: current use in Section B versus the past 12 months in Section F.

For respondents answering yes to any of F5–F7, please consider testing one follow-up:

“Thinking about the prescription medicines you took less of, skipped, delayed filling, or could not get because of cost during the past 12 months, what were those medicines intended to treat? Select all that apply.”

Suggested response categories:
• A mental health condition, such as depression or anxiety
• Opioid use disorder or another substance use disorder
• Another health condition
• Not sure
• Prefer not to answer

This item would help identify affordability barriers affecting behavioral health treatment. Cognitive testing should assess whether respondents understand the treatment categories and can report medicines used for multiple conditions. Respondents should receive this follow-up based on F5–F7, regardless of whether they currently take a mental health medication.

3. Consider a brief module on medication treatment continuity for opioid use disorder.

Section H measures alcohol, nicotine, and marijuana use, but the draft does not directly identify receipt of medication treatment for opioid use disorder or interruptions in that treatment. General prescription affordability questions also do not capture nonfinancial barriers to continuity.

If feasible within the questionnaire’s burden limits, please consider testing a brief module establishing past-year medication treatment specifically for opioid use disorder. Respondents reporting treatment could then be asked whether, during that period, they experienced a time when they wanted to continue treatment but could not obtain it. A conditional follow-up could distinguish cost or insurance problems, pharmacy or treatment-clinic availability, difficulty obtaining an appointment, and other barriers.

Specifying the treatment indication would be important because some medications used for opioid use disorder also have other uses. Wording should distinguish unwanted interruptions from treatment changes agreed upon with a clinician. If annual inclusion is not feasible, a periodic or sponsored module could be considered.

4. Evaluate measurement across collection modes and preserve interpretability over time.

Please test the proposed affordability follow-up and any treatment-continuity items across web, paper, and interviewer-administered formats. Clear skip instructions, understandable treatment categories, and privacy-sensitive wording will be particularly important for behavioral health questions. Documentation of wording, routing, and mode changes would help researchers assess comparability with earlier NHIS estimates.

These recommendations aim to preserve a concise questionnaire while improving its usefulness for studying medication access, affordability, and continuity, and identifying barriers associated with unwanted interruptions in treatment.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Oluwapelumi Odubunmi, MPH

The 2028 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) Questionnaire Redesign concerns me as a parent of a child with down syndrome. While the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) aims to reduce costs and respondent burden, the proposed changes threaten to create a massive data gap for individuals with lifelong, complex developmental disabilities.

The proposed modifications could directly skew longitudinal health data trends and obscure the reality of individuals like my daughter who relies on structured, integrated support:

1. The Erasure of "Age of Onset" Data

Historically, the NHIS included a foundational screening question asking whether a person's functional difficulties began before the age of 22.

The Impact on Trends: This specific metric is what allowed federal data trackers to distinguish a developmental disability (a condition an individual is born with or acquires in youth) from an acquired adult disability (such as an injury or age-related decline). Removing this item makes it nearly impossible to track longitudinal health, economic, and living trends specific to the lifelong developmental disability community

2. Drastic Cuts to Disability-Specific Questions

According to reviews by the Human Services Research Institute (HSRI), the draft proposal slashes the number of adult disability and functioning questions from 49 down to just 15.

The Impact on Trends: The draft removes targeted questions regarding fatigue, cognition, hearing aids, and mobility equipment like wheelchairs and scooters. Striking these queries will result in severe undercounting. Past papers co-authored by CDC statisticians already acknowledged that surveys missing these nuances could undercount the intellectual and developmental disability population by up to 75%

3. A Shift in How "Independence" and Care are Measured

The survey is shifting its focus heavily toward the Washington Group Short Set, which looks strictly at basic functional actions (seeing, hearing, walking, basic communicating).

The Impact on Trends: For individuals thriving through supported decision-making and customized community integration, a rigid, condensed survey fails to capture complex care structures. It leaves no room to document how a person with a rare genetic syndrome utilizes adaptive supports or community services to maintain independent living. Without data proving that these supports allow individuals to thrive in the least restrictive environment, justifying federal funding for integrated community programs becomes much harder for state agencies.

Please reconsider these changes.

Re: Docket No. CDC-2026-1387 — Proposed 2028 National Health Interview Survey Redesign

I am a professor of otolaryngology and public health. I support NCHS’s effort to sustain the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) as collection costs rise and household participation becomes more difficult. Shorter questionnaires and additional ways to respond may help. The redesign should also preserve the measures needed to identify hearing and communication needs, assess access to care, and interpret trends across the change in survey methods.

I ask NCHS to address four issues before finalizing the 2028 questionnaires.

1. Retain a minimal measure of hearing aid use. The proposed adult questionnaire retains difficulty hearing even when using a hearing aid (C2), but omits existing questions on whether respondents use hearing aids and how often they wear them. Hearing difficulty alone cannot show whether people receive and use this form of assistance. Please retain those two measures, or identify a shorter tested set that can measure hearing aid use alongside hearing difficulty.

2. Preserve language used in health care. The proposed questionnaire omits the existing measure of language used at the doctor’s office. A general communication difficulty item does not capture the language in which a person receives care. Please retain a brief measure of language used during health care encounters. It would support analysis of access and help researchers interpret differences in reported care across groups.

3. Address the early childhood measurement gap. In the proposed child questionnaire, children younger than 5 skip the section containing hearing difficulty (E3) and speech-understanding (E6). Please explain how NHIS will monitor hearing and communication needs in this age group and consider a brief, age-appropriate parent-reported measure. For older children, E6 combines difficulty being understood inside and outside the household. Please test whether this combined item retains the information provided by the separate existing questions.

4. Preserve the ability to identify head and neck cancers. The proposed adult cancer-type item (B12) names six cancer groups and places other types together. Earlier NHIS questionnaires identified several head and neck cancer types more specifically. Please retain a way to collect the specific cancer type, such as a follow-up for respondents selecting “other,” even when small counts limit what can appear in public-use files.

Finally, please publish results from testing that distinguish the effects of changed questions from the effects of web, paper, and interviewer administration. Report whether response, missingness, and key estimates differ by mode and by relevant population groups. Researchers will need this evidence to judge whether a change in an NHIS estimate after 2028 reflects a change in population health or a change in measurement.

NHIS has long been the gold standard population health survey, and is instrumental for understanding prevalence of health conditions, health care access and utilization and financial burden of health care NCHS has proposes a mixed-mode redesign from an field interviewer-administered survey to a paper and internet self-administered survey. NHIS asserts that this proposed redesign responds to “rising costs, growing difficulty in reaching households and the need for a more flexible and efficient survey.”
It is certainly true that survey costs are rising. However, there is not enough information to indicate that the proposed redesign would result in reducing costs. It would be helpful to see a full estimate of current and projected survey costs. Yet, reduced survey costs alone should not be a determine redesign if data quality is sacrificed, as it is likely to be with a self-administered survey on complex topics.
It is certainly true that survey researchers face growing difficulty reaching households and surveys, including federal surveys, have had declining response rates over time. Response rates to internet surveys are notoriously low, and significantly lower that response rates for surveys conducted in person. Further, given differences in digital literacy and high-speed internet and cellular access across the U.S., there is an increased likelihood of differential non-response, as some groups (younger, more highly educated, nonrural, persons without disabilities) may be more likely to respond and face fewer barriers to self-response than other groups (older, less educated, rural, persons with disabilities). Differential non-response would potentially introduce bias into estimates of population health and compromise data quality.
NCHS asserts that the transition to a self-administered dual mode NHIS will result in a more flexible and efficient survey. However, there is evidence that respondents use bots and AI to complete internet surveys, and current reCAPTCHA and other methods are not sufficient to ensure valid response. Clearly, AI response compromises data quality for a survey from which population health estimates are made. Additional resources would be needed to ensure validity of survey responses, reducing any “efficiencies” assumed to be generated by the redesign.
Nowhere in the FRN or the redesign does NCHS seem to consider and address the likely loss of data quality from the proposed redesign. The consequences of biased estimates provides a skewed picture of the health and health care access and utilization of the U.S. population and could misinform policy designed to improve population health and health care access as a result. Survey redesign should not come at the expense of data quality, especially when that survey is used to derive population estimates and inform policy.
Where is the testing and evidence in support of the changes the survey is making to mode of administration, or to question wording and omissions? Federal survey redesign in a several years process in which proposed changes to surveys undergo rigorous testing PRIOR to the announcement of changes in the Federal Register. Proposing a redesign without testing is irresponsible and wastes taxpaper money.

I urge the CDC to retain ME/CFS, Long COVID, and fatigue questions in the 2028 National Health Interview Survey. Removing them would interrupt national surveillance of disabling chronic illnesses, undermine long-term comparisons, and make it harder to measure their prevalence, severity, and impact on daily life.

I have post-vaccine Long COVID and ME/CFS. My illness began after COVID vaccination in 2022, before my first confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. I am largely housebound and unable to work. I experience severe cognitive dysfunction and post-exertional malaise (PEM), including delayed and prolonged symptom worsening after ordinary physical or cognitive activity. My exertional impairment has been documented through two-day cardiopulmonary exercise testing.

The proposed questionnaire cannot adequately capture disabilities like mine. A person may be physically capable of completing an activity but suffer significant deterioration afterward, or avoid the activity entirely to prevent that deterioration. Questions about walking, concentration, and self-care cannot capture this distinction. Similarly, counting missed workdays does not adequately measure disability among people who can no longer work.

I ask the CDC to:
1. Retain the existing ME/CFS questions measuring lifetime diagnosis and current illness, including questions for children. Include symptom-based measures to help identify people who remain undiagnosed.
2. Restore Long COVID questions measuring prevalence, ongoing symptoms, and limitations on daily activities, preserving comparability with previous survey years.
3. Retain fatigue measurements and add a specific measure of PEM, including delayed symptom worsening following physical or cognitive exertion and prolonged recovery.
4. Preserve and strengthen disability measurements to capture fluctuating function, activity avoidance, housebound status, cognitive impairment, and inability to work.
5. Record illness-onset chronology, including symptoms beginning after COVID vaccination or SARS-CoV-2 infection, so these experiences can be distinguished and studied rather than excluded by questions that assume infection preceded illness.

These measures are necessary to understand the population affected, the extent of disability, and the healthcare and support services people need. They also provide essential evidence for research priorities, resource allocation, and public policy.

A shorter survey should not come at the expense of accurately counting people with serious, disabling illnesses. I urge the CDC to preserve these measurements in the core survey so national surveillance remains continuous and meaningful.

CRDJ submits these comments in response to Docket No. CDC-2026-1387 concerning the National Center for Health Statistics’ proposed redesign of the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) beginning in 2028. NHIS is one of the federal government’s most important sources of population-level information about health, disability, health care access, and health outcomes. NCHS proposes to both shorten and revise the questionnaires and to shift from an interviewer-administered model to a sequential mixed-mode design beginning with online or paper self-response. NCHS has specifically invited comment on proposed additions and removals, data quality and usability, trend measurement, and the effects of the new collection method.

We are particularly concerned about the proposed changes affecting the federal government’s ability to identify and understand people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD). This concern extends beyond the loss of individual survey questions. Federal agencies have recently invested in improving national data about people with I/DD, including through questions designed to better identify adults whose age of onset, functional limitations, learning difficulties, and support needs are consistent with the population contemplated by the Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act of 2000 (“DD Act”), Pub. L. 106-402, 114 Stat. 1677 (2000). The proposed 2028 questionnaire would remove several of those measures before the newest questions have generated enough years of data to fully evaluate or use them.
These changes also do not occur in isolation. They are being proposed during a period of substantial change to the federal disability infrastructure, including the restructuring of HHS and repeated proposals to eliminate or reduce programs and research capacity associated with the DD Act. That context does not establish the purpose or motive behind the NHIS redesign. It does, however, make it especially important to understand what data capacity would be lost, what would replace it, and whether HHS has considered the cumulative effect of these changes on its ability to identify need, measure disparities, evaluate programs, enforce rights, and remain accountable to people with developmental disabilities.

CRDJ therefore urges NCHS to consider the proposed redesign through four related concerns:
•Reversing Hard-Won Progress: The proposed redesign would undo recent federal efforts to make people with I/DD more visible in national health data, removing newly developed measures before they have had sufficient time to establish a meaningful evidence base.
•Weakening the Disability Evidence Infrastructure: The loss of developmental-disability data cannot be evaluated separately from broader changes to the federal disability infrastructure, including repeated proposals to eliminate or reduce programs responsible for research, data, rights protection, systems change, and accountability.
•Compounding Inequities in Who Gets Counted: Reducing disability and functioning data will not affect everyone equally. The redesign risks further obscuring the experiences of people who live at the intersections of disability, race, poverty, language, geography, and other forms of marginalization.
•Accountability Before Redesign: NCHS has not yet provided the evidence, testing, or transparency necessary to demonstrate that the proposed redesign will preserve continuity, representation, and accountability for people with developmental disabilities, nor explained what will replace the federal data capacity it proposes to remove.

I wish to write to object to the changes being recommended to the current survey. People within the ID/D community already struggle to justify services and the deletion of key questions will increase the likelihood that more people with disabilities will go unserved or underserved. If anything, more questions would be a better direction than cutting and generalizing.

Re: Docket No. CDC-2026-1387, National Health Interview Survey

I am writing as a caregiver for someone with ME/CFS or Long Covid]. I am concerned that the proposed 2028 redesign of the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) leaves out ME/CFS and Long Covid.

The NHIS is where the national numbers for these illnesses come from. It’s how we know that about 1.3% of U.S. adults were living with ME/CFS in 2021–2022, and it tracked Long Covid from 2022 through 2025. The 2028 draft asks about other chronic conditions, but not ME/CFS or Long Covid, and it has no questions about fatigue. - until recently, simply engaging in active thought caused her to experience post-exertional malaise

She lays in bed all day unable to do anything. The suffering is profound.

Being counted matters. Without this data, it is harder to show how many people are affected, whether things are getting better, and why research and care deserve investment.

CDC says the redesigned survey can still add new topics. I urge CDC to include ME/CFS and Long Covid questions - especially on post-exertional malaise, keep questions on fatigue, and keep the disability questions which are currently proposed for removal.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I am a police officer and first responder. During the COVID-19 pandemic I served my community on the front lines, interacting with the public daily. Over time my condition progressed into what physicians later identified as dysautonomia and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). My illness has included severe fatigue, autonomic dysfunction, and significant blood glucose instability. During one episode my blood glucose dropped to 14 mg/dL, triggering a seizure while I was being transported to the ICU.

These health changes have significantly altered my life and made it difficult to continue in the profession I love. Despite these challenges, I continue working to remain a police officer.

I am sharing my experience not out of anger, but out of concern.

Across the country, individuals have reported symptoms following vaccination including autonomic dysfunction, neurological complications, and chronic fatigue-like syndromes. Many patients report difficulty obtaining recognition of their symptoms or finding physicians familiar with these conditions.

Patients living with these complications often struggle not only with complex medical symptoms but also with reporting systems and accessing appropriate care.

I respectfully ask that continued attention be given to: research into post-vaccine adverse events including dysautonomia and autonomic nervous system dysfunction; improved transparency and reporting within vaccine adverse event monitoring systems; support for clinicians researching and treating complex post-immune conditions; resources for patients experiencing serious long-term complications following vaccination; and consideration of policies related to manufacturer liability protections and patient recourse when harm occurs.

For patients whose lives have been altered by these conditions, this issue is not abstract—it is something we live with every day.

Public health trust depends on transparency, rigorous investigation of adverse events, and compassion for those experiencing complications.

To clarify the sequence of events, I have included the following timeline.

January–February 2021 — COVID-19 vaccination
I received my first two COVID-19 vaccine doses while serving as a frontline police officer during the pandemic. At that time I had never contracted COVID-19.

Post-vaccination symptom onset (2021)
Shortly after vaccination I developed multiple unexplained symptoms including severe fatigue, heart palpitations, muscle fatigue and weakness, muscle twitching, brain fog, peripheral neuropathy, gastrointestinal symptoms, muscle and joint pain, shortness of breath, sleep disturbances, visual disturbances, nausea, ringing in the ears (tinnitus), and chest pain. These symptoms significantly affected daily functioning and initially remained unexplained.

February 2022 — First COVID-19 infection
Approximately one year after symptom onset I contracted COVID-19. Symptoms worsened afterward.

March 2023 — Second COVID-19 infection
Following a second infection my condition deteriorated further.

My symptoms progressed into dysautonomia and ME/CFS with severe post-exertional malaise, leading to a significant decline in physical functioning.

Hospitalization for post-exertional malaise
I was hospitalized for four days and temporarily lost the ability to walk independently for approximately two weeks.

Hospitalization for hypoglycemia and seizures
About two and a half months later I experienced severe hypoglycemia and seizures requiring hospitalization and approximately four months off work.

Following further medical evaluation, physicians identified dysautonomia associated with Long COVID as the underlying condition.

Current status
I continue to live with dysautonomia and chronic fatigue-related symptoms while working to maintain my career as a police officer.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit my experience for the public record.

Respectfully,
Delaina Hartman
